lessons.title: Layered, hexagonal/clean, modular monolith vs microservices; REST API design
lessons.summary: Layers and ports organize code inside a deployable; the number of deployables is a separate choice. A module boundary that is a function call is cheaper than one that is a network call, which is why a solo developer starts with a modular monolith and a REST contract that states its concurrency rules.

examples.title: One module boundary, as a function call and as an HTTP call

annotations.note: The module boundary is a small interface declared by the caller (go.design.packages). Everything below implements it twice; placeOrders never changes. That is what keeps extracting a service later a wiring change.
In-process, billing is a struct behind a mutex. The call either returns or panics; there is no third outcome, and in a real app it could join the caller's database transaction.
The same method over HTTP gains a timeout, a request, a response body to close and new errors. Each is an obligation the in-process version never had (go.services.client).

The new outcome a network adds: the call failed, and the caller cannot know whether the effect happened. Retrying risks a double invoice; not retrying risks none. Only an idempotency key settles it (go.services.retries).

The billing service finished order 2 after the client gave up, so its ledger holds all three orders while the orders side saw a failure. Microservices turn this into a normal Tuesday: outboxes, idempotency and reconciliation jobs exist to repair it.

examples.title: REST: ETag and If-Match turn a lost update into 412

annotations.note: The version counts the note's states. Sent as a strong ETag ("1"), it lets a client say which state its edit is based on.
The check and the write must be one step, or two PUTs can both pass the check. The mutex is held for one request only, never while a user edits; in PostgreSQL the same step is one UPDATE (example 3).
428 Precondition Required (RFC 6585) makes the condition mandatory: a client that never read the note cannot blindly overwrite it.
If-Match uses the strong comparison, so a weak ETag (W/"1") never matches. Simplified: a full parser also accepts a list of ETags and If-Match: *.
A stale version is a false precondition: 412 Precondition Failed, per RFC 9110, and the method is not performed.
Two tabs read version 1. A saves first; B's write would have silently replaced A's text, and gets 412 instead. B must re-read (version 2) and merge before its PUT succeeds.

examples.title: The version column: two concurrent UPDATEs, one winner

annotations.note: The compare-and-set in one statement: the row changes only if its version is still the one the client read, and the version moves forward in the same UPDATE. This is optimistic locking, JPA's @Version without the framework.
B's UPDATE needs the row A has locked, so it waits.

Once A commits, B's blocked UPDATE re-checks its WHERE clause against the newly committed row (READ COMMITTED), finds version 2 and changes nothing: UPDATE 0, no version returned. The handler turns zero rows into 412.
A's text survived; B's was never written over it.

use_cases: Modular monolith: a product built by one person or one team, where modules need clean boundaries but not separate deploys
Extracting one service: when a module needs a different security boundary, runtime, scaling profile or release cadence (StackLab's sandboxed runner)
Microservices: many teams that must deploy independently, where coordination cost exceeds the cost of distributed systems
ETag + If-Match: any resource two clients (or two tabs) can edit: notes, settings, documents, admin forms
strengths: A modular monolith keeps calls in-process: no partial failure, one transaction across modules, and a refactor across a boundary is one commit and one deploy
Go enforces module boundaries at compile time (internal/, acyclic imports, unexported names), so a monolith doesn't decay into a ball of mud as easily as in languages without package privacy
HTTP already defines the concurrency contract: ETag, If-Match, 412 and 428 are understood by clients, proxies and tools, unlike a custom version field in a JSON body
Optimistic locking needs no held locks: no transaction stays open while a user edits, unlike SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
weaknesses: A monolith scales and deploys as one unit: a memory-hungry module, or one that must be isolated, takes the others with it
Module boundaries inside one process are a discipline; nothing stops a shortcut SQL join into another module's tables except review and lint
Microservices multiply operational work: per-service pipelines, versioned contracts, tracing across hops, and data that can no longer be joined or committed together
Optimistic locking under heavy contention fails often; hot rows need queuing or pessimistic locks (sql.transactions.row-locks)

pitfalls.title: Microservices to get modularity
pitfalls.detail: Splitting a codebase without clean module boundaries produces a distributed monolith: services that must deploy together and call each other synchronously, with all the network failure modes and none of the independence. Get the boundaries right in one process first.

pitfalls.title: Sharing tables across modules
pitfalls.detail: If billing reads orders' tables directly, the boundary is gone, whatever the packages say. Give each module its own tables (one schema per module works well in PostgreSQL) and cross the boundary through the module's API or a view it publishes.

pitfalls.title: PUT without a precondition
pitfalls.detail: Last write wins silently. For anything two clients can edit, return an ETag and require If-Match; answer 412 for a stale version and 428 for a missing one.

pitfalls.title: Verbs in REST paths for everything
pitfalls.detail: /api/createNote, /api/getNotes give up method semantics (GET is safe, PUT and DELETE are idempotent) that clients and proxies rely on. Model state as resources; keep RPC-style POST for real actions such as running code.

quiz.q: A remote call timed out. What do you know about its effect?
options: Nothing: it may or may not have happened
It will be rolled back automatically
quiz.why: The billing service invoiced order 2 after the client gave up. A timeout reports that the answer didn't arrive, not that the work didn't happen.

quiz.q: What is the main reason microservices exist?
options: They are faster than in-process calls
They let many teams deploy and scale parts independently
They remove the need for transactions
They make code easier to refactor
quiz.why: They trade in-process simplicity for independent deployment, scaling and ownership. That trade pays for organizations with many teams, rarely for one developer.

quiz.q: Tab B sends PUT with If-Match: "1" but the note is at version 2. Which status should it get?
quiz.why: RFC 9110: when an If-Match condition evaluates to false, the server must not perform the method and answers 412. 428 is for a request that carries no precondition at all.

quiz.q: Why is UPDATE ... WHERE version = $3 RETURNING version safe against two concurrent PUTs with the same version?
options: The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock, then re-checks the WHERE clause on the new row version and matches nothing
quiz.why: Under READ COMMITTED a blocked UPDATE re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the committed row; the version has moved, so it updates zero rows and the handler answers 412.

further_reading.title: Go: Organizing a Go module (internal/ and cmd/)
PostgreSQL: Concurrency control (READ COMMITTED and UPDATE re-checks)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three different decisions hide under "architecture":

1. **How code is organized inside one deployable.** Layered (transport, service,
   storage) or ports and adapters (a core that declares interfaces, adapters that
   implement them). go.design.layers covers this for Go and ts.architecture.folders for
   the frontend; this lesson takes it as known.
2. **How many deployables there are.** A **modular monolith** is one process, one deploy
   and usually one database, divided into modules with explicit public surfaces: Go
   packages with consumer-declared interfaces, `internal/`, each module owning its own
   tables. **Microservices** put modules in separate processes that deploy, scale and
   fail independently and talk over the network.
3. **What contract clients see.** For HTTP APIs, usually REST: resources named by URLs,
   uniform methods with defined semantics, status codes, and headers for caching and
   concurrency.

The second decision is the expensive one. Moving a boundary from a function call to a
network call adds failure modes that did not exist before: timeouts with unknown
outcomes, half-finished work on the other side, no shared transaction, contracts that
must be versioned, and traces that span processes. Microservices buy **independent
deployment and ownership** with that cost, which is why they fit organizations of many
teams (Conway's law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organization that
builds them). A solo developer has one team and one release train, so the benefit is near
zero and the cost is the same. Start with a modular monolith, keep the module boundaries
clean, and extract a service when a module needs something the process cannot give it:
a security boundary, a different runtime, separate scaling.

REST design follows from HTTP's own rules (RFC 9110). GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are **safe**;
PUT and DELETE are **idempotent**; POST is neither. Use `201 Created` with `Location` for
creation, `204` for success without a body, `404`, `409`, `412`, `422` for what they
mean, and one error format (problem details, RFC 9457) for all of them. Paginate with
cursors (go.services.pagination-streaming), evolve by adding fields, and protect
editable resources with **conditional requests**: an `ETag` on read, `If-Match` on
write. Not everything is a resource: an action such as "run this code" is an honest
`POST`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Spring Boot plus Spring Cloud made microservices the enterprise default for
  a decade; Spring Modulith is the same ecosystem's answer for modular monoliths. JPA's
  `@Version` is the optimistic locking the third example writes by hand, and its
  `OptimisticLockException` maps naturally to 412.
- **Python**: a Django project with several apps is a modular monolith; the discipline
  is to keep apps from importing each other's models freely.
- **JS/Node**: NestJS modules and Nx monorepos give module boundaries within one
  deployable; Express apps often have none, and splitting them into services is used
  to get boundaries the code never had.
- **C/C++**: a monolith is one binary linking several libraries; the boundary is a
  header. The difference with Go is that Go enforces package boundaries (and acyclic
  imports) in the compiler.

## How it works

The first example's numbers tell the story. In-process, three calls give three invoices
and three successes. Over HTTP, the second call takes longer than the client's 100 ms
budget, the client reports a timeout, and the server, unaware, finishes the work. The
two sides now disagree, and only extra machinery reconciles them: an idempotency key so
the client can safely retry (go.services.retries), an outbox so events are not lost
(design.patterns.classic), and a reconciliation job for what still slips through.

Conditional requests push the same problem, concurrent writers, into the protocol. The
server sends the version it has as an `ETag`. A client that wants to replace the resource
sends `If-Match` with the version it read. The server must evaluate the condition and
the write atomically: example 2 holds a mutex for the request, and with PostgreSQL it is
one `UPDATE ... WHERE version = $n` (example 3). Under READ COMMITTED, a second UPDATE
blocked on the same row re-checks its `WHERE` clause against the newly committed row
once the first commits, finds a different version and changes nothing. Zero rows means
the version moved or the note doesn't exist; both make `If-Match` false, so both become
412, and the client re-reads, merges and tries again.

## Design notes

StackLab is a modular monolith, with one deliberate extraction that was later folded
back. ADR-0007 puts all Go code in one module, split by feature under `server/internal/`;
the only interface is `httpapi.Runner`, declared by its consumer. The runner container
of Docker mode (ADR-0003) is the one service, and it exists for a security boundary, not
for scale: lesson code runs as a non-root user with memory, pid and network limits. When
local mode arrived, ADR-0008 kept the module (`runexec`) and the port, and made the
deployment boundary optional: one `if` in `main.go` picks `runexec` in-process or
`runclient` over HTTP. That is the modular monolith's promise working in reverse, and
ADR-0008 is explicit about the price: in local mode lesson code runs with the owner's
privileges.

The HTTP API is mostly resource-shaped: `PUT /api/notes/{lessonId}` replaces a note,
bookmarks have `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE`, and every error leaves through one `problem`
helper as RFC 9457 problem details. Two places are worth a critical look. Progress uses
verb sub-resources (`POST /api/progress/{lessonId}/viewed`), which is RPC in REST
clothing; the operations are idempotent (a status only moves up), and a `PUT` with the
status in the body would say so to every client. And notes carry no ETag, so two
browser tabs editing one note lose an update silently. For a single-user app that is a
fair trade; examples 2 and 3 are the fix if it ever bites. `POST /api/run` is an action,
and modelling it as one is the right call.

lessons.title: Where business rules live: app vs database
lessons.summary: Invariants about data belong in the database, where every writer obeys them and concurrency can't slip past them; policies that need the outside world belong in the app. Rules written twice drift, and "in the database" is only safe if it is a constraint or holds a lock.

examples.title: A read-then-write rule races, whether the app or a trigger does the reading

annotations.note: The application-side check: both sessions count 0 bookings, both decide there is a seat, both insert. Nothing conflicts, because they insert different rows, so both commit and course 1 is overbooked.
The same rule moved into the database as a trigger. It is still a read followed by a write, and the read sees only committed rows plus its own.

B's trigger counts 0 because A's row is not committed yet; under READ COMMITTED it is invisible to B's statement. Course 2 is overbooked exactly like course 1. Moving code into the database did not make it a constraint.
Sequentially the trigger refuses the third booking (P0001 is RAISE EXCEPTION's SQLSTATE). This is why such rules pass every single-user test and fail in production.
Two bookings each for one seat. PostgreSQL's docs warn about CHECK constraints that read other rows for the same reason: they appear to work in simple tests.

examples.title: A counter on the parent row plus a CHECK: the database decides, and serializes

annotations.note: The cross-row rule becomes a single-row one: courses.booked is maintained with every booking, and CHECK (booked <= seats), in the setup, states the rule where a CHECK can enforce it.
Incrementing the counter is a write to one row, so it takes that row's lock. The increment is relative (booked + 1): the database computes it, not the app.

B's increment waits for A's lock. When A commits, B re-reads the row (booked is now 1), computes 2, and the CHECK refuses it with SQLSTATE 23514 and the constraint's name, which the app maps to "course full" in one place.
One seat, one booking, and a counter that agrees. The race is gone because the rule is checked on the row that every competing writer must lock.

examples.title: One rule, four implementations, three answers; then one home for it

annotations.note: A rule as simple as "unique, ignoring case" depends on whose case mapping you use. JavaScript's toLowerCase applies Unicode's full mapping, so "İsmail" becomes a 7-character string; Go and this database's lower() do not.

Go's strings.ToLower and lower() in this C.UTF-8 database agree with each other and disagree with Turkish: IŞIL becomes işil, a different name from ışıl. ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase) and the ICU tr collation give the Turkish answer.
The rule gets one home: a unique index on the Turkish-aware expression. Every writer, including psql and the next service, now obeys the same definition.
IŞIL and Işıl are the same name as ışıl and are refused; işil, with a dotted i, is a different Turkish name and is accepted.

The app asks the home instead of re-implementing it: insert, and translate the violation by constraint name into a domain error. A pre-check for nicer UX should run the same SQL expression, never a Go copy of it.

use_cases: Database: invariants about stored data (NOT NULL, ranges, uniqueness, references, no overlaps, quotas kept as counters), because every writer and every concurrent transaction must obey them
Application: policies that need the outside world (payment authorization, emails, feature flags, the current user's permissions), change often, or need rich error messages
Both: the database enforces, the app pre-validates for UX with the same definition, and maps constraint violations to domain errors
Triggers: things that must happen on every write path (audit rows, outbox events, updated_at), not decisions
strengths: A constraint holds for every client, including psql sessions, migrations, batch jobs and services you haven't written yet; no application check can say that
Constraints are concurrency-safe by construction: unique indexes, exclusion constraints and single-row CHECKs are enforced under the locks PostgreSQL takes anyway
Constraint violations come back with a SQLSTATE and the constraint's name, so the app can map them to precise errors in one place
Application rules are easy to unit-test, to version with the code, to explain in an error message, and to change without a migration
weaknesses: A CHECK constraint sees only the row being written; cross-row rules need a counter, an exclusion constraint, a lock or SERIALIZABLE
Rules in the database are written in SQL or PL/pgSQL, tested only against a real PostgreSQL, and deployed by migration rather than with the code
Database errors are terse; without a mapping layer, users see 'violates check constraint' instead of 'the course is full'
A rule enforced in both places must be kept identical, or the two will disagree on edge cases (the Turkish İ/ı example)

pitfalls.title: Check-then-act in application code
pitfalls.detail: SELECT to check, then INSERT or UPDATE, is a race under READ COMMITTED. Make the database decide (a constraint, a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE booked < seats), lock the parent row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), or run the transaction SERIALIZABLE and retry on 40001.
pitfalls.bad:
n := countBookings(ctx, tx, course)  // two requests both see n = 0
if n < seats { insertBooking(ctx, tx, course, student) }

pitfalls.title: Assuming a trigger is a constraint
pitfalls.detail: A trigger that counts other rows runs under the same snapshot rules as application code, so it races the same way. Use it only with a lock (for example on the parent row) or under SERIALIZABLE.

pitfalls.title: Duplicating a rule in Go, TypeScript and SQL
pitfalls.detail: Three implementations drift: case mapping, rounding, time zones, trimming. Keep one authoritative definition and have the other layers call or mirror it from a single source (a shared schema, a generated validator, an endpoint), with tests that compare them.

pitfalls.title: Business decisions in triggers
pitfalls.detail: Sending email, calling services or applying pricing policy from a trigger hides behaviour from the code that caused it and makes it run inside the transaction. Keep triggers for audit and outbox rows (sql.server-side.triggers).

quiz.q: Why did the BEFORE INSERT trigger let both bookings for course 2 through?
options: B's statement could not see A's uncommitted row, so both counts were 0
The trigger was created after the inserts
RAISE EXCEPTION is only a warning
quiz.why: Under READ COMMITTED each statement sees rows committed before it started, plus its own. A trigger that reads other rows inherits that view and races like application code.

quiz.q: What made the counter + CHECK version safe?
options: Both sessions had to update the same course row, so the second waited, re-read it and failed the CHECK
quiz.why: The rule was moved onto a row every competing writer must lock. The blocked UPDATE re-evaluated booked + 1 against the committed value and the CHECK refused 2 > 1.

quiz.q: Which rule belongs in the application rather than the database?
options: An order's total is never negative
No two bookings for one room overlap
A refund needs the payment provider's approval
Every booking references an existing course
quiz.why: It depends on an external system and its response. The other three are invariants about stored data that a constraint (CHECK, EXCLUDE, FOREIGN KEY) enforces for every writer.

quiz.q: Under Turkish rules, which sign-up is a different user from 'ışıl'?
quiz.why: Turkish has dotted and dotless i as separate letters: I/ı and İ/i. 'işil' has a dotted i, so it is a different name; IŞIL, Işıl and ıŞıL all lower-case to ışıl.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: Constraints (the note on CHECK constraints that reference other rows)
PostgreSQL: Data consistency checks at the application level

lessons.body:
## Concept

A business rule is a statement that must stay true ("a course is never overbooked") or a
decision the system makes ("refunds over 1,000 TL need approval"). Where each one lives
is the most consequential line you draw, because it decides who can break it.

Split rules into two kinds:

- **Invariants about stored data.** Facts that must hold for every row at every moment,
  whoever writes: required fields, ranges, uniqueness, references, no overlapping
  bookings, a quota. They belong in the **database**, as constraints. Every client obeys
  them, psql and migrations included, and PostgreSQL enforces them correctly under
  concurrency.
- **Policies and workflows.** Rules that need the outside world (a payment provider,
  the current user, a feature flag, the clock in a time zone), that change with the
  business, or whose failure needs a careful explanation. They belong in the
  **application**, as code you can unit-test and deploy with the rest
  (ts.architecture.explicit-states shows a pure core for exactly this).

Two traps sit between them. First, **"in the database" is not the property that
matters; being a constraint is.** A trigger that counts rows is still a read followed by
a write, and races exactly like application code (example 1). PostgreSQL's own docs say
CHECK constraints must not read other rows for the same reason. Turn cross-row rules into
something the database enforces atomically: a counter on a parent row with a CHECK
(example 2), a unique index, an exclusion constraint, a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE
booked < seats`, a row lock, or SERIALIZABLE with retries.

Second, **a rule written twice drifts.** The app wants to validate early for a friendly
message, the frontend wants instant feedback, the database enforces. Three copies of
"ignoring case" gave three answers in example 3. Keep one authoritative definition and
make the others ask it, or generate them from one source.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Bean Validation (`@NotNull`, `@Size`) and JPA entity rules check objects in
  memory; they don't see concurrent transactions or other writers. Treat them as the
  friendly first check and the schema as the authority.
- **Python**: Django model validation runs only when your code calls `full_clean()`;
  `bulk_create` and raw SQL skip it. The database constraint is the one that cannot be
  skipped.
- **JS/TS**: zod at the trust boundary (ts.services.zod) is the right first check and the
  wrong last one: it validates shape, not uniqueness or capacity, which need the data.
  Also note that `toLowerCase()` in JavaScript applies Unicode's full case mapping and
  `toLocaleLowerCase("tr")` the Turkish one; Go's `strings.ToLower` applies neither.
- **C/C++**: an invariant in a class is protected by the type's methods within one
  process. A database is shared by processes you don't control, which is why the
  invariant has to live where they all meet.

## How it works

Under READ COMMITTED, each statement sees rows committed before it began plus its own
changes. In example 1 both sessions count bookings before either commits, so both see
zero; inserting different rows creates no conflict for PostgreSQL to detect. The trigger
version is the same read with the same snapshot.

Example 2 works because both sessions must update the same `courses` row. A row can be
updated by one transaction at a time, so B's `UPDATE` waits. When A commits, B does not
fail and does not use stale data: READ COMMITTED re-evaluates the updated row's new
version, computes `booked + 1 = 2`, and the CHECK, which only needs that one row, rejects
it. The error carries SQLSTATE 23514 and the name `courses_not_overbooked`, which is the
stable contract between schema and code.

Example 3's index works on an expression: `lower(username COLLATE "tr-x-icu")` uses ICU's
Turkish case rules, independent of the database's own C.UTF-8 locale. The app inserts
and translates the unique violation by constraint name, the same mapping go.errors.is-as-join and
go.postgres.repository-testing show for SQLSTATE 23505.

## Design notes

A practical default for each rule: write it as a constraint if it is a fact about stored
data and SQL can express it on one row or with an index; map its violation to a domain
error in the repository; pre-validate in the app or the UI only for user experience,
using the same definition. Write it as application code if it needs anything outside
the database or is a decision rather than a fact. Reach for a trigger only for things
every write path must do, such as audit and outbox rows, and keep decisions out of it.

StackLab leans on the database where it matters for the lesson runtime: the playground
role, schema-per-run and statement timeouts are enforced by PostgreSQL, not by Go code
trusting itself. Its own app data is simpler: learning progress, notes and bookmarks
have keys and NOT NULL, and the one rule with business flavour, "a lesson's status only
moves up" (viewed, ran, completed), lives twice: in a `CASE` inside `learningstore`'s
upsert and, for the offline fallback, in `RANK` in `src/features/learning/api.ts`. The two
have already drifted on an edge: marking a lesson completed again re-stamps
`completed_at` on the server (`WHEN excluded.status = 'completed' THEN now()`), while the
local version returns early and keeps the first time. Small, harmless here, and exactly
the drift this lesson warns about; a test that replays one sequence of events against
both is the cheap guard.

Cross-layer rules are where the Turkish locale bites first: case-insensitive uniqueness,
sorting, and search. Decide once which rules apply (`tr-x-icu`, `turkish` text search),
put that decision in the schema, and let the app ask the database instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Reliability: timeouts everywhere, retries with idempotency, graceful degradation, observability
lessons.summary: Four habits keep a system quiet at night: bound every wait, make retries safe with an idempotency key the database enforces, degrade optional parts instead of failing the page, and emit one structured event per request so failures explain themselves.

examples.title: The server's half of an idempotency key: two attempts race, one does the work

annotations.note: Claiming the key is the first statement of the transaction that does the work. RETURNING gives one row to the winner; ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING gives zero rows, not an error, to anyone else.
The retry arrives while the first attempt is still running. Its INSERT waits on the primary key's uniqueness check: PostgreSQL cannot tell yet whether A's key will commit.
The effect (the payment) and the record of it (payment_id on the key) are written in one transaction, so there is no moment where one exists without the other.
After A commits, B's INSERT returns zero rows. B charges nothing and reads the stored result, which is what the client should get back for every repeat of the request.

If the first attempt rolls back (a crash, a declined card), its key goes with it: B's waiting INSERT now succeeds and B does the work. A key that is claimed outside the work's transaction would stay claimed with no result behind it.

examples.title: Graceful degradation: a deadline per dependency, a fallback per panel, and a visible banner

annotations.note: A stand-in for fetch that honours an AbortSignal the way fetch does: one endpoint never answers, one returns 503, and /healthz says ok because, like most liveness checks, it checks nothing.
The result type records where a value came from. A degraded value that looks exactly like a live one is how stale data gets trusted.
Two separate failure paths: AbortSignal.timeout ends the wait, and the res.ok check turns a 503 into a failure, because fetch resolves its promise for any HTTP status.

Critical and optional dependencies are decided per call, not per app. The lesson has no fallback; the two optional panels run in parallel, each with its own budget, so the page waits for the slowest budget, not the sum.
Degradation must be visible: a banner for the user, a counter for you. A silent fallback hides an outage until someone notices wrong data.
A liveness probe at start-up says 200 while the API it guards answers 503. A one-time choice of "backend or offline mode" based on it would never notice.

examples.title: One structured event per request, the route pattern, and liveness vs readiness

annotations.note: Handlers add fields to the request's event instead of logging lines of their own. One line per request, with every field on it, can be filtered and counted; ten scattered lines per request have to be stitched together.

ServeMux sets r.Pattern on the request it receives. This middleware keeps a reference to that exact request (r was reassigned), so it can read the pattern afterwards; reading it from the original request would give "".
route is the pattern ("GET /notes/{id}"), not the path: a few distinct values instead of one per note, which is what metrics labels and dashboards need.
The clock is injected, so the example's durations are stable and a test can assert on them. Real code passes time.Now.

Liveness answers "is the process alive?" and checks nothing; failing it gets the process restarted. Readiness answers "should I get traffic?" and checks dependencies; failing it takes the instance out of rotation without a restart.
With the database down, /healthz stays 200 (a restart would not help) while /readyz turns 503, and the failed request says which dependency failed and how long it waited.

use_cases: Any call that leaves the process: HTTP clients, database queries, queue publishes; each gets a deadline, and every layer's deadline fits inside its caller's
Any POST a client may retry (payments, orders, sign-ups): an idempotency key enforced by a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect
Pages assembled from several sources: decide per panel what is critical, and give each optional one a budget and a fallback
Every service: one structured event per request with route, status, duration and dependency outcomes; separate liveness and readiness endpoints
strengths: PostgreSQL's unique index makes concurrent duplicate requests safe without any locking code in the app: the second attempt waits, then sees the first one's result
Go's context carries one deadline through every call that accepts it, the database driver included; TS's AbortSignal does the same for fetch, with AbortSignal.timeout as the one-liner
log/slog gives structured, levelled events in the standard library, unlike Java's split between SLF4J, Logback and MDC, or Python's add-on structlog
A degraded mode written as data (source: live, cached, default) is testable like any other state
weaknesses: Idempotency keys need storage, an expiry policy and care with requests that reuse a key with a different body
Every fallback is a second code path that runs rarely, so it is the least tested code in the system
Timeouts chosen without data are guesses: too short causes failures under normal load, too long lets queues pile up
Wide events cost log volume; high-cardinality fields (user IDs, paths) belong in logs and traces, not in metric labels

pitfalls.title: Retrying in every layer
pitfalls.detail: A client retrying 3 times, calling a service that retries 3 times, calling a database driver that retries 3 times, sends up to 27 attempts at the bottom. Retry in one layer, usually the one closest to the caller who knows the budget (go.services.retries).

pitfalls.title: Claiming the idempotency key in its own transaction
pitfalls.detail: If the key commits first and the work fails after, the key is burned: every retry sees 'already done' with no result. Claim the key in the same transaction as the effect, or store a pending state that a retry can resume.

pitfalls.title: A readiness check that is also the liveness check
pitfalls.detail: If /healthz pings the database, an outage makes the orchestrator restart every instance in a loop, which fixes nothing and adds cold starts. Liveness checks the process; readiness checks dependencies.

pitfalls.title: Logging the path as a metric label
pitfalls.detail: r.URL.Path makes one time series per lesson ID or user ID. Use r.Pattern (Go 1.23) for labels and keep the concrete path in the log event.
pitfalls.good: requests.WithLabelValues(r.Pattern).Inc() // "GET /notes/{id}"

quiz.q: A retry with the same idempotency key arrives while the first attempt is still running. What does its INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING do?
options: Waits until the first transaction ends, then returns zero rows if it committed
quiz.why: The uniqueness check can't decide until the first transaction commits or rolls back, so it waits. On commit it returns no row (DO NOTHING); on rollback it inserts.

quiz.q: Why does fetch need an explicit res.ok check for graceful degradation?
options: fetch rejects only on network errors and aborts; a 503 resolves normally
AbortSignal.timeout does not work with fetch
quiz.why: A fetch promise resolves for every HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx; only network failures and aborts reject it (ts.services.fetch).

quiz.q: The database is down. What should /healthz and /readyz answer?
quiz.why: The process is alive (restarting it won't fix the database), but it should not receive traffic it cannot serve. That is exactly the split between liveness and readiness.

quiz.q: A middleware passes r.WithContext(ctx) to the mux and then logs r.Pattern from the original r. What does it log?
quiz.why: ServeMux sets Pattern on the request it was given, which is the copy. Keep a reference to that copy (as the example does by reassigning r) and read it there.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Systems that don't page you share four habits. Each one has its own in-depth lesson;
here they are side by side, with the parts those lessons leave to this one.

1. **Timeouts everywhere.** Every wait has an end: `http.Client` and per-call contexts
   in Go (go.services.client), `AbortSignal.timeout` on `fetch` (ts.services.advanced),
   `statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` in
   PostgreSQL (go.postgres.bulk shows how a query ends under each). Deadlines shrink on
   the way down: a handler with 2 s gives its database call less, so it still has time to
   answer.
2. **Retries with idempotency.** Retry only what is transient, with capped, jittered
   backoff, in one layer (go.services.retries). A retried POST is safe only if the
   server recognizes the repeat, and the robust place to recognize it is a **unique
   constraint on the idempotency key, written in the same transaction as the effect**
   (example 1).
3. **Graceful degradation.** Decide per dependency what is critical. When an optional one
   fails or is slow, show a cached or default value, say so, and keep the page up. When a
   critical one fails, fail clearly. Shed load you cannot serve (a fast 503) rather than
   queueing it until everything times out.
4. **Observability.** Emit one structured event per request with the route pattern,
   status, duration and the outcome of each dependency, so that "what failed, where,
   how long did it wait" is a query, not an investigation. Expose liveness and readiness
   separately, so orchestrators restart only what a restart can fix.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Resilience4j (or Hystrix before it) packages timeouts, retries, circuit
  breakers and fallbacks as decorators. In Go and TS you write the same thing as a few
  functions around a call, which keeps the policy visible. MDC's per-request context
  is what the event in example 3 replaces.
- **Python**: `requests` has no default timeout either; `tenacity` is the usual retry
  library. `structlog` gives the per-request event style that `log/slog` has built in.
- **JS/Node**: `fetch` has no default timeout and does not reject on 5xx; the two lines
  in `load` are the fix for both. Promise-based fallbacks (`Promise.allSettled`, or a
  try/catch per panel as here) are the degradation tool.
- **C/C++**: `select`/`poll` timeouts and errno checks everywhere; Go's context and
  TS's AbortSignal are the same discipline with propagation built in.

## How it works

Example 1 relies on how a unique index treats concurrent inserts. When B inserts a key
that A has inserted but not committed, B cannot know whether the key will exist, so it
waits for A's transaction. If A commits, B's `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` skips the row and
`RETURNING` yields nothing; if A rolls back, B's insert proceeds. Because A wrote the
payment in the same transaction as the key, "key exists" and "payment exists" are always
true together. For effects outside the database (a card charge through a provider),
store the key with a `pending` state first, pass your key on to the provider's own
idempotency mechanism, and let a retry resume the pending operation.

Example 2's `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts with a `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`,
which lets the fallback say *why* it was used. Running the optional loads with
`Promise.all` over functions that never reject (they return a `Loaded` value instead)
gives the page the latest of the budgets, not their sum.

Example 3's middleware builds the event: it creates it, hands it to handlers through the
context, and logs it once after the handler returns. `r.Pattern` (Go 1.23) is the
matched routing pattern, the right key for grouping requests; the clock is a parameter,
so durations can be tested.

## Design notes

StackLab applies the habits unevenly, which makes it a useful review. Timeouts are
thorough: `http.Server` sets `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout` and
`IdleTimeout` in `main.go`; runexec bounds a run at 40 s and a queue wait at 10 s;
`runclient` has a 45 s client timeout; sqlrun sets `statement_timeout` and
`lock_timeout` on every SQL lesson session; the stores put a 3 s context on their queries.
Load shedding is real: at most two runs execute at once, and a third waits up to 10 s
for a slot, then gets `503 server busy` instead of joining an ever-longer queue. Degradation exists in two places: run history
is best effort (a failed insert is logged, the learner still gets the result), and the
frontend falls back to `localStorage` when the backend is unreachable.

That fallback is where the critical eye goes. `pickApi()` decides once, from a
`/healthz` probe with a 1.5 s timeout, and caches the answer for the life of the page. It
probes liveness, which checks nothing, so a backend whose database is down still wins
the probe. Until 2026-11-14 only an unreachable server selected the fallback, because
`fetch` resolves on any HTTP status: with the backend stopped, Vite's dev proxy answered
500 and the app kept the dead backend. A non-OK answer now counts as unreachable too. A backend that goes away after the first probe is never
re-checked, and progress saved to `localStorage` during an outage never syncs back. The
second example's shape (per call, with a budget, with the source recorded and shown) is
the direction to take if that ever matters.

Observability is minimal and adequate for one user: one `slog` line per request with
method, path, status and duration, plus `/healthz` and `/readyz` split correctly. The
first additions for a multi-user deployment would be a request ID in that line, the
route pattern next to the path, and dependency outcomes on the same event.

lessons.title: Security across the stack: validation, SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, secrets, least privilege
lessons.summary: Each layer has its own attack surface and one default defense: validate shape at the boundary, keep values out of SQL text, encode at the output sink, refuse cross-site writes, keep secrets out of code and logs, and give every process the least privilege that works.

examples.title: SQL: the part parameters can't cover, and the error message that leaks a secret

annotations.note: The value is a parameter, so the classic quote-breaking attack is gone. ORDER BY takes an identifier or an expression, not a value, so the sort column is concatenated: the injection point that survives in code written by people who know about $1.

The fix for anything that can't be a parameter: an allow-list mapping public keys to SQL the program wrote. The user's string never reaches the query, and an unknown key is a 400 before any SQL exists.

A stacked query fails, but only by luck of the protocol: with arguments, pgx uses the extended query protocol, which accepts one statement per query. pgx's Exec without arguments switches to the simple protocol, where both would run.
No second statement needed. A subquery in ORDER BY casts the secret to int, and PostgreSQL's error message quotes the value it failed to convert.
The output shows the secret inside an error. An API that returns err.Error() to the client has just published it; map errors to generic messages in one place and keep details in the server log.

examples.title: XSS: the same stored string through five output sinks

annotations.note: Both values would pass any reasonable input validation. XSS is not an input problem: the same string is harmless as text and dangerous as markup, so the defense belongs where it is output.

innerHTML parsed the comment and created an img element with an onerror handler. The example leaves out src so nothing loads; with any src, the handler would run as soon as the image failed, no click needed. textContent created no element.
React's default is the safe one: text children and attribute values are escaped, so the payload renders as visible text.
Escaping is correct and not enough: a javascript: URL contains nothing to escape, and React 18 (this app's version) renders the href as given. A click runs it.
dangerouslySetInnerHTML is innerHTML. If you must render user HTML, sanitize it with a maintained sanitizer first, and treat that as a dependency to keep patched.
URLs need an allow-list of schemes, checked with the URL parser rather than a prefix test: the parser lower-cases the scheme, strips leading spaces and encodes the Turkish host ışıl.dev as punycode.

examples.title: CSRF: a JSON endpoint on 127.0.0.1 is reachable from any page in the browser

annotations.note: A run endpoint with no cookies and no authentication. Its only credential is that it listens on 127.0.0.1, which keeps other machines out but not other origins: the browser on this machine can reach it.

A cross-site page can send POST with a text/plain body without a CORS preflight, but not with application/json. Requiring JSON turns the simple request into one the browser must preflight, and the preflight fails without CORS headers.

http.CrossOriginProtection (Go 1.25) rejects non-safe requests that the browser marks as cross-site with Sec-Fetch-Site, or whose Origin host differs from Host. Requests without either header (curl, other servers) pass.

What a page on evil.example can send with fetch and mode: "no-cors": the response is opaque to the page, but the server has already acted. Sec- headers are set by the browser and cannot be set by page scripts.
The undefended endpoint ran the cross-site request (200). Each defense blocks it (415, 403) while the app's own page and non-browser clients keep working.

use_cases: Boundary validation (zod in TS, a strict decoder plus checks in Go): reject malformed input early, with a useful 400
Parameters for every value in SQL; an allow-list for identifiers, sort keys and directions; generic error messages to clients
Output encoding by sink: React text and html/template by default, a URL scheme allow-list for href and src, a sanitizer for user HTML
CSRF protection on every state-changing endpoint a browser can reach, cookie-authenticated or merely local
Secrets from the environment or a secret store, typed so loggers redact them; least-privilege database roles per process
strengths: pgx and database/sql make the safe form the easy form: values go as $n arguments and travel separately from the SQL text
React and Go's html/template escape by default, so XSS requires an explicit opt-out (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, template.HTML) that review can grep for
Go 1.25's http.CrossOriginProtection gives token-free CSRF protection in one wrapper, built on headers browsers set and scripts cannot forge
PostgreSQL roles, GRANTs and row-level security enforce least privilege below the application, where a bug in the app cannot switch them off
weaknesses: No mechanism covers identifiers: table, column and sort names need allow-lists written by hand
Escaping is context-specific; HTML-escaping does nothing for a javascript: URL, a CSS value or a string inside a script
Header-based CSRF defenses assume a browser; non-browser clients need real authentication, and DNS rebinding needs a Host check
Least privilege costs setup: separate roles for migrations and the app, explicit GRANTs, and default privileges for tables created later

pitfalls.title: A masking function that masks the wrong half
pitfalls.detail: StackLab's maskDSN in cmd/stacklab/main.go used to cut the DSN at '@' and keep the part before it, which is postgres://user:password. The host was hidden and the password logged. A keyword-style DSN (password=...) has no '@' and was logged whole. net/url's Redacted (Go 1.15) replaces the password and keeps the rest; maskDSN uses it now.

pitfalls.title: Validation as an XSS defense
pitfalls.detail: Rejecting < and > on input breaks legitimate text (a lesson about generics) and still misses javascript: URLs and attribute contexts. Validate shape on input; encode for the sink on output.

pitfalls.title: Returning database errors to clients
pitfalls.detail: PostgreSQL error messages quote values, constraint and table names. Log them; send the client a stable message and a status from one mapping function, as StackLab's problem helper does.

pitfalls.title: One all-powerful database role
pitfalls.detail: An app connecting as a superuser or the table owner turns any injection into DROP TABLE or COPY ... TO PROGRAM. Migrate with an owner role; run the app with a role that has only the GRANTs it needs (sql.security-ops.roles).

quiz.q: Why can't the sort column be passed as $2?
options: Parameters stand for values; ORDER BY $2 would sort by a constant, not by the named column
It can; the example is just old-fashioned
quiz.why: A parameter is a value. Identifiers and keywords are part of the query's structure, so they must come from code, chosen through an allow-list.

quiz.q: React rendered <a href={website}> with website = "javascript:alert(1)" unchanged. Why didn't escaping help?
options: The string contains no characters that need escaping; the danger is the URL's scheme
quiz.why: Escaping makes the value parse as an attribute value, which it already does. Whether a URL is safe to follow is a separate rule: allow-list its scheme.

quiz.q: A backend with no CSRF defense listens on 127.0.0.1 and uses no cookies. Can a website the owner visits make it run code?
options: No: 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from the internet
No: without cookies there is no CSRF
Yes: the browser on this machine can send a simple cross-site POST to it
quiz.why: The browser is on the same machine. A text/plain POST needs no preflight, the server acts before the browser hides the response, and local reachability is the only credential.

quiz.q: Which header does http.CrossOriginProtection check first, and why can't page JavaScript fake it?
options: Sec-Fetch-Site; Sec- headers are forbidden request headers that only the browser sets
quiz.why: Browsers attach Sec-Fetch-Site to every request and scripts may not set Sec- headers. Without it, the Origin header is compared with Host.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: Message flow, extended query (one statement per Parse)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Security is easier to reason about as a list of surfaces, each with one default defense
that should be on unless you can say why not. The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's version
of this list; here it is by layer, for this stack.

- **Input (every boundary).** Validate shape early: types, lengths, formats, enums. zod
  at the TS trust boundary (ts.services.zod), a strict JSON decoder and explicit checks
  in Go (go.http.json-validation). Validation is about correctness and good errors; it is
  **not** the defense against injection or XSS, because safe input depends on where it
  ends up.
- **SQL.** Every value is a parameter (`$1`), never part of the SQL text
  (go.postgres.transactions shows the classic attack). What can't be a parameter
  (table and column names, sort keys and directions) comes from an allow-list in code.
  Error details go to the log, not the client.
- **Output (XSS).** Encode for the sink. React text and `html/template`
  (go.cli.templates) escape by default; `href` and `src` need a scheme allow-list;
  `innerHTML` and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` need a sanitizer or nothing at all.
- **Requests (CSRF).** A browser will send requests to any server it can reach, with
  whatever ambient credentials apply: cookies, or simply being on the same machine.
  Refuse cross-site state changes: `http.CrossOriginProtection` (Go 1.25), `SameSite`
  cookies (go.http.cors-cookies-httptest), and JSON-only bodies.
- **Secrets.** Out of the repository (only `.env.example` is committed here), out of
  logs (typed secrets with `slog.LogValuer`, as go.cli.slog shows; `url.URL.Redacted`
  for DSNs), out of error messages, and out of the frontend bundle entirely.
- **Privilege.** Every process and database role gets the least that works: an app role
  without DDL rights, a migration role that owns the schema, row-level security for
  tenant isolation (sql.security-ops.roles, sql.security-ops.rls), services bound to
  127.0.0.1 when nothing else needs them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `PreparedStatement` is the same idea as `$1`; JPA's Criteria API exists
  partly to avoid string-built JPQL. Spring Security's CSRF tokens are the synchronizer
  token pattern; Go's `CrossOriginProtection` reaches the same goal with Fetch metadata
  headers and no token.
- **Python**: DB-API placeholders (`%s` in psycopg) are parameters, unlike `%`
  formatting of the SQL string, which looks almost identical. Django and Jinja2
  autoescape HTML, with the same blind spot for `javascript:` URLs.
- **JS/Node**: template literals make string-built SQL tempting; use the driver's
  placeholders. On the frontend, React's escaping is the default you get for free.
- **C/C++**: buffer overflows are mostly gone in Go and TS; injection is the memory
  corruption of web code: data crossing into a context where it is interpreted as code.

## How it works

PostgreSQL has two ways to send a query. The simple protocol takes a string that may
hold several statements; the extended protocol parses one statement, then binds
parameter values separately, as data. pgx uses the extended protocol whenever there are
arguments, which is why `title; DROP TABLE api_keys` failed with "cannot insert multiple
commands into a prepared statement". That is a side effect, not a defense: the subquery
in ORDER BY needed no second statement, and the error message did the rest.

A "simple" cross-origin request is a GET, HEAD or POST whose headers and content type
(`text/plain`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`) a plain HTML
form could have produced. Browsers send it without asking the server first; CORS only
decides whether the page may *read* the response. Since 2023, every major browser also
attaches `Sec-Fetch-Site` (`same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site` or `none`), which
page scripts cannot set, and `CrossOriginProtection` rejects unsafe methods when it says
`cross-site`, falling back to comparing `Origin` with `Host`.

## Design notes

StackLab gets several defaults right. Every SQL value is a parameter; lesson SQL runs as
`playground`, created `NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE` precisely so `COPY ... TO
PROGRAM` is impossible (ADR-0008); errors leave through one `problem` helper and the run
handler's 502 says "details are in the log"; request bodies are capped with
`MaxBytesReader`; PostgreSQL is told to listen on `localhost` only; and only
`.env.example` is in the repository.

Reviewing StackLab for this lesson turned up three problems, in order of severity. All
three are fixed now; each is still worth knowing, because each was easy to miss:

1. **`POST /api/run` accepted cross-site requests.** It decoded JSON without checking
   `Content-Type` or `Origin`, and the server sent no CORS headers but had no CSRF
   check either. A page on any website the owner visited could send the third example's
   `text/plain` POST to `http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/run`; in local mode the code then ran
   in the backend process as the owner's Windows user. ADR-0003's threat model ("protect
   the owner from their own mistakes", void "if this app is ever exposed to a network")
   did not consider the browser as the path in. ADR-0011 closed it: `withRequestGuards`
   in `internal/httpapi/security.go` wraps the router in `http.CrossOriginProtection`,
   requires `application/json` on writes (415 otherwise) and allows only loopback `Host`
   values on `/api/` (403 otherwise). That last check stops DNS rebinding, where a
   hostile domain re-resolves to 127.0.0.1 and its requests look same-origin. Browsers
   have begun to restrict this: under Local Network Access, Chrome 142 and Edge 143 ask
   the user before a public page's `fetch()`, subresource or iframe request reaches a
   local or loopback address ([Chrome](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access),
   [Edge](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/ms-edge-local-network-access)).
   Microsoft's page says Edge has no plans to restrict main-frame navigation, which is
   what a plain form submission is, and the user can click Allow. It is the browser's
   policy, not your defense.
2. **`maskDSN` logged the password** (pitfall above). Low impact with the local
   `stacklab:stacklab` default, but it is the habit that matters once a real password is
   configured. It now parses the URL and logs `Redacted()`, masks `password=` in
   keyword-style DSNs, and logs a placeholder for anything it can't parse.
3. **Database privileges were wider than needed.** PostgreSQL grants `CONNECT` and
   `TEMPORARY` on every new database to `PUBLIC`, so `playground`, and with it every
   lesson, could connect to the app's database (not read its tables, which belong to
   `stacklab`). `setup-local-db.sql` now runs `REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE stacklab FROM
   PUBLIC`, and a connection attempt as `playground` fails with "permission denied for
   database". The app itself connects as `stacklab`, the owner of its schema, so app and
   migrations share one role; a separate migration role is the next step if the app ever
   leaves the owner's machine.

lessons.title: Paradigms side by side: Go, TS, SQL
lessons.summary: One report written three times: Go spells out the loop, the map and the sort; TypeScript describes shapes and lets the checker find mismatches; SQL describes the result and lets the planner choose. Each puts the same rule in a different place: run time, compile time, write time.

examples.title: Go: write the algorithm, check the value yourself

annotations.note: Go's way to spell an enum: a named type and some constants. The set is not closed. "pased" on line 63 is an untyped constant, and untyped constants are assignable to any type they can represent, so the compiler accepts it. Compare line 2 of the TS example.
You choose the data structure (a hash map) and how it is filled. A missing key yields the zero Tally, so there is no "first time" branch: Go's zero values do the work JavaScript's `?? 0` would.
The rule lives here, in code you wrote, and runs at run time. The compiler doesn't check that a switch covers every constant, so the default branch is what turns a bad value into an error value.
Map iteration order is random, so sorting is part of the algorithm, not a nicety. maps.Values with slices.SortedFunc (Go 1.23) collects and sorts in one call; cmp.Or (Go 1.22) chains the sort keys.
The bad value compiles and is found only when report runs, as an ordinary return value the caller must look at.

examples.title: TypeScript: describe the shapes, let the checker work

annotations.note: A literal union is a closed set the checker enforces on every expression it can see. This one type replaces Go's named type, its constants and its default branch, but only at compile time: it is erased before the code runs.
An interface names a shape, not a class. Any object with these three members is a Run, whoever built it; readonly is checked by the compiler only.

The same map-then-sort as Go, as a pipeline: Map.groupBy (ES2024) builds the map, filter counts, sort orders. It reads declaratively but runs exactly as written, in this process, over data already fetched. That is the difference from the SQL version.
Where Go compiled "pased", tsc refuses it (tsc 7.0.2 output). Mistakes in code are caught before anything runs.

Mistakes in data are not. JSON.parse returns any, the cast is accepted unchecked, and the run with status "pased" is silently counted as neither passed nor failed: the last output line. At a trust boundary, validate (lesson ts.services.zod) instead of casting.

examples.title: SQL: describe the result and the rule, let the database do the rest

annotations.note: The rule is part of the table. It is checked on every INSERT and UPDATE from every client: this script, a Go service, psql, a migration.
The whole report as a description: which groups, which counts, which order. FILTER (WHERE ...) counts only matching rows (PostgreSQL 9.4). There is no loop, no map and no variable to get wrong.

The plan shows the algorithm the Go example wrote by hand: HashAggregate is the map, Sort is slices.SortedFunc. On a bigger table with an index the planner may choose differently, and the query text stays the same.

The bad value is refused when it is written, with SQLSTATE 23514. In this runtime the first error ends the script; in an application, the Go layer translates this into a 4xx (lesson design.paradigms.errors).

use_cases: Deciding where a rule belongs: a CHECK or foreign key for invariants every client must respect, a Go switch for workflow decisions, a TS union for UI states and API shapes
Moving a report from a Go loop into one GROUP BY query, or reviewing a pull request that does
Translating an idiom when you switch languages mid-task: map plus sort in Go, Map.groupBy plus sort in TS, GROUP BY plus ORDER BY in SQL
strengths: Go: every step and its cost is on the page; a reviewer sees the map, the copy back into it and the sort, with no stream pipeline hiding allocations as in Java
TS: a misspelled status in source fails the build (TS2345), where Go compiles "pased" as a Status and only the default branch catches it, at run time
SQL: a CHECK constraint rejects bad data from every client, psql included; the Go and TS checks protect only their own code paths
SQL: the same query text can be run as a hash aggregate or a sort, chosen per data size; the algorithm in the Go loop is fixed when you write it
weaknesses: Go: no closed sets; named string types accept any constant, and the compiler doesn't check a switch for completeness
TS: types are erased, so data from JSON.parse, fetch or a cast is never checked unless you validate it
SQL: a bad value is refused at write time, far from the code that built it, as a SQLSTATE the application has to translate
The stack carries three spellings of one concept (Go constants, a TS union, a CHECK list) that drift apart unless one is generated from another or a test compares them

pitfalls.title: Casting data at the trust boundary
pitfalls.detail: A cast tells the checker to believe you. Everything after it is type-checked against a shape the data may not have, as the fromApi line shows. Parse unknown input with a schema instead.
pitfalls.good: const runs = RunList.parse(await res.json()); // a zod schema: throws on bad data

pitfalls.title: Treating a Go named type as a closed enum
pitfalls.detail: Status("pased") compiles, and so does any untyped constant where a Status is expected. Convert strings from outside through one function that returns an error for unknown values, and keep a default branch in every switch.
pitfalls.good: s, err := ParseStatus(r.FormValue("status")) // returns an error for anything but passed/failed

pitfalls.title: Fetching rows to aggregate them in application code
pitfalls.detail: The Go and TS versions need every run in memory first. Against a database, send the GROUP BY and receive three rows instead of three million (lesson sql.basics.set-based).

pitfalls.title: Expecting the same string order in all three
pitfalls.detail: Go's cmp.Compare and JavaScript's < compare bytes and UTF-16 code units, so "Çay" sorts after "Su". PostgreSQL orders by the column's collation; this database's default (the builtin provider) compares code points, so 'Çay' < 'Su' is false there too. Turkish alphabetical order needs a locale: Intl.Collator("tr") or localeCompare(b, "tr") in TS, golang.org/x/text/collate in Go, COLLATE "tr-x-icu" in SQL.

quiz.q: The value "pased" is offered to all three examples. Which one rejects it before any code runs?
options: Go: the named type Status rejects it
TypeScript, for the literal written in source
quiz.why: tsc rejects the literal at compile time. Go accepts the untyped constant and the switch catches it at run time; SQL refuses it when the row is written.

quiz.q: fromApi carries status "pased" through `as Run[]`. What happens?
options: JSON.parse throws because the data doesn't match Run
tsc reports an error on the cast
Nothing checks it; report counts the run as neither passed nor failed
quiz.why: Types are erased and a cast from any is unchecked; only a run-time validation would catch it.

quiz.q: Which version can switch from hashing to sorting without anyone editing it?
quiz.why: The query describes the result; the planner chooses HashAggregate or a sort from statistics and indexes. The Go and TS code run the algorithm they spell out.

quiz.q: Where must "status is passed or failed" live so that a psql session can't break it?
options: In a CHECK constraint on the table
quiz.why: Only the database sees every write. Application checks are for good error messages; the constraint is the guarantee.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Assignability

lessons.body:
## Concept

The three languages of this stack were designed around different ideas, and code reads
best when it follows the idea of the language it is written in.

- **Go is simple and explicit.** You write the algorithm: the loop, the map, the sort, the
  check, the error return. The language has few features and no hidden control flow (no
  exceptions, no inheritance, no implicit conversions between named types), so what a
  function does and what it costs is on the page. Rules live in code that runs.
- **TypeScript is structural and type-driven.** The runtime is JavaScript: dynamic,
  objects as bags of properties, functions as values. On top sits a type system that
  describes shapes, not classes. You design by writing the types first, a literal union
  for the statuses, a readonly array for the input, and the checker finds every place
  that disagrees. Types are erased, so they constrain the code you compile, never the
  data that arrives at run time.
- **SQL is declarative and set-based.** You describe the result and the invariants; the
  planner chooses the algorithms, and constraints guard every write from every client.
  The unit of work is a set of rows, and the data outlives every program that touches it.

The examples solve one small problem in each: group test runs by requirement, count
passes and failures, worst first. Then each is offered the same bad status, `"pased"`.
Go finds it at run time, in a branch you wrote. TypeScript finds it at compile time if
it is in the source, and not at all if it arrives as data. SQL finds it at write time,
whoever writes.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C**: Go is the closest relative here: structs are values, loops are explicit, errors
  are return values. It adds garbage collection, slices, maps, and interfaces that types
  satisfy without declaring it.
- **Java**: Go drops class hierarchies and exceptions; TypeScript keeps classes but rarely
  needs them, because any object of the right shape fits an interface; SQL resembles the
  Streams API in spirit, but it runs next to the data and picks its own execution plan.
- **C++**: TypeScript's structural checks feel like templates and concepts applied to
  every type, except that nothing is generated: the checker runs, then the types vanish.
- **Python**: TypeScript is JavaScript with a mypy that runs on every keystroke and
  blocks the build. Go shares Python's "one obvious way" culture, enforced by `gofmt` and
  a compiler.
- **JS**: TypeScript changes nothing at run time, which is both its strength (all your
  idioms carry over) and the reason the `fromApi` line goes unnoticed.

## How it works

The same concept, spelled three ways:

```text
concept           Go                          TypeScript                  SQL
record            struct (a value)            interface / type (a shape)  table row
collection        slice, map                  array, Map                  table (a set of rows)
closed set        named type + consts (open)  literal union (closed)      CHECK, enum, lookup table
grouping          loop + map                  Map.groupBy                 GROUP BY
ordering          slices.SortFunc             .sort / toSorted            ORDER BY
invariant         code and tests              types, at compile time      constraints, at write time
failure           error value                 throw, or a Result union    SQLSTATE error, rollback
who chooses       you                         you                         the planner
```

## Design notes

In a Go + TypeScript + PostgreSQL system, let each language do what it was built for.
Invariants that must hold whoever writes (not null, unique, references exist, status in
a set) belong in the schema, because only the database sees every write. Filtering,
joining and aggregating belong in queries, next to the data and its indexes. Go owns
workflows, side effects and I/O: calling other services, translating database errors
into API responses, deciding what happens next. TypeScript owns the UI's model, with
types that mirror the API contract and validation where data enters, because the types
will not be there at run time.

The price is that one concept now has three spellings: a CHECK list, Go constants and a
TS union. Make one of them the source and derive the others (sqlc generates Go from the
schema, an OpenAPI document generates TS types), or add a test that compares them.

Each language also has a style that fights it: getters and setters on Go structs, deep
class hierarchies in TypeScript, row-by-row loops around SQL. The rest of this module
takes one problem at a time (errors, polymorphism, concurrency, absence, immutability)
and shows each language's idiomatic answer next to the others; design.patterns.anti-patterns
collects the styles to avoid.

lessons.title: The same problem: error handling (Go errors vs TS exceptions/Result vs SQL constraints)
lessons.summary: One sign-up, three failure models: Go returns error values the caller inspects, TypeScript throws or returns a Result union, and PostgreSQL refuses the write with a SQLSTATE and aborts the transaction. Only the constraint still holds when two requests race.

examples.title: Go: errors are values, inspected with errors.Is and errors.AsType

annotations.note: Two kinds of expected failure: a sentinel answers "which failure?", an error type also carries details. Both are ordinary values; nothing is thrown and nothing unwinds.
The error result is in the signature, so every caller sees that Register can fail. It doesn't list which errors: that is documentation, the same gap a TS signature has for exceptions.
%w wraps the sentinel with context. The message gains "register ayse@example.com", and errors.Is still finds ErrEmailTaken underneath (lesson go.errors.errors-as-values).

The mapping to the outside world lives in one function. errors.AsType (Go 1.26) is the generic form of errors.As. In a real service this is the HTTP boundary, and it also logs the 500 case exactly once.

Nothing forces the check: write users.Register(email) as a bare statement and the program still compiles, and go vet stays quiet too. Third-party linters such as errcheck flag it; code review expects the check on the next line.

examples.title: TypeScript: the same rules, thrown and returned

annotations.note: The throwing version reads like Java or Python. The signature promises void, so tsc can't tell callers that this function fails, or how.

The catch variable is unknown (strict mode), so you narrow with instanceof and rethrow what you didn't expect. The catch block plays the role of Go's status function, but nothing in registerOrThrow's signature told the caller it was needed.
The Result version puts the failure modes in the return type. A caller can't treat the result as a success without checking ok first, which Go's (value, error) pair doesn't enforce.

satisfies checks that every Problem has a status without widening the object's type. Add "rate-limited" to Problem and this line stops compiling; Go's status function would fall through to 500 instead.

examples.title: SQL: the table refuses the write, even under a race

annotations.note: The failure modes are declared, not coded: NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK name the writes this table refuses, for every client.

Each refusal is an error with a SQLSTATE: 23505 unique_violation, 23514 check_violation. A Go repository maps the code (and the constraint name) to its own sentinel; pgx exposes both on *pgconn.PgError.
Both sessions ask "is it free?" and both get 0. This is the check an application does before inserting, and it proves nothing: the other request hasn't written yet.
The unique index decides. B's insert waits on A's uncommitted row, because A could still roll back. When A commits, B fails with 23505. Go's map check and TS's Set check would both have said yes.
An error inside a transaction aborts all of it: every further statement is refused with 25P02 until ROLLBACK. That is SQL's unwinding, and unlike an exception it also undoes the work already done.
The committed result, and a trace of the failures: ids 3, 4 and 6 were used by inserts that failed. Sequences are never rolled back, so treat identity values as unique, not gap-free.

use_cases: A sign-up or create endpoint: SQL UNIQUE and CHECK as the guarantee, Go mapping 23505 to 409 and InvalidError to 422, TS turning 409 and 422 into form messages
Choosing per failure: Go error or TS Result for outcomes callers must handle, panic or throw for bugs, a constraint for anything that must hold across all clients
Reviewing code that checks before writing (SELECT then INSERT) and replacing the check with a constraint plus error mapping
strengths: Go: the error result is in every signature and every propagation is a visible return, so there is no line that can throw unexpectedly as in Java or Python
TS Result: the success value is unreachable until ok is checked, and an exhaustive table over the Problem union makes a new failure a compile error
SQL: a constraint holds under concurrency and for every client; two racing requests can't both insert, which no application-side check can promise
SQL: an error rolls back the whole transaction, so a failure never leaves half the writes behind, unlike an exception thrown between two in-memory updates
weaknesses: Go: the compiler accepts an ignored error, and error is an interface, so the possible failures aren't listed anywhere a tool can check
TS exceptions: signatures can't declare what they throw, catch receives unknown, and libraries keep throwing even when your code returns Results
SQL: errors arrive as codes and constraint names that every layer above must translate; a 23505 means nothing to a user
SQL: an aborted transaction refuses everything until rollback, so an unhandled error poisons every later statement on that connection

pitfalls.title: Checking before writing instead of relying on the constraint
pitfalls.detail: A SELECT that finds no row doesn't reserve anything; the third example shows two sessions passing the same check. Insert, and map the unique violation; or use ON CONFLICT when a duplicate is not an error.
pitfalls.bad: if n, _ := countByEmail(ctx, email); n == 0 { insertUser(ctx, email) }
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING RETURNING id

pitfalls.title: Matching on message text
pitfalls.detail: Go's err.Error(), a JS error's message and PostgreSQL's message text are for humans, and PostgreSQL translates its messages to the server's lc_messages language. Match on identity: errors.Is, instanceof, the SQLSTATE code and the constraint name.
pitfalls.good: if pgErr, ok := errors.AsType[*pgconn.PgError](err); ok && pgErr.Code == "23505" { ... }

pitfalls.title: Carrying on after a failed statement in a transaction
pitfalls.detail: Every later statement fails with 25P02, and COMMIT on an aborted transaction rolls back and reports ROLLBACK instead of failing (pgx returns pgx.ErrTxCommitRollback). Return the error, or put the risky statement in a savepoint (lesson sql.transactions.acid-mvcc).

pitfalls.title: Letting one layer's vocabulary leak into the next
pitfalls.detail: A TS client that parses SQLSTATE codes, or a Go handler that wraps *pgconn.PgError with %w, couples every layer to the database driver. Translate once per boundary: SQLSTATE to sentinel in the repository, sentinel to status in the handler, status to a Problem union in the client.

quiz.q: Two requests register zeynep@example.com at the same moment. Each first runs SELECT count(*) and gets 0. What prevents a duplicate?
options: The UNIQUE constraint: one insert waits, then fails with 23505
READ COMMITTED isolation makes the second SELECT wait
quiz.why: Plain SELECTs never wait for writers under MVCC. The unique index makes the second insert wait for the first transaction and fail when it commits.

quiz.q: Where does the TS example tell tsc that registerOrThrow can fail?
options: In the catch clause of statusOf
quiz.why: TypeScript has no throws clause. The Result version moves the failures into the return type, where the checker can see them.

quiz.q: B's INSERT failed inside BEGIN. What does B's next SELECT do?
options: Fails with 25P02 until B ends the transaction
quiz.why: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction on an error; only ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint) makes the session usable again.

quiz.q: A new failure kind, "rate-limited", is added. Which version makes the compiler point at every place that needs a new case?
options: The TS Result version with satisfies Record<Problem, number>
quiz.why: The record must have a key for every member of the Problem union. Go's if-chain and the TS catch block both fall through to a default silently.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Working with Errors in Go 1.13
PostgreSQL docs: Appendix A. Error Codes

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every failure falls into one of three groups: expected and handled nearby (bad input,
a duplicate e-mail), expected but handled far away (a lost connection, a timeout), and
bugs. The three languages give honest, different answers.

- **Go returns errors as values.** The signature says a function can fail, the caller
  checks on the next line, and context is added with `%w` on the way up. Expected
  failures are sentinels or error types found with `errors.Is` and `errors.AsType`; bugs
  panic. Every propagation is a visible `return`, and nothing forces you to look.
- **TypeScript throws, or returns a union.** JavaScript can throw any value from any
  line, signatures don't say so, and `catch` receives `unknown`. For failures a caller
  must handle every time, a Result union moves them into the return type, where the
  checker makes callers look. Both channels coexist, because the platform and libraries
  throw.
- **SQL refuses the write.** Constraints declare which rows a table will never hold. A
  write that breaks one fails with a SQLSTATE code, and the failure aborts the whole
  transaction. Because the database sees every write, the constraint still holds when two
  requests race, which no check in Go or TypeScript can promise.

All three examples register the same three e-mails against a store that already holds
`ayse@example.com`: one succeeds, one is a duplicate, one is invalid. The SQL example then
runs the race that the in-memory versions can't see.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: checked exceptions put failures in signatures and force handling; Go puts
  them in signatures without forcing; TypeScript does neither. JDBC's
  `SQLException.getSQLState()` is the same five-character code that pgx exposes as
  `PgError.Code`.
- **Python**: TypeScript's exceptions behave like Python's, minus typed `except` clauses.
  psycopg raises `errors.UniqueViolation` for 23505, a class per SQLSTATE, where pgx
  gives one error type with a code field.
- **C**: Go's error values are return codes that carry a message and a chain of causes;
  SQLSTATE is the database's errno, the same on every client and every platform.
- **Rust and C++23**: `Result` and `std::expected` are TypeScript's Result union with
  language or library support; neither Go nor TypeScript has a `?` operator, so
  propagation is an explicit `return`.
- **JS**: nothing in TypeScript changes how `throw` works at run time; the Result union
  is a convention the type checker enforces.

## How it works

One failed sign-up crosses every layer, and each layer translates once:

```text
layer              receives                          produces
TS form            user input                        "must contain @" before sending (UX only)
```
