```text
Go handler         JSON body                         *InvalidError -> 422
Go repository      INSERT fails: SQLSTATE 23505,     ErrEmailTaken, wrapped with %w
                   constraint users_email_key
Go handler         errors.Is(err, ErrEmailTaken)     409 with a problem+json body
TS client          response.status 409               { ok: false, problem: "taken" }
TS form            Problem union                     "this e-mail is already registered"
```

No layer speaks another's vocabulary: the client never sees a SQLSTATE, and the handler
never imports the database driver.

## Design notes

Choose the mechanism per failure, not per codebase. Outcomes a caller must handle every
time (invalid input, a duplicate, "not found") are values: a Go error the caller inspects,
a TS Result the caller narrows. Bugs are panics or exceptions that travel to one boundary
which logs them once. Rules that must hold whoever writes are constraints, and the
application's own checks exist only to produce a better message earlier.

That last point is what the race in the SQL example proves. Validating in TypeScript and
again in Go is good UX and cheap defense, but "is this e-mail free?" can only be answered
by the database at the moment of the write. Let the INSERT fail, and give the constraint
a name the repository can map: the name says which rule broke, the SQLSTATE says what kind.

Transactions change what "handling" means in SQL. After an error the transaction is
dead; the only moves are ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint. In Go, that is the
`defer tx.Rollback(ctx)` of a WithTx helper (lesson go.postgres.transactions); in
TypeScript, it means a failed request should be retried or reported as a whole, never
patched up halfway.

lessons.title: The same problem: polymorphism (Go interfaces vs TS unions vs modeling variants in SQL)
lessons.summary: Discounts come in kinds: Go models them as an open set of types behind an interface, TypeScript as a closed union of tagged objects, SQL as rows with a kind column and a CHECK per shape. Each choice makes one kind of change cheap and leaves the other checked or unchecked.

examples.title: Go: an open set of types behind one method

annotations.note: The interface names the behavior, not the variants. Nothing lists which types implement it, so code in other packages can add discounts without editing this file (lesson go.interfaces.implicit).
Each variant is its own struct, so a Percent can't carry an amount: the illegal mix is unrepresentable here too. The builtin max (Go 1.21) clamps the price at zero.
The open set paying off: Chain is a new variant built from the others, and main's loop calls Apply on it without a single edit elsewhere. In TypeScript this would mean editing the union.

The other axis. An operation the interface doesn't have (here, naming the kind) needs a type switch, and Go has no sum types, so the compiler can't know the switch misses Chain. It falls through at run time.

json.Marshal writes the dynamic value's fields, not its type: {"Pct":15} doesn't say it was a Percent, and decoding it back into a Discount fails. At a boundary, a variant has to become tagged data again.

examples.title: TypeScript: a closed union of tagged objects

annotations.note: The union lists every variant, and each is plain data with a kind tag. This is the closed set Go can't declare, and the same shape as the table's rows and the API's JSON.
Each case narrows d, so d.percent exists only under "percent". There is no default branch on purpose: with the return type declared, a missing case is a compile error (lines 29-30).
JSON.stringify keeps the tag, so the value survives a round trip through an API or localStorage unchanged. Compare the Go example's {"Pct":15}.
A percent discount with an amount doesn't type-check (tsc 7.0.2 output). The SQL example's one_shape CHECK refuses the same row at run time.

The trade-off of a closed set: adding a variant means editing the union, and tsc then points at every switch that doesn't handle it. Go's Chain needed no edits, and its type switch got no warning either.

examples.title: SQL: a kind column, per-variant columns and a CHECK

annotations.note: Rows can't have methods, so the variant is data: a kind column with a closed set of values (the TS union's tags) and one nullable column per variant field.
This CHECK is the discriminated union, enforced on every write: a percent row has a percent and no amount, a fixed row the reverse. Without it, the table would accept any combination of NULLs.
The switch over kind is a CASE in each query that needs it. CASE has no exhaustiveness check: a kind with no WHEN gets NULL, silently, so the CHECK on line 4 is what keeps this CASE complete.
The row the TS checker rejected at compile time is rejected here at write time, with SQLSTATE 23514 and the constraint's name.

use_cases: Go interfaces for behavior supplied from elsewhere: storage backends, notifiers, payment providers, test fakes
TS unions for closed sets the UI must handle completely: request states, reducer actions, API payloads with a kind field
SQL kind column plus CHECK for variants that share most columns, such as discounts or payment methods; a table per variant when each carries a lot of data or its own foreign keys
strengths: Go: a new variant needs no edits anywhere else; Chain composes the existing discounts without them knowing it exists
TS: a switch over the tag is checked for completeness (TS2366), which neither Go's type switch nor SQL's CASE ever is
TS: variants are plain data, so JSON keeps the tag; Go's json.Marshal of an interface value loses which variant it was
SQL: the one_shape CHECK makes a mixed row impossible for every writer, a guarantee the TS type gives only to code tsc compiled
weaknesses: Go: no sum types; a type switch doesn't know the set of variants, so a forgotten case falls through to a default at run time
TS: only the module that owns the union can add a variant, and every switch over it must change in the same commit
SQL: a new kind makes every CASE without ELSE return NULL without warning, and nothing finds those queries for you
SQL: a single table grows a nullable column per variant field, and the shape CHECK has to be kept in step with the kind list

pitfalls.title: Serializing a Go interface value as it is
pitfalls.detail: json.Marshal writes {"Pct":15} with no variant name, and json.Unmarshal into a Discount field fails: "cannot unmarshal object into Go struct field Offer.Discount of type main.Discount". Put a kind field on the wire and switch on it when decoding, which gives the TS union's shape.
pitfalls.good: json.Marshal(wireDiscount{Kind: "percent", Percent: 15}) // {"kind":"percent","percent":15}

pitfalls.title: A default branch that switches off the exhaustiveness check
pitfalls.detail: With a default that returns a value, a new variant compiles and quietly takes that branch. Leave the default out (with a declared return type), or assign the narrowed value to never in it so a missing case is a compile error.
pitfalls.good: default: { const unhandled: never = d; throw new Error(`unknown discount ${JSON.stringify(unhandled)}`); }

pitfalls.title: PostgreSQL table inheritance for variants
pitfalls.detail: CREATE TABLE fixed_discounts (...) INHERITS (discounts) looks like subclassing, but the docs list the catch: unique constraints, primary keys and foreign keys apply to single tables, not their children. The same code can exist in two child tables, and no foreign key can point at "any discount". Use one table with a CHECK, or a base table plus a table per variant sharing its key.

pitfalls.title: Sealing a Go interface by convention only
pitfalls.detail: When the set of variants really is closed (AST nodes, protocol messages), add an unexported method to the interface, as go/ast does with exprNode(). Only types in your package can then satisfy it, and a type switch with a panicking default documents that the set is complete.

quiz.q: A new discount kind is added in all three languages. Where does a compiler point at the code that must handle it?
quiz.why: Only the TS union is a closed type the checker knows; Go's type switch and SQL's CASE fall through to a default or NULL at run time.

quiz.q: What does json.Marshal produce for a Percent{15} held in a Discount interface?
options: An error: interfaces can't be marshaled
quiz.why: Marshal encodes the dynamic value's exported fields; the type name is not part of the output.

quiz.q: Another package needs to add a discount type without editing yours. Which model allows that?
quiz.why: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly by any type with the methods. The union and the CHECK list every variant in one place.

quiz.q: After the kind CHECK is widened to allow 'bogo', what does the example's CASE return for a bogo row?
quiz.why: A CASE with no matching WHEN and no ELSE returns NULL.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Interface types
The Go Programming Language Specification: Type switches
TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing (discriminated unions, exhaustiveness checking)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Polymorphism is one operation over values of several kinds. Every design for it answers
two questions: who can add a new kind, and who can add a new operation, and which of
those changes the compiler checks. The three languages answer differently.

- **Go: an open set of types behind an interface.** The interface names the behavior;
  any type with the methods is a variant, in any package, without declaring it. Adding a
  variant is free. Adding an operation means a method on every type, or a type switch
  the compiler can't check, because Go has no sum types.
- **TypeScript: a closed union of tagged objects.** The union lists every variant, each
  is plain data with a literal `kind`, and a switch on the tag narrows to the variant's
  fields. Adding an operation is a new function with a switch the checker verifies;
  adding a variant means editing the union, after which tsc points at every switch that
  misses it. TypeScript can also do Go's style (objects with methods, matched
  structurally), and uses it for strategies and adapters (lesson ts.architecture.patterns).
- **SQL: variants are rows.** A row has no methods, so the kind is a column, each
  variant's fields are columns, and a CHECK states which columns go with which kind.
  Operations are CASE expressions in queries, and CASE checks nothing.

All three examples price the same 200,00 TL basket with the same discounts. Go then adds
a variant without editing anything; TypeScript shows what adding one costs; SQL refuses
a row whose shape doesn't match its kind.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: a Go interface is a Java interface without `implements`. The TS union is Java
  21's sealed interface with records and a pattern-matching `switch`, which the compiler
  also checks for completeness. JPA's inheritance strategies map to SQL designs:
  `SINGLE_TABLE` is this example, `JOINED` is a table per variant sharing the base key.
- **C++**: virtual functions are the Go side; `std::variant` with `std::visit` is the TS
  side, including the compile error when a visitor misses an alternative.
- **C**: the TS union and the SQL table are both the tagged union you write by hand
  (`struct { enum kind; union { ... }; }`), with the "forgot to check the tag" bug
  removed by the checker and by the CHECK respectively. Go's interface is a struct of
  function pointers that the compiler builds for you.
- **Python**: `typing.Protocol` is Go's model; dataclasses with `match` are the union,
  with completeness checked only by a type checker such as mypy (`assert_never`).
- **Rust**: `enum` with `match` is TypeScript's union; traits are Go's interfaces.

## How it works

The two axes, side by side (the "expression problem"):

```text
                     add a variant                         add an operation
Go interface         a new type, anywhere; no edits        a method on every type, or a
                                                           type switch nobody checks
TS union             edit the union; tsc flags every       a new function; its switch
                     switch that misses it                 is checked for completeness
SQL kind column      widen the CHECK, add columns; every   a CASE in the query; no ELSE
                     CASE silently yields NULL for it      means NULL for unknown kinds
```

At the boundaries between them, the closed, tagged form wins: JSON and table rows carry
a `kind` field, because data has no methods. A Go service decodes `{"kind":"percent",...}`
with a switch on the tag into its interface types, works with them through methods, and
encodes them back with the tag.

## Design notes

Pick the model by the change you expect. When other code must be able to plug in new
kinds (payment providers, storage backends, fakes in tests), use an interface: that is
what Go's are for. When the set is fixed and every consumer must handle every case
(request states, messages between client and server, the statuses of a run), use a
closed form: a TS union, and in Go an interface sealed with an unexported method plus a
type switch whose default panics, since the compiler won't check it for you.

Design the wire format as the TS union and let each side map it. The Go side converts
tags to types at the edge and keeps the conversion in one function, the same "translate
once per boundary" rule as for errors.

In the schema, a single table with a kind column and a shape CHECK suits variants that
share most columns. Move to a base table plus one table per variant when variants carry
many fields or need their own foreign keys, and to a jsonb payload when variant
attributes are numerous and rarely filtered on (lesson sql.tables-types.jsonb-arrays).
Avoid the "polymorphic foreign key" (a `target_type` plus `target_id` pair), which no
foreign key can check; sql.modeling.anti-patterns shows the alternatives.

lessons.title: The same problem: concurrency (goroutines vs the event loop vs MVCC)
lessons.summary: Twenty buyers, ten items: Go guards the counter with a mutex, TypeScript hides the bug behind an await on one thread, PostgreSQL fixes it with the check inside the UPDATE. Same bug, same cure in all three: make the check and the write one step.

examples.title: Go: parallel goroutines, a mutex around check and write

annotations.note: The mutex sits next to the state it guards, unexported, and only Reserve touches it. Callers can't forget to lock what they can't reach.

The check and the decrement form one critical section. Goroutines run in parallel on several threads and can be preempted almost anywhere, so without the lock two of them could both see left == 1: a data race, which `go run -race` reports (the race detector needs cgo and, except on macOS, a C compiler).
Results travel over a channel instead of a second shared counter: "channels orchestrate, mutexes serialize". The buffer of 20 means no buyer blocks on sending.
wg.Go (Go 1.25) starts each buyer and counts it. Which buyers win changes from run to run; how many never does, which is why the output prints counts only.

examples.title: TypeScript: one thread, and a race across await

annotations.note: No data race is possible here: one thread runs one task at a time. But await ends the synchronous step, all twenty buyers pass the check before the first decrement runs, and stock goes to -10. Nothing failed; nothing warned.

The fix needs no lock: code between two awaits can't be interrupted, so checking and decrementing in the same step is atomic. The cost moves to failure handling: a failed payment must put the item back.

Promise.all starts all twenty at once: concurrency without parallelism. They interleave only at awaits, which is why the output is the same on every run (lesson ts.async.event-loop shows the queue order).

examples.title: PostgreSQL: snapshots for readers, row locks for writers

annotations.note: Both transactions read 1, and neither waits: plain reads take no row locks under MVCC. This is the TS check before the await.

B's UPDATE waits for A's row lock, then runs once A commits. It writes the 0 the application computed from a stale read, so both buyers were told yes for one item: a lost update. The CHECK can't help, because 0 is a valid value.
A has written a new version but not committed. B's read doesn't wait: its snapshot still shows the committed version, 1. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

The check is inside the write. B waits for A's lock; after A commits, READ COMMITTED re-evaluates B's WHERE against the new version, finds 0, and B reports UPDATE 0: sold out. In Go, pgx returns that count as tag.RowsAffected().

use_cases: Stock, seats, quotas, coupon redemptions: any "take one if any are left" decision, made in one conditional UPDATE
Go: in-process shared state (caches, counters, connection bookkeeping) under a mutex next to the data, or owned by one goroutine fed by a channel
TS: UI state updated after an await, where a request that started earlier can finish later and overwrite newer data
strengths: Go: real parallelism on every core, with the mutex making the critical section explicit, and a race detector that ships with the standard toolchain (go test -race)
TS: run-to-completion makes every synchronous block atomic, so the fix needs no lock and no data race can corrupt memory
PostgreSQL: readers never wait for writers, and a conditional UPDATE is checked against the latest committed row, across every process and replica of your service
weaknesses: Go: nothing stops you from touching shared state without the lock; the race detector only finds races that happen during the run you test
TS: the race is invisible in the code's shape; moving one await or adding one fetch can turn a correct function into a lost update
PostgreSQL: under the default READ COMMITTED, read-then-write in the application loses updates silently; you have to choose a conditional write, a row lock or a stricter isolation level

pitfalls.title: Shared state without a lock in Go
pitfalls.detail: Called from twenty goroutines, the unguarded version can sell an item twice and is a data race, which the memory model leaves undefined. Run tests with -race.
pitfalls.bad: func (s *Stock) Reserve() bool { if s.left == 0 { return false }; s.left--; return true }
pitfalls.good: func (s *Stock) Reserve() bool { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); if s.left == 0 { return false }; s.left--; return true }

pitfalls.title: Locking the check and the write separately
pitfalls.detail: Two methods that each lock (Available, then Take) are each safe and together racy, exactly like a SELECT followed by an UPDATE or a check followed by an await. Make the operation the caller needs one locked method, one synchronous step, one statement.
pitfalls.good: if s.Reserve() { ... } // checks and takes under one lock

pitfalls.title: An in-process lock in a service with several instances
pitfalls.detail: A Go mutex guards one process's memory, and a TS variable one tab's. Two replicas behind a load balancer each keep their own count. Decide in the database: a conditional UPDATE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or an advisory lock (sql.transactions.row-locks).

pitfalls.title: Holding a transaction open across slow I/O
pitfalls.detail: Awaiting a payment API between BEGIN and COMMIT keeps the row locked and every other buyer waiting. Reserve and commit, call the payment service, then confirm or release the item in a second short transaction.

quiz.q: In the TS racy version, why do all twenty buyers succeed?
options: Two threads ran reserveRacy at the same time
Each buyer awaits after its check, so every check runs before any decrement
quiz.why: One thread runs the code, but await ends each synchronous step; all twenty checks see left === 10 before the first left-- runs.

quiz.q: B's UPDATE ... WHERE ... AND left_qty > 0 waited for A, then reported UPDATE 0. Why?
options: B's snapshot was taken before A's update
After A committed, B re-checked its WHERE against the new row version, where left_qty was 0
The CHECK constraint rejected the row silently
quiz.why: Under READ COMMITTED a blocked UPDATE re-evaluates its condition on the updated row once the other transaction commits; no row matched.

quiz.q: While A had updated 'fixed' but not committed, B ran SELECT left_qty. What happened?
options: B waited for A's commit, then saw 0
quiz.why: MVCC readers take no locks; B's snapshot shows the last committed version.

quiz.q: Your Go service runs as three replicas. Where must "is there an item left?" be decided?
options: In a sync.Mutex in each replica
In the browser, before sending the order
In the database, in the same statement that takes the item
quiz.why: Each replica has its own memory; only the database sees every buyer, and a conditional UPDATE makes the check and the write one step.

lessons.body:
## Concept

"Twenty buyers, ten items" is the same problem in all three languages: a check ("is
anything left?") followed by a write ("take one"). If anything can run between the two,
two buyers can pass the check for the last item. Each runtime decides what can run in
between, and that decides what the fix looks like.

- **Go: threads.** Goroutines run in parallel on several OS threads and can be preempted
  at almost any point. Any shared variable written by one goroutine and read by another
  needs synchronization, or it is a data race. The fix is a critical section: the check
  and the write under one mutex, or the state owned by a single goroutine that others
  talk to over a channel.
- **TypeScript: tasks.** One thread runs one task at a time, to completion. Memory can't
  be corrupted, and synchronous code is atomic. But every `await` ends the step, and other
  tasks run before the function continues. The fix is to do the check and the write in
  one synchronous step and await afterwards.
- **PostgreSQL: transactions.** Many sessions run at once, each in its own server
  process, isolated by MVCC: every statement reads a snapshot of committed rows, and
  writers of the same row queue on its lock. The fix is a write that carries its own
  check, `UPDATE ... WHERE left_qty > 0`, which is re-evaluated against the latest
  committed row when it has to wait.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/C++**: Go's model is yours, threads plus locks, with cheaper threads and a
  channel type built in. `sync.Mutex` is `ReentrantLock` without reentrancy and without
  `synchronized`; `defer mu.Unlock()` is a `lock_guard`.
- **Python**: the GIL hides some races in CPython threads (a single bytecode such as a
  list append is atomic); Go has no GIL, so the unguarded version breaks quickly.
  `asyncio` is the TypeScript model exactly: one thread, switches only at `await`.
- **JS/Node**: the TS example is plain JavaScript semantics. Node is the same model on
  the server; parallelism comes from Worker threads or more processes, each with its own
  memory unless you share a `SharedArrayBuffer`.
- **Databases you've used through an ORM**: Hibernate's optimistic locking (`@Version`)
  is the conditional UPDATE in disguise: `UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?`, and zero rows
  updated means someone else won.

## How it works

Where each runtime can interleave two buyers, and what makes a step atomic:

```text
             runs                                   atomic step                   guards for shared state
Go           goroutines on all cores, preempted     code between Lock and Unlock  mutex, channel ownership,
             almost anywhere                                                      sync/atomic
TypeScript   one thread, each task to completion    synchronous code between      nothing within a step; a
                                                    two awaits                    promise chain across awaits
PostgreSQL   one server process per connection,    one statement; a transaction  snapshots for reads, row
             all at once                            with row locks or             locks for writes, isolation
                                                    SERIALIZABLE                  levels
```

The same bug shows up in each column: Go's unguarded `left--`, TypeScript's check
before `await`, SQL's SELECT followed by an UPDATE of a computed value. The same cure
fixes all three: move the check into the atomic step.

## Design notes

A real deployment has all three at once: several browser tabs, several Go processes,
one database. In-process tools (a mutex, a single-threaded loop) protect one process's
memory, so any decision that involves shared business state, such as stock, seats or a
unique booking, belongs in the database, made by one statement or under a row lock. Go
and TypeScript keep their own concurrency tools for their own state: caches, in-flight
requests, UI state.

In SQL, prefer the conditional write: `UPDATE ... WHERE left_qty > 0` and look at the
row count. Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` when the decision needs several reads first, and
REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop when the invariant spans rows
(sql.transactions.serializable). Under REPEATABLE READ, the racy version's second
UPDATE would have failed with SQLSTATE 40001 instead of silently losing an update.

In Go, keep the mutex next to the data, unexported, with methods that lock; pass
ownership through channels when work moves between goroutines. In TypeScript, treat
every `await` as a place where the world changes: re-read what you checked, or do the
check and the change before awaiting.

lessons.title: The same problem: generics, and absence (zero values vs undefined/null vs NULL)
lessons.summary: "The cheapest offer" can be missing because the product isn't listed, has no offers, or has an unknown price. Go answers with zero values plus an ok bool, TypeScript with T | undefined, SQL with NULL in every type and no row at all.

examples.title: Go: a zero value plus a bool

annotations.note: A generic function can't return nil for a T that may be int64, and there is no Optional type: `var zero T` is the only "nothing" it can make. So absence travels as a second result, the comma-ok shape of map reads and type assertions. slices.Min (Go 1.21) would panic on an empty slice instead.
Reading a missing key yields the zero value, a nil slice, which ranges and measures exactly like an empty one. Only the comma-ok bool tells "ayran isn't listed" from "kahve has no offers".
Three situations, three branches. The free promotion prints 0 as a real price because ok, not the value, says whether there was one.
What the bools were for: without them, an unlisted product, a product without offers and a free offer all come back as 0. Never let a zero value stand for "missing" when zero is a valid answer.

examples.title: TypeScript: absence in the type, narrowed before use

annotations.note: The generic version returns T | undefined: the type itself says the result may be missing, and strictNullChecks makes callers narrow it. The catch: if T can itself be undefined, a missing result and a stored undefined look the same, where Go's bool would still tell them apart.
The guard is required, not cosmetic: [].reduce(f) with no initial value throws a TypeError.
Map.get returns number[] | undefined, and the early return narrows prices to number[] for the rest of the loop body. This is Go's comma-ok, expressed in the type instead of a second variable.
JavaScript's built-in answer for "the minimum of nothing" is Infinity, a number that looks like a price. And JSON has no Infinity, so it arrives at the server as null.
|| treats 0, "" and false as missing too, so the free offer turns into "no offers". ?? replaces only null and undefined.

examples.title: SQL: NULL in every type, and the difference between NULL and no row

annotations.note: A nullable column is SQL's third kind of absence, "unknown": the price exists but isn't known. In Go this column needs *int32 or sql.Null[int32], in TS number | null.

kahve has no offers, so the LEFT JOIN gives it one row of NULLs and min returns NULL. For su, min skips the NULL price and returns the free 0. count(column) counts non-null values, so offers and priced differ.
No row at all is a different answer from a NULL. In Go, QueryRow(...).Scan returns pgx.ErrNoRows here, which a repository translates to its own ErrNotFound.
Without GROUP BY, an aggregate always returns exactly one row, even over no input: min is NULL, count is 0. Code that expects "no row" for an unknown product never gets it.
coalesce is SQL's ??, and like min it works for any type. Use it to present absence, as here, not to store a made-up value in its place.

use_cases: Lookups that may find nothing: comma-ok or (T, bool) in Go, T | undefined in TS, an empty result in SQL, kept distinct from a found zero
Optional fields across the stack: a nullable column, a *T or sql.Null[T] field in Go, a JSON null, number | null in TS
Reports over groups that may be empty: LEFT JOIN plus aggregates, where NULL and count = 0 mean "nothing to measure"
strengths: Go: every variable is usable at its zero value, and no read of a missing map key or unset field can crash, unlike a null dereference in Java
TS: absence is part of the type under strictNullChecks, so the compiler makes callers handle undefined, which Go's zero values never force
SQL: aggregates skip unknown values by definition, so one missing price doesn't turn the whole minimum into NULL
weaknesses: Go: a zero value is indistinguishable from a real 0 or "" unless you add a bool, a pointer or sql.Null[T]
TS: two absent values (undefined and null) and falsy-based operators (||) make it easy to treat 0 as missing
SQL: NULL is in every column type unless you add NOT NULL, and it propagates through expressions and three-valued logic

pitfalls.title: A generic helper that returns a bare zero value
pitfalls.detail: The caller can't tell "no element" from an element equal to the zero value. Return (T, bool), as map reads and type assertions do.
pitfalls.bad: func MinOf[T cmp.Ordered](xs []T) T { var zero T; if len(xs) == 0 { return zero }; return slices.Min(xs) }
pitfalls.good: func MinOf[T cmp.Ordered](xs []T) (T, bool)

pitfalls.title: omitempty erasing a real zero on the way to TypeScript
pitfalls.detail: encoding/json's omitempty drops a 0 int64, so a free price disappears from the JSON and the TS client reads undefined: "no offers". Use a pointer, which encodes nil as null and 0 as 0.
pitfalls.good: Cheapest *int64 `json:"cheapest"` // nil -> null, 0 -> 0

pitfalls.title: Defaulting with || in TypeScript
pitfalls.detail: || replaces every falsy value: 0, "", false and NaN as well as null and undefined. Default with ?? unless replacing those is really what you mean.
pitfalls.good: const shown = cheapest ?? "no offers";

pitfalls.title: Expecting no row from an aggregate
pitfalls.detail: SELECT min(...) WHERE ... returns one row even when nothing matches, so pgx's QueryRow never reports ErrNoRows for it. Scan into a pointer and check for nil, or count the rows explicitly.

quiz.q: Why does MinOf return (T, bool) instead of just T?
options: Generic functions must return two values
The zero value of T can be a real answer, like a free price of 0
quiz.why: Without the bool, an empty input and a minimum of 0 return the same value.

quiz.q: How many rows does SELECT min(price_kurus) FROM offers WHERE product = 'ayran' return?
quiz.why: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; min over no input is NULL.

quiz.q: cheapest is 0, a free offer. What does `cheapest || "no offers"` evaluate to?
quiz.why: 0 is falsy, so || falls through to the right side; ?? would keep the 0.

quiz.q: su has offers 500, 0 and NULL. What does min(price_kurus) return for it?
options: NULL, because one price is unknown
quiz.why: Aggregate functions other than count(*) ignore NULL inputs.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: The zero value
The Go Programming Language Specification: Index expressions (comma-ok)

lessons.body:
## Concept

"Missing" is not one thing. In the example there are four products and four answers:
`ayran` isn't listed, `kahve` is listed with no offers, `simit` has a cheapest offer, and
`su` has a free one, so 0 is a real price. SQL adds a fifth case, an offer whose price is
unknown. Each language spells these differently, and the spelling shapes its generic code.

- **Go has zero values, not nulls.** Every type has a zero value, and a missing map key,
  an unset field and `var zero T` in generic code all produce it. Absence is therefore a
  separate signal: the comma-ok bool, a `(T, bool)` or `(T, error)` result, or a type
  that can say "nothing" (`*T`, `sql.Null[T]`) where a field may be absent.
- **TypeScript has two absent values in the type.** `undefined` is "never set" and `null`
  is "explicitly empty". Under strictNullChecks they belong to no other type, so a value
  that may be missing says so (`T | undefined`), and the checker makes you narrow before
  use. Generic code returns `T | undefined`.
- **SQL has NULL in every type, and empty results.** NULL means unknown and is a member of
  every column type unless NOT NULL removes it. Aggregates skip it, and over no input they
  return it (except `count`). Separately, a query can return no row at all, which is not
  the same answer as a row holding NULL.

Each language also has a built-in "minimum of nothing", and none of them is "nothing":
Go's `slices.Min` panics, JavaScript's `Math.min()` returns `Infinity`, and SQL's `min`
returns NULL.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `null` belongs to every reference type, as NULL belongs to every SQL type.
  Go's `(T, bool)` is an `Optional<T>` split into two values, and TypeScript under
  strictNullChecks works like Kotlin's `String` versus `String?`.
- **C/C++**: Go's zero values are C's zero-initialized statics applied to everything,
  so there is no uninitialized memory. `std::optional<T>` is the closest relative of Go's
  `(T, bool)`; `T | undefined` is an optional the compiler forces you to check.
- **Python**: `min([])` raises `ValueError`, much like Go's panic, and `min(xs, default=None)`
  is the TS `T | undefined` version. `dict.get(k)` returning `None` is `Map.get`.
- **JS**: TypeScript changes no run-time behavior: `Math.min()` is still `Infinity`,
  `[].reduce(f)` still throws, and `JSON.stringify` still turns `Infinity` into `null`.
- **Generics in general**: Java erases `T`, so every `T` can be null; C# has
  `default(T)`, which is Go's `var zero T`; TypeScript's `T | undefined` is ambiguous
  only when `T` itself includes `undefined`.

## How it works

The same situations, in each spelling:

```text
situation           Go                             TypeScript                SQL
not listed          offers[p]: nil, ok == false    Map.get -> undefined      no row
listed, no offers   MinOf -> (0, false)            minOf -> undefined        min() -> NULL, count 0
free offer          MinOf -> (0, true)             minOf -> 0                min() -> 0
price unknown       *int32 nil, sql.Null[int32]    number | null             NULL, skipped by min()
minimum of nothing  slices.Min panics              Math.min() is Infinity    min() is NULL
```

Crossing layers, the spellings have to be translated: a NULL column scans into a nil
pointer in Go (pgx refuses to scan NULL into a plain `int32`), `encoding/json` writes the
nil pointer as `null`, and TypeScript reads `number | null`.

## Design notes

Give each kind of absence one meaning and keep it through every layer. "Not listed" is
no row in SQL, a not-found error in Go and a 404 for the client. "No offers" is NULL from
the aggregate, a nil pointer in Go, `null` in JSON. A free offer is 0 everywhere, and no
layer may turn it into "missing": `omitempty` on an integer, `||` in TypeScript and
`coalesce(price, 0)` in SQL are the three usual ways it happens.

Prefer NOT NULL in the schema, and allow NULL only where "unknown" is a real state
(lesson sql.querying.null-logic). In Go, make types useful at their zero value, but don't
let the zero value stand for "not set" when zero is a legal value; use a pointer or
`sql.Null[T]` for those fields. In TypeScript, use `undefined` for "not provided" and
`null` only where the data carries it, typically JSON from a Go API and nullable columns.

For generic helpers, follow each language's convention: `(T, bool)` in Go, because a
type parameter has no nil; `T | undefined` in TypeScript, switching to a `{ found, value }`
result only when `T` may itself include `undefined`; and in SQL, the built-in
polymorphic functions (`min`, `coalesce`) already return NULL of whatever type they're
given.

lessons.title: The same problem: immutability
lessons.summary: A price changes, and last month's order must keep the old one: Go protects the old list by API and copy-on-write, TypeScript by readonly types and Object.freeze, SQL by an INSERT-only table. All three make a change a new value, and all three are shallow somewhere.

examples.title: Go: immutable by API, copy-on-write with maps.Clone

annotations.note: Go's const covers only compile-time constants, so a struct, map or slice can't be declared immutable. The guarantee comes from the API: an unexported field (outside this package, nobody can reach it) and a constructor that clones its input, so the caller keeps no alias to the map.

A change produces a new PriceList over a cloned map (maps.Clone, Go 1.21). The old list is never touched, so the order's snapshot and any goroutine reading it need no lock. The price is O(n) per change.
The trap: a value receiver looks like it works on a copy, but copying a struct copies the map header, not the map. Writing through it changes every copy (lesson go.composite.structs).
The order still says 1250 after the November change: With built a new list instead of editing the one the order holds.
"Changing a copy" changed november, because both structs point at one map. october is unaffected only because With cloned the map earlier.

examples.title: TypeScript: readonly for the checker, freeze for the runtime

annotations.note: Readonly<T> makes every property read-only to the checker, at no run-time cost. The const on line 4 is a different thing: it stops reassigning the name october, not writing to the object.
The TS form of With: spread copies october's properties into a new object and overrides one. It copies one level, which is all a flat price list needs.
A direct write is a compile error (tsc 7.0.2 output). This is where most of TypeScript's immutability lives: in the checker.

Types are erased and a cast removes readonly, so only Object.freeze stops the write at run time. ES modules are strict mode code, where the write throws a TypeError; sloppy-mode scripts ignore it silently.

Shallow, like Go's struct copy: the outer object is frozen and typed readonly, the nested prices object is neither, and tsc accepts the write. as const or a recursive readonly type, plus a deep freeze, are needed for nested data.

examples.title: SQL: an INSERT-only table, with history as a query

annotations.note: Each row is a fact that doesn't change: this sku cost this much from this date. The key includes valid_from, so a new price is a new row rather than a new value in an old one.

A statement-level trigger refuses the statements that would rewrite history; TRUNCATE triggers must be FOR EACH STATEMENT anyway. In production, REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE from the application's role first; the trigger also stops the owner's ad-hoc fixes.
The SQL form of With: insert the new version. The October row is still there for every order that was priced with it.
History is a query, not a copy you had to keep: the newest price on or before the order date. The primary key's index on (sku, valid_from) serves this lookup.
"Current" is also a query: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per sku in the ORDER BY order, here the newest. A view over this query gives the application a current_prices table to read.
The trigger's exception: SQLSTATE P0001, raise_exception. Because the script runs in one transaction, the error ends it.

use_cases: Prices, tax rates and exchange rates that orders and invoices must reproduce later: an INSERT-only table with valid_from, read with "newest on or before"
Configuration or price lists shared between goroutines: an immutable value swapped as a whole (atomic.Pointer), never edited in place
UI state in TypeScript and React: readonly types plus spread updates, so a changed reference means changed data
strengths: Go: an immutable value can be shared between goroutines without a mutex, since nobody writes it; a new version replaces the old one as a whole
TS: readonly turns accidental writes into compile errors at every call site at zero run-time cost, and spread makes a copy-on-write update one expression
SQL: an INSERT-only table keeps every past state answerable with a WHERE clause, and no client can rewrite what an order was charged
SQL: rows hold values and keys, never pointers, so copying a row can't alias anything, unlike Go maps and JS objects
weaknesses: Go: no deep or declared immutability; it is a convention guarded by package boundaries, and maps.Clone costs a full copy per change
TS: readonly is erased, a cast removes it, and both readonly and Object.freeze are shallow
SQL: "current state" becomes a query that needs an index, corrections need a convention of their own, and the table only grows

pitfalls.title: Handing out the internal map or slice
pitfalls.detail: A getter that returns the map gives every caller write access to state the type promised not to change. Return a clone, or an iterator, which has no way to write.
pitfalls.bad: func (p PriceList) All() map[string]int64 { return p.prices }
pitfalls.good: func (p PriceList) All() iter.Seq2[string, int64] { return maps.All(p.prices) }

pitfalls.title: Reading const as immutable
pitfalls.detail: In TypeScript, const forbids reassigning the binding; the object stays writable. In Go, const exists only for numbers, strings, booleans and runes known at compile time. Neither makes data read-only.
pitfalls.bad: const october = { simit: 1250 }; october.simit = 0; // compiles and runs
pitfalls.good: const october: Readonly<Record<string, number>> = Object.freeze({ simit: 1250 });

pitfalls.title: Updating in place where history matters
pitfalls.detail: UPDATE prices SET kurus = 1500 erases what October's orders were charged. Insert a new version with a validity date, or copy the price into the order line when the order is placed; PostgreSQL 18's temporal keys can enforce non-overlapping periods (lesson sql.modeling.temporal).
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE prices SET kurus = 1500 WHERE sku = 'simit';
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('simit', 1500, '2026-11-01');

pitfalls.title: Personal data in an append-only table
pitfalls.detail: Nothing can be erased from a table that refuses DELETE, but KVKK requires personal data to be erased, destroyed or anonymized once the reason to keep it ends. Keep personal data in mutable tables referenced by key, and keep append-only tables to facts about prices, amounts and states.

quiz.q: After november := october.With("simit", 1500), what does order.Prices.Price("simit") return?
options: 1250: With built a new list and left the order's one alone
quiz.why: With clones the map and writes to the clone; the order keeps a reference to the untouched October list.

quiz.q: copied := november; copied.SetInPlace("ayran", 0). Why does november's ayran become 0?
options: Copying the struct copied the map header, so both structs share one map
maps are copied lazily on first write
quiz.why: Struct assignment copies fields; a map field is a reference to the same hash table.

quiz.q: const october = { simit: 1250 }. What does october.simit = 0 do?
options: Throws a TypeError at run time
quiz.why: const only prevents reassigning october. readonly types or Object.freeze are needed to protect the object.

quiz.q: In the append-only table, how does simit's price change on 1 December?
options: DELETE the old row, INSERT the new one
quiz.why: Every change is a new fact; the trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE, and queries pick the newest row on or before a date.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Constants

lessons.body:
## Concept

The simit costs 12,50 TL in October and 15,00 TL from November. An order placed on 20
October must still say 12,50 when someone opens it in December. All three examples solve
this the same way: a change produces a new value and leaves the old one alone, so whoever
holds the old one can trust it. What differs is who enforces that.

- **Go enforces it by API.** `const` exists only for compile-time constants, so maps,
  slices and structs can't be declared read-only. An immutable type keeps its state in
  unexported fields, never writes it after construction, and offers methods that return a
  new value (`With`). Value semantics help, but shallowly: copying a struct copies its
  map and slice headers, not what they point to.
- **TypeScript enforces it in the checker, optionally at run time.** `const` fixes the
  binding, not the object. `readonly`, `Readonly<T>`, `ReadonlyArray<T>` and `as const`
  turn writes into compile errors and are erased. `Object.freeze` enforces at run time,
  one level deep. An update is a new object built with spread, sharing whatever didn't
  change.
- **SQL enforces it in the schema.** Tables are mutable by nature, but a table of facts
  can be append-only: a change is a new row with its validity date, history is a WHERE
  clause, and a trigger (or revoked privileges) refuses UPDATE and DELETE. Underneath,
  PostgreSQL already works this way: an UPDATE writes a new row version and leaves the
  old one for snapshots still reading it (lesson sql.transactions.acid-mvcc).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C++**: Go has no `const` member functions or `const T&` parameters; immutability is
  a property of the type's API instead. TypeScript's `readonly` is the closest thing to
  `const`, and like `const` on a pointer it says nothing about what the pointee allows.
- **Java**: an immutable Go type is a final class with private final fields and
  `withX` methods; Java records are shallowly immutable in the same way, since a record
  holding a `List` can't stop that list from being changed. `Object.freeze` resembles
  an unmodifiable collection, except that it locks the object itself instead of wrapping
  it, and a failed write throws only in strict mode.
- **Python**: frozen dataclasses and tuples are shallow too: a tuple holding a list holds
  a mutable list. `dataclasses.replace(p, simit=1500)` is `With`.
- **JS**: `const` was never immutability; TypeScript adds `readonly` on top without
  changing what runs. React's state rule ("never mutate, replace") is copy-on-write, and
  it is why `prev !== next` can mean "changed".

## How it works

```text
                   Go                            TypeScript                      SQL
fixed binding      const (compile-time values)   const                           -
no writes          unexported fields, no         readonly, Readonly<T> (tsc);    trigger, or REVOKE UPDATE,
                   setters (package boundary)    Object.freeze (run time)        DELETE, TRUNCATE
make a change      With: maps.Clone, then write  { ...old, simit: 1500 }         INSERT a new version
how deep           struct copy is shallow        spread, readonly and freeze     a row holds values and
                                                 are shallow                     keys, never pointers
the past           keep a reference to the old   keep a reference to the old     WHERE valid_from <= date
                   value                         object                          ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1
```

## Design notes

Immutability is how the three languages share data safely. In Go, a value nobody writes
can be read from any goroutine without a lock; the usual pattern for configuration or a
price list is to build a new value and swap it in whole with an `atomic.Pointer`, which is
what MVCC does with row versions. In TypeScript, treat any state other code can see as
immutable, put `readonly` in function signatures, and update by copying the path to the
change; React depends on it. Reserve `Object.freeze` for shared module-level data that
code outside the type system could write.

In the schema, choose per table. Facts (orders, payments, ledger entries, price and rate
histories, audit events) belong in append-only tables: they are never wrong, only
superseded or corrected by a later row. Current state that people edit (a user's
profile, a requirement's title) belongs in ordinary tables, with history kept by a
trigger or a temporal design when it matters (sql.modeling.temporal), not by soft
delete. An append-only table writes no dead row versions, so it doesn't bloat;
autovacuum still visits it, triggered by inserts since PostgreSQL 13, to freeze old rows.

Every form is shallow somewhere, so state the depth you mean. A Go type that holds a
slice must clone it on the way in and on the way out; a TypeScript `Readonly<T>` over
nested data needs a recursive type or `as const`; an SQL row that references a mutable
row by key is only as stable as that row, which is why an order line copies the price
instead of pointing at the current one.

lessons.title: Strategy, adapter, decorator/middleware, observer/pub-sub — idiomatically per language
lessons.summary: Four Gang of Four patterns in Go, TypeScript and SQL. The problems they solve are permanent; the interfaces, base classes and registries that Java needed to express them mostly disappear, and in SQL some patterns become data.

examples.title: Go: a strategy is a func type; decorators and an adapter are functions around it

annotations.note: The strategy "interface" is a function type, so any function of that shape is a strategy. The one-line Fee method is the http.HandlerFunc trick: it lets a plain function satisfy a one-method interface without a wrapper struct.

A decorator takes a FeeRule and returns one, so decorators nest freely and no abstract base class is needed. The outermost one decides first: freeAbove returns 0 before capped or the carrier are ever asked.

The adapter is a closure. Its real job is the boundary conversion: the SDK speaks float64 lira, the program speaks integer kuruş, and the rounding happens once, here, so float money never leaks inward.

The consumer declares the port it needs (go.design.packages). FeeRule satisfies it implicitly, and so would any struct with a Fee method: a strategy that needs state and several methods can grow into a struct without touching the caller.
The whole "pattern catalogue" is four lines of composition. In Java this is an interface, three strategy classes, an abstract decorator and two subclasses.

examples.title: TypeScript: decorator order is semantics, and what @ really does

annotations.note: A decorator as a higher-order function: same type in and out. It caches the Promise, not the value, so two concurrent calls for one word share a single in-flight lookup.

The same two decorators in two orders. logged outside cached sees every call (three lines); logged inside cached sees only misses (two lines). Middleware order in go.http.middleware is the same rule: the outer layer sees more.

A TS 5.0 standard decorator is a function from (method, context) to a replacement method. It runs once, when the class is defined. Angular and NestJS use the older experimentalDecorators form, whose signature differs.

This Map is created once per class definition, so every instance shares it. That is why b.computed stays 0 below: b got a's cached answer. Per-instance state needs a WeakMap keyed by this, or context.addInitializer.
Prints İĞNE twice and "computed: 1 0". The Turkish locale also turns i into İ, which plain toUpperCase() would not.

examples.title: SQL: strategy as rows, adapter as a view, observer as a trigger writing an outbox

annotations.note: In SQL a strategy becomes data: one row per rule. Adding a rule is an INSERT, not a deploy, at the price of the type checks and tests that code would get.
A view is an adapter: it renames Turkish legacy columns and converts lira to kuruş once, and every consumer queries orders in the shape it expects.

The join picks the strategy per row and CASE applies it. For the flat rule, total_kurus >= NULL is NULL, not true, so CASE falls through to the ELSE branch: NULL means "never free" without a special case.

A trigger is an observer on every ordinary write path: psql, migrations and every service fire it. The event row is written in the same transaction as the order, so a rolled-back order leaves no event. That is the outbox pattern.
One INSERT of two rows produced two events, because the trigger is FOR EACH ROW. A bulk load of a million rows writes a million outbox rows too.

use_cases: Strategy: pricing, sorting, retry policies, storage backends; a func type in Go, a function type or record of functions in TS, a rules table in SQL when non-developers change the rules
Adapter: wrapping a vendor SDK, a legacy table (a view) or a second backend behind the port your code declared
Decorator/middleware: logging, caching, auth, timeouts, metrics around a handler or a client call
Observer/pub-sub: UI stores, domain events, cache invalidation; an outbox table when the event must survive a crash
strengths: Go's implicit interfaces and func types make every pattern here a few lines: unlike Java, the strategy never declares that it implements anything, and a function can satisfy an interface through a method on its type
Decorators compose by plain function application in both Go and TS, so a stack of five is readable top to bottom, unlike five nested subclasses of an abstract decorator
SQL patterns are enforced for every client: a view or a trigger applies to psql, migrations and every service, which no application-level adapter can promise
An outbox row written in the same transaction as the change gives at-least-once delivery without a distributed transaction
weaknesses: Function types carry no name in error messages or stack traces: a panic inside a closure shows main.fromSDK.func1, not CarrierPricer.Fee
Strategies stored as rows lose compile-time checks; a misspelled rule name is a missed join, not a build error
Triggers are invisible from the application code: a reader of the INSERT has no hint that it also writes an outbox row
TS standard decorators apply only to classes and their members; a plain function still needs the higher-order-function form

pitfalls.title: Decorator order hides calls
pitfalls.detail: A cache outside the logger means cache hits never reach the log, so the log undercounts traffic. Put observers (logging, metrics) outermost unless you mean to measure only misses.
pitfalls.bad: handler := withCache(withLogging(api)) // hits are never logged
pitfalls.good: handler := withLogging(withCache(api)) // every request logged, hit or miss

pitfalls.title: Per-class state in a TS decorator
pitfalls.detail: The decorator function runs once per class definition. Anything it creates (a Map, a counter) is shared by every instance, as b.computed = 0 shows. Key per-instance state by this in a WeakMap.

pitfalls.title: An interface per strategy, declared up front
pitfalls.detail: Java habit: IFeeStrategy next to the only implementation. In Go, declare the interface in the consumer when a second implementation or a fake appears (go.design.packages); in TS a function type is already the interface.

pitfalls.title: NOTIFY treated as a durable queue
pitfalls.detail: NOTIFY is delivered at commit to sessions listening at that moment, and is gone otherwise. Use it to wake a worker, and keep the event itself in an outbox table the worker reads.

quiz.q: Which stack logs only cache misses?
quiz.why: The cache sits outside the logger, so a hit returns before the logger is reached. The outer layer sees more calls, the same rule as Go middleware.

quiz.q: How does http.HandlerFunc (or FeeRule above) let a plain function satisfy a one-method interface?
options: A compiler special case for functions
A named func type with a method that calls the function itself
An implements clause on the type
quiz.why: Methods can be declared on any named type, function types included. The method just calls f, and the type now has the method set the interface asks for.

quiz.q: An order and its 'order placed' event must be committed together or not at all. Which design gives that?
options: Publishing to a broker after COMMIT
An outbox row written in the same transaction
quiz.why: The outbox row commits or rolls back with the order. NOTIFY also waits for commit but is lost if no one is listening, and publishing after COMMIT can fail after the order is already saved.

quiz.q: Why did b.upper("iğne") leave b.computed at 0?
options: The decorator ran once per class, so a and b share its cache
Class fields are shared between instances
quiz.why: Standard decorators are evaluated when the class is defined. The returned method is on the prototype, and the Map it closes over is shared by every instance.

lessons.body:
## Concept

The *Design Patterns* book (1994) wrote its examples in C++ and Smalltalk. The problems
it names are still with us: swap an algorithm (**strategy**), fit a foreign shape to yours
(**adapter**), add behaviour around an object without changing it (**decorator**), tell
interested parties that something happened (**observer**). What changes from language to
language is how much ceremony the encoding needs.

- **Strategy.** Go: a `func` type, or a one-method interface when the strategy has state.
  TS: a function type, or a record of functions checked with `satisfies`
  (ts.architecture.patterns). SQL: a row in a rules table, chosen by a join and applied by
  `CASE`; the strategy becomes data.
- **Adapter.** Go: a closure or a small struct that wraps the foreign type and satisfies
  the interface your code declared; a method on a func type (`http.HandlerFunc`) adapts a
  plain function. TS: a function from their shape to yours. SQL: a view.
- **Decorator / middleware.** Go: `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` (go.http.middleware),
  or any function from `T` to `T`. TS: a higher-order function, and for class members the
  TS 5.0 `@` syntax. SQL has no clean equivalent: a view over a view adds columns, a
  `BEFORE` trigger rewrites a row on its way in.
- **Observer / pub-sub.** Observer is in-process and synchronous: the subject calls its
  listeners. Pub-sub puts something between them. Go: a slice of callbacks, or channels
  fanned out to goroutines. TS: `subscribe` returning an unsubscribe function, or
  `EventTarget`. SQL: a trigger is an observer inside the transaction, `LISTEN/NOTIFY` is
  pub-sub at commit, and an **outbox table** is pub-sub that survives a crash.

What disappears is the scaffolding: interfaces declared only so a class can implement
them, one class per variant, abstract decorator base classes, `Subject` and `Observer`
registries. What remains is a type and a few functions.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: since Java 8 a lambda is the idiomatic strategy (`Comparator<T>`), and Servlet
  filters are middleware. `java.util.Observable` has been deprecated since Java 9. Note
  that `@Transactional` is an annotation, metadata that Spring reads to generate a proxy
  (a decorator) at run time. A TS decorator is not metadata: it is code that runs when
  the class is defined and returns the replacement.
- **Python**: `@functools.lru_cache` is a higher-order function applied at definition
  time, which is exactly what a TS standard decorator is. Python's `@` also works on
  plain functions; TS's works only on classes and class members.
- **C++**: strategy is `std::function` or a template parameter (policy-based design);
  a decorator is a wrapper class holding the wrapped object. Go and TS closures replace
  the functor object and its captured fields.
- **JS**: Node's `EventEmitter` and the DOM's `EventTarget` are the observer pattern
  built in. TypeScript adds typed event maps; it adds no new pattern.

## How it works

Decorators compose like function application, so `logged(cached(upper))` means "call
`logged`'s wrapper, which calls `cached`'s wrapper, which may call `upper`". The outer
layer always runs; inner layers run only if outer ones pass the call on. That single rule
explains the TS output and the Go fee table: `freeAbove` answers 0 for a 720 TL order
before `capped` or the carrier SDK are asked.

A TS standard decorator receives the original method and a context object describing it
(`kind`, `name`, `static`, `private`, `addInitializer`). Whatever it returns replaces the
method on the prototype. Because that happens once, at class definition, state created
in the decorator body is per class.

In SQL, an `AFTER ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger runs inside the statement that fired it, in
the same transaction. The outbox row and the order row therefore commit or roll back
together; a separate worker reads the outbox and publishes. `NOTIFY` is also held until
commit, but it reaches only sessions that are listening at that moment, so it is a
wake-up call, not storage (go.services.listen-notify).

## Design notes

Start with the function. Promote a Go strategy to an interface with a struct behind it,
or a TS function to an object, when it needs a second method that shares state, a
lifecycle (`Close`), or an identity you want in logs and stack traces. Promote a
decorator stack into a named chain helper when the same stack appears in more than one
place, as Go routers do with middleware.

Patterns in SQL trade differently. A rules table lets an operator change pricing without
a deploy, but a typo in a rule name is a missed join rather than a compile error, so add
a foreign key from the orders to the rules. A view is the cheapest adapter there is, and
the right way to rename columns during a migration. A trigger as observer is powerful
and hidden: use it for things that must happen on every write path (an outbox, an
audit row), and keep business decisions out of it (sql.server-side.triggers,
design.architecture.business-rules).

StackLab shows most of these in production code, with one honest gap.
`httpapi.Runner` is a port with two adapters: `runexec` runs lessons in-process and
`runclient` adapts the Docker runner's HTTP API to the same method. `withLogging` in
`httpapi/middleware.go` is the decorator, wrapping the whole mux so even 404s are
logged. The frontend's `CodeRunner` is a strategy and `learning/store.ts` an observer
(ts.architecture.patterns reviews both). There is no pub-sub, because nothing needs one:
one user, one process. If a second process ever needed to react to runs, an outbox table
plus `LISTEN/NOTIFY` as the wake-up would be the boring first step, long before a broker.

lessons.title: Repository, factory/constructor, builder vs functional options, DI without frameworks
lessons.summary: Construction and wiring in Go, TypeScript and SQL: when a builder beats options, how a composition root replaces a DI container, and how PostgreSQL's search_path wires names, early or late.

examples.title: Go: a builder for a query assembled over several calls, with a sticky error

annotations.note: A builder is right when construction accumulates: a variable number of parts, added under conditions. Functional options (go.design.constructors) configure a value once from a fixed set of knobs, which this is not.

The builder owns the placeholder numbering. Callers write ?, the builder appends the value and writes $1, $2, so a value can never become SQL text and no hand-counted $3 can drift out of step with the args slice.

A chained method can't return an error without breaking the chain, so the first one is stored and every later call carries on. This is the errWriter idea from the Go blog's "Errors are values", and why bufio.Writer reports a failed write at Flush.
Build is the single exit, and the only place a caller has to check. The third form's sort key never reaches the SQL string.
The reason for the builder: parts are added in ifs. With a constructor or options, the caller would collect conditions and arguments in parallel slices and number placeholders by hand.

examples.title: TypeScript: a factory, a port, and React context as the injection channel

annotations.note: The port is a type the UI declares; the factory is a function that closes over its configuration (base URL, the fetch to use) and returns an object literal. No class, no new, no interface with an I prefix.
Context is React's injection mechanism. A null default plus a throwing hook turns "forgot to wire it" into an error naming the fix, instead of a component calling methods on undefined.
The component asks for a Progress and has no idea whether it talks HTTP or is a stub. Compare a component that imports a concrete client module: a test then has to mock the module or the network.
The composition root: the only lines that name concrete implementations. The fake is an object literal that fits the type; nothing had to be designed for testing beyond accepting the port.

examples.title: SQL: search_path binds names; the binding time decides who controls it

annotations.note: Two schemas, one table name: two implementations of the same "interface". Unqualified names are resolved through search_path, the database's wiring.
A function body written as a string is parsed when the function runs, so "lessons" is looked up in whatever search_path the caller has at that moment: late binding, the service-locator shape.
The SQL-standard body (RETURN or BEGIN ATOMIC, PostgreSQL 14) is parsed at CREATE time. The table is bound then, and recorded as a dependency, which the DROP TABLE at the end runs into.

SET search_path on the function keeps late lookup but fixes where it looks. PostgreSQL's docs ask for exactly this on SECURITY DEFINER functions, so a caller cannot slip a look-alike table or function in front.
The caller puts catalog_fixture first. Only the late-bound function follows it (1 instead of 21). For a test that is the point; for a privileged function it is a hijack.

The dependency recorded for minutes_bound blocks the drop (SQLSTATE 2BP01). The string-bodied functions recorded nothing: dropping the table would have succeeded and left them to fail at their next call.

use_cases: Builder: query and filter assembly, request construction with optional parts, report generation; anything built over several conditional calls
Functional options or an options object: configuring a client or server once, with defaults, from a known list of settings
Composition root plus constructor parameters (Go) or context and props (React): wiring an app with a real and a fake implementation of each port
search_path: schema-per-tenant or schema-per-test setups, and pinning it on every SECURITY DEFINER function
strengths: Wiring written as code is read like code: Go's run() and a React root show the whole dependency graph, unlike Spring's component scan, where you find a bean's implementation by searching annotations
Go builders need no library: methods returning the receiver plus a sticky error give fluent calls with one error check
A TS options object gets required-field checking from the type system, so the telescoping-constructor problem that builders solve in Java does not arise
PostgreSQL lets you choose the binding time per function: late (string body), early (SQL-standard body) or late in a fixed place (SET search_path)
weaknesses: A fluent Go builder hides errors until Build; code that forgets to call Build, or ignores its error, fails silently
React context is implicit: a component's dependencies are not in its props, and a missing provider surfaces only at render time
search_path is session-global state: any code that changes it changes name resolution for everything that follows, the same hazard as a mutable service locator
Hand-written wiring grows with the app; past a few dozen components, main becomes long (still readable, but long)

pitfalls.title: A builder where a struct literal would do
pitfalls.detail: If every part is known at the call site, a Config struct or options are clearer than a chain. Keep builders for construction that accumulates.
pitfalls.good: c := NewClient(u, WithTimeout(5*time.Second))

pitfalls.title: Service locator disguised as DI
pitfalls.detail: A module-level function that returns 'the' implementation (a cached singleton) is a locator: callers fetch their dependency instead of receiving it, and tests must mock the module. Pass the dependency in through a constructor, a prop or context.

pitfalls.title: SECURITY DEFINER without a pinned search_path
pitfalls.detail: The function runs with its owner's rights but resolves names through the caller's search_path. A caller who can create objects in any schema on the path can substitute a table or function the owner never meant to call.
pitfalls.good:
CREATE FUNCTION grant_badge(uid int) RETURNS void
  LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER
  SET search_path = app, pg_temp
  AS $$ INSERT INTO badges VALUES (uid) $$;

pitfalls.title: A repository interface with one implementation and no consumer that needs a substitute
pitfalls.detail: go.postgres.repository-testing: the repository is the type that owns the SQL; the interface is added by the consumer that needs a fake, not up front.

quiz.q: Which situation calls for a builder rather than functional options?
options: A client with six optional settings
A WHERE clause whose conditions depend on which form fields were filled in
A server that needs a logger and a database pool
A type whose zero value is useful
quiz.why: Options configure a value once from known settings. A builder accumulates parts across conditional calls, which is exactly a dynamic WHERE clause.

quiz.q: The Go builder stores the first error and keeps returning the receiver. Where must the caller check for errors?
quiz.why: Chained calls can't return errors without breaking the chain, so the error sticks and Build reports it, as bufio.Writer does at Flush.

quiz.q: After SET search_path = catalog_fixture, catalog_live, which function still sums catalog_live.lessons?
quiz.why: The SQL-standard body bound the table at CREATE time and the pinned function always looks in catalog_live; only the string body resolves names at call time.

quiz.q: In React, what is the injection channel that plays the role of Go's constructor parameters for deeply nested components?
quiz.why: A Provider at the composition root supplies the implementation; components read it with useContext, and a test wraps them in a Provider with a fake.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: CREATE FUNCTION (sql_body, SET, Writing SECURITY DEFINER Functions Safely)
PostgreSQL: Schemas and the schema search path

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every program constructs things and then connects them. The three languages split that
work differently.

**Construction.** Go has no constructor syntax: `New` functions return a ready value, the
zero value should be useful, and optional settings go in a `Config` struct or functional
options (go.design.constructors). TypeScript constructs with **factory functions** that
return object literals, an options object with defaults for the settings, and a class
when instances share methods or need `#private` state. In SQL the table definition is
the constructor: `DEFAULT`, identity columns and `CHECK` decide what a valid row is, and
`INSERT ... RETURNING` hands the constructed row back (sql.constraints.keys,
sql.modifying.returning-upsert).

**Builder vs options.** Options configure a value once, from a known list of knobs. A
builder **accumulates**: parts added over several calls, often inside `if`s and loops.
That makes builders rare in Go and TS application code and common in one place, query
construction. A Go builder cannot return an error mid-chain, so the first error sticks
and `Build` reports it.

**Repository.** One type owns the SQL for one part of the domain and speaks domain values
(go.postgres.repository-testing). In TS the equivalent is the API client module: the
only code that knows URLs and wire shapes. Inside the database, views and functions play
the same role: a stable interface in front of tables you want to be free to change.

**DI without frameworks.** Every dependency is created in one place, the **composition
root**, and handed to whatever needs it. Go hands it over as constructor parameters, React
as props or through context. PostgreSQL resolves unqualified names through
`search_path`, which is wiring too, with a choice of binding time.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Spring finds implementations by component scan and injects them by
  annotation. Here `main` (Go) or `main.tsx` (React) is the container, written out.
  Lombok's `@Builder` exists to escape telescoping constructors; Go's named struct
  fields and TS's options objects don't have that problem, so a builder there must earn
  its keep by accumulating.
- **Python**: keyword arguments with defaults are the TS options object. FastAPI's
  `Depends` injects through function parameters, which is close to how a React
  component receives a dependency from context through a hook.
- **C++**: a constructor always runs, and RAII ties construction to resource ownership.
  Go's `var x T` runs no code, so a type that needs set-up must be built by `New`, and a
  builder's `Build` is where invariants get checked.
- **JS/React**: you have used DI already: `QueryClientProvider` and React Router's
  `RouterProvider` deliver objects to deep components through context. Your own ports
  can travel the same way.

## How it works

PostgreSQL parses a function body written as a string constant at execution time, so
each unqualified name in it is looked up in the `search_path` of the session that calls
it. A SQL-standard body (`RETURN expr` or `BEGIN ATOMIC ... END`, PostgreSQL 14) is
parsed at `CREATE FUNCTION`: names are resolved once, stored as references to specific
objects, and tracked as dependencies. A `SET search_path` clause on the function
replaces the caller's path for the duration of the call and restores it afterwards.
The documentation's section on writing `SECURITY DEFINER` functions safely asks for that
clause, with `pg_temp` last, because a privileged function that resolves names through
the caller's path can be steered to objects the caller created.

React context works by looking up the component tree: `useContext` returns the value of
the nearest enclosing `Provider`, or the context's default when there is none. A `null`
default plus a hook that throws makes a missing provider fail loudly at the first render.

## Design notes

StackLab's backend has a textbook composition root: `run()` in `cmd/stacklab/main.go`
builds config, logger, pool, migrations, the runner (in-process or Docker, chosen by one
`if`), the router and the server, in that order. The wiring has a second, quieter root:
`httpapi.NewRouter(logger, db, runner)` builds `learningstore` and `runstore` itself from
`pool.Pool()`. The run path is injectable, so its handler can be tested with a fake
`Runner`; the learning handlers can only be tested against a real database. That is a
defensible choice for a single-database app (go.design.layers calls it flat on purpose),
and the fix if it ever pinches is mechanical: pass the stores in.

The frontend wires differently. `LessonNotes`, `LessonQuiz` and `learning/store.ts` call
`pickApi()`, a module-level factory that probes the backend once and caches the chosen
adapter in a module variable. That is a service locator: the components fetch their
dependency rather than receive it, and a test has to mock the module or intercept the
network. Providing the chosen API through context from `main.tsx`, as in the second
example, would make the choice visible in one place.

On the SQL side, prefer SQL-standard bodies for `LANGUAGE sql` functions that should
always mean the same tables, pin `search_path` on every `SECURITY DEFINER` function, and
treat a session-wide `SET search_path` as global state. The lesson runtime itself uses
it deliberately: each run's `search_path` is set to an empty schema of its own, which
is why your examples can create tables with common names without colliding.

lessons.title: Anti-patterns: Java getters/setters in Go, deep hierarchies in TS, god packages, anemic models
lessons.summary: Designs carried over from another language compile and run, and then fight you: Get/Set pairs and interfaces-per-struct in Go, inheritance trees in TypeScript, god packages, invariants scattered across services, and row-by-row loops against a set-based database.

examples.title: Go: Get/Set pairs and a rule in a service vs a type that guards its own invariant

annotations.note: Three Java habits at once: an I-prefixed interface declared next to its only implementation, Get on the getter, and a setter for a field that should never be set directly. Go's convention is the consumer declares the interface, when it needs one.

The anemic model: the data has no behaviour and the rule lives in a service. Any code holding an IAccount can call SetBalance, so the rule is a suggestion, and this one forgot to reject negative amounts.

The type owns the invariant. Unexported fields mean only this package can touch balance, so Withdraw is the only way to change it. Effective Go's naming: the getter is Balance; a setter, if one were justified, would be SetBalance.
Withdrawing -400 deposited 400, and SetBalance(-50) skipped the service. Both compile, and neither leaves a trace of which caller broke the rule.
The same three calls on Account: a bad amount and an overdraft are refused with errors the caller can test (errors.Is(err, ErrInsufficient)), and the balance only moves on success.

examples.title: TypeScript: an inheritance tree inherits the wrong answer; a union refuses to compile

annotations.note: Behaviour is spread over three levels: label in Item and SqlLesson, minutes in Item and Lesson. To know what any object does you read upward through every ancestor, and a change to Item reaches classes you have never opened.

The new class compiles, runs and is wrong: an exam inherits Lesson's formula and reports 4 minutes for 30 questions, while carrying an examples field of 0 that means nothing for it. Nothing forced anyone to decide what an exam's duration is.

The variants are plain data and the behaviour is one function with a case per variant. The declared return type is the exhaustiveness check: every path must return a number, so a variant without a case is a compile error.
SqlLesson's whole reason to exist becomes one boolean field read in one place. Variation that is data should be data, not a subclass.
The failure the class tree could not give you. The message is tsc's (checked with tsc 7.0.2), and it points at the switch that needs a decision.

examples.title: SQL: row by row from Go vs one statement over arrays vs one set-based UPDATE

annotations.note: A pgx QueryTracer sees every Query, QueryRow and Exec, which makes "how many statements did this code send?" a number instead of a guess. The same hook is where tracing and query logging plug in.
The ORM habit: load objects, change them in memory, save each one. 301 statements, each waiting for its reply before the next is sent, and outside a transaction each UPDATE is also its own commit.
When the rule must stay in Go, keep it there and still write once: two arrays and unnest turn 300 updates into one statement. pgx encodes a []string and a []int as PostgreSQL arrays.
