When the rule can be said in SQL, say it about all rows at once. Integer division truncates in both languages, so this matches newPrice exactly.
The three tables end up identical: same result, 301 statements against 1.

use_cases: Reviewing code from a team that is new to Go or TS: these are the shapes that show up first
Deciding whether a type needs methods that guard an invariant (money, state machines, quotas) or can stay plain data (DTOs, config, rows)
Replacing an inheritance tree with a discriminated union when variants are known and behaviour is spread across levels
Finding N+1 and row-by-row loops: count statements per request with a tracer before measuring anything else
strengths: Go's package-level privacy makes invariants cheap to enforce: unexported fields plus a few methods, with no need for Java's private/protected/package matrix
TS discriminated unions turn 'forgot a variant' into a compile error, where a class hierarchy turns it into a silently inherited default
Set-based SQL lets the database do in one statement, inside one transaction, what a loop does in hundreds of round trips
Each fix removes code: fewer interfaces, fewer classes, fewer statements
weaknesses: Go cannot stop code inside the same package from writing unexported fields directly, so a large package weakens every invariant it holds
A union with an exhaustive switch makes adding a variant touch every switch; a class hierarchy makes adding an operation touch every class. Pick by which change is more frequent
Set-based rewrites move logic into SQL text that Go's compiler does not check; keep such statements covered by tests on a real database

pitfalls.title: God package
pitfalls.detail: A package named after a layer or a mood (util, common, models, services) that everything imports. It cannot be understood alone, every change recompiles its importers, and it is where import cycles start. Split by feature and move helpers next to their only caller (go.design.packages).

pitfalls.title: Getters and setters for every field
pitfalls.detail: Plain data with no invariant should have exported fields and no methods. A type with an invariant should have unexported fields and operations, not setters. A Get/Set pair for every field is the worst of both: ceremony without protection.
pitfalls.bad:
func (u *User) GetEmail() string  { return u.email }
func (u *User) SetEmail(e string) { u.email = e }
pitfalls.good:
type User struct{ Email string } // plain data, or:
func (u *User) ChangeEmail(e string) error { /* validate, then set */ }

pitfalls.title: Inheritance for code reuse
pitfalls.detail: Extending a class to borrow two methods couples the child to every future change in the parent. In TS, prefer functions over the data, or composition; in Go there is no inheritance, and struct embedding promotes methods without making the outer type a subtype.

pitfalls.title: N+1 queries from a loop
pitfalls.detail: One query for the list, then one per item for its details. Fetch the details with one query (a JOIN, or WHERE id = ANY($1)) and match them up in Go.
pitfalls.good: rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE id = ANY($1)", customerIDs)

quiz.q: What does Effective Go say a getter for the unexported field owner should be called?
quiz.why: Upper-case Owner exports it; putting Get in the name is neither idiomatic nor necessary. A setter, if needed, would be SetOwner.

quiz.q: Exam extends Lesson and forgets to override minutes(). What happens?
quiz.why: An overridable method with a body is a default; nothing forces a subclass to decide. The union's switch, with a declared return type, does force it.

quiz.q: The row-by-row loop sent 301 statements outside a transaction. Besides round trips, what else multiplied?
options: Commits: each UPDATE committed on its own
quiz.why: Without BEGIN each statement is its own transaction, so 300 updates mean 300 commits, each waiting for its WAL record to reach disk under the default synchronous_commit.

quiz.q: The pricing rule exists only in Go code. What is the idiomatic way to write 300 new prices?
options: One UPDATE per row inside a transaction
One UPDATE ... FROM unnest($1, $2) with two arrays
Move the rule into a trigger
quiz.why: The rule stays in Go and the write is one statement. A transaction around the loop fixes the commits but not the round trips. Goroutines would need a connection each (a pgx.Conn is not safe for concurrent use) and still send 300 statements.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing (discriminated unions, exhaustiveness checking)

lessons.body:
## Concept

An anti-pattern here is a design that is good in the language it came from and fights the
one it was carried into. The code compiles and runs; the cost shows up as ceremony,
invariants nobody enforces, and changes that ripple further than they should.

- **Java getters and setters in Go.** Go has package-level privacy and no
  properties. Its answer to "how do I protect this field" is an unexported field plus
  methods that *do something* (`Withdraw`), not a `Get`/`Set` pair that exposes it
  anyway. Plain data with no invariant is a struct with exported fields and no methods.
  An `I`-prefixed interface next to its only implementation is the same habit: in Go the
  consumer declares the interface it needs.
- **Anemic models.** Data types without behaviour and every rule in a "service". It is
  not wrong in itself: rows, DTOs and JSON payloads should be plain. It becomes an
  anti-pattern when the data *has* an invariant and nothing in the type enforces it, so
  every caller must remember the rule.
- **Deep hierarchies in TypeScript.** Inheritance spreads one behaviour over several
  classes and lets new subclasses silently inherit wrong defaults. When the set of
  variants is known, a discriminated union plus functions with exhaustive switches keeps
  each behaviour in one place and makes "forgot a variant" a compile error.
- **God packages.** `util`, `common`, `models`, `services`: packages named after a layer
  or a feeling, imported by everything. In Go they also weaken encapsulation, because
  every file in a package can touch every unexported field (go.design.packages).
- **Row by row against SQL.** The database is set-based. Loading rows, changing them in
  a loop and saving each one (the ORM habit, and its cousin the N+1 query) turns one
  statement into hundreds of round trips and commits.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: JavaBeans conventions (`getX`/`setX`), interfaces per service, and abstract
  base classes are the source of most of these. Effective Go says outright that a getter
  for `owner` is `Owner`, not `GetOwner`. Records (Java 16) are closer to Go's plain data
  structs than beans are.
- **C++**: deep hierarchies with virtual functions, and the fragile base class problem,
  are familiar. `std::variant` plus `std::visit` is the C++ form of a discriminated union
  with exhaustive handling.
- **Python**: properties make getters invisible, so the habit shows up less. Python's
  `match` on dataclasses is the closest thing to a TS union switch, without the compile
  error.
- **JS**: ES2015 classes made inheritance look natural in JavaScript. React's documentation
  recommended composition over component inheritance long before hooks made function
  components the default.

## How it works

The union's exhaustiveness check comes from control-flow analysis. Inside `switch
(c.kind)`, each `case` narrows `c` to one variant; after the last case, `c` has type
`never`. With a declared return type of `number`, falling off the end of the function is
only allowed if that point is unreachable. Add a variant and the end becomes reachable,
and tsc reports TS2366. The class hierarchy has no such point: a subclass that does not
override simply uses the parent's method, which is the feature that produced the bug.

The statement counts come from round trips. pgx sends a statement and waits for its
result before the next call can use the connection, so N statements cost at least N
network round trips, plus N commits when each runs in autocommit mode. An `UPDATE ...
FROM unnest(...)` or a single set-based `UPDATE` costs one of each, however many rows it
touches.

## Design notes

Each fix has a limit worth knowing. Unexported fields protect an invariant only from
other packages; a 5,000-line package is one trust zone, which is another reason to keep
packages small. Unions make new variants expensive (every switch must change) and new
operations cheap; class hierarchies are the opposite. When third parties add variants
you don't control (plugins, a framework's components), an interface or a class is the
right tool. And set-based SQL moves logic out of the compiler's sight, so test it on a
real database (go.postgres.repository-testing).

StackLab is a fair test case. The backend has no `util` package and no interface without
a consumer; the shared packages, `platform` (database plumbing) and `runapi` (the run
request and response types), have a fixed direction: features import them, they import
no feature. The stores are concrete types used directly, which is not
anemic: they hold no invariants beyond what the schema enforces. On the frontend,
`CodeRunner` is the only class pair, and `RunState` is a discriminated union; the
learning feature's notes state is the place where three separate `useState` calls
(`body`, `loaded`, `saved`) recreate the "anything can be set" problem (ts.architecture.explicit-states).

When you review code from someone new to a language, these five shapes are the first to
look for. None of them is a bug by itself; each one makes the next bug more likely.

lessons.title: Step 1: Architecture and request lifecycle; contract-first API with OpenAPI
lessons.summary: TraceLite is one Go server, one PostgreSQL database and one React app, with openapi.yaml as the contract between them. A request goes browser, Vite proxy, ServeMux, handler, service, store, pgx, PostgreSQL and back; names change form at two well-defined places.

examples.title: One request through every layer, printed hop by hop

annotations.note: The wire type, abridged. Its json tags are where snake_case columns become camelCase members; nothing else in the request path renames anything.
A fixed id and a timestamp written in Istanbul time (+03), so the output is the same on every run. Step 2 has the real schema.
Go 1.22 patterns: the method and a named wildcard in the pattern itself. r.Pattern (Go 1.23) reports which pattern matched, which is also what TraceLite's request log records.
The id is parsed before any SQL runs, and travels to PostgreSQL as a parameter: the extended protocol sends the statement and the value separately.

r.Context() is passed down to pgx. If the browser goes away, the request's context is canceled and the call returns at once: by default pgx sets a deadline on the connection and closes it. Sending PostgreSQL a real cancel request is opt-in, through pgconn's CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler.

The error leg: an id that doesn't parse, or parses but names nothing (pgx.ErrNoRows), takes the same route and gets an RFC 9457 problem instead of a resource. Step 4 maps every error this way, in one function.
pgx returns timestamptz in the process's local zone ("Local"). The wire carries UTC with Z (06:30Z for 09:30+03), whatever zone the server runs in.

What vite.config.ts's server.proxy does: requests under /api go to the Go server; everything else, the app itself, Vite serves. The browser only ever talks to vite.URL, so the page and the API share one origin and the browser never sends a CORS preflight.

examples.title: The spec as the yardstick: checking a Go wire type against openapi.yaml

annotations.note: The Requirement schema from the spec below, reduced to what this check reads. The spec, not the Go struct and not the table, defines what a client receives.
The check runs on the encoded bytes, exactly what a handler would write, so struct tags, omitempty and custom marshalers are all part of what is checked.

Three kinds of drift: a required member missing, a member the spec doesn't know, and a value outside the enum. Step 14 turns this into a test; a production suite would load openapi.yaml into a JSON Schema validator, which also checks types, patterns and lengths. The idea is the same.
Each edit compiles, passes go vet and looks fine in a diff. Both change the wire, and neither changes the TypeScript client, which keeps reading parentId and description.
A struct conversion: the field names and types match, and since Go 1.8 tags are ignored when converting, so the same values are encoded both ways.
The third kind of drift is in the data, not the type: a display label in a field the spec defines as an enum of lowercase values.

use_cases: Starting a full-stack feature: write the operation and schemas into openapi.yaml first, then the migration, the store query, the handler and the client
Reviewing a change: a diff to openapi.yaml is a change to the contract and needs both sides
Debugging: following a request through the proxy, router, handler, store and database, one layer at a time
Local development with one origin: Vite proxies /api, so cookies, relative URLs and fetch work without CORS
strengths: The contract is a reviewed file in the repo, not whatever the Go structs happen to encode; TypeScript types are generated from it
One origin in development (Vite proxy) and production (the Go binary serves the app), so there is no CORS configuration to drift between them
Every layer has one job and one package; a bug report names a layer: decoding, rules, SQL, or rendering
Names change form in exactly two places, Go struct tags (SQL to Go to JSON) and nowhere in TypeScript, because the client uses the wire names directly
weaknesses: The Go wire types are written by hand next to the spec; only a test notices when they drift
Contract-first means writing YAML before code, which feels slow for a one-person project until the first client and server disagree
Three representations of a requirement (row, Go model, wire JSON) mean mapping code in the store and the handler
The Vite proxy hides cross-origin problems in development that a deployment on two origins would have

pitfalls.title: Letting the Go structs become the contract
pitfalls.detail: If the spec is updated from the code after the fact, a tag edit silently changes the API. Change openapi.yaml first, then the Go type, and let the contract test compare them.

pitfalls.title: Calling the Go server directly from the browser in development
pitfalls.detail: fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/...") from a page on :5173 is cross-origin and needs CORS headers that production never sends. Use relative URLs and the Vite proxy.
pitfalls.good: fetch("/api/requirements/" + id) // same origin; Vite forwards /api

pitfalls.title: snake_case leaking onto the wire
pitfalls.detail: A tag copied from the column name (json:"parent_id") breaks every client that reads parentId. Wire names are camelCase, always written as explicit tags.

pitfalls.title: Dropping the request context
pitfalls.detail: context.Background() in a handler's query keeps the handler waiting for a result after the client disconnected, holding a pooled connection. Pass r.Context() all the way to pgx.

quiz.q: In development, the browser loads the app from :5173 and calls /api/requirements/{id}. Who answers?
options: The Go server, through Vite's proxy, on the same origin
The Go server directly, with CORS headers
quiz.why: server.proxy forwards /api to the Go server; the browser only ever talks to the dev server's origin.

quiz.q: Where does parent_id become parentId?
options: In the json tag of the Go wire type
quiz.why: SQL keeps snake_case, sqlc maps columns to Go field names, and the wire type's json tags produce camelCase; the client uses the wire names unchanged.

quiz.q: Which file is the source of truth for the JSON a client receives?
quiz.why: Contract-first: the spec is written first and both sides conform to it. TypeScript types are generated from it; the Go types are checked against it.

quiz.q: A handler adds omitempty to description. What does example 2 report?
options: Nothing: the field still exists in Go
missing description, when the description is empty
quiz.why: omitempty drops the member when it is empty; the spec lists description as required.

further_reading.title: Go spec: conversions between struct types (tags ignored)

lessons.title: Step 2: Schema: hierarchical requirements, test cases, trace links, test runs
lessons.summary: TraceLite's first migration: requirements as a parent_id tree, test cases, trace links and test runs, with uuidv7 keys, named constraints the Go store can map, composite foreign keys that keep everything inside one project, and an index for every query.

examples.title: Migration 001's first two tables, verbatim, and each constraint refusing a row

annotations.note: goose's header (go.postgres.migrations-sqlc). The file is migrations/001_init.sql; this example runs its first two tables verbatim, and How it works shows all of it. Later steps add 002, 003, ... and never edit this one once it has run anywhere.

uuidv7() (PG 18) puts a millisecond timestamp in the leading bits, so new keys land at the right edge of the B-tree like a sequence would. Unlike bigint identity values, ids are safe to show in URLs, can be minted outside the database (the importer in step 7), and travel as JSON strings without the 2^53 problem.
A project owns its requirements: CASCADE removes them with it. parent_id NULL means top level. The tree is an adjacency list, the simplest model to write to.

Codes are identifiers, not prose: ASCII capitals, digits, single hyphens. COLLATE "C" compares bytes, so ORDER BY code, the keyset cursor and Go's string comparison agree on every server, whatever locale the database was created with.
char_length counts characters, not bytes; the Go service counts runes with utf8.RuneCountInString to match. A Turkish title of 200 characters can be 400 bytes (line 53).
text plus a CHECK instead of CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM: a value can be added or retired by replacing the constraint in a migration, while an enum value can be added and renamed but never dropped.

Every constraint has a chosen name, because the Go store maps violations by constraint name: requirements_code_key becomes 409, requirements_parent_fkey becomes 422 on #/parentId. Generated names would change if a column were renamed.

The parent must be in the same project. The pair (project_id, id) is already unique because id is, but a foreign key can only reference columns with a unique constraint, hence line 21. MATCH SIMPLE, the default, skips the check when parent_id is NULL, which is what lets top-level rows exist.
A row can't be its own parent. Longer loops (A under B under A) are not something a constraint can see; example 2 shows the check the store runs instead.
PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side of a foreign key, never the referencing side. This index serves the tree walk (children of a node) and the check that runs when a parent is deleted.

A lesson helper, not part of the migration. The EXCEPTION block runs the INSERT in a subtransaction, so a refused row is rolled back and the script continues; GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS reads the same fields a *pgconn.PgError carries in Go: Code and ConstraintName.

Lower case is refused rather than silently upper-cased: one canonical form, enforced where every writer passes. Line 50 is what "auth-login".toLocaleUpperCase("tr") produces: dotted capital İ, not ASCII, so it fails the same CHECK.
AUTH-LOGIN exists, but in project Ödeme. The composite key (Raporlama, AUTH-LOGIN's id) matches no row, so the database, not the application, rejects the cross-project parent.
ş is two bytes in UTF-8. The limit is 200 characters, so 400 bytes pass and 201 characters don't. A byte-based check in Go (len(title)) would have refused the first row.

Project names are prose, so their order depends on the collation: byte order puts Ödeme after Raporlama. The explicit COLLATE "C" keeps this output the same on servers created with different locales; a Turkish UI sorts with a Turkish collation instead.

examples.title: The requirement queries: the tree, a keyset page, the move check, deletes

annotations.note: Seeding by code, one INSERT per level: each level joins the codes of the level above. Step 7's CSV import resolves parent codes the same way, in bulk.

The tree endpoint's query. It starts at the project's roots, joins children on parent_id round by round (the requirements_parent index), and SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code gives each child a place right after its parent. The API returns this flat, ordered list with depth; the UI nests it (step 6).

GENERIC_PLAN (PG 16) plans a statement that still has $1, $2, $3 in it: exactly what the Go store prepares. The unique constraint's index on (project_id, code) both filters and delivers the order, so there is no Sort node and the scan stops after LIMIT rows, on every page.
One row more than the page size: the third row only says that a next page exists. The API returns two rows and a cursor holding the last code, AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT.

A move is legal unless the new parent is the moved row or one of its descendants. Walking up from the new parent costs one primary-key lookup per level, cheaper than collecting the moved row's whole subtree. CYCLE makes the walk finish even if bad data already contains a loop.

The foreign key is satisfied (every parent exists) and so is the CHECK (no row is its own parent), yet AUTH now hangs below its own grandchild. The loop has no root, so the tree query silently loses five requirements. This is why the store runs the move check, inside a transaction (step 3).
The cascade removes Raporlama's REPORT and REPORT-PDF in the same statement. The parent foreign key is checked at the end of that statement, when no orphan remains.

AUTH-LOGIN still has two children, so the default NO ACTION refuses: SQLSTATE 23503 on requirements_parent_fkey, which the API reports as 409 Conflict. Deleting a subtree is a deliberate operation, not a side effect.

examples.title: Trace links, latest runs, coverage per requirement, and evidence that survives a delete

annotations.note: The link carries project_id so that both foreign keys can be composite: a link between a requirement and a test case of different projects can't exist. The primary key's index starts with (project_id, requirement_id): the matrix of a project and the tests of a requirement. Line 19 serves the reverse direction and the check when a test case is deleted.

Test evidence doesn't disappear as a side effect: a test case with runs can't be deleted, and neither can its project, even through the cascade (line 66). Otherwise RESTRICT and the default NO ACTION differ only in that NO ACTION can be deferred until later in the transaction.

(test_case_id, finished_at DESC, id DESC) answers "latest run of this test case" with one index probe, and pages a test case's runs newest first. id breaks ties between runs that finished in the same microsecond.

Linking is idempotent: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING turns a repeated PUT into INSERT 0 0 instead of an error. project_id is taken from the requirement, and the composite foreign key checks the test case against it.
TC-1 failed, then passed; TC-3 passed, then failed. Only the latest run of each test case counts for coverage, so the order of finished_at matters, not the number of runs.
The trap: bool_and ignores NULL, and TC-4 has never run, so its latest result is NULL. AUTH-LOCKOUT's naive_all_passed is true although one of its two tests never ran.

TraceLite's coverage vocabulary, used from step 6 on: uncovered (no linked test), failing (a latest run failed), passing (every linked test's latest run passed), incomplete (anything else: never run, or last skipped). Counting the passes and comparing with count(*) treats NULL as not passed.
The join uses the primary key's leading columns, and LATERAL fetches one row per link through test_runs_latest: an index probe each, not a sort of all runs.

The cascade reaches test_cases, and test_runs_test_case_fkey refuses. RESTRICT raises SQLSTATE 23001 (restrict_violation), not the 23503 that NO ACTION raises (example 2's last statement), so the store maps both. The whole DELETE fails: no requirement or link is gone either.

use_cases: Any hierarchy users edit: requirements, documents and sections, categories, org units, bills of materials
Many-to-many links that must stay inside a tenant, project or workspace: carry the scope column and make both foreign keys composite
Evidence tables (test runs, audit records, payments) that must survive deletes elsewhere: ON DELETE RESTRICT
Public identifiers that appear in URLs and are created by importers or other services: uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()
strengths: Integrity lives in the database: an import script, a psql session and the API all hit the same CHECKs and keys, unlike validation kept only in Go or in an ORM's model classes
Composite foreign keys make cross-project links impossible without a trigger or a lookup in application code
Named constraints give the store a stable vocabulary: 23505 on requirements_code_key means duplicate code, whatever the message text
The adjacency list keeps writes to one row (insert, move, delete), while recursive CTEs answer subtree, ancestor and cycle questions in one round trip
weaknesses: No constraint can prevent a loop of two or more rows; the move check must run in every writer, in a transaction that serializes moves
uuid keys are 16 bytes against bigint's 8, in every index and foreign key, and are awkward to read in logs; codes are what people quote
Codes in byte order sort REQ-10 before REQ-2; numbered codes need zero padding or an ICU collation with numeric ordering
Carrying project_id in trace_links duplicates a fact the requirement already knows, and the extra unique constraints cost an index each

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNIQUE (project_id, id) to be redundant
pitfalls.detail: It is redundant for uniqueness, since id alone is unique, but a composite foreign key can only reference columns covered by a unique constraint or primary key. Without it, CREATE TABLE fails.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the index on the referencing column
pitfalls.detail: PostgreSQL indexes primary keys and unique constraints, not foreign key columns. Deleting a parent then scans the child table, and the tree walk does one sequential scan per level.
pitfalls.good: parent_id uuid REFERENCES requirements; CREATE INDEX requirements_parent ON requirements (parent_id);

pitfalls.title: bool_and over a LEFT JOIN
pitfalls.detail: Aggregates skip NULLs, so a test that never ran doesn't spoil bool_and. Count the matches and compare with the count of links instead.
pitfalls.good: count(*) FILTER (WHERE last.result = 'passed') = count(*)

pitfalls.title: Upper-casing codes with the user's locale
pitfalls.detail: In a Turkish locale, toLocaleUpperCase turns i into İ (U+0130), which the code CHECK rejects. Normalize identifiers with locale-independent toUpperCase() in TS or strings.ToUpper in Go.

pitfalls.title: Relying on uuidv7 order for display
pitfalls.detail: uuidv7 values sort by creation time to the millisecond, but two sessions in the same millisecond interleave randomly. Order lists by a real column (code, finished_at) and use id only as a tiebreaker.

quiz.q: Why can trace_links reference requirements (project_id, id) at all?
options: Because id is the primary key
Because the UNIQUE (project_id, id) constraint exists
Because both columns are NOT NULL
quiz.why: A foreign key must reference columns covered by a primary key or unique constraint. The primary key covers id alone, so the pair needs its own unique constraint.

quiz.q: UPDATE requirements SET parent_id = <id of its grandchild> WHERE code = 'AUTH'. What does PostgreSQL do with this schema?
options: Accepts it; the store's recursive check must catch it
quiz.why: The parent exists in the same project and isn't the row itself, so every constraint holds. Only a walk up the ancestors finds the loop.

quiz.q: A requirement has two children. DELETE FROM requirements WHERE id = <it>, and then DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = <its project>. Which succeed?
quiz.why: Deleting the parent alone leaves children pointing at nothing and fails with 23503. The project cascade deletes parent and children in one statement, and the check at the end of it finds no orphans (provided no test runs block it).

quiz.q: TC-4 is linked to a requirement and has no runs. Which coverage does TraceLite report if the requirement's other test passed?
quiz.why: A linked test without a passing latest run makes the requirement incomplete; bool_and would have said passing because it skips the NULL.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (foreign keys, MATCH SIMPLE, RESTRICT vs NO ACTION)
PostgreSQL docs: WITH queries, SEARCH and CYCLE

lessons.body:
## Concept

TraceLite stores four things, all inside a **project**:

- **requirements**, a tree: each row has an optional `parent_id` pointing at another
  requirement of the same project. A human-readable `code` (`AUTH-LOGIN`) is unique per
  project; the `id` is what URLs and foreign keys use.
- **test_cases**, a flat list per project, with the same kind of `code` (`TC-1`).
- **trace_links**, the many-to-many relation "this test case verifies this requirement".
  A test can verify several requirements, and a requirement can be verified by several
  tests.
- **test_runs**, the evidence: one row per execution of a test case, with a `result` of
  `passed`, `failed` or `skipped`. Only the latest run of a test case (by `finished_at`,
  then `id`) counts for coverage.

The schema enforces everything that a single row or a single foreign key can express:
code format, lengths in characters, allowed values, uniqueness per project, and "both
ends of every reference live in the same project". What it can't express (no loops in
the tree) is checked by one recursive query in the store, inside a transaction.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JPA/Hibernate**: `@ManyToOne` to the same entity plus `@OneToMany(mappedBy)` gives the
  same adjacency list, but walking it loads one level per query. Here the walk is one
  `WITH RECURSIVE` statement, and the tree is never loaded into memory to be checked.
- **Django/Rails**: model validations (`validates :code, uniqueness: true`) run in the
  application and race under concurrency; a unique constraint can't. TraceLite keeps
  the Go checks for friendly messages and lets the database have the last word.
- **ORM-generated migrations**: Django and Prisma diff models to produce DDL. Here the
  migration is SQL you write and review, and constraint names are chosen, because Go
  code switches on them.
- **C/C++**: a `parent` pointer in a struct with no owner of the invariant. The foreign
  key is the invariant "every parent pointer points at a live node of the same project",
  enforced on every write.

## How it works

The canonical migration, `migrations/001_init.sql`. Example 1 runs its first two tables
verbatim, example 3 its last two; later steps add tables and columns in migrations 002
and up, never by editing this file.

```sql
-- +goose Up
CREATE TABLE projects (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  name       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT projects_name_length CHECK (char_length(name) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  project_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE,
  parent_id   uuid,  -- NULL: top level
  code        text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL CONSTRAINT requirements_code_format
                CHECK (code ~ '^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(-[A-Z0-9]+)*$' AND char_length(code) <= 40),
  title       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT requirements_title_length CHECK (char_length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft'
                CONSTRAINT requirements_status_valid CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'approved', 'obsolete')),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_in_project UNIQUE (project_id, id),  -- target of same-project FKs
  CONSTRAINT requirements_not_own_parent CHECK (parent_id <> id),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_parent_fkey FOREIGN KEY (project_id, parent_id)
    REFERENCES requirements (project_id, id)
);
CREATE INDEX requirements_parent ON requirements (parent_id);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  project_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE,
  code        text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL CONSTRAINT test_cases_code_format
                CHECK (code ~ '^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(-[A-Z0-9]+)*$' AND char_length(code) <= 40),
  title       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT test_cases_title_length CHECK (char_length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT test_cases_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code),
  CONSTRAINT test_cases_in_project UNIQUE (project_id, id)
);
CREATE TABLE trace_links (  -- "this test case verifies this requirement"
  project_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  requirement_id uuid NOT NULL,
  test_case_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (project_id, requirement_id, test_case_id),
  CONSTRAINT trace_links_requirement_fkey FOREIGN KEY (project_id, requirement_id)
    REFERENCES requirements (project_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT trace_links_test_case_fkey FOREIGN KEY (project_id, test_case_id)
    REFERENCES test_cases (project_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE INDEX trace_links_test_case ON trace_links (project_id, test_case_id);
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  test_case_id uuid NOT NULL CONSTRAINT test_runs_test_case_fkey REFERENCES test_cases ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  result       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT test_runs_result_valid CHECK (result IN ('passed', 'failed', 'skipped')),
  finished_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  duration_ms  integer CONSTRAINT test_runs_duration_ms_valid CHECK (duration_ms >= 0),
  notes        text NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
);
CREATE INDEX test_runs_latest ON test_runs (test_case_id, finished_at DESC, id DESC);
```

Which query each index serves:

- `requirements_code_key (project_id, code)`: the flat list, paged by code (keyset), and
  lookups by code (imports, links by code).
- `requirements_parent (parent_id)`: children of a node (the tree walk) and the
  foreign-key check when a requirement is deleted.
- `trace_links` primary key `(project_id, requirement_id, test_case_id)`: the trace
  matrix of a project and the tests of one requirement. `trace_links_test_case`: the
  requirements of one test, and the check when a test case is deleted.
- `test_runs_latest`: the latest run per test case, and a test case's runs newest first.

Columns that are never absent are `NOT NULL` with a default (`description` is `''`, not
`NULL`), so the API never has to tell "missing" from "empty". The only nullable columns
are `parent_id` (top level) and `duration_ms` (a skipped run has none). Rows have no
`updated_at` trigger: the store's `UPDATE` statements set `updated_at = now()`
themselves; step 13 compares triggers with application events for the audit trail.

## Design notes

**Keys.** `uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()` rather than `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`,
following the ids lesson's rule for ids that leave the database: they appear in URLs and
JSON, the step 7 importer can assign them before rows exist, and they don't reveal how
many requirements a project has. Version 7 keeps inserts at the end of the index. People
never type ids; they type codes, which is why `code` exists separately and is unique per
project, not globally. Go reads uuid columns into `uuid.UUID` from the standard library
(Go 1.27); TypeScript sees branded strings (step 5).

**One project, enforced.** Carrying `project_id` into `trace_links` and making both
foreign keys composite costs a column and two unique constraints; the alternative, a
trigger or a check in Go before every insert, is code that must run in every writer and
races under concurrency. Same for `parent_id`: the composite key makes "parent in
another project" impossible, and the Go service only translates the error.

**What the database can't do.** No constraint sees a loop of two or more rows.
Rather than a trigger that walks the tree on every update, TraceLite has exactly one
operation that changes `parent_id` after creation (moving a requirement) and runs the
walk there, in a transaction that serializes moves per project (step 3).

**Deletes.** A requirement with children can't be deleted (409 in the API); a project
cascades through its requirements, test cases and links, but stops at test runs. That
asymmetry is deliberate: structure can be rebuilt, evidence can't. Steps that add tables
(jobs, audit) decide their own `ON DELETE` with the same question: is the child part of
the parent, or a record about it?

**Alternatives rejected.** `ltree` or a closure table would make subtree reads cheaper,
at the cost of rewriting paths or closure rows on every move; TraceLite's trees are small
and recursive CTEs are enough. A PostgreSQL `ENUM` for `status` and `result` would give
sqlc a Go type for free, but values can't be removed later; `text` plus a named `CHECK`
is changed by a migration like any other constraint.

lessons.title: Step 3: The store layer with sqlc, and transactions
lessons.summary: internal/store is sqlc's generated Queries plus one hand-written Store: a WithTx that binds the same queries to a transaction, one method per use case that needs one, and the translation of SQLSTATEs and constraint names into domain errors.

examples.title: The code sqlc generates for one requirement query, run on PostgreSQL

annotations.note: sqlc writes DBTX, the three methods its queries call. *pgx.Conn, *pgxpool.Pool and pgx.Tx all have them, so New takes any of the three, and the generated WithTx (example 2) rebinds existing Queries to a transaction.

The model mirrors the table, columns in table order. uuid.UUID is the standard library's (Go 1.27), through the overrides in sqlc.yaml; nullable parent_id becomes a pointer, which encodes as JSON null without a custom type. The real table has nine columns, and the timestamptz override turns created_at and updated_at into time.Time.

The input: named parameters (@name is sqlc.arg(name)) and RETURNING *, which sqlc expands into the column list at generation time (line 41), so a new column can't shift the Scan targets of an old query. The names become the fields of the Params struct.
The SQL is kept with its name comment, so pg_stat_activity and the server log show which query is running. Parameters are $1..$4 and travel separately from the text.

More than one parameter means a Params struct; ParentID *uuid.UUID sends NULL when nil. pgx encodes uuid.UUID because its underlying type is [16]byte and pgx treats a renamed type like its underlying type: no adapter, no driver.Valuer.
Here Queries gets a connection; cmd/tracelite hands it the pool, a test a transaction. Nothing in the generated code knows which, which is what makes WithTx in example 2 possible.
RETURNING * comes back as a full model: status is 'draft', the column default, and ParentID is nil for a top-level row.
Generated code returns pgx's errors untouched: a *pgconn.PgError with Code 23505 and ConstraintName requirements_code_key. Turning that into a store error is the Store's job (example 2).

examples.title: WithTx: all of a use case or none of it, and the statement that escapes

annotations.note: sqlc's generated WithTx: the same queries, bound to a transaction instead of the pool.

The Store keeps what can begin a transaction and the generated Queries bound to the pool. The real Store takes anything with a Begin method (How it works): Begin on a pgx.Tx creates a savepoint, so a test can wrap a whole Store in a transaction it rolls back.

pgx.BeginFunc is go.postgres.transactions' helper, ready-made: it commits when fn returns nil and rolls back when fn returns an error (or panics). fn receives Queries bound to the transaction, so every statement written with q is part of it.

The store's vocabulary. Callers test errors.Is(err, store.ErrDuplicateCode) and never see SQLSTATEs or *pgconn.PgError; the HTTP layer maps these errors to statuses in one place (step 4). The match is on the constraint name, never on the message text.
A use case with several writes that must happen together, like step 7's CSV import. It takes the Queries to write through as a parameter only so that the two runs below differ in one word.
Through q: the third row fails, fn returns the error, BeginFunc rolls back, and the first two rows go with it.
The bug: store.q is bound to the pool, so each INSERT commits on its own, outside the transaction. The use case reports the same error, but two of its three rows stay.

examples.title: Two moves at once: check-then-write races, the project lock serializes

annotations.note: Step 2's walk up from the new parent, as a function both sessions can call. The store's IsAncestorOrSelf is the same walk by id. It starts at the new parent itself, so a row moved under itself is caught here too, before the requirements_not_own_parent CHECK would be.
Both checks run before either move is committed, so both see the old tree and both answer false. The two UPDATEs change different rows, so neither waits for the other.
AUTH under EXPORT and EXPORT under AUTH: a loop with no root. Every row still has a parent in the same project, so no constraint objects, and the tree query would lose both requirements.

FOR UPDATE OF p locks the project's row, not the requirement: B moves a different requirement but needs the same lock, so it waits. Moves in other projects don't wait at all. No row at all would mean the requirement doesn't exist: ErrNotFound.

A's commit releases the lock and B's SELECT returns. Under READ COMMITTED each statement sees what was committed before it started, so B's check, a statement that starts after the lock was granted, sees A's move and answers true: ErrCycle, and B rolls back.

use_cases: Every query whose shape is fixed at compile time: CRUD, lists, the tree and cycle queries, reports
Use cases that read and then write: moving a requirement, linking with a check, recording a run and updating a summary
Translating constraint violations into errors the service and the HTTP layer understand
Tests against the real schema, with each test isolated by a transaction or by its own project
strengths: A misspelled column fails sqlc generate, not a request; the Scan targets can't drift from the SELECT list because both are generated together
One Queries type works on a pool, a connection and a transaction, so moving code into a transaction changes one line, unlike passing a Tx through every repository method by hand
Generated code is plain pgx without reflection; a debugger steps through it like your own code
Unlike Spring's @Transactional, the transaction boundary is a visible function call: the statements inside WithTx are exactly the ones in the closure
weaknesses: Dynamic SQL (optional filters, user-chosen sort columns) doesn't fit sqlc's one-query-one-method model; it stays hand-written beside the generated code
A row lock per project serializes all moves in that project; with heavy concurrent editing, SERIALIZABLE with retries would allow more parallelism
Error translation by constraint name couples the store to the migration's names; renaming a constraint is an API change for the store
Generated files must be regenerated and committed with every query or migration change

pitfalls.title: Using the pool inside WithTx
pitfalls.detail: A statement sent through s.q or the pool instead of the q passed to fn runs outside the transaction: it can't see the uncommitted rows and isn't rolled back. In example 2, two rows of a failed import stay.
pitfalls.bad: s.WithTx(ctx, func(q *Queries) error { return s.q.SetParent(ctx, arg) })
pitfalls.good: s.WithTx(ctx, func(q *Queries) error { return q.SetParent(ctx, arg) })

pitfalls.title: Check, then act, without a lock
pitfalls.detail: Two moves that each pass the cycle check can together close a loop, because neither sees the other's uncommitted update (example 3, part 1). Lock something both must lock (the project row) before checking, or use SERIALIZABLE and retry.

pitfalls.title: Matching error messages
pitfalls.detail: Message texts are for people and can be translated (lc_messages). Match the SQLSTATE and the constraint name: 23505 on requirements_code_key, 23503 on requirements_parent_fkey, 23001 on test_runs_test_case_fkey.
pitfalls.good: pgErr.Code == "23505" && pgErr.ConstraintName == "requirements_code_key"

pitfalls.title: pgtype values leaking out of the store
pitfalls.detail: Without overrides, sqlc's pgx/v5 output uses pgx's own types, such as pgtype.UUID and pgtype.Text, and every caller has to check .Valid. The overrides in sqlc.yaml give uuid.UUID, *uuid.UUID and time.Time instead.

quiz.q: Why does MoveRequirement lock the project row rather than the requirement being moved?
options: Locking a requirement row is not allowed
Two moves of different requirements can close a loop together; only a lock both must take serializes them
quiz.why: AUTH under EXPORT and EXPORT under AUTH touch different rows. The shared project row makes the second move wait and then see the first.

quiz.q: What does Store.db.Begin do when db is a pgx.Tx?
options: Starts a savepoint inside the outer transaction
quiz.why: pgx implements Begin on a Tx as a pseudo nested transaction, a SAVEPOINT; that's what lets a test wrap the whole Store in a transaction it rolls back.

quiz.q: sqlc reads the schema at generation time. What happens if a query names a column that the migrations don't have?
options: The generated method fails at run time
The column is scanned as NULL
quiz.why: sqlc parses the migrations and the queries together; an unknown column is a generation error, before any code runs.

quiz.q: Deleting a test case with runs fails. Which SQLSTATE does the store see?
quiz.why: test_runs_test_case_fkey is ON DELETE RESTRICT, which raises 23001; NO ACTION would raise 23503. Step 2 shows both.

further_reading.title: sqlc module page (README links the manual: overrides, query annotations)
PostgreSQL docs: Explicit locking, row-level locks

lessons.body:
## Concept

TraceLite's store has two halves in one package, `internal/store`:

- **Generated** by sqlc from `migrations/*.sql` and `queries/*.sql`: the `DBTX` interface,
  `Queries`, one model struct per table and one typed method per named query. Nobody
  edits these files.
- **Written by hand** in `store.go`: `Store`, which owns a `*pgxpool.Pool` and the
  generated `Queries`; `WithTx`, which runs a function against `Queries` bound to one
  transaction; one method per use case that needs more than one statement
  (`MoveRequirement`); and the store's errors.

A use case that is a single statement (create, get, list) needs no transaction of its
own: PostgreSQL runs every statement atomically. A use case that reads and then writes,
or writes several times, gets one `WithTx` call, and every statement inside goes through
the `q` it receives.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring Data**: a repository interface whose implementation is generated is
  similar, but Spring generates at run time from method names or JPQL. sqlc generates
  source code from SQL at build time, and `@Transactional`'s proxy becomes an explicit
  `WithTx(ctx, func(q) error)`.
- **Python/SQLAlchemy**: `with session.begin():` is the same boundary. The difference is
  that there is no session tracking objects: nothing is flushed implicitly, every
  statement is a method call you can see.
- **JS/Prisma**: `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)` has the same shape as `WithTx`;
  forgetting to use `tx` instead of `prisma` inside it is the same bug as using the pool
  inside `WithTx`.
- **C++ RAII**: the deferred `tx.Rollback(ctx)` inside `pgx.BeginFunc` plays the role of a
  destructor that rolls back unless `Commit` ran first.

## How it works

The project files for this step:

```text
sqlc.yaml
migrations/001_init.sql          # step 2, goose format
queries/requirements.sql         # -- name: ... :one / :many / :exec
internal/store/db.go             # generated: DBTX, New, Queries, WithTx
internal/store/models.go         # generated: Project, Requirement, TestCase, TraceLink, TestRun
internal/store/*.sql.go          # generated: one method per query
internal/store/store.go          # hand-written: Store, WithTx, use cases, errors (below)
```

`sqlc.yaml`. The two `uuid` overrides follow the pattern sqlc's "Overriding types" page
shows for `github.com/google/uuid` (one override for non-null columns, one with
`nullable: true`), pointed at Go 1.27's standard `uuid` package instead (it has no
`NullUUID`, so nullable columns become `*uuid.UUID`); the `timestamptz` override replaces pgx's own time type,
and `emit_pointers_for_null_types` turns the other nullable columns (`duration_ms`) into
pointers:

```yaml
version: "2"
sql:
  - engine: "postgresql"
    schema: "migrations"
    queries: "queries"
    gen:
      go:
        package: "store"
        out: "internal/store"
        sql_package: "pgx/v5"
        emit_pointers_for_null_types: true
        overrides:
          - db_type: "uuid"
            go_type: "uuid.UUID"
          - db_type: "uuid"
            nullable: true
            go_type:
              import: "uuid"
              type: "UUID"
              pointer: true
          - db_type: "pg_catalog.timestamptz"
            go_type: "time.Time"
```

The store's errors and what produces them. Later steps add to this list rather than
inventing a second mechanism:

- `ErrNotFound`: `pgx.ErrNoRows` from a `:one` query, or a project foreign key
  (`requirements_project_id_fkey`) when the project in the URL doesn't exist.
- `ErrDuplicateCode`: 23505 on `requirements_code_key` or `test_cases_code_key`.
- `ErrParentNotFound`: 23503 on `requirements_parent_fkey` during insert or update.
- `ErrHasChildren`: 23503 on `requirements_parent_fkey` during delete.
- `ErrCycle`: the move check in `MoveRequirement`.
- `ErrHasRuns`: 23001 on `test_runs_test_case_fkey` when a test case is deleted.
- `ErrNotInProject`: 23503 on `trace_links_test_case_fkey` or
  `trace_links_requirement_fkey`, a link across projects.

Times are `timestamptz`; pgx returns them in the process's local zone, and the HTTP layer
converts to UTC before encoding (step 4).

The one use case of this step that needs a transaction is moving a requirement. Its three
queries in `queries/requirements.sql` (example 3 runs the same statements by code, in two
sessions at once):

```sql
-- name: LockProjectOf :one
SELECT p.id FROM projects p JOIN requirements r ON r.project_id = p.id
WHERE r.id = @requirement_id FOR UPDATE OF p;

-- name: IsAncestorOrSelf :one
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id FROM requirements WHERE id = @node::uuid
  UNION ALL SELECT r.id, r.parent_id FROM requirements r JOIN up ON r.id = up.parent_id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT FROM up WHERE id = @ancestor::uuid);

-- name: SetParent :exec
UPDATE requirements SET parent_id = @parent_id, updated_at = now() WHERE id = @id;
```

And the hand-written half, `store.go`, minus the error variables listed above:

```go
// Store is what the service holds: one transaction per use case, the store's errors out.
type Store struct {
	db interface {
		Begin(context.Context) (pgx.Tx, error)
	} // the pool; a pgx.Tx in tests
	q *Queries // New(pool)
}

// WithTx commits when fn returns nil and rolls back otherwise.
func (s *Store) WithTx(ctx context.Context, fn func(q *Queries) error) error {
	return pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, s.db, func(tx pgx.Tx) error { return fn(s.q.WithTx(tx)) })
}

// MoveRequirement re-parents id under parent; nil makes it top level.
func (s *Store) MoveRequirement(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID, parent *uuid.UUID) error {
	return s.WithTx(ctx, func(q *Queries) error {
		if _, err := q.LockProjectOf(ctx, id); errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
			return ErrNotFound
		} else if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if parent != nil {
			cycle, err := q.IsAncestorOrSelf(ctx, IsAncestorOrSelfParams{Node: *parent, Ancestor: id})
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if cycle {
				return ErrCycle
			}
		}
		err := q.SetParent(ctx, SetParentParams{ParentID: parent, ID: id})
		if pgErr, ok := errors.AsType[*pgconn.PgError](err); ok && pgErr.ConstraintName == "requirements_parent_fkey" {
			return ErrParentNotFound // no such row, or one in another project
		}
		return err
	})
}
```

The order is the point. The lock comes first, in its own statement; the check runs after
the lock is granted, so it sees every move committed before; the write comes last. The
parent's existence isn't checked with a SELECT: the composite foreign key decides at the
write, where a concurrent delete can't slip in between, and the store translates its
constraint name.

The `::uuid` casts in `IsAncestorOrSelf` are for sqlc, not PostgreSQL. Inside this
recursive CTE, sqlc 1.31.1 can't resolve `id` to infer a parameter's type and stops with
`column reference "id" is ambiguous`, although PostgreSQL runs the query as is; a cast
gives sqlc the type without the lookup. Generated with sqlc 1.31.1 on 2026-11-14, these
queries give `IsAncestorOrSelfParams{Ancestor, Node uuid.UUID}` returning `(bool, error)`,
`SetParentParams{ParentID *uuid.UUID; ID uuid.UUID}` and
`LockProjectOf(ctx, requirementID uuid.UUID) (uuid.UUID, error)`, all importing the
standard `uuid` package; sqlc accepts the `CYCLE` clause and `FOR UPDATE OF p` as they are.

## Design notes

**Why a hand-written Store at all.** Generated `Queries` would be enough for single
statements, and the service could call them directly. The Store exists for the two
things generation can't give you: a transaction boundary around several queries, and one
place that turns database errors into the store's errors. Store methods that would only
forward to `Queries` are still written, because they are where the translation happens;
what is never written is a second, hand-made copy of a query.

**One transaction per use case, owned by the store.** The alternative is a service that
begins a transaction and passes it down. That leaks pgx types into the service and lets
any caller forget the boundary. TraceLite's rule: a use case that needs atomicity is one
Store method, and the service calls it once (go.design.layers calls this shaping the port
like the use case).

**Locking.** Moves lock the project row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. That serializes
tree edits per project, which is fine for a tool where a project is edited by a few
people. `SERIALIZABLE` would let independent moves run in parallel, at the price of
retry loops on SQLSTATE 40001; the transactions module covers both.

**Testing.** Store tests run against PostgreSQL with the real migrations, because the
rules that matter (composite keys, CHECKs, collation) live there. Single-statement tests
hand `Queries` a transaction and roll it back; tests of transactional behavior (commits,
concurrent moves) seed their own project and let the private schema be dropped
afterwards. Step 14 builds the full test setup on these two patterns. A Go test of two
concurrent moves can only assert the outcome: without the lock the race window is a few
milliseconds and the transactions still usually run one after the other. Forcing the bad
interleaving of example 3 takes a hook between check and write, as in go.design.layers.

lessons.title: Step 4: The REST API: CRUD, validation, problem-details errors, keyset pagination
lessons.summary: One vertical through TraceLite's API: the handler decodes strictly and maps errors in one function, the service holds the rules every entry point shares, the store speaks SQL; failures are RFC 9457 problems, and lists page with an opaque keyset cursor.

examples.title: POST a requirement: strict decoding, 404 for a malformed id, 201 with Location

annotations.note: The request body has its own type, with only what a client may send. id, status and timestamps aren't in it, so a client can't set them, and RejectUnknownMembers turns an attempt into a 400.

The wire type, abridged: camelCase names from openapi.yaml, uuid.UUID encoded as a string by its MarshalText, a pointer for the nullable parentId so it encodes as null, and no omitempty anywhere: every field is always present.
A path id that isn't a UUID can't name a resource, so it is a 404 like an unknown one, and the database is never asked.

encoding/json/v2, on by default in Go 1.27: UnmarshalRead requires exactly one JSON value, rejects duplicate names and invalid UTF-8, and matches names case-sensitively. MaxBytesReader caps the body at 64 KiB; the full decode helper from go.http.json-validation answers 413 when that cap is hit.

201 with a Location header naming the new resource, and the resource itself as the body, so the client needs no second request. The service and the store (examples 2 and 3, step 3) are left out here; a fixed id stands in for the one the database assigns.
"titel" is not a member of RequirementCreate. With v1 and no DisallowUnknownFields, this would have created a requirement with an empty title, or failed later with a confusing message.
v1 matched "Title" to the title field case-insensitively; v2 doesn't, so the member is unknown and the body is refused.

examples.title: The service: normalize, report every broken rule, and turn a store error into a field error

annotations.note: The service's answer to "what is wrong with this input": JSON Pointers into the request body, as in RFC 9457's own example. writeError (example 3) puts them into the problem's errors member.

The service normalizes (trims the title) and validates every field before touching the database, collecting all problems. Titles are counted in runes, like the CHECK's char_length; codes are ASCII, so len is right there.
The store says "parent not in this project"; the service knows that this is a fact about the parentId the client sent, so it becomes a field error, 422, not a 404.
The title arrives padded and reaches the store trimmed.
Both rules break, both are reported: İ (what "auth-login".toLocaleUpperCase("tr") produces) is not A-Z, and a title of spaces is empty once trimmed.
200 characters in 400 bytes pass, as they pass the CHECK. A byte count, len(title), would have refused them.

examples.title: writeError: every failure as an RFC 9457 problem, decided in one place

annotations.note: RFC 9457 problem details. type identifies the kind of problem, title is fixed per type, errors is TraceLite's extension member.
The one place where errors become statuses. Handlers never choose a status for an error themselves, so a new error kind can't come out as 422 from one endpoint and 500 from another.
A duplicate code is a conflict with existing state, 409, but it is still about one field, so the problem carries an errors entry and the form can mark the code input.
Anything unexpected is a 500 with no detail: the cause, which may name tables or constraints, goes to the log only (stderr here, which the output doesn't show).
For about:blank, RFC 9457 says the title should be the status code's standard phrase, so it comes from http.StatusText.
errors.Is looks through wrapping, so a store error wrapped with context on the way up still maps to 409.

examples.title: GET a list: limit, an opaque keyset cursor, and what a bad cursor gets

annotations.note: Every list in TraceLite has this shape: items, always an array, and nextCursor, always present, null on the last page. A client loops until nextCursor is null and never builds a cursor itself.
A stand-in for step 2's keyset query, so this example needs no database: the codes after the cursor, in byte order, at most limit of them. In TraceLite the store runs the SQL in the comment.
limit defaults to 50 (cmp.Or returns its first argument that isn't the zero value) and is capped at 200. A query parameter isn't content, so a bad one is 400, not 422.

The cursor format: the last item's sort key as a JSON array, in base64url without padding, so it needs no escaping in a query string. JSON keeps types (a timestamp keeps its microseconds); decoding into a Go array of the right length rejects a key of the wrong shape. No cursor means "", which sorts before every code, so the first page is the same query as every other page.
One row more than the page size. In SQL the extra row costs one index entry and replaces a count(*) over the whole project.
If the extra row came back, there is a next page, and the cursor is the sort key of the last row actually returned, not of the extra one.
json/v2's MarshalWrite. Unlike v1, a nil slice encodes as [] by default (FormatNilSliceAsNull restores null), so the empty page after the last code has "items":[] as the spec says.
The second and third cursors are the nextCursor of the response before them. The fourth, WyJaIl0, is ["Z"]: it sorts after every code, so the page is empty.

base64url of "not json", then of ["AUTH","AUTH-LOGIN"], two values for a one-value key. Both get the same answer: the server doesn't explain what it expected, because clients aren't meant to construct one. The cursor is readable to anyone who decodes it; opaque means clients must not depend on it, not that it is secret.

use_cases: Every resource endpoint in TraceLite: projects, requirements, test cases, links and runs follow these status codes, problem types and page shapes
Form submissions that show all field errors at once, from the errors array
Lists that a user scrolls or a client iterates: keyset pages stay fast and stable while rows are added
A second entry point (the CSV import in step 7, a CLI) that reuses the service's validation unchanged
strengths: The standard library's ServeMux (Go 1.22 patterns) routes methods and path parameters without a framework, and json/v2 makes strict decoding the default
One error-mapping function keeps statuses consistent across endpoints, unlike per-handler `http.Error` calls
Problem details let the TypeScript client handle every failure of every endpoint with one parser and one ApiError type
Keyset pages cost the same on page 1 and page 1,000 and never repeat or skip rows when others insert, unlike OFFSET
weaknesses: The Go wire types are a hand-kept copy of the spec; nothing but a test (step 1's contract check, step 14) notices drift
Three layers mean three shapes of the same data (row, model, wire) and mapping code between them
Keyset pagination can't jump to page 37 or show 'page 3 of 12' without an extra count
Only one sort order per list: another order needs another index and another cursor shape

pitfalls.title: Choosing statuses inside handlers
pitfalls.detail: Each handler deciding its own status drifts: the same duplicate is 400 here and 409 there. Return errors and map them in writeError.
pitfalls.good: writeError(w, err) // the one switch from error to problem

pitfalls.title: Matching JSON names case-insensitively by habit
pitfalls.detail: encoding/json (v1) matched "ID" to a field without a tag; json/v2 doesn't. Every wire field gets an explicit json tag in camelCase.
pitfalls.bad: var created struct{ ID string } // v2 leaves it empty for {"id": ...}
pitfalls.good: var created struct { ID string `json:"id"` }

pitfalls.title: Building the cursor from the extra row
pitfalls.detail: With limit + 1, the last row fetched is not returned. Encode the cursor from items[limit-1], or the next page skips a row.

pitfalls.title: Echoing database errors
pitfalls.detail: err.Error() from pgx names constraints and tables. Map known errors to problems and log the rest; a 500 carries no detail.

pitfalls.title: Times in the server's zone
pitfalls.detail: pgx returns timestamptz in the process's local zone, so on a machine in Turkey the JSON would say +03:00. Convert to UTC when mapping to wire types; the client's z.iso.datetime() accepts only Z.

quiz.q: The body is valid JSON but the title is only spaces. What does TraceLite answer?
options: 201, the database accepts an empty title
quiz.why: Decoding succeeded, the content breaks a rule: 422 with the validation problem type. The service trims, then counts characters.

quiz.q: POST /api/projects/{projectId}/requirements names a parentId that belongs to another project. Which status?
options: 422: a field of the body is invalid
quiz.why: The URL's project exists; the problem is the parentId field. The composite foreign key refuses it and the service reports #/parentId.

quiz.q: The page size is 2 and the query returns 3 rows. Which code goes into nextCursor?
options: None: there is no next page
quiz.why: The third row only proves a next page exists. The next page must start after the last row the client actually received.

quiz.q: A list endpoint gets ?cursor=<base64 of ["AUTH","AUTH-LOGIN"]> where the sort key has one value. What happens?
quiz.why: json/v2 requires a JSON array to have exactly as many elements as the Go array it decodes into; the handler answers 400 for any cursor it can't decode.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A request to TraceLite's API passes three layers, each in its own package:

- **`internal/httpapi`**: routes (`ServeMux` patterns), decodes the body strictly into a
  wire type, calls the service, maps every error to a problem in `writeError`, encodes
  the response. The wire types live here, as a hand-kept mirror of `openapi.yaml`.
- **`internal/tracelite`**: the service. Rules every entry point shares: normalization,
  field validation, translating store errors that are really about a field. The HTTP API
  and step 7's CSV import call the same methods.
- **`internal/store`**: step 3. SQL in, store errors out.

Failures are RFC 9457 problem details, served as `application/problem+json`. Lists are
pages with an opaque keyset cursor. Both shapes are the same for every resource, so the
TypeScript client (step 5) handles them once.

The examples take one vertical apart, a piece each: the handler's decoding (example 1),
the service's rules (example 2), `writeError` (example 3) and a list endpoint (example 4).
The store is step 3's, so the examples stand in for it rather than repeat it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Spring**: `@RestController` + `@Valid` + `@ControllerAdvice` returning `ProblemDetail`
  is the same layering, assembled by annotations. Here the handler calls the decoder and
  the service explicitly, and `writeError` is the `@ControllerAdvice`.
- **FastAPI**: pydantic validates on decode and answers 422 automatically, with its own
  error format. TraceLite returns RFC 9457 instead, and validates rules in the service so
  the importer gets them too.
- **Express**: an error-handling middleware `(err, req, res, next)` is the equivalent of
  `writeError`; the difference is that Go handlers return after writing the error, with
  no `next()` to forget.
- **Django REST Framework**: `CursorPagination` produces the same opaque, base64-encoded
  cursors; its `next` is a full URL, TraceLite's `nextCursor` is just the token.

## How it works

TraceLite's API conventions. Every later step follows them.

**Paths.** Everything is under `/api`. Collections that belong to a project are nested
under it; a single resource has a top-level path by its id:

- `GET|POST /api/projects`, `GET /api/projects/{projectId}`
- `GET|POST /api/projects/{projectId}/requirements` (list ordered by `code`)
- `GET /api/projects/{projectId}/requirement-tree` (whole tree, depth first, with `depth`)
- `GET|PATCH|DELETE /api/requirements/{requirementId}`
- `PUT /api/requirements/{requirementId}/parent` with `{"parentId": "<uuid>" | null}` (move)
- `GET|POST /api/projects/{projectId}/test-cases`, `GET|PATCH|DELETE /api/test-cases/{testCaseId}`
- `GET /api/projects/{projectId}/trace-links` (the matrix)
- `PUT|DELETE /api/requirements/{requirementId}/test-cases/{testCaseId}` (link, unlink; idempotent)
- `GET|POST /api/test-cases/{testCaseId}/runs` (newest first)

**JSON.** camelCase member names (`parentId`, `createdAt`); SQL stays snake_case and the
mapping happens in Go struct tags. Ids are UUID strings. Times are RFC 3339 in UTC with
`Z`: pgx returns `timestamptz` in the server's local zone, so `httpapi` calls `.UTC()`
when it maps the store's model to the wire type (step 1's example shows the difference). Every member of a resource is always present: absent values are `null`, empty lists
are `[]`, empty text is `""`. Enum values are lowercase strings (`draft`, `passed`).
`PATCH` bodies contain only the members to change, and `null` is not accepted in them;
moving is its own endpoint, so "absent" and "null" never have to be told apart.

**Statuses.** 200 for reads and updates, 201 with `Location` for creates, 204 for
deletes and for link and unlink. Errors:

- 400 `about:blank`: the body can't be decoded (syntax, wrong JSON type, unknown member,
  malformed UUID inside it) or a query parameter is invalid (`limit`, `cursor`).
- 404 `about:blank`: the id in the path is malformed or names nothing, including the
  project of a nested list: an unknown project gets a 404, not an empty page, so a typo
  in a URL is noticed.
- 409 `https://tracelite.example/problems/conflict`: the request contradicts current
  state: duplicate code (with `errors` on `#/code`), a requirement that still has
  children, a test case that has runs.
- 413 `about:blank`: the body is over the endpoint's limit (64 KiB for JSON).
- 422 `https://tracelite.example/problems/validation`: well-formed content that breaks a
  rule, with every failing field in `errors`.
- 500 `about:blank`: anything else, with no `detail`; the cause is logged.

**Problems.** `{"type", "title", "status", "detail"?, "errors"?}` where each error is
`{"pointer": "#/field", "detail": "..."}`. `title` is the status text for `about:blank`,
`Validation failed` and `Conflict` for the two TraceLite types. Clients branch on
`status` and `type`, never on text.

**Pages.** `?limit=` (1 to 200, default 50) and `?cursor=`. The response is
`{"items": [...], "nextCursor": "..." | null}`. The cursor is base64url (no padding) of a
JSON array holding the last item's sort key, in `ORDER BY` order: `["AUTH-LOGIN"]` for
lists by code, `["2026-11-13T06:30:00.123456Z", "<run id>"]` for runs newest first. The
server fetches `limit + 1` rows to know whether there is a next page.

## Design notes

**Why a service layer here.** go.design.layers warns against pass-through services.
TraceLite's service earns its place with one concrete reason: the CSV import (step 7) is
a second entry point that must apply exactly the same normalization and validation as
the API. Rules that only the database can check (uniqueness, same project) stay in the
schema and arrive as store errors; the service only decides which of those are field
errors.

**Validation in Go and in SQL.** The service checks formats and lengths to report every
field at once with a useful message; the CHECK constraints catch any writer that skips
the service. Keep the two in step: both count characters, both use the same code
pattern.

**Package choice.** `encoding/json/v2` is the default for new Go 1.27 code, as the JSON
lesson recommends: strict decoding without wrapper code and `[]` for nil slices. The
standard library's `ServeMux` covers TraceLite's routes, like StackLab's own `httpapi`.
A router, a problem-details package or a validation library were not added: each would
be a dependency to explain for a few dozen lines of code.

**Cursors.** Opaque, so the server can change what's inside without breaking clients;
base64url of JSON rather than a home-grown string format, so typed values survive and a
malformed one fails to parse. Not signed: a forged cursor can only start a page at a
different place in a list the caller may read anyway. If that ever stops being true,
sign it with an HMAC.

lessons.title: Step 5: Typed TS client from OpenAPI + zod, wrapped in TanStack Query hooks
lessons.summary: The client side of TraceLite's contract: types generated from openapi.yaml, zod schemas tied to them with satisfies and checked on every response, problems turned into one ApiError, and TanStack Query hooks that page with nextCursor and invalidate by project.

examples.title: Generated types and the zod schema tied to them: brands, satisfies, UTC times

annotations.note: What openapi-typescript writes into src/api/schema.d.ts, abridged: types only, no run-time code. format: uuid and date-time survive only as comments, a nullable member becomes T | null, and an enum becomes a union of literals.

Branded ids. z.uuid() validates the RFC 9562 layout, and .brand() adds a type-only tag, the technique of ts.type-level.branded with zod's symbol. A ProjectId can only come out of a parse, and a RequirementId can't be passed where a ProjectId is expected (line 49).

satisfies checks the schema against the generated type without widening it, so the inferred type keeps its brands. If the spec gains a required member, or the schema drops one, tsc fails here with TS1360. It doesn't catch a schema that is stricter than the spec, such as an enum with a value missing: a narrower type is still assignable.
z.iso.datetime() without options accepts only a Z suffix. That turns step 4's convention (times in UTC) into a check on every response.
The same instant with +03:00: a Go handler that forgot .UTC(). The value is right, the contract isn't, and the parse says where.

examples.title: request(): every response parsed, every failure one ApiError

annotations.note: One error type for every failed request, carrying the parsed problem. Callers branch on problem.status and problem.type, and forms read problem.errors. The field is declared, not a parameter property, which keeps the class within erasable syntax.
A body that isn't JSON (an HTML error page) becomes null instead of throwing a SyntaxError from inside the client.

Not every failure comes from TraceLite: a proxy, a gateway or the Vite dev server can answer 502 with HTML. The client builds an about:blank problem from the status, so callers still see one ApiError shape.
The success path validates too. A server that drifts from its own spec fails here, with a path to the bad member, instead of crashing a component three renders later.
One function per operation, with a path relative to the page: in development the Vite proxy forwards /api, in production the same Go binary serves both, so there is one origin.
The lesson iframe has no network, so this example replaces fetch itself and the client code stays as it is in the app. Step 14's tests intercept the same fetch calls with MSW instead.
A member that came out as CreatedAt instead of createdAt. The request succeeded on the server, and the client still refuses the response, because it no longer matches the contract.
"auth-login".toLocaleUpperCase("tr") is "AUTH-LOGİN", with a dotted capital İ. The server's 422 names the member, #/code, and the client passes the errors array through untouched.

examples.title: Query keys and an infinite query that follows nextCursor

annotations.note: The fake's cursor is readable to keep it short. TraceLite's is base64url of the last sort key, and the client never looks inside: it hands back what the server sent.

TraceLite's key scheme: keys start with the path of the resource they cache, ["projects", id, ...] for everything inside a project, and ["requirements", id] for a single requirement. A prefix then names a whole family of cached queries.

useInfiniteQuery stores pages, not items. initialPageParam null means "no cursor", and getNextPageParam hands the server's nextCursor back unchanged; null or undefined there means there is no next page, so hasNextPage becomes false and the button disappears.
The pages are flattened for display. Each page keeps its own cursor in the cache, which is what fetchNextPage continues from.

Invalidating ["projects", id] matches the list's key by prefix. An infinite query refetches every page it has loaded, in order from the first, so AUTH-2FA appears where the server's code order puts it; the client never guesses where a new item sorts.

examples.title: A create form: a mutation that invalidates, server errors under their field

annotations.note: After a successful create, the project prefix is invalidated: the list of example 3 and the requirement tree of step 6 both refetch. In the app this mutation is the hook useCreateRequirement in queries.ts, next to useRequirements.
The form's errors come straight from the problem: each errors entry has a JSON Pointer, and the field whose name it ends with shows it. Server rules stay on the server; the client renders them.

Codes are normalized with toUpperCase(), which is locale-independent. toLocaleUpperCase() without an argument uses the browser's locale, and in Turkish turns i into İ, which the server rejects (example 2).

Harness: the lesson's sandboxed iframe doesn't allow form submission, and the HTML spec returns before firing the submit event in that case. Dispatching the event is what a click on the Ekle button would trigger.
"auth-login" becomes AUTH-LOGIN, an existing code: 409, shown under the code input. The second code is new, and its i stays a plain I.

use_cases: Every TraceLite screen: lists, the tree, forms and the trace matrix read data through these hooks only
Forms that show server-side validation per field, from the problem's errors array
Infinite scroll and 'load more' over keyset-paginated endpoints
Catching contract drift in development and tests, before it reaches a component
strengths: One spec, two compile-time checks: the Go wire types are tested against it (step 1), the zod schemas must satisfy the generated types
Branded ids make passing a RequirementId where a ProjectId belongs a compile error, at no run-time cost
Every failure arrives as an ApiError with a typed problem, including failures from proxies that don't speak problem+json
TanStack Query turns cursors, pages, refetching and invalidation into a few lines, where a hand-written useEffect would also need race handling
weaknesses: The zod schemas are written by hand next to the generated types; satisfies catches missing and mistyped members but not a schema stricter than the spec
Validating every response costs CPU on large lists; a few thousand items per page is fine, a 50 MB export is not (step 8 streams instead)
Invalidating a whole project prefix refetches more than strictly changed, and an infinite query refetches every loaded page
Query keys are untyped arrays; the keys object is the only thing keeping them consistent

pitfalls.title: Annotating instead of satisfying
pitfalls.detail: const R: z.ZodType<Generated> = z.object(...) widens the schema to the generated type and drops the brands. satisfies checks the same thing and keeps the precise type.
pitfalls.good: const Requirement = z.object({ ... }) satisfies z.ZodType<components["schemas"]["Requirement"]>

pitfalls.title: Throwing the response body as the error
pitfalls.detail: A 502 from a proxy has an HTML body, and a 204 has none. Parse a problem when there is one, synthesize an about:blank problem from the status when there isn't, and keep one ApiError type.

pitfalls.title: Building cursors on the client
