  re-joins rooms, but can't know what was missed either; a refetch on reconnect is the
  same answer.
- **C/C++**: a producer thread and a set of bounded queues with a drop-on-full policy, the
  classic way to keep one slow consumer from stalling the others.

## How it works

The migration, `migrations/002_change_events.sql` (example 1 reads it from its fixture):

```sql
-- +goose Up
-- +goose StatementBegin
CREATE FUNCTION notify_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  project uuid;
BEGIN
  IF TG_TABLE_NAME = 'test_runs' THEN
    SELECT project_id INTO project FROM test_cases
    WHERE id = CASE TG_OP WHEN 'DELETE' THEN OLD.test_case_id ELSE NEW.test_case_id END;
  ELSE
    project := CASE TG_OP WHEN 'DELETE' THEN OLD.project_id ELSE NEW.project_id END;
  END IF;
  PERFORM pg_notify('tracelite_changes',
    json_build_object('projectId', project, 'topic', TG_ARGV[0])::text);
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;
-- +goose StatementEnd
CREATE TRIGGER requirements_notify AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON requirements
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_change('requirements');
CREATE TRIGGER trace_links_notify AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON trace_links
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_change('trace-links');
CREATE TRIGGER test_runs_notify AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON test_runs
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_change('test-runs');
```

- goose's `StatementBegin`/`StatementEnd` keep the function body, which contains
  semicolons, in one statement.
- `NEW` is null in a DELETE trigger and `OLD` in an INSERT, hence the `CASE` on `TG_OP`.
  `test_runs` has no `project_id`, so the function looks the project up through the test
  case.
- The payload names the project and the kind of change, nothing more: it must stay under
  8000 bytes, and the browser refetches anyway.
- The trigger fires for every writer: the API, step 7's importer, a psql session.

NOTIFY's rules, from the PostgreSQL documentation and shown in go.services.listen-notify:
a notification is delivered when its transaction commits and never if it rolls back;
identical channel-and-payload pairs within one transaction are delivered once; within a
transaction, notifications arrive in the order they were sent, and transactions arrive in
commit order.

The new endpoint, added next to the others in `openapi.yaml`:

```yaml
  /api/projects/{projectId}/events:
    parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/ProjectId" }]
    get:
      operationId: streamProjectEvents
      description: >
        Server-sent events. Event names: requirements, trace-links, test-runs, resync.
        Data: {"topic": <the event name>}. No ids; reconnecting clients refetch.
      responses:
        "200": { description: The stream, content: { text/event-stream: { schema: { type: string } } } }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant W as Writer (API, import, psql)
  participant P as PostgreSQL
  participant L as Go listener
  participant H as Hub
  participant B as Browser (EventSource)
  W->>P: INSERT INTO trace_links ... ; COMMIT
  P-->>L: NOTIFY tracelite_changes {"projectId", "topic": "trace-links"}
  L->>H: Publish(projectId, trace-links)
  H-->>B: event: trace-links (SSE, flushed)
  B->>B: invalidateQueries(["projects", id])
  B->>P: GET trace-links, coverage (through the API)
```

What each event refetches, by key prefix (step 5): all of them invalidate
`["projects", projectId]`, which covers the tree, the lists, the matrix's links and the
coverage. Topic-specific invalidation (`trace-links` only touching links and coverage) is
a later optimization; the topic is in the event so that it can be added without a
server change.

Where the gaps are, and what closes each:

| Gap | Closed by |
|---|---|
| between the first fetch and the stream opening | refetch on `open` |
| a network drop; EventSource reconnects by itself | refetch on `open` |
| a slow tab dropped by the hub; its response ends and EventSource reconnects | refetch on `open` |
| the listener's connection broke (database restart) | `resync` to every stream after `LISTEN` is active again |
| the server answered the reconnect with 404 or 503 | nothing automatic: the page shows that it is no longer live |

## Design notes

**Trigger, not application events.** The service could publish after each commit, but
then the importer, a psql fix and any future writer would each have to remember to. The
trigger makes "committed" and "notified" the same event. Step 13 weighs the same choice
for the audit history, where the trade-offs come out differently because the record
must survive.

**SSE, not WebSockets.** The browser never sends anything on this channel; mutations
already go through the REST API. SSE is a normal HTTP response, so it works through the
Vite proxy, carries the session cookie, and reconnects without code. A WebSocket would
add a second protocol and hand-written reconnection for no message the browser needs to
send.

Vite's [server.proxy docs](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-proxy) don't
mention SSE; they say the proxy "Extends http-proxy-3". http-proxy-3's response pass
pipes the backend's response straight into the browser's (`proxyRes.pipe(res)` in
`passes/web-incoming.js`, bundled into Vite 7.3.7's `dist/node/chunks/config.js`), so
each event goes through as the backend flushes it. A run on 2026-11-14 (Vite 7.3.7,
Node 24.22.0) showed it: a `text/event-stream` backend writing every 500 ms, read
through a Vite dev proxy, delivered its events at 1, 507, 1014 and 1520 ms.

**Hints, not data.** A payload with the new link would let the browser patch its cache
without a request, but then a missed or reordered event leaves the cache wrong until
the next full load. Refetching costs a few small requests per change and is always
right.

**Dedicated listener, bounded fan-out.** One connection serves every tab, and the hub
never blocks it; the policy for a slow tab is "drop and let it reconnect", which
EventSource implements on the client for free. The listener resyncs after every
`LISTEN`, not only after a reconnect: on a fresh server there are no streams to tell,
and if the first connection failed while tabs were already open, they need the refetch
too.

lessons.title: Step 10: External service: standards lookup with timeouts, retries, caching; outbound webhooks
lessons.summary: TraceLite calls a standards catalogue with a deadline per attempt, retries only what may go away, honors Retry-After within its own budget and serves a stale title rather than an error. It calls subscribers' webhooks the same way, signed with HMAC and carrying an event id that makes redelivery harmless.

examples.title: One attempt at the catalogue: its own timeout inside the caller's deadline, and what each answer means

annotations.note: Two errors callers test with errors.Is. ErrUnknownClause is an answer, which example 3 caches. errTransient marks what may go away; wrapping it with %w next to the cause keeps both visible.
context.WithTimeout derives from the caller's context, so an attempt ends at whichever comes first: its own 300 ms or the API request's deadline. TraceLite uses 2 s per attempt.
No answer at all (a refused connection, a reset, this attempt's timeout) is transient: the next attempt may well get through.
The status decides. 200 is the title, 404 an answer, 429 and 5xx may go away, and anything else is TraceLite's mistake, which no retry fixes.

A size limit on what is read back, so a broken catalogue can't make TraceLite read without end. The real catalogue answers JSON, and TraceLite decodes it without RejectUnknownMembers, unlike its own API: a client of someone else's API accepts members it doesn't know yet.
Retry-After is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date. This reads the seconds form; a date, or no header, counts as no wish at all.
The slow answer: the handler waits until the client gives up. The attempt fails after 300 ms whatever the catalogue does, which keeps the run deterministic.
The client's Timeout is only a backstop for code that forgets a context; http.DefaultClient has none. The client is built once and shared, so connections are reused.
The API request's budget: 2 s in all, shared by every attempt. The slow attempt spends 300 ms of it.

examples.title: Retrying what may go away: full jitter, Retry-After, and never a wait past the caller's deadline

annotations.note: The retry loop, as in go.services.retries: a bounded number of attempts, and a wait between them that the caller can cancel.
Only errTransient is retried. A 404 or a 400 fails the same way every time, so it returns at once.

Full jitter: a random wait between zero and a ceiling that doubles (200 ms, then 400 ms), so that many clients failing together don't retry together. Retry-After wins when it is longer; a server under load knows better.
A wait longer than the time left can only end in a timeout, so the loop gives up at once and the caller can fall back to its cache (example 3).

Three lookups: 503, a timeout, then 200 (three attempts, one answer); a 429 asking for 120 s against a 2 s budget; three 502s, which fail after the last attempt. The API answers 503 for the last two, unless the cache has an older title.

examples.title: The cache: answers for 24 hours, 404s for 10 minutes, and a stale title when the catalogue is down

annotations.note: One entry per reference. err holds ErrUnknownClause for a remembered 404, so a typo doesn't cost a call per keystroke.
Cache first. A fresh entry, including a remembered 404, answers without any call.
The call runs outside the lock: it may take the request's whole budget, and other lookups shouldn't wait for it. Two concurrent misses for one reference both call the catalogue (see Weaknesses).
An answer is kept for 24 hours, a 404 for 10 minutes, so a newly added clause appears soon.
The catalogue failed and an older title exists: it comes back marked stale. Degraded, not broken, and the UI can say so.
25 hours later the entry has expired, the catalogue fails, and the lookup returns the old title with stale: true.

examples.title: Outbound webhooks: one body signed per attempt; the receiver checks the MAC, the time and the event id

annotations.note: The envelope. id is minted once per event, when the failed run is recorded, and stays the same across every retry to every subscriber: it is the key receivers deduplicate by. data is abridged here.
go.services.webhooks-hmac's scheme: the timestamp is part of the signed bytes, so a captured request can't be replayed with a new time. Each webhook has its own secret.

sync.Map's LoadOrStore checks and records an id in one step, safe for concurrent requests. A real receiver inserts the id into a table in the transaction that does the work, with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
The header is "t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>". A malformed one leaves got empty, which can't match any MAC.
The receiver checks the HMAC over the raw bytes with hmac.Equal, which doesn't leak timing information, and refuses timestamps more than five minutes away from its own clock.

Deduplication by event id is the receiver's half of idempotency: TraceLite will deliver some events twice, and this is where twice becomes once. The duplicate still gets a 2xx, or the sender would keep trying.
Marshaled once: every attempt sends the same bytes. Marshaling again could even change them: encoding/json/v2 writes map entries in no particular order unless the Deterministic option is set.
Signed at each attempt, so the timestamp is fresh and a retry minutes later still falls inside the receiver's window.
The lost response: attempt 1 was processed, but its answer never reached TraceLite, which timed out and sent attempt 2. The receiver recognizes the id and does nothing twice.

Someone without the secret, and a captured request replayed later: both 401. The id check would catch the replay too, but only while the receiver still remembers the id; the window means it has to remember ids for minutes, not forever.

use_cases: Enriching your data from a third-party catalogue: standards, postal codes, exchange rates, VAT numbers
Notifying CI, chat or ticketing systems when a test run fails
Any server-to-server call where the other side can be slow, rate-limited or down for an hour
Keeping a page usable while a dependency is down, by showing slightly old data marked as such
strengths: Every call is bounded by the caller's deadline, so a slow catalogue slows the detail page by at most its budget and never hangs a handler
Full jitter spreads retries from many clients, and Retry-After is honored, so a struggling service isn't hammered back down
Cached answers, including 404s, cut traffic to the catalogue to roughly one call per reference per day
HMAC signatures with a timestamp and per-event ids give receivers authenticity, replay protection and exactly-once processing on top of at-least-once delivery
weaknesses: The in-memory cache is per process and empties on restart; several TraceLite instances would each call the catalogue
Concurrent misses for the same reference each call the service; golang.org/x/sync/singleflight would merge them into one call
In-process webhook retries die with the process; durable delivery needs the job table of step 11
Webhook URLs come from users, so the server makes requests to addresses users chose; a multi-user deployment must refuse private and loopback targets

pitfalls.title: http.DefaultClient and no context
pitfalls.detail: DefaultClient has no timeout, and a request without a deadline can hang a handler until the TCP connection dies. Derive a per-attempt context from the caller's.
pitfalls.good: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second); defer cancel(); req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", u, nil)

pitfalls.title: Retrying everything
pitfalls.detail: A 400 or 403 fails the same way every time, and a retried POST without an idempotency key may run twice. Retry timeouts, 429 and 5xx, and only operations that are safe to repeat.

pitfalls.title: Sleeping past the deadline
pitfalls.detail: A Retry-After of 120 s inside a 2 s request budget only produces a timeout two seconds later. Compare the wait with ctx.Deadline() and give up, or serve from the cache, at once.

pitfalls.title: Re-encoding the event per attempt
pitfalls.detail: Building the body again for a retry can change it: a new timestamp, or map entries in another order (encoding/json/v2 doesn't sort them unless the Deterministic option is set). Marshal once, sign per attempt, send the same bytes.

pitfalls.title: Treating a timeout as a failure to deliver
pitfalls.detail: A webhook that timed out may have been processed. Retry it with the same event id, and expect receivers to deduplicate; never mint a new id for a retry.

quiz.q: The catalogue answers 429 with Retry-After: 120, and the API request has 2 s left. What does the client do?
options: Gives up at once, and serves the cached title if there is one
quiz.why: Waiting longer than the budget can only end in a timeout. The client compares the wait with its deadline, and Lookup falls back to a stale entry.

quiz.q: A webhook delivery times out. Was the event processed?
options: Maybe: the receiver may have processed it and the answer been lost
quiz.why: That is why delivery is at least once, retries reuse the event id, and receivers deduplicate on it.

quiz.q: Why is a 404 from the catalogue cached?
options: So that repeated lookups of a wrong reference don't each call the service; for 10 minutes, not 24 hours
To return it as stale later
quiz.why: A negative answer is still an answer. A shorter lifetime lets a newly added clause appear soon.

quiz.q: Why is the timestamp inside the HMAC rather than only in a header?
options: So a captured request can't be replayed later with a fresh timestamp
quiz.why: If the time weren't signed, an attacker could change it freely and pass the receiver's tolerance check forever.

lessons.body:
## Concept

TraceLite talks to two kinds of outside services, and is polite to both the same way:

- **A standards catalogue it calls.** Requirements cite clauses of standards
  (`ISO27001:A.5.17`). Step 6's detail view gains a lookup that shows a clause's title,
  fetched through `GET /api/standards/{ref}`, which calls the catalogue. The browser never
  calls it directly: that would need CORS, would expose any API key, and would bypass the
  cache.
- **Webhooks it calls on behalf of users.** A project can register URLs that receive a
  signed POST when a test run fails, so a CI system or a chat channel hears about it.

Politeness has the same four parts in both directions:

1. **Bound every call.** A deadline per attempt, derived from the caller's context, and a
   size limit on what is read back.
2. **Retry only what may go away**, and only operations that are safe to repeat: network
   errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx. Wait with jittered backoff, or as long as Retry-After
   asks, but never past the caller's deadline.
3. **Remember answers.** A cache with expiry turns a daily-changing catalogue into a
   daily call, and a stale entry beats an error when the service is down.
4. **Make repeats harmless.** A retried webhook carries the same event id; receivers
   deduplicate on it. HMAC signatures prove the request came from TraceLite.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Resilience4j's Retry, TimeLimiter and a Caffeine cache are these pieces as
  annotations and decorators. Here each is a few visible lines, and the deadline comes
  from the incoming request's `context.Context` instead of a thread-local.
- **Python**: `requests` without `timeout=` waits forever, like `http.DefaultClient`;
  `urllib3.Retry(backoff_factor=..., respect_retry_after_header=True)` is the loop of
  example 2.
- **JS**: `fetch` with `AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` is `context.WithTimeout`;
  `AbortSignal.any([request, timeout])` composes the two deadlines that Go derives by
  passing the context down.
- **C/C++ (libcurl)**: `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS` per transfer plus your own retry loop; the
  shape is the same, the context that ties it to the caller's budget is not.

## How it works

The catalogue behind TraceLite's own endpoint:

```yaml
  /api/standards/{ref}:
    parameters: [{ name: ref, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string, maxLength: 64 } }]
    get:
      operationId: getStandardClause
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The clause; stale is true when the catalogue was unreachable and the title comes from the cache
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [ref, title, stale]
                properties: { ref: { type: string }, title: { type: string }, stale: { type: boolean } }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # the catalogue has no such clause
        "503": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # unreachable and nothing cached
```

The catalogue's URL and key come from configuration (`TRACELITE_STANDARDS_URL`), not from
the repo; the client is built once in `cmd/tracelite` and shared by every request.

Webhooks are registered per project, in `migrations/003_webhooks.sql`:

```sql
-- +goose Up
CREATE TABLE webhooks (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  project_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE,
  url        text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT webhooks_url_valid CHECK (url ~ '^https?://'),
  secret     text NOT NULL, -- the HMAC key; the receiver holds the same one
  events     text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{test-run.failed}'
               CONSTRAINT webhooks_events_valid CHECK (events <@ '{test-run.failed}'),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX webhooks_project ON webhooks (project_id);
```

- The secret is stored in clear because TraceLite must compute HMACs with it; a hash
  would be useless. `events` lists the types a subscriber wants, constrained to the ones
  that exist, so a later type is added by replacing the CHECK. Deleting a project
  cascades to its webhooks.
- One event type so far, `test-run.failed`, published by the service after a failed run
  has been committed. Body: `{"id", "type", "createdAt", "data": {"projectId", "testCase",
  "requirements", "finishedAt"}}`, marshaled once (example 4).
- The dispatcher sends it to every webhook of the project that lists the type
  (`WHERE project_id = $1 AND $2 = ANY (events)`). Each POST is an attempt like example
  1's: its own timeout (10 s) derived from the caller's context, the shared client, and
  the response body read (bounded) and closed, because the Transport reuses a keep-alive
  connection only after the body was read to the end and closed.
- Header `TraceLite-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<body>">`,
  computed for each attempt, and `Content-Type: application/json`. Receivers check the
  MAC and a five-minute window, and deduplicate on `id` (example 4).
- Responses: 2xx delivered. 410 Gone is the receiver saying "stop, for good", so the
  webhook is deleted (`DELETE FROM webhooks WHERE id = $1`). 429, 5xx and timeouts are
  retried with a loop like example 2's: delivery is at least once, since a timeout means
  "maybe processed". Any other 4xx stops this delivery: the receiver refused the request,
  and sending it again won't change its mind.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as TraceLite service
  participant D as Dispatcher
  participant R as Receiver
  S->>D: Publish(project, test-run.failed, id e1)
  D->>R: POST, TraceLite-Signature t=...,v1=...
  R->>R: verify, process e1, remember e1
  R--xD: (the response is lost)
  D->>D: attempt 1 timed out: wait, retry
  D->>R: POST, same body, fresh signature
  R-->>D: 200, e1 seen before, nothing done
```

## Design notes

**Stale beats broken.** The clause title is decoration on the detail page; showing
yesterday's title with a "stale" flag is better than an error box. Data that must be
current (a payment status, a permission) would fail closed instead. The choice is per
call, and the `Stale` field makes it visible to the UI rather than hiding it.

**A circuit breaker, not yet.** When a dependency is down for minutes, every request
still spends its first attempt finding out. A circuit breaker would skip the call for a
while after repeated failures. With a cache that serves most lookups and a 2 s budget,
TraceLite doesn't need one; the retry and cache code is where one would go.

**Webhooks belong in the job table.** Step 10's dispatcher retries in memory for a few
seconds. Real receivers are down for hours, and TraceLite restarts. Step 11 turns each
delivery into a row in a job table, inserted in the same transaction as the failed run
(so a committed run always gets its webhook, an outbox), with `run_after` holding the
next retry time on a schedule of minutes to hours. The signing, the event id and the
status handling stay exactly as here.

**User-chosen URLs.** A webhook URL makes TraceLite's server send requests wherever a user
points it. On a single-user local install that is the user's own business; a shared
deployment must resolve the host and refuse loopback, private and link-local addresses
before connecting, or a webhook becomes a way to reach internal services.

lessons.title: Step 11: Background jobs: job table + SKIP LOCKED + a Go worker pool, with graceful shutdown
lessons.summary: Work that must survive restarts is a row in a jobs table: SKIP LOCKED hands each job to one worker, a lease returns a dead worker's job, run_after spaces the retries. A Go pool drains on shutdown, and failed runs queue their webhooks in the same transaction.

examples.title: The queue: a one-statement SKIP LOCKED claim, a lease that outlives its worker, and a fenced finish

annotations.note: Declared where it is used: claim needs only QueryRow, which both a pool and a transaction have. The transaction is how this run holds w1's claim open while w2 claims.

The claim is one autocommitted statement: the subquery picks and locks a row, the UPDATE marks it running. The row lock lasts only for this statement; afterwards the lease in run_after keeps other workers away, and no transaction or connection stays open while the job runs.

run_after answers one question for every state: when may a worker take this job next? For a queued job it is the due time or the next retry; a claim sets it to the end of the lease, so a running job whose worker died becomes claimable again by itself, with no reaper. The lease token is new for every claim: a fencing token.

SKIP LOCKED: a claim passes over a row another claim is taking at this moment instead of waiting for that transaction to end. The docs call the resulting view of the table inconsistent, which a queue doesn't mind: any due job will do. The ORDER BY is the jobs_due index's order, so the claim reads that index from the start.
The fence. Every update after the claim names the lease token; zero rows means a later claim holds the job now, and the caller learns it as ErrLeaseLost and drops its result.

w1's claim is still uncommitted when w2 claims on another connection. w2 skips the row w1 has locked and gets chat at once; with plain FOR UPDATE it would wait for w1's commit, and claims would run one at a time.

w1 stops answering (a crash, a killed process, a frozen VM). Nothing notices: at 06:03:30 the lease still keeps everyone away, at 06:04:31 it has run out and the next claim gets ci back. The dead worker's attempt counts: this is attempt 2.
w1 resumes and reports success; the fence refuses it. w3, which holds the lease, finishes normally.

examples.title: The outbox: a failed run and its webhook deliveries commit together, or not at all

annotations.note: Enqueue is an INSERT inside the caller's transaction. A committed failed run always has its webhooks queued, and a rolled-back one never sends any. Step 10 published after the commit, so a crash in between lost the event.

The event is marshaled once, with its id, and stored as a string inside the payload. As a nested jsonb object it would come back with its keys reordered (jsonb doesn't keep key order); the string keeps the exact bytes that every attempt sends and signs.
One job per subscribed webhook, written by one INSERT ... SELECT: each receiver gets its own attempts, schedule and failure, so a dead chat server doesn't hold back the CI notification.
pgx.BeginFunc commits when the function returns nil and rolls back when it returns an error. Here a later step fails, and the second run takes its two deliveries with it.
One run, two jobs, and one event id between them: two deliveries of the same event, which receivers deduplicate on.

examples.title: A worker pool that drains on SIGTERM and gives back what it couldn't finish

annotations.note: Two contexts. stop is the signal: once it is canceled, no worker claims again. jobs is what running work sees; it is canceled only when the drain deadline passes, so a job that can finish in time does. context.WithoutCancel and context.AfterFunc are both Go 1.21.
sync.WaitGroup.Go (Go 1.25) starts a worker and counts it, so Wait returns when every worker has stopped.
Claim, run, claim again; when nothing is due, wait a moment. TraceLite polls every second; go.services.listen-notify shows how a NOTIFY could wake the workers instead.

The claim runs on jobs, not on stop: a claim already sent when the signal arrives may have committed in the database, and cancelling it could leave a job leased to a worker that never learns it got one.
pg_sleep stands in for step 8's report query. When the drain deadline cancels jobs, pgx cancels the running query.

A finished job is done. A job interrupted by shutdown is released: queued again at once, with its attempt given back, because a deploy is not the job's fault and shouldn't use up one of its six tries or wait for a lease to run out. Any other error is a retry (see How it works).
The outcome gets its own context: after the drain deadline the job's context is canceled, and an UPDATE sent with it would fail before reaching the database, leaving the job leased to nobody.
A background loop has nobody to return an error to, so it logs it. An ignored error here once hid a broken heartbeat in an earlier version of this step.

In cmd/tracelite this context comes from signal.NotifyContext. Here the "signal" is a timeout 100 ms in, when both workers have sent their claims: Raporlama (0.3 s) finishes inside the 700 ms drain, Ödeme (1.5 s) doesn't and is released, and Arşiv is never claimed. The next process finds both in the table and runs them.

examples.title: The finished report: 409 until it is done, then a download with Content-Length and ranges

annotations.note: A malformed id parses to the zero UUID, which matches no job: 404, as for any unknown path id.
Unknown job, or not a report: 404. A report that isn't done yet: 409 with the conflict problem type, whose detail tells the client what to do instead.

Step 8 had to stream and abort on failure. A finished file can be served properly: http.ServeContent sets Content-Length, takes the Content-Type from the name's extension, sends Last-Modified, answers Range requests with 206 and conditional requests with 304. The file name rule is step 8's.
A done report, as a worker leaves it: the file in result, stored by the same fenced UPDATE that marks the job done, so a worker that lost its lease can't publish a stale file.

A range from byte 29 to the end: the reply is 206 with Content-Range, which is how a download manager resumes a broken download. Content-Length counts bytes: the file has 75 characters and 76 bytes, because Ö takes two.

use_cases: Report and export generation that takes longer than a request should: queue it, answer 202, let the browser poll and download the finished file
Outbound webhooks and e-mail: queued in the same transaction as the change that triggers them (an outbox), delivered with retries over hours
Any slow, retryable task a request triggers (an import, thumbnails, e-mail), where the user can be told "queued" and come back later
A single-binary deployment with one PostgreSQL and no broker, where adding Redis or RabbitMQ would double the operational surface
strengths: Jobs commit and roll back with the data that caused them; with a broker, the message and the database write are two systems that can disagree after a crash
The queue is queryable with SQL: what is stuck, what failed and why, how many retries a receiver needed, with no extra tooling
SKIP LOCKED lets any number of workers in any number of processes claim concurrently without blocking each other or taking the same job
Leases and fencing make worker crashes boring: the job comes back by itself, and a late finisher can't overwrite its successor
weaknesses: Every claim, heartbeat and finish is a write: thousands of jobs per second would churn the table and its index, where a broker would not care
Polling adds up to a poll interval of latency and some idle queries; LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-ups remove the latency at the cost of a dedicated connection
Delivery is at least once: a worker that dies after a webhook POST but before finishing sends it again, so receivers must deduplicate
Done rows accumulate, including report files in bytea; a cleanup job and a retention rule are part of the design, not an afterthought

pitfalls.title: Holding a transaction open for the whole job
pitfalls.detail: Claiming with FOR UPDATE inside a transaction that lasts until the job ends also survives crashes (the lock dies with the connection), but it pins one connection per running job and keeps a transaction open for minutes, which holds back vacuum. Claim and commit; let the lease do the rest.

pitfalls.title: Finishing without the lease token
pitfalls.detail: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done' WHERE id = $1 lets a worker that lost its lease overwrite the successor's result or mark a retried job done. Every update after the claim must say AND lease_token = $2 and check the row count.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done' WHERE id = $1
pitfalls.good: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done', lease_token = NULL WHERE id = $1 AND lease_token = $2 -- 0 rows: lease lost

pitfalls.title: Publishing after the commit instead of in it
pitfalls.detail: Calling the webhook dispatcher after tx.Commit loses the event if the process dies in between, and calling it before the commit sends events for runs that then roll back. Insert the job inside the transaction.

pitfalls.title: Recording the outcome with the canceled context
pitfalls.detail: After the drain deadline the job's context is canceled, and pgx returns at once without sending the UPDATE. The job then stays leased until the lease expires. Write the outcome with context.WithoutCancel plus a short timeout.

pitfalls.title: A lease shorter than the job, with no heartbeat
pitfalls.detail: If a report can run longer than the lease, another worker claims it while it runs, and again after that. Extend the lease periodically (every third of it) and stop the work if the extension finds the lease gone.

quiz.q: A worker claims a webhook job, posts it, and is killed before it can record the result. What happens?
options: When the lease runs out, another worker claims it and posts the event again, with the same event id
PostgreSQL rolls the claim back when the connection drops
quiz.why: The claim committed, so nothing rolls back. run_after holds the lease's end; after it, the claim query sees a due job. Receivers deduplicate on the event id.

quiz.q: Why does the claim use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED rather than plain FOR UPDATE?
options: SKIP LOCKED is faster on small tables
So concurrent claims pass over a row being claimed instead of waiting for that claim's transaction to end
Plain FOR UPDATE can't be used with LIMIT
quiz.why: With plain FOR UPDATE every claim queues behind the one in progress; SKIP LOCKED gives each claimer a different due row at once.

quiz.q: SIGTERM arrives while a report has 3 minutes left and the drain is 20 seconds. What does TraceLite do?
options: Stops claiming, cancels the report after 20 seconds and releases it so the next process runs it at once
quiz.why: The drain bounds shutdown; Release puts the job back with run_after now and returns its attempt, because the interruption isn't the job's fault.

quiz.q: A failed run is recorded in a transaction that later rolls back. How many webhook deliveries are queued?
quiz.why: The job rows were inserted in the same transaction as the run (the outbox), so they roll back with it.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, the locking clause (SKIP LOCKED)
PostgreSQL docs: JSON types (jsonb doesn't keep key order)

lessons.body: ## Concept Some work doesn't belong in a request: a traceability report for a large project takes minutes, and a webhook receiver may be down for hours. Step 8 streamed the report while the browser waited; step 10 retried webhooks in memory for a few seconds. Both are lost when TraceLite restarts. Step 11 turns that work into rows. A **job** is a row in `jobs` with a `kind`, a `payload`, a `state` and a time, `run_after`, before which no one may take it. - **Enqueue** = `INSERT`, inside the transaction that made the work necessary. A failed test run and its webhook deliveries commit together: the **outbox** pattern. - **Claim** = one `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)`. Concurrent workers, in one process or several, each get a different job and never wait for each other. - **Lease**: the claim sets `run_after` to the end of a lease and a fresh `lease_token`. If the worker dies, the lease runs out and the job is due again. A worker still alive extends it with a heartbeat. Every later update must present the token (fencing). - **Retry**: a failed attempt puts the job back with `run_after` further in the future (1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, plus jitter); after the sixth attempt it is `failed`, with `last_error` kept. - **Shutdown**: on SIGTERM the pool stops claiming, lets running jobs finish within a drain period, cancels the rest through their context and releases them for the next process. The report endpoint becomes asynchronous: `POST` queues a job and answers **202 Accepted**, the browser polls the job, and the finished file is served with a real `Content-Length` and range support. ## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS - **Python/Celery, Ruby/Sidekiq, Node/BullMQ**: the same model (a queue, workers, retries with backoff, a dead state) on Redis or RabbitMQ. Enqueuing there is a second system: the task can be sent for a transaction that then rolls back, or lost when the process dies between commit and send. Here the queue is in the same database, so the job commits with the data. Celery's `acks_late` plus `visibility_timeout` is this lesson's lease. - **Java**: Quartz's JDBC job store and db-scheduler also keep jobs in tables, but claim them differently. db-scheduler's default `fetch` strategy claims with an optimistic `UPDATE … WHERE … AND version = ?`; its `lock-and-fetch` strategy uses `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, as this step does. Quartz moves a trigger from WAITING to ACQUIRED with a conditional `UPDATE`, and a clustered Quartz serializes acquiring and firing with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on one row of its `LOCKS` table: a cluster-wide mutex, not a lock per job (db-scheduler's README and `JdbcTaskRepository.pick`; Quartz's JobStoreTX configuration docs and `JobStoreSupport`). Spring's `@Async` is an in-memory pool, closer to step 10's dispatcher, and loses its work on restart. Graceful shutdown in Spring is a property; here it is two contexts. - **AWS SQS**: `run_after` is SQS's visibility timeout, `attempts` its receive count, and `failed` its dead-letter queue. The fencing token is what SQS's receipt handle does: a delete with an old handle doesn't remove a message someone else received. - **C/C++**: a thread pool over a shared work list, except that the list survives the process and the lock is a row lock taken for one statement. ## How it works `migrations/004_jobs.sql`; the examples create only the columns they use: ```sql -- +goose Up CREATE TABLE jobs ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), project_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE, kind text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT jobs_kind_valid CHECK (kind IN ('report', 'webhook')), payload jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued' CONSTRAINT jobs_state_valid CHECK (state IN ('queued', 'running', 'done', 'failed')), attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, run_after timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), -- no claim before this; a claim moves it to the lease's end lease_token uuid, -- new for every claim; finishing requires it last_error text NOT NULL DEFAULT '', result bytea, -- a finished report's file created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), finished_at timestamptz ); CREATE INDEX jobs_due ON jobs (run_after, id) WHERE state IN ('queued', 'running'); CREATE INDEX jobs_project ON jobs (project_id, created_at DESC); ``` One table for every kind of background work: the state, the attempts and the last error are columns anyone can query, unlike a queue that lives in a goroutine. `jobs_due` is a partial index over open jobs only, so done and failed rows pile up without slowing the claim; its order is the claim's `ORDER BY`, so the claim reads it from the start and stops at the first row it can lock. New endpoints in `openapi.yaml`: ```yaml /api/projects/{projectId}/traceability-report-jobs: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/ProjectId" }] post: operationId: queueTraceabilityReport responses: "202": description: Queued; poll the job named by Location headers: { Location: { schema: { type: string } } } content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Job" } } } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } /api/jobs/{jobId}: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/JobId" }] get: operationId: getJob responses: "200": { description: The job, content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Job" } } } } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } /api/jobs/{jobId}/file: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/JobId" }] get: operationId: getJobFile description: A finished report (step 8's TraceabilityReport); supports Range. responses: "200": { description: The file, headers: { Content-Disposition: { schema: { type: string } } } } "206": { description: The requested byte range } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } "409": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } # not done yet # components.parameters: JobId: { name: jobId, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string, format: uuid } } # components.schemas: Job: type: object required: [id, kind, state, attempts, lastError, createdAt, finishedAt] properties: id: { type: string, format: uuid } kind: { type: string, enum: [report, webhook] } state: { type: string, enum: [queued, running, done, failed] } attempts: { type: integer, minimum: 0 } lastError: { type: string } createdAt: { type: string, format: date-time } finishedAt: { type: [string, "null"], format: date-time } ``` A job's life: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> queued: INSERT (in the caller's transaction) queued --> running: claim (SKIP LOCKED), run_after = lease end running --> running: heartbeat extends the lease running --> done: handler ok (fenced UPDATE, result stored) running --> queued: retryable error, run_after = now + backoff running --> queued: shutdown: released, attempt given back running --> running: lease expired, claimed by another worker running --> failed: permanent error, or the sixth attempt failed ``` The code lives in a new package, `internal/jobs`: `Queue` (claim, extend, finish, release, plus `Enqueue(ctx, tx, …)` taking the caller's transaction) and `Pool`. Handlers are registered by kind: `report` (step 8's query, written into `result`) and `webhook` (one POST per attempt, signed as in step 10; the in-memory retry loop of step 10 is gone, because each claim is one attempt). Settings in `cmd/tracelite`: 4 workers, a poll every second, a 2-minute lease with a heartbeat every 40 s, a 20 s drain. What `Finish` writes, always fenced with `AND lease_token = $2` as in example 1: - The handler returned nil: `done`, with `finished_at`, and for a report the file in `result`, in the same UPDATE. - It returned a `Permanent` error (webhooks: a 4xx other than 410 and 429): `failed`, with `last_error`. Found with `errors.AsType[Permanent](err)` (Go 1.26). - Any other error (webhooks: 429, 5xx, a timeout): `queued` again with `run_after = now + schedule[attempts-1]`, where the schedule is 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, plus up to 10% jitter; after the sixth attempt, `failed`, keeping `last_error` for the UI. That is about nine hours in all, which covers a receiver's bad night but not a weekend. Unlike step 10's full jitter, a retry here must not come earlier than the schedule says; the spread only keeps a backlog from reaching a receiver in one burst when it comes back. - The pool is shutting down (example 3): released. While a handler runs, a heartbeat extends the lease every third of it (`UPDATE jobs SET run_after = $3 WHERE id = $1 AND lease_token = $2`). A report that takes longer than one lease keeps it; without the heartbeat another worker would claim the running report every two minutes. When the extension finds zero rows, the lease is lost and the heartbeat cancels the handler's context. Log its errors: an ignored error once hid a heartbeat that failed on every tick. The report endpoint answers before any work is done. RFC 9110's 202 Accepted means the request is valid and will be processed, not that it has been; `Location` names the job, and the body is the job as it stands, so the first poll is already answered: ```go mux.HandleFunc("POST /api/projects/{projectId}/traceability-report-jobs", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { project, _ := uuid.Parse(r.PathValue("projectId")) // a malformed id finds no project var j Job // the Job schema below, json tags in camelCase err := db.QueryRow(r.Context(), `INSERT INTO jobs (project_id, kind) SELECT id, 'report' FROM projects WHERE id = $1 RETURNING id, kind, state, attempts, last_error, created_at, finished_at`, project). Scan(&j.ID, &j.Kind, &j.State, &j.Attempts, &j.LastError, &j.CreatedAt, &j.FinishedAt) if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) { err = store.ErrNotFound // no such project } if err != nil { writeError(w, err) // step 4's: ErrNotFound is a 404, anything else a 500 return } j.CreatedAt = j.CreatedAt.UTC() w.Header().Set("Location", "/api/jobs/"+j.ID.String()) w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted) json.MarshalWrite(w, j) }) ``` Between the 202 and the work, TraceLite could be restarted, upgraded or switched off overnight. The request is a row in `jobs`, so the next process does it. Example 4 serves the finished file. Shutdown order in `main`: first `http.Server.Shutdown` (a request in flight may still enqueue), then the pool's drain, then the step 9 listener, then the database pool. Keep the sum under the supervisor's patience: `docker stop` waits 10 s by default before SIGKILL, systemd 90 s. In the browser, the report button posts, then polls the job until it ends, then offers the file as a plain link (TanStack Query v5 accepts a function for `refetchInterval`): ```tsx const job = useQuery({ queryKey: ["jobs", jobId], queryFn: () => request(Job, `/api/jobs/${jobId}`), refetchInterval: (q) => q.state.data?.state === "queued" || q.state.data?.state === "running" ? 1000 : false, }); // done: Raporu indir ``` ## Design notes **PostgreSQL as the queue.** TraceLite already runs one database and one binary; a broker would double what must be installed, backed up and monitored on a customer's machine. A jobs table handles hundreds of jobs a minute without strain, and its real advantage is transactional: enqueueing commits with the data. The trade-off reverses at high volume (thousands per second, many consumers), where claims and heartbeats become write load and a broker earns its place (go.services.grpc-brokers). **Leases rather than long transactions.** Holding the row lock for the whole job would also return a crashed worker's job (the lock dies with its connection), but it ties up a pooled connection and an open transaction per running job, for minutes. The lease costs two extra columns and a heartbeat, and lets a job outlive any one connection. **At least once, made harmless.** No queue can guarantee that a POST happened exactly once: a worker can die after the receiver processed the event and before the job is marked done. TraceLite redelivers with the same event id (step 10), and receivers deduplicate. Effects inside the database are better off: the report is written by the same fenced statement that marks the job done, so it is stored once. **Time comes from Go.** The queue reads its clock from a `now func() time.Time` (example 1 passes the time in and moves it by hand; example 3 and `cmd/tracelite` use `time.Now`). Several TraceLite processes would then need synchronized clocks, which NTP gives to well within the one-minute scale of leases and retries. Using the database's `now()` instead would give one clock and lose the testability. **Housekeeping.** Once a day the pool deletes done and failed jobs older than 30 days, and with them their report files; the UI says how long a report stays downloadable. A second POST while a report is still queued creates a second job; a partial unique index on `(project_id) WHERE kind = 'report' AND state IN ('queued', 'running')` would prevent that, at the price of one more rule to explain.

lessons.title: Step 12: Search across requirements (full-text + trigram)
lessons.summary: One search box, three matchers: a code prefix, Turkish words (stems or prefixes, lowered with Turkish rules on both sides) and a folded trigram key for typos and English keyboards. Results come in tiers, ranked, paged by a keyset cursor.

examples.title: Migration 005, and which matcher finds what people actually type

annotations.note: Both are trusted extensions: a role with CREATE privilege on the database, such as its owner, may create them without being a superuser (step 15 sets up that role). IF NOT EXISTS because another application may already have installed them in this database.

lower() follows the database's locale; TraceLite's runs on whatever the customer's server has, which, unless it is a Turkish locale, maps I to i. Naming the ICU Turkish collation makes the result the same everywhere: I to ı, İ to i. The function is the one place where that rule lives.
sql.search.trigram's folded key: ı, i, I and İ all become i, ş becomes s. It is the answer to users who type IKI ADIMLI or sifre, and it is used only for matching, never for display.

The query side. plainto_tsquery ANDs the stems of the typed words; the second half ANDs every word as a prefix (:*). || between two tsqueries is OR. The words are cut at anything that isn't a letter or a digit, and quote_literal makes each one a single lexeme, so no input can be read as tsquery syntax.

One stored vector, two spellings of every word: the Turkish stem and the word itself. The stemmer catches inflections (girişte is giriş); the words catch what it cuts too far (parola becomes parol) and make prefixes work. The title weighs A, the description B, for ranking.

One GIN index per matcher: the tsvector for words, a trigram index on the folded title for typos. Codes need no new index: the B-tree of requirements_code_key already serves prefix ranges (example 3).

tr_lower turned KARANLIK into karanlık before the stemmer saw it; lower() would have made it karanlik, a word nobody types. Stems and words differ in the description (kullan, kullanımı), and the stemmer errs on short words: gece (night) became geç (late), koyu (dark) became ko. The whole word is still there to match.

A user with caps lock on a Turkish keyboard types SIFIRLAMA with dotless I, and tr_lower gives sıfırla, the same lexeme as in the column. A user who has typed only paro gets a prefix query that already finds parola.

A code prefix is a range on codes: COLLATE "C" upper-cases only ASCII, as codes need (step 2's pitfall), and every code that starts with AUTH-L lies between AUTH-L and AUTH-L~, because the code CHECK allows only characters that sort before ~. An empty input would match every code, so the API refuses q="".

Each matcher finds what the others can't: auth-l only as a code; parolalar through its stem (parola, matching the word parola); paro and e-posta as prefixes; IKI ADIMLI and the typo sifirlma only through the folded trigram key. Trigrams look at titles only, which is why e-posta (in descriptions) isn't found that way.
The bug tr_lower prevents: lowered with the database's rules, SIFIRLAMA becomes sifirla, which is not in any vector, and caps-lock users find nothing.

examples.title: One query, three tiers, ranked, and paged by a keyset over the ranking

annotations.note: queries/search.sql, prepared exactly as pgx prepares it. Each row matched by any matcher gets a tier (1 code, 2 words, 3 similar) and an integer score; the order is tier, score descending, then code, which is unique per project and makes the order total.
Scores are ts_rank or word_similarity scaled to integers. Floats in a cursor would have to survive JSON and a round trip to compare equal; integers do. Code hits all score 0 and come in code order.

The typed text is turned into a prefix, a tsquery and a key once, in a one-row subquery, so each matcher's condition below is written once and compares a column with a value fixed for the whole query.
The keyset, as in step 4: a row comparison with the last row's key. Negating the score turns its descending order into ascending, so one row comparison expresses tier ASC, score DESC, code ASC.
A code hit comes first, then title hits by rank. AUTH-LOGIN outranks AUTH-RESET because its description mentions parolasıyla as well; the fourth row only says that a next page exists.

Page 2 continues from the cursor. Three rows tie on score, since each mentions the word once in its description; the code breaks the tie, the same way on every request. Three rows are fewer than four: this is the last page.
A typo plus an English keyboard: no code, no word matches, and the folded trigram key still finds the title, in tier 3.

examples.title: Which index serves which matcher, in the generic plans pgx ends up with

annotations.note: The range is the code matcher's form because it uses the B-tree with $2 unknown: both bounds are expressions of a parameter, which an index condition accepts.

The same matcher as LIKE: with a literal pattern the planner derives the same range itself, but here the pattern is only known at run time, so it reads every row of the project and filters. psql shows the good plan; the application, after five executions, may get this one.
tr_lower has been inlined, which keeps the expression usable in an index condition; EXPLAIN doesn't print its COLLATE. The GIN index answers @@ for any query value.
<% (word_similarity above pg_trgm.word_similarity_threshold, 0.6 by default) is served by the trigram GIN index through its commutator %>, with the exact score checked on the rows it returns.

Ordering by trigram distance is a different job: GIN can only filter, so this sorts the whole table. A GiST trigram index can return rows in distance order; TraceLite doesn't need it, since its similar tier is filtered first and sorted afterwards.

use_cases: A search box over records with short identifiers and prose fields: tickets, products, documents, requirements
Turkish or mixed-keyboard users: caps lock with dotless I, phones without Turkish letters, copy-pasted text
Type-ahead: prefixes of every word and of codes, answered from indexes on each keystroke after a short debounce
Search results in a paged API whose pages must stay stable while other users edit
strengths: No search engine to run or keep in sync: the vector is a generated column, updated in the same transaction as the row
Each failure mode of typing has its own matcher, and the tier says which one fired, so the UI can show 'did you mean' for tier 3
Turkish lowering lives in one SQL function used by the column and every query, so the two sides can't drift
Integer scores and a code tiebreaker give a total order that keyset pagination can use unchanged from step 4
weaknesses: Every page ranks all matches again; keyset pagination keeps pages stable, not cheap
ts_rank has no notion of rare words (no IDF), so a requirement that repeats a common word can outrank a better one
Two spellings per word make the vector and its GIN index roughly twice as large
The folded key merges distinct Turkish words (kır and kir), so tier 3 can return surprises; it is a fallback, ranked last

pitfalls.title: LIKE with a parameter for prefix search
pitfalls.detail: code LIKE $1 || '%' uses the B-tree only when the planner sees a constant pattern. pgx prepares statements, and after five executions PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan that scans the whole project. Write the prefix as a range, which an index condition accepts with parameters.
pitfalls.good: WHERE project_id = $1 AND code >= $2 AND code < $2 || '~'  -- codes contain only characters below ~

pitfalls.title: Lowering the document and the query differently
pitfalls.detail: If the column uses tr_lower and the query plain lower() (or Go's strings.ToLower), IŞIK becomes ışık in the column and işik in the query, and nothing matches. One SQL function, called on both sides.

pitfalls.title: Building tsquery text from user input
pitfalls.detail: to_tsquery('simple', $1 || ':*') fails with a syntax error on input like 'parola & (' and lets users write operators. Split the input into words in SQL, quote each with quote_literal, and append :* to each.

pitfalls.title: Floats in a keyset cursor
pitfalls.detail: A ts_rank of 0.6079271 that went through JSON and came back as a parameter may not compare equal to the value recomputed by the query, and the page boundary repeats or skips a row. Scale scores to integers before they become part of the sort key.

pitfalls.title: Searching on unaccent alone
pitfalls.detail: The folded key finds sifre for şifre, but also merges kır and kir and defeats the Turkish stemmer. Keep it as the last tier, after code and word matches.

quiz.q: A user with caps lock on types PAROLA SIFIRLAMA. Why does the word matcher find Parola sıfırlama only with tr_lower?
options: lower() maps I to i, giving sifirla, while the column holds sıfırla
quiz.why: The database's lowering isn't Turkish; tr_lower maps I to ı on both sides, so the lexemes agree.

quiz.q: Why does the code matcher use code >= $2 AND code < $2 || '~' instead of LIKE $2 || '%'?
options: With a parameter, the planner can't turn LIKE into an index range, and pgx's prepared statements may get a generic plan
quiz.why: B-tree prefix matching for LIKE requires a constant pattern at planning time; a range with parameters is an index condition in any plan.

quiz.q: Which matcher finds IKI ADIMLI typed on an English keyboard?
quiz.why: tr_lower makes it ıkı adımlı, which isn't iki adımlı; folding both sides with unaccent gives iki adimli, which the trigram index matches.

quiz.q: Why are scores scaled to integers before they go into the cursor?
options: So the cursor's value compares equal to the recomputed score, and pages neither repeat nor skip rows
quiz.why: The keyset condition compares the cursor with values the query computes again; integers survive the round trip exactly.

PostgreSQL docs: pg_trgm (word_similarity, operators, index support)
PostgreSQL docs: Index types (B-tree and LIKE)
PostgreSQL docs: PREPARE (custom and generic plans)

lessons.body:
## Concept

People don't search like a `WHERE` clause. They type half a code (`auth-l`), a word in
a different form than the title uses (`parolalar`), the start of a word (`paro`), a
title with caps lock on a Turkish keyboard (`PAROLA SIFIRLAMA`), or with no Turkish
letters at all, and with typos (`sifirlma`). TraceLite's search runs three matchers
over a project's requirements and merges them into one ranked list:

1. **Code prefix** (tier 1): `upper(q)` as a range over `code`, served by the existing
   `requirements_code_key` B-tree.
2. **Words** (tier 2): a stored `tsvector` holding, for title (weight A) and description
   (B), both the Turkish stem and the whole word of every word. The query asks for all
   typed words as stems, or all of them as prefixes. Both sides are lowered with
   Turkish rules by one function, `tr_lower`. Ranked with `ts_rank`.
3. **Similar** (tier 3): `word_similarity` between folded keys (`search_key`, which maps
   ş to s and ı, I, İ to i) of the input and the title, through a trigram index. Ranked
   by the similarity.

A row matched by several matchers counts in its best tier. Within a tier, a higher
score comes first; the code breaks ties. That sort key is also the cursor.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Elasticsearch/Lucene**: the three tiers are a `bool` query with `should` clauses
  (a `prefix` on a keyword field, a `match` on a Turkish-analyzed field, a `fuzzy`
  match), and the tiers stand in for boosts. Lucene scores with BM25 and has a Turkish
  lowercase filter; PostgreSQL's `ts_rank` has no IDF, and Turkish lowering is
  `tr_lower`. In exchange there is no index refresh and nothing to keep in sync.
- **Java/Hibernate Search, Python/django-watson**: both keep a search index next to the
  ORM. Here the index is a generated column, so a raw SQL update or the step 7 importer
  updates it too.
- **JS (Fuse.js, match-sorter)**: fuzzy search in the browser over data already
  loaded. Fine for a hundred rows; TraceLite searches on the server so that the page
  never needs all requirements.
- **Go**: `strings.ToLower` uses Unicode's default mapping (I to i), like the database's
  `lower()`; `golang.org/x/text/cases.Lower(language.Turkish)` is `tr_lower`'s
  equivalent. TraceLite lowers only in SQL, so Go never sees the question.

## How it works

`migrations/005_search.sql` is example 1's middle part. The endpoint, in `openapi.yaml`:

```yaml
  /api/projects/{projectId}/requirement-search:
    parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/ProjectId" }]
    get:
      operationId: searchRequirements
      parameters:
        - { name: q, in: query, required: true, schema: { type: string, minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 } }
        - { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit" }
        - { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor" }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Best matches first
          content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/SearchPage" } } }
        "400": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # q blank or too long, bad cursor
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
# components.schemas:
    SearchHit:
      allOf:
        - { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Requirement" }
        - type: object
          required: [match]
          properties: { match: { type: string, enum: [code, words, similar] } }
    SearchPage:
      type: object
      required: [items, nextCursor]
      properties:
        items: { type: array, items: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/SearchHit" } }
        nextCursor: { type: [string, "null"] }
```

The handler trims `q` and refuses it when blank (400; an empty prefix would match every
code), decodes the cursor into `[tier, score, code]` (step 4's format: base64url JSON,
the last row's sort key), runs `SearchRequirements` with `limit+1` and maps the tier to
`match`. The request path is the same as the list's; only the query differs.

Which index serves which matcher (example 3):

| Matcher | Condition | Index |
|---|---|---|
| code | `code >= $p AND code < $p \|\| '~'` | `requirements_code_key` (B-tree, from step 2) |
| words | `search @@ words_query($q)` | `requirements_search` (GIN on the tsvector) |
| similar | `search_key($q) <% search_key(title)` | `requirements_title_key` (GIN, `gin_trgm_ops`) |

For a project of a few hundred requirements the planner may well read the project's
rows through `requirements_code_key` and check all three conditions on each, which can
cost less than three index scans; the plan depends on the statistics. The GIN indexes start to matter in big projects, and they
are what make a search across all projects possible later.

In the browser, the search box waits 200 ms after the last keystroke, then runs a
`useInfiniteQuery` keyed `["projects", projectId, "search", q]` with
`placeholderData: keepPreviousData`, so the old results stay on screen while the new
ones load. The key sits under the project prefix, so step 9's events refresh open
results too. Each hit shows its `match` as a small label: `kod`, `kelime`, `benzer`.

## Design notes

**Three matchers, not one clever one.** A single trigram search over code, title and
description would find most things, ranked by an opaque similarity. Separate matchers
make each rule explainable ("codes match by prefix", "words match by stem or start",
"everything else by similarity") and let the UI say why a result is there. The order of
the tiers encodes what users mean: a typed code is a precise request; a fuzzy match is a
guess.

**Turkish rules in one function.** `tr_lower` names the ICU Turkish collation, so the
behavior doesn't depend on how the customer's PostgreSQL was initialized. The same
function lowers the stored vector and every query; Go code never lowers search text.
`search_key` deliberately does the opposite (it forgets Turkish letters) and is used
only where that is the point.

**Keyset over a ranking.** The cursor holds the last row's (tier, score, code). That
keeps pages stable when requirements are added between requests, and it is the same
cursor format as every other list. It doesn't make later pages cheaper: each page
ranks all matches again. A search returns tens of rows, not thousands, so that cost is
accepted; past that, a smaller `limit` on deep pages or a cap on matches would come
first.

**Not done here.** Highlighting the matched words is `ts_headline` (sql.search.fts),
called for the page's rows only. A "did you mean" for queries with no results would
offer the nearest word from `ts_stat` over the project's vectors, as the pg_trgm docs
suggest. Synonyms (şifre for parola) need a synonym dictionary file on the server, which
a migration can't install.

lessons.title: Step 13: Audit history: database trigger vs application events, and the trade-offs
lessons.summary: A row trigger records every change from every writer as a jsonb diff, with the user named per transaction through set_config. Application events record intent but only from code that remembers to write them. TraceLite keeps the trigger and lets the service label its changes.

examples.title: Migration 006: one trigger function, the actor from set_config, diffs as jsonb

annotations.note: One table for the history of requirements, test cases and links. Test runs aren't audited: they are insert-only evidence already, and step 2's RESTRICT keeps them.
now() is the transaction's start time, the same for every row it writes. xact (pg_current_xact_id, PG 13) groups those rows, so the UI can show "one save changed these four things".

No foreign key, unlike everything else in TraceLite. Step 2's question, whether the child is part of the parent or a record about it, has the second answer here: the record of a deleted project must survive the delete. row_id has no foreign key either, which is why the history at the end outlives AUTH-RESET.
to_jsonb(OLD) and to_jsonb(NEW) make one function work for every table. The timestamps are dropped: the audit row has its own, and an updated_at in every diff would hide what really changed.
The diff keeps only the members whose values differ, each as [old, new]. A save that changed nothing but updated_at produces no row, so the history shows edits, not clicks on Save.

The user comes from a setting the application puts in the transaction. current_setting with missing_ok true returns NULL if it was never set, but '' once any transaction on this connection has set it (example 3), hence nullif. Without a user, the database login stands in, marked db:.
The bridge between the two designs: the service may name what it is doing (move, import), and the trigger stores that label next to the facts.

AFTER ROW triggers on the audited tables. On the same table and event, triggers fire in alphabetical order of their names, so requirements_audit runs before step 9's requirements_notify; both belong to the same transaction.
trace_links has no id; TG_ARGV names the column that identifies the row in the history, and a link belongs to its requirement's.

set_config(name, value, is_local true) is SET LOCAL as a function: it takes the value as a parameter, and it ends with the transaction. Store.WithTx sends it first in every transaction (example 3). This runner keeps the whole script in one transaction, so each "request" below sets its own values.
A move, labelled by the service. Moving is just a parent_id change to the database; the label is what makes "moved under AUTH-LOGIN" readable in the history.
The same title saved again: at most updated_at differs, which the function ignores, so it returned without a row. Three UPDATEs, two entries in the history.
One DELETE, and the foreign key's cascade removed the link too. Both rows are recorded under Ayşe's name: a cascade runs as ordinary row deletes, triggers included.

The detail page's history: the full row for an insert or a delete, [old, new] pairs for updates. The link's rows appear because their row_id is the requirement, and all of it is still there after the requirement is gone.

examples.title: The same changes, recorded by a trigger and by application events: what each one misses

annotations.note: The rows exist before the trigger does, so both designs start with zero records.
Example 1's function without the label and the timestamp handling: the user, the code, and for an UPDATE the members that changed, as [old, new].

The application-events design: the service inserts one row per use case, in the same transaction as the change (step 11's outbox idea), with names a person can read: kind, the code at the time, and the parts of the change that matter.
After each step, mark stores how many records each design holds. A step that a design missed leaves its number where it was.
A use case through the service: both designs record it, the trigger as a diff, the service as an event.
A fix in psql, or a migration's data fix, is plain DML: the trigger records both rows, under the login role; the service never ran, so its log has nothing.
ADD COLUMN with a constant default fires nothing at all: since PG 11 the default is kept in the catalog, and no row is written.
Both designs live in the transaction, so both lose the attempt when it rolls back. Recording failed attempts means writing outside the transaction, which then also records things that never happened.
TRUNCATE removes rows without firing ON DELETE row triggers. An ON TRUNCATE statement trigger could record that it happened, not what was removed.
The tally: the trigger missed only what bypasses DML (DDL, TRUNCATE); the service missed every write that didn't go through it.

The same move, twice. The trigger knows the fact (parent_id went from one uuid to another); the event knows the meaning (moved from AUTH to AUTH-LOGIN), with codes, which stay readable after the requirement is deleted.

examples.title: Naming the user through a connection pool: session settings leak, transaction settings don't

annotations.note: The one place where the user reaches the database. Every store method that writes runs inside WithTx, so every audited write carries a user; a single autocommitted statement outside it would not.
A bind parameter, so a user name can't change the SQL. SET has no parameters; people who use it build the statement with Sprintf.
One connection makes the reuse certain. With a pool of 4 under load, the same thing happens to some requests, which is worse: the wrong name appears only sometimes.
The trigger in this example reports what it would record as a notice (the schema is at the end); pgx hands every notice to this function, so each record prints under the request that made it.
After WithTx commits, the setting is gone: the next write, from a path that named no one, is recorded as db:playground, a visible gap instead of a wrong name.
The setting now exists on this connection with the value '', not NULL, which is why the trigger wraps it in nullif.

The tempting version: SET names the user for the session. The setting stays on the connection after Ayşe's request returns it to the pool, and the next request's change is booked to her. Undoing it on every release (pgxpool has an AfterRelease hook) is a rule that must never be forgotten; a transaction-local setting needs no cleanup.

use_cases: Change history on a detail page: who changed the title, when, from what to what
Compliance questions (who approved this requirement, who removed that link) that must be answered for writes from psql, imports and migrations too
Attributing changes in a pooled-connection application without a database role per user
Deciding, for any cross-cutting record (audit, notifications, search indexing), whether the database or the application should produce it
strengths: The trigger sees every row written by INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, COPY and cascades, from any client: a forgotten code path shows up as a db: entry instead of a hole
Diffs are computed from OLD and NEW, so they are exact; an application event says what the code believed it changed
set_config(…, true) scopes the user to one transaction, which is the right lifetime with a connection pool; SET would leak to the next borrower
Audit rows commit and roll back with the change, so the log never claims a change that didn't happen
weaknesses: A row trigger runs once per row: a 10,000-row import writes 10,000 audit rows in 10,000 function calls; statement-level triggers with transition tables would batch them
The trigger records facts, not intent: a move is a parent_id change between two uuids until the service labels it
DDL, TRUNCATE, disabled triggers and session_replication_role = replica bypass it, and a table owner can disable it
Nothing records attempts that rolled back, in either design

pitfalls.title: SET instead of set_config(…, true) on a pooled connection
pitfalls.detail: A session-level setting outlives the request and is seen by the next one that borrows the connection, so its changes are attributed to the previous user. Set the user transaction-locally, first thing in every transaction.
pitfalls.good: tx.Exec(ctx, "SELECT set_config('tracelite.actor', $1, true)", user)

pitfalls.title: Testing current_setting(…, true) only for NULL
pitfalls.detail: Once a custom setting has been set on a connection, it exists there with the value '' after the transaction ends, and missing_ok no longer returns NULL. Treat '' as unset.
pitfalls.good: coalesce(nullif(current_setting('tracelite.actor', true), ''), 'db:' || session_user)

pitfalls.title: Writes outside the transaction helper
pitfalls.detail: A single statement sent through the pool, outside WithTx, runs in its own transaction where nobody set the user. Route every write through the helper, and treat db: entries in the log as bugs to find.

pitfalls.title: Auditing with BEFORE triggers
pitfalls.detail: A BEFORE trigger runs before constraints are checked and before later BEFORE triggers may change the row, so it can record values that are never stored. Audit in AFTER triggers, which see the row as written.

pitfalls.title: Copying secrets into the log
pitfalls.detail: to_jsonb(NEW) copies every column. Don't attach the generic trigger to tables like webhooks, whose secret would end up in the history; or remove such members in the function.

quiz.q: TraceLite's pool has 4 connections. A middleware runs SET tracelite.actor = <user> once per request. What goes wrong?
options: A later request on the same connection that doesn't set the user is recorded under the previous user's name
quiz.why: SET lasts for the session, which outlives the request; set_config(…, true) ends with the transaction.

quiz.q: A bulk load COPYs rows straight into requirements. Which design records them?
options: Only the trigger: COPY FROM fires row triggers
quiz.why: COPY FROM invokes the table's triggers and constraints; with application events, the loader would need to write its own event.

quiz.q: A migration runs ALTER TABLE requirements ADD COLUMN priority int NOT NULL DEFAULT 3. What does the audit trigger record?
options: One row for the whole table
quiz.why: DDL fires no row triggers, and a constant default is stored in the catalog rather than written into each row.

quiz.q: Why does the audit_log have no foreign key to projects?
options: The history must survive the project's deletion
uuid columns can't have foreign keys
quiz.why: It is a record about the project, not part of it; with CASCADE it would vanish, with RESTRICT no project could ever be deleted.
