PostgreSQL docs: Overview of trigger behavior (ordering, row vs statement)

lessons.body:
## Concept

The question "who changed this requirement, and what did it say before?" has two honest
answers.

**A database trigger** (migration 006). An `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE … FOR EACH
ROW` trigger on `requirements`, `test_cases` and `trace_links` writes one `audit_log`
row per changed row, with the diff as jsonb. The database doesn't know TraceLite's
users, so the application tells it: the first statement of every transaction is
`set_config('tracelite.actor', $1, true)`, and the trigger reads it back with
`current_setting`.

**Application events.** The service writes a `change_events` row for each use case
(`requirement.moved`, `requirement.renamed`) in the same transaction as the change, with
the user it already knows and the data a person wants to read.

They fail differently:

| | Trigger | Application events |
|---|---|---|
| Writes through the service | yes, as diffs | yes, as named use cases |
| Rows removed by a foreign key's `ON DELETE CASCADE` | yes, each one | only what the use case names |
| psql fixes, bulk SQL, migrations' data fixes | yes, user shown as `db:<role>` | no |
| COPY, and step 7's import (COPY to staging, then INSERT … SELECT) | yes: COPY FROM fires row triggers | only if the importer writes one |
| DDL (`ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT`), `TRUNCATE` | no | no |
| Rolled-back transactions | no (rolled back with them) | no (same) |
| Intent ("moved under AUTH-LOGIN") | only if the service labels it | yes |

TraceLite keeps the trigger as the record of what happened, because a history that
misses whole categories of writes can't answer an auditor. It borrows the one strength
of events: the service may label a change (`set_config('tracelite.action', 'move',
true)`), and the trigger stores the label next to the diff.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Hibernate Envers, Spring Data auditing**: entity listeners write revisions,
  which is the application-events design generated for you. They see what goes through
  the ORM, and nothing else. `@CreatedBy` comes from an `AuditorAware` bean, usually
  reading Spring Security's thread-local context; here the user travels in the
  `context.Context` and then in the transaction.
- **Python/django-simple-history, Rails/PaperTrail**: same model, same blind spots
  (`queryset.update()` in Django skips save signals, `update_all` in Rails skips
  callbacks). A trigger can't be skipped by choosing a different API call.
- **JS/Prisma middleware or extensions**: the same again, per client instance.
- **Change data capture (Debezium, logical decoding)**: reads the WAL, so it sees
  every committed change, like the trigger, without slowing the writer. It runs as a
  separate service and still can't name the application user unless the application
  writes it somewhere: the same problem `set_config` solves here.

## How it works

`migrations/006_audit.sql` is example 1's middle part. The store side, in
`internal/store/store.go`:

```go
// WithTx: step 3's helper; the actor comes from the request's context.
return pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, s.db, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
	if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx, "SELECT set_config('tracelite.actor', $1, true)", ActorFrom(ctx)); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return fn(s.q.WithTx(tx))
})
```

`ActorFrom` reads what a middleware put into the request's context. In a single-user
local install that is the owner's name from configuration (step 15); with
authentication, the signed-in user. A use case that wants a label sets
`tracelite.action` the same way inside its closure (`move` for moves, `import` for step
7's importer).

Bulk loads need nothing extra. PostgreSQL's COPY reference says that `COPY FROM` invokes
the destination table's triggers and check constraints, so a pgx `CopyFrom` inside
`WithTx` is recorded row by row under the loading user. Step 7's importer copies into a
staging table and then runs `INSERT … SELECT` into `requirements`, which the trigger sees
like any other insert.

The history endpoint, in `openapi.yaml`:

```yaml
  /api/requirements/{requirementId}/history:
    parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/RequirementId" }]
    get:
      operationId: getRequirementHistory
      parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit" }, { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor" }]
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Newest first, keyset-paged by id
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [items, nextCursor]
                properties:
                  items:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: object
                      required: [at, actor, action, table, op, changes]
                      properties:
                        at: { type: string, format: date-time }
                        actor: { type: string }
                        action: { type: string }
                        table: { type: string, enum: [requirements, test_cases, trace_links] }
                        op: { type: string, enum: [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE] }
                        changes: { type: object }   # the full row, or {column: [old, new]}
                  nextCursor: { type: [string, "null"] }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
```

It reads `audit_log` by `row_id` through `audit_log_row`, so it works for deleted
requirements too, as long as the client still has the id. The keys inside `changes` are
column names, snake_case, because they describe the table and not the wire format; the
detail page maps the few it shows (`title`, `status`, `parent_id`) to Turkish labels.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as Handler
  participant S as Store.WithTx
  participant P as PostgreSQL
  H->>S: MoveRequirement(ctx with actor "mehmet")
  S->>P: BEGIN
  S->>P: SELECT set_config('tracelite.actor', 'mehmet', true)
  S->>P: SELECT set_config('tracelite.action', 'move', true)
  S->>P: UPDATE requirements SET parent_id = ...
  P->>P: requirements_audit: INSERT INTO audit_log (actor mehmet, action move, diff)
  P->>P: requirements_notify (step 9): pg_notify, queued until commit
  S->>P: COMMIT (both, or neither)
```

## Design notes

**Same choice as step 9, different weights.** Step 9 chose a trigger for change
notifications because every writer must notify, and a lost or extra notification costs
only a refetch. For the audit trail the "every writer" argument is stronger still (a
history with holes is worse than none, because it is believed), and the cost of the
trigger's weakness, missing intent, is softened by the action label. If TraceLite's
history were mainly a product feature ("Ayşe moved this under AUTH-LOGIN") rather than a
record, application events would win, and a trigger could still backstop them.

**Row triggers and bulk writes.** A row trigger costs one function call and one insert
per changed row. For TraceLite's imports (thousands of rows, rarely) that is acceptable.
At larger scale, statement-level triggers with transition tables (`REFERENCING OLD TABLE
AS … NEW TABLE AS …`) write the whole statement's audit rows in one `INSERT … SELECT`;
the price is one trigger per event, because a trigger with transition tables can't be
attached to several events at once.

**What the trigger can't stop.** A table owner can `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER`, and
`session_replication_role = replica` disables ordinary triggers for a session (it needs
superuser or a granted SET privilege). The application's role owns the tables (it runs
the migrations), so an attacker with its password could bypass the audit. A stricter
setup migrates with an owner role, runs the application as a role without ownership, and
grants it only INSERT on `audit_log`: then the application can't rewrite history either.
TraceLite, installed on one machine for one team, doesn't go that far; it says so in its
installation notes.

**Retention.** Audit rows are small, but they are never updated and rarely read.
Requirements change slowly enough that years of history fit easily; if a project ever
needed limits, a range partition per year (sql.modeling.temporal) lets old years be
detached and archived without a `DELETE`.

lessons.title: Step 14: Testing the stack: Go integration tests, Vitest + MSW, one Playwright e2e test
lessons.summary: Each layer gets the test that can see its bugs: Go integration tests over HTTP against real PostgreSQL for rules, constraints and the contract; Vitest with MSW for the client's handling of real responses; one Playwright test for what only a browser decides.

examples.title: A Go integration test: the real router and handler against PostgreSQL, one project per test

annotations.note: The code under test, cut down to one rule. Whether a parent belongs to the same project is decided by the composite foreign key; the Go code can't know it without a query, and a fake store would simply answer 201.
The real decoder settings, as in step 4: an unknown member is a 400, which a test that calls the store directly never sees.

The store maps constraint names to answers. Whether that name exists, and fires for the rows the test sends, only a real database can tell: a migration that renames the constraint breaks this mapping without a compile error, and this test with it.

TestMain runs once per test binary: the pool, the migrations, the routes. In TraceLite it applies the real migrations with goose, so a migration that fails on PostgreSQL 18 fails the suite before any test runs.

This runner hands the test DATABASE_URL, an empty schema of its own. TraceLite's suite reads TEST_DATABASE_URL behind the integration build tag. pgxpool.New only parses the URL; the first query connects.

Isolation by data, not by transaction: the handler commits, so each test makes a project of its own (here a fresh project id; TraceLite inserts the projects row first). Tests never see each other's rows, and a failed test leaves its rows to inspect.

The request goes through the router, so the path pattern and PathValue are exercised too. TraceLite's suite serves the router with httptest.NewServer, which adds a real connection; the recorder runs the same routing and handler code without one.
t.Parallel is safe because nothing in the test depends on rows it didn't create, and nothing needs cleaning up afterwards.
The bug only this layer catches: AUTH exists, but in another project. The same request with the parent from the test's own project is the control: 201 there, 422 here.

examples.title: Vitest + MSW: step 5's client against the answers it will really get

annotations.note: Step 5's two boundaries: a failure becomes an ApiError holding a problem (made up when the body isn't one), and a success must parse. The tests below hit both through real fetch calls.
The one adaptation for Node: jsdom has a location, but Node's fetch doesn't resolve relative URLs against it. The browser build keeps fetch(path).
safeParse's data is undefined when the body isn't a problem, so ?? picks the made-up one. Either way the caller gets one shape to show.

No default handlers: each test installs the answer it needs, and resetHandlers removes it afterwards. MSW intercepts fetch at the network layer, so the request is built, serialized and sent exactly as in the browser.
A request no handler matches fails the test instead of leaving the machine (MSW 3's option name; MSW 2 called it onUnhandledRequest).
The server's 409 problem, as step 4 writes it, reaches the caller intact, pointer included; the form uses #/code to put the message next to its field.

What the browser gets when the Go server is down in development: the Vite proxy's 502 page, HTML, not a problem. request() makes an about:blank problem from the status line instead of crashing on JSON.parse.

Contract drift in a response: the Go side renamed a member. zod refuses it at the boundary, so the bug surfaces as a parse error naming parentId, not as an undefined deep in a component. The Go contract check (step 1) should have caught it first; this is the client's own line of defense.

examples.title: One Playwright test in Edge: the CSV export downloads under its Turkish name, with its BOM

annotations.note: A stand-in for the project page. In TraceLite, playwright.config's webServer starts cmd/tracelite against a test database and the test opens the real page; this runner has no app server, so the test serves the page itself.

A real HTTP server on a free port, rather than ts.testing's page.route. While writing this lesson, the page.route version failed: in Chromium-based browsers a download started by a link with the download attribute never reaches page.route's handler (Playwright issue 22650), so the request went to the network and the file was named after the URL. A real server answers with the real Content-Disposition, so the test measures the browser, not the interception.

The download event and its file name are decided by the browser: the download attribute, Content-Disposition, RFC 6266's filename* with percent-encoded UTF-8. jsdom can't download at all, and no Go test can see what Edge does with the header.
The saved bytes: the BOM is still there (Excel on Turkish Windows needs it, step 8), and so are ';' and CRLF.

use_cases: Deciding where a new test goes: the layer whose bug it is, not the one that is easiest to test
Integration tests that hit the real database through the real HTTP handler, in parallel, without cleanup code
Testing the browser client's error handling (problems, proxy errors, drift) without a running backend
One end-to-end test for the behavior only a browser has: downloads, focus, real rendering, navigation
strengths: The Go test exercises decoding, rules, SQL, constraint names and encoding together, against the same PostgreSQL major version that ships
Per-test projects make database tests parallel and order-independent, with no truncation between tests
MSW keeps the client code unmodified, so fetch, headers, JSON parsing and zod run exactly as in the browser
A single, targeted Playwright test stays fast and stable, unlike an e2e suite that re-tests what lower layers already cover
weaknesses: Integration tests need PostgreSQL running; they live behind the integration build tag so go test ./... stays fast without one
Per-test data accumulates in the test database; drop and recreate it per run (TestMain or the CI job)
MSW handlers are written by hand and can drift from the server; the Go contract test is what keeps both sides honest
The e2e test here uses a stand-in page; the real one needs a build, a server and a database in CI, which is minutes, not seconds

pitfalls.title: Testing database rules with a fake store
pitfalls.detail: An in-memory fake accepts the cross-project parent, the duplicate code in another casing, the 201-character title: the rules live in constraints it doesn't have. Fakes are for the layers above the store; the store and the handlers that map its errors are tested against PostgreSQL.

pitfalls.title: Rolling back a transaction around a handler test
pitfalls.detail: The handler takes a pool and commits; wrapping the test in a transaction would need the handler to accept that transaction, which production code never does. Give each test its own project instead.

pitfalls.title: Relative URLs in Node tests
pitfalls.detail: Node's fetch throws on fetch('/api/...'), even under jsdom. Resolve against location.href in the test's fetch (or inject a base URL); don't change production code to absolute URLs, which would bring back CORS (step 1).

pitfalls.title: page.route as a stand-in for download responses
pitfalls.detail: In Chromium-based browsers, Edge included, a download started by a link with the download attribute bypasses page.route: the handler never runs and the request goes to the network (Playwright issue 22650, closed without a fix). Serve downloads from a real HTTP server in the test (or the real app via webServer).

pitfalls.title: An e2e test per feature
pitfalls.detail: Browser tests are slow and break on timing and markup; a suite that re-checks validation messages and coverage numbers through the browser duplicates the Go and Vitest tests and fails more often. Keep e2e for what only the browser decides.

quiz.q: A requirement is created with a parent from another project and the API answers 201. Which test should have caught it?
options: The Go integration test against PostgreSQL
quiz.why: The rule is a composite foreign key and its mapping in the store; only a test that runs the real handler against the real schema sees both.

quiz.q: The Go side changes a tag to json:"parentID". Which tests fail?
options: The Go contract check, and the client's zod parse when it meets such a response
quiz.why: The contract check compares encoded responses with the spec; zod is the client's own check at the boundary. Nothing at compile time sees a tag.

quiz.q: Why does each Go test create its own project?
options: The handler commits, so tests isolate by data; separate projects let them run in parallel without seeing each other
quiz.why: Rolled-back transactions don't work for code that commits; per-test data does.

quiz.q: What does the Playwright test check that the other two can't?
options: That the CSV has the right columns
What the browser does with the response: a download named by Content-Disposition's filename*, with the BOM intact
quiz.why: Columns and status are Go-testable; the download decision and file name are made by the browser.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A bug lives in one layer, and the cheapest test that can see it belongs to that layer.
TraceLite has three kinds of tests:

1. **Go integration tests** (`internal/httpapi`, build tag `integration`): the real
   router, handlers, service and store, over HTTP with `httptest`, against PostgreSQL 18
   with the real migrations. Every response is checked against `openapi.yaml`'s
   schemas. Each test creates its own project, so tests run in parallel and need no
   cleanup.
2. **Vitest + Testing Library + MSW** (`web/src/**/*.test.tsx`): components and the API
   client against MSW handlers that answer like the Go server does, including problem
   documents, proxy error pages and drifted responses. Example 2 tests the client;
   components add Testing Library on top, as step 6's matrix test does.
3. **One Playwright test** (`web/e2e/`), in Microsoft Edge, for what only a browser
   decides. TraceLite's is the export download.

Below them, plain unit tests stay where they already are (the tree's `nest` and
`tallies` from step 6, the CSV parser from step 7, the queue's `Finish` with a fake
clock from step 11). Which layer catches which bug:

| Bug | Caught by |
|---|---|
| a rule in Go (code format, title length in characters) | Go unit test of the service, and the integration test |
| a constraint, or its name in the store's mapping (cross-project parent, duplicate code) | Go integration test |
| a migration that doesn't apply, a query that doesn't plan | Go integration test (TestMain runs the migrations) |
| response drift from the spec (omitempty, a tag typo, local time) | Go contract check; then the client's zod parse |
| the client mishandles a 409 problem, a 502 HTML page, a drifted body | Vitest + MSW |
| the matrix shows the wrong state after a failed toggle (step 6) | Vitest + Testing Library |
| tree nesting, coverage roll-up, CSV quoting, retry schedule | Go or Vitest unit tests |
| the export doesn't download, or downloads under a garbled name | Playwright |

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring**: `@SpringBootTest` with Testcontainers and MockMvc is example 1;
  here the database is the one you run, `httptest` plays MockMvc's part, and `TestMain`
  sets both up, replacing `@BeforeAll` at the suite level. Spring's
  `@Transactional` test rollback is the pattern this lesson avoids for code that
  commits.
- **Python/pytest**: a session-scoped fixture for the database, a function-scoped one
  for the project; `responses` or `respx` mock HTTP the way MSW does for the browser.
- **JS**: Jest + MSW is the same idea as Vitest + MSW; Cypress or Playwright for e2e.
  Playwright's own test runner, not Vitest, drives the browser.
- **C/C++**: a test binary per layer with a fixture process; Go's `TestMain` is the
  fixture, and `go test` builds and runs it.

## How it works

The files:

```text
internal/httpapi/*_integration_test.go   //go:build integration; TEST_DATABASE_URL
internal/httpapi/contract_test.go        loads openapi.yaml, checks every recorded response
internal/tracelite/*_test.go             the service's rules, with a fake store
web/src/**/*.test.tsx                    Vitest, jsdom, Testing Library, MSW handlers in web/src/test/
web/e2e/export.spec.ts                   Playwright, Edge (channel "msedge")
web/playwright.config.ts                 webServer: builds and starts cmd/tracelite on a test database
```

Commands, from the repository root:

```text
go test ./...                                         unit tests, no database needed
go test -tags integration -count=1 ./...              + integration tests (TEST_DATABASE_URL)
npm --prefix web test                                 vitest run
npm --prefix web run e2e                              playwright test
```

Example 1 keeps one handler and one rule; the suite has the same shape with every
route. It serves the router with `httptest.NewServer`, so requests cross a real
connection; the example's `httptest.NewRecorder` runs the same routing and handler code
without one. `contract_test.go` is step 1's contract check turned into a test: every
response the integration tests record is compared with its schema in `openapi.yaml`
(required members present, no undocumented ones, enum values, times ending in `Z`). A
`json:"parentID"` tag or an `omitempty` on `description` fails there, in Go, before any
client sees the response.

`-count=1` turns off Go's test cache, which would otherwise skip integration tests
whose Go code didn't change even though the database did. The integration suite
creates a fresh database per run (`CREATE DATABASE tracelite_test_<pid>` from
TestMain, dropped at the end), so per-test projects never pile up across runs.

The Playwright configuration in the project (not runnable here):

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  testDir: "e2e",
  use: { channel: "msedge", baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:8081" },
  webServer: {
    // The binary built by the CI step, not `go run`: on Windows, killing go run
    // leaves its child server running (StackLab's scripts/dev.mjs has the story).
    command: process.platform === "win32" ? "..\\bin\\tracelite.exe" : "../bin/tracelite",
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/projects",
    env: { TRACELITE_ADDR: "127.0.0.1:8081", DATABASE_URL: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL ?? "" },
  },
});
```

## Design notes

**The pyramid, by bug.** The table above decides where a test goes. Most tests are Go
tests because most of TraceLite's rules are in Go and SQL; the client's tests are
about turning answers into screens; the browser test covers the one behavior nobody
else can observe. Adding a second e2e test needs a reason of the same kind: something
the browser decides.

**Real database, isolated by data.** Rolling each test back would be faster, but
TraceLite's handlers commit, and the tests should run the code that ships. A project
per test gives isolation for free, because every table hangs off a project and every
query filters by one (step 2's same-project rule). It also documents that the API
really is project-scoped: a query that forgot its project filter would make parallel
tests interfere and fail.

**Contract checks on both sides.** The Go check compares responses with the spec; zod
compares them again in the browser; MSW handlers are written from the spec too. None of
them is generated from the others, which is the point: a mistake has to be made three
times to slip through.

**What the e2e test found.** The first version of example 3 answered the download with
`page.route`, as ts.testing does for JSON. For the `download`-attribute link the route
handler never ran: the request went past it to the network, Edge named the file after
the URL, and the test failed. Served by a real HTTP server, the same headers gave the
right name. The lesson for test design: an interception layer is part of the system
under test, and for browser-decided behavior it can change the answer.

This is a known Chromium-side gap, not an Edge quirk. Playwright issue
[#22650](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/22650) reports that downloads
using the anchor's `download` attribute "cannot be mocked"; a maintainer reproduced it
and reported it upstream to Chromium, and it was closed for low activity without a fix;
[#38585](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/38585) (2025) found the same in
Chromium and WebKit but not Firefox. A probe run through this app's ts-test runtime on
2026-11-14 (Playwright 1.65.0, Edge 157.0.4341.46) counted the route handler's calls
for the export URL: 0 for the `<a download>` link, whose request went to the network
instead, and 1 for the same link without the attribute, which then downloaded as
`Ödeme gereksinimleri.csv`.

lessons.title: Step 15: Packaging: one binary embedding frontend + migrations; cross-compiling; customer-machine setup
lessons.summary: TraceLite ships as one executable per platform: the built React app and the migrations are embedded, configuration comes from the environment, and the binary migrates, serves and shuts down in a fixed order. A customer installs PostgreSQL and one file.

examples.title: web/dist inside the binary: files, client-side routes and the API on one origin

annotations.note: A //go:embed pattern is relative to the Go file's directory and can't contain "..", so cmd/tracelite can't reach web/dist. TraceLite has a tiny package web (web/web.go) next to dist; this one-file example keeps the directive in main.

all: keeps names starting with _ or ., which a plain directory pattern skips (go.files-io.embed). The build output here has one: when two lazy chunks import CommonJS packages, a Vite build puts the shared interop helper in _commonjsHelpers-hash.js (Rollup writes the helper module's leading NUL as _). Without all:, the binary would ship an app that can't load it.
Read once at start: a binary built before npm run build fails here, at startup, with a message that says what to do, instead of serving 404s.

A real file is served by http.FileServerFS (Go 1.22): it sets Content-Type, Last-Modified (the embed time is zero, so none here) and handles ranges. Files under assets/ carry a content hash in their names, so they may be cached for a year: a new build has new names.

After a deploy, a tab opened before it asks for the previous build's chunk. Answering with index.html would make the browser parse HTML as JavaScript; a 404 lets the app notice and reload. Anything with a file extension, or under assets/, is a file or nothing.
Every other path is a client-side route (step 6), answered with the app. index.html is revalidated on every load, because it is the one file that names the current assets.
Embedded names keep their directory (web/dist/index.html); fs.Sub makes dist the root. The migrations travel the same way (example 3), because goose reads the root of the FS it is given.

Unknown API paths stay problems: a typo in a fetch URL must produce a 404 problem, not an HTML page that zod then fails to parse with a confusing message. ServeMux picks the most specific pattern, so /api/ only gets what no real API route matched, and / only what isn't under /api/.
FileServerFS redirects /index.html to /, and / is answered by the route handler, with no-cache. The output shows where the redirect ended.

examples.title: Configuration from the environment, refused all at once; the version a binary reports

annotations.note: The linker sets the variable at release time with -X (shown running in go.performance.cross-compile). This runner builds without -ldflags and outside Git, so the output says dev.

debug.ReadBuildInfo reads what go build recorded, such as the commit as vcs.revision. A support call starts with tracelite --version, and this is what it prints. TraceLite's Version also reports vcs.modified and the module version from a Git tag (How it works).
Three of the five settings; the other two have safe defaults (How it works). TRACELITE_OWNER is step 13's actor for an installation without logins: the name recorded in the audit history.
Load takes getenv instead of calling os.Getenv, so a test passes a map, as main does here twice. The default address is the safe one: loopback only.

TraceLite has no authentication (step 1), so listening on all interfaces would publish every project to the network. The binary refuses unless the operator says, in a variable named for what it does, that something in front of it checks users. ":8080" has an empty host, which means every interface.
errors.Join (Go 1.20) keeps every problem; printing it gives one per line. A service that stops at the first error makes the customer restart it once per mistake.
url.URL.Redacted replaces the password with xxxxx, so the startup log line can show which database it connected to without leaking how. StackLab's maskDSN does the same.

examples.title: The binary's life: migrate before listening, then stop HTTP, jobs, listener and pool, in that order

annotations.note: In TraceLite this directive lives in migrations/migrations.go, next to the files, for the same reason as web/web.go (example 1).

A stand-in for goose, which isn't in this runner's module set. goose also records each applied version in goose_db_version, runs each file in a transaction, and with a session locker lets two starting processes migrate one at a time (go.postgres.migrations-sqlc).

Migrate before listening: a request never meets a schema older than the code. If a migration fails, the process exits and the service manager shows the error. goose runs each file in a transaction, so the failed one leaves nothing behind, while the ones before it stay applied; the old binary still runs if they were additive (design notes).
Step 11's pool gets its own context, derived without cancellation, because it must outlive the signal until HTTP has stopped.
A request that is still running when the signal arrives, so the output can show what happens to it.
The signal has canceled ctx, so the shutdown deadline is derived without its cancellation; 10 s for HTTP plus step 11's 20 s drain stays inside systemd's default 90 s stop timeout.

The reverse of the start, in dependency order. HTTP first: Shutdown closes the listener and waits for requests in flight, which may still enqueue jobs or write. Then the jobs drain (step 11), then the step 9 listener, then the pool that everything used.
The request that was running at the signal was answered with 200 before the server stopped: a deploy or a reboot doesn't turn into errors in someone's browser.

use_cases: Shipping an internal tool or a small product to machines you don't control: one file per OS, no runtime to install besides the database
Serving a single-page app and its API from one origin in production, as the Vite proxy does in development
Upgrades by replacing a file: the new binary migrates the database at startup
Support: a version command and a startup log line that say exactly which build and configuration is running
strengths: One artifact per platform: no Node, no web server, no copying of static files or migration scripts that can drift from the code
Cross-compiling is two environment variables: pgx is pure Go, so CGO_ENABLED=0 builds Windows and Linux binaries from one machine
Same origin in production: no CORS, cookies just work, and the router decides in one place what is API and what is app
Configuration is validated as a whole before anything starts, and the binary refuses unsafe settings instead of logging a warning nobody reads
weaknesses: The binary must be rebuilt for a UI change; there is no hot-swapping of static files (by design)
go build depends on npm run build having run first; a CI pipeline or a Makefile must order them
Self-migration at startup suits one instance; several instances need goose's session locker or a separate migration step
Windows services need code (golang.org/x/sys/windows/svc) or a wrapper; a plain console program isn't one

pitfalls.title: //go:embed dist without all:
pitfalls.detail: Files whose names start with _ or . are silently left out. Build tools generate such names; the app then fails in production only. Use all:dist, and keep secrets out of dist.
pitfalls.good: //go:embed all:dist

pitfalls.title: Answering every unknown path with index.html
pitfalls.detail: The SPA fallback must not cover /api/ or missing assets. Otherwise a mistyped endpoint returns HTML with 200, and after a deploy an old tab gets HTML for a JavaScript chunk.

pitfalls.title: Caching index.html
pitfalls.detail: index.html names the hashed assets of the current build. With a long cache lifetime, browsers keep loading the previous build after an upgrade. Cache assets for a year, revalidate index.html always.

pitfalls.title: Stopping the database pool before the HTTP server
pitfalls.detail: Closing in the order things were started (or in no order, from deferred calls in random places) lets requests in flight fail with 'closed pool'. Stop in reverse dependency order: HTTP, jobs, listener, pool.

pitfalls.title: Listening on 0.0.0.0 by default
pitfalls.detail: Docker images often listen on all interfaces because the container network is the boundary. A binary on a customer's Windows machine has no such boundary; default to 127.0.0.1 and make wider exposure an explicit decision.

quiz.q: Why does TraceLite answer GET /assets/index-A1old000.js with 404 instead of index.html?
options: A tab from before a deploy asks for an old chunk; HTML would be parsed as JavaScript, while a 404 lets the app reload
quiz.why: The fallback is for client-side routes only; anything that looks like a file is a file or a 404.

quiz.q: Where does the //go:embed directive for web/dist live?
options: In a small package inside web/, because patterns can't contain ..
quiz.why: Embed patterns are relative to the source file's directory and may not climb out of it.

quiz.q: SIGTERM arrives. Why is the HTTP server stopped before the job pool?
options: Requests in flight may still enqueue jobs; the pool must keep running until they are done
The job pool needs the HTTP server
quiz.why: Stop consumers after their producers: HTTP produces jobs, the pool consumes them, and both use the database pool, which closes last.

quiz.q: Which command builds a Linux binary on the Windows development machine?
options: It can't be done without WSL
Setting GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 for go build
quiz.why: Go cross-compiles by environment variables; with no cgo dependency, the result is a static Linux executable.

further_reading.title: Go: Environment variables GOOS, GOARCH, CGO_ENABLED

lessons.body:
## Concept

The product TraceLite set out to be is **one executable plus PostgreSQL**. Everything
else is inside the executable:

- **The web app**: `npm run build` writes `web/dist`; `//go:embed all:dist` in package
  `web` puts it into the binary; a handler serves files, answers client-side routes
  with `index.html`, and keeps `/api/` for the API. One origin, as in development.
- **The migrations**: `//go:embed *.sql` in package `migrations`; at startup goose
  applies whatever the database doesn't have yet, before the server listens.
- **Configuration**: environment variables, validated together at startup, with safe
  defaults (loopback address) and a refusal for unsafe ones.
- **Its identity**: a version set with `-ldflags -X` at release, plus the Git revision
  that `go build` records, printed by `tracelite --version` and in the first log line.

Because pgx is pure Go, `CGO_ENABLED=0` cross-compiles the same source into a Windows
`.exe` and a static Linux binary from one machine. On the customer's machine: install
PostgreSQL 18, create a role and a database, put the binary somewhere, register it as a
service with its environment, start it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring Boot**: the fat JAR is the same idea (app, static resources from
  `src/main/resources/static`, Flyway migrations), but it needs a JVM on the target. A
  Go binary needs nothing; jlink or GraalVM native-image get Java close, with more
  build machinery.
- **Python/Django**: `collectstatic` plus a web server for static files, a WSGI server,
  a virtualenv, and `manage.py migrate` as a separate step. PyInstaller can bundle an
  interpreter, with platform-specific builds and a large result.
- **Node/Express**: `express.static` plus a catch-all route is this handler; shipping
  means Node plus `node_modules` on the target, or a single-executable build (Node SEA),
  which is still experimental.
- **C/C++**: a static binary with resources compiled in (`xxd -i`, or `#embed` in C23),
  and a cross-toolchain per target. Go's cross-compiler ships with the language.

## How it works

The repository, as it ends after fifteen steps:

```text
openapi.yaml  sqlc.yaml  go.mod
cmd/tracelite/main.go        config, logger, pool, migrate, store, service, jobs, listener, router, server
migrations/                  001_init … 006_audit (.sql) + migrations.go: //go:embed *.sql
internal/store/              sqlc output + store.go (WithTx sets the actor, step 13)
internal/tracelite/          rules, CSV import (7), report generation (8, 11)
internal/httpapi/            router, handlers, problems, cursors, SSE (9), SPA fallback (15)
internal/events/             LISTEN connection and hub (9)
internal/jobs/               queue, pool, report and webhook handlers (10, 11)
web/                         Vite + React; web.go: //go:embed all:dist
web/src/api/  web/src/features/  web/e2e/
```

The migrations package has one unit test of its own: the embedded names, in order, must
start with `001_`, `002_` and so on, so a duplicated or skipped number fails CI rather
than a customer's upgrade.

Configuration is five environment variables, read once at startup (example 2 shows
three of them):

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | required; `postgres://` or `postgresql://`; logged with the password redacted |
| `TRACELITE_OWNER` | required; the actor of a single-user install (step 13) |
| `TRACELITE_ADDR` | default `127.0.0.1:8080`; a non-loopback address needs `TRACELITE_ALLOW_REMOTE=yes` |
| `TRACELITE_WORKERS` | job workers, 1-32, default 4 (step 11) |
| `TRACELITE_STANDARDS_URL` | the standards catalogue (step 10); optional |

`tracelite --version` prints `main.version` when the release set it with `-X`;
otherwise the module version that `go build` records from Git (since Go 1.24: the tag, or
a pseudo-version from the commit). Then comes the commit, `vcs.revision`, with
`, modified` when `vcs.modified` says the tree had uncommitted changes.

One more endpoint, for service managers and monitoring:

```yaml
  /api/health:
    get:
      operationId: getHealth
      responses:
        "200": { description: "Up: {status: ok, version, database: ok}" }
        "503": { description: "The database doesn't answer" }
```

A release, from the Windows development machine (PowerShell):

```text
npm --prefix web ci
npm --prefix web run build                      # web/dist, must exist before go build
go test ./... ; go test -tags integration -count=1 ./...
$env:CGO_ENABLED = "0"
$env:GOOS = "windows"; $env:GOARCH = "amd64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=1.0.0" -o dist/tracelite-1.0.0-windows-amd64.exe ./cmd/tracelite
$env:GOOS = "linux"
go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=1.0.0" -o dist/tracelite-1.0.0-linux-amd64 ./cmd/tracelite
```

`-trimpath` removes local paths (reproducible builds, go.performance.docker-vulns);
`-s -w` leave out the symbol table and DWARF data, which makes the file smaller and
debuggers less useful, while panics still print function names and lines.

Setting up a customer's Windows machine:

```text
1. winget install PostgreSQL.PostgreSQL.18        (the installer creates the service)
2. psql -U postgres:
     CREATE ROLE tracelite LOGIN PASSWORD '<generated>';
     CREATE DATABASE tracelite OWNER tracelite TEMPLATE template0 ENCODING 'UTF8';
   then, connected to tracelite:  SELECT show_trgm('ığdır');  -- six entries, or step 12's
   typo search treats Turkish letters as separators (see sql.search.trigram)
3. Copy tracelite.exe to C:\Program Files\TraceLite\
4. Register it as a service, with DATABASE_URL, TRACELITE_OWNER (and TRACELITE_ADDR if
   not 127.0.0.1:8080) in the service's environment; start it; open http://127.0.0.1:8080
5. Back up: a scheduled task running pg_dump -Fc tracelite every night, kept off the machine
6. Upgrade: stop the service, replace the .exe, start it; the new binary migrates first
```

The role owns its database, so its migrations may create tables and the trusted
extensions of step 12. On Linux the same binary runs under systemd:

```ini
[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/tracelite/tracelite
EnvironmentFile=/etc/tracelite/env
User=tracelite
Restart=on-failure
# SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after TimeoutStopSec (90 s by default)
```

Windows is the odd one out: the Service Control Manager talks to a service through a
control handler, and a plain console program registered with `sc.exe create` doesn't
answer, so the start fails after a timeout. TraceLite's `main` asks
`svc.IsWindowsService()` (from `golang.org/x/sys/windows/svc`) and, when true, runs under
`svc.Run`, whose Stop request cancels the same context that Ctrl+C cancels on a
console. The alternative without code is a service wrapper such as WinSW or NSSM.

The service details are documented behavior, not run here. The SCM waits for a new
service process to call `StartServiceCtrlDispatcher`, which
[its reference page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsvc/nf-winsvc-startservicectrldispatcherw)
says to do "within 30 seconds"; a console program never calls it, so the start fails
with error 1053, `ERROR_SERVICE_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`: "The service did not respond to the
start or control request in a timely fashion"
([system error codes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/system-error-codes--1000-1299-)).
[golang.org/x/sys/windows/svc](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sys/windows/svc)
(v0.50.0) has `IsWindowsService() (bool, error)` and `Run(name, handler)`, which makes
that call for you.

<!-- VERIFY: how step 4 puts variables into the service's environment. NSSM's and Elastic's docs use a REG_MULTI_SZ value Environment (one NAME=value per line) under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>; no Microsoft documentation of that value was found (2026-11-14), and it can't be tried here without creating a service (admin rights). -->

StackLab, the app running these lessons, is packaged differently on purpose:

| | StackLab, Docker mode | StackLab, local mode (ADR-0008) | TraceLite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frontend | Vite dev server in a `node` container | Vite dev server, started by `npm start` | built `web/dist`, embedded, served by the binary |
| Migrations | embedded in `cmd/stacklab` | embedded | embedded |
| Backend | `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath` in a distroless image | `go build` to `.bin/` by `scripts/dev.mjs` | one cross-compiled file per OS |
| Database | PostgreSQL containers | PostgreSQL 18 Windows service | PostgreSQL 18 on the customer's machine |
| Why | a development tool for one person: the UI changes daily, Vite's hot reload matters more than an artifact | the same, without containers | a product: one file to install, upgrade and support |

## Design notes

**Embed, don't deploy files next to the binary.** A directory of static files beside the
executable can be edited, half-copied or left from the previous version. Embedding makes
the UI and the migrations part of the build that the version names, and a customer's
"which version are you running?" has one answer.

**Self-migration, with a way back.** Migrating at startup is right for one instance per
database, which is every TraceLite installation. Each migration is additive where it can
be (step 11's jobs table, step 12's columns, step 13's log), so the previous binary still
runs against the new schema if an upgrade has to be undone; a migration that breaks that
rule says so in its release notes. Several instances would need goose's session locker,
or a separate `tracelite migrate` step run once per release.

**What the fifteen steps built.**

| Step | Added |
|---|---|
| 1 | The architecture, the request lifecycle, `openapi.yaml` as the contract |
| 2 | The schema: projects, a requirement tree, test cases, trace links, test runs; migration 001 |
| 3 | The store: sqlc queries, `WithTx`, constraint names turned into errors |
| 4 | The REST API: strict JSON, RFC 9457 problems, keyset cursors |
| 5 | The typed client: generated types, zod at the boundary, TanStack Query hooks |
| 6 | The UI: the requirement tree, the detail form, the trace matrix with coverage |
| 7 | CSV import: Turkish Excel files, all or nothing, errors by line |
| 8 | Streaming exports: CSV for Excel and the traceability report |
| 9 | Live updates: triggers, LISTEN/NOTIFY, a hub, server-sent events |
| 10 | The outside world: a cached standards catalogue and signed webhooks |
| 11 | Background jobs: a job table, SKIP LOCKED, leases, retries, graceful shutdown |
| 12 | Search: codes, Turkish words and typos, ranked and paged |
| 13 | Audit history: a trigger, the user through `set_config`, and its trade-offs |
| 14 | Tests at every layer, each catching what the others can't |
| 15 | One binary with the app and migrations inside, and a way onto a customer's machine |

lessons.title: var vs :=, zero values, constants and iota
lessons.summary: Every Go variable starts at a usable zero value, := declares while = assigns, and constants are exact compile-time values that iota can enumerate.

examples.title: Zero values are usable, not just empty

annotations.note: There is no "uninitialized" state: var gives every field its zero value ("", 0, false, nil). Unlike C, no garbage; unlike Java, a string field is "" rather than null.
A nil slice is a valid empty slice (append allocates on demand) and a nil map reads as empty. Only writing to a nil map panics, as the comment on the next line says.
:= declares and infers the type, inside functions only. With several names on the left it needs at least one new one; the others are plainly assigned, which is how n changes from 3 to 4 here.
Both right-hand values are read before either variable is written, so a swap needs no temporary.

examples.title: The := shadowing bug and its one-character fix

annotations.note: Inside the block, := declares brand-new result and err that hide the outer ones. The outer variables are never written, and it compiles because the inner ones are used. Default go vet doesn't report it.
= assigns the variables declared on lines 16-17. When a block should update outer state, declare first and assign inside.

examples.title: Typed enums with iota, and untyped constants

annotations.note: iota is the line index inside one const block, starting at 0. A line without an expression repeats the previous one, type included, so all four constants are Level values.
A String method makes Level a fmt.Stringer, so fmt prints names. The fallback keeps an unknown value like Level(7) debuggable.
The blank identifier skips iota's 0; the repeated expression then yields 1<<10, 1<<20 and 1<<30.
Untyped constants are exact values of arbitrary precision. 1<<100 never exists at run time; only the result 4 has to fit in an int.
The untyped 2 takes its type from time.Second, a time.Duration. The same with a variable n would need time.Duration(n): the next lesson.

use_cases: var x T when the zero value is what you want, or a declaration without an obvious initial value
:= for nearly every local variable, especially results of calls: v, err := f()
const + iota for enum-like sets (log levels, states) with a String method
Untyped constants for unit math such as KB/MB or timeouts (2 * time.Second)
strengths: Zero values remove a whole class of null checks: a zero sync.Mutex, bytes.Buffer or empty struct is ready to use, unlike Java fields that start as null
Constants are checked at compile time with exact arithmetic, so 1<<100 overflow mistakes surface as compile errors rather than wrapped values at run time
Declaration forms are few: var, :=, const. No let/var/const scoping puzzles as in pre-ES6 JavaScript
weaknesses: iota enums are just integers: any int converts to Level, and nothing checks a switch for exhaustiveness the way TypeScript's never does
:= in an inner scope silently shadows outer variables, and the default go vet doesn't report it
A zero value isn't always meaningful: 0 retries or an empty name may be a real setting or a forgotten field, and the type can't tell you which

pitfalls.title: Shadowing err or a result inside if/for blocks
pitfalls.detail: x, err := f() inside a block creates new variables; the outer ones keep their old values. Declare outside and use = inside when the block should update them.
pitfalls.good: if ok { result, err = lookup(k) }

pitfalls.title: Writing to a nil map
pitfalls.detail: Reading a nil map is fine, writing panics. Initialize maps with make (or a literal) before the first write.
pitfalls.good: m := make(map[string]int); m["a"] = 1

pitfalls.title: Relying on iota values in storage
pitfalls.detail: Inserting a new constant in the middle renumbers everything after it. Persist names (or explicit numbers), not iota positions.

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println print for a struct field `Tags []string` that was never assigned?
quiz.why: The field's zero value is a nil slice, and fmt prints a nil slice as [].

quiz.q: `a, err := f()` appears inside an if block while a and err are already declared outside. What happens?
options: The outer a and err are assigned
New a and err are declared for the block; the outer ones are untouched
quiz.why: The block is a new scope, so := declares fresh variables there. The 'no new variables' error only applies within the same scope.

quiz.q: In `const ( A = iota * 10; B; C )`, what is C?
quiz.why: B and C repeat the expression iota * 10 with iota = 1 and 2.

The Go Programming Language Specification: The zero value

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go has three ways to introduce a name: `var x T` (zero value), `x := expr` (declare and
infer, inside functions only) and `const`. There is no uninitialized memory: every
variable starts at its type's zero value, and the standard library designs types so that
the zero value works (a zero `sync.Mutex` is unlocked, a zero `bytes.Buffer` is empty and
ready). Constants are compile-time values with exact arithmetic; `iota` numbers the lines
of a `const` block, which is how Go spells enums.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: no uninitialized locals and no constructors; `var c Config` is fully initialized.
- Java: no `null` for strings or numbers. Only pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions
  and interfaces have `nil` as their zero value.
- Python: names are declared, not created on first assignment, and a typo in an
  assignment is a compile error instead of a new variable.
- JS/TS: `:=` is roughly `let` with inference, but there is no `undefined`. A `const`
  in Go must be a compile-time value; JS `const` only forbids reassignment.
- Java/TS enums are their own types with a closed set of values. Go's `iota` constants
  are named integers: nothing stops `Level(7)`.

## Design notes

Prefer `:=` for locals and `var` when the zero value is the point (`var buf
bytes.Buffer`). Make your own types useful at their zero value where you can: then
callers never need a constructor for the common case. For enums, add a `String` method
and handle the unknown case explicitly, because the compiler won't check that a
`switch` covers every constant. Watch for `:=` inside `if`/`for` blocks whenever you mean
to update an outer variable; it is the most common beginner bug that compiles cleanly.

lessons.title: Basic types and explicit conversion
lessons.summary: Go never converts between numeric types for you, not even int to int64. Every conversion is visible, and named types like Celsius carry meaning the compiler enforces.

examples.title: Mixing numeric types needs a conversion, and conversions have rules

annotations.note: int and int64 are distinct types even where int is 64 bits wide. The commented line is a compile error; the conversion makes the widening visible at the exact spot it happens.
The same for float64 and int. Untyped constants are the exception: price * 3 compiles, because the literal 3 takes on float64.
Float to int truncates toward zero: -2.9 becomes -2, not -3. Use math.Floor or math.Round first when you mean those.
Narrowing a variable keeps the low bits: 200 fits uint8 but reads as -56 in int8. With a constant, int8(200) is a compile error instead.
Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^32 here. Nothing panics on integer overflow in Go, signed or unsigned.
Integer division truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the dividend: -3 and -1. Python floors instead and gives -4 and 1.

examples.title: Named types, time.Duration and strconv

annotations.note: Celsius and Fahrenheit share float64 underneath, so converting between them is allowed, but only when written out. Assigning one to the other is the bug the type exists to catch.
time.Duration is a named int64 counting nanoseconds. An int variable must be converted before multiplying, and a bare 2 is two nanoseconds.
strconv.Itoa formats digits; string(rune(65)) is the code point "A". Writing string(n) for an int n is the classic mix-up, and go vet flags it.
Parsing returns the zero value plus an error that names the function and the input: no exception, no NaN.
strconv follows Go syntax, not a locale. A Turkish decimal comma ("3,14") is a syntax error, so normalize user input at the boundary.

use_cases: Converting between int sizes at API boundaries (database int64 ids, len() int results)
Named types for units and identifiers: type UserID int64, type Celsius float64
time.Duration arithmetic for timeouts and backoff
strconv for parsing and formatting numbers from flags, query strings and CSV
strengths: No implicit conversions means no silent truncation or sign changes hidden in arithmetic, unlike C's usual arithmetic conversions
Named types give unit and ID safety for free: passing a UserID where an OrderID is expected doesn't compile, unlike TypeScript's structural number aliases
Parsing errors are values that say what failed and on which input
weaknesses: Conversions add noise in numeric code, e.g. float64(len(xs)) in every average
Integer overflow wraps silently at run time; there is no checked arithmetic as in Rust's debug builds
Named types over the same base convert freely when written out, so a careless Fahrenheit(c) still compiles

pitfalls.title: string(n) on an integer
pitfalls.detail: It produces the character with that code point, not decimal digits. Use strconv.Itoa or fmt.Sprint.
pitfalls.good: s := strconv.Itoa(65) // "65"

pitfalls.title: Expecting float-to-int to round
pitfalls.detail: int(f) truncates toward zero. Round explicitly with math.Round when you need it.

pitfalls.title: Narrowing without a range check
pitfalls.detail: int32(x) on an out-of-range int64 keeps the low bits and changes the value. Check the range first when the input isn't under your control.

quiz.q: var a int = 1; var b int64 = 2. Does a + b compile?
options: Yes, int is 64 bits on amd64
No: mismatched types int and int64
quiz.why: Distinct types never mix in arithmetic, whatever their size on the platform.

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println(int(-2.9)) print?
quiz.why: The fraction is discarded: truncation toward zero.

quiz.q: What is time.Duration(5)?
quiz.why: Duration counts nanoseconds; write 5 * time.Second for seconds.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go's basic types are `bool`, `string`, sized integers (`int8`…`int64`, `uint8`…`uint64`,
plus `int`/`uint` at the platform's word size), `float32`/`float64`, and aliases `byte`
(`uint8`) and `rune` (`int32`). Values of different types never mix: you write the
conversion `T(x)` yourself. A *named type* such as `type Celsius float64` is a new type
with the same underlying representation; it converts to and from `float64` explicitly,
never implicitly.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: no integer promotion and no usual arithmetic conversions. `int + int64` is a
  compile error, so a sign or width change always shows up as a conversion in the code.
- Java widens `int` to `long` automatically; Go doesn't widen at all. There is no
  boxing either: no `Integer` objects.
- Python: Go integers have a fixed size and wrap on overflow, and integer `/` and `%`
  truncate toward zero where Python's `//` and `%` floor.
- JS/TS: no single `number` type. TS `type UserId = number` is only an alias, while Go's
  `type UserID int64` is a distinct type the compiler checks.

## Design notes

Convert at the boundary and keep one type inside: parse strings with `strconv` where
input enters, convert database `int64` ids once in the store layer, and let named types
(`UserID`, `Celsius`, `time.Duration`) carry meaning through the rest of the code. When
a conversion narrows a value you don't control, check the range first: Go wraps silently
on overflow. For user-facing numbers in Turkish (decimal comma, dot as thousands
separator), normalize the text before `strconv.ParseFloat`, which only accepts Go syntax.

lessons.title: Strings, bytes and runes — UTF-8 all the way down
lessons.summary: A Go string is a read-only byte slice holding UTF-8. len counts bytes, range walks runes, and case conversion is locale-blind — which matters if your users write Turkish.

examples.title: len counts bytes; range counts runes

annotations.note: len(s) is the byte length: 4 for "DİL", because İ encodes as two bytes. utf8.RuneCountInString counts the 3 characters.
range decodes UTF-8 and yields each rune with the byte offset where it starts: 0, 1, 3. The offsets skip 2, the second byte of İ.
Indexing returns a single byte (0xC4, half of İ). Decode from that offset to get the whole character back.

examples.title: Case conversion ignores locale until you ask for Turkish

annotations.note: strings.ToLower maps I to i whatever the user's language. The stdlib has the Turkish and Azeri mapping as unicode.TurkishCase: I becomes ı and İ becomes i (strings.ToUpperSpecial goes the other way).
Naive lowercasing turns both DIL and DİL into "dil", so a search for one finds the other. strings.EqualFold has no Turkish mode either: EqualFold("DİL", "dil") is false.

use_cases: Processing user input that is not pure ASCII: names, cities, addresses
Deciding between byte offsets (wire formats, file slices) and rune counts (UI limits)
Understanding why len('İ') == 2 and range treats it as one rune
strengths: One encoding everywhere: source and string literals are UTF-8 and the standard library assumes it; no separate wide-char type
range over a string just works for iteration; no manual decoder loops
Explicit byte/rune split makes costs visible instead of hidden in a locale setting
weaknesses: len and slicing are byte-based; s[:1] can cut a rune in half and produce invalid UTF-8
Locale rules are opt-in: Turkish needs strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s), other languages golang.org/x/text/cases, and EqualFold has no Turkish mode
Rune is an alias for int32, not a distinct type — the name suggests more safety than it delivers

pitfalls.title: Indexing a string gives a byte, not a character
pitfalls.detail: s[1] on "DİL" returns the first byte of İ (0xC4), which prints as garbage. Use []rune(s) or utf8.DecodeRuneInString when you need a whole character.

pitfalls.title: Counting characters with len
pitfalls.detail: len(s) is bytes. For UI length limits use utf8.RuneCountInString(s) — 'DİL' is len 4 but 3 runes.

quiz.q: What is len("DİL")?
quiz.why: İ encodes as two UTF-8 bytes, so the byte length is 4 even though there are 3 runes.

quiz.q: What does range yield for each iteration over a string?
quiz.why: range decodes UTF-8 and yields the starting byte index of each rune plus the rune itself — which is why indices skip over continuation bytes.

quiz.q: On a machine with a Turkish OS locale, what does strings.ToLower("ISTANBUL") return?
quiz.why: ToLower never consults the OS locale, so you always get 'istanbul'. Turkish rules need strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s).

further_reading.title: Go blog: Strings, bytes, runes and characters in Go

lessons.body:
## Concept

A Go string is a read-only slice of bytes, and those bytes are UTF-8. That
single decision explains most of this lesson: `len` counts bytes, indexing
gives bytes, and the `range` clause is the one construct that decodes runes
for you. A rune is a Unicode code point — `int32` under the alias — and the
conversion cost between "what the user sees" (runes) and "what the machine
stores" (bytes) is always visible in Go.

The second half is about case: Go's `strings` functions do simple, locale-blind
mapping. That is predictable and fast, but wrong for Turkish, where uppercase
`I` lowercases to dotless `ı` and dotted `İ` lowercases to plain `i`. The
standard library has that mapping as `unicode.TurkishCase`, used through
`strings.ToLowerSpecial` and `strings.ToUpperSpecial`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

C gives you `char*` and no encoding opinion — you already know the pain Go
avoids. Java and C# hide UTF-16 behind a `char` type, so you get a *different*
surprise (surrogate pairs) instead. Python 3 and JavaScript strings are
code-point-ish abstractions where indexing usually does what you mean; Go is
closer to the metal: bytes in memory, explicit decode on demand. If you have
fought `wchar_t` or ICU locale structs, Go's "one encoding, no guesses" stance
is a relief: Turkish casing is one stdlib call, and `golang.org/x/text` covers
other languages' rules when you need them.

## Design notes

The stdlib refuses to guess locales, so `strings.ToLower` never consults the
OS locale — the same binary behaves identically in Istanbul and Oslo. The
trade-off: correctness for Turkish users is *your* job, via
`strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` wherever text is normalized
for comparison or search. This matches Go's general philosophy of explicit
dependencies over ambient environment.

lessons.title: if with init, the one for, switch without fallthrough, labels
lessons.summary: Go has one loop (for), an if that can declare variables for its own scope, and a switch whose cases never fall through unless you say so.

examples.title: if with an init statement, and switch without break

annotations.note: Handle the error and return early. The happy path stays at the left margin instead of nesting inside else branches.
A switch with no tag is a tidier if/else-if chain: cases are tested top to bottom and the first true one wins.
The init statement declares v and ok for the if and its else only. The comma-ok form tells a missing key apart from a stored zero.
Cases end on their own: no break, and no accidental fall-through as in C or Java. One case can list several values.
fallthrough jumps into the next case body without testing its condition, which is why the second line prints. It must be the last statement in a case; real code rarely needs it.

examples.title: One for for everything, labeled break, per-iteration variables

annotations.note: Since Go 1.22, range accepts an integer and counts 0..n-1.
A for with only a condition is Go's while loop; with nothing at all it loops forever.
A label names the outer loop, so break outer leaves both loops at once. No flag variable, no goto.

Since Go 1.22 every iteration has its own i, also in the three-clause form, so the closures print 0 1 2. A module whose go.mod says go 1.21 or older still gets the old shared variable and prints 3 3 3.

use_cases: if v, err := f(); err != nil { ... } for errors that matter only in this branch
Tagless switch for range checks and classification
for range over slices, maps, strings, channels, integers and iterator functions
Labeled break/continue for nested searches
strengths: One loop keyword covers counting, while, infinite and range loops; less syntax to remember than C's for/while/do-while
Cases never fall through by accident, the bug Java and C need break (and linters) to prevent
Init statements keep helper variables scoped to the branch that uses them
weaknesses: No ternary operator: a one-line choice becomes a four-line if/else
switch is not exhaustive over iota constants or interface types; the compiler never warns about a missing case
The loop-variable fix depends on the go version in go.mod, so old modules keep the old behavior

pitfalls.title: break inside switch inside for
pitfalls.detail: A plain break in a switch case leaves the switch, not the loop. Label the loop and break the label.
pitfalls.good: loop: for { switch { case done: break loop } }

pitfalls.title: Assuming per-iteration variables in an old module
pitfalls.detail: The Go 1.22 loop semantics follow the go line in go.mod. Code in a module declaring go 1.21 still shares one variable across iterations.

pitfalls.title: Reading a missing map key without comma-ok
pitfalls.detail: m[k] returns the zero value for a missing key, indistinguishable from a stored zero. Use v, ok := m[k] when the difference matters.

quiz.q: In Go, what happens at the end of a switch case body?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
quiz.why: Cases never fall through unless the body ends with fallthrough.

quiz.q: for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { fs = append(fs, func() int { return i }) } in a module declaring go 1.27. What do the closures return?
quiz.why: Since Go 1.22 each iteration has its own i.

quiz.q: How do you leave two nested loops at once?
options: A label on the outer loop and break label
quiz.why: break and continue accept a label naming an enclosing loop.
