The Go Programming Language Specification: Switch statements

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go keeps three control structures and makes each do more. `if` and `switch` accept an
init statement whose variables live only in that statement. `switch` evaluates cases top
to bottom, stops at the first match and never falls through by default; without a tag it
replaces if/else-if chains. `for` is the only loop: three-clause, condition-only (while),
bare (forever) or `range`. Labels let `break` and `continue` target an outer loop.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/Java: no parentheses around conditions, braces are mandatory, and `switch` needs no
  `break`. There is no `do-while` and no ternary `?:`.
- Python: `range` over an integer works like `range(n)`; labeled `break` covers what
  Python does with flags or `for/else`.
- JS: the Go 1.22 loop variable behaves like `let` in a JS `for` loop (one binding per
  iteration). The pre-1.22 behavior was JS's `var`.

## Design notes

Use the init form when a value only matters for one branch (`if err := f(); err != nil`).
Return early on errors instead of nesting the success path in `else`; this is the shape
most Go code has, and reviewers expect it. Prefer a tagless `switch` over long
if/else-if chains. Keep `fallthrough` for the rare case where one case is a strict
superset of the next, and leave a comment when you use it.

lessons.title: Functions: multiple returns, named results, variadic, closures
lessons.summary: Go functions return several values, and (value, error) is the idiom every API follows. Variadic parameters are slices, and closures capture variables, not copies.

examples.title: (value, error), named results and the min/max builtins

annotations.note: The error is a second return value, so the caller can't use the result without at least seeing it. On failure, return the zero value plus the error.
Named results document what comes back and start at their zero value. A naked return returns them as they are, handy here, confusing in long functions. min and max are builtins since Go 1.21.
q and err exist only inside each if. errors.Is compares against the ErrDivByZero sentinel, which keeps working when someone wraps the error.
The standard library uses the same (value, error) shape everywhere, so callers handle every failure the same way.

examples.title: Variadic parameters are slices; closures keep state

annotations.note: Inside the function nums is a plain []int. sum() with no arguments gets a nil slice, which ranges zero times.
xs... passes the slice itself, not a copy, so double writes into the caller's backing array. Callers who don't expect that get a surprise.
The closure captures the variable count, not its value at creation. Each call to counter makes a new count, so counters don't share state.
Arguments are evaluated left to right, so the output is 1 2 3 1: the second counter starts fresh.
Functions are values: assign them, pass them, return them. A function type like func(string) string is often all the interface you need.

use_cases: (T, error) results for anything that can fail: parsing, I/O, lookups
Named results when a deferred function must adjust them (see the defer lesson)
Variadic helpers: fmt.Println, append, slices.Concat, option lists
Closures for counters, memoization, and callbacks passed to sort or http handlers
strengths: Errors are visible in every signature; unlike Java's unchecked exceptions, a call that can fail looks different from one that can't
Multiple returns remove out-parameters (C) and throwaway tuple or result classes (Java)
Closures are lightweight and capture by reference, like JS closures, with no 'effectively final' rule as in Java lambdas
weaknesses: No default parameters and no overloading: options become structs, variadic option functions, or several functions with different names
if err != nil repeats in every caller; there is no ? operator as in Rust
Variadic calls with slice... share the caller's backing array, an aliasing rule that is easy to forget

pitfalls.title: Ignoring the error with _
pitfalls.detail: v, _ := f() compiles and silently drops failures. Reserve _ for errors that genuinely can't happen, and say why in a comment.

pitfalls.title: Naked returns in long functions
pitfalls.detail: A bare return far from the result declarations hides what is returned. Keep naked returns for short functions.

pitfalls.title: Expecting xs... to copy
pitfalls.detail: The callee receives the caller's slice; writes are visible to the caller. Copy with slices.Clone when that's not wanted.

quiz.q: Inside func f(nums ...int), what is the type of nums?
quiz.why: A variadic parameter is an ordinary slice inside the function.

quiz.q: c1, c2 := counter(), counter(); fmt.Println(c1(), c1(), c2()). What prints?
quiz.why: Each counter() call creates its own captured count variable.

quiz.q: What should a function return together with a non-nil error?
options: The zero value of the result type, unless the docs say otherwise
quiz.why: Callers must not use the result when err != nil; returning the zero value makes accidental use harmless.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Function types
The Go Programming Language Specification: Min and max

lessons.body:
## Concept

A Go function can return several values. The convention for anything that can fail is
`(result, error)` with the error last; callers check it before touching the result. Results
can be named, which documents them and lets a `defer` change them. A final parameter
`...T` accepts any number of `T` and arrives as a `[]T`. Functions are first-class
values, and function literals are closures over the variables they mention.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: multiple returns replace out-parameters and `errno`.
- Java: no checked or unchecked exceptions for ordinary failures; the error is part of the
  return type. No overloading and no default arguments.
- Python: multiple returns look like tuple returns, but they aren't a tuple value; you
  can't store `f()` in one variable when f returns two results.
- JS/TS: closures work the same way (capture by reference). Rest parameters `...xs`
  correspond to variadic `...T`.

## Design notes

Return errors, don't print them: the caller knows whether a failure matters. Keep
signatures small; when you need optional parameters, take an options struct rather than
inventing overloads. Name results when they clarify (`(lo, hi int)`) or when a deferred
function must touch them, and otherwise leave them unnamed. When a function only needs
one behavior from its caller, accept a function value instead of an interface.

lessons.title: defer: LIFO order and when arguments are evaluated
lessons.summary: defer schedules a call for when the function returns, in reverse order, with its arguments evaluated immediately. Deferred closures can rewrite named results; os.Exit skips them all.

examples.title: Last in, first out, and arguments evaluated at defer time

annotations.note: Deferred calls run when main returns, not at the end of each loop iteration, and in reverse order. A loop that opens a file per iteration and defers Close keeps every file open until return.
The arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when the defer statement runs, so this line prints 1 although x is 2 by then.
A closure reads x when it finally runs, so it prints 2. Pick the form that captures the value you mean.

examples.title: Deferred closures can change named results, and recover from panics

annotations.note: The return statement assigns port and err first; then the deferred closure runs and can replace err. One place adds context to every error path.
All three returns pass through the deferred wrapper, including the range check added later. Nobody can forget the context.
recover stops a panic only when called directly by a deferred function. Here the integer division by zero becomes an ordinary error value.

examples.title: os.Exit (and log.Fatal) skip deferred calls

annotations.note: This cleanup never prints: the expected output has a single line.
os.Exit ends the process immediately, without running deferred calls. log.Fatal and log.Fatalf call os.Exit(1), so in a server they skip the cleanup you deferred.

use_cases: Releasing resources right after acquiring them: defer f.Close(), defer mu.Unlock(), defer rows.Close()
Adding context to every error of a function in one deferred closure
Turning a panic into an error at a boundary (an HTTP handler, a worker goroutine)
Timing a function: defer logDuration(time.Now())
strengths: Cleanup sits next to the acquisition, so it can't drift away from it, unlike a finally block at the bottom of a long Java method
Runs on every return path and during panics, which try/finally also does, but without the extra nesting
Argument evaluation at defer time makes defer logDuration(time.Now()) work with no closure
weaknesses: Defers are per function, not per block: in loops they pile up until the function returns
os.Exit and log.Fatal bypass them, so cleanup depends on how the program ends
An error returned by a deferred Close is easy to ignore; handling it needs a named result and a closure

pitfalls.title: defer in a loop
pitfalls.detail: Each iteration's defer waits for the function to return. Move the loop body into its own function so each defer runs per iteration.
pitfalls.bad: for _, p := range paths { f, _ := os.Open(p); defer f.Close() }
pitfalls.good: for _, p := range paths { if err := process(p); err != nil { return err } } // process defers Close

pitfalls.title: log.Fatal in a function with defers
pitfalls.detail: It calls os.Exit(1); deferred cleanup never runs. Return the error and exit from main after cleanup instead.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a deferred call to see later changes
pitfalls.detail: defer fmt.Println(x) captures x now. Use a closure if you want the value at return time.

quiz.q: x := 1; defer fmt.Println(x); x = 2. What prints when the function returns?
quiz.why: Arguments are evaluated when the defer statement executes.

quiz.q: Three defers A, B, C are registered in that order. In which order do they run?
quiz.why: Deferred calls run last in, first out.

quiz.q: Where does recover() stop a panic?
options: Only when called directly by a deferred function
quiz.why: Called anywhere else, recover returns nil and the panic continues.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

lessons.body:
## Concept

`defer f(args)` schedules `f` to run when the surrounding function returns, whether it
returns normally or panics. Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order. The function
value and its arguments are evaluated when the `defer` statement executes; only the call
is delayed. Because deferred functions run after the return values are set, a deferred
closure can read and change named results, and it is the only place where `recover`
stops a panic.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/JS: `defer` replaces most `try/finally` blocks, and it sits next to the
  acquisition instead of at the end of the method.
- Python: similar to a `with` block's exit, but tied to the function, not to a block.
- C++: like a destructor-based scope guard (RAII), but explicit and scoped to the whole
  function.
- `os.Exit` skipping defers matches Java's `System.exit` skipping `finally` and Node's
  `process.exit`. Python's `sys.exit` differs: it raises `SystemExit`, so `finally` and
  `with` blocks still run.

## Design notes

Write the `defer` on the line right after a successful acquisition (`f, err :=
os.Open(p); if err != nil { return err }; defer f.Close()`). If a loop acquires
resources, put the loop body in its own function. Use `recover` only at boundaries you
own, such as an HTTP handler or a worker goroutine, and convert the panic to an error
there; recovering everywhere hides bugs. In `main`, prefer returning errors to a single
exit point over calling `log.Fatal` deep in the code, so deferred cleanup still runs.

lessons.title: Pointers without arithmetic; new(expr) vs &T{}
lessons.summary: Go passes everything by value; a pointer is how a callee changes the caller's data. There is no pointer arithmetic, returning &local is safe, and Go 1.26's new(expr) points at any value.

examples.title: Copies vs pointers, and why returning &local is safe

annotations.note: A struct parameter is a full copy. The increment changes the copy, which disappears when the function returns.
With a pointer the callee changes the caller's struct. c.Hits is shorthand for (*c).Hits: no -> operator.
In C this would return a dangling pointer. Go's escape analysis sees that c outlives the call and allocates it on the heap; go build -gcflags=-m prints "moved to heap: c".
Copying a pointer copies the address: alias and p name the same struct, so the write through alias shows up through p.
The zero value of a pointer is nil. Dereferencing it panics, and pointer arithmetic doesn't exist outside package unsafe.

examples.title: Pointers to values for optional fields; new(expr) in Go 1.26

annotations.note: A pointer field can say "not set", which "" and 0 can't. This is the usual shape for PATCH requests and optional JSON fields.
&"api" and &0 don't compile: only addressable operands, such as variables, have an address. Codebases wrote this generic helper to copy the value into a variable first.
Since Go 1.26, new accepts an expression and returns a pointer to a new variable holding its value, which retires the helper.
new(int) still works and points at a zeroed int; new(7) points at a fresh int holding 7.
&T{...} remains the idiomatic way to get a pointer to a new struct: taking the address of a composite literal is allowed on purpose.

use_cases: Letting a function modify its argument: func (c *Counter) Inc()
Avoiding copies of large structs in hot paths (measure first)
Optional values: *string and *int fields for PATCH bodies and nullable columns
Constructors returning *T: func NewServer(cfg Config) *Server
strengths: No pointer arithmetic and garbage collection: no buffer overruns or use-after-free through pointers, unlike C
Escape analysis decides stack vs heap, so returning &local is safe and idiomatic
Value semantics are the default, so a copy never aliases by accident, unlike Java and JS where every object is a reference
weaknesses: nil pointer dereferences still crash at run time; the type system can't mark a pointer as non-nil
Pointer vs value is a choice at every API, and a struct that mixes both kinds of methods confuses readers
Heap allocations caused by escaping pointers cost garbage-collection time in hot code

pitfalls.title: Taking the address of a loop element copy
pitfalls.detail: In for _, v := range items, v is a copy; &v points at that copy, not into the slice. Use &items[i] to point into the slice.
pitfalls.bad: for _, v := range items { ptrs = append(ptrs, &v) }
pitfalls.good: for i := range items { ptrs = append(ptrs, &items[i]) }

pitfalls.title: Using pointers 'for speed' by default
pitfalls.detail: Small structs are cheap to copy, and a pointer can force a heap allocation. Use pointers when you need sharing or mutation, and measure before optimizing.

pitfalls.title: Dereferencing optional fields without a nil check
pitfalls.detail: *p.Name panics when Name is nil. Check first, or give the type a method that does.

quiz.q: func inc(c Counter) { c.Hits++ } is called with a variable c. Does the caller's c.Hits change?
options: No, the function got a copy
quiz.why: Go passes arguments by value; only a pointer lets the callee modify the caller's struct.

quiz.q: Is `func newT() *T { t := T{}; return &t }` safe?
options: No, t lives on the stack
Yes, escape analysis moves t to the heap
quiz.why: The compiler allocates variables whose address escapes on the heap.

quiz.q: Which expression gives a *int pointing at 5 in Go 1.26?
quiz.why: new(expr) creates a variable initialized to the value and returns its address; &5 doesn't compile.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Address operators
The Go Programming Language Specification: Allocation

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every assignment and every function argument in Go copies the value. A pointer `*T`
holds the address of a `T`; `&x` takes an address and `*p` dereferences, while field
access and method calls dereference automatically. There is no pointer arithmetic, and
the garbage collector owns memory: the compiler's escape analysis puts a variable on the
heap when its address outlives the function, so returning `&local` is safe. `new(T)`
returns a pointer to a zeroed `T`; since Go 1.26 `new(expr)` returns a pointer to a new
variable holding the value of `expr`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: no arithmetic, no dangling pointers, no `->`, no `free`. `&local` is safe.
- Java/Python/JS: objects there are always references. In Go a struct is a value until you
  take its address, so `b := a` copies the whole struct.
- TS: `?:` optional properties correspond to pointer fields (`*string`), where `nil` means
  absent and `""` is a real value.

## Design notes

Use a pointer when the callee must modify the value, when the value must be shared, or
when it is genuinely large; otherwise pass values. Pick one receiver kind per type
(usually pointer receivers for anything with mutable state). Pointer fields are the
standard way to express "optional" in structs that map to JSON or SQL, and `new(expr)`
removes the boilerplate of filling them. Let escape analysis do its job and check
`-gcflags=-m` only when a profile points at allocations.

lessons.title: fmt verbs, tabwriter tables, stdout vs stderr, exit codes
lessons.summary: fmt's verbs format any value, and widths count runes, not bytes; text/tabwriter aligns columns for you. A tool writes results to stdout, diagnostics to stderr, and reports failure through an exit code set in exactly one place.

examples.title: The verbs you actually use, and what a mistake prints

annotations.note: A String method makes the type a fmt.Stringer. Inside it, convert to the underlying type before formatting: Sprintf("%v", c) would find the String method again and recurse until the stack overflows.
%+v adds field names, the everyday debugging verb. %#v prints Go syntax you can paste into a test. %T names the dynamic type, which is what you want when an interface holds something unexpected.
%v and %s call String. %.2f does not: fmt uses String only for the string-like verbs (%v %s %q %x %X), so a numeric verb formats the underlying float64.

%q quotes and escapes, %+q also escapes everything non-ASCII. % x shows that İ is the two bytes c4 b0. Width 8 pads "İzmir" with three spaces: fmt counts runes (5), not bytes (len is 6), unlike C's printf.
fmt prints maps in key-sorted order (since Go 1.12), so the output is stable and testable. Ranging over a map is still deliberately random.
A wrong verb, a missing argument and an extra argument all compile and run; the output carries a %! marker. go vet's printf check reports all three lines, and go test runs that check automatically.

examples.title: Padding by bytes, by runes, and with text/tabwriter

annotations.note: Padding computed with len counts bytes. İ, ğ and ı take two bytes each, so the İstanbul and Iğdır rows come out one and two columns short.
A fmt width counts runes, so a fixed %-10s lines up, as long as you know the widest value in advance.

tabwriter buffers tab-terminated cells, measures every column, then pads. The last cell of each line has no tab after it, so it is not padded and no line ends in spaces. Forget Flush and nothing is printed.

examples.title: run() returns the exit code; main is one line

annotations.note: The program takes its arguments and writers as parameters and returns an int. Nothing inside touches os.Args, os.Stdout or os.Exit, so a test calls it with buffers and checks all three outputs.
Usage errors go to stderr with code 2, the code flag.ExitOnError uses. An unrecovered panic also exits with 2, and log.Fatal with 1.
The "tool: cause" prefix tells the user which program in a pipeline failed. stdout stays empty, so x=$(sum 40 two) captures nothing instead of an error message.

The stderr line appears in the run panel but not in the compared output, exactly as a pipe would skip it. os.Exit sits in main, after run has returned, so every defer inside run (closing files, flushing a bufio.Writer) has already happened. Here the code is 0.

use_cases: list and status commands that print aligned columns with text/tabwriter
%q around user input in error messages, so empty strings, trailing spaces and invisible characters show up
%+v and %T while debugging; %#v to turn a value you printed into a test fixture
A run(args, stdout, stderr) int entry point that table-driven tests call directly
strengths: Widths and precision count runes, so %-10s aligns İstanbul and Iğdır; C's printf counts bytes and misaligns them
%v prints any value, nested structs, slices and maps included, with no toString to write as in Java; maps come out key-sorted
Format mistakes never crash or corrupt memory as they can in C: they print a %! marker, and go vet (also run by go test) flags them first
Aligned tables need no dependency: text/tabwriter is in the standard library, where Python reaches for third-party tabulate
weaknesses: The compiler accepts any verb for any argument; only go vet catches %d with a string, so skip vet and the mistake ships
tabwriter assumes every rune is one column wide: emoji, East Asian wide characters and combining accents misalign. The package is frozen
os.Stdout has no buffer: each Printf is a write system call. A tool printing 100,000 lines needs a bufio.Writer, which C stdio and Python give you for free when stdout is a pipe

pitfalls.title: Errors and progress on stdout
pitfalls.detail: Anything on stdout becomes input for the next program in the pipe. Results go to stdout; usage, warnings, progress and errors go to stderr.
pitfalls.good: fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "mytool: %v\n", err)

pitfalls.title: os.Exit or log.Fatal deep in the code
pitfalls.detail: Both skip deferred calls, so a deferred bufio.Writer.Flush never runs and the last block of output is lost. Return errors up to run and exit only in main.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting tabwriter's Flush
pitfalls.detail: The writer cannot pad a column before it has seen every row, so it holds everything until Flush. No Flush, no table.

pitfalls.title: Exit codes outside 0-125
pitfalls.detail: os.Exit's docs ask for [0, 125] for portability: shells use 126 and 127 themselves and report a process killed by a signal as a status above 128.

quiz.q: What does fmt.Printf("%d\n", "42") do?
quiz.why: fmt reports bad verbs in its output instead of failing. go vet's printf check would have flagged the call.

quiz.q: fmt.Printf("[%-8s]", "İzmir"). How many spaces follow İzmir?
quiz.why: fmt widths count runes: İzmir is 5 runes (6 bytes), so 3 spaces pad it to 8.

quiz.q: Your tool prints "processing 3 files..." while it works. Where should that line go?
quiz.why: It is a diagnostic. On stdout it would end up in the file or the next command of a pipeline.

quiz.q: A helper three calls deep finds a bad argument. What is the idiomatic way to end with exit code 2?
options: Return an error up to run, which returns 2 to main
quiz.why: os.Exit and log.Fatal skip deferred cleanup, and a panic dumps a stack trace on the user. Exiting only in main keeps defers running and run testable.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A command-line tool talks through three channels. **stdout** carries the result: it is
what `|`, `>` and `$(...)` capture. **stderr** carries everything meant for the human
(usage, progress, warnings, errors); pipes pass it by. The **exit code** is what shells,
`&&`, Makefiles and CI read: 0 is success, anything else is failure.

`fmt` formats any value through verbs: `%v` for the default form, `%+v` and `%#v` for
more detail, `%q` for quoted strings, `%d`, `%x`, `%f` with width and precision flags.
Widths count runes, not bytes, which matters as soon as a Turkish name meets a column.
`text/tabwriter` computes column widths from the data, so tables align without you
measuring anything.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: the verbs look familiar, but there are no length modifiers (`%ld`, `%zu`); fmt
  knows each argument's type at run time. A mismatch prints a marker instead of
  undefined behaviour. Unlike stdio, `os.Stdout` is never buffered by Go.
- Java: `String.format` ≈ `fmt.Sprintf`, `toString()` ≈ a `String() string` method,
  `System.err` ≈ `os.Stderr`, `System.exit` ≈ `os.Exit` (both skip cleanup).
- Python: `print(..., file=sys.stderr)` ≈ `fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, ...)`, `repr()` ≈
  `%q`/`%#v`. `sys.exit(2)` raises `SystemExit`, so `finally` blocks run; `os.Exit` does
  not run deferred calls.
- Node: `console.log`/`console.error` map to stdout/stderr. Setting `process.exitCode`
  and returning is the same idea as `run` returning a code; `process.exit()` is `os.Exit`.

## Design notes

Keep `main` to one line, `os.Exit(run(os.Args[1:], os.Stdout, os.Stderr))`, and put the
program in `run`. Three things follow: deferred cleanup inside `run` always happens
before the process exits, tests drive the whole tool with `strings.Builder`s, and the
exit code is decided in exactly one place. Use 1 for "it failed" and 2 for "you called
it wrong", the code the `flag` package already uses.

When a tool prints a lot, wrap stdout once in `bufio.NewWriter` inside `run` and
`defer` its `Flush`; that is safe precisely because `run` returns normally. Write
errors as `tool: what failed: cause`, with `%q` around anything the user typed, so an
empty argument or a trailing space is visible in the message.

lessons.title: flag and subcommands, environment variables, stdin
lessons.summary: A FlagSet per command parses an explicit argument slice and returns errors instead of exiting; environment variables feed flag defaults, so flags win. stdin is just an io.Reader.

examples.title: The flag syntax rules, run against a FlagSet

annotations.note: flag.Parse() parses os.Args into package-level globals and, on error, exits with code 2. A FlagSet with ContinueOnError returns the error instead, so the same function serves main and a table-driven test.
XxxVar binds a flag to a struct field. The default and the help text are part of the definition, and flag builds the usage message from them: look at the stderr pane.
One dash or two are the same flag, and -name=value and -name value both work. Typed flags parse on the spot: 1.5s becomes a time.Duration, and "many" is rejected as an int.
Parsing stops at the first non-flag argument, so -v after a.txt is a file name. GNU getopt and Python's argparse accept flags after positionals; Go does not.
A boolean flag is switched off only with -v=false: in "-v false" the false would be a positional argument. "--" ends the flags, so a file name that starts with a dash survives.

With ContinueOnError, flag has already printed the error and the usage to fs.Output() (stderr by default); the caller only picks the exit code. -h and -help return flag.ErrHelp, which by convention exits 0.

examples.title: Subcommands, and an environment variable as the flag's default

annotations.note: A map from subcommand name to function is all the dispatch a small tool needs. strings.ToUpperSpecial with a nil SpecialCase has no overrides, so it is plain Unicode casing; unicode.TurkishCase maps i to İ and ı to I.
Start from the built-in default and replace it with the environment value if there is one. An empty variable counts as unset here.

One FlagSet per subcommand, named after it, so subcommands can define different flags. The value so far becomes the flag's default: an explicit -lang overwrites the environment, and -h shows the effective default. SetOutput sends flag's messages to the injected stderr.
flag checks syntax, not meaning: "de" is a valid string. Validate after parsing and treat a bad value as a usage error, code 2.
A map-backed getenv lets tests run without touching the process environment, which is global: testing's t.Setenv refuses to run in parallel tests for exactly that reason.
os.LookupEnv has exactly the parameter's type. os.Setenv changes this process and the children it starts later, never the shell that started it.

examples.title: A tiny wc: stdin is an io.Reader
examples.stdin:
Merhaba dünya
İstanbul'da yağmur var
çay mı, kahve mi?

annotations.note: count never mentions os.Stdin. main passes stdin, a test passes strings.NewReader, and a file argument would pass an *os.File: the same accept-a-Reader shape as in the reading-files lesson.
ScanLines strips "\n" and a "\r" before it, so CRLF input from Windows tools counts the same as LF input from Unix ones.
chars matches wc -m and bytes matches wc -c, minus the newlines. They differ by 5 here because ü, İ, ğ, ç and ı take two bytes each in UTF-8.

os.Stdin is an ordinary *os.File. Run without a pipe, the program waits for the user to type and end the input, which looks like a hang; tools that default to stdin usually say so in their usage text.

use_cases: Internal tools and one-off migrations where a dependency for argument parsing isn't worth it
git-style tools with subcommands (tool import, tool export), each with its own flags
Twelve-factor services: configuration from environment variables, overridable by flags during development
Unix filters that read stdin and write stdout, so they compose with grep, sort and jq
strengths: No dependency for small tools: flag, os and bufio are in the standard library, while the JDK has no argument parser at all
Typed flags (Int, Duration, Bool) parse and validate in one step: -timeout 1.5s arrives as a time.Duration, not a string to parse later
Usage text is generated from the definitions, so -h can't drift from the code
With a FlagSet, an injected getenv and an io.Reader, the whole CLI runs in-process in a test, with no subprocess
weaknesses: No GNU conventions: -v and --v are the same flag, there are no short/long aliases (-v/--verbose) and no combined short flags (-xvf)
Flags must come before positional arguments; users used to GNU tools put them last and get them treated as file names
No required flags, no subcommand tree, no config-file binding: you write the checks, or reach for a third-party package once the CLI grows

pitfalls.title: Flags after positional arguments
pitfalls.detail: tool report.txt -v leaves -v in fs.Args(). Document flags-first usage, or check Args() for leftovers that start with a dash.

pitfalls.title: Turning a boolean off with a separate word
pitfalls.detail: -dry-run false sets dry-run to true and adds "false" as a positional argument.
pitfalls.good: tool -dry-run=false input.csv

pitfalls.title: os.Getenv can't tell unset from empty
pitfalls.detail: Both return "". Use os.LookupEnv when an empty value means something different from a missing one.

pitfalls.title: flag.Parse in init() or in a library
pitfalls.detail: Since Go 1.13 test flags are registered when the test binary starts, so a package that parses flags during initialization can break go test. Parse once, in main or run, and keep flag definitions out of libraries.

pitfalls.title: Turkish text piped from Windows PowerShell 5.1
pitfalls.detail: Text piped into a native program is encoded with $OutputEncoding, which defaults to US-ASCII there: İ and ı arrive as '?'. Set $OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new() first.

quiz.q: fs defines a bool flag -v. What does fs.Parse([]string{"report.txt", "-v"}) leave you with?
options: An error: flags must come first
quiz.why: Parsing stops at the first non-flag argument without error; everything after it, -v included, is positional.

quiz.q: A bool flag defaults to true. How does the user switch it off?
quiz.why: Boolean flags take a value only in the -flag=value form; in -color false, false is a positional argument.

quiz.q: The casing tool has -lang and reads CASING_LANG. Which order of precedence does it implement?
quiz.why: The environment value becomes the flag's default, and an explicit flag overwrites the default.

quiz.q: Why does run take getenv func(string) (string, bool) instead of calling os.Getenv?
options: Tests can pass a map without changing the process-wide environment
quiz.why: The environment is global to the process; os.Setenv in one test leaks into others and blocks t.Parallel. Injection keeps tests independent.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A command-line program has three inputs: its arguments, its environment and its
standard input. The `flag` package turns arguments into typed values; a `FlagSet`
does it for an explicit slice, which is how you build subcommands and how you test.
`os.LookupEnv` reads the environment and tells "unset" from "empty". `os.Stdin` is an
`*os.File`, so everything that reads an `io.Reader` reads stdin.

The common shape is precedence: a built-in default, overridden by an environment
variable, overridden by a flag. With `flag` that takes three lines, because the
environment value simply becomes the flag's default.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: GNU `getopt` permutes arguments and supports `-xvf`; `flag` does neither and
  stops at the first positional argument. `getenv` returning `NULL` for unset is what
  `os.LookupEnv`'s boolean gives you.
- Python: `argparse` is the closer match (stdlib, generated help, subparsers), but it
  accepts options after positionals. `os.environ.get` ≈ `os.LookupEnv`.
- Java: there is no argument parser in the JDK; `flag` plays the role of picocli or
  commons-cli for small tools. `System.getenv` returns `null` for unset, like
  LookupEnv's `false`.
- Node: `process.argv.slice(2)` ≈ `os.Args[1:]`, `process.env` ≈ the environment,
  `process.stdin` ≈ `os.Stdin`, but in Go reading it is plain blocking code.

## Design notes

Keep `main` as the only place that touches the process: `os.Exit(run(os.Args[1:],
os.LookupEnv, os.Stdin, os.Stdout, os.Stderr))`. Everything else takes its inputs as
parameters, so a table-driven test calls `run` with a slice, a map-backed `getenv` and a
`strings.Reader`, in parallel, with no subprocess.

Stay with `flag` while the tool is small. Since Go 1.16, `fs.Func` handles a repeatable
flag (`-H a -H b`) without writing a `flag.Value` type. When you need GNU-style
`--long`/`-s` pairs, nested subcommands, shell completion or config-file binding,
that is the point to adopt a CLI library, not before. For anything you pipe in from
Windows, remember the shell decides the encoding: make it UTF-8 and the Go side needs
nothing special.

lessons.title: text/template vs html/template
lessons.summary: text/template and html/template share one template language and one API. html/template adds escaping that depends on where each value lands (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript), which is what stops XSS.

examples.title: A text report: range, else, with, methods and a FuncMap

annotations.note: {{range}} and {{with}} rebind the dot: to each Item, then to the Note. {{else}} runs when the slice is empty, and {{with}} skips its body for an empty Note. A dash inside the braces ({{- or -}}) trims the whitespace on that side, which is how a text template keeps control over its newlines.
.Total calls the method on Item, and printf is a built-in function with fmt's verbs. There is no arithmetic in the language: anything beyond comparisons is a method or a function you register.
Functions must be registered before Parse, which otherwise fails with function "upper" not defined. Must turns a parse error into a panic, the right reaction to a broken template constant.

Field names are resolved at Execute time, by reflection. The typo compiles, parses, and fails halfway through the output. Render into a buffer when a partial result would hurt, like a half-written HTTP response.

examples.title: The same template through both packages

annotations.note: One value in five contexts. Each needs its own escaping: entities in the body and in attributes, percent-encoding in a query string, JavaScript string syntax inside script, and a scheme check in href.

text/template copies the bytes, so the quote closes the attribute and the script tag runs. html/template turns the javascript: URL into #ZgotmplZ, and percent-encodes ş as %c5%9f, its two UTF-8 bytes.
Both types have the same constructors and Execute method, which makes switching packages a one-line import change, and makes picking the wrong one easy to miss.

examples.title: Layouts with block and Clone; template.HTML for trusted markup

annotations.note: {{block}} defines a named template and calls it in place, so the layout renders on its own with the defaults. A page redefines the blocks it needs with {{define}}.
The field's type decides the escaping. A string is escaped; a template.HTML is trusted and inserted as is. Use it only for markup your code produced or a sanitizer returned.

Clone copies the set of named templates, so each page gets its own title and content while base stays untouched. Clone returns an error once the template has been executed: build all pages at startup.
Converting user input to template.HTML disables the protection for that value: the onerror handler is now live in the page.

use_cases: text/template: generated Go code (go generate), config files, plain-text emails, reports
text/template: user-chosen output formats, the --format '{{.Name}}' flag several Go CLIs offer
html/template: server-rendered pages, HTML emails, admin screens without a frontend build
strengths: Escaping follows the context: html/template knows whether {{.}} sits in a body, an attribute, a URL or a script. Jinja2 or Handlebars autoescaping applies one HTML-entity escape everywhere, which does not make a javascript: URL or a value inside script safe
One template language and one API for both packages: learn it once, switch the import for HTML
Standard library, no build step; with embed.FS and ParseFS (Go 1.16) the templates ship inside the binary
Deliberately small language (no assignment to fields, no arithmetic), which keeps business logic in Go code
weaknesses: No compile-time checking: a misspelled field fails at Execute, while TSX checks every prop at compile time
Minimal expressions: no + or -, so even an index+1 needs a registered function
Typed strings (template.HTML, template.URL, template.JS) switch escaping off wholesale; a careless conversion reintroduces XSS
Whitespace control with {{- and -}} is fiddly when the output is plain text

pitfalls.title: Importing text/template for HTML
pitfalls.detail: The two packages have the same API, so the compiler can't tell you picked the wrong one, and an editor's auto-import may choose either. Check the import in every file that renders HTML.
pitfalls.good: import "html/template"

pitfalls.title: template.HTML(userInput)
pitfalls.detail: The conversion tells html/template the value is safe. Use typed strings only for constants, your own templates' output or a sanitizer's output.

pitfalls.title: Partial output on error
pitfalls.detail: Execute writes as it goes. In an HTTP handler, a failure halfway means a half page with status 200 already sent. Execute into a bytes.Buffer, then write it.

pitfalls.title: Missing map keys print <no value>
pitfalls.detail: With map data, text/template prints <no value> for an absent key instead of failing. Set t.Option("missingkey=error") to make it an error.

pitfalls.title: Unexported fields
pitfalls.detail: Templates use reflection and can't read lowercase fields: Execute fails with "name is an unexported field of struct type".

quiz.q: html/template renders <a href="{{.}}"> with the value javascript:alert(1). What comes out?
quiz.why: In a URL attribute, html/template only allows safe schemes; anything else is replaced by the marker #ZgotmplZ.

quiz.q: A template contains {{.Custmer}} (typo) and the data is a struct. When does the problem surface?
quiz.why: Fields are resolved by reflection while executing; Parse only checks syntax and function names.

quiz.q: When is converting a string to template.HTML appropriate?
options: For a user's bio that contains formatting
For markup your own code built or a sanitizer returned
quiz.why: template.HTML is inserted verbatim. It must never carry untrusted input.

quiz.q: You switch a working program from text/template to html/template. What usually has to change besides the import?
options: The templates need a new syntax
Usually nothing: the package adds the escaping itself
quiz.why: The packages share the template language and API; html/template adds the right escapers to each action by itself.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`text/template` is a small template language: `{{.Field}}` prints data, `{{range}}`,
`{{if}}` and `{{with}}` control the flow, pipelines pass values through functions like
shell pipes. Data comes in as any Go value and is read by reflection at execution time.

`html/template` wraps the same engine. It works out, for every action, where the
value will land (element text, attribute, URL, CSS, JavaScript) and inserts the
matching escaper. The template author is trusted; the data passed to `Execute` is
not. That is the whole defence against cross-site scripting, and it costs one import
line.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: Jinja2 has more expression power (arithmetic, filters, inheritance with
  `extends`). Go's `{{block}}` plus `Clone` covers layouts with less. Jinja2's
  autoescaping is one HTML-entity escape; Go's is context-aware.
- Java: Thymeleaf escapes `th:text` by default; `template.HTML` plays the role of
  its unescaped `th:utext`.
- JS/React: JSX escapes text children much as html/template does, and
  `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is the analogue of `template.HTML`. Template literals
  with string concatenation are the analogue of text/template: no escaping at all.
- C: think of text/template as a typed, reflective `printf` over whole documents.

## Design notes

Parse all templates once at startup, with `template.Must`, so a broken template stops
the program before it serves anything. Keep logic in Go: pass a view struct that
already holds the formatted values, rather than registering many functions. For a
site, put the layout and the pages in files, embed them with `embed.FS` and parse
them with `ParseFS`, cloning the layout per page as in the third example.

Use `text/template` only for output that is not HTML: code, configs, plain-text mail.
Anything a browser will render, including an "internal" admin page, goes through
`html/template`, and every `template.HTML` conversion deserves a code-review comment
saying where the markup came from.

lessons.title: log/slog: levels, attributes, handlers, JSON output
lessons.summary: log/slog (Go 1.21) logs a message plus typed key-value attributes; a Handler turns each record into text for people or JSON for machines. Loggers carry context with With, levels change at run time with a LevelVar.

examples.title: The same calls through TextHandler and JSONHandler

annotations.note: ReplaceAttr sees every attribute before it is written, including the built-in time, level and msg. Returning a zero Attr drops it. The same hook renames keys or masks personal data for a whole handler.
Before SetDefault, the top-level functions go through the old log package: stderr, its timestamp format, nothing in the compared output.

The call sites don't know the format; the Handler decides. Switching a service to JSON is a one-line change at startup. The Debug call produces nothing, because a handler's default minimum level is Info.

Alternating keys and values. TextHandler quotes a value only when it contains spaces, non-printing characters, quotes or "=", so İzmir stays bare and "Ayşe Yılmaz" is quoted. JSON keeps the UTF-8 as is, without \u escapes.

Typed constructors (slog.Duration, slog.Int) can't get out of step the way loose key-value pairs can. Group nests attributes: db.table in text, a nested object in JSON. A Duration is "1.5s" in text but nanoseconds (1500000000) in JSON.
An error value is written as its Error() string in both formats. Use a consistent key such as "err" so you can search for it.

examples.title: With, WithGroup, a LevelVar, and LogValuer for redaction

annotations.note: A type with a LogValue method decides its own log form, and the built-in handlers resolve it before writing. Token logs as REDACTED and User as its ID, without the e-mail, and no call site has to remember.
A LevelVar is a Leveler you can change while the program runs; its zero value is Info. HandlerOptions.Level also accepts a fixed level such as slog.LevelWarn.
With returns a new logger that adds request_id and method to every record. Pass reqLog down the request instead of repeating the IDs at each call.
The first Debug is dropped, the second appears: same code, level changed by level.Set with no restart.
WithGroup prefixes the keys of later attributes: payment.amount in text, a "payment" object in JSON. Attributes added earlier by With stay outside the group.
A key without a value compiles; the handler prints !BADKEY. go vet's slog check reports the call ("missing a final value").

examples.title: One logger, two audiences: NewMultiHandler (Go 1.26) and SetDefault

annotations.note: Each handler has its own minimum level and format. stdout stands in for a log collector here; a CLI whose stdout carries results sends all logs to stderr instead.

NewMultiHandler (Go 1.26) passes each record to every handler that is enabled for its level. Before 1.26 this took a small hand-written Handler. SetDefault makes the logger the target of slog.Info and friends.
Both records reach the JSON handler; only the warning reaches the text handler, which is the line in the stderr pane.
After SetDefault, log.Printf output becomes an Info record on the same handler, so old code joins the structured stream unchanged while you migrate it.

use_cases: Services: one JSON object per line on stdout, for a collector such as Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch
Request-scoped loggers: logger.With("request_id", id) created in middleware and passed down
Raising verbosity in production for a while with a LevelVar, without a restart
Migrating a codebase from log.Printf gradually: SetDefault routes the old calls through the new handler
strengths: In the standard library since Go 1.21, so most programs need no logging dependency; in Java, java.util.logging, SLF4J and Log4j still compete
Call sites are format-agnostic: the Handler chooses text or JSON, and switching is one line at startup
Redaction lives on the type (LogValuer), not at hundreds of call sites
Logger.LogAttrs with typed attributes avoids allocations, so logging on hot paths stays cheap
weaknesses: Key-value arguments are ...any: a missing value compiles and prints !BADKEY; only go vet catches it
Arguments are evaluated before the level check: Debug("x", "dump", expensive()) pays for expensive() even when Debug is off
The built-in handlers ignore the context.Context: getting a request or trace ID from ctx into the output needs a small custom Handler
TextHandler joins group keys with dots without escaping, so a.b.c is ambiguous to a parser; use JSON when machines read the logs

pitfalls.title: Unpaired keys and values
pitfalls.detail: The variadic list is untyped. Run go vet, whose slog check catches it (the vet subset that go test runs does not include it), or use slog.String, slog.Int and friends.
pitfalls.good: logger.Info("login", slog.String("user", name))

pitfalls.title: Paying for disabled debug logs
pitfalls.detail: Arguments are computed before the handler checks the level. Wrap expensive values in a LogValuer, or guard the call with logger.Enabled(ctx, slog.LevelDebug).

pitfalls.title: Durations in JSON are nanoseconds
pitfalls.detail: slog.Duration becomes an integer in JSON (1500000000) but 1.5s in text. Pick a unit in the key (took_ms) or convert in ReplaceAttr so dashboards agree.

pitfalls.title: Secrets and personal data in logs
pitfalls.detail: Log an e-mail address once and it is in every backup of your log store. Give sensitive types a LogValue method, or mask keys in ReplaceAttr.

quiz.q: JSONHandler logs slog.Duration("took", 1500*time.Millisecond). What appears in the output?
quiz.why: A Duration is an int64 count of nanoseconds, and the JSON handler writes the number; TextHandler writes the String form.

quiz.q: logger.Info("login", "user") has a key without a value. What happens?
options: The record is logged with !BADKEY=user; go vet warns
quiz.why: The arguments are ...any, so the compiler accepts it. The handler marks the stray value, and vet's slog check reports the call.

quiz.q: Where does a type-wide rule like "never log the API token" belong?
options: In a LogValue method on the token type
In a comment above the struct
quiz.why: The built-in handlers resolve LogValuer values before writing, so the rule holds wherever the value is logged.

quiz.q: After slog.SetDefault(l), what happens to log.Printf calls?
options: They still print in the old format to stderr
They become Info records on l's handler
quiz.why: SetDefault also redirects the log package's default logger to l's Handler, at the level set by SetLogLoggerLevel (Info by default).

lessons.body:
## Concept

A structured log record is a level, a message and a list of typed attributes, not one
formatted string. `log/slog` (Go 1.21) separates the two halves: a `Logger` collects
records at call sites, and a `Handler` decides which records to keep and how to write
them. The standard library ships `TextHandler` (`key=value` lines for people) and
`JSONHandler` (one JSON object per line for machines). Because messages stay constant
and the variables become attributes, you can search for `msg="payment failed"` and
group by `err` instead of writing regular expressions over prose.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `Logger` ≈ an SLF4J logger, `Handler` ≈ a Logback appender plus encoder,
  `With` ≈ MDC values, but explicit and passed as a value instead of thread-local.
- Python: `logging` with a JSON formatter and `extra={...}`; `logger.With` is closer to
  structlog's `bind`. Levels are numbers in both (slog: Debug -4, Info 0, Warn 4, Error 8).
- Node: very close to pino: one JSON object per line, child loggers (`pino.child`) ≈
  `With`, levels filtered before formatting.
- C/C++: no standard equivalent; spdlog-style sinks are the `Handler` idea.

## Design notes

Configure logging once in `main`: build the handler (JSON in production, text in a
terminal) with a `LevelVar` as its level, and pass the `*slog.Logger` to the
components that log, as a constructor parameter. `slog.SetDefault` is for the parts you
don't control, such as libraries still calling `log.Printf`. Request-scoped attributes
come from `With` in the HTTP middleware.

Keep messages constant and put variables in attributes. Choose key names once
(`err`, `user_id`, `request_id`) and stick to them: the log store indexes keys, not
your intentions. For a CLI, logs and diagnostics go to stderr so stdout stays clean for
results, as in the fmt lesson; for a service, the collector usually reads stdout.

lessons.title: Slices and maps: len/cap, append, aliasing, nil maps, comma-ok
lessons.summary: A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) over an array, so slicing shares memory and append may or may not. A map returns the zero value for missing keys, tells you with comma-ok, and iterates in random order.

examples.title: Slices share their backing array until append runs out of room

annotations.note: arr[1:3] copies nothing: s points at arr[1], has length 2, and capacity 4 because arr has four elements from index 1 on.
Writes through s land in arr. append with spare capacity writes into the same array too, overwriting arr[3], which other code may still be using.
Two more elements don't fit, so append allocates a new array and copies. From then on s and arr are independent. Whether append copied depends on capacity, not on anything visible at the call.
The classic bug: a and b both append into base's spare capacity, so the second append overwrites the first. a[3] is 2, not 1.
base[:3:3] sets capacity to 3, so each append must copy and a and b get their own arrays. slices.Clone(base) is the other way out.

examples.title: Maps: comma-ok, key normalization, random order, nil maps

annotations.note: A missing key yields the zero value, not an exception or undefined. The second result, ok, is the only way to tell "stored 0" from "not there".

Keys are compared byte for byte, so case-insensitive keys need a normalized form. strings.ToLower maps ILIK to ilik, merging lukewarm with bone marrow; unicode.TurkishCase maps I to ı and İ to i, which is right for Turkish text and wrong for English.
fmt sorts map keys when printing (since Go 1.12), which is why this output is stable. That says nothing about range.
The runtime randomizes iteration order on purpose, so code that depends on it breaks in tests instead of after an upgrade. slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (Go 1.23) gives a stable order.
A nil map behaves like an empty one for reads, len, delete and range, but storing into it panics. A struct with a map field needs a constructor or a lazy make.

examples.title: Passing slices to functions, range copies, nil vs empty

annotations.note: The slice header is copied into the parameter, but it points at the caller's array, so element writes are visible to the caller.
append changes the parameter's length (and maybe its pointer); the caller's header is untouched. If the caller's slice had spare capacity, the new element even lands in its array, invisibly.
Return the slice, exactly like append: xs = add(xs, 4). The compiler rejects a bare append(xs, 4) whose result is unused.
The range value is a copy of each element. To change elements, index: for i := range xs { xs[i] *= 10 }.
A nil slice and an empty one both have length 0 and work with range and append. They differ in == nil and in encoding/json, which writes null for nil and [] for empty; API clients often care.

use_cases: Slices: every ordered collection, buffers, results of queries, function arguments of variable length
Maps: lookups by key, counting, grouping, de-duplication; map[K]struct{} as a set
Full slice expression or slices.Clone: handing out part of a slice that the receiver may append to
Sorted keys of a map: stable output for logs, tests, golden files and APIs
strengths: Slicing is O(1) and copies nothing, unlike Python's or JavaScript's slice, which copy
comma-ok separates a missing key from a stored zero value without exceptions (Python's KeyError) or undefined
Zero values are usable: a nil slice can be appended to and ranged over, a nil map can be read, so empty collections need no setup in most code
Randomized map order makes order-dependent code fail early, in tests, unlike Java's HashMap whose order merely happens to be stable
weaknesses: Whether append shares or copies depends on capacity, so aliasing bugs appear only for some inputs
No ordered map in the standard library; sorted output means sorting the keys
Maps are not safe for concurrent writes: the runtime aborts with 'concurrent map writes'. Use a sync.Mutex or sync.Map
nil and empty slices look the same in Go code but differ in JSON (null vs [])

pitfalls.title: Two appends into one slice's spare capacity
pitfalls.detail: Both results share the array and the second append overwrites the first. Cap the capacity with s[:len(s):len(s)] or copy with slices.Clone before appending.
pitfalls.good: a := append(slices.Clone(base), 1); b := append(slices.Clone(base), 2)

pitfalls.title: Writing to a nil map in a zero-value struct
pitfalls.detail: var c Cache; c.items["k"] = v panics. Initialize the map in a constructor (NewCache) or with if c.items == nil { c.items = map[string]V{} }.

pitfalls.title: Keeping a small slice of a large array
pitfalls.detail: header := data[:16] keeps the whole data array reachable. Copy what you keep (slices.Clone) when the source is big.

pitfalls.title: Changing a struct stored in a map
pitfalls.detail: m[k].Count++ does not compile (cannot assign to struct field in map): map values are not addressable. Read, modify and store back, or store pointers.
pitfalls.good: v := m["a"]; v.Count++; m["a"] = v

quiz.q: base := make([]int, 3, 10); a := append(base, 1); b := append(base, 2). What is a[3]?
quiz.why: Both appends write index 3 of base's array, which has room. a and b share it, so the second write wins.

quiz.q: m is map[string]int without the key "k". What does v, ok := m["k"] give?
quiz.why: Missing keys yield the zero value; ok reports whether the key was present.

quiz.q: In Python a[1:3] creates a new list. What does a[1:3] create in Go?
options: A slice that shares a's backing array
quiz.why: Slicing builds a new header over the same array; writes through either are visible to both.

quiz.q: var m map[string]int. Which operation panics?
quiz.why: A nil map behaves like an empty read-only map; only storing into it panics.

further_reading.title: Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of 'append'
The Go Programming Language Specification: Slice expressions

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go's two built-in collections cover nearly everything. A **slice** `[]T` is a
three-word header: a pointer into an underlying array, a length, and a capacity (how
many elements the array has from that pointer on). Slicing makes a new header over
the same array; `append` writes into the spare capacity when there is some and
allocates a bigger array when there isn't. An array `[N]T` is a fixed-size value that
is copied on assignment, and you rarely use it directly.

A **map** `map[K]V` is a hash table with comparable keys. Reading a missing key
returns the zero value of `V`; `v, ok := m[k]` tells you whether the key was there.
Iteration order is unspecified and deliberately randomized. Maps and slices are both
cheap to pass around: you copy a small header, not the data.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python/JS**: `a[1:3]` and `arr.slice(1, 3)` copy; Go's `a[1:3]` aliases. Python
  dicts and JS `Map` keep insertion order; Go maps keep none.
- **Java**: a slice is like `ArrayList.subList`, a view that writes through, except
  that `append` may silently detach it. A missing map key gives a zero value, not
  `null`, and deleting during `range` is allowed instead of throwing
  `ConcurrentModificationException`.
- **C**: a slice is `struct { T *ptr; size_t len, cap; }` passed by value, and
  `append` is a `realloc` that may move the data. The same rule applies: after a
  possible reallocation, use the returned value.
- **C++**: like `std::vector`, but a sub-slice is a view (`std::span`) that can still
  grow into its parent's storage.

## How it works

```
arr := [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
s := arr[1:3]          s = {ptr: &arr[1], len: 2, cap: 4}

arr  [ 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 ]
           ^ s[0]
           |--len--|
           |------cap------|
```

`append(s, x)` checks `len < cap`. If so, it stores `x` at `arr[3]` and returns a
header with `len` 3, same pointer. If not, it allocates a larger array, copies, and
returns a header pointing there. The growth factor is an implementation detail; the
spec only promises a "sufficiently large" array.

## Design notes

Every slice rule follows from "the header is a value, the array is shared". So:
always assign the result of `append`; return slices from functions that grow them;
and when you hand out a slice of your internal state, give a copy (`slices.Clone`) or
cap it (`s[:n:n]`) so the receiver cannot write into your array. Preallocate with
`make([]T, 0, n)` when you know the size. For maps, decide the key's canonical form
before inserting: for user-entered Turkish text that means choosing between
`strings.ToLower` and `strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` based on the
text's language, not the server's locale.

lessons.title: The slices and maps packages, copy, clear
lessons.summary: Since Go 1.21 the generic slices and maps packages, plus the min, max and clear built-ins, replace most hand-written search, sort, de-dup, filter and merge loops. Go 1.23 iterators connect them.

examples.title: Search and sort without writing the loop

annotations.note: Three loops you no longer write. Index returns -1 when absent; Max panics on an empty slice, so check len first when it can be empty.

Sort works in place on any ordered element type. BinarySearch needs sorted input and returns where the value is (or would be inserted) plus whether it was found, instead of Java's negative-index encoding.

The comparison returns negative, zero or positive, like Java's Comparator. cmp.Or (Go 1.22) returns its first non-zero argument, which turns "by region, then by population" into one expression. SortFunc is not stable; use SortStableFunc to keep input order of ties.
IndexFunc and ContainsFunc take a predicate. IndexFunc returns -1 when nothing matches, so check before indexing.

String order is byte order of the UTF-8 encoding, so Ç (0xC3...) and İ (0xC4...) sort after Z. Turkish alphabetical order needs a collator: golang.org/x/text/collate with language.Turkish, outside the standard library.

examples.title: Edit in place: Compact, Insert, Delete, DeleteFunc, copy, clear

annotations.note: slices.Values turns tags into an iterator and Sorted collects it into a new sorted slice, leaving tags alone (slices.Sort would sort in place). Compact, like Unix uniq, only drops adjacent repeats, hence the sort first.
Insert shifts elements up and may reallocate: always use the result, as with append.
Delete shifts the tail down in the same array and zeroes the freed slots (Go 1.22), which also lets the garbage collector reclaim what they pointed to. before still covers four slots and shows that.
DeleteFunc is an in-place filter: no second slice, but the input's array is reused, so don't keep using the old slice.
copy copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements and returns that count. It never grows dst: a destination made with make([]T, 0, n) has length 0 and receives nothing.
Slices cannot be compared with == (only with nil), so slices.Equal does it. Clone allocates a new array, so writes to c don't reach nums.
clear on a slice sets each element to its zero value and keeps the length. To empty a slice for reuse, use s = s[:0] instead.

examples.title: maps: Clone, Copy, Keys, DeleteFunc, Equal, Collect, clear

annotations.note: Clone then Copy is the merge-with-defaults idiom: keys from user overwrite. Clone is shallow: a value that is a slice or map is shared between the clone and the original.
maps.Keys and maps.Values return iterators (iter.Seq), not slices, and in random order. slices.Sorted collects and sorts in one call; slices.Collect collects without sorting.
DeleteFunc removes every entry the predicate accepts. Maps can't be compared with ==, so maps.Equal compares keys and values.
Iterators compose: slices.All yields index/element pairs and maps.Collect builds a map from any key/value sequence.
clear on a map deletes every entry and the map stays writable, unlike assigning nil. That matters when other code holds the same map.

use_cases: Membership, position and extremes: slices.Contains, Index, IndexFunc, Max, Min
Sorting by several keys: slices.SortFunc with cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(...), ...)
De-duplicating: slices.Sort then slices.Compact, or collect into a map[T]struct{}
Configuration merges and copies: maps.Clone, maps.Copy; stable output with slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))
Resetting a cache or buffer without reallocating: clear(m), s = s[:0]
strengths: Generic and type-checked: slices.SortFunc receives typed elements, unlike sort.Slice's index-based less function, and its docs note it is usually faster
One idiom for everything ordered: cmp.Compare and cmp.Or give Java Comparator chaining without a builder API
Iterators (Go 1.23) connect the packages: maps.Keys feeds slices.Sorted without an intermediate slice in your code
In-place operations (Delete, Compact, DeleteFunc) avoid allocations, and zero the tail so the GC can reclaim it
weaknesses: In-place operations mutate the shared array: other slices of it see shifted or zeroed elements
No locale-aware string sorting in the standard library; Turkish order needs golang.org/x/text/collate
No map/filter/reduce returning new slices: a transformation is still a loop, or DeleteFunc for filtering in place
maps.Clone and slices.Clone are shallow; deep copies are hand-written

pitfalls.title: Compact without sorting
pitfalls.detail: Compact only removes adjacent duplicates: [go sql go] stays as it is. Sort first, or use a map if order must be kept.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring the result of Insert, Delete, Compact or DeleteFunc
pitfalls.detail: They return the new slice header; the old variable keeps the old length and now sees shifted or zeroed elements.
pitfalls.good: s = slices.Delete(s, 0, 1)

pitfalls.title: copy into a zero-length destination
pitfalls.detail: copy(dst, src) with dst := make([]T, 0, len(src)) copies nothing. Use make([]T, len(src)), or simply slices.Clone(src).

pitfalls.title: Sorting user-visible Turkish names with slices.Sort
pitfalls.detail: Byte order puts Çorum and İzmir after Zonguldak. Collate with golang.org/x/text/collate (language.Turkish), or sort in PostgreSQL with a Turkish ICU collation.

quiz.q: s := []string{"go", "sql", "go"}; s = slices.Compact(s). What is s?
quiz.why: Compact only collapses runs of adjacent equal elements. Sort first to remove all duplicates.

quiz.q: dst := make([]int, 0, 3); n := copy(dst, []int{1, 2, 3}). What is n?
quiz.why: copy copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements; len(dst) is 0. Capacity doesn't count.

quiz.q: What does clear(s) do to a slice of length 3?
options: Zeroes the three elements, length stays 3
quiz.why: For slices, clear zeroes elements up to the length. For maps it deletes all entries.

quiz.q: How do you sort cities by region, then by population descending?
options: slices.SortFunc with cmp.Or(strings.Compare(a.Region, b.Region), cmp.Compare(b.Pop, a.Pop))
quiz.why: cmp.Or returns the first non-zero comparison, so the population only breaks ties within a region; swapping a and b sorts descending.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Built-in functions (copy, clear)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go 1.21 added generic `slices` and `maps` packages, the `cmp` package with
`cmp.Compare` (and `cmp.Or` in 1.22), and the `min`, `max` and `clear` built-ins. Go
1.23 added iterators, so `maps.Keys`, `slices.Values` and `slices.All` produce
sequences that `slices.Sorted`, `slices.Collect` and `maps.Collect` consume. Together
they cover the loops every codebase used to repeat: search (`Contains`, `Index`,
`BinarySearch`), sort (`Sort`, `SortFunc`, `SortStableFunc`), edit in place (`Insert`,
`Delete`, `DeleteFunc`, `Compact`, `Reverse`), compare (`Equal`) and copy (`Clone`). The
older built-ins remain: `copy` moves elements between slices, `clear` resets a map or
zeroes a slice.

Before Go 1.21 you would have written `sort.Slice(s, func(i, j int) bool {...})` or a
loop for each of these. `go fix` (Go 1.26) rewrites many such loops for you, as the
modernizers lesson shows.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(City::region).thenComparing(...))` becomes
  `slices.SortFunc` with `cmp.Or`. `Arrays.binarySearch` encodes "not found" as a
  negative insertion point; `slices.BinarySearch` returns `(pos, found)`.
- **Python**: `sorted(xs, key=...)` has no direct equivalent: Go comparison functions
  are three-way, so compare the derived keys with `cmp.Compare`. `{**defaults, **user}`
  is `maps.Clone` plus `maps.Copy`.
- **JS**: `filter` returns a new array, `slices.DeleteFunc` filters in place.
  `Object.assign` ≈ `maps.Copy`; `structuredClone` is deep, `maps.Clone` is shallow.
- **C++**: `std::sort`, `std::lower_bound` and `std::unique` map to `Sort`,
  `BinarySearch` and `Compact`, except that `Compact` returns the shortened slice
  instead of an iterator you must pass to `erase`.

## Design notes

Reach for the library before writing a loop; it states intent in one line and its
edge cases (empty input, ties, zeroing) are documented. Remember which calls mutate:
`Sort`, `Delete`, `Compact`, `Insert` and `DeleteFunc` work on the slice you pass,
while `Sorted`, `Clone` and `Collect` allocate. Pick ordered output deliberately:
`fmt` sorts map keys for you, `range` and `maps.Keys` never do. For text shown to
users, byte order is rarely the right order; when the data lives in PostgreSQL, sort
there with a Turkish collation, and in Go use `golang.org/x/text/collate`.

lessons.title: Structs, embedding, tags, value vs reference semantics
lessons.summary: A struct is a value: assignment copies its fields, shallowly. Embedding promotes another type's fields and methods without inheritance or virtual dispatch, and tags attach metadata that encoding/json and database libraries read through reflection.

examples.title: Struct values, comparison, map keys, shallow copies

annotations.note: The zero value is a usable Point, with no constructor. Keyed literals keep compiling when fields are added; positional ones like Point{3, 4} are fine only for small, stable types, and vet flags them for struct types from other packages. q := p copies the struct, so q.X = 100 leaves p alone.
== compares field by field when every field is comparable, so a struct makes a natural composite map key, without the hashCode and equals pair Java needs.
The copy is shallow: r2 got its own Name but shares the Stops array with r1, so r1 sees {9 9}. Route has a slice field, which also makes r1 == r2 a compile error: slices are not comparable.
An anonymous struct type for a one-off shape, the standard layout of a table-driven test. %+v prints field names.
struct{} occupies no memory, so map[string]struct{} is the idiomatic set; the comma-ok read is the membership test.

examples.title: Embedding promotes fields and methods, without virtual dispatch

annotations.note: This is the difference from inheritance. Summary's receiver is the embedded Audit, which knows nothing about Order, so a.Label() calls Audit.Label even when reached through o: "audit v2", not "order 7". There is no template method by overriding; use an interface field or a function value.
An embedded field has a type and no name; its name is the type's name, so o.Audit is still reachable. Audit's fields and methods are promoted: o.By and o.Touch work as if Order declared them.
A method declared on Order hides the promoted one with the same name: the shallowest depth wins, for fields and methods alike.

New in Go 1.27: promoted fields can be keys in a composite literal. Before, you wrote Order{ID: 7, Audit: Audit{By: "ayşe", Version: 1}}; the compiler reports the version needed if the go line is older, and go fix's embedlit modernizer rewrites the old form once it isn't.
Touch has a pointer receiver. o is addressable, so o.Touch means (&o.Audit).Touch and changes o's embedded Audit in place.

examples.title: Struct tags drive encoding/json and database mapping

annotations.note: A tag is a raw string literal of key:"value" pairs; the compiler doesn't interpret it, and go vet's structtag check catches malformed ones. json renames fields; db is read by libraries such as pgx or sqlx.

omitempty drops false, 0, "", nil and empty collections, but never a struct, so the zero Joined time is still written. omitzero (Go 1.24) drops zero values and uses an IsZero method when the type has one, as time.Time does.
json:"-" keeps a field out of JSON entirely. That is the tool for exported fields; unexported ones are skipped anyway.

encoding/json falls back to a case-insensitive match, so "NAME" fills Name. encoding/json/v2 (Go 1.27) matches exactly unless you pass MatchCaseInsensitiveNames. If a client sends both "name" and "NAME", v1 keeps whichever comes last, without an error.
Tag.Lookup separates "absent" from "empty". This loop is, in miniature, how a row-to-struct mapper finds its column names.

use_cases: Domain records, request and response bodies, configuration: a struct per shape
Composite map keys: map[Point]int, map[struct{ user, day string }]int
Mixing in shared fields and helpers (timestamps, audit info, a sync.Mutex) by embedding
Mapping to JSON and database columns with tags instead of hand-written conversion code
strengths: Values by default: a copied struct can't be changed behind your back (except through its pointer, slice and map fields), unlike Java objects, which are always references
Comparable structs work with == and as map keys with no equals/hashCode to write or get wrong
Embedding reuses fields and methods without a class hierarchy; there is no fragile base class, because the embedded type never calls back into the outer one
Tags keep wire names and column names next to the field they describe, like Java annotations but read only at runtime through reflect
weaknesses: Copies are shallow and silent: a struct with a slice or map field shares that data with every copy
Tags are unchecked strings: a typo like json:"naem" or a missing colon compiles; go vet catches syntax, not misspelled names
Embedding exposes the embedded type's whole method set, so embedding *sync.Mutex or a big type widens your API by accident
Large structs passed by value cost a copy on every call; pass pointers when they are big or must be mutated

pitfalls.title: Expecting virtual dispatch through embedding
pitfalls.detail: A method of the embedded type always calls the embedded type's methods. If behavior must vary, put an interface or a func field in the struct.

pitfalls.title: Modifying a copy in a range loop
pitfalls.detail: for _, o := range orders { o.Total = 0 } changes copies. Index instead, or store pointers.
pitfalls.good: for i := range orders { orders[i].Total = 0 }

pitfalls.title: omitempty on a struct or time.Time field
pitfalls.detail: It never omits structs, so a zero time is encoded as 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z. Use omitzero (Go 1.24) or a pointer field.

pitfalls.title: Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex
pitfalls.detail: The copy gets its own, possibly locked, mutex and protects nothing. go vet's copylocks check reports it; pass such structs by pointer.

quiz.q: type Base struct{}; func (Base) Name() string { return "base" }; func (b Base) Hello() string { return b.Name() }. type D struct{ Base } with its own Name returning "d". What does D{}.Hello() return?
quiz.why: Hello's receiver is the embedded Base, so it calls Base.Name. Embedding promotes methods; it doesn't make them virtual.

quiz.q: r2 := r1 where Route has Name string and Stops []Point. After r2.Stops[0] = p, what does r1.Stops[0] hold?
quiz.why: Assignment copies the slice header, not the array; both Routes share Stops.

quiz.q: Which struct can be used as a map key?
quiz.why: Map keys must be comparable; slices and maps aren't, and neither is a struct containing them.

quiz.q: A time.Time field tagged json:"at,omitempty" holds the zero time. What does json.Marshal do?
quiz.why: omitempty doesn't apply to structs. omitzero does, using time.Time's IsZero method.

The Go Programming Language Specification: Composite literals

lessons.body:
## Concept

A struct is a sequence of named fields, and a struct value *is* its fields: no header,
no hidden pointer, no identity. Assigning, passing or returning a struct copies every
field. That copy is shallow: pointer, slice and map fields are copied as references,
so the copy shares what they point to. A struct is comparable with `==`, and usable as
a map key, when all its fields are.

**Embedding** a type (a field with a type but no name) promotes its fields and methods
to the outer struct, so `o.By` means `o.Audit.By` and `o.Touch()` means
`o.Audit.Touch()`. It is composition with shorter syntax: the embedded value never
learns about the struct around it, so there is no overriding and no virtual dispatch.
Polymorphism comes from interfaces instead.

**Tags** are string literals after a field's type. The compiler ignores them;
packages such as `encoding/json` read them through `reflect` to choose names and
options.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: there are no classes, only structs with methods. Values instead of
  references by default, `==` instead of `equals`/`hashCode`, embedding instead of
  `extends` (without `super` and without overriding), tags instead of annotations.
- **C**: a struct is laid out like a C struct and copied by value, as in C. Embedding
  is the "first member is the base struct" trick, made official and given promoted
  names.
- **C++**: closest to a struct with public members. Embedding resembles inheritance
  in which no method is `virtual`, minus the implicit upcast: an `Order` is not an
  `Audit`, you pass `o.Audit` explicitly.
- **Python/JS**: no dynamic attributes; the field set is fixed at compile time. A JS
  object spread `{...a}` is shallow in the same way a Go struct copy is.

## Design notes

Make the zero value useful (`var buf bytes.Buffer` works, so should your types), and
prefer keyed literals so adding a field never breaks callers. Embed to reuse
behavior you would otherwise forward method by method, but only when the embedded
type's whole method set belongs in your API; otherwise use a named field. When a
struct holds a mutex, slices that must not be shared, or is large, give it pointer
methods and pass `*T`. Tags are a contract with another system (an API, a table):
keep them stable, test them with a round trip, and remember that `encoding/json`
matches names loosely while `encoding/json/v2` is strict.

lessons.title: Goroutines and channels: unbuffered, close, ranging
lessons.summary: A goroutine is a concurrently running function; a channel passes values between goroutines. An unbuffered channel is a handoff: both sides wait until the value changes hands.

examples.title: Three workers receiving from one channel
examples.nondeterminism_note: Which worker takes which job is the scheduler's decision and varies run to run. Sorted-lines comparison makes the check about the *set* of events: every job 1-6 handed to some worker, each exactly once. Output is also post-sorted in the example itself for a fully stable lesson view.

annotations.note: Launching three goroutines is just `go f()`. Each runs the same loop; the runtime schedules them on OS threads for you.
An unbuffered channel send blocks until a receiver takes the value: the sender knows the work was handed off, unlike a queue drop.
Close signals "no more values". The range loop ends when the channel is closed AND drained. Only the sender should close: a send on a closed channel panics, and so does closing it twice.

wg.Wait() blocks until the counter hits zero. The counter was incremented before `go` ran the goroutine — decrementing happens in the goroutine. Workers share the map only to collect results, under a mutex; the channel itself passed each job to exactly one worker.

use_cases: Fan-out work across workers while results stream back through a channel
Signaling completion (close a done channel) without locks
strengths: Goroutines are cheap (KB-scale stacks): thousands are normal, unlike Java's thread-per-request
Channels pass ownership of data between goroutines: no lock to forget
The compiler checks send/receive direction in typed channels
weaknesses: Wrong ownership (who closes, who reads) produces deadlocks or panics at runtime, not compile time
A nil channel blocks forever; a send on a closed channel panics
Unbuffered channels couple sender to receiver timing; sometimes you want a buffer

pitfalls.title: Closing a channel from the receiver side
pitfalls.detail: The sender then panics on send. Close belongs to the sender: it means 'I will send no more'.
