pitfalls.title: Forgetting wg.Wait() or leaking goroutines
pitfalls.detail: main returning kills all goroutines instantly, half-finished. Use WaitGroup or range over the channel.

pitfalls.title: Sharing a variable across goroutines instead of sending it
pitfalls.detail: Concurrent map writes and read/write races are real. Race detector: go test -race.

quiz.q: What does a receive from a closed channel yield after it is drained?
quiz.why: Closed + drained channels return zero values with ok=false; that's how range terminates.

quiz.q: Who should close a channel?
quiz.why: Close means 'no more sends coming', which only the sender can know.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`go f()` starts a goroutine: a function running concurrently with the caller. Channels are
typed conduits: `ch <- v` sends, `v := <-ch` receives. An unbuffered channel makes both
sides wait for the handoff; a closed channel signals "no more values", and `for v := range ch`
ends when the channel closes.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: goroutines ≈ virtual threads; channels ≈ BlockingQueue, but first-class in the
  language with select (later lesson) and no checked InterruptedException.
- C/C++: no mutex to forget, no data race through the channel — the value itself moves.
- JS: like posting messages to a Web Worker, but with shared memory processes cheaply and
  many goroutines instead of two isolated heaps.

## Design notes

Share memory by communicating: send the data, don't guard it with a mutex when ownership
actually transfers. A useful rule this lesson plants: whoever *sends* owns the channel and
closes it; receivers only read. When several senders exist, wrap close in a sync.Once or
collect via WaitGroup first — covered in the sync lesson.

lessons.title: select: timeouts, default, and multiplexing
lessons.summary: select waits on several channel operations at once and runs one that can proceed. A timer channel gives you timeouts, default gives you non-blocking sends and receives, and a for-select loop merges many inputs.

examples.title: A timeout is just another case

annotations.note: Capacity 1 is what makes the timeout safe. With an unbuffered channel the goroutine would block forever on line 18 once await had given up: one leaked goroutine per timed-out call.
select blocks until one case can proceed. time.After returns a channel that receives once after the duration, so a timeout is an ordinary case, not a special language feature.
The reply wins here: the goroutine can send at once, and a one-second timer is nowhere near firing.

Nothing arrives within 50ms, so the timer case runs. The slow call isn't stopped by the timeout; closing slow lets it finish, and its send lands in the buffer nobody reads. Stopping the work itself is what context is for (lesson 4).

examples.title: default for non-blocking sends and receives, and random choice

annotations.note: default runs when no other case is ready, so this select never blocks. On a full buffer the send case isn't ready and the event is dropped: load shedding instead of backpressure.

A non-blocking receive drains what is buffered and stops. Without default the third receive would block forever, and with no other goroutine alive the runtime would stop the program with "all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!".

Both channels are closed, so both cases are always ready. The spec requires a uniform pseudo-random choice, so after 1000 rounds both counters are positive (missing one has probability 2^-999). Case order gives no priority.

examples.title: for-select over several inputs, nil channels to switch cases off

annotations.note: time.After is called once, before the loop, so the second covers the whole merge. Called inside the select it would create a fresh timer on every iteration: an idle timeout that never fires while messages keep trickling in.

A receive from a closed channel is always ready and yields ok == false. Without the nil assignment this case would win again and again, spinning the loop. A nil channel never proceeds, which switches the case off.
continue applies to the for loop. break here would only leave the select, the same trap as break inside a switch.
Values from one channel arrive in the order they were sent. Across channels there is no order, so the output is grouped per source rather than printed as received.

use_cases: Timeouts around any channel operation: a worker's reply, a result from a pool, a lock implemented as a channel
Load shedding: try-send with default to drop metrics or audit events instead of blocking the request path
Event loops: one goroutine owns some state and reacts to commands, ticker ticks and shutdown arriving on different channels
Merging streams: fan-in of several producers, with nil channels switching off the finished ones
strengths: Waiting on several queues, a timer and a shutdown signal is one statement. Java has BlockingQueue.poll(timeout) for a single queue and nothing built in for many
The random choice among ready cases prevents starvation by construction; there is no fairness flag to remember, unlike Java's ReentrantLock(true)
Sends and receives are both cases, so backpressure (block) and load shedding (default) are the same construct with one line changed
weaknesses: No priority: when a shutdown channel and a busy work channel are both ready, select may keep picking work. Preferring one needs an explicit check first
Like Promise.race, select doesn't stop the work behind the losing case; the slow goroutine keeps running unless a context tells it to stop
The cases are fixed in source code. Waiting on a dynamic number of channels needs reflect.Select or a fan-in goroutine per channel

pitfalls.title: time.After inside the loop is an idle timeout, not a deadline
pitfalls.detail: Each iteration creates a new timer, so the timeout only fires after that long without any message. Create the timer (or a context with a deadline) once, before the loop.
pitfalls.bad: for { select { case m := <-in: handle(m); case <-time.After(5 * time.Second): return } }
pitfalls.good:
deadline := time.After(5 * time.Second)
for { select { case m := <-in: handle(m); case <-deadline: return } }

pitfalls.title: break leaves the select, not the loop
pitfalls.detail: Inside a for-select, break ends the select statement only and the loop goes round again. Use return, or a labeled break.
pitfalls.good:
loop:
	for { select { case <-done: break loop } }

pitfalls.title: for-select with an empty default spins
pitfalls.detail: A default that does nothing turns a blocking wait into a busy loop that burns a CPU core. Drop the default and let select block.
pitfalls.bad: for { select { case m := <-in: handle(m); default: } }
pitfalls.good: for m := range in { handle(m) }

pitfalls.title: Unbuffered result channel plus a timeout leaks the sender
pitfalls.detail: After the timeout nobody receives, so the worker blocks on its send forever. Give the result channel capacity 1, or have the worker select on ctx.Done() too.
pitfalls.good: result := make(chan string, 1)

quiz.q: Two cases of a select are ready at the same moment. Which one runs?
options: The first one in source order
quiz.why: The spec requires a uniform pseudo-random choice among the cases that can proceed, which is why case order can't express priority.

quiz.q: Inside a select, what does a receive from a nil channel do?
options: Never proceeds, so the case is effectively disabled
quiz.why: Communication on a nil channel never proceeds. Setting a finished input to nil is the standard way to switch its case off.

quiz.q: for { select { case m := <-in: handle(m); case <-time.After(time.Minute): return } }. When does this return?
options: One minute after the loop started
After one minute without any message on in
quiz.why: time.After runs again on every iteration, so each message restarts the minute. For a deadline, create the timer once before the loop.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Select statements

lessons.body:
## Concept

`select` is a `switch` whose cases are channel operations, sends or receives. On entry
it evaluates every channel expression once. If one or more cases can proceed, it picks
one **uniformly at random** and runs it. If none can, it runs `default` if there is one,
and otherwise blocks until some case becomes ready. A `nil` channel never proceeds, and
an empty `select {}` blocks forever.

Three idioms cover nearly every use:

- **Timeout**: add `case <-time.After(d):` next to the operation you are waiting for.
- **Non-blocking**: add `default:` to try a send or receive without waiting.
- **Multiplexing**: a `for { select { ... } }` loop that reacts to whichever input is
  ready, including a shutdown signal.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C**: the name is no accident: it is `select(2)`/`poll`/`epoll` for typed channels.
  One difference: those report readiness and you do the read afterwards, while Go's
  `select` performs the send or receive itself, so the value is already yours when the
  case body runs.
- **Java**: there is no language equivalent. `BlockingQueue.poll(timeout)` covers one
  queue; `CompletableFuture.anyOf` covers futures. `select` mixes queues, timers and
  shutdown signals in one wait.
- **Python**: `asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` and `asyncio.wait_for`
  play this role for awaitables. Python cancels the loser with `task.cancel()`; Go
  uses a `context` for that.
- **JS**: `Promise.race([fetch(url), timeout(5000)])` is a `select` with a `time.After`
  case, with the same catch: the race doesn't abort the slow `fetch`. That takes an
  `AbortController`, which is what `context` is in Go.

## How it works

`time.After(d)` creates a timer and returns its channel, which receives the current time
once `d` has passed. Because it's an ordinary channel, a timeout is an ordinary case.

Go 1.23 changed timers in two ways (your `go.mod` says `go 1.27`, so you have both).
Timers that are no longer referenced are garbage collected even if they haven't fired,
so `time.After` in a loop no longer piles up live timers. Before Go 1.23 the docs told you
to use `time.NewTimer` and `Stop` instead. Timer channels are also unbuffered now, so
after `Stop` or `Reset` returns, no stale value can be received. Go 1.27 removed the
`asynctimerchan` GODEBUG that could switch the old behaviour back on.

Order within one channel is guaranteed: values arrive in the order they were sent.
Across the cases of a `select` there is no order at all.

## Design notes

Put the timeout at the caller, and give the worker a result channel with capacity 1 so
it can always finish its send and exit. A timeout only stops the waiting, not the work:
to stop the work, pass a `context.Context` and select on `ctx.Done()` inside the worker.
That is the next lesson, and in real code `ctx.Done()` replaces most hand-made `quit`
channels.

A goroutine that owns some state and runs a `for`-`select` over command channels is
Go's actor: nothing else touches the state, so it needs no mutex. It is a good fit when
the state changes in response to messages. When many goroutines just read and update a
shared structure, a mutex (lesson 3) is simpler.

If one case must win, such as shutdown over work, don't rely on case order. Check it
first with a non-blocking select, or test `ctx.Err()` at the top of the loop.

lessons.title: sync: WaitGroup (and wg.Go), Mutex/RWMutex, Once/OnceValue, atomic
lessons.summary: When goroutines share memory instead of passing it, package sync guards it: WaitGroup waits for them, Mutex and RWMutex serialise access, OnceValue runs initialisation exactly once, and sync/atomic handles lone counters and flags.

examples.title: wg.Go starts and counts goroutines; a Mutex guards the shared map

annotations.note: The mutex sits next to the data it guards, and both are unexported: callers go through add and can't forget the lock. The zero Mutex is unlocked and ready, so there is no constructor.

Lock, then defer Unlock on the next line, so an early return or a panic can't leave it locked. Go's Mutex isn't reentrant: calling add from inside add would block forever, where Java's synchronized would let the same thread in again.

wg.Go (Go 1.25) adds 1 before the goroutine starts and calls Done when the function returns. The older wg.Add(1); go func() { defer wg.Done() ... }() form is what go fix's waitgroupgo analyzer rewrites into this. Each iteration has its own line variable (Go 1.22), so no copy is needed.
Every goroutine's return happens before Wait returns, so their writes are visible here and reading the map without the lock is safe. Before Wait, it would be a data race.

examples.title: OnceValues for lazy initialisation, errors included

annotations.note: atomic.Int32 (Go 1.19) is the typed form: the value can only be reached through atomic methods, unlike a plain int32 handed to atomic.AddInt32 and read directly elsewhere.

OnceValues (Go 1.21) returns a function that runs f at most once. Callers that arrive while it runs wait for it, then everyone gets the same values. It replaces sync.Once plus package-level variables for the result and the error.
Each goroutine writes its own element of a pre-sized slice. Distinct elements are distinct memory locations, so this needs no lock and is race-free.

The error is cached too: three calls, one dial. If a failed attempt should be retried later, OnceValues is the wrong tool; keep the connection in a mutex-guarded field that stays nil until a dial succeeds.

examples.title: RWMutex for read-mostly data, atomics for counters

annotations.note: RWMutex admits many readers or one writer. It helps only when reads dominate: a waiting Lock blocks new RLock calls, so with frequent writes readers queue behind every writer anyway.
Several readers hold RLock at the same time, so c.hits++ on a plain int here would be a data race. RLock protects reading the map, not writing the counters; that's why the counters are atomics.
Writes take the exclusive lock. Concurrent writes to a Go map can crash the program with "fatal error: concurrent map writes", a fatal error rather than a panic, so recover can't catch it.
The 100 goroutines interleave differently on every run, yet the totals are fixed: 50 readers times two hits, 50 misses for "fr", and 2 + 50 entries.

use_cases: WaitGroup: wait for a batch of goroutines that report through shared memory or not at all; when they can fail, use errgroup (lesson 6)
Mutex: a map or struct that many request goroutines update, such as an in-memory cache, a session table or per-client rate-limit state
RWMutex: read-mostly data such as a routing table or a feature-flag set reloaded once a minute
OnceValue/OnceValues: lazy initialisation of templates, compiled regexps or a client, instead of init() or a hand-written nil check under a lock
atomic: counters, flags, and swapping in a new immutable config snapshot with atomic.Pointer[T]
strengths: Zero values are ready to use: var mu sync.Mutex and var wg sync.WaitGroup need no constructor, unlike Java's new ReentrantLock()
go vet catches copied locks (copylocks) and wg.Add called inside the new goroutine (waitgroup); javac and C++ compilers check neither
OnceValue is lazy, thread-safe initialisation in one line, without Java's double-checked locking and its volatile subtleties
Atomics are sequentially consistent, the semantics of C++'s default std::atomic and Java's volatile, so there are no memory orderings to choose
weaknesses: Nothing ties a mutex to the data it guards. Unlike Rust's Mutex<T>, the compiler can't tell you a field was read without the lock; only the race detector can, at run time
No reentrancy: a goroutine that locks a mutex it already holds blocks forever
No lock timeouts like Java's tryLock(timeout, unit); TryLock exists, but its own docs call correct uses rare

pitfalls.title: Copying a value that contains a lock
pitfalls.detail: A value receiver or a struct passed by value copies the mutex, and each copy locks independently, which protects nothing. Use pointer receivers; go vet's copylocks check reports the copy.
pitfalls.bad: func (c cache) get(k string) string { c.mu.RLock(); defer c.mu.RUnlock(); return c.data[k] }
pitfalls.good: func (c *cache) get(k string) string { c.mu.RLock(); defer c.mu.RUnlock(); return c.data[k] }

pitfalls.title: Calling wg.Add inside the goroutine
pitfalls.detail: Wait may run before the goroutine has called Add and return early. Call Add before the go statement, or let wg.Go do both; go vet's waitgroup analyzer (Go 1.25) reports the misplaced Add.
pitfalls.bad: go func() { wg.Add(1); defer wg.Done(); work() }()
pitfalls.good: wg.Go(work)

pitfalls.title: Locking the same mutex twice in one call chain
pitfalls.detail: A locked method that calls another locked method on the same value blocks forever. Split it into a public method that locks and an unexported helper that assumes the lock is held.
pitfalls.bad: func (s *Store) Move(a, b string) { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); s.Delete(a); s.Put(b) } // Delete and Put lock s.mu too
pitfalls.good: func (s *Store) Move(a, b string) { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); s.deleteLocked(a); s.putLocked(b) }

pitfalls.title: Holding a lock across I/O
pitfalls.detail: An HTTP call or a database query under a mutex serialises every caller behind the slowest request. Copy what you need, unlock, then do the I/O.

quiz.q: A method holds mu.RLock() and increments a plain int field. Is that safe?
options: No: several readers can hold RLock at once, so the increment races
quiz.why: RLock is shared. Writes need Lock, or the counter needs to be an atomic.

quiz.q: The function passed to sync.OnceValues returned an error on its first call. What do later calls return?
options: The same error, without calling the function
quiz.why: OnceValues runs the function once and caches both results, the error included.

quiz.q: A method holding s.mu.Lock() calls another method of s that also calls s.mu.Lock(). What happens?
options: It works, the lock is reentrant
quiz.why: Go's Mutex has no owner and no reentrancy, so the second Lock waits for an Unlock that never comes.

quiz.q: Many goroutines increment one shared counter. What is the simplest correct choice?
quiz.why: A lone counter is what atomics are for. A plain int races, and sync.Map is a map for specific access patterns, not a counter.

further_reading.title: Go 1.25 release notes: WaitGroup.Go and the waitgroup vet check

lessons.body:
## Concept

Lesson 1 passed data between goroutines through channels. The alternative is to share
memory and guard it. Package `sync` and `sync/atomic` provide the tools:

- **`WaitGroup`**: wait until a set of goroutines has finished. `wg.Go(f)` (Go 1.25)
  starts `f` in a goroutine and counts it; `wg.Wait()` blocks until all have returned.
- **`Mutex`**: one goroutine at a time in the critical section. **`RWMutex`**: many
  readers or one writer.
- **`Once`**, **`OnceFunc`**, **`OnceValue`**, **`OnceValues`** (the last three since
  Go 1.21): run something exactly once, on first use, safely from any goroutine.
- **`sync/atomic`**: typed atomics such as `atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool` and
  `atomic.Pointer[T]` (Go 1.19) for single values.

The types (`WaitGroup`, `Mutex`, `RWMutex`, `Once`, the atomics) are ready to use as zero
values and must not be copied after first use.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `Mutex` ≈ `ReentrantLock` without the reentrancy, and there is no
  `synchronized` keyword, so a lock is always an explicit field. `WaitGroup` ≈
  `CountDownLatch` with a counter you can increase. `OnceValue` replaces lazy holders
  and double-checked locking. `atomic.Int64` ≈ `AtomicLong`.
- **C/C++**: `Mutex` ≈ `std::mutex`, with `defer mu.Unlock()` in place of
  `std::lock_guard`. Go atomics are always sequentially consistent, like
  `std::atomic` with the default `memory_order_seq_cst`; there is no relaxed mode.
- **Python**: `threading.Lock` maps directly. The difference: goroutines run in parallel
  on all cores, with no GIL serialising them, so a missing lock corrupts data quickly.
- **JS**: one event loop never needs locks between callbacks. Go's goroutines are
  preemptively scheduled across threads, so any shared write needs one of these tools.

## How it works

The guarantees come from the Go memory model, which defines "synchronizes before":
an `Unlock` synchronizes before the next `Lock`, the return of a `wg.Go` function before
the `Wait` it releases, and the return of a `Once` function before any `once.Do` call
returns. Without such an edge, a write in one goroutine and a read in another are a
**data race**: the read may see the old value or the new one, and for multiword values
such as strings, slices and interfaces a torn mix that can corrupt memory. Lesson 6
shows how the race detector finds them.

Typed atomics are the safer form. `var n int64` plus `atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)` compiles
fine next to a plain `n++` somewhere else; `var n atomic.Int64` has no plain access at
all. In the Go 1.27 toolchain, `go fix`'s `atomictypes` analyzer rewrites the old form
into the new one.

## Design notes

Channels or mutexes? Use a channel when ownership moves, such as handing a job to a
worker or passing a result back. Use a mutex when several goroutines need short access
to the same structure, like a cache or a counter table. "Share memory by communicating"
is the default, not a ban: a mutex around a map is simpler than a goroutine that owns
the map and serves requests over channels.

Keep critical sections small and free of I/O. Put the mutex in the struct it protects,
unexported, with methods that lock, so callers can't forget. Prefer `Mutex` over
`RWMutex` until reads clearly dominate.

`sync.Map` is not a general replacement for a map plus a mutex. Its docs say most code
should use a plain map, and name the two cases it is optimized for: keys written once
and read many times, and goroutines working on disjoint key sets. Otherwise a plain map
with a mutex keeps type safety and lets you maintain other invariants under the same
lock.

lessons.title: context: cancellation, deadlines, values used sparingly
lessons.summary: A context.Context carries a cancellation signal, an optional deadline and a few request-scoped values down the call chain. Every function that does I/O takes it as its first parameter and stops when ctx.Done() is closed.

examples.title: Deadlines, explicit cancellation, and causes

annotations.note: This select is the whole contract: do the work, but stop waiting once ctx.Done() is closed. net/http, database/sql and pgx do the same inside every call that takes a ctx.
Wrap ctx.Err() with %w, so callers can still ask errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) and tell a timeout from a real failure.
WithTimeoutCause (Go 1.21) attaches a reason. ctx.Err() still reports DeadlineExceeded, so existing checks keep working; context.Cause returns the reason for logs and error messages.

Call cancel on every path, even after success: it stops the timer and detaches the child from its parent. Deferring it on the next line is the idiom, and go vet's lostcancel check reports a dropped CancelFunc.

Cancellation is a request, not a kill. query stops only because it selects on ctx.Done(); a function that ignores its ctx runs to the end regardless. Calling a CancelFunc twice, or from several goroutines, is safe.
When the work beats the deadline, the context never fires and the result comes back as usual.

examples.title: Cancellation flows down the tree; WithoutCancel and AfterFunc

annotations.note: Every With... call wraps a parent, so contexts form a tree. In a server the root is r.Context(), which net/http cancels when the client disconnects or the handler returns.
Canceling cacheCall leaves request and dbCall alone. Cancellation flows from parent to children, never up or sideways.
WithoutCancel (Go 1.21) keeps the parent's values but drops its cancellation and deadline. Use it for work that must finish after the request is gone, and give that work a timeout of its own.

AfterFunc (Go 1.21) runs the callback in a new goroutine once the context is canceled. It is how you connect a blocking call that takes no ctx, for example closing a connection to unblock a read. The closed channel only fixes the output order.
One call reached every descendant: the hour-long dbCall is canceled too. The audit context isn't, and still carries the user value.

examples.title: Values with unexported key types and typed accessors

annotations.note: The key's type is unexported, so only this package can construct the key. Another package's key with the same underlying 0 has a different type and can't collide with it.
Export typed helpers, not the key, as the context docs recommend. Callers never see the any, and a missing value yields the zero value rather than a failed type assertion.

Values are for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries: a request ID, a trace span, the authenticated user. What a function needs to do its job belongs in its parameters, where the compiler checks it.
A key matches only if both type and value are equal, so authKey("user"), logKey("user") and the plain string "user" are three different keys. That is why the docs warn against built-in key types.

use_cases: Per-request deadlines in HTTP handlers: derive from r.Context() so a disconnected client stops the database query it started
Outgoing calls with a budget: context.WithTimeout around an HTTP request, a pgx query or a gRPC call
Graceful shutdown: signal.NotifyContext cancels a root context on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, and everything derived from it winds down
Request-scoped metadata that middleware adds and logging reads: request ID, trace span, authenticated user
strengths: One convention across the standard library and the ecosystem: net/http, database/sql, pgx and gRPC all take ctx first, unlike Java, where each API has its own timeout and interrupt story
Cancellation propagates through the whole call tree from one cancel() call, including into goroutines started deeper down
Deadlines compose: a child can only shorten its parent's deadline, so a 100ms handler budget can't be exceeded by a callee asking for 5s
weaknesses: Cooperative only: code that never checks ctx.Done() or passes ctx on can't be cancelled, and nothing in the type system tells you
ctx is threaded by hand through every signature, which is noisier than the implicit propagation of Python's contextvars or Java's ThreadLocal
Values are untyped (any) and invisible in signatures, so they turn into hidden parameters when overused

pitfalls.title: Storing a Context in a struct
pitfalls.detail: The context docs say to pass it explicitly to each function instead. A stored ctx outlives the request it belonged to, and callers can't give individual calls their own deadline.
pitfalls.bad: type Repo struct { ctx context.Context; db *pgxpool.Pool }
pitfalls.good: func (r *Repo) FindUser(ctx context.Context, id int64) (User, error)

pitfalls.title: Using context.Background() deep in the call chain
pitfalls.detail: It cuts the chain: the request's deadline and cancellation no longer reach the query. Background belongs in main, tests and top-level setup; elsewhere pass the ctx you were given, or context.TODO() while refactoring.

pitfalls.title: Optional parameters in context values
pitfalls.detail: A page size or a feature flag hidden in the context is a parameter the compiler can't check. Use a function argument or an options struct.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting cancel
pitfalls.detail: Without cancel, a WithTimeout child and its timer stay alive until the timeout fires or the parent is canceled; with WithCancel, until the parent is canceled. go vet's lostcancel check reports it.
pitfalls.good:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, time.Second)
defer cancel()

quiz.q: A child context is canceled. What happens to its parent?
options: Nothing: cancellation only flows to descendants
quiz.why: Canceling a context cancels it and its children; parents and siblings are untouched.

quiz.q: ctx was created with WithTimeoutCause(parent, d, myErr) and the deadline passed. What does ctx.Err() return?
quiz.why: Err keeps reporting DeadlineExceeded so existing checks still work; context.Cause(ctx) returns myErr.

quiz.q: A function receives ctx but never selects on ctx.Done() and never passes ctx on. What does canceling ctx do to it?
quiz.why: A context only signals. Work stops when code observes Done or hands ctx to an API that does.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A `context.Context` is an immutable value that carries three things down a call chain:
a **cancellation signal** (`Done()` returns a channel that is closed on cancel), an
optional **deadline**, and a few **request-scoped values**. You never modify a context;
you derive a child from it:

- `context.WithCancel(parent)` returns a child and a `cancel` function.
- `context.WithTimeout(parent, d)` / `WithDeadline(parent, t)` cancel automatically.
- `WithCancelCause` (Go 1.20) and `WithTimeoutCause` / `WithDeadlineCause` (Go 1.21)
  record why; `context.Cause(ctx)` reads it back.
- `context.WithValue(parent, key, val)` attaches one value.

When a context is canceled, every context derived from it is canceled too. After that,
`ctx.Err()` returns `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded`.

The convention is strict: anything that does I/O or may block takes
`ctx context.Context` as its **first parameter** and passes it on.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: `AbortController`/`AbortSignal` is the closest match. `signal` ≈ `ctx`,
  `controller.abort(reason)` ≈ `cancel(cause)`, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` ≈
  `WithTimeout`, and `fetch(url, { signal })` ≈ passing `ctx` to `http.NewRequestWithContext`.
- **Java**: there is no single equivalent. `Thread.interrupt()` is per thread,
  `Future.cancel(true)` per task, and every API has its own timeout parameters.
  `context` is one mechanism used everywhere, and it's explicit rather than a flag
  on the thread.
- **Python**: `asyncio` cancels a task by raising `CancelledError` inside it. Go has no
  exceptions to inject: the callee has to check `ctx.Done()` or `ctx.Err()`.
  `contextvars` covers the values part.
- **C/C++**: closest to passing a cancellation token around by hand, as in C++20's
  `std::stop_token`, with deadlines built in.

## How it works

`Done()` returns a channel that is **closed**, never sent on, when the context is
canceled. A closed channel is ready for every receiver, so one `cancel()` wakes any
number of goroutines selecting on `<-ctx.Done()`. That's why the cancellation check is
a `select` case, the pattern from the previous lesson.

Deadlines only get shorter. `WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second)` under a parent that
expires in 100ms still expires in 100ms. A handler's budget therefore holds no matter
what its callees ask for.

For incoming HTTP requests, `r.Context()` is canceled when the client's connection
closes, when an HTTP/2 request is canceled, or when `ServeHTTP` returns. Deriving every
query's context from it means a disconnected client stops the database work it started.

## Design notes

Context is plumbing, so keep it boring:

- First parameter, named `ctx`, never stored in a struct, never `nil` (use
  `context.TODO()` if you're unsure which context to use).
- `context.Background()` belongs at the top: in `main`, in tests (or `t.Context()`,
  Go 1.24) and in long-lived background loops.
- Call `cancel` on every path, usually with `defer` on the next line.
- Values only for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries, behind an unexported
  key type with typed accessors. If a function needs a value to do its job, it's a
  parameter.
- Pick the timeout where the budget is known, usually at the edge (the handler or the
  job runner), and let deeper layers inherit it rather than invent their own.

`errgroup` (lesson 6) builds on this: its context is canceled as soon as one goroutine in
the group fails, so its siblings stop early.

lessons.title: Patterns: worker pool, fan-out/fan-in, pipelines, semaphores, rate limiting
lessons.summary: Most concurrent Go programs combine a few shapes: pipelines of stages joined by channels, fan-out to workers and fan-in of their results, a bound on how many things run at once, and a limit on how often they start.

examples.title: A pipeline with fan-out, fan-in and a cancellation path

annotations.note: A stage returns a receive-only channel and starts the goroutine that fills it. That goroutine owns the channel, so it closes it, and downstream range loops end cleanly.
Every send also selects on ctx.Done(). If the consumer stops reading, a plain send would block forever and leak this goroutine; with the select, one cancel() releases it.
Fan-out: three workers range over the same channel and each value goes to exactly one of them. A slow stage gets parallel without any change to the stages around it.

Fan-in needs one extra goroutine that waits for all workers and then closes out. Closing inside a worker would make the others panic on their next send; never closing would leave main's range loop waiting forever.
If main returned early, say on the first bad value, the deferred cancel would unblock every stage still trying to send. Without it, those goroutines would leak.
Workers finish in any order. When order matters, carry an index with each value or write results into a slice by index, as the next example does.

examples.title: Bounding concurrency: worker pool vs semaphore

annotations.note: The tracker only measures concurrency. time.Sleep stands in for I/O so that tasks overlap; nothing here depends on it for ordering.
Each index is written by exactly one goroutine, and wg.Wait orders those writes before the Println, so the slice needs no lock and the results keep input order.

Worker pool: a fixed set of goroutines and one job channel; the concurrency is the number of workers. It suits workers that hold something costly, such as a connection or a large buffer, and reuse it across jobs.

Semaphore: one goroutine per job and a channel of capacity 3 as the gate. The send acquires a slot and blocks while three are taken; the deferred receive releases it. All ten goroutines exist at once, but only three work at a time.

examples.title: Rate limiting: a steady ticker and a token bucket

annotations.note: A loop that waits for a tick before each request can't go faster than the ticker. Only lower bounds on elapsed time are reliable, so that is all the example prints.
The bucket is a buffered channel of tokens. Starting it full lets a burst of three requests through without waiting.

The refill goroutine adds one token per tick and drops it when the bucket is full, so idle time can't bank more than three requests. The done channel stops it; without that, every limiter you create leaks a goroutine and a ticker.
The first three requests take the burst; the next two wait for refills. In production, golang.org/x/time/rate's Limiter.Wait(ctx) does this and lets a waiting request be canceled.

use_cases: Pipeline: parse, enrich, write, e.g. read a CSV export, look up each row, then batch inserts into PostgreSQL
Worker pool: a fixed number of workers, each holding a database connection, processing jobs claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Semaphore: cap concurrent calls to an external API, or concurrent image resizes at the number of cores
Rate limiting: stay under a third-party quota such as 50 requests per second
strengths: Built from language parts (goroutines, channels, select), with no executor framework to configure, unlike Java's ThreadPoolExecutor and its queue and rejection policies
Unbuffered channels give backpressure for free: a fast stage waits for a slow one, where Java's Executors.newFixedThreadPool queues work in an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue
A buffered channel is a semaphore with no extra type, and goroutines are cheap enough that one per item behind a semaphore is a sound design
weaknesses: Every pattern needs a cancellation path and a clear owner for every close. Getting either wrong deadlocks or leaks at run time; the compiler doesn't notice
Fan-out loses order; restoring it means carrying indexes or sequence numbers
No rate limiter in the standard library: bursts, per-key limits and Wait(ctx) come from golang.org/x/time/rate or your own code
Each channel hop is a synchronisation. When the per-item work is tiny, a plain loop can beat a pipeline; measure before splitting cheap work into stages

pitfalls.title: Closing a shared output channel in a worker
pitfalls.detail: The first worker to finish closes it and the others panic with "send on closed channel". Close it from one goroutine after wg.Wait().
pitfalls.bad: wg.Go(func() { for n := range in { out <- n * n }; close(out) })
pitfalls.good: go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()

pitfalls.title: One goroutine per item with no bound
pitfalls.detail: Ten thousand URLs become ten thousand simultaneous connections, file descriptors and memory spikes. Bound it with a pool, a semaphore or errgroup.SetLimit (lesson 6).
pitfalls.bad: for _, u := range urls { go fetch(u) }
pitfalls.good:
g.SetLimit(8)
for _, u := range urls { g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, u) }) }

pitfalls.title: Stages without a cancellation path
pitfalls.detail: When the consumer returns early, every upstream goroutine blocks on its next send forever. Select on ctx.Done() for each send and defer cancel() in the consumer.

pitfalls.title: Rate limiting with time.Sleep
pitfalls.detail: Sleeping after each request makes the rate drift by the request's own duration, and nothing can cancel the sleep. Use a ticker, or rate.Limiter.Wait(ctx).

quiz.q: In a fan-in, who should close the merged output channel?
options: One goroutine that waits for all workers, then closes it
quiz.why: Only after every sender is done is it safe to close; a closing worker would make the others panic on send.

quiz.q: A pipeline's consumer returns after the first bad value. What keeps the upstream goroutines from leaking?
options: Each send also selects on ctx.Done(), and the consumer cancels
quiz.why: Blocked goroutines are never collected. They exit only if something unblocks them, and ctx.Done() is that something.

quiz.q: slots := make(chan struct{}, 3) is used as a semaphore. What does slots <- struct{}{} do when three tokens are already in it?
options: Blocks until another goroutine receives one
quiz.why: A send on a full buffered channel blocks; receiving a token is the release.

further_reading.title: Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation

lessons.body:
## Concept

Four shapes cover most concurrent Go code:

- **Pipeline**: stages connected by channels. Each stage is a goroutine that receives
  from its input, does one thing, sends to its output, and closes the output when done.
- **Fan-out / fan-in**: several goroutines read the same channel (fan-out); their
  outputs are merged back into one channel (fan-in).
- **Bounded concurrency**: a **worker pool** (N goroutines pulling from a job channel) or
  a **semaphore** (one goroutine per job, a buffered channel admitting N at a time).
- **Rate limiting**: start work no faster than a fixed rate, with a ticker or a token
  bucket.

The rules that make them safe are the same everywhere: the goroutine that sends on a
channel owns it and closes it, every blocking send also watches `ctx.Done()`, and the
consumer cancels when it stops early.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C / Unix**: a pipeline is `grep | sort | uniq` inside one process, with channels as
  the pipes and blocking sends as their backpressure.
- **Java**: a worker pool is `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` without the executor:
  the job channel is the queue and `close` is `shutdown()`. A semaphore is
  `java.util.concurrent.Semaphore`.
- **Python**: `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n)` ≈ worker pool; `asyncio.Semaphore` ≈
  the channel semaphore. Goroutines run in parallel, so CPU-bound stages scale across
  cores.
- **JS**: bounding concurrency is what `p-limit` or chunked `Promise.all` do; Node's
  `stream.pipeline` is the pipeline. There, everything shares one thread; here, each
  stage can run on its own core.

## How it works

The pipeline example has this shape:

```
        ┌─► worker 1 ─┐
gen ────┼─► worker 2 ─┼──► out ──► main
        └─► worker 3 ─┘
```

Each value from `gen` goes to exactly one worker, because a receive takes the value off
the channel. The merged `out` must be closed exactly once, after all three workers have
stopped sending, which is why a fourth small goroutine waits on the WaitGroup and then
closes it.

A worker pool and a semaphore bound concurrency the same way, from different ends: the
pool creates N goroutines and feeds them jobs; the semaphore creates one goroutine per
job and lets N through a gate. A third option is `errgroup.Group.SetLimit` (next lesson),
which adds error handling. `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` offers a weighted semaphore
whose `Acquire(ctx, n)` can be canceled.

## Design notes

Start with the simplest thing: a loop. Add a pipeline when stages have different costs
and you want them to overlap, such as reading the next CSV rows while the database
insert of the previous batch is in flight. Add fan-out only to the slow stage.

Prefer a semaphore or `errgroup.SetLimit` when jobs are independent and short-lived;
prefer a worker pool when workers hold a resource (a connection, a buffer, a
prepared statement) worth reusing.

Make every stage cancelable, and make ownership obvious from the signature: return
`<-chan T` from the function that creates and closes the channel, and accept `<-chan T`
in stages that only read.

lessons.title: errgroup with limits, data races, -race, goroutine leaks
lessons.summary: errgroup runs a group of goroutines, cancels the rest when one fails, bounds how many run at once, and returns the first error. The race detector finds unsynchronised memory access; the goroutineleak profile (Go 1.27) finds goroutines that can never finish.

examples.title: errgroup.WithContext and SetLimit: first error wins, the rest are canceled

annotations.note: WithContext returns the group and a derived context. It is canceled when the first task returns an error, or when Wait returns, so it must not be used after Wait.
With a limit, g.Go blocks until fewer than two tasks are running: the semaphore from the previous lesson, built in. Set it before the first Go.
Each task writes only its own status[i], so collecting results needs no mutex. i and page are fresh in every iteration (Go 1.22), so each closure sees its own values.

Page 2 fails at once and cancels ctx; page 1 can only end through that cancellation. Pages 3 to 5 get a slot only after one of the first two has returned, which is after the cancel, so they start on a canceled context. That ordering, not timing, makes the output the same on every run.
The group keeps only the first non-nil error. Page 1's context.Canceled comes after page 2's failure, so Wait reports the real cause rather than the cancellation it triggered.
Wait returns only after every task has returned, failure or not, so no goroutine outlives the call. x/sync v0.25.0 cancels the context with the error as its cause, which context.Cause reads back.

examples.title: Finding a goroutine leak with the goroutineleak profile

annotations.note: The fix is room for every sender: each goroutine completes its send and exits, and the unread answers are garbage collected along with the channel. Having each sender also select on ctx.Done() works too.
first returns after one receive. On an unbuffered channel, each of the other replicas waits on its send for a receiver that will never come, and keeps its stack and everything it references alive.

The goroutineleak profile (an experiment in Go 1.26, always available since Go 1.27) runs a special GC cycle. A goroutine blocked on a channel or lock that no runnable goroutine can reach can never wake, so it is reported. WriteTo with debug=1 prints the leaked stacks.
The losing replicas need a moment to reach their send, so this polls with a bound instead of trusting a fixed sleep. A goroutine that a live goroutine could still unblock is never counted.
Two leaked goroutines per call. In a server that calls first on every request, the goroutine count only ever grows.

use_cases: Fetch several independent resources for one request (user, orders, recommendations) and fail fast if one fails
Process a batch with bounded parallelism: g.SetLimit(8) instead of a hand-written semaphore
Run go test -race in CI on Linux for every package that starts goroutines
Expose /debug/pprof/goroutineleak (net/http/pprof, Go 1.27) next to /debug/pprof/goroutine in services, or check the profile in tests
strengths: Structured concurrency in a few lines: no goroutine outlives Wait, and one failure cancels its siblings, which Promise.all does not do: the other promises keep running
SetLimit and TryGo cover bounded parallelism without a separate semaphore
The race detector reports races with both stacks and the goroutine creation site, where a C++ or Java data race just yields wrong numbers now and then
Leak detection uses the garbage collector's reachability, so it finds leaks no test asserted on, without changing the code
weaknesses: errgroup is in golang.org/x/sync, not the standard library: one go get away, but a dependency
Only the first error is returned; to report every failure, collect errors yourself and errors.Join them
-race needs cgo and a C compiler, costs 5-10x memory and 2-20x time per the docs, and only finds races on code paths that actually ran
The leak profile misses goroutines blocked on primitives reachable from globals or from running goroutines; a clean profile is not proof

pitfalls.title: Using the group's context after Wait
pitfalls.detail: WithContext's context is canceled when Wait returns, even on success. Any later call made with it fails with context.Canceled. Derive follow-up work from the parent context.

pitfalls.title: Expecting errgroup to recover panics
pitfalls.detail: A panic in a task crashes the program like any goroutine panic. The x/sync v0.25.0 source explains why it doesn't propagate panics to Wait. Recover inside the task if it calls code that may panic.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring ctx inside the tasks
pitfalls.detail: Cancellation only helps if tasks pass ctx to their I/O calls or select on ctx.Done(). A task that ignores ctx keeps the whole Wait waiting.
pitfalls.good: g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, url) })

pitfalls.title: Treating a quiet program as race-free
pitfalls.detail: A racy counter can print the right total a thousand times in a row and lose updates under load. Races on strings, slices or maps can even corrupt memory. Only -race, or reasoning about happens-before, tells you the code is correct.

quiz.q: errgroup.WithContext: task A returns an error while task B is waiting on <-ctx.Done(). What happens?
options: Wait returns immediately with A's error
B keeps running; Wait returns when B finishes on its own
ctx is canceled, B returns, and then Wait returns A's error
quiz.why: The first error cancels the group's context; Wait still waits for every task, then returns the first error.

quiz.q: go test ./... passes 100 times in a row. Is the code race-free?
options: Not necessarily: run go test -race, and even then only executed paths are checked
quiz.why: Races often produce correct-looking output. The race detector finds them only on code paths the tests actually run.

quiz.q: Which goroutine does the goroutineleak profile report?
options: A goroutine blocked on a channel or lock that no runnable goroutine can reach
Any goroutine blocked for more than a minute
Every goroutine still running when main returns
quiz.why: Reachability is the test: if nothing that can run can ever reach the primitive, the blocked goroutine can never wake.

further_reading.title: Go 1.27 release notes: goroutine leak profile

lessons.body:
## Concept

**errgroup** (`golang.org/x/sync/errgroup`) is a `WaitGroup` that understands errors:

- `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(parent)` creates a group and a context.
- `g.Go(func() error {...})` starts a task; `g.SetLimit(n)` caps how many run at once,
  and `g.TryGo` starts one only if a slot is free.
- `g.Wait()` waits for all tasks and returns the first non-nil error. The first error
  also cancels `ctx`, so well-behaved siblings stop early.

That's **structured concurrency**: goroutines are started inside a scope and none
outlive it. Two tools find the bugs that slip through anyway:

- A **data race** is two goroutines accessing the same memory, at least one writing,
  with no happens-before ordering between them. `go test -race` and `go run -race`
  detect races while the code runs.
- A **goroutine leak** is a goroutine blocked forever. Go 1.27's `goroutineleak` profile
  reports the ones that provably can never wake up.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: `await Promise.all(tasks)` rejects on the first failure, but the other
  promises keep running. errgroup also cancels them, the way an `AbortController`
  shared by all the fetches would.
- **Java**: errgroup is close to `StructuredTaskScope` (still a preview API) set to shut
  down on the first failure: fork tasks, join, get the first exception, siblings cancelled.
- **Python**: `asyncio.TaskGroup` (3.11) is the same idea, cancelling the rest when one
  task fails. It reports all failures in an `ExceptionGroup`; errgroup keeps only the
  first error.
- **C/C++**: ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) is the engine behind Go's `-race`.
  The memory model is milder than C++'s: a racy read of a single word sees some value
  actually written there, as in Java. But races on multiword values (strings, slices,
  interfaces, maps) can corrupt memory, so a race report is always a bug, never noise.

## How it works

`-race` instruments every memory access at compile time and checks happens-before at
run time. Take a goroutine and `main` that both increment a counter without a lock:

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	hits := 0
	done := make(chan bool)
	go func() {
		hits++ // line 9
		done <- true
	}()
	hits++ // line 12
	<-done
	fmt.Println(hits)
}
```

Built normally, it prints `2` and looks fine. `go run -race main.go` still prints `2`,
but also writes a report to stderr that names both accesses and where the goroutine was
started, and the program exits with status 66 (addresses, paths, and which access is
the "Previous" one vary by run):

```
==================
WARNING: DATA RACE
Read at 0x00c000012128 by goroutine 7:
  main.main.func1()
      /home/you/race/main.go:9 +0x2e

Previous write at 0x00c000012128 by main goroutine:
  main.main()
      /home/you/race/main.go:12 +0x8c

Goroutine 7 (running) created at:
  main.main()
      /home/you/race/main.go:8 +0x7a
==================
Found 1 data race(s)
exit status 66
```

This report was not captured on the owner's machine (no C compiler, so no `-race`); it
shows the documented format. The [race detector article](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector)
says a report holds "stack traces for conflicting accesses, as well as stacks where the
involved goroutines were created", and its `exitcode` option defaults to 66, which
`go run` prints as `exit status 66`. The exact lines (`Read at 0x... by goroutine N:`,
`Previous write at 0x... by main goroutine:`, `Goroutine N (running) created at:`,
`Found 1 data race(s)`) are the ones Go 1.27.4's own tests expect, in
`src/runtime/race/output_test.go` (cases `simple` and `midstack_inlining_traceback`).
The goroutine number, addresses, paths, frame names and line numbers above are
illustrative, not observed.

Under `go test -race`, the failing test also reports `race detected during execution
of test`. The race detector needs cgo, and on Windows a MinGW-w64 C compiler (runtime
version 8 or later). Without one, `go run -race` stops with `go: -race requires cgo;
enable cgo by setting CGO_ENABLED=1`, and with `CGO_ENABLED=1` cgo reports that `gcc`
was not found. The lesson runner doesn't build with `-race`, which is why the runnable
examples show a leak rather than a race; run `-race` in CI on Linux.

The leak profile works through the garbage collector. If goroutine G is blocked on a
channel or mutex that no runnable goroutine can reach, nothing can ever unblock G. It
was an experiment in Go 1.26 (`GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile`) and is always
available from Go 1.27, both as `pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")` and as
`/debug/pprof/goroutineleak` from `net/http/pprof`.

## Design notes

Reach for errgroup whenever you'd write a `WaitGroup` plus an error variable plus a
mutex. Pass the group's `ctx` into every task, write results into a pre-sized slice by
index, and return wrapped errors so `Wait` tells you which task failed. Add it to a
module with `go get golang.org/x/sync`.

Make `go test -race ./...` part of CI for any package that starts goroutines, and
write tests that actually exercise the concurrent paths; the detector can't see code
that didn't run. Leaks are cheapest to find in tests: check `runtime.NumGoroutine()` or
the `goroutineleak` profile at the end, or run the test under `testing/synctest`
(next lesson), which fails a test whose goroutines are deadlocked. In production,
watch the goroutine count over time; a line that only goes up is a leak.

lessons.title: testing/synctest: deterministic time for concurrent tests
lessons.summary: synctest.Test runs a test in a bubble with a fake clock that jumps forward whenever every goroutine in it is blocked. Timeouts, backoff and heartbeats are tested instantly and exactly, with no clock interface in the production code.

examples.title: Seven seconds of backoff in zero real time

annotations.note: Ordinary production code: time.After and a context deadline, nothing test-specific. synctest swaps the clock underneath, so there is no Clock interface to inject.
synctest.Test (Go 1.25) runs the function in a bubble. Goroutines started inside belong to it, and the time package inside uses a fake clock that starts at midnight UTC on 2000-01-01.
retry waits 1s, 2s and 4s. Whenever every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, the clock jumps to the next timer, so seven seconds of waiting take no real time: the PASS line shows (0.00s).
Fake time is exact, so the test asserts equality. With real time it could only check "at least 7s, not much more", and every run would cost seven seconds.
Deadlines are timers too. The context fires at exactly 5s, in the middle of the 4s wait that would have ended at 7s, and retry returns the cause.

examples.title: Checking state just before and after a timeout with synctest.Sleep

annotations.note: The goroutine under test. Its timer belongs to the bubble's clock. Since Go 1.23, Reset on an unfired timer needs no Stop-and-drain dance: no stale value can arrive afterwards.

When the test function returns, t.Context() is canceled and the goroutine exits. synctest.Test waits for every goroutine in the bubble, and fails the test if they are deadlocked, so a leaked goroutine can't go unnoticed.
Beat is an unbuffered send to the watchdog goroutine. The clock can't move until that goroutine is blocked again, so its Reset happens at exactly 20s.
synctest.Sleep (Go 1.27) is time.Sleep followed by synctest.Wait: the clock moves, then every other goroutine in the bubble runs until it blocks. On Go 1.25 and 1.26, write those two calls.

At 50s the test's sleep and the watchdog's timer fire at the same fake instant. After a plain time.Sleep, which goroutine runs first is unpredictable and the check could see dead == false; the Wait inside synctest.Sleep lets the watchdog finish its turn first.

use_cases: Retry and backoff: assert the exact schedule (1s, 2s, 4s) without waiting seven seconds
Timeouts, TTL caches, heartbeats and debouncers: check the state just before and just after the boundary
Code built on context.WithTimeout, time.AfterFunc or tickers whose tests used to need long sleeps or an injected clock
HTTP timeouts over an in-memory network: net.Pipe, or httptest.NewTestServer (Go 1.27)
strengths: No clock abstraction in production code: it keeps calling time.Now and time.After, where Java tests typically need a java.time.Clock passed in
Time advances by itself when everything is blocked, unlike Vitest or Jest fake timers, where the test calls advanceTimersByTime(ms) and has to know how far
Assertions are exact (got == 7*time.Second), with no tolerance windows and no flaky sleeps on a loaded CI machine
A bubble whose goroutines end up deadlocked fails the test instead of hanging until the go test timeout
weaknesses: Only blocking inside the bubble counts. Real network I/O, system calls and mutex waits aren't durably blocking, so code under test needs in-memory fakes such as net.Pipe
Go 1.25 or later (synctest.Sleep: 1.27); projects stuck on older toolchains still need an injected clock
Bubble rules take some learning: no t.Run or t.Parallel inside, and channels and timers created in a bubble panic when used from outside

pitfalls.title: Real network I/O inside the bubble
pitfalls.detail: A goroutine reading from a TCP socket isn't durably blocked, so the clock won't advance past it and Wait keeps waiting. Use net.Pipe or httptest.NewTestServer, whose in-memory network works with synctest.

pitfalls.title: Channels created outside the bubble
pitfalls.detail: Only operations on channels created inside the bubble count as durably blocking. Create the system under test inside the synctest.Test function, not in a package variable or TestMain.

pitfalls.title: time.Sleep when another goroutine wakes at the same instant
pitfalls.detail: Two goroutines woken at the same fake time run in unpredictable order. Follow the sleep with synctest.Wait, or use synctest.Sleep (Go 1.27).
pitfalls.good:
synctest.Sleep(30 * time.Second)
if !w.Dead() { t.Fatal("alive") }

pitfalls.title: Copying examples written for the Go 1.24 experiment
pitfalls.detail: Go 1.24 had synctest.Run behind GOEXPERIMENT=synctest. Go 1.25 replaced it with synctest.Test(t, f); Run is not in the Go 1.27 package.

quiz.q: When does the fake clock inside a synctest bubble advance?
options: When every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked
Only when the test calls synctest.Wait
quiz.why: The clock jumps to the next pending timer once nothing in the bubble can make progress without time passing.

quiz.q: Which of these does not count as durably blocking?
options: Receiving from a channel created in the bubble
sync.WaitGroup.Wait after Add was called in the bubble
quiz.why: A mutex can be released by a goroutine outside the bubble, so a goroutine waiting on one is not durably blocked.

quiz.q: What does synctest.Sleep(d) do?
options: Sleeps for d of real time
Moves the clock by d without blocking
quiz.why: Its docs define it as exactly those two calls: advance the fake clock, then let the other goroutines settle.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Testing concurrent code with timeouts used to mean one of two compromises: real sleeps
(slow and flaky) or a clock interface threaded through production code.
`testing/synctest` (Go 1.25) removes both.

`synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ... })` runs the function in a **bubble**. Every
goroutine started inside belongs to the bubble, and inside it the `time` package runs on
a **fake clock** that starts at midnight UTC, 2000-01-01. The clock only moves when
every goroutine in the bubble is **durably blocked**, meaning only another goroutine in
the same bubble could wake it. Then it jumps straight to the next timer.

Two helpers control the timing inside a test:

- `synctest.Wait()` blocks until every other goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked,
  so you can assert on state once the system has settled.
- `synctest.Sleep(d)` (Go 1.27) is `time.Sleep(d)` followed by `synctest.Wait()`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: Vitest's `vi.useFakeTimers()` and Jest's fake timers replace `setTimeout`,
  but the test drives them with `advanceTimersByTime(ms)`. In a bubble the clock
  advances on its own whenever nothing else can happen, across all goroutines.
- **Java**: the usual approach is injecting a `java.time.Clock` or a fake
  `ScheduledExecutorService`, plus Awaitility-style polling. synctest needs neither:
  production code keeps calling `time.Now` and `time.After`.
- **Python**: `freezegun` or `time-machine` freeze `time.time()`, but a thread that is
  sleeping still sleeps in real time. The bubble controls sleeps, timers and deadlines
  together.
- **C++**: comparable to templating code on a clock type, done by the runtime instead.

## How it works

The runtime tracks every goroutine in the bubble. A goroutine is durably blocked when it
is blocked on a send, receive or `select` over channels created in the bubble, on
`time.Sleep`, on `sync.Cond.Wait`, or on `sync.WaitGroup.Wait` when `Add` was called in
the bubble. Locking a `sync.Mutex`, network I/O and system calls are not durably
blocking, because something outside the bubble could end them.

When every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked:

1. if the test is in `synctest.Wait`, `Wait` returns;
2. otherwise, while the test function is still running, the clock jumps to the next
   time that would wake a goroutine;
3. if there is no such time, the bubble is deadlocked: `synctest.Test` panics and the
   test fails.

`synctest.Test` returns only after every goroutine in the bubble has exited. Inside the
bubble, `t.Context()` has a `Done` channel that belongs to the bubble, and `t.Run`,
`t.Parallel` and `t.Deadline` must not be called.

These examples run with `go test -v`. Real time per test is milliseconds, while the
logged fake time is seconds.

## Design notes

Write production code against the real `time` and `context` APIs, and let tests decide
how time passes. Reserve injected clocks for the cases synctest doesn't cover, such as
code that has to block on real I/O.

A useful test shape: start the system inside the bubble, `synctest.Sleep` to just
before the interesting moment and assert nothing has happened yet, then to just after
and assert that it did. `synctest.Wait()` on its own is the way to assert "this has
not happened": once it returns, nothing else can happen without time moving.

Fake networks keep tests inside the bubble: `net.Pipe` for raw connections, and
`httptest.NewTestServer` (Go 1.27), whose in-memory network suits synctest, for HTTP.

lessons.title: Package design: by feature, small API surface, no util packages
lessons.summary: A package is Go's unit of naming, privacy and dependency, and the compiler refuses import cycles. Give each package one job and a name that says it, group code by feature, and when two packages need each other, move the code or let the consumer declare an interface.

examples.title: A util package grows an import cycle; one job per package removes it

annotations.note: util starts innocently with Slug, which needs nothing of ours. OrderURL is where it breaks: a "shared helper" that takes a domain type has to import the domain package, and that package already imports util. Grab-bag packages attract exactly this kind of code.

The go command names the whole loop and the file behind each edge. The spec makes a package importing itself, directly or indirectly, illegal, so this fails on the first build, not at run time as a circular import can in Python or with ES modules.

slug has one job and a name that says it, and imports only strings, so any package can use it without risking a loop. A real slug function has decisions to make (should ş and ı become s and i?) and tests to prove them: one more reason it deserves its own package.
URL needs nothing but an Order, so it is a method on Order. Most functions in a util package belong to the package that owns their main argument.
The same program, rearranged, builds (a nil error). The edges now point one way: order imports slug, and slug imports only strings.

examples.title: Two packages that need each other: the consumer declares an interface

annotations.note: A genuine two-way need. No code is misplaced here, so moving a function can't fix it: written the direct way, with order calling email.Confirm(o), it fails with example 1's import cycle error. The fix has to change the direction of one edge.
order states what it needs, in its own terms, with the one method it calls. It no longer knows email exists: a test can pass a fake, and an SMS sender can be added without touching this package.

email imports order for the Order type and satisfies Notifier without naming it. Implicit satisfaction is what makes consumer-side interfaces possible; in Java, Sender would need "implements order.Notifier" and the dependency would point back again.
main is the one package that knows both sides and makes the concrete choice. StackLab's cmd/stacklab/main.go does the same when it hands httpapi either a runexec.Executor or a runclient.Client.

go list with a template prints the import graph: order imports nothing from the module, email depends on order, and only the root package depends on both. The same command in review or CI shows when a change adds an edge that shouldn't exist.

use_cases: A feature in a service: one package (internal/order) holding its types, rules and storage, instead of an order file in each of models/, services/ and handlers/
A helper two features share: a small package named for what it does (slug, money, clock), or a copied three-line function
Two packages that need each other: move the misplaced code, merge the packages, or declare an interface in the package that makes the call
Reviewing structure: go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} -> {{.Imports}}' ./... shows every edge of the graph
strengths: Import cycles are a compile error, so the package graph is acyclic by construction; Java compiles cyclic packages happily and needs ArchUnit or JDepend to catch them
Every call site carries the package name (order.New, slug.Make, http.Server), so identifiers stay short without Java's OrderServiceImpl or Python's from-import ambiguity
Interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so the consumer can declare the abstraction it needs without editing the implementing package
An unused import is a compile error, so removing a dependency removes the edge for real
weaknesses: Splitting a package later means renaming identifiers at every call site and exporting names that used to be private
There is no visibility level between package-private and exported, apart from internal/ directories; a helper two sibling packages share must be exported from a third
The cycle error shows the loop, not the fix; choosing between moving, merging and inverting is a design decision
Consumer-declared interfaces multiply: three packages may each declare a one-method interface over the same concrete type

pitfalls.title: A util, common or helpers package
pitfalls.detail: The name says nothing about the contents, so everything lands there, including helpers that take domain types, and the package starts importing the packages that import it. Put each function with the type it works on, or in a package named for its one job.
pitfalls.good: url := o.URL() // and slug.Make(name) for the helper with a job of its own

pitfalls.title: Packages per layer
pitfalls.detail: models/, services/, handlers/ spreads one feature across three packages, makes every change touch all of them, and turns models into a package everyone depends on. Group by feature; layers can live inside a feature package.
pitfalls.good: internal/order, internal/customer, internal/billing

pitfalls.title: Stutter
pitfalls.detail: The package name is already part of every reference, so repeating it in the identifier is noise.
pitfalls.good: order.New(...), order.Service

pitfalls.title: Breaking a cycle with a types package
pitfalls.detail: Moving every struct into a shared types or models package silences the compiler but keeps the coupling: now every package depends on one that changes for every feature. Move behaviour to its owner or invert the dependency instead.

pitfalls.title: Exporting by default
pitfalls.detail: Every exported name is a promise to every importer. Start lower-case and export when a second package needs it; put shared implementation details under internal/.

quiz.q: Package order imports util, and someone adds a util function that takes an order.Order. What happens?
options: It builds; Go resolves the cycle lazily
go build fails with import cycle not allowed
It builds, but initialization order becomes undefined
quiz.why: The spec forbids a package importing itself directly or indirectly, and the go command reports the loop with the file behind each edge.

quiz.q: order.Service needs to send notifications that package email implements. Where should the Notifier interface live?
options: In email, next to the implementation
In order, the package that calls it
quiz.why: Interfaces belong with their consumer (Go Code Review Comments). email satisfies it implicitly, so order no longer imports email and the cycle is gone; a shared interfaces package becomes one more thing everyone depends on.

quiz.q: Package order's main type is Order. Which constructor reads best at call sites?
quiz.why: Callers always write the package name, so order.New already says what it builds; the same reasoning gives http.Server rather than http.HTTPServer.

quiz.q: Why is an internal/models package holding every struct a design smell?
options: Package names may not be plural
Every feature depends on it, it changes for every feature, and it tends to grow helpers that import feature packages
quiz.why: Plural names are legal and binary size is unaffected; the problem is coupling. A package with no single job becomes the hub of the graph and the usual place for cycles to start.

further_reading.title: Go Code Review Comments: Package Names and Interfaces
Go at Google: Language Design in the Service of Software Engineering (dependencies)
The Go Programming Language Specification: Import declarations

lessons.body:
## Concept

A Go package is one directory compiled as a unit, and it is three things at once:

- the unit of **naming**: callers always write `pkg.Name`, so the package name is
  half of every identifier (`order.New`, `slug.Make`, `http.Server`);
- the unit of **privacy**: lower-case names are visible in every file of the package
  and nowhere else;
- a node in the **import graph**, which the compiler requires to be acyclic.

Good package design follows from those facts. Give each package one job and name it
for what it provides. Group code by feature (`order`, `customer`, `runexec`) rather
than by kind (`models`, `services`, `utils`). Export only what other packages need.
The Go blog puts the naming rule bluntly: "Packages named `util`, `common`, or `misc`
provide clients with no sense of what the package contains."

When two packages need each other, the compiler stops you, and the fix is one of three:

1. **Move** code that is in the wrong package (a helper that takes an `Order` belongs
   with `Order`).
2. **Merge** the packages if they are really one feature.
3. **Invert** the dependency: the package that makes the call declares a small
   interface for what it needs, and the other package satisfies it without being
   imported.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: a package is a namespace, javac compiles mutually dependent packages
  together, and "package by layer" (`controller`, `service`, `repository`) with links
  in both directions is common. A Go package is closer to a small module: many types
  and files, one purpose, one-way dependencies.
- **Python**: circular imports are legal until they aren't. Depending on import order
  you get `ImportError: ... partially initialized module` at run time. Go reports
  every cycle at build time, whatever the order.
- **JS/TS**: ES modules allow cycles through live bindings and fail at run time with a
  TDZ `ReferenceError` or an `undefined` import. Barrel files make such cycles easy
  to create; Go has no barrels, because the directory is the package.
- **C/C++**: forward declarations let two headers refer to each other. Go has no
  cross-package forward declarations; a package sees only what it imports.

## How it works

The compiler builds a package from its own sources plus the compiled export data of
its direct imports, which therefore have to be built first. A cycle would have no
first package, so the spec rules it out ("It is illegal for a package to import itself,
directly or indirectly"). The same ordering drives initialization: imported packages
are initialized before the package that imports them, and `init` functions run in
that order. An acyclic graph is also what lets the go command build independent
packages in parallel and cache each one by content.

## Design notes

StackLab's backend is the case study. ADR-0007 puts all Go code in one module, with
`server/internal/` split **by feature**: `gorun` and `sqlrun` run lessons, `runexec`
dispatches to them, `runclient` talks to the Docker runner, `learningstore` and
`runstore` own their SQL, `httpapi` owns HTTP. The layered alternative
(`handlers/`, `services/`, `models/`) was rejected because it scatters one feature
across three directories. `platform` is the closest thing to a shared package, and it
works because its direction is fixed: features import it, it imports no feature.

`httpapi` declares the `Runner` interface it calls. `runexec.Executor` and
`runclient.Client` both satisfy it without importing `httpapi` or each other, and
`cmd/stacklab/main.go`, the only package that knows all three, picks one. That is the
inversion from the second example at production scale.

Start with fewer, larger packages and split when a part has its own vocabulary, its
own reason to change and a small surface towards the rest. A package boundary is an
API: everything that crosses it must be exported, documented and kept stable, so a
split that needs twenty exported names in both directions is in the wrong place.

lessons.title: Constructor injection, functional options, useful zero values
lessons.summary: Go has no constructors, only functions named New. Make the zero value usable where you can, pass every dependency to New explicitly and wire them in main, and pick a Config struct or functional options for optional settings.

examples.title: Zero values that work, and zero values that only look safe

annotations.note: Neither field needs setup: a zero sync.Mutex is unlocked, and a nil map reads as empty. That makes var t Tally a complete, valid value, the way var mu sync.Mutex is.
Writing to a nil map panics, so the first write creates it. This lazy initialization is the usual price of a useful zero value, and the mutex makes it safe under concurrent use.

The property composes: Report holds a Tally, so the zero Report is ready too. Don't copy a Tally once it is in use: the copy shares the map but gets its own lock (go vet's copylocks check reports this).
bytes.Buffer, strings.Builder and sync.WaitGroup have no constructors either. wg.Go (Go 1.25) adds the goroutine to the group and starts it, replacing the Add(1)/go/defer Done() pattern.
A zero http.Client never times out, and a zero http.Server sets no deadline for reading headers. Usable, but wrong for production; StackLab's main.go sets every server timeout for this reason.

examples.title: Constructor injection: the store and the clock are parameters

annotations.note: The interface sits next to its consumer and has one method, the one Notes calls. A pgx-backed store, an in-memory map and a failing fake all satisfy it without importing this package.
Every dependency is a parameter of NewNotes, so the signature is the full list of what Notes needs. No package-level variables, no container, no reflection: wiring is ordinary code in main.
Time is a dependency too. A func() time.Time field lets tests freeze the clock, which is why the output below is deterministic; production passes time.Now.
Wrap with the context the caller can't see (which lesson) and %w, so errors.Is and errors.As still reach the store's error.
A failing dependency is one line, with no mocking library: write a type with the method. That is the payoff of small consumer-declared interfaces.

examples.title: Functional options vs a Config struct, and the explicit-zero problem

annotations.note: An Option is a function that modifies the value under construction. Adding WithProxy later adds a function; no existing call breaks, which is why libraries such as grpc-go take ...Option.
Defaults are set first, options applied after, in the order given. Options can also validate: make them func(*Client) error and have New return (*Client, error).

The Config struct is the simpler design and the more common one in the standard library (tls.Config, slog.HandlerOptions). cmp.Or (Go 1.22) returns its first non-zero argument: default-if-zero in one expression.
With options, WithRetries(0) says "zero retries" and gets it.
With a Config, Retries: 0 is indistinguishable from "not set", so the caller silently gets 2. Fix it with a *int field, a documented negative sentinel, or options.

use_cases: Types whose zero value works: counters, buffers, caches with lazily created maps, anything guarded by a sync.Mutex field
Services: NewService(store Store, now func() time.Time, log *slog.Logger), constructed once in main and passed down
Application settings: one Config struct filled from the environment in one function, as StackLab's config.Load does
Library clients with many optional, evolving settings: New(addr, WithTimeout(d), WithRetries(n))
strengths: Dependencies are ordinary parameters, so main.go reads as the dependency graph; Spring and Guice build the same graph from annotations at run time
A usable zero value removes 'forgot to initialize' bugs: var mu sync.Mutex is ready, where C needs pthread_mutex_init and Java a constructor call
Functional options let a library add settings without breaking callers, the job Java does with builders and overloaded constructors
Fakes are plain types with one method, so tests need no mocking framework
weaknesses: No default parameter values or keyword arguments: optional settings need a Config struct or options, more ceremony than Python's def connect(timeout=10)
A struct literal bypasses the constructor: Notes{} compiles and panics on first use with a nil store
A Config struct can't tell 'unset' from an explicit zero
Functional options are harder to discover in go doc and impossible to print: the settings live inside closures

pitfalls.title: Dependencies in package-level variables
pitfalls.detail: A global pool set in init() hides the dependency from every signature, makes tests share state, and ties startup order to import order. Create it in main and pass it in.
pitfalls.good: func NewStore(pool *pgxpool.Pool) *Store { return &Store{pool: pool} }

pitfalls.title: Zero meaning both 'unset' and 'zero'
pitfalls.detail: Config{Retries: 0} gets the default when the caller meant none. Use options, a pointer field, or a documented sentinel such as -1 for 'none'.

pitfalls.title: Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex
pitfalls.detail: Passing Tally by value copies the lock and the map header: both copies now point at one map, guarded by two unrelated locks. Use pointer receivers and pass *Tally; go vet's copylocks analyzer reports the copy.
pitfalls.good: func show(t *Tally) { fmt.Println(t.Count("go")) }

pitfalls.title: Constructors that return interfaces by reflex
