pitfalls.detail: Return the concrete type and let each consumer declare the interface it needs. Returning an interface hides methods and forces callers to type-assert; Effective Go reserves it for types that exist only to implement one interface, like crc32.NewIEEE returning hash.Hash32.
pitfalls.good: func NewNotes(s NoteStore) *Notes

pitfalls.title: Trusting the zero value of http.Client and http.Server
pitfalls.detail: Both mean 'no timeout'. Set Client.Timeout (or per-request contexts) and the server's ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout and IdleTimeout.

quiz.q: Which zero value is not ready to use for its main purpose?
quiz.why: Reading a nil map returns zero values, but assigning to one panics. The other three are documented as ready to use when zero.

quiz.q: A constructor computes retries := cmp.Or(cfg.Retries, 2). What does Config{Retries: 0} produce?
quiz.why: cmp.Or returns the first argument that isn't the zero value, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'not set'.

quiz.q: Where should the database pool be created in a Go service?
options: In an init() function of the store package
In main, or a function main calls, and passed to constructors
quiz.why: Creating it at the top and passing it down keeps every dependency visible in signatures, lets main decide what to build (real pool or fake), and lets tests construct their own.

quiz.q: A zero-value http.Client calls a server that accepts the connection and never answers. What happens?
options: It fails after a 30-second default timeout
It waits until the request's context is cancelled or the connection drops, which may be never
quiz.why: Client.Timeout zero means no timeout. Set it, or give each request a context with a deadline.

further_reading.title: Effective Go: Allocation with new (useful zero values)
Effective Go: Constructors and composite literals

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go has no constructor syntax. A constructor is a function, by convention `New` or
`NewThing`, that returns a ready value (usually a pointer) and sometimes an error.
Three habits decide how construction looks in Go code:

- **Make the zero value useful.** If `var x T` can be a valid `T`, callers need no
  constructor at all. `sync.Mutex`, `bytes.Buffer`, `strings.Builder` and
  `sync.WaitGroup` work this way; your types can too, by treating zero fields as
  "empty" or "default" and creating maps lazily.
- **Inject dependencies through the constructor.** When a type needs a store, a
  clock, a logger or an HTTP client, `New` takes them as parameters, typed as small
  interfaces the type itself declares. `main` builds the concrete things once and
  passes them down. There is no container and no annotation; the wiring is code.
- **Choose a shape for optional settings.** Required dependencies are positional
  parameters. Optional settings go in a `Config` struct whose zero fields mean
  "default", or in functional options (`New(addr, WithTimeout(d))`) when there are
  many of them, they evolve, or an explicit zero must be expressible.

When the zero value can't be valid (a dependency is required, a goroutine must start,
input must be checked), write `New` and return `(*T, error)` if construction can fail.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: no overloading, so telescoping constructors and builders turn into a
  `Config` struct or options. No Spring or Guice: `main` is the composition root,
  written out by hand, and an unused dependency is visible in a signature rather
  than hidden in an annotation.
- **Python**: no default arguments or keyword arguments. A struct literal with named
  fields, `Config{Timeout: 45 * time.Second}`, is the closest thing to
  `Client(timeout=45)`, and omitted fields are zero.
- **JS/TS**: an options object with `??` defaults is a `Config` struct with `cmp.Or`,
  with one difference: `??` distinguishes `undefined` from `0`, `cmp.Or` does not.
- **C++**: a constructor always runs. In Go, `var x T` and `T{}` never run code, so
  either the zero value is valid or callers must be told to use `New`. Unexported
  fields stop other packages from setting them, but not from writing `T{}`.

## Design notes

StackLab follows these rules throughout `server/`. `config.Load` fills one `Config`
struct from the environment and applies every default in one place.
`runexec.New(playgroundDSN, nodeProject)`, `runclient.New(baseURL)` and
`httpapi.NewRouter(logger, db, runner)` take their dependencies as plain parameters,
and `cmd/stacklab/main.go` constructs everything in order, so reading `run()` from
top to bottom is reading the dependency graph. CLAUDE.md states it as a convention:
constructor injection, interfaces declared by the consumer, no globals, no DI framework.

StackLab uses no functional options, and that is a choice, not an omission: each
constructor has two or three parameters, all required. Options earn their keep in
libraries with many optional settings and callers you can't update, which is where
you meet them (grpc-go's dial options, for instance). A reasonable default order is:
positional parameters for what is required, a `Config` struct for a handful of
optional settings, options when the list is long or keeps growing. Use one of the
two per constructor, not both.

lessons.title: Layered vs hexagonal: handler/service/store trade-offs
lessons.summary: A handler that calls a store is a fine design until rules, a second entry point or tests without a database appear. Then a service with ports declared by the core pays for itself, and its ports must keep each invariant in one call.

examples.title: Flat: the handler talks to the store, and that's enough

annotations.note: A concrete store with no interface in front of it. With one implementation and tests that run against a real database, an interface would only add a file to read.
The handler decodes, calls the store, and encodes. There is no rule to put anywhere else, so a service layer here would be a pass-through: three files for one map write.
PUT is idempotent here: the second request changes nothing. When the domain is this thin, the database (a primary key, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) holds the rules and the Go code stays flat.

examples.title: Rules and two entry points: a core with a port, adapters around it

annotations.note: The core owns its errors and declares the port it needs. It imports no net/http and no pgx, so it reads as the feature's rules and runs in a test with a slice for storage.

The rules: a well-formed id, at most maxBookmarks bookmarks. They hold no matter who calls, which is the reason this layer exists. Note the shape: count, then add. The next example shows what that costs.

The HTTP adapter translates: path value in, status code out. Domain errors become statuses in this one switch; the core never mentions HTTP. (StackLab's httpapi likewise sends every error response through one helper, problem.)
A second driving adapter. An import job, a CLI command or a queue consumer gets the same rules for free. Without the core, each would copy the validation, and copies drift.
Wiring stays in main: the storage adapter is built here and handed to the core, and the core to the router. Swapping memStore for a pgx store changes this line and nothing else.

examples.title: A port shaped like CRUD splits an invariant; shape it like the use case

annotations.note: The gate makes both requests count before either adds, the interleaving that two concurrent HTTP requests can produce. It is only there so the race happens on every run instead of occasionally.
The service's rule spans two store calls. Each call is safe on its own, but nothing makes the pair atomic, so two requests both see 2 and both add.

The fix is in the port's shape, not in the service: AddWithin does the check and the insert as one operation. In PostgreSQL that means one transaction that locks the user's row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or SERIALIZABLE with a retry; a count inside the INSERT statement is still racy under READ COMMITTED.
Same requests, same starting data: four bookmarks with the split port, three plus one rejection with the atomic one. Which request wins varies between runs; the totals don't.

use_cases: Flat (handler -> store): CRUD endpoints, internal tools, one entry point, rules enforced by database constraints
Layered (handler -> service -> store): business rules that span several store calls, transactions, more than one entry point
Ports and adapters: a core tested without a database, several drivers (HTTP, CLI, queue consumer), storage that may change
Mixed: most features flat, the two or three with real rules get a service; consistency within a feature matters more than across them
strengths: Consumer-declared interfaces make ports nearly free in Go: the core declares Store, the pgx package satisfies it without importing the core, unlike Java's ports, which the adapter must implement by name
One place maps domain errors to HTTP statuses, so a new error can't leak as a 500 from one handler and a 400 from another
Rules in a core run in microseconds in tests, with no database or HTTP server
Package boundaries enforce the layering: a core package that imports nothing from net/http or pgx can't call them by accident, unlike a folder convention in a JS project
weaknesses: Every layer adds types, constructors and mapping code; for CRUD that is cost without benefit
Ports shaped like tables (Get, Insert, Count) push invariants into services, where concurrent requests break them
Transactions don't fit neatly: a service that needs two store calls in one transaction needs a store method for the use case or a way to pass a transaction down
Mapping between transport, domain and storage structs multiplies when each layer gets its own type for the same data

pitfalls.title: A pass-through service
pitfalls.detail: A service whose methods only call the store with the same arguments is a layer of indirection with no rule in it. Call the store from the handler until a rule appears.
pitfalls.bad: func (s *Service) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Note, error) { return s.store.Get(ctx, id) }
pitfalls.good: note, err := h.store.Get(r.Context(), id) // in the handler, until there is a rule

pitfalls.title: Check-then-act across two port calls
pitfalls.detail: Count then Insert, Get then Update: each call is correct, the pair isn't. Give the port a method per use case that runs in one transaction, or enforce the invariant with a constraint.
pitfalls.bad: n, _ := store.Count(ctx); if n < limit { store.Add(ctx, id) }
pitfalls.good: err := store.AddWithin(ctx, id, limit) // one transaction inside the store

pitfalls.title: Driver types leaking into the core
pitfalls.detail: A core that checks pgx.ErrNoRows or *pgconn.PgError is coupled to the driver. The store translates them into the core's own errors (ErrNotFound, ErrDuplicate).

pitfalls.title: An interface for every struct
pitfalls.detail: Interfaces belong where there is a second implementation or a test that needs a substitute. StackLab's stores are concrete; only httpapi.Runner, with two implementations, is an interface.

pitfalls.title: Layers as packages named after layers
pitfalls.detail: handlers/, services/, repositories/ packages recreate the layer cake across the whole app and invite import cycles. Keep the layers inside each feature package, or one package per feature with sub-packages only when it grows.

quiz.q: A feature has three CRUD endpoints, one entry point, and its only rule is a unique constraint in the database. Which shape fits?
options: Handlers calling a concrete store directly
A domain core with ports for storage and HTTP
quiz.why: There is no rule for a service to hold and only one implementation of storage. Add layers when rules, a second entry point or substitutes appear.

quiz.q: A service enforces 'at most 3 bookmarks' with store.Count followed by store.Add. What goes wrong under load?
options: Two concurrent requests can both see 2 and both add, ending with 4
quiz.why: Each call is atomic, the pair isn't. Make check and insert one store operation in one transaction, or enforce the limit in the database.

quiz.q: In ports and adapters, who declares the Store interface?
options: The storage adapter, next to the SQL
quiz.why: Ports belong to the core; adapters satisfy them. In Go this is the ordinary consumer-declared interface, satisfied implicitly.

quiz.q: Where should a domain error such as ErrLimit become HTTP 409?
options: In the core, by returning the status code
In the HTTP adapter, in one mapping function or switch
quiz.why: The core stays transport-agnostic, so the CLI and the import job can use it; one mapping point keeps statuses consistent.

further_reading.title: Organizing a Go module (server project layout)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three shapes cover most Go services:

- **Flat**: HTTP handlers call a store (or run SQL) directly. Right for CRUD, admin
  tools and anything whose rules live in database constraints.
- **Layered**: a transport layer (decode, validate shape, map errors to statuses), a
  service layer (business rules, transactions, orchestration) and a storage layer
  (SQL). Each layer calls only the one below.
- **Ports and adapters** (hexagonal, Alistair Cockburn's term): a core of rules
  declares *ports*, interfaces for what it needs from the outside (storage, mail,
  clocks). *Adapters* implement them (a pgx store) or drive the core (an HTTP
  handler, a CLI, a queue consumer, a test). Dependencies point inward: the core
  imports neither `net/http` nor `pgx`.

In Go the step from layered to hexagonal is small. If the service declares the `Store`
interface it uses and the pgx package satisfies it, you already have a port and an
adapter. The real decisions are how many layers a feature gets, and what shape the
ports have.

Add structure when you can name what it buys: rules that aren't just validation, a
second entry point, tests that must run without a database, a transaction across
several statements. Without one of those, a layer is a pass-through, and a
pass-through is cost.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring**: `Controller -> Service -> Repository`, each with an interface and an
  `Impl`, is the default from the first endpoint. Go code usually starts flat, adds a
  service when a rule appears, and declares an interface only where a consumer needs
  a substitute.
- **Python**: Django puts rules on models (active record); FastAPI and Flask apps often
  stay flat with SQLAlchemy in the route. Both map directly onto the shapes above.
- **JS/TS**: NestJS enforces modules, controllers and providers; Express leaves it to
  you. Unlike a folder convention, a Go package boundary is enforced by the compiler:
  a core package without a `pgx` import cannot call pgx.
- **"Clean architecture"** adds more rings (entities, use cases, interface adapters),
  each with its own types. In Go that usually means mapping code nobody needs; take
  the dependency rule and skip the ceremony.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  http["HTTP handler"] --> core["Bookmarks (rules)"]
  job["import job / CLI"] --> core
  test["test"] --> core
  core -->|"Store port"| pg["pgx store"]
  core -->|"Store port"| mem["memory store"]
```

Arrows are calls; the Go imports point the same way except at the ports: the pgx
store imports the core (for its types and errors), the core imports nothing from
it. `main` is the only package that sees both ends and connects them.

A port's shape decides where invariants live. A port mirroring a table (`Get`,
`Insert`, `Count`) leaves every rule that touches two rows to the service, which then
runs several statements without a shared transaction, as the third example shows. A
port shaped like the use case (`AddWithin`, `ReserveSeat`, `TransferFunds`) lets the
adapter run the whole thing in one transaction with the right locks, and keeps the
core free of transaction handles.

## Design notes

StackLab's backend is mostly flat, on purpose. `httpapi` handlers call
`*learningstore.Store` and `*runstore.Store` directly: one database, no rule beyond
what the schema enforces, nothing to swap. The run path is the
exception, and it is exactly where a port pays: `httpapi.Runner` has two adapters,
`runexec` in local mode and `runclient` in Docker mode, chosen in `main`. Every error
response leaves through one function, `httpapi`'s `problem` helper, so the error shape
stays uniform.

That mix is the recommendation. Choose a shape per feature, for the program you have:
flat until a rule, a second driver or a test without a database asks for more; a
service with use-case-shaped ports when it does. Moving from flat to layered later is
a mechanical refactor in Go (extract the rule, declare the interface where it is
called); undoing premature layers is harder, because every caller has learned them.

lessons.title: A little copying is better than a little dependency; Go proverbs, examined
lessons.summary: The Go proverbs are design advice, not law. Some are enforced by tools, some hold almost always, and some bend: copy a five-line helper rather than import a module, but depend on maintained code for protocols and crypto, and use a mutex when a channel only adds ceremony.

examples.title: What one helper from a utility module brings with it

annotations.note: The function we want needs no imports; its neighbour needs net/http. Go imports whole packages, so every importer of strutil compiles net/http and runs its package initialization, whichever function it calls.

A require line, and a replace pointing at a local directory so the demo works offline. With a real module this line also brings a go.sum entry, a version your users must accept as a minimum, and every advisory govulncheck will report against it.

Five lines with a source and license note. It counts runes, not bytes: s[:12] on "Merhaba dünya" would cut ü's two UTF-8 bytes in half, while this returns "Merhaba düny…". Small, pure, stable and tested code is what the proverb is about.
go list -deps prints every package the build compiles; GOOS and GOARCH are fixed so the count is the same on Windows and Linux. 190 packages against 60, and crypto/tls among them, for one function.
The linker drops functions nothing calls, so the binary grows less than the package count. The rest of the cost stays: compile time, init code, upgrades and advisories.

examples.title: Before copying or depending, check the standard library

annotations.note: Grouping needs no helper. slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (Go 1.23) replaces the "keys, sorted" function that used to be copied into every project, or imported from a lodash-style library.
A two-key sort: cmp.Compare gives -1/0/+1, and cmp.Or (Go 1.22) returns the first non-zero, so the second key only decides ties. Swapping a and b in the first Compare sorts descending.
slices.Compact removes adjacent duplicates, so sort first. The pair is the standard spelling of "unique".
slices.Chunk returns an iterator over sub-slices that share the original's backing array: no copies, and range-over-func reads it like any loop.
strings.Cut (Go 1.18) replaced Index-and-slice code; min and max are built-ins since Go 1.21. Most "util" functions in older Go codebases now have a standard-library name.

examples.title: Share memory by communicating, or guard it with a mutex? The same counter twice

annotations.note: The channel version: one goroutine owns the map, and nobody else touches it, so no lock is needed. It runs forever: a real version needs a Close method or a context to stop it, which the mutex version doesn't.
A read is a request with a reply channel, two channel operations and a goroutine hop for what is a field access in the other version.
The mutex version: state with a guard. Effective Go itself says the channel approach "can be taken too far" and that a reference count may be best done with a mutex around an integer.
maps.Clone returns a shallow copy. Returning c.counts itself would hand callers the guarded map, and their reads would race with Inc.
Both pass the same concurrent workload with the same result. Pick by clarity: channels to hand off work and ownership, a mutex for shared state such as caches and counters.

use_cases: Copy: a short, pure, stable function (truncate, clamp, a retry loop) when the alternative is a module dependency
Depend: crypto, protocols, database drivers, parsers of formats you don't control, anything that receives security fixes
Look in the standard library first: slices, maps, cmp, strings and iterators replace most helper libraries since Go 1.21-1.23
Mutex for state (caches, counters, registries); channels for handing off work, ownership and results
strengths: Go's standard library covers HTTP, JSON, crypto, SQL interfaces, templates and testing, so many services need a database driver and little else, unlike a typical npm or Maven tree
Modules make a dependency's cost visible: one require line, checksums in go.sum, go list -deps and go mod graph to see what came with it
The proverbs give a shared vocabulary for review comments, the way the Zen of Python does
weaknesses: Copied code doesn't get upstream fixes, and govulncheck can't see it, because it scans module versions and their symbols
The proverbs predate generics and modules (2015); some, such as interface{} says nothing, read differently now
Slogans get applied without their context: 'share memory by communicating' has produced many channel-based counters that a mutex would do better

pitfalls.title: Copying security-sensitive code
pitfalls.detail: A hand-copied JWT check or a copied parser loses every future fix and is invisible to govulncheck. Depend on maintained code for crypto, protocols and formats from outside.

pitfalls.title: Copying without the license notice
pitfalls.detail: MIT and BSD licenses require keeping the copyright and permission notice with substantial copies. Put it in a comment next to the code, with the source and version.

pitfalls.title: Re-implementing what the standard library has
pitfalls.detail: Hand-written contains, keys, unique and chunk helpers are common in pre-1.21 code. Since Go 1.26, go fix rewrites many such loops (its slicescontains, mapsloop and minmax analyzers).
pitfalls.bad: func contains(xs []string, x string) bool { for _, v := range xs { if v == x { return true } }; return false }
pitfalls.good: slices.Contains(xs, x)

pitfalls.title: A goroutine and two channels for a counter
pitfalls.detail: An owner goroutine needs a lifecycle (start, stop, leak checks) and makes every read a round trip. For plain shared state a mutex is shorter and faster.

pitfalls.title: Returning a guarded map or slice
pitfalls.detail: The lock protects the field, not values handed out: callers keep reading the same map while Inc writes to it.
pitfalls.bad: func (c *MutexCounter) Snapshot() map[string]int { c.mu.Lock(); defer c.mu.Unlock(); return c.counts }
pitfalls.good: return maps.Clone(c.counts)

quiz.q: Which is the strongest case for adding a dependency rather than copying code?
quiz.why: Signature verification is security-sensitive and receives fixes; a copy would miss them, and govulncheck couldn't flag it. The other two are small, pure and stable.

quiz.q: Your app imports example.com/strutil only to call Truncate, but strutil also imports net/http. What does your build include?
options: net/http and everything it imports, compiled and initialized, although the linker drops unused functions
Nothing extra until FetchJSON is called
quiz.why: Go imports whole packages: every imported package is compiled and initialized at startup. Dead-code elimination happens later, at function level, in the linker.

quiz.q: What does Effective Go say about 'share memory by communicating'?
options: The approach can be taken too far; a reference count may be best done with a mutex around an integer
quiz.why: Effective Go introduces the slogan and immediately warns against overdoing it; the Go wiki's advice is to use whichever is most expressive or simple.

quiz.q: You copy 20 lines from an MIT-licensed library. What do you keep with them?
options: Nothing; 20 lines are too few to matter
The copyright and permission notice, plus a note of the source
quiz.why: The MIT license requires the notice in all copies or substantial portions; recording the source and version also tells future readers where fixes would come from.

further_reading.title: Go at Google: Language Design in the Service of Software Engineering (dependency hygiene)
Go wiki: Use a sync.Mutex or a channel?
How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks

lessons.body:
## Concept

The Go proverbs are nineteen one-liners from Rob Pike's talk at Gopherfest SV in 2015
(collected at go-proverbs.github.io). They compress design advice, and like all
slogans they hold in the context they came from. Read them in three groups:

- **Enforced or near-universal.** "Gofmt's style is no one's favorite, yet gofmt is
  everyone's favorite", "Errors are values", "Cgo is not Go", "With the unsafe package
  there are no guarantees", "Clear is better than clever". Tools enforce the first,
  and arguing with the others rarely ends well.
- **Strong defaults that bend.** "A little copying is better than a little dependency"
  holds for short, pure, stable code and fails for crypto, protocols and parsers.
  "Don't communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating" is followed in
  the list by "Channels orchestrate; mutexes serialize", which already admits the
  bend. "Make the zero value useful" works until a type needs a dependency or a limit.
  "Don't panic" allows `regexp.MustCompile` at start-up.
- **Changed by later Go.** "interface{} says nothing" predates generics: with type
  parameters (Go 1.18), code that is truly generic no longer needs `interface{}`,
  though `any` in an API still says nothing. The copying proverb predates modules
  (Go 1.11): a dependency then was an unversioned GOPATH checkout, now it is a
  checksummed, versioned requirement, cheaper but not free.

The copying proverb comes from how Go itself was built. The 2012 "Go at Google" talk
says "Dependency hygiene trumps code reuse" and cites the `net` package carrying its
own integer-to-decimal conversion to avoid depending on the formatted I/O package.
The habit persists: in Go 1.27, `go list -f '{{.Imports}}' net` shows neither `fmt`
nor `strconv`; `net` uses a small internal package instead.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS/npm**: the opposite culture. Micro-packages such as left-pad, and dependency
  trees of hundreds of packages, are normal; Go teams treat each new module as a
  decision. Go also runs no install scripts when fetching modules.
- **Java**: Guava and Apache Commons are reflexive imports. Go's `slices`, `maps`,
  `strings` and `cmp` packages cover much of what they are imported for.
- **Python**: the proverbs play the role of the Zen of Python (`import this`), and
  "batteries included" matches Go's standard library.
- **C/C++**: copying a header-only library into the tree is common because package
  management is hard. Go's module cache and minimal version selection make
  versioned dependencies easy, so copying is a choice, not a workaround.

## Design notes

StackLab applies the proverb as policy. CLAUDE.md asks before any dependency outside
an allow-list. ADR-0008 rejected Windows Job Objects because they need
`golang.org/x/sys`; `taskkill /T` "is boring and ships with Windows". When the runner
later also had to kill what a program leaves running after it exits, which `taskkill`
can't find, gorun took Job Objects after all, without the dependency: three kernel32
functions loaded through the standard library's `syscall.NewLazyDLL`, a little copying
in place of `golang.org/x/sys/windows`. ADR-0001 chose
the standard library router over a framework, and the config package reads
environment variables without a config library. The counter-examples are just as
deliberate: StackLab depends on pgx and goose, because nobody should copy a
PostgreSQL wire-protocol implementation or a migration engine.

A workable rule: copy when the code is short, has no state, won't need security
fixes and you can test it; keep the license notice and the source next to it.
Depend when the code implements a protocol, a format you don't control, or
cryptography. Before either, search the standard library.

Copying values has its own version of the trade-off, seen in the third example:
`maps.Clone` and `slices.Clone` are shallow. Handing out a copy of the map protects
the counter's internals; handing out the map itself shares them, lock or no lock.

lessons.title: Errors as values: wrapping with %w and adding context
lessons.summary: Errors are ordinary values you return and check. Wrap them with %w to add context without losing the cause, and inspect them later with errors.Is.

examples.title: Wrapping adds context; errors.Is still finds the cause

annotations.note: os.ReadFile already says "open users.txt" — but not who wanted it or why. Wrapping adds the loadConfig frame; it doesn't discard anything.
%w (not %v) is what makes wrapping work: it embeds the original error so errors.Is/As can unwrap. %v would only format text.

The text after the last colon comes from the operating system: "no such file or directory" on Linux and macOS, "The system cannot find the file specified." on Windows. That is why this example's check only looks at the parts Go produced.
errors.Is walks the whole chain with ==, so a sentinel like fs.ErrNotExist matches even three wrappers deep, on every OS. A string match on the message would be brittle and locale-hostile.

use_cases: Boundary functions that translate low-level errors into your domain
Adding what the operation was doing (query, file, service) without losing WHY it failed
strengths: Unlike Java checked exceptions, the compiler won't force you to handle the error — errcheck-style linters fill that role
Wrapping keeps one error chain instead of exception hierarchies; the cause and the context travel together
Sentinels like fs.ErrNotExist are comparable values: errors.Is is precise string-free matching
weaknesses: Nothing enforces checking a returned error; ignoring one is a silent bug
Deeply wrapped chains can produce noisy messages if every layer adds context
No stack trace by default: you add context deliberately instead

pitfalls.title: Wrapping with %v instead of %w
pitfalls.detail: The message looks right, but errors.Is/As can no longer see the cause. Always %w when you want unwrapping.

pitfalls.title: Checking err == fs.ErrNotExist on a wrapped error
pitfalls.detail: == only matches the immediate value. Wrapped errors must be inspected with errors.Is.

pitfalls.title: Adding context twice
pitfalls.detail: "open users.txt: open users.txt". Wrap where you add new information, not to re-log what the message already says.

quiz.q: Which verb preserves the wrapped error for errors.Is?
quiz.why: %w embeds the error value; %v and %s only format its message into the new string.

quiz.q: errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) on err = fmt.Errorf("load: %w", fmt.Errorf("open: %w", fs.ErrNotExist))?
quiz.why: errors.Is walks Unwrap() repeatedly until it finds a match or the chain ends.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A Go error is an ordinary value returned alongside your result: `value, err := doThing()`.
You check it, add context with `fmt.Errorf` and `%w`, and pass it up. `errors.Is` and
`errors.As` inspect the wrapped chain without knowing how many layers added context.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/Python/JS: exceptions unwind for you. In Go the `if err != nil` check is the unwind
  — visible, local, and impossible to trigger from a line you didn't expect to throw.
- C: errno plus return codes, but the error carries a message and an identity (`==`-able
  sentinels) instead of a global mutable code.
- Rust: `Result<T, E>` with `?` ≈ `(T, error)` with `if err != nil`; Go's `return err` is
  the explicit version of `?`.

## Design notes

Add context at each layer that knows something new ("loading config", "querying orders for
user 42"), and let `errors.Is`/`As` answer inspection questions at the top. Handle the error
once: either respond to it meaningfully or wrap and pass it up — logging it *and* returning
it produces duplicate log lines for one failure. This lesson's strategy across layers
(sentinel vs typed errors, where to recover) is its own later lesson.

lessons.title: errors.Is, errors.As, errors.Join; sentinels vs error types
lessons.summary: Sentinels answer "which failure?", error types carry data, and errors.Is, errors.As and errors.AsType find either anywhere in a wrapped tree. Whatever you wrap with %w becomes your API, so translate driver errors at the boundary.

examples.title: Sentinels with errors.Is, error types with errors.AsType and errors.As

annotations.note: A sentinel is matched by identity, so its message text plays no part. Exporting one makes it API: callers will depend on it. io.EOF and sql.ErrNoRows are the standard library's best-known sentinels.
An error type carries fields the caller can act on. Error has a pointer receiver, so *ValidationError is the error type, and it is the type to ask for below.
== compares only the outermost value, the wrapper fmt.Errorf built on line 23. errors.Is walks the chain, comparing each link with == or asking the link's own Is method.
A type assertion has the same blind spot as ==: it sees only the outer wrapper, so one more layer of context breaks it. Never type-assert errors you didn't just create.
errors.AsType (Go 1.26) returns the first *ValidationError in the chain, already typed. errors.AsType[ValidationError] wouldn't compile: the value type has no Error method.
errors.As does the same through a pointer to a target variable; code written before Go 1.26 uses it. Passing verr instead of &verr panics at run time, and go vet's errorsas check reports it.

examples.title: errors.Join and several %w build a tree that Is and As search

annotations.note: Limits on names and places should count characters. len counts UTF-8 bytes: "Şanlıurfa" is 9 runes but 11 bytes, and a byte limit of 10 would reject a valid Turkish city.
Collect, then join once. errors.Join drops nil values and returns nil when nothing is left, so the valid path (line 40) needs no special case.
A joined error prints one line per error, which suits logs. An API that returns a list of field errors can get the parts through the Unwrap() []error method that Join's result implements.
Is and As search the whole tree depth-first, so each check finds its error whichever branch holds it.
Since Go 1.20 fmt.Errorf accepts several %w, and the result unwraps to all of them. errors.Unwrap only follows Unwrap() error, so it returns nil here: inspect with Is and As, never by hand.

examples.title: Translating a driver error at the repository boundary

annotations.note: A stand-in so the example needs no database. The real type is pgx's *pgconn.PgError, and SQLSTATE 23505 is unique_violation in PostgreSQL's error code table.
%w passes the driver type through, so callers can, and will, write errors.AsType[*pgconn.PgError]. Your service now depends on pgx, and changing the storage breaks code that never touched SQL.
The translation: %w on ErrEmailTaken, %v on the driver error. The message keeps the SQLSTATE and constraint name for the log; the only link callers can inspect is the sentinel you chose to promise.
Other driver errors stay opaque too: the caller logs them and answers 500. If callers must detect something from below, such as context.Canceled, wrap that one on purpose.
The same text, a different API: errors.Is succeeds only on the translated error, and only the leaky one exposes the driver type.

use_cases: Sentinels for conditions callers branch on: ErrNotFound, ErrEmailTaken, io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows
Error types when callers need data: the field that failed validation, a retry-after duration, an HTTP status from an upstream API
errors.Join for form validation that reports every field at once, and for cleanup that fails after the main operation failed
Translating pgx or HTTP-client errors into domain errors inside the repository or client package
strengths: Matching is by identity or type, never by message text, so messages can change (or be localized) without breaking callers, unlike parsing exception messages
errors.Is and errors.As walk any depth of wrapping, so each layer can add context without breaking inspection further up
Exposure is an explicit choice at each call site: %w makes the cause inspectable, %v keeps only its text, and the message reads the same either way
errors.AsType is checked at compile time: asking for a type that doesn't implement error fails to build instead of panicking
weaknesses: Nothing tells the caller which sentinels and types a function can return; it lives in doc comments, unlike Java's throws clause
Every exported sentinel and error type is API surface you have to keep
Trees from errors.Join and several %w have no single cause: errors.Unwrap returns nil, and order of the search matters when two links match

pitfalls.title: Comparing with == or asserting the type
pitfalls.detail: err == ErrNotFound and err.(*MyErr) both fail as soon as any layer wraps the error. Use errors.Is and errors.AsType (errors.As before Go 1.26).

pitfalls.title: Matching on err.Error() text
pitfalls.detail: Messages are not API, and OS text differs by platform and language: on Windows, Go asks for the English message and falls back to the system language when it isn't available. Match sentinels and types instead.

pitfalls.title: Passing a non-pointer to errors.As
pitfalls.detail: errors.As(err, verr) panics at run time; it needs &verr. go vet's errorsas check catches it, and errors.AsType makes the mistake impossible.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping driver errors with %w out of habit
pitfalls.detail: Callers start depending on *pgconn.PgError and SQLSTATE codes. Translate to your own sentinel with %w and keep the driver error as %v text.

quiz.q: err := fmt.Errorf("load: %w", ErrNotFound). What does err == ErrNotFound return?
quiz.why: err is the wrapper fmt.Errorf created; only errors.Is looks inside it.

quiz.q: When is an error type better than a sentinel?
options: When the caller needs data about the failure, such as which field
When the error is returned from many places
quiz.why: A sentinel only identifies the failure; a type carries fields the caller can use.

quiz.q: err := errors.Join(errA, errB). What does errors.Unwrap(err) return?
quiz.why: errors.Unwrap only calls Unwrap() error; Join's result has Unwrap() []error, which Is and As use instead.

quiz.q: Your repository gets a *pgconn.PgError with code 23505. What should it return?
quiz.why: Callers get an inspectable domain sentinel and the full text for logs, without depending on the driver's type.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Working with Errors in Go 1.13 (Whether to wrap)
Go 1.20 Release Notes: wrapping multiple errors

lessons.body:
## Concept

There are two ways to make an error something callers can inspect. A sentinel is a
package-level value, `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`, checked with
`errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)`. It answers "which failure was it?". An error type is a
struct with an `Error` method, checked with `errors.AsType[*ValidationError](err)` (Go
1.26) or `errors.As(err, &target)`. It answers "which failure, and with what details?".

Both functions search the chain `%w` builds, and since Go 1.20 that chain can be a tree:
`errors.Join` and `fmt.Errorf` with several `%w` produce errors with several children,
searched depth-first. A type can also customize matching with an `Is(error) bool` method.
That is why the previous lesson's `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` worked on Linux and
Windows alike: `syscall.Errno` has an `Is` method that maps each OS's own "file not
found" codes to `fs.ErrNotExist`.

The design rule comes from the Go blog: wrapping with `%w` makes the wrapped error part
of your API. Wrap what you are willing to support; format the rest with `%v`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `catch (ValidationException e)` looks only at the thrown exception;
  `errors.AsType[*ValidationError](err)` is that catch plus a walk down `getCause()`.
  `errors.Is` is the same walk looking for one specific instance. `errors.Join` plays
  the role of suppressed exceptions, but as an ordinary value.
- Python: `except ValidationError as e:` maps to `AsType`, `raise DomainError() from e`
  to `%w`, and `ExceptionGroup` (3.11) to `errors.Join`.
- JS/TS: `err instanceof ValidationError` plus `err.cause` (ES2022) is the same search
  done by hand; `AggregateError` corresponds to `errors.Join`.
- C: errno values are sentinels without a chain, and `strerror` text was never meant to be
  matched either.

## Design notes

Prefer, in this order: opaque errors (the caller only checks `err != nil`), then sentinels
for the few conditions callers really branch on, then error types when they need data.
Every exported sentinel and type is a promise, so add them when a caller needs one, not
in advance. Translate at package boundaries: the repository turns `*pgconn.PgError` with
SQLSTATE 23505 into `ErrEmailTaken`, the HTTP layer turns `ErrEmailTaken` into 409, and
neither knows the other's vocabulary. The next lesson puts that mapping in one place and
adds the panics that slip past it. Never match on `err.Error()` text: on Windows, Go
asks the OS for English messages and falls back to the system language, so the same
failure can read differently on different machines.

lessons.title: panic/recover and an error strategy across layers
lessons.summary: Errors are for failures a correct program expects; panics are for bugs. Recover only at boundaries you own, the top of a goroutine and the top of a request, and let every other layer return errors upward.

examples.title: Errors for input, panics for bugs, and what recover hands you

annotations.note: Must functions panic by convention (regexp.MustCompile, template.Must). Use them only on inputs fixed in the source: a typo then fails the first test run or program start, never a request.
recover returns any, so a type switch sorts it. A runtime.Error is a failure the runtime detected, such as a nil map write or an index out of range: always a bug, never a condition to handle.

One mistake, two APIs. Compile returns an error because its input may come from a user; MustCompile panics because its input is code. Its panic value is a plain string, so it lands in the default case.
Nothing at this level can handle these sensibly. The right response is a 500 at the boundary, a log entry with the stack, and a fix.
Before Go 1.21, panic(nil) made recover return nil, so a boundary checking r != nil let the panic vanish. Now it raises *runtime.PanicNilError; GODEBUG=panicnil=1 restores the old behavior.

examples.title: Recover at the top of each goroutine and report a typed error

annotations.note: A distinct type lets callers tell bugs from failures with errors.AsType. A failure can be retried or shown to the user; a bug needs its stack logged and someone told.

The deferred recover must run in the goroutine that panics. A recover in main, or in the function that started the goroutine, never sees this panic, and an unrecovered panic in any goroutine ends the whole process.
debug.Stack() still includes the panicking line here, because the deferred function runs on top of the panicking frames. Once it returns they are gone, so capture the stack now, not later.
sync.WaitGroup.Go (Go 1.25) bundles Add, go and Done, and its documentation says f must not panic: hence safely. Each goroutine writes only its own slot, and Wait makes the writes visible.
Three outcomes: success, an ordinary failure, and a bug. Without safely, job 2 would have crashed the program and taken the other results with it.

examples.title: One place for status codes, logging and recovery in an HTTP server

annotations.note: Handlers return an error, as in the Go blog's appHandler pattern. They don't write error responses themselves; ServeHTTP does, once, for every route.
The request boundary. http.ErrAbortHandler means "abort this response quietly", so it is re-panicked for net/http to handle; swallowing it would turn a deliberate abort into a logged 500.
The single place errors become status codes. errors.Is finds ErrNotFound however deeply it was wrapped. Unexpected errors are logged here, once, and the client gets a 500 without internals.
Without a boundary of your own, net/http recovers the panic, logs a stack trace to the server's error log (see stderr), and closes the connection. The client gets no status code at all.

/raw: a dropped connection. /users/7: a mapped 404, not logged, because it isn't a server problem. /users/0: a recovered 500. stderr shows both logs; it is never compared, which is just as well, since it holds a port number and timestamps.

use_cases: Must helpers for constants: regexp.MustCompile, template.Must, parsing embedded config at startup
Panicking on a violated invariant: the default branch of a switch over your own enum, an impossible state in a state machine
Recovering at the top of worker goroutines, consumers and scheduled jobs so one bad item doesn't stop the process
Recovery middleware in HTTP and gRPC servers that logs the stack and answers 500
strengths: Expected failures stay ordinary values, so control flow is visible in the code, unlike exceptions that can come out of any call
A panic is loud: it carries a stack trace and, unrecovered, stops the process instead of leaving it running in a corrupted state
Boundaries are explicit: you can point at the two or three places in a codebase where recover is allowed
weaknesses: An unrecovered panic in any goroutine kills the whole process, unlike Java or Python, where an uncaught exception ends only its thread
Each goroutine needs its own recover boundary and nothing adds one for you: even sync.WaitGroup.Go only documents that f must not panic
recover works only when called directly by a deferred function, a rule that is easy to break with a helper

pitfalls.title: Expecting main's recover to catch a goroutine's panic
pitfalls.detail: recover only sees panics in its own goroutine. Put the deferred recover inside the function the goroutine runs.
pitfalls.good: go func() { defer logPanic(); work() }()

pitfalls.title: Calling a recover helper from a deferred closure
pitfalls.detail: defer logPanic() works when logPanic calls recover. defer func() { logPanic() }() does not: recover is then called by logPanic, not directly by the deferred function, and returns nil.

pitfalls.title: Recovering deep inside the code
pitfalls.detail: A recover in the middle of a call chain hides the bug and leaves state half-updated: a mutex held, a transaction open, a slice half-written. Recover at boundaries, fail that unit of work, log the stack.

pitfalls.title: Panicking for expected failures in a library
pitfalls.detail: Callers can only handle it with recover. "Not found", invalid input and timeouts are errors; the Code Review Comments say: don't use panic for normal error handling.

pitfalls.title: Swallowing http.ErrAbortHandler
pitfalls.detail: httputil.ReverseProxy and others panic with it to abort a response. A recovery middleware should re-panic it, not log a 500.

quiz.q: A goroutine started by main panics. main has defer func() { recover() }(). What happens?
quiz.why: recover only stops a panic in its own goroutine; an unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the program.

quiz.q: Which situation calls for a panic rather than an error?
options: A user submits an invalid email
A switch over your own enum reaches a value that can't exist
quiz.why: Only the impossible enum value is a bug in the program; the rest are failures a correct program must expect.

quiz.q: An HTTP handler panics and no middleware recovers it. What does the client get?
options: No response: the connection is closed
quiz.why: net/http recovers per request, logs the stack and closes the connection (or resets the HTTP/2 stream); it sends no status.

quiz.q: Where should HTTP status codes be chosen?
options: In one place at the HTTP boundary, from errors.Is and errors.AsType
quiz.why: Lower layers return domain errors; one boundary maps them to status codes, so the mapping stays consistent and the layers stay independent of HTTP.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Defer, Panic, and Recover
The Go Blog: Error handling and Go (the appHandler pattern)
The Go Programming Language Specification: Handling panics
package net/http: Handler (panic behavior) and ErrAbortHandler
Go Code Review Comments: Don't Panic

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go has two failure channels. Errors carry failures a correct program must expect: bad
input, a missing row, a timeout, an upstream returning 503. Panics signal bugs: a nil map
write, an index out of range, a broken invariant, a constant regular expression that
doesn't compile. A panic unwinds its goroutine, running deferred calls on the way; if
nothing recovers it, the program prints the panic value and a stack trace and exits with
status 2.

`recover` belongs at boundaries you own, where one unit of work may fail without taking
the rest down: the top of each goroutine you start, and the top of each request. There
the panic becomes a logged bug report plus an ordinary error or a 500. Everywhere else,
let it propagate. The defer lesson showed the mechanics of `recover`; this lesson is
about where it goes.

Errors travel the other way. Each layer returns them upward with context, translates
the ones that cross a package boundary, and exactly one place, the HTTP boundary or
`main`, decides what the outside world sees and logs the failure once.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/Python: a panic is like an unchecked exception that nobody is meant to catch, and
  `recover` is the catch at the thread or request boundary. The difference that bites:
  an uncaught exception in a Java or Python thread ends only that thread, while an
  unrecovered panic in any goroutine ends the whole process.
- Node: closer to Go. An uncaught exception crashes the process, and so does an unhandled
  promise rejection by default since Node 15.
- React: an error boundary is the UI-side version of the HTTP recover boundary: it stops
  one broken subtree from blanking the whole page (lesson ts.errors.result).
- C++: an unrecovered panic is like `std::terminate` after an uncaught exception, except
  that Go runs the panicking goroutine's deferred calls first.

## How it works

```text
layer            returns                               decides
repository       domain errors with context            driver errors -> ErrEmailTaken (%w) + text (%v)
service          domain errors with more context       business rules; knows nothing about HTTP
HTTP boundary    status code and body                  errors.Is/AsType -> 4xx/5xx; logs 5xx once;
                                                       recover -> log stack, 500
goroutine top    an error in a channel or slot         recover -> *PanicError with the stack
main             exit code                             logs once; os.Exit(1) after cleanup
```

Only the last three rows contain `recover` or `log`. A request handler that starts its
own goroutines needs a goroutine boundary inside them as well: the HTTP boundary only
covers the handler's own goroutine.

## Design notes

Panic for programmer errors only: violated invariants, unreachable branches of your own
switches, and `Must` calls on constants. Library code should never panic on bad input,
because its callers can only handle that with `recover`. At each boundary, log the panic
value together with `debug.Stack()` from inside the deferred function, since the
panicking frames are gone once that function returns. Fail that unit of work and keep
the process running. A recovered handler can only send a 500 if it hasn't written the
response headers yet; after that, logging and closing is all that's left. Keep
`log.Fatal` and `os.Exit` in `main`, after cleanup, as the defer lesson explained. And
map errors to status codes in one place, so a new domain error needs one new case, not a
hunt through every handler.

lessons.title: Reading files: whole file vs streaming
lessons.summary: Use os.ReadFile when the file comfortably fits in memory; stream it with bufio.Scanner when it might not, or when one pass is all you need.

examples.title: Read the whole file with os.ReadFile

annotations.note: One call opens, reads and closes the file. The error is an ordinary return value: nothing forces you to check it, but ignoring it is a bug.
string(data) copies the bytes. That's fine for a config file. For a 500 MB export it doubles memory, which is the cue to stream instead.

examples.title: Stream line by line with bufio.Scanner

annotations.note: defer schedules f.Close() for when main returns, on every return path. But log.Fatalf calls os.Exit, which skips deferred calls: harmless in a tiny program, a real bug in a server.
Memory use stays constant no matter how big the file is: one line at a time.
Scan returns false both at end of file and on error. Only sc.Err() tells the two apart, so this check isn't optional.
Go randomizes map iteration order on purpose. slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (iterators, Go 1.23) gives stable output.

use_cases: os.ReadFile: config files, small JSON/CSV, templates, test fixtures
bufio.Scanner: logs, large CSV exports, uploaded files, anything of unknown size
strengths: os.ReadFile is one call and closes the file for you; there's no resource to leak
Scanner uses constant memory regardless of file size
Both build on io.Reader, so the same scanning code works on files, network connections, gzip streams and HTTP bodies, without Java's InputStream class hierarchy
weaknesses: os.ReadFile holds the whole file in memory, and converting to string copies it again
Scanner's default maximum token size is 64 KB; longer lines stop the scan with bufio.ErrTooLong
Errors have to be checked in two places: at Open and after the loop

pitfalls.title: Skipping sc.Err()
pitfalls.detail: A too-long line ends the loop early and looks like EOF. Always check sc.Err(); raise the limit with sc.Buffer(...) if you need to.

pitfalls.title: Relative paths resolve against the working directory
pitfalls.detail: They don't resolve against the source file. In servers, resolve paths from configuration.

pitfalls.title: Untrusted file names can escape a directory
pitfalls.detail: "../../etc/passwd". Use os.Root (Go 1.24) or filepath.IsLocal before opening user-supplied paths.

quiz.q: sc.Scan() returned false. What do you know?
quiz.why: Scan reports false for both EOF and errors; Err() returns nil only at a clean EOF.

quiz.q: You must read a 2 GB CSV on a 4 GB machine. Which do you reach for?
quiz.why: os.ReadFile would need the file (plus its string copy) in memory; Scanner holds one line.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go gives you two levels of file reading. `os.ReadFile` returns the whole content as
`[]byte`. `os.Open` returns an `*os.File`, which is an `io.Reader`, and you consume it
piece by piece, usually through `bufio.Scanner` (line by line) or `bufio.Reader`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: `Path.read_text()` ≈ `os.ReadFile`; `for line in f:` ≈ the `Scanner` loop.
- Java: `Files.readAllBytes` vs `BufferedReader.lines()`. There are no checked exceptions:
  errors are return values, and linters (`errcheck`) catch the ones you ignore.
- C: a `fgets` loop without buffer overflows. An over-long line becomes an error, not memory corruption.
- Node: `fs.readFileSync` vs `readline` over a stream. Go's version is synchronous code
  that doesn't block other goroutines.

## Design notes

Accept an `io.Reader`, not a file name: `func countLevels(r io.Reader) (map[string]int, error)`.
Opening the file stays at the edge of the program (`main`, an HTTP handler), and the logic
works on files, request bodies, gzip streams and `strings.NewReader` in tests. This is Go's
everyday form of dependency inversion, and it's why `io.Reader` is the most important
interface in the standard library. The exercise has you do exactly this refactor.

lessons.title: Writing files: atomic writes, permissions, bufio.Writer
lessons.summary: Buffer many small writes with bufio.Writer and always Flush; check the error from Close on files you wrote. To replace a file that matters, write a temp file in the same directory and rename it over the target.

examples.title: bufio.Writer, the Close error, O_APPEND and O_EXCL

annotations.note: os.Create truncates an existing file to zero bytes before you write anything. From this line on, the old content is gone, which is the problem the second example solves.

A buffered write can succeed in memory and fail when the OS finally writes it (disk full, network drive). Close is where that surfaces, so for files you write, join its error into the result instead of a bare defer f.Close().

bufio.Writer collects small writes and hands them to the file 4096 bytes at a time. The output shows the file holding exactly one full buffer while 2583 bytes still sit in memory: return without Flush and the tail of the report is silently lost.
OpenFile is the general form behind Open and Create. O_APPEND makes every write land at the current end of file, which is what log files want. The 0o644 is used only if the file is created.

O_CREATE|O_EXCL creates the file only if it doesn't exist, in one step, with no gap between checking and creating. Use it for lock files and to avoid overwriting a user's file. Test the error with errors.Is and fs.ErrExist: the message text differs between Windows and Linux.

examples.title: Temp file plus rename versus writing in place

annotations.note: The naive version: truncate, then write. If the process dies, the disk fills or the encoder fails in between, the file holds a prefix of the new content and the old content is gone.
The temp file goes in the target's directory, not os.TempDir(): a rename cannot move a file to another file system or volume, and /tmp is often a separate one (tmpfs, or a different Docker volume).
On any error after this point, close and delete the temp file. A hard crash skips this cleanup, so a stray "atomic.json.tmp-123" can still appear; a recognizable name lets a startup job remove them.

CreateTemp creates the file with mode 0o600. Without this Chmod, every save would silently tighten the target from 0o644 to 0o600. On Windows only the owner-write bit is used, as the read-only attribute.

Sync asks the OS to put the data on stable storage before the rename makes it visible under the real name. Without it, a power cut right after the rename can leave a correctly named but empty file on some file systems.
The in-place file is now invalid JSON; the atomic one still has version 1, because the failed write never got the real name.

use_cases: bufio.Writer: CSV and report exports, any loop that writes many small pieces
Temp file plus rename: config and state files, caches, generated assets, anything another process reads while you write
O_APPEND: log and audit files several writers append to
O_CREATE|O_EXCL: lock files and "don't overwrite the user's file" saves
strengths: os.WriteFile covers the small case in one call, like Python's Path.write_text or Node's fs.writeFileSync
bufio.Writer wraps any io.Writer (file, socket, gzip stream), not just files, unlike Java's separate BufferedWriter and BufferedOutputStream classes
The atomic pattern needs only CreateTemp, Sync, Close and Rename from the standard library
weaknesses: The standard library has no WriteFileAtomic; you write (and test) the helper yourself
Errors surface late: a buffered write succeeds in memory and fails at Flush or Close, so both must be checked
Permission bits are Unix concepts: on Windows only the owner-write bit does anything (it maps to the read-only attribute)

pitfalls.title: Forgetting Flush
pitfalls.detail: bufio.Writer holds up to 4096 bytes in memory. Return without Flush and the end of the file is missing, with no error anywhere.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring Close on a file you wrote
pitfalls.detail: defer f.Close() discards the error. For files you read that's fine; for files you wrote, join Close's error into the function's result.
pitfalls.good: defer func() { err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()) }()

pitfalls.title: Truncating a file that matters, then writing it
pitfalls.detail: os.WriteFile and os.Create truncate first. The os.WriteFile docs say it outright: a failure mid-operation can leave the file partially written. Write a temp file and rename it.

pitfalls.title: Temp file in os.TempDir()
pitfalls.detail: Rename across file systems fails (EXDEV on Linux, and Windows refuses to move across volumes). Create the temp file in the target's directory.

pitfalls.title: Losing the original permissions
pitfalls.detail: CreateTemp uses 0o600 and rename keeps the temp file's mode, so call f.Chmod(perm) before renaming.

quiz.q: A function writes 300 short lines through bufio.NewWriter(f) and returns without calling Flush. What ends up in the file?
options: All 300 lines: Close flushes the buffer
Only the bytes that filled whole 4096-byte buffers
quiz.why: Closing the *os.File knows nothing about the bufio.Writer wrapped around it; whatever is still buffered is lost.

quiz.q: Why must the temp file be created in the target's directory?
options: Rename can't move a file across file systems or volumes
So the file inherits the directory's permissions
quiz.why: os.TempDir() is often another file system or volume, where rename fails. Same directory means same file system.

quiz.q: You save config.json (mode 0o644) with CreateTemp plus Rename and no Chmod. What mode does it have afterwards on Linux?
quiz.why: Rename replaces the directory entry with the temp file, mode included. CreateTemp creates files with 0o600 before umask.

further_reading.title: package os: WriteFile, CreateTemp, Rename, OpenFile

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three layers, from simple to safe:

- `os.WriteFile(name, data, perm)` writes a whole `[]byte` in one call. It creates or
  **truncates** the file, so a failure halfway leaves it partially written.
- `os.Create` or `os.OpenFile` give you an `*os.File`, an `io.Writer`. Wrap it in a
  `bufio.Writer` when you make many small writes, and call `Flush` at the end.
- To replace a file that something else depends on, write a temp file in the same
  directory, `Sync` and `Close` it, then `os.Rename` it over the target. Until the rename,
  readers see the complete old file; after it, the complete new one.

The `perm` argument (`0o644`, `0o600`) is only used when the file is **created**, and the
process umask is subtracted from it on Unix (a umask of `022` turns `0o666` into `0o644`).
On Windows only the owner-write bit means anything: without it the file gets the
read-only attribute. That's why the examples never print modes: they would differ by OS.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: `os.OpenFile` flags are `open(2)`'s (`O_APPEND`, `O_CREATE`, `O_EXCL`, `O_TRUNC`),
  and `bufio.Writer` is the buffering `stdio` does for `FILE*`, made explicit. As with
  `fclose`, the close can be where a write error shows up.
- Java: no atomic write either. The idiom is `Files.createTempFile(dir, ...)`, write, then
  `Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE)`; Go's `os.Rename` is that move. Java's checked
  `IOException` on `close()` forces you to think about a failed close; in Go only you (and
  linters such as `errcheck`) notice a dropped `Close` error.
- Python: `os.replace(tmp, target)` is the same rename, and `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=...)`
  is `os.CreateTemp(dir, pattern)`, mode `0o600` included.
- Node: `fs.writeFileSync` truncates and writes like `os.WriteFile`; there's no built-in
  atomic write there either (npm packages such as `write-file-atomic` do this dance).

## How it works

`writeAtomic` in the second example, step by step:

1. `os.CreateTemp(dir, "atomic.json.tmp-*")` creates a new file with a random name and
   mode `0o600`. Several processes can do this at once without colliding.
2. Write the content. Nobody reads this name, so a crash here only leaves a stray temp file.
3. `f.Chmod(perm)`, then `f.Sync()` so the bytes are on stable storage, then `f.Close()`.
4. `os.Rename(tmp, target)` swaps the name. On Linux and macOS, `rename(2)` within one file
   system is atomic: other processes see the old file or the new one, never a mix.

Go's own docs for `os.Rename` add a caveat: "Even within the same directory, on non-Unix
platforms Rename is not an atomic operation." On Windows the pattern still guarantees the
target is never a half-written file, because the new content is complete before it gets
the name; just don't rely on readers never seeing a gap. Replacing a file that another
Windows process holds open (an editor, an antivirus scan) can also fail, so retry or report.

## Design notes

Accept an `io.Writer` (or a `func(io.Writer) error`, as `writeAtomic` does) in code that
produces content, and decide at the edge whether it goes to a file, a buffer in a test, or an
HTTP response. Reserve the atomic dance for files that are read while you write or must
survive a crash; for an export the user downloads once, `bufio` plus a checked `Close` is
enough. On Linux, a rename is durable only after the parent directory is synced too
(`fsync` on the directory), which databases do and most applications skip; PostgreSQL's
write-ahead log is the industrial version of the same idea.

lessons.title: Composing readers and writers: io.Copy, TeeReader, MultiWriter, LimitReader
lessons.summary: io.Reader and io.Writer have one method each, so small adapters wrap them like Unix pipes: MultiWriter fans out, TeeReader taps, LimitReader caps, MultiReader concatenates and io.Pipe connects a writer to a reader.

examples.title: Copy once to two places; read once for two consumers

annotations.note: sha256.New returns a hash.Hash, which is an io.Writer. MultiWriter sends every chunk to the file and to the hash, so the checksum costs no second pass over the data. Swap the strings.Reader for an HTTP body and nothing else changes.
io.Copy counts bytes, not characters: İ, Ş, ı and ğ take two bytes each in UTF-8, hence 69 bytes for 64 characters. Size limits and Content-Length are in bytes.

TeeReader copies whatever its consumer reads into the hash. The hash sees only what was actually read: if the loop stopped early, the checksum would cover a prefix, so check sc.Err before trusting it.
Sum(nil) appends the digest to nil and returns it; it doesn't reset the hash. bytes.Equal compares the two 32-byte results.

examples.title: LimitReader with the +1 trick, byte limits vs characters, MultiReader

annotations.note: LimitReader returns a plain EOF at the limit, so a body of exactly max bytes and a much longer one look the same. Reading max+1 bytes and checking the length tells them apart without reading the rest.
Kastamonu is exactly 9 bytes and passes. Eskişehir is 9 characters but 10 bytes, so a 9-byte limit rejects it: limits are in bytes.

Cutting at a byte count can split a character: the third byte is the first half of ı. Trim previews with a rune-aware loop, or back off to a boundary with utf8.RuneStart, before showing them to a user.
MultiReader reads each reader to EOF, then moves to the next. Typical uses: prepend a header, stitch file parts together, or put back bytes you already consumed to sniff a format.

examples.title: Your own Writer, and io.Pipe between a producer and a consumer

annotations.note: A type satisfies io.Writer by having this method; there is nothing to declare. Return len(p) and nil on success: a Writer that reports fewer bytes than len(p) must also return an error.

io.Pipe connects code that wants an io.Writer (the encoder) with code that wants an io.Reader (io.Copy) without a temp file or a buffer of the whole output. Each side must run in its own goroutine, or the first Write blocks forever.
Always close the writer side. CloseWithError(nil) gives the reader EOF; a real error reaches the reader as its Read error, so a failed producer can't look like a short, successful stream.
Each Encode is one Write, the pipe hands it to one Read, and io.Copy passes it on: three records, three writes.

use_cases: Hashing or counting while copying: checksums of uploads, progress bars, metrics
Logging to the console and a file at once with io.MultiWriter
Capping untrusted input: io.LimitReader for files and streams, http.MaxBytesReader for request bodies
io.Pipe: streaming an encoder's output (JSON, gzip, CSV) into an HTTP request or upload without a temp file
strengths: Two one-method interfaces cover files, sockets, HTTP bodies, hashes, compressors and buffers, without Java's InputStream/Reader class hierarchies and their adapters
Adapters are values you nest, like a Unix pipeline, and they cost a function call per chunk, not a thread or an event loop
io.Copy uses WriterTo/ReaderFrom when the types have them; on Linux, file-to-file and file-to-socket copies can then go through copy_file_range, splice or sendfile
weaknesses: Blocking calls keep backpressure simple, but io.Pipe needs a second goroutine and leaks it if a side never closes
Wrapping hides capabilities: io.MultiWriter has no ReadFrom, so a copy through it loses the zero-copy path a bare *os.File would get
LimitReader stops silently with EOF, so it can't tell you the input was too large; you need the +1 check or http.MaxBytesReader

pitfalls.title: Trusting LimitReader to report oversize input
pitfalls.detail: It truncates and returns EOF. Read max+1 and compare, or in HTTP handlers use http.MaxBytesReader, which returns a *http.MaxBytesError.
pitfalls.bad: data, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, max)) // a 2 GB body becomes a valid-looking prefix

pitfalls.title: Never closing the PipeWriter
pitfalls.detail: The reader waits for EOF forever and both goroutines leak. Close it on every path, with CloseWithError(err) so failures propagate.

pitfalls.title: Checksum from a TeeReader whose consumer stopped early
pitfalls.detail: The hash covers only what was read. Drain the rest (io.Copy(io.Discard, r)) or treat an early stop as an error.

pitfalls.title: Cutting text by bytes
pitfalls.detail: A byte limit can split a multi-byte character such as ş, which then shows up as \xc5 or U+FFFD. Limit storage by bytes, but cut display text at rune boundaries.

quiz.q: io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, 1024)) returns exactly 1024 bytes and no error. What do you know about r?
quiz.why: LimitReader reports EOF at the limit whether or not r had more. Ask for 1025 to find out.

quiz.q: A goroutine writes to an io.PipeWriter and returns without closing it. What happens to the io.Copy reading the other end?
options: It gets EOF when the goroutine exits
quiz.why: Pipes have no idea the writer goroutine ended; only Close or CloseWithError ends the stream.

quiz.q: You need a SHA-256 of an upload while saving it to disk, in one pass. Which composition?
quiz.why: MultiWriter duplicates each chunk to both writers; io.TeeReader(body, hash) as the source would work too.

further_reading.title: Effective Go: Interfaces and other types

lessons.body:
## Concept

`io.Reader` (`Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)`) and `io.Writer` (`Write(p []byte) (n int,
err error)`) are the whole contract. Because they are this small, the `io` package can offer
adapters that take readers or writers and return new ones:

- `io.Copy(dst, src)` moves bytes until EOF, in 32 KB chunks or through a fast path.
- `io.MultiWriter(w1, w2, ...)` writes every chunk to all of them (Unix `tee`).
- `io.TeeReader(r, w)` returns a reader that also writes what it reads into `w`.
- `io.LimitReader(r, n)` stops with EOF after `n` bytes.
- `io.MultiReader(r1, r2, ...)` reads one after another, as one stream.
- `io.Pipe()` gives a connected reader and writer: what one goroutine writes, another reads.

Code that accepts an `io.Reader` or `io.Writer` works with all of these, and with files,
network connections, HTTP bodies, `bytes.Buffer`, hashes and compressors.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Unix shell: this is `cat a b | tee file | head -c N`, as values in one process.
- Java: `InputStream`/`OutputStream` decorators (`BufferedInputStream`, `DigestInputStream`,
  `SequenceInputStream`) do the same job, but through a class hierarchy, and with a
  separate `Reader`/`Writer` family for characters. Go has one family, for bytes; text is
  bytes that happen to be UTF-8.
- Python: file-like objects are duck-typed the same way, but `shutil.copyfileobj` has no
  standard tee or limit wrapper; you write a small class.
- Node: closest to `stream.pipeline` with `PassThrough` and transform streams, minus events
  and callbacks. A Go `Read` blocks its goroutine; it doesn't block the process, so plain
  sequential code gets backpressure for free.

## How it works

`io.Copy` first looks for shortcuts: if `src` has a `WriteTo` method, or `dst` has
`ReadFrom`, it lets them do the copy. `*os.File` has both, and on Linux they use
`copy_file_range`, `splice` or `sendfile`, so file-to-file and file-to-socket copies may never
pass through your process's memory. Otherwise `io.Copy` loops over a 32 KB buffer.

`io.Pipe` has no buffer at all: a `Write` blocks until `Read` calls have taken every byte.
That makes it a synchronization point between two goroutines, which is why the producer in
the third example runs in its own goroutine and closes the writer when it is done.

## Design notes

Make functions take the narrowest interface they need (`io.Reader`, not `*os.File`), and
compose at the call site: the hash, the size limit and the progress counter are wrappers the
caller adds, not parameters of your parser. Put limits at the trust boundary, where untrusted
bytes enter (an HTTP handler, an upload, an archive entry), and keep them in bytes, because
memory and disks are measured in bytes; convert to characters only for display. Reach for
`io.Pipe` when one API insists on a `Writer` and the next on a `Reader`; if both sides are
yours, a direct function call with an `io.Writer` is simpler.

lessons.title: Directories: ReadDir, WalkDir, path vs path/filepath, os.Root
lessons.summary: os.ReadDir lists one level and filepath.WalkDir a whole tree, both in byte order. Use path for "/" names, path/filepath for OS paths, and os.Root (Go 1.24) to open user-supplied names without escaping a directory.

examples.title: ReadDir for one level, WalkDir for a tree, io/fs for "/" names

annotations.note: MkdirAll is mkdir -p: it creates missing parents and succeeds if the directory already exists. Forward slashes work in os calls on Windows too; paths you get back from filepath use backslashes there.

ReadDir returns fs.DirEntry values sorted by name as bytes: uppercase Z before lowercase n, and İ (0xC4 0xB0) after every ASCII letter. Fine for deterministic output, wrong for a Turkish user's list, which needs collation (golang.org/x/text/collate).
A non-nil err means WalkDir couldn't read path (permissions, a vanished directory). Returning it stops the whole walk; returning nil skips that directory and carries on.
fs.SkipDir on a directory skips its subtree without reading it, so node_modules costs nothing. fs.SkipAll (Go 1.20) ends the walk early without an error.
filepath.WalkDir hands you OS paths: data\raporlar\Ocak.csv on Windows. ToSlash makes the printed form the same everywhere.

os.DirFS("data") is the same directory as an fs.FS. Names are relative to it and always use "/", which is what embed.FS, zip archives and fstest.MapFS use too, so code written against fs.FS works with all of them.

examples.title: path vs path/filepath, Join, IsLocal and Localize

annotations.note: The path package is pure string manipulation with "/" on every OS. Use it for URL paths and io/fs names; using it on Windows file paths would mishandle backslashes and drive letters.
filepath uses the OS separator. Rel computes the path of p relative to "data". Printing through ToSlash keeps the output identical on Windows and Linux.
Join calls Clean, which resolves ".." lexically. With a name taken from a request, uploads/../../etc/passwd becomes ../etc/passwd: Join is not a security boundary.

IsLocal (Go 1.20) is true only for a non-empty, relative name that stays inside the directory it is joined to; a/../b stays inside, so it passes. It checks the string only: a symlink inside the tree can still point outside.

Localize (Go 1.23) takes an io/fs-style name, as in a URL, and gives an OS path, or an error for names that aren't valid fs paths (.., leading /) or that the OS can't represent, such as a\b on Windows.

examples.title: os.Root keeps every lookup inside one directory

annotations.note: OpenRoot (Go 1.24) opens the directory once and keeps a handle to it. Every method on root resolves names relative to that handle and refuses any step that leaves it.
Writes stay inside as well. Names such as kasım are UTF-8 strings in Go; on Windows the os package converts them to the UTF-16 the system calls expect, so the same code works on both.
The naive Join plus os.ReadFile leaks secret.env twice. root.ReadFile refuses both: ".." may not climb above the root, and neither may absolute names or symlinks that point outside it.

use_cases: Listing a folder for a UI or an API: os.ReadDir
Indexing, cleanup and import jobs over a tree: filepath.WalkDir with SkipDir for vendor and node_modules
Serving or reading user-named files (uploads, report downloads, archive extraction): os.Root or os.OpenInRoot
Code that should work on disk, in embed.FS, in a zip and in tests: accept an fs.FS
strengths: WalkDir avoids an lstat per entry (unlike the older filepath.Walk), and DirEntry.Info only stats when you ask
Deterministic order out of the box: ReadDir and WalkDir sort by name, unlike Node's fs.readdir or Python's os.scandir, which return directory order
os.Root resolves names with openat-style lookups, so it is safe against symlink tricks that a lexical check like IsLocal (or Java's normalize().startsWith()) misses
weaknesses: Two path packages that look alike; mixing them up compiles and fails only on Windows
Byte-order sorting is wrong for display: İ, Ç, Ş sort after z
os.Root confines names, not resources: it doesn't stop bind mounts, /proc files or device files on Unix, as its docs say

pitfalls.title: filepath.Join as a sandbox
pitfalls.detail: Join cleans .. away from the result; it never refuses. Use os.Root (or at least filepath.IsLocal) for names that come from users, archives or URLs.
pitfalls.good: f, err := root.Open(r.PathValue("name")) // root, _ := os.OpenRoot(uploadDir)

pitfalls.title: path where filepath was meant
pitfalls.detail: path.Join("C:\\data", "x") treats the whole "C:\\data" as one name. Use filepath for anything the OS opens, path for URLs and fs.FS names.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive file systems
pitfalls.detail: NTFS (Windows) and macOS's default APFS treat Rapor.csv and rapor.csv as one file; Linux ext4 sees two. Code that dedupes or looks up names behaves differently in Docker than on your machine.

pitfalls.title: Returning err from the WalkDir callback by reflex
pitfalls.detail: One unreadable directory then aborts the whole walk. Decide: stop, or log and return nil to skip it.

quiz.q: filepath.Join("uploads", "../../etc/passwd") returns what?
quiz.why: Join cleans the result lexically. It doesn't confine anything, which is why user-supplied names need os.Root or IsLocal.

quiz.q: Which package do you use to join the parts of a URL path or an embed.FS name?
options: either; they're the same on Linux
quiz.why: URL and io/fs names always use "/". filepath would produce backslashes on Windows.
