quiz.q: filepath.IsLocal(name) is true. Is opening filepath.Join(dir, name) now safe against escaping dir?
options: Only lexically: a symlink inside dir can still lead outside
quiz.why: IsLocal checks the string. os.Root checks each step against the real file system, symlinks included.

lessons.body:
## Concept

- `os.ReadDir(dir)` reads one directory and returns `[]os.DirEntry` (an alias of
  `fs.DirEntry`), sorted by name. A `DirEntry` knows its name and type from the directory
  read; `Info()` fetches size and times only if you call it.
- `filepath.WalkDir(root, fn)` visits a whole tree in lexical order, calls `fn` for every
  directory and file, and lets `fn` prune with `fs.SkipDir` or stop with `fs.SkipAll`.
  It doesn't follow symbolic links.
- `path` handles `"/"`-separated names (URLs, `io/fs`, `embed.FS`, zip entries) on every
  OS; `path/filepath` handles the OS's own paths, with `\` and drive letters on Windows.
- `os.Root` (Go 1.24, with `MkdirAll`, `ReadFile`, `WriteFile`, `Rename` and more in 1.25)
  opens a directory and then refuses any name that would leave it, through `..`, an
  absolute path or a symlink.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: `opendir`/`readdir` plus `nftw`; `os.Root` is the `openat`-relative-to-a-dirfd
  discipline, wrapped so every method uses it.
- Java: `Files.list` and `Files.walk` (lazy streams, unsorted) vs Go's sorted slices.
  `path.normalize().startsWith(base)` is the lexical check that `filepath.IsLocal` replaces,
  with the same symlink blind spot.
- Python: `os.scandir` ≈ `os.ReadDir` (both avoid a stat per entry), `os.walk` ≈ `WalkDir`,
  `posixpath` vs `os.path` ≈ `path` vs `filepath`.
- Node: `fs.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` ≈ `ReadDir`; `path.posix` vs `path` ≈
  `path` vs `filepath`. Node has no equivalent of `os.Root`.

## How it works

`os.Root` resolves a name one component at a time from the directory handle it holds (on
Unix with `openat(2)` and `O_NOFOLLOW`, following symlinks itself). `..` may not climb
above the root, a leading `/` (or `C:` on Windows) is rejected, and symlinks are followed
only if they are relative and their target stays inside. Because it never builds a full
path string and then opens it, there is no gap between "checked" and "opened" for an
attacker to swap a directory for a symlink (the docs list the few exceptions, such as
`Root.Chmod` on Unix). On Windows it also refuses reserved device names such as `NUL` and
`COM1`. `root.FS()` gives the same protection behind the `fs.FS` interface; `os.DirFS`
does not, as its own documentation warns.

## Design notes

Keep the OS at the edge. Functions that only read files can take an `fs.FS`, and `main`
decides whether that is `os.DirFS(dir)`, `root.FS()`, an `embed.FS` or a zip archive;
tests pass a `fstest.MapFS`. For anything that turns user input into a file name (download
endpoints, upload storage, archive extraction), open an `os.Root` once at startup for the
directory and route every access through it; `filepath.IsLocal` is a good input check but
not a substitute. Sort for display with locale-aware collation, and remember that the same
two names can be one file on your Windows machine and two in the Linux container.

lessons.title: embed.FS: shipping static assets in the binary
lessons.summary: A //go:embed directive makes the compiler copy files into the binary as a string, a []byte or a read-only embed.FS. Because embed.FS is an fs.FS, templates and HTTP file servers use it directly: one file to deploy.

examples.title: string, embed.FS, the hidden-file rule and all:

annotations.note: The directive sits directly above a package-level variable. For a string or []byte it must match exactly one file, and the file's content becomes the variable's value at compile time.

Naming a directory embeds its whole subtree except names that start with . or _, so editor backups and .env files stay out. The all: prefix turns that filter off, which is how secrets end up in a binary.
The binary doesn't read version.txt at run time; the compiler already did. Changing the file changes nothing until the next go build.
Embedded names are slash-separated, relative to the package directory, and include the directory you named: static/app.css, not app.css.
A file excluded by the pattern simply isn't there: Open returns an error wrapping fs.ErrNotExist.

examples.title: ParseFS and FileServerFS on embedded files, a MapFS in tests

annotations.note: Two variables, two patterns. templates/*.tmpl matches files only; a * pattern would also match .hidden files at that level, unlike a bare directory name.
The handler depends on fs.FS, the interface, so the embedding decision stays in main. This is what lets the last request run against an in-memory test file system.
http.FileServerFS (Go 1.22) serves any fs.FS. StripPrefix removes /static/ from the URL so the remaining path matches names in the sub-tree.
ParseFS takes path.Match patterns over the FS. fs.Sub returns the static directory as its own FS, so names lose the static/ prefix.
r.PathValue returns the decoded name, Ayşe, and html/template escapes it for HTML: the <script> attempt arrives as text.
_draft.html is on disk next to the source but was never embedded, so the file server answers 404.
fstest.MapFS is a map from names to files that satisfies fs.FS, so a test can swap the assets without touching disk or the build.

use_cases: Single-binary deployment: HTML templates, CSS, JS and a built SPA inside one executable (or one FROM scratch image)
SQL migrations embedded next to the code that runs them
Default config files, license texts, test fixtures and seed data
strengths: No path resolution at run time: the binary works from any working directory, unlike reading ./templates relative to where the process started
Plugs into everything that takes an fs.FS: html/template.ParseFS, http.FileServerFS, fs.WalkDir, migration tools

Built into the go command, no bundler, resource compiler or build step, unlike Java resources (which need the JAR packaging) or Node, which needs a bundler or its experimental single-executable feature
weaknesses: Every change needs a rebuild; in development you usually want os.DirFS for live edits
Read-only, and files carry no modification time, so http.FileServer can't send Last-Modified or answer 304 on its own
The binary grows by the size of the files, and patterns can't reach outside the package directory (no .., no parent folders)

pitfalls.title: all: embeds secrets
pitfalls.detail: all:static includes .env, .git leftovers and _drafts. Prefer a plain directory pattern and a build step that writes only what should ship. You need all: when a framework's output uses _ names (SvelteKit's _app, Next.js's _next).

pitfalls.title: Assets outside the package directory
pitfalls.detail: //go:embed ../web/dist is an invalid pattern. Put a tiny package next to the assets (web/embed.go exporting an fs.FS) and import it.

pitfalls.title: Building before the frontend exists
pitfalls.detail: A pattern that matches nothing fails the build ("pattern dist: no matching files found", or "cannot embed directory dist: contains no embeddable files" for an empty directory). Build the frontend first in CI and in the Dockerfile.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the directory prefix
pitfalls.detail: static.ReadFile("app.css") fails: the name is static/app.css. Use fs.Sub to serve a directory as the root.

quiz.q: //go:embed static is above an embed.FS. Which of static/app.css, static/_draft.html, static/.env end up in the binary?
quiz.why: Directory patterns skip names that start with . or _; the all: prefix would include them.

quiz.q: You edit a template file while the compiled server is running. When do users see the change?
options: After a rebuild and a restart
quiz.why: The compiler copied the file into the binary; the running program never reads the file on disk.

quiz.q: Why should newHandler take an fs.FS instead of an embed.FS?
options: embed.FS can't be passed to functions
So tests and development can pass fstest.MapFS or os.DirFS
quiz.why: Depending on the interface keeps the decision about where files come from in main.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`//go:embed pattern` above a package-level variable tells the compiler to read files from the
package directory (or below it) at build time and store them in the binary:

- `string` or `[]byte`: exactly one file, its content.
- `embed.FS`: any number of files and directories, as a read-only file system that
  implements `fs.FS`, `fs.ReadDirFS` and `fs.ReadFileFS`.

Patterns use `/` on every OS and may not contain `.`, `..` or a leading `/`. A directory
pattern takes the whole subtree except names beginning with `.` or `_`; `all:dir` takes
everything. The program never looks for those files at run time, so it works from any
working directory, in a `FROM scratch` container, or copied to another machine.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: C23 (and C++26) add `#embed` for one file; before that, `xxd -i` or linker tricks.
  `embed.FS` adds the directory tree and a file-system API on top.
- Java: like resources on the classpath (`getResourceAsStream`), but there's no JAR or
  classloader: the files are bytes in the executable, and the API is the same `fs.FS` you'd
  use for a directory.
- Python: `importlib.resources` for package data, minus the packaging metadata you need to
  get the files into the wheel.
- Node: the closest is a bundler inlining assets, or Node's single executable applications
  (still experimental). In Go it's part of the plain `go build`.

## How it works

The `go` command finds the `//go:embed` lines, checks the patterns, and hands the matching
files to the compiler, which stores their contents in the binary's read-only data. An
`embed.FS` value is just a sorted list of names and contents, so `Open`, `ReadDir` and
`ReadFile` are lookups in memory. Its files report a zero modification time; `go list
-json` shows each package's `EmbedPatterns` and `EmbedFiles` if you want to see what was
matched.

## Design notes

Put embedded assets behind a small package that exports an `fs.FS` (for example a `web`
package next to the frontend's `dist/`), and make every consumer take `fs.FS`. Then `main`
chooses: the embedded files in production, `os.DirFS("web/dist")` behind a `-dev` flag for
live editing, `fstest.MapFS` in tests. Since embedded files have no modification time, give
built assets content-hashed names (Vite does this by default) and serve them with a long
`Cache-Control`, or add an `ETag` middleware; otherwise browsers have nothing to revalidate
against and download them again.

lessons.title: CSV and JSON: encoding/csv, encoding/json (and json/v2, Go 1.27)
lessons.summary: encoding/csv reads and writes RFC 4180 records; Turkish Excel adds ';', a BOM or windows-1254. encoding/json streams with Decoder and defers decoding with RawMessage. Go 1.27 ships encoding/json/v2, stricter by default.

examples.title: CSV from and for Turkish Excel: ';', BOM, decimal comma, windows-1254

annotations.note: With Turkish regional settings ',' is the decimal separator, so Excel separates CSV fields with ';'. Saving as "CSV UTF-8" adds a byte order mark; plain "CSV (Comma delimited)" ("Virgülle ayrılmış") is written in windows-1254 instead.

Comma is the field separator: any rune except CR, LF and U+FFFD. ReadAll loads every record; for large files call Read in a loop, which holds one record at a time. Quoted fields, doubled quotes and CRLF are handled for you.

encoding/csv doesn't strip the BOM, so the first header is U+FEFF followed by Müşteri and a lookup by "Müşteri" fails. Strip it from the first field, or peek at the first three bytes with bufio.Reader before parsing.
1.250,50 is Turkish notation for 1250.50, and strconv only knows the English form. Remove the thousands dots, swap the comma, and parse money into integer kuruş rather than float64.

In windows-1254, 0xDD is İ and 0xDE is Ş; followed by ASCII letters, neither byte forms valid UTF-8, so Go shows replacement characters. Decode such files with golang.org/x/text/encoding/charmap, which is not in the standard library.
For Excel: write the BOM yourself, then set Comma and UseCRLF. Without the BOM, a double-clicked UTF-8 file opens in the ANSI code page and ş turns into two odd characters (ÅŸ in windows-1252).

The writer quotes the field that contains ';' and doubles the quotes inside it. csv.Writer is buffered: WriteAll flushes and returns any error; if you call Write yourself, finish with Flush, which returns nothing, and then check w.Error().

examples.title: Streaming a large array with Decoder, RawMessage for mixed payloads

annotations.note: json.RawMessage keeps the bytes of data undecoded. The envelope is decoded once, and the switch decides which struct the payload becomes; unknown types keep their raw JSON for logging or forwarding.
JSON numbers are decoded into whatever type the field has. Keep money in integer kuruş (or a decimal string): float64 can't represent values like 0.10 exactly.

Token reads one syntactic piece, here the opening bracket, and More reports whether another element follows. Decode then reads one element. Memory is bounded by the largest element, not the whole array.
Each payload is decoded only after its type is known. With interface-based decoding (map[string]any) you'd get float64 numbers and type assertions everywhere instead.

Reading the closing bracket proves the array really ended. On a truncated upload either Decode or this Token fails (which one depends on the implementation), so a cut-off file is never accepted as a shorter one.

examples.title: encoding/json vs encoding/json/v2 on the same input

annotations.note: Both packages are named json, so one import needs an alias. In Go 1.27, encoding/json is itself implemented on top of v2 with options that keep the old behavior.
v2 redefines omitempty as "omit if it encodes as an empty JSON value" (null, "", {}, []), so 0 is kept. Use omitzero, which means the same in v1 and v2, to drop zero numbers and booleans.
Classify errors with errors.Is and errors.As. The v2 docs say the text of its errors may change over time, and v1 messages may differ since 1.27 moved v1 onto the v2 implementation.
A nil slice: v1 writes null, v2 writes []. Frontends that call .map() on the field stop crashing; consumers that check for null must be updated.

On the same bytes v1 keeps the last duplicate, replaces the invalid byte with U+FFFD and ignores the unknown member, all silently. v2 rejects duplicates and invalid UTF-8 by default; unknown members take RejectUnknownMembers (v1: Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields).
v1 always sorted map keys; v2 writes them in unspecified order unless you pass Deterministic(true). Snapshot tests and signatures over JSON need that option.

use_cases: Importing bank statements, e-invoice exports and price lists that users export from Excel
Generating CSV reports that open correctly in Turkish Excel with a double click
Streaming large JSON exports or NDJSON logs without loading them into memory
Webhook or event envelopes whose payload shape depends on a type field (RawMessage, jsontext.Value)
strengths: Decoding goes straight into typed structs with the standard library alone, where Python's json.load gives you dicts and Java needs Jackson or Gson as a dependency
Decoder and csv.Reader read from any io.Reader, so a 2 GB upload streams with flat memory
v2 rejects duplicate names and invalid UTF-8 by default, the inputs where two parsers can disagree about what a document means
v1 and v2 share one implementation in 1.27, so both can live in one program and a migration can go type by type
weaknesses: The standard library has no charset conversion: windows-1254 needs golang.org/x/text
encoding/csv returns [][]string; types, headers and validation are yours to write
Two JSON packages with different defaults: moving a struct from v1 to v2 changes nil slices, omitempty, map order and name matching
Reflection-based: a misspelled tag compiles and silently leaves a field empty

pitfalls.title: The BOM in the first header
pitfalls.detail: Excel's "CSV UTF-8" starts with EF BB BF, which becomes part of the first field. Strip it before mapping headers to columns.
pitfalls.bad: idx := slices.Index(header, "Müşteri") // -1: the field is BOM + "Müşteri"
pitfalls.good: header[0] = strings.TrimPrefix(header[0], "\xEF\xBB\xBF")

pitfalls.title: Reading windows-1254 as UTF-8
pitfalls.detail: Every İ, Ş, Ğ, ı, ş, ğ becomes U+FFFD (v1) or an error (v2, PostgreSQL). Check utf8.Valid on a sample and decode the stream instead.
pitfalls.good: r := csv.NewReader(charmap.Windows1254.NewDecoder().Reader(f)) // golang.org/x/text/encoding/charmap

pitfalls.title: Parsing 1.250,50 with strconv
pitfalls.detail: strconv.ParseFloat fails on Turkish number formatting, and float64 is the wrong type for money anyway. Normalize the string and parse integer kuruş.

pitfalls.title: time.Duration under v2
pitfalls.detail: v1 encodes a Duration as nanoseconds; v2 has no default representation and returns an error. Pass jsonv1.FormatDurationAsNano(true) (the option lives in encoding/json), or wrap the field in a type with its own MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON.

pitfalls.title: Expecting v2 to sort maps
pitfalls.detail: Without json.Deterministic(true), the same map can encode to different bytes on each run.

quiz.q: A Turkish user uploads an Excel "CSV UTF-8" file. record[0][0] of the header doesn't equal "Müşteri" although it prints like it. Why?
options: The field starts with a byte order mark
quiz.why: The BOM (U+FEFF) is invisible when printed, but encoding/csv keeps it as part of the first field.

quiz.q: {"name":"a","name":"b"} is unmarshaled into a struct. What do v1 and v2 do by default?
options: v1 keeps "b" silently, v2 returns an error
quiz.why: v2 rejects duplicate names unless you pass jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(true).

quiz.q: Why read the closing ] with dec.Token() after the dec.More() loop?
options: To detect a truncated or malformed array
quiz.why: The loop can end without seeing ]: with the pre-1.27 implementation, More just returns false on a broken stream. The final Token is the explicit check.

quiz.q: Is encoding/json/v2 usable in Go 1.27 without setting GOEXPERIMENT?
options: Yes, it ships enabled; GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 opts out
quiz.why: It was experimental in Go 1.25 and 1.26 and became available by default in 1.27.

lessons.body:
## Concept

**CSV.** `csv.NewReader(r)` parses RFC 4180 records from any `io.Reader`: quoted fields,
doubled quotes, embedded newlines, and CRLF turned into LF. Set `Comma` for `;` or tab files,
`FieldsPerRecord` to enforce a column count, `LazyQuotes` for sloppy producers.
`csv.NewWriter(w)` is buffered: `Flush` (or `WriteAll`), then check `Error`. It works on bytes
and knows nothing about character sets.

**JSON (v1).** `json.Marshal`/`Unmarshal` map structs through field tags. For streams, use
`json.NewDecoder(r)`: `Decode` reads one value at a time (NDJSON), and `Token` plus `More`
walk into a large array element by element. `json.RawMessage` holds a value's bytes to
decode later. `Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields` makes decoding strict.

**JSON v2 (Go 1.27).** `encoding/json/v2` (`Marshal`, `Unmarshal`, `MarshalWrite`,
`UnmarshalRead`, all taking options) and `encoding/json/jsontext` (tokens, `Value`, a
streaming `Encoder`/`Decoder`) were behind `GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2` in Go 1.25 and 1.26 and ship
enabled in 1.27. The v1 package now runs on the v2 implementation with options that keep v1
behavior; `GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2` restores the old implementation for now. v1 is not
deprecated, and you don't have to migrate.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: `csv.reader(f, delimiter=";")` ≈ `csv.NewReader` with `Comma`; Python's
  `encoding="utf-8-sig"` strips the BOM, Go has no such switch. `json.load` builds dicts;
  Go decodes straight into typed structs.
- Java: Jackson's `@JsonProperty` ≈ struct tags; Jackson's streaming `JsonParser` ≈
  `Decoder.Token`. Jackson fails on unknown properties by default; both Go packages ignore
  them unless you ask (`DisallowUnknownFields`, `RejectUnknownMembers`).
- JS: `JSON.parse` keeps the last duplicate key and has no schema, which is why the TS track
  validates with zod. Go v1 behaves like `JSON.parse` on duplicates; v2 refuses them.
- C/C++: no standard library support at all; Go's tag-driven mapping replaces hand-written
  visitors or code generators.

## How it works

The v1/v2 differences that change output or acceptance by default, from the `encoding/json`
"Migrating to v2" docs (v1 first; the option that controls it in parentheses):

- Name matching: case-insensitive vs case-sensitive (`MatchCaseInsensitiveNames`).
- Duplicate names: last one wins vs error (`jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames`).
- Invalid UTF-8: replaced with U+FFFD vs error (`jsontext.AllowInvalidUTF8`).
- nil slice and map: `null` vs `[]` and `{}` (`FormatNilSliceAsNull`, `FormatNilMapAsNull`).
- `omitempty`: omits empty Go values (0, false, "") vs empty JSON values (null, "", {}, []).
- Map keys: sorted vs unspecified order (`Deterministic`).
- `time.Duration`: nanoseconds vs an error (`FormatDurationAsNano` in `encoding/json`).
- `<`, `>` and `&` in strings: escaped for HTML vs written as is (`jsontext.EscapeForHTML`).

In v2, `json.RawMessage`'s role is played by `jsontext.Value` (v1's `RawMessage` is now an
alias of it), and the streaming loop is `jsontext.NewDecoder` with `json.UnmarshalDecode`.
`UnmarshalRead` reads its reader to EOF and expects exactly one value, unlike v1's
`Decoder.Decode`. If you tried the experiment in 1.25 or 1.26: in 1.27 the `inline` tag
option is called `embed`, and the `format` and `unknown` options are gone. Only `format`
fails loudly; a leftover `inline` or `unknown` is ignored, so the field is quietly no
longer flattened.

## Design notes

Treat imports as a trust boundary. For CSV from users: sniff the encoding (`utf8.Valid` on
the first few KB, allowing for a character cut off at the end of the sample), decode
windows-1254 if needed, strip the BOM, map headers by name rather than position, and
validate each row into a typed struct with its line number (`Reader.FieldPos`) in the error;
or load the raw rows into a staging table and let SQL validate them. For JSON, new code can
use v2 for its stricter defaults. To move existing types, call v2 with
`jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1()` first and add v2 behaviors one option at a time after it (later
options win), with a round-trip test per type. Whatever you pick, decode into structs at the
edge and keep `map[string]any` out of the core.

Where the Excel facts come from. Microsoft documents two: a comma decimal separator
"forces Excel to use a semi-colon for the list separator"
([Import or export text files](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/import-or-export-text-txt-or-csv-files-5250ac4c-663c-47ce-937b-339e391393ba)),
and a UTF-8 CSV opens normally "if it was saved with BOM"
([Opening CSV UTF-8 files correctly](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/opening-csv-utf-8-files-correctly-in-excel-8a935af5-3416-4edd-ba7e-3dfd2bc4a032)).
The rest was observed on 2026-11-14 with Excel for Microsoft 365 (build 16.0.20527.20196)
on an en-US Windows, with Excel's own separators set to decimal `,` and thousands `.`, as
Windows's tr-TR locale has them. "CSV UTF-8" starts with `EF BB BF` and writes `;`,
`1250,5` and CRLF row ends. "CSV (Comma delimited)" is written in the Windows ANSI code
page: windows-1252 on that machine, where ş, ı and İ became `?`. Turkish Windows's ANSI
code page is 1254
([code page identifiers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/intl/code-page-identifiers)).
So a file with `?` in place of Turkish letters was saved as plain CSV on a non-Turkish
Windows, and no decoder brings them back: ask for "CSV UTF-8". Double-clicked, a UTF-8 file
without a BOM showed `Müşteri` as `MÃ¼ÅŸteri`, its bytes read as windows-1252.

lessons.title: Binary data, byte order, gzip and zip
lessons.summary: encoding/binary turns fixed-size integers and structs into bytes in an explicit byte order. gzip streams are an io.Writer and io.Reader you stack on files; zip archives need random access and untrusted entry names.

examples.title: Decoding a sensor packet by offsets and with binary.Read

annotations.note: Only sized types: uint8, int16, uint32, [2]byte. A plain int has no fixed size, and binary.Read/Write reject it with "some values are not fixed-sized".

The same four bytes are 123456 or 1088553216 depending on the order you read them in. Network protocols and Modbus registers are big-endian, plenty of device protocols are little-endian, and x86 and ARM machines are little-endian in practice. The order is a property of the protocol, never of the machine.

binary.Read fills the fields in declaration order and never inserts padding, so binary.Size is the wire size: 12 here. A C struct with a uint8 followed by a uint32 is usually 8 bytes in memory; through encoding/binary it is 5.
0xFF83 read into an int16 is -125: two's complement comes for free when the field has a signed type. Scaled integers (tenths of a degree) are how devices avoid floats on the wire.
binary.Append (Go 1.23) appends the encoding to a slice; Encode and Decode work on a byte slice you already have. Before 1.23 you wrote into a bytes.Buffer with binary.Write.
A packet cut short returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF; io.EOF means no bytes at all. On a TCP stream that's how you tell "connection closed between packets" from "closed in the middle of one".
A uvarint uses 7 bits per byte and the top bit as "more follows", so 5 takes one byte and 2^32 takes five. Signed values use Varint, which zigzag-encodes them so small negative numbers stay short.

examples.title: gzip as a Writer and a Reader, its Latin-1 header, and Close

annotations.note: gzip.Writer wraps the file; fmt.Fprintf doesn't know it is compressing. Close flushes the compressor and writes the footer, a CRC-32 and the length; closing the file does neither.

gzip.Reader is an io.Reader, so the Scanner from the reading-files lesson works unchanged and memory stays flat. The CRC is checked when the stream ends, so a damaged file fails at sc.Err, after you've already seen its lines: treat data as tentative until EOF.

The gzip header's name and comment must fit in Latin-1 (U+0001 to U+00FF). ü and ç fit; Ş, ş, Ğ, ğ, İ and ı don't, so a Turkish file name in the header fails at the first Write. Leave Name empty or transliterate it.
Flush makes the data so far decodable (useful on a network stream), but without Close there's no footer: the reader returns every byte and then io.ErrUnexpectedEOF.

examples.title: Writing a zip, reading raw entries, extracting safely with CopyFS

annotations.note: Create compresses with Deflate and returns an io.Writer for that one entry; finish writing it before the next Create. Nothing checks the name, so this archive really contains ../../evil.txt, the classic "zip slip" payload.
The central directory, the index of all entries, lives at the end of the file and is written by zw.Close. Without it the archive can't be opened. Then close the file and check that error too.

zip.OpenReader needs random access because it reads that index first. zr.File holds names as stored: Go sets the UTF-8 flag (bit 0x800) for Şubat.csv automatically, and the hostile name is there verbatim. Joining zf.Name onto a target directory yourself is the vulnerability.

zip.Reader is also an fs.FS whose listing cleans stored names: a leading / and leading ../ are dropped, so ../../evil.txt appears as evil.txt while zf.Name above keeps the original. os.CopyFS (Go 1.23) extracts through that view and won't overwrite existing files.

use_cases: Device and industrial protocols over serial or TCP: fixed headers, big-endian fields, scaled integers
File formats with binary headers: PNG chunks, WAV, custom record files
Compressed exports and logs (.csv.gz) streamed to disk, S3 or an HTTP response
Zip uploads and downloads: bundling several reports, importing an archive a user sends
strengths: Byte order is an explicit argument, so you can't accidentally depend on the machine's endianness the way a C memcpy into a struct does

gzip, flate and zlib are plain io.Writer/io.Reader wrappers, so csv.NewReader(zr) or json.NewDecoder(zr) works directly; Java needs an InputStreamReader between GZIPInputStream and a text parser because bytes and characters are separate hierarchies
zip.Reader is an fs.FS: fs.WalkDir, http.FileServerFS and os.CopyFS work on an archive without extracting it
weaknesses: binary.Read/Write use reflection; for hot paths decode by offsets with BigEndian.Uint32 and friends
Compressed bytes are not stable across Go releases (Go 1.27 changed the flate encoder), so never hash or compare compressed output in tests
zip needs io.ReaderAt and the total size, so it can't be read from a pipe or a streaming HTTP body; use archive/tar plus gzip for true streams

pitfalls.title: Extracting with filepath.Join(dir, zf.Name)
pitfalls.detail: Entry names are attacker-controlled: ../../ climbs out of dir. Extract through the fs.FS view (os.CopyFS), or check filepath.IsLocal and use os.Root. GODEBUG=zipinsecurepath=0 makes OpenReader report such names as ErrInsecurePath.
pitfalls.good: err := os.CopyFS(dir, zr) // names come from the cleaned fs.FS view

pitfalls.title: Trusting declared sizes
pitfalls.detail: UncompressedSize64 is a number from the archive; a zip bomb lies or simply expands to gigabytes. Wrap each entry in io.LimitReader and enforce a total budget.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting Close on gzip.Writer or zip.Writer
pitfalls.detail: gzip loses its footer and readers report unexpected EOF; zip loses its central directory and can't be opened at all.

pitfalls.title: Using int in binary structs
pitfalls.detail: int is 32 or 64 bits depending on the platform, so encoding/binary refuses it. Use int32, uint16 and the like, matching the protocol spec.

quiz.q: The bytes 00 01 E2 40 are documented as a big-endian uint32. What does binary.LittleEndian.Uint32 give?
quiz.why: Byte order is a reading convention, not something the bytes carry; reading big-endian data little-endian silently gives a different number.

quiz.q: You wrote a .csv.gz with gzip.NewWriter(f), called zw.Flush() and f.Close(). What does a reader see?
quiz.why: Flush emits the compressed data; only Close writes the footer with the CRC and length.

quiz.q: Why can't you read a zip archive directly from an HTTP response body?
options: zip is not an io.Reader format; it needs io.ReaderAt and the size, because the index is at the end
zip.Reader only opens files by name
quiz.why: The central directory sits at the end of the file. Save the body to a temp file (or buffer it within a size limit) first, or use tar.gz for streaming.

quiz.q: A gzip header Name of "Şubat.csv" makes the first Write fail. Why?
options: Header strings must be in Latin-1, and Ş is outside it
quiz.why: RFC 1952 stores the name in ISO 8859-1; Go accepts U+0001 to U+00FF and rejects the rest.

further_reading.title: Go 1.27 release notes: compress/flate output changes

lessons.body:
## Concept

- **encoding/binary** converts between Go values and bytes. `binary.BigEndian` and
  `binary.LittleEndian` read and write `uint16/32/64` at given offsets (`Uint32(b)`,
  `PutUint32(b, v)`, `AppendUint32`). `binary.Read`, `Write`, and since Go 1.23 `Append`,
  `Encode` and `Decode`, handle whole fixed-size structs and slices, packed field by field.
  `Uvarint`/`Varint` give the variable-length integers protobuf also uses.
- **compress/gzip** wraps an `io.Writer` (`gzip.NewWriter`) or `io.Reader`
  (`gzip.NewReader`); everything you know about streams applies. `Close` finishes the file.
- **archive/zip** reads and writes multi-file archives. Reading needs random access
  (`zip.OpenReader` or `zip.NewReader(io.ReaderAt, size)`); entries open as readers, and the
  archive is also an `fs.FS`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: instead of casting a buffer to a packed struct (and fighting alignment,
  endianness and strict aliasing), you name the byte order and the decoder copies field by
  field. `binary.BigEndian.Uint32` is `ntohl` plus the load.
- Java: `ByteBuffer.order(ByteOrder.BIG_ENDIAN).getInt()` ≈ `BigEndian.Uint32`;
  `GZIPOutputStream` ≈ `gzip.Writer`, but in Go the same `io.Writer` interface covers it, no
  separate stream class tree. `ZipFile` ≈ `zip.OpenReader`.
- Python: `struct.unpack(">2sBBIhH", pkt)` is exactly the `Reading` struct (`>` =
  big-endian); `gzip.open` and `zipfile.ZipFile` ≈ these packages. Python's
  `ZipFile.extractall` sanitizes names; Go's equivalent is extracting through the `fs.FS`
  view with `os.CopyFS`.
- JS: `DataView.getUint32(offset, littleEndian)` takes the byte order as a flag too;
  `DecompressionStream("gzip")` ≈ `gzip.NewReader`. There's no zip in the platform.

## How it works

A gzip file is a 10-byte header (optionally followed by a name and a comment in ISO
8859-1), a DEFLATE stream, and an 8-byte footer with the CRC-32 and the uncompressed length. The reader
decompresses as you read and checks the footer at the end, which is why errors in a
damaged file arrive last. Several gzip members can be concatenated, and `gzip.Reader` reads
through all of them unless you call `Multistream(false)`.

A zip file is a sequence of local entries (header plus compressed data) followed by the
**central directory**, an index of all entries, and an end record pointing to it. Readers
start from the end, which is why `zip` needs `io.ReaderAt` and the size, why
`zip.Writer.Close` is essential, and why an entry can be read without decompressing the
others. Bit 11 of an entry's flags marks the name as UTF-8; Go's writer sets it for
non-ASCII names, and its reader reports names from tools that used a legacy code page
through `FileHeader.NonUTF8`.

Go 1.27 changed the DEFLATE encoder for speed, so gzip, zip and PNG output from 1.27 can
differ byte for byte from 1.26. Decompressing still gives identical data; only the
compressed bytes moved, which is why these examples print contents, never compressed sizes.

## Design notes

Write protocol decoders as functions over `[]byte` (or an `io.Reader` plus
`io.ReadFull` for one frame), with the byte order and field offsets taken from the spec, and
test them against captured packets. Prefer explicit offsets for hot paths and
`binary.Read` for readability elsewhere. For compressed exports, stack writers
(`csv.Writer` → `gzip.Writer` → file or `http.ResponseWriter`; `csv.Writer` already
buffers) and finish them in the order you write through them: flush the CSV writer, close
the gzip writer, then close the file. Treat every archive from outside as hostile: extract through the
`fs.FS` view or an `os.Root`, limit bytes per entry and in total, and cap the entry count.

The archive/zip docs only say that `Reader.Open` takes paths "with no leading / or ../
elements"; they don't say how stored names are listed. That comes from the source:
`toValidName` in `archive/zip/reader.go`, called from `initFileList`, turns backslashes
into slashes, cleans the path, then strips a leading `/` and every leading `../`, while
`File.Name` keeps the name as stored. A run on Go 1.27.4 (2026-11-14) showed it: entries
`../../evil.txt` and `/abs.txt` walked as `evil.txt` and `abs.txt`, and
`Open("evil.txt")` worked. The zip example's exact output pins this.

lessons.title: Type parameters, constraints, ~, comparable, cmp.Ordered
lessons.summary: A type parameter list says which types a function or type accepts; the constraint says what the body may do with them. Inference fills in the type arguments at most call sites, so Set[T] and Stack[T] read like ordinary code.

examples.title: Constraints, ~ for defined types, cmp.Ordered, and inference

annotations.note: A constraint is an interface, here one that lists types instead of methods. The ~ matters: int64 alone means exactly int64, so Kurus (line 15) would be rejected. ~int64 admits every type whose underlying type is int64. Interfaces like this exist only as constraints; var n Number does not compile.
The body is checked once, against the constraint, not per call as with C++ templates. += compiles because every type in Number supports it. var total T is how you spell "the zero value of T".
cmp.Ordered (Go 1.21) is the set of types that support < : integers, floats and strings, each with ~. The built-in min and max (also Go 1.21) accept such a T directly.

To appears only in the result, so nothing can infer it. Explicit type arguments fill the list from the left, which is why To comes first: the caller names To and inference supplies From. To(x) is legal because every type in Number converts to every other.

No type arguments at these call sites. Untyped constants default to int and float64; the []Kurus argument makes T Kurus, so the sum is a Kurus and prints through its String method. Passing strings fails at compile time, at the call.
One Clamp serves ints, Kurus and strings. Strings order by their UTF-8 bytes, not by the Turkish alphabet: ç is 0xC3 0xA7 and sorts after z. The standard library has no locale collation.
The result is a real []float64, not a []any. Go generics are not erased, which is why %T can print the instantiated type.

examples.title: Set[T comparable] and Stack[T any]

annotations.note: comparable is the constraint for == and !=, exactly what map keys need. struct{} values take no memory, so the map is a set.
A constructor function exists mostly for inference: callers write SetOf("a", "b") and get a Set[string] without naming the type.
A method on a generic type repeats the type parameter in the receiver, Set[T], but never the constraint: that comes from the type declaration.

Sorting needs <, which comparable does not promise, and a receiver cannot tighten T's constraint. A function with a stricter constraint can still take a Set[T]. Sorting also makes the random map order deterministic.
An empty stack has nothing to return; var zero T gives the zero value for any T. Where Java would return null, Pop returns that zero value plus false: the comma-ok idiom of map lookups.
For strings, == compares bytes: "izmir" is not "İzmir". The sorted output puts Iğdır before İzmir because I is the byte 0x49 and İ starts with 0xC4.

Inference applies to generic functions, never to generic types, so a Stack needs its type argument spelled out. var st Stack[rune] is also ready to use: the zero value of the struct is an empty stack.
Ranging over a string yields runes, so ş and ı are pushed whole and the word reverses correctly. The final Pop returns the zero rune and false.

examples.title: comparable accepts interface types, and the check moves to run time

annotations.note: Since Go 1.20, interface types such as any satisfy comparable, because == is defined on interfaces. A go.mod declaring go 1.19 rejects Set[any] at compile time.

A map insert hashes the key's dynamic value, and a []int can be neither hashed nor compared, so the insert panics. The compile-time guarantee only holds when the type argument is a concrete comparable type.

use_cases: Containers whose code is the same for every element type: Set[T], Stack[T], an LRU cache, a ring buffer
Algorithms over slices and maps: Clamp, Sum, a Convert or GroupBy helper, the slices and maps packages themselves
Replacing any plus type assertions in helpers where the caller's type should flow through to the result
strengths: The body is type-checked once against its constraint, so a mistake is reported in the generic code, not as a wall of template errors at a call site as in C++
Unlike Java's erased generics, a Set[int] stores plain ints with no boxing, and T exists at run time: var zero T, T(x) and %T all work
Inference keeps most call sites free of type arguments: SetOf("a", "b"), Sum(prices...)
Constraints are ordinary interfaces, so there is one concept to learn rather than Java's bounded wildcards or C++'s SFINAE
weaknesses: Operators can't be overloaded, so a constraint like Number can only list built-in types; a user-defined Decimal struct can never be added with +
Generic types are never inferred: there is no Java diamond (new Stack<>()), you write Stack[rune]
A method can't demand more of T than the type declared, so stricter operations (Sorted) end up as package-level functions
cmp.Ordered compares strings by bytes; there is no locale-aware ordering for Turkish in the standard library

pitfalls.title: Forgetting ~ in a constraint
pitfalls.detail: int64 | float64 means exactly those two types. A defined type such as type Kurus int64 is rejected; the compiler even hints "possibly missing ~ for int64".
pitfalls.bad: type Number interface { int | int64 | float64 }
pitfalls.good: type Number interface { ~int | ~int64 | ~float64 }

pitfalls.title: Trusting comparable with interface type arguments
pitfalls.detail: Set[any] compiles, then panics with "hash of unhashable type" the first time someone adds a slice, map or func. Prefer a concrete key type, or derive a comparable key (an ID, a string) from the value.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive Turkish keys
pitfalls.detail: Keys compare bytes, so normalize before inserting. strings.ToLower is not Turkish-aware: it maps I to i, turning "IĞDIR" into "iğdir". Use the Turkish case mapping.
pitfalls.good: set.Add(strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, city))

pitfalls.title: Using a constraint as a variable type
pitfalls.detail: An interface with type terms (| or ~) is a constraint only: var n Number fails with "cannot use type Number outside a type constraint". Use the type parameter T, or a method-only interface if you need a variable.

quiz.q: type Celsius float64. Which constraint accepts Celsius as a type argument?
quiz.why: float64 alone means exactly float64; ~float64 admits every type whose underlying type is float64.

quiz.q: s := Set[any]{}; s.Add([]int{1}). What happens with Set[T comparable] map[T]struct{}?
quiz.why: The type argument is any, which satisfies comparable since Go 1.20. The slice is the dynamic value, hashed at run time, and slices can't be hashed.

quiz.q: Why does func Convert[To, From Number](xs []From) []To list To first?
options: To can't be inferred from the arguments, and explicit type arguments fill the list from the left
quiz.why: Convert[float64](ints) names To; From is inferred from ints. With From first, the caller would have to name both.

quiz.q: Why is Sorted a function instead of a method on Set[T comparable]?
options: A method can't require more of T (cmp.Ordered) than the type declaration (comparable)
quiz.why: The receiver's type parameters take their constraints from the type. Go 1.27 generic methods can add new type parameters, but they can't tighten T.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type parameter declarations

lessons.body:
## Concept

A type parameter list in square brackets makes a function or type generic:
`func Sum[T Number](xs ...T) T`. Each parameter has a constraint, which is an
interface. The constraint does two jobs: it limits the type arguments callers may
pass, and it limits what the body may do with values of type `T`. Three constraints
cover most code. `any` allows every type but only assignment and passing around.
`comparable` allows `==` and `!=`, which is what map keys need. `cmp.Ordered` (Go
1.21) allows `<` and friends on integers, floats and strings. When you need your own,
list types with `|`, and write `~T` to include every type whose underlying type is `T`.

At a call site, inference works out the type arguments from the ordinary arguments,
so `SetOf("a", "b")` is a `Set[string]`. You write type arguments yourself only when
there is nothing to infer from: for generic types (`Stack[rune]`) and for type
parameters that appear only in the result (`Convert[float64](ints)`).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C++: closer to C++20 concepts than to templates. The body is checked once against
  the constraint; there is no specialization, no SFINAE and no non-type parameters
  (`Array<T, N>` has no Go equivalent).
- Java: no erasure and no boxing. `Set[int]` stores ints, `var zero T` works, and
  there are no wildcards: Go has no subtyping between `[]Circle` and `[]Shape` for
  variance rules to describe.
- TypeScript: `[T any]` instead of `<T>`, and `[T Number]` instead of
  `<T extends Number>`. TS generics are erased after type checking; Go's exist in the
  compiled program (`%T` prints `[]float64`). Go has no conditional or mapped types:
  a constraint describes a set of types and nothing more.
- Python: like a `TypeVar` with a bound, except the compiler enforces it and the
  program won't build if a call breaks it.

## Design notes

Start with concrete code. Reach for a type parameter when you are about to copy a
function for a second element type, or when a helper takes `any` and every caller
follows it with a type assertion. Pick the weakest constraint the body needs: `any`,
then `comparable`, then `cmp.Ordered` or your own union. Put type parameters that
can't be inferred first, so callers name one type and let inference do the rest.
Before writing your own container, check the `slices` and `maps` packages: most
"generic utility" code in older projects is now one standard library call. The
standard library still has no set type, so a small `Set[T comparable]` like the one
here is reasonable. The next lesson covers methods with their own type parameters
(new in Go 1.27) and how to recognize code where an interface is the better tool.

lessons.title: Generic methods (Go 1.27) and when an interface wins
lessons.summary: Since Go 1.27 a method can declare its own type parameters, which makes left-to-right chains like list.Filter(even).Map(strconv.Itoa) possible. Such methods never satisfy interfaces, so interfaces still own run-time polymorphism.

examples.title: A method with its own type parameter, and the function it replaces

annotations.note: E comes from the receiver; F is Map's own type parameter, declared after the method name exactly as on a function. In a module whose go.mod says go 1.26 or older this line fails with "generic method requires go1.27 or later".
Before Go 1.27 the only option was a package-level function. It still works, and it is still how the slices and maps packages are shaped.
Same result, two shapes. The nested calls read inside out: the last step, label, is written first. The chain reads in execution order. F is inferred at each step from the function argument.

Used as a value, a generic method must be instantiated first, like a generic function. List[int].Map[string] is a method expression: an ordinary func whose first parameter is the receiver. nums.Map without type arguments, or a target type to infer them from, does not compile.

Go 1.27 added N as a method on *rand.Rand, next to the older generic function rand.N. Int is inferred from the argument, so a time.Duration bound yields a time.Duration. Only the types are printed; the values depend on the generator.

examples.title: Generic methods don't satisfy interfaces and are invisible to reflect

annotations.note: An ordinary method. It satisfies fmt.Stringer the usual way (line 26).
A generic method on a generic type. Called directly, U is inferred from strconv.Itoa (line 24).

Writing Convert[U any] inside an interface is a compile error ("interface method must have no type parameters"), so an interface can only name one instance. Even that is not enough: a generic method never satisfies an interface method.

The commented line fails to compile: "wrong type for method Convert, have Convert[U any](func(int) U) Box[U], want Convert(func(int) string) Box[string]". The assertion from any compiles and answers false at run time.
reflect can't instantiate code at run time, so it lists String only. Anything that finds methods by reflection, such as text/template's {{.Convert}}, can't call a generic method.

examples.title: Over-genericized code, the interface fix, and where a type parameter pays

annotations.note: A type switch on any(s) inside a generic function means the behavior differs per type, which is what methods are for. The set is closed, the compiler can't check the switch is exhaustive (hence the panic), and the logic duplicates the Area methods.
Total only calls Area, so a plain interface parameter is enough. One slice holds both shapes, and a shape added in another package works without touching Total.
Here the type parameter does work: Largest returns S, the caller's own type. It also accepts a []Circle as is, while Total([]Circle{...}) doesn't compile, because []Circle is not a []Shape.
Circle | Rect is not a type. Unions exist only inside constraints, so no variable or slice can hold "a Circle or a Rect". Unlike TypeScript, Go has no union types; mixed values need an interface.
c is a Circle, so c.R needs no type assertion. With an interface result the caller would get a Shape back and have to assert.

use_cases: Fluent APIs on your own types: query builders, result lists, pipelines that change the element type step by step
Typed operations that belong to one type's namespace instead of the package's: (*rand.Rand).N, List.Map vs a MapList function
Adding a stricter type parameter next to a looser receiver: Set[T comparable] can have SortedBy[K cmp.Ordered](key func(T) K)
Interfaces, still, for run-time polymorphism: mixed collections, plugins, ports in a layered design, test fakes
strengths: Operations chain left to right in execution order, where pre-1.27 code nested MapList(MapList(...)) inside out
No package-level name clashes: List.Map and Tree.Map instead of MapList and MapTree

Interfaces stay simple and fast: dynamic dispatch never needs code generated at run time, so Go keeps pure ahead-of-time compilation, where C# typically instantiates generic virtual methods in its JIT
weaknesses: A generic method never satisfies an interface; Java and C# both allow generic interface methods (<R> R accept(Visitor<R> v))
Invisible to reflect, so text/template and other reflection-driven code can't call them
Requires go 1.27 in go.mod, which raises the minimum Go version for every user of a library that adopts them
As values they must be instantiated: nums.Map alone is not a func value

pitfalls.title: Expecting a generic method to implement an interface
pitfalls.detail: A type with Read[B ~[]byte](p B) (int, error) does not implement io.Reader, although Read[[]byte] would match. Methods that must satisfy an interface stay non-generic; put type parameters on the type or on the interface instead.
pitfalls.good: func (r *Src) Read(p []byte) (int, error)

pitfalls.title: A type parameter that only calls methods
pitfalls.detail: If the body only calls methods of T and T never appears in the result, the type parameter adds nothing over an interface parameter.
pitfalls.bad: func Describe[T fmt.Stringer](v T) string { return v.String() }
pitfalls.good: func Describe(v fmt.Stringer) string { return v.String() }

pitfalls.title: Type switches inside generic code
pitfalls.detail: switch any(v).(type) in a generic function means the behavior is per type. Give the types a method and accept an interface; the set stays open and the compiler checks each implementation.

pitfalls.title: Union constraints of your own structs
pitfalls.detail: [T Circle | Rect] looks like a sum type but isn't one: you can't store a Circle | Rect anywhere. If you need a value that is one of several types, use an interface (optionally with an unexported marker method to close the set).

quiz.q: Which declaration compiles in a module whose go.mod says go 1.27?
options: type Mapper interface { Map[F any](func(int) F) []F }
func (l List[E]) Map[F any](f func(E) F) List[F]
quiz.why: Methods of concrete types may declare type parameters since Go 1.27; interface methods still may not.

quiz.q: type Src struct{} has func (Src) Read[B ~[]byte](p B) (int, error). Does Src implement io.Reader?
options: No, a generic method never satisfies an interface method
quiz.why: Interface satisfaction compares method signatures, and a generic method's signature has type parameters. Go 1.27 defines it this way so that no code has to be instantiated at run time.

quiz.q: func Describe[T fmt.Stringer](v T) string { return v.String() }. What would you write instead?
quiz.why: The body only calls a method and T never flows back out, which is exactly what an interface parameter expresses.

quiz.q: When does a type parameter beat an interface parameter?
options: When the function only calls methods
When the caller's concrete type must come back out, as in Largest[S Shape](xs []S) S
quiz.why: With an interface result the caller gets a Shape and must assert; with S they get their own type back.

further_reading.title: Go 1.27 Release Notes: changes to the language
The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

lessons.body:
## Concept

Since Go 1.27 a method may declare type parameters of its own, after the method name
and in addition to any its receiver type has:
`func (l List[E]) Map[F any](f func(E) F) List[F]`. Calls infer them like function
calls; used as a value, the method must be instantiated first. Two rules decide where
the feature fits. Interface methods still can't declare type parameters, and a generic
method never satisfies an interface method. reflect can't see generic methods either.
So generic methods organize code around a type and make chains read left to right;
they never take part in run-time polymorphism.

That leaves the older and more frequent question: should this code have a type
parameter at all, or is an interface the right tool?

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `<R> List<R> map(Function<T, R> f)` has always been allowed, interface methods
  included, because erasure compiles one body for every `R`. Go compiles real
  instantiations, so it would have to know every `R` an interface call could need.
- C#: generic virtual methods exist; the runtime typically instantiates them on
  demand in its JIT. Go has no JIT.
- C++: member function templates can't be virtual, for the same reason as Go's rule.
- TypeScript: generic methods are unrestricted because types are erased. TS also has
  real union types; Go's `Circle | Rect` exists only inside a constraint.
- Python: duck typing makes the question moot; `typing.Protocol` is the closest thing
  to a Go interface.

## How it works

Put a value whose type has `func (Empty) Nop[T any](x T) T` into an `any`, then ask
`x.(interface{ Nop(string) string })`. Saying yes would mean running `Nop[string]`,
code nobody compiled, because the compiler can't see which assertions will happen at
run time. The Go FAQ lists the ways out: recompile at link time, add a JIT, fall back
to a slow boxed version, or rule that generic methods never satisfy interfaces. The
FAQ entry predates Go 1.27 and rejects all four. Go 1.27 took the last one, on the
grounds that methods are worth having for code organization even without interfaces.
That makes a generic method an ordinary compile-time instantiation, the same
machinery generic functions use.

## Design notes

Use a generic method when an operation belongs to one of your types and you would
otherwise name a package function after the type (`MapList`, `MapTree`), or when a
chain reads better than nesting. Keep package functions for operations that apply to
many types, which is why `slices` and `maps` stay as they are. Any method that has to
satisfy an interface (`io.Reader`, `fmt.Stringer`, your own repository port) must be
non-generic; if it needs a type parameter, put it on the type or the interface
(`type Converter[T, U any] interface{ Convert(T) U }`).

Signs of over-genericized code: a type parameter used only to call methods on it; a
type switch on `any(v)` inside a generic function; a union constraint of your own
struct types; a type parameter that is only ever instantiated with one type. The
opposite smell is a helper taking `any` and forcing every caller to assert. The Go
team's rule of thumb holds: write the concrete code first, and add a type parameter
when you are about to write the same code again for another type.

lessons.title: The handler model and ServeMux patterns
lessons.summary: An http.Handler is one method, ServeHTTP, and everything in net/http, the router included, is built from it. Since Go 1.22 ServeMux matches methods and wildcards and picks the most specific pattern, so most services need no router library.

examples.title: Handlers, HandlerFunc, and the ResponseWriter's order of operations

annotations.note: No base class and no registration magic: a type with a ServeHTTP method is a Handler. Its fields are shared by every request, and requests run concurrently (one goroutine per connection), so fields must be read-only or protected by a mutex.

PathValue returns the segment already percent-decoded: %C4%B0zmir arrives as İzmir, and the client encoded the ş in Ayşe by itself. The value is always a string; turning it into an int and answering 400 when that fails is your job.

The ResponseWriter is a stream, not a response object you return: headers, then status, then body. A header set after WriteHeader or the first Write is silently ignored, because it has already been sent.

Handle takes a Handler. HandleFunc takes a function and converts it to http.HandlerFunc, a function type whose ServeHTTP method calls the function itself. That one-line adapter is why plain functions work.
httptest.NewServer accepts any Handler and serves it on a loopback port. The mux is just another Handler, which is why middleware can wrap the whole router.

show(http.Get(...)) passes both results straight through: Go allows f(g()) when g's results match f's parameters. greeter set no Content-Type, so net/http sniffed one from the first 512 bytes. /users/7 matches no pattern and gets the mux's plain-text 404.

examples.title: Wildcards, subtrees, {$}, and the most specific pattern wins

annotations.note: Request.Pattern (Go 1.23) is the pattern that matched. Log and count by it: "GET /posts/{id}" is one value per route, while raw paths produce one value per ID and blow up your metrics.

Registration order is irrelevant. ServeMux picks the most specific matching pattern, the one that matches a strict subset of the other's requests, so /posts/latest beats /posts/{id} even though it was registered second.
"/" matches every path, the classic accidental catch-all; "/{$}" matches only the root. /posts/42/comments lands in "/" because {id} matches exactly one segment.
/docs has no pattern, but "GET /docs/" owns that subtree, so the mux redirects to /docs/ and http.Get follows the redirect. Register "/docs" separately if you want to answer it yourself.

examples.title: 405 with Allow, HEAD for free, and conflicts caught at registration

annotations.note: Recovering here is only so the output can show the messages. In a real program, let the panic stop startup: a broken routing table should never serve a request.

HEAD is served by the GET handler and the server drops the body. PUT matches the path but no method, so the mux answers 405 with an Allow header instead of a misleading 404. Methods are case-sensitive: "get" is not GET.

"GET /" is narrower in method, "/index.html" narrower in path, so neither is more specific: a conflict, whichever comes first. Renaming a wildcard makes a duplicate, and wildcards must be whole segments.

use_cases: JSON APIs and internal services: method + path patterns cover what chi or gorilla/mux were used for before Go 1.22
Health and readiness endpoints, admin pages and webhooks next to the main API on one mux
Mounting a sub-application under a prefix with "/admin/" and http.StripPrefix
Tests: the router is a Handler, so httptest exercises the whole routing table without a network
strengths: One interface for everything: routers, middleware, file servers and test servers all take and return http.Handler, unlike Java's split between Servlet, Filter and the container
Precedence by specificity, not registration order, and ambiguous route sets panic at startup instead of misrouting in production, unlike Express's first-match rule
405 with an Allow header and HEAD support come for free
Blocking code per request: no callbacks or async/await, yet requests run concurrently on goroutines
weaknesses: No typed or regex constraints: {id} matches any segment, and parsing "abc" into an int is your code, unlike Flask's <int:id> or Spring's @PathVariable conversion
No route groups or reverse routing (building a URL from a route name); you nest muxes, wrap handlers, and build URLs by hand
The ResponseWriter's ordering rules fail silently: late headers are dropped, a second WriteHeader only logs a warning
The default 404 and 405 bodies are plain text; an API that answers JSON errors must register its own "/" fallback

pitfalls.title: Forgetting return after an error response
pitfalls.detail: http.Error writes a response; it does not stop the handler. The code below it still runs, appends to the body, and the server logs "superfluous response.WriteHeader call".

pitfalls.title: Setting headers after the body
pitfalls.detail: Header().Set after WriteHeader or the first Write has no effect. Set Content-Type, Location and cookies before writing anything.

pitfalls.title: A go.mod older than 1.22
pitfalls.detail: The go line sets the GODEBUG defaults, so a module saying go 1.21 gets the old mux: "GET /posts/{id}" is not a method pattern and every request 404s, silently. go vet does report PathValue as requiring go1.22.

pitfalls.title: "/" when you meant the home page
pitfalls.detail: "/" matches every path that nothing else claims, including typos, so they get your home page with a 200. Use "/{$}" (or "GET /{$}") for the root alone.

pitfalls.title: Lowercase methods in patterns
pitfalls.detail: "get /users" registers a pattern for a method literally named get. A GET request then receives 405 with "Allow: get". Use http.MethodGet or uppercase strings.

quiz.q: You register "GET /posts/latest" first and "GET /posts/{id}" second. Which handler serves GET /posts/latest?
options: GET /posts/latest, because it is more specific
quiz.why: ServeMux ignores order and picks the pattern that matches a strict subset of the other's requests; a literal segment is narrower than a wildcard.

quiz.q: Only "GET /items/{id}" is registered. What does PUT /items/1 get?
options: 405 Method Not Allowed with "Allow: GET, HEAD"
quiz.why: The path matches a pattern with another method, so the mux answers 405 and lists the methods that would work; GET implies HEAD.

quiz.q: What happens when you register both "GET /" and "/index.html"?
quiz.why: One is narrower in method, the other in path; neither matches a subset of the other's requests, so they conflict and Handle panics.

quiz.q: A handler calls w.WriteHeader(201) and then w.Header().Set("Location", "/users/7"). What does the client see?
quiz.why: The status line and headers are sent on WriteHeader; later changes to the header map are ignored.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Routing Enhancements for Go 1.22

lessons.body:
## Concept

The whole server side of `net/http` rests on one interface:

```go
type Handler interface {
	ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)
}
```

A router is a `Handler` that picks another `Handler`. Middleware is a function that takes a
`Handler` and returns one. `http.FileServerFS`, `http.TimeoutHandler` and
`httptest.NewServer` all speak the same type. `http.HandlerFunc` is a function type with a
`ServeHTTP` method that calls the function, so any `func(w, r)` becomes a `Handler` by a
plain conversion.

The `ResponseWriter` is a stream with a fixed order: set headers, then write the status
(`WriteHeader`, or implicitly 200 on the first `Write`), then write the body. The server
gives each connection its own goroutine, so handlers run concurrently and write blocking,
sequential code.

`http.ServeMux` has understood patterns of the form `[METHOD ][HOST]/[PATH]` since Go 1.22:

- `{name}` matches one path segment, `{name...}` the rest of the path, and `r.PathValue`
  returns the decoded value.
- A trailing slash (`/docs/`) matches a subtree; `{$}` matches the end of the path only.
- A method in the pattern restricts it; `GET` also matches `HEAD`. A path that matches only
  under another method gets **405** with an `Allow` header.
- When several patterns match, the **most specific** wins: the one whose matches are a
  strict subset of the other's. If neither is more specific, registering the second one
  **panics**, whatever the order.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `ServeHTTP` is `HttpServlet.service(req, resp)` without the container. The
  server is a library you start from `main`. Spring's `@GetMapping("/posts/{id}")` maps to
  `mux.HandleFunc("GET /posts/{id}", ...)`, but there is no reflection: `PathValue` gives
  you a string and `strconv.Atoi` is yours to call.
- **Node/Express**: `app.get('/posts/:id', ...)` dispatches to the first registered match;
  ServeMux ignores order and rejects ambiguous route sets at startup. Express handlers share
  one thread, while Go handlers run in parallel: a map shared between requests needs a
  `sync.Mutex`.
- **Python**: WSGI's `app(environ, start_response)` has the same shape as `ServeHTTP`.
  Flask's `<int:id>` converters have no equivalent; validate inside the handler.
- **C/C++**: no event loop and no callbacks on readiness. Each connection reads blocking in
  its own goroutine, and the runtime multiplexes those goroutines over a few OS threads.

## How it works

    net.Listener ── Accept ──> one goroutine per connection
                                   │ reads a request
                                   ▼
                     server.Handler.ServeHTTP(w, r)      your root Handler (usually middleware)
                                   ▼
                     ServeMux: clean the path, find the most specific pattern
                       ├─ match           -> handler(w, r) with r.Pattern and PathValue set
                       ├─ subtree root    -> redirect to the path with a trailing slash
                       ├─ other method    -> 405 + Allow
                       └─ nothing         -> 404 (or your "/" pattern)

## Design notes

Start with `http.ServeMux`; reach for a router library only for what it lacks: typed or
regex segment constraints, route groups with their own middleware, and URL building from
route names. StackLab itself uses the standard mux (ADR-0001): every route is registered in
one function, `NewRouter` in `server/internal/httpapi/router.go`, which reads like a table
of contents of the API. A test that merely builds the router catches conflicting patterns,
because they panic at registration.

Two shapes for handlers with dependencies coexist there. A struct whose methods are
handlers (`learningHandlers`) suits a group sharing the same store and logger. A function
that returns an `http.HandlerFunc` closure (`handleReady(logger, pool)`) suits a one-off.
Both are constructor injection without globals.

Before Go 1.22, handlers checked `r.Method` by hand and cut IDs out of `r.URL.Path` with
`strings.TrimPrefix`, which is why chi and gorilla/mux were near-universal. Code like that
still works, but new code should put the method and wildcards in the pattern. Check the
`go` line in `go.mod`: below 1.22 the old matching applies (GODEBUG `httpmuxgo121=1`), and
the new patterns quietly fail to match.

lessons.title: JSON helpers, validation, problem-details errors (RFC 9457)
lessons.summary: Decode request bodies strictly (size cap, unknown fields, one value), validate business rules at the edge, and answer failures as application/problem+json. Go 1.27's encoding/json/v2 makes the strict part the default.

examples.title: A strict decode helper and what each bad body gets back

annotations.note: MaxBytesReader caps what the server will read. Past the limit, Read returns *http.MaxBytesError, and a real server also closes the connection after the response, so a client can't stream gigabytes into a JSON endpoint. A plain io.LimitReader would just truncate and look like malformed JSON.

By default encoding/json ignores keys it doesn't know, so a client's typo ("agee") silently becomes the zero value. Rejecting unknown fields turns that into a 400 the client developer sees immediately.
Decode reads one value and stops; the rest of the body is never looked at. A second Decode must hit io.EOF, otherwise the body held more than one value. Trailing whitespace is fine.

The one place decode errors become statuses. Messages are written for the client: the raw UnmarshalTypeError text names Go structs and types, an internal detail. A body over the limit is 413, not 400. The remaining errors describe only the client's own input, so they pass through. errors.As fits a switch; errors.AsType returns two values and doesn't.
The handler states intent; the helpers carry the rules. Every endpoint that takes JSON calls the same two functions, so the API rejects bad input the same way everywhere.

null decodes without error and leaves the struct at its zero value ("hello  (0)"). Decoding proves the syntax, not the content: that is what validation in example 3 is for. Strict v1 also accepts duplicate and differently cased keys; example 2 shows why that matters and what v2 does instead.

A ResponseRecorder calls the handler directly, with no server and no socket; the decode errors are the same ones a real server would see. Lesson go.http.cors-cookies-httptest covers this way of testing.

examples.title: encoding/json/v2 (Go 1.27): strict by default

annotations.note: This is the hardened v1 decoder from example 1, still the most common form in existing code, including StackLab's own run handler.
UnmarshalRead consumes the whole reader and requires exactly one value, so the trailing-data check comes built in. RejectUnknownMembers is the v2 spelling of DisallowUnknownFields.

v2 picks "cannot" or "unable to" for a SemanticError's message at random, once per process, so that nobody matches on the text. Branch on errors.Is(err, json.ErrUnknownName) or on the error's fields; JSONPointer says where in the body the problem is.

A parser differential: a proxy that reads the first "name" and a Go service that reads the last one disagree about who the request is for. v2 rejects duplicate names and matches names case-sensitively.

A client that sends Windows-1254 (or ISO-8859-9) instead of UTF-8 turns ş into byte 0xFE. v1 replaces it with U+FFFD and stores "Ay�e" for good; v2 rejects the body, so the client learns about its encoding bug at once.

examples.title: Validation at the edge, answered as problem details

annotations.note: RFC 9457 defines type, title, status, detail and instance, and allows extension members; clients must ignore members they don't know. The errors array with pointer and detail follows the RFC's own validation example.

Rules that types can't express live in one method. All failures are collected rather than returned at the first one. "Gülşen Çağlayıcı" is 16 characters but 22 bytes: a len(name) > 20 check would have rejected a valid name. PostgreSQL's varchar(20) counts characters too.
mail.ParseAddress also accepts "Name <addr>" forms, so the parsed address must equal the input. Format checks stop here; whether the mailbox exists is a confirmation e-mail's job, not a regex's.

The Content-Type header is set before WriteHeader, because headers set afterwards are dropped. Problems get application/problem+json, so a client can tell an error body from a resource without looking at the status first. Taking the status from p itself keeps the status member and the real response status from disagreeing.
With type "about:blank" the problem means no more than its status code, and the RFC says title should then be the status phrase. StackLab's httpapi.problem function writes this form for every error.

422: the JSON was well-formed but the content breaks the rules. 400 stays for bodies that can't be parsed. A custom type URI names the kind of problem, and clients switch on type, never on title or detail text.

use_cases: Every JSON endpoint: one decode helper and one error writer keep a whole API consistent
Form submissions from a React client that highlights each invalid field from the errors array
Public APIs where clients in other languages need a documented, machine-readable error format
Endpoints behind a proxy or gateway, where duplicate keys and case-folding would let two parsers disagree
strengths: Struct tags plus a decode helper replace a framework's binding layer; nothing is reflected that you can't see
Problem details is a standard format, so a client handles every error of every endpoint with one code path, unlike ad-hoc {"error": ...} bodies
MaxBytesReader and *MaxBytesError make the size limit a typed, testable error instead of a truncated body
Go 1.27's encoding/json/v2 rejects duplicate names, invalid UTF-8 and trailing data by default, without the wrapper code v1 needs
weaknesses: v1's defaults are lenient (unknown keys ignored, case-insensitive matching, duplicates accepted, invalid UTF-8 replaced) and each needs explicit handling
v1's unknown-field error has no exported type; you can only match its text (v2 has json.ErrUnknownName, and scrambles its message wording so nobody matches text)
No declarative validation in the standard library: unlike zod or Bean Validation, the rules are hand-written code (or a third-party validator)
A missing field and a zero value decode to the same thing; telling them apart needs pointer fields or json/v2's options

pitfalls.title: Reading an unbounded body
pitfalls.detail: json.NewDecoder(r.Body) reads as much as the client sends. Wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader with a limit per endpoint.
pitfalls.good: json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)).Decode(&in)

pitfalls.title: Counting bytes instead of characters
pitfalls.detail: len(s) is bytes. A 20-character Turkish name can be 30 bytes. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for user-facing limits, and keep byte limits for storage and transport.

pitfalls.title: Echoing internal errors to clients
pitfalls.detail: err.Error() from encoding/json mentions Go struct and type names, and a database error can reveal table names. Map errors to client messages in one place and log the original.

pitfalls.title: Validating before decoding finished
pitfalls.detail: Validate the decoded struct, not the raw map. And remember that a body of null decodes without error, so required-field checks belong in validation, not in the decoder.

pitfalls.title: Choosing the status by habit
pitfalls.detail: 400 for bodies you can't parse, 413 for bodies over the limit, 415 for a wrong Content-Type, 422 for well-formed bodies that break the rules. The problem's status member must match the real response status.

quiz.q: A client sends {"name":"Ayşe"} {"name":"Eve"} to a handler that calls dec.Decode(&in) once. What happens with plain encoding/json (v1)?
options: It fails with a syntax error
in.Name is "Ayşe" and the rest is ignored
It fails with an unknown field error
quiz.why: Decode reads one value from the stream and stops. Only a second Decode (expecting io.EOF), or v2's UnmarshalRead, detects the trailing value.

quiz.q: The body is well-formed JSON but the e-mail is invalid. Which status fits best?
quiz.why: The syntax was fine; the content breaks a rule. 400 is for bodies that can't be parsed at all.

quiz.q: What does v1 encoding/json do with {"name":"a","NAME":"b"} decoded into a struct with a `json:"name"` field?
quiz.why: v1 matches keys case-insensitively and lets a later duplicate overwrite an earlier one; DisallowUnknownFields doesn't help, because NAME is not unknown. v2 rejects this input.

quiz.q: Why should a client branch on the problem's type rather than its title?
options: type is the stable identifier; title and detail are human-readable text that may change or be translated
quiz.why: RFC 9457 makes type the primary identifier of the problem kind; title is a human-readable summary.

further_reading.title: package encoding/json: Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields and the v1/v2 differences

lessons.body:
## Concept

The edge of an HTTP service is where untrusted bytes become typed values. Three steps,
always in this order:

1. **Decode strictly.** Cap the body size, reject unknown fields, accept exactly one JSON
   value. A failure here is the client's syntax problem: 400, or 413 for size.
2. **Validate.** Check the rules the type system can't express: lengths in characters,
   formats, ranges, cross-field rules. Collect all failures. A failure here is 422.
3. **Answer machine-readably.** RFC 9457 "Problem Details for HTTP APIs" (it obsoletes RFC
   7807) defines a JSON object with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`,
   served as `application/problem+json`, plus any extension members you need, such as an
   `errors` array of JSON Pointers to the bad fields.

Below the edge, code works with values that are already valid. Services and repositories
don't re-check that an e-mail looks like one.

Go 1.27 ships `encoding/json/v2`. The v1 package is now implemented on top of it with
options that keep v1's historical behavior, and its documentation encourages new code to
use v2, whose defaults are the strict ones.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript/zod**: `schema.safeParse(body)` decodes and validates in one declarative
  step. In Go, decoding is driven by struct tags and validation is ordinary code, usually a
  `validate()` method. More typing, nothing hidden (lesson ts.services.zod).
- **Java/Spring**: `@Valid @RequestBody` with Bean Validation annotations, and
  `ProblemDetail` (Spring 6) for RFC 7807/9457 responses. Go has no annotations; the
  handler calls the helpers explicitly.
- **Python/FastAPI/pydantic**: a model class validates on construction and FastAPI answers
  422 with a list of field errors automatically. In Go you build that response yourself,
  which also means you choose its format.
- **Jackson (Java)**: a plain `ObjectMapper` fails on unknown properties. v1
  `encoding/json` ignores them, and so does v2 unless you pass `RejectUnknownMembers(true)`.

## Design notes

Write the helpers once per service: a `decodeJSON` (size limit, unknown fields, single
value, error mapping), a `writeJSON` and a `writeProblem`. StackLab's backend has the last
one as `problem(w, status, detail)` in `server/internal/httpapi/router.go`, and its run
handler decodes with `MaxBytesReader` and `json.NewDecoder`, the v1 form of example 1.

For new code on Go 1.27, `json.UnmarshalRead(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, n), &v,
json.RejectUnknownMembers(true))` gives you the single-value check, duplicate-name
rejection, case-sensitive matching and UTF-8 validation without wrapper code. Moving an
existing API from v1 to v2 is a behavior change for clients, so test it against real
traffic first: a client that sends `"Email"` instead of `"email"` worked yesterday.

Keep validation next to the type it validates, as a method, and keep it free of HTTP: it
returns field errors, and the handler decides that they become a 422. The same method then
serves a CLI import or a queue consumer. Return all field errors at once; a form that
reveals one error per submit is a frustrating form. Finally, never put `err.Error()` from
a lower layer into `detail` unfiltered: log it, and send the client a message written for
the client.

lessons.title: Middleware as function wrappers: logging, recovery, request ID, timeouts
