lessons.summary: Middleware is a function from http.Handler to http.Handler. Wrapping order is the whole design: request ID outside logging, logging outside recovery. Wrapped ResponseWriters need Unwrap, and timeouts only help handlers that watch their context.

examples.title: The middleware type, a chain helper, and a request ID in the context

annotations.note: The whole abstraction is one function type. No framework interface, no next() callback: a middleware receives the next Handler and returns a new one that calls it, or doesn't.
chain applies the list back to front (slices.Backward, Go 1.23), so the code reads in request order. Without it you write a(b(c(app))), which is fine for two layers and unreadable for six.
Code before next.ServeHTTP runs on the way in, code after it on the way out. The output shows the onion: outer, inner, handler, inner, outer.
A key of an unexported type can't collide with another package's key, which a plain string like "requestID" can. The context documentation says so explicitly.

Configuration arrives through the outer function (here the ID generator), the classic closure-based constructor. Behind your own proxy you may reuse the X-Request-ID it sends instead; accept it only from that proxy and cap its length, otherwise clients choose what lands in your logs.
A request is never modified in place: WithContext returns a shallow copy carrying the new context. Go has no thread-local storage, so this is how per-request data travels, explicitly.
Handlers run on many goroutines at once, so even a counter needs atomic.Int64 or a mutex. In production, crypto/rand.Text (Go 1.24) returns an unguessable ID.
A ResponseRecorder runs the whole chain without a server: ServeHTTP is just a method call, which is also why middleware is easy to test.

examples.title: A status-recording access log, panic recovery, and why wrappers need Unwrap

annotations.note: A ResponseWriter can't tell you the status afterwards, so the logger wraps it. Embedding the interface forwards everything else. The default must be 200, because a handler that only calls Write never calls WriteHeader.

The wrapper hides the real writer's optional methods (Flush, SetWriteDeadline, Hijack). http.ResponseController (Go 1.20) follows Unwrap to find them. StackLab's own statusRecorder gained this method after its absence silently broke the run route's deadline.
One log line per request, written after the handler returns, when the status is known. Log the duration here too in real code; it is left out only to keep the output stable.

The request boundary from the panic lesson as a reusable layer. It sits inside logging, so the access log records the 500 it writes. Placed outside, the panic would unwind through logging and that request would never be logged. A production recoverer also re-panics http.ErrAbortHandler, the value a handler panics with to abort a response on purpose.

struct{ http.ResponseWriter }{w} is a wrapper without Unwrap. The same Flush call works through statusRecorder and fails with http.ErrNotSupported through the bare wrapper. For a streaming endpoint that means a response that never streams.
The chain reads outside-in: logging(recoverer(mux)). Middleware that must see every request, including 404s and 405s, wraps the mux; middleware for one route wraps that route's handler.

examples.title: http.TimeoutHandler and handlers that do or don't watch their context

annotations.note: The client got its 503 long ago, but this goroutine keeps working until the sleep ends, and its write fails with ErrHandlerTimeout. A timeout layer can't stop code; it can only tell the code to stop.

TimeoutHandler gives the handler a context with a deadline. Selecting on r.Context().Done(), or passing r.Context() to database and HTTP calls, which do the same, stops the work when the client is no longer waiting.
TimeoutHandler buffers the whole response so it can replace it with a 503 at any moment. That is also why it doesn't support Flush: never put it in front of a streaming or SSE endpoint.
The handlers report through a channel, so main prints their side after the client's. Without that, the order of the lines would depend on scheduling.

use_cases: Access logs, metrics and tracing that wrap every route, including the mux's own 404s and 405s
Request IDs that tie a client's error report to every log line of that request
Recovering panics per request into a 500 plus a logged stack
Per-route policies: a body limit or a TimeoutHandler on one endpoint, authentication on a sub-mux
strengths: No framework: a middleware is a plain function, testable with httptest and composable with any router that speaks http.Handler
Order is visible in one expression, unlike annotation- or registration-order-driven filter chains in Java containers
Context values carry request-scoped data explicitly through every layer and goroutine, where Java's MDC and Python's thread-locals rely on thread affinity
weaknesses: Wrapping ResponseWriter hides optional interfaces; every wrapper needs Unwrap, and older code that type-asserts w.(http.Flusher) still breaks behind a wrapper
context.Value is untyped: a typo in the key type or a wrong assertion yields the zero value, not a compile error
No error return from handlers: error mapping needs a convention of your own (the appHandler pattern) or panics
A timeout can't preempt a goroutine; a handler that ignores its context keeps running after the client has its 503

pitfalls.title: A ResponseWriter wrapper without Unwrap
pitfalls.detail: Flush, SetWriteDeadline and Hijack then fail with http.ErrNotSupported. Streaming stalls and per-route deadlines silently don't apply.
pitfalls.good: func (r *rec) Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter { return r.ResponseWriter }

pitfalls.title: Recovery outside logging
pitfalls.detail: The panic unwinds through the logging middleware's ServeHTTP before anything recovers it, so the log line after next.ServeHTTP never runs. Put recovery inside logging, or log from a defer.

pitfalls.title: Strings as context keys
pitfalls.detail: context.WithValue(ctx, "user", u) collides with any other package that uses "user". Declare type ctxKey struct{} and expose typed getters.

pitfalls.title: Context values for dependencies
pitfalls.detail: Databases, loggers with configuration and feature flags belong in constructor arguments. The context documentation limits values to request-scoped data that transits processes and APIs.

pitfalls.title: TimeoutHandler on a streaming endpoint
pitfalls.detail: It buffers the response and doesn't support Flush, so an SSE stream or a large download is held back and then cut off with a 503. Use the context deadline or ResponseController.SetWriteDeadline for those routes.

quiz.q: srv := chain(app, a, b) with the chain helper from example 1. In which order do the layers see the request?
quiz.why: chain wraps back to front, so the first listed middleware is outermost: it sees the request first and the response last.

quiz.q: Recovery middleware wraps logging middleware (recoverer(logging(mux))). A handler panics. What does the access log show?
quiz.why: The panic unwinds through logging before recovery catches it, so logging's code after next.ServeHTTP never runs.

quiz.q: A middleware wraps w in a struct that embeds http.ResponseWriter and has no other methods. The handler calls http.NewResponseController(w).Flush(). Result?
quiz.why: Embedding the interface only promotes Header, Write and WriteHeader. Without Flush or Unwrap on the wrapper, ResponseController can't reach the real writer.

quiz.q: TimeoutHandler answered 503. What happens to a handler that called time.Sleep and never looks at r.Context()?
options: It keeps running; its later writes return http.ErrHandlerTimeout
Its output is appended to the 503
quiz.why: Go can't kill a goroutine from outside. The deadline is a request to stop that only context-aware code honors.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Go Concurrency Patterns: Context

lessons.body:
## Concept

A middleware is any function `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`. It returns a handler that
runs code before calling `next.ServeHTTP`, after it, around it, or instead of it. Stacked
middleware form an onion: the outermost layer sees the request first and the response
last.

Three mechanics carry most real middleware:

- **Context values** pass per-request data inward: a request ID, the authenticated user.
  The middleware builds a new request with `r.WithContext(context.WithValue(...))`; handlers
  read it with a typed getter.
- **ResponseWriter wrappers** observe the response: a struct embeds the original writer
  and overrides `WriteHeader` to record the status. Since Go 1.20 such a wrapper should also
  have `Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter`, so `http.ResponseController` can still reach the real
  connection's `Flush`, deadlines and `Hijack`.
- **`defer` + `recover`** turns a panic in one request into a logged 500.

Order is a design decision, not a detail. A sound default from the outside in: request ID,
logging, recovery, then per-route concerns (authentication, body limits, timeouts), then
the handler.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: a Servlet `Filter.doFilter(req, res, chain)` is the same onion, with
  `chain.doFilter` as `next.ServeHTTP` and `HttpServletResponseWrapper` as the status
  recorder. SLF4J's MDC keeps the request ID in a thread-local; Go has no goroutine-local
  storage, so the context is passed explicitly, and it keeps working across goroutines.
- **Express**: `app.use((req, res, next) => ...)` is the closest relative. Express passes
  errors with `next(err)` to an error middleware; Go handlers have no error return, so you
  either adopt the appHandler pattern from the panic lesson or recover panics.
- **Python**: WSGI middleware wraps the application callable, exactly like a Go middleware
  wraps a Handler. Django's `get_response` style is the same idea.
- **C/C++**: think of it as function composition over one callback type, with closures
  holding the configuration.

## Design notes

Keep the chain in one place, next to the routing table, so a reader can see what every
request goes through. StackLab's `NewRouter` ends with
`withLogging(logger)(withRecovery(logger)(withRequestGuards(logger, withProblemFallbacks(mux))))`:
logging outermost, so even 404s and recovered panics are logged with their status, then
recovery, then the request guards around the mux. Its `statusRecorder` has the `Unwrap`
method this lesson explains, added after the run route's extended write deadline silently
failed behind the wrapper; the recoverer's own wrapper has it for the same reason.

Write middleware as constructors that take their dependencies (`requestID(newID)`,
`logging(log, next)`), not as code that reaches for globals. Put request-scoped data in the
context, dependencies in constructor arguments. A small `chain` helper is enough; you don't
need a library for it.

Timeouts come in three layers, and this lesson covers the middle one. Server-wide timeouts
on `http.Server` protect the connection (next lesson). Per-request deadlines, through
`TimeoutHandler` or a middleware that wraps the context, limit how long the work may take.
Per-call deadlines on each database or HTTP call protect against one slow dependency. All
three only work if handlers pass `r.Context()` down to every call that can block.

lessons.title: Server timeouts, graceful shutdown, static files with embed
lessons.summary: The zero http.Server has no timeouts, so one slow client can hold a connection forever: set them. Shut down with Server.Shutdown, which drains requests but cancels none, and ship static assets inside the binary with embed and FileServerFS.

examples.title: What ReadHeaderTimeout and WriteTimeout do, and what the client sees

annotations.note: The slowloris attack in miniature: valid but unfinished headers, sent by a client that then just waits. Each such connection pins a goroutine and a file descriptor; a few thousand of them exhaust a server without sending much traffic.
errors.AsType (Go 1.26) finds the net.Error and returns it typed. A read deadline that passes is a timeout; anything else here means the server hung up.
httptest.NewServer, like http.ListenAndServe, uses a zero http.Server: every timeout is zero, which means none. That is the dangerous default this lesson is about.
NewUnstartedServer exposes the *http.Server as Config, so a test can set fields before Start. ReadHeaderTimeout closes the connection without any response, not even a 408.

WriteTimeout is not a request timeout with a polite answer: when it passes, the client gets a closed connection and no status at all, while the handler's write succeeded into a buffer and it never learned. Use it as a backstop, and per-request deadlines (previous lesson) for answers.

examples.title: Shutdown drains in-flight requests; long-lived ones need a signal

annotations.note: Listening on 127.0.0.1:0 lets the OS choose a free port; the listener knows which. Binding to 127.0.0.1 rather than ":8080" keeps a development server off the network.
Shutdown does not cancel request contexts and does not wait for hijacked connections such as WebSockets. A context canceled from RegisterOnShutdown gives streams and long polls their stop signal.

BaseContext is the root of every request's context on this server, so canceling it reaches every handler at once. RegisterOnShutdown functions run in their own goroutines when Shutdown starts; they should start the goodbye, not wait for it.

Always give Shutdown a deadline. Without one, a single stuck request blocks the process forever; with one, Shutdown returns the context's error and you can call srv.Close() to cut the remaining connections.
Serve returns http.ErrServerClosed immediately, while two requests are still running. A main that returns at that moment kills them mid-response: main must wait for Shutdown, not for Serve.
The stream ended because RegisterOnShutdown canceled its context. The report finished its work and got its 200: drained, not dropped. Only then did Shutdown return nil.

examples.title: Serving embedded files with fs.Sub and http.FileServerFS

annotations.note: //go:embed is read at compile time: the files must sit next to the source, and the build fails if they are missing. Embedding a directory skips names starting with "." or "_" (_draft.html below); the "all:static" pattern would include them.

Forgetting fs.Sub is the classic bug: every URL then needs a /static/ segment, or nothing matches. StackLab's backend hit the same trap with its embedded migrations; main.go's migrationsFS exists for it.
FileServerFS (Go 1.22) takes any fs.FS: embed.FS, os.DirFS, or a testing/fstest.MapFS in tests. StripPrefix removes /assets/ so the remaining path matches names inside the FS.

Content-Type comes from the extension. Last-Modified is empty because embedded files have a zero ModTime, so browsers can't revalidate with If-Modified-Since. index.html redirects to its directory, and a directory without an index gets a listing.

use_cases: Any production http.Server: ReadHeaderTimeout always, the others according to the slowest legitimate request
Rolling deploys and container restarts: SIGTERM, stop accepting, drain, exit before the orchestrator's kill deadline
Single-binary tools and admin UIs that carry their HTML, CSS and JavaScript (or a built React app) inside the executable
Embedding SQL migrations or templates so a distroless image needs nothing but the binary
strengths: Shutdown is built in and correct by default (stop accepting, close idle, wait for active), where many stacks need a library or careful signal handling
Per-route exceptions without a second server: http.ResponseController.SetWriteDeadline extends one handler's deadline
embed.FS is an fs.FS, so the same code serves embedded files in production and os.DirFS or fstest.MapFS in development and tests
One static binary with its assets: no working-directory surprises, unlike Java resources resolved at run time or Node's static folders
weaknesses: Safe timeouts are opt-in: http.ListenAndServe and the zero http.Server have none, unlike Node's 60 s headersTimeout and 300 s requestTimeout (since Node 18)
Server-wide ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout can't tell a slow upload or a stream from an attack; long routes need per-request handling
Shutdown neither cancels handlers nor tracks WebSockets; long-lived work needs BaseContext or RegisterOnShutdown wiring
Embedded files have no modification time, so FileServerFS sends no Last-Modified; caching needs ETags or fingerprinted file names

pitfalls.title: http.ListenAndServe in production
pitfalls.detail: It uses a zero http.Server, so there is no way to set timeouts. Build an http.Server and set at least ReadHeaderTimeout.
pitfalls.good:
srv := &http.Server{Addr: "127.0.0.1:8080", Handler: mux,
	ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second, IdleTimeout: time.Minute}

pitfalls.title: Exiting when ListenAndServe returns
pitfalls.detail: After Shutdown starts, ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed at once. If main returns there, in-flight requests die. Wait for Shutdown to return.

pitfalls.title: Treating ErrServerClosed as a failure
pitfalls.detail: It is the expected result after Shutdown or Close. Check errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) before logging an error or exiting non-zero.

pitfalls.title: A global WriteTimeout shorter than your slowest route
pitfalls.detail: The client of a long export or SSE stream gets a dropped connection, and the handler's writes may look successful. Extend the deadline for that route with http.NewResponseController(w).SetWriteDeadline, which needs Unwrap on any wrapping middleware.

pitfalls.title: Expecting dotfiles and _files in an embedded directory
pitfalls.detail: //go:embed static skips names starting with . or _. Frameworks that emit _app.js or similar need //go:embed all:static.

quiz.q: What are the timeouts of a server started with http.ListenAndServe(addr, mux)?
options: None: every timeout is zero, meaning no deadline
quiz.why: ListenAndServe builds a zero http.Server, and a zero timeout means no timeout. Set them on your own http.Server.

quiz.q: A handler takes longer than the server's WriteTimeout. What does the client see?
options: The connection closes without a response
quiz.why: The write deadline expires on the connection; the buffered response can't be sent and the connection is closed. No status line reaches the client.

quiz.q: Shutdown(ctx) is called while an SSE handler waits on r.Context().Done(). Without further wiring, what happens?
options: The handler's context is canceled at once
Shutdown waits for the handler until ctx expires
quiz.why: Shutdown waits for active connections but cancels nothing. Cancel a BaseContext from RegisterOnShutdown to end such handlers.

quiz.q: Why does FileServerFS over an embed.FS send no Last-Modified header?
options: Embedded files have a zero modification time, and ServeContent omits a zero time
quiz.why: embed.FS reports a zero ModTime; ServeContent only sets Last-Modified for a non-zero time. Use an ETag or fingerprinted names for caching.

lessons.body:
## Concept

An `http.Server` is configuration plus a loop that accepts connections. Its zero value,
which `http.ListenAndServe` uses, has **no timeouts**: a client that sends headers slowly,
never finishes a body, or never reads the response holds a goroutine and a socket for as
long as it likes. Four fields bound the phases of a connection:

| Field | Bounds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ReadHeaderTimeout` | reading the request line and headers | set it always; the slowloris defense |
| `ReadTimeout` | reading the whole request, body included | blunt for uploads; often left to per-request limits |
| `WriteTimeout` | from the end of the headers to the end of the response | effectively caps handler time; the client gets no response when it fires |
| `IdleTimeout` | waiting for the next request on a keep-alive connection | falls back to `ReadTimeout` when zero |

Header size has a limit by default: `MaxHeaderBytes` defaults to 1 MB, and Go 1.27 added
`MaxHeaderValueCount` (default 500 values). One route can relax the server-wide deadlines
with `http.NewResponseController(w).SetWriteDeadline(...)` (Go 1.20).

**Graceful shutdown** is `srv.Shutdown(ctx)`: close the listeners, close idle connections,
wait for active requests to finish. `Serve` returns `http.ErrServerClosed` as soon as it
starts, so `main` must wait for `Shutdown` to return. Shutdown never cancels a request's
context and ignores hijacked connections, so streams and WebSockets need their own signal.

**Static files** can live in the binary: `//go:embed static` fills an `embed.FS` at compile
time, `fs.Sub` drops the directory prefix, and `http.FileServerFS` (Go 1.22) serves it with
content types, range requests and conditional GETs.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Node**: `http.createServer` has defaults: `headersTimeout` 60 s and, since Node 18,
  `requestTimeout` 300 s. Go starts at zero, and you choose. Draining on SIGTERM is your
  code in both: `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` there, `signal.NotifyContext` here.
- **Java**: a servlet container ships preconfigured connection timeouts and its own
  graceful-shutdown setting. In Go the server is a struct in your `main`, and so is its
  lifecycle.
- **Python**: gunicorn or uvicorn own the timeouts and the SIGTERM handling outside your
  code. In Go there is no separate application server: your binary is it.
- **C/C++**: `go:embed` is what `xxd -i` or C23's `#embed` do for a byte array, but it
  produces a read-only file system with directories, not one blob.

## Design notes

StackLab's `cmd/stacklab/main.go` is a complete lifecycle to read: `ReadHeaderTimeout` 5 s,
`ReadTimeout` and `WriteTimeout` from configuration (15 s), `IdleTimeout` 60 s;
`signal.NotifyContext` for Ctrl+C and SIGTERM; `ListenAndServe` in a goroutine, ignoring
`ErrServerClosed`; and `Shutdown` with a 10 s budget. The run route is the one exception
to the 15 s write deadline: it extends its own deadline with `ResponseController`, because
a lesson run may take longer.

Pick the drain budget from the slowest request you are willing to wait for, and keep it
below the time your process manager waits before killing the process. If `Shutdown` returns
`context.DeadlineExceeded`, call `srv.Close()`, log, and exit. For a service behind a load
balancer, fail the readiness check first (StackLab has `/readyz`), so traffic stops arriving
before the listener closes.

For embedded assets, decide on caching explicitly. With content-hashed file names, as a
Vite build emits, serve them with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. For
fixed names, compute a hash per file at startup and set it as the `ETag` header before
calling the file server; `ServeContent` then answers `If-None-Match` with 304. A single-page
app also needs a fallback that serves `index.html` for unknown paths outside `/api/` and
`/assets/`.

lessons.title: File upload (multipart, size limits), streaming download, SSE, WebSockets
lessons.summary: Request and response bodies are streams: read uploads part by part under a size cap, write downloads and Server-Sent Events as they are produced, and flush. WebSockets leave HTTP after a 101 handshake; the standard library stops there.

examples.title: Streaming a multipart upload under a size limit

annotations.note: The cap goes on the whole body before anything reads it. Every part, header and boundary counts, so one limit covers files and fields.

MultipartReader hands out parts in order as they arrive. Its alternative, ParseMultipartForm (also called by r.FormValue and r.FormFile, with 32 MB of memory), reads the whole body first: memory up to the limit, temp files for the rest.
On HTTP/1.x a handler should finish reading the body before it writes the response. Collecting the report and writing it at the end also keeps a 413 possible until the last byte.
io.Copy moves the part in 32 KiB chunks straight into the hash. Swap the hash for an os.File from os.CreateTemp or an object-storage writer and memory use stays the same for a 5 GB file.

FileName() is the client's claim, passed through filepath.Base, which depends on the OS. "../../etc/passwd" arrives as "passwd". Never use it as a path: store under a name you generate, and keep the original (here "rapor-İş.csv", UTF-8) only as metadata.
The client streams too: multipart.Writer writes into a pipe from a goroutine while http.Post reads the other end. Closing the pipe with mw.Close()'s error ends the body, or fails it.
200,000 bytes against a 64 KiB cap: the server stops reading, answers 413 and closes the connection. Go's client returns that response even though it never finished sending the body.

examples.title: Server-Sent Events: flush per event, stop when the client leaves

annotations.note: text/event-stream is what makes a browser's EventSource accept the response. no-cache keeps proxies and the browser from storing a live stream.
The wire format: "field: value" lines, a blank line ends the event. id lets EventSource send Last-Event-ID when it reconnects, so the server can resume; event picks the listener; data is the payload.
Without Flush the event sits in a 4 KiB buffer until it fills. ResponseController.Flush reports when flushing is impossible, for example behind a middleware wrapper without Unwrap.
A stream runs until someone ends it. The request context is canceled when the client disconnects, so the select is the only way out. Without it this goroutine would loop forever.
No Content-Length (-1), so HTTP/1.1 uses chunked encoding: each flush sends a chunk. Any download written with io.Copy(w, src) without a length is streamed the same way.
Canceling the request context closes the connection. The server notices only because it was waiting on r.Context().Done(); a handler that never looks would find out at its next failed write.

examples.title: The WebSocket upgrade handshake with net/http, and one raw frame

annotations.note: The only cryptography in the handshake, and it isn't security: it proves the server understood the WebSocket request, so a misconfigured plain HTTP server can't accidentally accept one.
426 Upgrade Required with an Upgrade header tells a plain HTTP client which protocol this endpoint wants.

Browsers send Origin on WebSocket requests but enforce nothing, so checking it is the server's job. Skipping the check enables cross-site WebSocket hijacking: another site's page opens a socket with your user's cookies.
Hijack takes the TCP connection away from net/http: no more headers, timeouts or Shutdown tracking. It works only on HTTP/1.x; HTTP/2 connections don't support it.
A minimal frame: FIN plus opcode 1 (text), then a length byte. The length counts bytes: "Merhaba dünya" is 14 bytes but 13 characters, and text frames must be valid UTF-8.
The sample key from RFC 6455. Real clients send 16 random bytes in base64; the expected accept value s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo= is printed in the RFC and on MDN, so you can check the computation.
Since Go 1.12 the client hands back a 101 response whose Body is also an io.Writer: the raw connection, readable and writable.

use_cases: Uploads of CSV imports, images and documents, written to disk or object storage without holding them in memory
Exports and backups streamed with io.Copy or http.ServeContent (which adds Range and conditional requests)
SSE for one-way live updates: job progress, notifications, log tails, LLM token streams
WebSockets for two-way, low-latency traffic: chat, collaborative editing, games
strengths: io.Reader and io.Writer make streaming the default shape: MultipartReader, io.Copy and Flush compose without callbacks, unlike Node's stream events or Java's servlet async API
Size limits are one wrapper (MaxBytesReader) with a typed error
SSE needs nothing beyond net/http: a header, a format and Flush; the browser's EventSource adds reconnection and Last-Event-ID for free
weaknesses: No WebSocket implementation in the standard library: Hijack gives you a raw connection, and framing, masking, ping/pong and the close handshake are a library's job
Hijacked connections are invisible to Server.Shutdown and to server timeouts; you manage their lifecycle yourself
Streams fight with server-wide WriteTimeout, TimeoutHandler and buffering middleware such as compression, which need per-route exceptions
SSE is one-way, text-only, and over HTTP/1.1 limited to six connections per browser and domain

pitfalls.title: r.FormValue on an upload endpoint
pitfalls.detail: It calls ParseMultipartForm(32 MB) for you: up to 32 MB in memory and the rest in temp files, before your code sees a byte. Use MultipartReader for large or untrusted uploads.

pitfalls.title: Trusting the file name and Content-Type of a part
pitfalls.detail: Both come from the client. Generate the storage name, keep the original for display, and sniff the type with http.DetectContentType on the first 512 bytes if it matters.
pitfalls.good: f, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, "upload-*") // original name goes to metadata

pitfalls.title: Writing an SSE stream without Flush
pitfalls.detail: The events wait in the server's buffer and arrive in bursts or at the end. Flush after every event, and check that no middleware hides Flush.

pitfalls.title: A non-ASCII download name in Content-Disposition
pitfalls.detail: filename="rapor-İş.csv" in a raw header is not portable. mime.FormatMediaType("attachment", map[string]string{"filename": name}) produces filename*=utf-8''rapor-%C4%B0%C5%9F.csv, the RFC 2231 encoding browsers understand.

pitfalls.title: Accepting WebSocket upgrades from any origin
pitfalls.detail: CORS doesn't apply to WebSockets. Compare Origin against an allow-list before upgrading, or any site can open a socket with your users' cookies.

quiz.q: An upload handler calls r.FormFile("file") on a 2 GB upload. What happens before the call returns?
options: The whole body is parsed: up to 32 MB in memory, the rest in temp files
It fails: the body is too large
quiz.why: FormFile calls ParseMultipartForm with 32 MB of memory if the form isn't parsed yet, which consumes the entire body.

quiz.q: An SSE handler writes events but never calls Flush. What does the browser see?
options: Events in bursts when the buffer fills, or at the end
quiz.why: Small writes sit in the server's response buffer until it fills or the handler returns; Flush pushes them out.

quiz.q: Which statement about WebSockets in Go's standard library is true?
options: net/http can perform the upgrade through Hijack, but framing, masking and control frames need code of your own or a library
quiz.why: The standard library has no WebSocket package; after the 101 the connection is yours. Shutdown doesn't track hijacked connections.

quiz.q: Why must a WebSocket server check the Origin header itself?
options: Browsers don't send Origin on WebSocket requests
Browsers don't apply CORS to WebSocket connections
quiz.why: Browsers send Origin but don't block the connection; without a server-side check, any site can connect with the user's cookies (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).

further_reading.title: package golang.org/x/net/websocket (and the alternatives its docs recommend)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A request body is an `io.Reader` and a response is an `io.Writer`. As long as you keep
them that way, memory use doesn't depend on the size of what passes through. Buffering
creeps in through convenient calls: `io.ReadAll(r.Body)`, `r.FormFile`, a JSON encoder
fed one giant slice.

**Uploads.** Cap the body with `http.MaxBytesReader`, then walk the parts with
`r.MultipartReader()` and `NextPart()`, copying each file part into its destination with
`io.Copy`. Exceeding the cap surfaces as `*http.MaxBytesError`: answer 413.

**Downloads.** `io.Copy(w, src)` streams. Without a known length, HTTP/1.1 switches to
chunked encoding. For files and seekable data, `http.ServeContent` adds `Content-Length`,
range requests (resumable downloads) and conditional GETs.

**Server-Sent Events.** A response that never ends: `Content-Type: text/event-stream`,
events made of `id:`, `event:` and `data:` lines, each event ended by a blank line and
followed by a `Flush`. The browser's `EventSource` parses them, and reconnects on its own
with a `Last-Event-ID` header. A line starting with `:` is a comment, useful as a
keep-alive through proxies.

**WebSockets.** A GET with `Upgrade: websocket` and a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; the server
answers `101 Switching Protocols` with `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, and from then on both sides
exchange binary frames on the same TCP connection. `net/http` gets you to the 101 through
`Hijack`. Everything after it is yours or a library's.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Node**: `req` and `res` are streams there too, and `busboy` or `multer` stream
  multipart. `res.write` + `res.flushHeaders` is the SSE counterpart. `ws` and Socket.IO
  are separate packages, as in Go.
- **Java**: Servlet 3.0's `request.getParts()` buffers to disk like `ParseMultipartForm`;
  Spring's `SseEmitter` wraps the SSE format. Java EE/Jakarta has a standard WebSocket API
  (JSR 356), which Go's standard library has no equivalent of.
- **Python**: Starlette's `StreamingResponse` and `request.stream()` play the same roles;
  WebSockets need an ASGI server, never WSGI.
- **C/C++**: think `sendfile` and a write loop; `io.Copy` uses such fast paths when both
  sides allow it.

## How it works

What a WebSocket library adds after the handshake, all of it from RFC 6455:

- **Masking**: client-to-server frames are XOR-masked with a fresh 4-byte key, and a server
  must close the connection on an unmasked client frame. Server frames are unmasked.
- **Lengths**: 0-125 fit in the second byte; 126 means a 16-bit length follows, 127 a
  64-bit one.
- **Fragmentation**: a message may span frames (opcode 0, continuation), the last with FIN.
- **Control frames**: ping (0x9), pong (0xA) and close (0x8) with a status code and the
  close handshake; pings keep idle connections alive through NATs and proxies.
- **Checks and limits**: UTF-8 validation of text messages, maximum message sizes, one
  writer at a time per connection, optional `permessage-deflate` compression, Origin
  checks and subprotocol negotiation.

`golang.org/x/net/websocket` exists outside the standard library, and its own documentation
points to more actively maintained packages, github.com/gorilla/websocket and
github.com/coder/websocket.

## Design notes

Choose the simplest transport that fits. Polling suits data that changes every few
minutes. SSE suits server-to-client updates: it is plain HTTP, so cookies, CORS,
compression and HTTP/2 multiplexing work unchanged, and the browser reconnects for you.
Choose WebSockets when the client sends a steady stream too, and accept the cost: a
library, Origin checks, your own heartbeat, and connections that `Shutdown` doesn't see.

Long-lived responses need the server configured for them: a write deadline extended for
that route (or none), no `TimeoutHandler`, no buffering middleware, and a context that
`RegisterOnShutdown` cancels, as in the previous lesson. For uploads, decide the limit per
endpoint, stream into the destination, and record the client's file name only as metadata.

lessons.title: CORS, cookies, and httptest
lessons.summary: CORS is the server telling browsers which other origins may read its responses; it stops no request. Cookies carry sessions, so they need HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and CSRF protection. httptest runs all of it in tests without a network.

examples.title: A CORS middleware: preflights, an allow-list, and what it doesn't stop

annotations.note: The key fact about CORS: the server only labels responses. The browser decides whether the page's JavaScript may read them. curl, Go programs and attackers' scripts ignore the labels entirely.

Reflect the request's Origin only when it is on the list, and add Vary: Origin so a cache never serves one origin's permission to another. "*" also works, but never together with cookies or other credentials.

A preflight is an OPTIONS request with Access-Control-Request-Method. The browser sends one before a PUT, a DELETE, or a POST with Content-Type: application/json, and sends the real request only if the answer allows it. Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer.
CORS wraps the mux, not the route. The mux only knows "PUT /notes/{id}", so a preflight reaching it would get 405 and the browser would never send the PUT.
For the other site the preflight succeeds as an HTTP exchange but carries no permission, so a browser stops there. A non-browser client simply sends the PUT, and the handler runs.

A sandboxed iframe without allow-same-origin has an opaque origin, sent as the string "null". StackLab's TS runner iframe is exactly that. Never allow-list "null": every sandboxed iframe, data: URL and file: page in the world has that same origin.
Three executions, not one: the handler ran for every PUT. Protect state-changing endpoints with authentication and CSRF defenses; CORS only protects the response from being read.

examples.title: Session cookies, non-ASCII values, and CSRF protection (Go 1.25)

annotations.note: The usual session cookie. The value is a random ID pointing at server-side state, so the cookie carries nothing worth reading. SameSite=Lax withholds it from cross-site POSTs and subrequests but keeps it on ordinary links into your site.
The __Host- prefix is a promise browsers enforce: such a cookie is rejected unless it is Secure, has Path=/ and no Domain, so a sibling subdomain can't set or overwrite it.

Cookie values allow only a subset of ASCII. net/http drops the bytes of ş and logs a warning on stderr; the log even shows the first byte as Å, UTF-8 read as Latin-1. Encode such values (base64url, or percent-encoding) and decode them on the way back.
Deleting a cookie is setting it again with the same name, path and domain and an expiry in the past. In Go, MaxAge < 0 sends Max-Age=0.

CrossOriginProtection rejects every method except GET, HEAD and OPTIONS when a browser sends it from another origin, judged by Sec-Fetch-Site or, failing that, Origin versus Host. Requests without either header (curl, server to server) pass, so it complements authentication.
srv.Client() trusts the TLS test certificate; a cookiejar makes the client keep and resend cookies like a browser, Secure ones included, because the server speaks HTTPS.
A browser sets Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site when another site's form posts here. The 403 means the logout never happened: the next /me still finds the session.

examples.title: Testing handlers with ResponseRecorder and NewTestServer (Go 1.27)

annotations.note: The fastest handler test: build a request with httptest.NewRequest, call ServeHTTP with a ResponseRecorder, inspect the result. The whole router runs, 405 included, with no socket and no goroutine. The CORS middleware from example 1 is tested the same way: set Origin on the request and check Access-Control-Allow-Origin in the result.

httptest.NewRequest builds a server-side request (Host example.com unless the target is absolute) and panics on bad input, which is what you want in a test. http.NewRequest builds a client request instead.

rec.Header() is the live map a handler mutates; rec.Result().Header is a snapshot of what was sent at the first write. Assert on the snapshot, or a header set too late will look correct. http.Error sets text/plain itself, which is why the error rows expect it.

NewTestServer (Go 1.27) runs a real server and client over an in-memory network: any host name reaches it, no port is opened, and t.Cleanup shuts it down. It also fails the test if a handler panics. httptest.NewServer is the loopback alternative when a test needs a real address.

use_cases: An API used by a browser app on another origin, such as a Vite dev server on :5173 calling a backend on :8080 without a proxy
Cookie-based sessions for server-rendered pages and same-site SPAs
CSRF protection for any cookie-authenticated endpoint that changes state
Handler, middleware and router tests that run in milliseconds without ports
strengths: CORS is a few headers in one middleware; no framework configuration DSL like Spring's CorsConfiguration
http.CrossOriginProtection (Go 1.25) gives token-free CSRF protection in one wrapper, unlike Django's or Spring Security's synchronizer tokens
http.Cookie models every attribute (SameSite, Partitioned since Go 1.23) and SetCookie validates what it writes
httptest covers three levels, recorder, in-memory server and loopback server, all in the standard library, where Java needs MockMvc or a test container
weaknesses: CORS mistakes fail silently on the server: the request succeeds, only the browser console complains
Invalid cookie bytes are dropped with a log line, not an error; nothing stops a deploy
CrossOriginProtection relies on headers that only browsers send, so it is a browser-facing defense, not authentication
A ResponseRecorder skips the transport: connection handling, Flush and Hijack behavior need a test server

pitfalls.title: Allowing the null origin
pitfalls.detail: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null admits every sandboxed iframe, data: URL and file: document, including hostile ones. Serve such clients through a proxy or a data: URL design instead.

pitfalls.title: Reflecting any Origin with credentials
pitfalls.detail: Echoing whatever Origin arrives plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true lets every website read authenticated responses. Compare against an explicit allow-list.

pitfalls.title: CORS middleware inside the router
pitfalls.detail: With method patterns, OPTIONS reaches no route and the mux answers 405, so every preflighted request fails. Wrap the mux.

pitfalls.title: Treating CORS as access control
pitfalls.detail: Simple requests, such as a form POST, are sent cross-origin without any preflight, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely. Authenticate, and protect cookie-based state changes against CSRF.

pitfalls.title: Non-ASCII in cookie values
pitfalls.detail: "Ayşe" becomes "Aye" with only a log line to show for it. Base64url- or percent-encode the value.

quiz.q: A page on https://evil.example calls fetch("https://api.example/notes/1", {method: "PUT"}). Your server answers the preflight without Access-Control-Allow-Origin. What happens?
options: The PUT is sent and its response hidden
The browser never sends the PUT
The PUT is sent without cookies
quiz.why: PUT is not a simple method, so the browser preflights first and stops when the preflight grants nothing.

quiz.q: Why does a sandboxed iframe (sandbox="allow-scripts", no allow-same-origin) send Origin: null?
options: Its document gets an opaque origin, which serializes as null
quiz.why: Without allow-same-origin the sandbox gives the document a unique opaque origin, and opaque origins serialize as "null".

quiz.q: http.SetCookie(w, &http.Cookie{Name: "n", Value: "Ayşe"}). What reaches the browser?
options: n=Aye, with a warning logged by net/http
quiz.why: Cookie values are limited to a subset of ASCII; net/http drops the invalid bytes and logs, so encode non-ASCII values.

quiz.q: What does an httptest.ResponseRecorder test not exercise?
options: The real HTTP transport: connections, serialization, Flush and Hijack
quiz.why: ServeHTTP is called directly with a recorder, so routing and middleware run, but no connection or wire format is involved; use a test server for those.

lessons.body:
## Concept

An **origin** is scheme + host + port: `http://127.0.0.1:5173` (Vite) and
`http://127.0.0.1:8080` (the Go backend) are different origins. Browsers let a page *send*
many cross-origin requests (links, forms, images, simple fetches) but not *read* the
responses, unless the server opts in with CORS headers:

- **Simple requests** (GET, HEAD, POST with a form or plain-text body) are sent directly;
  the browser shows the response to the page only if `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matches.
- **Preflighted requests** (PUT, DELETE, JSON bodies, custom headers) start with an
  `OPTIONS` request; the real one follows only if the preflight answer allows it.
- With cookies (`credentials: "include"`), the server must name the exact origin and send
  `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`; `*` is rejected.

The `Origin` header is the string `null` for **opaque origins**: documents in an
`<iframe sandbox>` without `allow-same-origin`, `data:` and `file:` documents, and requests
after cross-origin redirects.

**Cookies** carry sessions automatically, which is both their convenience and their
danger. `HttpOnly` hides them from scripts, `Secure` keeps them off plain HTTP, `SameSite`
limits cross-site sending, and the `__Host-` prefix pins them to one host. Because the
browser attaches them to requests other sites trigger, cookie-authenticated state changes
need **CSRF** protection; since Go 1.25 that is `http.CrossOriginProtection`.

**httptest** tests all of this without a network: `NewRecorder` and `NewRequest` call a
handler directly, `NewTestServer` (Go 1.27) runs a real client and server over an in-memory
network, and `NewServer`/`NewTLSServer` listen on loopback.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS/React**: you have met CORS as a red console error. This is the other side: the
  server's headers decide, and the browser enforces. The Express `cors` package is the same
  middleware as example 1.
- **Java/Spring**: `@CrossOrigin` and `CorsConfiguration` generate these headers; Spring
  Security's CSRF tokens solve what `CrossOriginProtection` solves with `Sec-Fetch-Site`.
  `MockMvc` corresponds to the `ResponseRecorder` style, a random-port `@SpringBootTest` to
  `httptest.NewServer`.
- **Python**: Django's CSRF middleware uses tokens; `flask-cors` and Starlette's
  `CORSMiddleware` add the headers. Flask's `test_client()` calls the app without a socket,
  like a recorder.
- **C/C++**: a non-browser client never sees CORS at all, which is the point to remember.

## How it works

StackLab's TS runner, `src/features/runner/browserTs.ts`, is a worked example of the
null origin:

    <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" srcdoc="...lesson...">
      - no allow-same-origin   -> opaque origin, Origin: null, no access to the app's
                                  DOM, storage or cookies
      - CSP default-src 'none' -> no fetch at all, so lessons stay deterministic
      - libraries              -> data: URLs in an import map (ADR-0010), which need
                                  neither CORS nor a CSP exception

The app itself avoids CORS too: the Vite dev server proxies `/api` to the backend, so the
browser only ever talks to one origin, and the backend sends no CORS headers at all. If a
lesson iframe were allowed to call the API, the backend would have to allow `null`, which
would also allow every other sandboxed document on the web.

## Design notes

Avoid CORS when you can: serve the frontend and the API from one origin, in development
through a proxy as StackLab does, in production behind one reverse proxy. When you need
it, keep an explicit allow-list, reflect only listed origins, add `Vary: Origin`, answer
preflights before routing, and keep `Allow-Credentials` off unless the client sends
cookies.

For sessions, store a random ID in a `__Host-` cookie with `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and
`SameSite=Lax`, keep the data on the server, and wrap state-changing routes in
`CrossOriginProtection`. Generate IDs with `crypto/rand.Text`. Keep tokens for third-party
API clients in the `Authorization` header instead: no cookies, no CSRF, but the client has
to store the token somewhere scripts can reach.

Test at the cheapest level that covers the behavior: recorder tests for routing,
validation, status codes and headers; `NewTestServer` when the client side matters
(cookies in a jar, redirects, TLS); loopback servers only for code that needs a real
address. Lesson go.testing.fakes-httptest goes further with fakes and golden files.

lessons.title: Methods: value vs pointer receivers and method sets
lessons.summary: A receiver is passed like any other argument: a value receiver gets a copy, a pointer receiver shares the caller's value. Pick one kind per type, because mixed receivers let the compiler accept code that silently works on copies.

examples.title: Value receivers copy, pointer receivers share

annotations.note: IncCopy compiles, runs and changes nothing the caller can see: the receiver is an ordinary parameter, copied like any other. The compiler doesn't warn. Counter mixes both kinds only to show the difference; the next example shows why real types shouldn't.
Go takes the address for you when the variable is addressable, so value and pointer methods look identical at the call site. That is also why the lost increment on line 15 is easy to miss in review.
range hands you a copy of each element. Since Go 1.22 k is a fresh variable per iteration, but it is still a copy, so Inc changes nothing in the slice. Indexing (line 26) reaches the element itself.

Map elements are not addressable, so Go can't insert the &: the commented call fails with "cannot call pointer method Inc on Counter". Copy out, modify, store back, or keep *Counter values in the map.

examples.title: Mixed receivers: interfaces and method values capture copies

annotations.note: With String on the value, both Hits and *Hits satisfy fmt.Stringer. That looks convenient, and it is the trap: the compiler now accepts code that quietly works on a copy.
Storing h in an interface copies it. A method value with a value receiver evaluates and saves the receiver immediately, the same rule as a defer's arguments. Both print hits=0 after the increment.
With pointer receivers throughout, the copy can't happen by accident: the commented assignment fails with "method String has pointer receiver", and v.String binds &v, so all three agree.
The one hole: fmt.Println takes any and looks for String at run time. A Visits value has no String in its method set, so fmt prints the raw struct. Pass &v, or hand *Visits around everywhere.

examples.title: Methods on slices and maps, and nil pointer receivers

annotations.note: A slice value is a small header (pointer, length, capacity). A value receiver could overwrite existing elements, but its append would be lost with the copied header. Growing needs *Tags, and consistency moves String to *Tags too.
Map, channel and func values already refer to shared state, so value receivers are idiomatic for them. Writing to a nil map still panics, which is why line 40 makes one.

A pointer-receiver method may run with a nil receiver: it is only a parameter. Here nil means "empty tree", so the recursion needs no nil checks at the call sites. Java would throw a NullPointerException before the method body ran.
empty.Sum() is a legal call on a nil pointer. Lesson go.interfaces.assertions shows what happens when such a nil pointer is stored in an interface.

use_cases: Pointer receivers for anything with mutable state or a sync.Mutex inside: services, repositories, caches, builders
Value receivers for small immutable values: time.Time-style types, Celsius, Money, IDs
Methods on non-struct types: http.HandlerFunc is a func type with a ServeHTTP method; http.Header is a map type
nil receivers as a cheap default: an empty tree or list that still answers Len and Sum
strengths: Unlike Java or JS, where a method always receives a reference, a value receiver guarantees the method can't change the caller's data; time.Time relies on that
Methods attach to any named type, so a plain function becomes an http.Handler through http.HandlerFunc instead of a wrapper class
A method value binds its receiver: f := c.Inc keeps working when passed around, unlike JS where const f = obj.method loses this
nil receivers are legal, so a nil pointer can be a working empty value instead of needing a null-object class
weaknesses: Call sites look the same for both receiver kinds, so a wrong value receiver is invisible where the method is used
The compiler accepts a value receiver that modifies its copy; only review, tests and go vet's copylocks check (for mutexes) catch it
Mixing receivers is legal: the one-kind-per-type rule is a convention from the FAQ and review guidelines, not a compiler check

pitfalls.title: A value receiver on a struct that holds a sync.Mutex
pitfalls.detail: Each call locks its own copy of the mutex, so nothing is protected. go vet reports "passes lock by value".
pitfalls.bad: func (s Store) Get(k string) string { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); return s.m[k] }
pitfalls.good: func (s *Store) Get(k string) string { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); return s.m[k] }

pitfalls.title: Calling a mutating method on a range copy
pitfalls.detail: for _, c := range items gives copies; c.Inc() changes the copy. Index into the slice, or store pointers.
pitfalls.good: for i := range counters { counters[i].Inc() }

pitfalls.title: fmt ignores a pointer-receiver String on a value
pitfalls.detail: fmt.Println(v) prints the raw struct when String is declared on *T. Pass &v. The same applies to Error methods and errors.

pitfalls.title: Naming the receiver this or self
pitfalls.detail: Go convention is a short name derived from the type, the same in every method: (c *Counter), (t *Tree).

quiz.q: func (c Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }. After var c Counter; c.Inc(); c.Inc(), what is c.n?
quiz.why: A value receiver is a copy; both increments change copies that are discarded.

quiz.q: Inc has a pointer receiver. Which call does not compile?
options: c.Inc() on a local variable c
quiz.why: Go inserts & only for addressable operands, and map elements are not addressable.

quiz.q: Hits has Inc with a pointer receiver and String with a value receiver. var s fmt.Stringer = h; h.Inc(); fmt.Println(s) prints what?
quiz.why: Assigning h to the interface copied it; Inc changed h, not the copy inside s.

quiz.q: type Stack []int needs a Push that appends. Which receivers should Stack's methods use?
options: Pointer for Push, value receivers for the rest
quiz.why: append changes the length, which only a pointer receiver can report back; the FAQ then asks for the same kind on every method.

further_reading.title: Go FAQ: Should I define methods on values or pointers?
Go FAQ: Why do T and *T have different method sets?
Go Code Review Comments: Receiver Type
The Go Programming Language Specification: Method sets
The Go Programming Language Specification: Method values

lessons.body:
## Concept

A method is a function with a receiver: `func (c *Counter) Inc()`. The receiver is a
parameter like any other, so a value receiver (`c Counter`) gets a copy and a pointer
receiver (`c *Counter`) shares the caller's value. Methods can be declared on any named
type defined in the same package: structs, but also slices, maps, functions and numbers
(not pointer or interface types). They can't be added to types from other packages, such
as `int` or `time.Time`.

The method set of `T` holds its value-receiver methods; the method set of `*T` holds
both kinds. Method sets decide which interfaces a type satisfies (the next lesson). At
call sites Go hides the difference: it takes `&c` for you when `c` is addressable, and
dereferences a pointer when the method wants a value.

The working rule is one decision per type, not per method. If any method must mutate the
receiver, or the type holds a mutex, or it is large, every method gets a pointer
receiver. If the type is a small value that never changes in place, every method gets a
value receiver.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/Python/JS: `this` and `self` are always references. Go's value receivers are the
  unusual part, as the Go FAQ itself points out.
- C++: a pointer receiver is like a non-const member function; a value receiver is like a
  member function that receives its own copy of `*this`. There is no `->`: Go takes
  addresses and dereferences at call sites automatically.
- JS: `const f = obj.method; f()` loses `this`. In Go, `f := c.Inc` is a method value
  with the receiver bound; for a value receiver, the receiver is copied at that moment.
- Python: the receiver is an explicit parameter like `self`, but you name it after the
  type (`c`, `t`), never `this` or `self`.

## How it works

    you have                                  value-receiver method   pointer-receiver method
    addressable T (variable, slice element)   x.M()                   (&x).M(), inserted by Go
    non-addressable T (map element, literal)  x.M()                   compile error
    *T                                        (*p).M(), inserted      p.M()
    T assigned to an interface needing M      ok, holds a copy        compile error: use &x

The last row has a reason: an interface holds its own copy of a `T`, and a pointer
method changing that copy would change nothing you can see. The FAQ's example is `io.Copy(buf, os.Stdin)` with a `bytes.Buffer` value,
which would copy into a copy of `buf`.

## Design notes

Decide per type, in this order, which follows the Go FAQ and the Code Review Comments.
A type that mutates, holds a `sync.Mutex`, or is large gets pointer receivers on every
method. Map, channel and func types get value receivers. Small immutable values get
value receivers. When in doubt, use pointers. The standard library's honest exception is
`time.Time`: value receivers everywhere except `UnmarshalJSON`, `UnmarshalText`,
`UnmarshalBinary` and `GobDecode`, which must write into the value. That is the one good
reason to mix. Mixing for convenience brings back the copies example 2 shows, and the
compiler won't point them out.

lessons.title: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly
lessons.summary: A Go type satisfies an interface just by having its methods — no implements declaration. Small interfaces plus value vs pointer receivers shape idiomatic Go APIs.

examples.title: Satisfaction without declaration; receiver rules

annotations.note: Account satisfies Teller just by having a Balance method; nothing says "implements". Teller is declared where it is used and asks for one method, and small interfaces are easy to satisfy.
No implements keyword anywhere: Account converts to Teller, and Celsius prints through its String method, by method set alone.
Meter has a pointer receiver (line 23), so only *Gauge has it in its method set: var m Meter = &g compiles, var m Meter = g would not.

use_cases: Accepting narrow interfaces in functions so callers can pass anything with the right method
io.Reader/io.Writer composition: your types plug into the whole stdlib for free
Testing: a small interface is trivially satisfied by a fake
strengths: Decoupling without ceremony: packages never import each other just to name a shared interface
Interfaces defined at the consumer are as small as that consumer needs
Retrofitting: existing types gain new interface compatibility without edits
weaknesses: No self-documentation: nothing at the type's declaration lists what it satisfies
Method-set rules (value vs pointer receivers) are subtle and fail at compile time far from the cause
Accidental satisfaction: a type can match an interface by coincidence with wrong semantics

pitfalls.title: Storing a value where the pointer satisfies the interface
pitfalls.detail: If methods use pointer receivers, T does not satisfy the interface — only *T does. A slice of values fails to compile where a slice of pointers works.

pitfalls.title: Declaring interfaces next to implementations, Java-style
pitfalls.detail: Go style is to declare the interface where it is USED, with only the methods that call site needs. Big Java-style interfaces force implementers to promise more than anyone relies on.

quiz.q: How does a Go type declare that it implements an interface?
quiz.why: Satisfaction is implicit and structural: the method set is the contract.

quiz.q: type S has a method with a pointer receiver. Which satisfies interface I { m() }?
quiz.why: Pointer-receiver methods belong only to the pointer's method set, so *S satisfies I and S does not.

quiz.q: Where is it idiomatic to declare an interface?
options: In the package that consumes it
quiz.why: Consumer-declared interfaces stay minimal and decouple packages.

further_reading.title: Go blog: The Laws of Reflection (method sets)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go interfaces are satisfied *implicitly*: a type implements an interface when
its method set contains the interface's methods — no `implements` keyword, no
registration. This inverts the usual dependency direction. The interface is
declared by whoever needs it, often with just one or two methods, and any type
that happens to fit can be used without knowing about the interface.

The fine print is method sets: methods with a value receiver belong to both
`T` and `*T`; methods with a pointer receiver belong only to `*T`. So a type
whose methods use pointer receivers satisfies an interface only through its
pointer.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

Java (and C#, TypeScript) demand an up-front `implements` declaration — the
type must import and name its interface, creating a compile-time dependency
from implementation to abstraction. C++ does it with abstract base classes and
the same coupling. Python/JS have structural typing at runtime (duck typing)
but no compiler to check it; Go is "duck typing with a proof": structural like
Python, but verified statically. If you have ever written `class Foo implements
Bar` only to satisfy a linter, Go deletes that line.

## Design notes

The standard library's tiny interfaces (`io.Reader` is one method) only work
because satisfaction is implicit: your type becomes an `io.Reader` the moment
it has a matching `Read`, with zero declarations. Consumer-side declaration
keeps interfaces minimal — an interface with 30 methods where callers use 2 is
a Java habit, not a Go one.

lessons.title: Type assertions, type switches, any, and the nil-interface trap
lessons.summary: An interface value is a (dynamic type, value) pair. Assertions and type switches read the type back out, and an interface holding a nil pointer is not a nil interface.

examples.title: Comma-ok assertions, the panicking form, and type switches

annotations.note: In each single-type case, x has that case's type. Cases are tried in order, so a value that is both an error and a Stringer takes whichever case comes first. fallthrough isn't allowed in a type switch.
case nil matches only an interface with no dynamic type at all. An interface holding a nil pointer skips it, which example 3 shows.
With two types in one case Go can't give x a single static type, so x stays any. Split the case when you need int arithmetic.
Here x is a string. len counts bytes, so the Turkish "ağaç" is 6 bytes but 4 runes: ğ and ç take two bytes each in UTF-8.
Cases can name interfaces, not just concrete types. time.Duration has a String method, so 90s lands in the Stringer case and prints 1m30s.
The one-result form v.(int) panics on a mismatch. The message names both types; any is an alias, so the runtime still spells it interface {}. Use this form only where a mismatch would be a bug.
The comma-ok form never panics: a mismatch gives the zero value and false, the same shape as a map lookup.

examples.title: Asserting to an interface to discover an optional capability

annotations.note: Asserting to an interface type asks whether the dynamic value also has these methods. Signatures must match exactly: http.Flusher's Flush returns nothing, so a ResponseWriter wouldn't match this one.

The standard library downcasts this way itself: io.WriteString checks for io.StringWriter, and io.Copy for WriterTo and ReaderFrom. The parameter stays the narrow io.Writer; the extra method is optional.
Proof that the upgrade ran: the report lines appear after "(... can flush)", because bufio held them until Flush.

examples.title: The trap: a non-nil error holding a nil pointer

annotations.note: Returning verr converts a *ValidationError to error, and the interface records the type even when the pointer is nil. The result is not nil, so every caller's if err != nil fires.

The fix is at the source: declare the result as error and return the literal nil. Functions that return *ValidationError instead recreate the trap as soon as a caller stores the result in an error variable.
fmt makes it worse: %v prints <nil> because fmt catches the panic of Error on a nil receiver, while err == nil is false. %T shows the dynamic type. Calling err.Error() yourself would panic.
Every interface type behaves this way. Only the assertion x.(*int) reveals the nil pointer inside; short of package reflect, there is no operator that asks whether the dynamic value is nil.

use_cases: Walking JSON decoded into any: encoding/json stores float64, string, bool, nil, []any and map[string]any, and a type switch takes them apart
Optional capabilities: io.WriterTo and io.ReaderFrom in io.Copy, http.Flusher behind an http.ResponseWriter
Classifying the value recover() returns: runtime.Error, error, or anything else
Heterogeneous messages or AST nodes where the set of types is open
strengths: Checked at run time, unlike a C cast: a failed assertion returns false or panics with both type names, never reinterprets memory
Type switches give each case a correctly typed variable, much like TypeScript's narrowing, but over real runtime types instead of erased ones
Asserting to an interface lets a function accept the narrow io.Writer and still use extra methods when the value has them
weaknesses: The compiler can't check a type switch for exhaustiveness: interfaces are open, so a new type silently falls to default
Every assertion is a spot where static typing ends; code full of any and switches gets the costs of dynamic typing without its brevity
Wrapper types hide capabilities: a logging ResponseWriter wrapper drops http.Flusher unless it forwards it (http.ResponseController, Go 1.20, finds it through the wrapper's Unwrap method)

pitfalls.title: Returning a typed nil pointer as an error
pitfalls.detail: The interface holds (type *T, value nil) and compares unequal to nil. Return the literal nil on success and declare results as error, never as *MyError.
pitfalls.bad: var e *MyErr; if bad { e = &MyErr{} }; return e
pitfalls.good: if bad { return &MyErr{} }; return nil

pitfalls.title: Type-asserting a wrapped error
pitfalls.detail: err.(*MyErr) only looks at the outermost error. Once someone wraps it with %w, the assertion fails. Use errors.As or errors.AsType (lesson go.errors.is-as-join).

pitfalls.title: The one-result assertion on data you don't control
pitfalls.detail: v.(string) panics on a mismatch, and JSON numbers decoded into any are float64, never int. Use the comma-ok form for input.

pitfalls.title: Comparing interfaces that hold slices or maps
pitfalls.detail: == on two interfaces compares dynamic types and values, and panics with "comparing uncomparable type []int" when both hold the same dynamic type and that type can't be compared.

quiz.q: var x any = "7"; n, ok := x.(int). What happens?
quiz.why: The comma-ok form never panics; on a mismatch it returns the zero value and false.

quiz.q: func f() error { var p *MyErr; return p }. What is f() == nil?
quiz.why: The interface holds the dynamic type *MyErr with a nil value, and an interface is nil only when it has no type.

quiz.q: In switch x := v.(type) { case int, int64: ... }, what is x's type inside that case?
options: The type of v (for example any)
quiz.why: With more than one type in a case, x keeps the type of the switched expression.

quiz.q: Which assertion checks whether a writer can also flush?
quiz.why: Asserting to an interface type tests the dynamic value's method set without naming its concrete type.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type assertions
The Go Programming Language Specification: Type switches
Go FAQ: Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?
Effective Go: Interface conversions and type assertions
The Go Blog: The Laws of Reflection

lessons.body:
## Concept

An interface value holds two things: a dynamic type and a value of that type. A type
assertion `x.(T)` reads them back. If `T` is a concrete type, it asks "is the dynamic
type exactly `T`?"; if `T` is an interface, it asks "does the dynamic value also have
these methods?". The one-result form panics on a mismatch; the comma-ok form `v, ok :=
x.(T)` returns the zero value and `false`. A type switch, `switch x := v.(type)`, runs
the same test against several types in order.

`any` is an alias for `interface{}` (Go 1.18): every type satisfies it, so it carries no
static information at all.

An interface is `nil` only when it has no dynamic type. Store a nil pointer in it and the
interface is no longer nil: it has a type, and the value happens to be a nil pointer.
This is the most common way to return an error that looks like `<nil>` but fails
`err != nil`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `if (o instanceof Foo f)` corresponds to `f, ok := o.(*Foo)`, and pattern-matching
  `switch` to a type switch. A failed one-result assertion panics, like a failed cast
  throws `ClassCastException`.
- C/C++: closer to `dynamic_cast` than to `static_cast`: it's checked, and the comma-ok
  form returns `false` instead of a null pointer. There's no unchecked cast outside
  package `unsafe`.
- TypeScript: `typeof`/`instanceof` narrowing is the same idea, but TS types are erased
  and narrowing is the compiler trusting your check. Go assertions test real runtime
  types, so `as`-style lying isn't possible.
- Python: `isinstance` plus duck typing. Asserting to an interface is the static-typed
  version of `hasattr(w, "flush")`.

## How it works

    statement                           interface holds                    err == nil
    var err error                       (type: none,   value: none)        true
    var p *MyErr; var err error = p     (type: *MyErr, value: nil)         false
    var err error = &MyErr{}            (type: *MyErr, value: an address)  false

The middle row exists on purpose. A nil `*Tree` can have working methods (the previous
lesson's `Sum`), so an interface holding one is a usable value, and Go can't treat it as
"nothing".

## Design notes

Reach for static types first: accept the narrowest interface that works, and use type
parameters (Go 1.18) when the caller knows the concrete type. Keep `any` and type
switches for data that really is heterogeneous: JSON decoded into `any`, values from
`recover()`, messages in a protocol. Asserting to an interface for an optional capability
is idiomatic and widely used in the standard library, so there's no shame in it, but
wrappers hide capabilities they don't forward. For errors, use `errors.As` or
`errors.AsType` instead of assertions, because they see through wrapping. And never
return a concrete pointer type where the caller expects an `error`: return the
interface, and return `nil` literally.

lessons.title: Range over int and range over functions (iter.Seq/Seq2)
lessons.summary: Since Go 1.23, range accepts a function that pushes values into a yield callback. Break and return still mean what they always meant, the iterator must stop when yield returns false, and iter.Pull turns push into pull.

examples.title: A push iterator, early exit, and Seq2 from the standard library

annotations.note: An iter.Seq[int] is only a named func(yield func(int) bool). The iterator owns the loop and its state lives in local variables; the range body becomes yield. The deferred cleanup runs when the iterator returns, whether the sequence ended or the consumer stopped.

The output interleaves iterator and body on one call stack: no goroutine, no buffer. break makes the pending yield call return false, Countdown returns, and its cleanup prints before the next statement after the loop runs.
Seq2 yields pairs. slices.Backward walks from the end and yields the original indexes, without copying or reversing the slice.
maps.Keys yields keys in random order; slices.Sorted collects and sorts them, the usual way to print a map deterministically. Sorting is by bytes, so çay lands after simit.

examples.title: The yield contract, and why return and defer still behave

annotations.note: careless keeps calling yield after the body has finished. It compiles, and it even works for every loop that runs to the end.
The contract: check what yield returns and stop when it is false.
The compiler turns the body into a function, yet return v returns from firstPositive. break, continue, return, goto and labels keep their ordinary meaning.
The defers belong to deferInBody, not to the synthesized yield function: they run after "loop done", last in first out, exactly as in a plain for loop.
The early return makes yield return false, careless calls it again, and the runtime panics. The bug is in the iterator, but it shows up in the first loop that stops early.

examples.title: iter.Pull for consuming two sequences in lockstep

annotations.note: A range loop drives one push iterator. Merging needs "the next value from whichever side is smaller", so both sides must be pulled on demand.
Pull runs the iterator on a separate coroutine and returns next and stop. If you stop pulling before the end, stop lets the iterator return and run its own cleanup; defer stop() is the idiom.
A textbook merge written against next. Merge still returns a push iterator, so its callers simply range over it.
slices.Values turns a slice into a Seq; slices.Collect drains a Seq into a new slice.
next returns a value and ok. After the end it keeps returning the zero value and false, and calling stop then is still allowed.

use_cases: Exposing a collection without exposing its storage: All() iter.Seq2[K, V] on a cache, tree or ordered map
Producing lines, rows or API pages lazily, with early exit and cleanup kept inside the iterator
iter.Pull for lockstep work: merging, zipping or comparing two sequences
for i := range n for plain counted loops (Go 1.22)
strengths: Unlike a Java Iterator with hasNext/next, the iterator is an ordinary loop whose state lives in local variables; a tree walk needs no explicit stack
Push iterators need no generator objects and no goroutines: the loop body runs as an ordinary function call on the same stack
One range syntax covers slices, maps, strings, channels, integers and functions, and the standard library speaks iter.Seq (maps.Keys, slices.Values, strings.Lines)
weaknesses: The yield contract is checked only at run time: an iterator that ignores false compiles and panics later, in someone else's loop
Walking two sequences at once needs iter.Pull, which switches coroutines on every value and needs a stop call
The standard library has no Map, Filter or Take for iter.Seq; you write those adapters yourself (next lesson)
Panics in the loop body show the iterator's frames in the stack trace, which makes traces deeper than for a plain loop

pitfalls.title: Ignoring what yield returns
pitfalls.detail: Every yield call must be checked. A Seq that calls yield after false panics with "range function continued iteration after function for loop body returned false".
pitfalls.good: for _, v := range items { if !yield(v) { return } }

pitfalls.title: Dropping stop from iter.Pull
pitfalls.detail: If you stop calling next before the sequence ends, the iterator stays suspended, holding whatever it opened. Always keep stop and defer it.
pitfalls.good: next, stop := iter.Pull(seq); defer stop()

pitfalls.title: Replacing iterators with goroutines and channels
pitfalls.detail: Before Go 1.23 a lazy sequence was often a goroutine sending on a channel. It is slower, and the goroutine leaks when the consumer stops early. Return an iter.Seq instead.

pitfalls.title: A go line older than 1.23
pitfalls.detail: Range over a function follows the language version in go.mod: with go 1.22 the compiler reports "cannot range over ... requires go1.23 or later".

quiz.q: The body of a range-over-func loop runs break. What does the iterator observe?
options: The pending yield call returns false
Nothing; further values are silently ignored
quiz.why: The iterator must check that result and return; its defers then run as usual.

quiz.q: What does return x do inside the body of a range-over-func loop?
options: Returns from the synthesized yield function only
Returns from the enclosing function, as in any for loop
quiz.why: The compiler preserves the meaning of return, break, continue, goto and defer in the body.

quiz.q: When do you need iter.Pull?
options: To consume two sequences in lockstep, or take values one at a time on demand
quiz.why: range drives one push iterator to completion or break; Pull lets the consumer decide when to ask for the next value.

quiz.q: An iterator keeps calling yield after it returned false. When is that caught?
options: At run time: that yield call panics
Never; the extra values are dropped
quiz.why: The yield function the compiler synthesizes checks its state and panics.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements with range clause

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go 1.22 let `range` count over an integer and gave every iteration fresh variables
(see the control-flow lesson). One detail worth adding: in `for i := range n`, `i`
has the type of `n`, so ranging over a `uint8` gives `uint8` values. Go 1.23 added the
third form: `range` over a function. The function must have one of three shapes:
`func(yield func() bool)`, `func(yield func(V) bool)` or `func(yield func(K, V) bool)`.
Package `iter` names the last two `Seq[V]` and `Seq2[K, V]`.

Such a function is a push iterator. It runs its own loop and calls `yield` once per
element; the compiler turns the loop body into that `yield`. When the body breaks or
returns, `yield` returns false and the iterator must stop. Sometimes the consumer
needs to decide when to take the next value, for example to walk two sequences
together. `iter.Pull` converts a push iterator into a pull pair: `next` to take one
value, `stop` to end early.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: a `Seq` is a generator turned inside out. A Python generator suspends at
  `yield` until someone calls `next()`; a Go iterator calls `yield`, and the loop body
  runs inside that call. `iter.Pull` gives you the `next()` style.
- JS: close to a generator consumed by `for...of`, where `break` calls the iterator's
  `return()`. There is no generator object, though: a `Seq` is a plain function, and
  calling it again usually walks the sequence again.
- Java: `Iterator<T>` is pull, with state in fields between `hasNext()` and `next()`.
  `Iterable.forEach(Consumer)` is push but can't stop early; `yield`'s bool result is
  what Go adds.
- C++: like a visitor callback that returns "keep going". C++23's `std::generator` is
  the coroutine-based pull equivalent.

## How it works

The compiler rewrites `for v := range seq { body }` into roughly
`seq(func(v V) bool { body; return true })`. A `break` becomes `return false`.
Extra bookkeeping makes `return`, labeled `break`, `goto` and `defer` in the body act
on the enclosing function, and makes the synthesized `yield` panic if it is called
again after returning false. No goroutine is involved. `iter.Pull` is different: it
runs the iterator on a coroutine and switches stacks on every `next`, which is why it
costs more and needs `stop`.

## Design notes

Give collection types methods that return `iter.Seq` or `iter.Seq2`, conventionally
named `All`, `Keys`, `Values` or `Backward`, instead of exposing the underlying slice
or map. Callers range over them, or collect with `slices.Collect`. Check every `yield`.
Prefer push; reach for `iter.Pull` only when you consume two sequences at once or
