hand out values on demand, and always `defer stop()`. Code from before Go 1.23 often
used a goroutine and a channel for the same job. Replacing it with an iterator removes
the goroutine leak on early exit and the scheduling cost per element.

lessons.title: Writing your own iterators; helper functions in slices/maps/strings
lessons.summary: strings.Lines, strings.SplitSeq and slices.Values hand out iter.Seq values; small adapters such as Filter, Map and Take compose them into lazy pipelines that stop the producer as soon as the consumer is done.

examples.title: strings.Lines, SplitSeq and FieldsSeq over Turkish text

annotations.note: strings.Lines (Go 1.24) yields every line with its "\n", unlike bufio.Scanner, which strips it. The lines concatenate back to the exact input; trimming is your job when you parse.
TrimSuffix removes the newline Lines kept, and Cut splits once at the first ";". A CRLF file would still leave "\r" at the end of each line.
The Turkish case mapping turns i into İ, so simit prints as SİMİT. strings.ToUpper would give SIMIT.
SplitSeq yields the same pieces as strings.Split but never builds the []string. For three tags that's style; inside a loop over a large export it removes one allocation per line.
FieldsSeq splits on runs of Unicode whitespace, like strings.Fields. slices.Collect turns any Seq into a slice when you do need one.
Lines and SplitSeq are documented as single-use: the second pass over the same value yields nothing, hence 4 and then 0. Call strings.Lines again for a second pass; it's cheap.

examples.title: Filter, Map and Take as generic adapters, composed lazily

annotations.note: An adapter takes a Seq and returns a Seq. Filter's only real duty is the yield check: when downstream stops, it stops pulling from upstream.
Map changes the element type, so it needs two type parameters. This function-over-Seq shape is the one the standard library uses.

Take returns right after the n-th value and never pulls the next one. Its counter lives inside the returned func, so every range starts from zero; decrementing the captured n instead would make the Seq single-use.
The predicate prints a trace. It counts letters with RuneCountInString; len counts bytes, and len("ılık") is 6, so a byte check would let a four-letter word through.

Building the pipeline runs nothing. The range pulls one value at a time through Filter, Map and Take; after the second match, Take's return sends false back up the chain, so ıhlamur and kiraz are never checked.

examples.title: An All() method on your own collection, consumed by maps and slices

annotations.note: A plain unbalanced binary search tree: just enough structure to be worth iterating over.
The convention from package iter: a collection exposes All() returning a Seq2 of key and value. Callers never see nodes or pointers.

In-order traversal is three lines with yield in the middle. The bool result carries "stop" up the recursion, so one false from yield unwinds every level. A Java Iterator for the same walk needs a class with an explicit stack.
Inserting from a map gives a random order and a different tree shape on each run, yet the in-order walk is always sorted, so the output is deterministic.
break after plate 34: walk returns false at every level and no further node is visited.
All returns a standard Seq2, so maps.Collect, maps.Values and slices.Sorted work with no glue code. Byte order puts Iğdır (I) before İstanbul (İ).

use_cases: Parsing text line by line without building a []string: strings.Lines, SplitSeq, FieldsSeq, and the same functions in package bytes
All, Keys, Values or Backward methods on your own collections
Small adapters (Filter, Map, Take) over database rows, file lines or API pages, where stopping early saves real work
slices.Collect, slices.Sorted and maps.Collect at the end of a pipeline when you need a materialized result
strengths: Lazy and early-exiting by construction: Take(..., 2) stops the producer after two matches, which a chain of slice-returning helpers can't do
Everything meets at one type, iter.Seq, so your adapters, your collections and the standard library helpers plug into each other
A tree iterator is a recursive function with yield in the middle, where Java needs an Iterator class with an explicit stack; Python's generators are the closest match
weaknesses: The standard library has no Map, Filter or Take for iter.Seq as of Go 1.27, so every project writes or imports its own
Nested calls read inside out: Take(Map(Filter(src, long), upper), 2) names the last step first
Single-use iterators such as strings.Lines and SplitSeq look like reusable values; a second range silently yields nothing
iter.Seq has no error channel: a sequence that can fail needs a convention, such as yielding (value, error) pairs through a Seq2

pitfalls.title: Forgetting that strings.Lines keeps the line ending
pitfalls.detail: Each line ends in "\n" (except possibly the last), and a Windows file with CRLF endings leaves "\r\n". Trim before comparing or parsing.
pitfalls.good: line = strings.TrimRight(line, "\r\n")

pitfalls.title: Ranging twice over a single-use iterator
pitfalls.detail: strings.Lines, SplitSeq and iterators over readers are single-use. Call the function again for each pass, or collect once with slices.Collect.
pitfalls.bad: lines := strings.Lines(s); n := count(lines); for l := range lines { ... }
pitfalls.good: n := count(strings.Lines(s)); for l := range strings.Lines(s) { ... }

pitfalls.title: Keeping adapter state outside the returned func
pitfalls.detail: Variables declared in the outer function are shared by every range over the Seq. Declare counters and cursors inside the func(yield ...) so each loop starts fresh.

pitfalls.title: Measuring Turkish text with len
pitfalls.detail: len counts bytes: len("ılık") is 6, len("Iğdır") is 7. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for letters, or range over the string.

quiz.q: for line := range strings.Lines("a\nb"): which values does line take?
quiz.why: Lines keeps each terminating newline; the last line has none because the input doesn't end in one.

quiz.q: Take(Map(Filter(src, keep), f), 2) runs over a src with a million elements. How many does src produce?
options: All million, then Take keeps two
Only as many as needed until Take has its two values
quiz.why: Each value travels through the whole chain before the next is read, and Take's false stops src. Exactly two only if the first two both pass the filter.

quiz.q: lines := strings.Lines(text); a := count(lines); b := count(lines). What is b?
options: 0, because Lines returns a single-use iterator
quiz.why: The documentation says single-use; per package iter's convention, calling it again after it finished yields nothing.

quiz.q: Why does the tree's walk method return a bool?
options: So a false from yield stops the whole recursion, not just the current level
quiz.why: Without it, the parent call would carry on to the right subtree and call yield again after false, which panics.

further_reading.title: package iter: naming conventions, single-use iterators

lessons.body:
## Concept

Since Go 1.23 the standard library hands out sequences as `iter.Seq[V]` and
`iter.Seq2[K, V]`: `slices.Values` and `slices.All` over a slice, `maps.Keys` and
`maps.All` over a map, and since Go 1.24 `strings.Lines`, `strings.SplitSeq`,
`strings.FieldsSeq` (and their `bytes` twins) over text. At the other end,
`slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted` and `maps.Collect` turn a sequence back into a slice
or map.

Writing your own takes two forms. A collection gets a method such as `All()` that
returns a Seq built around its internal walk. An adapter is a function that takes a
Seq and returns a new one (`Filter`, `Map`, `Take`). Adapters compose into lazy
pipelines: nothing runs until a `range` pulls, values travel through the whole chain
one at a time, and the first `false` from the consumer stops the producer.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: like `Stream.filter().map().limit()`, lazy and short-circuiting. Go has no
  stream type: adapters are plain functions over `iter.Seq`, and there is no parallel
  mode.
- Python: like `itertools` with generators: `filter`, `map` and `islice` over a
  generator. Go's `Take` is `islice(seq, n)`.
- JS/Node: close to iterator helpers (`.filter().map().take()`) or a Node stream
  pipeline, but synchronous and without backpressure: the consumer's loop drives
  everything.
- C++: C++20 `std::views::filter | transform | take` composes lazily the same way.

## Design notes

Expose iteration through methods that return `iter.Seq` or `iter.Seq2`, named after
what they walk (`All`, `Keys`, `Values`, `Backward`, or a domain name like `Cities`).
Document single-use iterators, as `strings.Lines` does. Inside every iterator and
adapter, check `yield` and keep mutable state inside the returned function. Keep
adapters few and boring; three or four cover most needs, and when the standard library
already has a function (`slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted`, `maps.Collect`), use it at
the end of the pipeline. Go 1.27's generic methods would let you wrap a Seq in your
own type and chain `.Filter(...).Map(...)` left to right, but the standard library
stays with functions over `iter.Seq`, which work with every sequence without
wrapping. For text, remember the Turkish rules from earlier lessons: count letters with
`utf8.RuneCountInString`, and change case with `unicode.TurkishCase`.

lessons.title: pprof: CPU and heap profiling, escape analysis (-gcflags=-m)
lessons.summary: pprof samples where a program spends CPU time and where it allocates, down to the source line; go build -gcflags=-m explains why a value lives on the heap. Profile a benchmark or a running service, fix the top entry, measure again.

examples.title: A CPU profile finds the quadratic loop nobody suspected

annotations.note: One loop, one append: it reads as linear. slices.Contains scans out on every iteration, so it is O(n²), and nothing on the page looks expensive. This is why guessing fails.
format uses fmt and reflection, the usual suspect in a code review. It doesn't appear in the profile at all.

While profiling is on, the runtime records the running goroutine's stack 100 times per second of CPU time. Overhead is low enough for production, but it is a sample: a 200 ms run gives about 20 stacks.

-top lists functions; -cum sorts by cumulative time (the function plus everything it calls) instead of flat time (the function's own instructions). cum finds the expensive path, flat the instructions burning the time.
The table is real pprof output; only the header (binary path, date, sample count) is cut. Timings differ on every run, which is why this example is checked with "contains".

examples.title: A heap profile names the function and the line that allocate

annotations.note: By default the runtime records one allocation per 512 KiB allocated, on average, and pprof scales the samples up. Rate 1 records every allocation so the numbers are exact and repeatable; it is far too slow for production.
2,000 concatenations, each copying everything so far: about 20 MB allocated to build a 20 KB string. The CSV parsing that looks busier allocates less than 0.1 MB.
A heap profile reports as of the last completed GC, so collect first. go test -memprofile does the same before writing its profile.

alloc_space counts every byte allocated since start; the default, inuse_space, counts only what is still live, which here is almost nothing. Use alloc_* to find churn that keeps the GC busy, inuse_* to find memory that is retained or leaking.
-list takes a regular expression and prints the source of matching functions with per-line totals: the profile points at line 29, not just at render.

examples.title: go build -gcflags=-m: the compiler's heap decisions, one per function

annotations.note: "moved to heap: p": the address is returned, so p must outlive the call. One allocation per NewPoint, which is fine unless NewPoint is in a hot loop.
"&Point{...} does not escape": taking an address costs nothing when the pointer never leaves the function; the struct stays on the stack.
The slice is returned, so its backing array must be on the heap.

"does not escape" is not "never allocates". The size is known only at run time; since Go 1.25 the compiler keeps a small buffer on the stack and falls back to the heap when n doesn't fit (in an AllocsPerRun test on Go 1.27, 32 bytes fit and 33 did not).
Nothing escapes, yet buf is moved to the heap: a 1 MiB variable is too large for a goroutine stack frame.
fmt.Sprint takes ...any, so p.X is converted to an interface and "escapes". The variadic slice itself stays on the stack ("... argument does not escape").
-gcflags=-m applies to the packages named on the command line; -m=2 explains each decision, and -gcflags=all=-m includes every dependency. The example filters out the "can inline" lines.
Positions are file:line:column in esc.go, whose first line is line 12 of this file: esc.go:8:2 is the p := Point{x, y} on line 19 here.

use_cases: A slow benchmark: go test -bench=Name -cpuprofile cpu.out, then go tool pprof -top or -http=:8081 cpu.out
A service using too much CPU or memory: import net/http/pprof on a localhost-only listener and pull a 30-second profile
GC pressure: a heap profile with -sample_index=alloc_space, then -gcflags=-m on the hot package to see why values escape
Goroutine leaks: the goroutine profile, and since Go 1.27 the goroutineleak profile
Profile-guided optimization: commit a representative CPU profile as default.pgo next to main
strengths: Built into the runtime and the go command: no agent, no separate profiler install, unlike Java's async-profiler or JFR setup
Sampling keeps CPU profiling overhead low enough to run in production, unlike Python's instrumenting cProfile
Profiles carry symbols and inlining information, so -list maps samples to source lines, inlined calls included
Escape decisions are printable on demand, where the JVM's escape analysis happens invisibly in the JIT
weaknesses: A profile is a statistical sample: short runs and rare paths can be missing or noisy
Heap profiles show where memory was allocated, not who holds it now; finding a retention path needs reasoning or a heap dump
-gcflags=-m output changes between Go versions, so don't build tooling that parses it
The CPU profile shows on-CPU time; time spent waiting for locks, I/O or the database needs the block, mutex or trace views

pitfalls.title: Optimizing without a profile
pitfalls.detail: The expensive code is often the innocent-looking loop, not the reflection-heavy formatter. Profile a benchmark or production first, fix the top entry, and measure again.

pitfalls.title: Exposing net/http/pprof on the public listener
pitfalls.detail: The blank import registers /debug/pprof/ on http.DefaultServeMux. Serve that mux on 127.0.0.1 only, separately from the application's own mux.
pitfalls.bad: import _ "net/http/pprof" // and the public server uses DefaultServeMux
pitfalls.good: go func() { log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", nil)) }() // app uses its own mux

pitfalls.title: Reading inuse_space when hunting garbage
pitfalls.detail: The default heap view shows live memory. Short-lived garbage that drives GC cost appears only under alloc_space or alloc_objects.

pitfalls.title: Taking 'does not escape' as 'no allocation'
pitfalls.detail: Variable-size make and very large locals can still use the heap. Confirm with testing.AllocsPerRun or -benchmem.

pitfalls.title: Profiling with the race detector or coverage on
pitfalls.detail: -race and -cover change the code being measured. Profile a normal build.

quiz.q: In pprof -top, main.handle has flat 0 and cum 95%. What does that mean?
options: It does almost no work itself; functions it calls account for 95% of the samples
quiz.why: flat counts samples where the function was executing its own code; cum counts samples where it was anywhere on the stack.

quiz.q: You want the code that creates the most short-lived garbage. Which heap view?
quiz.why: inuse_* shows what is still live; garbage has already been collected and appears only in the alloc_* totals.

quiz.q: -gcflags=-m prints 'make([]byte, n) does not escape'. Can that line still allocate on the heap?
options: Yes: with a size known only at run time, a large n falls back to the heap
quiz.why: 'Does not escape' means the slice doesn't outlive the function. Since Go 1.25 a small stack buffer covers small sizes; larger ones are heap allocated. Large fixed-size locals are moved to the heap too.

quiz.q: How should a production service expose pprof?
options: Register net/http/pprof on the public mux behind a feature flag
Serve http.DefaultServeMux with the pprof handlers on a localhost-only listener
Write a CPU profile to disk continuously
quiz.why: Profiles reveal internals and a CPU profile request costs CPU for its duration; keep the endpoint off the public listener and reach it through SSH or kubectl port-forward.

further_reading.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector: optimization guide

lessons.body:
## Concept

pprof is Go's built-in profiler, in three parts: the runtime collects samples,
`runtime/pprof`, `net/http/pprof` and `go test` write them as profile files, and
`go tool pprof` reads and presents them. The profiles you will use most:

- **cpu**: where on-CPU time goes, sampled 100 times per second.
- **heap**: allocations by call stack, viewable as `inuse_space`/`inuse_objects`
  (live now) or `alloc_space`/`alloc_objects` (since start).
- **goroutine**, **block**, **mutex**: what goroutines are doing and where they wait.
  Go 1.27 adds **goroutineleak**, goroutines blocked on something no runnable
  goroutine can ever reach.

The workflow is a loop: reproduce the load (a benchmark, or a real service under
traffic), collect a profile, read the top entries, change one thing, measure again.
A benchmark run from the scratch module behind the first example, on the author's
machine:

```
$ go test -bench=Dedupe -benchmem -cpuprofile cpu.out
BenchmarkDedupe-32   625   1860894 ns/op   60032 B/op   14 allocs/op
$ go tool pprof -list Dedupe cpu.out
ROUTINE ======================== example.com/report.Dedupe in .../report.go
         0      1.11s (flat, cum) 97.37% of Total
         .          .      5:func Dedupe(ids []int) []int {
         .          .      6:	var out []int
         .          .      7:	for _, id := range ids {
         .      1.11s      8:		if !slices.Contains(out, id) {
         .          .      9:			out = append(out, id)
```

Replacing the scan with a `map[int]struct{}` set brought it to 87524 ns/op, 21 times
faster, at 207802 B/op and 31 allocs/op: CPU and memory profiles can pull in
opposite directions, so measure both. `go tool pprof -http=:8081 cpu.out` opens the
same data in a browser, with a flame graph as the default view since Go 1.26.

When a heap profile points at a line, `go build -gcflags=-m` tells you why the value
there lives on the heap: it escapes (returned, stored, captured, converted to an
interface) or is too large for the stack.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: JFR and async-profiler give similar sampled CPU and allocation views; in
  Go there is nothing to attach, the profiler is in every binary. The JVM's escape
  analysis is a JIT detail you can't easily see; Go prints its decisions at compile
  time.
- **Python**: `cProfile` instruments every call and distorts timings; pprof samples,
  like py-spy. Python has no stack allocation to reason about at all.
- **JS/Node**: Chrome DevTools and `node --cpu-prof` are sampling CPU profilers too.
  V8 heap snapshots show the object graph; Go's heap profile shows allocation sites
  instead, which is better for finding churn and worse for finding who retains what.
- **C/C++**: `perf` works on Go binaries, but pprof understands goroutines, inlined
  frames and Go symbol names without extra setup. There is no `new` vs stack choice:
  escape analysis makes it for you.

## How it works

For CPU profiles the runtime interrupts threads running Go code at 100 Hz and
records the current goroutine's stack; pprof merges identical stacks and counts
them. **flat** is the samples where a function was at the top of the stack, **cum**
those where it appeared anywhere. Inlined calls are kept as separate frames marked
`(inline)`, which is why `slices.Index` shows up with all the flat time although it
was compiled into `dedupe`.

For heap profiles, `mallocgc` records a stack for one allocation per
`runtime.MemProfileRate` bytes (512 KiB by default) and pprof scales the counts
back up. Profiles are only updated at the end of a GC cycle, so a profile can lag
the program by up to two cycles; collecting first gives a current one.

To profile a service, the blank import registers handlers on
`http.DefaultServeMux`. If the application serves its own mux, as StackLab's does,
serve the default mux on a separate localhost listener:

```go
import _ "net/http/pprof"

go func() { log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", nil)) }()
```

```
go tool pprof http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/heap
```

## Design notes

Keep the profile loop cheap and routine. Benchmarks with `b.Loop` and `-benchmem`
make the CPU and allocation cost of hot functions visible in review; `pprof` explains
the numbers; `-gcflags=-m` explains the allocations. Fix the top entry, not the one
you expected, and keep the benchmark so the fix stays fixed.

A CPU profile from production is also a build input. Saved as `default.pgo` in the
main package's directory, it is picked up by `go build` (the default `-pgo=auto`),
which then inlines and devirtualizes more aggressively along the hot paths; the
Go 1.22 notes report 2 to 14% gains for most programs. The profile must come from
representative load, and it is worth refreshing when the code changes a lot.

lessons.title: Reducing allocations; sync.Pool (and when not to use it); the Green Tea GC
lessons.summary: Every heap allocation costs once in malloc and again in GC work, and the collector runs more often the faster you allocate. Count allocations with AllocsPerRun or -benchmem, fix the hot sites with capacity and reuse, use sync.Pool only for churned buffers, and know what Green Tea changed.

examples.title: Count allocations per operation, then remove them

annotations.note: testing.AllocsPerRun runs f, then reports the average number of heap allocations per call, as a whole number. It pins GOMAXPROCS to 1 while measuring, and the counts are stable for a given program and Go version, which makes them good test assertions: a test can fail when a hot path starts allocating.
Eight ids, eight allocations: every += builds a new string holding everything so far, and the previous one becomes garbage. For long loops the copying is quadratic as well.
strings.Builder grows by doubling: 4 allocations here. Grow with a good estimate makes it one, and strings.Join computes the exact size itself.
The same doubling for slices: append without capacity allocates at 1, 2, 4 and 8 elements. When the final length is known, make([]T, 0, n) allocates once.

Two allocations: the result string, and 1234 boxed into an interface for the ...any parameter. Values 0 to 255 are boxed for free (the runtime keeps a static table), which is why small numbers can make this look cheaper in a test than in production.
The strconv.Append* family writes into a caller-owned buffer. Reusing buf[:0] keeps the capacity, so steady state is zero allocations: the pattern behind fast loggers and encoders.
m[string(key)] with a []byte key doesn't allocate: the compiler recognizes the conversion inside a map index. s := string(key) followed by m[s] does allocate when s escapes.

examples.title: sync.Pool for buffers: Reset, cap the size, store pointers

annotations.note: New runs when the pool is empty. A pool holds any, so it is usually a package-level variable with one concrete type inside, recovered by a type assertion on Get.
Get may return an object some other request used. Forgetting Reset appends to the previous request's data, which in a server means leaking one user's output into another's response.
A pool should hold objects of similar cost. One huge request would otherwise park a huge buffer in the pool for good; fmt drops buffers over 64 KiB for exactly this reason (Go issue 23199).

Four allocations without the pool (the buffer doubling from 64 bytes, plus the result string), one with it: only the String() copy is left. A real saving only when this runs thousands of times a second.
Put takes any. A slice header is three words, not a pointer, so storing it in an interface allocates on every Put, which defeats the pool. staticcheck reports this as SA6002.
Pool a pointer to the slice instead (or a *bytes.Buffer): pointers fit in an interface without allocating.

examples.title: Allocation drives GC frequency; GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT set the pace

annotations.note: 64 MiB of short-lived garbage, never more than 4 KiB alive. Live heap stays tiny, yet the collector must run repeatedly, because the pacer triggers on growth since the last cycle, not on total memory.
NumGC counts completed cycles. Only booleans and zeros are printed: the exact number depends on heap sizes and timing, the fact that it is above zero does not.
The same work without allocating: no cycles at all. This is the real payoff of reducing allocations; the cheaper malloc is a bonus.
debug.SetGCPercent(-1) is GOGC=off. With no memory limit either, the heap just grows, which is fine for a short batch job and fatal for a server.
SetMemoryLimit (GOMEMLIMIT, Go 1.19) is a soft limit: as the heap approaches it, the GC runs regardless of GOGC. Containers commonly set it a little below the memory limit, with GOGC at its default.

use_cases: Hot request paths: build responses with strings.Builder or append-style APIs and a known capacity
Encoders, loggers, template renderers: pooled *bytes.Buffer with Reset and a size cap
Regression tests: assert testing.AllocsPerRun(100, f) == 0 on a zero-allocation fast path
Containers: GOMEMLIMIT 5-10% under the container limit, so the GC works harder before the OOM killer acts
strengths: Allocation counts are deterministic for a given program and Go version, so they can be asserted in tests; Java's TLAB allocation is cheap too, but per-call counts aren't a standard test assertion there
Escape analysis keeps many values on the stack automatically; there is no new vs stack choice to make as in C++
Two knobs, GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT, instead of the JVM's collector choice plus dozens of -XX flags
Green Tea arrived as a default with no code change: the same binary, rebuilt with Go 1.26 or later, spends less time marking
weaknesses: No manual memory management: the GC is the only way memory comes back (the arena package exists only behind GOEXPERIMENT=arenas)
Allocation sites are invisible in source; you need -gcflags=-m or a profile to see what escapes
sync.Pool gives no retention guarantee: anything in it may be dropped at any GC
Interfaces box values: an any parameter can allocate where a concrete type would not

pitfalls.title: Pooling everything
pitfalls.detail: Small structs allocate in tens of nanoseconds; Get/Put, the type assertion and Reset can cost as much. Pool objects that are large or expensive to build and churned across many goroutines, and keep the pool only if a benchmark shows the gain.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting Reset on a pooled object
pitfalls.detail: A pooled buffer still holds the previous user's bytes. Reset immediately after Get, not before Put, so a path that forgets Put can't leak data.
pitfalls.good:
b := pool.Get().(*bytes.Buffer)
b.Reset()
b.WriteString(user)

pitfalls.title: Putting non-pointer values in a Pool
pitfalls.detail: Put([]byte) allocates a box for the slice header on every call. Pool *[]byte or *bytes.Buffer.
pitfalls.good: pool.Put(&buf) // pool of *[]byte

pitfalls.title: Returning a pooled object to the caller
pitfalls.detail: Once Put runs, another goroutine may get and overwrite the object. Return a copy (b.String(), bytes.Clone) and Put the original.

pitfalls.title: Optimizing without a measurement
pitfalls.detail: A heap profile (alloc_space or alloc_objects) and -benchmem show where allocations happen. Code that runs once per request rarely matters next to the database round trip.

quiz.q: What does testing.AllocsPerRun(1000, f) return?
options: The average number of heap allocations per call, as a whole number
quiz.why: It reads runtime.MemStats.Mallocs before and after, divides by the run count with integer division, and pins GOMAXPROCS to 1 while measuring.

quiz.q: A pool is declared as sync.Pool{New: func() any { return make([]byte, 0, 512) }}. What is wrong?
options: Put with a []byte allocates, because a slice header is boxed into an interface
Slices can't be stored in a Pool
quiz.why: Only pointer-shaped values fit in an interface without allocating; pool *[]byte instead (staticcheck SA6002).

quiz.q: A program allocates 64 MiB of short-lived garbage while keeping 4 KiB alive. With default settings, does the GC run?
options: No, the live heap is tiny
Yes, repeatedly: the next cycle starts when the heap grows by GOGC percent over the last live heap
Only when the OS runs low on memory
quiz.why: The pacer's trigger is growth since the last collection. Allocation rate, not live size, decides how often it runs.

quiz.q: Which statement about Green Tea is correct for Go 1.27?
options: It must be enabled with GOEXPERIMENT=greenteagc
It is the default collector since Go 1.26 and changes how marking scans small objects; programs need no changes
It replaces GOGC with a new tuning variable
quiz.why: Go 1.25 shipped it as an experiment, Go 1.26 made it the default. GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT work as before.

further_reading.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector
The Green Tea Garbage Collector (Go blog)
Go 1.26 Release Notes: Green Tea garbage collector

lessons.body:
## Concept

A heap allocation costs twice: once in `mallocgc`, which is fast, and again in the
garbage collector, which has to mark what is live and sweep what isn't. The second
cost depends on *how often* the collector runs, and that depends on allocation rate:
with the default `GOGC=100`, a new cycle starts when the heap has grown by roughly
100% over what was live after the previous one (the GC guide has the exact formula).
Fewer allocations mean fewer cycles.

The workflow is measure, locate, fix:

1. **Measure**: `go test -bench . -benchmem` (or `b.ReportAllocs()`) reports
   allocations per operation; `testing.AllocsPerRun` does the same in a plain test.
2. **Locate**: a heap profile with `-sample_index=alloc_space` or `alloc_objects`
   ranks allocation sites; `go build -gcflags=-m` explains why a value escapes.
3. **Fix** with a few standard moves: give slices and builders their capacity up
   front, append into reused buffers (`buf[:0]`, `strconv.AppendInt`), keep hot paths
   free of `any` parameters, and stop returning pointers to small values that could
   be returned by value.

`sync.Pool` is the last of these tools, not the first. It keeps a per-processor set of
reusable objects that the runtime may drop at any GC. It pays off for buffers and
encoders that many goroutines create and discard at a high rate: `fmt` uses one for
its printers.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++**: no `free`, no arenas in the standard library, no custom allocators.
  The equivalent of "allocate less" is the same; the equivalent of a free list is
  `sync.Pool`, which the GC may empty.
- **Java**: generational collectors make short-lived garbage almost free. Go's
  collector is not generational and doesn't move objects, so short-lived garbage still
  costs mark and sweep work; escape analysis (which Java also has) and reuse matter
  more. Tuning is `GOGC` and `GOMEMLIMIT`, not a collector zoo and `-XX` flags.
- **Python/JS**: reference counting (CPython) or a generational GC (V8) with no
  control over layout. Go gives you value types, slices with capacity and stack
  allocation, so you can often avoid the allocation instead of hoping the collector
  is fast.

## How it works

Go's collector is concurrent, non-moving mark-and-sweep. The **pacer** decides when to
start a cycle from `GOGC` and the memory limit, and mutator goroutines help with
marking when they allocate quickly ("assists"), which is how allocation-heavy code
pays for GC in its own latency. `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` prints one line per cycle; from
the third example on the author's machine:

```
gc 1 @0.066s 0%: 0+1.1+0 ms clock, 0+0.59/2.3/0+0 ms cpu, 3->4->1 MB, 4 MB goal, 0 MB stacks, 0 MB globals, 32 P
```

The `3->4->1 MB, 4 MB goal` part reads: heap at start, heap at end, live heap after
marking, and the target that triggered the cycle.

**Green Tea** changes the mark phase. The classic collector follows pointers object by
object, jumping around memory. Green Tea tracks *pages* of small objects instead: the
work list is a queue of pages, and scanning a page handles every marked object on it
in one pass, which uses CPU caches better and contends less across cores. It shipped
as an experiment in Go 1.25 (`GOEXPERIMENT=greenteagc`) and became the default in
Go 1.26, where the release notes expect a 10 to 40% reduction in GC overhead for
GC-heavy programs, and about 10% more on amd64 CPUs from Intel Ice Lake or AMD Zen 4
on, which get vector instructions for scanning. Some workloads gain little, and
some (one object per page to scan at a time) can be slower.

The opt-out is a build-time flag, and the binary records it. The Go 1.26 notes say
the opt-out "is expected to be removed in Go 1.27"; the 1.27 notes don't mention it,
and the Go 1.27.0 toolchain still accepts it:

```
$ GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc go build -o app .
$ go version -m app
app: go1.27.0-X:nogreenteagc
	...
	build	GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc
```

Go 1.27 also made small allocations cheaper on the malloc side: the compiler now calls
size-specialized allocation routines, up to 30% faster for some objects under 80
bytes (opt-out `GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc`).

## Design notes

Neither Green Tea nor faster malloc changes the advice. They lower the price of each
allocation and each cycle; avoiding the allocation still removes both. Start with
the profile, fix the top few sites with capacity and reuse, and assert the result
with `AllocsPerRun` in a test so it stays fixed.

Treat `sync.Pool` as an optimization with a maintenance cost: every pooled type needs
Reset discipline, a size cap and a benchmark that justifies it. In a container that
runs only your program, set `GOMEMLIMIT` 5 to 10% below the container's memory limit
(the GC guide's rule of thumb, leaving room for memory the runtime doesn't track) and
leave `GOGC` at its default. `GOGC=off` with only a limit lets the heap run up to the
limit and then collect hard; the guide advises against it when the memory is shared
with other programs.

lessons.title: Cross-compilation and the single binary: GOOS/GOARCH, CGO_ENABLED=0, ldflags
lessons.summary: Any Go toolchain builds for any supported OS and CPU: set GOOS and GOARCH. With CGO_ENABLED=0 the result is one self-contained file per target. Stamp versions with -ldflags -X, or since Go 1.24 let go build take them from your Git tags.

examples.title: GOOS decides which files are compiled: suffixes and //go:build

annotations.note: StackLab's gorun package has this shape: proc_unix.go uses process groups, proc_windows.go a Job Object. Each target compiles exactly one of them, and both must keep building, which is why CLAUDE.md asks for go vet with GOOS=linux as well as on Windows.
A file name ending in _GOOS, _GOARCH or _GOOS_GOARCH (before .go and an optional _test) carries an implicit build constraint. No comment needed.

unix is a build tag (Go 1.19), not a GOOS, so the _unix suffix means nothing: without this line proc_unix.go would be compiled on Windows too. StackLab's file says //go:build !windows instead, which also admits plan9 and wasm targets where its Unix syscalls don't exist.
GOOS, GOARCH and CGO_ENABLED are ordinary environment variables for one command. go list doesn't compile anything, so asking about four targets takes a moment.
plan9 matches neither file, so killTree would be undefined there. go list shows it before a release build fails on it; go tool dist list prints every supported target (47 in Go 1.27).

examples.title: Four targets from one machine, with a version stamped in by the linker

annotations.note: -X works only on a package-level string variable that is uninitialized or initialized to a constant string. A const, or a var initialized by a function call, is silently left alone.

-s drops the symbol table and, since Go 1.22, implies -w (no DWARF debug info), so "-s -w" is now redundant. Smaller files; stack traces still have function names and lines, which come from a separate table.

No cross toolchain, no sysroot: the Go compiler and linker target every port. CGO_ENABLED=0 keeps it that way and makes Linux binaries fully static. -trimpath removes local file system paths, so the binary doesn't reveal the build machine's directories.

debug/buildinfo reads the record that go version -m prints, from an ELF, PE or Mach-O file alike. With -trimpath the -ldflags setting is left out on purpose (Go issue 52372), since linker flags can contain local paths; without -trimpath it is recorded.
Only the build for this machine can run here. Name Windows outputs with .exe yourself: -o uses the name exactly as given.

examples.title: Since Go 1.24, go build takes the version from Git

annotations.note: The program reads its own version at run time. Main.Version used to be (devel) for every local build, which is why -X main.version was the standard trick.
A clean checkout of a tagged commit: the tag becomes the main module's version, exactly what go install example.com/app@v1.4.2 would record.
Uncommitted changes add +dirty, so a binary built from a modified tree can't pass for the release.

A commit after the tag gets a pseudo-version: the next patch number, the commit time and the first 12 characters of the commit hash (masked here). -buildvcs=false turns stamping off, and without a repository (a Docker build that copies only the source) there is nothing to stamp: Main.Version is (devel) again.

An untracked file counts as a modification, so a binary written into the repository would make the next build +dirty. Release builds write to a dist/ directory listed in .gitignore, or outside the checkout.

The demo pins git's identity and clock and ignores your git configuration (no signing, no line-ending conversion), so the history and the pseudo-version's timestamp are the same on every run. go build itself calls git to read the revision, so it gets the same environment.

use_cases: Release matrix: linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 for servers, darwin/arm64 for Macs, windows/amd64 for Windows users, all from one CI job
Container images: CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath, copied into a scratch or distroless image
Developing on Windows, deploying to Linux: GOOS=linux go vet ./... and go build catch Unix-only code before CI does
Version reporting: debug.ReadBuildInfo() in a --version flag or a /version endpoint; go version -m on a binary in the field
strengths: Cross-compiling is two environment variables, unlike C/C++ cross toolchains and sysroots or Rust's per-target linker setup
With CGO_ENABLED=0 the output is one file with no runtime to install, unlike Java (a JVM), Python (an interpreter and site-packages) or Node (node_modules)
Build metadata (Go version, dependencies with checksums, VCS revision, build flags) is embedded in every binary and readable without running it
go:embed puts templates, migrations and static assets in the same file, so deployment is a copy
weaknesses: cgo breaks the easy path: cross-compiling with cgo needs a C cross compiler and the target's libc
Binaries are larger than C equivalents (a hello world is about 1.5 MB stripped) because the runtime and GC are linked in
Build constraints are checked per target: code for a target you never build can rot unnoticed
-X takes strings only and fails silently on a typo in the import path or variable name

pitfalls.title: Expecting _unix.go to be Unix-only
pitfalls.detail: unix is a build tag, not a GOOS, so the suffix is ignored. Add a //go:build unix line (or a GOOS-specific suffix such as _linux).
pitfalls.good: //go:build unix

pitfalls.title: go env -w GOOS=linux on a development machine
pitfalls.detail: go env -w writes to the user's Go environment file, so every later build, test and run cross-compiles. Set GOOS for one command instead.
pitfalls.good: PowerShell: $env:GOOS='linux'; go build ...; Remove-Item Env:GOOS (bash: GOOS=linux go build ...)

pitfalls.title: A dynamically linked binary in a scratch image
pitfalls.detail: With cgo enabled (the default where a C compiler exists, as in the golang image), a program that imports net or os/user links against libc and fails to start in FROM scratch with a confusing 'no such file or directory'. Build with CGO_ENABLED=0.

pitfalls.title: -X on a variable that isn't a plain string
pitfalls.detail: -X ignores constants and variables initialized by function calls, without an error. Use var version = "dev" and check the result with go version -m or a --version flag.
pitfalls.good: var version = "dev"

quiz.q: On Windows, what do you need to build a linux/arm64 binary of a pure-Go program?
options: WSL and a Linux Go toolchain
Only GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 for the go build command
quiz.why: The Go toolchain targets every port itself. Cgo is disabled by default when cross-compiling; a C cross compiler is needed only if you turn it back on.

quiz.q: gorun/proc_unix.go has no //go:build line. When is it compiled?
options: On every target, because unix is not a GOOS value and the suffix is ignored
quiz.why: Only _GOOS, _GOARCH and _GOOS_GOARCH suffixes are implicit constraints. unix exists as a build tag since Go 1.19, so write //go:build unix.

quiz.q: go build -ldflags='-X main.version=v1.4.2' runs, but the program still prints dev. Which declaration explains it?
quiz.why: -X sets string variables that are uninitialized or initialized to a constant string; it can't change a constant, and it doesn't report that.

quiz.q: With Go 1.27, a clean checkout of the commit tagged v1.4.2 is built with plain go build. What is debug.ReadBuildInfo().Main.Version?
quiz.why: Since Go 1.24 go build sets the main module version from VCS tags; a later commit gets a pseudo-version and uncommitted changes add +dirty.

further_reading.title: Go 1.24 Release Notes (version from VCS tags)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every Go toolchain contains a compiler and linker for every supported target. Pick
one with two environment variables:

```
GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s" -o dist/stacklab-linux-arm64 ./cmd/stacklab
```

In PowerShell, which is what this machine runs, set them for the session and remove
them afterwards:

```
$env:GOOS = "linux"; $env:GOARCH = "arm64"; $env:CGO_ENABLED = "0"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s" -o dist/stacklab-linux-arm64 ./cmd/stacklab
Remove-Item Env:GOOS, Env:GOARCH, Env:CGO_ENABLED
```

The pieces:

- **GOOS/GOARCH** select the target; `go tool dist list` prints all of them. The
  same variables pick files: `_linux.go`, `_windows_amd64.go` and `//go:build` lines.
- **CGO_ENABLED=0** keeps C out of the build. Cgo is off by default when
  cross-compiling or when no C compiler is on the PATH (this Windows machine builds
  with `CGO_ENABLED=0` for that reason), and on by default for native builds where
  one exists. Pure-Go builds for Linux are fully static.
- **-trimpath** removes your directories from the binary; **-ldflags="-s"** drops the
  symbol table and DWARF.
- **Version stamps**: `-ldflags="-X main.version=v1.4.2"` sets a string variable at
  link time. Since Go 1.24, `go build` in a Git checkout records the tag (or a
  pseudo-version, with `+dirty` for uncommitted changes) as the main module's version,
  next to the `vcs.revision`, `vcs.time` and `vcs.modified` settings it has recorded
  since Go 1.18. `go version -m ./app` prints all of it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++**: no cross toolchain, sysroot or static glibc to fight, as long as cgo is
  off. Turning cgo on brings all of that back.
- **Java**: the JAR is portable and the JVM is not. A Go binary is the native-image
  end of that trade: one file per OS and CPU, no runtime to install, start-up in
  milliseconds.
- **Python/Node**: PyInstaller and Node's single executable applications bundle an
  interpreter with your code. Go's output is compiled code plus a small runtime, and
  the dependency tree is linked in, not shipped beside it.
- **JS bundlers**: `-trimpath` and `-s` are Go's equivalent of a production build;
  there is no separate minify step, and dead code is removed by the linker.

## Design notes

StackLab's `server/Dockerfile` builds with `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath` and
copies the result into a distroless static image; the migrations travel inside the
binary via `go:embed`, so the image needs no volume for them. On the owner's Windows
machine the same code builds natively, and `proc_unix.go`/`proc_windows.go` keep the
one OS-specific piece behind build constraints.

For release versions, prefer the Go 1.24 VCS stamp when you build from a tagged
checkout: it can't drift from the tag, and `+dirty` exposes local builds. Keep
`-X` for what Git doesn't know, such as a CI build number, and for builds without a
repository: a Docker build that copies only the source tree has no `.git`, so
Main.Version falls back to `(devel)`. Either way, expose the result (a `--version`
flag, a `/version` endpoint, a startup log line) so that "which build is running?"
has an answer.

Build for every target you ship on every change, even if you test on one: a
`GOOS=linux go vet ./...` step on a Windows machine, or a CI matrix, catches the
file that only compiles on one side.

lessons.title: Multi-stage Docker builds, govulncheck, a release checklist
lessons.summary: Build in a golang stage, ship only the static binary in a scratch or distroless stage, and the image holds little more than your code. govulncheck reports the known vulnerabilities your code actually reaches, and -trimpath makes the binary the same wherever it is built.

examples.title: What the build stage produces: a Linux binary with nothing to load

annotations.note: With cgo enabled, the default in the golang image because it ships a C compiler, a program importing net is linked against the system libc. That binary then fails in FROM scratch with "no such file or directory": the missing file is the dynamic loader, not your binary.
Inside a container, listen on all interfaces (":8080"); restricting access is the job of the port mapping, such as 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 in Compose, which is how StackLab publishes its ports.
The command a Dockerfile's build stage runs. CGO_ENABLED=0 selects Go's own DNS resolver and user lookup, so nothing from libc is needed; -trimpath and -s keep paths and symbols out of the image.
A dynamically linked ELF has a PT_INTERP header naming its loader (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 on amd64 glibc systems) and a list of needed shared libraries. This one has neither.
"Can run" is about loading. A scratch image still lacks CA certificates, the time zone database and /etc/passwd; distroless static has all three, which is why StackLab uses it.

examples.title: -trimpath makes two checkouts build the same bytes

annotations.note: Same source, same Go version, same flags; only the directory differs, as it does between a laptop and a CI runner.
Without -trimpath, absolute source paths are compiled into the binary (for stack traces and debug info), so the hashes differ and the binary tells anyone who reads it where you keep your code.

With -trimpath the paths become module paths and the two builds are byte-for-byte identical. Anyone can rebuild a tagged release and compare checksums; the Go project verifies its own toolchain releases this way.
Reproducibility also needs the same toolchain and flags: pin the Go version (the go and toolchain lines in go.mod, the image tag or digest) and keep the build command in one script.

use_cases: Service images: a golang build stage, a distroless/static or scratch final stage, a non-root USER
CI gate: govulncheck ./... fails the build when reachable code calls a vulnerable function
Auditing a binary you didn't build: govulncheck -mode=binary ./app and go version -m ./app
Verifiable releases: -trimpath builds from a tag, with published SHA-256 checksums anyone can reproduce
strengths: A static Go binary makes the final image tiny and nearly empty: no shell, no package manager, no interpreter for an attacker to use, unlike a JRE or Node base image
govulncheck reports only vulnerabilities in functions your code can reach, where npm audit, pip-audit and most dependency scanners report every vulnerable version in the tree
Standard-library vulnerabilities are part of the report and are fixed by a Go upgrade, because the binary records which Go built it
Since Go 1.25 the runtime sets GOMAXPROCS from the container's CPU limit on Linux, a job that used to need a third-party package
weaknesses: scratch has no CA certificates, time zone data or users: TLS, time.LoadLocation and user lookups fail until you add them
Distroless images have no shell, so debugging means a debug image variant or an ephemeral debug container
govulncheck needs the vulnerability database (vuln.go.dev, or a mirror via -db), so offline CI needs a local copy
Reachability analysis is static: calls through reflection are invisible, and interface calls are approximated

pitfalls.title: Building with cgo for a scratch image
pitfalls.detail: The golang image has gcc, so cgo is on by default and anything importing net links libc dynamically. Set CGO_ENABLED=0 in the build stage.
pitfalls.good: RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o /out/app ./cmd/app

pitfalls.title: Time zones in scratch
pitfalls.detail: time.LoadLocation("Europe/Istanbul") returns 'unknown time zone' in an image without tzdata. Use distroless/static, or embed the database with a blank import of time/tzdata (about 450 KB) or -tags timetzdata.
pitfalls.good: import _ "time/tzdata" // in package main

pitfalls.title: Copying the whole context before go mod download
pitfalls.detail: COPY . . first invalidates the dependency layer on every source change. Copy go.mod and go.sum, download, then copy the source; or use BuildKit cache mounts for the module and build caches.

pitfalls.title: Running as root in the final image
pitfalls.detail: Add USER nonroot:nonroot (distroless) or a numeric USER for scratch. StackLab's server image switches to distroless's nonroot user, and its Compose file runs the runner container as uid 65532.

pitfalls.title: Scanning once at release time
pitfalls.detail: New advisories appear for code you already shipped. Run govulncheck in CI on every change and on a schedule against the main branch and released binaries.

quiz.q: A Go service built with plain go build in the golang image fails in FROM scratch with 'no such file or directory'. Why?
options: Cgo was enabled, so the binary is dynamically linked and its loader and libc are missing from the image
quiz.why: The golang image includes a C compiler, so cgo is on by default; net then links libc. CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a static binary.

quiz.q: govulncheck ./... lists a vulnerability in its Informational section, with no call stack. What does that mean?
options: A vulnerable package is imported, but none of your code reaches the vulnerable function
quiz.why: Source mode traces calls to vulnerable functions. Without a call path, the vulnerable code is imported but not reachable from yours; govulncheck's own wording is that you may not need to take any action. Upgrading is still the tidy fix.

quiz.q: Two CI runners build the same tag in different directories and get different SHA-256 sums. What is the usual cause?
options: Absolute source paths are embedded; build with -trimpath
The linker embeds the build time
quiz.why: Go records no timestamps; with the same toolchain, flags and -trimpath, builds are byte-for-byte reproducible.

quiz.q: How does govulncheck know which standard-library vulnerabilities apply to a compiled binary?
options: It can't; it only checks modules
From the Go version recorded in the binary's build info
quiz.why: Every binary records the Go version that built it (go version -m prints it), and the standard library is versioned with Go.

further_reading.title: Tutorial: Find and fix vulnerable dependencies with govulncheck
Perfectly Reproducible, Verified Go Toolchains (Go blog)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A Go service image is usually two stages: one with the full toolchain that builds a
static binary, and one with almost nothing that runs it. The final stage doesn't need
Go, a shell or a package manager, so it is small and offers little to an attacker.

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s" -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

`AS build` names the stage and `COPY --from=build` takes only the binary from it.
Copying `go.mod` and `go.sum` before the source keeps the dependency layer cached
until they change, and the BuildKit cache mounts keep the module cache and build
cache between builds (the paths are those of the official golang image, as in
Docker's own Go example). `FROM scratch` works too, if you add what the binary needs
from the file system: CA certificates, time zone data, a non-root user.

**govulncheck** checks code against the Go vulnerability database:

```
go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
govulncheck ./...                # source: call stacks from your code to vulnerable functions
govulncheck -mode=binary ./app   # a built binary: Go version and module versions it records
```

In source mode it reports a vulnerability only when your code can reach the vulnerable
function, and it exits non-zero when it finds one, which is what makes it a CI gate.
The fix is an upgrade: `go get example.com/mod@fixed-version` for a module, a newer Go
for the standard library.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: the image needs a JRE (or a `jlink` runtime) plus the JAR; a Go image is
  the binary and, with distroless, CA certificates and tzdata. OWASP Dependency-Check
  matches versions; govulncheck also checks whether you call the affected code.
- **Node**: multi-stage builds exist to drop devDependencies and build tools, but
  `node_modules` and the runtime still ship. `npm audit` reports every vulnerable
  version in the tree, reachable or not.
- **Python**: slim images still carry an interpreter and site-packages; `pip-audit`
  works at the package-version level like `npm audit`.
- **C/C++**: a static musl build gets close to the Go result, with more effort; Go
  gets there with `CGO_ENABLED=0`.

## How it works

govulncheck reads the vulnerability database (vuln.go.dev), where every entry names
the affected module, versions and, where known, the vulnerable functions. In source
mode it builds a call graph of your packages and reports entries whose functions are
reachable from your code, with an example call stack; entries for code you import but
don't reach are listed separately as informational. In binary mode it reads the build
information every Go binary carries (the same record `go version -m` prints) and the
binary's symbols, so it works on artifacts you didn't build, but it can't show call
stacks. Requests to the database contain only module paths, not your code.

Reproducibility comes from what Go leaves out: no build timestamps, and with
`-trimpath` no host paths. The Go blog's recipe for programs that don't need cgo is
exactly `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath`, and the second example confirms it. The Go
project holds its own toolchain to the same standard: since Go 1.21, release builds
are rebuilt from source every night and must match the published archives bit for
bit.

## Design notes

StackLab's `server/Dockerfile` follows this shape: a `golang:${GO_VERSION}` build
stage with `go.mod`/`go.sum` copied first, `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath`, a
`gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13` final stage, `USER nonroot:nonroot`, and
migrations embedded with `go:embed` so the image needs no extra files. One Dockerfile
builds two programs through a `SERVICE` build argument.

A release checklist that fits on one screen:

1. `go mod tidy` leaves no diff; `go mod verify` passes.
2. `gofmt -l .` prints nothing; `go vet ./...` passes, with `GOOS=linux` too when
   you develop on Windows.
3. `go test -race ./...` passes. The race detector needs cgo, so run it on Linux CI
   (or with a C compiler installed); on this Windows machine without one, `-race`
   refuses to start.
4. `govulncheck ./...` passes.
5. Build every target with `-trimpath`, `CGO_ENABLED=0` and a version stamp from the
   tag; publish SHA-256 checksums beside the files.
6. Check the artifacts: `go version -m` shows the expected Go version, module
   versions and VCS revision; `govulncheck -mode=binary` passes.
7. Build the image from a pinned base (a version tag, ideally a digest), run as
   non-root, tag it with the version rather than only `latest`.
8. In the deployment, set `GOMEMLIMIT` below the container's memory limit. Since
   Go 1.25, `GOMAXPROCS` follows the CPU limit by itself.

lessons.title: database/sql vs native pgx; pgxpool sizing and lifecycle
lessons.summary: For a PostgreSQL-only service use pgx's native API with one pgxpool per process; use database/sql where a library demands *sql.DB, and bridge the two. Size the pool from the server's connection budget, and give every connection back.

examples.title: A pool of two connections, and what happens when both are taken

annotations.note: ParseConfig is the only way to get a Config (NewWithConfig panics on a hand-built one) because it fills in the defaults: MaxConns is the greater of 4 and runtime.NumCPU(), MaxConnLifetime 1 hour, MaxConnIdleTime 30 minutes. The same settings can ride in the URL as pool_max_conns=10&pool_max_conn_lifetime=30m.

NewWithConfig returns without connecting, so a wrong password or host would only surface on the first request. Ping at startup makes the deploy fail instead. This app's platform.NewPool does exactly that.
A Query borrows a connection and keeps it until its rows are closed (or Next returns false). The two connections are two server processes, which is why each one costs the database real memory.

The pool is empty, so the third query waits in Acquire until its context gives up. Without a deadline it would wait forever: a leaked Rows in a handler looks exactly like this, as a hang, not an error.

Closing rows hands the connection back and the queued work proceeds. The deferred pool.Close() blocks until every connection is returned, so a leak would also hang shutdown; rows2.Close() is not optional.

examples.title: database/sql over the pgx driver, and the bridges between the two APIs

annotations.note: Importing stdlib registers the "pgx" driver with database/sql in its init function. Code that needs nothing else from it imports it as _; here it is also used by name, for the two bridges below.

*sql.DB is a pool despite its name, and its default is no limit on open connections (MaxIdleConns defaults to 2). Under a traffic spike it opens connections until PostgreSQL refuses them, so always set the limits yourself.

Same query, two APIs: database/sql adds Context-suffixed methods, pgx takes ctx first. Scanning an array into []string through database/sql needs Go 1.27 and pgx 5.11+ (driver.RowsColumnScanner); older code wraps the target with pgtype.Map.SQLScanner.
Raw lends you the *pgx.Conn under a database/sql connection, so choosing database/sql never locks you out of COPY, batches or LISTEN. The connection is pinned to conn until conn.Close().

The other direction: OpenDBFromPool wraps the pgx pool as *sql.DB for a library such as goose. It sets MaxIdleConns to 0 so database/sql doesn't sit on connections the pgx side needs, and closing it leaves the pool open.

use_cases: pgxpool: HTTP services, workers and CLIs that only talk to PostgreSQL, especially when they need COPY, batches, LISTEN/NOTIFY or arrays, jsonb and ranges as Go values
database/sql with the pgx driver: libraries that require *sql.DB (goose, sqlx, many ORMs) and code that must also run on another database
A single *pgx.Conn: one-shot CLIs and scripts, and the dedicated connection a LISTEN loop holds for its whole life
strengths: Unlike JDBC plus HikariCP, the pool ships with the driver: one module gives you connections, pooling, health checks and lifetime rotation
The native API exposes PostgreSQL itself (COPY, batches, notifications, numeric, intervals, ranges) instead of the common subset database/sql must offer across databases
The bridges work both ways (stdlib.OpenDBFromPool, (*sql.Conn).Raw), so the choice is never all or nothing
pgxpool's default ceiling is bounded at max(4, NumCPU); database/sql's is unlimited
weaknesses: Native pgx code is PostgreSQL-only: switching databases means rewriting the data layer, where database/sql code would mostly need SQL dialect changes
The two APIs look alike but differ in semantics: database/sql rolls a transaction back when its context is cancelled, pgx's Begin uses the context only for BEGIN itself
MaxConns is per process; nothing in Go knows how many replicas share the server's max_connections, so the arithmetic is yours to write down

pitfalls.title: Leaving rows open
pitfalls.detail: Every open pgx.Rows holds a pool connection. Return early without Close and the pool drains, later queries hang until their deadline, and pool.Close() at shutdown blocks. Defer Close right after the error check, or use pgx.CollectRows and ForEachRow, which close for you.

pitfalls.title: Sharing one *pgx.Conn between goroutines
pitfalls.detail: A *pgx.Conn is not safe for concurrent use; a second caller arriving mid-query typically fails with "conn busy". Use pgxpool, or give each goroutine its own connection.

pitfalls.title: Trusting database/sql's pool defaults
pitfalls.detail: MaxOpenConns defaults to unlimited and MaxIdleConns to 2: a burst opens connections until PostgreSQL refuses with SQLSTATE 53300 (too_many_connections), and after it all but two are closed again. Call SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns and SetConnMaxLifetime explicitly.

pitfalls.title: A pool per request or per repository
pitfalls.detail: Each pool opens its own server processes and multiplies your share of max_connections. Build one pool in main, inject it, close it after the HTTP server has drained.

pitfalls.title: PgBouncer in transaction mode
pitfalls.detail: pgx caches named prepared statements per connection. PgBouncer 1.21+ supports that when max_prepared_statements > 0; with an older PgBouncer, set ConnConfig.DefaultQueryExecMode to pgx.QueryExecModeExec.

quiz.q: On a 2-core laptop, how many connections can a pool from pgxpool.New(ctx, url) open, with no pool_max_conns in the URL?
quiz.why: ParseConfig sets MaxConns to the greater of 4 and runtime.NumCPU().

quiz.q: max_connections is 100 with the default 3 superuser slots. Three replicas of your service and a reporting job that holds 10 connections share the server. What is the largest MaxConns per replica that cannot exhaust it?
quiz.why: (100 - 3 - 10) / 3 = 29. Every replica's pool draws on the same server budget.

quiz.q: A handler calls pool.Query, then returns early on a validation error without closing the rows. What happens as traffic continues?
options: Nothing: the garbage collector closes the rows
The pool runs dry and later queries wait until their context expires
PostgreSQL drops the idle connection after 30 minutes and the pool heals
quiz.why: pgx has no finalizer on Rows: the connection stays checked out until Close, so each early return leaks one.

quiz.q: goose needs a *sql.DB; the rest of the service uses a pgxpool. What keeps a single pool?
options: sql.Open("pgx", url) next to the pool
quiz.why: OpenDBFromPool serves database/sql from the pgx pool's connections; sql.Open would build a second pool with its own connections.

further_reading.title: package stdlib: pgx as a database/sql driver
package database/sql: DB and its pool settings
PostgreSQL: Architectural fundamentals (a process per connection)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go has two ways to talk to PostgreSQL, and pgx serves both. **database/sql** is the
standard library's database-neutral interface: you program against `*sql.DB` and plug
in a driver; `github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib` registers one called `"pgx"`. **Native
pgx** (`pgx.Conn`, `pgxpool.Pool`) skips that layer. It only speaks PostgreSQL, and in
exchange gives you COPY, batches, LISTEN/NOTIFY, every PostgreSQL type through `pgtype`,
and generic helpers such as `pgx.CollectRows`.

The choice is simple:

- A service that only uses PostgreSQL: native pgx with one `pgxpool.Pool`.
- A library demands `*sql.DB` (goose, sqlx, most ORMs), or you must support other
  databases: database/sql with the pgx driver.
- Both: keep the pgx pool and lend it out with `stdlib.OpenDBFromPool`.

A `*pgx.Conn` is one connection, which on the server is one process, and it is not safe
for concurrent use. `pgxpool.Pool` is: create it once in `main`, pass it to whatever
needs it, and close it at shutdown. Every query borrows a connection until its rows are
closed.

**Sizing.** `MaxConns` is a per-process ceiling. The real budget is the server's
`max_connections` (default 100) minus `superuser_reserved_connections` (default 3) and
`reserved_connections` (default 0), and every replica, migration job, cron script and
`psql` session draws on it: replicas × `MaxConns` + everything else must fit. Once the
server's CPUs and disks are busy, more connections don't add throughput: queries queue
on the server instead of in your pool, and each extra connection is another process
holding memory. Start from the default, watch `pool.Stat().EmptyAcquireCount()`
and `EmptyAcquireWaitTime()` (acquires that waited because the pool was empty), and grow
it only while the database still has headroom.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `pgxpool.Pool` is HikariCP's `DataSource` and the driver in one. `*sql.DB` is
  JDBC with the pool built in: it's a `DataSource`, not a `Connection`, despite the name.
  There's no try-with-resources; closing rows is your job, or `CollectRows`'s.
- Python: native pgx is closer to asyncpg (PostgreSQL-only API) and database/sql to
  DB-API drivers such as psycopg; `pgxpool` plays `psycopg_pool`'s role. Placeholders are
  `$1, $2`, never `%s` or `?`.
- Node: `pg.Pool` is the same idea. The difference is that Go code calling the pool is
  ordinary blocking code; many goroutines share it with no `async` anywhere.
- C: libpq gives you one `PGconn` and no pool. pgx's own libpq-level layer is `pgconn`,
  reachable through `conn.PgConn()`.

## How it works

The pool's lifecycle settings, all on `pgxpool.Config` (defaults from `ParseConfig`):

- `MaxConnLifetime` (1 h) and `MaxConnLifetimeJitter` (0): connections are retired by
  age, so a long-running service eventually reconnects, for example to a new primary
  after a DNS change; jitter keeps them from all expiring at once.
- `MaxConnIdleTime` (30 min) and `HealthCheckPeriod` (1 min): the background check closes
  idle connections that are too old or too quiet.
- `MinConns` and `MinIdleConns` (0): keep warm connections ready so a request doesn't pay
  for the TCP and authentication handshake. `MinIdleConns` arrived in pgx 5.7.3.
- On `Acquire`, a connection that sat idle for at least a second is pinged first, so a
  connection the server dropped is replaced instead of failing your query.

The connection string also carries session settings: parameters pgx doesn't recognise
become `RuntimeParams`, sent at connect time. That is how this runner gives your program
its own schema: its `DATABASE_URL` carries `search_path=run_...`. `application_name` (to
find your service in `pg_stat_activity`) and `statement_timeout` work the same way.

## Design notes

One pool per database per process, built at the edge and injected: this app's
`server/internal/platform/platform.go` parses the URL, applies `MaxConns`, `MinConns` and
`MaxConnLifetime` from configuration, pings, and returns the pool; `main.go` defers
`pool.Close()`, which runs after the HTTP server has drained. That order matters, because
`Close` waits for every borrowed connection.

The app's migrations show the database/sql bridge in practice:
`server/internal/platform/migrate.go` gives goose a short-lived `*sql.DB` built with
`sql.OpenDB(stdlib.GetConnector(...))` from the pool's connection config, and closes it
when the migrations are done. `stdlib.OpenDBFromPool` would have shared the pool's
connections instead. Both are fine; what you avoid is a second long-lived pool nobody
counted against `max_connections`.

lessons.title: Querying and scanning: CollectRows, RowToStructByName, NULL handling
lessons.summary: pgx.CollectRows with RowToStructByName turns rows into typed structs and does the close-and-check bookkeeping for you. Give every nullable column a type that can say NULL (*string, pgtype.Text), because pgx refuses to scan NULL into a zero value.

examples.title: CollectRows, RowTo and CollectOneRow, and how strict name mapping is

annotations.note: Fields match columns by name, ignoring case and, for untagged fields, underscores (pgx 5.5.2+), so BirthYear finds birth_year. A db:"col" tag pins the name, db:"-" skips the field, unexported fields are ignored.

Exec with no arguments uses PostgreSQL's simple protocol, which takes several statements in one string: handy for setup. With arguments, pgx sends one statement and the values separately, which is what makes parameters injection-proof (next lesson).

CollectRows loops, scans, closes the rows and checks rows.Err(): the four steps a hand-written loop gets wrong. Ignoring Query's error is the documented style here, because CollectRows returns the same error.
RowTo[T] covers single-column results. CollectRows always returns a non-nil slice, so zero rows encode to JSON as [] rather than null.

No row is an error, not a zero User. pgx.ErrNoRows wraps sql.ErrNoRows (pgx 5.7+), so either check works. Translate it to your own ErrNotFound at the repository boundary, as the errors module did with *pgconn.PgError.

Name mapping is strict: a column without a field fails, and so does a field without a column. With SELECT *, an ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN breaks binaries already deployed. RowToStructByNameLax only forgives missing columns, not extra ones; list the columns.

examples.title: NULL in, NULL out, and the aggregate that returns NULL

annotations.note: Nullability goes into the type. *string reads naturally and encodes to JSON null; pgtype.Text is what sqlc generates for pgx. sql.NullString and sql.Null[string] (Go 1.22) work too, because pgx accepts any sql.Scanner.
A nil pointer, an untyped nil or pgtype.Text{} is sent as NULL. The empty string is a value: Gül is known to have no phone, Ömer's is unknown, and the database keeps the difference.
NULL into a plain string is an error that names the column. pgx won't invent "" for you; JDBC's getString would have handed you null, and getInt a silent 0.
The two rows keep "" and NULL apart. A NULL pgtype.Text still has String == "", so check Valid first; with *string, forgetting the nil check panics on dereference instead of printing a fake value.
Except for count, aggregates over zero rows return NULL: sum of nothing is NULL, not 0. Here coalesce is honest, because no orders really means a quantity of 0.

use_cases: CollectRows + RowToStructByName: list endpoints, reports, anything that maps rows onto a struct
RowTo[T]: single-column results such as ids or names
QueryRow / CollectOneRow: lookups by key, where no row becomes a domain-level not found
ForEachRow: large results processed row by row without building a slice
strengths: Unlike a JDBC ResultSet loop, CollectRows closes the rows and checks the error in one call, so the two classic mistakes can't happen
Mapping mistakes are loud: an extra or missing column is an error, unlike encoding/json, which silently leaves unknown fields at their zero value
NULL cannot become a zero value by accident: scanning it into string or int64 fails and names the column
Generics give typed results ([]User) without an ORM or code generation
weaknesses: Names are matched at run time: a typo in a db tag or a column alias is a runtime error, which sqlc (lesson 5) moves to generation time
RowToStructByName matches columns by reflection (cached per struct and column list); a hand-written Scan, which sqlc generates, skips even that
Three spellings of a nullable value (*T, pgtype.T, sql.Null[T]) invite a codebase that mixes all of them

pitfalls.title: SELECT * into a struct
pitfalls.detail: Adding a column to the table breaks every RowToStructByName over SELECT * until the struct catches up. List the columns you map.
pitfalls.bad:
rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT * FROM users")
users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
pitfalls.good:
rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users")
users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])

pitfalls.title: coalesce to make NULL go away
pitfalls.detail: coalesce(phone, '') merges "unknown" with "known to be empty". Use it where NULL really means zero (an aggregate over no rows); elsewhere scan into a nullable type.

pitfalls.title: Reading pgtype.Text.String without Valid
pitfalls.detail: A NULL pgtype.Text has String == "". Check Valid first, or use *string so a NULL can't pass for a value.

pitfalls.title: A hand-written loop without rows.Err()
pitfalls.detail: Next returns false at the end and on a network error alike. Without the Err check, a failure halfway through looks like a short result.
pitfalls.good: users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])

pitfalls.title: Building an IN list by hand
pitfalls.detail: Pass a Go slice as one parameter and compare with = any($1). IN ($1) compares against the whole array, and string-joining ids into the SQL is the injection the next lesson is about.
pitfalls.bad: q := "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id IN (" + strings.Join(ids, ",") + ")"
pitfalls.good: rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = any($1)", ids)

quiz.q: A query uses SELECT * with RowToStructByName[User]. A colleague adds a nullable column to the table. What happens to the binary already deployed?
options: Scanning fails: the struct has no field for the new column
The column lands in the nearest matching field
quiz.why: Every column must have a field (and every field a column); extra columns are an error even with the Lax variant.

quiz.q: Which Go type honestly represents a nullable text column?
quiz.why: Both can say NULL. Scanning NULL into string is an error in pgx, and "" would conflate unknown with empty anyway.

quiz.q: SELECT max(created_at) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1, for a customer with no orders, scanned into a time.Time. What happens?
options: An error: cannot scan NULL into *time.Time
quiz.why: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; over zero input rows its value is NULL. Scan into *time.Time or use coalesce.

quiz.q: CollectOneRow found no rows. Which checks are true?
options: Both errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) and errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)
err is nil and the value is the zero struct
quiz.why: Since pgx 5.7, pgx.ErrNoRows unwraps to sql.ErrNoRows.

further_reading.title: package pgtype: PostgreSQL types and their Go mappings
PostgreSQL: Aggregate functions (NULL over no rows)

lessons.body:
## Concept

`Query` returns `pgx.Rows`, a cursor over the result that holds a connection until it is
closed. Don't loop over it by hand; hand it to a collector together with a function that
turns one row into a value:

- `pgx.CollectRows(rows, fn)` returns `[]T`; `CollectOneRow` returns the first `T` or
  `pgx.ErrNoRows`; `CollectExactlyOneRow` also fails with `ErrTooManyRows`.
- `fn` is usually `pgx.RowTo[T]` (one column), `pgx.RowToStructByName[T]` (columns to
  fields by name) or `RowToStructByPos[T]` (by position). The `RowToAddrOf...` variants
  return `*T`.
- `ForEachRow` scans into variables you provide and calls a function per row: no slice.

All of them close the rows and check `rows.Err()`. `QueryRow(...).Scan(...)` remains the
shortest way to read one row into variables.

Go has no null string or null int, so a nullable column needs a type that can hold
NULL: a pointer (`*string`, nil for NULL), a `pgtype` value (`pgtype.Text`, with `Valid`),
or `sql.Null[T]`. Scanning NULL into a plain `string` or `int64` is an error, which is the
point: the struct you scan into should say what the schema says.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: JDBC's `getInt` returns 0 for NULL unless you remember `wasNull()`; Go makes you
  pick a NULL-capable type up front, and fails loudly if you didn't. `CollectRows` with
  `RowToStructByName` is roughly Spring's `BeanPropertyRowMapper` without the framework.
- Python: psycopg hands back `None` for NULL in any column. Go strings can't be `nil`, so
  `*string` or `pgtype.Text` plays `None`'s role.
- JS/TS: node-postgres puts `null` in the row object and TypeScript believes whatever type
  you declared. pgx checks every value as it scans.
- C: libpq's `PQgetisnull` is the `Valid` flag of `pgtype.Text`, minus the struct.

## Design notes

Treat the struct as the contract with the schema: `NOT NULL` columns get plain types,
nullable ones get `*T` (or `pgtype.T` if you follow sqlc's output), and the query lists its
columns. Pick one nullable spelling per codebase; pointers are plain Go and encode to JSON
`null`, as does `pgtype.Text`.

`coalesce` is for places where NULL really means zero, such as the sum of no rows.
Turning an unknown phone number into `""` loses information you can't get back.

Keep `pgx.ErrNoRows` inside the repository: return your own `ErrNotFound` (wrapped with
`%w`) so callers never import pgx, which is the translation rule from the errors module.

Text comparison is exact: `WHERE city = $1` matches `İzmir` byte for byte. For
case-insensitive Turkish matching, remember this database's builtin `C.UTF-8` locale
lowercases `I` to `i`, never `ı`; Turkish rules need an explicit ICU collation such as
`lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`, which the `sql.search` module covers.

lessons.title: Transactions: a WithTx helper, deferred rollback, injection-safe parameters
lessons.summary: Wrap writes that belong together in one helper that begins, defers the rollback and commits only on success, and run every statement through the tx it hands you. Values always travel as $1 parameters; identifiers come from an allow-list.

examples.title: A WithTx helper and a transfer that must not half-happen

annotations.note: The consumer declares the one method it needs, so WithTx accepts a connection, a pool, or a transaction (which then nests as a savepoint). pgx.BeginFunc takes the same shape.
