pgx uses Begin's context for the BEGIN statement only; cancelling it later does not roll anything back. database/sql's BeginTx, by contrast, watches the context for the life of the transaction.

The deferred Rollback covers every early return and a panic in fn. After Commit it just returns ErrTxClosed. If ctx is already cancelled the ROLLBACK can't be sent; pgx then closes the connection and the server rolls back on its own.
Commit only when fn succeeded, and return Commit's error: a commit can fail (a serialization failure, a deferred constraint, a dropped connection), and then nothing was saved.
The credit runs first on purpose: when the debit fails, Çağrı already has the money inside the transaction, and only the rollback takes it back. Note every statement goes through tx, never the pool.
The CHECK (balance >= 0) violation, SQLSTATE 23514, becomes a domain error at the boundary, as in the errors module; callers test errors.Is(err, ErrInsufficientFunds), not SQLSTATE codes.
The second transfer fails and both balances are exactly as the first one left them: the credit and the failed debit were one unit.

examples.title: The same input as a parameter and concatenated into SQL

annotations.note: With an argument, pgx sends the statement and the value separately (the extended protocol): the server has parsed the SQL before it sees the value, so no value can change the statement's shape. Nobody is called "nobody' OR 'a' = 'a", so nothing changes.

Concatenated, the quote closes the literal and OR 'a' = 'a' makes the WHERE true for every row. Exec without arguments even uses the simple protocol, which runs several statements: '; DROP TABLE accounts; -- would have worked as well.

Identifiers can't be parameters. pgx.Identifier.Sanitize quotes them and doubles embedded quotes, so the input becomes one strange table name that doesn't exist (42P01). It stops injection, not misuse: an allow-list of names is still the better design.

examples.title: An error aborts the whole transaction; a savepoint contains it

annotations.note: After any error PostgreSQL rejects every further statement in the transaction with SQLSTATE 25P02 until it ends. Logging the error and carrying on achieves nothing; the second email is never inserted.
COMMIT on an aborted transaction is accepted and performs a ROLLBACK. pgx reports that as ErrTxCommitRollback, which is the only reason you learn the "successful" work was thrown away.
BeginFunc on a Tx starts a SAVEPOINT (pgx calls it a pseudo nested transaction); on error it rolls back to the savepoint only, and the outer transaction stays usable.
Expected errors are handled, everything else still aborts the outer transaction. For this exact case INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is simpler; savepoints are for failures SQL can't express.

use_cases: Any write that touches more than one row or table and must not half-happen: transfers, orders with order lines, a user plus their default settings
Read-modify-write sequences, together with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE isolation (sql.transactions module)
Savepoints for imports that skip or record bad rows without abandoning the whole batch
strengths: Unlike Spring's @Transactional, nothing is implicit: the tx is a value you pass, so the statements inside are visibly the ones that use it
One defer covers every exit path, including panics, which Java needs a finally block or try-with-resources for
PostgreSQL runs most DDL inside transactions too, so a schema change and its data fix can commit or roll back together, which MySQL cannot do
Parameters are a protocol feature, not string escaping: the value never becomes SQL text
weaknesses: Passing tx explicitly means every function in the unit takes it as a parameter (or works on an interface both pool and tx satisfy)
pgx does not tie the transaction to Begin's context; code ported from database/sql that relied on cancel-means-rollback must roll back itself
After an error the transaction is unusable; recovering mid-transaction needs savepoints, which other databases don't require

pitfalls.title: Using the pool inside the transaction
pitfalls.detail: pool.Exec runs on a different connection in its own implicit transaction: it commits immediately, even if fn later fails, and it can't see the tx's uncommitted rows.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring Commit's error
pitfalls.detail: defer tx.Commit(ctx) drops the error. A commit can fail (40001 serialization_failure under SERIALIZABLE, a deferred constraint, a lost connection), or report ErrTxCommitRollback after a swallowed error; either way nothing was saved.

pitfalls.title: Formatting values into SQL
pitfalls.detail: fmt.Sprintf with '%s', and hand-written quote escaping, both turn data into code. Pass every value as $n. For dynamic ORDER BY columns or table names, map user choices to constants.
pitfalls.bad: q := fmt.Sprintf("SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY %s", r.URL.Query().Get("sort"))

pitfalls.title: LIKE patterns from user input
pitfalls.detail: A parameter stops injection but not wildcards: % and _ in the input still match anything. Escape them (backslash is LIKE's default escape character) or use starts_with(name, $1).

pitfalls.title: Slow work inside a transaction
pitfalls.detail: An open transaction holds a connection and its row locks, and keeps VACUUM from cleaning up. Make HTTP calls and other slow work before Begin or after Commit; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is the server's backstop.

quiz.q: Inside WithTx's callback you call pool.Exec instead of tx.Exec, and later the callback returns an error. What happens to the pool.Exec write?
options: It is rolled back with the transaction
It is committed: it ran on another connection, outside the transaction
pgx returns an error because the pool is busy
quiz.why: The pool hands out a different connection, where the statement runs and commits on its own.

quiz.q: A statement inside a transaction fails with a unique violation. You log it and run another INSERT on the same tx. What does PostgreSQL do?
options: Rejects it with SQLSTATE 25P02 until the transaction ends
Rolls back automatically and runs the INSERT in a new transaction
quiz.why: An aborted transaction ignores every command until ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT).

quiz.q: Which is safe against SQL injection?
quiz.why: Only the parameter keeps the value out of the SQL text. strconv.Quote makes a double-quoted Go string, which PostgreSQL reads as an identifier.

quiz.q: defer tx.Rollback(ctx) runs after tx.Commit(ctx) succeeded. What does it do?
options: Nothing: it returns ErrTxClosed, which the defer ignores
quiz.why: Rollback on a closed Tx is a documented no-op that returns ErrTxClosed, which is why the deferred call is safe.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: Pattern matching with LIKE (escape characters)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A transaction makes several statements one unit: all of them commit or none do. In pgx,
`Begin` returns a `pgx.Tx` bound to one connection; every statement of the unit must go
through that `tx`, and the transaction ends with `Commit` or `Rollback`. Getting the
ending right on every path (errors, early returns, panics) is the part people get wrong,
so put it in one helper:

```go
tx, err := db.Begin(ctx)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer tx.Rollback(ctx) // no-op after Commit
if err := fn(tx); err != nil {
    return err
}
return tx.Commit(ctx)
```

`pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, db, fn)` is exactly this, ready-made. Two PostgreSQL behaviours shape
the code inside `fn`. First, an error aborts the whole transaction: later statements fail
with SQLSTATE 25P02 until it ends, so you either return the error or isolate the risky
statement in a savepoint (`tx.Begin`). Second, values are never part of the SQL text: you
write `$1, $2` and pass the values as arguments. Identifiers (table and column names)
can't be parameters, so choose them from a fixed list in your code.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: JDBC's `setAutoCommit(false)` plus commit, and rollback in `finally`, is the same
  shape with `defer` as the `finally`. Spring's `@Transactional` hides the connection in a
  thread-local; Go has no thread-locals, so the transaction is an explicit parameter.
  `$1` is `PreparedStatement`'s `?`.
- Python: psycopg 3's `with conn.transaction():` is `WithTx`, with a closure instead of a
  context manager. `cursor.execute(sql, (name,))` is the safe form there too; Python's
  `%` operator on the SQL string is the unsafe one.
- JS/TS: `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)` and knex's `transaction(trx => ...)`
  use the same callback shape as `WithTx`.
- C: libpq has no helper; you send `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` yourself, and `PQexecParams` is
  how values stay separate from the SQL.

## Design notes

The service layer decides what one unit of work is ("transfer" is two updates), so the
transaction belongs there, not inside each repository method. Repositories take an
interface that both the pool and a `pgx.Tx` satisfy (`Exec`, `Query`, `QueryRow`), so the
same code runs inside or outside a transaction; sqlc generates exactly that interface,
`DBTX`, in lesson 5. Pass the transaction as a value; hiding it in a `context.Context`
makes it invisible in signatures and easy to bypass.

Keep transactions short: no HTTP calls or user think-time between `Begin` and `Commit`.
The default isolation level is READ COMMITTED; `BeginTx(ctx, pgx.TxOptions{IsoLevel:
pgx.Serializable})` buys stronger guarantees at the price of retrying on SQLSTATE 40001,
which the `sql.transactions` module demonstrates with two live sessions.

lessons.title: CopyFrom bulk loads, batches, context timeouts and cancellation
lessons.summary: CopyFrom streams rows over the COPY protocol and loads 100k rows in one all-or-nothing statement; a Batch sends many statements in one round trip. Give every query a deadline, and choose whether it is enforced by closing the connection, by a cancel request, or by the server's statement_timeout.

examples.title: 100,000 rows with CopyFrom, and a load that fails as a whole

annotations.note: CopyFrom runs COPY ... FROM STDIN in binary format: one statement, rows streamed without a round trip each. pgx's own docs say it can beat INSERT with as few as 5 rows. The program prints no timing because it varies; the run panel's duration covers the whole program, connect and summary query included.
CopyFromSlice asks for one row at a time, so nothing holds 100k []any at once. CopyFromFunc does the same for sources without a length, such as a csv.Reader; CopyFromRows wraps a ready [][]any.

A single bad row fails the whole COPY and loads nothing: the row 100001 before the duplicate is gone too. The aborted rows still take disk space until VACUUM. COPY's ON_ERROR ignore doesn't help here: it only applies to text and csv input, and pgx sends binary.
Under this database's C.UTF-8 locale, ORDER BY city puts İstanbul and İzmir after Muğla, because İ (U+0130) sorts by code point. The ICU collation tr-x-icu gives the order a Turkish reader expects.

examples.title: A Batch is one round trip and one implicit transaction

annotations.note: Queue only records the statement; nothing is sent yet. The callback sees each result in order. Capturing name is safe because since Go 1.22 every loop iteration has its own variable.
SendBatch sends everything at once, and Close reads every result and runs the callbacks. Close must happen before the connection is used again, and its error is the batch's error.
Without an explicit BEGIN, the batch runs as one implicit transaction: the duplicate rolls back the "sql" insert queued before it, and the DELETE after it never executes, so its callback never runs.
The table shows only batch 1's rows. array_agg needs its own ORDER BY for a deterministic order, and pgx scans the text[] straight into a []string.

examples.title: Three ways a slow query ends, and what each leaves behind

annotations.note: The default: when the context expires, pgx sends PostgreSQL a cancel request and closes the connection. The error wraps context.DeadlineExceeded; a pool simply discards the dead connection, a lone *pgx.Conn must reconnect.

CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler asks the server to cancel and waits for its answer, so the connection survives. The error is then the server's 57014, not DeadlineExceeded: check ctx.Err() to know a deadline caused it. DeadlineDelay caps how long it waits.

statement_timeout is enforced by the server alone, with no client context involved; RuntimeParams makes it the session default on every connection (on a pool: cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams). The connection stays healthy.
Call cancel as soon as the work is done, not only on error: a context with a timer holds resources until it fires or is cancelled.

use_cases: CopyFrom: imports, seeding test data, nightly loads from another system, copying between databases
Batch: many small independent statements per request (several inserts, a read after a write) without paying a round trip each
Context deadlines: every query in a request handler, bounded by the request's own deadline
statement_timeout: a server-side ceiling for a role or service, so one bad query can't run for hours
strengths: COPY is PostgreSQL's fastest way in, and pgx exposes it with Go values; database/sql has no equivalent without Raw
A batch removes round trips without string-building a multi-row INSERT, and each statement keeps its own parameters
Cancellation is a context, the same mechanism as for HTTP calls, so a client disconnect can stop the query it started
Unlike JDBC's setQueryTimeout (whole seconds, set per statement), one context carries a single deadline through every call of a request, HTTP and SQL alike
weaknesses: COPY is all or nothing and stops at the first bad row; reporting which rows were bad needs validation first or a staging table
CopyFrom needs binary encodings for every column: enum and other custom types must be registered with the connection first
The default cancellation closes the connection, which costs a reconnect; the polite handler opens an extra connection to deliver the cancel request, which PostgreSQL's protocol makes inherently racy

pitfalls.title: Queries without a deadline
pitfalls.detail: context.Background() in a handler lets a slow query outlive the request. Use the request's context (r.Context()) and, for long work, context.WithTimeout on top of it.

pitfalls.title: Using the connection before closing the batch
pitfalls.detail: BatchResults must be closed before the connection runs anything else; until then the connection is busy reading the batch's results.

pitfalls.title: Creating a table and using it in the same batch
pitfalls.detail: With the default exec mode pgx may prepare every queued statement before running any of them, so a statement that refers to a table created earlier in the batch can fail. Run DDL first, then the batch.

pitfalls.title: Building one giant INSERT string
pitfalls.detail: Concatenating VALUES (...) rows risks injection and runs into the 65535 bind-parameter limit if you parameterize it. CopyFrom has neither problem.

quiz.q: The 60,000th row of a 100,000-row CopyFrom violates a CHECK constraint. How many rows are in the table afterwards?
quiz.why: COPY is one statement: an error aborts it, and the rows it had already written stay invisible until VACUUM removes them.

quiz.q: A batch queues INSERT a, INSERT b (which fails), INSERT c, with no BEGIN. What is committed?
quiz.why: SendBatch runs the queued statements in one implicit transaction unless the batch contains its own transaction control.

quiz.q: With pgx's default settings, a query's context deadline expires. What happens to the connection?
options: pgx sends a cancel request and closes it
quiz.why: The default handler interrupts the network read and closes the connection, after asking the server to cancel the query.

quiz.q: You want slow queries stopped but connections kept. Which options do that?
quiz.why: Both make the server cancel the statement (57014) and leave the connection usable; a context deadline with the default handler closes it.

further_reading.title: package pgx: CopyFrom, CopyFromSlice, Batch, SendBatch
PostgreSQL: statement_timeout and other client settings

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three tools for doing a lot, or for giving up on time.

**CopyFrom** uses PostgreSQL's COPY protocol: one `COPY ... FROM STDIN` statement, then
the rows streamed in binary. No per-row round trip, no per-row statement. You hand it a
`CopyFromSource`: `CopyFromRows` for a `[][]any`, `CopyFromSlice(n, fn)` to produce row
`i` on demand, `CopyFromFunc` for a stream of unknown length. Being one statement, it is
all or nothing.

**Batch** queues ordinary statements, each with its own parameters, and `SendBatch` sends
them together. Results come back in order, to callbacks or to `BatchResults`. Without its
own `BEGIN`, the batch runs as one implicit transaction.

**Cancellation** is a context. Every pgx call takes one; when it expires, what happens
depends on the connection's context-watcher handler: by default pgx asks the server to
cancel and closes the connection; `CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler` asks and keeps it.
Independently, the server's `statement_timeout` cancels any statement running longer than
the limit, and the connection stays usable either way.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: CopyFrom is the PgJDBC `CopyManager` with typed values instead of CSV text; a
  Batch is closer to pipelining than to `addBatch`, because each statement can return rows.
  A context replaces `Statement.setQueryTimeout` and `cancel()` with one mechanism.
- Python: psycopg 3's `cursor.copy()` and `executemany` are the equivalents; asyncio's
  `wait_for` around a query plays the context's role.
- Node: `pg-copy-streams` adds COPY to node-postgres; an `AbortSignal` passed down the call
  chain is the closest thing to a context.
- C: libpq's `PQputCopyData` and pipeline mode are the same protocol features, which pgx
  implements natively rather than wrapping libpq; `PQcancel` is the cancel request.

## Design notes

Put deadlines where the work starts: an HTTP handler passes `r.Context()` down, so a
client that disconnects cancels its queries; background jobs set `context.WithTimeout`.
Add `statement_timeout` as a server-side backstop for the whole service, set on the
pool's `ConnConfig.RuntimeParams` or with `ALTER ROLE ... SET statement_timeout`, so a
forgotten context can't run a query for hours. `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` inside a
transaction raises or lowers it for one unit of work.

For imports, validate in Go before CopyFrom, or COPY into a staging table without
constraints and move the good rows with one `INSERT ... SELECT`; the
`sql.files-movement` module shows the staging pattern. Measure with your own data and
indexes: every index on the target table is maintained row by row during the load, which
is why PostgreSQL's bulk-loading advice suggests creating indexes after a large initial
load.

lessons.title: goose migrations and the sqlc workflow
lessons.summary: Schema changes are numbered SQL files applied in order and recorded in a version table; on PostgreSQL each one commits or rolls back as a whole. sqlc turns annotated queries into typed Go methods over a DBTX interface, checked against that same schema at generation time.

examples.title: What goose does underneath, in 30 lines, over an fs.FS

annotations.note: The version table is the whole memory of the system: a file runs once per database, ever. This demo records file names; goose's table, goose_db_version, records the version number parsed from the name and when each version was applied.
Order comes from the file names, so zero-pad sequential prefixes (010 after 009, not after 001). goose parses the number and sorts by it; goose create uses timestamp prefixes unless you pass -s.

Recording the file first, in the same transaction as the change, means the two commit or roll back together. A second instance migrating at the same moment blocks on the primary key, then finds the row and skips. goose offers an advisory lock for this instead.

No arguments, so pgx uses the simple protocol and the whole file runs in one call. goose splits files into statements itself, which is why function bodies need -- +goose StatementBegin / StatementEnd.

A real service embeds the directory and passes fs.Sub(embedded, "migrations"), exactly as this app's main.go does. The files keep goose's required -- +goose Up header, so goose could run them unchanged.

Schema and data change together: add the column nullable, backfill it, then require it. On a large table SET NOT NULL scans the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; the zero-downtime variants are in the sql.security-ops module.
The first ALTER succeeds, the second fails, and PostgreSQL rolls back both: transactional DDL. MySQL commits each DDL statement implicitly and would have left city behind.

Ayşe's row got its name from the backfill, and city does not exist: migration 003 left nothing behind, and because its row in schema_migrations rolled back too, a fixed 003 will run on the next deploy.

examples.title: The code sqlc generates for one :many query, and how you call it

annotations.note: DBTX is declared by the generated code, the consumer, and *pgx.Conn, *pgxpool.Pool and pgx.Tx all satisfy it. WithTx rebinds the same queries to a transaction: q.WithTx(tx) inside the WithTx helper from lesson 3.
Models come from the schema: phone is nullable, so it becomes pgtype.Text. With emit_pointers_for_null_types: true in sqlc.yaml it would be *string instead.

You write the SQL with a name and a command (:one, :many, :exec, plus :batchexec for pgx batches and :copyfrom for COPY). The constant keeps the name comment, so server logs and pg_stat_activity show which query is running.

The loop CollectRows would run, spelled out with positional Scan: no reflection, and columns and fields can't drift apart because both come from the same query. var items stays nil for zero rows, which encodes to JSON null.

The calling code has no SQL and no Scan, and a typo in a column name fails at sqlc generate instead of at run time. The NULL phone prints as { false}: pgtype.Text's String and Valid fields. Zero rows give a nil slice, as the Muğla line shows.

use_cases: goose (library mode): a service that migrates itself at startup from embedded files, like this app
goose (CLI): a separate deploy step that runs before new instances start, when several replicas share one database
sqlc: CRUD and reporting queries whose shape is known at compile time, which is most of a typical service
Hand-written pgx next to sqlc: dynamic filters and sort orders, COPY pipelines with custom sources
strengths: The SQL that runs in production is the SQL in the pull request, unlike an ORM's generated DDL and queries
PostgreSQL's transactional DDL makes each migration all or nothing; MySQL commits every DDL statement implicitly
sqlc checks queries against the schema at generation time: a renamed column breaks sqlc generate, not a request in production
Generated code is plain pgx with positional Scan: no reflection, no runtime magic, readable in a debugger
weaknesses: Queries that change shape at run time (optional filters, user-chosen sorting) don't fit one static SQL string; they need several queries, sqlc.narg tricks, or hand-written code
One more tool in the build: generated files must be regenerated and committed whenever a query or migration changes
Down migrations are rarely tested and often can't restore dropped data; in practice a bad migration is fixed by a new one

pitfalls.title: Editing a migration that already ran
pitfalls.detail: Its version is recorded, so the edit never runs where the old version did, and databases silently drift apart. Write a new migration; the app's own migrations say so in their header.

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a migration
pitfalls.detail: It cannot run inside a transaction block, and goose wraps each migration in one. Put -- +goose NO TRANSACTION at the top of that file, and keep it to that one statement.

pitfalls.title: Several replicas migrating at startup
pitfalls.detail: goose's locking is off unless you pass WithSessionLocker (for example lock.NewPostgresSessionLocker(), a PostgreSQL advisory lock). Enable it, or run migrations as a separate deploy step.

pitfalls.title: Editing generated code
pitfalls.detail: The next sqlc generate overwrites it. Change the SQL or sqlc.yaml (type overrides, emit_pointers_for_null_types) and regenerate.

pitfalls.title: Semicolons inside function bodies
pitfalls.detail: goose splits a file on semicolons. Wrap CREATE FUNCTION and DO blocks in -- +goose StatementBegin and -- +goose StatementEnd.

quiz.q: Migration 007 ran in production yesterday. Today you spot a wrong column type in it. What do you do?
options: Delete the 007 row from the version table and redeploy
quiz.why: 007 never runs again where it already ran; only a new version reaches every database the same way.

quiz.q: The second statement of a goose migration fails on PostgreSQL. What state is the schema in?
options: The first statement's change is kept
As before the migration: it ran in one transaction
quiz.why: goose runs each migration in a transaction by default, and PostgreSQL rolls DDL back like any other change.

quiz.q: How does sqlc know that users.phone is nullable?
options: It connects to the database at run time
It parses the schema, which can be your migrations directory, when you run sqlc generate
From a struct tag you write
quiz.why: sqlc reads the DDL (ignoring down migrations) and derives the Go types from it before any code runs.

quiz.q: Why does generated code take a DBTX instead of a *pgxpool.Pool?
options: So the same Queries work on a pool, a single connection or a transaction
quiz.why: All three satisfy the three-method interface; WithTx swaps a transaction in.

further_reading.title: sqlc module page (README; the full manual is linked from the Concept section)
PostgreSQL: ALTER TABLE (SET NOT NULL, locking)

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Migrations.** The schema's history is a directory of numbered SQL files in the repo.
A tool applies the ones a database hasn't seen yet, in order, and records each version
in a table. A file that has run is never edited again; a change is a new file. goose is a
common choice: files start with `-- +goose Up` (an optional `-- +goose Down` section
undoes them), it records versions in `goose_db_version`, and on PostgreSQL it runs each
migration in a transaction, so a failure leaves nothing half-applied. It works as a CLI
or as a library inside your binary.

**sqlc.** You write queries in `.sql` files, each named and given a cardinality:

```sql
-- name: ListUsersByCity :many
SELECT id, email, city, phone FROM users WHERE city = $1 ORDER BY email;
```

`sqlc generate` parses them against the schema (it can read your migrations directory
directly) and writes Go: a struct per table, a `Queries` type over a `DBTX` interface, and
one typed method per query. A query that names an unknown table or column fails at
generation time. The generated code is ordinary pgx; there is no runtime library.

The workflow: write a migration, write or change a query, run `sqlc generate`, call the
new method, commit all of it together. sqlc's manual covers the details:
[getting started with PostgreSQL](https://docs.sqlc.dev/en/latest/tutorials/getting-started-postgresql.html),
[using goose migrations as the schema](https://docs.sqlc.dev/en/latest/howto/ddl.html) and
[query annotations](https://docs.sqlc.dev/en/latest/reference/query-annotations.html).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: goose is Flyway with SQL migrations. sqlc resembles jOOQ's code generation in that
  types come from the schema, but you write plain SQL instead of a query DSL. Unlike
  JPA/Hibernate, nothing writes SQL for you at run time.
- Python: Alembic and Django can generate migration files from models; goose files are
  SQL you write. aiosql (named queries in `.sql` files with `-- name:` comments) is the
  nearest relative of sqlc, minus the generated types.
- JS/TS: Prisma Migrate plus Prisma Client is the closest pair, except that sqlc starts
  from SQL rather than a schema DSL; PgTyped (TypeScript types generated from SQL) is the
  direct analogue.
- C: PostgreSQL's ECPG preprocessor, embedded SQL turned into C calls, is the old form of
  the same idea.

## How it works

This app migrates itself at startup. `server/cmd/stacklab/main.go` embeds the files with
`//go:embed migrations/*.sql` and passes `fs.Sub(embedded, "migrations")`, because goose
only reads the root of the FS it is given. `server/internal/platform/migrate.go` builds a
`*sql.DB` from the pool's connection config (goose speaks database/sql, lesson 1) and
runs:

```go
provider, err := goose.NewProvider(goose.DialectPostgres, sdb, fsys)
// ...
_, err = provider.Up(ctx) // applies every version newer than the database's
```

A minimal `sqlc.yaml` for pgx:

```yaml
version: "2"
sql:
  - engine: "postgresql"
    queries: "query.sql"
    schema: "migrations"
    gen:
      go:
        package: "store"
        out: "internal/store"
        sql_package: "pgx/v5"
```

## Design notes

Self-migrating at startup suits a single instance like this app. With several replicas,
either enable goose's session locker or run migrations as their own deploy step, and
write migrations that the previous release can live with: add a column before the code
that uses it ships, drop it only after the code that read it is gone.

sqlc covers the static queries, which is most of them. Keep hand-written pgx (with
`CollectRows`) beside it for genuinely dynamic SQL, and wrap the generated `*Queries` in
your own store type only when you need a boundary, which is the next lesson's question.

lessons.title: The repository pattern (and when it's overkill); testing DB code on real Postgres
lessons.summary: A repository is a concrete type that owns its SQL and speaks domain values and errors; an interface appears only where a consumer needs a substitute. The rules that matter live in the database, so test repositories on a real PostgreSQL, one rolled-back transaction per test.

examples.title: The same service over a fake and over PostgreSQL

annotations.note: The consumer declares the interface, with only the method it calls. The repository doesn't name it and doesn't need to: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly.

The repository owns the SQL and translates driver errors at the boundary: callers see ErrEmailTaken, never SQLSTATE 23505 or a *pgconn.PgError. It is a concrete struct; nothing here needs an interface of its own.
A fake encodes what you believe the database does: here, exact-match uniqueness. It is fast and fine for testing signup's own logic, but it can't tell you whether the belief is true.
The real rule: a unique index on the expression lower(email). This is behaviour of your system that lives only in the schema, along with CHECK constraints, NULL semantics, collations and triggers.

Same service, two stores, two answers. A test suite built on the fake stays green while production returns "email already registered", which is why the repository itself must be tested against PostgreSQL.

examples.title: A table-driven test on real PostgreSQL, one rolled-back transaction per case

annotations.note: The repository asks for the one method it uses. *pgxpool.Pool, *pgx.Conn and pgx.Tx all have it, which is what lets a test hand it a transaction instead of the pool.

Connect and migrate once per test binary. Without DATABASE_URL the tests skip instead of failing, so go test ./... still works on a machine without a database. TestMain may return; the wrapper exits with m.Run's result.

Every test runs inside its own transaction, and Cleanup rolls it back: no test sees another's rows and nothing needs deleting. t.Context() (Go 1.24) is canceled just before cleanups run, so the rollback gets context.Background().
Table-driven: each case names the situation and the error it expects. The second case is the one the fake in the first example got wrong; the unique index answers it.
After the expected 23505 the transaction is aborted (lesson 3). That is fine because the case ends here; a test that keeps going after an expected error needs a savepoint.

use_cases: A concrete repository (or sqlc's Queries) called directly: CRUD services with one database and little logic, which is most of them
A consumer-declared interface plus a fake: business logic with real branching that should be unit-tested in microseconds
Interfaces with two real implementations, like this app's httpapi.Runner (in-process runner and Docker runner client)
Integration tests on real PostgreSQL: every repository, every query with constraints, NULLs or collations involved
strengths: Unlike Java's interface-per-repository habit, Go's implicit interfaces let the consumer define the seam later, without touching the repository
Transactional DDL and cheap transactions make rolled-back tests fast enough to run on every change against a local PostgreSQL
Error translation in the repository keeps driver types out of services and handlers, so storage can change behind a stable API
Tests against the real database pin down behaviour no fake reproduces: expression indexes, constraint names, collations, NULL comparisons
weaknesses: Integration tests need a running PostgreSQL and a migrated schema; CI must provide one
A transaction per test can't cover code that must commit or that needs two sessions (lock waits, LISTEN/NOTIFY); those need a schema per test or cleanup
Interfaces added too early hide which implementation runs and multiply files for no gain

pitfalls.title: Mocking the driver
pitfalls.detail: A mocked pgx asserts the SQL text you expected to send, not what PostgreSQL does with it, so it passes while a constraint, a typo in a column or a NULL breaks production. Test repositories against PostgreSQL.

pitfalls.title: An interface per struct, by reflex
pitfalls.detail: A UserRepository interface beside its only implementation, declared by the producer, mirrors every method and protects nothing. Let each consumer declare the few methods it needs, when it needs a substitute.

pitfalls.title: Rolling back with t.Context() in Cleanup
pitfalls.detail: t.Context() is already canceled when cleanup functions run, so the ROLLBACK can't be sent and pgx closes the connection instead. Use context.Background() there.

pitfalls.title: Parallel tests that insert the same unique value
pitfalls.detail: Uncommitted rows are invisible to other transactions, but a unique index still makes the second insert wait until the first transaction ends. Give parallel tests distinct values.

pitfalls.title: Tests that depend on committed data
pitfalls.detail: Seeding shared rows that every test reads couples the tests to their order. Create what a test needs inside its own transaction.

quiz.q: Your fake user store passes every test, but production rejects "Ayse@Example.com" after "ayse@example.com". Why?
options: The fake has a bug in its map
The unique index on lower(email) is a database rule the fake never knew
quiz.why: A fake encodes your assumptions; the schema holds the actual rule, and only a test on PostgreSQL checks it.

quiz.q: A service has one storage implementation (sqlc over PostgreSQL) and almost no logic. Does it need a UserRepository interface?
options: Yes, always program to an interface
No: call the concrete store or Queries; add a small interface when a consumer needs a substitute
quiz.why: An interface earns its place with a second implementation or logic worth testing in isolation; otherwise it is indirection.

quiz.q: Which context should the rollback in t.Cleanup use?
quiz.why: t.Context() is canceled just before cleanups run, so a rollback using it can't reach the server.

quiz.q: Code under test calls WithTx(ctx, db, fn), and the test passes its own pgx.Tx as db. What happens?
options: It fails: you can't begin inside a transaction
Begin on a Tx creates a savepoint; the code's commit releases it, and the test's rollback still undoes everything
The inner commit makes the data permanent
quiz.why: pgx.Tx.Begin starts a pseudo nested transaction backed by a savepoint, so the outer rollback wins.

further_reading.title: package testing: TestMain, T.Cleanup, T.Context, T.Skip
package pgx: Tx and pseudo nested transactions

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **repository** is the type that owns the SQL for one part of the domain. It takes
domain values in, returns domain values and domain errors out (`User`, `ErrEmailTaken`),
and nothing above it imports pgx. In Go it is a plain struct with a constructor, often a
thin layer over sqlc's `Queries`.

Whether it also needs an **interface** is a separate question, answered by its consumers.
Add one when a consumer needs a substitute: business logic you want to unit-test with a
fake, or a second real implementation. The consumer declares it, with only the methods it
calls, and the repository satisfies it without knowing. Without such a consumer, an
interface is ceremony: one implementation, a mirror of its methods, and one more hop when
reading the code. That is when the pattern is overkill, and with sqlc's typed methods it
often is.

**Testing.** A repository's behaviour is half Go and half schema: unique indexes,
constraints, NULL handling, collations. Only a real PostgreSQL tests the second half, so
test repositories against one. The standard shape: connect and migrate once, give each
test a transaction, roll it back in `t.Cleanup`, and skip when no database is configured.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: Spring Data generates an implementation behind `interface UserRepository`; in Go
  you write the struct, and interfaces come from consumers. Testcontainers plus a
  `@Transactional` test (rolled back by default in Spring tests) is the same
  real-database, rolled-back-transaction technique.
- Python: Django's `TestCase` wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back; pytest
  fixtures with teardown play `t.Cleanup`'s role.
- JS/TS: mocking the database client in Jest tests the mock. The real-database approach
  is the same as here: a test database and a transaction or truncate per test.
- C: swapping in a fake object file at link time is the C version of a fake, with the
  same blind spot.

## Design notes

This app shows both sides. `httpapi.Runner` is an interface declared by its consumer,
the HTTP layer, because two real implementations exist: `runexec.Executor` runs lessons
in-process, `runclient.Client` forwards them to the Docker runner. The stores
(`*learningstore.Store`, `*runstore.Store`) are concrete and used directly, because there
is one database and nothing to swap.

Its database tests follow the integration pattern: `sqlrun_test.go` and
`multisession_test.go` in `server/internal/sqlrun` carry `//go:build integration` and read
`TEST_DATABASE_URL`, skipping when it is unset, while the unit tests in `split_test.go`
beside them have no tag. `go test ./...` stays fast, and `go test -tags integration ./...` runs the honest
suite against the local playground database. This lesson's runtime passes
`DATABASE_URL` instead and has no tags, which is why the example skips on the variable
alone.

A transaction per test covers code that accepts a `DBTX`-style interface. Code that
commits on its own can still run inside it if it begins from something you pass in:
`Begin` on a `pgx.Tx` makes a savepoint. Code that needs two sessions, waits on locks or
uses LISTEN needs committed data instead: a schema per test (what this runner does for
every run) or truncating tables between tests.

Case-insensitive rules carry a locale: `lower()` in this C.UTF-8 database maps `I` to
`i`, so a unique index on `lower(username)` treats `IŞIL` and `ışıl` as different users,
while `lower(username COLLATE "tr-x-icu")` would not. Behaviour like that is exactly what
a test on the real database pins down.

lessons.title: http.Client without timeouts is a bug; per-request context
lessons.summary: http.Get and the zero http.Client wait forever. Give every client a Timeout as a backstop, give every call a context derived from the work that asked for it, and close (ideally drain) every response body so connections are reused.

examples.title: Client.Timeout and a per-call deadline: two ways a call gives up

annotations.note: The server cancels r.Context() when the client's connection closes. That is how /hang ends once the client gives up, and it's the signal your own handlers should watch. A handler that never returns would also block srv.Close.

For an outgoing request the context covers the whole exchange: getting a connection, sending, the headers and reading the body. http.Get and http.Post take no context, one more reason to keep them out of service code.
Do returns an error only when no response arrived. When err is nil you own resp.Body and must close it. The defer goes after the error check, because resp is nil on error.
A 404 or a 503 is a successful round trip as far as Do is concerned. Turning statuses into errors is your job, and belongs in one helper.
io.LimitReader is the client-side MaxBytesReader: a misbehaving upstream can't make you buffer more than you planned for.

http.Get uses DefaultClient, whose Timeout is zero: no limit. DefaultTransport only bounds dialing (30 s) and the TLS handshake (10 s); a server that accepts the connection and never answers holds your goroutine for good.

Client.Timeout covers connecting, redirects, headers and body, and is the backstop for every call made with this client. /hang fails after one second with "Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers".

Every Do error is a *url.Error carrying the method and URL, which is what you want in logs. Here the port is random, so only the cause is printed. errors.AsType is Go 1.26. errors.Is sees through the wrapper either way.
The per-call budget. /stall sends its headers, so Do returns 200, and the deadline then interrupts the body read. Whichever ends first, the context or Client.Timeout, wins.
cancel releases the context's timer even when the call ends early. go vet's lostcancel check reports a cancel function that is never called.

examples.title: Closing and draining bodies decides whether connections are reused

annotations.note: The server's view: StateNew fires once per accepted TCP connection, so the counter is exactly how many connections the client opened.
A Client's Transport is its connection pool. One client for the program means one pool; a new Transport per request would open a connection (and do a TLS handshake) for every call.
An unclosed body keeps its connection busy and a transport goroutine alive, so every call dials again. Under load this ends in "too many open files" or exhausted ephemeral ports.

Closing an unread body says the rest isn't wanted. Rather than read 1 MiB nobody needs, the Transport closes the connection, and the next request dials a new one. For large bodies that is the right trade.

Read to EOF, then close: the connection goes back to the idle pool and the next two requests reuse it. Since Go 1.27 Close also drains unread bodies "up to a conservative limit" (release notes); reading to EOF yourself doesn't depend on where that limit lies.

examples.title: A handler's outgoing call: budget, status mapping, cancellation

annotations.note: The upstream only sees its connection close, so its context reports Canceled in both slow cases. A deadline doesn't travel over plain HTTP; gRPC sends it along as a header (lesson 7).

The outgoing call's context comes from r.Context(): it ends after 300 ms, or earlier if our own caller disconnects. Using context.Background() here would let the work outlive the request that asked for it.
Our deadline becomes 504 Gateway Timeout, any other transport failure 502 Bad Gateway. The caller learns which hop failed, and the message reveals nothing about the upstream.

The caller leaves after 100 ms, well inside the gateway's budget. Cancellation travels the whole chain: caller to gateway (its r.Context()), gateway to upstream (the closed connection), and every hop stops working. The caller's error is context.Canceled, not DeadlineExceeded, so code can tell "not wanted" from "too slow".

use_cases: Every call from a service to another HTTP API: payment providers, internal services, object storage, webhooks you send
Handlers that fan out to upstreams and must answer within their own deadline (a gateway or BFF)
CLIs and jobs that call APIs and must fail with a clear error instead of hanging in CI
strengths: One context carries the deadline and the caller's cancellation through every layer (HTTP calls, SQL queries, your own functions), where Java and Python configure timeouts per library, each with its own API
The Transport pools and reuses connections for you, and the same Client is safe to share between goroutines
Errors keep their cause: errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) works through *url.Error and your own %w wrapping
httptest makes slow, hanging and broken upstreams a few lines of code, so timeout paths get tested
weaknesses: The defaults are unsafe: http.Get, http.Post and the zero Client never time out
Statuses are not errors, so every call site (or one helper) must check StatusCode
Connection reuse depends on how you treat the body, which is invisible until a load test or a file-descriptor limit finds it
Client.Timeout includes reading the body, which is wrong for long downloads; those need a context and a progress check instead

pitfalls.title: Calling with http.Get in service code
pitfalls.detail: It uses DefaultClient (no timeout) and takes no context. Build a client once, with a Timeout, and make requests with NewRequestWithContext.
pitfalls.good:
client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second} // once, at startup

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
resp, err := client.Do(req)

pitfalls.title: Deferring Close before checking the error
pitfalls.detail: On error resp is nil, and the deferred resp.Body.Close() panics when the function returns.

pitfalls.title: A new Client or Transport per request
pitfalls.detail: Each Transport has its own pool, so nothing is reused and idle connections pile up. Share one client per upstream. If you fan out to one host from many goroutines, raise Transport.MaxIdleConnsPerHost: the default is 2.

pitfalls.title: defer cancel() inside a loop
pitfalls.detail: Deferred calls run when the function returns, not at the end of the iteration, so every iteration's timer lives until the loop is done. Put the body of the loop in its own function, or call cancel() explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Draining without a limit
pitfalls.detail: io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) on an error response from a broken upstream can read gigabytes. Drain through io.LimitReader and accept losing the connection beyond that.

quiz.q: client.Do(req) gets back a 503 Service Unavailable. What is err?
quiz.why: Do returns an error only for transport and policy failures. Any status, including 4xx and 5xx, is a response with a nil error.

quiz.q: Client.Timeout is 2 s. Do returns after 1.5 s with the headers; the body needs 3 s more. What happens?
options: The body is read in full: the timeout already passed its check
Reading the body fails at the 2 s mark
Do waits for the whole body before returning
quiz.why: The timer keeps running after Do returns and interrupts the body read. That's why Client.Timeout is wrong for long downloads.

quiz.q: Inside an HTTP handler, which context should an outgoing call use?
options: context.Background(), so a client disconnect can't break the call
quiz.why: Deriving from r.Context() stops the call when the caller leaves, and the timeout keeps it inside the handler's own budget.

quiz.q: You read 100 bytes of a 1 MiB response and call Close. What happens to the connection?
options: It goes back to the idle pool
The Transport reads the remaining bytes, then reuses it
It is closed; the next request dials a new one
quiz.why: Unread data that is not small is not drained: the Transport closes the connection. Go 1.27 drains only small bodies, up to a conservative limit.

further_reading.title: Go 1.27 release notes: Response.Body drains on close

lessons.body:
## Concept

Calling another service comes with three obligations: **bound the wait**, **stop when
nobody needs the answer any more**, and **release what you opened**.

`http.Get`, `http.Post` and `http.DefaultClient` do none of the first two. A
`Client` with a zero `Timeout` has no limit, and `DefaultTransport` only bounds dialing
(30 s) and the TLS handshake (10 s). An upstream that accepts the connection and then
never answers keeps your goroutine, and whatever it holds (a request slot, a database
transaction), forever. That is why the title calls it a bug rather than a style issue.

Two layers bound a call, and whichever ends first wins:

- **`Client.Timeout`**: a ceiling for everything a call does, including redirects and
  reading the body. Set it once per client, as a backstop.
- **The request's context**: `http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, ...)`. It carries this
  call's budget (`context.WithTimeout`) and the caller's cancellation. In a handler it is
  derived from `r.Context()`, so the call stops when the caller disconnects.

Releasing what you opened means: when `Do` returns a nil error, close `resp.Body`. Read
it to EOF if you want the connection back in the pool. And use one client per upstream
for the life of the program, because its `Transport` *is* the connection pool.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: requests doesn't time out by default either; you pass `timeout=` on every
  call, and its read timeout is per gap between bytes, not a total. Go's context
  replaces that argument, is a total, and also carries cancellation, which requests
  has no API for.
- **Java**: `java.net.http.HttpClient` blocks forever unless the request sets
  `HttpRequest.Builder.timeout(...)`; `connectTimeout` is a separate builder setting.
  In Go both the deadline and cancellation travel in the one context.
- **JS**: `fetch` has no timeout option: you pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (the
  equivalent of `WithTimeout`) or an `AbortController` signal (`WithCancel`). Like Go's
  `Do`, `fetch` doesn't fail on a 404 either (lesson ts.services.fetch).
- **C**: libcurl's `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` defaults to 0, meaning no limit, the same trap
  with a different spelling.

## How it works

What each knob bounds, from the bottom up:

- `net.Dialer.Timeout` (in `Transport.DialContext`): the TCP connect.
- `Transport.TLSHandshakeTimeout`: the TLS handshake.
- `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout`: from the request being written to the response
  headers. It does not include the body.
- `Client.Timeout` and the request's context: the whole call, body included. The timer
  keeps running after `Do` returns, which is how `/stall` in example 1 fails during
  `io.ReadAll`.

When the context ends, the Transport closes the connection (on HTTP/1.1) and returns an
error that wraps `context.DeadlineExceeded` or `context.Canceled`. The server on the
other end notices the closed connection and cancels its own `r.Context()`, which is how
cancellation crosses a process boundary without any protocol support.

## Design notes

Build one client per upstream at startup and pass it in through a constructor, wrapped
in a small type with real methods (`GetUser(ctx, id)`): status checks, size limits,
decoding and error mapping then live in one place instead of at every call site. For
custom pool settings, start from `http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone()` and
change what you need; a hand-written `&http.Transport{}` loses the proxy, dial and
HTTP/2 defaults.

Think of deadlines as a budget that shrinks on the way down. A handler with 2 s to
answer should give its upstream call less than that, so it still has time to answer
504 instead of being cut off itself. Plain HTTP doesn't transmit deadlines, so each hop
sets its own; gRPC does transmit them (lesson 7).

`Client.Timeout` is wrong for large downloads, because it caps the body as well. Use a
context there, and cancel it when no progress is made for a while (lesson 3). Since
Go 1.27, closing an unread `Response.Body` drains small remainders for you, so a plain
`defer resp.Body.Close()` usually keeps connections reusable; draining explicitly, with a
limit, makes it deterministic.

lessons.title: Retries with backoff and jitter; 429 and Retry-After; idempotency
lessons.summary: Retry only failures that may go away, only requests that are safe to repeat, and only inside the caller's deadline: exponential backoff with full jitter, the server's Retry-After when it sends one, and an Idempotency-Key for POSTs.

examples.title: Exponential backoff, with and without jitter

annotations.note: The ceiling doubles per attempt and is capped, so a long outage doesn't turn into hour-long sleeps. Clamping attempt before the shift matters too: see the last two lines of output.
A seeded PCG source makes this output repeatable. Production code uses the top-level rand.N, which is randomly seeded per process, so two replicas never share a sequence.
Without jitter every client that failed together retries together: an overloaded service gets the same spike again at 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms. That synchronized wave is what keeps it down.

Full jitter: a uniformly random wait below the ceiling. Rand.N is a generic method, new in Go 1.27 together with generic methods themselves; it accepts time.Duration directly, so there is no int64 conversion.
100ms << 40 overflows int64 into a negative Duration. time.Sleep returns at once for it, turning backoff into a hot loop, and Rand.N panics on a non-positive argument.

examples.title: Retry-After: delay-seconds or an HTTP-date

annotations.note: strconv.Atoi accepts a sign, and the header's grammar doesn't: a negative value is treated as no hint rather than as "retry immediately".
There is no Retry-After parser in net/http, but http.ParseTime reads all three date formats HTTP allows: the preferred IMF-fixdate and the obsolete RFC 850 and asctime formats.

Measuring the date against the response's own Date header cancels out clock skew between the two machines; the local clock is only the fallback. A date in the past means "retry now", not a negative wait.

examples.title: A retry loop that honours 429/503 and Retry-After within a budget

annotations.note: This example gives up on network errors. A GET could be retried after one too; a request that isn't idempotent can't, because the server may have acted on it before the connection died (example 4).
Close the body before waiting, so the connection is back in the pool during the sleep instead of held by a goroutine that's doing nothing.
Retry statuses that mean "try later": 429 and 503 here, 502 and 504 as well for idempotent requests. A 400 or 404 will be just as wrong the second time.
The server's hint wins over our own schedule. Without one, back off with full jitter as in example 1.
When the server asks for longer than our budget allows, fail now and say why. Sleeping until the deadline would fail anyway, later, with a less useful error.
The wait itself watches ctx, so a caller that gives up isn't kept waiting by a sleep. time.Sleep can't be interrupted; a select on a timer and ctx.Done() can.

examples.title: A lost response, a retried POST, and the Idempotency-Key that saves it

annotations.note: The server's half of the contract: the first request with a key does the work and stores the result under the key; every repeat gets the stored result back. In a real service the key row and the charge commit in one transaction, with a unique constraint on the key.

The charge is committed, then the connection dies: http.ErrAbortHandler makes the server drop the connection without answering. To the client this looks exactly like a request that never arrived; nothing on its side can tell the two apart.
A new request per attempt: the first send consumes the body. For a bytes.Reader, NewRequest also sets GetBody, which the Transport uses when it replays a request itself.
crypto/rand.Text (Go 1.24) returns at least 128 random bits as text. The IETF draft recommends a UUID or a similar random identifier.
A new server per run also means a fresh connection. On a reused connection, net/http's Transport would itself retry this POST once: it treats any request with an Idempotency-Key header as idempotent.
One key per logical operation, sent unchanged with every attempt of that operation. A fresh key per attempt would defeat the point.

use_cases: Calls to rate-limited third-party APIs (payment, SMS, e-mail providers) that answer 429 with Retry-After
Internal calls during deploys and failovers, when a few 502/503 responses are expected
Payment, order and booking endpoints, where a client must be able to retry a POST without doing it twice
Background jobs that sync with an external API and must survive transient outages
strengths: The whole policy is a short loop you can read, with no annotation magic like Spring's @Retryable
Context makes the overall budget explicit: the loop stops when the caller's deadline arrives, not after a fixed attempt count
math/rand/v2's seeded PCG and Rand.N make jittered schedules testable and repeatable
Idempotency keys turn at-least-once delivery into exactly-once effects, which no amount of client-side cleverness can
weaknesses: No retry policy in the standard library; the Transport's built-in retry covers only one narrow case
Retries add load exactly when the upstream is struggling; without jitter, caps and a budget they prolong outages
Idempotency needs the server's cooperation (key storage, replay, expiry); the client alone can't make a POST safe
Retry-After has two formats and no parser in net/http

pitfalls.title: Retrying everything
pitfalls.detail: A POST that timed out may have succeeded. Retry automatically only GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE (idempotent by RFC 9110), or requests carrying an idempotency key the server honours. Never retry 4xx other than 408 and 429.

pitfalls.title: Retrying at every layer
pitfalls.detail: A handler retries 3 times a service call that retries 3 times a database call that retries 3 times: 27 attempts per user request during an outage. Retry in one layer, usually the one closest to the failing call, and make the rest fail fast.

pitfalls.title: Sleeping with time.Sleep
pitfalls.detail: It ignores cancellation and keeps the goroutine (and whatever it holds) busy after the caller left.

pitfalls.title: A new idempotency key per attempt
pitfalls.detail: Generate the key when the user's action starts (and persist it with the pending operation if the client can crash), not inside the retry loop.

pitfalls.title: Unclamped exponentials
pitfalls.detail: base << attempt overflows for large attempts and produces a negative or zero Duration. Clamp the exponent and cap the result.

quiz.q: Your POST /payments timed out after the request was fully sent. What do you know about the payment?
options: It failed: no response means no effect
It succeeded: the request was sent
Nothing: it may or may not have happened
It will be rolled back by TCP
quiz.why: The server may have committed and lost the response, as in example 4. Only an idempotency key makes a retry safe.

quiz.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: To make the average wait shorter
To spread out clients that failed at the same moment, so their retries don't arrive together
quiz.why: Plain exponential backoff keeps synchronized clients synchronized; random waits spread the load over the whole interval.

quiz.q: A 429 says Retry-After: 120 and your context has 30 s left. What should the client do?
options: Fail now with an error that mentions the server's requested wait
quiz.why: No attempt within the budget can succeed. Failing at once frees the caller and reports the real cause.

quiz.q: Which request does net/http's Transport retry by itself after a network error on a reused connection?
options: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, or any request with an Idempotency-Key header, if its body can be replayed
quiz.why: The Transport documentation lists exactly these conditions. It's one retry for a stale keep-alive connection, not a retry policy.

further_reading.title: package net/http: Transport (when it retries by itself)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A retry turns a transient failure into a success, and a permanent one into extra load.
Four questions decide whether to retry:

1. **Is the failure transient?** 429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable say
   "later" outright; 502 and 504 usually mean a proxy lost its upstream for a moment;
   connection errors often mean a restart. Other 4xx statuses won't change on a retry.
2. **Is the request safe to repeat?** An idempotent request has the same effect whether
   it runs once or five times: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are defined that way by
   RFC 9110. A POST isn't, unless it carries an **idempotency key** that the server uses
   to recognize the repeat and answer with the original result.
3. **How long to wait?** Exponential backoff, capped, with **jitter**, so that clients
   that failed together don't retry together. If the server sends `Retry-After`, that
   wins.
4. **When to stop?** After a few attempts, and always when the caller's context ends.
   Retries happen inside the deadline, never in addition to it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Spring Retry's `@Retryable` and Resilience4j's `Retry` configure the same
  knobs (attempts, backoff, which exceptions) declaratively. In Go it's a loop you write
  once in your client type, and the context replaces the separate total-timeout setting.
- **Python**: urllib3's `Retry`, mounted into a requests `Session` through `HTTPAdapter`,
  has `total`, `backoff_factor`, `status_forcelist` and `allowed_methods`. Those names
  map directly onto the loop in example 3.
- **JS**: `fetch` never retries. The usual hand-written loop with `await new
  Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms))` is example 3 with an `AbortSignal` in place of the
  context (lesson ts.services.advanced).
- **C**: nothing built in; libcurl leaves retries to the application as well.

## How it works

net/http's `Transport` does retry by itself, in one narrow case: a network error on a
**reused** keep-alive connection, for a request that is idempotent and whose body can
be replayed. Its documentation counts GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as idempotent, and
also any request whose header map contains `Idempotency-Key` or `X-Idempotency-Key`.
That covers a server closing an idle connection just as you reuse it; it is not a policy
for 503s.

The `Idempotency-Key` header is specified in an IETF draft
(draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header, not yet an RFC). It recommends a UUID or a
similar random value per operation, and says the server should answer 409 Conflict while
a request with the same key is still being processed, 422 when a key is reused with a
different payload, and 400 when a required key is missing. Payment providers have used
the same header for years.

## Design notes

Retry in one layer only, usually the client type that wraps the upstream; everything
above it should fail fast. Bound the extra load: a few attempts, a capped backoff, and in
busy systems a retry budget (for example, retries may add at most 10% to the request
rate) or a circuit breaker that stops calling an upstream that keeps failing.

The idempotency key is the client's half of a contract. The server's half is a table
keyed by the idempotency key, written in the same transaction as the effect, with a unique
constraint so two concurrent attempts can't both win (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, lesson
sql.modifying.returning-upsert), and an expiry after which keys are forgotten. Generate
the key when the operation starts, not per attempt, and store it with the pending
operation if the client can crash between attempts.

Keep the policy testable: inject the random source (and, if you like, the sleep
function), as the examples do with a seeded `rand.Rand`, and a test can assert the
exact schedule without waiting for it.

lessons.title: Cursor pagination and streaming large responses
lessons.summary: Wrap a paged API in an iterator that follows the cursor and fetches lazily; prefer cursors over offsets, which skip and repeat rows while others write. Stream big downloads to disk through a hash, with a stall watchdog instead of a total timeout.

examples.title: A paged API as an iter.Seq2 that fetches pages on demand

annotations.note: The usual page shape: the items plus an opaque cursor for the next page, absent on the last one. The client never parses the cursor; it only sends it back.
iter.Seq2 (Go 1.23) lets callers write a plain for-range over every item and never see pages. Paging and cursors stay in one function.
An error is yielded as a value, once, and then the sequence ends. That is the common convention for Seq2[T, error]: the caller decides whether to stop or log and continue.
When yield returns false the caller has left its loop (break, return, panic). The iterator must stop right there; calling yield again panics at run time.
The cursor here is just the last ID, base64-encoded so clients treat it as opaque. Real APIs often also sign or encrypt it, so they can change what's inside without breaking clients.

The IDs are Turkish licence-plate codes, and pages are ordered by ID: behind this API runs a keyset query, WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3. Ordering by name would be harder: compared byte by byte, İstanbul and İzmir sort after Konya, because İ is a two-byte character beyond ASCII. Names need a Turkish collation (golang.org/x/text/collate).
fetch is a parameter, so a fake API can stand in for the real one. In a client type it's the method that sends lesson 1's GET with a context and decodes the JSON page.
Laziness pays off: the loop stops at Bursa, the iterator returns, and the third page is never requested.

examples.title: Offset pages repeat and skip rows when the data changes; cursors don't

annotations.note: OFFSET counts positions. The returned page is a copy, as it would be after a JSON round trip; returning a subslice would let the in-place DeleteFunc below change page 1 after the fact.
A keyset cursor names the last row seen. Rows inserted before it or deleted after it can't shift the next page.

A new post at the top pushes everything down one position, so the offset client sees post 8 twice. A deleted post pulls everything up, so post 7 is never seen at all. Neither failure produces an error.

examples.title: Stream 10 MB to disk through a hash; rename only when verified

annotations.note: Write to a temp file next to the target, and rename only when the file is complete and verified. A failed download never leaves a half-written cities.csv for someone else to read.
io.Copy moves the body through one 32 KiB buffer, and MultiWriter feeds each chunk to the file and the hash, so memory stays flat whether the body is 10 MB or 10 GB. io.ReadAll would hold all of it.

Content-Digest (RFC 9530) carries a hash of the bytes as sent. A body that ends early looks like a normal end of stream to io.Copy (no Content-Length here); only the digest catches it, and the file is not renamed into place.
Each line is 30 characters but 34 bytes: İ, Ş and ı take two bytes each in UTF-8. Sizes, Content-Length and offsets are always in bytes.

examples.title: Bound stalls, not total time: a watchdog that cancels with a cause

annotations.note: A reader that wraps a reader: every chunk that arrives pushes the stall deadline back. This bounds "no progress", which is what you actually care about for a download of unknown duration.
The transfer takes 2 s, longer than the 1 s idle limit, and is never cut off: only a gap without data counts.
Clone keeps DefaultTransport's settings and adds a bound on the wait for headers. There is deliberately no Client.Timeout, which would also cut off a slow but healthy 10 GB download.
WithCancelCause (Go 1.20) lets the watchdog say why it cancelled. The Transport reports context.Cause from the body read, so the error the caller sees is errStalled, not a bare "context canceled".
The watchdog starts once the headers are in; until then the Transport's ResponseHeaderTimeout is in charge.

use_cases: Syncing every record from a SaaS API (customers, invoices, tickets) into your database
Exports and backups that are larger than the memory of the process downloading them
Infinite-scroll feeds and admin tables whose data changes while users page through it
strengths: Range-over-func iterators let a paged API look like a slice to its callers, and stop fetching when they stop reading
io.Reader composition (wrappers, MultiWriter, TeeReader) builds a streaming pipeline in a few lines, with constant memory
Keyset pagination is stable under concurrent writes and as fast on the last page as on the first
A cancel cause makes timeouts self-describing: the error says stalled, not just canceled
weaknesses: Cursors can't jump to page 37 or show a total page count; offsets can, at the cost of correctness and speed
Iterator errors need a convention (Seq2 with error), since a for-range has no error return
Streaming means the caller sees partial data before it is validated; the temp-file-and-rename discipline is on you
There's no built-in progress or stall timeout on Response.Body; you wrap the reader yourself

pitfalls.title: Reading a large body with io.ReadAll
pitfalls.detail: It holds the whole response in memory, growing the buffer by repeated reallocation along the way. Stream to the destination with io.Copy, and cap what you accept with io.LimitReader if the size is untrusted.
pitfalls.good: n, err := io.Copy(f, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, maxBytes))

pitfalls.title: Writing the final file in place
pitfalls.detail: A download that fails halfway leaves a truncated file under the real name, and the next run or another process trusts it. Write to a temp file in the same directory and rename after verification, so readers see the old file or the new one, never half of one (go.files-io.writing).

pitfalls.title: Verifying a digest after transparent decompression
pitfalls.detail: If the Transport asked for gzip itself, it decompresses the body for you and deletes Content-Encoding (resp.Uncompressed is true). Your hash then covers decoded bytes, while Content-Digest covers the gzip bytes that were sent. Set Transport.DisableCompression, or request the encoding explicitly, when you verify digests.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting to stop the iterator
pitfalls.detail: An iterator that ignores yield's false return keeps fetching pages nobody reads, and calling yield after it returned false panics. Return as soon as yield says stop.

pitfalls.title: Parsing or constructing cursors on the client
pitfalls.detail: Cursors are opaque by contract; the server may change their format at any time. Store and send them back verbatim, URL-encoded.

quiz.q: A client pages through /posts?offset=N newest first. A new post is published between page 1 and page 2. What does the client see?
options: The last post of page 1 again at the top of page 2
The new post at the top of page 2
quiz.why: Everything moved down one position, so offset 3 now points at what used to be the third row. Keyset cursors don't move with positions.

quiz.q: In a for c, err := range cities(...) loop the caller hits break. What must the iterator function do?
options: Fetch the rest of the pages so the connection can be reused
Call yield once more with io.EOF
quiz.why: yield returning false means the loop is over; calling yield again panics, and the iterator should stop fetching.

quiz.q: Why is Client.Timeout a poor fit for a 5 GB download?
options: It caps the whole exchange including the body, so a slow but healthy download is cut off
quiz.why: Client.Timeout includes reading the body. A stall watchdog bounds the absence of progress instead of the total time.

quiz.q: What does io.Copy(io.MultiWriter(file, hash), resp.Body) hold in memory?
options: One buffer of a fixed size
quiz.why: Neither side implements WriterTo or ReaderFrom here, so io.Copy loops over a single 32 KiB buffer and writes each chunk to both destinations.

lessons.body:
## Concept

APIs that return collections hand them out in pages, and there are two ways to say
"the next page":

- **Offset**: `?offset=40&limit=20`, "skip 40 rows". Simple, and lets a UI jump to any
  page, but the server still reads and discards the skipped rows, and positions shift
  whenever someone inserts or deletes: rows are repeated or silently skipped.
- **Cursor (keyset)**: `?cursor=...`, where the cursor encodes the last row you saw, and
  the server continues *after* it (`WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`). Stable under
  concurrent writes, and as fast on page 10,000 as on page 1, but only forward (and
  backward), with no "page 37".

On the client, wrap the paging in an **iterator** (`iter.Seq2[T, error]`, Go 1.23):
callers range over items, pages are fetched only as the loop asks for more, and a
`break` stops the fetching.

Large responses are **streams**. `resp.Body` is an `io.Reader`; copy it to its
destination in chunks instead of reading it into memory. Downloads get two extra
guards: write to a temp file and rename only after verifying (size, digest), and bound
*stalls* rather than total time, because a healthy 10 GB transfer may take an hour.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: a generator that `yield`s items and fetches the next page inside the loop
  is exactly `iter.Seq2`; `requests.get(url, stream=True)` with `iter_content()` is the
  streaming half.
- **Java**: you would implement `Iterator<T>` or `Spliterator` (or a reactive
  `Flux`) for the pages; `InputStream.transferTo(OutputStream)` is `io.Copy`.
- **JS/TS**: an `async function*` generator consumed with `for await`, and
  `response.body` as a `ReadableStream` piped through a `TransformStream` (lesson
  ts.services.advanced). Go's version is synchronous code; the goroutine blocks, nothing
  else does.
- **C**: a `read()` loop into a fixed buffer, plus `rename(2)` for the atomic replace:
  the same design, with the error handling done by hand.

## How it works

A range-over-func loop calls the iterator once, passing `yield`; each `yield(item, nil)`
runs the loop body. A `break` in the body makes `yield` return false, and the iterator
must return then. That's how the stop propagates without channels or goroutines: the
whole thing is ordinary function calls on one stack.

In example 4, the stall watchdog is a `time.AfterFunc` that cancels the request's
context with a cause. Cancelling the context makes the Transport close the connection
and fail the pending `Read` on the body; the error the Transport reports is
`context.Cause(ctx)`, so `io.Copy` returns `errStalled` itself.

## Design notes

When you design the API (the server side), prefer cursors for anything that is written
to while being read, and make them opaque: base64 at least, signed if clients could
gain anything by forging them. Order by a unique key, or by a tuple ending in one
(`ORDER BY created_at, id` with `WHERE (created_at, id) > ($1, $2)`), or ties at page
boundaries produce the same skip-and-repeat bugs as offsets. The SQL side, including the
index that makes this fast, is in sql.indexes.stats-pagination.

On the consuming side, an iterator is the right boundary: the sync job that needs every
invoice writes `for inv, err := range client.Invoices(ctx)`, and retries (lesson 2) live
inside `fetch`. Keep the cursor of the last completed page, and a crashed sync can resume
where it stopped instead of starting over.

For downloads, decide what "done" means before starting: a byte count, a digest, or both.
Then nothing else may see the file until it is done. The same pattern (temp file, fsync
if durability matters, rename) is in go.files-io.writing.

lessons.title: Webhooks with HMAC signature verification
lessons.summary: A webhook is an unauthenticated POST until you prove otherwise. Verify an HMAC over the raw body and a timestamp with hmac.Equal, reject stale timestamps, deduplicate by event ID, and only then parse and act.

examples.title: Verify signature and freshness, and see which replay still gets through

annotations.note: HMAC-SHA256 with a secret shared only by sender and receiver. The timestamp is part of the signed message, so an attacker can't take a captured request and simply put a fresh timestamp on it.

The header may carry several v1 signatures: during a rotation the sender signs with both the old and the new secret. Signatures are compared as decoded bytes, so upper- or lowercase hex doesn't matter.
The freshness window limits replays to five minutes. It also requires roughly synchronized clocks on both sides (NTP); the window absorbs the difference.

hmac.Equal takes the same time whether the first or the last byte differs. With bytes.Equal or ==, response times leak how many leading bytes of a guess were right, and the MAC can be found byte by byte.
verify takes "now" as a parameter, so tests and this example control the clock without sleeping.
The receiver accepts two secrets while a rotation is in progress, so events signed with the old one keep verifying until the sender has switched.
A copy of a valid request, replayed inside the window, passes every check here. Senders also deliver at least once on their own, so the event ID has to decide: see How it works.

Fail closed: no header, a bad header, an old timestamp and a wrong MAC all end in a rejection. The reason is printed for the demo; a real receiver logs it and answers with a bare 403, which tells a prober nothing.

examples.title: Why the MAC must be checked on the bytes received, not a re-encoding

annotations.note: Python's json.dumps escapes non-ASCII characters by default, so ş travels as a six-character escape. The sender signed exactly these bytes.

Decoding and re-encoding gives the same JSON value but different bytes: Go writes ş as UTF-8, escapes <, > and & for HTML safety, and sorts map keys. Any framework that hands you a parsed object instead of the raw body has the same problem.

Only the received bytes verify. A receiver built on the shortcut rejects valid events whenever the encodings differ (here: Turkish letters, the HTML characters and the key order), and such a check tends to get "fixed" by switching verification off.
After decoding, "Ayşe Çelik" is 10 characters and 12 bytes in UTF-8. On the wire it was longer still: each escape is six bytes.

use_cases: Payment, shipping and e-mail providers notifying you of events (payment succeeded, parcel delivered, message bounced)
Git hosting and CI systems triggering builds and deployments
Your own service sending webhooks to customers: the same scheme, from the signing side
strengths: crypto/hmac and crypto/sha256 are in the standard library, and hmac.Equal is constant-time, so the whole scheme is a few dozen lines without dependencies
Verification needs no network round trip or key server, unlike checking a token against an identity provider
Reading the body as []byte first makes 'verify the raw bytes' the natural order in Go, unlike frameworks that parse JSON before your handler runs
weaknesses: A shared secret has to be stored on both sides and rotated by hand; a leak on either side lets anyone forge events
Every provider has its own header format, signed-message layout and encoding (hex or base64), so each needs its own small verifier
