Tests run against the same PostgreSQL version and extensions as production, where an in-memory substitute such as H2 or SQLite in Java and Python stacks differs in SQL dialect and locking
Plain env vars and flags (TEST_DATABASE_URL, -tags, -count=1) work the same locally, in CI and in a container
weaknesses: Tagged files are invisible to go build, go vet and gopls unless they get the tag too, so they can stop compiling without anyone noticing
go test ./... runs package test binaries in parallel (-p defaults to GOMAXPROCS); packages sharing one database need separate schemas or -p 1
Committed test data needs explicit cleanup or isolation, which costs time and code that the rollback-per-test technique avoids
Needs a running PostgreSQL: a service in CI, a local install or a container, plus migrations

pitfalls.title: Pointing tests at DATABASE_URL
pitfalls.detail: Tests that TRUNCATE tables must never pick up the development or production connection string by accident. Read a variable only tests use, such as TEST_DATABASE_URL, as this app does.

pitfalls.title: Letting the tagged files rot
pitfalls.detail: go vet ./... and the editor skip files behind the tag. Run go vet -tags integration ./... in CI (it needs no database), and set gopls's buildFlags to ["-tags=integration"].

pitfalls.title: Trusting a cached result
pitfalls.detail: A database test that passed is cached as long as its binary, files and environment are unchanged, even if the schema changed underneath. Run integration tests with -count=1.

pitfalls.title: Skipping silently in CI
pitfalls.detail: If TEST_DATABASE_URL is missing in CI, every database test skips and the job is green. Fail when the tag is set and the variable isn't, or check the skip count.

pitfalls.title: Old-style constraints
pitfalls.detail: Code from before Go 1.17 has // +build integration lines. gofmt adds the equivalent //go:build line; the //go:build form is the one to write.

quiz.q: A file starts with //go:build integration. What does plain go test ./... do with it?
options: Doesn't compile it, so its tests don't exist in that run
Runs its tests and skips them at runtime
quiz.why: Build constraints exclude the file from the package unless the tag is set with -tags integration.

quiz.q: Why add -count=1 when running the integration suite?
options: To run each test once instead of twice
To bypass the test cache, which can't know the database changed
quiz.why: go test caches passing results keyed on the binary, flags, files read and env vars; external state such as a database isn't part of the key.

quiz.q: The code under test commits its own transactions. How do you isolate tests?
options: Wrap each test in a transaction and roll back
Reset the tables (TRUNCATE) or use a schema per test
quiz.why: A rollback can't undo what the code already committed in its own transactions; committed data has to be cleared or kept in separate schemas.

quiz.q: Where should one-time setup such as connecting and migrating go?
options: At the start of every test
quiz.why: TestMain runs once per test binary, wraps all tests, can stop with a clear error before any test runs and can clean up after m.Run; init has no place for teardown.

further_reading.title: go command: testing flags (-count, -short, test caching)
PostgreSQL: SELECT, The Locking Clause (SKIP LOCKED)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Split the test suite in two along what it needs:

- **Unit tests** need nothing outside the process. They run on every `go test ./...`,
  in seconds, on any machine.
- **Integration tests** need a real PostgreSQL. They live in files whose first line is
  `//go:build integration`, so they are compiled only with
  `go test -tags integration ./...`.

Inside the tagged files, a second gate says where the database is: an environment
variable such as `TEST_DATABASE_URL`, with tests skipping (locally) or failing (in CI)
when it is missing. Expensive setup happens once per package in `TestMain`: connect,
run the migrations, call `m.Run()`, close. Each test then gets a clean state, by a
rolled-back transaction when the code under test accepts one, or by resetting tables
or using its own schema when the code commits.

A third, lighter gate is `testing.Short()`: true under `go test -short`, for tests that
are slow but need nothing external.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Maven runs `*IT.java` with Failsafe in a later phase, or JUnit 5 `@Tag`s
  filter at runtime. A Go build tag works at compile time: the tests don't exist in the
  default build. Testcontainers starts a database per run; in Go you pass a URL to one
  you already run, or start a container in `TestMain`.
- **Python**: `@pytest.mark.integration` with `-m integration`, and a session-scoped
  fixture for the connection, is the same split; `TestMain` is the session fixture.
- **JS/TS**: separate Vitest or Jest configs or projects for integration tests, often
  with `globalSetup` doing what `TestMain` does here.
- **C/C++**: like a CMake option or `#ifdef` that compiles a test target only when
  asked for.

## How it works

The go command decides which files belong to a package before compiling. A file whose
`//go:build` expression is false for this build is left out entirely, so tags work for
any condition: `integration`, `linux`, `go1.27`. `-tags a,b` adds tags. The constraint
must precede the package clause and be followed by a blank line; one `//go:build` line
per file.

This app does exactly this. `server/internal/sqlrun/sqlrun_test.go`,
`multisession_test.go` and `server/internal/runexec/runexec_integration_test.go` carry
`//go:build integration` above the package clause and skip unless `TEST_DATABASE_URL` is
set, while `split_test.go` beside them has no tag:

```
cd server
go test ./...                                    # unit tests only
# the playground database from .env.example:
$env:TEST_DATABASE_URL = "postgres://playground:playground@127.0.0.1:5432/playground"
go test -tags integration -count=1 ./...         # plus the PostgreSQL suite
```

(`$env:` is PowerShell; in bash it is `TEST_DATABASE_URL=... go test ...`.) The
`Makefile` also runs `go test -tags integration ./internal/gorun/`, where the tag guards
tests that compile and run real programs and so need a Go toolchain rather than a
database.

The lesson runtime has no flags, so example 2 has no tag. It reads `DATABASE_URL`, which
the runner sets to the playground database with an empty schema of its own, dropped
after the run. That is also why the example can commit freely.

## Design notes

Keep the default `go test ./...` hermetic and fast; it is what runs on every save. Make
the integration suite easy to run on demand (one documented command, one environment
variable) and mandatory in CI, where a missing database must fail the job rather than
skip it. Run `go vet -tags integration ./...` in the fast pipeline too: it compiles the
tagged files without needing a database.

Choose isolation by what the code under test does. If it takes a `DBTX`-style interface,
give each test a transaction and roll it back (go.postgres.repository-testing). If it
commits, as a job queue or anything with its own transactions must, reset tables before
each test, or give each test (or each package, when `go test ./...` runs packages in
parallel) its own schema and set `search_path`. A test schema per package also stops
two packages from truncating each other's tables mid-run.

Test the behaviour only the database can give you: constraints, collations (a unique
index on `lower(name)` treats `IŞIL` and `ışıl` as different users in a `C.UTF-8`
database), locks, isolation levels, `SKIP LOCKED`. Everything above that line is
better served by fakes and fast unit tests.

lessons.title: What changed from Go 1.21 to 1.27 and how to spot old code
lessons.summary: Seven releases changed everyday Go: per-iteration loop variables, range over ints and functions, wg.Go, os.Root, errors.AsType, new(expr), json/v2 and a standard uuid package. Knowing which version brought what tells you how old a piece of code, or a blog post, is.

examples.title: Go 1.21 loop semantics, reproduced on Go 1.27

annotations.note: A //go:build line naming a Go release sets the language version of this one file (in modules at go 1.21 or later). Here it brings back the pre-1.22 loop semantics on a 1.27 toolchain. Delete the line and run again: all three outputs become Adana Bursa Çorum / 0 1 2.
Before Go 1.22, one variable c served every iteration. Each closure captured that variable, not its value, and saw its last value after the loop: Çorum three times.
The fix everyone wrote for ten years. In code whose go line is 1.22 or later it is redundant, and go fix (the forvar analyzer) removes it. Seeing it is a reliable sign the code predates 1.22.
The same applies to three-clause loops: all three pointers point at one i, which ended at 3. Since Go 1.22, each iteration gets a copy of i, and the increment applies to the next copy.

examples.title: Go 1.21 to 1.24: built-ins, sorted keys, iterators, range over int

annotations.note: The old way to iterate a map in order: copy the keys, sort.Strings, loop. Still correct, just longer than it needs to be.
An iterator is a plain function of type iter.Seq[int]: it calls yield for each value and must return when yield returns false. No channel, no goroutine, no interface.
Range over an int (Go 1.22) replaces for i := 0; i < limit; i++.
Byte order, both ways: İ is U+0130, encoded as C4 B0, so İzmir sorts after Muğla. Turkish alphabetical order needs a collator such as golang.org/x/text/collate, whatever the Go version.
min and max are built-ins since Go 1.21 and take any number of ordered arguments; cmp.Or (Go 1.22) returns its first non-zero argument, handy for defaults from configuration.
break inside a range-over-func loop makes yield return false, and Evens stops. A million-element range is never materialized.
strings.SplitSeq (Go 1.24) yields the parts without allocating the slice that strings.Split builds. strings.Lines and FieldsSeq are its siblings.

examples.title: Go 1.24 to 1.27: wg.Go, new(expr), os.Root, errors.AsType, json/v2, uuid

annotations.note: wg.Go (Go 1.25) does Add(1), starts the goroutine and calls Done when it returns. The closure can use i directly because loop variables are per iteration since 1.22.
new(true) (Go 1.26) allocates a variable with that initial value. Old code has helpers such as func ptr[T any](v T) *T for optional fields like this one.

os.Root (Go 1.24) resolves every name inside its directory and refuses ../.env. errors.AsType (Go 1.26) returns the typed error and a bool, instead of declaring a target and passing its address to errors.As.
In Go 1.27 encoding/json runs on the v2 implementation but keeps v1 behaviour: the duplicate key is accepted and the last value wins. encoding/json/v2 rejects it by default.

The standard library's uuid package (Go 1.27; import path "uuid"). New is currently NewV4; NewV7 starts with a millisecond timestamp, so ids sort by creation time and index well as primary keys. Parse also accepts braces, urn:uuid: and upper case.

use_cases: Reading code or a blog post and dating it: n := n in loops, sort.Strings on map keys, wg.Add(1) before go func
Reviewing a pull request in a module at go 1.27 that still uses pre-1.22 idioms copied from older code
Upgrading a service: raise the go line, run the tests, run go fix ./... until its diff is empty
Choosing dependencies: uuid v4/v7, JSON strictness and errgroup-free fan-out no longer need third-party modules
strengths: Language changes are gated per module by the go line (and per file by //go:build go1.N), so old code keeps its meaning after a toolchain upgrade; Java and C++ change semantics only through compiler flags for the whole build
The compiler names the release a feature needs ("requires go1.22 or later"), and vet's stdversion check does the same for library APIs
go fix (rewritten in Go 1.26) applies most modernizations mechanically: rangeint, forvar, minmax, waitgroupgo, errorsastype, newexpr, stringsseq, omitzero
The Go 1 compatibility promise means old idioms still compile and run; modernizing is a choice, not a migration deadline
weaknesses: Old idioms stay valid, so codebases mix styles for years; reviewers have to know both
Library APIs aren't gated by the compiler: a module at go 1.21 can call errors.AsType and only vet (stdversion, run by go test since 1.27) notices
The uuid package covers versions 4 and 7 only; name-based v5 or other versions still need a module such as github.com/google/uuid

Behaviour changes that aren't syntax (timer channels in 1.23, encoding/json on the v2 engine in 1.27) need release-note reading; GODEBUG settings and GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 roll some back, but only for a few releases (asynctimerchan is gone in 1.27)

pitfalls.title: Removing x := x without raising the go line
pitfalls.detail: The copy is only redundant when the module (or file) is at go 1.22 or later. In a go 1.21 module, removing it brings the shared-variable bug back.

pitfalls.title: Concluding from the toolchain version
pitfalls.detail: Building with Go 1.27 doesn't give a module 1.27 semantics; its go line does. A module at go 1.21 built with Go 1.27 still shares loop variables.

pitfalls.title: Hand-written ptr helpers and Add/Done pairs in new code
pitfalls.detail: They still work, but each has a one-call replacement with fewer ways to go wrong (a forgotten Done, an Add inside the goroutine).
pitfalls.good: wg.Go(func() { work(i) })

pitfalls.title: Assuming encoding/json became strict in 1.27
pitfalls.detail: The v1 package now runs on the v2 engine, but with v1 semantics: duplicate names, case-insensitive matching and invalid UTF-8 are accepted as before. Strict defaults come from importing encoding/json/v2.

quiz.q: A closure inside for _, v := range items captures v. When does every closure see the last item?
options: When the module's go line (or the file's //go:build go1.N) is below 1.22
quiz.why: Per-iteration variables are a language change gated by the language version, not by the installed toolchain.

quiz.q: Which release added each? wg.Go, os.Root, errors.AsType, package uuid.
quiz.why: The API files of the Go 1.27 distribution list WaitGroup.Go in go1.25, os.OpenRoot in go1.24, errors.AsType in go1.26 and package uuid in go1.27.

quiz.q: In Go 1.27, what does encoding/json (v1) do with {"name":"a","name":"b"}?
options: Rejects it: v1 now uses v2 rules
Accepts it; the last value wins
quiz.why: v1 is backed by the v2 implementation but preserves v1 behaviour; only encoding/json/v2 rejects duplicate names by default.

quiz.q: Your module says go 1.21 and calls errors.AsType. What happens on Go 1.27?
options: It builds; go vet and go test report errors.AsType requires go1.26 or later
quiz.why: The compiler gates syntax by language version; standard-library symbols are checked by vet's stdversion analyzer.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Go changes slowly and keeps old code compiling, so code written for Go 1.20 still runs
on Go 1.27. What changes is what idiomatic code looks like. The releases from 1.21
(August 2023) to 1.27 (August 2026), by what you meet daily:

- **1.21**: built-ins `min`, `max`, `clear`; packages `slices`, `maps`, `cmp`,
  `log/slog`; `sync.OnceFunc`/`OnceValue`; the `go` line in `go.mod` becomes a
  minimum requirement, and toolchains can switch themselves.
- **1.22**: each loop iteration gets its own variables; `for i := range n`;
  `math/rand/v2`; `net/http` patterns with methods and wildcards (`"GET /users/{id}"`,
  `r.PathValue`); `cmp.Or`.
- **1.23**: range over functions (`iter.Seq`, `iter.Seq2`), with iterator helpers in
  `slices` and `maps` (`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))`); timers whose channels need no
  draining; package `unique`.
- **1.24**: generic type aliases; `os.Root`; `testing.B.Loop` and `T.Context`;
  `strings.Lines`, `SplitSeq`, `FieldsSeq`; the `omitzero` JSON tag option; `tool`
  directives in `go.mod`; a Swiss-table map implementation.
- **1.25**: `sync.WaitGroup.Go`; `testing/synctest`; `GOMAXPROCS` that respects
  container CPU limits on Linux; experimental Green Tea GC and `encoding/json/v2`.
- **1.26**: `new(expr)`; `errors.AsType`; generic types that refer to themselves in
  their constraints; Green Tea GC on by default; `go fix` rebuilt around modernizers.
- **1.27**: generic methods; struct literal keys that name promoted fields;
  `encoding/json/v2` and `jsontext` without an experiment flag, with `encoding/json`
  running on the v2 engine; package `uuid`; `httptest.NewTestServer`.

The stdlib UUID the curriculum mentions is real: `import "uuid"` (no domain in the path),
with `New` (currently version 4), `NewV4`, `NewV7`, `Parse`, `MustParse`, `Nil`, `Max`
and `Compare`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: comparable to the jump from Java 8 to 21 (records, `var`, switch
  expressions, virtual threads), except Go gates language changes per module through
  `go.mod` rather than with `--release` for the whole build.
- **Python**: the loop-variable change fixes Go's version of the late-binding closure
  trap (`lambda: i` in a loop), which Python still has.
- **JS**: the same story as `var` versus `let` in `for` loops: ES2015 gave each
  iteration its own binding, and Go 1.22 did the same almost nine years later.
  `iter.Seq` plays the role of generator functions, without `function*`.
- **C++**: like moving between `-std=c++17` and `-std=c++20`, chosen by each module
  instead of each build.

## How it works

Every file is compiled at a **language version**: the `go` line of its module, or a
`//go:build go1.N` constraint on the file. The compiler rejects newer syntax and names
the release it needs, as these real errors for a module at `go 1.21` show:

```
cannot range over 3 (untyped int constant): requires go1.22 or later (-lang was set to go1.21; check go.mod)
new(42) requires go1.26 or later (-lang was set to go1.21; check go.mod)
generic method requires go1.27 or later (-lang was set to go1.21; check go.mod)
```

Standard-library additions are not compile errors. They are reported by vet's
`stdversion` analyzer, which `go test` runs by default since Go 1.27:

```
main.go:23:5: sync.(*WaitGroup).Go requires go1.25 or later (module is go1.21)
main.go:25:16: errors.AsType requires go1.26 or later (module is go1.21)
main.go:26:11: uuid.NewV7 requires go1.27 or later (module is go1.21)
```

Behaviour changes in the runtime and library follow the `go` line too, through
**GODEBUG** defaults. Built with Go 1.27, `panic(nil)` in a module at `go 1.20` still
recovers as `nil`; at `go 1.21` it recovers as `runtime error: panic called with nil
argument`. These settings are temporary: Go 1.27 removed `asynctimerchan`, so pre-1.23
timer channels are gone whatever the go line says.

### Spotting old code

Signs that code predates a release, with the `go fix` analyzer that rewrites it:

- `x := x` inside a loop: before 1.22 (`forvar`).
- `for i := 0; i < n; i++` with `i` only counting: before 1.22 (`rangeint`).
- if/else to clamp values, `sort.Slice` on basic types: before 1.21 (`minmax`, `slicessort`).
- `for _, s := range strings.Split(...)`: before 1.24 (`stringsseq`).
- `wg.Add(1)` with `defer wg.Done()` in the goroutine: before 1.25 (`waitgroupgo`).
- `var pe *fs.PathError; errors.As(err, &pe)`: before 1.26 (`errorsastype`).
- `func ptr[T any](v T) *T { return &v }`: before 1.26 (`newexpr`).
- `json:",omitempty"` on a `time.Time` or struct field: before 1.24 (`omitzero`).
- `context.WithCancel(context.Background())` in tests: before 1.24 (`testingcontext`).
- `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++` in benchmarks, `github.com/google/uuid` for v4 or v7 ids,
  channels used as generators, `filepath.Join` plus prefix checks on user paths:
  no fixer; change by hand.

A real `go fix -diff` on such code (module at go 1.27) rewrote the loop, the WaitGroup,
the `errors.As` and the pointer helper in one pass, and removed `i := i` on the second:

```
-	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
+	for i := range n {
 		i := i
-		wg.Add(1)
-		go func() {
-			defer wg.Done()
+		wg.Go(func() {
 			out[i] = i * i
-		}()
+		})
```

## Design notes

Upgrade in this order: raise the `go` line (`go get go@1.27.0`), run the tests, then
run `go fix ./...` until it reports nothing, and commit that mechanical diff
separately. The language-version gate means the first step can change behaviour (loop
variables, GODEBUG defaults), which is why tests come before the cleanup.

When you read Go elsewhere, date it before copying it. Advice to write `v := v`, to
drain a timer before `Reset`, to call `rand.Seed`, or to pick a third-party router for
path parameters was correct once and is noise now. The opposite also holds: code
using `wg.Go` or `new(expr)` needs at least the release that introduced them, which
matters for libraries whose users may be on older toolchains.

Some decisions don't change with versions. Sorting strings still compares bytes, so
`İzmir` sorts after `Muğla`; Turkish order still needs a collator. And a UUID in the
standard library doesn't change the database side: PostgreSQL 18 has its own
`uuidv7()`, so decide which side generates ids and keep it to one.

lessons.title: The go command: mod, run, build, test, vet, fmt, doc
lessons.summary: One binary builds, runs, tests, vets, formats and documents Go code. A package is a directory of files compiled together; a module is a tree of packages under one go.mod, versioned as a unit.

examples.title: go mod init makes a module of packages; go list, go run and go doc show it

annotations.note: An import path is the module path plus the package's directory: example.com/hello + greet. There are no relative imports inside a module, so moving a directory means updating its import paths.

go mod init writes go.mod with the module path and a go line, the Go version the module needs. Every directory below it belongs to the module, down to the next directory with its own go.mod. go mod tidy would add requirements for imported modules; there are none here.

go list -m lists modules, plain go list lists packages. ./... means this directory and everything below it. The output shows that the import path and the package name are different things: the root package is imported as example.com/hello but declares package main.
go run . compiles the main package in the current directory into a temporary binary and runs it (since Go 1.24 that binary is cached). Use go build when you want a file to ship.
go doc prints doc comments from source, exported identifiers only. go doc -u adds unexported ones; go doc strings.Cut works for any package or symbol, standard library included.
The program drives the real go command from inside a lesson. It pins GOTOOLCHAIN=local and GOPROXY=off so a stray version line can never trigger a download.

examples.title: The compiler accepts it; go vet, go test and go fmt do not

annotations.note: Two problems the compiler doesn't care about: a %d verb fed a string, and four-space indentation where gofmt uses tabs.
go build with several packages, or a non-main package, compiles and discards the results: a pure compile check. Silence means success, as with most go subcommands.
vet's printf analyzer checks format strings against argument types and exits with status 1, which is what fails a CI step.
go test runs a high-confidence subset of vet (printf, errorsas, stdversion and a few more) before the tests, and refuses to run them if vet complains: "[build failed]", no test executed.
With -vet=off the test runs and shows the bug: fmt never panics on a wrong verb, it writes %!d(string=Ayşe) into the output. Vet found it without running anything.
go fmt runs gofmt -l -w on the packages and prints each file it rewrote. In CI, run gofmt -l . and fail if it prints anything.
Test timings change on every run, so the demo strips them. That is also why the go-test runtime compares output with "contains".

examples.title: What go build records inside the binary

annotations.note: Every module-mode binary carries this record. go version -m ./app prints it without running the program, which is how scanners such as govulncheck find out which Go and which dependency versions built it.
The toolchain's version, such as go1.27.1. It differs between machines, which is why this example's expected output is a regex.

(devel) means "built from a local directory, version unknown". go install example.com/tool@v1.2.3 records v1.2.3, and since Go 1.24 go build in a Git checkout records the tag or a pseudo-version. Dependencies are listed with versions and checksums; this program has none, because the standard library is not a module dependency.

Build settings include the target platform. Inside a Git checkout go build also adds vcs.revision, vcs.time and vcs.modified (Go 1.18; -buildvcs=false turns that off). The lesson runs in a temp dir, so there is nothing to stamp.

use_cases: Day-to-day loop: go run . while developing, go test ./... before committing, go build -o bin/app ./cmd/app for a release
CI gate: gofmt -l . must print nothing, then go vet ./... and go test -race ./...
Dependencies: go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0 to add or upgrade, go mod tidy to drop unused ones and fill go.sum
Command-line tools: go install example.com/tool@latest puts a binary in GOBIN; go get -tool and go tool (Go 1.24) track dev tools in go.mod
Finding out which Go built a binary: go version -m ./app
strengths: One binary replaces what Java splits across Maven or Gradle plugins and JS splits across npm scripts, ESLint, Prettier and Jest, with no config file to keep in sync
No build scripts: the import graph is the build graph, and neither fetching nor building runs dependency code, unlike npm install hooks or Gradle build scripts
Build and test caches are keyed by content (sources, flags, compiler), not timestamps, so go test ./... after a one-line change only rebuilds and reruns what depends on it
gofmt has no style options, so formatting debates and formatter configuration files don't exist
weaknesses: There is no task runner: code generation, migrations or Docker images go into go generate directives, a Makefile or scripts
vet's default analyzers are deliberately conservative; unchecked errors and many other bugs need staticcheck or golangci-lint, separate installs
A cached ok is not a fresh run: a test that talks to a database is cached like any other unless you pass -count=1

pitfalls.title: go run main.go in a multi-file package
pitfalls.detail: Naming files compiles only those files, so helpers in other files of package main are undefined. Run the package instead.
pitfalls.good: go run .

pitfalls.title: Treating vet findings as style nits
pitfalls.detail: The compiler doesn't check format verbs, struct tags or misuse of errors.As; vet does, and go test runs the important analyzers anyway. Keep go vet ./... green.

pitfalls.title: Believing a cached test result
pitfalls.detail: "ok example.com/x (cached)" means the test binary and its inputs were unchanged, so the old result was replayed. Use -count=1 when the test depends on something outside the module.

pitfalls.title: A module path without a dot
pitfalls.detail: Import paths without a dot in the first element are reserved for the standard library. Use your repository path (github.com/you/app) or example.com/...; the names example and test are reserved for local experiments.

quiz.q: go.mod says module example.com/shop. Which import path does the package in the directory tax/ have?
quiz.why: An import path is the module path joined with the package's directory inside the module; Go has no relative imports in module mode.

quiz.q: go build ./... in a module with three library packages prints nothing. What happened?
options: Everything compiled and the results were discarded: it was a compile check
Three binaries were written next to the packages
quiz.why: When building several packages or a non-main package, go build only checks that they compile. Use -o or a single main package to get a binary.

quiz.q: go test fails with a fmt.Sprintf vet message and runs no tests. Why?
options: go test runs every vet analyzer
go test runs a high-confidence subset of vet, including printf, before running tests
The test file has a syntax error
quiz.why: go help test lists the subset (atomic, bools, buildtag, directive, errorsas, ifaceassert, nilfunc, printf, stdversion, stringintconv, tests). -vet=off disables it, -vet=all runs everything.

quiz.q: How do you make go test run tests again instead of printing (cached)?
quiz.why: -v and -run are on the list of cacheable flags, so results can still be replayed. -count is not, and -count=1 is the documented idiom for bypassing the cache.

further_reading.title: How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks

lessons.body:
## Concept

The `go` command is compiler driver, dependency manager, test runner, linter,
formatter and documentation viewer in one binary. It works on two units:

- A **package** is one directory of `.go` files that share a `package` clause and are
  compiled together. It is the unit of import and of visibility.
- A **module** is a tree of packages with a `go.mod` at its root. It is the unit of
  versioning: you require, upgrade and publish modules, never single packages.
  `go.mod` names the module (its path), the Go version it needs, and the modules it
  requires; `go.sum` records checksums of every module that contributes to the build.

A package's import path is the module path plus its directory, so the code layout on
disk *is* the import graph, and the import graph is the build graph. Commands take
package patterns: `.` is the package in the current directory, `./...` is it and
everything below, and `example.com/hello/greet` is an import path.

| You want to | Command |
|---|---|
| start a module | `go mod init example.com/app` |
| add or upgrade a dependency | `go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0` |
| make go.mod and go.sum match the imports | `go mod tidy` |
| run while developing | `go run .` |
| build a binary | `go build -o bin/app ./cmd/app` |
| test, check, format | `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go fmt ./...` |
| read docs offline | `go doc strings.Cut`, `go doc -all ./greet` |
| install a CLI tool | `go install example.com/tool@latest` |
| inspect settings | `go env`, `go env GOPATH` |

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Maven or Gradle, Checkstyle, Javadoc and the JUnit runner are all built in,
  with no plugin configuration. `go.mod` is like the dependency section of a POM, but
  versions are minimums: minimal version selection picks the highest minimum anyone
  requires, deterministically, without a separate lock file.
- **JS/Node**: `go.mod` ≈ `package.json` without `scripts`; `go.sum` holds hashes, not a
  resolved tree. There is no `node_modules`: downloaded modules live once per version
  in a shared, read-only module cache.
- **Python**: no virtualenv. Two projects needing different versions of a library
  simply get different directories in the module cache. `gofmt` is Black without the
  options.
- **C/C++**: no headers, no Makefile or CMake for the build itself. The build cache is
  keyed by content hashes, so there are no stale objects to `make clean` away.

## How it works

`go build` and `go test` hash every input (sources, flags, compiler version) and look
the result up in the build cache (`go env GOCACHE`). `go test` additionally caches
passing results: when nothing it tracks has changed, it replays the old output with
`(cached)` instead of a duration. Since Go 1.24, the binaries `go run` builds are
cached too, so a second `go run .` starts almost instantly.

## Design notes

The tool is opinionated on purpose: one layout rule (directory = package), one
formatter with no options, one test runner, and vet analyzers chosen for few false
positives. That makes every Go repository look alike, which is the point: a new
codebase builds with `go build ./...` and tests with `go test ./...`, with nothing to
read first. The cost is that anything outside that loop, such as generating code or
building images, lives in a Makefile or `go generate` directives. A reasonable CI
gate is `gofmt -l .` (must print nothing), `go vet ./...`, then `go test -race ./...`,
plus staticcheck or golangci-lint if the team agrees on one.

lessons.title: Modules, packages, internal/, and the cmd/ layout
lessons.summary: Go has two visibility levels, decided by the first letter of a name, plus internal/ directories that the go command enforces. Applications put binaries under cmd/ and everything else under internal/.

examples.title: Exported means "starts with an upper-case letter", and libraries obey it

annotations.note: No public or private keywords: Name and City are exported, password is visible only inside this package, in every file of it. There is no class-private or protected level.
encoding/json is another package, so it cannot touch password and silently leaves it out. A struct whose fields are all lower-case marshals to {} and never gets filled by Unmarshal.
fmt also uses reflection, but only reads, and it prints unexported fields too. Logging a struct with %+v can leak a secret that json.Marshal would have dropped.
reflect applies the same rule through StructField.IsExported. reflect.TypeFor[T]() (Go 1.22) gets the type without needing a value.

The spec says "a Unicode upper-case letter (category Lu)". İ is one, so İlçe is exported; dotless ı is lower-case. Names starting with _ or with a letter that has no case, such as 日, can never be exported. (The %-6s width counts runes, not bytes, so İlçe pads correctly.)

examples.title: cmd/ for binaries, internal/ for shared code, and an unexported name

annotations.note: A typical application module. Each directory under cmd/ is a package main that builds one binary named after the directory; keep main small (configuration, wiring) and put the logic in internal/.
Package vat's API is Of. round is an implementation detail that other packages cannot call, so it can change without breaking them.
Three packages, one module. A binary is addressed by its directory: go run ./cmd/shopd here, go install example.com/shop/cmd/shopd@latest for someone installing it from elsewhere.

go build ./... type-checks every package. cmd/peek reaches for an unexported function and fails to compile; the message names the rule. Importing internal/vat itself is fine: both packages live in example.com/shop.

examples.title: go.work joins two local modules; internal/ still stops outsiders

annotations.note: A library module and an app that uses it, both on disk. Without a workspace the app would need a require line and a published version, or a replace directive pointing at ../shop.
go.work: a go line and one use directive per module directory. go work init ./app ./shop writes this file for you; go work use adds more modules later.
No go.work yet, and app/go.mod doesn't require example.com/shop, so the import cannot be resolved. The error suggests go get, which would need a published module.
The go command looks for go.work in the current directory and its parents. Both modules are now main modules: the import resolves to the code on disk, with no edit to either go.mod.
internal/ is enforced across modules: only example.com/shop and the packages below it may import example.com/shop/internal/vat. A workspace does not lift that rule.

use_cases: Application: cmd/<binary>/main.go for each executable, internal/<feature>/ for the code, nothing importable by other modules
Library: the package at the module root (import example.com/lib), helpers in internal/ so you can change them without breaking users
Hiding a field or helper: start its name with a lower-case letter; the compiler enforces it at every use site in other packages
Developing a library and an app together: go work init ./app ./lib, without touching either go.mod
strengths: Visibility shows at every use site: shop.Gross is public and round is private without looking at a declaration, unlike Java modifiers or TypeScript export lists
internal/ is enforced by the go command, unlike Python's _module convention or a JS package's undocumented files
No build configuration: the directory tree is the package graph, so a new binary is a new directory under cmd/
go.work replaces the old habit of temporary replace directives in go.mod, which tended to get committed by accident
weaknesses: Only two visibility levels plus internal/: no protected and no class-private, so a struct's invariants are guarded from other packages but not from the rest of its own package
Changing visibility means renaming the identifier at every use site; gopls rename does it, plain search and replace may not
Import paths are absolute (module path + directory), so moving a package rewrites every import of it

pitfalls.title: Lower-case struct fields and encoding/json
pitfalls.detail: json.Marshal skips unexported fields and Unmarshal never sets them, without an error. Export the field and control its JSON name with a tag.
pitfalls.good: type User struct { Name string `json:"name"` }

pitfalls.title: Printing structs that hold secrets
pitfalls.detail: fmt's %v and %+v print unexported fields. Give the type a String or slog LogValue method that redacts, or log selected fields only.

pitfalls.title: Assuming sub-directories share privileges
pitfalls.detail: example.com/shop/vat cannot see unexported names of example.com/shop. Nesting directories means nothing to the compiler; only the internal/ rule depends on paths.

pitfalls.title: Committing go.work
pitfalls.detail: A checked-in go.work can override a developer's own workspace and makes CI test versions users won't get. Keep it local, or run CI with GOWORK=off.

quiz.q: Which of these identifiers is exported?
quiz.why: İ (U+0130) is in Unicode category Lu, so İl is exported. _ is not a letter, and 日 has no case, so names starting with it can never be exported.

quiz.q: Module example.com/shop has a package in internal/vat. Who can import it?
options: example.com/shop and the packages below it
Any module in the same go.work
quiz.why: Code in or below internal/ is importable only by code rooted at internal's parent, here example.com/shop. A workspace does not change that.

quiz.q: json.Marshal(struct{ name string; Age int }{"Ayşe", 30}) returns?
quiz.why: encoding/json only sees exported fields; name is dropped without an error.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Exported identifiers
Tutorial: Getting started with multi-module workspaces

lessons.body:
## Concept

A package is a directory; every file in it declares the same package name and sees
everything the others declare. Across packages there are exactly two levels of
visibility, and the name itself says which: an identifier whose first character is
an upper-case letter is **exported**, anything else is visible only inside its
package. That covers types, functions, constants, variables, struct fields and
methods alike.

The go command adds one more rule based on paths: a package in or below a directory
named `internal` can be imported only by code rooted at the parent of that
directory. That is how a module keeps packages for itself while still splitting its
code into many packages.

The common layout follows from those two rules:

```
shop/                     module example.com/shop
├── go.mod
├── cmd/
│   ├── shopd/main.go     go build ./cmd/shopd  -> binary "shopd"
│   └── shopctl/main.go
└── internal/
    ├── orders/           example.com/shop/internal/orders
    └── vat/
```

A library puts its public package at the module root instead, so users import
`example.com/lib`, and keeps helpers in `internal/`. A workspace file, `go.work`,
lets several local modules build together while you change them in step.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: exported ≈ `public`, unexported ≈ package-private. There is no `protected`
  and no class-private: every file in the package can touch a struct's lower-case
  fields. Like Java, `com.x.shop.vat` gets no special access to `com.x.shop`.
  `internal/` plays the role of packages a JPMS module does not export.
- **C/C++**: no headers to curate. Capitalization does what `static` and the header's
  contents do in C.
- **Python**: `_name` is a convention that anyone can ignore; Go's rule is checked by
  the compiler. There is no `__init__.py`: the directory is the package.
- **JS/TS**: the capital letter replaces the `export` keyword, `internal/` replaces a
  `package.json` `exports` map, and `go.work` resembles npm or pnpm workspaces.

## Design notes

Start with one package and split when a part has a clear name and API, by feature
(`internal/orders`, `internal/billing`) rather than by layer (`models`, `utils`).
Callers write the package name at every call, so `vat.Of` reads well and
`vat.VATOf` stutters. Import cycles are compile errors, which pushes the dependency
graph into layers whether you planned them or not. The official layout guide does not
use a `pkg/` directory; it is a community habit, and `internal/` gives the protection
`pkg/` only implies. Treat `go.work` as a local tool: it is for editing modules
together, and CI should build each module the way its users will (`GOWORK=off`).

lessons.title: go fix modernizers and the toolchain directive
lessons.summary: go fix rewrites code to newer idioms, but only as far as the module's go line allows. The go line is both the language version and the minimum toolchain; the toolchain line and GOTOOLCHAIN decide which compiler actually runs.

examples.title: go fix only applies what the go line allows

annotations.note: The module declares go 1.21. Every fixer checks this version, or a //go:build go1.N line on the file, before suggesting anything.
any (Go 1.18) and the min built-in (Go 1.21) are allowed at 1.21, so the first diff rewrites both functions.
for i := range n and dropping n := n both need Go 1.22. Before 1.22 the loop shared one n across iterations, so n := n was required: without it every deferred call would print the last name.
-diff prints a unified diff and exits with status 1 when there is anything to fix, which makes it usable as a CI check. Squares and PrintAll are untouched.
go get go@1.22.0 is the documented way to raise the go line. From now on the module compiles with Go 1.22 semantics, including per-iteration loop variables.
The second diff holds the 1.22 fixes. Removing n := n is safe only now, because the go line changed what the loop means.
strings.Lines (Go 1.24) yields each line with its newline; the ---/+++ diff headers hold absolute temp paths and are skipped.

examples.title: The go line is a language version and a minimum toolchain

annotations.note: Ranging over an int is Go 1.22 syntax. The installed compiler knows it; whether it accepts it depends on the module.
With go 1.21 the compiler runs with -lang=go1.21 and names the version the feature needs. This is how to check a since: claim: lower the go line and read the error.
Since Go 1.21 the go line is a hard requirement. With GOTOOLCHAIN=local the go command refuses a module that needs a newer Go than itself.

With auto, the default, it tries to download that toolchain as the module golang.org/toolchain, verified against the checksum database. Go 1.99 doesn't exist and GOPROXY=off blocks the network, so it fails.

GOTOOLCHAIN in the environment wins over go env -w settings and the default in $GOROOT/go.env, which is auto in standard distributions. The expected output is a regex because the error names the local Go version and platform.

examples.title: //go:fix inline: a deprecation that migrates its callers

annotations.note: The old function is rewritten as a call to the new one and marked //go:fix inline. The Deprecated: paragraph makes editors and staticcheck flag uses; the directive lets go fix remove them.
The caller, which could just as well live in another module that depends on this one.
-inline selects one fixer (go tool fix help lists them all). Each call to Format is replaced by Format's body with the arguments substituted; the inliner keeps evaluation order and side effects.
After applying, the program prints the same thing: the fix changes the code, not its behavior.

use_cases: After raising a module's go line: go fix ./... in its own commit, so the mechanical diff is reviewed separately
CI check that new code uses current idioms: go fix -diff ./... fails when it has suggestions
Renaming or replacing an API in a library: keep the old function as a //go:fix inline wrapper and let callers migrate with go fix
Making every developer and CI build with at least a given compiler: toolchain go1.27.1 in go.mod; GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.1 in CI for an exact version
strengths: Fixes are gated by the file's language version, so go fix never suggests syntax or APIs the module can't use, unlike a codemod that targets the latest release
Built on the vet analysis framework and shipped with the toolchain: no plugin to install, and new modernizers arrive with each Go release
//go:fix inline turns a deprecation notice into an automatic migration, which Java's @Deprecated or JSDoc's @deprecated cannot do
Toolchain switching downloads checksum-verified compilers on demand, so go.mod alone states which Go a project needs, like .nvmrc plus nvm but built into the go command
weaknesses: Only patterns the fixers recognize get rewritten: a hand-rolled max loop or an if/return clamp stays as it is
The toolchain line is a minimum, not a pin: a developer with a newer Go installed still uses that newer Go
GOTOOLCHAIN=auto downloads compilers from the module proxy, which locked-down networks block; there you need GOTOOLCHAIN=local and the right version installed

pitfalls.title: Concluding that old code is already modern
pitfalls.detail: With an old go line, go fix silently skips everything newer. Raise the go line first, then run go fix.

pitfalls.title: Raising a library's go line casually
pitfalls.detail: Since Go 1.21 every module that requires yours must declare at least your go version. Keep a library's go line as low as its code allows; applications can use the newest.

pitfalls.title: Treating the toolchain line as an exact pin
pitfalls.detail: It only takes effect when the local Go is older. For identical builds, set GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.1 in CI or build in an image with that exact version.

pitfalls.title: Writing a //go:fix inline wrapper with extra logic
pitfalls.detail: The inliner copies the body into every caller. Keep the wrapper a single call to the new API, or callers inherit logging, defaults or other surprises.

quiz.q: A module declares go 1.21 and has for i := 0; i < n; i++ loops. go fix -diff ./... shows no rangeint changes. Why?
options: Ranging over an int needs Go 1.22, and the go line says 1.21
go fix only rewrites code in the main package
quiz.why: Fixers only suggest features allowed by the file's language version. Raise the go line (go get go@1.22.0) and run go fix again.

quiz.q: go.mod says go 1.25.0 and toolchain go1.27.1. The developer has Go 1.28.0 installed and GOTOOLCHAIN=auto. Which Go builds the module?
quiz.why: The toolchain line is used only when the default toolchain is older than it. A newer local toolchain wins.

quiz.q: Why does go fix remove n := n inside a range loop only when the go line is at least 1.22?
options: Go 1.22 gave each iteration its own variable, but only in modules declaring go 1.22 or later
quiz.why: Loop-variable semantics follow the module's go line. Under 1.21 semantics, removing the copy would make every closure see the last value.

quiz.q: What does //go:fix inline on func Format(k int) string { return Lira(k) } do?
options: The compiler inlines Format for speed
go fix rewrites calls to Format into calls to Lira
go vet reports every call to Format as an error
quiz.why: The directive is for the inline fixer. Compiler inlining is automatic and unrelated.

lessons.body:
## Concept

**go fix** was rewritten in Go 1.26 as the home of *modernizers*: analyzers, built on
the same framework as `go vet`, whose suggested fixes move code to newer idioms
without changing behavior (`interface{}` to `any`, three-clause loops to
`range n`, hand-written loops to `slices.Contains`, `sort.Slice` to `slices.Sort`,
and a few dozen more). `go fix ./...` applies them, `go fix -diff ./...` previews,
`go tool fix help` lists them, and a flag such as `-rangeint` selects one. Go 1.27
added `atomictypes`, `embedlit`, `slicesbackward` and `unsafefuncs`, renamed
`waitgroup` to `waitgroupgo` and removed `fmtappendf`.

Every fix is limited by the **language version** of the file it edits: the `go` line
of its module, or a `//go:build go1.N` constraint on the file. That `go` line does three
jobs at once:

1. It sets the language version the compiler enforces for the module's packages.
2. Since Go 1.21 it is a hard minimum: an older toolchain refuses the module.
3. It feeds toolchain selection.

The optional **toolchain** line names a *suggested* toolchain, used only when the
installed Go is older. **GOTOOLCHAIN** controls switching: `auto` (the default,
short for `local+auto`) uses the installed Go unless `go.mod` asks for newer and then
downloads it; `local` never switches; `go1.27.1` always uses exactly that version;
`go1.27.1+auto` starts from it and may still go higher.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: `go fix` is `pyupgrade --py311-plus` built into the toolchain, with the
  target version read from the project (`go` line ≈ `requires-python`) instead of a
  flag.
- **Java**: the `go` line is like `--release 21` for the language, and the toolchain
  line like a Gradle toolchain spec that is fetched automatically. Modernizers resemble
  OpenRewrite recipes, without the plugin.
- **JS/TS**: codemods (jscodeshift) are third-party and version-blind. `engines` in
  `package.json` usually only warns; the `go` line is enforced. The toolchain line
  plus `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` is what `.nvmrc` plus nvm or Volta does, without an extra
  tool.
- **C/C++**: `-std=c++20` is per build; the `go` line travels with the module, so
  every consumer compiles it with the same language rules.

## Design notes

Upgrade in two steps: raise the `go` line (`go get go@1.N.0`), run the tests, then run
`go fix ./...` and commit its diff separately so reviewers see a purely mechanical
change. Libraries should keep their `go` line as low as their code allows, because
it becomes a requirement for every module that depends on them; applications can
track the newest release. For reproducible builds, the toolchain line sets a floor
for everyone, and CI pins the exact compiler with `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.1` or a
versioned build image. Since Go 1.27, `go test` also runs vet's `stdversion` check,
which flags standard library symbols newer than the file's `go` version, the API
counterpart of the compile error in example 2. When you deprecate an API you own,
express the old function in terms of the new one and mark it `//go:fix inline`:
the deprecation then migrates its own callers.

lessons.title: How main.go wires dependencies
lessons.summary: StackLab's backend has no DI framework: server/cmd/stacklab/main.go calls constructors in order and passes each result to the next. One consumer-declared interface, httpapi.Runner, lets one if switch between running lessons in-process and in the Docker runner.

examples.title: The dependency graph in miniature: config, logger, runner, router

annotations.note: A plain struct and a Load function, no config library. The real `config.Load` reads `os.Getenv` directly; taking `getenv` as a parameter here lets one program show both modes, and is the shape you'd want if config ever got tests (it has none today).

The interface lives with its consumer, `internal/httpapi/run.go`. `runexec` and `runclient` never import httpapi and never name Runner: they satisfy it because their Run methods have the right signature. A Java-style `implements` would make both implementations depend on the HTTP package.
Constructors return concrete types (`*Executor`, `*Client`), not Runner. `cmd/runner` uses `*runexec.Executor` directly, with no interface at all; only the backend, which has two choices, needs one.

The parameter list is the dependency list. The real signature is `NewRouter(logger, pool *platform.DB, runner Runner)`, and it builds the run-history and learning stores from `pool.Pool()` itself, so those two are not injectable from outside. Only the runner is.
The entire run-mode switch (ADR-0008) is one if. The real main also builds `runexec.New(...)` first and replaces it in Docker mode, which is cheap: New only allocates a two-slot channel.
`%T` prints the dynamic type behind the interface value. The handler code was identical in both runs; only the value handed to NewRouter changed.

examples.title: run() error, defers in reverse order, and the shutdown context

annotations.note: `main` only calls `run` and turns its error into `os.Exit(1)`. `os.Exit` and `log.Fatal` skip deferred calls, so calling them inside run, after the pool opened, would leave the pool unclosed.

The real line is `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)`. One context then bounds the pool's first connect, the migrations, and the wait below. On Windows, Ctrl+C arrives as `os.Interrupt`, and closing the console window arrives as SIGTERM.
Defer right after each successful acquire. The first start fails in Migrate and still prints "pool: closed": every later return path releases what was acquired before it.

In main.go, `ListenAndServe` runs in a goroutine and sends a startup failure (port 8080 taken) on this channel. The buffer of 1 lets that goroutine finish even if nobody reads. select waits for whichever comes first: a broken server or a signal.

The drain budget must start from `context.Background()`. ctx is already cancelled by the signal, so anything derived from it is born cancelled and `srv.Shutdown` would give up at once, cutting off in-flight requests. main.go gets this right.

When run returns here, its deferred calls run last-in, first-out: the two cancels, then `pool.Close`, then stop. The output shows "server drained" before "pool: closed", so a request still finishing during the drain can use the database.

use_cases: Reading a Go service for the first time: open `cmd/<name>/main.go` and read the dependency graph top to bottom before any package
Swapping an implementation per environment (in-process runner locally, HTTP client in Docker) with one interface and one if
Building handlers in tests with fakes instead of a database or a runner process
strengths: The whole graph is ordinary code: Go to Definition works on every edge, and a missing dependency is a compile error, not a startup failure in Spring's or Guice's container
Structural interfaces let the consumer define the seam after the fact: `runexec` and `runclient` were written without knowing `httpapi.Runner` exists
Startup order is visible: config, logger, signal context, pool, migrations, runner, router, server. Teardown order follows from the defers
weaknesses: Manual wiring grows by hand. Every new store or service is another constructor call and parameter; there is no autowiring

Only half-injected: `NewRouter` builds `runstore` and `learningstore` from the pool itself, and handlers hold concrete `*platform.DB` and store types. A test can build the real router without a database only by passing `platform.NewDB(nil)` and sending requests that never reach a store, which is what the one router test does
`slog.SetDefault(logger)` sets process-wide state next to the explicitly passed logger. Code that calls `slog.Info` directly uses the global and bypasses injection
`config.Load` reads `os.Getenv` directly and only validates integers: an empty or wrong database URL fails later, at the pool's ping, not at load

pitfalls.title: Deriving the shutdown context from the signal context
pitfalls.detail: The signal already cancelled it, so `Shutdown` returns immediately and drops in-flight requests. Start the drain budget from `context.Background()`.
pitfalls.good: shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)

pitfalls.title: log.Fatal deep inside startup
pitfalls.detail: It calls `os.Exit`, which skips every deferred `Close`. Return the error to `main`, which is the only place that exits.

pitfalls.title: Declaring the interface next to its implementation
pitfalls.detail: A `runexec.Runner` interface would make httpapi import runexec, and runclient would have to import runexec to say it implements it. Declare small interfaces where they are used.

pitfalls.title: Handing go:embed's FS straight to goose
pitfalls.detail: go:embed keeps the `migrations/` prefix and goose only reads the FS root, so the backend died with "no migrations found". main.go wraps it in `fs.Sub`, and `main_test.go` guards that contract.

quiz.q: Where is `httpapi.Runner` declared, and why there?
options: In runexec, next to the main implementation
In httpapi, the package that calls Run, so neither implementation depends on HTTP code
In runapi, the shared wire-format package
In main.go, where the choice is made
quiz.why: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so the consumer can declare the smallest interface it needs. runexec and runclient compile without knowing it exists.

quiz.q: main.go derives the 10 s drain budget from `context.Background()`, not from the signal context. What would deriving it from the signal context do?
options: Give Shutdown an already-cancelled context, so it stops waiting at once and in-flight requests are cut off
quiz.why: A context derived from a cancelled parent is cancelled from birth. The example prints exactly that: context canceled versus <nil>.

quiz.q: Which of these does `NewRouter` construct itself instead of receiving it from main?
quiz.why: router.go calls `runstore.NewStore(pool.Pool())` and `learningstore.NewStore(pool.Pool())`. That is why a test can fake the runner but not the stores.

further_reading.title: Effective Go: Interfaces and other types

lessons.body:
## Concept

`server/cmd/stacklab/main.go` is about 140 lines, and its package comment states the
rule: main only wires dependencies, "config -> logger -> pool -> router -> server". Read
`run()` top to bottom and you have the backend's whole object graph:

1. `config.Load()` builds a `Config` from environment variables, with defaults for local
   mode, so `npm start` needs no environment at all.
2. `platform.NewLogger(...)` builds an `*slog.Logger`, also installed with `slog.SetDefault`.
3. `signal.NotifyContext` gives the context that bounds startup I/O and the shutdown wait.
4. `platform.NewPool(ctx, ...)` opens the pgx pool for the `stacklab` database, wrapped in
   `platform.NewDB(pool)`.
5. `platform.Migrate` applies the embedded goose migrations before anything is served.
6. The runner: `runexec.New(...)` (in-process, local mode) unless `STACKLAB_RUNNER_URL` is
   set, then `runclient.New(url)` (the Docker runner container).
7. An `http.Server` with explicit timeouts whose handler is
   `httpapi.NewRouter(logger, db, runner)`.
8. Serve in a goroutine, wait for a server error or a signal, then `Shutdown` with 10 s.

That is constructor injection with nothing else: no container, no reflection, no
annotations. Each constructor takes what it needs as parameters and returns a concrete
type. The only interface on the graph is `httpapi.Runner`, declared in
`internal/httpapi/run.go` by the code that calls it, because it is the only dependency
with two implementations.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Spring and Guice build this graph by reflection from annotations; Dagger
  generates it at compile time. main.go is roughly what Dagger would generate, written
  and read by hand. There is no `implements`: `*runexec.Executor` satisfies
  `httpapi.Runner` because it has a matching `Run` method.
- **Python**: FastAPI's `Depends` or module-level singletons. The Go habit is to avoid
  package-level state and pass things explicitly, which is also why `slog.SetDefault`
  here stands out.
- **JS/TS**: NestJS has a decorator-driven container; plain Node code often uses module
  singletons (`import { db } from './db'`). Go's version is closer to a hand-written
  composition root in an `index.ts`.
- **C++**: the same constructor injection you would write by hand, minus abstract base
  classes. The interface can be declared after the implementations exist, by the code
  that needs it.

## How it works

The runner choice is the one place the graph branches:

```go
var runner httpapi.Runner = runexec.New(cfg.PlaygroundDatabaseURL, cfg.NodeProjectDir)
if cfg.RunnerBaseURL != "" {
	runner = runclient.New(cfg.RunnerBaseURL)
}
```

Both `runexec.Executor.Run` and `runclient.Client.Run` return
`(*runapi.Result, *runapi.Error, error)`, so the handler code in `run.go` never knows
which one it has. `cmd/runner/main.go`, the Docker runner's own main, wires the same
`runexec` package behind a different HTTP shell, which is how ADR-0008 keeps the two
modes from drifting.

Shutdown is the graph in reverse. `run()` defers `stop()`, then `pool.Close()`, then the
drain budget's `cancel()`. When the signal arrives, `srv.Shutdown` drains first, and only
when `run` returns do the defers close the pool, so requests finishing during the drain
still have a database.

## Design notes

What the file gets right: one readable composition root, a `run() error` that keeps
`os.Exit` out of reach of the defers, explicit `http.Server` timeouts (Go's zero values
mean no deadline), and a self-migrating start, so a fresh database comes up correct.

What it doesn't, read honestly:

- **The injection stops at the router.** `NewRouter` receives `*platform.DB` and builds
  `runstore.NewStore(pool.Pool())` and `learningstore.NewStore(pool.Pool())` inside, and
  the handlers hold concrete store types. The doc comment on `platform.DB` used to say it
  exists so handlers depend on "an interface declared by the consumer", but no such
  interface exists: `handleReady` takes `*platform.DB`. The comment now says so. The
  `Runner` seam is real; the database seam is aspirational. The one test that builds the
  router (`TestRouterAnswersUnmatchedRequestsWithProblems` in `middleware_test.go`)
  passes `platform.NewDB(nil)` and sends only requests that never reach a store
  (unmatched paths and `/healthz`).
- **The next step** would be small consumer-declared interfaces in httpapi (`pinger`,
  `runHistory`, `learningStore`) and a `NewRouter` that receives the stores built in
  main. That is a few lines in each file and buys handler tests without a database.
- **No framework is the right call at this size.** With fewer than ten constructors,
  explicit wiring costs a few lines per dependency and is never wrong silently. A
  generated-wiring tool starts paying off when the graph has dozens of nodes and several
  binaries share it.

Compare `go.design.constructors` for the pattern itself and `go.http.server-lifecycle`
for the timeout and shutdown details.

lessons.title: The HTTP layer and middleware chain
lessons.summary: internal/httpapi is a standard-library ServeMux with fifteen routes, wrapped in logging, panic recovery and three request guards; one problem() function writes every error, the mux's own 404 and 405 included, as RFC 9457 JSON. The run route answers 200, 400, 502 or the runner's status; a failing program is a 200.

examples.title: router.go and middleware.go in small: patterns, logging, problem details

annotations.note: The real `statusRecorder`. The default is 200 because a handler that only calls Write never calls WriteHeader. Unwrap lets http.ResponseController reach the real connection: embedding the ResponseWriter interface forwards Header, Write and WriteHeader and hides everything else (How it works tells the bug its absence caused).
`withLogging(logger)` returns a `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`, so the logger is captured by a closure and the result composes with any other wrapper. The real one also logs the duration.

Every error a handler writes goes through this one function: one shape, `application/problem+json`, with `type: about:blank`, which RFC 9457 defines as "the status code says it all". Changing the error format means changing one function.
Go 1.22 patterns put the method and a `{lessonId}` wildcard in the pattern string, read back with `r.PathValue`. ADR-0001 chose this over chi or gin: the router is itself lesson material.
Each handler caps its own body: 64 KiB for the learning routes, 2 MiB for the run route. There is no global body-size middleware.

The middleware wraps the mux, not individual routes, so it also sees the requests the mux rejects itself: the 405 and 404 lines are logged. The real router puts recovery (example 4) and the request guards (example 2) between the two, and one more wrapper around the mux (example 5).

What a bare mux does: it writes 405 (with `Allow: GET, HEAD, PUT`, since a GET pattern also serves HEAD) and 404 itself, as plain text, never reaching problem(). The real router had this gap in "one error shape" until withProblemFallbacks (example 5) took both over. `/api/lessons/{id}` is the route docs/ARCHITECTURE.md describes; it does not exist.

examples.title: security.go in small: three guards in front of the code-running API

annotations.note: `http.CrossOriginProtection` (Go 1.25) is the outer guard; the real deny handler also logs and answers through problem(). The order of the wrappers is the order a request meets them.

Against DNS rebinding: a hostile name re-pointed at 127.0.0.1 makes the browser treat the attacker's page as same-origin, but the Host header still carries that name. Only /api/ is checked, because Compose probes /healthz by container name.
Any port is fine: the Vite proxy forwards the browser's Host, which names port 5173, not 8080.
A cross-site page can't send application/json without a CORS preflight, which this server never approves. Bodyless POSTs (progress, bookmarks) have Content-Length 0 and pass.
A form or fetch from another site: the browser labels it with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site, and CrossOriginProtection answers 403 before any handler runs.
Without Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin, CrossOriginProtection assumes a same-origin or non-browser request and lets it through; the JSON-only check is what stops a text/plain body here.
The browser believes it is same-origin, so the first two guards pass; the Host check doesn't.

examples.title: POST /api/run: one handler, every outcome mapped to a status

annotations.note: `Run` returns three things. `*RunError` is "the runner said no" (busy, runtime unsupported): pass its status through. `error` is "the run machinery broke". Two channels instead of one error and an `errors.As`, at the cost that forgetting one check still compiles.
A fake behind the consumer-declared interface: three cases, no mocking library. The last line is the important one: a program that fails to compile is a successful run, a 200 with exitCode 1.

400 for what the client can fix: a body that isn't JSON, or one that fails `runapi.Request.Validate` (runtime required, at most 32 files, names of at most 128 bytes, 1 MiB of sources, timeout 0 to 15 s).
502 with a generic detail: the real cause (a pgx error naming host and port) goes to the log only. The learner learns which side failed, not the infrastructure's internals.
A refusal keeps its status: 503 "server busy" when both run slots are taken, 501 for a ts-test lesson in Docker mode.
The real handler records run history first, unless the request carries `X-Stacklab-No-History` (verify-lessons sets it). A failed insert is logged as a warning and the result is still returned.

examples.title: withRecovery in small: a panic becomes a 500, unless the reply has started

annotations.note: The recovery needs one fact the ResponseWriter doesn't expose: has the handler written anything? The real writeTracker also has Unwrap, so the run route's write deadline still works through it, and FlushError, because a flush sends the status line too.

The deferred function runs while the panic unwinds, so recover() stops it here. http.ErrAbortHandler is how a handler asks net/http to drop the connection without logging; recovering it would turn a deliberate abort into a 500, so it goes back up untouched.

The real one logs through slog with method, path, the panic value and `debug.Stack()`. Called inside the deferred function, it still shows the frames that panicked, because the stack hasn't unwound yet.

After a write the status line may already be on the wire, and a 500 can't replace it. Returning normally would end a half-written body as if it were complete; re-panicking with ErrAbortHandler makes net/http drop the connection, so the client sees a broken reply instead.
Nothing written yet: the client gets the same problem JSON as every other error. In NewRouter this sits just inside withLogging, so the access log records the 500 too.
This recover stands in for net/http's own, one level up in the connection's goroutine. With ErrAbortHandler it closes the connection silently; with any other value it logs `http: panic serving ...`.

examples.title: withProblemFallbacks in small: the mux's own 404 and 405 as problem JSON

annotations.note: The mux answers with http.Error, which sets text/plain and calls WriteHeader before writing its text. This writer swaps that WriteHeader for problem(). For a 405 the mux has already set Allow, so the header survives into the problem reply.
http.Error writes "404 page not found" after WriteHeader; once problem() has answered, that text is dropped instead of being appended to the JSON.

ServeMux.Handler returns an empty pattern when no route will handle the request, so only the mux's own replies (404, 405, or a path-cleaning redirect, which passes through) get the rewriting writer. A catch-all "/" route can't do this: it matches every method, so DELETE /api/notes/x would get its 404 instead of a 405.
A matched route's reply is never touched, even a 404 in another format. StackLab's handlers have no 404 of their own; this one is here to show where the wrapper stops.

use_cases: Reading any Go service's HTTP layer: find the mux, the middleware wrapped around it, and the one function errors go through
Long-running endpoints (runs, exports, reports) that need a longer write deadline than the server default
Deciding which failures are 4xx, which are 5xx, and which are a 200 carrying a failed result
Protecting a localhost service that runs code or holds private data from the other websites open in the same browser
strengths: Fifteen routes in one flat list in `router.go`: method, path and handler, greppable, with no annotations or route groups to chase as in Spring MVC or NestJS
One error shape for every error the API writes (handlers, guards, recovered panics, the mux's own 404 and 405): RFC 9457 problem details from one function
A compile error or failing test is a 200 result, not an HTTP error, so the UI never confuses "your code failed" with "the server failed"
Infrastructure errors are logged in full and summarized to the client, so pgx messages with hosts and ports never reach the page
Cross-site protection is the standard library's `http.CrossOriginProtection` plus two short wrappers: no CSRF tokens, sessions or token endpoint
weaknesses: Recovery can only answer a panic that happens before the handler writes. After that it aborts the connection, and the client sees a broken reply rather than a 500

The 404/405 rewrite leans on two ServeMux behaviours: an empty pattern from `Handler` when nothing matched, and `http.Error` calling `WriteHeader` before it writes. If either changed, text/plain would come back quietly; a router test (`middleware_test.go`) is what would notice
Status mapping happens per handler, not in one function over typed errors: every store failure becomes a 500 with a hand-written message
No request IDs: the log line for a failed run and the problem JSON the browser saw can only be matched by time and path

pitfalls.title: A ResponseWriter wrapper without Unwrap
pitfalls.detail: SetWriteDeadline, Flush and Hijack then fail with `http.ErrNotSupported` through `http.ResponseController`. Ignoring that error is how the run route silently kept the 15 s deadline.

pitfalls.title: Treating 127.0.0.1 as private
pitfalls.detail: A loopback listener keeps other machines out, not other websites: any page open in the browser can send requests to it, and a text/plain or form POST needs no CORS preflight. An endpoint that acts on a request (runs code, writes data) needs cross-origin protection even on localhost.

pitfalls.title: Returning 4xx/5xx for failing user code
pitfalls.detail: The program failing is the expected outcome of a lesson about errors. Reserve HTTP errors for requests the server could not process.

pitfalls.title: Assuming middleware sees panics
pitfalls.detail: A panic unwinds through every middleware outside the recover, so the code after `next.ServeHTTP` never runs there. Without `withRecovery`, `withLogging` would never write that request's line. A recovery middleware belongs inside the logging one, which is where NewRouter puts it.

pitfalls.title: Answering a panic with 500 after the handler wrote
pitfalls.detail: The status line may already be on the wire. A second WriteHeader only logs "superfluous response.WriteHeader call", and returning normally ends a half-written body as if it were complete. Re-panic with `http.ErrAbortHandler` so net/http drops the connection.
pitfalls.bad: defer func() { if v := recover(); v != nil { problem(w, 500, "internal server error") } }()

pitfalls.title: A catch-all "/" route for problem 404s
pitfalls.detail: It matches every method and every path, so the mux never gets to answer 405: GET /api/run would become a 404. Wrap the mux and rewrite only the replies it writes when no pattern matched.

quiz.q: With the app running, what does `GET /api/run` return?
options: 405 text/plain with `Allow: POST`, written by the ServeMux
quiz.why: Only `POST /api/run` is registered, so the mux decides on 405 and sets `Allow: POST` itself. No handler runs; `withProblemFallbacks` sees that no pattern matched and swaps the mux's plain-text body for problem().

quiz.q: A website the owner has open sends a text/plain POST to http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/run. In a current browser, what stops it?
options: Nothing needs to: other sites can't reach 127.0.0.1
CrossOriginProtection: the browser marks it Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site, and the guard answers 403
CORS: the browser refuses to send it
quiz.why: Loopback keeps other machines out, not other pages in the same browser, and a text/plain POST needs no preflight, so it is sent. The browser labels it cross-site and the outer guard rejects it; in a browser that sends no such header, the JSON-only guard would answer 415.

quiz.q: Why did the run route need `statusRecorder.Unwrap`?
options: So the access log could read the status code
So http.ResponseController could reach the real connection and extend its write deadline
So the JSON encoder could flush
quiz.why: Without Unwrap, SetWriteDeadline returned ErrNotSupported, the 15 s WriteTimeout stayed in force, and slow runs lost their response.

quiz.q: A handler panics before writing anything. What does the browser get?
options: No response: net/http logs the panic and closes the connection
quiz.why: `withRecovery` recovers it, logs the panic with its stack, and answers through problem(). Without it, net/http would recover the panic itself, log `http: panic serving ...` and close the connection, and the client would read EOF. That is still what happens when the handler had already started writing.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`internal/httpapi` is the backend's whole HTTP surface, in five files:

- `router.go`: `NewRouter` registers fifteen routes on a standard `http.ServeMux` (health,
  readiness, `POST /api/run`, and twelve progress, notes, bookmarks, quiz and history
  routes), wraps the mux, and defines `problem()`.
- `middleware.go`: `statusRecorder` and `withLogging`, `withRecovery` (panics to 500), and
  `withProblemFallbacks` (the mux's own 404 and 405 to problem JSON).
- `security.go`: `withRequestGuards`, three checks that keep other websites away from
  the API (ADR-0011).
- `run.go`: the `Runner` interface and `handleRun`.
- `learning.go`: one `learningHandlers` type for the per-lesson state routes.

The whole chain is the last line of `NewRouter`:
`withLogging(logger)(withRecovery(logger)(withRequestGuards(logger, withProblemFallbacks(mux))))`.
A request meets `withLogging` → `withRecovery` → `http.CrossOriginProtection` →
`requireLoopbackHost` → `requireJSONBody` → `withProblemFallbacks` → `ServeMux` (method +
path match, or its own 404/405, rewritten as problem JSON) → handler → decode with
`http.MaxBytesReader` → call a store or the runner → write JSON with `writeJSON`, or an
error with `problem`. Logging sits outermost so that rejected and panicking requests show
up in the log too; recovery sits just inside it, so the log line says 500.

"The lessons applied" is accurate for the router (ADR-0001's Go 1.22 patterns), for
middleware as a function wrapper with an `Unwrap`-capable recorder, for recovery and for
problem details. It is partial elsewhere: `go.http.middleware` also teaches request IDs
and timeouts, and this app has neither as middleware (its timeouts are the
`http.Server` fields).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java (Spring MVC)**: routes are annotations spread across controllers, and errors map
  through `@ControllerAdvice`. Here routes are one list of `mux.HandleFunc` calls, and
  each handler calls `problem()` itself. Spring 6's `ProblemDetail` writes the same wire
  format (RFC 7807, which RFC 9457 replaced).
- **Python (Flask/FastAPI)**: an unhandled exception becomes a 500 by default. In Go a
  panic is not that: without recovery middleware, net/http drops the connection, which
  is why `NewRouter` has `withRecovery`.
- **JS (Express)**: `app.use(logger)` is `withLogging(logger)(mux)`. Express has
  `next(err)` and error-handling middleware; Go handlers return nothing, so error mapping
  is a convention you choose (here: call `problem` and return).
- **C++**: no standard HTTP server to compare with; the closest analogue is a request
  dispatcher wrapped in a decorator that records the response code.

## How it works

**The guards.** In local mode `POST /api/run` runs lesson code as the owner's Windows
user. Listening on 127.0.0.1 keeps other machines out, but not other websites: any page
open in the owner's browser can send requests to 127.0.0.1, and a `text/plain` POST needs
no CORS preflight. Each guard closes one door, and each answers through `problem()`:

- 403 for an unsafe request the browser marks as cross-site, through `Sec-Fetch-Site`
  or an `Origin` that doesn't match `Host`. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS always pass.
- 415 for an unsafe request whose body isn't `application/json`, which a cross-site page
  can't send without a preflight. This catches the same attack in a browser that sends
  neither header.
- 403 for an `/api/` request addressed to anything but `localhost` or a loopback IP,
  which stops DNS rebinding.

CORS is not one of them: it controls who may read a response, not who may send a simple
request. ADR-0011 also rejected CSRF tokens, which need a session and a token endpoint.

**The run route** is where the status mapping is most deliberate. `handleRun` produces
one of:

1. **400**: the body isn't JSON, exceeds 2 MiB, or fails `req.Validate()`. (A body with
   any other `Content-Type` never gets this far: `requireJSONBody` answers 415.)
2. **502**: `Run` returned an `error`. The runner container (Docker) or the playground
   database (local) failed. Logged in full, summarized to the client.
