3. **The refusal's status**: `Run` returned a `*runapi.Error`, which runexec uses for 503
   "server busy" and 501 (ts-test in Docker mode, or a runtime with no case in its switch).
   In Docker mode `runclient` passes the runner's refusal through with its detail, and
   turns a runner 500 into an `error`, so that case is a 502 as in local mode.
4. **200**: everything else, including programs that don't compile, panic, exit non-zero
   or time out. Those facts are fields of the result (`exitCode`, `timedOut`,
   `diagnostics`), which the UI's `judge.ts` interprets.

**The write deadline.** The server's `WriteTimeout` of 15 s counts from the request, and
a run can take much longer: up to 10 s waiting for one of runexec's two run slots, then
up to its 40 s run budget (20 s to compile plus 15 s to run fits inside). So before
calling the runner the handler lifts its own write deadline
(`SetWriteDeadline(time.Time{})`), and once the run is over it sets a fresh one for the
reply, 10 s (`replyWriteBudget`). Nothing is written in between, and the run's length is
the Runner's business. An earlier version set 45 s up front (`runWriteBudget`, matching
runclient's HTTP timeout), which forgot the wait for a slot: a run that queued and then
used its whole budget lost its reply. `http.ResponseController` (Go 1.20) finds
`SetWriteDeadline` by following `Unwrap` through wrappers, so the deadline calls work
through `withLogging` and `withRecovery` only because `statusRecorder` and
`writeTracker` have that method. When `statusRecorder` first shipped it didn't: the call
returned `http.ErrNotSupported`, the error was ignored, the 15 s deadline stayed, and on
slow runs the server dropped the connection mid-reply, which the browser reported as
"socket hang up". Today `run.go` logs a warning when a deadline call fails,
`middleware_test.go` pins the `Unwrap` behaviour, and `run_test.go` checks that a run
longer than the server's `WriteTimeout` still gets its reply.

What is not here, despite older docs: no `/api/lessons` or `/api/source` routes (content
never touches the backend, see `inside.codebase.content-pipeline`), no `/mock/*` proxy, no
CORS (the Vite dev server proxies `/api` so the browser stays same-origin), and no
embedded frontend.

## Design notes

- **Errors are mapped per handler, not centrally.** CLAUDE.md asks to "map to HTTP status
  in one place (httpapi)". The package is the one place, but there is no single function
  from error to status: each learning handler logs and writes a 500 with its own message.
  That is fine while every store error really is a 500. When a store grows a meaningful
  error (not found, conflict), a sentinel such as `learningstore.ErrNotFound` plus one
  `writeError(w, err)` doing `errors.Is` would keep the mapping in one function.
- **Recovery inside logging.** `withRecovery` sits just inside `withLogging` and turns a
  panic into a logged 500 problem response instead of a dropped connection (example 4).
  It answers only when the handler hasn't written yet; otherwise it re-panics with
  `http.ErrAbortHandler`, which also passes through untouched when a handler raises it.
  Its `writeTracker` needs `Unwrap` for the same reason `statusRecorder` does.
- **The mux's own 404 and 405 are problem JSON.** A catch-all `"/"` route is not the fix:
  it matches every method, so it would also swallow the requests that should get a 405.
  `withProblemFallbacks` asks `mux.Handler` first; an empty pattern means no route
  matched, and only then does a writer rewrite 404 and 405 through `problem()` (example
  5). Before it, a client had to handle two error formats.
- **The three-value `Run` signature** keeps refusals and failures apart without
  `errors.As`, and both runners implement it. The cost is a convention the compiler
  can't enforce: check `err` first, then the refusal, then use the result.

lessons.title: The runner sandbox and its threat model
lessons.summary: ADR-0003 promised timeouts, output caps, a process-tree kill and two run slots; internal/gorun and internal/runexec deliver them in both modes. The container limits exist only in Docker mode: in local mode (ADR-0008), lesson code runs as you, with your files, network and environment.

examples.title: A runaway program: the deadline kills it, the cap keeps 40 bytes

annotations.note: gorun's `cappedBuffer`, with the cap cut from 64 KB to 40 bytes. It is an `io.Writer` the output is copied into as it arrives, so the cap is enforced while the output streams in, not after the program has filled memory.
Past the cap it still reports success. Returning an error would stop the copying goroutine, the pipe would fill, and the program would block on its next write: a hang instead of a truncation.

The cut backs up to a character boundary. Byte 40 is the first half of the two-byte "ı", so the output ends in "sat", not in half a letter that the JSON encoder would turn into U+FFFD on its way to you. The check looks at the buffer, not only at p, because a character can arrive split across two writes.
A UTF-8 character is at most four bytes, so only the last three can start one that isn't finished. `utf8.FullRune` counts invalid bytes as whole, so binary output is cut where it is.

The real `runProcess` in miniature: a context deadline (5 s by default, at most 15), output caps per stream, and `WaitDelay` (gorun's `pipeGrace`, 2 s) bounding how long Wait keeps reading after the process is gone. The real one also reads the pipes itself and kills the whole process tree whenever the run ends (example 2).

Check the context before the exit code. A killed process reports exit status 1 on Windows and "signal: killed" (-1) on Linux; gorun normalizes every timeout to `timedOut: true, exitCode: -1` so the UI and the judge see the same thing on both.

examples.title: Why the whole process tree must die, and why WaitDelay exists

annotations.note: The lesson program starts a process of its own that inherits its stdout, then hangs. This is the shape of gorun's own `TestRunTimeoutKillsChildren`.

`exec.CommandContext`'s default Cancel kills only the direct child. gorun replaces it in `proc_unix.go` (own process group, SIGKILL to the negative PID) and `proc_windows.go` (a Job Object per run, ended with TerminateJobObject), which a single cross-platform file can't show.

With `WaitDelay` 0, Run reads the pipe until EOF, and EOF only comes when every holder of the write end has exited, including the orphaned grandchild 3 s later. With 300 ms, Run closes the pipe and returns. The os/exec docs describe exactly this case.

A tree kill done by hand: the grandchild told us its PID, so we can kill it. Without that it would have run to the end on its own. gorun doesn't need the PID: after Wait returns it kills whatever is left in the program's process group or Job Object, so a lesson program that exits normally can't leave a background process behind either.

examples.title: At most two runs at once: a channel as a semaphore

annotations.note: A buffered channel of empty structs is the semaphore: sending takes a slot, receiving frees it, `cap` is the limit. runexec uses exactly this, with `maxConcurrent = 2`.

Three ways out of the wait: a slot, the request's context (the browser went away), or `queueWait` (10 s in runexec). The last two become 503 "server busy". `time.After` in a one-shot select is fine; since Go 1.23 an unfired timer no longer leaks.
The slot is released by defer, so a panicking or failing run can't keep it forever.
Waiting on `len(e.slots)` makes the demo deterministic: runs 1 and 2 hold both slots before run 3 asks. Without it, the scheduler could let run 3 in first.

use_cases: Running code you didn't write, or wrote carelessly, without letting it hang or flood the process that started it
Any os/exec call in a server: a deadline, capped output, a bounded Wait, and a tree kill
Bounding concurrent expensive work (builds, conversions, renders) with a channel semaphore and a 503 when full
strengths: Every limit is a constant at the top of `gorun.go` or `runexec.go`, readable in one screen, and exercised by `gorun_test.go` (timeout, tree kill, output cap)
One package, `runexec`, serves both modes: the Docker runner and the in-process backend can't disagree about timeouts or caps
Compile errors, panics and timeouts come back as data (`exitCode`, `timedOut`, `truncated`, `diagnostics`), never as HTTP errors
Unlike a Java `Process.destroy()`, which ends only the direct child, every run's end kills descendants on both operating systems: on timeout, on a cancelled request, and after a normal exit
weaknesses: Local mode has no isolation at all: lesson code runs as the owner, can read and delete any of the owner's files, reach the network and the `stacklab` database on 127.0.0.1:5432, and inherits the backend's environment variables

A process that leaves the tree escapes the kill: `setsid` on Unix; on Windows one started through WMI, or in the instant between the program's start and its assignment to the Job Object. runProcess then stops reading its output after 2 s
The compile step (`goBuild`, `goVet`) uses plain `exec.CommandContext`: on its 20 s timeout only the `go` command itself is killed, not the compiler processes it started
Docker mode's real limits (memory, pids, CPU, read-only root, no internet) live in `docker-compose.yml`; nothing in Go checks they are there

pitfalls.title: Trusting exec.CommandContext to stop a program
pitfalls.detail: Its default Cancel kills one process. Children survive and can hold the output pipe open, so Wait blocks until they exit. Set `cmd.Cancel` to kill the tree and `cmd.WaitDelay` to bound Wait, and kill what is left after Wait returns too: Cancel only fires while the program runs.
pitfalls.bad:
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, bin)
cmd.Stdout = &buf
err := cmd.Run()
pitfalls.good:
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, bin)
tree := newProcessTree(cmd) // sets cmd.Cancel; proc_unix.go / proc_windows.go
cmd.WaitDelay = pipeGrace
cmd.Stdout = stdoutPipe
err := cmd.Start()
tree.started()
err = cmd.Wait()
tree.killLeftovers()

pitfalls.title: An io.Writer that errors when full
pitfalls.detail: exec stops copying, the pipe fills, and the child blocks on write until the timeout. Swallow the excess and record that you did.

pitfalls.title: Reading ExitCode for a timeout
pitfalls.detail: It differs by OS (1 on Windows, -1 on Unix for a kill). Check `ctx.Err()` first and report the timeout as such.

pitfalls.title: Reading ADR-0003 as a description of local mode
pitfalls.detail: Its container limits apply to Docker mode only (ADR-0008). Locally, the per-run hygiene in gorun and runexec is all there is.

quiz.q: A lesson program prints in an endless loop. What stops it?
options: The run deadline (5 s by default): the context fires and the process tree is killed
Docker's memory limit, in both modes
quiz.why: The cap only stops storing output; it keeps accepting writes so the program never blocks. The deadline kills it.

quiz.q: With `WaitDelay` 0, why can Run block long after the killed child has exited?
options: A grandchild that inherited stdout still holds the pipe, so EOF never arrives until it exits
Run always waits for the full timeout
quiz.why: Run waits for the copying goroutine, which ends at EOF. WaitDelay bounds that wait. gorun removes the cause instead: it reads the pipes itself and kills the tree as soon as the program has exited, so EOF follows at once.

quiz.q: Which of these protections exists in local mode (npm start)?
options: The run timeout and the output cap
quiz.why: Memory, network and filesystem limits come from docker-compose.yml. Timeouts, caps, the tree kill and the two slots are Go code in gorun and runexec, so they apply in both modes.

lessons.body:
## Concept

ADR-0003 states the threat model plainly: the sandbox protects the owner from their own
mistakes (infinite loops, fork bombs, huge output, deleted files, runaway memory), not
from a determined attacker. ADR-0008 then moved the default run mode out of the container
and into the backend process. So the useful question is: which promise lives in which
place, and does it still hold when you run `npm start`?

In Go code, so in **both modes**:

- **Fresh temp dir per run**: `newWorkDir` uses `os.MkdirTemp`, removed by
  `defer os.RemoveAll`. File names must pass `filepath.IsLocal`, which on Windows also
  rejects `C:x`, `\x` and device names like `NUL`. ts-test runs under `.lesson-runs/` in
  the project instead, so Node finds the app's `node_modules`.
- **Timeouts**: `compileTimeout` 20 s; run `defaultRunTTL` 5 s, at most `maxRunTTL` 15 s
  (`runapi.Validate` rejects more); go-test gets 35 s; ts-test takes `timeout_s` the
  same way, but 15 s when it is unset, because starting Vitest or Edge is part of the
  run; the whole request `runBudget` 40 s in runexec.
- **Output caps**: `OutputCap` 64 KB per stream with `[output truncated]`, cut back to a
  whole character so Turkish text doesn't end in half a letter, and `truncated` in the
  result.
- **Tree kill whenever a run ends**: on timeout, on a cancelled request, and after a
  normal exit that left processes behind (`processTree` in `proc_unix.go` and
  `proc_windows.go`).
- **Two concurrent runs**: runexec's `slots` channel, 10 s queue wait, then 503.
- **Offline builds**: `GOPROXY=off`, so `go build` can't download anything.

In `docker-compose.yml`, so in **Docker mode only**: `user: "65532:65532"`,
`read_only: true` with tmpfs for `/tmp` and `/work`, `mem_limit: 512m`, `cpus: 1`,
`pids_limit: 128`, and networks marked `internal: true`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/POSIX**: `setpgid` plus `kill(-pgid, SIGKILL)` is the classic way to kill a tree;
  `proc_unix.go` does exactly that through `SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true}`. Windows has no
  process groups to signal; its equivalent is a Job Object, which every descendant
  joins automatically.
- **Java**: `Process.destroy()` ends one process; you need `ProcessHandle.descendants()`
  to find the rest. Go's `exec.CommandContext` has the same one-process default.
- **Python**: `subprocess.run(timeout=...)` kills the direct child only; its children
  survive, as with Go's default Cancel. `start_new_session=True` plus `os.killpg` is the
  POSIX fix, the same idea as `Setpgid`.
- **Node**: `child_process.spawn` with `detached: true` and `process.kill(-pid)` is the
  Unix pattern; `scripts/verify-lessons.mjs` does that for the headless browser, and
  `taskkill /T /F` on Windows.

## How it works

`gorun.runProcess` is the one function every server runtime goes through, Go programs,
`go test`, Node for ts-node and Vitest or Playwright for ts-test:

```go
runCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, ttl)
cmd := exec.CommandContext(runCtx, name, args...)
tree := newProcessTree(cmd) // Setpgid (Unix); cmd.Cancel kills the tree
cmd.WaitDelay = pipeGrace   // 2 s
cmd.Stdout = stdoutW        // an os.Pipe; gorun copies the read end into a 64 KB cappedBuffer
runErr := cmd.Start()
tree.started()              // Windows: put the program in a new Job Object
runErr = cmd.Wait()         // returns when the program exits
tree.killLeftovers()        // whatever it left running
```

The context comes from the HTTP request, so closing the browser tab cancels the run too.
The result records `TimedOut` from `runCtx.Err()` and normalizes the exit code to -1.

gorun reads the pipes itself rather than handing exec an `io.Writer`. With a Writer,
Wait keeps copying until every process holding the pipe has exited, so a background
child left by the program would hold up the run until `WaitDelay` gave up, and only then
could it be killed. With the pipe's write end passed as an `*os.File`, Wait returns as
soon as the program exits, the leftovers are killed right then, and the copies reach EOF.

On Windows the kill is `TerminateJobObject`: the program joins a fresh Job Object right
after it starts, and every process it starts later joins it too. `taskkill /T` finds
descendants through their parent, so it can't reach the children of a program that has
already exited; it remains only as the fallback when no job can be created. The three
kernel32 functions come from the standard library's `syscall.NewLazyDLL`, so the
dependency ADR-0008 wanted to avoid (`golang.org/x/sys`) is still not needed.

## Design notes

Read against the threat model, the code is honest about local mode: ADR-0008 lists what
is lost and accepts it for a single-user app bound to 127.0.0.1. What that means in
practice deserves to be said plainly:

- **A local lesson program is just a program you ran.** It runs as you, sees your files
  (`~/.ssh`, the repo), can reach the internet, and inherits the backend's environment
  (`cmd.Env` is nil, so `os.Environ()`), including any `STACKLAB_*` variables you set. It
  can also connect to the app database with the default credentials in `config.go`.
- **Docker mode is less isolated than its comments say.** `cmd/runner/main.go` says "The
  backend is its only network peer", but in `docker-compose.yml` the runner sits on
  `backend-net` together with `app-db` and `mocksvc`, and on `runner-net` with
  `playground-db`. And the playground role there is created by the postgres image from
  `POSTGRES_USER`, which the image documents as a superuser, so the "non-superuser role"
  of ADR-0003 holds only in local mode (`scripts/setup-local-db.sql`).
- **A small gap worth closing:** give `goBuild` and `goVet` the same `processTree`, so a
  compile that times out takes the compiler processes with it.
- **If the app ever leaves 127.0.0.1, none of this is a sandbox.** ADR-0003 already says
  so: rebuild the runner on gVisor, Firecracker or a separate host.

lessons.title: The SQL runner's transaction-and-rollback technique
lessons.summary: For the sql runtime, internal/sqlrun sends BEGIN, CREATE SCHEMA and SET LOCAL as one message, runs your statements one by one, and always ends with ROLLBACK, so even your CREATE TABLE never existed. A guard refuses COMMIT and ROLLBACK so your script can't end the sandbox early.

examples.title: Where your script actually runs

annotations.note: `sqlrun.Run` sends this as one simple-protocol message through its `quiet` helper, so none of it appears in your output. `sandboxSQL` builds the SET lines; scope LOCAL means they end with the transaction.

The name is `run_<unix nanos>_<8 hex>`: the time lets the janitor age leftovers, the random part keeps two runs in the same clock tick apart (Windows' wall clock is coarse). current_setting shows the SET LOCAL values; 5000 ms displays as 5s.

An xid exists because CREATE SCHEMA wrote catalog rows. transaction_timestamp() is fixed at BEGIN; statement_timestamp() is this statement's arrival. They differ because the runner's BEGIN was an earlier message.
search_path resolves unqualified names, so the table lands in the run's schema. Nothing here names the schema, which is what lets one example file run unchanged on every run.

PostgreSQL answers a nested BEGIN with a WARNING and keeps the one transaction going. Notices print under their statement in the text output. The dangerous counterpart, your own ROLLBACK or COMMIT, is refused: example 3.

examples.title: Uncommitted DDL is invisible, and its names are reserved until it ends

annotations.note: Session A plays sqlrun.Run: a transaction that creates a table and rows. This runtime itself sandboxes differently: its run_ schema is committed and dropped afterwards, because two sessions must share it.
B uses the same schema, yet the table doesn't exist for it: catalog rows are MVCC rows like any other, and A's aren't committed. `to_regclass` returns NULL where `'scratch'::regclass` would raise.

B's CREATE TABLE has to insert the same (name, schema) key into the system catalogs' unique indexes, where A's uncommitted entry already sits. B waits for A's outcome. A rolls back, so B goes ahead; had A committed, B would have failed with a duplicate-key error.
A sees B's new, empty table: A's two rows were never visible to anyone, and after ROLLBACK they are dead tuples waiting for VACUUM.

examples.title: Your own ROLLBACK is refused; savepoints still work

annotations.note: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes the DROP and stays inside the one transaction. Its command tag is also ROLLBACK, which is why the guard reads the statement's leading keywords, not the tag the server sends back.

`refuseTxControl` (internal/sqlrun/guard.go) matches the first keyword after any comments and refuses the statement before it is sent. The result carries the reason, a DETAIL and a HINT, and `runPhase` stops the phase as it does for any error.
Never sent. Before the guard, the ROLLBACK above ended the runner's transaction, and this statement ran in autocommit mode in public, without timeouts: anything it created would have persisted.

use_cases: Running untrusted or exploratory SQL against a shared database without leaving anything behind
Test isolation: one transaction per test, rolled back at the end, instead of truncating tables
Per-run schemas when a transaction is not possible (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, two sessions): create, use, DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE
strengths: PostgreSQL's DDL is transactional: CREATE TABLE, ALTER and CREATE SCHEMA roll back with the data, unlike MySQL or Oracle, where DDL commits implicitly
Cleanup can't be forgotten: there is nothing to delete, and if the backend dies mid-run the server rolls back when the connection drops
No naming collisions between runs: each one resolves unqualified names into its own schema through search_path
Statement-at-a-time execution on the simple protocol attributes every result, notice and error to its statement, and stops at the first error, as psql with ON_ERROR_STOP does
weaknesses: The sandbox is the transaction, so a `sql` example can't show transaction control: COMMIT and ROLLBACK are refused, and lessons about transactions use `sql-nontx` or `sql-multisession`
The guard is a keyword list (COMMIT, END, ABORT, ROLLBACK without TO, PREPARE TRANSACTION). The transaction-status check behind it catches what the list misses, but only after that statement has run
Rolled-back is not free: every run writes catalog rows that become dead tuples, and burns a transaction ID. Harmless at one user's pace, worth knowing at scale
In Docker mode the playground role is a superuser (the postgres image creates `POSTGRES_USER` as one), so lesson SQL could write server files with COPY, which no rollback undoes

pitfalls.title: COMMIT or ROLLBACK in a `sql` runtime example
pitfalls.detail: It would end the runner's transaction, so sqlrun refuses it and stops the run. Use `sql-nontx` for scripts with their own transaction control, and `SAVEPOINT` / `ROLLBACK TO` inside a `sql` example.

pitfalls.title: Expecting statements after an error to run
pitfalls.detail: The first error aborts the transaction, so sqlrun stops the phase there. A later statement could only fail with 25P02 (current transaction is aborted).

pitfalls.title: Plain SET instead of SET LOCAL inside the sandbox
pitfalls.detail: Inside a transaction both are undone by ROLLBACK, but SET outlives a COMMIT and stays for the session. SET LOCAL is the one that is scoped to the transaction by definition.

quiz.q: Why can the sql runtime roll back a script that creates tables and a schema?
options: PostgreSQL's DDL is transactional: catalog changes commit or abort with the transaction
sqlrun records every CREATE and drops it afterwards
The playground database is recreated after every run
quiz.why: Catalog rows are MVCC rows. Example 2 shows another session can't see uncommitted DDL, and ROLLBACK makes it never have existed.

quiz.q: A `sql` example ends with `COMMIT; CREATE TABLE t (id int);`. What happens?
options: Both run, and t is rolled back with everything else
The COMMIT is refused before it is sent, the run stops there, and nothing persists
quiz.why: sqlrun's guard refuses statements that would end the sandbox transaction. Without it, the COMMIT would have committed the run_ schema, ended SET LOCAL, and let t autocommit in public.

quiz.q: In example 2, why does B's CREATE TABLE wait instead of succeeding or failing at once?
options: B holds a table lock A needs
A's uncommitted catalog entry occupies the same unique-index key, and whether it's a duplicate depends on A's outcome
quiz.why: A unique-index insert that meets an in-progress entry waits for that transaction. Rollback frees the key, commit makes it a duplicate-key error.

quiz.q: Why does sqlrun open its own connection per run instead of using a pool?
options: Pools are slower for short scripts
Transaction state and SET LOCAL live on a connection; a dedicated one guarantees the run sees no one else's state, and closing it rolls back whatever is left
quiz.why: Session.Close's comment says it: any open transaction is rolled back by the server. A pooled connection would need resetting before reuse.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: Schemas and the search path

lessons.body:
## Concept

The promise in `internal/sqlrun/sqlrun.go`'s package comment is "nothing ever persists".
For the `sql` runtime, `Run` keeps it like this:

1. runexec opens a fresh `pgx.Conn` to the playground database, as the non-superuser
   `playground` role (local mode). One connection per run, no pool.
2. `Run` sends one message: `BEGIN; CREATE SCHEMA run_<nanos>_<hex>; SET LOCAL search_path
   TO it; SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 5000; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 2000;`.
3. It defers `ROLLBACK`, with `context.WithoutCancel` and a 5 s budget, so the cleanup
   runs even when the run's own context has expired.
4. It splits the lesson's `setup`, then your script, at top-level semicolons (psql's
   rules, dollar quotes and `BEGIN ATOMIC` function bodies included) and sends each
   statement on its own, after refusing
   any that would end the transaction (`guard.go`). The first error ends the phase.
5. It renders the results as text (command tag, notices, table) for the expected files.

There is no cleanup code that deletes what you created, because there is nothing to
delete: PostgreSQL's DDL is transactional, so the schema, your tables and your rows are
uncommitted catalog and heap rows that ROLLBACK turns into dead tuples nobody ever saw.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring tests**: `@Transactional` on a test class rolls back after each test,
  the same technique. Here the schema is part of the transaction too, which is only
  possible because PostgreSQL's DDL is transactional; MySQL's and Oracle's commit
  implicitly.
- **Python/Django**: `TestCase` wraps each test in a transaction for the same reason, and
  `TransactionTestCase` exists for code that needs real commits: StackLab's `sql-nontx`.
- **JS**: test runners often truncate tables between tests. A rollback is cheaper and
  needs no list of tables to clean.
- **C/C++ with libpq**: the multi-statement first message is `PQexec` with several
  statements; pgx's `PgConn().Exec(...).ReadAll()` is the same simple-protocol call.

## How it works

The three SQL modes share one idea, a `run_` schema per run, and differ in how it goes
away:

- **`sql`** (`Run`): schema and settings inside the transaction (`SET LOCAL`); ROLLBACK
  removes everything.
- **`sql-nontx`** (`RunNonTx`): autocommit, needed for `VACUUM` and
  `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which refuse to run in a transaction block. Settings are
  session-level; a deferred `dropSchema` sends ROLLBACK (in case your script left a
  transaction open) and `DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE`.
- **`sql-multisession`** (`RunMulti`): the schema is committed so both sessions see it,
  setup commits, and cleanup rolls back B first, since B may hold locks the DROP would
  wait on.

Go lessons that import pgx get the same treatment through `ScratchSchema`: an empty
committed schema, passed to the program as `DATABASE_URL` with a `search_path`
parameter, dropped after the run. Committed schemas can outlive a crash, so the
non-transactional modes start with `dropStaleSchemas`: drop every `run_` schema this role
owns whose name-encoded timestamp is older than ten minutes. `Run` doesn't call it,
because a rolled-back run can't leave one behind.

If the backend dies mid-run, nothing is left either: the connection drops and the server
aborts its open transaction.

## Design notes

The technique had one real hole: the sandbox and the learner's script share a
transaction. A `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` in a `sql` example ended the sandbox, and every
later statement autocommitted in `public`, without timeouts, as a role allowed to
create there. `internal/sqlrun/guard.go` now closes it in two layers:

- **Refuse transaction control in `sql` mode.** A statement whose leading keyword is
  `COMMIT`, `END`, `ABORT`, `ROLLBACK` (but not `ROLLBACK TO`) or `PREPARE TRANSACTION`
  is never sent; the result explains why and points to `sql-nontx`. Example 3 shows it.
- **Check after each statement** that the session is still in a transaction. The server
  reports it with every ReadyForQuery message, and pgx exposes it as
  `PgConn().TxStatus()`: `'T'` in a transaction, `'E'` in a failed one, `'I'` when the
  script has ended it. On `'I'` the run stops and `Run` drops the schema, which may have
  been committed.

The same file refuses `COPY ... FROM STDIN` in every mode: the server would wait for
the client to stream rows, which this runner can't do, so the run used to hang until
its time budget ran out. A third layer sits in the database itself. Since PostgreSQL 15,
`public` is owned by `pg_database_owner`, a role whose only member is the current
database's owner, and `playground` owns its database, so it could create in `public`. A
`REVOKE` can't take that away from the owner, so `scripts/setup-local-db.sql` ends with
`ALTER SCHEMA public OWNER TO postgres`: `playground` keeps `USAGE` and loses `CREATE`.
An escape that slipped past both checks would fall back to the default search path, and
its unqualified `CREATE` would now fail instead of persisting.

The Docker mode caveat belongs here too. ADR-0003 says SQL runs "with a non-superuser
role owning only sandbox objects", but `docker-compose.yml` creates `playground` through
the postgres image's `POSTGRES_USER`, which the image makes a superuser. A rollback
can't undo what a superuser does outside the database, such as `COPY ... TO` a file.
Local mode's `scripts/setup-local-db.sql` gets this right with `NOSUPERUSER`.

lessons.title: Content loading and full-text indexing
lessons.summary: Lessons go from files to the page through a build script, not a database: scripts/build-lessons.mjs validates content/ and writes an index plus one file per lesson for the frontend. There is no lessons table, no full-text index and no Ctrl+K search; this lesson shows what exists and what the planned index would take.

examples.title: contentcheck in small: collect every error, write nothing if there is one

annotations.note: The real script reads the ids from `content/curriculum.yaml`, and its allow-list has nine hosts (go.dev, pkg.go.dev, typescriptlang.org, developer.mozilla.org, react.dev, postgresql.org, nodejs.org, with www. variants). The H2 list is copied verbatim.

contentcheck scans every example file for LEARN markers, this one included. A literal marker naming a non-curriculum id here failed this very lesson's check while it was being written, hence the escape.

The frontmatter regex is the real one. The real parser is the `yaml` package, and validation against `lesson.schema.json` is a hand-written subset validator (about 80 lines) instead of ajv, as the script's comment explains.
The directory decides the id: `<track>/<module>/<NN-slug>` must be `track.module.slug`. `--filter` matches on the directory too, so a lesson with a broken id can still be selected and checked.
The real H2 check, verbatim: the headings present must appear in the fixed order, and the optional "How it works" may be missing.

The real marker regex: only id-shaped arguments count, so prose such as `LEARN(<lesson-id>)` in CLAUDE.md isn't a marker. On an unfiltered run the real script also scans `server/`, `src/` and `scripts/`.
Errors are collected, not thrown, so one run reports all of them. Any error means exit 1 and no file written: the frontend never imports a half-valid bundle.

examples.title: The generated module, the lookups, and the search that doesn't exist

annotations.note: The shape of `content/lessons.bundle.json` and of the private bundle verify-lessons reads: every lesson's frontmatter plus `dir` and `body`, and three maps keyed by path: example sources, expected outputs, fixtures. Until 2026-11-14 the frontend imported this whole object as one `.ts` module; it now gets the same data split per lesson.

A lookup by id, `Array.find` over every lesson, as the app's old `lessonById` did. `load.ts` now keeps the index in a Map by id, and its imports are typed by assertion (`index as LessonSummary[]`, `import.meta.glob<Lesson>`): no runtime check, it trusts the generator that validated the data.

The sidebar and lesson list come from `curriculum.yaml`; the content comes from the generated lesson data. `LessonPage` joins them by id, and a curriculum lesson with no content renders the "not authored yet" box.

The key schemes: `<dir>/<file>` for sources, `<dir>/<example id>` for expected output (a lesson's own file drops the `<dir>/`). Fixtures lose their `fixtures/` prefix on the way to the runner, so the program opens `seed.csv` in its working directory.

`toLowerCase` turns "İ" into "i" plus a combining dot, so "izolasyon" misses. `toLocaleLowerCase('tr')` fixes that and breaks the other side: "I" becomes "ı", so a query typed on a non-Turkish keyboard misses. A search has to fold İ, I, ı and i to one letter.
The proof: U+0069 U+0307, two code points for one visible letter. `.length` is 2, and a naive `startsWith` or highlight offset is off by one.

examples.title: The lessons table and search index the docs planned (not built)

annotations.note: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md's ERD: a `search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` column with a GIN index, so the vector is computed on write and every query is an index lookup. Weights mark title (A) above body (B).

Read what the stemmer did: "satırları" in the body became `satır`, but the title's "Satır" became `sa`. PostgreSQL's Turkish (Snowball) stemmer is aggressive and not always consistent; measure it on your vocabulary before relying on it.

`kilit` matched "kilitleri" in one title and "kilitler" in the other body, and the title match ranks higher. `websearch_to_tsquery` accepts what people type (quotes, or, -word) without raising syntax errors.

Lowercasing uses the database's own case mapping. This one (builtin C.UTF-8, see `scripts/setup-local-db.sql`) maps I to i, so "YALITIM" becomes `yalit` and misses the `yalıt` stored for "Yalıtım". The same trap as the JS filter, one layer down.
PostgreSQL 18 made generated columns VIRTUAL by default (computed on read), and those can't be indexed, which is why the ERD insists on STORED. The script stops here: an error ends a sql run.

use_cases: Content that should be reviewed like code: files in the repo, validated by a script, turned into a generated module
Small, read-only data sets a frontend can ship whole (docs, help text, a few hundred records) instead of serving through an API
Deciding between a client-side filter and server-side full-text search for a Ctrl+K box
strengths: No moving parts at runtime: lessons render with the backend down, and a broken lesson.md is caught by the build script, not by a user
Content diffs are ordinary text diffs, and every check (schema, ids, links, LEARN markers) runs before anything is written
`verify-lessons` builds a private bundle with `--out` and `--filter`, so several authors can check their own lessons without racing on the shared files
weaknesses: Each lesson is a separate chunk: opening one costs a request and a loading state, and a page that outlives a rebuild can ask for a chunk file that no longer exists (it shows an error and asks for a reload)
Nothing regenerates it automatically: not `npm start`, not `npm run build`'s prebuild. After editing content you run `node scripts/build-lessons.mjs` yourself

No search of any kind, and lesson ids join three places (curriculum.yaml, the generated lesson data, app-db rows) with no foreign key: renaming an id silently orphans its progress, notes and bookmarks
The import is typed with `as`, so a generator bug that changes the shape surfaces as an `undefined` deep in a component, not as an error at load

pitfalls.title: Expecting an edited lesson.md to show up
pitfalls.detail: The page reads the generated files. Run `node scripts/build-lessons.mjs` (Vite then hot-reloads), or `npm run gen:curriculum` after editing curriculum.yaml.

pitfalls.title: Renaming a lesson id
pitfalls.detail: Progress, notes, bookmarks, quiz answers and run history are keyed by the id as text. Treat ids as immutable, as the schema's description says.

pitfalls.title: Lowercasing Turkish with one function
pitfalls.detail: Neither `toLowerCase` nor `toLocaleLowerCase('tr')` makes İ, I, ı and i match each other, and neither does PostgreSQL's `lower` under a non-Turkish locale. Fold explicitly on both sides of the comparison.
pitfalls.good:
const fold = (s: string) => s.toLocaleLowerCase('tr').replace(/ı/g, 'i').normalize('NFD').replace(/\p{M}/gu, '');
fold(title).includes(fold(query))

quiz.q: When you open a lesson, where does its text come from?
options: Generated files bundled by Vite: an index in the main chunk, the lesson itself in a chunk of its own
The backend reads content/ on each request
quiz.why: There is no lessons route or table. `load.ts` imports `lessonIndex.generated.ts` for the header and loads `generated/<id>.json` with import() for the content.

quiz.q: You fix a typo in a lesson.md while `npm start` is running. What makes the page show it?
options: Nothing, the backend re-indexes content on change
Running `node scripts/build-lessons.mjs`; Vite then reloads the regenerated module
quiz.why: No watcher, SSE event or startup loader exists. The build script is the only writer of the generated files.

quiz.q: Why does the query IZOLASYON miss the title İzolasyon with both JavaScript lowercasings?
options: toLowerCase maps İ to i plus a combining dot, and the Turkish locale maps I to ı: neither gives plain i on both sides
quiz.why: The example prints both results and the two code points of the lowercased İ.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL: Tables and indexes for text search

lessons.body:
## Concept

The curriculum's goal for this lesson is "files to lessons table to Ctrl+K". Two of those
three don't exist. What exists is shorter:

1. **Files.** `content/<track>/<module>/<NN-slug>/` holds `lesson.md` (YAML frontmatter
   plus prose), `examples/`, `expected/` and `fixtures/`. `content/curriculum.yaml` holds
   the full plan, including lessons nobody has written yet.
2. **Two generators, run by hand.** `npm run gen:curriculum` turns curriculum.yaml into
   `src/features/curriculum/curriculum.generated.ts` (sidebar, tracks, paths).
   `node scripts/build-lessons.mjs` validates every lesson and writes
   `content/lessons.bundle.json` (everything), `src/features/lessons/lessonIndex.generated.ts`
   (each lesson's title, header facts and unconfirmed claims) and
   `src/features/lessons/generated/<lesson id>.json` (one lesson's full content).
3. **A static import and a lazy one.** `src/features/lessons/load.ts` imports the index,
   which Vite bundles into the app. It lists the lesson files with `import.meta.glob`, so
   Vite emits each as its own chunk, and `LessonPage` loads one with `import()` when the
   lesson opens: the header renders from the index at once, the tabs when the chunk
   arrives.

The backend never sees lesson content. Its migrations
(`server/cmd/stacklab/migrations`) create `schema_info`, `runs`, `progress`, `notes`,
`bookmarks` and `quiz_answers`, each keyed by `lesson_id text` without a foreign key,
because there is no `lessons` table to reference. There is no `tsvector` column, no
search endpoint, and no Ctrl+K handler anywhere in `src/`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Static site generators** (Hugo, Jekyll, Sphinx, Docusaurus) are the closest model:
  Markdown in, a validated build artefact out, no database. StackLab's artefacts are a
  JavaScript module and one JSON file per lesson instead of HTML pages.
- **Java**: comparable to resources processed at build time into generated classes
  (annotation processors, protobuf). The generated file is checked in, like
  `curriculum.generated.ts`, so the app builds without running the generator first.
- **C/C++**: `xxd -i` or `#embed` (C23) turns a file into data in the binary; here the
  "binary" is the JS bundle. Go's `embed.FS` is the backend equivalent and is used for
  migrations, not content.
- **Python**: like loading a validated YAML file at import time, except the validation
  happens once at build time instead of on every start.

## How it works

`build-lessons.mjs` walks `content/`, and for each `lesson.md` it checks the frontmatter
against `lesson.schema.json`, the id against the directory, unique ids, that every
`prerequisites` and `compare_with` id exists, that example, fixture and expected files
exist, the H2 order, official-docs-only links, `nondeterminism_note` on `check: none`,
and LEARN markers. On success it writes the bundle and the frontend's files, each only
when its content changed, so an unchanged lesson doesn't reload open tabs; on any error
it writes nothing and exits 1.

Three flags exist for `npm run verify:lessons`, which never touches the shared files:
`--out <file>` writes only a private bundle, `--filter a,b` (with `--out`) restricts the
run to lessons whose directory matches, and `--allow-missing-expected` turns a missing
expected file into a warning while you generate it. verify-lessons then sends every
example to `POST /api/run` with `X-Stacklab-No-History` (or runs it in headless Edge for
ts-browser) and judges the output with the UI's own `judge.ts`, twice.

## Design notes

The docs describe a different design. ADR-0004 decided that "the backend loads and
indexes it into app-db at startup (upsert on content hash, delete removed lessons) so
search and the lessons table still work", with a `cmd/contentcheck` and a dev-mode file
watcher pushing an SSE `content-changed` event. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` draws the
`lessons` table with its `search` column. None of it was built: contentcheck is a Node
script, and what shipped is the alternative ADR-0004 rejected, "content in the frontend
bundle". The README's "it runs as part of the build" is also out of date: `prebuild`
runs `copy-wasm.mjs` and `build-lesson-libs.mjs` only.

For one user and a couple of hundred lessons, the shipped design is the boring, right
one: no loader to keep in sync, nothing to fail at startup, lessons readable with the
backend down. Its costs were a large main chunk, until the content was split per lesson
on 2026-11-14 (4.7 MB of first-chunk JavaScript before, 0.48 MB after), and no search.
If you add Ctrl+K, there are two honest options:

- **Client-side**, over the lesson index already in memory: titles and summaries are
  there (add tags to the index to search them too); fold Turkish casing as in example 2's pitfall, and it is instant with no
  backend change. This is where to start.
- **Server-side**, as drawn: a loader that upserts lessons by content hash at startup,
  the STORED tsvector with a GIN index, a search route. Worth it only if search must
  cover lesson bodies, which sit in per-lesson chunks the page doesn't load, or needs
  ranking and stemming.
  Example 3 shows what to check first: the `turkish` stemmer's quirks and the database's
  I/ı case mapping.

Either way, if lessons ever become rows, give `progress` and `notes` a foreign key with
`ON UPDATE CASCADE`, so an id rename stops orphaning learning state.

lessons.title: The TS CodeRunner strategy: ServerRunner vs BrowserTsRunner
lessons.summary: The Run button calls runnerFor(runtime).run(request) and never asks where the code runs. The interface is one line; the real work is making a browser iframe honor the same contract as a backend process, including when a run is over.

examples.title: One interface, two runners, one factory: the shape of CodeRunner.ts

annotations.note: The whole strategy interface, as in src/features/runner/CodeRunner.ts. Everything that differs between runtimes hides behind one async method that takes the wire request and returns the wire result.

ServerRunner's error contract: a non-2xx answer is a refusal (busy, unsupported runtime), so it throws with the problem body's detail. The real class calls the global fetch; this one takes it as a parameter because the lesson iframe has no network.

A stand-in for BrowserTsRunner. The real one transpiles in a worker and runs the module in a sandboxed iframe; this one imports a data: URL in the same page, which keeps the shape and drops the isolation. Note that a crash resolves with exit 1: failing lesson code is a result, not an error.
The factory is the only place that knows the mapping. In the app, ts-browser goes to the browser and all eight other runtimes, ts-node and ts-test included, go to the server.

The caller's two branches are the ones RunPanel.tsx turns into { kind: 'done' } and { kind: 'failed' }. A thrown TypeError from the lesson would have been the wrong kind of failure; the runner turns it into a result.

examples.title: When is a browser run over? A fixed delay vs the pending-timer rule

annotations.note: A virtual clock so the output is exact. The real shim (IFRAME_SHIM in browserTs.ts) wraps window.setTimeout and setInterval and keeps the ids of pending timers in a Set; pending here plays that role.
An interval that is never cleared keeps the run alive, as it would keep a Node process alive. The shim counts intervals as pending until clearInterval.

The real marker is a line appended after the lesson module's last statement, window.__stacklabMainDone(), so it runs after every top-level await. A throw skips it and the error handler marks the main part done instead.
The rule the runner used before: finish a fixed delay after the frame loaded. Anything logged later is silently lost, and the expected file would record the truncated output as correct.

Today's rule: done when the main part ran and no timer is pending. The shim then waits two more task turns: promise continuations can start new timers, and the unhandledrejection event for a promise rejected in the last task arrives a task later. This miniature has no promises, so it skips both. The 10 s ceiling is BrowserTsRunner's default timeout.

use_cases: Reading src/features/runner/ before adding a runtime: a new server runtime needs a case in runexec.execute and nothing in the frontend beyond the Runtime union
Debugging a ts-browser lesson that passes in Node but not in the app: different strategy, different console formatting and timeout
A model for any UI that must run work in two places (local and remote) behind one call
strengths: RunPanel never branches on where code runs, so fetch, problem details, workers and iframes stay out of the view; unlike a switch in the component, a third strategy would touch only runnerFor
The same BrowserTsRunner class runs in the app and in verify.html, so scripts/verify-lessons.mjs checks the code the learner uses, not a copy
The iframe's opaque origin and CSP are enforced by the browser, which is a stronger boundary than any check the app could write itself
Like Go's implicit interfaces, structural typing means implements CodeRunner is an extra compile-time check, not a requirement
weaknesses: The two strategies honor the same type, not the same behavior: the browser runner ignores fixtures, stdin and setup, uses only the first file, defaults to a 10 s timeout (server: 5 s) and reports a timeout as exit 124 (server: -1)
No output cap in the browser: truncated is always false, and a logging loop floods postMessage until the timeout fires; the server caps each stream at 64 KB
Browser runs never reach the backend, so they are missing from run history
Module-level singletons (serverRunner, browserTsRunner) are created at import; fine in a browser app, but a unit test can't swap fetch without patching globals

pitfalls.title: Rejecting for failing lesson code
pitfalls.detail: If a runner threw on a compile error or an uncaught exception, RunPanel would show a red 'failed' banner instead of the output and the exit code. Only machinery failures reject; everything the lesson did is a RunResult.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ts-browser and ts-node to print the same thing
pitfalls.detail: The browser shim formats values itself: strings as-is, Map, Set and Error readably, everything else as JSON. Node uses util.inspect. console.log({ a: 1 }) prints {"a":1} in one and { a: 1 } in the other, so an expected file recorded under one runtime fails under the other.

pitfalls.title: Hiding the iframe with display: none
pitfalls.detail: The runner keeps the frame rendered, 1x1 and transparent, because Edge throttles a hidden cross-origin frame: requestAnimationFrame stops (Microsoft documents this), and in Edge 157 its timers woke up only about once a second. Async lessons would get slow and their timing claims wrong.

quiz.q: A ts-browser example has a syntax error. What does BrowserTsRunner.run do?
options: Rejects, so RunPanel shows the 'failed' banner
Resolves with exitCode 1 and the esbuild message as a diagnostic
Resolves with exitCode 0 and empty output
quiz.why: transpile() rejects inside run(), and run() catches it and returns a RunResult with exit 1 and one diagnostic. Only machinery failures reject.

quiz.q: Why is the lesson iframe sandboxed with allow-scripts but without allow-same-origin?
options: So the lesson runs in an opaque origin and can't touch the app's DOM, storage or cookies
So the iframe can fetch the lesson libraries itself
quiz.why: Without allow-same-origin the frame's origin is opaque ('null'). That is also why the libraries arrive as data: URLs: the frame couldn't fetch them from the app's origin.

quiz.q: A ts-browser lesson starts a setInterval and never clears it. What does the learner see?
options: The run ends when the module's last statement finishes
The run ends at the 10 s timeout with exit 124 and a timed-out note
quiz.why: A pending interval keeps the run alive, as in Node. The runner's own timer then fires, removes the iframe and reports a timeout.

quiz.q: Which runner executes a ts-node lesson?
options: ServerRunner: runnerFor sends everything except ts-browser to POST /api/run
quiz.why: runnerFor only checks for 'ts-browser'. ts-node runs in Node on the backend side (gorun.RunNode), with Node's own console formatting.

further_reading.title: MDN: setTimeout, reasons for longer delays than specified

lessons.body:
## Concept

`src/features/runner/CodeRunner.ts` is the strategy pattern in about 40 lines: an
interface with one method, two implementations and a factory.

```ts
export interface CodeRunner {
  run(req: RunRequest): Promise<RunResult>;
}
export function runnerFor(runtime: RunRequest['runtime']): CodeRunner {
  return runtime === 'ts-browser' ? browserTsRunner : serverRunner;
}
```

`RunPanel.tsx` builds a `RunRequest` from the editor and calls
`runnerFor(example.runtime).run(...)`. It still looks at the runtime for the editor
language, the stdin box and SQL tables, but never to decide where code runs.

- **`ServerRunner`** posts the request to `/api/run`. Vite proxies that to the Go
  backend, which runs the code in-process in local mode (`internal/runexec`, ADR-0008)
  or forwards it to the runner container in Docker mode. Eight runtimes take this path:
  `go`, `go-test`, `go-server`, `ts-node`, `ts-test`, `sql`, `sql-nontx` and
  `sql-multisession`.
- **`BrowserTsRunner`** (`browserTs.ts`) handles `ts-browser`: it transpiles in a Web
  Worker and runs the result in a sandboxed iframe. Nothing reaches the backend.

The interface is the easy part. The contract behind it is the hard part: **resolve with a
`RunResult` for anything the lesson code did** (compile errors, crashes, timeouts) and
**reject only when the machinery refused or broke**. RunPanel relies on that split: a
resolved result becomes `{ kind: 'done' }` with the output, a rejection becomes
`{ kind: 'failed' }` with a banner. The server side gets most of the contract from the
operating system, which supplies exit codes, stdout and stderr, and the end of a process.
The browser runner has to build each of these itself.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: the same shape as a `Comparator` or a JDBC `Driver`: an interface, classes,
  a factory. The difference is structural typing: `implements CodeRunner` asks the
  compiler to check the class, but any object with a matching `run` is a `CodeRunner`.
- **Go**: the backend repeats the pattern one layer down. `httpapi.Runner` is declared by
  its consumer in `httpapi/run.go`; `runexec.Executor` (in-process) and
  `runclient.Client` (HTTP to the container) satisfy it without naming it, and `main.go`
  picks one from `STACKLAB_RUNNER_URL`. The frontend strategy chooses *where* (browser or
  server); the backend one chooses *how* (in this process or in a container).
- **C++**: a pure virtual base class, or `std::function` when there's one method. TS has
  both options too; ts.architecture.patterns argues that the stateless `ServerRunner`
  could just as well be a function.
- **Python/JS**: a `Protocol` or plain duck typing. The type adds a compile-time check,
  nothing at run time.

## How it works

What `BrowserTsRunner.run` does for one ts-browser example:

1. **Transpile off the main thread.** `esbuild.worker.ts` loads esbuild-wasm once (about
   14 MB of WebAssembly) and answers `{ id, code, loader }` messages with
   `{ id, ok, js | error }`. The id pairs answers with requests on the shared worker. The
   output is an ES module (`format: 'esm'`, `target: 'es2022'`), because lessons use
   top-level `await`. Types are stripped, not checked.
2. **Resolve libraries.** If the module imports `react`, `zod` or another library from
   ADR-0010, the runner fetches `/lesson-libs/manifest.json` and `bundle.js` once and
   builds an import map of `data:` URLs. The iframe can't fetch them itself (next step).
3. **Build the frame.** `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">` with a `srcdoc` holding a CSP
   `<meta>` (`default-src 'none'`, scripts only inline or `data:`), the import map, the
   shim and the module, followed by `window.__stacklabMainDone()`. Without
   `allow-same-origin` the frame's origin is opaque: no access to the app's DOM,
   `localStorage` or cookies, and with the CSP no network at all.
4. **Keep it running at full speed.** The frame is 1x1 px, transparent and fixed in the
   corner rather than `display: none`. The comment in `browserTs.ts` records why: a hidden
   cross-origin frame (the sandbox's opaque origin makes it one) is throttled. Microsoft
   documents that Edge throttles cross-origin frames that are `display: none` or outside
   the viewport, and that such frames "lose access to `requestAnimationFrame` and
   `ResizeObserver`" ([iframe throttling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/edge-learnmore-iframe-throttling-display)).
   Timers aren't on that page; a run in Edge 157.0.4341.46 (headless and headed,
   2026-11-14) showed them too. In a `display: none` sandboxed frame, a 10 ms
   `setInterval` fired a few times in the first 80 ms, then once a second, and
   `requestAnimationFrame` stopped after three callbacks; the 1x1 frame got about 300
   ticks and 180 frames in the same 3 s.
5. **Collect output.** The shim replaces `console.*` and posts every call to the parent;
   `log`/`info`/`debug` become stdout, `warn`/`error` stderr, an uncaught error or
   unhandled rejection stderr plus exit 1. One exception: React 18's development build
   replays a failed render inside a `react-invokeguardedcallback` event so that devtools
   see it, which also reaches the window's error handler even when an error boundary
   catches it. The shim ignores errors reported during that event; React rethrows the
   ones no boundary caught, and those count. The parent drops any message whose
   `e.source` isn't its own frame, and the `switch` over the message type ends in a
   `never` check.
6. **Decide when it's over** (example 2): when the main part has run and no timer is
   pending, or at the timeout (`timeoutS`, default 10 s). An unhandled rejection doesn't
   end the main part; the module keeps running. Then the frame is removed, which also
   kills an infinite loop inside it, and the result is resolved.

`ServerRunner` is ten lines by comparison: `fetch`, a problem-details error path, and
`(await res.json()) as RunResult`. That cast trusts the backend completely; the contract
lesson (inside.codebase.contract) shows where that trust is misplaced.

## Design notes

The pattern earns its keep in two places. The run logic holds no list of server
runtimes, so the backend went from three runtimes to eight without touching it. And
because the strategy is a plain object that doesn't
depend on React, `src/verify/browserVerify.ts` can expose the real
`BrowserTsRunner` to headless Edge, so `npm run verify:lessons` tests what the learner
runs.

The strategies share a type, not a behavior, and the differences are worth knowing
before you debug a lesson:

- The browser runner reads only the first file and ignores `fixtures`, `stdin` and
  `setup`. Its default timeout is 10 s (the server's run timeout is 5 s), and it reports
  a timeout as exit 124 where gorun reports -1. Both fail the "matches expected" check.
- It has no output cap: `truncated` is always `false`.
- Its `console.log` formatting is the shim's `fmt` (strings as-is, `Map`/`Set`/`Error`
  readable, everything else as JSON). `ts-node` lessons get Node's `util.inspect`, so the
  same line can print differently under the two runtimes.
- Browser runs are never recorded in run history; only `handleRun` on the backend writes
  history.

Comments drift like this one did: until 2026-11-14 the doc comment at the top of
`CodeRunner.ts` said `ServerRunner` "proxies go/sql/ts-node through the backend to the
runner container (ADR-0003)", which predated ADR-0008 and named three runtimes of eight.
It now says what happens: the backend runs the code itself in local mode and forwards it
to the runner service in Docker mode.

Classes are justified for `BrowserTsRunner`: it owns a worker, a request counter and a
lazily built import map, and the class keeps that state in one place. `ServerRunner` has
no state. If you ever need to test `RunPanel` without a backend, the module-level
singletons are the obstacle: pass the runner in (a prop or a context) rather than
patching the global `fetch`.

Two alternatives were possible here. A `switch (runtime)` inside RunPanel would have
spread transport details through the view. Sending ts-browser to the server as well
would have needed a browser on the backend, which is exactly what verify-lessons starts
for itself, and a far heavier way to run a learner's three lines of TypeScript.

lessons.title: The API contract and type generation
lessons.summary: There is no openapi.yaml and no generated code here: the run API's contract is the Go package runapi, mirrored by hand in types.ts and trusted with a cast. This lesson reads where that mirror drifted, how two of the drifts were found and fixed, and what would catch the next one.

examples.title: The Go half: nil slices become null, and unknown fields pass silently

annotations.note: The tags are the contract. A plain slice field is always present but can be null; a pointer with omitempty is absent when nil, which the TypeScript mirror spells sql?: ... The mirror has to get both rules right by hand.

gorun initializes its slices to []; this copy loop, the shape of runexec.fromGorun, starts from a nil slice and appends nothing when there is nothing to copy. The producer was right, and the adapter in between undid it.

Until the fix, a clean Go run and every SQL run said "diagnostics": null on the wire, where types.ts promises Diagnostic[]. An empty slice is all the fix takes (the "fixed" line). The backend now swaps one in inside runapi.Result's MarshalJSON, the one type every producer shares; the learning handlers do the same with if rows == nil.
This is how httpapi's handleRun decodes: a misspelled field is dropped without a word, and the run gets the default timeout.
runapi.Decode does exactly this, with a comment saying drift should fail loudly in development. Nothing calls it: the backend, cmd/runner and runclient all decode leniently.

examples.title: The TypeScript half: a cast, a type guard and two zod schemas on the real response

annotations.note: Copied from a real POST /api/run response in local mode (a Go hello world), from before the fix. Every server run without compile errors or written files carried these two nulls; the same run now sends [] for both. Any other producer (an older backend, a proxy, a test double) can still send this.

This is ServerRunner's (await res.json()) as RunResult. The cast compiles and checks nothing; the TypeError surfaces wherever the field is first used. Nothing in the UI reads files or diagnostics, which is why nobody noticed the nulls while the backend sent them.

The type guard that runapi.go's package comment used to say the frontend has (it was never written; the comment now describes the cast). It catches the drift but only answers false: no field name and no path, and it is a third hand-written copy of the shape to keep in sync.

Annotating the schema with the mirror type ties them together: if types.ts and the schema disagree, tsc rejects this line. At run time zod reports each failing field with its path. zod is already an app dependency (ADR-0010), so this costs no new package.

The tolerant alternative: accept null and hand the app []. It would have kept the UI working against the old backend, but it also hides the drift. The fix went into the producer instead; a strict schema in development is what would catch the next drift.

examples.title: The error half: how runclient lost the runner's problem detail

annotations.note: runclient.Run's order of operations before the fix: decode into Result first, then look at the status. An RFC 9457 problem body decodes into Result without error, because unknown fields are ignored, and the detail was never read.

Choosing the shape by status first keeps the detail. The runner's problem body and runapi.Error have the same fields, so one Decode fills it. runclient.Run does this now, with one exception: a 500 is the runner itself failing, so it becomes an error and the backend answers 502, as it does in local mode.

The last hop is ServerRunner in the browser: it shows the problem's detail, or the status text when the detail is empty. Before the fix, Docker mode turned "ts-test lessons run only in local mode" into "Not Implemented", and "server busy" into "Service Unavailable".

use_cases: Adding a field to RunResult: change runapi.go and types.ts in the same commit, and decide null vs [] vs absent explicitly
Deciding whether a two-language project needs OpenAPI or code generation, or a contract test is enough
Reviewing any Go JSON API for nil slices, omitempty on required fields, and lenient decoding
strengths: One Go package (runapi) is shared by the backend, cmd/runner, runclient and runexec, so the Go side cannot drift from itself
Problem details (application/problem+json) are written in one place, httpapi.problem, so every error has the same shape
The mirror is small (about a dozen types) and readable; there is no generator to install, configure or upgrade
Empty lists are [] on the wire, normalized in one place (runapi.Result's MarshalJSON), and runapi_test.go fails if any list in a Result encodes as null
SQL cells travel as *string in Go and string | null in TS, so NULL never looks like an empty string; that part of the mirror is exact
weaknesses: Nothing checks types.ts against runapi.go: not tsc, not a test, not the browser at run time

Go's encoding/json writes nil slices as null and ignores unknown fields unless asked, so drift is silent in both directions. Result's MarshalJSON covers the nulls for the run API only; a new response type has to remember the rule again
Both fixed drifts shipped first and were found by people reading the code while writing lessons, not by a test or a type check

Comments describe checks that don't exist (a discriminated union in gorun.go, a strict Decode that nothing calls), which is worse than no comment. runapi.go's promised type guard was the third, corrected since

pitfalls.title: Appending into a nil slice and marshaling it
pitfalls.detail: A struct field that starts nil and receives no elements is null in JSON. Initialize it, or set it to an empty slice just before encoding.
pitfalls.bad: out := Result{}; for _, d := range in { out.Diagnostics = append(out.Diagnostics, d) }
pitfalls.good: out := Result{Diagnostics: make([]Diagnostic, 0, len(in))}

pitfalls.title: A MarshalJSON on an embedded type
pitfalls.detail: Methods of an embedded struct are promoted, MarshalJSON included. Give StatementResult a MarshalJSON and StepResult, which embeds it, encodes as the statement alone, losing step, session and the rest. runapi fills in the embedded lists from Result's MarshalJSON instead.

pitfalls.title: Decoding an error body into the success type
pitfalls.detail: With unknown fields ignored, any JSON object decodes into any struct without error. Check the status first, then decode into the shape that status promises.

pitfalls.title: Treating `as` as validation
pitfalls.detail: JSON.parse(...) as RunResult tells the compiler to stop checking. Validate at the boundary (zod, or a guard) at least in development, or accept that the first symptom will appear far from its cause.

pitfalls.title: Believing the comment
pitfalls.detail: runapi.go said the frontend validates with a type guard (corrected since); gorun.go says the TS side mirrors Result as a discriminated union. Neither was true. Check claims about other files against those files.

quiz.q: A Go struct with no MarshalJSON method has a field Diagnostics []Diagnostic `json:"diagnostics"` that is never assigned. What does json.Marshal write?
quiz.why: A nil slice encodes as null. [] needs an empty, non-nil slice (runapi.Result's MarshalJSON swaps one in just before encoding); omitting the key needs omitempty.

quiz.q: A client posts {"runtime":"go","timeoutSecs":15} to /api/run. What happens?
options: The field is ignored and the default timeout applies
The backend maps timeoutSecs to timeoutS
quiz.why: handleRun uses a plain json.Decoder. Only DisallowUnknownFields, which runapi.Decode sets but nobody calls, would reject it.

quiz.q: Which of these catches "files": null before the UI uses it?
options: tsc, because RunResult declares files: WrittenFile[]
The as RunResult cast in ServerRunner
A zod schema or type guard applied to the parsed body
quiz.why: Types are erased at run time, and a cast is an instruction to the compiler, not a check. Only code that runs on the value can see null.

quiz.q: Where is this app's openapi.yaml?
options: There is none: runapi.go is the source and types.ts a hand-written mirror
quiz.why: The curriculum, ADR-0001 and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md describe an OpenAPI contract and a generated client, but none was ever written.

further_reading.title: package encoding/json: nil slices, omitempty, DisallowUnknownFields

lessons.body:
## Concept

The curriculum's goal for this lesson is "one openapi.yaml, two languages". That file
does not exist, and neither does any generated code. The contract for the run API, the
one every Run button press goes through, is:

- **`server/internal/runapi/runapi.go`**: Go structs with JSON tags (`Request`, `Result`,
  `StatementResult`, `StepResult`, `SQLStmtError`, `Error`). The backend's handler, the
  Docker runner binary, `runclient` and `runexec` all import it, so the Go side cannot
  disagree with itself.
- **`src/features/runner/types.ts`**: a hand-written TypeScript mirror (`RunRequest`,
  `RunResult`, the `Runtime` union and the rest). Nothing compares it with the Go file.
  `ServerRunner` trusts it with `(await res.json()) as RunResult`.
- **Errors**: RFC 9457 problem details, written by `httpapi.problem` as
  `{ type, title, status, detail }` with `application/problem+json`. `ServerRunner`
  reads `detail`.

The learning endpoints (progress, notes, bookmarks, quiz) follow the same pattern:
structs in `learningstore`, a mirror in `src/features/learning/api.ts`, a generic
`req<T>()` that casts.

Drift found while writing the lessons (the first and the last are fixed now, the second
in part):

1. **`null` where arrays are declared.** A clean Go run, and every SQL run, returned
   `"diagnostics": null, "files": null`; `types.ts` says `Diagnostic[]` and
   `WrittenFile[]`. `gorun` initializes both slices, and `runexec.fromGorun` rebuilds them
   by appending onto nil (example 1). The learning handlers knew this rule and turned
   nil into `[]` before encoding; the run path didn't. The fix is a `MarshalJSON` on
   `runapi.Result` that writes every empty list as `[]` (SQL statements, columns, rows
   and notices too), so every producer is covered, plus `runapi_test.go`, which fails if
   any list in a `Result` encodes as `null`.
2. **A validator that isn't there.** `runapi.go`'s package comment said the frontend
   checks the shape "with a zod-free type guard in Phase 3". No guard was ever written;
   the comment now says the frontend trusts the response with a cast. `gorun.go` still
   says "the TS side mirrors it as a discriminated union on TimedOut/ExitCode"; the TS
   `RunResult` is a plain interface (the union in `types.ts` is `RunState`, a UI state).
3. **A strict decoder nobody calls.** `runapi.Decode` sets `DisallowUnknownFields` "so wire
   drift fails loudly in dev", but every decoder on the path is lenient.
4. **A lost error detail in Docker mode** (example 3). `runclient` now reads the problem
   body whenever the status isn't 200, and its tests pin "server busy" and the ts-test
   refusal.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++**: two programs sharing a header compile against one definition. Here each
  language has its own copy, so this is closer to two teams agreeing a struct layout by
  email.
- **Java**: Jackson fails on unknown properties by default
  (`FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES`), and deserialization builds real objects. Go's
  `encoding/json` ignores unknown fields unless you call `DisallowUnknownFields`, and
  TypeScript's `JSON.parse` builds plain objects whose declared type is never checked.
- **Python**: pydantic models validate on parse. A TS interface is the type hint without
  the validator: zod is what brings the pydantic half back.
- **Go**: the encoder rules to remember are nil slice or map → `null`; `omitempty` drops
  `false`, `0`, `""`, nil and empty slices; a pointer with `omitempty` is absent when nil.
  Each one changes the TypeScript type you must write.
- **JS**: `as` is the everyday way to get a typed object out of `fetch`. It works until
  the server changes.

## How it works

How one `runapi` field maps to its mirror, and where each rule shows up in this API:

- `string`, `bool`, `int`/`int64` map to `string`, `boolean`, `number`. An `int64` is
  exact in JavaScript only up to 2^53 - 1; `durationMs` and `rowsAffected` never get
  close.
- `*SQLResult` with `omitempty` maps to `sql?: {...}`: absent for non-SQL runs, never
  `null`.
- `[]StepResult` with `omitempty` maps to `steps?: StepResult[]`: absent when empty.
- `[]Diagnostic` without `omitempty` maps to `Diagnostic[] | null` under encoding/json's
  default rule, and the mirror says `Diagnostic[]`. That gap was the drift.
  `Result.MarshalJSON` closes it on the Go side by never writing `null` for a list, which
  makes `Diagnostic[]` exact.
- `[][]*string` maps to `(string | null)[][]`: a nil pointer is SQL NULL. This one is
  exact, and the SQL lessons depend on it.
- `SQLStmtError.Pos int32` with a comment "0 when it didn't say" maps to `pos: number`:
  the "absent" case is a sentinel value, not `undefined`.

The two mirrors are compiled separately: `go build` sees only Go, `tsc` sees only
TypeScript. Agreement between them is a property of the running system, so the only
things that can check it run: a test that decodes real responses, or validation at the
boundary (example 2).

## Design notes

For one endpoint and about a dozen types, generation (OpenAPI with oapi-codegen and
openapi-typescript, as ts.services.openapi describes) would cost more than it saves. The
boring fixes, in order of value:

1. **Fix the producer.** Done. The empty lists are normalized in `runapi.Result`'s
   `MarshalJSON` rather than in `runexec.fromGorun` and the SQL paths: one place covers
   every producer, including the next one. `runclient` decodes the problem body when the
   status isn't 200. Two small changes, and the mirror became true.
2. **One contract test.** Half done: `runapi_test.go` encodes a `Result` whose every list
   is nil and fails on any `null`. The other half, golden JSON responses that a
   TypeScript type test checks with `satisfies RunResult`, would catch the next drift in
   the other direction.
3. **Validate at the boundary in development.** A zod schema annotated with
   `z.ZodType<RunResult>` in `ServerRunner`, strict in development. It also gives the
   learner a readable error instead of a `TypeError` three components away.
4. **Make the comments true.** Done for `runapi.go`, whose package comment now describes
   the cast instead of a type guard. Still to do: the discriminated-union sentence in
   `gorun.go` (delete it, or write the code it describes), and `runapi.Decode` (call it
   in the handlers, or delete it).

The docs share the drift. ADR-0001 says "the OpenAPI contract stays hand-maintained for
the TypeScript side"; `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` describes an `openapi-fetch` client, zod
validation at the trust boundary and a multipart `POST /run`; the Makefile's `gen`
target promises "(Phase 3+) sqlc/OpenAPI types". None of this exists. The request body is
JSON, the client is `fetch` plus a cast, and there is no `sqlc` either. When the docs
and the code disagree, the code is what runs; this lesson describes the code.

lessons.title: This repo's test pyramid
lessons.summary: This repo's tests are shaped less like a pyramid than a top-heavy vase: a thin base of unit tests, a thick layer of integration tests against the real toolchains and PostgreSQL, and a lesson verifier that runs every example. Handlers, learningstore and the UI have no tests; the frontend has three small Vitest files.

examples.title: The base: a table-driven unit test, after sqlrun/split_test.go

annotations.note: A pure function: string in, slice out, no I/O. That is what makes it cheap to test in hundreds of cases. sqlrun's real splitter keeps the same property while handling dollar quotes and nested comments.

Ranging over a string yields runes. The Turkish case below is there because a byte-wise splitter can cut a multi-byte character in half; the real table has an "İ in an identifier before $" row for the same reason.
Each row is one behavior with a name. Adding a regression is one line, which is why the real file has twenty rows for the splitter alone.
t.Run gives every row its own name in the output and its own failure. Since Go 1.22 each iteration has its own tc, so the closure is safe even if the subtest ran in parallel.

examples.title: The missing layer: handleRun tested through httptest with a fake Runner

annotations.note: The seam already exists in the app: httpapi.Runner is declared by its consumer, and router.go's comment says handlers stay "testable with fakes". Only run_test.go uses it, with a slow fake that checks the reply outlives the server's WriteTimeout.
A miniature of handleRun: the same order of checks, the same status mapping (machinery error 502, refusal passed through) and the same no-history header that verify-lessons sends.
The fake returns whatever a row puts in it. There is no mocking library and no generated code, only a type that has the method.
httptest.NewRequest and NewRecorder run the handler in-process with no listener and no network. The whole table runs in microseconds, which is what the base of a pyramid should cost.

examples.title: The next frontend unit test: judge.ts in Vitest

annotations.note: A copy, because a lesson can't import repo files. The real src/features/runner/judge.ts is a pure function too, shared by the run panel and scripts/verify-lessons.mjs, so a test of it guards both the badge and the verifier.

it.each is Vitest's table-driven test. The second row documents a surprise: judge.ts's comment says trailing whitespace never decides a verdict, but only whitespace at the very end of the output is trimmed.
A non-zero exit fails every check, including contains. This is the rule that makes a crashing example red even when its output happens to match.

use_cases: Deciding which test to write for a change: a splitter rule (unit), a status code (handler), a lock wait (integration), a lesson (verify)
Running the right suite before committing: go test ./... is seconds; -tags integration needs Go, Node, Edge and TEST_DATABASE_URL
Planning where tests would pay off most in this codebase: handlers, stores and the frontend
strengths: The runners are tested against the real things they drive: the go toolchain, Node, Microsoft Edge and PostgreSQL. A mocked exec.Command would test nothing that matters about a process-tree kill or a deadlock
verify-lessons judges with the UI's own judge.ts and the real BrowserTsRunner, and runs every example twice, so a flickering 'matches expected' badge is a failure
Integration tests sit behind //go:build integration, so go test ./... stays fast and needs no database, like a Maven surefire/failsafe split but enforced by the compiler
Tests name the bug they guard (the goose embed path, the ResponseController unwrap), which makes them read like a changelog of real incidents
weaknesses: One handler test, for the run route's write deadline: the 400/502/503 mapping, the history header and every learning endpoint are tested only by hand
One store test: run history's trim to the newest rows. learningstore's 'progress only moves forward' upsert has none

Three small Vitest files cover the lesson-markdown parser, the lesson data and the backend probe; components, judge.ts, the runners and the rest of the learning API have none, and no end-to-end test drives the app. Testing Library, MSW and Playwright are used by ts-test lessons only
No CI: every suite runs only when someone runs it, and the integration suite needs a fully set-up machine

pitfalls.title: Pure tests trapped behind the integration tag
pitfalls.detail: A build tag applies to the whole file. gorun_test.go's TestCappedBufferStopsButDoesNotBlock, TestSeedRejectsPathEscape and TestNodeEntry need no toolchain, but go test ./... never runs them. Move such tests to an untagged file.

pitfalls.title: Tagged files that no longer compile
pitfalls.detail: go test ./... and go vet ./... skip files behind a build tag, so a refactor can break the integration suite silently. Run go vet -tags integration ./... as well.

pitfalls.title: Reading verify-lessons as an end-to-end test of the app
pitfalls.detail: It drives verify.html and the backend API, not the lesson page. RunPanel, navigation, progress and notes are outside it.

pitfalls.title: A green go test ./... after a runner change
