pitfalls.detail: The runner's behavior lives in integration tests and in verify-lessons. A change to gorun or sqlrun needs go test -tags integration ./... and npm run verify:lessons before it is known to work.

quiz.q: You change how handleRun maps a refusal to a status code. Which existing test tells you if you broke it?
options: None: no test checks how handleRun maps errors to statuses
quiz.why: httpapi's tests cover the middleware (logging, recovery) and the request guards around stub handlers, and the real router only for requests no route matches. handleRun's one test (run_test.go) checks its write deadline with a fake Runner that answers 200; the status mapping and the learning handlers have no tests.

quiz.q: Why are gorun's timeout tests integration tests rather than unit tests with a mocked exec.Command?
options: What they guard is how real processes and process trees die on Windows and Linux; a mock would only check that a function was called
quiz.why: The behavior under test lives in the OS and the toolchain. Mocking it would remove the thing being tested.

quiz.q: Which command runs TestCappedBufferStopsButDoesNotBlock?
quiz.why: It lives in gorun_test.go, which starts with //go:build integration, so only a build with that tag compiles it.

quiz.q: What does npm run verify:lessons check that the Go tests don't?
options: That every lesson example runs, twice, through the real runners and matches its expected output
quiz.why: It is a content-level end-to-end check of the runners. The UI itself has no automated test.

further_reading.title: Go blog: Using Subtests and Sub-benchmarks

lessons.body:
## Concept

The textbook pyramid has many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in
the middle and a handful of end-to-end tests on top. Here is what this repo actually
has, layer by layer.

**Static checks.** `npm run typecheck` (tsc 7), `npm run lint` (ESLint with type-aware
rules), `go vet ./...` (CLAUDE.md asks for it with `GOOS=linux` as well, because gorun
has per-OS files) and contentcheck (`scripts/build-lessons.mjs`: lesson schema, ids,
prerequisites, LEARN markers, official-docs links).

**Go unit tests**, no build tag, `go test ./...`: thirty tests in eleven files.

- `sqlrun/split_test.go`: the statement splitter (twenty named cases, among them
  SQL-standard `BEGIN ATOMIC` bodies that must stay one statement while a plain `BEGIN;`
  still splits), the A:/B: script parser, and the SQL text renderer, including column
  alignment with `İstanbul` and `Ağrı`.
- `sqlrun/guard_test.go`: SQL lessons may not end the runner's transaction
  (`COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `END`) or start `COPY ... FROM STDIN`.
- `gorun/scaffold_test.go`: the pgx lesson module pins the same versions as
  `server/go.mod`; `UsesPgx` detection.
- `gorun/unit_test.go`: the output cap cuts on a character boundary (a `ğ` or `İ` split
  across two writes included), ts-test's time limit, and the color variables it drops
  from the inherited environment.
- `runexec/runexec_test.go`: an unknown runtime is a 501 refusal, not a 502.
- `httpapi/middleware_test.go`: the logging and recovery middleware keep
  `http.ResponseController` working (an `httptest` server with a short `WriteTimeout`);
  a panic becomes a 500 problem reply, or an abort once the handler has written; the
  real router, built with a nil pool, answers unmatched requests with problem 404 and
  405 and keeps `Allow`.
- `runapi/runapi_test.go`: no list in a `Result` encodes as `null`, SQL NULL cells stay
  `null`, and marshaling leaves the value alone.
- `runclient/runclient_test.go`: against an `httptest` runner, refusals keep their status
  and detail ("server busy"), and a runner 500 becomes an error.
- `httpapi/run_test.go`: a run that takes longer than the server's `WriteTimeout` still
  gets its reply, through a fake `Runner` and the real logging middleware.
- `httpapi/security_test.go`: the request guards (ADR-0011), one case per attack next to
  the callers that must keep working (the browser through Vite, verify-lessons, health
  probes), plus `isLoopbackHost`.
- `cmd/stacklab/main_test.go`: goose sees every embedded migration, each has a
  `-- +goose Up` line, and logged connection strings hide their passwords.

**Go integration tests**, `//go:build integration`, `go test -tags integration ./...`:
41 tests in six files, against real tools. `gorun` builds and runs real programs
(the whole process tree dies on timeout, on a cancelled request and after a normal exit
that left a child behind, 64 KB output caps that keep UTF-8 whole, path escapes,
`go test` mode, Node type stripping, offline `x/sync`); its tree tests start the test
binary itself as the lesson program, so they need no compiler and run on Linux too;
`nodetest_test.go` runs Vitest, MSW, a typecheck and Playwright in Edge, without colors
and within `timeout_s`; `sqlrun` and `multisession` run against PostgreSQL through
`TEST_DATABASE_URL` (rollback, NULL vs `''`, `BEGIN ATOMIC` functions, `VACUUM` in
non-transactional mode, the stale-schema janitor, lock waits, a deterministic
deadlock); `runexec` checks
that a pgx lesson's schema is dropped afterwards; `runstore` checks, in a schema of its
own built from the real migration, that run history keeps only the newest rows. The
database tests skip when
`TEST_DATABASE_URL` is unset.

**Lesson verification**, `npm run verify:lessons` (needs `npm start`): every example
of every lesson, run twice, through the running backend's `POST /api/run`, and for
ts-browser through the real `BrowserTsRunner` in headless Edge. Verdicts come from the
UI's own `judge.ts`; annotation line ranges are checked too.

**Frontend unit tests**, `npm test` (`vitest run --dir src`): three files.
`shared/ui/markdownBlocks.test.ts` covers the lesson-markdown parser (pipe tables, HTML
comments); `features/lessons/unverified.test.ts` checks that every lesson's unconfirmed-claim
markers become warning boxes in the right tab, and that the generated lesson index matches
the lesson files; `features/learning/api.test.ts` checks the `/healthz` probe that picks
the backend or the localStorage fallback.

**Missing**: tests for HTTP handlers beyond `run_test.go`'s write deadline (`handleRun`'s
status mapping, the twelve learning routes),
for `learningstore` (`runstore` has one, for the trim), for `config`, for the frontend's components,
runners, `judge.ts` and the rest of the learning API, and an end-to-end test that drives the app's UI.
There is no CI.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: no Mockito. Go tests use hand-written fakes behind small interfaces declared
  by the consumer (go.testing.fakes-httptest); `httptest.NewRecorder` replaces
  MockMvc. The surefire/failsafe split becomes a build tag.
- **Python**: `@pytest.mark.integration` is close to a build tag, with one difference: a
  pytest marker deselects tests that were still imported, while a tagged Go file isn't
  compiled at all in the default run. A compile error in it goes unnoticed until someone
  runs with the tag.
- **JS**: Vitest + Testing Library + MSW + Playwright is the standard stack, and it's
  all installed here, used only by ts-test lessons. Many JS teams prefer a "trophy"
  with integration tests as the widest layer; this repo has that shape on the Go side
  by necessity, and barely a base on the frontend.
- **C/C++**: think GoogleTest for the pure parts and a ctest label for the slow ones;
  the slow ones here start real compilers and a real browser.

## How it works

```sh
cd server
go test ./...                      # unit: seconds, needs only Go
go test -tags integration ./...    # needs go and node on PATH, npm install,
                                   # Microsoft Edge, and TEST_DATABASE_URL
                                   # (the playground database) for sqlrun/runexec
cd ..
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm test                           # Vitest over src/
npm run verify:lessons             # needs npm start; add --filter <id prefix>
```

The Makefile's `test` target runs the unit tests plus the integration tests for
`internal/gorun` only. The README mentions `-tags integration` for gorun and sqlrun.

Why the middle layer is the thickest: what gorun and sqlrun promise lives outside Go
code. A process tree dies (or doesn't) on Windows because of a Job Object; a deadlock
forms because PostgreSQL's detector runs after `deadlock_timeout`. A unit test with a
mocked process or a mocked connection would check that the code calls the mock, not
that the promise holds. ADR-0009 makes the same argument for verify-lessons: it runs
the real runners, because re-implementing them for the check "would check a copy of the
runtime rules, not the code learners use".

## Design notes

The shape is right where it is thick and wrong where it is empty. Handlers, stores and
the frontend are exactly the parts where unit and handler tests are cheapest, and
bugs there are found only by clicking. The drift in inside.codebase.contract
(`"files": null`, a lost error detail in Docker mode) was the kind a handler-level test
catches the first time it runs; both were found by reading, and the fixes came with the
tests that would have caught them (`runapi_test.go`, `runclient_test.go`).

What I'd add, cheapest first:

1. **A handler test for `POST /api/run`'s status mapping** with a fake `Runner`
   (example 2). The interface already exists for this, and `run_test.go` already uses
   one for the write deadline. `runstore.Store` is a concrete type in
   `runService`, so recording needs a small consumer-declared interface too.
2. **Store tests behind the integration tag**, on `TEST_DATABASE_URL`, for the
   progress upsert that never downgrades. Run history's trim has one already
   (`runstore/store_integration_test.go`); it shows the pattern: a schema of its own,
   built from the real migration file, dropped in `t.Cleanup`.
3. **Move the remaining pure tests out of `gorun_test.go`** into the untagged
   `unit_test.go`, so the default run covers the cap's write-and-discard behavior and the
   path-escape check too.
4. **More Vitest for the pure frontend functions**, next to the three that exist:
   `judge.ts` (example 3), `bareImports` in `browserTs.ts`, the learning API's
   localStorage adapter. Then `RunPanel` with MSW standing in for `/api/run`, as ADR-0005 already
   promises ("component tests mock the API layer with MSW").
5. **One Playwright smoke test of the app**: open a lesson, press Run, see "matches
   expected". The same headless Edge verify-lessons uses would do.

Two documents promise tests that don't exist: ADR-0005 (component tests with MSW, e2e
tests that drive the URL) and ADR-0003 (a "fork bomb contained" runner test; gorun has
the process-tree kill test, not a fork bomb).

lessons.title: The Compose topology: who can talk to whom
lessons.summary: A network boundary only protects what it separates. Reading docker-compose.yml as data shows the sandboxed runner can reach the app database; local mode, the default, has no network boundaries at all apart from loopback, database roles and the browser iframe.

examples.title: docker-compose.yml as data: who can reach whom, and the one-line fix

annotations.note: Everything in docker-compose.yml that decides reachability: each service's networks, its published port, and one bind address that matters. frontend has no networks key, so Compose puts it on default.
Membership is the whole rule. Containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other on every port; there is no per-port filter. The only extra check is what the process binds to.
internal: true removes the route out. A service has egress when at least one of its networks is not internal; here that is default.
mocksvc's main.go listens on 127.0.0.1:8091. Inside a container that is the container's own loopback, so no other service can connect, whatever networks they share.
The finding. runner sits on backend-net, which is how app-db is reachable to it, so lesson code in the sandbox can open a connection to the learner's data. The password is in the same compose file.
Both databases publish a port to 127.0.0.1 while sitting on internal networks only. The compose file's own comment says Docker publishes nothing for such a container; the host can't use these ports.
The backend already reaches the runner over runner-net, so dropping backend-net from the runner loses nothing it needs.

examples.title: The tightest boundary in the app: what lesson code in the iframe cannot reach

annotations.note: sandbox="allow-scripts" without allow-same-origin gives the frame an opaque origin, serialized as "null". It is same-origin with nothing, not even another frame built the same way.

The frame's CSP is default-src 'none' with no connect-src, so every fetch is refused before a packet leaves, including one to the app's own backend. Scripts may only be inline or data: URLs, so a CDN import fails too.
The opaque origin owns no storage and can't see the parent's DOM. Even a bug that ran untrusted code here couldn't read the learner's notes in localStorage.
No 'unsafe-eval' in script-src, so eval and new Function throw. That is why the runner hands the iframe the transpiled module as an inline script and the libraries as data: URLs.
The only way out. BrowserTsRunner accepts a message only when e.source is its own frame and the data carries __stacklab_run: true; this one is ignored.

use_cases: Reviewing docker-compose.yml before running Docker mode: list what each service must reach, then compare with what it can reach
Judging what a lesson program could do on your machine in local mode, where it runs as you
Designing a sandbox for untrusted code in the browser: opaque origin, CSP, a single message channel
strengths: Compose networks are declarative: the whole reachability graph is in one file and can be checked as data, unlike host firewall rules spread across machines
internal: true removes the route out entirely, so the runner and both databases have no internet access in Docker mode
Every published port binds 127.0.0.1, so nothing in either mode is reachable from the LAN, unlike Docker's default of publishing on all host addresses
The lesson iframe's boundary is enforced by the browser in both modes: no network, no app storage, no eval
weaknesses: In Docker mode the runner shares backend-net with app-db, so the sandbox can reach the app database whose credentials sit in the compose file
In local mode lesson programs run as the owner with full network access: the internet, the backend API and both databases on 127.0.0.1:5432
Default credentials (stacklab/stacklab, playground/playground) live in config.go, the setup script and the compose file; fine for 127.0.0.1, wrong anywhere else
Docker mode is not exercised by any test or by verify-lessons, so the topology above has not been run since ADR-0009 and ADR-0010

pitfalls.title: Putting a service on a network for convenience
pitfalls.detail: Membership grants every port to every other member. The runner on backend-net is the example: it never talks to app-db, but it can.

pitfalls.title: 127.0.0.1 inside a container
pitfalls.detail: Loopback is per network namespace. A server listening on 127.0.0.1 in a container is reachable only from that container; listen on :8091 (all interfaces of the container) and let the networks decide.
pitfalls.good: http.ListenAndServe(":8091", mux) // reachable only via the networks it joins

pitfalls.title: Publishing without a host address
pitfalls.detail: "5432:5432" publishes on every host address, which can expose the database to the network. This file always writes 127.0.0.1:5432:5432.

pitfalls.title: Trusting the diagram instead of the file
pitfalls.detail: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md says the backend is the only service with an outbound path and reverse-proxies mocksvc. The frontend container has an outbound path too, and there is no /mock route.

quiz.q: In Docker mode, can lesson code in the runner container connect to app-db:5432?
options: No: the runner is on an internal network
Yes: runner and app-db both sit on backend-net
quiz.why: internal: true blocks traffic to other networks, not between members. Both services are members of backend-net.

quiz.q: The backend and mocksvc share two networks. Why can't the backend reach http://mocksvc:8091?
options: mocksvc listens on 127.0.0.1, which inside its container is its own loopback
quiz.why: Publishing is for the host. Between containers, what matters is a shared network and a process listening on an address that network reaches.

quiz.q: In local mode, what stops a Go lesson from connecting to the stacklab database?
options: Nothing technical: same machine, and the default credentials are in config.go
quiz.why: Lesson SQL from the sql runtimes runs as playground, but a Go program opens its own connections as whoever it likes. ADR-0003's threat model accepts this for a single-user, local-only app.

quiz.q: Why does fetch('/healthz') fail inside a ts-browser lesson even though the app serves it?
options: The frame's CSP leaves connect-src at default-src 'none'
The backend sends no CORS headers
quiz.why: The CSP blocks the request before it is sent. CORS would only matter if the CSP let it through.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A network boundary is a list of who may open a connection to whom. It is coarse and
cheap, and it protects only what it actually separates. StackLab has three topologies,
and the one you run by default has the fewest boundaries.

**Local mode** (ADR-0008, `npm start`). One machine: Vite on `127.0.0.1:5173`, the Go
backend on `127.0.0.1:8080`, one PostgreSQL service holding both databases. Lesson Go and
Node programs are child processes of the backend, running as you, with your network.
The boundaries that remain:

- **Bind addresses.** Everything listens on loopback. `scripts/setup-local-db.sql` sets
  PostgreSQL's `listen_addresses = 'localhost'`, because the Windows installer listens on
  every interface.
- **Database roles.** SQL from the `sql*` runtimes runs as `playground`, a
  non-superuser (sql.security-ops.roles), so it can't run `COPY ... TO PROGRAM`.
- **The browser sandbox** for ts-browser lessons (example 2).

Nothing separates a lesson program from the app: a Go lesson can call the backend API,
reach the internet, or connect to the `stacklab` database with the default credentials
in `server/internal/config/config.go`. ADR-0003's threat model, protecting the owner from
their own mistakes rather than from an attacker, is what makes that acceptable.

**Docker mode** (`docker-compose.yml`, optional). Six services, three networks:
`default`, plus `backend-net` and `runner-net`, both `internal: true`. Example 1 reads
the file as data:

- `frontend` reaches `backend` over `default` (Vite proxies `/api` to
  `http://backend:8080`).
- `backend` is on all three networks: app-db over `backend-net`, the runner over
  `runner-net`, the internet over `default`.
- `runner` needs `playground-db` (over `runner-net`) and nothing else. It also sits on
  `backend-net`, which puts `app-db` within its reach. That is the boundary this
  topology was meant to draw, and it isn't drawn.
- `mocksvc` binds `127.0.0.1:8091` inside its container, so no other service can reach
  it. Nothing calls it yet (ADR-0008).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Cloud networking**: a Compose network is a security group with one rule, "members may
  talk to members on any port". Kubernetes NetworkPolicy can filter by port and
  direction; Compose can't.
- **Java/Python services**: `localhost` in a container means the container itself. A
  server that binds `127.0.0.1` is unreachable from its neighbors, which is the opposite
  of what you want for a service and exactly what you want for a debug port.
- **JS**: the browser has the most precise boundary in this app. Same-origin policy
  decides what a page may read, CSP decides what it may load or connect to, and
  `sandbox` decides its origin. ts.services.realtime-cors covers CORS, which only comes
  into play when the CSP lets a request through.
- **C/C++**: think of `bind()` addresses and `iptables` rules. Compose generates the
  rules from network membership; you never write them.

## How it works

What the Docker documentation guarantees, and what the examples rely on:

- [Compose networks](https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/networks/):
  `internal: true` creates "an externally isolated network", and services without a
  `networks` key join the implicit `default` network.
- [`docker network create --internal`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/network/create/):
  "Containers on an internal network may communicate between each other, but not with
  any other network", and firewall rules drop traffic to or from other networks.
- [Bridge networks](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/): containers
  on the same user-defined bridge "effectively expose all ports to each other".
- [Port publishing](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/port-publishing/): publishing
  to `127.0.0.1` means "only the Docker host can access the published container port";
  without an address, Docker publishes on all host addresses.

What the documentation doesn't settle: `app-db` and `playground-db` publish
`127.0.0.1:5432` and `:5433` but sit on internal networks only. The comment on the
backend's `networks` in the compose file says "Docker publishes nothing for a container
that sits on internal networks only", and ADR-0008 lists "internal-network port
publishing" among the reasons local mode replaced Docker. If that holds, the two
published database ports are dead, and `psql` from the host can't reach them.
<!-- VERIFY: Docker's network docs say internal networks drop traffic to/from other networks but do not state that published ports of an internal-only container are unreachable; the claim rests on the compose comment and ADR-0008. -->

The lesson iframe (example 2) is built by `BrowserTsRunner`: `sandbox="allow-scripts"`
without `allow-same-origin` (opaque origin), and a CSP of
`default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline' data:; worker-src blob:; img-src data: blob:; style-src 'unsafe-inline'`.
`connect-src` isn't listed, so it falls back to `default-src 'none'`.

## Design notes

Least privilege for networks works like least privilege for database roles: list what
each service must reach, then give it exactly the networks that cover that list. For this
file:

- `runner` on `runner-net` only (the fix in example 1). The backend still reaches it there.
- Better still, a third internal network for the sandbox's own dependencies:
  `runner-net` for backend and runner, `sandbox-net` for runner, `playground-db` and
  `mocksvc`. Then the backend can't reach the playground database either, which it
  never needs in Docker mode.
- `mocksvc` listening on `:8091`, once something calls it.

The documentation has drifted from the file. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` says the backend is
"the only service with an outbound path" (the `frontend` container is on `default` too,
which it needs for `npm install`) and that the backend reverse-proxies `/mock/*` to
mocksvc (the router has no such route). The compose comment says internal members have
no published ports "except where the owner inspects them directly", which describes the
two database ports that probably can't be reached.

Docker mode has not been run since today's runner changes (ADR-0009, ADR-0010), and
nothing tests it. One thing to fix before relying on it: the final stage of
`runner/Dockerfile` is the Node image plus the runner binary, `ca-certificates` and
`curl`. No step installs the Go toolchain the runner invokes as `go`, although the
stage's comment says one does. This is read from the Dockerfile and `gorun.go`, not run.
What a Go lesson would get follows from the code: `goBuild` reports only the build's
captured output, and a `go` that can't be started prints nothing, so a `go` or
`go-server` lesson would fail with exit code 1 and an empty stderr. `go-test` starts
`go` through `runProcess`, which appends the start error:
`gorun: exec: "go": executable file not found in $PATH`.

In local mode the network is not the boundary, and pretending otherwise would be
dishonest. What holds is that nothing listens beyond 127.0.0.1. If the app ever leaves
this machine, ADR-0003 says the runner must be rebuilt (gVisor, Firecracker or a
separate host), and the first network rule to add is the one example 1 is missing:
lesson code must not be able to reach the app's data.

lessons.title: What I'd change at 10x scale
lessons.summary: "10x" means three different things for a single-user local app: ten times the lessons, the runs, or the learners. Each breaks something different first: serial verification (and the statically imported lesson bundle, until it was split per lesson), the two run slots, and a schema that has no user in it.

examples.title: Arithmetic first: today's measurements multiplied by 10

annotations.note: Every input is a measurement, not a guess: the size of the generated bundle file, the example count in it, and the mean durationMs of 59 server examples in a verify run. An estimate is only as honest as the numbers going into it.
verify-lessons awaits each server example before sending the next, and runs everything twice to catch nondeterminism, so its time grows linearly with the content and nothing overlaps.

The bundle column was the crack that users would feel: all of it was imported statically, so at 10x a 37 MB module would have sat in the main chunk. Since 2026-11-14 each lesson is a chunk of its own, and the main chunk holds only an index of about 0.46 KB per lesson.
Throughput is slots divided by service time. Two slots at about a second per run is plenty for one person and a ceiling for anything more.

examples.title: The two run slots under load, in fake time

annotations.note: runexec.go's values. Two slots kept the 512 MB runner container honest in Docker mode and keep a burst of runs from stalling the PC in local mode. Both are reasons about one machine and one person.
The admission select from Executor.Run, minus the ctx.Done case: take a slot, or give up after queueWait. A full buffered channel is the semaphore; the deferred receive gives the slot back.
time.Since inside a synctest bubble reads the fake clock, so the waits are exact: 3.2 s for the tenth learner at 0.8 s per run, which is five rounds of two.
synctest.Test (Go 1.25) runs each scenario in its own bubble; the clock jumps whenever every goroutine is blocked. Thirty learners and ten seconds of queueing take no real time.

examples.title: The second learner: a schema without a user

annotations.note: The real table. lesson_id alone is the key, which is exactly right for one learner: no joins, no user table, nothing to authenticate.
learningstore's upsert, minus its completed_at bookkeeping. It never moves status backwards, so one learner's 'completed' absorbs the next learner's 'viewed'.
Mehmet has never run the lesson, and the dashboard says he completed it. More slots or more servers can't fix this; only a different key can.

The migration a second learner forces: a user column, a value for every existing row (the default fills them, then is dropped so new rows must say who they belong to), and a new primary key. notes, bookmarks, quiz_answers and runs need the same, and every query and handler with them.

use_cases: Before an "it won't scale" discussion: name the axis (content, runs or users) and the first number that breaks
Deciding what to fix if StackLab grows to the full curriculum and beyond, or is shared with a second learner
A template for capacity reviews: measure, multiply, find the bottleneck, then change the design
strengths: Most of the design is fine at 10x: the stdlib HTTP server, one PostgreSQL holding a few megabytes, contentcheck reading files, the per-run schema sandbox
Admission control exists: a full queue answers 503 after 10 s instead of piling up goroutines and processes until the machine stalls
The single-user schema is a deliberate simplification (migration 003 says so), which kept every learning query a primary-key lookup
Because content is files (ADR-0004), moving lessons out of the main bundle needed no data migration, only a different generator output and loader
weaknesses: The lesson index is still eager: about 0.46 KB per lesson in the main chunk, roughly 1 MB at ten times the curriculum (the full lessons would have been 37 MB)
verify-lessons is serial and runs everything twice: minutes today, hours at 10x, and it competes with the learner for the same two run slots
Two slots and a 10 s queue: fine for one person, 503s for a classroom

No user anywhere (schema, API, auth), lesson code running inside the backend process, and a run history table that is written on every run and read by no screen (each insert now trims it to the newest 1,000 rows)

pitfalls.title: Scaling the wrong axis
pitfalls.detail: More run slots don't help a second learner whose progress overwrites the first's, and a user table doesn't shrink the bundle. Name which 10x you mean before choosing the fix.

pitfalls.title: Raising maxConcurrent as the fix
pitfalls.detail: Each Go run is a compile plus a process; each SQL run opens its own connection (two for multisession). More slots move the bottleneck to CPU and to PostgreSQL's max_connections; size them to cores and keep the queue.

pitfalls.title: Treating a multi-user version as a scaling exercise
pitfalls.detail: ADR-0003 says the sandbox is void once the app is exposed beyond 127.0.0.1. A second learner on another machine needs authentication and a real isolation boundary (a container or VM per run), not tuning.

quiz.q: Thirty learners press Run at the same moment and each run takes 3 s. How many see "server busy"?
options: None: they queue until a slot frees
22: two runs start every 3 s, and everyone still waiting at 10 s gets a 503
quiz.why: Batches start at 0, 3, 6 and 9 s, so 8 learners are served; the other 22 hit queueWait at 10 s.

quiz.q: Which change is needed for a second learner but not for 10x the lessons?
options: A user_id in the progress key
quiz.why: With lesson_id as the only key, two learners share one progress row. Content size has nothing to do with it.

quiz.q: Until 2026-11-14, why did the lesson bundle grow the main JavaScript chunk instead of being loaded per lesson?
options: types.ts imported lessons.bundle.generated.ts statically, so the bundler had to include all of it up front
quiz.why: A static import is part of the module graph at build time. Now load.ts lists one JSON file per lesson with import.meta.glob and loads it with import(), so each lesson is its own chunk.

quiz.q: What limits throughput first if verify-lessons runs while you study?
options: The two run slots in runexec, which the learner's Run button shares
quiz.why: Both go through POST /api/run and the same Executor; verify retries 503s, the learner waits or sees "server busy".

lessons.body:
## Concept

Nobody runs a personal learning app at ten times its load, so the useful question is:
ten times *what*? Three axes, each with a different first crack.

**10x the content** (about 2,300 lessons). Until 2026-11-14,
`src/features/lessons/types.ts` did `import bundleData from './lessons.bundle.generated'`:
every lesson's prose, examples, expected outputs and fixtures as one module in the main
chunk. The bundle measured on 2026-11-13 held 122 lessons in 1.98 MB, about 16 KB each,
so the planned 229 lessons needed 3.7 MB and ten times that 37 MB, downloaded and parsed
before the first page renders (example 1). That crack is fixed (Design notes, item 1).
The one that remains is `npm run verify:lessons`: it runs each example twice, one at a
time, which is minutes today and hours at 10x.

**10x the runs** (one learner, much more running, or verify running while you study).
`internal/runexec` admits two runs at once and refuses after a 10 s wait with
503 "server busy" (example 2). verify-lessons and the Run button share those two slots.

**10x the learners.** This is a change of kind, not of scale. `progress`, `notes`,
`bookmarks` and `quiz_answers` are keyed by `lesson_id` alone (example 3); there is no
user and no authentication; and in local mode lesson code runs in the backend process
as the owner's OS user (ADR-0008). ADR-0003 says plainly that exposing the app voids the
sandbox's threat model.

Two numbers hold up fine: the database (a few megabytes of progress and run history) and
the Go HTTP layer, which serves one person's clicks without noticing.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with two threads, a bounded wait and a
  `RejectedExecutionException`. In Go it is a buffered channel and a `select` with a
  timer, and the rejection is a value (`*runapi.Error`), not an exception.
- **Python**: the same arithmetic as sizing Gunicorn workers: throughput is workers
  divided by service time. Queueing theory (Little's law) says the queue grows without
  bound once arrivals per second exceed that.
- **JS**: code splitting is the standard answer to a big bundle: `import()` per route
  or per lesson, `React.lazy` for components. Vite emits a separate chunk for every
  dynamic import.
- **C/C++**: a back-of-envelope estimate before a profiler. Example 1 is that envelope.

## How it works

Admission control in `runexec.Executor.Run`:

```go
select {
case e.slots <- struct{}{}:      // a free slot: run now
	defer func() { <-e.slots }()
case <-ctx.Done():               // the client went away
	return nil, busy(), nil
case <-time.After(queueWait):    // 10 s without a slot
	return nil, busy(), nil      // 503 "server busy"
}
```

With two slots and a service time of S seconds, the most the backend can admit is 2/S
runs per second, about 120 a minute for 1 s Go runs (example 1 takes the mean of 59
measured server examples: Go programs about 0.85 s, `go test` about 2.9 s, SQL about
35 ms). Anyone who waits longer than 10 s gets a 503. verify-lessons retries a 503 (up to
30 attempts); the Run button shows the error.

One budget used not to add up under load: `httpapi` extended the write deadline for
`/api/run` to 45 s up front, to cover runexec's 40 s run budget, but not the up to 10 s
spent waiting for a slot first, so a run that queued and then used its whole budget
could have its reply cut off. The handler now lifts the deadline while the run (queue
wait included) is in progress and sets a fresh 10 s one for writing the reply, so no
budget has to be added up. Docker mode still has fixed limits that leave the queue out:
`runclient`'s 45 s HTTP timeout and the runner container's 45 s `WriteTimeout`.

## Design notes

What I'd change, in the order the cracks appear:

1. **Split the lesson bundle.** Done on 2026-11-14: the main chunk keeps an index
   (titles, header facts, unconfirmed claims; the sidebar and paths read the curriculum
   module) and each lesson loads with a dynamic `import()` from a chunk of its own. The
   first chunk went from 4.7 MB to 0.48 MB of JavaScript. Serving lessons from the
   backend, as ADR-0004 planned, stays the option if search ever needs the lesson bodies.
2. **Verify only what changed.** Hash each lesson directory and skip unchanged ones,
   the way ADR-0004's planned `content_hash` upserts would have. Running server examples
   two at a time gains at most 2x, because the slots are the limit.
3. **Size the slots to the machine.** Make `maxConcurrent` configurable and default it
   from the number of cores, and give verify a lower priority than the Run button (a
   separate slot, or no retries during interactive use).
4. **Bound run history.** Done in the most boring form: `runs` gets the code and the full
   result JSON on every run, and each insert now deletes all but the newest 1,000 rows
   in the same transaction (`runstore.DefaultKeep`). Still open: no screen reads
   `/api/history`. A history screen would want the last N per lesson instead; until one
   exists, history could also be dropped.
5. **For a second learner, stop and redesign.** A users table and `user_id` in every
   learning key (example 3), authentication, and lesson execution outside the backend
   process: the Docker runner, or gVisor/Firecracker as ADR-0003 suggests. That is a
   different application with the same lessons.

What I would not change: the stdlib router, pgx, the per-run `run_` schemas, content as
files, the strategy split between browser and server runners. They are what made this
small app easy to read, and none of them is the first thing to break.

lessons.title: GROUP BY, HAVING, FILTER (WHERE ...)
lessons.summary: GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group, and aggregates summarize each group; WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. FILTER (WHERE ...) restricts the input of one aggregate, so several conditional counts come out of a single pass.

examples.title: One row per group, what count(*) counts, and WHERE vs HAVING

annotations.note: count(*) counts rows, count(duration_ms) only non-NULL values. avg skips NULLs too and divides by what it kept: export averages 900 over its one timed run, not 450 over two. avg of an integer column returns numeric, so search's 77.5 rounds to 78 instead of truncating.
WHERE removes rows before any group exists. export has no failed run, so it never becomes a group. An aggregate here is an error (SQLSTATE 42803): there is nothing to aggregate yet.

HAVING runs on the finished groups, so it can test aggregates: auth has one failure and is dropped. It can't use the output name failures, because the SELECT list is computed after it; repeat the expression.
Aggregates without GROUP BY treat all input as one group, and one group gives one row even when it is empty: count is 0, sum is NULL.
Add GROUP BY and the same empty input makes no groups at all: SELECT 0. A report that needs a row for every suite has to start from a list of suites and LEFT JOIN the runs (example 3).
A suite has several statuses, and PostgreSQL refuses to pick one. Group by status too, count it with FILTER (next example), or, if any value really will do, say so with any_value(status) (PG 16).

examples.title: FILTER for side-by-side counts, its CASE equivalent, and ratio traps

annotations.note: Each FILTER restricts the input of its own aggregate only. Unlike WHERE, it doesn't remove rows from the other columns or groups: export stays, with failed = 0. One scan produces the whole pivot.

The pre-9.4 spelling, still needed on databases without FILTER. It depends on an easy-to-miss detail: count(CASE ... END) works because a CASE without ELSE yields NULL, which count skips. Add ELSE 0 and it counts every row.
count returns bigint, and bigint / bigint is integer division: 2 / 3 is 0. No error, no warning, a column of zeros.
100.0 is numeric, so the whole expression is computed in numeric. round(value, digits) exists for numeric only; with a double precision value it fails to resolve.

export has no failed run, so the filtered sum sees no input: NULL, while count says 0. Every aggregate except count returns NULL on empty input; coalesce turns it into the 0 a chart or an API client expects.

examples.title: count(*) after a LEFT JOIN, grouping by the key, and Turkish İ/ı in lower()

annotations.note: REQ-EXPORT has no tests, so the LEFT JOIN gives it one row padded with NULLs. count(*) counts that row (1); count(t.id) counts matched tests (0). Count a column of the optional side that is never NULL in real rows, its primary key.

Grouping by the primary key makes every other column of requirements functionally dependent on it, so r.code may appear in SELECT without being grouped (PG 9.1). Group by the identity, not by a label that might repeat.

This database uses the builtin C.UTF-8 locale, where lower() applies Unicode simple case mapping: İ becomes i and I also becomes i. So 'DİYARBAKIR' turns into 'diyarbakir', which doesn't equal 'diyarbakır'. Iğdır splits the same way.

lower() follows the collation of its input. With tr-x-icu it applies Turkish rules (I to ı, İ to i), and each city becomes one group. The result carries the collation too, so ORDER BY sorts the keys in Turkish order.

use_cases: Reports and dashboards: runs per suite, failures per requirement, orders per customer per month
Pivot-style status columns (passed / failed / skipped) with FILTER, in one query instead of three or a client-side pivot
Data-quality checks with HAVING: duplicate e-mail addresses (HAVING count(*) > 1), requirements with fewer than two tests
Case-insensitive duplicate reports on names and cities, with the Turkish collation when the text is Turkish
strengths: The summary is computed next to the data: one row per group crosses the network, instead of every row being fetched and folded in Go or TS
FILTER puts several conditional aggregates into one scan and reads like the question; Java's Collectors need a filtering(...) downstream collector per column
Ambiguous selects are an error (SQLSTATE 42803) rather than an arbitrary pick, and any_value() (PG 16) makes 'any value will do' explicit
Grouping by a primary key lets you select every column of that table without listing them all in GROUP BY
weaknesses: NULL rules differ per aggregate: count gives 0 on empty input, sum, avg, min and max give NULL, and avg divides by the non-NULL count
Integer arithmetic on counts truncates silently: bigint / bigint is bigint
WHERE can't see aggregates and HAVING can't see SELECT aliases, so filtered totals repeat their expression or move to an outer query
Grouping compares text exactly; case-insensitive grouping needs an explicit normalization, and the correct one depends on the language

pitfalls.title: count(*) after a LEFT JOIN
pitfalls.detail: The NULL-padded row of an unmatched parent is still a row, so count(*) reports 1 where the answer is 0. Count a NOT NULL column of the optional side.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT r.code, count(*) FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id
pitfalls.good: SELECT r.code, count(t.id) FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.detail: count(*) is bigint, so passed / total is 0 for anything under 100%. Bring a numeric in first. A FILTERed denominator can be 0 (a suite with only skipped runs), so guard it with nullif or the query fails with division by zero.
pitfalls.good: round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE status <> 'skipped'), 0), 1)

pitfalls.title: An output name that shadows a column in GROUP BY
pitfalls.detail: GROUP BY accepts output column names, but when an input column has the same name, the input column wins (ORDER BY makes the opposite choice). This query groups by the raw city and returns 'diyarbakır' twice, with no error.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT lower(city) AS city, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city
pitfalls.good: SELECT lower(city) AS city_key, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY lower(city)

pitfalls.title: sum() of nothing is NULL
pitfalls.detail: A group whose FILTER matches no row, or a query with no input, gets NULL from sum, avg, min, max and array_agg; only count returns 0. Use coalesce where the consumer expects a number.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive grouping of Turkish text
pitfalls.detail: In the default C.UTF-8 collation lower() maps I to i, so 'DİYARBAKIR' and 'Diyarbakır' land in different groups. PG 18's casefold() doesn't fix it: in this database it leaves İ unchanged ('dİyarbakir'). Name the Turkish collation.
pitfalls.good: GROUP BY lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")

quiz.q: REQ-EXPORT has no test cases. What do count(*) and count(t.id) return for it in `requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id`?
quiz.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps REQ-EXPORT as one row with NULLs on the test side. count(*) counts that row; count(t.id) skips the NULL.

quiz.q: What does `SELECT count(*), sum(duration_ms) FROM test_runs WHERE false` return?
quiz.why: Without GROUP BY the input forms one group even when it is empty. count of nothing is 0; sum of nothing is NULL.

quiz.q: You want one row per suite with its number of failed runs, including suites with no failures. Which do you use?
options: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') ... GROUP BY suite
Either; they return the same rows
quiz.why: WHERE removes the rows before grouping, so a suite without failures has no rows left and disappears. FILTER only limits what that one aggregate sees.

quiz.q: A suite has 2 passed runs out of 3. What is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*)`?
quiz.why: Both counts are bigint, and integer division truncates toward zero. Multiply by 100.0 (numeric) first.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Aggregate Expressions (FILTER, ORDER BY, DISTINCT)
PostgreSQL docs: The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses
PostgreSQL docs: Collation Support (lower and upper follow the collation)

lessons.body:
## Concept

`GROUP BY` collapses all rows that share the grouping values into one output row, and
aggregate functions (`count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, ...) summarize the rows of each
group. Once a query groups, every expression in the SELECT list must be one of three
things: a grouping expression, an aggregate, or a column functionally dependent on a
grouped primary key. Anything else would need PostgreSQL to pick one value out of many,
and it refuses.

Two filters sit on either side of the grouping. `WHERE` decides which **rows** go in;
`HAVING` decides which **groups** come out, and can therefore test aggregates.
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` (PG 9.4) is a third, narrower one: it decides which rows a single
aggregate sees, so `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')` next to a plain `count(*)`
gives failures and totals from the same pass.

Most aggregates ignore NULL inputs. `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` counts non-NULL
values, and on empty input every aggregate except `count` returns NULL.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** pandas `df.groupby('suite').agg(...)` is the same idea.
  `itertools.groupby` only merges *adjacent* equal keys, so it needs sorted input;
  `GROUP BY` doesn't.
- **Java:** `runs.stream().collect(groupingBy(Run::suite, counting()))`. Each FILTER
  column would be its own `filtering(r -> ..., counting())` downstream collector.
- **JS:** `Object.groupBy(runs, r => r.suite)` (ES2024) builds the arrays and you reduce
  each one. SQL fuses grouping and reducing, and never materializes the groups' rows
  for you to look at.
- **Go:** a `map[string]*stats` filled in a loop, then sorted keys for stable output.
  The database does the same with a hash table or a sort, next to the data.
- In all of these, reading a field from "the group" without reducing it is something
  your code decides (the first element?). SQL makes you choose explicitly: group by it,
  aggregate it, or `any_value()` it.

## How it works

The clauses run in this logical order, which explains most of the rules above:

1. `FROM` and joins build the input rows.
2. `WHERE` keeps the rows for which its condition is true. No aggregates exist yet.
3. `GROUP BY` forms the groups; aggregates (with their `FILTER`s) are computed per group.
4. `HAVING` keeps the groups for which its condition is true.
5. The `SELECT` list is evaluated, output names come into existence.
6. `ORDER BY` sorts, and it may use those output names.

`HAVING` runs before step 5, so it can't refer to `failures`; it repeats `count(*)`.
PostgreSQL lets `GROUP BY` use output names as an extension, but an input column with
the same name takes precedence (see the pitfalls).

## Design notes

Prefer `FILTER` to `CASE` inside aggregates. It states the condition once, can't be
broken by a stray `ELSE 0`, and produces the same single-pass plan. Keep `CASE` for code
that must run on databases without `FILTER`.

Group by identities, not labels: `GROUP BY r.id` and select `r.code`, rather than
`GROUP BY r.code`, which silently merges two requirements if codes ever repeat.

Ratios are numeric work: bring in `100.0` or a cast before dividing, `nullif` any
denominator that can be zero, and round last.

Case-insensitive grouping is a normalization decision, and for Turkish text the default
one is wrong. `lower()` and `upper()` follow the collation of their input, so name it:
`lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`. Even that assumes Turkish typing: `IZMIR` typed on an
English keyboard becomes `ızmır` under Turkish rules. When the input is mixed, normalize
once on the way in instead of in every query.

lessons.title: string_agg, array_agg, jsonb_agg
lessons.summary: Aggregates can build values: string_agg joins text, array_agg collects an array, jsonb_agg and jsonb_object_agg build JSON. Put ORDER BY inside the call, handle the NULLs a LEFT JOIN brings in, and aggregate each child list on its own to avoid join fan-out.

examples.title: string_agg and array_agg: element order, NULLs, DISTINCT, Turkish sorting

annotations.note: string_agg skips NULL inputs (Giriş has no owner); array_agg keeps them as NULL elements. ORDER BY inside the call orders the elements; the query's own ORDER BY only sorts the result rows. Without it the element order is unspecified.
DISTINCT removes duplicates before collecting, and FILTER drops the NULL that array_agg would otherwise keep. Can owns two tests and appears once.

The elements are compared in the column's collation. This database's default, C.UTF-8, compares code points, so Ç (U+00C7), İ (U+0130) and Ş (U+015E) sort after every ASCII letter and Giriş comes first. tr-x-icu gives the Turkish alphabet: C, Ç, ..., G, ..., I, İ, ..., S, Ş.
With no input rows array_agg returns NULL, not an empty array, and so do string_agg and jsonb_agg. coalesce supplies the empty value a client can iterate over.
SQLSTATE 42P10. Can has two ids, so "the distinct owners ordered by id" isn't defined. Order by the aggregated value, or remove duplicates in a subquery first.

examples.title: jsonb_agg and jsonb_build_object: a nested document per row, and the empty-list trap

annotations.note: REQ-EXPORT's padding row has t.id and t.title NULL, but the object built from them is not NULL: [{"id": null, "title": null}]. jsonb_agg_strict (PG 16) skips NULL inputs and wouldn't catch this either.
jsonb_build_object takes alternating keys and values. Each test row becomes one object, and jsonb_agg collects them in t.id order.
FILTER (WHERE t.id IS NOT NULL) drops the padding row, so the aggregate sees no input and returns NULL, and coalesce turns that into []. The same two steps apply to array_agg with '{}'.

The whole response document comes out of the database; the Go or TS layer can pass it through. jsonb doesn't preserve key order, so keys appear in jsonb's storage order, not the order of the call. Use the json variants if the text order matters.

jsonb_object_agg(key, value) builds an object; keys must not be NULL, and with jsonb a duplicate key keeps its last value. Aggregates can't be nested, so jsonb_object_agg(status, count(*)) is an error; count in a grouped subquery first.

examples.title: Two child lists: join fan-out, and one subquery per list

annotations.note: Each test row pairs with each tag row of the same requirement, and the aggregates see all 6 pairs: count says 6, every tag appears twice. REQ-EXPORT gets {NULL} from its padding row. count(DISTINCT t.id) and array_agg(DISTINCT g.tag) would hide the damage but still build the product, and array_agg(DISTINCT t.title) would also merge two different tests that happen to share a title.

ARRAY(subquery) is a correlated subquery per requirement, so each list is built from its own table with its own ORDER BY, and nothing multiplies. It returns {} when the subquery finds no rows. For JSON, the same shape is (SELECT coalesce(jsonb_agg(...), '[]') FROM ... WHERE ... = r.id), or a LATERAL subquery per child.

use_cases: API list endpoints that return parent rows with nested children as JSON, in one query instead of 1 + N
Exports and reports with a readable cell such as 'Can, Zeynep' (string_agg) or a tag list (array_agg)
Lookup maps sent to a frontend: jsonb_object_agg(code, label) gives {"REQ-1": "Login", ...}
Collecting ids to pass on in one parameter: array_agg(id) feeding = ANY($1) in a later query
strengths: One query returns the response shape, so the ORM-style 1 + N queries (one per parent for its children) disappear
ORDER BY inside the aggregate gives deterministic lists with the collation you choose, including Turkish order
jsonb_build_object and jsonb_agg produce valid JSON with correct escaping; there is no string concatenation to get wrong
string_agg skips NULLs, unlike JS's join (empty string) or Java's String.join (the text "null")
weaknesses: NULL behaviour differs per function: string_agg skips NULLs, array_agg and jsonb_agg keep them, and all return NULL for no rows
Over a LEFT JOIN, the padding row ends up in the list ({NULL}, or an object of nulls) unless you FILTER it out
Every collected value is built in memory and a single value is capped at 1 GB, so whole-table exports belong in COPY or a streamed cursor, not one jsonb_agg
JSON built in SQL is untyped to the application; Go or TS still needs a schema check (struct tags, zod) on the way in

pitfalls.title: ORDER BY in the wrong place
pitfalls.detail: The query's ORDER BY sorts result rows, not the elements of an aggregate. Inside the call it goes after all arguments: string_agg(title ORDER BY title, ', ') parses as a one-argument string_agg and fails with function string_agg(text) does not exist.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT string_agg(title ORDER BY title, ', ') FROM test_cases
pitfalls.good: SELECT string_agg(title, ', ' ORDER BY title) FROM test_cases

pitfalls.title: jsonb_agg over a LEFT JOIN
pitfalls.detail: A parent without children yields [{"id": null, ...}], or [null] when you aggregate a bare column. Filter the padding row out and coalesce the empty case.
pitfalls.good: coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id)) FILTER (WHERE t.id IS NOT NULL), '[]')

pitfalls.title: Two child lists from two joins
pitfalls.detail: Joining tests and tags to the same requirement multiplies them, and every list and count is inflated. DISTINCT hides it at a cost. Aggregate each child in its own subquery.
pitfalls.bad: FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON ... LEFT JOIN tags g ON ... GROUP BY r.id
pitfalls.good: SELECT r.code, ARRAY(SELECT ... FROM test_cases t WHERE t.requirement_id = r.id ORDER BY ...), ARRAY(SELECT ... FROM tags g WHERE g.requirement_id = r.id ORDER BY ...) FROM requirements r

pitfalls.title: Code-point order for Turkish names
pitfalls.detail: Under C.UTF-8, Çağla, İrem and Şule sort after Zeynep. Name the collation in the aggregate's ORDER BY, or declare the column with it.
pitfalls.good: string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name COLLATE "tr-x-icu")

quiz.q: owner holds 'Zeynep', NULL and 'Can' (in id order). What does `string_agg(owner, ', ' ORDER BY id)` return?
quiz.why: string_agg concatenates the non-NULL inputs only; the NULL contributes neither a value nor a delimiter.

quiz.q: REQ-EXPORT has no tests. What does `jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id))` give for it after `requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ... GROUP BY r.id`?
quiz.why: The LEFT JOIN supplies one padding row, and jsonb_build_object turns its NULLs into an object, which jsonb_agg collects.

quiz.q: A requirement has 2 tests and 3 tags. Joined to both tables and grouped by requirement, what does count(t.id) return?
quiz.why: Each test row pairs with each tag row of the same requirement, so the group holds 2 x 3 rows, all with a non-NULL t.id.

quiz.q: Which call returns the titles in alphabetical order?
options: string_agg(title, ', ') with ORDER BY title at the end of the query
quiz.why: Element order is set inside the call, after all arguments. The query-level ORDER BY sorts rows, and the third form is a call to a one-argument string_agg that doesn't exist.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Aggregate Expressions (ORDER BY inside the call)
PostgreSQL docs: JSON Types (json vs jsonb, key order, duplicate keys)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Not every aggregate reduces a group to a number. Some collect it:

- `string_agg(value, delimiter)` joins text,
- `array_agg(value)` builds an array,
- `jsonb_agg(value)` builds a JSON array, and `jsonb_object_agg(key, value)` a JSON object.

They follow the same rules as `count`: one result per group, computed after `WHERE`. What
is new is that their result depends on the **order** of the input, and that order is
unspecified unless you write `ORDER BY` inside the call.

Together with `jsonb_build_object`, they turn a parent-child relationship into a nested
document in one query: one row per requirement, its tests as a JSON array. That is the
shape an API returns, and it replaces the "one query for the parents, one per parent for
the children" pattern ORMs fall into.

Two things go wrong regularly. NULLs: `string_agg` skips them, `array_agg` and
`jsonb_agg` keep them, and a LEFT JOIN supplies one for every parent without children.
Fan-out: joining two child tables to the same parent multiplies their rows before any
aggregate sees them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** `', '.join(sorted(names))` is `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`,
  except that `join` raises `TypeError` on `None` where `string_agg` skips it. `sorted()`
  on `str` compares code points, like C.UTF-8 here; Turkish order needs a collation
  library, as it needs `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` here.
- **JS:** `[a, null, b].join(', ')` turns the null into an empty string (`"a, , b"`);
  `Intl.Collator('tr')` is the browser's Turkish collation.
- **Java:** `Collectors.joining(", ")` appends the text `null` for null elements;
  `Collator.getInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"))` sorts Turkish.
- **Go:** `strings.Join(slices.Sorted(...), ", ")`, and `golang.org/x/text/collate` for
  Turkish order. A `jsonb_agg` result scans into `json.RawMessage` and can go straight
  into the HTTP response.
- **ORMs:** eager-loading two collections through joins hits the same fan-out as
  example 3, which is why ORMs usually load each collection with a query of its own.

## Design notes

Build JSON in SQL when the response is a projection of the query: list endpoints,
exports, dashboards. The application passes the bytes through and stays thin. Build
objects in Go or TS when the data feeds domain logic that wants typed values. Either way,
make empty lists `[]`, never `null`: `coalesce(... FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL),
'[]')`.

Give each child list its own subquery (`ARRAY(...)`, a scalar `(SELECT jsonb_agg(...)
...)`, or `LATERAL`). One `GROUP BY` over two child joins is wrong by construction, and
`DISTINCT` inside the aggregates only hides it.

Prefer `jsonb_agg` and `jsonb_build_object` unless you need the exact text (key order,
duplicate keys) that the `json` variants keep. For Turkish text, put the collation where
the ordering happens (`ORDER BY name COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` inside the aggregate) or on the
column, if Turkish order is what the column means everywhere.

lessons.title: GROUPING SETS/ROLLUP/CUBE, DISTINCT ON
lessons.summary: GROUPING SETS computes several GROUP BYs in one pass: ROLLUP adds subtotals along a hierarchy, CUBE every combination, and GROUPING() tells a subtotal's NULL from a NULL in the data. DISTINCT ON, a PostgreSQL extension, keeps the first row of each group in ORDER BY order.

examples.title: ROLLUP subtotals, and GROUPING() to label them

annotations.note: ROLLUP (suite, browser) means GROUPING SETS ((suite, browser), (suite), ()): every prefix of the list, which fits a hierarchy (browsers within a suite). One query returns 5 detail rows, 3 suite subtotals and the grand total.

A column that isn't part of a row's grouping set comes back NULL. auth now has two rows with browser NULL: the API tests (2 runs, 70 ms) and the suite subtotal (4 runs, 530 ms). Without GROUPING(browser) in the ORDER BY, even their relative order would be unspecified.

GROUPING(browser) = 1 marks the rolled-up rows, so coalesce only ever sees the NULLs that came from the data. A plain coalesce(browser, 'all browsers') would have labelled the API tests as a subtotal.

With several arguments GROUPING returns a bitmask, rightmost argument in the lowest bit, 1 meaning "not grouped here": 0 is a detail row, 1 a suite subtotal, 3 the grand total. ROLLUP never produces 2 (browser without suite); CUBE does.

Sorting on GROUPING() places each subtotal after its details and the total last, whatever NULL ordering is in effect. suite and browser here are the input columns, not the labels, which would sort 'all suites' among the real names.

examples.title: GROUPING SETS instead of UNION ALL, CUBE, and the one-scan plan

annotations.note: Each set in the list is an independent GROUP BY: per suite, per status, and () for the total. The docs define it as the UNION ALL of those queries, with NULL in the columns a set doesn't use.
CUBE (suite, status) expands to all four subsets, so it adds the per-status totals (level 2) that ROLLUP leaves out. With n columns that is 2^n groupings; CUBE of five columns asks for 32.
MixedAggregate: one Seq Scan feeds a hash table per column (Hash Key: suite, Hash Key: status) plus a running total for (). The UNION ALL spelling would scan test_runs three times.

examples.title: DISTINCT ON: the latest run per test case, ties, and the portable alternative

annotations.note: Two runs of Export in the same second: a tie on ran_at. Real data has these (retries, batch imports), and they decide whether the query is deterministic.

DISTINCT ON (test_case) keeps the first row of each test_case group in ORDER BY order. The leading ORDER BY items must be the DISTINCT ON expressions; the ones after them pick the winner: newest ran_at, and for the tie the higher id. Drop id DESC and the docs call the chosen row unpredictable.
The inner ORDER BY is tied to the DISTINCT ON groups. To present the winners in a different order, wrap the query and sort outside.

row_number() (window functions get their own module) numbers the rows of each partition in the given order, and rn = 1 keeps the first. It is standard SQL, and it turns into "latest three per test" with rn <= 3, which DISTINCT ON can't do.
SQLSTATE 42P10. The sort would order rows by ran_at alone, so rows of one test case aren't adjacent and "first of the group" has no meaning.

use_cases: Report exports with subtotals and a grand total: per suite and browser, per suite, overall (ROLLUP)
Dashboard tiles that each need a different breakdown (per status, per suite, total) from one query (GROUPING SETS)
Cross-tab margins: row totals, column totals and the corner total (CUBE over two columns)
Latest row per key with DISTINCT ON: last run per test, current price per product, newest address per customer
strengths: Several groupings come out of one scan of the data; the UNION ALL equivalent reads the table once per grouping
GROUPING() distinguishes subtotal rows from NULLs in the data, which no amount of coalesce can
DISTINCT ON returns whole rows, not just the max: the latest run's status, duration and id together, without joining max(ran_at) back to the table
Grouping sets, ROLLUP, CUBE and multi-argument GROUPING are standard SQL (features T431-T434 in PostgreSQL's conformance list)
weaknesses: Result rows have different meanings in one column set, so every consumer must check GROUPING() or a level column
CUBE grows as 2^n; a few extra columns produce far more groupings than anyone reads
DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL extension and only keeps one row per group; top-N needs row_number() or LATERAL
DISTINCT ON sorts its whole input (or reads an index in that order); with few keys and many rows each, LATERAL ... LIMIT 1 over an index reads far less

pitfalls.title: Labelling subtotals with coalesce
pitfalls.detail: coalesce(browser, 'all') can't tell a subtotal's NULL from a NULL in the data, so detail rows get mislabelled as totals. Test GROUPING().
pitfalls.good: CASE WHEN GROUPING(browser) = 1 THEN 'all browsers' ELSE coalesce(browser, 'api') END

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT ON without a complete tie-breaker
pitfalls.detail: When two rows tie on every ORDER BY item after the DISTINCT ON expressions, either may be kept, and the answer can change between runs. End the ORDER BY with a unique column.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) * FROM test_runs ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC
pitfalls.good: SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) * FROM test_runs ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC, id DESC

pitfalls.title: Combining ROLLUPs repeats grouping sets
pitfalls.detail: Several grouping items multiply into their Cartesian product, so GROUP BY ROLLUP (a, b), ROLLUP (a, c) contains (a, b) and (a, c) twice and (a) three times, and their rows repeat accordingly. GROUP BY DISTINCT (PG 14) removes the duplicate sets.
pitfalls.bad: GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser), ROLLUP (suite, status)
pitfalls.good: GROUP BY DISTINCT ROLLUP (suite, browser), ROLLUP (suite, status)

pitfalls.title: Expecting the subtotal rows in the right place
pitfalls.detail: Without ORDER BY, grouping-set rows come out in whatever order the plan produces them. Sort on GROUPING() and the grouping columns explicitly.

quiz.q: Which grouping sets does `GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)` compute?
quiz.why: ROLLUP takes every prefix of its list, down to the empty set. All subsets, including (browser) alone, is CUBE.

quiz.q: A ROLLUP result row has browser NULL. How do you tell whether it is a subtotal?
quiz.why: GROUPING(browser) is 1 only when browser is not part of the row's grouping set; a NULL in the data gives 0.

quiz.q: What does GROUPING(suite, status) return on the grand-total row?
quiz.why: Neither column is grouped, so both bits are set: 2 for suite plus 1 for status.

quiz.q: What happens with `SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, passed FROM test_runs ORDER BY ran_at DESC`?
options: It returns the latest run per test case
It fails: the DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions
It returns one arbitrary run per test case
quiz.why: DISTINCT ON relies on the sort placing each group's rows together, so the ORDER BY must start with test_case (SQLSTATE 42P10).

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP
PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, DISTINCT clause (DISTINCT ON)
PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, GROUP BY clause (GROUP BY DISTINCT)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A report rarely wants just one level of summary. It wants runs per suite and browser,
per suite, and overall. Plain `GROUP BY` gives one level per query. **Grouping sets**
(PG 9.5) give several in one result:

- `GROUPING SETS ((a), (b), ())` lists the groupings explicitly. Each set behaves like
  its own `GROUP BY`, and its rows have NULL in the columns the set doesn't use.
- `ROLLUP (a, b)` is shorthand for every prefix, `(a, b), (a), ()`: subtotals down a
  hierarchy.
- `CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for every subset, `(a, b), (a), (b), ()`: the margins of a
  cross-tab.
- `GROUPING(a, b)` returns a bitmask saying which columns are rolled up in the current
  row, so a subtotal's NULL can be told from a NULL in the data.

**DISTINCT ON** answers a different summary question: not "how many per group" but
"which row per group". `SELECT DISTINCT ON (key) ... ORDER BY key, preference` keeps the
first row of each key in that order: the latest run per test case, with all its
columns. It is a PostgreSQL extension; `row_number()` is the standard equivalent.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Spreadsheets and BI tools:** a pivot table with subtotals and a grand total is
  `ROLLUP`; "totals for rows and columns" is `CUBE` over the two pivot axes.
- **Python:** pandas `pivot_table(..., margins=True)` adds the `All` row and column, as
  `CUBE` over two columns does. "First row per group" is
  `df.sort_values(...).drop_duplicates('test_case')`, which keeps the first occurrence:
  the same sort-then-keep-first algorithm as `DISTINCT ON`.
- **Java, JS, Go:** you would run one grouping pass per level, or add subtotals in a
  second loop. Grouping sets compute every level from one scan.
- **JS:** latest per key is usually a `reduce` into a `Map` that replaces an entry when a
  newer one arrives. That compares two rows at a time; `DISTINCT ON` sorts once and keeps
  the first of each run of equal keys.

## How it works

`GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ())` is defined as the `UNION ALL` of three
queries: `GROUP BY suite` with `status` as NULL, `GROUP BY status` with `suite` as NULL,
and the ungrouped total. The executor computes them together: example 2's plan is one
scan feeding a hash table per set (`MixedAggregate`).

Grouping items combine as a Cartesian product: `GROUP BY suite, ROLLUP (browser,
status)` means `GROUPING SETS ((suite, browser, status), (suite, browser), (suite))`.
That is how you get subtotals *within* each suite without a grand total.

`DISTINCT ON` runs after the sort: rows arrive ordered by the `DISTINCT ON` expressions
first, and a `Unique` step keeps the first row of each run of equal keys. That is why
the `ORDER BY` must start with those expressions.

## Design notes

Use grouping sets when the database is the reporting engine: CSV exports, admin
summaries, dashboard tiles. Always return `GROUPING()` (or a level column derived from
it) so the consumer never has to guess what a NULL means, and always sort explicitly.
Prefer `GROUPING SETS` that list exactly the levels you need over `CUBE`, which grows as
2^n.

For "one row per group", pick by shape. `DISTINCT ON` is the shortest when you need
one row per key and run on PostgreSQL only; always end its `ORDER BY` with a unique
column. `row_number()` is portable and extends to top-N. When there are few keys and
many rows per key, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... ORDER BY ran_at DESC LIMIT 1)` over an index
on `(test_case, ran_at DESC)` reads one index entry per key instead of every row (see the
LATERAL lesson).

lessons.title: Client/server, databases vs schemas vs roles
lessons.summary: One PostgreSQL server (a "cluster") holds many databases; a connection is one role inside one database, and schemas are namespaces within it, resolved through search_path. Roles live above all databases, which is why they can own databases and schemas alike.

examples.title: Who and where is this connection?

annotations.note: pg_stat_activity has one row per server process. 'client backend' is a process serving a client, as opposed to background processes such as the checkpointer. The server starts one per connection, which is why opening a connection is expensive and why Go and Node apps keep a pool of them (pgxpool, pg.Pool) instead.
session_user is the role that logged in. current_user is the role privileges are checked against; it moves away from session_user after SET ROLE and inside SECURITY DEFINER functions.

The path holds only the sandbox schema, yet current_schemas(true) lists pg_catalog first: when the path doesn't name it, pg_catalog is searched implicitly, before everything else. That is how upper(), now() and every built-in type resolve without a prefix.

examples.title: Same table name, two schemas: search_path picks

annotations.note: A schema is a namespace, not a separate store: creating one needs no new connection, and queries can combine tables from different schemas freely, as the last query does.

The same unqualified name, tickets, means a different table after each SET: the first schema on the path that has a match wins. SET LOCAL lasts until the transaction ends; a plain SET would last for the whole session, which matters when connections are pooled.
refunds has no prefix, so it lands in the current schema: the first existing schema on the path, billing by now. Migration tools and ORMs that create unprefixed tables depend on this setting.
A qualified name never consults the path. Code that must not be redirected by someone else's search_path (functions, migrations) qualifies its names or sets the path explicitly.

examples.title: Cluster-wide vs per-database, read from the catalogs

annotations.note: relisshared marks catalogs stored once for the whole server: pg_authid holds the roles, pg_database the databases. pg_class (tables) and pg_namespace (schemas) exist separately inside every database, so a connection can only ever see its own database's.

In a new database (PG 15+) public belongs to pg_database_owner, a role whose one implicit member is the current database's owner. Before 15 the bootstrap superuser owned it and every role could create objects in it; clusters upgraded from 14 keep those old permissions. StackLab's setup-local-db.sql hands the playground's public to postgres: lesson code runs as the database owner, and this way it can use public but not create objects in it.
The playground role owns the playground database. That ownership, not superuser rights, is what lets StackLab's runner create a throwaway schema for every run.

The first part of a three-part name is the database (the SQL standard calls it the catalog), and it may only name the one you are connected to. Reaching another database takes a second connection or an extension such as postgres_fdw.

use_cases: One database per application; schemas inside it for parts that must still be joined (app, audit, reporting)
Separate databases for unrelated projects on one server, so they cannot see each other's tables
Distinct roles for running migrations (owns the schema) and for the app itself (only the privileges it needs)
strengths: Schemas are cheap namespaces you can join across. What MySQL calls a database is closer to a PostgreSQL schema; a PostgreSQL database is a harder boundary
Roles cover users and groups with one concept (since 8.1): grant privileges to a group role, then grant the group to login roles
Databases are isolated by construction: a connection to one cannot read another by accident, no matter what SQL it sends
weaknesses: No cross-database queries: data that must be joined has to live in one database, or go through postgres_fdw
One server process per connection makes connections expensive; hundreds of idle ones cost real memory, so applications need a pool
search_path is implicit session state: the same SQL text can reach different tables under different settings

pitfalls.title: Planning on cross-database joins
pitfalls.detail: Coming from MySQL or SQL Server, it's natural to split modules into databases and join across them. In PostgreSQL that fails with 'cross-database references are not implemented'. Use schemas in one database for anything you'll join.

pitfalls.title: permission denied for schema public on a fresh database
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 15 ordinary roles can no longer create objects in public; only the database owner can. A migration that ran on an old server fails on a new one. Have the database owner run migrations, or create a schema for the app and grant CREATE on it.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE TABLE users (...);  -- as a role that doesn't own the database
pitfalls.good: CREATE SCHEMA app AUTHORIZATION app_owner;  -- then create tables in app

pitfalls.title: A SET that outlives your request
pitfalls.detail: SET search_path (or any SET) changes the server session, and a pooled connection carries it into the next request that borrows it. Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction, or configure the setting per role with ALTER ROLE ... SET.

quiz.q: Your Go service needs to join orders (database shop) with users (database auth) on the same server. What happens?
options: It works: write shop.public.orders JOIN auth.public.users
It fails: a connection reaches one database; put both in one database (two schemas) or use postgres_fdw
It works as long as both databases have the same owner
quiz.why: Every connection is bound to one database, and a three-part name may only name that one. Schemas are the joinable unit.

quiz.q: search_path is billing, support and both schemas have a tickets table. What do SELECT * FROM tickets and CREATE TABLE refunds (...) use?
options: billing.tickets, and refunds is created in billing
support.tickets, and refunds is created in support
An ambiguity error, and refunds is created in public
quiz.why: Lookup walks the path in order and takes the first match; creation goes to the first existing schema on the path.

quiz.q: Where do roles live?
options: At the cluster level, shared by every database on the server
quiz.why: Roles are global to the cluster (pg_authid is a shared catalog), which is why a role can own a database and objects in several databases.

quiz.q: On a new PostgreSQL 18 database, a role that doesn't own the database runs CREATE TABLE public.t (id int). What happens?
options: The table is created; public is open to everyone
permission denied for schema public: since PG 15 only the database owner (via pg_database_owner) can create there by default
The table is created in the role's own schema instead
quiz.why: PG 15 removed PUBLIC's CREATE privilege on public and made pg_database_owner its owner.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Schemas (including the search path and usage patterns)

lessons.body:
## Concept

PostgreSQL is a server program. Clients (psql, your Go service through pgx, a GUI) connect
to it over TCP or a local socket, and every connection names two things: a **role** to
log in as and a **database** to work in. The server starts a separate process for each
connection; that process holds your session's state (settings, the open transaction)
until you disconnect.

The containers, from the outside in:

- **Cluster**: one running server with its data directory, usually one port. The
  docs call it a "database cluster"; it has nothing to do with multi-node clustering.
- **Database**: an isolated collection of schemas. A connection is bound to exactly
  one, and no query can reach into another.
- **Schema**: a namespace inside a database, holding tables, views, functions, types
  and sequences. Schemas cannot nest, and joining across them is ordinary SQL.
- **Role**: a user, a group, or both. Roles live at the cluster level, next to the
  databases rather than inside them, so one role can own objects in many databases.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **MySQL**: `CREATE SCHEMA` is a synonym for `CREATE DATABASE` there, and you can join
  across them. That unit corresponds to a PostgreSQL *schema*. A PostgreSQL database is
  a much harder wall.
- **Go and Java packages, C++ namespaces**: a schema is the same idea: `billing.tickets`
  vs `support.tickets`, like `billing.Ticket` vs `support.Ticket`. `search_path` is like
  a list of C++ `using namespace` directives, except that where C++ reports an
  ambiguity, PostgreSQL silently takes the first match.
- **Python's `sys.path`** is a closer analogy still: an ordered search list that the
  environment can change under you. Code that must be robust qualifies its names.
- **Node and Go connection handling**: a connection is a server process, not a cheap
  socket. That's why `pgxpool` and `pg.Pool` exist, and why a `SET` on a pooled
  connection leaks into whichever request borrows it next.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  client1["psql"] -- "role + database" --> server
  client2["Go service (pgxpool)"] -- "role + database" --> server
  subgraph server["cluster: one server, one data directory"]
    roles["roles (shared by all databases)"]
    subgraph db1["database: playground"]
      s1["schema: public"]
      s2["schema: run_… (one per lesson run)"]
    end
    subgraph db2["database: stacklab"]
      s3["schema: public"]
    end
  end
```

Name resolution happens when a statement is parsed. An unqualified `tickets` is looked
