up in each schema on `search_path`, in order. `pg_catalog`, home of the built-in
functions and types, is searched first unless the path places it explicitly. The
default path is `"$user", public`: a schema named after your role if one exists, then
`public`. New objects without a prefix go into the first schema on the path that exists.

Every StackLab SQL run sits inside this picture: the runner connects as the
`playground` role to the `playground` database, creates schema `run_<id>`, sets the
path to it, runs your SQL in one transaction and rolls it back.

## Design notes

Choose the boundary by asking whether the data will ever be joined. Unrelated
applications get separate databases, and the docs recommend exactly that for projects
that should be unaware of each other. Parts of one application (core tables, an
audit trail, reporting views) get schemas in one database, so a report can join them
and one transaction can span them.

The PG 15 change to `public` is part of the same design: a database is owned by
someone, and by default only that owner may create objects in the shared schema. The
security module builds on this with a least-privilege application role. It is also why
StackLab's local setup makes the playground role the owner of its database instead of a
superuser: owning the database is enough to create schemas in it, and nothing more is
handed out.

lessons.title: psql essentials: \d, \dt, \x, \timing, \e
lessons.summary: psql's backslash commands are answered by psql itself, mostly by sending catalog queries it writes for you. Learn the dozen you'll use daily, and the SQL behind \d, which you can reuse anywhere psql isn't.

examples.title: \d without a pattern, as the SQL psql sends

annotations.note: The identity columns bring sequences with them, and \d lists them next to the tables: GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is backed by a sequence the table owns.
COMMENT ON stores documentation in the catalog. \dt+ and \d+ show it in their Description column, so a colleague browsing in psql sees it without opening your repository.
The core of what psql runs for \d, trimmed. Start psql with -E (or \set ECHO_HIDDEN on) and it prints the full query before every meta-command: the quickest way to learn the catalogs.

pg_table_is_visible is true when the table's schema is on the search path and no earlier schema has the same name. It is why \dt lists nothing for tables in schemas outside your path; \dt *.* shows every schema.

examples.title: \d orders: columns, constraints, and the portable way

annotations.note: format_type prints the names psql shows, with modifiers: character varying(80), timestamp with time zone. pg_get_expr turns a stored default back into SQL text. Identity columns have no default expression; their attidentity flag says how values arrive.
Positive attnum skips system columns (ctid, xmin, ...). A dropped column only becomes invisible; its slot stays in pg_attribute, flagged attisdropped, until the table is rewritten.

pg_get_constraintdef reconstructs the definition rather than returning what you typed, hence (total >= (0)::numeric). Since PG 18 NOT NULL is stored here too, as contype 'n' constraints with their own names.

information_schema is the SQL standard's catalog: the same query works on other databases. The price: data_type drops the (80) and (10,2) into separate columns, and every Postgres-specific type collapses to ARRAY or USER-DEFINED.

examples.title: Stored names: folding, quotes, and a Turkish letter

annotations.note: Unquoted names fold to lower case; quoted ones are stored exactly. The fold covers ASCII letters only: in this UTF-8 database Şubeler keeps its capital Ş, so şubeler (with ş) is a different name.

Identifiers are limited to 63 bytes, not characters, and each Turkish letter outside ASCII takes two bytes in UTF-8. This 55-character name is one byte too long, so the server cuts it and says so only in a NOTICE.
length counts characters, octet_length bytes: 7 and 8 for Şubeler. The long name came back at 63 bytes, without its final m.
to_regclass parses its argument as SQL would, folding PAYMENTS to payments and keeping "Invoices" as written, and returns NULL instead of raising an error when nothing matches.
Unquoted, Invoices means invoices, which doesn't exist. psql patterns follow the same rule: \dt Invoices finds nothing; \dt "Invoices" finds the table.

use_cases: Inspecting a server you reached over SSH, where there is no GUI: \dn, \dt app.*, \d app.orders
Running migration and seed scripts: psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f migrate.sql
Learning the catalogs: psql -E prints the SQL behind every meta-command, ready to reuse in Go or TS tooling
strengths: Ships with every PostgreSQL install and needs nothing but a terminal, unlike GUI clients
Meta-commands are thin wrappers over catalog queries you can see (-E) and copy, not a black box
\x auto switches to one-field-per-line only when a row is wider than the screen; \gx does it for a single query
weaknesses: Meta-commands exist only in psql: pgx, node-postgres and every GUI need the catalog queries instead
Its output is formatted for humans, so scripts should query the catalogs or information_schema rather than parse \d
On Windows, the console code page can garble Turkish characters until it matches what psql expects

pitfalls.title: \dt shows nothing, yet the app works
pitfalls.detail: Without a pattern, \d commands list only objects visible on your search_path. The app's tables are probably in another schema: \dn lists schemas, \dt app.* or \dt *.* finds them.

pitfalls.title: NULL and the empty string look identical
pitfalls.detail: By default psql prints nothing for NULL. Set a visible marker once in your psqlrc.
pitfalls.good: \pset null '(null)'

pitfalls.title: A missing semicolon
pitfalls.detail: SQL is sent only at ';' (or \g). Until then psql keeps buffering, and the prompt changes from playground=> to playground-> to say so. Backslash commands, by contrast, end at the newline.

pitfalls.title: Turkish characters garbled in the Windows console
pitfalls.detail: psql warns at startup when it detects a problematic console code page. The docs' fix: switch the console to your Windows code page (cmd.exe /c chcp 1254 on Turkish Windows, 1252 on Western European ones) and set the console font to Lucida Console.

quiz.q: \dt lists no tables, but the application reads and writes them fine. What's the most likely reason?
options: psql lacks privileges to see them
They live in a schema that isn't on your search_path; try \dt *.*
\dt only shows tables created in the current session
quiz.why: Without a pattern, \d commands show only objects visible on the search path. *.* matches every schema.

quiz.q: What does starting psql with -E do?
options: Runs every statement in its own transaction
Prints the catalog queries that backslash commands send
quiz.why: -E is the same as \set ECHO_HIDDEN on: psql shows each hidden query before running it. Expanded output is -x.

quiz.q: After CREATE TABLE "Invoices" (id int), which psql command lists it?
quiz.why: Patterns fold to lower case like unquoted SQL names; double quotes stop the folding.

quiz.q: Why can't your Go code send \d orders through pgx?
options: Meta-commands are interpreted by psql and never reach the server; send the catalog query instead
quiz.why: The server only understands SQL. psql turns \d into catalog queries before anything is sent.

lessons.body:
## Concept

psql reads two kinds of input. SQL is buffered until a `;` and then sent to the server.
Backslash commands (meta-commands) end at the newline and are handled by psql itself;
many of them are just catalog queries psql writes for you. That is why StackLab's runner
can't execute `\d`: it only speaks SQL to the server, as your Go code does. The examples
run the SQL those commands stand for instead.

The working set:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `\l`, `\c db` | list databases; reconnect to another one (a new connection) |
| `\dn`, `\dt`, `\dv`, `\di`, `\df`, `\du` | list schemas, tables, views, indexes, functions, roles |
| `\d name`, `\d+ name` | describe one object; `+` adds sizes, comments and more |
| `\x`, `\x auto`, `\gx` | expanded output (one field per line): toggle, only when too wide, or for one query |
| `\timing` | toggle printing how long each statement took |
| `\e`, `\ef fn` | edit the query buffer (or a function) in your editor |
| `\i file.sql` | run a file as if you'd typed it |
| `\?`, `\h CREATE TABLE` | help for meta-commands; SQL syntax help |

Patterns work on every `\d` command: `\dt app.*` lists tables in schema `app`, `\dt *.*`
lists tables in all schemas, and an `S` (`\dtS`) includes system objects.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python's or Node's REPL**: psql is that for SQL, with `\d` in place of `dir()` and
  `help()`, and `\i file.sql` to load a script into the session.
- **The `go` command**: psql ships with the server the way `go` ships with Go. GUI
  clients are optional; psql is always there, including on a server you reach over SSH.
- **Reflection** (Java's `Class.getDeclaredFields`, Go's `reflect`): the system catalogs
  are the database describing itself in tables, and `\d` is a pretty-printer over them.
  `information_schema` is the portable, standardized layer on top, with less detail.
- **Windows**: psql is a console program, and the console has its own code page. If psql
  warns about it at startup, fix that first (see the pitfall), or Turkish letters may
  come out garbled.

## How it works

`\timing` prints how long each statement took as psql saw it, so the number includes the
network and transferring the result, but not printing it. The docs say only "how long
each SQL statement takes"; psql's source (src/bin/psql/common.c, function
ExecQueryAndProcessResults) starts the clock before sending the query and stops it once
the result has arrived, before printing. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, covered in the indexes
module, works the other way round: its Execution Time is measured inside the server and,
per the docs, includes neither planning (reported separately) nor sending rows to the
client. When `\timing` is much larger, the gap is planning plus getting the rows to you.
On PostgreSQL 18.7 here, 300,000 generated rows sent to `\o NUL` took 135 to 184 ms by
`\timing`, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of the same query reported 61 to 81 ms.

`\e` opens the current query buffer (or, if it's empty, the last query) in an editor:
`PSQL_EDITOR`, `EDITOR` or `VISUAL`, whichever is set first, else `vi` on Unix and
`notepad.exe` on Windows. When you save and quit, any complete statement in the buffer,
one ending in `;`, runs at once. Your personal settings go in `~/.psqlrc`, or
`%APPDATA%\postgresql\psqlrc.conf` on Windows; `\x auto`, `\timing on` and a
`\pset null` marker are common first lines.

Patterns follow SQL's identifier rules: unquoted letters fold to lower case, double
quotes keep them. In SQL itself, in a UTF-8 database, the server's fold only touches
ASCII letters, as the `Şubeler` example shows. The docs say only that unquoted names "are
always folded to lower case"; the server's source (src/backend/parser/scansup.c, function
downcase_identifier) lowers A to Z and leaves every byte of a multibyte character alone.
With Turkish table names in SQL, quote them or keep them all lower case.

psql's own fold for patterns is cruder. It goes byte by byte through the C library's
`isupper`/`tolower` in the client's locale (src/fe_utils/string_utils.c, function
patternToSQLRegex), which can change a byte inside a UTF-8 letter. Observed with psql 18.7
on StackLab's Windows machine (locale en-US, code page 1252; console code page 437 or 65001;
client encoding UTF8): `\dt Şubeler`, and even `\dt şubeler`, fail with `invalid byte
sequence for encoding "UTF8"`, while `\dt "Şubeler"` and `\dt *ubeler` find the table.
In a pattern, double-quote any name with a non-ASCII letter, lower case included.

## Design notes

psql's split between SQL and meta-commands is the useful lesson here: the database
describes itself in ordinary tables, and every tool, from psql to pgAdmin to your own
health check, is just querying them. When you need schema facts in code (a migration
check, a test asserting an index exists), copy the query `psql -E` shows you, or use
`information_schema` if it must also run on another database. Don't scrape `\d` output:
it is formatted for people and changes between versions.

lessons.title: SQL as a declarative, set-based language (vs loops in Go/TS)
lessons.summary: A query describes the rows you want; the planner picks the loops, hash tables and sorts. Statements act on every qualifying row at once, against the table as it was when they started, so stop writing the loop and write the result.

examples.title: The question as one query, and the plan the server chose

annotations.note: Each clause states a property of the answer: which rows (WHERE), grouped how (GROUP BY), which groups survive (HAVING), in what order. None says how to compute it. GROUP BY and HAVING get their own lesson in the aggregation module.

A half-open range, from the first of the month up to (not including) the first of the next, stays correct when the column later becomes a timestamp; BETWEEN ... '2026-11-30' would then miss that day's afternoon.

EXPLAIN prints the plan instead of running the query. Bottom-up: scan and filter the table, sort by customer, sum each run of equal names (GroupAggregate), keep groups of 500 or more, sort by the sum. On other data the planner may pick a HashAggregate, which is your Go map, or an index. The query text would not change. COSTS OFF hides the estimates, which shift with table statistics.

examples.title: One statement, every row, one snapshot

annotations.note: Every right-hand side is computed from the row as it was before the UPDATE, so the two assignments don't see each other. Go's a, b = b, a works the same way; Java needs a temporary variable.

The SELECT reads a snapshot taken when the statement started: 3 rows in, 3 rows added. A JavaScript for...of that pushes onto the array it iterates never ends. Go's range evaluates the slice once and stops after 3, the semantics every SQL statement has.

The crack: PostgreSQL checks a non-deferrable UNIQUE as each row is written, not at the end of the statement as the SQL standard asks. pos 1 becomes 2 while the old 2 still exists, so the statement fails, and fails whole: no row moves. A DEFERRABLE constraint (constraints module) gets the end-of-statement check.

examples.title: Diff two lists with EXCEPT, INTERSECT and UNION

annotations.note: supplier_file has no key and lists B-7 twice: tables are bags (multisets), not sets. UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove duplicates unless you add ALL.
EXCEPT is set difference. In Go you'd build a map from one side and loop over the other; here the planner picks hashing or sorting, and there is no map to get wrong.
INTERSECT keeps rows present on both sides. B-7 comes out once even though the file has it twice.
UNION has to sort or hash every row to find duplicates. When duplicates are impossible, or are real data (two identical payments), UNION ALL is both correct and cheaper.

use_cases: Reports and dashboards: filter, group, sort in one query instead of fetching rows and folding them in Go or TS
Bulk changes: one UPDATE or DELETE for every qualifying row, not a loop issuing one per row
Reconciling lists (import vs catalog, expected vs actual) with EXCEPT and INTERSECT
strengths: The planner chooses algorithms from statistics and indexes; adding an index can speed a query up without touching its text, which a hand-written loop can't offer
One statement is atomic: it applies to all qualifying rows or to none, so there is no half-finished loop to clean up after an error
Set operators express list diffs in a line, where Go needs a map and two loops and Java a HashSet and removeAll
weaknesses: You don't pick the plan directly (core PostgreSQL has no per-query hints, only crude enable_* settings); when the planner misestimates, you fix statistics, indexes or the query's shape
Work with per-row side effects outside the database (call an API, send an e-mail) doesn't fit in one statement
PostgreSQL's row-by-row UNIQUE check breaks the all-at-once model for updates that permute key values

pitfalls.title: One statement per row from the application
pitfalls.detail: A Go or TS loop that sends an UPDATE per item makes N round trips and N statements, and leaves half the rows changed if it fails midway outside a transaction. Send the whole set in one statement: UPDATE ... FROM over arrays passed through unnest, with one entry per sku (the modifying module shows why that matters).
pitfalls.bad: for _, it := range items { db.Exec(ctx, "UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - $1 WHERE sku = $2", it.Qty, it.SKU) }
pitfalls.good: UPDATE stock s SET qty = s.qty - i.qty FROM unnest($1::text[], $2::int[]) AS i(sku, qty) WHERE s.sku = i.sku

pitfalls.title: Expecting rows in insertion order
pitfalls.detail: A table has no order. Without ORDER BY, rows come back in whatever order the chosen plan produces, and that changes with updates and plans.

pitfalls.title: UNION where UNION ALL was meant
pitfalls.detail: UNION silently merges identical rows. Two identical 100 TL payments become one, and the total is wrong.

quiz.q: nums holds 1, 2, 3. What does INSERT INTO nums SELECT n + 3 FROM nums leave behind?
options: An endless loop, stopped by statement_timeout
An error: a table can't be read and written in one statement
quiz.why: The SELECT sees the table as of the statement's start, so it reads 3 rows and inserts 3.

quiz.q: What does UPDATE t SET a = b, b = a do?
options: Sets both columns to the old b
Swaps a and b in every row
Fails: a column is used after being assigned
quiz.why: Right-hand sides use the old values of the row, like Go's a, b = b, a.

quiz.q: What does the text of a SELECT decide?
options: The rows and order of the result
Whether a hash table or a sort is used
The order in which the table is read from disk
quiz.why: The query is a description of the result. The algorithms are the planner's choice, visible with EXPLAIN.

quiz.q: Which query lists skus in the supplier's file that we don't stock?
options: SELECT sku FROM supplier_file UNION SELECT sku FROM stock
SELECT sku FROM supplier_file INTERSECT SELECT sku FROM stock
SELECT sku FROM supplier_file EXCEPT SELECT sku FROM stock
quiz.why: EXCEPT returns rows of the first query that the second doesn't have: set difference.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
PostgreSQL docs: CREATE TABLE, non-deferred uniqueness constraints

lessons.body:
## Concept

SQL is declarative: a query describes the rows you want, and the planner decides how to
produce them. Which index, which join algorithm, hash table or sort, in which order to
read the tables: all of that is chosen per query from statistics, and `EXPLAIN` shows
the choice.

The unit of work is the set of rows (strictly a bag, since duplicates are allowed), not
the row. An `UPDATE` changes every row its `WHERE` matches, in one atomic step, and
every expression in it reads the table as it was when the statement started. The habit
to build: when you're about to write a loop around the database, ask what the result
looks like and write that.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

The November report as imperative Go:

```go
spent := map[string]int64{} // in kuruş: never float for money
for _, o := range orders {  // every row, fetched over the network first
	if !o.Placed.Before(nov1) && o.Placed.Before(dec1) {
		spent[o.Customer] += o.TotalKurus
	}
}
var out []row
for c, s := range spent {
	if s >= 500_00 {
		out = append(out, row{customer: c, spent: s})
	}
}
slices.SortFunc(out, func(a, b row) int { return cmp.Compare(b.spent, a.spent) })
```

Here you chose the algorithm (a hash map), the memory (all rows in the process) and the
order of operations. The SQL version states the result and lets the server pick, next to
the data and its indexes.

- **TS's `filter`/`reduce`, Java Streams, Python comprehensions** look declarative, but
  they still run as written, in your process, after every row has been fetched. The
  planner can do what they can't: reorder steps, use an index, or skip reading most of
  the table.
- **N+1 queries**: a loop that runs one query per item is a loop the database cannot see
  or optimize. It's the most common performance bug in application code that talks to
  SQL.
- **Halloween problem**: C++ iterator invalidation and JS's endless `for...of` over a
  growing array don't exist inside one SQL statement; the snapshot rule prevents them.

## Design notes

"Set-based" doesn't mean "one giant statement for everything". Loops still have a
place, one level up: batch a ten-million-row backfill into chunks of a few thousand rows,
each chunk a single set-based `UPDATE`, so locks stay short and progress is visible. Per-row
work outside the database (an HTTP call per customer) belongs in application code.
What disappears is the loop *inside* the data work: filtering, joining, grouping and
diffing are the database's job, and it does them better because it knows the data's
size, its indexes and its statistics.

lessons.title: NOT NULL, DEFAULT, primary keys and UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT
lessons.summary: Constraints are invariants the database checks on every write, from every client. NOT NULL and DEFAULT shape columns, a primary key names the row, and UNIQUE (with NULLS NOT DISTINCT since PG 15) guards the real-world identity a surrogate key can't.

examples.title: DEFAULT fills omitted columns; an explicit NULL is not omitted

annotations.note: PRIMARY KEY means NOT NULL plus UNIQUE plus "this is the row's identity": one per table, and the default target of foreign keys. The identity column generates it (previous module).
NOT NULL DEFAULT is the usual pair. The default spares every INSERT from naming the column; NOT NULL stops a later UPDATE from setting it to "no value".
Leave a column nullable only when NULL has a meaning you can name. Here it does: the ticket is unassigned.
Both rows get status 'open'. The DEFAULT keyword asks for the default explicitly, which helps in a multi-row VALUES list where only some rows carry a value.
The ORM trap: a client that always lists every column sends NULL for "not set", so the DEFAULT never fires. Omit the column or write DEFAULT. The error carries SQLSTATE 23502 (not_null_violation).

examples.title: Surrogate keys identify rows; UNIQUE keeps the real-world identity

annotations.note: A natural key is data that already identifies the thing. It reads well wherever it is referenced: users.currency below says TRY with no join. The price is paid when it changes, because every referencing row must change too. ISO codes almost never change; e-mail addresses do.
The identity column makes every row distinct, so the same person signs up twice. A surrogate key answers "which row", never "which person".
The common shape: a meaningless, immutable id for references, and the natural key declared unique next to it.

A UNIQUE constraint takes plain columns only. lower(email) is an expression, so it becomes a unique index, which enforces the same rule. lower() uses the database's case rules: under C.UTF-8, I lowers to i, never to ı (see the pitfalls).
The e-mail address changed and the id did not, so anything pointing at users.id is untouched. With email as the primary key, every referencing row would need the update.

'Ayse.Yilmaz@Example.com' and the stored address have the same lower(), so the index rejects it (SQLSTATE 23505, unique_violation). The error names the index: give constraints and indexes names your error mapping can recognise.

examples.title: UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG 15) for optional key columns

annotations.note: By default a unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct, so two "global" theme rows coexist and every lookup of the global default becomes a coin toss. The SQL standard leaves this choice to each database, and they differ.

NULLS NOT DISTINCT makes (NULL, 'theme') equal to (NULL, 'theme') for this constraint only; NULL = NULL in a query is still NULL. Before PG 15 the workaround was a second, partial unique index: (key) WHERE tenant_id IS NULL.
The second global theme row now fails with the same SQLSTATE 23505 as any other duplicate.

use_cases: NOT NULL DEFAULT for status fields, flags and counters, so no code path can leave them unset
Surrogate identity key plus UNIQUE on the natural key: users (email), products (sku), requirements (project_id, code)
Natural primary keys for small, stable, standard codes: ISO 4217 currencies, ISO 3166 countries
NULLS NOT DISTINCT for 'global default plus per-tenant override' tables and other keys with an optional part
strengths: Unlike a check in a Go handler or a zod schema, a constraint also covers psql sessions, migration scripts and the second service that writes the same table
Uniqueness holds under concurrency: two transactions inserting the same e-mail can't both commit, which an application-side SELECT-then-INSERT can't promise
Violations come back with a SQLSTATE (23502, 23505) and the constraint name, so the API can map them to a precise 409 or 422 in one place
weaknesses: Every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE is a B-tree index that each INSERT and key UPDATE must maintain
A DEFAULT applies only when the column is omitted; clients that always send every column bypass it
Case-insensitive or partial uniqueness needs a unique index, which can't be attached as a table constraint with ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX
A natural primary key that changes has to be rewritten in every referencing row

pitfalls.title: Sending NULL and expecting the DEFAULT
pitfalls.detail: Only an omitted column or the DEFAULT keyword gets the default. An explicit NULL is stored as NULL, or rejected by NOT NULL.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO tickets (title, status) VALUES ('x', NULL);
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO tickets (title) VALUES ('x');  -- or VALUES ('x', DEFAULT)

pitfalls.title: Treating the surrogate key as the uniqueness rule
pitfalls.detail: An identity primary key makes every row distinct, duplicates included. Declare UNIQUE on whatever identifies the thing in the real world.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive keys under the wrong case rules
pitfalls.detail: lower() follows the database's case rules. StackLab's databases use C.UTF-8, which maps I to i, so lower('IŞIK') is 'işik' and never collides with 'ışık'. When Turkish rules define identity (user names, product names), index the Turkish lowercase. For e-mail addresses the default rules are what you want.
pitfalls.good: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(username COLLATE "tr-x-icu"));

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNIQUE to reject a second NULL
pitfalls.detail: Under the default NULLS DISTINCT, any number of rows may hold NULL in a unique column. Use NOT NULL, or NULLS NOT DISTINCT on PG 15+.

quiz.q: status is `text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open'`. What does `INSERT INTO tickets (title, status) VALUES ('x', NULL)` do?
quiz.why: An explicit NULL is a value, so the DEFAULT doesn't apply and NOT NULL rejects it. Only an omitted column or the DEFAULT keyword gets the default.

quiz.q: users has `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY` and `email text NOT NULL`, nothing else. What stops two rows with the same e-mail?
quiz.why: The primary key is on id, which is different for every row. Only a UNIQUE constraint or unique index on email (or lower(email)) prevents the duplicate.

quiz.q: A table has `UNIQUE (tenant_id, key)` without NULLS NOT DISTINCT. How many rows with (NULL, 'theme') can it hold?
quiz.why: NULLs are distinct by default, so the constraint never considers two of these rows equal.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A constraint is a rule the database checks on every INSERT and UPDATE, whoever sends
them. The four in this lesson cover most of a table's shape:

- **NOT NULL**: the column always has a value.
- **DEFAULT**: not a constraint strictly, but its partner: the value used when an INSERT
  leaves the column out.
- **PRIMARY KEY**: the row's identity. Unique and not null, one per table, and what
  foreign keys point at by default.
- **UNIQUE**: no two rows share these values. NULLs count as distinct unless you say
  `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+).

A key is either **natural** (data that already identifies the thing: an ISO currency
code, an e-mail address) or **surrogate** (a generated number or UUID with no meaning).
The usual design is a surrogate primary key for references plus a UNIQUE constraint on
the natural key, because a surrogate key by itself never stops a duplicate.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: Bean Validation's `@NotNull` runs in the JVM, for that one application. `NOT NULL`
  runs in the database, for every client, including psql and the next service someone
  writes.
- Go: a struct field always holds a value; an unset `int` is `0` and is sent as `0`. To
  get the column's DEFAULT, the INSERT has to leave the column out. To store NULL, the
  field needs a pointer or a nullable type.
- TypeScript: a nullable column is `string | null` under `strictNullChecks`, and NOT NULL
  is the database's non-optional property. SQL has no `undefined`: a value is either
  sent or the column is omitted.
- Python/JS: a UNIQUE constraint behaves like a set keyed on its columns, except that
  NULL never equals NULL unless you ask for `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.

## Design notes

Application validation exists for good error messages; the constraint is the guarantee.
Two app instances can both "check that the e-mail is free" and both insert, while a
unique index lets exactly one of them commit. Map the SQLSTATE (23505
`unique_violation`, 23502 `not_null_violation`) to an HTTP status in one place and
let the constraint name pick the message.

Pick natural primary keys only when the value is small, standard and practically never
changes. Everything people can edit (e-mail addresses, requirement codes like REQ-12,
user names) gets a surrogate id plus UNIQUE. A requirements table, for example, keys
on `id` and declares `UNIQUE (project_id, code)`, so renaming REQ-12 touches one row
and every trace link to it survives.

PostgreSQL 18 records NOT NULL as a constraint in `pg_constraint`, with a name such as
`tickets_status_not_null`, and like a CHECK it can now be added `NOT VALID` and
validated later. What NOT NULL enforces is unchanged.

lessons.title: Foreign keys and ON DELETE choices, CHECK, deferrable constraints
lessons.summary: A foreign key makes the database refuse orphans and decide what deleting a parent does to its children. CHECK states rules about a single row, and DEFERRABLE moves a check to the end of the statement or the transaction.

examples.title: CASCADE, SET NULL and RESTRICT, each where it fits

annotations.note: CASCADE models composition: a requirement can't outlive its project. The cascaded deletes run inside the parent's DELETE, recursively, so one statement can remove a whole tree. Reserve it for children that really are part of the parent.

SET NULL models a loose association, and the column must be nullable for it to work. PG 15+ accepts a column list, ON DELETE SET NULL (author_id), so a composite key like (tenant_id, author_id) can keep its tenant_id.

RESTRICT and the default NO ACTION both refuse to delete a referenced row. The difference: NO ACTION is checked at the end of the statement, or later if the constraint is deferred, so a statement or transaction can still fix things; RESTRICT can never be deferred.

The referenced side always has an index (a foreign key must point at a primary key or unique constraint). The referencing columns get none automatically, and without one every DELETE on projects scans all of requirements looking for children.
Deleting user 11 sets owner_id to NULL on 101 and 200. Deleting project 2 then takes requirement 200 with it. One DELETE each, and no application code walked the relationships.

Requirement 100 has a test run, so RESTRICT refuses. PG 18 reports this as SQLSTATE 23001 (restrict_violation); NO ACTION, and RESTRICT before PG 18, use 23503 (foreign_key_violation), the same code an INSERT with a missing parent gets.

examples.title: CHECK constraints, and why NULL slips through them

annotations.note: A column CHECK with an IN list is the lightweight alternative to an enum type or a lookup table (compared in the tables and types module).
duration_ms >= 0 rejects negative numbers, but NULL >= 0 is NULL, and a CHECK only fails on false. Unknown passes.

A table constraint can compare columns of the same row. It can't look at other rows or tables: PostgreSQL assumes a CHECK gives the same answer for the same row forever, and only re-checks on INSERT and UPDATE. Cross-row rules belong in UNIQUE, EXCLUDE or a foreign key.
When NULL must not slip through, say so: duration is required unless the run was skipped. IS NOT NULL is never unknown, so this CHECK means exactly what it says.
Row 2 has NULL duration and NULL finished_at: the first two checks evaluate to unknown and pass; duration_unless_skipped is true because the status is 'skipped'.
finished_at is before started_at, so the named table constraint fails with SQLSTATE 23514 (check_violation). The name in the message is the reason to name table constraints.

examples.title: DEFERRABLE: check at the end of the statement, or at COMMIT

annotations.note: A plain UNIQUE in PostgreSQL is checked row by row, so the UPDATE on line 9 would fail with 23505 as soon as row 1 moved to pos 2 while row 2 still held it. DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE checks at the end of the statement instead, as the SQL standard specifies, at some cost in speed.
Every row moved one place and the end state is unique, so the statement succeeds. This is the shape of every "reorder the list" feature.
INITIALLY DEFERRED postpones the foreign key check to COMMIT. Each transaction starts in that mode; SET CONSTRAINTS changes it for the current transaction only.

The child row arrives before its parent, which is what imports and circular references need. Switching to IMMEDIATE runs the pending checks right there. StackLab rolls every script back and never reaches COMMIT, so this is how the lesson makes the check happen.

The orphan is accepted, and the error surfaces at SET CONSTRAINTS, not at the INSERT that caused it. In an application the same error would come from COMMIT and abort the whole transaction: that distance between cause and error is the price of deferring.

use_cases: ON DELETE CASCADE for parts of an aggregate: a project's requirements, an order's lines
ON DELETE SET NULL for optional associations such as owner or assignee
RESTRICT (or NO ACTION) where history must survive: test runs, invoices, audit rows
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED for bulk imports in arbitrary order and for circular references
CHECK for value ranges, allowed states and simple cross-column rules
strengths: Unlike JPA's cascade settings, which only run when the ORM performs the delete, ON DELETE actions fire for every client, including a psql session
The database decides atomically: no window where a concurrent request inserts a child under a parent that is being deleted
CHECK and FK violations have their own SQLSTATEs (23514, 23503, and 23001 for RESTRICT in PG 18), so the API can tell 'invalid value' from 'missing parent'
weaknesses: Referencing columns are not indexed automatically; forgetting the index makes parent deletes scan the child table
CASCADE can delete far more than the statement names, and nothing in the DELETE says so
NOT NULL and CHECK can't be deferred, and deferrable constraints can't serve as ON CONFLICT arbiters
A CHECK sees one row only; rules across rows need UNIQUE, EXCLUDE, a foreign key or a trigger

pitfalls.title: CHECK passes on NULL
pitfalls.detail: A CHECK fails only when its expression is false. With a nullable column, NULL makes most expressions unknown, and unknown passes. Add NOT NULL or write the NULL case into the expression.
pitfalls.good: duration_ms int NOT NULL CHECK (duration_ms > 0)

pitfalls.title: No index on the foreign key column
pitfalls.detail: Deleting or re-keying a parent looks for children in the referencing table. Without an index on the referencing columns, that is a sequential scan per deleted parent row.
pitfalls.bad: project_id int REFERENCES projects  -- and nothing else
pitfalls.good: project_id int REFERENCES projects; CREATE INDEX ON requirements (project_id);

pitfalls.title: Reaching for CASCADE by default
pitfalls.detail: CASCADE turns an accidental delete of a parent into silent data loss in every child table. Use it for true composition; prefer RESTRICT or NO ACTION for anything that is evidence or history.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a deferred error at the INSERT
pitfalls.detail: With INITIALLY DEFERRED, the violating INSERT succeeds and COMMIT fails. Code that only checks errors on each statement must also check the commit.

quiz.q: test_runs.requirement_id references requirements ON DELETE RESTRICT. What happens on DELETE of a requirement that has runs?
quiz.why: RESTRICT refuses the delete outright and can't be deferred; PG 18 reports it as SQLSTATE 23001.

quiz.q: A column has CHECK (qty > 0) and no NOT NULL. Is a row with qty = NULL accepted?
quiz.why: NULL > 0 is NULL, and a CHECK only rejects rows for which the expression is false.

quiz.q: An FK is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. An INSERT creates an orphan. When is the error raised?
options: At the end of the INSERT statement
At COMMIT, or at SET CONSTRAINTS ... IMMEDIATE if that comes first
quiz.why: Deferred constraints are checked at commit; switching them to IMMEDIATE checks all pending changes at that moment.

quiz.q: Which constraints can be declared DEFERRABLE?
options: UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE and foreign keys
quiz.why: NOT NULL and CHECK are always checked immediately, per row; the other four accept DEFERRABLE.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (foreign keys, check constraints)
PostgreSQL docs: CREATE TABLE (referential actions, DEFERRABLE)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **foreign key** says "this column's value must exist as a key in that table". The
database refuses rows that point nowhere, and when the parent is deleted, the
`ON DELETE` action decides what happens to the children:

| Action | Child rows when the parent is deleted |
|---|---|
| `NO ACTION` (default) | The delete fails if children remain when the check runs (end of statement, or later if deferred) |
| `RESTRICT` | The delete fails; never deferred |
| `CASCADE` | Deleted too |
| `SET NULL` / `SET DEFAULT` | The referencing columns are set to NULL or their default |

A **CHECK** constraint is a boolean expression over one row, and the row is rejected only
when it evaluates to false. **DEFERRABLE** constraints (UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE and
foreign keys) can be checked later than usual: at the end of the statement
(`INITIALLY IMMEDIATE`) or at COMMIT (`INITIALLY DEFERRED`).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/JPA: `cascade = CascadeType.REMOVE` and `orphanRemoval` run only when the ORM
  performs the delete. `ON DELETE CASCADE` runs for every client, including a bulk
  `DELETE` statement and a psql session.
- Go/TS: the check-then-insert you would write in a service (`SELECT` the parent, then
  `INSERT` the child) races with a concurrent delete. The foreign key closes that window.
- C++ ownership is a good mental model: CASCADE is a member owned by value, SET NULL is a
  weak pointer that gets reset, RESTRICT refuses to destroy something still referenced.

## How it works

When each constraint is checked:

| Constraint | Checked |
|---|---|
| NOT NULL, CHECK | Per row, as it is written; never deferrable |
| UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE (not deferrable) | Immediately as each row is written |
| Foreign key (not deferrable) | At the end of each statement |
| Any `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` | At the end of each statement |
| Any `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` | At COMMIT, or at `SET CONSTRAINTS ... IMMEDIATE` |

The first two rows explain the reorder example: a plain UNIQUE sees the intermediate
duplicate, while the deferrable one only sees the final state.

## Design notes

Choose the ON DELETE action from the domain, not from convenience: is the child part of
the parent (CASCADE), associated with it (SET NULL), or evidence that must outlive any
cleanup (RESTRICT)? The same question decides whether you need soft delete instead.

Deferral is a tool for the few places that need it, such as imports and circular
references. Deferred errors arrive at COMMIT, far from the statement that caused them,
so don't make constraints deferrable by default.

PostgreSQL 18 adds `NOT ENFORCED` for CHECK and foreign key constraints: the constraint
is recorded but never checked. That documents a rule the application enforces itself;
it is not a cheaper way to get the guarantee.

lessons.title: Generated columns (virtual by default in PG 18, vs STORED) and exclusion constraints
lessons.summary: A generated column derives its value from the rest of the row: virtual (the PG 18 default) computes it on read, STORED on write. Exclusion constraints generalize UNIQUE to other operators, so "no two bookings overlap" becomes a declaration.

examples.title: A virtual and a stored generated column side by side

annotations.note: No keyword means VIRTUAL in PG 18: no storage, computed whenever the column is read, like a column of a view. PG 12 to 17 had only stored generated columns and required the STORED keyword, so DDL written without it is PG 18+ only.

STORED computes the value on INSERT and UPDATE and writes it to disk: it costs space and write time, reads are free, and it can be indexed. Either kind may use only immutable functions and the current row: no subqueries, no other generated columns.
The INSERT never mentions the generated columns, and the UPDATE of vat_pct changes gross_cents with no trigger. Writing one yourself fails with SQLSTATE 428C9: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value.

lower('Iğdır') gives 'iğdır' under the database's C.UTF-8 rules, not the Turkish 'ığdır'. lower(name COLLATE "tr-x-icu") is allowed in a generation expression and gives 'ığdır'. A STORED column bakes the rules in at write time. Also note gross_cents: integer division truncates, so put the rounding rule into the expression.
pg_attribute.attgenerated tells the kinds apart: 'v' virtual, 's' stored, empty for ordinary columns.

The stored column takes a normal B-tree index. PG 18 rejects an index on a virtual column (SQLSTATE 0A000), and also a UNIQUE constraint on one. To index such a value, make it STORED or index the expression itself.

examples.title: EXCLUDE ... WITH &&: no two bookings overlap

annotations.note: A real schema would use tstzrange (see the time zones lesson). tsrange keeps the printed output independent of the session's time zone.

For any two rows, during && during must not be true. A B-tree can only answer equality and ordering, so overlap needs a GiST index, which the constraint creates. Range types bring their own GiST support: no extension needed.
Half-open ranges [start, end) make back-to-back bookings legal: one ends at 10:00, the next starts at 10:00, and they share no instant. With a closed upper bound, 10:00 would belong to both.
11:00 to 12:00 overlaps Mehmet's booking, so the insert fails with SQLSTATE 23P01 (exclusion_violation). A UNIQUE constraint can't express this: the two ranges are not equal.

examples.title: Per room, live bookings only: = and && with btree_gist

annotations.note: btree_gist adds GiST support for scalar types such as text and int. Without it the CREATE TABLE fails: data type text has no default operator class for access method "gist". CREATE EXTENSION is transactional, so here it is rolled back with everything else; a real database installs it once, in a migration.
Two rows conflict only when room = room AND during && during. The WHERE clause makes the constraint partial: cancelled bookings don't take part, which no UNIQUE constraint can express.
Same time, different rooms: the = comparison is false, so there is no conflict.
Cancelling booking 1 takes it out of the constraint, so booking 3 can claim an overlapping slot in Galata.
10:00 to 11:00 overlaps booking 3 (09:30 to 10:30) in the same room, so the insert fails with SQLSTATE 23P01.

use_cases: STORED: normalized lookup keys such as lower(name) or a slug that you filter or sort on and must index
VIRTUAL: derived values read now and then, such as gross from net and VAT, display names or unit conversions
EXCLUDE: room and resource booking, non-overlapping validity periods for prices or tax rates, one active assignment per person at a time
strengths: Unlike a computed property on a Go struct or a TS class, the value is the same for every reader: reports, other services and psql
A virtual column costs no storage, and adding one never rewrites the table (adding a STORED one does)
An exclusion constraint replaces the application's 'look for an overlap, then insert', which races: two concurrent overlapping inserts can't both commit
weaknesses: PG 18 can't index virtual columns or put UNIQUE on them; anything you search by needs STORED or an expression index
Virtual columns may use only built-in functions and types, and are recomputed on every read
Changing a STORED column's expression (ALTER COLUMN ... SET EXPRESSION) rewrites its existing data
Exclusion constraints need a GiST index, btree_gist for = on scalar columns, and can't be arbiters for ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE

pitfalls.title: Indexing a virtual column
pitfalls.detail: In PG 18 a generated column without a keyword is virtual, and CREATE INDEX on it fails with 'indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported'. Decide the kind when you create the column.
pitfalls.bad: name_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (lower(name))  -- then CREATE INDEX ... (name_key)
pitfalls.good: name_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (lower(name)) STORED

pitfalls.title: Closed ranges for back-to-back slots
pitfalls.detail: '[09:00,10:00]' and '[10:00,11:00)' overlap at 10:00, so the second booking is rejected. Use half-open '[)' ranges, which is also what tsrange(a, b) builds by default.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting btree_gist
pitfalls.detail: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, ...) on a text or int column needs the btree_gist extension. It is trusted, so the database owner can install it without superuser rights.

pitfalls.title: Case rules frozen into a stored key
pitfalls.detail: A STORED lower(name) is computed with the rules in force at write time. Under C.UTF-8, 'IĞDIR' becomes 'iğdir'. If Turkish rules matter, write lower(name COLLATE "tr-x-icu") in the expression.

quiz.q: In PG 18, what does `total int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (price * qty)` (no keyword) create?
quiz.why: Virtual is the default in PG 18. PG 12 to 17 required the STORED keyword, so they reject this line.

quiz.q: Which generated column can you index in PG 18?
quiz.why: Indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported in PG 18; a stored one indexes like any other column.

quiz.q: Bookings '[09:00,10:00)' and '[10:00,11:00)' in the same room, with EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&). What happens to the second insert?
options: It fails: the ranges touch at 10:00
It succeeds: half-open ranges that only touch don't overlap
quiz.why: The first range excludes 10:00 itself, so && is false and the constraint is satisfied.

quiz.q: Why does `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` with room text need btree_gist?
options: GiST has no built-in operator class for = on text
quiz.why: Ranges have GiST support built in; btree_gist supplies GiST operator classes for scalar types like text and int.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Range Types (constraints on ranges)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **generated column** is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression)`, computed from other columns
of the same row and never written directly. PG 12 introduced the **STORED** kind,
computed on write and kept on disk. PG 18 adds **VIRTUAL**, computed on read with no
storage, and makes it the default. The expression may use only immutable functions and
the current row.

An **exclusion constraint** generalizes UNIQUE: for any two rows, comparing them with the
listed operators must not return true for all of them. UNIQUE is the special case where
every operator is `=`. With `&&` (overlaps) on a range column, "no double booking"
becomes a constraint, and a `WHERE` clause can limit it to some rows.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python/TS: a virtual column is a `@property` or getter, computed on access. A stored
  column is a field that the database recomputes on every write, so it can never go stale.
- Java/Go: a computed field on an entity or struct only exists in that one program. A
  generated column gives the same value to every reader, including SQL reports.
- Overlap checks in application code (load the bookings of that room, compare intervals,
  insert) race under concurrency, much like an unlocked check-then-act on a shared map.
  The exclusion constraint is checked through its index and holds across transactions.

## Design notes

Choose the kind by how the value is used. Virtual suits values that are cheap to compute
and rarely filtered on; it adds nothing to writes or disk. Stored suits values you index,
search or sort by, or that are expensive to compute, at the price of storage and write
time.

PG 18 also adds temporal keys: `PRIMARY KEY (room, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` behaves like
`EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` and needs btree_gist for the same
reason. Reach for plain EXCLUDE when you need what a key can't express: a `WHERE`
clause, as with cancelled bookings, or operators other than `=` and `&&`. The temporal
data lesson covers WITHOUT OVERLAPS and PERIOD foreign keys.

lessons.title: COPY ... FROM/TO vs \copy
lessons.summary: COPY moves rows in bulk between a table or query and a stream. With a file name the server opens the file on its own disk, which takes a privileged role; with STDIN/STDOUT the data rides the client connection, and that is all psql's \copy and pgx's CopyFrom/CopyTo do.

examples.title: TO STDOUT goes to the client; a file name goes to the server's disk

annotations.note: The rows leave as COPY data messages after the statement, not as a result set. psql would print a header line and two CSV rows here; this runner, like a plain query call in any driver, never asks for them and keeps only the tag. Drivers have a separate API for it: pgx's PgConn().CopyTo, psycopg's cursor.copy(), PgJDBC's CopyManager.

COPY (query) TO accepts a SELECT, VALUES, or INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE with RETURNING. COPY table TO works only on plain tables and (since PG 18) populated materialized views; for a view or a partitioned table, wrap it in a SELECT.

USAGE asks whether the role's privileges apply to you right now. The playground role has none of the three on purpose: the docs warn they "could be used to gain superuser-level access", and TO PROGRAM would let lesson SQL run shell commands on this machine.

The privilege check comes first, so the path is never even looked at. With the role, the server would look for C:/Users/ayse/... on its own disk, which is your laptop only if the server runs there. psql's \copy requirements FROM 'C:/Users/ayse/Downloads/requirements.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER) reads the file on the client and needs no role.

examples.title: COPY ... FROM STDIN from Go: CSV, a BOM, and a windows-1254 file

annotations.note: PgConn().CopyFrom sends the statement, then copies the io.Reader to the server in chunks; the server parses CSV, not the client. Any reader works: an os.File, an upload's request body, a gzip.Reader. pgx.CopyFrom (the Go/Postgres module) is the other API: Go values, binary format.

HEADER MATCH (PG 15) checks that the header names the table's columns, in order, instead of skipping the first line unseen. A file whose columns were reordered in Excel then fails loudly instead of loading one column's values into another.

Two CSV rules decide NULL vs empty: an unquoted empty field is NULL, a quoted one ("") is the empty string. The ';' inside quotes is data. The output shows REQ-2's title as 'Rapor; PDF', its priority as NULL, and REQ-3's title as ''.

Excel's "CSV UTF-8" starts with a byte order mark, and COPY treats it as data: the error says got "code", expected "code" because an invisible U+FEFF precedes the first. HEADER true would discard it along with the header line; with no header it would end up inside REQ-4's code.

0xDD is İ and 0xFE is ş in windows-1254, Turkish Excel's "CSV (Comma delimited)" encoding; neither starts valid UTF-8, so the load fails at the first one. ENCODING 'WIN1254' makes the server convert while it reads. Without the option COPY assumes client_encoding, which defaults to the database encoding: UTF8 here.

examples.title: COPY ... TO STDOUT from Go: text, CSV, and a file Turkish Excel opens

annotations.note: CopyTo writes each piece of COPY data to the io.Writer as it arrives, so memory stays flat whether the export to an http.ResponseWriter has three rows or fifty million. COPY has no ORDER BY of its own; the query form adds one.
The text format, COPY's default: tab-separated, NULL as \N, and backslash escapes for tab, newline and backslash itself. It is unambiguous and what pg_dump uses, but no spreadsheet reads it.

CSV quotes only what needs it: the field holding a tab and quotes, with the quotes doubled, and TC-3's empty string as "" so it reads back as '' rather than NULL. FORCE_QUOTE (col) or * quotes every non-NULL value if a consumer insists.

For Turkish Excel: a BOM written by Go before the data, ';' as the delimiter and a decimal comma made in SQL. For a legacy consumer that wants windows-1254, drop the BOM and add ENCODING 'WIN1254'; the server then converts on the way out.

use_cases: Loading a CSV export from another system or from Excel: \copy in psql, PgConn().CopyFrom in a Go service
Streaming a large CSV download straight from a query to an HTTP response with CopyTo
Seeding a database and moving tables between databases (COPY ... TO STDOUT piped into COPY ... FROM STDIN)
Server-side COPY from a file for a DBA on the database host, where the file already lives on the server
strengths: One statement for the whole load, with no per-row parse, plan or round trip; the docs call it almost always faster than INSERT, even prepared and batched
The server parses CSV, quoting, NULLs and encodings itself, so a client can stream an uploaded file through without parsing it
Unlike MySQL's LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE, client-side loading needs no server switch: STDIN is part of the protocol, and \copy is just psql using it
COPY (query) TO exports any result, including joins and RETURNING output, not only whole tables
weaknesses: All or nothing: by default one bad row aborts the whole load and reports only the first error
CSV in PostgreSQL's dialect only: one delimiter character, no decimal-comma numbers, no DD.MM.YYYY dates unless DateStyle says so
Server-side files need roles the docs warn can lead to superuser access, and the file has to be on the database host
Plain query APIs can't use it: the client needs the COPY sub-protocol (psql, pgx, psycopg, PgJDBC's CopyManager)

pitfalls.title: COPY FROM 'C:\...' typed into a GUI client or a Go program
pitfalls.detail: The server opens that path, on the server's machine. Either it fails with "permission denied to COPY from a file" or, as a superuser, it reads whatever happens to be at that path on the server. Read the file on the client side instead.
pitfalls.bad: COPY requirements FROM 'C:/Users/ayse/Downloads/requirements.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);
pitfalls.good: \copy requirements FROM 'C:/Users/ayse/Downloads/requirements.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

pitfalls.title: \copy is one line
pitfalls.detail: psql takes the entire rest of the line as \copy's arguments, without variable interpolation. For a long export query, write the SQL COPY ... TO STDOUT over several lines and end it with \g file.
pitfalls.good:
COPY (SELECT code, title FROM requirements ORDER BY code)
  TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)
\g requirements.csv

pitfalls.title: Empty Excel cells arrive as NULL
pitfalls.detail: Excel writes an empty cell as nothing between two delimiters, which CSV COPY reads as NULL, so a NOT NULL text column rejects the row. FORCE_NOT_NULL (column) reads unquoted empty values as empty strings instead.

pitfalls.title: A windows-1254 file read as UTF-8
pitfalls.detail: Excel's plain "CSV" save on Turkish Windows is windows-1254. COPY fails with invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8" at the first İ, ş or ğ; ENCODING 'WIN1254' fixes it without converting the file first.

pitfalls.title: Granting pg_read_server_files to the application role
pitfalls.detail: It lets the role read any file the PostgreSQL service account can read, including server configuration. Stream through the connection instead; the app never needs it.

quiz.q: You run psql on your laptop against a database server elsewhere and execute COPY t FROM '/home/me/data.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv). What happens?
options: psql reads /home/me/data.csv from the laptop and sends it
The server looks for /home/me/data.csv on its own filesystem, and only if your role may read server files
It fails because COPY needs STDIN
quiz.why: Files named in SQL COPY are opened by the server process. \copy is the client-side variant.

quiz.q: COPY ... FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv) reads the line REQ-2;;"" with DELIMITER ';' into three text columns. What are the second and third values?
quiz.why: In CSV, an unquoted empty field is NULL and a quoted empty field is the empty string.

quiz.q: Which of these needs no special role or superuser rights?
quiz.why: \copy runs COPY t TO STDOUT and psql writes the file with your own OS permissions; the other two act on the server.

quiz.q: A Turkish user's CSV fails with: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0xdd 0x7a. What's the cheapest correct fix?
options: Add ENCODING 'WIN1254' to the COPY options
Change the database encoding to WIN1254
quiz.why: 0xDD is İ in windows-1254. COPY converts from the ENCODING option to the database encoding while it reads.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`COPY` moves many rows in one statement between a table (or, outbound, a query) and a
stream in one of three formats: `text` (the default: tab-separated, `\N` for NULL),
`csv`, or `binary`. Where the stream comes from or goes to is the part that matters:

- **`FROM STDIN` / `TO STDOUT`**: the data travels over your client connection. Any role
  that may `INSERT` into (or `SELECT` from) the table can do this.
- **`FROM 'file'` / `TO 'file'`**: the *server process* opens a path on the *server's*
  filesystem, as the operating-system account PostgreSQL runs under. That needs
  superuser or the predefined role `pg_read_server_files` / `pg_write_server_files`.
- **`PROGRAM 'command'`**: the server runs a shell command and reads or writes its
  pipe. Superuser or `pg_execute_server_program`.

psql's `\copy` is not a different command. It sends `COPY ... FROM STDIN` (or
`TO STDOUT`) and pipes a local file through the connection, with your own file
permissions. pgx's `PgConn().CopyFrom` and `CopyTo` do exactly the same with an
`io.Reader` or `io.Writer`, which is why the loading and exporting examples here are Go
programs: this app's SQL runner, like a plain query call in any driver, doesn't speak
the copy sub-protocol. It shows only the command tag for `TO STDOUT`, and a
`COPY ... FROM STDIN` in it would wait for data until the run times out.

The options you'll use most: `HEADER` (`true` skips the first line, `MATCH` checks it
against the column names, PG 15), `DELIMITER`, `NULL`, `ENCODING`, `FORCE_QUOTE`,
`FORCE_NULL` and `FORCE_NOT_NULL` (CSV only), a column list, and `WHERE` on
`COPY FROM` to filter rows on the way in. `ON_ERROR` comes in the next lesson.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **MySQL**: `LOAD DATA INFILE` vs `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` is the same server-file vs
  client-file split as `COPY ... FROM 'file'` vs `\copy`. SQL Server has it as
  `BULK INSERT` (server) vs the `bcp` tool (client).
- **Java**: PgJDBC's `CopyManager.copyIn(sql, reader)` is `PgConn().CopyFrom`; JDBC's
  `addBatch` is still one INSERT per row.
- **Python**: psycopg 3's `with cur.copy("COPY t FROM STDIN") as copy: copy.write(...)`
  is the same conversation; `executemany` is not.
- **C**: libpq's `PQputCopyData` and `PQgetCopyData` are the C API for it.
- **Node**: `pg-copy-streams` turns COPY into a Node stream you can `pipeline()` a file
  or an upload into.

## How it works

`COPY ... FROM STDIN` is a short conversation inside the normal protocol. The client
sends the statement; the server answers "send me copy data" and waits; the client sends
the bytes in chunks of any size (they don't have to align with rows), then "done" or
"fail"; the server answers with the tag, `COPY 3`. `TO STDOUT` is the mirror image.
A client that sends the statement but doesn't take part gets only the tag, or, for
`FROM STDIN`, a server waiting for data that never comes.

Parsing happens on the server, after encoding conversion: input is read in the
`ENCODING` option's character set, or the session's `client_encoding` without it, and
converted to the database encoding, even when the server reads the file itself. That
is why a windows-1254 file fails under `client_encoding` UTF8 (the default in a UTF-8
database), and why one option fixes it.

Rows are inserted as they are parsed, with the table's constraints and triggers applied.
If row 90,001 fails, the statement fails and the 90,000 rows before it stay behind as
dead rows that take space until `VACUUM`. `binary` is the fastest format and the one
pgx's `CopyFrom` uses, but the docs call it less portable across architectures and
PostgreSQL versions, and it can't read into a column of a different type.

## Design notes

Decide by where the file lives. On your machine: `\copy`, or a driver's
`COPY ... FROM STDIN`. Already on the database server, and you're the DBA:
server-side `COPY` saves a network hop, at the price of a role the docs say "could be
used to gain superuser-level access". Application roles never need it, and code that
streams through the connection works wherever the database runs.

In a Go service, pick the API by what you hold. Rows already parsed into Go values:
`pgx.CopyFrom` with binary encoding. A CSV upload you trust to be well formed:
`PgConn().CopyFrom(ctx, r.Body, ...)` streams it through without parsing it in Go.
Exports: `CopyTo(ctx, w, "COPY (query) TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)")` into an
`http.ResponseWriter` is a streaming download in a few lines.

Don't COPY files from people straight into the real table. One malformed row aborts the
load and reports a single error, and the format rules (decimal commas, DD.MM.YYYY,
`Geçti` vs `KALDI`) are richer than any COPY option. Load into a staging table and
validate there, which is the next lesson. For speed, the docs' advice for big loads:
create indexes after loading a fresh table, consider dropping foreign keys during huge
loads, and `ANALYZE` afterwards.

The Excel side was observed, not documented: on 2026-11-14, Excel for Microsoft 365 (build
16.0.20527.20196), with its decimal separator set to `,` as on Turkish Windows, wrote "CSV
UTF-8" starting with `EF BB BF`, wrote an empty cell as nothing between two separators
(`Kaya, Ltd.;;99,9`), and wrote "CSV (Comma delimited)" in the Windows ANSI code page,
windows-1252 on that en-US machine. Turkish Windows's ANSI code page is 1254
([code page identifiers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/intl/code-page-identifiers)).
The PostgreSQL side is in the COPY docs (with the default settings a NULL "is written as an
unquoted empty string", and "Reading values follows similar rules"), and the examples show
that rule, the BOM kept as data and ENCODING 'WIN1254' at work on 18.7.

lessons.title: CSV import through a staging table with validation
lessons.summary: Load the file as text into a staging table, compute typed values and a list of problems per row in one view, then move only the clean rows and report the rest with row numbers. COPY's ON_ERROR ignore is the quick alternative, and the example shows what it can't catch.

examples.title: Which casts you can trust with Turkish input

annotations.note: The same text is March 4 under MDY and April 3 under DMY, and 31.12.2026 is valid only under DMY. DateStyle's built-in default is ISO, MDY, but initdb sets it from the server's lc_time locale, so one import can mean different dates on two servers. Build YYYY-MM-DD yourself: ISO dates read the same under every DateStyle.

pg_input_is_valid and pg_input_error_info (PG 16) run the type's input check without raising an error, so nothing aborts. '1.250' passes: it is 1.25 to PostgreSQL and 1250 to a Turkish reader. Valid input isn't necessarily the value the user meant, so check the format first.

lower() follows the collation's case rules. Under the default ones I lowers to i, so KALDI becomes kaldi and matches neither spelling; tr-x-icu applies Turkish rules (I to ı, İ to i) and all three rows agree.

An ordinary cast has no soft mode: the error aborts the statement and the transaction, and this runner stops here the way psql does with ON_ERROR_STOP. COPY behaves the same by default, which is why the validation below never casts before checking.

examples.title: Stage as text, validate in one view, report, then move the clean rows

annotations.note: Text columns and no constraints: every line of the file lands, and the rules run afterwards, in SQL you can query. \copy with a column list leaves row_no out, so the identity numbers rows in the order COPY reads them: the numbers you report back. A quoted field with a line break makes rows and file lines differ.

Each CASE yields a reason or NULL, and array_remove drops the NULLs, so '{}' means clean. One row can collect several reasons (TC-5 has two), so the user fixes the file in one pass instead of one error per attempt.
The first and third rules repeat the target's foreign key and its CHECK (seconds >= 0). Left to the INSERT, the first violation would fail the whole statement, naming a constraint rather than a row.
The primary key, checked twice: against the file itself (both TC-7 rows are rejected, since nothing says which is right) and against the table, which makes re-running the same file harmless.
regexp_match returns the captured groups or NULL. A date that isn't DD.MM.YYYY, an ISO date included, yields NULL instead of a guess. Numbers lose their thousands dots and get a decimal point.

A cast runs only when pg_input_is_valid says it will succeed, so the view itself can never raise an error: 31.11.2026 fits the pattern but isn't a date. The regex insists on Turkish grouping, so 1.250,5 is 1250.5 and a bare 1.250 would be 1250, never 1.25.
KALDI is accepted thanks to the Turkish collation; Gecti, typed without the ç, is rejected rather than guessed at.

Report first. A view is evaluated on every read: after the INSERT the good rows are in test_runs and would come back as "already imported". One statement with a data-modifying CTE also works, since all its parts see the same snapshot.

examples.title: COPY ON_ERROR ignore, LOG_VERBOSITY and REJECT_LIMIT, and what they miss

annotations.note: TC-3 (month 13) and TC-4 (decimal comma) fail type conversion. TC-2 doesn't: under MDY, 09.11.2026 is a perfectly good September 11.
Pinned so the example gives the same result on every server; the point stands for whatever DateStyle yours has.
Skipped rows are reported as NOTICEs, which pgx hands to OnNotice rather than returning them from CopyFrom. The line numbers count the header line.

ON_ERROR ignore (PG 17) skips rows whose values fail conversion, and the tag counts only what was loaded: COPY 3 of 5. Without verbose you get just the summary notice; LOG_VERBOSITY silent (PG 18) drops that too.
REJECT_LIMIT (PG 18): the second bad row exceeds the limit of 1 and the whole COPY fails as if ignore weren't there. A guard for feeds: skip the odd bad row, refuse a file that is mostly garbage.
ignore covers conversion errors only. A CHECK violation or a missing column still aborts the whole COPY, and nothing from that file is loaded, not even TC-1.
TC-2 sits in the table as 2026-09-11. ON_ERROR can tell bad syntax from good, not a wrong value from a right one; that takes rules, which is what the staging view is for.

use_cases: Importing test results, requirement lists or price lists that people export from Excel, with an error report they can act on
Nightly feeds from another system: stage, validate, move, and keep the rejects for someone to look at
Loading into a table with row-level security, which COPY FROM doesn't support: COPY into staging, then INSERT ... SELECT
Machine-generated files where an occasional malformed row may be dropped: COPY with ON_ERROR ignore and a REJECT_LIMIT
strengths: Every rule sees the whole file and the real tables at once: duplicates within the file and references to existing rows are one EXISTS or window function, where a Go or Python loop would have to load the lookup tables first
Collects every problem of every row in one pass, unlike COPY or a constrained INSERT, which stop at the first error
The soft checks (pg_input_is_valid) use the server's own parsers, so a value that passes is exactly what the column will accept
Bad rows never touch the real table: no dead rows from a failed load, no partially imported file
weaknesses: The data is written twice (staging, then target); for very large, trusted feeds, COPY straight into the table is faster
Every constraint of the target has to be mirrored as a rule, and the two can drift apart when the schema changes
SQL regexes and CASE chains get long; messages meant for end users (and in Turkish) are easier to build in application code
ON_ERROR ignore is quick but blind: it reports bad rows only as NOTICEs and lets wrong-but-parseable values through

pitfalls.title: Casting DD.MM.YYYY straight to date
pitfalls.detail: The result depends on DateStyle: 03.04.2026 becomes March 4 on a server with MDY. Match the pattern and build an ISO date.
pitfalls.good:
SELECT make_date(d[3]::int, d[2]::int, d[1]::int)
FROM staging, regexp_match(run_on, '^(\d\d)\.(\d\d)\.(\d{4})$') AS d;

pitfalls.title: Treating "valid" as "correct"
pitfalls.detail: pg_input_is_valid('1.250', 'numeric') is true, and the value is 1.25. Check the Turkish format with a regex before converting, so the dot is read as a thousands separator.

pitfalls.title: lower() without the Turkish collation
pitfalls.detail: Under the default case rules KALDI lowers to kaldi, which matches no label. Apply tr-x-icu, or compare against a fixed list of accepted spellings.
pitfalls.bad: CASE lower(result) WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END
pitfalls.good: CASE lower(result COLLATE "tr-x-icu") WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END

pitfalls.title: Expecting ON_ERROR ignore to clean a file
pitfalls.detail: It skips type-conversion failures only. A CHECK, NOT NULL, unique or foreign key violation still aborts the whole COPY, and values that parse but mean something else (09.11.2026 under MDY) go straight in.

pitfalls.title: Reading the validation view after the move
pitfalls.detail: The view re-runs its checks on every read; once the clean rows are in the target, they look like duplicates. Report before moving, do both in one statement, or store the verdicts in a staging column.

quiz.q: With DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY', what does SELECT '03.04.2026'::date return?
options: An error: the format is ambiguous
quiz.why: Ambiguous day/month input follows DateStyle's field order, and MDY reads 03 as the month. Nothing warns you.

quiz.q: COPY ... WITH (FORMAT csv, ON_ERROR ignore) reads 1,000 rows; row 500 violates a CHECK constraint. What ends up in the table?
options: 1,000 rows, with row 500's value set to NULL
quiz.why: ON_ERROR only applies to errors converting input values to column types. A constraint violation aborts the statement as usual.

quiz.q: Why collect the problems in an array instead of a CASE that returns the first failing rule?
options: A row can break several rules, and the user should see them all in one report
quiz.why: array_remove(ARRAY[...], NULL) keeps every reason that applies; a single CASE stops at its first true branch.

quiz.q: In a UTF-8 database with default case rules, which expression maps both KALDI and Kaldı to 'kaldı'?
quiz.why: Only Turkish case rules lower I to dotless ı; the default rules give kaldi.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: System Information Functions (pg_input_is_valid, pg_input_error_info)
PostgreSQL docs: Date/Time Types, date input and DateStyle

lessons.body:
## Concept

Never `COPY` a file from people straight into the table it belongs in. Use three steps:

1. **Load** the file into a staging table whose columns are all `text`, with no
   constraints, plus a row number. `\copy` in psql or `PgConn().CopyFrom` in Go. The
   load can't fail on content, so every line arrives.
2. **Validate** with one query, usually a view: compute the typed value of each field (or
   NULL), and a list of problems per row. Formats are checked with regular expressions,
   "would this cast work?" with `pg_input_is_valid` (PG 16), references with `EXISTS`
   against the real tables, duplicates within the file with a window function, and
   duplicates against the target with `EXISTS` again.
3. **Move and report**: `INSERT ... SELECT` the rows without problems, and give the
   others back to the user with their row numbers and reasons.

Whether a bad row means "skip it" or "refuse the whole file" is a policy decision, and
both are one `WHERE` clause away: the example imports the clean rows; adding
`AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM checked WHERE problems <> '{}')` makes it all or nothing.

COPY's own alternative is `ON_ERROR ignore` (PG 17), with `LOG_VERBOSITY verbose`
to name the skipped rows and `REJECT_LIMIT` (PG 18) to cap them. It skips rows whose
values fail type conversion and nothing else: no format rules, no references, no
duplicates, no CHECK constraints.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python/pandas**: `read_csv(dtype=str)` followed by `pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")`
  is the same shape: everything as text first, then a conversion that yields a missing
  value instead of raising. `pg_input_is_valid` is that `errors="coerce"`, in SQL.
- **Java**: Bean Validation reports every constraint violation of an object, not the
  first. The `problems` array does that for every row of a file in one query.
- **TS**: zod's `safeParse` returns all issues instead of throwing (see
  `ts.services.zod`); a staging view is `safeParse` over a whole table.
- **Go**: the `go.files-io.csv-json` lesson validates per field while reading with
  `csv.Reader`. That is the better place for format checks with exact line and column
  positions; SQL is better at the rules that need other rows: duplicates and
  references, checked without loading lookup tables into Go.
- **ETL tools** (SSIS, Talend): their "error output" of rejected rows is here just the
  rows `WHERE problems <> '{}'`.

## How it works

Staging as text works because conversion is where COPY and INSERT fail fast. A text
column accepts any string, and with no constraints there is nothing else to violate.
The checks then use functions that report instead of raising: `pg_input_is_valid(text,
type)` returns false where the cast would throw, and `pg_input_error_info` returns the
message, detail and SQLSTATE it would have thrown. Both take a type name with modifiers,
such as `'numeric(6,2)'`, so they also catch overflow. The docs note they only work this
way for types whose input function reports soft errors; the built-in date and numeric
types used here do.

Three Turkish traps sit in this path. Dates: an ambiguous date like `03.04.2026` is read
in DateStyle's field order (built-in default `ISO, MDY`, though initdb picks one from
the server locale); `YYYY-MM-DD` input means the same everywhere. Numbers:
PostgreSQL only reads a decimal point, and `1.250` is a valid number with a different
meaning. Case: `lower` and `upper` follow the collation, and only Turkish rules (`COLLATE
"tr-x-icu"`) map I to ı and İ to i.

For real loads, the staging table can be `TEMPORARY` (private to the session, dropped
at its end) or `UNLOGGED` (no write-ahead log, so faster, but emptied after a crash).
Either fits data you can reload from the file. COPY can fill staging from a Turkish
Excel file directly:
`\copy staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) FROM 'kosular.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true, DELIMITER ';', ENCODING 'WIN1254')`.

## Design notes

Keep the verdicts. A staging table with an `import_id` and a `problems` column filled
by `UPDATE ... FROM checked` survives the request, so the UI can offer the rejected
rows as a CSV with an extra "Hata" column, which is what people fixing a spreadsheet
actually want. Delete old imports on a schedule.

Mirror every constraint of the target as a rule, or the move can still fail as a
whole, but keep the constraints too: they are the guarantee, the rules are the error
messages. Two imports of the same file at the same moment can both pass the
"already imported" check; the primary key still stops the second one, and
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in the move, or an advisory lock around the import (the
transactions module), turns that into a clean outcome.

Split the work by what each side is good at: the Go handler checks encoding, header
and field formats while it streams the upload and can point at line and column; SQL
checks what needs the database: references, duplicates, existing rows. Keep
`ON_ERROR ignore` for machine feeds where dropping the odd malformed row is acceptable,
and always give it a `REJECT_LIMIT`, so a feed that suddenly changed its format fails
instead of loading 3 rows out of 30,000.

lessons.title: Exporting results; pg_dump/pg_restore; generating test data with generate_series
lessons.summary: generate_series plus INSERT ... SELECT seeds 100,000 realistic, reproducible rows in one statement. pg_dump exports a database as a consistent snapshot, as a SQL script for psql or an archive for pg_restore; query results leave through COPY.

examples.title: 100,000 test runs in one statement, skewed, correlated and reproducible

annotations.note: generate_series is a row source: every expression on i becomes a column. Indexing an array with [1 + i % 5] cycles through sample values; the 1 + is there because SQL arrays start at 1.
One INSERT ... SELECT, one round trip, INSERT 0 100000. A client loop would send 100,000 statements; even batched, it moves data the server could have made itself.

u is spread evenly over [0, 1); squaring it piles values up near 0, so low ids get most runs: REQ-001 has 7,273, REQ-003 2,236. Real data is skewed like this, and plans and index choices change with it; i % 200 would give every requirement exactly 500.
One run every 257 seconds from 1 January, about ten months. The +03 in the literal fixes the instant whatever the session's TimeZone is.

Both columns come from v, so they are correlated: the slowest 10% of runs are the failures (average 24.78 s against 4.13), the way timeouts look in real test results. The fourth power gives a long tail of slow runs.
md5 makes realistic-looking strings: a 10-digit hex "commit" shared by 25 consecutive runs. Every fourth tester is NULL, an automated run, so queries meet NULLs the way they will in production.
