The md5 of the row number, read as bytes, gives two numbers between 0 and 1 that look random and are identical on every run, on every server: a reproducible stand-in for random(), with no seed to manage.
Check what you generated: counts, distinct values, ratios, ranges. AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul' turns the timestamptz into Turkish local time before taking the date, independent of the session.

examples.title: random() with setseed, and the date trap in generate_series

annotations.note: setseed takes a value between -1 and 1 and restarts the session's generator, so the same statements after the same seed fill identical tables. random(min, max) is PG 17; before that, floor(random() * 6) + 1.
Without a new seed the generator just continues. Reorder two statements in a seed script and every table after them changes.

Comparing tables keeps this output stable. The values themselves are not promised across versions: PG 15's release notes say its new random() algorithm gives different results "even for the same seed value".

There is no date version of generate_series, so dates resolve to the timestamptz one: days are stepped in the session's time zone, and you get timestamps back. Cast to date, or add an integer series to a date: date '2026-11-01' + i.

examples.title: The text format pg_dump uses, and a table streamed between two connections

annotations.note: Both connections use the same URL so the example is self-contained; the pattern is for two different databases: production to a reporting database, an old server to a new one.
COPY's text format: tab-separated, \N for NULL, escapes for tabs and newlines inside values. A plain-format pg_dump stores table data in this form.

io.Pipe connects CopyTo's io.Writer to CopyFrom's io.Reader. Rows flow from one server to the other as they are read, with no temporary file: what pg_dump -t runs src | psql dst does, inside one program.
A failed source reaches the reader as an error rather than EOF; pgconn then aborts the COPY on the destination, so a half-read table is never loaded as if it were complete.
EXCEPT ALL in both directions compares the tables as multisets on the server, without fetching 50,000 rows into Go.

use_cases: Seeding a development or test database with enough skewed, realistic data to make EXPLAIN plans meaningful
Reproducible benchmark data: the same script gives the same rows on every machine and every run
Copying a database or a single table to another server: pg_dump/pg_restore, or COPY streamed between connections
Exporting a report as CSV from psql (\copy, --csv) or from code (CopyTo)
strengths: 100,000 rows in one statement, made where they are stored, instead of a Faker loop in Python or Java inserting row by row
Deterministic generators (arithmetic, md5) need no seed and can't drift between versions or sessions
pg_dump takes a consistent snapshot without blocking readers or writers, unlike stopping the application to copy files
The custom format keeps a table of contents: pg_restore can restore one table, reorder items, or work in parallel, which a mysqldump-style SQL script can't
weaknesses: Realism is hand-made: names, distributions and correlations are only as good as the expressions you write
pg_dump is a logical copy of one database: no roles or tablespaces (pg_dumpall --globals-only has those), no point-in-time recovery, slow to restore for large databases
Statistics are not dumped by default in PG 18, so a restored database needs ANALYZE before its plans mean anything
A dump can't be loaded into an older major version without editing, and pg_dump refuses to dump a server newer than itself

pitfalls.title: Seeding from a client loop
pitfalls.detail: 100,000 single-row INSERTs are 100,000 statements. Generate the rows in SQL, or use CopyFrom when the data really comes from the program.
pitfalls.bad: for i := range 100_000 { conn.Exec(ctx, "INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES ($1, ...)", i, ...) }
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO test_runs SELECT i, ... FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS i;

pitfalls.title: setseed through a connection pool
pitfalls.detail: The seed belongs to one session. With pgxpool, SELECT setseed(...) and the INSERT that follows can run on different connections. Put them in one transaction, or on one acquired connection.

pitfalls.title: Looking at plans right after seeding
pitfalls.detail: Until ANALYZE runs (yourself, or autovacuum eventually), the planner guesses row counts. The docs recommend ANALYZE after any bulk load.
pitfalls.good: ANALYZE test_runs;

pitfalls.title: Restoring a custom-format dump with psql
pitfalls.detail: -Fc writes a compressed archive, not SQL. pg_restore reads it; pg_restore -f - turns it into a script if you need one.
pitfalls.good: pg_restore -d tracelite_copy tracelite.dump

pitfalls.title: Restoring into a database whose roles don't exist
pitfalls.detail: The dump sets object owners; on another server those roles may be missing and every ALTER ... OWNER fails. Create the roles first (pg_dumpall --globals-only), or restore with --no-owner so the restoring user owns everything.

quiz.q: Which pg_dump formats can pg_restore restore in parallel with -j?
quiz.why: The pg_restore docs: only the custom and directory archive formats are supported with -j, and the input must be a regular file or directory.

quiz.q: A seed script calls setseed(0.5) and then fills tables with random(). Does it produce the same data on PostgreSQL 14 and 18?
options: Yes, the seed fixes the sequence
No: PG 15 changed random()'s algorithm, so the same seed gives different values
Only on the same operating system
quiz.why: The PG 15 migration notes say random() results differ from prior versions even for the same seed. md5- or arithmetic-based generators don't have this problem.

quiz.q: What does generate_series(date '2026-11-01', date '2026-11-03', interval '1 day') return?
quiz.why: There is no date variant; the dates are converted for the timestamptz variant, which steps in the session's time zone.

quiz.q: pg_dump -Fc -d tracelite -f tracelite.dump made an archive. How do you read the SQL it contains without a database?
options: Unzip it: it is gzip-compressed SQL
quiz.why: Without -d, pg_restore writes the script it would run; -f - sends it to standard output.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Populating a Database (ANALYZE afterwards)

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Generating data.** `generate_series(1, 100000)` is a table of 100,000 integers, and
`INSERT ... SELECT` turns any query into rows. Every column is an expression on the
counter: arithmetic for ids, dates and cycles, arrays for sample values, `md5` for
strings and for numbers that look random but come out the same every time. Real data
is skewed, correlated and has NULLs, and test data that has none of the three gives
plans and bugs that production never sees.

**Exporting results.** A query result becomes a file through COPY, as in the first
lesson. From psql there are three ways:

```
\copy (SELECT code, title FROM requirements ORDER BY code) TO 'requirements.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)
psql -X -d tracelite --csv -c "SELECT code, title FROM requirements ORDER BY code" -o requirements.csv
COPY (SELECT ...) TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER) \g requirements.csv
```

The third allows a query over several lines. From code, it's `CopyTo` into a file or an
HTTP response.

**pg_dump and pg_restore.** `pg_dump` exports one database: definitions and data, as
a consistent snapshot, without blocking readers or writers. The default plain format
is an SQL script that psql replays. The custom format (`-Fc`, compressed) and the
directory format (`-Fd`) are archives that `pg_restore` reads selectively,
in any order, and in parallel. Roles and tablespaces belong to the whole cluster, so
they come from `pg_dumpall --globals-only`. The usual commands:

```
# plain SQL script, replayed by psql into a database created from template0
pg_dump -d tracelite -f tracelite.sql
createdb -T template0 tracelite_copy
psql -X -d tracelite_copy --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on -f tracelite.sql

# custom format: restore everything with 4 jobs, or look inside first
pg_dump -Fc -d tracelite -f tracelite.dump
pg_restore -d tracelite_copy -j 4 tracelite.dump
pg_restore -l -f toc.list tracelite.dump
pg_restore -L toc.list -d tracelite_copy tracelite.dump
pg_restore -f - --schema-only tracelite.dump

# one table's rows as INSERT statements, for another database product
pg_dump -d tracelite -t test_runs --data-only --inserts -f test_runs.sql
```

`pg_restore -l` lists the archive's table of contents; edit the list (delete lines, or
comment them out with `;`) and `-L` restores just those items, in that order. On
Windows the tools live in `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin`. Pass `-f` instead of
redirecting with `>` in PowerShell: Microsoft's about_Redirection page for Windows
PowerShell 5.1 says redirected byte streams are treated as strings, which "results in
corrupted data". Reproduced here with Windows PowerShell 5.1 and pg_dump 18.7:
`pg_dump -Fc ... > bad.dump` wrote a UTF-16 file (it starts with the bytes FF FE) that
`pg_restore -l` rejects as "not a valid tar archive", while `-f good.dump` works. Text
suffers too: a TOC list written with `pg_restore -l ... > toc.list` came out UTF-16, and
`pg_restore -L` warned "line ignored", restored nothing and still exited with 0.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Faker** (Python), **Datafaker** (Java), **@faker-js** (JS): great names and
  addresses, but a loop in the client inserting row by row. `generate_series` makes the
  rows where they are stored; arrays of sample values cover most needs, and a
  Faker-made CSV loaded with COPY covers the rest.
- **Go**: seeding test databases with `for i := range n { db.Exec(...) }` is the habit to
  drop. One SQL statement, or `CopyFrom` with `CopyFromSlice` (the Go/Postgres
  module) when the program computes the values.
- **MySQL**: `mysqldump` writes an SQL script like pg_dump's plain format. The custom
  format adds what a script can't: a table of contents for selective, reordered,
  parallel restores.
- **SQL Server**: `BACKUP DATABASE` is a physical backup. pg_dump is logical, closer
  to generating scripts; PostgreSQL's physical backups (`pg_basebackup`, WAL archiving)
  are in the security and operations module.
- **Shell**: `generate_series` is `seq` inside the database, and a plain dump piped into
  psql (`pg_dump -h host1 db | psql -X -h host2 db`, straight from the docs) is the same
  idea as the Go pipe in the third example.

## How it works

Three ways to make values from a row number, from most to least reproducible:

- **Arithmetic on i**: `i % 5`, `i * interval '257 seconds'`, `i / 25`. Exact, but
  regular: cycles show up as patterns, and `i % 200` gives every group the same count.
- **Hashing i**: `md5(i::text)` read as bytes (`decode(..., 'hex')`, `get_byte`). It
  looks random, involves no state, and gives the same values on every server and
  version, since md5 is a fixed algorithm.
- **random() with setseed()**: random() is volatile (evaluated per row) and keeps its
  state per session. After `setseed`, the docs promise the same sequence again within
  the session; across versions they don't, and PG 15 did change it.

A plain-format dump is the schema as `CREATE` statements, then each table's rows as a
`COPY ... FROM stdin;` command followed by the rows in COPY's text format and a line
holding only `\.`, then indexes and the constraints not written inline (primary keys,
unique and foreign keys; NOT NULL and CHECK stay in `CREATE TABLE`). That inline data is
why psql, which knows to feed it to the COPY, replays dumps, and why a driver can't
simply execute the file. pg_dump 18.7 also wraps the script in psql's `\restrict` and
`\unrestrict` meta-commands (the `--restrict-key` option). The docs describe the parts:
data is dumped as COPY unless `--inserts`, `--section` splits pre-data, data and
post-data (indexes, triggers, most constraints), and the COPY page says psql ends in-line
data at `\.`. A dump of a small schema from PostgreSQL 18.7 showed exactly this order,
with `\N` for NULL and `\t` for a tab inside a value.

pg_dump reads everything from one snapshot, taken when it starts, which is how it
stays consistent while others write; only operations that need an exclusive lock, such
as most forms of `ALTER TABLE`, have to wait for it. Statistics are not dumped by default in PG 18 (`--statistics` adds them), so run
`ANALYZE` after a restore. A dump loads into newer major versions; pg_dump refuses to
dump a server newer than itself, so after upgrading a server, upgrade the client tools
too.

## Design notes

Keep seed scripts in the repository as SQL: one `INSERT ... SELECT FROM
generate_series` per table, the row count in one place, and deterministic generators,
so tests and benchmarks on different machines see the same data. Make the data look
like production in shape (skew, NULL rates, correlations, Turkish text) rather than
copying production rows, which drags personal data into places it doesn't belong.
Run `ANALYZE` after seeding, before you read a single `EXPLAIN`.

Use pg_dump for moving a database to another server or version, for a schema snapshot
(`--schema-only`) to diff in review, and for pulling one table out. The docs say it is
"generally not the right choice" for regular backups of production databases:
physical backups with WAL archiving restore faster and to any point in time. For
moving one table between live databases from code, the streamed COPY of the third
example avoids temporary files altogether.

lessons.title: How B-trees work; EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers
lessons.summary: A B-tree finds a row in a few page reads at any table size, but only EXPLAIN tells you whether the planner uses it, and only EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which really runs the statement, tells you what it cost: rows, loops and pages touched.

examples.title: EXPLAIN predicts, EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes and measures

annotations.note: 20,000 orders, 20 per customer, and customer 42's rows are 1,000 ids apart, so each sits on a different page. ANALYZE the command collects the statistics the planner estimates from; it has nothing to do with EXPLAIN's ANALYZE option below. In production autovacuum runs it for you; this sandbox table is uncommitted and invisible to autovacuum.
Seq Scan with a Filter: read every row, test the condition on each. COSTS OFF hides the estimates (cost, rows, width) so the output is stable; "How it works" reads a full cost line.
A B-tree on customer_id: the keys in sorted order, each pointing at the row's physical location (its TID, block and offset) in the table.

A bitmap scan, in two steps: the Bitmap Index Scan collects the locations of all matching rows, then the Bitmap Heap Scan reads those table pages in physical order, each once. Recheck Cond is the condition it re-tests when it has to, for example when the bitmap grew too large to remember individual rows.

Now with actuals. rows=20.00 loops=1: PG 18 prints row counts with two decimals because they are averages per loop. Heap Blocks: exact=20 is the 20 rows on 20 pages. Buffers counts 8 kB pages: hit means found in PostgreSQL's shared buffer cache, read means fetched from the operating system (its file cache or the disk). Nothing had read the new index's two pages through the cache yet; in the DELETE below they are hits. Since PG 18 ANALYZE implies BUFFERS; on older servers write EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Index Searches (also new in 18) counts descents of the tree.

Plain EXPLAIN only plans the DELETE. With ANALYZE it executes, and the 20 rows are really gone; the Delete node reports 0 rows because there is no RETURNING. Outside a sandbox, wrap it in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK. Running the plain EXPLAIN first has a side benefit: the measured run finds the planner's lookups cached, so PG 18 has no "Planning: Buffers" section to print.

examples.title: Tree depth from buffer counts: 100, 10,000 and 200,000 rows

annotations.note: Same shape, three sizes. A PRIMARY KEY is backed by a unique B-tree index, and the inserts went through it, so its pages are in the cache and every buffer below is a hit.
The first plan in a session reads catalog data and each index's metapage (which records where the root is). Planning these lookups once here keeps that out of the measurements below.

2, 3 and 4 pages: one per tree level plus one heap page for the row. 100 keys fit on one page that is root and leaf at once. 10,000 need about 30 leaf pages under a root. 200,000 need about 550 leaves, more than one root page can point to, so a level of internal pages appears. With 4-byte keys a page holds roughly 400 entries, so three levels cover tens of millions of rows.

A range descends once (Index Searches: 1) and then follows the leaf level's sibling links: 6 index pages are 2 to descend plus the 4 leaves holding keys 1000 to 1999. The 1,000 rows themselves sit on 6 heap pages. The planner picked a bitmap scan; the index walk is the same either way.

examples.title: An index the planner is right to ignore

annotations.note: 7919 is prime, so (g * 7919) % 1000 hits every amount from 0 to 999 exactly 20 times, scattered over the table. Physical order and amount are unrelated, as for most columns that aren't timestamps or ids.
Same index, same query shape, two plans: 1% of the rows (200) goes through the index, 90% (18,000) doesn't. The planner compares estimated costs per query, using the statistics from line 10.
147 pages: every page of the table once, in physical order, which the operating system can read ahead. Rows Removed by Filter: 2000 is the price of not using the index: cheap here.

SET LOCAL lasts until the transaction ends. enable_seqscan = off doesn't forbid sequential scans; it makes the planner avoid them whenever another plan exists (PG 18 marks a node it had to use anyway with "Disabled: true"). The forced bitmap scan reads the same 147 table pages plus 18 index pages: more work for the same answer.

A plain Index Scan walks the index in amount order and jumps to the table for each row: 18,018 page accesses, each table page visited about 120 times. With a cold cache each jump can be a random disk read, which is why random_page_cost (4.0 by default) is priced above seq_page_cost (1.0).

use_cases: Before adding an index: EXPLAIN the slow query and look for a Seq Scan whose Filter throws most rows away (Rows Removed by Filter)
After adding one: EXPLAIN ANALYZE inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, on production-sized data, to confirm the new plan and that it touches fewer buffers
A plain B-tree serves =, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, ORDER BY and min/max on its column, and anchored LIKE 'abc%' under the C collation or with text_pattern_ops
Reviewing an ORM's generated query: the plan shows whether its WHERE clause can use any index at all
strengths: Lookup cost grows with tree depth, not table size: 4 pages for 200,000 rows here and only a few more for billions, while a Seq Scan grows linearly
Keys stay sorted, so one B-tree answers equality, ranges, ORDER BY and min/max; a hash structure (Java HashMap, Python dict, PostgreSQL's hash index) answers only equality
EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives exact per-node row and page counts for one real execution, more precise than a sampling profiler, and hit + read is the same total whether the cache was warm or cold
No hints needed: add or drop an index and the planner re-decides per query from statistics, without touching the SQL
weaknesses: Every index slows every INSERT and every UPDATE of an indexed column, and takes disk and cache space
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement in full: a 10-minute query takes 10 minutes, and writes happen unless you roll back
A plan reflects this data volume and these statistics; the plan on a 100-row development table says nothing about production
Timing every node costs overhead (significant on some systems, the docs warn); TIMING OFF keeps row and buffer counts without it

pitfalls.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write, in autocommit
pitfalls.detail: ANALYZE executes the statement, so the rows really change. Wrap it in a transaction and roll back.
pitfalls.bad: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE placed_at < '2025-01-01';
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE placed_at < '2025-01-01'; ROLLBACK;

pitfalls.title: Judging an index on a toy table
pitfalls.detail: The docs: on a table that occupies one disk page you'll nearly always get a sequential scan, index or not. Generate realistic volumes with generate_series, ANALYZE, then read the plan.

pitfalls.title: Comparing timings instead of buffers
pitfalls.detail: The second run is faster because the pages are now cached. Buffers (hit + read) counts the same work either way, so compare those, and use timings only on the same cache state.

pitfalls.title: enable_* settings as a fix
pitfalls.detail: enable_seqscan = off and friends are diagnostic switches for seeing what an alternative plan costs. Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction; turned off server-wide they distort every query's plan.

quiz.q: In autocommit, you run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42`. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; EXPLAIN never modifies data
The rows are deleted and the plan is printed
The rows are deleted only if BUFFERS is also given
quiz.why: ANALYZE executes the statement and discards only its output. Use BEGIN ... ROLLBACK around it.

quiz.q: A primary-key lookup on a 200,000-row table shows `Buffers: shared hit=4`. What are the 4?
options: Three index levels plus one table page
quiz.why: A lookup reads one page per tree level, then the heap page holding the row. Index Searches: 1 shows it was a single descent.

quiz.q: `amount < 900` matches 90% of the rows and there is an index on amount. Why does the planner choose a Seq Scan?
options: Fetching 90% of the rows through the index visits table pages in random order, many times each; reading every page once is less work
B-tree indexes can't evaluate range conditions
quiz.why: The forced index scan touched 18,018 pages against 147 for the Seq Scan. B-trees handle ranges fine; the range was just too wide.

quiz.q: What does `Buffers: shared read=2` tell you?
options: Two pages weren't in PostgreSQL's buffer cache and were requested from the operating system
Two pages were certainly read from disk
quiz.why: A read may still be served by the OS file cache; PostgreSQL only knows its own cache missed. Turn on track_io_timing to see how long those reads took.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: EXPLAIN (options: ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING, SUMMARY)
PostgreSQL docs: B-Tree Indexes (implementation: levels, page splits, deduplication)
PostgreSQL docs: Planner Cost Constants (seq_page_cost, random_page_cost)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A table in PostgreSQL is a **heap**: rows sit in 8 kB pages in no particular order. An
index is a separate structure that maps values to row locations (a **TID**: block number
and offset). The default kind, and the one behind every `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE`, is a
**B-tree**: keys kept sorted in pages, with internal levels above the leaves. A lookup
starts at the root and reads one page per level. A page holds hundreds of keys, so the
tree stays shallow: three levels reach tens of millions of rows.

Whether a query uses the index is the **planner's** decision, made per query from
statistics. Two commands show it:

- `EXPLAIN` prints the chosen plan with estimates. Nothing runs; it's cheap and safe.
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the statement and adds what really happened: rows per node,
  loops, and (by default since PostgreSQL 18) **buffers**, the pages each node touched.

Read the plan before you trust an index: the planner may ignore it, and sometimes it is
right to.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java's `TreeMap`, C++'s `std::map`:** sorted, O(log n), ranges and ordered
  iteration. A B-tree is the on-disk version: nodes are pages with hundreds of keys, so
  the cost is a handful of page reads rather than dozens of pointer hops.
- **`HashMap`, Python `dict`, JS `Map`:** equality only, no order. PostgreSQL has hash
  indexes too, and they're rarely the right choice for the same reason.
- **Profilers:** `EXPLAIN` is reading what the compiler intends to emit; `EXPLAIN
  ANALYZE` is a precise profiler for one execution, with exact counts instead of samples.
- **If you've read MySQL advice:** InnoDB stores the table inside its primary-key tree.
  PostgreSQL doesn't; every index, the primary key included, points into the heap, so an
  index scan always pays for the trip to the table (lesson 2's index-only scans are the
  exception).

## How it works

```text
                 [ root: 1 .. 200000 ]                  level 2
                 /                    \
      [ internal: 1 .. ]         [ internal: .. 200000 ]  level 1
       /      |       \               ...
  [leaf] <-> [leaf] <-> [leaf] <-> ... <-> [leaf]        level 0: keys + TIDs
     |         |  \
   heap      heap  heap     table pages, in insertion order, not key order
```

Leaves are linked to their neighbours, so a range scan descends once and then walks
sideways. Page splits add leaves as the table grows; when the root itself splits, the
tree gains a level. That's the whole reason lookup cost barely moves with table size.

A plan is a tree of nodes, printed with indentation; each node pulls rows from the nodes
indented below it, so start reading at the innermost line. With costs on, a node reads:

```text
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..378.00 rows=20 width=14)
```

`378.00` is the estimated total cost in abstract units: the table's 128 pages at
`seq_page_cost` (1.0), plus 20,000 rows at `cpu_tuple_cost` (0.01), plus 20,000
evaluations of the filter at `cpu_operator_cost` (0.0025). `0.00` is the start-up cost
(work before the first row, such as a sort). `rows=20` is the estimate you compare with
`actual rows` from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`; a large gap means bad statistics, the subject of
lesson 5. The planner picks the cheapest total among the plans it considers.

## Design notes

A workflow that holds up:

1. `EXPLAIN` the query first. Look for the scan type on the big tables and for filters
   that discard most rows.
2. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` it inside `BEGIN ... ROLLBACK`, on realistic data volumes. Compare
   estimated and actual rows, then look at Buffers. `TIMING OFF` and `SUMMARY OFF` are
   what keep this sandbox's output stable; on a real investigation, keep the timings.
3. Change one thing (an index, the query, `ANALYZE`) and compare Buffers again.

Indexes are not free: each one is updated by every `INSERT`, and by every `UPDATE` that
changes an indexed column. Add them for queries you have measured, not for columns that
look important. The planner rejecting an index for a wide range is usually correct;
the fix for a slow wide query is a different index or a different query, which the rest
of this module covers.

lessons.title: Reading plans: seq/index/index-only/bitmap scans, nested loop/hash/merge joins
lessons.summary: The planner picks one of four ways to read each table and one of three ways to join each pair, per query, from estimated row counts. Each choice tells you what it believed; EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you whether it was right.

examples.title: One table, six plans: seq, index, index-only, bitmap, BitmapOr, ordered

annotations.note: value is a scrambled permutation (the 7919 trick from the previous lesson) and sensor_id repeats every 200 rows: neither follows the physical order of the table.

90% of the rows match, so the planner reads every page once and tests the Filter on each row. A Seq Scan is always on the menu; every other plan needs an index that matches the condition or the ORDER BY.
Index Scan: descend the tree, then fetch each match from the table. Unbeatable for a handful of rows, expensive per row for many.

Index Only Scan: the query needs only id, and the index holds it, so the table can be skipped for pages the visibility map marks all-visible. B-trees always support this; GiST and SP-GiST only for some operator classes; GIN never, because its entries hold only parts of the values.

Bitmap scan: 200 matches scattered over the table. The bitmap orders their locations by page, so each page is read once, in physical order. That also means the index order is lost: an ORDER BY on top of a bitmap scan needs its own Sort.

A single index scan can only use conditions joined by AND on its own columns. Here each index builds a bitmap and BitmapOr merges them. AND conditions on two indexes combine the same way (BitmapAnd), though one composite index usually beats that (next lesson).
No Sort node: the index hands rows over in value order, and Limit stops pulling after five. The cost is the same on 20,000 rows or 20 million, which is what keyset pagination (lesson 5) builds on.

Heap Fetches: 100. The visibility map of a brand-new table has no bits set (VACUUM sets them, and these uncommitted rows aren't visible to anyone else anyway), so every row is checked in the table. Only 3 buffers, because the 100 rows share one heap page next to 2 index pages. On a vacuumed table that changes slowly, Heap Fetches drops toward 0, and only then does index-only pay off.

examples.title: The three join methods, each where it fits

annotations.note: Ten orders per customer, scattered over the table. The index on orders.customer_id is explicit: a foreign key doesn't create one.

Nested Loop: the first child (outer) yields 3 customers; the second child (inner) runs once per outer row with that row's id plugged in, which is why its Index Cond mentions c.id. The IN list became = ANY(array), a single index scan for all three keys.

Hash Join: the Hash node reads customers once into an in-memory hash table keyed on id, then all 20,000 orders stream past it. No index needed, each table read once. HashAggregate then groups by city with a second hash table.

Merge Join: both inputs arrive sorted on the join key (customers from its primary key, orders from orders_customer), so one merge pass joins them, and the result is already in c.id order: no Sort node for the ORDER BY.

examples.title: One join, three methods: what the rejected plans would have cost

annotations.note: The same tables as before, but now 500 customers qualify: too many for one index lookup each, so the planner hashes them instead.

120 buffers: customers' 11 pages and orders' 109, each read once. Batches: 1 means the hash table fit in memory; the limit is work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier (4MB × 2.0 by default), and a hash table past it spills to temporary files in more batches. Planning: Buffers counts pages the planner itself read while choosing.

Nested Loop, forced: the inner Index Scan ran 500 times (loops=500, Index Searches: 500). actual rows=10.00 is per loop, so 5,000 rows in total. Each loop reads 2 index pages and 10 table pages: 6,011 page accesses, 50 times the hash join. With 3 outer rows (previous example) the same shape was the cheapest plan; the method depends on the row counts, not on the query text.

Merge Join, forced: customers gets an explicit Sort (500 rows in memory), orders comes sorted from its index at one page jump per row: 20,005 accesses. It reads 19,981 orders and stops: past the last İzmir customer (id 1998) there's nothing left to merge.
All three methods off, and a join is still required. enable_* only discourages, so the planner takes the cheapest disabled plan and PG 18 marks it Disabled: true; older versions printed no marker.

use_cases: Diagnosing a slow endpoint: find the node where actual rows, loops or buffers explode, and compare its actual rows with the estimate
Deciding between a composite index and two single-column indexes combined with BitmapAnd
Checking that ORDER BY ... LIMIT stops early on an index instead of sorting the whole table
Explaining why one customer's page is fast and a whole city's report is slow: the join method changes with the row counts
strengths: The algorithm is chosen per query from statistics: the same join is a nested loop for 3 customers and a hash join for 500, which a hand-written loop in Go or an ORM can't do
Bitmap scans combine any number of single-column indexes for AND/OR conditions and still read each table page only once
Index order replaces sorting: index scans and merge joins deliver ordered rows, so ORDER BY ... LIMIT can stop after a few rows
Rejected alternatives are measurable: switch a method off with SET LOCAL and compare buffers in the same transaction
weaknesses: Every choice is only as good as the row estimates: a nested loop planned for 3 outer rows that meets 50,000 is the classic slow query
Core PostgreSQL has no per-query hints; the enable_* switches are coarse and apply to everything in the session or transaction
Index-only scans depend on the visibility map, so on a busy table they degrade into index scans until VACUUM catches up
Hashes and sorts are bounded per node by work_mem (hashes: times hash_mem_multiplier) and spill to temporary files beyond it

pitfalls.title: Reading actual rows without loops
pitfalls.detail: On the inner side of a nested loop, actual rows is the average per execution. rows=10.00 loops=500 is 5,000 rows. Multiply before comparing with the estimate or blaming the node.

pitfalls.title: Reading Buffers as per-node work
pitfalls.detail: A node's Buffers include all of its children. The Aggregate's 120 in the hash join plan is the two Seq Scans' 11 + 109, not 120 more.

pitfalls.title: Expecting an index-only scan right after a bulk load
pitfalls.detail: Until VACUUM has set the visibility map, every row is checked in the table (Heap Fetches). After a large load, vacuum and analyze explicitly instead of waiting for autovacuum.
pitfalls.good: VACUUM (ANALYZE) readings;

pitfalls.title: Raising work_mem server-wide for one report
pitfalls.detail: work_mem applies per sort or hash node, per session, so a global increase multiplies across every concurrent query. Raise it for the one transaction that needs it.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; SELECT ...; COMMIT;

quiz.q: An inner Index Scan shows `actual rows=10.00 loops=500`. How many rows did it produce in total?
quiz.why: Actual rows is the per-loop average; multiply by loops.

quiz.q: Why does a Bitmap Heap Scan need a separate Sort for ORDER BY, even on an indexed column?
options: It visits rows in physical page order, so the index order is lost
quiz.why: The bitmap is laid out by page so each page is read once; the docs note that any ordering of the original indexes is lost.

quiz.q: An Index Only Scan reports `Heap Fetches` equal to the number of rows. What usually fixes it in a real database?
options: VACUUM, so the visibility map marks pages all-visible
quiz.why: The table can be skipped only for all-visible pages, and VACUUM is what records them.

quiz.q: You join every row of two large tables on a key with no index, and the output order doesn't matter. Which method do you expect?
quiz.why: One pass over each table, no index or sort needed. A nested loop would rescan the inner side per row; a merge join would have to sort both sides first.

PostgreSQL docs: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes
PostgreSQL docs: Query Planning settings (enable_*, cost constants)

lessons.body:
## Concept

For each table in a query the planner considers a **Seq Scan** (always possible) and an
index-based scan for every index whose columns match a condition or the `ORDER BY`. For
each pair of inputs it considers three join methods. It estimates the cost of the
combinations and runs the cheapest. The menu:

- **Seq Scan**: every page, once, in order. Right for a large fraction of the table.
- **Index Scan**: descend, then one table fetch per match. Right for a few rows, or when
  the index order saves a sort.
- **Index Only Scan**: answer from the index alone, for pages the visibility map marks
  all-visible.
- **Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan**: collect matching locations first, read each
  page once in physical order. The middle ground, and the way to combine indexes.
- **Nested Loop**: for each outer row, run the inner side. Right when the outer side is
  small and the inner side has an index.
- **Hash Join**: build a hash table on one side, stream the other. Right for large,
  unsorted inputs.
- **Merge Join**: walk two inputs sorted on the key. Right when both arrive sorted, or the
  output must be sorted anyway.

None of them is good or bad by itself. A plan is a statement about row counts: a nested
loop says "the outer side is small". Your job when reading it is to check that belief.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

You've written all three joins by hand:

- **Nested loop:** `for c in customers: for o in index[c.id]` in Python, or a lookup in a
  `TreeMap` per outer element in Java. Without the index it is JS's
  `customers.map(c => orders.filter(o => o.customerId === c.id))`, O(n·m).
- **Hash join:** build a `HashMap<Integer, Customer>` (Go: `map[int]Customer`) from the
  smaller list, then loop over the larger one and probe it.
- **Merge join:** the merge step of merge sort, over two lists sorted by the same key.

The difference is that you choose once, when you write the code, while the planner
chooses per execution from estimated sizes. An ORM that loads customers and then queries
each one's orders is running a nested loop from the application, with a network round
trip per inner lookup: the N+1 problem of lesson 5.

## How it works

Reading `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output, node by node:

- **`actual rows=10.00 loops=500`**: rows are averages per loop. Since PG 18 they are
  printed with two decimals, because an average needn't be whole.
- **`Index Searches: 500`** (new in PG 18): descents of the tree across all loops. On the
  inner side of a nested loop that's one per outer row. A range is one search; an
  `= ANY(...)` list can take up to one per element, fewer when neighbouring keys share a
  leaf page.
- **`Buffers`**: cumulative, a node's count includes its children's.
- **Hash**: `Buckets`, `Batches`, `Memory Usage`. One batch means it fit in memory.
- **Sort**: `Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 25kB` fit in `work_mem`; `external merge
  Disk: ...` did not.
- **`Heap Fetches`**: table visits an index-only scan couldn't skip.
- **`Rows Removed by Filter`**: rows read and thrown away; a large number on a selective
  query is the classic sign of a missing or unusable index.

Two more nodes you'll meet: **Memoize** (PG 14+) sits between a nested loop and its inner
scan and caches inner results per key when the same keys repeat; **Gather** with
`Parallel Seq Scan` below it means the work was split across worker processes, which
starts once a table passes `min_parallel_table_scan_size` (8 MB by default).

## Design notes

Read a slow plan in this order:

1. Find the node with the largest actual rows × loops, or the largest Buffers.
2. Compare its actual rows with the estimate (`EXPLAIN` without `COSTS OFF`). A tenfold
   gap is the usual root cause: the planner picked a nested loop for "3 rows" and got
   thousands. Fix the estimate (`ANALYZE`, extended statistics, lesson 5) before
   anything else.
3. If the estimate is right and the plan is still slow, the fix is an index that matches
   the query (lesson 3) or a different query shape.

`enable_*` switches belong between steps 2 and 3: confirming what the alternative would
cost, as in the third example. The docs call them a crude method and a temporary
solution, and core PostgreSQL has no per-query hints. A plan you had to force today
breaks silently when the data changes tomorrow; a correct estimate keeps adapting.

lessons.title: Composite index column order, partial and expression indexes, covering (INCLUDE)
lessons.summary: Start from the query, not the table: equality columns first, then one range or sort column; a WHERE clause to index only the rows you search; an expression to index what you compare; INCLUDE to answer from the index alone.

examples.title: (shop_id, placed_on) vs (placed_on, shop_id) for the same query

annotations.note: g / 100 is integer division: 100 consecutive orders per day, and g % 100 + 1 spreads them over 100 shops. Dates rather than timestamptz keep the plan text short and independent of the server's time zone setting.

Entries are sorted by day first, so the only contiguous stretch for this query is "March and April, every shop": about 6,100 entries, checked one by one for shop_id = 7. shop_id still appears in the Index Cond, but it filters inside the scanned range instead of narrowing it. 60 buffers: the 39 table pages holding the 61 rows, and about 20 index pages mostly full of other shops' entries. The Planning section counts pages the planner itself read while choosing the plan.

Sorted by shop first, shop 7's two months are one contiguous run of 61 entries: the Bitmap Index Scan reads 2 index pages instead of about 20. The table side (39 pages for 61 rows) is identical, since both indexes find the same rows. Each measured run follows a plain EXPLAIN of the same query, so planner lookups are already cached.

A prefix of the key is an index too: shop_id alone works, and within one shop the entries are already in placed_on order, so ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT reads the run backwards and stops after 10. An index on (placed_on, shop_id) could do neither of these well.
total isn't in the index, so its order is unknown: all of shop 7's rows are fetched and sorted (a top-N sort that keeps only 10). An index on (shop_id, total) would serve this query instead.

examples.title: Partial index for the hot rows; expression index for Turkish lower-casing

annotations.note: The full index has an entry for all 20,000 rows; the partial one only for the 400 open tickets, and it shrinks further as tickets close. Fewer pages to cache, and nothing to maintain when closed tickets change. pg_relation_size takes the index name, resolved via search_path, so other schemas' objects can't interfere.

The plan shows no condition at all: every entry in the partial index is open by construction. The planner used it because the query's WHERE implies the index's WHERE. It proves that at planning time, so the condition must be in the SQL text, not a $1 parameter.
The databases here use the builtin C.UTF-8 locale, whose lower() maps I to i. Turkish rules map I to ı (and İ to i), which is what a Turkish user typing "ısparta" expects to match.

The index stores lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu") for every row, computed once per insert or update. ANALYZE also gathers statistics on the expression itself, which helps the estimate for queries on it.

The query repeats the indexed expression, collation included. EXPLAIN shows the collation change as (city)::text rather than spelling out COLLATE, so read the index definition, not the plan, to see it.

lower(city) is a different expression: Seq Scan, and with the default rules 'ISPARTA-8' becomes 'isparta-8', so nothing matches. Choosing the collation is a correctness decision first and an indexing one second.

examples.title: INCLUDE: an index-only scan, and what payload columns can't do

annotations.note: In the transactional sql runtime nothing is ever committed, so the visibility map stays empty and an index-only scan still visits every row (previous lesson). Here VACUUM can mark the pages all-visible. If another transaction in the database was open while it ran, some pages may stay unmarked and Heap Fetches would be above 0.
20 table pages for 20 rows, because the index only knows where customer 42's rows are, not their totals.
Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0: 2 index pages plus 1 hit on the visibility map, against 22 pages before. INCLUDE columns sit in the leaf entries only; they are not part of the key.
Payload never guides a scan: a condition on total can't use either index. If you need to search or sort by total, make it a key column.

79 pages against 21. The key-only index stores each customer_id once with a list of 20 row pointers (deduplication); the docs state that INCLUDE indexes never deduplicate, and every entry also carries its numeric total.
Uniqueness applies to the key columns only. A plain UNIQUE (email, name) would have accepted this row, since the pair differs; with INCLUDE, name is stored but not compared. SQLSTATE 23505.

use_cases: (tenant_id, created_at) for 'this tenant's latest items' in multi-tenant apps; (status, priority) for a work queue
Partial: open tickets, pending jobs, rows WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; partial UNIQUE for 'one active subscription per user'
Expression: case-insensitive lookups (lower(email)), Turkish-aware search keys, jsonb fields (data->>'sku')
INCLUDE: a hot lookup that needs one or two extra small columns, served by an index-only scan
strengths: One composite index serves every query on a prefix of its columns, and returns rows in key order, unlike a hash map keyed by the whole tuple
A partial index costs nothing for rows outside its WHERE: no space, and no maintenance when those rows change
An expression index makes a computed comparison as cheap as a column comparison, with no extra column in the table
UNIQUE ... INCLUDE enforces uniqueness on the key and serves index-only scans for the payload, with one index instead of two
weaknesses: Column order serves some queries and not others: (a, b) helps a alone but not b alone (short of PG 18's skip scan, next lesson)
Partial and expression indexes only match queries written to fit them: the same predicate, the same expression and collation, with no parameters in the predicate
Every index adds write cost, and an UPDATE touching any indexed column, INCLUDE columns too, gives up HOT (in-place) updates
INCLUDE indexes never deduplicate and repeat payload in every entry, so they can be several times larger

pitfalls.title: Range or sort column first
pitfalls.detail: The range column decides where the scan starts and stops; any column after it only filters entries inside that stretch. Put equality columns first.
pitfalls.good: CREATE INDEX ON orders (shop_id, placed_on);

pitfalls.title: A partial index's condition sent as a parameter
pitfalls.detail: Matching happens at planning time. pgx prepares and caches statements by default, and after five executions PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan that knows only $1, which can't imply the predicate. Keep the predicate's value literal in the SQL.
pitfalls.bad: rows, err := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE status = $1 ORDER BY opened_on LIMIT 10", "open")
pitfalls.good: rows, err := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open' ORDER BY opened_on LIMIT 10")

pitfalls.title: Expression or collation mismatch
pitfalls.detail: An index on lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu") does nothing for lower(city), upper(city) or city ILIKE ..., and those also compare differently. Pick one normalization, put it in a STORED generated column or a SQL function, and use it everywhere.

pitfalls.title: One partial index per category
pitfalls.detail: The docs warn against a set of indexes like ON t (data) WHERE category = 1, = 2, ...: the planner has to test each one. Use one index on (category, data), or partitioning for truly large tables.

pitfalls.title: Wide INCLUDE columns
pitfalls.detail: Payload is copied into every leaf entry. A long text column bloats the index, and a value too large for an index entry makes the INSERT fail.

quiz.q: Which index serves `WHERE shop_id = $1 AND placed_on >= $2 ORDER BY placed_on LIMIT 20` best?
options: Separate indexes on shop_id and placed_on
quiz.why: Equality first makes the shop's rows one contiguous run, already in placed_on order, so the scan starts at $2 and stops after 20. Two separate indexes would need a bitmap, which loses the order.

quiz.q: There's a partial index `ON tickets (opened_on) WHERE status = 'open'`. A prepared statement running `WHERE status = $1 ...` has switched to a generic plan. Can it use the index?
options: No, the plan is made without knowing $1, so it can't prove the predicate
quiz.why: The docs: matching takes place at planning time, so parameterized clauses don't work with a partial index.

quiz.q: The index is on `lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`. What does `WHERE lower(city) = 'ısparta-8'` do?
options: Uses the index and finds the row
Uses the index but finds nothing
Seq Scan, and under C.UTF-8 rules finds nothing
quiz.why: It's a different expression, so the index doesn't apply; and default lower() maps I to i, giving 'isparta-8'.

quiz.q: With `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) INCLUDE (name)`, can two rows share an email if their names differ?
quiz.why: INCLUDE columns are payload; the uniqueness condition applies only to the key columns.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Indexes and ORDER BY
PostgreSQL docs: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes
PostgreSQL docs: PREPARE (generic vs custom plans)

lessons.body:
## Concept

An index is a sorted copy of some expression of each row, plus a pointer back. Four knobs
decide what it is good for:

- **Column order** (composite indexes). Entries are sorted by the first column, then the
  second within it, and so on. The docs' rule: equality conditions on leading columns,
  plus a range on the first column without an equality, limit the part of the index
  that's scanned. Conditions on later columns only filter inside that part. So:
  **equality columns first, then one range or `ORDER BY` column**.
- **`WHERE`** (partial indexes). Only rows matching the predicate get entries. The query
  must imply the predicate, provably, at planning time.
- **Expressions**. Index `lower(email)`, `(data->>'sku')`, `date_trunc('day', at)`. The
  query must use the same expression.
- **`INCLUDE`** (covering indexes, PG 11+). Extra columns stored in the leaf entries so an
  index-only scan can answer without the table. Not searchable, not part of uniqueness.

The design question is never "which columns are important?" but "which queries run
often, and what exactly do they filter, sort and return?"

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java's `Comparator.comparing(Order::shopId).thenComparing(Order::placedOn)`**, or Go's
  `slices.SortFunc` with `cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(a.ShopID, b.ShopID), a.PlacedOn.Compare(b.PlacedOn))`,
  is exactly the order of a `(shop_id, placed_on)` index. A `TreeSet.subSet(from, to)` over
  it is the range scan: contiguous only when the leading part of the key is fixed.
- **Python:** `bisect` on a list of `(shop_id, placed_on)` tuples finds shop 7's March in
  one step; on `(placed_on, shop_id)` tuples, shop 7's rows are interleaved with 99 other
  shops.
- **JS:** a `Map` keyed by `name.toLocaleLowerCase('tr-TR')` is an expression index. A
  lookup with `name.toLowerCase()` uses a different key function and misses, which is
  the collation mismatch from the second example.
- **Covering index:** a denormalized cache inside the index. Like any cache, it costs space
  and must be kept in sync on every write; PostgreSQL does the syncing for you.

## How it works

The two indexes of the first example, as their leaf entries are ordered:

```text
(shop_id, placed_on):  ... (6, 2026-07-19) | (7, 2026-01-01) ... (7, 2026-03-01) ... (7, 2026-04-30) ... | (8, ...)
                                                                 \___ one run of 61 entries ___/

(placed_on, shop_id):  (2026-03-01, 1) (2026-03-01, 2) ... (2026-03-01, 7) ... (2026-04-30, 100)
                       \___ 6,100 entries scanned, each checked for shop_id = 7 ___/
```

`INCLUDE` vs adding the column to the key: `(customer_id, total)` would also cover the
query, and could additionally search and sort by `total`. INCLUDE columns don't need a
B-tree operator class, are kept out of the upper levels of the tree, and stay out of
uniqueness checks, which is why `UNIQUE (email) INCLUDE (name)` exists.

Since PG 18, a B-tree can sometimes use `(a, b)` for a condition on `b` alone by skipping
through the distinct values of `a`. That **skip scan** is the next lesson's topic; it
softens the column-order rule but doesn't replace it.

## Design notes

Work from the query list (lesson 5 shows where to get it: `pg_stat_statements`), one
query shape at a time:

1. Equality columns of the `WHERE` first. Among them, prefer the order that lets other
   queries share the index as a prefix (`tenant_id` first in a multi-tenant schema).
2. Then the one column that is a range or the `ORDER BY`. A second range column after it
   only filters.
3. If the query touches a small, well-defined subset (open, pending, not deleted), make it
   partial, and keep that condition literal in the SQL.
4. If it compares a computed value, index the expression, or store it in a `STORED`
   generated column when several queries need it (the generated-columns lesson). For
   Turkish text, put the collation inside the expression.
5. Only for hot, read-mostly lookups: `INCLUDE` the one or two small columns the query
   returns, then confirm `Heap Fetches` stays near zero in production.

Then merge: an index on `(a, b)` makes a separate index on `(a)` redundant. Each index you
keep slows every write, so drop the ones no query uses (`pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan`
tells you which, see the monitoring lesson).

lessons.title: GIN (jsonb, arrays, full-text, trigram), BRIN for time series, skip scan (PG 18)
lessons.summary: GIN indexes the parts inside a value (jsonb keys, array elements, words, trigrams); BRIN stores one min/max per block range, tiny and only useful when physical order follows the column; PG 18's skip scan lets a B-tree serve queries that omit its leading column.

examples.title: GIN on jsonb and arrays: which operators it serves, and which it doesn't

annotations.note: 200 brands with 100 products each, four colors, and two tags per product: a label and one of 100 categories. Every marka-7 product happens to be siyah, so the containment query below matches 100 rows.

jsonb_ops makes an entry for every key and every value. @> looks up the entries for brand, marka-7, color and siyah and intersects their row lists. GIN is always read through a bitmap scan: it yields row locations in no useful order. The recheck matters here, because keys and values are indexed separately: a row holding "siyah" under some other key would also be a candidate.
Key existence (?, ?| and ?&) is served by jsonb_ops only. No product has a discount key, and the index says so without touching the table.

->> returns text, and text = text belongs to B-tree, not to the GIN operator class. Write the condition as attrs @> '{"brand": "marka-7"}', or give the key a B-tree expression index on (attrs ->> 'brand'), or, if every row has it, a real column (the JSON module's indexing lesson).

jsonb_path_ops stores one hash per value together with the keys leading to it, instead of separate key and value entries: 24 pages instead of 37, and more specific lookups. The price: only @>, @? and @@, no key-existence operators.
The array operator class serves @>, <@, && and =. 'kategori-7' = ANY (tags) asks the same question as tags @> ARRAY['kategori-7'], but the planner only matches operators, not meanings: Seq Scan.

examples.title: GIN for words (turkish full-text search) and for substrings (pg_trgm)

annotations.note: The turkish configuration lower-cases, drops stop words and stems: kitapları becomes kitap, kitapçılar (booksellers) becomes kitapçı, a different stem. Stemming is heuristic: yeni (new) became ye, which is also the verb "eat". The query kitaplar stems to kitap, so it matches kitapları but not kitapçılar.
An expression index: to_tsvector('turkish', body) is computed on every insert and update, and GIN keeps, for each stem, the list of rows containing it.
kitap & dün intersects two of those row lists: 1,000 articles (every 20th one) mention books and yesterday.

The one-argument to_tsvector uses the default_text_search_config setting, so its result can change with a SET; it can't be indexed and doesn't match the indexed expression. The docs require the configuration name in both places; a STORED generated tsvector column avoids repeating it in every query.

pg_trgm is a trusted extension, so the non-superuser playground role may create it; the rollback removes it again. Each word is padded with two spaces in front and one behind, then cut into three-character pieces.

A leading % defeats any B-tree, hence the Seq Scan. With the trigram index the pattern's own trigrams are looked up, and the candidates are rechecked with ILIKE: 223 titles. A pattern too short to contain a trigram can't narrow anything down and becomes a full index scan.

pg_trgm asks the database's LC_CTYPE, fixed at CREATE DATABASE, which characters are letters. The playground's is a real locale, so ı and ğ are letters and ığdır has six trigrams, printed in hex because a trigram holding non-ASCII letters is stored as a 3-byte hash. Under LC_CTYPE 'C' every non-ASCII letter is a separator: ığdır shrinks to the trigrams of d and r, exactly those of dür, and vs_dur becomes 1.

pg_trgm lower-cases each word with the database's default collation, C.UTF-8 here, which maps I to i, not ı. IĞDIR becomes iğdir and shares no trigram with ığdır, so a similarity search for the capitalised name scores the real one 0.

examples.title: BRIN on an append-only table, and a PG 18 skip scan

annotations.note: EXPLAIN prints timestamptz constants in the session's time zone. Pinning it keeps the output identical on servers configured for UTC.
Rows arrive in time order, four sensors per minute, as in a log or an IoT feed: the physical position of a row follows its timestamp.

pg_stats.correlation compares the column's order with the physical row order: 1.00 for at, 0.25 for the cycling sensor_id, 0.00 for the scrambled value. BRIN only helps a column like at. On large tables ANALYZE works from a random sample and such numbers shift slightly between runs; on this small table they come out the same every time.

3 pages of BRIN against 32 of B-tree for a 128-page table: BRIN keeps one min/max per range of 8 pages, a B-tree one entry per row. The default range is 128 pages (1 MB of table); 8 suits this small table.

BRIN can only say "this range may contain matches", so the scan is always lossy: Heap Blocks: lossy=8 is one whole range, and Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1016 are its rows outside the hour. 13 buffers in all (8 table pages, 5 index pages). The Bitmap Index Scan's actual rows=80.00 is not a row count; BRIN knows pages, not rows. The Planning section is pages the planner itself read.

The index leads with sensor_id and the query doesn't mention it. Before PG 18 that condition couldn't narrow the scan: all 79 pages, or a Seq Scan. PG 18's skip scan repositions once per distinct sensor_id (Index Searches: 6 for 4 sensors) and reads 19 index pages. The plan never says "skip scan"; Index Searches above 1 for a single range condition is the sign.

use_cases: GIN, jsonb_path_ops: filtering semi-structured attributes with @> (product specs, event payloads, settings)
GIN on arrays: tags, labels, permission lists queried with @> (has all) and && (has any)
GIN on tsvector: full-text search in Turkish or English, the engine behind a site search box
GIN with pg_trgm: LIKE/ILIKE '%fragment%' and fuzzy similarity search on names and titles
BRIN: huge append-only tables queried by time range (logs, audit trails, sensor readings), where a B-tree would cost gigabytes
Skip scan: an existing (tenant_id, created_at) index serving an occasional query on created_at alone, when there are few tenants
strengths: GIN answers 'contains this element/key/word' questions that no B-tree can, like Lucene's inverted index but inside your transactions
One GIN index on a jsonb column serves containment queries on any key, without an index per attribute
BRIN is orders of magnitude smaller than a B-tree and nearly free to maintain on append-only data
Skip scan (PG 18) can save you a second index for queries that omit the leading column, with no change to the SQL
weaknesses: GIN only serves its own operators (@>, ?, &&, @@, LIKE via trigrams): ->> equality, = ANY and ranges fall back to other indexes or a Seq Scan
GIN is always a bitmap scan: no ordered output, no index-only scans, and inserts are expensive because one row adds many entries
BRIN is lossy and useless once physical order stops following the column (updates, out-of-order loads); newly appended ranges stay unsummarized until VACUUM or brin_summarize_new_values()
Skip scan pays off only when the skipped column has few distinct values; with many, the planner still prefers a Seq Scan or another index

pitfalls.title: Writing = ANY where @> would use the index
pitfalls.detail: Both ask whether the array contains a value, but only the operator form matches the GIN operator class.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT id FROM products WHERE 'kategori-7' = ANY (tags);
pitfalls.good: SELECT id FROM products WHERE tags @> ARRAY['kategori-7'];

pitfalls.title: ->> equality against a GIN-indexed jsonb column
pitfalls.detail: attrs ->> 'brand' = 'x' compares text, which GIN can't serve. Rewrite it as containment, or add a B-tree expression index on (attrs ->> 'brand') for a key you always filter on.
pitfalls.good: WHERE attrs @> '{"brand": "marka-7"}'

pitfalls.title: Full-text queries without the configuration
pitfalls.detail: An index on to_tsvector('turkish', body) serves only queries that spell the same two-argument call. Store the tsvector in a generated column, or wrap the expression in one SQL function used everywhere.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on a column that doesn't follow the physical order
pitfalls.detail: If rows are updated, deleted and refilled, or loaded out of order, every range's min/max spans nearly everything and BRIN excludes nothing. Check pg_stats.correlation first; near 1 or -1 is what BRIN needs.

pitfalls.title: Trusting pg_trgm with Turkish letters without checking
pitfalls.detail: pg_trgm skips characters it doesn't consider alphanumeric, and the database's LC_CTYPE decides which those are. Under LC_CTYPE 'C' every non-ASCII letter (ı, ğ, ş, ü...) is a separator: show_trgm('ığdır') returns only the trigrams of d and r, similarity('ığdır', 'dür') is 1, and similarity() and trigram index lookups on Turkish words get much weaker (LIKE results stay correct, since candidates are rechecked). The playground has a real LC_CTYPE. On another server, check datctype in pg_database and run show_trgm('ığdır'): six entries is right. LC_CTYPE can't be changed later; fixing it means a new database.

quiz.q: There is a GIN index on `tags text[]`. Which condition can use it?
quiz.why: Only the array operators of the GIN operator class (@>, <@, &&, =) are indexable; = ANY and subscripts are not.

quiz.q: Which question can a `jsonb_path_ops` GIN index NOT answer?
quiz.why: jsonb_path_ops hashes values together with their paths, so there is no entry for a key on its own; key existence needs jsonb_ops.

quiz.q: Why is BRIN a good fit for `created_at` on a 500 GB append-only events table?
options: It finds single rows faster than a B-tree
Rows arrive in time order, so each block range covers a narrow time span, and one summary per range keeps the index tiny
It supports ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10
quiz.why: BRIN works through correlation with the physical order; it is lossy and gives no ordering, but costs almost nothing to store and maintain.

quiz.q: PG 18, index on `(tenant_id, created_at)`, query `WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 hour'`. When does skip scan make this efficient?
options: When tenant_id has few distinct values
Only if the query also uses ORDER BY tenant_id
quiz.why: Skip scan does one index search per distinct tenant_id; the docs note it's chosen when there are so few distinct leading values that most of the index can be skipped.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: GIN Indexes (built-in operator classes, fast update)
PostgreSQL docs: jsonb Indexing (jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops)
PostgreSQL docs: Tables and Indexes for text search

lessons.body:
## Concept

A B-tree sorts whole values. Three other tools cover what sorting can't:

- **GIN** (Generalized Inverted Index) breaks each value into parts and indexes the parts:
  the keys and values of a `jsonb` document, the elements of an array, the stems of a
  `tsvector`, the trigrams of a string (with `pg_trgm`). For each part it keeps the list
  of rows containing it, so "which rows contain X and Y?" is a lookup and an
  intersection. It serves only its operator class's operators (`@>`, `?`, `&&`, `@@`,
  trigram `LIKE`), and is always read through a bitmap scan.
- **BRIN** (Block Range INdex) stores one small summary, usually min and max, per range of
  table pages. A query skips every range whose summary rules it out. It is tiny and
  cheap, and it only works when a column follows the physical row order, which
  append-only time series do by nature.
- **Skip scan** (PostgreSQL 18) isn't a new index type: a B-tree on `(a, b)` can serve a
  condition on `b` alone by searching once per distinct value of `a`. Before 18, such a
  query could only read the whole index or the whole table.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Lucene / Elasticsearch:** GIN is the same idea, an inverted index from term to
  postings. With `tsvector` and the `turkish` configuration you get stemmed full-text
  search inside your transactions, with no second system to keep in sync.
- **Java/Go:** a GIN index is a `Map<String, Set<Long>>` (Go: `map[string][]int64`) from
  element to row ids, maintained on every write. A `jsonb_path_ops` index keys that map
  by a hash of path and value.
- **Parquet or columnar stores:** BRIN is the per-row-group min/max statistics that let a
  reader skip whole chunks, applied to a heap table.
- **Python:** skip scan is a loop of `bisect` calls over a list sorted by
  `(sensor_id, at)`: for each distinct sensor, jump to `(sensor, from)` and read until
  `to`, instead of reading the whole list.

## How it works

GIN is a B-tree of keys whose leaves hold row lists (posting lists, or posting trees
when a key is very common). A single row can add dozens of entries, which makes writes
expensive; by default (`fastupdate`) new entries go to a pending list first and are
merged in bulk later, so searches also scan that list until it's flushed. GIN can't
return rows in any order and can't do index-only scans.

BRIN has a range map and one summary tuple per range of `pages_per_range` pages. A scan
returns every page of every range whose summary might match, and the executor rechecks
each row: always lossy. Pages appended after the index was built belong to unsummarized
ranges until `VACUUM` (or autovacuum, or `brin_summarize_new_values()`) summarizes them;
the `autosummarize` storage parameter is off by default. Besides `minmax`, there are
`minmax-multi`, `bloom` and `inclusion` operator classes for data with outliers or for
equality-heavy queries.

Skip scan, in the docs' words, generates "a dynamic equality constraint internally,
that matches every possible value in an index column". The planner chooses it when it
expects so few distinct leading values that most leaf pages can be skipped. It is
visible only as `Index Searches` greater than 1 in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.

## Design notes

- **jsonb:** GIN with `jsonb_path_ops` for `@>` filters on varied keys. A key that every
  query filters on deserves a B-tree expression index or, better, its own column (the
  JSON module's indexing lesson); GIN can't do ranges or ordering on it.
- **Arrays:** GIN, and write the query with `@>` or `&&`.
- **Text:** GIN on a stored, generated `tsvector` column for words; GIN with
  `gin_trgm_ops` for substrings and typos. GiST trigram indexes also support
  nearest-neighbour ordering (`ORDER BY name <-> 'query' LIMIT 10`), which GIN can't.
- **Time series:** BRIN on the timestamp of an append-only table, with `pages_per_range`
  tuned to how narrow your typical query window is. Keep a B-tree for point lookups.
- **Skip scan** relaxes the column-order rule from the previous lesson for low-cardinality
  leading columns; it doesn't remove it. Check `Index Searches` and buffers before you
  drop the second index you thought you needed.

Turkish text needs one check per tool: the `turkish` FTS configuration stems Turkish
suffixes but lower-cases with the database's rules (here C.UTF-8, which maps I to i).
`pg_trgm` lower-cases the same way and takes its idea of a letter from the database's
`LC_CTYPE`, as the last query of the second example and the pitfall show. The search
module covers both in depth.

lessons.title: Statistics and ANALYZE; keyset vs OFFSET pagination; the N+1 problem; pg_stat_statements
lessons.summary: Keep the planner's statistics current and teach it about correlated columns; page with a keyset cursor instead of OFFSET; fetch a page's children in one statement instead of one per row; and use pg_stat_statements to find which queries actually cost the most.

examples.title: Estimates vs reality: correlated columns, then a stale table

annotations.note: 20,000 addresses spread evenly over ten districts, and each district lies in exactly one city. Real data is full of such dependencies: postcode and city, product and category, tenant and plan.

ANALYZE stores per-column statistics in pg_statistic (readable through the pg_stats view): most common values with their frequencies, a histogram, the number of distinct values, correlation. Autovacuum normally runs it; this sandbox table is invisible to autovacuum.

EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) returns the plan as data; "Plan Rows" is the estimate that text format prints as rows=... when costs are on. The helper then counts the real rows. Machine-readable plans are also how monitoring tools consume EXPLAIN.

Alone, each condition is estimated exactly from the most-common-values list: 20% and 10% of the rows. Together the planner multiplies them, assuming independence: 0.2 × 0.1 × 20,000 = 400, where the truth is 2,000. A fivefold underestimate is how a nested loop gets planned for an input that turns out large.

CREATE STATISTICS asks the next ANALYZE to measure how strongly one column determines the other; now the estimate is exact. Functional dependencies only help equality and IN conditions with constants; the mcv and ndistinct kinds cover combinations and GROUP BY estimates.

ANALYZE last saw five cities covering every row, so a sixth is estimated at 1 row while 5,000 exist. The planner does scale its row counts to the table's current size, but the distribution it knows is stale.
Fixed. Autovacuum would analyze the table eventually, once enough rows have changed, but a job that loads data and queries it right away should run ANALYZE itself.

examples.title: Keyset vs OFFSET: the same page, the cost of getting there, and a moving feed

annotations.note: Pins the session time zone, which decides how timestamptz values and constants are printed, so the output is the same on any server.
created_at alone isn't unique, so it can't mark a position: id is added as a tiebreaker, and the index on (created_at, id), read backwards, delivers exactly ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC.

Identical rows. OFFSET counts positions from the top; the keyset query asks for rows that sort after the last one the reader saw, whose sort key the client kept as its cursor. The row comparison is lexicographic: created_at earlier, or the same created_at and a smaller id.

actual rows=8005: the index scan produced 8,005 entries so that Limit could throw 8,000 of them away. The docs put it plainly: rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed. The cost grows with the page number. (Heap Fetches is the visibility-map effect from lesson 2.)
The row comparison became an Index Cond, so the scan starts at the cursor and stops after 5 entries: 3 buffers, on page 2 or page 2 million.

OFFSET is positional. One post arriving at the top shifts everything down, so page 2 begins with 19998, which the reader already saw on page 1. A deleted post would make one silently disappear instead.
The keyset query continues right after 19998, whatever happened above the cursor in the meantime.

examples.title: N+1 queries, and the one-statement alternatives

annotations.note: 1 + N statements: what lazy loading in an ORM, or a Go loop calling QueryRow per post, sends. Each one is a cheap index lookup; the cost is the round trip and the per-statement overhead, paid N times. A 50-post page means 51 statements per request.

One statement per page. The ids travel as a single array parameter; from Go, pgx sends a []int32 as int[]. The SQL text stays the same for any page size, so it's one prepared statement and one pg_stat_statements entry.
Or let the database join: the page and its counts in one query. LEFT JOIN keeps posts without comments, and count(c.id) gives 0 for them where count(*) would give 1.

The per-row shape can hide inside a single statement too: SubPlan 1 runs once per outer row (loops=3, Index Searches: 3). No round trips, so it's far cheaper than N+1 from the application, but it is still N lookups. The join form lets the planner choose a hash join when the page is large.

use_cases: Run ANALYZE right after bulk loads, imports and big deletes, before the next query depends on them
CREATE STATISTICS for columns filtered together that depend on each other: city and district, tenant and plan, country and currency
Keyset pagination for feeds, infinite scroll, public API cursors and batch jobs that walk a whole table
Batching child lookups with = ANY($1) or a join in every list endpoint
pg_stat_statements as the first stop when the database is slow: which normalized queries take the most total time
strengths: Statistics make the planner adapt to the data without hints; extended statistics fix the independence assumption for the columns that need it
Keyset pagination costs the same on every page and stays correct while rows are inserted, unlike OFFSET, which gets slower and shifts
A batched query costs one round trip for any page size, where N+1 grows linearly with it
pg_stat_statements aggregates every execution per normalized query, so a 0.05 ms query run a million times shows up next to the one slow report
weaknesses: Statistics are approximate and sampled on large tables; they go stale between autovacuum runs, and extended statistics must be declared by hand
Keyset pagination can't jump to page 37, needs an index matching the ORDER BY exactly, and gets complicated for mixed sort directions
Batching moves the fan-out into the application: results arrive keyed by parent id and must be stitched back together
pg_stat_statements needs shared_preload_libraries and a server restart, and isn't available in this sandbox

pitfalls.title: Querying right after a bulk load
pitfalls.detail: Until ANALYZE runs, the planner estimates new values from old statistics: 1 row for 5,000 in the example. Analyze in the same job.
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO addresses SELECT ... FROM staging; ANALYZE addresses;

pitfalls.title: A keyset cursor without a unique tiebreaker
pitfalls.detail: With ORDER BY created_at alone, rows sharing the boundary timestamp are skipped or repeated across pages. Add the primary key to both the ORDER BY and the cursor.
pitfalls.bad: WHERE created_at < $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
pitfalls.good: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20

pitfalls.title: Comparing the cursor columns separately
pitfalls.detail: created_at < $1 AND id < $2 is not the same as the row comparison: it drops rows with the same created_at and a smaller id, and rows with an earlier created_at but a larger id.

pitfalls.title: N+1 in a Go loop
pitfalls.detail: One QueryRow per item is a round trip per item. Collect the ids, send them as one array, and map the results back by id.
pitfalls.bad: for i := range posts { conn.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT count(*) FROM comments WHERE post_id = $1", posts[i].ID).Scan(&posts[i].Comments) }
pitfalls.good: rows, err := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT post_id, count(*) FROM comments WHERE post_id = ANY($1) GROUP BY post_id", ids)

pitfalls.title: count(*) for 'page X of Y' on every request
pitfalls.detail: An exact total reads the whole matching set each time. Fetch LIMIT n + 1 rows to know whether a next page exists, and show totals only where they are cheap or can be approximate.

quiz.q: city = 'İstanbul' matches 20% of 20,000 rows and district = 'Kadıköy' 10%. Without extended statistics, how many rows does the planner estimate for both conditions together?
quiz.why: It assumes independence and multiplies: 0.2 × 0.1 × 20,000. The real answer is 2,000, because Kadıköy is always in İstanbul.

quiz.q: `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 8000`: how many rows must the server produce?
quiz.why: Skipped rows still have to be computed; with a matching index the scan can stop after offset + limit rows, but not before.

quiz.q: Which condition fetches the next page after cursor ($1, $2) for `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`?
quiz.why: Row comparison is lexicographic, matching the sort; the separate comparisons drop valid rows, and > goes the wrong direction for a descending order.

quiz.q: In pg_stat_statements, what does an N+1 pattern usually look like?
options: One query with a huge mean_exec_time
A simple lookup with an enormous calls count and a tiny mean_exec_time, high in total_exec_time
quiz.why: Each execution is fast; the damage is in the count. Sorting by total_exec_time surfaces it.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Statistics Used by the Planner (including extended statistics)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Four habits that keep a working schema fast once real traffic arrives:

- **Statistics.** Every plan rests on row estimates, and every estimate comes from
  `ANALYZE`'s summary of the data. Stale statistics (after a bulk load) and the
  independence assumption (for correlated columns) are the two common ways estimates
  go wrong. Fix the first with `ANALYZE`, the second with `CREATE STATISTICS`.
- **Keyset pagination.** `OFFSET n` makes the server produce and discard `n` rows, and the
  pages shift when rows are inserted or deleted. A keyset cursor, `WHERE (created_at, id)
  < ($1, $2)` with a matching index, starts exactly where the last page ended.
- **No N+1.** Loading a list and then querying once per item turns one request into N+1
  round trips. Fetch children for the whole page at once, with `= ANY($1)` or a join.
- **Measure the workload, not one query.** `pg_stat_statements` records every normalized
  statement's call count, total and mean time, rows and buffers, so you optimize what
  actually costs the most.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **ORMs:** N+1 is the classic lazy-loading trap. Hibernate's answer is `JOIN FETCH` or
  batch fetching; Django's is `select_related` (a join) and `prefetch_related` (a second
  query with `IN (...)`); GraphQL servers in JS use DataLoader to batch per request. In Go
  there is usually no ORM, so N+1 is visible: a `QueryRow` inside a `for` loop.
- **REST APIs:** `?page=37&size=20` maps naturally to `OFFSET`; the `next_cursor` tokens of
  many public APIs are keyset pagination with the sort key encoded inside. Clients of
  such an API just pass the token back (the Go and TypeScript services lessons build such
  clients).
- **Profilers:** `pg_stat_statements` is a sampling-free aggregate profiler for the whole
  database, the equivalent of looking at cumulative time per function instead of one
  stack trace.

## How it works

How the planner turns statistics into a row count (the docs' row estimation examples):

- `col = value` with `value` in the most-common-values list: its stored frequency.
- A value not in that list: the frequency left over after the common values, spread
