  evenly over the remaining distinct values. If the common values covered every row, the
  leftover is nothing, hence the estimate of 1 row for a city ANALYZE never saw.
- Ranges: the position of the constant within the histogram's equal-frequency buckets.
- `AND`: the selectivities multiplied, unless extended statistics say otherwise.

On large tables `ANALYZE` reads a random sample whose size grows with the statistics
target (`default_statistics_target`, 100 by default; per column with `ALTER TABLE ...
ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS`). Raise it for skewed columns whose rare values matter.

`pg_stat_statements` must be listed in `shared_preload_libraries` (a server restart),
then created per database with `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`. The sandbox
doesn't load it, so here is the query you'd run first, as a sketch:

```sql
SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 3) AS mean_ms,
       rows,
       shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read AS buffers,
       query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Constants are replaced by `$1`, `$2`, ... so every execution of the per-post comment
lookup lands in one row: an N+1 shows up as a simple query with a huge `calls` and a tiny
`mean_ms`, near the top of `total_ms`. Since PostgreSQL 18, `IN` lists that differ only
in length are also merged into one entry, shown as `IN ($1 /*, ... */)`. Seeing other
users' query texts needs the `pg_read_all_stats` role; `pg_stat_statements_reset()`
starts a fresh measurement, for example after a deploy.

## Design notes

- Make `ANALYZE` part of every job that bulk-loads or bulk-deletes. Autovacuum catches up
  on its own schedule, which is too late for the job's own next query.
- Declare extended statistics when `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows a large gap between estimated
  and actual rows on a multi-column condition, not preemptively.
- Default to keyset pagination for anything a user scrolls or a program iterates; the
  same cursor technique drives batched backfills (`WHERE id > $last ORDER BY id LIMIT
  1000`). Keep `OFFSET` for small, bounded lists where "page 7 of 12" matters. Encode the
  cursor as an opaque token so clients can't depend on its contents.
- Design list endpoints as one query per level: the page, then the children of all its
  rows. TraceLite's API (step 4) builds its list endpoints on keyset pagination.
- Turn on `pg_stat_statements` (and `track_io_timing`) in every environment you care
  about. Rank by `total_exec_time` before tuning anything; the slowest single query is
  often not the most expensive one.

lessons.title: Inner, left/right/full outer, cross and self joins
lessons.summary: A join pairs rows from two tables by a condition. INNER keeps matched pairs; LEFT, RIGHT and FULL also keep unmatched rows, padded with NULLs; CROSS pairs everything; a self join pairs a table with itself.

examples.title: INNER vs LEFT, and where the filter on the optional side goes

annotations.note: A nullable foreign key: a test case may exist before anyone links it. A NULL key never matches anything, not even another NULL, so the smoke test can't take part in a join on requirement_id.
JOIN means INNER JOIN. A row without a partner disappears from either side: Export CSV has no tests, the smoke test has no requirement.

LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side's columns with NULL when nothing matched. Add WHERE t.id IS NULL and this becomes the "requirements without tests" report. To list unlinked tests instead, put test_cases on the left.

WHERE runs after the join. On the padded rows t.automated is NULL, NULL is not true, so those rows go, and so does Password reset, whose only test is manual. The LEFT JOIN has quietly become an INNER JOIN.

In ON, the condition decides what counts as a match before the padding happens, so every requirement stays. Rule of thumb: conditions on the optional side go in ON, filters on the preserved side go in WHERE. For inner joins the two placements are equivalent.

examples.title: FULL for reconciliation, CROSS + LEFT for expected-versus-actual

annotations.note: FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides: logout was planned but never reported, signup was reported but never planned. coalesce picks whichever side has the key, so the sort works for every row.

CROSS JOIN produces every browser with every locale (2 x 2 = 4 rows): the runs that should exist. LEFT JOIN the runs that do exist, and a NULL marks firefox/tr-TR as never tested. The same shape finds missing days in a time series.
A CROSS JOIN of N and M rows yields N x M rows. Here that is the point; when it happens by accident (a comma join with a forgotten WHERE), it is the classic exploding result.

examples.title: Self joins: parent lookup and duplicate pairs, with Turkish case rules

annotations.note: parent_id references the same table. One level up is a self join; walking the whole tree needs a recursive CTE (subqueries and CTEs module).
The aliases c and p give one table two roles. LEFT keeps the root requirements, whose parent is NULL.
To compare rows of one table with each other, join it to itself. a.id < b.id keeps each unordered pair once and never pairs a row with itself; a.id <> b.id would list every pair twice.
Under the database's C.UTF-8 rules lower('KAYIT FORMU') is 'kayit formu', with a dotted i, so it never equals 'kayıt formu'. With COLLATE "tr-x-icu", I lowers to ı and the duplicate is found.

use_cases: INNER: the everyday 'rows with their parent' query, such as test cases with their requirement
LEFT ... WHERE right.id IS NULL: coverage gaps, orphans, customers without orders
FULL: reconciling two sources such as a test plan and CI results, or a ledger and a bank statement
CROSS + LEFT: expected-versus-actual matrices (browser x locale, day x sensor)
Self join: parent and child in one table, duplicate detection, comparing a row with its neighbour
strengths: Declarative: you state the condition, and the planner chooses a nested loop, hash join or merge join from table statistics, where Go or TS code would hard-wire one strategy
Outer joins make missing data visible as NULL-padded rows instead of rows that silently aren't there
A join condition can be any boolean expression: ranges, lower(), inequalities, not just key equality
weaknesses: NULL-padded rows meet three-valued logic: a WHERE on the optional side undoes the outer join
Joining a parent to two independent child tables multiplies rows (2 tests x 3 comments = 6 rows per requirement) and inflates counts and sums
RIGHT JOIN reads backwards; swapping the tables gives the same result as a LEFT JOIN, which most code standardizes on

pitfalls.title: Filtering the optional side in WHERE
pitfalls.detail: The NULL-padded rows fail the condition and vanish, turning the outer join into an inner one. Move the condition into ON.
pitfalls.bad: FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id WHERE t.automated
pitfalls.good: FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id AND t.automated

pitfalls.title: Fan-out from two one-to-many joins
pitfalls.detail: requirements JOIN test_cases JOIN comments returns tests x comments rows per requirement, so count(*) and sum() come out multiplied. Aggregate each child separately (subqueries, or LATERAL in this module's last lesson).

pitfalls.title: Comma joins hide a missing condition
pitfalls.detail: FROM a, b with a forgotten WHERE clause is a cross join. Explicit JOIN ... ON keeps the condition next to the table it belongs to, and leaving out ON is a syntax error.
pitfalls.bad: FROM requirements r, test_cases t  -- WHERE forgotten
pitfalls.good: FROM requirements r JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id

pitfalls.title: Expecting NULL keys to match
pitfalls.detail: NULL = NULL is unknown, so rows with a NULL key never join, not even to each other. Model 'not linked' deliberately and use an outer join where it matters.

quiz.q: `requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id WHERE t.automated`: what happens to requirements that have no tests?
quiz.why: Their padded t.automated is NULL, WHERE keeps only true, so they are filtered out after the join.

quiz.q: Which join returns unmatched rows from both tables?
quiz.why: FULL JOIN pads whichever side is missing, so rows that exist on only one side appear either way.

quiz.q: browsers has 4 rows and locales 5. How many rows does browsers CROSS JOIN locales return?
quiz.why: A cross join is the Cartesian product: 4 x 5 = 20.

quiz.q: In a self join looking for duplicate titles, why `a.id < b.id` rather than `a.id <> b.id`?
options: It reports each pair once instead of twice
quiz.why: <> keeps both (x, y) and (y, x); < keeps only one ordering and still excludes pairing a row with itself.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A join combines two tables into pairs of rows for which a condition holds. The kinds
differ only in what happens to rows that find no partner:

| Join | Matched pairs | Unmatched left rows | Unmatched right rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[INNER] JOIN` | kept | dropped | dropped |
| `LEFT [OUTER] JOIN` | kept | kept, right side NULL | dropped |
| `RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN` | kept | dropped | kept, left side NULL |
| `FULL [OUTER] JOIN` | kept | kept | kept |
| `CROSS JOIN` | every combination, no condition | | |

A self join is not a separate kind: it is any of the above with the same table on both
sides under two aliases.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python/pandas: `merge(how="inner" | "left" | "right" | "outer" | "cross")` maps
  one-to-one onto these joins, including the NaN padding (NULL here).
- Go/TS: a join is the nested loop or the map lookup you would write by hand (build a
  map by `requirementId`, then probe it per row). The planner picks between those
  strategies from table sizes; you only state the condition.
- JS: an inner join is a `flatMap` that emits one pair per match; a left join is the same
  `flatMap` emitting `{ ...r, test: null }` when the match list is empty.
- Java/JPA: forgetting to join is what produces the N+1 query problem. One join is one
  round trip.

## Design notes

Before writing an outer join, decide which side may be missing and put the preserved
table first, then use LEFT JOIN consistently; mixing LEFT and RIGHT in one query is hard
to read. Conditions on the optional side belong in ON, filters on the preserved side in
WHERE.

Keep join conditions on keys the schema declares (foreign key to primary key) wherever
possible: they are indexed and they can't drift. Expression joins such as `lower(a.title)
= lower(b.title)` are legitimate for analysis and clean-up, and the Turkish example shows
why their collation has to be chosen on purpose.

lessons.title: Many-to-many via junction tables; semi-joins (EXISTS); anti-joins (NOT IN NULL trap)
lessons.summary: A many-to-many relationship is a table of links. EXISTS asks "is there at least one?" without repeating rows, and NOT EXISTS asks "is there none?" safely, while NOT IN returns nothing once its subquery yields a NULL.

examples.title: The trace-link table: composite key, cascades, idempotent linking

annotations.note: The junction table needs no id of its own: the pair is the identity. The composite primary key forbids duplicate links, makes both columns NOT NULL and builds an index starting with requirement_id. Attributes of the link itself (who linked, when, which kind) go here too.
CASCADE on both sides: a link means nothing once either end is gone. Compare the RESTRICT on test runs in the foreign keys lesson, where the child was evidence.

A multicolumn B-tree is most efficient for conditions on its leading column, so the key index serves "tests of this requirement". The reverse question, "requirements of this test", gets its own index.
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (from the modifying-data module) skips the duplicate: INSERT 0 0. Linking becomes idempotent, so a retried API request doesn't fail.
Two joins walk the relationship: requirement to link to test case. Each requirement appears once per linked test; REQ-EXPORT has no links and drops out of the inner joins.
Deleting test 11 removes its links to both requirements in the same statement: (1, 11) and (2, 11) are gone.

examples.title: Semi-joins with EXISTS, and 'verified' as EXISTS plus NOT EXISTS

annotations.note: last_passed NULL means "never run". A nullable boolean has three states, and every query on it has to handle the third (line 33).
The join repeats a requirement once per link. SELECT DISTINCT would hide that, but it still builds every pair first, and it stops working the moment you also select a column from the link side.

EXISTS returns each requirement at most once and can stop at the first matching link. The select list inside is ignored; SELECT 1 is the convention. r.id IN (SELECT requirement_id FROM trace_links) is the same semi-join, and PG 18 plans both identically here.
"Every linked test passed" is written as "no linked test failed to pass", plus EXISTS so a requirement without tests isn't verified vacuously. REQ-RESET is out because test 12 never ran.
IS NOT TRUE counts NULL as not passed. With last_passed = false, test 12's NULL would match nothing and REQ-RESET would wrongly count as verified.

examples.title: The NOT IN NULL trap, and NOT EXISTS as the fix

annotations.note: A legitimate nullable foreign key: ad-hoc runs belong to no test case. Nothing about the schema hints at the trap below.
While the subquery returns only 10, 10 and 12, NOT IN is correct: Locked account (11) never ran.

The same query, after one NULL arrived: 11 NOT IN (10, 10, 12, NULL) is 11 <> 10 AND ... AND 11 <> NULL, which is NULL, and WHERE keeps only true. Every row fails the same way: no rows, no error, no warning.
The trap in isolation. Without the NULL the answer is true; with it, NULL.

NOT EXISTS asks whether a matching row exists, and the NULL row simply doesn't match. EXPLAIN shows it as an Anti Join; NOT IN can't be planned that way because of its NULL semantics and runs as a filter over a hashed SubPlan.

LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is the same anti-join. Test a column that is never NULL in real rows (r.id, the primary key); testing a nullable column would also keep matched rows that happen to hold NULL there.

use_cases: Trace links between requirements and test cases, tags on articles, users in groups, products in categories
EXISTS: 'has at least one' filters, such as requirements with tests or customers with an open order
NOT EXISTS: coverage gaps, never-run tests, orphan detection, and 'all X satisfy Y' written as 'no X violates Y'
strengths: The junction table's composite primary key makes links unique and indexed, with no surrogate id
EXISTS never duplicates outer rows and may stop at the first match, unlike JOIN plus DISTINCT
NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and is planned as an anti-join
weaknesses: Every many-to-many traversal costs two joins, and the reverse direction needs its own index
NOT IN (subquery) is only correct while the subquery can never yield NULL, and it is not planned as an anti-join
EXISTS can't return columns of the inner table; when you need them, you need a join or LATERAL

pitfalls.title: NOT IN over a nullable column
pitfalls.detail: One NULL in the subquery result makes NOT IN NULL for every row, and the query returns nothing. Use NOT EXISTS, which also plans better.
pitfalls.bad: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT test_case_id FROM test_runs)
pitfalls.good: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id)

pitfalls.title: JOIN plus DISTINCT for an existence question
pitfalls.detail: It builds every pair and then removes duplicates; EXISTS asks the actual question and returns each outer row once.

pitfalls.title: A junction table without a unique pair
pitfalls.detail: A surrogate id with no UNIQUE (requirement_id, test_case_id) lets the same link be inserted twice, and every count over links is then wrong. Make the pair the primary key or at least unique.

pitfalls.title: Checking a nullable column in LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
pitfalls.detail: WHERE r.test_case_id IS NULL can't tell 'no match' from 'matched a row whose column is NULL'. Check a NOT NULL column of the right side, usually its primary key.

quiz.q: test_runs.test_case_id contains one NULL. What does `SELECT ... FROM test_cases WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT test_case_id FROM test_runs)` return?
options: The test cases that never ran
quiz.why: For every row, x NOT IN (..., NULL) is either false or NULL, never true, so WHERE keeps nothing.

quiz.q: A requirement has five linked tests. How many times does it appear in `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trace_links l WHERE l.requirement_id = r.id)`?
quiz.why: EXISTS is a semi-join: it only asks whether a match exists, so each outer row appears at most once.

quiz.q: What is the result of `SELECT 11 NOT IN (10, NULL)`?
quiz.why: 11 <> 10 is true, 11 <> NULL is NULL, and true AND NULL is NULL.

quiz.q: Why does the junction table use `PRIMARY KEY (requirement_id, test_case_id)`?
options: Every table needs an integer id
It forbids duplicate links and indexes lookups by requirement
quiz.why: The pair is the link's identity; the key enforces uniqueness and its index leads with requirement_id. Cascading comes from the foreign keys.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Subquery Expressions (EXISTS, IN, NOT IN)
PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (foreign keys, with a many-to-many example)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Relational tables have no "list of ids" column that the database can check. A
many-to-many relationship (a requirement is verified by many test cases, a test case
covers many requirements) is a table of its own with one row per link: a **junction**
table. Its primary key is the pair, and it has a foreign key to each side.

Two query shapes go with it. A **semi-join** returns rows of A that have at least one
match in B, each at most once: `EXISTS` or `IN (subquery)`. An **anti-join** returns rows
of A with no match in B: `NOT EXISTS`, or `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.key IS NULL`. `NOT IN`
looks like an anti-join and isn't one when NULLs are involved.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/JPA: `@ManyToMany` generates exactly this join table and hides it. Mapping it as
  its own entity is what lets you add attributes to the link.
- Go/TS: in code you would keep a slice or `Set` of ids on one side. In a table that is
  the comma-separated-list (or id array) anti-pattern: no foreign key can check it.
- JS: `EXISTS` is `tests.some(...)`, `NOT EXISTS` is `!tests.some(...)`, and the
  "verified" query is `tests.length > 0 && tests.every(t => t.lastPassed === true)`.
  `Array.prototype.includes` is two-valued, so JS has no equivalent of the NOT IN trap.

## Design notes

Prefer EXISTS and NOT EXISTS for "has any" and "has none" questions, and reserve joins
for when you need columns from both sides. Treat `NOT IN (subquery)` as a review
finding unless the column is declared NOT NULL; even then NOT EXISTS says the same thing
and is planned as an anti-join. `NOT IN` over a literal list (`status NOT IN ('done',
'dropped')`) is fine as long as no NULL can appear in the list.

Name the junction table after the relationship (`trace_links`) once the link has
meaning of its own, and give it the index for the reverse direction from the start.

lessons.title: LATERAL joins
lessons.summary: A LATERAL subquery or function in FROM can read columns of the items before it, so it runs per row and may return any number of rows and columns: top-N per group, expanding arrays and series, and naming intermediate expressions.

examples.title: The latest two runs per test case with LEFT JOIN LATERAL

annotations.note: This index matches the subquery's WHERE and ORDER BY. On a large table, each per-test lookup can then read just the newest two index entries and stop, however many runs the test has.

For each test case t, the subquery runs with t.id bound and returns up to two rows of two columns. A scalar subquery in the SELECT list could return one value at most, and a plain join can't apply a LIMIT per group.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true: the correlation lives inside the subquery, so ON has nothing left to test, and true keeps Export CSV with NULLs. CROSS JOIN LATERAL would drop it.
Without LATERAL, each FROM item is evaluated on its own and can't refer to its neighbours, so t.id is an invalid reference (SQLSTATE 42P01).

examples.title: Expanding each row: unnest WITH ORDINALITY and generate_series

annotations.note: unnest is a set-returning function. In FROM, functions may always use columns of earlier items, so LATERAL is optional for them; it is written here for clarity. WITH ORDINALITY (PG 9.4) adds a bigint position starting at 1, so the array's order survives as data.
An empty array produces no rows, so REQ-3 vanished above. LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps it with a NULL tag.
Each sprint expands into one row per day, computed from its own starts and ends. generate_series has no date variant, so the dates are promoted to a timestamp type and d::date converts back.

examples.title: LATERAL as a let binding for computed values

annotations.note: A subquery without FROM computes one row from r's columns. m.ms is now a name that SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY can all use, instead of the same expression written three times.
extract(epoch FROM interval) gives seconds; times 1000 and the cast give whole milliseconds.
ORDER BY may use an output column name (over_budget_ms) because it is evaluated after the SELECT list. WHERE is evaluated before it.
Hence the error: the alias ms doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs (SQLSTATE 42703). Repeating the expression, a subquery or CTE, or the LATERAL above are the ways around it.

use_cases: Top-N per group: latest runs per test case, last three orders per customer
Expanding arrays, jsonb arrays (jsonb_array_elements) and generated series per row
Calling a set-returning function with arguments taken from each row
Naming an intermediate computation once and using it in WHERE and ORDER BY
strengths: Returns several columns and several rows per outer row, which a scalar subquery can't
Top-N per group with ORDER BY ... LIMIT inside can read a few index entries per group, where a window function ranks every row first
Combines with LEFT JOIN ... ON true to keep outer rows that produce nothing
weaknesses: It is a per-row loop: with many outer rows and no supporting index, the subquery runs that many times
CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops outer rows whose subquery or function returns nothing
When nothing depends on the current row, a plain join or a window function says the same thing more simply

pitfalls.title: Correlating in ON instead of inside the subquery
pitfalls.detail: With the condition in ON, the subquery's ORDER BY ... LIMIT 2 picks the newest two runs of the whole table, and ON then keeps only the ones belonging to t. Most test cases get nothing. Put the correlation inside and write ON true.
pitfalls.bad: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM test_runs ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 2) r ON r.test_case_id = t.id
pitfalls.good: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 2) r ON true

pitfalls.title: LIMIT without ORDER BY
pitfalls.detail: Inside the subquery, LIMIT 2 without ORDER BY returns two arbitrary rows. 'Latest' needs an ORDER BY, ideally backed by an index.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL where rows may produce nothing
pitfalls.detail: Empty arrays, test cases without runs and NULL arguments make the outer row disappear. Use LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true when every outer row must stay.

quiz.q: Why `ON true` in `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id ...) last ON true`?
options: The correlation is inside the subquery, and true keeps outer rows without matches
It turns the join into a cross join
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN needs an ON clause; the matching already happened inside, so ON true just preserves outer rows that got no inner rows.

quiz.q: A requirement has tags '{}'. What does `CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(r.tags)` produce for it?
quiz.why: unnest of an empty array returns no rows, and a cross join with nothing is nothing. LEFT JOIN ... ON true would keep it.

quiz.q: Do you need the LATERAL keyword for `FROM requirements r, unnest(r.tags)`?
options: No, function calls in FROM may reference earlier items anyway
quiz.why: For functions the keyword is optional; for subqueries it is required.

quiz.q: Why does `SELECT x * 2 AS y FROM t WHERE y > 10` fail?
options: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list defines y
quiz.why: Output aliases exist only after SELECT is computed; ORDER BY can use them, WHERE can't.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A subquery in FROM is normally evaluated independently: it can't see the other items in
the FROM list. Marked `LATERAL`, it may reference columns of the items to its left, so
it is evaluated once for each of their rows, and whatever it returns, zero rows or many,
each with several columns, is joined to that row. Function calls in FROM behave this way
without the keyword.

Three patterns cover most uses: top-N per group (`ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` inside), expanding
a row into several (`unnest`, `generate_series`, `jsonb_array_elements`), and naming a
computed value so later clauses can use it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- JS/TS: `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` is `flatMap`:
  `cases.flatMap(t => runs.filter(r => r.caseId === t.id).sort(byNewest).slice(0, 2))`.
  `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is the same `flatMap` that emits one padded row when the
  inner list is empty.
- Go: it is the nested loop with a query per row, except it runs as one statement in one
  round trip instead of N+1 queries.
- Python: a nested comprehension where the inner iterable depends on the outer variable:
  `[(t, r) for t in cases for r in latest_runs(t, 2)]`.

## Design notes

Reach for LATERAL when the right-hand side depends on the current row and must return
more than one value. For a single value per row, a scalar subquery reads more simply.
For ranking or running totals over the whole set, window functions (a later module) are
the tool; LATERAL wins for top-N when an index lets each group stop after N rows.

Keep the correlation inside the subquery and the ON clause `true`. A condition moved
into ON is applied after the subquery's LIMIT, which silently changes the answer.

lessons.title: json vs jsonb; the operators ->, ->>, @>, ?
lessons.summary: -> walks a jsonb document and keeps jsonb, ->> ends the walk with text; a JSON null and a missing key are different things. @> tests whether a document contains a shape, ? whether a key or string element exists. ||, -, #-, jsonb_set and subscripts change documents, with traps around NULL.

examples.title: Navigating a document: ->, ->>, #>>, array indexes, and JSON null vs SQL NULL

annotations.note: -> returns jsonb: number_jsonb is the JSON number 108, still of type jsonb. ->> returns text: main, without the quotes. Walk with -> and use ->> only at the last step, when you want the value.
#>> takes the whole path as a text array. Event 2 has no agent, and the docs' rule applies: extraction operators return NULL instead of failing when the document doesn't have the requested structure.
JSON array positions are 0-based, unlike SQL arrays (1-based), and -1 is the last element. Event 2's empty tags array has no element 0, which is NULL again rather than an error.

Event 1 has "retry_of": null, event 2 has no such key. -> returns the JSON value null for the first (a real jsonb value, so IS NULL is false) and SQL NULL for the second. ->> turns both into SQL NULL. Only ? and jsonb_typeof tell them apart.
'9' > '100' as text, because the character 9 sorts after 1, so event 2 passes a filter it should fail. The same happens in ORDER BY on a ->> value.
Two correct forms: cast the text (an expression index can serve this one, see the indexing lesson), or compare jsonb with jsonb, which compares numbers numerically.
SQLSTATE 42883: there is no text = integer operator. Compare with a string ('108'), cast, or ask with containment: payload @> '{"build": {"number": 108}}'.

examples.title: @> containment and the ? existence operators, and what json lacks

annotations.note: Containment is anchored at the root: the pattern's shape must match the document's from the top. {"branch": "main"} would need a top-level branch key, and no event has one.
Array containment ignores order and duplicates: ["smoke", "nightly"] is contained in ["nightly", "smoke"]. Event 2 has only smoke.

A string is not a one-element array: {"tags": "smoke"} matches nothing. The docs' exception, an array containing a bare primitive, shows up when you compare the array itself, as payload -> 'tags' @> '"smoke"' does.

A pattern element matches any array element that contains it: some result has status failed. A pattern object with two keys must find both in the same element; status from one result and test from another don't combine.
? looks at top-level keys only. branch lives under build, so nested_key is false everywhere; payload -> 'build' ? 'branch' would be true.
On an array, ? tests for string elements; ?| means any of the list, ?& all of it. Strings only: '[1, 2]'::jsonb ? '1' is false.
jsonb compares numbers as numbers and objects key by key, so the two documents are equal. It still prints 120.0 as written: JSON numbers are stored as numeric, which keeps trailing zeros.
SQLSTATE 42883. json stores the text and offers only the extraction operators (->, ->>, #>, #>>): no containment, existence, equality or GIN index. Cast to jsonb, or store jsonb in the first place.

examples.title: Changing documents: shallow ||, subscripts, jsonb_set, - and #-, and the NULL trap

annotations.note: || merges top-level keys, and the right side's value wins whole: notify lost email. The docs say it outright: || does not operate recursively.
Subscript assignment (PG 14) creates or replaces one nested value. The right-hand side must be jsonb, hence the quoted 'true'.
jsonb_set does the same with a text[] path, and adds the key because create_if_missing defaults to true. All earlier steps of the path must exist, or the document comes back unchanged.
- removes a top-level key, #- removes the value at a path. Both are ordinary operators, applied left to right here.

to_jsonb(NULL) is SQL NULL, and jsonb_set returns NULL when given one. In an UPDATE that sets the whole column to NULL, or fails if it is NOT NULL. jsonb_set_lax (PG 13) writes a JSON null by default, or deletes the key, raises an error or returns the document unchanged.

use_cases: Reading fields from stored webhook payloads, third-party API responses and event logs
Filtering semi-structured rows by shape: events on branch main with any failed result (@>)
Per-project settings and feature flags: test for a key (?), change one nested value (subscripts, jsonb_set)
String lists inside documents, such as tags: ?| for any of, ?& for all of
strengths: @> says 'has this nested shape' in one operator that a GIN index can serve, where Go or Java code would decode and walk the tree
Extraction never throws on a missing key or a different shape; it returns NULL, which suits documents whose structure varies
jsonb comparisons are semantic: key order, whitespace and 120 vs 120.0 don't matter, unlike comparing JSON text
Partial updates (subscripts, jsonb_set, -, #-) happen inside one UPDATE, without a read-modify-write round trip through the application
weaknesses: ->> returns text, so numbers and dates need casts, and a forgotten cast compares strings without any error
A missing key, a JSON null and a mistyped path all come back as NULL through ->>, so a typo in a key name fails silently
|| is shallow and jsonb_set returns NULL for a NULL value: two easy ways to lose data in an UPDATE
Changing one key writes a new version of the whole row and locks it, so big, frequently updated documents contend

pitfalls.title: Comparing ->> output as text
pitfalls.detail: '9' > '100' is true for strings. Cast the extracted text, or compare jsonb values.
pitfalls.good: WHERE (payload -> 'build' ->> 'number')::int > 100

pitfalls.title: Testing a JSON null with -> ... IS NULL
pitfalls.detail: -> returns the JSON value null, which is not SQL NULL. If null and missing mean the same to you, test the ->> result; if they differ, use ? or jsonb_typeof.
pitfalls.good: WHERE payload ->> 'retry_of' IS NULL

pitfalls.title: Deep merge with ||
pitfalls.detail: The right-hand object replaces the left one's nested objects whole. Set the nested value instead.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE project_settings SET prefs = prefs || '{"notify": {"slack": true}}'
pitfalls.good: UPDATE project_settings SET prefs['notify']['slack'] = 'true'

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set with a value that may be NULL
pitfalls.detail: A NULL parameter makes jsonb_set return NULL, and the UPDATE erases the document (or fails on NOT NULL). Use jsonb_set_lax and say what NULL should mean.
pitfalls.good: SET prefs = jsonb_set_lax(prefs, '{theme}', to_jsonb($1::text), true, 'delete_key')

pitfalls.title: Casting a JSON null on older servers
pitfalls.detail: Since PostgreSQL 18, (payload -> 'retry_of')::int returns NULL for a JSON null; earlier versions raise an error. Code that must also run on older servers should cast the ->> text instead.

quiz.q: payload is {"retry_of": null}. What does `payload -> 'retry_of' IS NULL` return?
quiz.why: -> returns the JSON value null, a non-NULL jsonb value. ->> would return SQL NULL.

quiz.q: What does `'{"tags": ["a", "b"]}'::jsonb @> '{"tags": "b"}'` return?
options: true, because b is in the array
false, because inside an object a string doesn't match an array
quiz.why: Containment compares structure from the root; the primitive-in-array exception only applies when the array itself is compared, as in payload -> 'tags' @> '"b"'.

quiz.q: build.number is 9 in one row and 108 in another. Which condition selects only 108?
quiz.why: The first compares text ('9' > '100' is true); the third looks for a top-level number key, which doesn't exist.

quiz.q: prefs is {"notify": {"email": true, "slack": false}}. What is `prefs || '{"notify": {"slack": true}}'`?
quiz.why: || merges only the top level; the right side's notify object replaces the left one whole.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: json and jsonb operators
PostgreSQL docs: jsonb Containment and Existence
PostgreSQL docs: JSON processing functions (jsonb_set, jsonb_set_lax)

lessons.body:
## Concept

The jsonb lesson in the types module showed the storage difference: `json` keeps an exact copy of the
input text, `jsonb` stores it parsed (keys deduplicated and reordered, whitespace gone).
For querying, the consequence is that `json` only has the four extraction operators;
everything else in this lesson is `jsonb`-only. Use `json` when the exact text matters,
for example a webhook body whose signature was computed over its bytes, and `jsonb` for
everything you query.

The operators, by job:

- **Navigate:** `->` takes a key or a 0-based array index (negative counts from the
  end) and returns `jsonb`; `->>` does the same and returns `text`; `#>` and `#>>` take a
  whole path as `text[]`. A path that doesn't exist yields NULL, never an error.
- **Null:** a key holding JSON `null` is not the same as a missing key. `->` returns
  the jsonb value `null` for the first and SQL NULL for the second; `->>` returns SQL
  NULL for both.
- **Test:** `@>` asks whether the left document contains the right one's shape (`<@`
  is the reverse). `?`, `?|` and `?&` ask whether a string exists as a top-level key or
  as a string element of an array.
- **Change:** `||` merges or concatenates (shallowly), `-` and `#-` delete, `jsonb_set`
  and subscript assignment (`doc['a']['b'] = ...`, PG 14) replace one nested value.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS:** `payload #>> '{build,agent,os}'` is `payload?.build?.agent?.os`, with NULL for
  `undefined`. JSON null versus a missing key is JS's `null` versus `undefined`, and
  `payload ? 'retry_of'` is `'retry_of' in payload`.
- **Python:** `->` chains are `d.get('build', {}).get('agent')`; `?` is `key in d`;
  `@>` is a recursive "is a subset of" check that you would otherwise write by hand.
- **Go:** decoding into a struct, a `*int` field is nil both for `null` and for a
  missing key, so Go can't tell them apart without `json.RawMessage` or a map lookup;
  SQL can, with `?`. pgx uses `$1` placeholders, so the `?` operators cause no trouble.
- **Java:** JDBC uses `?` as the parameter placeholder. With PgJDBC, write the operators
  as `??` in a `PreparedStatement`, or use `@>`, which has no question mark.
- **Everyone:** `->>` hands you text. Comparisons and sorting on it are text operations
  until you cast, whereas a JSON decoder in your language would have given you 108 as a
  number.

## Design notes

Filter with operators an index can serve and extract in the `SELECT` list. `WHERE
payload @> '{"build": {"branch": "main"}}'` and `WHERE payload -> 'build' ->> 'branch' =
'main'` ask the same question, but only the first can use a GIN index on `payload` (the
GIN lesson); the second needs an expression index of its own (the indexing lesson in this
module).

Decide once what "absent" means. If a JSON `null` and a missing key mean the same thing,
strip nulls on write (`jsonb_strip_nulls`) or always test the `->>` result; if they
differ, test with `?` and say so in a comment.

Update narrowly: subscripts or `jsonb_set` for nested values, `jsonb_set_lax` when the
new value comes from a parameter that may be NULL, and `||` only for top-level keys.
Every one of these writes a new version of the whole row and takes its row lock. A key
that several writers update independently, or that every query filters on, has outgrown
the document; the indexing lesson shows how to promote it to a column.

PostgreSQL 18 changed one detail: casting a JSON `null` to a scalar type, as in
`(payload -> 'retry_of')::int`, now returns NULL; earlier versions raise an error.

lessons.title: SQL/JSON path and JSON_TABLE (PG 17)
lessons.summary: SQL/JSON path (PG 12) walks and filters inside a document: [*], ? (@ ...), $variables, lax or strict. PG 17's JSON_TABLE turns a document into typed rows, with NESTED PATH for child arrays, and JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY and JSON_EXISTS extract with explicit ON EMPTY and ON ERROR behaviour.

examples.title: jsonpath: filters, variables, @?, and lax vs strict mode

annotations.note: Read the path left to right: $ is the document, .suites[*] every suite, .tests[*] every test, ? (...) keeps the tests whose status is "failed", .title takes their title. jsonb_path_query is set-returning: one output row per match, so report 2, with no failure, has no row at all. The values are jsonb, hence "Çıkış" in quotes.

$max is a path variable, supplied as a jsonb object: the jsonpath form of a bind parameter, so no value is spliced into the path text. Report 2's "slow" is a string, "slow" > 500 is unknown in SQL/JSON's three-valued logic, and the filter drops the test without a word.
@? asks "does the path return anything?". Together with @@ (for predicates such as '$.build > 100') it is the form a GIN index on report can serve; the path functions are not.
size() counts array elements: 2 and 1. Lax mode makes an exception for size() and type() and doesn't unwrap the array first; otherwise size() would run on each suite object and return 1.
No [*] anywhere: in lax mode an accessor applied to an array is applied to each element. Convenient, and also why a lax path accepts data shaped differently from what you expected.
Lax mode also suppresses the missing-key error. Only Çıkış has an error key; the other tests contribute nothing.

SQLSTATE 2203A. strict mode raises structural errors, here a test without an error key, instead of skipping them. Use it when the document has a contract; for optional keys in strict mode, filter with exists (@.error) first.

examples.title: JSON_TABLE: one row per test, NESTED PATH, and an import that fails loudly

annotations.note: JSON_TABLE (PG 17) sits in FROM and is joined laterally to each ci_reports row, so it can read r.report. The row path $.suites[*] makes one row per suite.
FOR ORDINALITY numbers the rows from 1. Each NESTED PATH has its own counter, so test_no restarts in every suite; together they keep the document's order as data.
NESTED PATH makes child rows joined to their parent: one row per test, suite columns repeated. export has no tests and still appears once, with NULL test columns, as a LEFT JOIN would show it.
In report 2, Giriş's "slow" and Çıkış's missing ms both come out NULL: a column defaults to NULL ON EMPTY and NULL ON ERROR, so a type error and an absent value look the same.
An EXISTS column is true when its path finds anything: a cheap "has an error" flag that doesn't extract the value.
For loading, the row path starts at $ to pick up build once, then nests suites and tests. The JSON_TABLE output feeds INSERT ... SELECT directly: the document becomes rows in one statement.
DEFAULT 0 ON EMPTY fills a missing ms; ERROR ON ERROR turns "slow" into SQLSTATE 22P02, and the whole INSERT fails instead of storing a silent NULL. A failed import is better than a wrong dashboard.

examples.title: JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY, JSON_EXISTS: RETURNING, PASSING, ON EMPTY, ON ERROR

annotations.note: JSON_VALUE returns one scalar, as text unless RETURNING names a type: the JSON string "108" becomes the integer 108.
RETURNING timestamptz parses the ISO 8601 string. The Z (UTC) instant is displayed in the session's time zone: 09:12+03.

ON EMPTY applies only when the path finds nothing: report 2 has no owner and gets 'nobody'. Report 1's owner is JSON null, which is an item; JSON_VALUE turns it into SQL NULL and the default isn't used.
JSON_QUERY returns JSON. A path that yields several items needs WITH WRAPPER to collect them into an array; without it, several items are an error, and errors become NULL by default.
PASSING binds the SQL value 500 to $max: the standard spelling of the vars argument in example 1.
ON ERROR and ON EMPTY default to NULL, so "more than one value", "not a scalar" and "not there" are three different problems with the same answer.
SQLSTATE 22034 names the actual problem. Wherever a NULL would be stored or displayed as if it were data, ask for ERROR ON ERROR.

use_cases: Importing JSON exports and API responses into tables with one INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM JSON_TABLE
Questions about nested arrays without unnesting by hand: failed tests inside suites inside a CI report
Parameterized filters over stored payloads: tests slower than $max, events of a given type
Typed extraction with validation in a staging step: JSON_VALUE ... RETURNING date ERROR ON ERROR
strengths: One path expression replaces chains of ->, jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL joins for nested arrays
JSON_TABLE yields typed columns and ordinality, so a document becomes rows that join, group and insert like any table
Path variables ($max, PASSING) keep values out of the path text, as bind parameters do for SQL
Per column or call you choose what missing or malformed data means (NULL, DEFAULT, ERROR), which is more control than a JSON decoder's all-or-nothing
weaknesses: Lax mode and the NULL defaults hide malformed data: a misspelled key or a string where a number belongs simply disappears
jsonpath is a second language inside SQL, with its own syntax (==, &&, like_regex), its own three-valued logic and its own case rules
JSON_TABLE and the SQL/JSON query functions need PostgreSQL 17; older servers need jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL for the same job
Index support comes only through operators (@?, @@, @>, ?); the path functions and JSON_TABLE in a WHERE clause read every document

pitfalls.title: Using lax mode as validation
pitfalls.detail: Lax paths unwrap arrays and skip missing keys, so a document of the wrong shape returns less data instead of an error. Use strict mode, or ERROR ON ERROR, where shape matters.
pitfalls.good: jsonb_path_query_array(report, 'strict $.suites[*].tests[*].ms')

pitfalls.title: Building a path from user input
pitfalls.detail: Concatenating a value into the path lets the value change the path's structure (a quote ends the string literal). Pass it as a variable.
pitfalls.good: jsonb_path_exists(report, '$.suites[*] ? (@.name == $name)', jsonb_build_object('name', $1))

pitfalls.title: JSON_TABLE columns that swallow errors
pitfalls.detail: By default a wrong type becomes NULL, indistinguishable from a missing value. Say ERROR ON ERROR on required columns of an import.
pitfalls.good: ms int PATH '$.ms' DEFAULT 0 ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR

pitfalls.title: jsonb_path_query in the SELECT list drops rows
pitfalls.detail: It is set-returning: a document with no match produces no row at all. Use jsonb_path_query_array or jsonb_path_query_first to keep one row per document.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive like_regex and Turkish letters
pitfalls.detail: flag "i" pairs letters by the database's default collation, not Turkish rules; under StackLab's builtin C.UTF-8 locale that is Unicode's simple case mapping. On StackLab's PostgreSQL 18.7, '^izmir' with flag "i" matches IZMIR but not İzmir, and '^ığdır' matches Iğdır. For Turkish case-insensitive search, extract the text and use the search module's ICU tools.

quiz.q: In lax mode, what does `$.suites.tests.title` return for {"suites": [{"tests": [{"title": "A"}]}]}?
quiz.why: In lax mode an accessor applied to an array is applied to each of its elements; strict mode would raise an error instead.

quiz.q: A JSON_TABLE column `ms int PATH '$.ms'` meets "ms": "slow". What happens by default?
quiz.why: Column-level ON ERROR defaults to NULL; ERROR ON ERROR makes it fail with SQLSTATE 22P02.

quiz.q: The report has "owner": null. What does `JSON_VALUE(report, '$.owner' DEFAULT 'nobody' ON EMPTY)` return?
quiz.why: The path found an item, the JSON null, so the result isn't empty; JSON_VALUE returns SQL NULL for a JSON null.

quiz.q: Why pass `'{"max": 500}'` as the vars argument instead of concatenating 500 into the path?
options: The value can't change the path's structure: it is the jsonpath form of a bind parameter
quiz.why: Variables are values, never syntax, exactly like $1 in a prepared SQL statement.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: The SQL/JSON Path Language
PostgreSQL docs: Strict and Lax Modes

lessons.body:
## Concept

The operators from the previous lesson address one value at a time. For nested arrays
("every failed test in every suite") and for turning documents into rows, PostgreSQL
implements two layers of the SQL standard.

**SQL/JSON path** (PG 12) is a small language, passed as a `jsonpath` value, that
addresses items inside one document: `$` is the document, `.key` a member, `[n]` and
`[*]` array elements, `? (condition)` a filter in which `@` is the item being tested,
`$name` a variable, and methods such as `.size()`, `.type()` and `.datetime()`. A path
runs in **lax** mode (the default: arrays are unwrapped automatically, structural errors
such as missing keys are suppressed) or **strict** mode (they are raised). The functions
are `jsonb_path_query` (one row per item), `jsonb_path_query_array`,
`jsonb_path_query_first`, `jsonb_path_exists` and `jsonb_path_match`, plus the
operators `@?` and `@@`.

**SQL/JSON query functions** (PG 17) use the same paths with standard syntax and
explicit error handling:

- `JSON_VALUE` extracts one scalar and casts it with `RETURNING`.
- `JSON_QUERY` extracts JSON (`WITH WRAPPER` collects several items into an array).
- `JSON_EXISTS` tests whether the path finds anything.
- `JSON_TABLE` turns a document into rows: a row path, typed columns with their own
  paths, `FOR ORDINALITY`, `EXISTS` columns, and `NESTED PATH` for child arrays.

Each of them lets you choose what happens `ON EMPTY` (the path found nothing) and `ON
ERROR` (wrong type, several items where one was expected, a structural error in strict
mode): `NULL` (the default for values), `DEFAULT expr`, or `ERROR`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript/JS:** the path in example 1 is
  `report.suites.flatMap(s => s.tests).filter(t => t.status === 'failed').map(t => t.title)`.
  `JSON_TABLE` is what you'd do with zod and a loop: parse, check each field's type,
  emit rows. The difference is the default: zod throws on a bad field, `JSON_TABLE`
  quietly writes NULL until you say `ERROR ON ERROR`.
- **Python:** `pandas.json_normalize(report, record_path=['suites', 'tests'],
  meta=['build'])` is `JSON_TABLE` with nested paths.
- **Go:** `encoding/json` decoding "slow" into an `int` field reports an
  `UnmarshalTypeError`. `ERROR ON ERROR` gives you that strictness inside SQL; the default
  is more lenient than Go.
- **XML users:** jsonpath plays the role of XPath, and `JSON_TABLE` is the JSON
  counterpart of `XMLTABLE`, which PostgreSQL also has.

## How it works

`JSON_TABLE` behaves like a set-returning function in `FROM`: it is evaluated for each
row of the tables before it, which is why it can read `r.report` without the `LATERAL`
keyword. The row path produces parent rows; each `NESTED PATH` produces child rows that
are joined to their parent, and a parent without children is kept with NULL child
columns. Sibling `NESTED PATH`s at the same level are combined with `UNION`, not
multiplied.

In a filter, comparisons follow SQL/JSON's three-valued logic: comparing a string with a
number yields *unknown*, and the filter keeps only items for which the condition is
true. That is how report 2's `"ms": "slow"` vanished from example 1 without an error.

## Design notes

Use `JSON_TABLE` at the boundary. When a document arrives (an import, a webhook, an
export from another system), turn it into rows once and work relationally from there.
Per column, decide the contract: required fields get `ERROR ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR`,
optional ones `DEFAULT ... ON EMPTY`. A parent without children still yields one row
with NULL child columns, so an import of tests should filter `WHERE title IS NOT NULL`
or treat that row deliberately.

Prefer strict mode or explicit `ERROR ON ERROR` where the document has a contract; keep
lax mode for exploring heterogeneous data. Pass values as variables, never by string
concatenation.

For filters on stored documents that must be fast, write them with `@?`, `@@` or `@>`,
which a GIN index can serve (next lesson). The path functions and `JSON_TABLE` in a
`WHERE` clause read every document.

Case-insensitive `like_regex` (flag "i") folds case through the database's default
collation: the source compiles the regex with it (src/backend/utils/adt/jsonpath_exec.c,
function executeLikeRegex). StackLab's database uses the builtin `C.UTF-8` locale, whose
case mapping the docs (Locale Support) call the "simple" variant, and the regex engine
applies it per character (src/backend/regex/regc_pg_locale.c, pg_wc_tolower and
pg_wc_toupper): a lower-case i in the pattern matches i and I, never İ, and ı matches I.
Observed on PostgreSQL 18.7: '^izmir' matched izmir and IZMIR but not İzmir, '^ığdır'
matched ığdır, Iğdır and IĞDIR. Another database may have another default collation:
`datlocprovider` in `pg_database` names the provider, and `datlocale` (for libc,
`datctype`) the locale.

lessons.title: Indexing jsonb, building JSON responses in SQL, when a real column wins
lessons.summary: GIN serves containment and jsonpath matches; ranges and sorting on one key need a B-tree on the exact expression the query writes. json keeps the key order you build, jsonb normalizes it. A key that every row has and every query uses wants to be a real, typed, constrained column.

examples.title: GIN for @? and a B-tree expression index for ranges and ORDER BY ... LIMIT

annotations.note: Priority 1 is on 1 % of the tickets, the kvkk label on 2 %: selective conditions, the case where an index pays off.
jsonb_path_ops, the smaller GIN operator class from the GIN lesson: it serves @>, @? and @@, but not the key-existence operators.

A B-tree on an expression. Anything that isn't a plain column or a function call needs its own parentheses, hence the doubled ones. The cast makes it an index of integers, so ranges and sorting compare numbers, not text.
The docs: a new expression index gets statistics only after ANALYZE. Until then the planner has no idea how common priority 1 is and falls back to default estimates.
The jsonpath filter is answered from the GIN index. The plan prints the path in canonical form ($."labels"[*]?(@ == "kvkk")): a jsonpath value is stored parsed, like jsonb.
The 200 priority-1 tickets come from tickets_priority. GIN couldn't help here: <= isn't one of its jsonb operators.

An Index Scan in index order feeds the LIMIT directly: no Sort, and the first five entries read are the answer. For a deterministic top five, add a tie-breaker and index (((doc ->> 'priority')::int), id).

(doc -> 'priority')::int casts jsonb to int (allowed since PG 11) and gives the same numbers, but the planner matches expressions, not meanings: Seq Scan. Keep the indexed expression in one place, such as a view, or promote the key to a column (example 3).

examples.title: Building JSON responses: json vs jsonb key order, whole rows, timestamps, big ids

annotations.note: json_build_object returns json: keys in call order, printed as "key" : value with spaces around the colon. jsonb_build_object returns jsonb: keys stored shorter first (id, code, owner, title) and printed in jsonb's canonical "key": value form. Both are valid JSON; choose json when a client or a snapshot test depends on key order. Turkish text goes out as UTF-8, not as \u escapes.

to_jsonb(row) names keys after columns, so renaming a column renames an API field. - 'id' drops a key; jsonb_strip_nulls drops REQ-2's null owner. For public APIs list the fields explicitly: with to_jsonb, a column added later, say password_hash, would leak.
timestamptz becomes an ISO 8601 string in the session time zone, "2026-11-13T09:00:00+03:00": what JavaScript's Date and Go's time.Time (RFC 3339) parse.

9007199254740993 is exact in jsonb, whose numbers are numeric. A browser's JSON.parse returns 9007199254740992: JavaScript numbers are doubles, exact only up to 2^53 - 1. Send bigint ids as strings, or keep them below that limit.
The subquery-per-list shape from the aggregation lesson: each list is aggregated on its own, and coalesce turns "no tests" into [] instead of NULL.

examples.title: Promoting a key to a STORED generated column with NOT NULL and a foreign key

annotations.note: customer_id and total are in every order; gift_note and coupon only in some. That split is the design question of this lesson.

A STORED generated column computes its value on every write of doc and stores it: a real int column that can be NOT NULL, carry a foreign key and be indexed. doc stays the single source of truth, and the column can never disagree with it. Adding a stored generated column rewrites the table, so on a big table plan it like any rewriting migration.
PostgreSQL 18 makes a generated column VIRTUAL unless you say STORED, and a virtual column can't be indexed or carry a foreign key (both fail with SQLSTATE 0A000). Here STORED is not optional.
The join uses a typed, indexed, constrained column; total still comes out of the document. If every report sums totals, total is the next key to promote.
What remains in the document is genuinely optional data: notes and coupons that vary per order.

SQLSTATE 23503: the foreign key runs on write. A missing customer_id would fail NOT NULL (23502) and a non-numeric one the cast (22P02), also at INSERT time. jsonb alone would have accepted all three.

use_cases: GIN (jsonb_path_ops): filtering event payloads or product attributes by varying keys with @> or jsonpath
B-tree expression index: one hot key used for ranges, sorting or top-N, while the rest stays in the document
JSON built in SQL: API responses with nested lists, CSV-free exports, snapshots for an audit log
STORED generated columns: promoting stable keys of ingested documents (customer, type, created time) to typed, constrained, indexed columns
strengths: One GIN index serves containment and jsonpath filters on any key, without an index per attribute
Expression indexes give one key B-tree powers (ranges, ORDER BY ... LIMIT) and planner statistics, without changing the table
SQL-built JSON is escaped correctly and arrives in one round trip; the Go or TS layer can pass it through
A generated column turns a document field into a real column (types, NOT NULL, foreign keys, statistics) while the document stays the source
weaknesses: GIN can't do ranges or ordering, and an expression index serves only the exact expression it was built on
Statistics on keys inside a document exist only for indexed or declared expressions; everything else is estimated with defaults
json and jsonb render keys differently, and to_jsonb(row) couples API field names to column names
Promotion costs a table rewrite for a stored generated column, and every promoted key is one more place a schema change must reach

pitfalls.title: Writing the expression differently from the index
pitfalls.detail: (doc -> 'k')::int and (doc ->> 'k')::int mean the same thing, but only the indexed spelling uses the index. Put the expression in one view or function, or make it a column.
pitfalls.good: CREATE INDEX ON tickets (((doc ->> 'priority')::int)); ... WHERE (doc ->> 'priority')::int <= 1

pitfalls.title: A generated column without STORED in PostgreSQL 18
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 18 the default is VIRTUAL, computed on read, and a virtual column can't have an index or a foreign key. Say STORED when the column exists to be indexed or referenced.
pitfalls.bad: ADD COLUMN customer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((doc ->> 'customer_id')::int)
pitfalls.good: ADD COLUMN customer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((doc ->> 'customer_id')::int) STORED

pitfalls.title: bigint ids as JSON numbers for JavaScript clients
pitfalls.detail: Ids above 2^53 - 1 lose precision in JSON.parse without any error. Send them as strings (t.id::text), or use ids that stay below the limit.

pitfalls.title: to_jsonb(row) as a public API
pitfalls.detail: Every column, including ones added later, becomes a field. Build the object from an explicit list of keys.
pitfalls.good: SELECT jsonb_build_object('id', u.id::text, 'name', u.name) FROM users u

pitfalls.title: Expecting jsonb to keep the key order you built
pitfalls.detail: jsonb stores keys shorter-first and then bytewise, so id comes before code whatever you wrote. Use the json variants (json_build_object, json_agg) when order matters to a consumer.

quiz.q: There is a GIN index on `doc` (jsonb_path_ops). Which condition can it serve?
quiz.why: jsonb_path_ops supports @>, @? and @@. Ranges are B-tree work, and key existence needs the default jsonb_ops class.

quiz.q: The index is on `((doc ->> 'priority')::int)`. Does `WHERE (doc -> 'priority')::int = 1` use it?
options: No, the planner matches the indexed expression, not its meaning
quiz.why: Index matching is syntactic on the expression tree; -> plus a jsonb-to-int cast is a different expression.

quiz.q: `jsonb_build_object('title', 'x', 'id', 1)` prints as?
quiz.why: jsonb stores keys shorter first; the third form is what json_build_object would print.

quiz.q: Every order has a customer_id that reports join on and that must reference customers. Where should it live?
options: In the jsonb document, with a GIN index
In a column (or a STORED generated column) with NOT NULL and a foreign key
In a VIRTUAL generated column with a foreign key
quiz.why: Only a stored column can be NOT NULL, indexed and referenced by a foreign key; PG 18 rejects foreign keys and indexes on virtual generated columns.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE STATISTICS (statistics on a single expression)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three decisions come with every `jsonb` column.

**How to index it.** The GIN lesson covered the whole-document index: `jsonb_ops` (all
keys and values, serves `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?`, `@@`) and the smaller
`jsonb_path_ops` (`@>`, `@?`, `@@`). GIN finds documents that *contain* something. It
can't answer ranges or sorting, so a key used with `<`, `BETWEEN` or `ORDER BY` needs a
**B-tree expression index** on exactly the expression the query writes, such as
`((doc ->> 'priority')::int)`. An expression index also gives the planner statistics
for that expression after `ANALYZE`; `CREATE STATISTICS ... ON (expression)` (PG 14)
gives the statistics without the index.

**How to build JSON for clients.** `json_build_object`/`jsonb_build_object`, `to_jsonb`
on a row, and the aggregates from the aggregation lesson produce the response document
in SQL. `json` output keeps your key order; `jsonb` output is canonical: keys shorter
first, one space after the colon. Dates become ISO 8601 strings, numbers stay exact
numerics, which JavaScript can't always represent.

**When a column wins.** If every row has the key and queries filter, join, sort or
aggregate on it, or it must be `NOT NULL`, unique or a foreign key, it should be a
column. A `STORED` generated column extracts it from the document on every write, so
ingested payloads stay intact and the column can't drift from them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS/TS:** `JSON.parse` turns every number into a double. Ids above
  `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1) come back rounded, without an error, so bigint ids
  travel as strings. On the way in, a jsonb column is `unknown` until zod has checked it;
  a promoted column is a type the database already checked.
- **Go:** `encoding/json` decodes a JSON number into `float64` when the target is `any`,
  with the same precision problem; a struct field of type `int64`, or the `,string` tag
  option, keeps it exact. pgx can scan a SQL-built JSON column straight into
  `json.RawMessage` and the handler can write it out unchanged.
- **Java:** a jsonb column is like a `Map<String, Object>` field in an entity: flexible,
  and invisible to every constraint and index you'd put on a real field. Promoting a key
  is the same refactoring as replacing a map entry with a typed field.
- **Document databases:** there you index paths inside documents. Postgres gives you
  that (GIN, expression indexes) and also lets you move a hot path into a typed,
  constrained column without leaving the table.

## How it works

The planner considers an expression index when the query contains the indexed
expression itself; an equivalent spelling doesn't count, as the last plan of example 1
shows: `(doc -> 'priority')::int` missed the index that `(doc ->> 'priority')::int` used.
In return, the docs point out, the search is as fast as on a plain column, because the
expression's values are stored in the index and not recomputed (they are computed on
every insert and non-HOT update instead). It also explains why the
generated column is the robust solution: every query writes `customer_id`, and there is
nothing to spell differently.

Without statistics on an expression, the planner falls back to fixed guesses. The
`CREATE STATISTICS` docs give 0.5 % selectivity for equality and range conditions in
that case. A key whose values are very skewed (one tenant with half the rows) is
exactly where that guess goes wrong, and where an expression index or a column, both of
which `ANALYZE` measures, fixes the plans.

## Design notes

Structured where it's stable, JSON where it isn't. Walk each key of a document through
three questions: does every row have it, do queries filter, join, sort or aggregate on
it, and does it need a constraint? Any yes makes it a candidate column. What stays in
the document is the long tail: optional attributes, integration-specific fields, the raw
payload kept for replay.

When the document is the record (an order received from a shop, a webhook you must be
able to replay), promote with a `STORED` generated column and leave the document
untouched. When the application owns the data, make it an ordinary column, backfill it,
and remove the key from the document, so there is one source of truth.

For responses, let SQL build the shape when the response is a straightforward
projection of the data: one round trip, correct escaping, and no N+1 queries. Choose
`json` when key order is part of the contract, list keys explicitly instead of
`to_jsonb(row)` for anything public, and send bigint ids as strings to JavaScript
clients.

lessons.title: From entities to tables: normalization 1NF to BCNF by fixing a messy spreadsheet
lessons.summary: Normalization is "one fact, one place". Find the functional dependencies in the data, give each determinant a table keyed by it, and the keys and foreign keys you declare are those dependencies, enforced on every write.

examples.title: A test log spreadsheet as a table, and its three anomalies

annotations.note: No key and every column nullable: the shape of a spreadsheet. Its real key is (test_code, run_on), one run per test per day. A normalized table holds only columns that depend on its whole key, and here four columns don't.
REQ-1's title is stored in three rows and Mehmet's e-mail in two. Every repetition is a copy that can disagree with the others, and row 3 already does.

A functional dependency check: group by the determinant and count the distinct values that should depend on it. Run it against any import before you design the tables. Every row it returns is a contradiction a person has to resolve.
Without a key, nothing rejects a half-empty row. count(*) now says 5 and count(run_on) says 4, so every aggregate over the sheet has to know which rows aren't really runs.
REQ-2 lived only inside TC-3's run row. Deleting a run shouldn't delete a requirement, but in this shape it does, and nothing reports it.

examples.title: Decompose to 3NF: one table per determinant, then rebuild the sheet with joins

annotations.note: The title depended on the run only through req_code (a transitive dependency, which 3NF forbids). Now req_code is the key of a table that holds the title once. Codes as primary keys keep this example short; the keys lesson explains why a real schema adds a surrogate id and keeps UNIQUE (code).

test_code determines req_code, but test_code is only part of the run's key (test_code, run_on). Storing req_code per run was the 2NF violation. It now lives once per test case, and the foreign key is the link between the two tables.
tester determines the e-mail: the second 3NF fix. UNIQUE (email) also declares the reverse, one address per tester, which the spreadsheet couldn't express at all.
What's left needs the whole key: who ran this test on this day, and the result. The composite primary key is the sheet's implicit key, now enforced, and the CHECK closes the result vocabulary.
1NF: 'smoke, payment' was two values in one field. One row per tag can be matched exactly, counted and referenced. The anti-patterns lesson shows what the comma-separated version breaks.

Normalizing doesn't resolve contradictions, it exposes them. DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per req_code in ORDER BY order, the newest run's title. A plain SELECT DISTINCT req_code, req_title would produce two REQ-1 rows and fail on the primary key.
string_to_table (PG 14) splits on the comma, trim drops the space, and DISTINCT removes TC-1's tags, which the sheet repeated for each of its two runs.

Joining along the foreign keys gives the sheet's columns back: the decomposition is lossless, because each split was on a determinant that became the key of its new table. Every run now shows the one current title.
The dependency req_code -> req_title is now a primary key, so a second title is a duplicate key: SQLSTATE 23505.

examples.title: Beyond 3NF: a dependency whose determinant is not a key

annotations.note: Two candidate keys: (test_code, lab) and (test_code, tester). Every column belongs to one of them, and 3NF only restricts columns that belong to none, so this table is in 3NF.
BCNF's rule is stricter: every determinant must be a candidate key. tester determines lab but isn't a key here, so the fact is repeated per assignment, and the update anomaly is back.

testers is keyed by the determinant. UNIQUE (name, lab) follows from the primary key, but a foreign key must point at a unique constraint or index on exactly its columns; without it the FK below fails with SQLSTATE 42830.

The textbook BCNF split is assignments (test_code, tester), with no lab. That loses "one tester per test per lab", which then spans two tables and can't be a key. Keeping lab as a copy tied to testers by a composite foreign key keeps both rules declarable: deliberate, controlled redundancy, the subject of the next lesson.

ON UPDATE CASCADE carries the changed (name, lab) pair into every assignment, in the same statement. A move to 'ios' would fail with 23505 instead: TC-1 on iOS is Mehmet's, and the primary key still holds.
Zeynep works in android, so (Zeynep, ios) matches no tester row: SQLSTATE 23503. The copy can't drift from its source.

use_cases: Designing tables from a spreadsheet, a CSV export or a legacy table: list the dependencies first, then derive the tables
Cleaning an import: the GROUP BY ... HAVING count(DISTINCT ...) > 1 check lists every contradiction to resolve before loading
Reviewing a schema: a column that depends on part of a key, or on another non-key column, is an update anomaly waiting to happen
Deciding where a new column goes: next to the key that determines it
strengths: A rename or an e-mail change is a one-row UPDATE; in a flat table or a document store it is a multi-row update that a forgotten WHERE or a partial failure leaves inconsistent
The dependencies become PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE and REFERENCES declarations checked on every write, instead of invariants each Go or TS service has to remember
Things exist on their own: a requirement without tests or a tester without runs is a row, not a NULL-padded line
Narrow, keyed tables are what B-tree indexes, joins and the planner's per-column statistics are built for
weaknesses: Reads need joins: the spreadsheet comes back only by joining four tables, which reports and ORMs pay for on every read
BCNF can cost a rule: a dependency that ends up spanning two tables can't be a key and needs a composite foreign key, a trigger or application code
Normalization knows only the current value: a normalized title is today's title, so values that must be frozen (prices on invoices) need a deliberate copy
Over-splitting, such as a table per attribute, adds joins without removing any redundancy; stop where the dependencies stop

pitfalls.title: Loading with SELECT DISTINCT and trusting the result
pitfalls.detail: DISTINCT over (code, title) gives one row per distinct pair, so a contradiction becomes a duplicate key, or, with no key declared, a duplicate entity. Run the dependency check first and resolve what it finds.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO requirements SELECT DISTINCT req_code, req_title FROM sheet;
pitfalls.good: SELECT req_code FROM sheet GROUP BY req_code HAVING count(DISTINCT req_title) > 1;  -- resolve these, then load

pitfalls.title: Adding an id column and calling it normalized
pitfalls.detail: A surrogate key makes every row distinct, duplicates included, and leaves the dependencies among the other columns untouched. Every anomaly from example 1 survives it.
pitfalls.bad: ALTER TABLE sheet ADD COLUMN id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY;
pitfalls.good: requirements (code PRIMARY KEY, title), test_runs PRIMARY KEY (test_code, run_on), ...: the keys the dependencies imply

pitfalls.title: Normalizing away a snapshot
pitfalls.detail: The price on an order line or the title a test had when it ran may look like copies, but they are different facts: the value at that time. Replacing them with a join to the current value rewrites history.

pitfalls.title: Treating BCNF as the goal
pitfalls.detail: A decomposition that loses a business rule is worse than a controlled copy. Keep the copy and tie it to its source with a composite foreign key, as in example 3.

quiz.q: The sheet's key is (test_code, run_on), and req_code depends on test_code alone. Which normal form does that violate?
quiz.why: A non-key column that depends on part of a composite key is a partial dependency, which is exactly what 2NF forbids.

quiz.q: How do you check whether tester -> tester_email holds in imported data?
options: SELECT DISTINCT tester, tester_email FROM sheet
GROUP BY tester HAVING count(DISTINCT tester_email) > 1 returns no rows
quiz.why: The dependency holds when every tester has exactly one e-mail, so group by the determinant and look for more than one. UNIQUE (tester_email) checks the reverse direction.

quiz.q: lab_assignments in example 3 is in 3NF but not in BCNF. Why?
options: tester determines lab, and tester is not a candidate key
It has a composite primary key
quiz.why: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. 3NF lets this pass because lab is part of a candidate key, (test_code, lab).

quiz.q: Decomposing on a dependency X -> Y produces what?
options: A table keyed by X that holds Y, and X as a foreign key where Y used to be
A CHECK constraint relating X and Y
quiz.why: The determinant becomes a key, so each X maps to one Y by construction, and the original table keeps only the reference.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (primary keys, unique, foreign keys)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A table models one kind of thing, and every non-key column states a fact about that
thing. Normalization is the discipline that keeps it that way, phrased in terms of
**functional dependencies**: `X -> Y` holds when each value of `X` comes with exactly one
value of `Y` (a requirement code has one title; a tester has one e-mail address). `X` is
the **determinant**.

Data in which a determinant is not a key stores the same fact many times, and that
causes three **anomalies**:

- **Update**: a fact changed in one copy but not the others (REQ-1 has two titles).
- **Insertion**: a fact can't be recorded without an unrelated one (a requirement with
  no test run yet).
- **Deletion**: removing one fact removes another (the only run of TC-3 was the only
  record of REQ-2).

The cure is always the same move: give the determinant its own table, keyed by it, and
replace the copies with a foreign key. The normal forms name which dependencies are
left to remove.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Any OO language:** a class with `customerName` and `customerEmail` fields on every
  `Order` is the same smell as the spreadsheet; you would extract a `Customer` and hold
  a reference. Normalization is that refactoring, with a test (the dependency check)
  for when it's needed.
- **Java/JPA:** entities with `@ManyToOne` already produce normalized tables. The trap is
  the other direction: an `@Embedded` value object copied into many rows is
  denormalized, which is fine for a snapshot and a bug for shared data.
- **Document databases and JSON APIs:** a nested document per order is the
  spreadsheet again. It reads in one go, and every write to a shared value has to find
  all the copies.
- **Python/pandas:** `df.groupby('req_code')['req_title'].nunique() > 1` is the
  dependency check of example 1, and `drop_duplicates` is the `SELECT DISTINCT` you
  shouldn't trust blindly.

## How it works

The normal forms, as a checklist for each table (a candidate key is any minimal set of
columns that identifies a row):

1. **1NF**: every field holds one value; no lists in a cell, no `tag1, tag2, tag3`
   columns.
2. **2NF**: no non-key column depends on just part of a composite key (req_code on
   test_code alone).
3. **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column (req_title on req_code,
   tester_email on tester). The usual summary: every non-key column depends on the key,
   the whole key, and nothing but the key.
4. **BCNF**: every determinant is a candidate key, key columns included (tester -> lab
   in example 3).

The procedure that gets you there:

1. Name the entity each row is about and its real key.
2. List the dependencies; confirm them on real data with the `GROUP BY ... HAVING
   count(DISTINCT ...) > 1` check.
3. For each dependency whose determinant isn't a key, move the dependent columns to a
   table keyed by the determinant, and reference it.
4. Declare everything: the primary keys, UNIQUE constraints and foreign keys you end up
   with are the dependencies, and from then on the database rejects every write that
   would break one.

Splitting on a determinant that becomes a key is always lossless: joining back gives
exactly the original rows. Going from 3NF to BCNF, however, can lose a dependency, as in
example 3.

## Design notes

Aim for 3NF by default, check for BCNF, and treat every remaining copy as a decision you
can name. In practice the dependencies come from the domain, not from the data you
happen to have: four rows can't prove that a tester has one lab, only that no
counterexample exists yet. Ask whoever owns the rules.

Normalized does not mean "everything gets a surrogate id". Example 2 uses codes as keys
for brevity; a real TraceLite schema keys requirements by `id`, declares
`UNIQUE (project_id, code)`, and references the id, because codes get renamed. The
dependencies, and therefore the tables, are the same either way.

When a split would lose a rule, as in example 3, keep the redundant column and make the
database maintain it: a composite foreign key with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` turns a copy
into something that can't drift. The next lesson covers deliberate denormalization in
general, including the copies that aren't redundant at all, such as a price at the
time of sale.

lessons.title: When to denormalize; naming conventions, keys and audit columns
lessons.summary: A stored copy of derivable data is a cache: decide what keeps it right before you add it. A value copied at the time of an event is not a copy at all. Conventions for names, keys and audit columns make every table predictable.

examples.title: A stored 'last result': one write path, how it drifts, and a reconciliation query

annotations.note: The copy answers "what happened last" without reading test_runs, which matters on a list of thousands of test cases. It is also a second place where that fact lives; the rest of the example is what that costs.

One statement inserts the run and updates the copy, so both commit or neither does. The last condition lets the copy only move forward: an older run arriving late (a retry, an import) can't overwrite a newer result. If two writers race, the second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock and, under READ COMMITTED, re-checks this WHERE against the updated row.
Any writer that skips the write path causes drift: bulk imports, psql sessions, a second service. Nothing fails. The copy is simply wrong from now on.
The view defines the copy once, in terms of its source. id DESC breaks ties between two runs on the same day, so "latest" is deterministic.

A reconciliation query: recompute, compare, list the differences. IS DISTINCT FROM is NULL-safe; with <> TC-2's NULL against 'passed' would be unknown and the row would be missed. Zero rows is the invariant: run it on a schedule or in integration tests.

The repair reuses the view, so there's one definition of the truth. A trigger on test_runs or a materialized view would need no write path discipline at all, at their own costs (triggers and views lessons).

examples.title: A snapshot is a different fact: the price and KDV rate on the order
