annotations.note: The foreign key stays. The copied columns freeze the terms; the reference keeps the identity (which product this was). It also means a product with orders can't be deleted, only retired with a flag.

These look like copies of products.price and products.vat_pct, but they record the terms of this order. An invoice that changes when the price list changes is a bug, and in accounting a legal problem.
A value derived from the same row is the cheap kind of denormalization: a generated column is recomputed by the database on every write and can't be written by hand, so it can't drift.
The INSERT takes the copy itself. The client sends a SKU and a quantity, never a price, so a stale screen or a tampered request can't set what the customer pays.
products says what is true today. Turkey's general KDV rate rose from 18% to 20% in July 2023, and every order from before kept 18.
net_if_joined is what a "fully normalized" design reports for order 1: 298.00 instead of the 258.00 that was charged. Here the join is the bug, and the copy is the correct model.

examples.title: Naming conventions, generated constraint names, audit columns and identifier folding

annotations.note: No single convention matters; consistency does. With id everywhere and <singular>_id for references, every join condition is predictable: test_cases.project_id = projects.id. Plural table names also sidestep reserved words: CREATE TABLE user and CREATE TABLE order are syntax errors, users and orders are fine.
Audit columns are timestamptz (the time zones lesson explains why). now() is the start time of the transaction, so every row written in one transaction shares one created_at.
current_user is the database role. Behind a connection pool it is the application's role for every request, here playground. Store the end user explicitly, as a column the application fills.

Generated names follow <table>_<columns>_<suffix>: pkey, key for UNIQUE, fkey, check. Errors carry the constraint name, so the API's error mapping can key on it; write CONSTRAINT name ... wherever you want to choose it. PG 18 also lists NOT NULL constraints here (contype 'n'), which the filter hides.
updated_at = created_at even after the UPDATE, because a DEFAULT applies to INSERT only. Either every UPDATE sets updated_at = now() itself, or a BEFORE UPDATE trigger does (triggers lesson).

Quoted "TestRuns" keeps its capitals, so every query must quote it forever. Unquoted Ürünler shows the folding rule as this UTF-8 database applies it: Fiyat became fiyat, but the non-ASCII Ü stayed upper case.
ürünler with a lower-case ü is a different name: SQLSTATE 42P01. Lower-case ASCII snake_case avoids both traps; Turkish belongs in the data and in comments, not in identifiers.

use_cases: Lists that show an aggregate on every row (last result, open defect count, member count), read far more often than written
Snapshots of the terms at the time of an event: prices and tax rates on order lines, a test case's title in a signed-off test report
Carrying a parent key down (project_id on test_runs) to filter or index without a join, tied to its source by a composite foreign key
Audit columns (created_at, created_by, updated_at) on every table, so 'when did this row change' doesn't need a log search
strengths: A stored aggregate turns a per-row subquery into a column read, which an ORM-driven list page would otherwise repeat for every row
A snapshot keeps documents reproducible: an invoice printed again in five years says what it said, with no history tables
Kept by the same statement (a data-modifying CTE) or by the database (generated column, composite FK with ON UPDATE CASCADE), a copy is as atomic as the write it depends on
Predictable names and audit columns let tooling, error mapping and a reviewer find their way around any table
weaknesses: Every copy needs a write path to keep it right, and imports, psql sessions or a second service that skip it cause silent drift
Reads get cheaper and writes get dearer: each recorded run now also updates, and row-locks, its test case
Drift isn't an error. You only find it with a reconciliation query that somebody has to remember to run
PostgreSQL accepts any name, quoted or not; conventions hold only as far as review and linting enforce them

pitfalls.title: Denormalizing before measuring
pitfalls.detail: A join on indexed keys is cheap. Copy a value when EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data shows the join or the aggregate is the problem, not in advance.

pitfalls.title: updated_at with only a DEFAULT
pitfalls.detail: The default fills it on INSERT and never again, so every row looks untouched. Set it in every UPDATE, or let a trigger do it.
pitfalls.bad: updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()  -- and nothing else
pitfalls.good: UPDATE test_cases SET title = $1, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $2;  -- or a BEFORE UPDATE trigger

pitfalls.title: current_user as the audit user
pitfalls.detail: Behind a connection pool, every row records the application's database role. Record the person explicitly.
pitfalls.bad: created_by text NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user
pitfalls.good: created_by bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users  -- filled by the application

pitfalls.title: Quoted and non-ASCII identifiers
pitfalls.detail: ORMs and GUI designers that quote mixed-case names make every hand-written query quote them too, and unquoted Turkish letters don't fold the way the ASCII ones do.
pitfalls.good: CREATE TABLE test_runs (...);  CREATE TABLE products (...);

pitfalls.title: Identifiers longer than 63 bytes
pitfalls.detail: Longer names are truncated with only a NOTICE, and two names that share their first 63 bytes collide. The limit is in bytes: ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü take two bytes each in UTF-8.

quiz.q: test_cases.last_result is kept up to date by the endpoint that records runs. A CSV import inserts into test_runs directly. What happens?
quiz.why: Nothing connects the copy to its source except the write path, and the import didn't use it. Only a reconciliation query, a trigger or a materialized view would notice.

quiz.q: order_lines.unit_price is copied from products.price when the order is placed. Is that a normalization violation?
options: Yes: the price depends on the SKU
No: it is the price agreed for that order, a different fact from today's list price
quiz.why: unit_price depends on the order line, not just the SKU. Replacing it with a join would reprice old orders.

quiz.q: A column is `updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`. A row is updated. What does updated_at hold?
options: Its old value: defaults apply only to INSERT
quiz.why: A DEFAULT is used when an INSERT omits the column (or says DEFAULT). Updates need an explicit SET or a trigger.

quiz.q: In a UTF-8 database you run `CREATE TABLE Ürünler (id int)` and then `SELECT * FROM ürünler`. What happens?
options: It works: unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive
quiz.why: Folding lower-cased only the ASCII letters, so the table is named Ürünler with a capital Ü, and ürünler is a different name.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Identifiers and Key Words
PostgreSQL docs: Data-Modifying Statements in WITH
PostgreSQL docs: Current Date/Time (now() and transaction time)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Denormalizing means storing a fact in more than one place on purpose, usually to make
reads cheaper. Three different things go by that name, and they deserve different
treatment:

- **A derived copy**: a value you could compute from other rows (the last result of a
  test case, a count of open defects). It is a cache. It needs a source of truth, a
  mechanism that keeps it right, and a way to detect when it isn't.
- **A derived value within one row** (a line total from quantity and price). A
  generated column covers this, and the database keeps it right for you.
- **A snapshot**: a value copied at the time of an event (the price on an order line).
  It looks like a copy but records a different fact, and normalizing it away would be
  the bug.

The rest of the lesson is the boring part that makes schemas readable: naming
conventions, key naming, and the audit columns every table should carry.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Caching:** a derived column is a cache inside the database. Everything you know
  from caches applies: invalidation is the hard part, and a stale entry fails silently.
  The difference is that it can be updated in the same transaction as its source, which
  an external cache never can.
- **Java/JPA:** Hibernate's `@Formula` and a `@Transient` getter are the "compute on
  read" choice; a counter field updated in a service method is the "store it" choice,
  and every bulk JPQL `UPDATE` or native query bypasses it.
- **Go and TS:** with pgx or a query builder, the write path is a function you call. Put
  the copy's update in the same SQL statement (a data-modifying CTE), not in a second
  call that a later refactor can drop.
- **Naming:** Go wants `ProjectID`, TS wants `projectId`, SQL wants `project_id`. Keep
  each language's convention and map at the boundary (struct tags, a mapping layer);
  don't quote `"projectId"` into the database.

## Design notes

Before adding a derived copy, measure, then answer four questions in the migration's
comment: what is the source of truth; what keeps the copy right; what detects drift;
what repairs it. The mechanisms, from most to least help from the database:

1. **Generated column**, when the value comes from the same row.
2. **Composite foreign key with `ON UPDATE CASCADE`**, when the copy is a key from a
   parent row (the BCNF example in the previous lesson).
3. **Materialized view**, when a periodically refreshed result is acceptable.
4. **Trigger**, when the copy must change in the same transaction as its source and
   every writer must be covered.
5. **Application write path**, the cheapest to build and the easiest to bypass.

Conventions this codebase follows, as a starting point:

- Lower-case ASCII `snake_case` for every identifier; never quoted names.
- Plural table names (`test_runs`), which also avoids the reserved `user` and `order`.
- `id` as the primary key; `<singular>_id` for foreign keys (`project_id`).
- `_at` for `timestamptz` columns, `_on` for `date` columns, `is_`/`has_` for booleans.
- Explicit `CONSTRAINT` names wherever error mapping depends on them; otherwise the
  generated `_pkey`, `_key`, `_fkey`, `_check` names.
- `created_at`, `updated_at` and, where it matters, `created_by`/`updated_by` holding
  the application's user id. A full change history is a different tool: history tables
  (next lesson) or an audit trigger (triggers lesson).

lessons.title: History and temporal data: PG 18 WITHOUT OVERLAPS, history tables, a bitemporal introduction
lessons.summary: A temporal table stores each fact with the period it was true. PG 18's WITHOUT OVERLAPS keys and PERIOD foreign keys enforce "one at a time" and "only while the parent exists"; a second period, the time the database knew it, makes past reports reproducible.

examples.title: A temporal primary key: one owner per requirement at any moment

annotations.note: The key compares requirement_id with = and valid_at with &&, both in one GiST index, and GiST has no built-in = for int or text. Without btree_gist the CREATE TABLE fails with SQLSTATE 42704 (no default operator class for access method "gist"). The docs call btree_gist the expected way to use this feature.

WITHOUT OVERLAPS on the last column means: no two rows with the same requirement_id whose periods overlap. The docs describe it as behaving like EXCLUDE USING gist (requirement_id WITH =, valid_at WITH &&). The column must be a range or multirange, and empty ranges are rejected (SQLSTATE 23514).
Half-open [start, end) ranges let one period end exactly where the next begins. No upper bound means "still true": the current row is the one where upper_inf(valid_at) holds.
@> answers "what was true on that day" in one predicate. A multicolumn GiST index can serve conditions on any of its columns, so the key's own index helps here too.

PG 18 has no temporal UPDATE (the standard's FOR PORTION OF), so changing a fact from a date onwards is your code: shorten the current row, then insert the new one, in one transaction. The key is checked as each row is written, so the reverse order fails.
The primary key is backed by a GiST index named after the constraint. A key made only of equality columns would be a B-tree.

Selin's May to July overlaps Ayşe's period and Mehmet's. The error is an exclusion violation, SQLSTATE 23P01, not 23505 like an ordinary duplicate key: error mapping that only knows 23505 will let it through as a 500.

examples.title: A PERIOD foreign key, and a temporal join

annotations.note: In a temporal table id alone is no longer unique; (id, period) is. The rename is a new version row, so both names are kept along with when each applied.

PERIOD makes the last column special: the reference holds when the referenced rows with that id, taken together, cover the whole referencing period. The other side needs a WITHOUT OVERLAPS key. Only NO ACTION is supported; CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT and RESTRICT are rejected for PERIOD foreign keys (SQLSTATE 0A000).
No single project row covers March to September; Checkout and Payments together do, so the reference holds. Splitting a version, as a rename does, never breaks the memberships that span it.

The temporal join: match on the key and on overlap (&&), then intersect the periods with *. The result is temporal too: Ayşe was on Checkout until July and on Payments after, which neither table says on its own.

Project 2 ends on 1 April, so April to July is uncovered: SQLSTATE 23503, the ordinary foreign key error. The other direction is guarded as well: shortening or deleting a project version that a membership still needs fails with the same code.

examples.title: Bitemporal: what was true, and when the database knew it

annotations.note: Two time axes. valid_at (application time) is when the price holds in the world, and the business may set it in the past or future. recorded_at (system time) is when the database held the belief, and only the system sets it. It is a daterange with literal dates here so the output is reproducible; a real table uses tstzrange starting at now().
WITHOUT OVERLAPS takes a single range column. With two axes the rule is "no two rows for one SKU overlap in both periods at once", which is EXCLUDE with two && operators.
Nothing is deleted, and the only change to an old row is the upper bound of recorded_at. The belief "129.00, open-ended" was what the database said from January to March, and it stays queryable.
A correction is the same move. The typo row keeps its recorded period, 1 to 20 March: exactly when an invoice could have used it.

Three answers for the same day, all correct: 129.00 as known in February, 149.00 as known on 15 March (what an invoice printed then shows), 139.00 as known today. Reproducing an old report means filtering recorded_at by the report's date.
This row overlaps the current 139.00 row in valid_at (from 15 March) and in recorded_at (from 20 March): SQLSTATE 23P01. A correction has to close the old belief first, as lines 27-28 do.

use_cases: Ownership, assignments and memberships over time: who was responsible for REQ-12 when the defect shipped
Price lists, tax rates and tariffs with future-dated changes: enter next month's prices today
Contracts, employment and insurance cover, where corrections are backdated and old reports must stay reproducible (bitemporal)
Audit questions such as 'what did the screen show on 15 March' (system time, history tables)
strengths: A temporal key makes 'one owner at a time' a declaration; in Go or TS the same rule is a SELECT-then-INSERT that races
A PERIOD foreign key checks coverage against all referenced versions together, which a hand-written trigger would need range aggregation and locking to get right
Range operators make as-of filters (@>), overlap tests (&&) and temporal joins (*) one predicate each, and GiST indexes serve them
Bitemporal rows reproduce past reports exactly, without restoring a backup or replaying a log
weaknesses: No temporal UPDATE or DELETE in PG 18: splitting a period takes two or three statements of your own, in the right order
PERIOD foreign keys support only NO ACTION, so retiring a parent means closing or deleting the children first
Temporal keys need btree_gist and a GiST index, which is larger and slower to maintain than a B-tree
Tables grow with every change, and every query needs a time predicate; forgetting it silently returns all versions

pitfalls.title: Querying a temporal table without a time predicate
pitfalls.detail: Every version comes back, so project 1 appears twice and joins multiply rows. Say which moment you mean, or read through a view of current rows.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT name FROM projects WHERE id = 1;
pitfalls.good: SELECT name FROM projects WHERE id = 1 AND valid_at @> current_date;

pitfalls.title: Closed upper bounds
pitfalls.detail: daterange is stored in the canonical [) form, so '[2026-01-01,2026-06-01]' becomes [2026-01-01,2026-06-02) and overlaps a row starting on 1 June. Write half-open ranges; daterange(a, b) builds [a, b) by default.

pitfalls.title: Inserting the new version before closing the old one
pitfalls.detail: The key sees two open periods and fails with 23P01. Shorten the current row first, then insert, inside one transaction.

pitfalls.title: Mapping only 23505 to 409 Conflict
pitfalls.detail: Violations of WITHOUT OVERLAPS keys and EXCLUDE constraints are SQLSTATE 23P01 (exclusion_violation). Map it next to 23505, or the API answers a conflict with a 500.

pitfalls.title: History that outlives the erasure duty
pitfalls.detail: History tables and closed versions keep personal data after the current row is anonymized. KVKK Article 7 erasure and anonymization requests have to reach the history too.

quiz.q: projects has PRIMARY KEY (id, valid_at WITHOUT OVERLAPS) with rows for id 1 valid [2026-01-01,2026-07-01) and [2026-07-01,). A membership references project 1 with PERIOD for [2026-03-01,2026-09-01). Is it accepted?
options: No: no single project row covers it
Yes: the two rows together cover it
quiz.why: A PERIOD reference is satisfied when the combined periods of the matching referenced rows cover the referencing period completely.

quiz.q: Which SQLSTATE does an overlapping insert into a WITHOUT OVERLAPS primary key raise?
quiz.why: The key is enforced like an exclusion constraint, so it reports exclusion_violation. 23514 is what an empty range gets.

quiz.q: The owner of requirement 2 changes on 1 October. How do you record that in PG 18?
options: UPDATE ... FOR PORTION OF valid_at FROM '2026-10-01'
Shorten the current row to end on 1 October, then insert the new owner from 1 October
Insert the new owner from 1 October, then shorten the current row
quiz.why: PG 18 has no FOR PORTION OF. The key is checked per row, so the old period must end before the new one is inserted.

quiz.q: In a bitemporal table, what does recorded_at answer?
options: When the fact is true in the world
When the database held that belief
When the row was last read
quiz.why: recorded_at is system time. valid_at is application time, which the business can set in the past or future.

PostgreSQL docs: Range Functions and Operators
PostgreSQL docs: Unsupported SQL features (T180, T181)

lessons.body:
## Concept

An ordinary table holds the current state: an UPDATE overwrites the past. When the past
matters, a schema can keep time along one or two axes:

- **Application time** (valid time): when a fact is true in the world. Each row carries
  a period, typically a `daterange` or `tstzrange` named `valid_at`, and a change of
  owner, name or price is a new row with a new period. The business sets these
  periods, including in the past and the future.
- **System time** (transaction time): when the database held a row. Only the system
  sets it. The classic form is a **history table**: the current table stays as it is,
  and every UPDATE or DELETE copies the old version, stamped with its system period,
  into a `_history` table.
- **Bitemporal**: both at once, for domains where facts are corrected after the fact
  and you must still answer "what did we believe then".

PostgreSQL 18 adds the constraints application time needs: `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE`
with `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` on a range column, and foreign keys with `PERIOD`. The SQL
standard's system-versioned tables (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`, feature T180) and temporal
`UPDATE ... FOR PORTION OF` are not part of PG 18.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java:** `effectiveFrom`/`effectiveTo` fields with a service that checks for
  overlaps is the hand-written version of example 1, and it races under concurrency.
  Hibernate Envers is a history-table implementation (audit tables filled by the ORM),
  so it misses writes that bypass the ORM; a database trigger doesn't.
- **Go and TS:** there's no temporal library to reach for, which is fine: keep the
  rules in the database (keys, PERIOD foreign keys) and the period splitting in one
  store function that runs its statements in a transaction.
- **Event sourcing:** an append-only event log is system time taken to the extreme.
  A bitemporal table is its relational cousin: you never lose a belief, but you can
  still query state with plain SQL instead of replaying events.
- **Python/JS dates:** a range `[start, end)` is the same half-open convention as
  `range(a, b)` and `Array.prototype.slice`: adjacent periods share a boundary
  without overlapping.

## How it works

`WITHOUT OVERLAPS` turns the key into an exclusion constraint over a GiST index: equal
on the leading columns and overlapping (`&&`) on the period is a conflict, reported as
SQLSTATE 23P01. Empty periods are rejected. Scalar key columns need btree_gist.

A `PERIOD` foreign key compares the leading columns for equality and requires the
referenced rows' periods, taken together, to cover the referencing period. Deleting or
shortening a referenced version is checked the same way (NO ACTION is the only
action PG 18 accepts for it).

Changing a temporal fact from a date onwards is a split you write yourself, inside a
transaction:

1. Shorten the row that is current at that date: `upper = change date`.
2. Insert the new version from the change date.
3. If the change ends before the old period did, insert the remainder of the old
   version after it.

A history table for system time is usually maintained by an `AFTER UPDATE OR DELETE`
trigger that inserts the old row with `tstzrange(previous change, now())`. The triggers
lesson and TraceLite's audit step build one; the design questions are the same as here.

## Design notes

Pick the axis from the question the business asks. "Who owned REQ-12 on 15 March?" is
application time: add `valid_at` and a `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` key. "What did this record look
like before Mehmet edited it?" is system time: a history table, filled by a trigger so
no writer can skip it. "What did the invoice of 15 March say, given that we corrected the
price on 20 March?" is bitemporal, and rare enough that you should be sure before paying
for it.

Keep reads of the present cheap. Most queries want current rows only; give them a view
(`WHERE upper_inf(valid_at)` or `valid_at @> current_date`), or keep a plain current
table and put only the past in a history table. A soft-delete flag is the degenerate
case of all this: one transition, no period.

History is personal data too. Anonymizing a customer's current row leaves their old
versions in history tables and closed periods, so erasure under KVKK Article 7 has to
cover them, and a retention policy should say how long history is kept at all.

lessons.title: Anti-patterns: EAV, polymorphic foreign keys, comma-separated lists, jsonb for everything
lessons.summary: EAV tables, polymorphic target_type/target_id pairs, lists in strings and jsonb-only tables all move the schema out of the database's sight. Each one gives up types, NOT NULL, foreign keys or statistics, and every reader pays for the checks the writer skipped.

examples.title: Entity-attribute-value: everything fits, nothing is checked

annotations.note: EAV turns columns into rows, so the schema becomes data. The database can no longer say what a test case has: one text column holds every value, so there are no types, no NOT NULL for a required attribute, no CHECK, no DEFAULT, and no foreign key from a value.

'high' isn't a number and 'prority' isn't an attribute, and both are accepted. With columns, the first is a type error at INSERT and the second a "column does not exist" error in the query that misspells it.

Reading an entity back is a pivot: one FILTER aggregate per attribute, every value still text. TC-3 has no priority and nothing says why. Filtering on two attributes takes a join or subquery per attribute.

The attributes every test case has become ordinary columns: priority a smallint with a range check, automated a boolean with a default. Adding one is an ALTER TABLE, which is the point: the change is reviewed and visible.
What really varies per customer goes into one jsonb column. It is still unchecked inside (the jsonb lesson shows what to constrain), but it is one column next to typed ones, not the whole model.
The typed column rejects 'high' at the INSERT, SQLSTATE 22P02: at write time, once, where EAV accepted it and left the problem to every reader.

examples.title: Polymorphic target_type/target_id, and the exclusive arc that replaces it

annotations.note: Rails' polymorphic belongs_to, Django's GenericForeignKey and Hibernate's @Any produce this shape. A foreign key references one table, and target_id points into a different one per row, so nothing checks it.
Both mistakes are accepted: a comment on a test case that never existed, and one whose test case was just deleted. There is no foreign key to attach ON DELETE CASCADE to either.
Every read joins every possible target conditionally. A third target type means changing every such query.

An exclusive arc: one nullable foreign key per target type, each with real integrity and its own ON DELETE action, and a CHECK that exactly one is set. num_nonnulls (PG 9.6) counts its non-null arguments, so none or both fails with SQLSTATE 23514.
Each reference column needs its own index, for "comments on this test case" and for the cascade. That cost grows per target type, which is why many targets call for another design (Design notes).
Deleting test case 1 removes its comment in the same statement: CASCADE works because the reference is real.
Test case 9 doesn't exist: SQLSTATE 23503. The polymorphic table accepted the same row on line 17.

examples.title: Ids in a string, ids in a document, ids in a junction table

annotations.note: A list in a string, the textbook 1NF violation. It is still common wherever a multi-select is saved as one field.

LIKE '%1%' matches the 1 in 12, so TC-3 is reported as covering REQ-1. Delimiter tricks such as ',' || req_ids || ',' LIKE '%,1,%' fix this query and break on TC-3's space after the comma, and no B-tree index helps a leading wildcard.

jsonb parses the list into numbers, and @> '1' is exact: by a special rule of jsonb containment, an array contains a primitive value that is one of its elements. A GIN index on doc would serve the equivalent doc @> '{"req_ids": [1]}'.
Integrity is now a query that unpacks every document, run after the fact. Nothing stopped 99 on the way in, and nothing will stop REQ-12 from being deleted while documents still point at it.

The junction table makes each link a row with a foreign key on both sides. The primary key forbids duplicate links, and the index on requirement_id serves the reverse lookup (the many-to-many lesson).
"Which tests cover REQ-1" is an indexed equality, exact by construction.
SQLSTATE 23503 at write time. Deleting REQ-12 while links exist is refused too, unless you declare ON DELETE CASCADE.

use_cases: Custom fields per customer: typed columns for the common ones, one jsonb column for the long tail, CHECK constraints on the keys you rely on
Comments, attachments or watchers on two or three entity types: an exclusive arc; on many types: a table per target or a shared parent table
Many-to-many links such as test cases to requirements: a junction table with two foreign keys
Where jsonb is right: payloads stored as received (webhooks, imports) and attributes that genuinely differ from row to row
strengths: Typed columns reject bad values once, at write time, instead of every reader casting text and failing at read time
Real foreign keys refuse dangling references and run ON DELETE actions for every client, which an ORM-level polymorphic association can't promise for psql or a second service
A junction table answers both directions with indexed equality lookups; a list in a string needs parsing on every row
The corrected designs show up in the schema, so \d, sqlc, ORMs and new team members all see the model
weaknesses: A new attribute is a migration (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN) instead of an INSERT; jsonb stays the escape hatch for what you can't predict
An exclusive arc adds a column, an index and a CHECK term per target type, so it stops scaling after a handful of targets
Reading a list back from a junction table costs a join, and an ORM may hide that join behind lazy loading
A jsonb column inside a typed table still needs CHECK constraints or validation for whatever the code relies on

pitfalls.title: EAV for flexibility
pitfalls.detail: Every value becomes text, required attributes can't be enforced, and each attribute in a filter is another join. Since jsonb exists, there is little reason left to build EAV in PostgreSQL.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE TABLE attrs (entity_id int, attr text, value text, PRIMARY KEY (entity_id, attr));
pitfalls.good: priority smallint NOT NULL CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 4), extra jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'

pitfalls.title: A type column plus an id column
pitfalls.detail: No foreign key, no cascade, orphans after every delete in a target table. Use one real reference per target type, or another of the designs below.
pitfalls.bad: target_type text NOT NULL, target_id int NOT NULL
pitfalls.good: requirement_id int REFERENCES requirements, test_case_id int REFERENCES test_cases, CHECK (num_nonnulls(requirement_id, test_case_id) = 1)

pitfalls.title: Searching a list with LIKE
pitfalls.detail: Substring matching finds 1 inside 12 and can't use a B-tree index. Store one row per element.
pitfalls.good: WHERE requirement_id = 1  -- on a junction table

pitfalls.title: jsonb as the whole row
pitfalls.detail: A table of (id, data jsonb) gives up types, NOT NULL, foreign keys and per-field statistics: without an expression index or CREATE STATISTICS on the expression (PG 14), the planner uses default estimates for filters like data ->> 'status' = 'open'. Every update also rewrites and row-locks the whole document.

quiz.q: How would you make priority required for every test case in example 1's EAV table?
options: NOT NULL on the value column
No constraint can: a missing attribute is a missing row
quiz.why: Constraints check the rows that exist. An attribute nobody inserted has no row to check; only a trigger or application code could notice.

quiz.q: Why can't comments_poly declare a foreign key on target_id?
options: A foreign key references exactly one table, and target_id points into a different table depending on target_type
Foreign keys can't be NOT NULL
quiz.why: REFERENCES names one table. A value whose target table depends on another column is outside what a foreign key can express.

quiz.q: Which row does CHECK (num_nonnulls(requirement_id, test_case_id) = 1) reject?
quiz.why: Two non-null arguments make num_nonnulls return 2. The arc allows exactly one target.

quiz.q: req_ids is text holding '1,12' or '12, 99'. Which query reliably finds the tests for requirement 1?
options: Neither: store the links in a junction table and query WHERE requirement_id = 1
quiz.why: The first matches 12, the second breaks on spaces and other formatting. Only one row per link makes the lookup exact and indexable.
