lessons.body:
## Concept

The four designs in this lesson share one move: they take structure the database could
check and hide it inside data.

- **Entity-attribute-value (EAV)**: a table of `(entity_id, attr, value)`, so any
  attribute can be added without a migration. Every value is text, and the list of
  attributes lives in the rows.
- **Polymorphic association**: `target_type` plus `target_id`, so one comments table can
  point at requirements or test cases. A foreign key can't point at "one of several
  tables", so nothing checks the reference.
- **Lists in a string**: `'1,12'` in a text column. Matching, counting and integrity all
  require parsing.
- **jsonb for everything**: a table of `(id, data jsonb)`. Parsed and indexable, but
  without types, NOT NULL, foreign keys or per-field statistics.

Each is chosen for flexibility, and each makes every write unchecked and every read
responsible for the checks. The test to apply to any design: can the database reject a
wrong value or a dangling reference at write time? If not, all readers inherit the job.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go and TS:** EAV and jsonb-only tables are `map[string]any` and
  `Record<string, unknown>` persisted. You wouldn't model a domain type that way in
  code; a struct or an interface with real fields is the column list.
- **Rails, Django, Hibernate:** polymorphic `belongs_to`, `GenericForeignKey` and `@Any`
  make the polymorphic pattern one line of code. The ORM enforces the reference only
  for writes it performs; the database sees an unconstrained integer.
- **WordPress and Magento:** `wp_postmeta` and Magento's product attributes are the
  well-known EAV schemas. They exist because plugins define attributes at runtime, and
  they pay for it in pivot queries and caches. An application with a known domain
  doesn't have that excuse.
- **MongoDB:** a jsonb-only table is a document store inside PostgreSQL. You keep
  transactions and joins, but give up exactly the parts that made a relational
  database worth choosing.

## Design notes

For custom fields, use typed columns for every attribute the code knows about and one
`jsonb` column for the rest. Add CHECK constraints for the jsonb keys the code depends
on; when a key earns several checks, promote it to a column.

For references to several kinds of parent, choose by the number of target types:

- **Exclusive arc** (example 2): two or three targets. Each gets a real foreign key and
  index, and one CHECK keeps exactly one set.
- **A table per target** (`requirement_comments`, `test_case_comments`): any number of
  targets, simplest constraints, and a `UNION ALL` view when you need all comments.
- **A shared parent table**: an `items (id)` table that requirements and test cases each
  reference one-to-one, and comments reference `items`. One foreign key on the comment
  side, at the price of an extra table and join.

For lists, a junction table is the default. `text[]` is acceptable for plain labels that
reference nothing (the jsonb and arrays lesson); ids in a string or a document never
are.

jsonb is the right tool for data whose shape you don't control or can't predict. When
every row has the field, or you filter, join or sum on it, it is a column.

lessons.title: Multi-tenant patterns: tenant column, schema per tenant, database per tenant, and RLS
lessons.summary: Tenants can share tables (a tenant_id column), share a database (a schema each) or get a database each. With shared tables, put tenant_id into every key and foreign key, and let row-level security add the tenant filter that a query might forget.

examples.title: Shared tables: tenant_id in every key and every foreign key

annotations.note: projects keeps a global id as its primary key and also declares UNIQUE (tenant_id, id). That looks redundant, but a foreign key can only reference a unique constraint on exactly its columns, and (tenant_id, id) is the pair children must match.
The naive foreign key checks that project 10 exists somewhere. Güney's requirement now sits in Kuzey's project, and every join from it puts Kuzey's data on Güney's pages.
Codes are unique per tenant, so both tenants have a REQ-1. A plain UNIQUE (code) would let one customer's naming block another's, and the duplicate key error would tell them the other code exists.

The composite foreign key puts the tenant into the reference: a requirement's project must belong to the requirement's tenant. Do the same in every child table, and the tenant boundary becomes a property of the schema instead of each query.
Indexes lead with tenant_id, because every query filters by it. This one also serves the foreign key when projects are deleted.

Column tenancy's weak spot: isolation is a WHERE clause every query has to remember. The second query stands for any admin page, report or bug: both tenants in one result, and no error. Example 3 moves the filter into the database.
(2, 10) matches no row in projects: SQLSTATE 23503. The naive table accepted the same row on line 19.

examples.title: Schema per tenant: search_path does the isolation, migrations multiply

annotations.note: Each tenant gets the same tables in its own schema. Isolation is name resolution: an unqualified requirements is one tenant's table, and there is no tenant_id to forget. StackLab runs every SQL example the same way, in a throwaway schema on the search_path.

SET LOCAL lasts until the transaction ends. A plain SET would stay on the pooled connection and serve the next request, possibly another tenant's, from this schema. Behind a transaction-mode pooler, transaction-scoped settings are the only safe kind.
Anything across tenants (billing, usage dashboards, support queries) becomes a UNION over every schema, generated by code that knows the list of schemas.
A migration is now one per tenant, and each can fail on its own. The catalog query is the drift check you'll need: tenant_kuzey has 3 columns, tenant_guney 2.
The new code is deployed everywhere, and the tenant whose migration didn't run gets SQLSTATE 42703 while the others work. Every deploy becomes a fleet rollout.

examples.title: Row-level security: the database adds the tenant filter

annotations.note: The default takes the tenant from the session setting, so inserts don't name it. current_setting without a second argument raises an error when the setting doesn't exist (SQLSTATE 42704): a request that forgot to set its tenant fails instead of seeing everything.

ENABLE turns policies on for everyone except superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and the table's owner. The role running this script owns the table, as an application role that runs its own migrations would, so FORCE is what makes the policy apply to it. Enabled with no policy at all, the table shows no rows (default deny).

One policy for every command. USING filters the rows that SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE can see; without a WITH CHECK clause the same expression also checks the rows INSERT and UPDATE write. The RLS lesson in the security module covers per-command policies.
Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS ignore every policy, FORCE or not. Check the application's role once, in a test; playground has neither attribute.

set_config(name, value, true) is SET LOCAL as a function: it ends with the transaction, and unlike SET it accepts a query parameter, so the tenant id travels as $1 rather than spliced into SQL text. Custom setting names need a dot: PostgreSQL accepts any two-part name.
Tenant 2 sees only its own row, though the query has no WHERE. The policy applies to every query on the table, including ones written by someone who never heard of tenants.
Tenant 1's row is invisible, so the UPDATE matches nothing: UPDATE 0, no error. Policies filter silently on read; they raise errors only for rows being written.
tenant_id came from the column default, that is from the setting, so the new row belongs to tenant 2.

A row for tenant 1 fails the policy's check: SQLSTATE 42501. Note what RLS doesn't hide: unique and foreign key checks bypass policies, so inserting id 1 here would fail with a duplicate key and reveal that the row exists. Keys that include tenant_id avoid that leak.

use_cases: Shared tables with tenant_id and RLS: SaaS with many small tenants, such as a hosted TraceLite; the usual default
Schema per tenant: tens to a few hundred tenants that need per-tenant restore, customization or contractual separation

Database per tenant: a few large or regulated tenants that need their own backups, resource limits, versions or server; for example to keep a tenant's personal data in Turkey, where KVKK Article 9 regulates transfers abroad
Offboarding and erasure requests: DELETE ... WHERE tenant_id = $1 across tables, DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE, or DROP DATABASE
strengths: With shared tables, composite foreign keys make cross-tenant references impossible in the schema, not just unlikely in the code
RLS covers every query on the table, including reports and ad-hoc SQL run as the app role, unlike Hibernate filters or Rails default scopes, which only cover ORM queries
Schema tenancy needs no tenant_id in queries, and one tenant can be dumped or restored with standard tools (pg_dump --schema)
Database tenancy gives the strongest boundary: separate connections, privileges, backups and resource limits per tenant
weaknesses: Shared tables without RLS depend on every query remembering WHERE tenant_id, and the one that forgets leaks without an error
Schema tenancy multiplies tables, indexes and migrations by the number of tenants, and cross-tenant reports need a UNION per schema
Database tenancy needs a connection pool per database, since a connection is bound to one database, and cross-tenant queries need postgres_fdw or an export
RLS adds a predicate to every query, doesn't hide anything from unique and foreign key checks, and is skipped by superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and, without FORCE, the owner

pitfalls.title: Session-level SET behind a connection pool
pitfalls.detail: A plain SET stays on the connection after the request, and the pool hands that connection to the next request. Set the tenant per transaction.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true); ... COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys that leave out tenant_id
pitfalls.detail: A reference by id alone checks existence, not ownership, so one tenant's row can point at another's.
pitfalls.good: FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, project_id) REFERENCES projects (tenant_id, id)

pitfalls.title: ENABLE without FORCE
pitfalls.detail: If the application connects as the table's owner, which is common when it runs its own migrations, ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY alone protects nothing. Use separate owner and application roles (the roles lesson), and FORCE anyway.

pitfalls.title: An empty setting is not a missing one
pitfalls.detail: Once a session has used app.tenant, the setting keeps existing with an empty value after the transaction ends, so current_setting('app.tenant', true) returns '' rather than NULL. Make sure both NULL and '' match no rows, and never coalesce to a default tenant.

pitfalls.title: Global unique keys under RLS
pitfalls.detail: Unique and foreign key checks bypass policies, so a duplicate key error can confirm that another tenant's row exists. Put tenant_id into unique keys over tenant data.

quiz.q: requirements has FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects (id), and both tables have tenant_id. What stops tenant 2's requirement from pointing at tenant 1's project?
quiz.why: The foreign key only checks that the project exists. Referencing (tenant_id, id) makes ownership part of the check.

quiz.q: The application connects as the table's owner. RLS is enabled with a tenant policy but not forced. What do its queries see?
options: All rows: the owner bypasses RLS
quiz.why: Table owners bypass row security unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

quiz.q: Why call set_config('app.tenant', $1, true) inside each transaction instead of running SET app.tenant once per connection?
options: The local setting ends with the transaction, so a pooled connection can't carry one tenant's id into another request
quiz.why: A session-level SET outlives the request on a pooled connection. A transaction-local setting is gone at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and set_config also takes the value as a parameter.

quiz.q: With app.tenant = 2 and the tenant_isolation policy, `UPDATE requirements SET code = 'X' WHERE id = 1` targets tenant 1's row. What happens?
quiz.why: USING hides the row, so the UPDATE finds nothing to change. Errors come only from rows being written that fail the check.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Configuration Settings Functions (set_config, current_setting)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A multi-tenant application serves many customers (tenants) from one deployment. The
database has to keep their data apart, and there are three places to draw the line:

- **Shared tables, tenant column**: every table has `tenant_id`. Cheapest and densest;
  one schema, one migration, one pool. Isolation is a predicate on every query, which
  you either write yourself or let row-level security add.
- **Schema per tenant**: the same tables in a schema per tenant, chosen per request
  with `search_path`. Isolation is name resolution; the cost is N copies of every
  table, index and migration.
- **Database per tenant**: a database (or server) each. Isolation is the connection
  itself. Not demonstrated here: the playground role can't create databases, which is
  itself an example of the least privilege an application role should have.

**Row-level security (RLS)** is the database's half of the tenant-column design: a
policy such as `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int` is added to every query
on the table, so a query that forgets the tenant still sees only one.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Hibernate:** Hibernate's multi-tenancy offers the same three strategies: a
  separate database, a separate schema, or a discriminator column (`@TenantId` in
  Hibernate 6). Its filters only cover queries Hibernate runs; RLS also covers native
  queries, reports and psql.
- **Rails:** acts_as_tenant (column) and Apartment (schema per tenant) are the two
  well-known gems; both work at the ORM level.
- **Go:** there is no framework to do this for you, which keeps it visible. A
  middleware resolves the tenant from the authenticated request and puts it into the
  `context.Context`; the store's `WithTx` helper begins the transaction and runs
  `SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true)` before anything else.
- **Node:** the tenant often lives in `AsyncLocalStorage` for the duration of a
  request. The database setting has to have exactly that lifetime, which is why it is
  transaction-local and not set once per pooled connection.

## How it works

One request, in the tenant-column design with RLS:

1. Authenticate and resolve the tenant (never from a client-supplied header alone).
2. `BEGIN`, then `SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true)`.
3. Run the queries. Policies filter what they read and check what they write; column
   defaults fill `tenant_id` on insert.
4. `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. The setting is gone, and the connection goes back to the
   pool clean.

If step 2 is skipped, `current_setting('app.tenant')` raises an error on a fresh
connection; on a connection that has used the setting before, it returns an empty
string, which fails the `::int` cast. Either way the request fails rather than leaking.

## Design notes

Start with shared tables, `tenant_id` in every table, and RLS as defence in depth:

- Put `tenant_id` first in primary keys or alongside them in UNIQUE constraints, in
  every foreign key, and first in indexes. Cross-tenant references then become
  impossible, and every tenant-scoped query has an index to narrow on.
- Separate the role that owns the tables (runs migrations) from the role the
  application uses, give the application role neither superuser nor `BYPASSRLS`, and
  still `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
- Write one integration test per table that sets tenant A and asserts that tenant B's
  rows are invisible and unwritable.

Move to a schema or a database per tenant when a tenant needs something shared tables
can't give: its own restore point, its own resource limits, contractual or legal
separation, or a location. Having `tenant_id` in every key makes that move a copy of
the rows `WHERE tenant_id = $1`, not a redesign.

Offboarding is part of the design. Under KVKK, a customer that leaves may be owed
erasure of the personal data you processed for them: with shared tables that's a
`DELETE` per table, children first or by `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `tenants`; with
schemas a `DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE`; with databases a `DROP DATABASE`. Backups and
history tables (temporal lesson) hold copies too.

lessons.title: Highlights from PG 16 to 18: uuidv7, virtual generated columns, OLD/NEW in RETURNING, temporal constraints, skip scan, async I/O, JSON_TABLE, MERGE ... RETURNING
lessons.summary: Three releases changed a lot of standing advice: UUID keys, generated columns, audit queries, non-overlap constraints, composite index design, JSON import and MERGE. A tour with small runnable proofs, each feature tagged with its version and linked to the lesson that covers it in depth.

examples.title: PG 18 table definitions: temporal keys, uuidv7, virtual columns, NOT NULL as constraints

annotations.note: btree_gist gives int a GiST equality operator class. For key columns that aren't ranges, the docs call adding it the expected way to use WITHOUT OVERLAPS.

PG 18 temporal primary key: requirement_id may repeat as long as the valid ranges don't overlap. It is enforced like the exclusion constraint you had to write by hand before 18 (requirement_id WITH =, valid WITH &&), and foreign keys can now reference it.

uuidv7() (PG 18) puts a timestamp in the leading bits, so new keys arrive roughly in order at the end of the B-tree instead of at random places. The old advice, gen_random_uuid() or the uuid-ossp extension, gives random v4 keys (sql.tables-types.ids).

No keyword now means VIRTUAL (PG 18): computed when read, no storage. Before 18 the STORED keyword was required, so old DDL can't silently change meaning. Virtual columns may use built-in functions and types only.

PG 18 temporal foreign key: the rows with the same requirement_id must together cover the whole ran period. The referenced key must be declared WITHOUT OVERLAPS, and ON DELETE CASCADE and friends aren't supported here.
This run spans the switch between two versions. Neither covers it alone; together they do, and that is what PERIOD checks.
uuid_extract_version (PG 17) reads the version back; duration_s is computed on read.
The temporal key's index is GiST, the uuid key's is B-tree. Also new in 18: every NOT NULL is a named row in pg_constraint (contype n), and ALTER TABLE can add one as NOT VALID.
attgenerated is 'v' for virtual, 's' for stored.
SQLSTATE 23P01, exclusion_violation: the docs describe WITHOUT OVERLAPS as enforced by an EXCLUDE constraint rather than a unique one, and the error says so. Catch 23P01 in Go, not 23505.

examples.title: IS JSON (16), JSON_TABLE (17), MERGE ... RETURNING (17) with old/new (18)

annotations.note: PG 16 IS JSON: validate text before casting it instead of catching a cast error. It can also test for ARRAY or SCALAR, and WITH UNIQUE KEYS.
PG 17 JSON_TABLE: the SQL-standard way to turn a JSON document into typed rows. Before 17 you combined jsonb_array_elements or jsonb_to_recordset with ->> per field (sql.json.path-table).
One statement: parse the CI report, merge it into test_cases and return what changed. A MERGE with RETURNING can sit in WITH like any data-modifying statement, which is how its output gets sorted.
TC-1 matches with an unchanged status: no action, so no RETURNING row.
PG 17 WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE acts on target rows the source doesn't mention. Before 17 that took a second statement.
merge_action() (PG 17) names the action behind each row; old and new (PG 18) give both sides, with old NULL for the insert. Before 17 a MERGE returned only its row count.

examples.title: Skip scan, EXPLAIN's new defaults, and the async I/O settings (PG 18)

annotations.note: status leads the index and the query never mentions it. Before 18 a B-tree could serve this query only by reading the whole index, so the advice was "filter column first, or a second index".
271 pages of index, for comparison with what the scan touches below.
The answer. Running the query once first also keeps one-time catalog lookups out of the EXPLAIN output below.

Index Searches: 7 (a PG 18 EXPLAIN line): the scan jumped from one status value to the next, touching 23 index buffers instead of 271 pages. Buffers appears without asking for it, and row counts print with two decimals: both new in 18.

PG 18 asynchronous I/O lets a backend queue several reads at once for sequential scans, bitmap heap scans and VACUUM. worker (the default) hands them to io_workers background processes; io_uring needs a Linux build with liburing; sync means no AIO. The effective_io_concurrency default rose to 16. A tuned server shows other values.

use_cases: Reviewing old advice before applying it: Stack Overflow answers, ORM defaults and blog posts written for PostgreSQL 9 to 15
Planning an upgrade: which features you gain, and which incompatibilities (the release notes' Migration section) you must handle
Choosing a minimum supported server version for software you ship, such as TraceLite on a customer's machine
strengths: Several features replace extensions or hand-written workarounds: uuidv7 instead of uuid-ossp, WITHOUT OVERLAPS instead of a hand-written EXCLUDE, JSON_TABLE instead of jsonb_to_recordset chains
RETURNING old/new and MERGE ... RETURNING make audit-style writes one statement, without triggers
Skip scan and async I/O speed up existing queries without changing them
One major version a year, five years of support for each, and fix-only minor releases at least every three months make upgrades plannable
weaknesses: Features depend on the server version, not on your client: code using uuidv7() fails on a PG 17 server with no compile-time warning
Defaults moved: generated columns are virtual unless you say STORED, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints BUFFERS, so old expected outputs and scripts can differ
Some new features are first versions: temporal foreign keys support no CASCADE or SET NULL actions, virtual columns can't use user-defined functions
Managed services and Linux distributions trail the newest release, so 'available in PostgreSQL' and 'available on your server' differ

pitfalls.title: Following advice without its version
pitfalls.detail: 'Use uuid-ossp for UUIDs', 'generated columns are always stored', 'MERGE can't return rows', 'a composite index is useless without its first column': each was true for some versions. Check the release notes for when it changed.

pitfalls.title: Using a feature newer than the oldest server you support
pitfalls.detail: Check at startup or in a migration, and fail with a clear message instead of a syntax error halfway through. server_version_num is an integer: 180007 for 18.7.
pitfalls.good: SELECT current_setting('server_version_num')::int >= 180000 AS has_pg18;

pitfalls.title: Catching unique violations from a temporal key
pitfalls.detail: A WITHOUT OVERLAPS conflict is an exclusion violation, SQLSTATE 23P01, not unique_violation 23505. Error mapping written for plain keys misses it and returns a 500.

pitfalls.title: Assuming a virtual column is indexed or stored
pitfalls.detail: Virtual is the default now. If you need to index the value or read it often from a large table, say STORED explicitly, as before 18.
pitfalls.good: price_gross int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (price_net * 120 / 100) STORED

quiz.q: On PG 18, `CREATE TABLE t (a int, b int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a * 2))` creates b as...
options: A syntax error: STORED is required
quiz.why: PG 18 made VIRTUAL the default. Before 18, STORED was required, so the same statement failed.

quiz.q: Which version added RETURNING to MERGE, and which added old/new in RETURNING?
quiz.why: PG 17 added MERGE ... RETURNING with merge_action(); PG 18 added the old and new aliases for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.

quiz.q: An index on (status, ran_on); the query filters only on ran_on. What changed in PG 18?
options: Nothing, the leading column must be constrained
The B-tree can skip from one status value to the next instead of reading the whole index
PostgreSQL creates a second index automatically
quiz.why: Skip scan lets multicolumn B-tree indexes be used without conditions on the leading columns; it pays off when those columns have few distinct values.

quiz.q: Inserting an overlapping period into a table with `PRIMARY KEY (id, valid WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` fails with which SQLSTATE?
quiz.why: WITHOUT OVERLAPS is enforced like an EXCLUDE constraint on a GiST index, so a conflict is an exclusion violation.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE TABLE (WITHOUT OVERLAPS, PERIOD, VIRTUAL)

lessons.body:
## Concept

PostgreSQL ships one major version a year. Much of what you'll read online predates the
last three, and some of it is now wrong. The headline changes, with the old advice they
retire:

**PostgreSQL 16 (2023)**

- SQL/JSON constructors (`JSON_OBJECT`, `JSON_ARRAY`, `JSON_ARRAYAGG`,
  `JSON_OBJECTAGG`) and the `IS JSON` predicate.
- `ANY_VALUE()`; integer literals in hex, octal and binary (`0x1F`) and underscores in
  numbers (`1_000_000`); `pg_input_is_valid()` to test a cast without an error.
- `pg_stat_io` for I/O statistics; parallel `FULL` and right outer hash joins.

**PostgreSQL 17 (2024)**

- `JSON_TABLE` and `JSON_EXISTS`/`JSON_QUERY`/`JSON_VALUE`: "parse JSON in the app" is
  no longer the only clean option.
- `MERGE ... RETURNING` with `merge_action()`, `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`, and `MERGE`
  on updatable views.
- `COPY ... ON_ERROR ignore`, `transaction_timeout`, incremental backups, the
  `MAINTAIN` privilege, and the builtin `C.UTF-8` collation provider (the one local
  mode's playground database uses).

**PostgreSQL 18 (2025)**

- `uuidv7()`: time-ordered UUID keys without an extension.
- Generated columns are **virtual** by default.
- `RETURNING old.*, new.*` in `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `MERGE`.
- Temporal constraints: `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE ... WITHOUT OVERLAPS` and foreign keys
  with `PERIOD`.
- B-tree **skip scan**; an **asynchronous I/O** subsystem; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes
  `BUFFERS` by default.
- `NOT NULL` constraints stored in `pg_constraint` (nameable, addable `NOT VALID`);
  `CHECK` and foreign keys can be `NOT ENFORCED`; `pg_upgrade` keeps planner
  statistics; `casefold()`; MD5 passwords deprecated; data checksums on by default in
  new clusters.

The examples prove the ones you'll touch in everyday schema and query work; the linked
lessons go deeper.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Language versions:** like checking whether advice targets Java 8 or Java 21, or
  Go before 1.22's loop variable change, check which PostgreSQL version a piece of SQL
  advice assumes. The go.timeline lesson does the same tour for Go.
- **Runtime, not compile time:** a Go program built with a newer toolchain still runs;
  SQL that uses `uuidv7()` fails on a PG 17 server at execution. The database is the
  runtime, and its version is a deployment fact your code should check.
- **Release cadence:** one major version a year, each supported for five years, with
  fix-only minor releases at least every three months. Minor upgrades (18.6 to 18.7) are
  binary replacements; major upgrades go through `pg_upgrade`, dump and restore, or
  logical replication.

## Design notes

Decide a minimum server version deliberately and write it down, as this curriculum does
with `since`. For an application you host, take the newest major version your platform
offers; for software installed on someone else's machine (TraceLite's packaging step),
support what they can realistically run and check `server_version_num` at startup.

Read the "Migration to Version N" section of each release's notes before upgrading: it
lists the incompatibilities, such as the virtual default for generated columns, MD5
deprecation warnings, `AFTER` triggers running as the queuing role, and `VACUUM` and
`ANALYZE` processing inheritance children by default in 18.

Adopt new features where they remove code or extensions: `uuidv7()` for new
UUID-keyed tables, `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` for validity periods, `RETURNING old/new` for
audit-style writes, `JSON_TABLE` for imports. Don't rewrite working code just because a
newer form exists, and keep the old idiom in mind when you read other people's schemas.

lessons.title: Multi-row INSERT, INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM, DELETE ... USING
lessons.summary: Write sets, not rows: many rows per INSERT, rows produced by a query, and UPDATE and DELETE driven by a join. One statement, one round trip, all rows or none.

examples.title: Many rows per INSERT: VALUES lists and unnest over arrays

annotations.note: Three rows, one statement: one round trip, one parse, and all or nothing, since a CHECK failure in any row inserts none of them. The tag reads INSERT 0 3; the 0 is a leftover OID field and is always 0 now.
DEFAULT works per value, so one statement can mix explicit values and column defaults. Columns left out of the list get their default (or NULL) too.

unnest with several arrays in FROM zips them into rows. From Go you pass three slices as parameters, so the SQL text is the same for 3 rows or 3,000: nothing to build, nothing to inject. Arrays of different lengths are padded with NULLs, so check lengths first.

examples.title: INSERT ... SELECT: convert and load from a staging table

annotations.note: Load raw text first, convert in SQL second. A bad row then fails in a query you can inspect and rerun, not halfway through a load.
The rows to insert are a query's result: zero, two or a million of them, inserted by one statement. The tag counts what the query produced (INSERT 0 2), not what staging held.

Turkish number format: drop the thousands dot, then turn the decimal comma into a point, before casting. Cast first and '1.250,00' fails; worse, a thousands-only value such as '1.250' would cast happily to 1.25.
NOT EXISTS skips skus already on sale, so rerunning the load adds nothing. Two loads running at the same moment could still both insert; ON CONFLICT (next lesson) closes that gap.

examples.title: UPDATE ... FROM, DELETE ... USING, and the subquery trap

annotations.note: The target is joined to price_list, and each joined row becomes one update. XYZ-99 matches no product and changes nothing. UPDATE 2 counts target rows.
The join must give at most one source row per target row. With two price_list rows for TEA-01, only one would be applied, and the docs say which one is not predictable. Here sku is the primary key.
USING is DELETE's FROM: join to the list, delete what matches. WHERE p.sku IN (SELECT sku FROM discontinued) is the standard spelling and equally fine here.

A SET with a subquery and no WHERE updates every row; where the subquery finds nothing, the value is NULL. BAK-01 has no new price, and only NOT NULL stops it from losing its price. Add WHERE EXISTS (...) or use FROM.

use_cases: Inserting a batch from Go or TS in one statement: unnest over one array parameter per column
Imports: COPY or INSERT raw rows into a staging table, then INSERT ... SELECT with conversion and filtering
Applying a list to a table: new prices with UPDATE ... FROM, removals with DELETE ... USING
strengths: One statement per batch is one round trip and atomic, unlike a loop of single-row INSERTs that leaves half the rows written if it fails outside a transaction
A join in UPDATE or DELETE states "apply this list" directly, where an ORM typically loads each row into memory and saves it back
Array parameters keep the SQL text constant whatever the batch size, so the driver can reuse one prepared statement
weaknesses: UPDATE ... FROM and DELETE ... USING are PostgreSQL extensions; the portable subquery forms are wordier and easy to get wrong
One huge statement holds its row locks until commit and makes one big transaction; very large backfills need batching
Binding one parameter per value hits the protocol's 16-bit parameter count on big multi-row VALUES; arrays need one parameter per column

pitfalls.title: A source with duplicate keys in UPDATE ... FROM
pitfalls.detail: Each target row is updated at most once, with one of its matching source rows chosen unpredictably. Make the source unique first (a key, GROUP BY, or DISTINCT ON).

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the join condition
pitfalls.detail: UPDATE ... FROM without a WHERE linking the tables joins every target row to every source row: all rows are updated, each with an arbitrary source row.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE products p SET price = l.new_price FROM price_list l;
pitfalls.good: UPDATE products p SET price = l.new_price FROM price_list l WHERE l.sku = p.sku;

pitfalls.title: Running a big UPDATE or DELETE blind
pitfalls.detail: psql has no undo. Run it inside BEGIN, check the count in the command tag (UPDATE 3, not UPDATE 30000), then COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

pitfalls.title: Building multi-row INSERT text in code
pitfalls.detail: Concatenating values into SQL invites injection and produces a new statement text per batch size. Pass arrays to unnest, or use COPY (pgx's CopyFrom) for very large loads.

quiz.q: price_list has two rows for TEA-01 (235 and 240). What does UPDATE products p SET price = l.new_price FROM price_list l WHERE l.sku = p.sku do to TEA-01?
options: Applies both, so the last one wins
Applies one of them; which one is not predictable
quiz.why: A target row is updated at most once per statement, and the docs say which joined row gets used is not readily predictable.

quiz.q: Which statement sets price to NULL for every product missing from price_list?
options: UPDATE products p SET price = l.new_price FROM price_list l WHERE l.sku = p.sku
UPDATE products SET price = (SELECT l.new_price FROM price_list l WHERE l.sku = products.sku)
DELETE FROM products p USING price_list l WHERE l.sku = p.sku
quiz.why: Without a WHERE, the subquery form updates every row, and a subquery that finds nothing yields NULL.

quiz.q: INSERT INTO t (a) SELECT ... reports INSERT 0 2. What is the 0?
options: The number of rows that failed
A legacy OID field, always 0 today
The id of the first inserted row
quiz.why: The tag is INSERT oid count; tables WITH OIDS are gone, so oid is always 0.

quiz.q: A Go service must insert 5,000 rows in one statement without building SQL text. What fits?
options: A loop of 5,000 single-row INSERTs inside one transaction
fmt.Sprintf one VALUES list with all the rows
quiz.why: One parameter per column carries every row; the text never changes. The loop is 5,000 round trips; Sprintf invites injection.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` take sets, like `SELECT` returns them:

- **Multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES`**: many rows in one statement.
- **`INSERT ... SELECT`**: the rows to insert are the result of a query (a staging
  table, another table, `unnest` over arrays sent by the app).
- **`UPDATE ... FROM`**: join the target to other tables; each target row that joins
  is updated using the joined values.
- **`DELETE ... USING`**: the same join, deciding what to delete.

Each is one statement: atomic, one round trip, and reported by a command tag with a
count (`INSERT 0 3`, `UPDATE 2`, `DELETE 2`), which drivers expose as rows affected
(`CommandTag.RowsAffected()` in pgx).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **ORMs** (JPA, Django, Prisma): `for p in products: p.price = new[p.sku]; p.save()` is
  N selects and N updates. `UPDATE ... FROM` is the same intent in one statement, and
  the database does the matching.
- **JDBC's `addBatch()`**: batching saves round trips but still executes the statement
  N times. `unnest` over arrays is one execution with one parameter per column.
- **Go**: `for _, it := range items { tx.Exec(...) }` is the habit to break. Pass one
  slice per column (`[]string` for the skus, and so on) and let `unnest` turn them into
  rows. For tens of thousands of rows and more, pgx's `CopyFrom` (the Go/Postgres
  module) is faster still.
- **SQL Server and MySQL** also allow joins in `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, each with its own
  syntax. PostgreSQL's is `FROM` for `UPDATE` and `USING` for `DELETE`; neither is
  standard SQL.

## Design notes

Prefer a two-step shape for anything that comes from outside: land raw rows in a staging
table, then move them with one `INSERT ... SELECT` (or `UPDATE ... FROM`) that converts,
validates and filters. The conversion lives in a query you can rerun and inspect instead
of in a loop. Keep the source side of every join unique on the join key, because
PostgreSQL won't stop you when it isn't. When an insert must also cope with rows that
already exist, the next lesson replaces `NOT EXISTS` with `ON CONFLICT`, which is safe
under concurrency.

lessons.title: RETURNING, upsert with ON CONFLICT, MERGE
lessons.summary: RETURNING reads back what you wrote in the same statement. ON CONFLICT makes an insert an upsert; MERGE expresses insert/update/delete in one pass with a join condition.

examples.title: Upsert stock levels and read back the affected rows

annotations.note: One statement: insert the new sku, refresh the existing one. The conflict target (sku) must be a unique constraint — a conflict the database never sees can't be upserted.
qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty: existing row plus incoming amount. EXCLUDED is the row that *would have* been inserted.
RETURNING fires once per affected row, after the update or insert — including OLD/NEW in PG 18 for both sides of the change.
MERGE joins source to target and picks an action per row. Use it when the decision is "match by X, then insert/update/delete"; plain ON CONFLICT when it's just insert-or-update.

use_cases: Idempotent ingest: re-running a load must not duplicate rows
Counters and stock: qty = qty + n without read-modify-write races (with FOR UPDATE or in one statement)
API responses that echo the written rows without a second round-trip
strengths: Atomic: no window where a concurrent reader sees the old value between your UPDATE and INSERT
RETURNING eliminates the follow-up SELECT and its race
MERGE covers insert+update+delete in one declarative pass (PG 17 adds MERGE ... RETURNING)
weaknesses: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING hides *why* nothing happened; you still need RETURNING to know
MERGE requires PG 15+; ON CONFLICT remains the portable workhorse
Uperts on hot rows serialize on the row lock — batch bursts can queue

pitfalls.title: ON CONFLICT without a conflict target
pitfalls.detail: DO UPDATE needs (sku) — without it the statement can't know which unique constraint to arbitrate.

pitfalls.title: Assuming RETURNING shows the pre-image
pitfalls.detail: It returns the new row. PG 18's RETURNING OLD/NEW gives both, explicitly.

quiz.q: What does EXCLUDED refer to in ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE?
options: The row that would have been inserted
quiz.why: EXCLUDED carries the proposed insert, so you can combine it with the current row.

quiz.q: RETURNING in an UPDATE gives you…
quiz.why: Default is the post-image; PG 18 adds RETURNING OLD.* / NEW.* for both sides.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` turns a would-be duplicate into an update (`DO UPDATE`) or a no-op
(`DO NOTHING`); `RETURNING` streams the affected rows back out of the same statement.
`MERGE` (PG 15+) joins a source and picks per-row actions.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- App code: the SELECT-then-INSERT-else-UPDATE dance is a race; ON CONFLICT does it in one
  atomic statement.
- Go/TS: RETURNING replaces the "insert, then query by id" round trip — one statement, one
  network hop, no interleaving window.

## Design notes

Upserts are the idiomatic answer to *idempotency*: replaying an event stream or a CSV load
must converge, not duplicate. But decide conflict behavior deliberately — DO NOTHING can
mask bugs where the same key means different things. When the logic grows beyond
insert-or-update (deletes, conditions across tables), that's MERGE's shape.

lessons.title: Soft-delete trade-offs
lessons.summary: A deleted_at column turns DELETE into UPDATE and keeps the row. In exchange, every query, unique constraint and foreign key has to learn what "deleted" means, and the data is still there when the law says it must go.

examples.title: deleted_at instead of DELETE, and the first two things it breaks

annotations.note: A nullable timestamptz rather than a boolean: it records when, and NULL means live. Being NULL-based, the filter is IS NULL; a deleted_at = NULL test would match nothing.
Soft delete is an UPDATE: it writes a new row version, fires UPDATE triggers rather than DELETE ones, and leaves every byte of personal data in place.
The table's default answer is now wrong. Each query, report, export and admin screen must add the filter, and the one that forgets shows deleted accounts without any error.
UNIQUE (email) covers deleted rows too, so the old account blocks the new one (SQLSTATE 23505). The next example narrows it.

examples.title: A partial unique index and a view of live rows

annotations.note: A partial index holds only rows matching its WHERE, so uniqueness applies among live rows only. It's an index, not a constraint: ON CONFLICT must repeat the predicate to use it (ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and a foreign key can't reference it.
The view puts "live" in one place. The app reads live_users and can no longer forget the filter. A simple view like this is also updatable, so UPDATEs through it work too.
Selin's old row has deleted_at set, so it isn't in the index, and the new row doesn't collide with it.
Among live rows the rule still holds. The message says "unique constraint" but names the partial index, users_email_live: no constraint exists, only the index.

examples.title: Foreign keys don't know about deleted_at

annotations.note: A foreign key checks that the parent row exists, and a soft-deleted row exists. CASCADE never fires, and order 13 is accepted for a customer the app considers gone.
The report counts Can's three orders as if nothing happened. Whether that's right (revenue happened) or wrong (active customers) is a decision every join now has to make explicitly.
Anonymizing keeps the row, so orders and invoices stay intact, but removes what identifies the person. That is often the honest version of "delete my account" when records must be retained.
A real DELETE is what ON DELETE CASCADE was declared for: Can's orders go with him, in the same statement.

use_cases: Undo windows: a user can restore something for 30 days before a purge job deletes it for real
Records that others reference and that must outlive deactivation (customers on invoices), usually combined with anonymization
Sync to offline or mobile clients, which must learn that a row was deleted (a tombstone) instead of simply never seeing it again
strengths: Restoring is an UPDATE, while undoing a hard DELETE means restoring a backup
Child rows keep a valid parent, so history (orders, invoices) stays joinable without an archive
Partial unique and partial regular indexes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) keep uniqueness and hot-path indexes about live rows only
weaknesses: Every query must filter; the forgotten filter fails silently by showing deleted data, unlike a missing row, which fails loudly
Constraints stop meaning what they say: UNIQUE needs a partial index, and foreign keys and ON DELETE actions ignore the flag
Deleted rows never leave: tables and non-partial indexes keep growing, and personal data stays stored

pitfalls.title: Treating the flag as erasure
pitfalls.detail: GDPR, and in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, Article 7), can oblige you to erase, destroy or anonymize personal data. A deleted_at flag hides the data; it doesn't remove it from the table, the backups or the replicas. Plan a purge or an anonymizing UPDATE.

pitfalls.title: A plain UNIQUE on a soft-deleted table
pitfalls.detail: Deleted rows keep their values, so re-registering with the same e-mail fails. Use a partial unique index over live rows.
pitfalls.good: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

pitfalls.title: Filtering in some queries but not others
pitfalls.detail: Point the application at a view (live_users) or, for stronger guarantees, row-level security, so forgetting the filter is impossible rather than unlikely.

pitfalls.title: Partial indexes and parameters
pitfalls.detail: The planner uses a partial index only when the query's WHERE provably implies the predicate at planning time. Write deleted_at IS NULL literally (or read through the view); a parameter like deleted_at IS NOT DISTINCT FROM $1 won't match.

quiz.q: users has UNIQUE (email) and a deleted_at column. Selin deletes her account (deleted_at set) and signs up again. What happens?
options: The sign-up works: deleted rows are ignored by constraints
Unique violation: the constraint still sees her old row
quiz.why: Constraints know nothing about the flag. A partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL limits uniqueness to live rows.

quiz.q: orders references customers ON DELETE CASCADE. A customer is soft-deleted. What happens to the orders?
options: Nothing: the parent row still exists, so no foreign key action fires
quiz.why: Foreign key actions react to DELETE and UPDATE of the key, not to other columns changing.

quiz.q: A customer asks you to erase their personal data under KVKK. Their orders must be kept for tax reasons. What fits?
options: Set deleted_at; the data is hidden from the app
Keep the row and replace the personal columns with NULL or placeholders (anonymize)
DELETE the customer and let CASCADE remove the orders
quiz.why: The flag hides but retains the data; a cascade destroys records you must keep. Anonymizing keeps the references and removes the person.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Views (CREATE VIEW, updatable views)
PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (foreign keys and ON DELETE)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Soft delete replaces `DELETE` with `UPDATE ... SET deleted_at = now()`. The row stays;
"deleted" becomes a convention that every reader has to honor. Teams pick it for undo,
for audit, and to keep history (orders, invoices) attached to a customer who left.

The price is that the database's own guarantees no longer line up with what the
application means:

- **Queries** see deleted rows unless each one filters them out.
- **Unique constraints** count deleted rows; you need a partial unique index.
- **Foreign keys** check only that the parent row exists. `ON DELETE` actions never
  fire, and new children can attach to a "deleted" parent.
- **Storage and privacy**: the data, personal data included, never leaves.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **ORMs**: Rails' paranoia/discard, Django packages, Hibernate's `@SQLDelete` and
  `@SQLRestriction` add the filter for you, but only to queries that go through the ORM.
  Raw SQL, reports, BI tools and psql still see every row. A view or row-level security
  enforces the rule in the database, where all of them pass.
- **Go and TS**: there is no ORM magic to lean on with pgx or a query builder, so the
  filter lives in each hand-written query. That is the strongest argument for a view
  such as `live_users` from day one.
- **Garbage collection**: soft-deleted rows are like objects you never release because
  something might still point to them. A retention policy and a purge job are the GC.

## Design notes

First decide what "deleted" means in your domain. Often it's really a state
(`closed`, `cancelled`, `archived`) that deserves a `status` column and its own rules,
not a generic flag. When it is deletion, the usual alternatives are:

- **Hard delete plus archive**: move the row to an `_archive` table in the same
  statement (`WITH gone AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) INSERT INTO ... SELECT * FROM gone`)
  so the live table keeps honest constraints.
- **Anonymize**: keep the row for its references, wipe the personal columns. This is
  how a "delete my account" request can coexist with records you must retain.
- **History tables** (modeling module) when you need what was true at any point in time,
  not just "gone or not".

If you do soft-delete, make it complete: a partial unique index, a view for live rows,
indexes with `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` on hot paths, an explicit decision per foreign
key, and a purge job with a retention period. Privacy law sets the hard limit: KVKK
Article 7 requires personal data to be erased, destroyed or anonymized once the
reasons for processing it no longer exist, and a flag does none of those.

lessons.title: SELECT/WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT
lessons.summary: The everyday query: name the columns, filter rows with WHERE, sort with a deterministic ORDER BY, cut with LIMIT. Clauses run in a fixed logical order, NULLs sort first under DESC, and the default sort order is not Turkish alphabetical.

examples.title: Columns, filters, and when each clause runs

annotations.note: Name the columns you need: the result's shape stays under your control when someone adds a column. ORDER BY may use the alias stock_value because sorting happens after the SELECT list is computed.
AND binds tighter than OR, so this is outdoor OR (kitchen AND in stock), and the out-of-stock Hamak comes back. The same precedence as && over || in Go, Java and JS; SQL just makes it easier to miss.
IN (a, b) means = a OR = b, grouped for you. With the parentheses implied, the AND applies to both categories.
BETWEEN includes both ends. With timestamps that is a trap: BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-30' stops at midnight on the 30th. Use a half-open range there (>= start AND < next start).
Logically, FROM and WHERE run before the SELECT list exists, so WHERE can't see its aliases (SQLSTATE 42703). Repeat the expression, or wrap the query in a subquery and filter outside.

examples.title: ORDER BY, NULL placement, ties, LIMIT and pages

annotations.note: Without ORDER BY, rows come back in whatever order the plan produces. Here that is storage order, and the UPDATE wrote deniz's new row version after the others. It is repeatable on this tiny table, which is exactly why code that relies on it passes tests and breaks later.
NULL sorts as if larger than any value: last under ASC, first under DESC. Emre, who hasn't played, tops the leaderboard.
umut and zeynep tie at 85. Without the id tie-breaker either could be cut at LIMIT 2, and the choice can change with the plan. A unique last sort key makes the result, and every page, deterministic.
OFFSET pages only work over the same deterministic order. The skipped rows are still computed, so deep pages get slower; keyset pagination (indexes module) avoids that.

FETCH FIRST is the SQL-standard spelling (LIMIT is PostgreSQL's and MySQL's); WITH TIES (PG 13) also returns rows that tie with the last one. Ties have no order among themselves, so the outer ORDER BY fixes the display.

examples.title: Sorting Turkish names: code points vs tr-x-icu

annotations.note: StackLab's local databases use the builtin C.UTF-8 collation, which orders by code point, as Go's string comparison does. Fast and the same on every OS, but Çorum lands after Zonguldak and Ağrı after Ankara.

tr-x-icu is ICU's Turkish collation: Ç after C, ğ after g, I before İ. An index on name is built in the column's collation and can't serve this ORDER BY; declare the column COLLATE "tr-x-icu", or add an index with that collation, if this is the order you sort by.
Collation decides comparisons, not just sorting: "before J" is 4 cities by code point and 6 by Turkish rules, because Ç and İ come before J in the Turkish alphabet.

use_cases: List screens: filter, sort by a user-chosen column plus a unique tie-breaker, LIMIT for the page size
Leaderboards and "top N" widgets: ORDER BY ... DESC NULLS LAST, FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES
Turkish-facing lists (cities, customer names) sorted with COLLATE "tr-x-icu"
strengths: WHERE runs next to the data and can use indexes; a Go or TS .filter() runs after every row has crossed the network
NULLS FIRST/LAST and FETCH ... WITH TIES state edge cases declaratively that hand-written comparators usually get wrong
Besides the database default, collation is a per-column or per-query choice, like passing a Turkish Intl.Collator to sort()
weaknesses: Written order (SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE) differs from evaluation order, which is why aliases fail in WHERE
No order without ORDER BY: tests on small tables can pass while relying on an order nothing promises
OFFSET pagination recomputes every skipped row, so deep pages get slower; keyset pagination needs more care

pitfalls.title: SELECT * in application queries
pitfalls.detail: Every column travels to the app, a new column changes every result, and an index-only scan would need every column in the index. Name the columns.

pitfalls.title: Mixing AND and OR without parentheses
pitfalls.detail: a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c). Parenthesize, or use IN for alternatives on one column.
pitfalls.bad: WHERE status = 'new' OR status = 'paid' AND total > 100
pitfalls.good: WHERE status IN ('new', 'paid') AND total > 100

pitfalls.title: Paging without a unique tie-breaker
pitfalls.detail: ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20 can repeat or skip rows when timestamps tie. End the ORDER BY with a unique column.
pitfalls.good: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20

pitfalls.title: DESC puts NULLs on top
pitfalls.detail: NULLS FIRST is the default for DESC. Say NULLS LAST when missing values belong at the bottom.

quiz.q: SELECT price * qty AS total FROM items WHERE total > 100 fails with 'column "total" does not exist'. Why?
options: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list, so the alias doesn't exist yet
quiz.why: Logical order is FROM, WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. ORDER BY can use the alias; WHERE can't.

quiz.q: How does PostgreSQL read WHERE a = 1 OR a = 2 AND b = 3?
options: It's a syntax error without parentheses
quiz.why: AND binds tighter than OR, as && does over || in Go and JS.

quiz.q: ORDER BY rating DESC on a column with some NULLs puts the NULL rows…
quiz.why: NULL sorts as larger than any value, and NULLS FIRST is the default for DESC.

quiz.q: With ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET n, some rows show up on two pages and others on none. The fix?
options: Add a unique tie-breaker: ORDER BY created_at, id
Use FETCH FIRST instead of LIMIT
quiz.why: Rows with equal created_at have no defined order, so each page query may arrange them differently. A unique last key fixes the order.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A `SELECT` is written in one order and evaluated in another:

1. `FROM`: where the rows come from
2. `WHERE`: keep the rows that satisfy the condition
3. `SELECT` list: compute the output columns (and their aliases)
4. `ORDER BY`: sort, by output columns, aliases or any expression
5. `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` (or `FETCH FIRST`): cut the result

(`GROUP BY` and `HAVING` slot in between 2 and 3; they get their own lesson.) Most
surprises in this lesson follow from that order: aliases don't exist in `WHERE`, and
nothing is ordered until step 4. A result without `ORDER BY` has no order you may rely
on, so `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns *some* rows, not the first ones.

Sorting text depends on a collation. StackLab's local-mode databases use the builtin
`C.UTF-8` collation, which compares Unicode code points: fast, identical on every OS, and not
alphabetical for Turkish. `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` asks for Turkish rules where you need them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS arrays**: `WHERE` is `.filter()`, the `SELECT` list is `.map()`, `ORDER BY` is
  `.sort()`, `LIMIT/OFFSET` is `.slice()`. The difference is where they run: next to
  the data, possibly through an index, before anything crosses the network.
- **Comparators**: `ORDER BY points DESC NULLS LAST, id` is Java's
  `Comparator.comparing(...).reversed().thenComparing(...)` or Go's
  `cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(b.points, a.points), cmp.Compare(a.id, b.id))`, with NULL
  placement built in. Like Go's `slices.SortFunc`, SQL's sort is not stable: rows that
  compare equal come out in any order.
- **String order**: Go compares strings byte by byte and JS's `<` compares UTF-16 code
  units; for Turkish letters both give the same order as `C.UTF-8`, Ç after Z. The
  equivalents of `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` are `Intl.Collator('tr')` and Java's
  `Collator.getInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"))`.
- **Python**: `sorted(rows, key=...)[:10]` sorts everything, then slices. PostgreSQL
  takes `LIMIT` into account when planning and can stop early, for example by reading
  just the first entries of a matching index.

## Design notes

Give every query an explicit `ORDER BY` that ends in a unique column whenever the order
is visible to someone: a UI list, an export, a page. It costs little and turns
"usually right" into "always right". For Turkish-facing data, decide the collation in
the schema (`name text COLLATE "tr-x-icu"`) when it's the only order you'll ever sort
by, so indexes and comparisons follow it; keep the code-point default when the column
holds identifiers, codes or e-mails, where linguistic order has no meaning and code
point order is cheaper.

lessons.title: NULL and three-valued logic
lessons.summary: NULL means "unknown", not "empty". Any comparison with NULL yields unknown, which WHERE treats as false — the root of most NULL surprises, and the reason IS DISTINCT FROM and COALESCE exist.

examples.title: x <> 'a' doesn't match NULL; IS DISTINCT FROM does

annotations.note: brin's email is NULL, and NULL <> 'cay@example.com' evaluates to unknown, not true. WHERE keeps only true — so NULL rows vanish.
IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a value you can compare: NULL is distinct from 'cay@example.com', so brin appears. It's the null-safe inequality.
COALESCE substitutes a display value for NULL. Don't use it to "fix" data in UPDATEs — store what you mean, render what you mean.

use_cases: Audit queries where 'not X' must include missing values (IS DISTINCT FROM / IS NULL)
Display defaults (COALESCE(nickname, name))
Deduplication guards (NULLIF in unique-safe upserts)
strengths: Three-valued logic is mathematically consistent: unknown propagates honestly through AND/OR/NOT
IS DISTINCT FROM and IS NULL give you exact, index-friendly null handling
CHECK constraints treat unknown as pass, so partial data isn't rejected by mistake
weaknesses: Every predicate silently returns unknown on NULL: aggregates skip NULLs, NOT IN has its famous trap
NULL = NULL is not true, so joins and DISTINCT behave in ways SQL newcomers don't predict

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL
pitfalls.detail: x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is never true: unknown compares kill the whole list. Use NOT EXISTS.

pitfalls.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)
pitfalls.detail: COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows. Mixing them misreports totals.

pitfalls.title: Writing WHERE col = NULL
pitfalls.detail: Never true. NULL predicates are IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

quiz.q: SELECT 1 WHERE NULL <> 1 returns?
quiz.why: NULL <> 1 is unknown, and WHERE only passes true.

quiz.q: Which is the null-safe version of a <> b?
options: a != b OR a IS NULL
quiz.why: IS DISTINCT FROM compares with NULL-as-a-value in one expression, index-friendly and readable.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Comparison Functions (IS DISTINCT FROM)

lessons.body:
## Concept

SQL has three logical values: true, false, and unknown. NULL compared to anything is
unknown, and WHERE-style filters keep only true. `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`
and `COALESCE` exist to handle unknowns deliberately.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- TS: null and undefined are values you can ===; SQL NULL is the *absence of a value*, and
  it isn't equal to itself. `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true.
- Go: a NULLable column ≈ a pointer you must nil-check; the database forces the check in
  every predicate instead of panicking later.
- C: not a sentinel like NULL pointer dereference — it's a third truth value in the logic.

## Design notes

Schema design decides where NULL is meaningful: a missing value that means "not yet known"
earns NULL; one that means "none" deserves a real value (empty array, false, 0). Constraints
(NOT NULL) then encode the decision, so queries can rely on it. The NOT IN trap is an
anti-join lesson in disguise — covered properly with EXISTS in the joins module.

lessons.title: LIKE/ILIKE/regex, CASE, string and date functions
lessons.summary: Compute in the database instead of in the app: case-insensitive matching with ILIKE, conditional labels with CASE, and formatted output with to_char.

examples.title: ILIKE, CASE labels and to_char formatting

annotations.note: ILIKE lowercases both sides with the database's case rules. StackLab's databases use the builtin C.UTF-8 locale, so Ş/ş and İ/i fold, but Turkish I/ı never pair up: 'ISPARTA' ILIKE 'ısparta' is false. Appending COLLATE "tr-x-icu" switches to Turkish rules.
A searched CASE without ELSE yields NULL when no branch matches, which is why Quiet day gets a NULL label.
Dy and Mon always print English abbreviations. The TM prefix (TMDy, TMMon) translates them using the server's lc_time setting instead.

use_cases: Search boxes: ILIKE '%term%' over names and titles
Reports: CASE labels, to_char formatted dates, grouped totals
strengths: Shaping happens once, in the database, close to the data and its indexes
CASE works everywhere an expression does: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, aggregates
to_char formats dates in the query itself; with the TM prefix, month and day names follow the server's lc_time
weaknesses: Leading-wildcard ILIKE cannot use a btree index; large tables need pg_trgm or full-text search
ILIKE follows the database's case rules: under the default (non-Turkish) mapping, I and ı never match; Turkish rules need COLLATE "tr-x-icu"
Heavy string formatting in SQL moves presentation logic away from the app

pitfalls.title: CASE without ELSE returning NULL
pitfalls.detail: Rows matching no branch come back NULL, which then fails comparisons and concatenation downstream. Add an ELSE when 'other' means something.

pitfalls.title: Trusting to_char for machine-readable output
pitfalls.detail: to_char is presentation and depends on session settings; keep timestamps raw in the wire format and format in the client when the app must compute on them.

quiz.q: Which operator matches case-insensitively?
quiz.why: ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive LIKE; standard SQL has no equivalent.

quiz.q: What does a CASE expression without ELSE return when no branch matches?
quiz.why: A missed CASE yields NULL, which then interacts with three-valued logic downstream.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every row you ship to the app is a row the app must re-shape. Postgres can do
the shaping: `ILIKE` for case-insensitive search, `CASE` for conditional labels,
`to_char` for formatted dates, and the string functions (`upper`, `left`,
`split_part`) for light text munging. The result reads like a tiny report
written in SQL.

`CASE` comes in two forms — searched (`CASE WHEN cond THEN ...`) and simple
(`CASE x WHEN v THEN ...`) — and both return NULL when nothing matches and no
ELSE is given, which connects back to three-valued logic.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

If you reach for the application layer for formatting, this is the lesson that
moves that code. Python: think of `CASE` as a per-row conditional expression
(`x if cond else y`); `to_char` is `strftime` with Postgres's own format
specifiers — note they differ from strftime's codes. Java: `String.format`
lives in the database now, and the format survives whichever client queries
next. JavaScript: this is the work you'd otherwise do in a `.map()` after
fetching — doing it in SQL means less data over the wire and one less place
for the formatting to drift.

## Design notes

Postgres deliberately blurs "expression" and "report": CASE is an expression, so
it sorts, filters and aggregates like any other value; to_char exists so that a
report can come out of the database already formatted (with TM-prefixed patterns,
in the server's lc_time language). The split to keep in mind
is data versus rendering — keep the wire format raw (timestamptz, plain text)
and reach for these functions for evidence-shaped queries and human output, not
for storage formats.

lessons.title: Full-text search: tsvector, tsquery, ranking, a stored tsvector with GIN
lessons.summary: Full-text search reduces documents and queries to normalized lexemes and matches them with @@. Parse what users type with websearch_to_tsquery, order hits with ts_rank, and keep a STORED tsvector column under a GIN index.

examples.title: Documents, queries and @@: four query parsers and prefix matching

annotations.note: The english configuration lowercases, drops stop words and stems: exports becomes export, archived becomes archiv, every becomes everi. Lexemes are index keys, not words. Dropped stop words still count as positions (are was 10, so archiv is 11), which keeps phrase distances honest.

Only to_tsquery reads operators from its input (&, |, !, <-> and parentheses). plainto_tsquery ANDs the words, phraseto_tsquery chains them with <-> (followed by), and websearch_to_tsquery understands quotes, or and a leading dash. All four run the words through the configuration first, so signed is looked up as sign.
exported cases matches because both sides were stemmed to export and case. A quoted phrase has to appear in that order, so "test linked" fails, and -linked excludes the document.

A prefix (:*) is stemmed like any other query word. The stemmer leaves migrati as it is, and the stored lexeme migrat doesn't start with migrati, so the search fails mid-word although migr and migration succeed. The simple configuration doesn't stem: every prefix of migrations matches.

Two words without an operator are a syntax error for to_tsquery (SQLSTATE 42601). A search box fed into it fails on the first space, quote or stray parenthesis. websearch_to_tsquery never raises a syntax error, which, in the docs' words, makes it possible to use raw user-supplied input.

examples.title: Weights, ts_rank and ts_rank_cd, and ts_headline snippets

annotations.note: Both functions return float4. Rounding keeps the display stable. A rank has no unit and no fixed scale: compare ranks within one query, never across queries.

ts_rank_cd (cover density) scores the shortest stretches of text that contain all the query terms, so it needs positions and returns 0 for a stripped vector. Both functions put REQ-2, where the words share a sentence, above REQ-3, where they are a sentence apart.

setweight labels every title lexeme A and every body lexeme B, and || appends the body's lexemes after the title's. The flat vector has no labels, so all its lexemes count as D. With the default weights (D 0.1, C 0.2, B 0.4, A 1.0) REQ-1's rank grows exactly tenfold and the others fourfold: the title match moves REQ-1 far ahead.
REQ-4 mentions the audit log but not export. websearch_to_tsquery ANDs the words, so REQ-4 doesn't match and is never ranked.

ts_headline parses the original text again, which costs more than the match itself: call it only for the rows you display. MaxFragments=2 lets REQ-3's snippet show both distant matches, joined by "...". The default markers are and , and the output is not safe HTML.

examples.title: A stored tsvector column with GIN, and what ranking costs

annotations.note: The vector is computed on every INSERT and UPDATE and kept in the row. The expression must be immutable: to_tsvector('english', ...) is, the one-argument form (which depends on a setting) is only stable. Write STORED: in PG 18 a generated column without it is virtual, and virtual columns can't be indexed.
A stored vector shows the labels and the concatenation: title lexemes at positions 1 to 4 with A, body lexemes from 5 on with B. can and the are stop words, so positions 6 and 8 are missing.
For each lexeme, GIN keeps the rows that contain it. It stores no weight labels, so a query that filters on them (export:A) rechecks every candidate row.

The planner folds websearch_to_tsquery into a constant. The Bitmap Index Scan finds all 4,000 matches, the Sort needs ts_rank for every one of them, and only then does Limit keep 5. A GIN index can't hand rows back in rank order, so ranking costs grow with the number of matches, not with LIMIT.

Every fifth row has both words in its title. Rows 5, 25, 45... also say export in the body, which puts them first. Equal ranks are common in real data too: the id tiebreaker keeps pages from reshuffling.

use_cases: Search boxes over prose: requirement titles and descriptions in TraceLite, articles, tickets, product descriptions, help pages
A Ctrl+K palette over a few thousand records (lessons, documents, commands), with prefix matching for the word being typed
Filtering by words inside SQL, combined with ordinary WHERE conditions, joins and permissions in the same query
strengths: Unlike a separate Elasticsearch cluster, the index is updated in the same transaction as the row: a committed requirement is searchable at once, a rolled-back one never was, and there is no sync job
Unlike ILIKE '%export%', it matches words after normalization: exported finds exports, and stop words don't count
websearch_to_tsquery accepts whatever a user types (quotes, or, -) without raising errors
One STORED tsvector column with a GIN index serves every query; queries name the column, so they can't drift from the indexed expression
weaknesses: ts_rank uses only the document and the query: unlike BM25 in Lucene or Elasticsearch, it doesn't know how rare a word is across the table (no IDF)
GIN finds matches but can't return them in rank order; every match is ranked before LIMIT applies
No typo tolerance: exprot finds nothing (pg_trgm, two lessons on, covers typos)
Stemmers are rule-based per language; prefixes go through them too, so type-ahead needs an unstemmed vector

pitfalls.title: Passing raw user input to to_tsquery
pitfalls.detail: to_tsquery parses its own query language. Two words without an operator are a syntax error (SQLSTATE 42601), and parentheses, quotes or ! in the input change the query.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT id FROM requirements WHERE search @@ to_tsquery('english', $1);
pitfalls.good: SELECT id FROM requirements WHERE search @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1);

pitfalls.title: Prefix search through a stemmer
pitfalls.detail: A prefix is stemmed first: migrati:* stays migrati and misses the stored lexeme migrat. For type-ahead, match the unfinished last word against a simple (unstemmed) vector, built from a word your code has split and quoted.
pitfalls.good: to_tsvector('simple', title) @@ to_tsquery('simple', 'migrati:*')

pitfalls.title: A generated tsvector without STORED (PG 18)
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 18 a generated column without a keyword is virtual, and CREATE INDEX on it fails with 'indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported'. PG 12 to 17 required STORED, so old snippets work as written; new ones that drop the keyword don't.
pitfalls.bad: search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body))
pitfalls.good: search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED

pitfalls.title: Rendering ts_headline output as HTML
pitfalls.detail: The docs warn that ts_headline output is not guaranteed safe for web pages: it removes only some tags from the document, so it is no defence against XSS. Pick markers that can't occur in the text, escape the snippet, then turn the markers into <mark> elements (in React, render text nodes).

pitfalls.title: Searching identifiers with full-text search
pitfalls.detail: The parser reads REQ-104 as the word req and the signed integer -104, so a search for 104 finds nothing. Match codes on their own column with = or pg_trgm, and keep FTS for prose.

quiz.q: A user types into a search box. Which function should receive that text?
quiz.why: websearch_to_tsquery never raises a syntax error and understands quotes, or and a leading dash; to_tsquery fails on plain multi-word input.

quiz.q: The title is labeled A, the body B, default weights. export appears once in REQ-1's title and once in REQ-2's body; the rows are otherwise alike. Which ranks higher for export?
quiz.why: Default weights are D 0.1, C 0.2, B 0.4, A 1.0: the title occurrence is weighted 1.0, the body occurrence 0.4.

quiz.q: There is a GIN index on search. What does it do for ORDER BY ts_rank(search, q) DESC LIMIT 10?
options: Returns the 10 best rows directly, in rank order
Finds all matching rows; each is ranked and sorted before LIMIT applies
Nothing: GIN can't be used together with ORDER BY
quiz.why: GIN answers which rows match. It keeps no ranks, so the executor ranks every match and sorts before the limit.

quiz.q: The user has typed migrati. Why does to_tsquery('english', 'migrati:*') miss a document about migrations?
options: Prefix matching needs a GiST index
The fragment stays migrati after stemming, and the stored lexeme migrat doesn't start with it
The :* syntax only works in websearch_to_tsquery
quiz.why: Query words, prefixes included, go through the configuration's stemmer; use an unstemmed simple vector for type-ahead.

PostgreSQL docs: Controlling Text Search (parsing queries, ranking, headlines)
PostgreSQL docs: Tables and Indexes (a generated tsvector column)
PostgreSQL docs: Text Search Functions and Operators
PostgreSQL docs: Preferred Index Types for Text Search

lessons.body:
## Concept

Full-text search is two data types and an operator. A `tsvector` is a document reduced
to its **lexemes**, normalized words with their positions. A `tsquery` is a query reduced
the same way, plus operators: `&`, `|`, `!` and `<->` (followed by). `vector @@ query`
says whether the document satisfies the query.

A **text search configuration** does the reducing. Its parser splits text into typed
tokens (words, numbers, e-mail addresses...), and for each token type it lists
dictionaries that lowercase the token, drop it as a stop word or stem it. `english`
turns *exports*, *exported* and *exporting* into `export`. The next lesson compares
`english`, `turkish` and `simple`.

On top of matching:

- **Parsing user input:** `websearch_to_tsquery` reads quotes, `or` and `-` and never
  raises a syntax error. `to_tsquery` is the full query language, for queries your code
  builds, including prefixes (`migr:*`).
- **Ranking:** `ts_rank` and `ts_rank_cd` score a match. `setweight` labels lexemes
  A to D so that a title counts more than a body.
- **Snippets:** `ts_headline` marks the matching words in the original text.
- **Speed:** a `tsvector` column, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED`, under a GIN index.

**StackLab has no search yet.** `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` plans a
`search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` column on a `lessons` table, the
engine for a Ctrl+K palette. Today the lessons are bundled into the frontend at build
time, and the app database has neither that table nor a search endpoint. The third
example builds the planned design on TraceLite requirements instead.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Lucene / Elasticsearch:** a configuration is an analyzer (tokenizer plus filter
  chain), a `tsvector` is the analyzed field, GIN is the inverted index, and
  `websearch_to_tsquery` is a simple query-string parser. Two differences matter. The
  index lives in your transaction, so there is no refresh interval and no second system
  to keep in sync. And `ts_rank` looks at one document and the query only: unlike BM25
  it has no IDF, so a word that appears in every row weighs as much as a rare one.
- **Java/Go:** don't build `to_tsquery` input by concatenating user text. It's the same
  mistake as concatenating SQL, except it yields syntax errors and wrong queries instead
  of injection. Pass the text as a parameter to `websearch_to_tsquery`.
- **Python/JS:** `ILIKE '%export%'` is `s.includes('export')`: it finds *exporter* but
  not *exported* when the user typed *exports*. Full-text search matches words after
  normalization, which is what people expect from a search box. Substrings and typos are
  `pg_trgm`'s job, two lessons on.

## How it works

1. The parser splits the text into typed tokens; `ts_debug` shows them. A requirement
   code like `REQ-104` becomes the word `req` and the signed integer `-104`.
2. For each token, the configuration's dictionaries run in order until one recognizes it.
   It returns lexemes, or an empty list for a stop word. Snowball stemmers recognize
   every word, so they come last.
3. `to_tsvector` collects the lexemes, sorted and de-duplicated, with positions (and
   weights after `setweight`). Stop words leave gaps in the positions.
4. A GIN index on the column maps each lexeme to the rows that contain it. `&` intersects
   those row lists and `|` unions them. Ranking needs positions and weights, which the
   index doesn't keep, so it reads the stored vector of every matching row.

## Design notes

- **Store the vector.** A STORED generated column parses the text once per write. The
  docs list two advantages over an expression index on `to_tsvector('english', body)`:
  queries name the column instead of repeating the expression (and its configuration),
  and rechecks read the stored vector instead of parsing the text again. The expression
  index is smaller. Write `STORED` explicitly (PG 18 defaults to virtual).
- **Name the configuration in every call**, queries included. Without it,
  `default_text_search_config` decides, and the next lesson shows that silently finding
  nothing.
- **Search box text** goes to `websearch_to_tsquery`. A Ctrl+K palette that searches as
  you type also needs a prefix for the unfinished last word, and prefixes don't survive
  stemming: keep a `simple` vector for that, and build the prefix query from a word your
  code has split and quoted.
- **Rank what you display.** Order by `rank DESC, id` so that equal ranks don't reshuffle
  between pages. When thousands of rows match, ranking them is the cost; narrow the
  candidates with ordinary filters first.
- **Identifiers aren't prose.** Requirement codes, ticket numbers and version strings go
  in their own column, matched with `=` or `pg_trgm`.
- **Size matters less than you think, both ways.** For a few hundred lessons the planner
  will scan the stored vectors sequentially and that is fine; the GIN index pays off as
  the table grows. Past millions of documents, or when you need relevance tuning,
  synonyms per tenant or faceting, a dedicated search engine starts to earn its upkeep.

lessons.title: The turkish, english and simple FTS configurations; Turkish text gotchas
lessons.summary: A query must use its document's configuration: turkish stems Turkish suffixes, english and simple barely touch Turkish words, and a mismatch finds nothing without an error. to_tsvector lowercases with the database's rules, so İ/ı need lower(... COLLATE "tr-x-icu") on both sides.

examples.title: One sentence, three configurations, and a query in the wrong one

annotations.note: turkish strips plural and case endings (raporlar, testleri) and the past tense (hazırlandı, bitti), and drops ve and the da split off İstanbul'da as stop words. english and simple produce the same vector for this sentence: neither knows Turkish stop words, and the English stemmer finds nothing English to strip here.
The column holds turkish stems, with the configuration named, as an index or generated column requires.
