initdb sets default_text_search_config from the server's locale: english on this English-language Windows machine, possibly turkish on a server installed with a Turkish locale, and the built-in simple when no configuration matches. SET LOCAL pins it for this transaction, so the example behaves the same on any server.

A query that names no configuration is parsed with the default, english. rapor happens to come out unchanged and works; raporlar stays raporlar and şifre becomes şifr, and neither is in the column. No error, no warning, just missing rows, and a test that only searches for base forms passes.
simple only lowercases, so it finds a row only when the user happens to type the stem itself: rapor and şifre.

examples.title: İ/ı: lowercase the Turkish way, on both sides

annotations.note: The turkish configuration lowercases each word with the database's rules before stemming. Here (builtin C.UTF-8) both I and İ become i: IĞDIR turns into iğdir, which the stemmer cuts to ik; ığdır becomes ık; mixed Iğdır becomes iğdır and is left alone. One city, three lexemes. lower(... COLLATE "tr-x-icu") maps I to ı and İ to i first, and all three spellings meet at ık.
The flip side is IZMIR, typed on an English keyboard: Turkish rules make it ızmır, which no longer matches İzmir. Each lowering is right for one way of typing and wrong for the other.
to_tsvector ignores the collation of its argument: ISPARTA still becomes ispar. A column declared COLLATE "tr-x-icu" doesn't make full-text search Turkish; lower() is what reads the collation.
lower() is immutable, with or without the COLLATE, so the Turkish lowering can live in a generated column and under an index.

The query must be lowered the same way as the column. raw_query works only when the user typed lowercase Turkish; lowered, every Turkish spelling finds its rows. igdir, typed without Turkish letters, finds nothing either way: no lowering turns g into ğ. That case belongs to unaccent and pg_trgm, in the next lesson.

examples.title: Where the turkish stemmer goes wrong, and prefixes as a second net

annotations.note: rapor is the stemmer at its best: three forms, one lexeme. hata and gereksinim show its failure mode. The bare word ends in letters that look like a suffix (-ta as in kitapta, -im as in kitabım), so hata is cut to ha and gereksinim to gereks, while hatalar and gereksinimler are cut back to the real root. Singular and plural end up as different lexemes.

ts_debug shows each token, its type, the dictionary that took it and the result. The apostrophe is a separator, so TraceLite'ın yields traceli (the final -te is read as a suffix too) and ın, and İstanbul'da yields istanbul and the stop word da. Proper-noun suffixes become loose lexemes like ın.

A stem search for hata finds only the singular. A prefix on unstemmed words finds every form, because Turkish adds suffixes at the end, and it also finds Hatay, a city. Prefixes trade misses for false hits; rank stem matches above prefix-only ones.

use_cases: TraceLite installations with Turkish requirement texts: turkish configuration over the description, with Turkish lowering
Names, codes and tags (people, cities, product codes): the simple configuration, no stemming
Search-as-you-type over Turkish titles: a simple vector for prefixes next to the stemmed one
strengths: A built-in Turkish stemmer and stop word list: raporlar, raporları and raporların all find rapor with no extra setup, unlike LIKE
ts_debug shows exactly which token went through which dictionary, so a missed match can be explained rather than guessed at
Configurations are SQL objects: CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION ... (COPY = turkish) and ALTER MAPPING change behaviour per database without code
weaknesses: The stemmer is rule-based: some common words split into several lexemes (hata/ha, gereksinim/gereks, kullanıcı/kullanıç)
No Turkish-aware lowercasing inside the configuration: it uses the database's case rules, which map I to i under C.UTF-8
Unlike Lucene's Turkish analysis chain, there is no apostrophe handling: suffixes after an apostrophe become separate lexemes
A wrong or missing configuration in a query raises no error; the only symptom is missing rows

pitfalls.title: Querying in a different configuration than the document
pitfalls.detail: The column was built with turkish; a query without a configuration uses default_text_search_config, which depends on how the server was installed. raporlar then finds nothing, silently.
pitfalls.good: WHERE search @@ plainto_tsquery('turkish', $1)

pitfalls.title: Expecting COLLATE to make full-text search Turkish
pitfalls.detail: to_tsvector ignores the collation of its input and lowercases with the database's rules. Only lower() reads the collation, so lowercase explicitly before handing the text over.
pitfalls.good: to_tsvector('turkish', lower(title COLLATE "tr-x-icu"))

pitfalls.title: Lowering only the document
pitfalls.detail: With Turkish lowering in the column, the column holds ık for IĞDIR, but plainto_tsquery('turkish', 'IĞDIR') produces ik. Put the lowering in one SQL function and call it for the column and for every query.
pitfalls.good: WHERE search @@ plainto_tsquery('turkish', lower($1 COLLATE "tr-x-icu"))

pitfalls.title: Putting unaccent in front of the turkish stemmer
pitfalls.detail: The unaccent docs show ALTER MAPPING ... WITH unaccent, french_stem. The same recipe weakens the Turkish stemmer, whose rules read ı, ğ, ö and ü: tested here, gözlüklerini becomes gozlukler instead of gözlük, ağacı stays agaci instead of ağaç, and ığdır becomes igi. Keep the stemmed vector Turkish and add a folded one next to it if users type without Turkish letters.

pitfalls.title: Trusting the stemmer with your domain vocabulary
pitfalls.detail: hata (error) and gereksinim (requirement) are the words a TraceLite user searches for most, and both split into several lexemes. Run your vocabulary through to_tsvector('turkish', word) once and add a prefix match or a synonym dictionary where it fails.

quiz.q: The column holds to_tsvector('turkish', title). The app runs WHERE search @@ plainto_tsquery($1) on a server whose default configuration is english. What does a search for raporlar return?
options: The matching rows: Postgres converts the query to turkish
Nothing, silently: the query keeps raporlar, the column holds rapor
quiz.why: Configurations are applied, not checked. The english stemmer leaves raporlar alone, and that lexeme isn't in the column.

quiz.q: In this database (builtin C.UTF-8), what does to_tsvector('turkish', 'IŞIK') contain?
quiz.why: The configuration lowercases with the database's rules, which map I to i; ş lowercases normally. lower('IŞIK' COLLATE "tr-x-icu") would give ışık.

quiz.q: Why does a turkish-configuration search for hata miss a requirement titled 'Raporlama modülündeki hatalar'?
options: The stemmer cuts hata to ha but hatalar to hata, so query and document get different lexemes
Turkish words need a GiST index
quiz.why: The stemmer works by suffix rules; when a bare word ends like a suffix, it is cut too far.

quiz.q: A user types IZMIR on an English keyboard. Which lowering, applied to both sides, lets it match İzmir?
quiz.why: C.UTF-8 maps I and İ to i, so both become izmir. Turkish rules turn IZMIR into ızmır. For users who type both ways, the next lesson folds ı and i together.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Dictionaries (simple, Snowball, synonym, Ispell)
PostgreSQL docs: Testing and Debugging Text Search (ts_debug)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A configuration is the language of a search, and it has to be the same on both sides of
`@@`. Three matter for Turkish text:

- **`turkish`**: Snowball's Turkish stemmer and a Turkish stop word list. It removes
  plural, case, possessive and tense suffixes (*raporları* → `rapor`, *bitti* → `bit`)
  and drops words like *ve*, *da* and *için*.
- **`english`**: the English stemmer and stop words. On Turkish text it mostly does
  nothing, and now and then applies an English rule (*şifre* → `şifr`).
- **`simple`**: lowercase, nothing else. No stop words, no stemming: right for names,
  codes and tags, and as the prefix companion of a stemmed vector.

Three Turkish traps follow, and none of them raises an error:

1. **Configuration mismatch.** A document built with `turkish` and a query parsed with
   another configuration match only where both happen to produce the same lexeme.
2. **Lowercasing follows the database, not Turkish.** Each word is lowercased with the
   database's case rules before the stemmer sees it. StackLab's databases use the builtin
   `C.UTF-8` locale, which maps both `I` and `İ` to `i`, so *IĞDIR*, *Iğdır* and *ığdır*
   become three different lexemes. `lower(text COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`, applied to the
   column and to the query, fixes this for text typed with Turkish letters.
3. **The stemmer is suffix rules, not a dictionary.** It handles regular nouns well and
   cuts some words too far: *hata* becomes `ha` while *hatalar* becomes `hata`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java:** `"TITLE".toLowerCase()` uses the JVM's default locale, and on a Turkish
  machine returns `tıtle`: the classic Turkish locale bug. PostgreSQL errs the other way.
  It never applies Turkish rules unless the expression names a Turkish collation.
  `toLowerCase(Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"))` corresponds to `lower(x COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`.
- **Go:** `strings.ToLower` applies Unicode's default mapping, like `C.UTF-8`;
  `strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` applies Turkish rules.
- **Python/JS:** `str.lower()` and `toLowerCase()` use Unicode's full case mapping, so
  `'İ'` becomes `i` plus a combining dot (two code points), while `C.UTF-8`'s simple
  mapping gives a plain `i`. Text lowered in the app and text lowered in Postgres can
  differ byte for byte: lowercase in one place. `toLocaleLowerCase('tr')` applies
  Turkish rules.
- **Lucene / Elasticsearch:** the Turkish analysis chain has a Turkish lowercase filter
  and an apostrophe filter that drops the suffix after an apostrophe. PostgreSQL's
  `turkish` configuration has neither: you add the lowercasing yourself, and
  *TraceLite'ın* leaves a lexeme `ın` behind.

## Design notes

**Choose per field.** Turkish prose gets `turkish`; names, codes and tags get `simple`.
For rows in different languages, store the configuration in a column:
`to_tsvector(lang, body)` with `lang regconfig` is still immutable and indexable. A query
then ORs the languages it might be in: `plainto_tsquery('turkish', $1) ||
plainto_tsquery('english', $1)`.

**Normalize in one place.** The Turkish lowering has to happen identically for the column
and for every query. Put it in an SQL function and call it on both sides, rather than
lowering in Go or TypeScript on one side and in SQL on the other.

**Stems and words, together.** Stems catch *kitabı* for *kitap* (consonant change, which
a prefix misses); prefixes catch *hatalar* for *hata* (which the stemmer misses). Keep
both, and rank by the stem match:

```sql
search_stems tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS
  (to_tsvector('turkish', lower(title COLLATE "tr-x-icu"))) STORED,
search_words tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS
  (to_tsvector('simple', lower(title COLLATE "tr-x-icu"))) STORED
-- GIN on both; $1 is the lowered input, $2 a prefix query built from its last word
WHERE search_stems @@ plainto_tsquery('turkish', $1)
   OR search_words @@ to_tsquery('simple', $2)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_stems, plainto_tsquery('turkish', $1)) DESC, id
```

**Know your users' keyboards.** Turkish lowering is right when people type Turkish
letters. If many type `IZMIR` or `igdir`, no lowering helps; fold both sides to ASCII
for matching (the next lesson's `unaccent` key) and accept that *kır* and *kir* become
the same word.

**Custom dictionaries are possible, at a price.** A synonym dictionary can map your
domain's problem words, and Ispell/Hunspell dictionaries for Turkish exist, but their
files must live in the server's `tsearch_data` directory: an operations task, not
something an application migration can ship.

lessons.title: pg_trgm similarity, ICU collations and case-insensitive matching, unaccent
lessons.summary: pg_trgm scores strings by shared three-letter pieces: it forgives typos, not ş typed as s. An unaccent search key in an IMMUTABLE wrapper folds those away (merging ı and i), and nondeterministic ICU collations make =, LIKE and UNIQUE case-insensitive with Turkish rules.

examples.title: Trigrams, similarity, % and <->, on Turkish city names

annotations.note: pg_trgm is a trusted extension, so the non-superuser playground role may create it; the rollback removes it again.

Each word is lowercased, padded with two spaces in front and one behind, and cut into three-character pieces. The six entries for ığdır are its six trigrams; those containing non-ASCII letters print as hex codes. Which characters count as letters depends on the database's LC_CTYPE (see the pitfalls): with LC_CTYPE C, this database used to return only four trigrams, around d and r.

similarity is shared trigrams divided by all distinct trigrams of both strings: Antlya and Antalya share 5 of 10. % compares it with pg_trgm.similarity_threshold (default 0.3), and a trigram index can serve %.
<-> is the distance, 1 - similarity. ORDER BY distance LIMIT 1 is a "did you mean" lookup; name breaks ties. A GiST trigram index can return rows in this order directly, GIN can't.

IZMIR finds İzmir at 1.00, because pg_trgm lowercases with the database's rules (C.UTF-8 maps I and İ to i). Turkish letters are another matter: sanliurfa reaches only 0.25, below the % threshold; igdir lands on İzmir (0.20) rather than Iğdır; ızmır, which is what Turkish lowercasing makes of IZMIR, shares almost nothing with İzmir.

examples.title: A folded search key: unaccent in an IMMUTABLE wrapper, under a trigram index

annotations.note: unaccent replaces characters by a rules table (unaccent.rules): ş to s, ı to i, İ to I, ğ to g. In Turkish these are letters of their own, not accented ones; the table doesn't care, which is exactly what input typed on an English keyboard needs.

unaccent is STABLE and index expressions need IMMUTABLE, hence the wrapper; IMMUTABLE is our promise to reindex if unaccent.rules ever changes. The RETURN body (SQL-standard, PG 14) is parsed now and records its dependencies. A quoted body would be parsed at run time, and since PG 17 CREATE INDEX, REINDEX and ANALYZE run with a safe search_path: tested here, such a wrapper fails with 'text search dictionary "unaccent" does not exist'.

10,000 generated village names give the planner a reason to use the index. The index stores the trigrams of search_key(name): every I variant (I, ı, İ, i) becomes i, and ş, ğ, ç, ö, ü lose their marks.
Every ASCII spelling now finds its city at 1.00, and ızmır meets İzmir. Istambul still scores 0.50: folding fixes letters, trigrams fix typos, and the two combine.
search_key('SANLIURFA') is computed once at plan time, and search_key(name) is exactly the indexed expression, so the GIN index answers %. A query spelled lower(unaccent(name)) wouldn't match it.
The price: kır (countryside) and kir (dirt), ılık (lukewarm) and ilik (bone marrow) share a key. Use the key to find candidates; display, rank and compare with the original text.
Indexing unaccent directly fails: functions in an index expression must be IMMUTABLE (SQLSTATE 42P17).

examples.title: Nondeterministic ICU collations: Turkish case-insensitive =, LIKE and UNIQUE

annotations.note: ks-level2 compares letters and accents but ignores case; ks-level1 ignores accents too. tr uses the Turkish case pairs (I/ı, İ/i) and treats ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü as letters of their own; und, the root locale, uses Unicode's defaults. deterministic = false is what allows different strings to compare equal.

tr_ci pairs ISPARTA with ısparta and İZMİR with izmir, but not IZMIR with izmir. und_ci does the opposite: I pairs with i, and İ counts as I with a dot accent, equal to i only at level 1. Çeşme equals cesme only under und_ai, because Turkish treats ç and ş as letters at every level. Iğdır never equals igdir: even the root collation keeps ı apart. No collation is the folded key of the previous example.

On the column, the collation makes every comparison Turkish and case-insensitive, with no lower() in the queries, and the primary key index follows it. citext would apply the database's lower() instead, which maps I to i.
IŞIK finds ışık. LIKE with a nondeterministic collation is new in PG 18; ILIKE, SIMILAR TO and regular expressions still refuse such collations (ILIKE fails with SQLSTATE 0A000).
The primary key compares with the column's collation, so DENİZ is a duplicate of Deniz: case variants can't register as separate users.

use_cases: "Did you mean": the nearest city, product or customer name to a misspelled query (ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT 5)
Search boxes used from English keyboards or phones without Turkish letters: igdir, sanliurfa, IZMIR
Case-insensitive identities with Turkish rules: usernames, tags, city names in a UNIQUE column
Substring search (LIKE '%fragment%') on titles and codes, with a trigram index
strengths: Typo tolerance with no external engine: similarity, % and <-> work per row and are indexable with GIN or GiST
unaccent folds Turkish letters that Unicode normalization keeps: ı has no decomposition, so Python's NFKD trick leaves it alone; unaccent maps it to i
A nondeterministic collation moves case-insensitivity into the schema: =, LIKE (PG 18), UNIQUE and the index agree, and no query can forget a lower()
weaknesses: Trigram similarity knows nothing about language: ş and s, ı and i are simply different characters, so ASCII-typed Turkish scores low without folding
unaccent is STABLE: indexing it needs an IMMUTABLE wrapper, a promise Postgres doesn't check
Folding merges distinct Turkish words (kır and kir)
Nondeterministic collations cost performance, rule out B-tree deduplication, and don't support ILIKE, SIMILAR TO or regular expressions

pitfalls.title: pg_trgm on a database with LC_CTYPE C
pitfalls.detail: pg_trgm decides which characters are letters through the database's LC_CTYPE, fixed at CREATE DATABASE. Before StackLab's playground database was recreated, it had LC_CTYPE C, and show_trgm('ığdır') returned only {"  d","  r"," d "," r "}: ı and ğ counted as separators, weakening similarity and trigram index lookups on Turkish words. Run show_trgm('ığdır') on a new server: six entries is right. Fixing it means a new database; scripts/fix-playground-ctype.sql does that for the playground.

pitfalls.title: Indexing unaccent() directly
pitfalls.detail: unaccent is STABLE, so CREATE INDEX fails with 'functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE'. Wrap it, and use the wrapper in both the index and the queries.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE INDEX ON places USING gin (lower(unaccent(name)) gin_trgm_ops);
pitfalls.good: CREATE INDEX ON places USING gin (search_key(name) gin_trgm_ops);

pitfalls.title: A wrapper whose body is a string
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 17, CREATE INDEX, REINDEX, ANALYZE and VACUUM run with a safe search_path, so a quoted body can't find an unaccent installed in another schema: 'text search dictionary "unaccent" does not exist'. Use a RETURN body, which is parsed when the function is created, or schema-qualify the function and the dictionary.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS 'SELECT lower(unaccent(''unaccent''::regdictionary, $1))';
pitfalls.good: CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT RETURN lower(unaccent('unaccent'::regdictionary, $1));

pitfalls.title: Expecting an accent-insensitive collation to fold Turkish letters
pitfalls.detail: und-u-ks-level1 equates Çeşme with cesme but keeps ı apart from i; tr-u-ks-level1 equates neither, because in Turkish they are letters. For users typing without Turkish letters, compare folded keys instead.

pitfalls.title: ILIKE on a nondeterministic column
pitfalls.detail: ILIKE doesn't support nondeterministic collations and fails with SQLSTATE 0A000. Since PG 18, plain LIKE does, and it is already case-insensitive under such a collation.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT username FROM users WHERE username ILIKE 'den%';
pitfalls.good: SELECT username FROM users WHERE username LIKE 'den%';

quiz.q: Why does sanliurfa score only 0.25 against Şanlıurfa?
options: ş and ı are different characters from s and i, so most trigrams differ
The similarity threshold is set too low
quiz.why: pg_trgm lowercases but doesn't fold letters; folding both sides with unaccent makes them identical.

quiz.q: CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (lower(unaccent(name)) gin_trgm_ops) fails. Why?
options: unaccent is STABLE, and index expressions need IMMUTABLE functions
Only a superuser may index unaccent
quiz.why: unaccent depends on a dictionary that could change. An IMMUTABLE wrapper is the accepted workaround, with the duty to reindex if the rules change.

quiz.q: Under a nondeterministic collation with locale tr-u-ks-level2, which pair compares equal?
quiz.why: Turkish case pairs are I/ı and İ/i; level 2 still distinguishes accents, and in Turkish ç and ş are separate letters anyway.

quiz.q: username text COLLATE tr_ci (nondeterministic). What does WHERE username ILIKE 'den%' do on PG 18?
options: Raises an error: ILIKE doesn't support nondeterministic collations
quiz.why: PG 18 added LIKE support for nondeterministic collations, not ILIKE. Use LIKE, which is case-insensitive under this collation.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Pattern Matching (LIKE with nondeterministic collations)
PostgreSQL docs: CREATE FUNCTION (SQL-standard function bodies)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Full-text search matches words. People also expect a search box to forgive two other
things, and Postgres has a tool for each, plus one for case:

- **Typos:** `pg_trgm` cuts strings into trigrams and measures their overlap.
  `similarity()` gives a score, `%` tests it against a threshold, `<->` is the distance
  for "did you mean" ordering, and GIN or GiST trigram indexes serve `%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE`
  and regular expressions.
- **Letters typed differently:** `unaccent` maps characters through a rules table, so
  *sanliurfa* and *Şanlıurfa* get the same key. It is STABLE, so indexing it takes an
  IMMUTABLE wrapper.
- **Case:** a nondeterministic ICU collation such as `tr-u-ks-level2` makes `=`, `LIKE`
  (PG 18), `UNIQUE` and indexes ignore case, with Turkish case pairs.

The Turkish angle is that people write *Iğdır* at least three ways: *Iğdır*, *IĞDIR*
and *igdir*. A collation handles case, trigrams handle typos, and only a folded key
handles a keyboard without Turkish letters. `pg_trgm` itself lowercases with the
database's rules (`C.UTF-8` here, I to i), and decides what counts as a letter through
the database's `LC_CTYPE`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** `similarity` is in the spirit of `difflib.SequenceMatcher.ratio()`, but
  computed next to the data and indexable. The usual accent strip,
  `unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', s)` followed by dropping combining marks, turns ş into s
  but leaves ı alone (ı has no decomposition); `unaccent`'s table maps it to i.
- **Java:** a `Collator` for `Locale.forLanguageTag("tr")` with strength `SECONDARY` is
  `tr-u-ks-level2`; `PRIMARY` is level 1. Postgres applies the same idea (with ICU's
  rules) to `=`, `UNIQUE` and indexes rather than only to `compare()`.
- **JS:** `new Intl.Collator('tr', { sensitivity: 'accent' })` corresponds to
  `tr-u-ks-level2`, and `sensitivity: 'base'` to level 1.
- **Go:** `golang.org/x/text/collate` with `language.Turkish` and `collate.IgnoreCase`
  gives the same comparisons in application code.

## Design notes

Pick the tool by the job:

- **Display and sort:** the original text, ordered with `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"`.
- **Identity and uniqueness** (usernames, tags): a nondeterministic Turkish collation on
  the column. The citext docs themselves recommend nondeterministic collations over
  citext, which lowercases with the database's rules and so pairs I with i.
- **Finding:** a folded key (`lower(unaccent(...))` in an IMMUTABLE wrapper) with a
  trigram index, matched with `%` or `LIKE`. Store it as a generated column
  (`name_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (search_key(name)) STORED`) if many queries use it.
- **Words in prose:** full-text search with the `turkish` configuration. The pg_trgm docs
  suggest combining the two: collect the words of your documents with
  `ts_stat('SELECT to_tsvector(''simple'', body) FROM ...')`, index that word list with
  trigrams, and offer the nearest word when a search finds nothing.

**GIN or GiST.** Both serve filtering (`%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE`, regex). Choose GiST when
you need `ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT n` served from the index: the docs note that GIN
can't return rows by distance.

**Thresholds are per session.** `%` uses `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` (0.3). Short
strings have few trigrams, so one typo moves their score a lot; test the threshold on
your real names, or order by `<->` with a `LIMIT` instead of filtering with `%`.

**casefold() isn't the Turkish answer either.** PG 18's `casefold()` follows the
collation: under this database's `C.UTF-8` it leaves İ as it is (`dİyarbakir`), with
`COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` it gives `diyarbakır`. For Turkish text, the collation decides.

**Letters come from LC_CTYPE, not the collation.** The pg_trgm docs don't say how it
finds words; the source does. Its letter test (contrib/pg_trgm/trgm.h, macro ISWORDCHR)
calls `t_isalnum_with_len` (src/backend/tsearch/ts_locale.c), which asks the C library
under the database's LC_CTYPE, whatever the collation provider; when LC_CTYPE is C it
tests single bytes, so every non-ASCII letter is a separator. Observed on PostgreSQL 18.7
here: `show_trgm('ığdır')` has six trigrams under today's LC_CTYPE 'English_United
States.1252', and had four, only those of d and r, under the playground's earlier
LC_CTYPE 'C' (the pitfall). What PostgreSQL 18 moved to the collation provider is
lower-casing: its release notes name pg_trgm under the change to full text search, and
contrib/pg_trgm/trgm_op.c now lower-cases with `str_tolower` and the default collation
where 17 used libc. On another server, check `datctype` in `pg_database`.

lessons.title: Roles and privileges: GRANT, default privileges, a least-privilege app user
lessons.summary: A role's attributes decide what it may do to the server; privileges decide what it may do to each object; ownership is a third, irrevocable power. Run the app as a role that owns nothing, and give it exactly the grants its queries need.

examples.title: The sandbox role: what it is, and what it may not do

annotations.note: Attributes are switches on the role itself, set by CREATE ROLE and ALTER ROLE, not by GRANT. Not a superuser, so every permission check applies; no CREATEROLE or CREATEDB, so it can't mint identities or databases; no BYPASSRLS, so row-level policies (next lesson) bind it.

'USAGE' asks whose privileges this role holds without SET ROLE. pg_database_owner is a predefined role whose one implicit member is the current database's owner. Since PostgreSQL 15 it owns every new database's public schema, so by default whoever owns a database controls its public schema.

EXECUTE inside an EXCEPTION block runs in a subtransaction: a failure is undone and reported, and the list goes on. Only SQLSTATE 42501 (insufficient_privilege) is caught, so any other error still stops the script and 'allowed' really means allowed. Successful statements stay in effect until the run's final ROLLBACK.
Identity management is closed: no new roles, no new attributes for itself, and no switching into a role it is not a member of, not even a predefined one such as pg_read_all_stats.

The reason this role is not a superuser (ADR-0008): COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs a shell command as the operating-system account the server runs under, here on your own machine. Only superusers and members of pg_execute_server_program may. psql's \copy runs on the client instead and is open to everyone.
No server files and no password hashes. pg_authid is readable by superusers only; pg_roles is the public view of it, with the password column always reading ********.
Logging settings have context 'superuser' in pg_settings: an ordinary role can neither silence nor flood the server log.

Inside its own database the owner is strong: it creates schemas, and on a fresh database it could drop public through pg_database_owner. StackLab's setup gave the playground's public to postgres, so that drop is refused here. That is the intended blast radius: one database, where each sql run is rolled back and each sql-nontx run's schema dropped. Nothing outside it.

examples.title: GRANT and REVOKE, down to columns; ownership survives REVOKE ALL

annotations.note: relacl stays NULL until the first GRANT or REVOKE. NULL means the built-in default: every privilege for the owner, none for anyone else. Tables give PUBLIC nothing by default; functions do (example 3).

A column grant: a reporting role can see who a customer is without the national ID. has_table_privilege is false because there is no table-wide SELECT; the column checks see the grant. The role name 'public' asks about the PUBLIC pseudo-role, which every role belongs to.

The app-role pattern, played on ourselves because this sandbox can't create roles: INSERT, UPDATE of name only, no DELETE or TRUNCATE. An owner may revoke its own ordinary privileges, and always keeps the grant options to give them back.

An aclitem reads grantee=privileges/grantor, and an empty grantee is PUBLIC. r SELECT, a INSERT, w UPDATE, d DELETE, D TRUNCATE, x REFERENCES, t TRIGGER, m MAINTAIN (PostgreSQL 17). psql's \dp prints the same strings.
Both succeed through column grants. The UPDATE needs UPDATE on name and, because its WHERE reads id, SELECT on id, which PUBLIC (so every role, this one included) holds.

The right to alter or drop an object comes with ownership and can't be revoked. A service that connects as the owner of its tables can always DROP them, whatever you REVOKE: that is why the owner and the app are separate roles.
SQLSTATE 42501. * expands to every column, including tckn (never granted) and email (added after the grants, so nobody has it yet). New columns stay private until someone grants them.

examples.title: Default privileges for future objects, and the sequence trap

annotations.note: Defaults differ by object type. A new schema and a new table give PUBLIC nothing, but every new function is executable by PUBLIC. Harmless for a pure function; for a SECURITY DEFINER function, which runs with its owner's rights, it's an open door.

Default privileges belong to the creating role (here the current one) and are applied when an object is created. In production the creator is the migration role: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner IN SCHEMA tracelite GRANT ... TO tracelite_app.

The documented way to drop PUBLIC's EXECUTE on future functions. It has to be global: per-schema defaults are added to the global ones, so a per-schema REVOKE can't take away what the global default grants.
pg_default_acl is what psql's \ddp lists. Kind r is tables, f functions; the global entry has schema OID 0. The function entry now holds only the owner's EXECUTE.

The new table got the default grants and the new function lost PUBLIC's EXECUTE, while projects, created earlier, kept its old ACL. Defaults never touch existing objects; GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA does that, once, in the same migration.

The identity column's INSERT succeeds without any sequence privilege. serial calls nextval(), which needs USAGE or UPDATE on the sequence: SQLSTATE 42501. An app role built from table grants alone fails on its first INSERT into a serial table; grant ON SEQUENCES too, or use identity columns.

use_cases: A separate owner role for migrations and a login role with DML only for the running service
A read-only reporting or BI role with column grants that leave out personal data (TCKN, phone, address), one of the technical measures KVKK Article 12 asks for
A monitoring login that is a member of pg_monitor instead of a superuser
Auditing a database: who can read or change what, from relacl, attacl, has_*_privilege and information_schema.table_privileges
strengths: Privileges are enforced by the server on every statement, whatever the client: an ORM, psql or an injected query all hit the same check, unlike permission checks in application code
Grants reach down to single columns, so personal data can be hidden from a role without a view or a second table
Roles are users and groups in one concept: grant privileges to a NOLOGIN group role, then grant the group to login roles
Predefined roles (pg_monitor, pg_read_all_data, pg_maintain, pg_signal_backend) give operational powers without superuser
weaknesses: Ownership can't be restricted: the owner can always ALTER, DROP and re-grant, so least privilege depends on the app not owning anything
Default privileges are per creating role and only affect future objects, two details that make 'the app can't read the new table' a classic deploy failure
PUBLIC gets EXECUTE on every new function and CONNECT and TEMPORARY on every new database unless you revoke them
Roles are cluster-wide and not dumped by pg_dump: they live in migrations or provisioning scripts outside the database's own backup

pitfalls.title: The service connects as the owner of its tables
pitfalls.detail: REVOKE does nothing against ownership, and table owners bypass row-level security unless FORCE is set. An SQL injection or a bad migration in the service can DROP or rewrite anything it owns. Own the schema with a NOLOGIN role; log in as a role that owns nothing.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE TABLE requirements (...);  -- run by the role the service logs in as
pitfalls.good: CREATE SCHEMA tracelite AUTHORIZATION tracelite_owner;  -- migrations SET ROLE tracelite_owner; the service logs in as tracelite_app

pitfalls.title: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES run as the wrong role
pitfalls.detail: Default privileges apply to objects created by the role they were set for. Run by an admin without FOR ROLE, they cover the admin's future tables, not the ones the migration role creates, and the app gets 'permission denied' after the next deploy.
pitfalls.bad: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA tracelite GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO tracelite_app;  -- as postgres
pitfalls.good: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner IN SCHEMA tracelite GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO tracelite_app;

pitfalls.title: Forgetting sequences
pitfalls.detail: TABLES defaults don't cover sequences. serial columns need USAGE on their sequence; identity columns don't. Grant both kinds explicitly.
pitfalls.good: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner IN SCHEMA tracelite GRANT USAGE ON SEQUENCES TO tracelite_app;

pitfalls.title: A SECURITY DEFINER function anyone can call
pitfalls.detail: New functions are executable by PUBLIC, and a SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner's privileges. Revoke PUBLIC in the same transaction that creates it, and pin its search_path with pg_temp last so callers can't shadow the objects it uses.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; CREATE FUNCTION ... SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = tracelite, pg_temp; REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION ... FROM PUBLIC; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION ... TO tracelite_app; COMMIT;

quiz.q: Your service logs in as the role that owns its tables. You run REVOKE DELETE, TRUNCATE ON requirements FROM that role. What can the service still do?
options: DROP TABLE requirements, or GRANT DELETE back to itself
quiz.why: Altering and dropping come with ownership and can't be revoked, and owners always hold the grant options to restore their own privileges.

quiz.q: As tracelite_owner you run ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA tracelite GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO reporting. Which tables can reporting read?
options: Tables tracelite_owner creates in tracelite from now on
Tables any role creates in tracelite from now on
quiz.why: Default privileges apply at creation time, to objects created by the role they belong to. Existing tables need GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA.

quiz.q: Why does lesson SQL here run as a non-superuser?
options: A superuser can run shell commands and read files on the machine through COPY ... TO PROGRAM and the file functions
Superusers are slower because every check is logged
quiz.why: Superusers bypass all permission checks, including the ones that keep SQL inside the database. ADR-0008 runs lessons on the owner's own machine, so that boundary matters.

quiz.q: An app role has INSERT on a table whose id column is serial, and no other grant. What does its INSERT do?
quiz.why: serial's default calls nextval(), which needs USAGE or UPDATE on the sequence. An identity column would have succeeded.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Privileges (including the ACL abbreviations)
PostgreSQL docs: Access Privilege Inquiry Functions
PostgreSQL docs: Writing SECURITY DEFINER Functions Safely

lessons.body:
## Concept

PostgreSQL answers "may this connection do that?" with three independent mechanisms:

- **Role attributes** are cluster-wide switches on the role: `SUPERUSER`, `CREATEROLE`,
  `CREATEDB`, `BYPASSRLS`, `LOGIN`. A superuser bypasses every check except the right to
  log in.
- **Privileges** are granted per object: `CONNECT` on a database, `USAGE` on a schema,
  `SELECT`/`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` on a table or on single columns, `EXECUTE` on a
  function. `PUBLIC` is an implicit group containing every role, present and future.
- **Ownership** is the third power. The owner of an object holds all privileges by
  default, can always grant them again, and alone can `ALTER` or `DROP` it. That right
  can't be granted or revoked.

Least privilege follows directly: the role your service logs in with should own nothing
and hold only the grants its queries need. A separate role owns the schema and runs the
migrations.

The sandbox you have been using is built exactly this way. `scripts/setup-local-db.sql`
creates `playground` with `NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE` and makes it the owner of
the `playground` database, nothing more. Ownership is enough for the runner
(`server/internal/sqlrun`) to create a throwaway `run_...` schema per run; the missing
superuser bit is what keeps lesson SQL from reaching your machine (ADR-0008).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Unix:** a superuser is root. Ownership works like a file owner's right to `chmod`:
  the owner can always restore its own permissions, so revoking privileges from an owner
  is a seatbelt, not a lock. Predefined roles such as `pg_monitor` or `pg_signal_backend`
  are closer to Linux capabilities: one specific power without root.
- **Java/Spring:** many services ship with `spring.datasource.username=postgres`. Flyway
  and Liquibase can run migrations with their own credentials; that split (owner for DDL,
  app role for DML) is what this lesson builds.
- **MySQL:** accounts are `user@host` and roles came late (8.0). In PostgreSQL a user is
  simply a role with `LOGIN`, groups are roles too, and host rules live separately in
  `pg_hba.conf`.
- **Application-level checks:** an `if user.isAdmin` in your code protects one code path.
  A missing `GRANT` protects the data from every code path, including an injected query.

## How it works

A statement passes several gates, in this order: the `LOGIN` attribute and `pg_hba.conf`
at connect time, `CONNECT` on the database, `USAGE` on each schema it names, the
privilege on each table or column it touches (`SELECT` on every column a `WHERE` reads,
too), and finally row-level security policies. A superuser passes every gate after login.

A least-privilege setup for TraceLite needs a superuser (or a `CREATEROLE` role) once, so
it can't run in this sandbox. As a provisioning script:

```sql
CREATE ROLE tracelite_owner NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE tracelite_migrator LOGIN PASSWORD '...' IN ROLE tracelite_owner;
CREATE ROLE tracelite_app LOGIN PASSWORD '...';

CREATE DATABASE tracelite OWNER tracelite_owner;
\c tracelite
REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE tracelite FROM PUBLIC;          -- CONNECT, TEMPORARY by default
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE tracelite TO tracelite_app, tracelite_migrator;
CREATE SCHEMA tracelite AUTHORIZATION tracelite_owner;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA tracelite TO tracelite_app;

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner IN SCHEMA tracelite
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO tracelite_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner IN SCHEMA tracelite
  GRANT USAGE ON SEQUENCES TO tracelite_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE tracelite_owner
  REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC;
```

Migrations log in as `tracelite_migrator` and start with `SET ROLE tracelite_owner`, so
every table is owned by the `NOLOGIN` role and picks up its default privileges. The
service logs in as `tracelite_app`: it can read and write rows, and can't `DROP`,
`ALTER`, `TRUNCATE`, or create anything. Roles are cluster-wide, so `pg_dump` of the
database doesn't contain them; keep this script (or `pg_dumpall --globals-only`) with
your backups.

## Design notes

- **Who owns, who logs in.** One `NOLOGIN` owner per schema, one login role per kind of
  client: the service, a reporting role with column grants that leave out personal data,
  a monitoring role in `pg_monitor`. KVKK Article 12 obliges a data controller to take
  technical measures against
  [unlawful access to personal data](https://www.kvkk.gov.tr/Icerik/6601/Obligations-Concerning-Data-Security-);
  "the reporting role cannot read the TCKN column" is such a measure, and it is enforced
  by the database rather than by every report author.
- **Grant to groups, not people.** Create `tracelite_readonly` as a `NOLOGIN` role, grant
  privileges to it, and grant the role to logins. Removing a person is then one `REVOKE`.
- **Revoke PUBLIC's defaults** on databases (`CONNECT`, `TEMPORARY`) and functions
  (`EXECUTE`). Since PostgreSQL 15 the `public` schema no longer lets every role create
  objects; a cluster upgraded from an older release, or a restored dump, keeps the old, open grant.
- **StackLab itself** keeps it simple: the app's own `stacklab` role owns the `stacklab`
  database and runs its own migrations, which is acceptable for a local single-user tool.
  The lesson sandbox is where the line is drawn. In local mode `playground` is an ordinary
  role, so these outputs hold. In the optional Docker mode the image creates `playground`
  as its container's superuser: the container is the boundary there, and these examples
  would print `allowed` throughout.

lessons.title: Row-level security for multi-tenant isolation
lessons.summary: A policy turns "WHERE tenant_id = ?" into a property of the table: every query gets it, including the one somebody forgets to filter. Make it fail closed, force it on the owner, scope your keys by tenant, and set the tenant per transaction.

examples.title: One policy, every query: reads, silent writes, and a rejected insert

annotations.note: ENABLE switches policies on; with none defined the table would deny everything. A policy without FOR or TO covers every command and every role. current_setting(..., true) returns NULL rather than an error when the variable was never set, and nullif turns the empty string a session is left with later (example 3) into NULL as well.
3 rows. Table owners bypass policies by default, and this session owns the table, as a service that runs its own migrations would.

FORCE applies the policies to the owner too. Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles still skip them; nobody else does. With no tenant set the answer is zero rows, not all rows: failing closed is the property that matters.

set_config(name, value, true) is SET LOCAL as a function call: the value lasts until the transaction ends, and unlike SET it accepts a bind parameter ($1) from the driver. The SELECT has no tenant filter and still returns only Acme's projects.

The rewriter adds the policy's USING expression to the query, and the plan shows it as an ordinary Filter. current_setting() is stable, so with an index on (tenant_id, ...) the same predicate becomes an Index Cond, exactly like a hand-written WHERE. Lead your indexes with tenant_id.

UPDATE 0, DELETE 0: a command only sees rows the policy lets it see, and the rest are skipped without an error. A handler that maps "no rows affected" to 404 then gives the same answer for "doesn't exist" and "belongs to someone else", which is what you want.

Change the variable and you change the tenant. That is the trust model: any session that can run SQL as this role can call set_config. A policy keyed on a setting protects against a forgotten WHERE in your own code, not against an attacker who can run arbitrary SQL as the app role.
SQLSTATE 42501. A policy with only USING applies it as WITH CHECK too, so INSERT and UPDATE can't produce a row outside the current tenant. Write a separate WITH CHECK only when the two must differ.

examples.title: Constraint checks look past policies: scope the keys by tenant

annotations.note: A global UNIQUE (code) and a single-column foreign key: the schema an application had before it became multi-tenant, with RLS added on top.

Unique and foreign key checks always see every row, so that integrity holds whatever the policies say. INSERT 0 0 just told Acme that some tenant uses the code RAIL; without ON CONFLICT the duplicate-key error would say the same. The docs call these covert channels.

The foreign key check found project 3, which Acme can't see, so the row went in: Acme's requirement now hangs off Globex's project, and the join shows Acme a dangling reference. Worse for Globex: it can no longer delete its own project, because of a referencing row it can't see.

Tenant-scoped keys. Codes are unique per tenant, and the foreign key carries tenant_id, so a requirement can only point at a project of its own tenant. UNIQUE (tenant_id, id) exists to be the target of that composite key.

Acme can now use RAIL too, so the probe above tells nothing any more. The primary key on id is still global; let an identity column assign ids (GENERATED ALWAYS) so a client can't pick an id to test for.
SQLSTATE 23503: there is no project (1, 3), because project 3 belongs to tenant 2. The database refuses the cross-tenant reference whatever the application does.

examples.title: Tenant context on a reused connection: transaction-local or leaked

annotations.note: The pattern for a pooled service: begin, set the tenant with is_local = true, run the request's queries, commit. In Go it lives in the one helper that starts transactions: tx.Exec(ctx, "SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true)", tenantID).

After COMMIT the local value is gone, but the variable now exists in this session and reads as an empty string, not NULL. nullif maps it back to NULL, so a request that forgot the tenant sees nothing.
is_local = false is a plain SET: it lasts for the rest of the session, and with a pool that means for whichever requests get this connection next.

The leak. Request 4 belongs to another user, set no tenant, and reads tenant 2's projects, because a pool hands the same server session to the next borrower with its settings intact. Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode it is worse: consecutive transactions of one client may not even share a server connection.

Without nullif, the empty leftover reaches the bigint cast and every query on the table fails with SQLSTATE 22P02, on every connection that ever had a tenant set. Still closed, but as an error instead of an empty result. RESET leaves the same empty value that COMMIT did.

use_cases: Shared-schema multi-tenant SaaS: every tenant's rows in the same tables, separated by tenant_id and enforced by policies
Defence in depth under an application that already filters by tenant: a forgotten WHERE in a report or an ad-hoc admin query returns nothing instead of everyone's data
Per-user visibility rules (own rows, or rows of my team) when users map to database roles, keyed on current_user
Read-only analysts or support staff who may query production but only for the customers they are assigned, a KVKK-style data minimisation measure
strengths: Enforced below every client: ORM queries, raw SQL, reports and psql sessions all get the same predicate, unlike Hibernate filters or Rails default scopes, which only cover queries that go through them
Fails closed when written with current_setting(..., true): no tenant means no rows, not all rows
Policies are plain SQL predicates, so the planner uses ordinary indexes on tenant_id
Writes are checked as well: WITH CHECK stops a request from creating or moving rows into another tenant
weaknesses: Superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and (without FORCE) table owners skip every policy, so the role setup decides whether RLS means anything
Unique and foreign key checks ignore policies: global keys leak existence and allow cross-tenant references unless keys include tenant_id
A tenant kept in a session variable is only as trustworthy as the code that sets it; anyone who can run SQL as the app role can switch tenants
Hidden rows make UPDATE and DELETE silently affect nothing, which can mask bugs; and views run with their owner's policies unless created WITH (security_invoker = true) (PostgreSQL 15+)

pitfalls.title: Enabling RLS without FORCE while the app owns the tables
pitfalls.detail: The owner bypasses policies, so everything keeps working and nothing is isolated. Either connect as a non-owner role (the roles lesson), or add FORCE, or both.
pitfalls.bad: ALTER TABLE projects ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;  -- app connects as the owner
pitfalls.good:
ALTER TABLE projects ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE projects FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

pitfalls.title: current_setting without missing_ok, or without nullif
pitfalls.detail: current_setting('app.tenant') raises an error when the variable was never set; after a transaction-local set, the variable reads '' for the rest of the session and a bare ::bigint cast fails. Use the two-argument form and map '' to NULL.
pitfalls.good: USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant', true), '')::bigint)

pitfalls.title: Setting the tenant for the session on a pooled connection
pitfalls.detail: SET app.tenant or set_config(..., false) outlives the request and is inherited by the next borrower of the connection. Set it with is_local = true inside the request's transaction, every time.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true); ... COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: A view owned by the table owner
pitfalls.detail: By default a view reads its tables with its owner's privileges and policies. If the owner bypasses RLS (no FORCE), every user of the view bypasses it too. Create views over RLS tables WITH (security_invoker = true).
pitfalls.good: CREATE VIEW open_requirements WITH (security_invoker = true) AS SELECT ... FROM requirements WHERE status = 'open';

pitfalls.title: Backing up as the app role
pitfalls.detail: pg_dump sets row_security = off so a backup can't silently miss rows; a role that can't bypass RLS gets an error instead of a partial dump. Back up as a role with BYPASSRLS (or a superuser), never with --enable-row-security by accident.

quiz.q: RLS is enabled with a tenant policy, the service connects as the role that owns the tables, and FORCE is not set. What does a query without a tenant filter return?
quiz.why: Table owners bypass row security unless the table is set to FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

quiz.q: Tenant 1 runs UPDATE projects SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 3, and project 3 belongs to tenant 2. What happens?
options: new row violates row-level security policy
quiz.why: USING decides which existing rows the command can see; invisible rows are skipped silently. The WITH CHECK error only fires for rows the command produces.

quiz.q: Policies isolate tenants, yet tenant 1 managed to insert a requirement pointing at tenant 2's project. What fixes it?
options: A foreign key on (tenant_id, project_id) referencing projects (tenant_id, id)
FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on requirements
quiz.why: Foreign key checks bypass row security; only a key that includes tenant_id keeps references inside one tenant.

quiz.q: Why set_config('app.tenant', $1, true) rather than SET app.tenant = ... in a pooled Go service?
options: The value ends with the transaction instead of leaking to the next borrower, and set_config takes a bind parameter
quiz.why: is_local = true scopes the value to the transaction; SET is a utility command with no $1 parameters, so the value would have to be spliced into SQL text.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: ALTER TABLE (ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY)
PostgreSQL docs: Configuration Settings Functions (current_setting, set_config)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Row-level security (RLS) attaches **policies** to a table. A policy has a `USING`
expression, which decides which existing rows a command can see (`SELECT`, and the rows
an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` can touch), and a `WITH CHECK` expression, which every new or
changed row must satisfy. Once `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is set, the planner adds the
policies to every query on the table, and a table with RLS enabled but no policy denies
everything.

For a shared-schema multi-tenant design (tenancy patterns are compared in the modeling
module), the policy is the tenant filter itself:

```sql
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON projects
  USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant', true), '')::bigint);
```

The service sets `app.tenant` at the start of each transaction from the authenticated
request. From then on, a query that forgets `WHERE tenant_id = $1` is still correct,
because the database filters for it.

Who is exempt matters as much as the policy: superusers and `BYPASSRLS` roles always,
and the table's owner unless the table is set to `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **ORM tenant filters** (Hibernate's `@TenantId` and filters, Rails' default scopes and
  tenant gems, a Django manager that adds `.filter(tenant=...)`) work on queries that go
  through the ORM. A raw SQL report, a migration script or a psql session skips them.
  A policy is applied by the server to all of them.
- **Middleware that sets request context** (a Go `context.Context` value, a Java
  `ThreadLocal`, an `AsyncLocalStorage` store in Node) has a database twin here: the
  transaction-local setting. Both must be set at the start of every request, and both
  leak if they outlive it.
- **Unix permissions** decide per file; policies decide per row, and the check runs
  inside the query, so the planner can still use indexes.

## How it works

- **Combining policies.** Policies are per command (`FOR SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`,
  `DELETE`, or `ALL`) and per role (`TO ...`, default `PUBLIC`). Permissive policies
  (the default) are combined with `OR`; `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies are combined with
  `AND` on top. A tenant rule plus "support staff see only open tickets" is a permissive
  policy and a restrictive one.
- **Order of evaluation.** Policy predicates run before conditions from the user's
  query, so a user-written function in `WHERE` can't observe rows the policy hides.
  Functions marked `LEAKPROOF` (such as `=` on integers and text) may run earlier, which
  is what lets the planner use an index on the user's own conditions.
- **Indexes.** With an index on `(tenant_id, id)`, `EXPLAIN` on the first example's
  table shows the policy as `Index Cond: (tenant_id = (NULLIF(current_setting(...),
  ''))::bigint)`, the same plan a hand-written filter gets.
- **What policies don't cover.** `TRUNCATE` and `REFERENCES` act on the whole table,
  and unique, primary key and foreign key checks always see every row (example 2).
- **Backups.** `pg_dump` sets `row_security = off`, which doesn't bypass anything; it
  makes any query that a policy would filter fail instead of returning fewer rows. The
  backup role therefore needs `BYPASSRLS`.

## Design notes

- **Where the tenant comes from.** Only from the authenticated session in the service,
  never from a request body or a URL. Set it in the one helper that opens transactions,
  with `set_config(..., true)`, and run every request in a transaction, reads included.
- **Two roles, belt and braces.** The service logs in as a role that doesn't own the
  tables (the roles lesson), so policies apply to it by default, and `FORCE` covers the
  day someone runs the service as the owner. Migrations, backups and support tooling use
  roles that bypass RLS on purpose.
- **Keys carry the tenant.** `UNIQUE (tenant_id, code)`, foreign keys on `(tenant_id,
  parent_id)`, indexes that start with `tenant_id`. In TraceLite, projects, requirements,
  test cases, runs and trace links all carry `tenant_id`, and every link between them
  includes it.
- **Session variable or database role.** Keying policies on `current_user` (one role
  per tenant or per user) is a stronger boundary, because a role can't be switched with
  a function call, but it costs a role per tenant and a connection pool per role. The
  session variable is the common compromise: it protects against bugs in your own
  queries, not against SQL injection with full statement control, which needs to be
  prevented anyway (parameters, never string concatenation).
- **In this sandbox** `playground` owns every table it creates, which is why the examples
  need `FORCE`. In the optional Docker mode the playground role is the container's
  superuser, and superusers bypass all policies: these examples assume local mode.

lessons.title: Connection limits and pooling (the PgBouncer concept); shared_buffers and work_mem basics
lessons.summary: Connections are processes and their number is fixed at server start; memory is one shared cache sized at start plus per-operation budgets that multiply under load. Pool connections, keep work_mem modest and raise it per transaction, and know what a pooler does to session state.

examples.title: The first knobs: who can change them, and when it takes effect

annotations.note: context is the column to read first. postmaster: set at server start, a change needs a restart. superuser: a superuser (or a role granted SET on it) may change it per session. user: any session may change it for itself. The built-in defaults: shared_buffers 16384 pages of 8kB = 128MB, effective_cache_size 4GB, work_mem 4MB, maintenance_work_mem 64MB, 100 connections of which 3 are kept for superusers. initdb may write lower values into postgresql.conf if the machine can't support these.
work_mem is a per-operation budget, so raising it for one heavy transaction is safe and normal. SET LOCAL ends with the transaction; a plain SET would stay with the connection.

A session that sits idle inside an open transaction for 30 seconds is terminated. Such sessions hold their locks and stop VACUUM from removing dead rows; this timeout is the server-side guard against a client that forgot to commit. Set it per role rather than globally.

SQLSTATE 55P02. shared_buffers is one shared memory area allocated at start, and max_connections sizes shared structures too, which is why both need a restart. Plan them; you can't tune them on the fly.

examples.title: work_mem decides whether a sort spills to disk

annotations.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query, and FORMAT JSON returns the plan as data, so the helper can return only the facts that are the same on every machine: the sort method and where it ran. The query text is spliced into SQL: fine for a lesson helper, never for user input.

external merge on Disk: the sort didn't fit in the default 4MB, so it wrote sorted runs to temporary files and merged them. Not an error, only slower; it shows up as temp_files in pg_stat_database and, with log_temp_files set, in the server log.
quicksort in Memory: 8MB is enough. In production this is the knob for one report or batch job, raised with SET LOCAL in its own transaction.
top-N heapsort keeps only the best 20 rows in a heap: 27kB, whatever the table's size. A missing LIMIT, or a missing index that would deliver the order, is often the real reason a sort spills.

examples.title: Session state, and what a pooler must reset between clients

annotations.note: Six kinds of session state: a setting, a custom variable, a prepared statement, a temporary table, a session-level advisory lock and a LISTEN. All of them belong to the server session, not to the client code that created them.
Everything is still there. A pool that hands this server session to another client as it is gives that client 256MB of work_mem, tenant 1 (the leak from the RLS lesson) and a lock it never took.

DISCARD ALL bundles RESET ALL, DEALLOCATE ALL, UNLISTEN *, pg_advisory_unlock_all(), DISCARD TEMP and a few more, and can't run inside a transaction block. It also reset this sandbox's own search_path, which is why the script only reads after it.
A clean session. The price is that the next client starts cold: no prepared statements, no cached plans. That is the trade PgBouncer's session mode makes on every client switch.

use_cases: Sizing max_connections and per-process pools for a service with several replicas, a worker, and cron jobs on one server
Putting PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of many short-lived clients (serverless functions, dozens of small services) that would otherwise exhaust max_connections
Giving a nightly report or an index build more memory (SET LOCAL work_mem, maintenance_work_mem) without raising it for every session
Setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout per role so one stuck client can't hold locks indefinitely
strengths: Unlike a JVM heap, most memory is budgeted per operation: work_mem, hash_mem_multiplier and maintenance_work_mem can be raised for one transaction without a restart
Operations that exceed work_mem spill to temporary files and finish, slower but correct, instead of failing
A pooler such as PgBouncer lets thousands of client connections share a few dozen server processes, with no change to the SQL in transaction mode as long as no session features are used
pg_settings documents every knob's unit, default and context, so a configuration review is a query
weaknesses: Each connection is a server process: opening one is expensive, and max_connections, fixed at start, caps the whole server
work_mem is per sort or hash node per session, so the worst case is work_mem × nodes × sessions; there is no global cap
shared_buffers and max_connections need a restart, so getting them wrong costs a maintenance window
Transaction pooling breaks session features (SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, temp tables that outlive a transaction) silently rather than with an error

pitfalls.title: Raising max_connections instead of pooling
pitfalls.detail: More connections than the server has CPUs and disks to serve add contention, not throughput, and every slot sizes shared memory. Keep max_connections modest, size each process's pool from the budget (the pgx lesson does the arithmetic), and add PgBouncer when the number of client processes outgrows it.

pitfalls.title: A global work_mem raise
pitfalls.detail: A server-wide 256MB looks harmless until 100 sessions each run a query with three sort and hash nodes. Keep the global value small and raise it where a known heavy query runs.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; -- the report; COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: Session features behind transaction pooling
pitfalls.detail: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, a SET, a PREPARE or a pg_advisory_lock() lands on whichever server session ran that transaction; your next transaction may get another one, and another client may inherit it. Use SET LOCAL or set_config(..., true), pg_advisory_xact_lock, and a direct connection for LISTEN.
pitfalls.bad: SET statement_timeout = '2s';  -- through a transaction-mode pooler
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s'; ...; COMMIT;  -- or ALTER ROLE tracelite_app SET statement_timeout = '2s'

pitfalls.title: Timeouts in postgresql.conf
pitfalls.detail: The docs advise against setting statement_timeout, lock_timeout or transaction_timeout in postgresql.conf, because they would hit every session, maintenance and migrations included. Set them per role or per transaction.

quiz.q: Which of these needs a server restart to change?
quiz.why: shared_buffers has context postmaster: the shared memory is allocated at start. The others have context user.

quiz.q: work_mem is 64MB and 50 sessions each run a query with two sorts and one hash join (hash_mem_multiplier 2.0). Roughly how much memory may those operations use at the same time?
quiz.why: Each sort may use work_mem and each hash work_mem × 2: (2 × 64 + 128) MB per session, times 50.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of a nightly report shows Sort Method: external merge. What's the first fix to try?
options: Raise work_mem in postgresql.conf for everyone
SET LOCAL work_mem for the report's transaction (or add a LIMIT or an index that delivers the order)
quiz.why: The spill is about one operation's budget. Raising it globally multiplies across every session; shared_buffers is a cache, not sort memory.

quiz.q: A Go service behind PgBouncer in transaction mode runs SET app.tenant = '7' and then its queries, each in its own transaction. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: PgBouncer replays SET for every transaction
The setting stays on the server session that ran it, so later transactions may miss it and other clients may inherit it
quiz.why: PgBouncer's docs list SET as unsupported in transaction pooling; only a handful of reported parameters are tracked. Use set_config(..., true) inside each transaction.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Resource Consumption (shared_buffers, work_mem, hash_mem_multiplier)
PostgreSQL docs: Client Connection Defaults (statement, lock and idle timeouts)
PostgreSQL docs: effective_cache_size and other planner settings

lessons.body:
## Concept

Two resources run out first, and both are fixed more rigidly than you might expect.

**Connections.** Every connection is a server process. `max_connections` (default 100)
is set at server start, and PostgreSQL sizes parts of its shared memory from it;
`superuser_reserved_connections` (3) and `reserved_connections` (0) are carved out of it.
Every replica's pool, every worker, migration job and psql session shares that budget.

**Memory** comes in two kinds:

- `shared_buffers` is the shared page cache, allocated once at start (default 128MB). On
  a dedicated server with 1GB or more of RAM the docs suggest starting at 25% of memory;
  beyond about 40% it rarely helps, because PostgreSQL also relies on the operating
  system's file cache. `effective_cache_size` only tells the planner how much cache to
  assume; it allocates nothing.
- `work_mem` (default 4MB) is the budget for **one** sort or hash operation before it
  spills to temporary files. A query can run several such operations at once, hashes get
  `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0), and every session has its own.
  `maintenance_work_mem` (64MB) does the same for `VACUUM`, `CREATE INDEX` and adding
  foreign keys.

A **connection pool** keeps a few connections open and lends them out. An application
pool (pgxpool) does that inside one process; a **pooler** such as PgBouncer sits between
many client connections and a few server connections, for all clients at once.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java:** HikariCP, Node's `pg.Pool`, `psycopg_pool` and pgxpool are all application
  pools. PgBouncer is the same idea moved out of process, so twenty service instances
  can share forty server connections instead of opening twenty pools of twenty.
- **Threads vs processes:** MySQL serves a connection with a thread; PostgreSQL starts a
  process for each one. Opening a connection is correspondingly expensive, which is why
  poolers are standard equipment rather than an optimisation.
- **Memory model:** `shared_buffers` behaves like a JVM heap fixed with `-Xms = -Xmx` at
  start; `work_mem` is closer to a per-request buffer limit in C, with a defined fallback
  (an external merge sort on disk) instead of an out-of-memory failure.

## How it works

The arithmetic to keep in mind:

- **Connections:** replicas × pool size + workers + jobs + admin sessions ≤
  `max_connections` − reserved slots. The `go.postgres.pgx` lesson works an example.
- **Memory:** `shared_buffers` + sessions × (sort/hash nodes per query × `work_mem`) +
  maintenance operations × `maintenance_work_mem`, plus the operating system's file
  cache, must fit in RAM. The per-session term is the one that surprises people.

PgBouncer has three pool modes
([features](https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html),
[configuration](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html)):

- **session** (the default): a client keeps one server connection until it disconnects;
  then PgBouncer runs `server_reset_query`, `DISCARD ALL` by default, before the next
  client gets it. Every feature works; you save connection setup, not connections.
- **transaction**: a client gets a server connection only for the duration of a
  transaction. The reset query is not used. Per the PgBouncer docs, `SET`/`RESET`,
  `LISTEN`, `PREPARE`/`DEALLOCATE`, `WITH HOLD` cursors, session-level advisory locks,
  `LOAD` and temp tables that outlive a transaction are not supported. Protocol-level
  prepared statements (the kind pgx uses) work when `max_prepared_statements` is
  non-zero.
- **statement**: transaction pooling that also forbids multi-statement transactions.

## Design notes

- **Pool in the process, and pool in front when processes multiply.** One pgxpool per
  process, sized from the server's budget. Add PgBouncer in transaction mode when the
  number of processes (replicas, serverless functions, many small services) makes the
  sum outgrow `max_connections`, and write the code for it from day one: transaction-
  scoped settings, `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, a direct connection for `LISTEN`.
- **Memory defaults to change on a real server:** `shared_buffers` toward 25% of RAM;
  `effective_cache_size` to what the OS will actually cache; `work_mem` modest globally
  and raised per transaction; `maintenance_work_mem` larger, since few maintenance
  operations run at once.
- **Timeouts per role:** `ALTER ROLE tracelite_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
  = '60s'` and a `statement_timeout` suited to the service, not in postgresql.conf.
- **StackLab's runner** shows the other end of the spectrum. `sqlrun` opens one
  connection per run (two for multisession) and `runexec` closes it afterwards: no pool,
  so one learner's `SET`s, temp tables and locks can't reach the next run. This example's
  `DISCARD ALL` shows how much a pool would otherwise have to reset. Runs are short, at most two
  at a time (ADR-0008), and each one sets its own `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout`
  (`sandboxSQL` in `server/internal/sqlrun/sqlrun.go`): `SET LOCAL` for the
  transactional runtime, session-level for `sql-nontx`, where the connection is closed
  afterwards anyway.

lessons.title: Backups and PITR (concepts); zero-downtime migrations (add, backfill, NOT VALID + VALIDATE)
lessons.summary: A dump is a snapshot; a base backup plus archived WAL can be rolled forward to any moment, which is what you need after a bad DELETE. Schema changes go out in small steps: expand, add constraints NOT VALID, build indexes concurrently, backfill in committed batches, validate, and only then contract.

examples.title: What the WAL records, and what recovery can bring back

annotations.note: relpersistence p (permanent) and u (unlogged). An unlogged table's data never enters the WAL: it is truncated after a crash, not replicated to standbys, and left out of base backups except for an empty initialization fork. Fine for scratch data you can reload, never for an audit log.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) counts the WAL a statement generated. Only the record count is returned: the byte count includes full-page images, which depend on when the last checkpoint happened.

2003 records for 1000 rows: one per heap insert, one per index entry, and a few more. The unlogged table wrote none. (With wal_level = minimal, a table created in the same transaction would skip row logging too; the default, replica, is the minimum for archiving.)

A logical backup is different: pg_dump reads tables with SQL, so it includes unlogged tables' rows unless you pass --no-unlogged-table-data. Physical backups and PITR see only what the WAL and the data files hold.

SQLSTATE 42501: restricted to superusers by default, though EXECUTE can be granted, for example to a deploy role. recovery_target_name later stops replay at that mark. Keep names unique: recovery stops at the first restore point with a matching name.

examples.title: A concurrent unique index: the failed build, the cleanup, and the wait

annotations.note: CONCURRENTLY takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE instead of SHARE, so inserts, updates and deletes go on during the build. It pays with two table scans, several waits, and no transaction block. SQLSTATE 23505: ayse@ and Ayse@ collide under lower().

The failed build left an invalid index behind. indisready is false because it failed in the first scan, so it isn't even maintained. A failure in the later validation scan would leave it ready: updated on every write and, the docs warn, still enforcing uniqueness. Either way queries ignore it, and psql's \d marks it INVALID.

INSERT 0 1: an index that isn't ready enforces nothing, so a third spelling of the same address got in. Leftovers are worth a monitoring query: SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid.

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY removes the leftover without blocking the table. The data fix is the real migration step; here the mixed-case duplicates are deleted, in TraceLite you would merge the accounts.
REPEATABLE READ keeps the snapshot of its first query until COMMIT, like a long report or a pg_dump. B never touches the index or writes anything.

A waits. Before it can mark the index valid, a concurrent build waits for every transaction holding a snapshot older than its last scan, a read-only one included. pg_stat_progress_create_index names the phase.
B commits, A finishes, the index is valid and enforces uniqueness. One forgotten idle-in-transaction session can stall every concurrent index build: look at pg_stat_activity before you start one.

examples.title: A foreign key on a live table: NOT VALID, batched backfill, VALIDATE

annotations.note: Table locks are held until the transaction ends, so a query right after each ALTER, inside the same transaction, shows what the ALTER took.
Expand. A nullable column without a default is a catalog-only change (the ALTER TABLE lesson lists what rewrites and what doesn't).

ADD FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables, which blocks writes to both; NOT VALID skips the scan of existing rows, so that lasts a moment. From here on every insert and update must reference an existing project. AccessShareLock, a plain SELECT's mode, conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

A procedure may COMMIT inside its loop when CALL runs in its own transaction (PostgreSQL 11+). Each batch's row locks are released at once, a lock wait or failure costs one batch, and autovacuum can clean up behind it. Real backfills use batches of a few thousand rows and often pause between them.

VALIDATE takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on requirements, which lets reads and writes continue, and only ROW SHARE on projects, exactly as the ALTER TABLE docs list. The long scan of existing rows happens here, off the critical path.

use_cases: Recovering from a bad DELETE or a destructive migration to the minute before it happened (PITR)
Moving one database between servers or major versions, or keeping a portable copy, with pg_dump/pg_restore
Deploying schema changes to tables that serve traffic: new columns, foreign keys, unique indexes, type changes
Long data backfills that must not hold locks or bloat one giant transaction
strengths: Continuous archiving gives recovery to any moment since the base backup, not just to the last nightly copy
pg_dump produces a consistent snapshot of a live database without blocking readers or writers
NOT VALID + VALIDATE and CONCURRENTLY split a blocking operation into a short strong lock and a long weak one, so most changes need no maintenance window
Transactional DDL means a failed migration step rolls back cleanly, unlike MySQL, where DDL commits implicitly
weaknesses: PITR needs setup in advance (wal_level, archive_mode, a reliable archive), and restore time grows with the amount of WAL to replay since the base backup
pg_dump is per database and doesn't include roles; a restore also needs pg_dumpall --globals-only and rebuilds every index
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can fail halfway and leave an invalid index, and waits for every transaction holding an older snapshot
Zero-downtime changes take several deploys (expand, backfill, contract) and the application must work with both schemas in between

pitfalls.title: Backups that were never restored
pitfalls.detail: A backup is only proven by a restore. Restore to a scratch server on a schedule, replay WAL to a target, and run a few sanity queries; measure how long it took.

pitfalls.title: Migrations without lock_timeout
pitfalls.detail: Even the brief SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE of ADD FOREIGN KEY waits behind a long transaction, and every query queues behind the waiting ALTER. Set a short lock_timeout and retry.
pitfalls.good:
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE requirements ADD CONSTRAINT requirements_project_fk FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects NOT VALID;

pitfalls.title: One huge UPDATE as the backfill
pitfalls.detail: A single UPDATE of ten million rows holds every row lock until it commits, doubles the table with dead versions before VACUUM can act, and loses everything on failure. Commit in batches.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE requirements r SET project_id = p.id FROM projects p WHERE p.code = r.project_code;
pitfalls.good: CALL backfill_project_id(5000);  -- COMMIT after each batch

pitfalls.title: Ignoring an invalid index after a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
pitfalls.detail: Retrying with the same name fails because the leftover exists; an index left ready keeps costing every write. Drop it (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY) or REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY, after fixing the data.

pitfalls.title: Contracting too early
pitfalls.detail: Dropping the old column in the same deploy that stops writing it breaks the old application version still serving requests. Drop it in a later deploy, after a backup or restore point.

quiz.q: A DROP TABLE committed at 14:32 yesterday must be undone. Which setup lets you recover the database as it was at 14:31?
options: A base backup plus a continuous WAL archive
quiz.why: PITR restores the base backup and replays archived WAL up to a recovery target. The dump loses everything after 02:00; the replica replayed the DROP within moments.

quiz.q: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fails on duplicate values. What is left?
options: An invalid index that must be dropped (or rebuilt) after fixing the data
A valid index without the duplicate rows
quiz.why: The build runs in several transactions; a failure leaves the catalog entry behind, marked invalid.

quiz.q: Which lock does ALTER TABLE requirements ADD FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects NOT VALID take on projects?
options: SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, which briefly blocks writes to projects
