PostgreSQL docs: tcn, triggered change notifications
PostgreSQL docs: Packaging Related Objects into an Extension

lessons.body:
## Concept

**LISTEN/NOTIFY** is a publish/subscribe channel built into PostgreSQL. A session runs
`LISTEN channel`; any session runs `NOTIFY channel, 'payload'` (or `pg_notify(channel,
payload)`), and every session listening on that channel in the same database receives
the message. Three properties define it:

- **Transactional:** notifications are delivered when the sending transaction commits,
  and never if it rolls back. `LISTEN` and `UNLISTEN` also take effect at commit.
- **Ephemeral:** nothing is stored for absent listeners. A session that isn't listening
  at that moment never sees the message.
- **Small:** the payload is text shorter than 8000 bytes in the default configuration.

Put a trigger behind it and the database becomes an **event source**: every committed
change announces itself, whoever made it. The contrib extension `tcn` packages that
trigger.

**Extensions** package SQL objects (types, functions, operators, index operator classes)
so they install with one `CREATE EXTENSION` per database and drop with one `DROP
EXTENSION`. The files must already be on the server. Since PG 13, extensions marked
**trusted** (they give no access outside the database) can be created by any role with
`CREATE` on the database; the rest need a superuser. About fifty modules ship with
PostgreSQL itself, and a large outside ecosystem, such as PostGIS for geospatial data and
pgvector for vector similarity search, builds on the same mechanism.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Redis pub/sub:** the same fire-and-forget fan-out with no persistence, plus one thing
  Redis can't do: delivery tied to the commit of the transaction that wrote the data.
- **Kafka or RabbitMQ:** durable, acknowledged, replayable. NOTIFY is none of these. Use
  it as a doorbell next to a table, the way an outbox table wakes a relay.
- **Spring's `@TransactionalEventListener`:** its default phase, after commit, is the
  semantics NOTIFY gives you natively, and across processes.
- **npm, pip, Go modules:** extensions are packages, but they are installed into the
  server by whoever controls its files, and enabled per database. `CREATE EXTENSION` is
  closer to loading an installed shared library than to `npm install`.

The Go side, receiving notifications with pgx, catching up after reconnects and folding
of duplicates, is go.services.listen-notify. The SQL runners here don't display
asynchronous messages, so example 3 is a small Go program.

## How it works

Notifications go through one server-wide queue (8 GB in a standard installation). A message
stays queued until every listening session has read it, and sessions read only between
transactions, so a listener stuck in a long transaction stops the queue's cleanup; the
log warns when the queue is half full, and a full queue makes `NOTIFY` fail at commit.
Within one transaction, identical channel-and-payload pairs are delivered once and the
rest in the order sent; transactions are delivered in commit order.

An extension is a control file plus versioned SQL scripts in the server's extension
directory. `CREATE EXTENSION` runs the script for the default (or requested) version,
creating the objects in the extension's schema (by default the first schema on
`search_path`), and records each object as a member in `pg_depend`. `ALTER EXTENSION ...
UPDATE` runs the upgrade scripts. Extensions that need shared memory or hooks, such as
pg_stat_statements, must also be listed in `shared_preload_libraries`, which takes a
server restart.

## Design notes

Treat NOTIFY as a wake-up call, never as the data. The table holds the events; the
payload is an id or empty; the listener, on every (re)connect, runs `LISTEN`, then catches
up from the table, then waits. Use `pg_notify` with bind parameters, one channel per
purpose, and a dedicated connection for listening. When you need durability,
acknowledgements, replay or fan-out across many services, that is a message broker's job.

Choose extensions like dependencies, because they are. Prefer trusted contrib modules,
check that each one exists on every target (local mode, Docker, a managed service's
allow-list), create them in the first migration, and decide which schema they live in.
The CREATE EXTENSION docs advise installing only into schemas where untrusted roles
can't create objects. An extension written in C runs inside the server process: before
adopting a third-party one, trust it as you would trust the server itself.

lessons.title: Scalar and correlated subqueries; CTEs for readability; MATERIALIZED choice
lessons.summary: A scalar subquery is an expression: it must return at most one row (none means NULL), and a correlated one is evaluated per outer row. CTEs name the steps of a query; since PG 12 a side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined, and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED override the planner's choice.

examples.title: Uncorrelated vs correlated scalar subqueries, and the more-than-one-row error

annotations.note: The subquery doesn't refer to the outer query, so it runs once (EXPLAIN shows it as an InitPlan) and its result, 357.5, is compared with every row. Writing WHERE duration_ms > avg(duration_ms) instead is an error: aggregates aren't allowed in WHERE.
t.id comes from the outer row and acts as a constant during each evaluation. count without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, so Export CSV gets 0, not NULL.
A subquery that finds no row yields NULL: Export CSV has never run. ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 makes "latest" explicit and guarantees at most one row, whatever the data looks like.

SubPlan 1 hangs under the scan of test_cases: PostgreSQL executes it once per outer row, and here each execution scans test_runs. An index on test_runs (test_case_id) turns each call into a lookup; for a report over every test case, a join with GROUP BY lets the planner choose a hash join instead.
SQLSTATE 21000, raised at run time by the first outer row whose subquery returns two rows. With one run per test in development data this query works; it breaks on the data that matters.

examples.title: The same query as nested derived tables and as named CTE steps

annotations.note: Reading starts at the innermost SELECT (line 18) and works outward, and each name (per_case, f) appears after the code it names. One more step and the indentation is deeper than the logic.
WITH names each step before it is used, so the query reads top to bottom, and any step can be checked on its own by selecting from it.

Both CTEs are referenced once and have no side effects, so PG 12+ inlines them: EXPLAIN shows the identical plan for both versions, with flaky's WHERE turned into a filter on the aggregate. The names cost nothing.

examples.title: Inlined, MATERIALIZED, referenced twice, NOT MATERIALIZED: four plans

annotations.note: Inlined: a single Index Scan on test_runs. The CTE's condition (NOT passed) and the outer one (id = 4) were merged, and the primary key answers id = 4 directly.

MATERIALIZED: the CTE runs on its own (Seq Scan, every failed run), its result is stored, and CTE Scan applies id = 4 to that. Before PG 12 every CTE behaved like this, which is where the advice "CTEs are an optimization fence" comes from.
Two references: by default the CTE is materialized, computed once and read by two CTE Scans. That pays off when the CTE is expensive and each reference needs most of its rows.

NOT MATERIALIZED copies the CTE into both places: two Seq Scans of test_runs, each with the filter. That pays off when each reference needs only a few rows that an index can find, and costs duplicate work when it doesn't.

use_cases: Comparing each row with a table-wide value: runs slower than the average, prices above the category median
Small per-row lookups in a SELECT list: the latest status, a count, a label from another table
Reports and migrations written as named steps (WITH) that a reviewer can follow and test step by step
Forcing or preventing materialization when EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the planner's default choice is the slow one
strengths: A scalar subquery can go anywhere a value can: SELECT list, WHERE, ORDER BY, even inside another expression
CTEs make multi-step queries read in order, and since PG 12 a single-use CTE costs nothing: same plan as the nested version
MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED give an explicit, documented override instead of rewrite tricks to fool the planner
Unlike variables in Go or TS, the steps are not executed one by one: the planner optimizes the whole query
weaknesses: The at-most-one-row rule is checked at run time, per execution, so a missing LIMIT or aggregate only fails on some data
A correlated subquery in the SELECT list runs once per outer row; over large outer sets a join or LATERAL can be much cheaper
A CTE referenced twice is materialized by default, so outer filters can't use the base table's indexes unless you say NOT MATERIALIZED
MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED are PostgreSQL extensions, so portable SQL can't state the choice

pitfalls.title: A scalar subquery that can return two rows
pitfalls.detail: It works while every outer row matches at most one row, then fails with SQLSTATE 21000. Make 'at most one' structural: ORDER BY with LIMIT 1, an aggregate, or a lookup by unique key.
pitfalls.bad: (SELECT r.passed FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id)
pitfalls.good: (SELECT r.passed FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id ORDER BY r.run_no DESC LIMIT 1)

pitfalls.title: Several correlated subqueries for one report
pitfalls.detail: Each scalar subquery in the SELECT list is its own SubPlan, run per outer row: three columns mean three probes per test case. Aggregate once with a join and GROUP BY (or one LATERAL subquery) and select the columns from there.

pitfalls.title: Pre-PG 12 folklore about CTEs
pitfalls.detail: 'CTEs are an optimization fence' was true until PG 11. Today a single-use, side-effect-free CTE is inlined. If old code relied on the fence to force an evaluation order, it now needs MATERIALIZED to keep that behaviour.
pitfalls.bad: WITH x AS (SELECT ...)  -- relies on the pre-12 fence
pitfalls.good: WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...)

pitfalls.title: Volatile functions keep a CTE materialized
pitfalls.detail: A CTE that calls random(), nextval() or clock_timestamp() is not side-effect-free, so it is never inlined, even when referenced once. That is correct (inlining could change how often the function runs), but it also means outer filters don't reach the base table.

quiz.q: A scalar subquery in the SELECT list finds no row for some outer row. What happens?
options: The query fails with 'more than one row returned'
quiz.why: A scalar subquery that returns no rows yields NULL; only more than one row is an error.

quiz.q: When does `(SELECT r.passed FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id)` fail?
options: When some test case has more than one run
When some test case has no runs
quiz.why: The error is raised at run time by an execution that returns two or more rows. No rows gives NULL.

quiz.q: `WITH x AS (SELECT * FROM t WHERE NOT passed) SELECT * FROM x WHERE id = 4`, x referenced once, no volatile functions, PG 18. What does the planner do?
options: Inlines x, so id = 4 can use the index on t
Computes x in full, then filters it
quiz.why: Since PG 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is folded into the outer query and optimized with it.

quiz.q: A CTE is referenced twice and each reference needs one row by primary key. What does NOT MATERIALIZED change?
options: The CTE is stored in a temporary table
Each reference is inlined, so each can use the index instead of scanning a stored result
quiz.why: NOT MATERIALIZED forces inlining even for multiple references, at the risk of computing the CTE twice.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Subquery Expressions (EXISTS, IN, ANY)
PostgreSQL docs: WITH Queries, SELECT in WITH

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **subquery** is a `SELECT` inside another statement. Used where a single value is
expected, it is a **scalar subquery**: one column, at most one row. No row means NULL;
two rows are a run-time error. A subquery that refers to columns of the outer query is
**correlated**: those columns act as constants during each evaluation, so logically it
runs once per outer row. (`EXISTS` and `IN` subqueries, from the joins module, are
usually turned into semi- and anti-joins by the planner; a scalar subquery in the
SELECT list runs as a per-row SubPlan, as example 1's plan shows.)

A **common table expression** (`WITH name AS (...)`) gives a subquery a name, so a query
with several steps reads top to bottom instead of inside out. Whether a CTE is actually
computed as a separate step is the planner's decision. Since PG 12, a non-recursive CTE
without side effects that is referenced once is **inlined**: folded into the main query
and optimized together with it. Referenced more than once, it is **materialized**:
computed once, stored, and scanned. `MATERIALIZED` and `NOT MATERIALIZED` override that
default.

The goal is to structure queries without fear. Through PG 11 every CTE was materialized,
an "optimization fence", and much of the advice you will find online still dates from
then.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python/JS:** CTEs look like naming intermediate results
  (`const perCase = ...; const flaky = perCase.filter(...)`). The difference is that
  nothing runs step by step: the planner sees the whole query. Inlined is a lazy,
  fused pipeline (generators, Java streams); materialized is a list built in the middle
  (`list(...)`, `.collect(toList())`).
- **Java Streams:** `MATERIALIZED` is the explicit `.collect()` in the middle of a
  pipeline; `NOT MATERIALIZED` asks the planner to keep fusing even though two consumers
  read the same intermediate result.
- **C/C++:** inlining a function versus calling it once and caching the result; same
  trade-off, decided by the planner unless you say otherwise.
- **Correlated subqueries** are the nested loop you would write in code:
  `for t in cases: n = sum(1 for r in runs if r.case_id == t.id)`. An index on the
  inner column makes each probe cheap; a join plus `GROUP BY` lets the database pick a
  hash join instead of looping.

## How it works

A CTE stays materialized (computed once, then read through `CTE Scan` nodes) when any
of these holds:

- it is referenced more than once (unless `NOT MATERIALIZED`),
- it is written `MATERIALIZED`,
- it is recursive (next lesson) or contains a data-modifying statement (the lesson after),
- it calls a volatile function or locks rows (`FOR UPDATE`).

Otherwise it is inlined like a subquery in `FROM`, and conditions from the outer query
can be pushed down into it and onto its tables' indexes. `EXPLAIN` tells you which
happened: a `CTE Scan` node means materialized.

## Design notes

Write CTEs for any query with more than one logical step, and name each step after
what it contains (`per_case`, `flaky`). The single-use case costs nothing, so the only
question left is the multi-use case: `EXPLAIN` it, and add `NOT MATERIALIZED` when every
reference only needs a few rows an index can find.

Reach for `MATERIALIZED` rarely and deliberately: when `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows that
the inlined plan is worse (typically a misestimate the fence happens to fix), or when
old code depended on the pre-12 fence. Leave a comment saying why.

Use scalar subqueries for small, per-row lookups, and make "at most one row" structural
(an aggregate, `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`, or a unique key). When a report needs several
values from the same child table, or runs over every row of a large table, aggregate
once with a join and `GROUP BY`, or use one `LATERAL` subquery, instead of one scalar
subquery per column.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs: requirement hierarchies and trace chains, with the CYCLE clause
lessons.summary: WITH RECURSIVE runs a start query, then repeats a step query on the rows the previous round produced until a round returns nothing: enough to walk requirement trees down and up, and trace graphs. SEARCH orders the result depth- or breadth-first, and CYCLE (PG 14) stops paths that revisit a node.

examples.title: A requirement tree: walking down with SEARCH DEPTH FIRST, and walking up

annotations.note: The non-recursive term runs once and produces the starting rows, here just AUTH at depth 0.
UNION ALL keeps every row. A tree has no duplicates to discard, so the cheaper ALL is right; graphs are another matter (example 2).

In each round, subtree stands for the rows the previous round produced, not everything so far. Round 1 finds AUTH's children, round 2 their children, round 3 finds nothing and the query stops. Each round joins on parent_id, so a real table wants an index on it.

SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code (PG 14) adds a column, ord, that sorts every child right after its parent and siblings by code. Without it the rows come out breadth-first, which the docs call an implementation detail it is "perhaps unsound" to rely on.

Walking up is the same shape with the join reversed: each round finds the parent of the last row. It stops after AUTH, whose NULL parent_id matches nothing. The primary key index serves this direction.

examples.title: A trace graph with a cycle: the naive loop, CYCLE, and UNION

annotations.note: Without line 22 this query never ends: SYS-2 leads to SYS-3, SYS-3 back to SYS-2, and every lap produces rows that differ in hops. With the guard it ends at 6 hops, having reached SYS-2 three times and TC-10 four times. A depth limit bounds the damage; it doesn't detect the cycle.

CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path adds two columns. path records the codes visited on the way to each row; when a step reaches a code already on its path, that row is emitted with is_cycle = true and not extended. Here SYS-2 at hop 3 closes the loop and the walk ends.
path is an array of row values, so ORDER BY path lists every route as a depth-first outline. TC-10 appears twice, once per route: in a graph, reachable through several paths is normal.

UNION discards rows that duplicate any earlier result row. With only the node itself in each row, a revisited node is a duplicate and the loop runs dry. Add hops or a path to the row and that protection is gone, which is why the CYCLE version needs CYCLE.

examples.title: Coverage per top-level requirement: carry the root down, then aggregate

annotations.note: Each round copies root_id from parent to child, so every requirement ends up tagged with its top-level ancestor. Anything derivable from the parent can be carried the same way: depth, a path, an inherited owner.

Test 10 is linked to AUTH-LOGIN and to AUTH-LOGIN-2FA, both inside AUTH's subtree: 4 links but 3 distinct tests. Rolling up over a hierarchy needs DISTINCT, or a test is counted once per requirement it covers.
FILTER from the GROUP BY lesson: failing tests per root, in the same pass as the totals.
LEFT JOINs keep EXPORT even though nothing below it has tests; its counts are 0, because count skips the NULL padding.

use_cases: Requirement and document hierarchies: everything under a requirement, the breadcrumb of ancestors, outlines in reading order
Traceability chains: from a stakeholder need through system requirements to the tests that verify it, and back
Org charts, category trees, threaded comments, bill-of-materials explosions
Impact analysis on dependency graphs: what is affected if this component changes
strengths: The whole walk is one query and one round trip, instead of one query per level from Go or TS
The tree stays a plain parent_id column with a foreign key, so writes are simple and integrity is enforced
SEARCH and CYCLE (PG 14) are standard SQL and replace hand-written path arrays and ANY() checks
Values can be carried down the walk (root, depth, path), so roll-ups need no second pass
weaknesses: UNION ALL over cyclic data never terminates; safety has to be written into every graph query
Each round is a join, so deep trees cost one join per level, and an unindexed parent_id means one table scan per level
Row order is undefined without SEARCH or an explicit ORDER BY on a path
Read-heavy, deep hierarchies can be cheaper with a materialized path (the ltree extension) or a closure table, at the cost of more complex writes

pitfalls.title: UNION ALL over a graph without a cycle check
pitfalls.detail: One bad link (A to B, B to A) makes the query run until a timeout or a resource limit stops it. Add CYCLE, or use UNION when each row is just the node.
pitfalls.bad: WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (SELECT 'STK-1'::text AS code, 0 AS hops UNION ALL SELECT l.to_code, r.hops + 1 FROM reach r JOIN trace_links l ON l.from_code = r.code) SELECT * FROM reach
pitfalls.good: WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (... same ...) CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path SELECT * FROM reach

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNION to stop a walk that carries a depth
pitfalls.detail: UNION only drops rows that are entirely equal. (SYS-2, 1) and (SYS-2, 3) differ, so a cycle repeats forever. The docs make the same point for depth and path columns.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the output order
pitfalls.detail: Rows currently come out breadth-first, but the docs call that an implementation detail. Use SEARCH DEPTH FIRST or SEARCH BREADTH FIRST and ORDER BY the column it creates.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT as a loop guard
pitfalls.detail: A LIMIT in the outer query does stop runaway recursion in PostgreSQL, because only the rows fetched are computed. The docs recommend it for testing only: other systems might work differently.

pitfalls.title: Double counting in roll-ups
pitfalls.detail: A test linked to several requirements in one subtree is reached once per link. Count DISTINCT test ids, or deduplicate before aggregating.
pitfalls.good: count(DISTINCT l.test_case_id)

quiz.q: During one round of the recursive term, what does the self-reference (subtree in example 1) contain?
options: Only the rows the previous round produced
quiz.why: The working table holds the previous round's new rows; each round's output replaces it, and the query stops when a round adds nothing.

quiz.q: The trace links contain a cycle. Which version is guaranteed to terminate?
options: UNION ALL with CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path
quiz.why: Rows with a growing hops value are never equal, so neither UNION nor UNION ALL stops. CYCLE checks the code against the path and stops extending a path that revisits it.

quiz.q: Why does example 3 count DISTINCT test ids per root?
options: A test linked to two requirements in the same subtree would otherwise count twice
quiz.why: The walk reaches the test once per linked requirement. Distinct ids count each test once per root.

quiz.q: What does SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code SET ord give you?
options: A column to ORDER BY so each child follows its parent, siblings by code
A guarantee that the CTE's output is already sorted
quiz.why: SEARCH only adds the ordering column; you still ORDER BY it. Cycle detection is CYCLE's job.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, WITH clause (SEARCH and CYCLE syntax)

lessons.body:
## Concept

`WITH RECURSIVE` defines a CTE in two parts joined by `UNION ALL` (or `UNION`): a
**non-recursive term** that produces the starting rows, and a **recursive term** that
refers to the CTE itself. Despite the name, it is a loop, not recursion: the start rows
form the first round; each further round runs the recursive term against the previous
round's rows only; all rounds together are the result; the loop stops when a round
produces no rows.

That loop walks a **tree** stored as `parent_id`: down (children of the last round) or
up (the parent of the last row). It also walks a **graph**, such as trace links from
stakeholder needs through system requirements to test cases. Graphs bring two things
trees don't: a node reachable by several paths, and cycles. A cycle makes a `UNION ALL`
walk run forever.

PG 14 added two standard clauses after the CTE: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST | BREADTH FIRST BY
col SET ordcol` adds a column to sort by, and `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` tracks
the path and stops extending a path when it revisits a node.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Any language:** this is the breadth-first frontier loop you have written many
  times: `frontier = [start]; while frontier: frontier = children_of(frontier);
  result += frontier`. The working table is `frontier`. `CYCLE` is a per-path `visited`
  check; `UNION` is a global `visited` set over whole rows.
- **Go and TS services:** without this, you either query once per level (N round trips)
  or load the whole table and build a `map[int][]int` of children in memory. The
  recursive CTE runs the loop next to the data and returns only the result.
- **Java/JPA:** a self-referencing `@OneToMany children` collection is lazy by default,
  so walking down issues one query per node whose children you touch. A native query
  with `WITH RECURSIVE` replaces the walk.
- **Python:** `networkx.descendants(G, 'STK-1')` returns the set of reachable nodes,
  which is what the `UNION` version of example 2 computes.

## How it works

Example 1, round by round:

1. Start: `AUTH` (depth 0).
2. Children of `AUTH`: `AUTH-LOGIN`, `AUTH-RESET` (depth 1).
3. Children of those: `AUTH-LOGIN-2FA`, `AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT` (depth 2).
4. Children of those: none. Stop.

With `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`, each round also drops rows equal to any row already
produced; that is what lets the node-only walk in example 2 terminate. `CYCLE` is
documented as a rewrite of a hand-written pattern: carry an array of visited keys,
mark a row whose key is already in it, and don't extend marked rows. `SEARCH` is a
similar rewrite that carries a sort key.

## Design notes

For hierarchies, start with an adjacency list (`parent_id REFERENCES` the same table)
and recursive CTEs: writes stay trivial, the foreign key keeps the tree honest, and
reads are one query. Index `parent_id` for downward walks. Consider a materialized path
(the `ltree` extension) or a closure table only when deep, read-heavy trees show up in
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.

For graphs, make every traversal cycle-safe, even if the application is supposed to
prevent cycles: one bad link must not turn a page load into a timeout. Use `UNION` when
you need the set of reachable nodes, and `CYCLE` when you need paths, depths or
per-path data.

Carry what you need down the walk (root id, depth, path) and aggregate afterwards, and
remember that in a graph, or a roll-up over a tree with many-to-many links, the same
leaf arrives once per path: count distinct ids.

lessons.title: Data-modifying CTEs
lessons.summary: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE can sit in a WITH clause, and their RETURNING rows feed the next step: moving rows, inserting a parent with its children, or updating with an audit trail becomes one atomic statement. All parts read one snapshot, so they see each other's changes only through RETURNING.

examples.title: Move rows to an archive, and insert a parent with its children

annotations.note: LIKE ... INCLUDING ALL copies columns, defaults, constraints and indexes, so the archive has the same column order and its own primary key: archiving the same run twice would fail loudly.

DELETE ... RETURNING * hands the removed rows to the INSERT. It is one statement, so it commits or fails as a whole: no window where a run is deleted but not yet archived, and no second copy if a client retries a half-finished pair of statements.
RETURNING * yields the columns in table order, which matches the archive because LIKE copied it. Once the two tables can drift, list the columns on both sides.
The main statement can itself be an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. With no RETURNING of its own, the client sees only its command tag: INSERT 0 2.

req's RETURNING carries the generated id into the second INSERT, with no round trip to the client in between. The foreign key on test_cases holds: a non-deferrable constraint is checked after the whole command, and by then the requirement row exists.
req has one row and VALUES has two; the comma join pairs the new id with each child title.

examples.title: One snapshot: the table shows the old state, RETURNING the new; get-or-create

annotations.note: The UPDATE runs, but every part of the statement reads the snapshot taken before any of it ran, so the outer scan of test_cases still sees failed. The docs are explicit: RETURNING is the only way for a WITH sub-statement's changes to reach the rest of the statement.
A later statement always sees the changes of earlier statements in the same transaction, at any isolation level: the update is visible.
kvkk is new: the INSERT returns its row ('created'), and the SELECT, reading the old snapshot, finds nothing, so there is no duplicate line.
security already exists: DO NOTHING returns no row, and the SELECT finds the existing one ('found'). Either way the caller gets the id in one round trip.
SQLSTATE 0A000. A data-modifying statement may only be in a WITH attached to the top-level statement, not in a subquery's own WITH.

examples.title: Update and audit in one statement with RETURNING old/new (PG 18)

annotations.note: status <> 'passed' leaves out rows the update wouldn't change, so the log records real changes only: Logout is neither updated nor logged.
old.status and new.status (PG 18) are the row before and after the update. Before PG 18, an UPDATE's RETURNING could only show the new values.
The second step reads the first one's RETURNING. The audit rows and the update commit or fail together, and the audit logic is visible in the query instead of hidden in a trigger.
The main query reads logged's RETURNING, so the client receives exactly what was written to the log.

use_cases: Archiving: DELETE ... RETURNING into an archive or history table in one atomic statement
Creating an aggregate in one round trip: a requirement and its test cases, an order and its lines, with generated ids flowing through RETURNING
Audit trails without triggers: UPDATE ... RETURNING old.*, new.* (PG 18) feeding an INSERT into a log table
Get-or-create for tags, labels and lookup values: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, falling back to a SELECT
strengths: Several writes are one statement: atomic even in autocommit, one round trip from Go or TS, no transaction plumbing in the application
Generated ids travel through RETURNING instead of being read back by the client and sent again
Each data-modifying step runs exactly once and to completion, whether or not anything reads its output
With PG 18's old/new in RETURNING, before-and-after values come from the same statement that changed them
weaknesses: All parts share one snapshot, so a step can't see another step's changes in the tables; only RETURNING carries them
Sub-statements run concurrently with each other and the main query, in no guaranteed order
Two steps modifying the same row is unsupported: only one change takes effect, and which one is hard to predict
Long chains get hard to debug: a step can't be run on its own without performing its write

pitfalls.title: Reading the table instead of RETURNING
pitfalls.detail: The main query and the other steps read the snapshot from before the statement. A SELECT on the modified table shows the old rows; read the CTE.
pitfalls.bad: WITH u AS (UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'retest' WHERE status = 'failed' RETURNING id) SELECT id, status FROM test_cases WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM u)
pitfalls.good: WITH u AS (UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'retest' WHERE status = 'failed' RETURNING id, status) SELECT id, status FROM u

pitfalls.title: Two steps touching the same row
pitfalls.detail: The docs say updating the same row twice in one statement is not supported: only one modification happens, and which one is hard to predict. Deleting a row another step updated performs only the update. Merge the changes into one UPDATE.
pitfalls.bad: WITH a AS (UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'passed' WHERE id = 1), b AS (UPDATE test_cases SET title = 'Login (SSO)' WHERE id = 1) SELECT 1
pitfalls.good: UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'passed', title = 'Login (SSO)' WHERE id = 1

pitfalls.title: Get-or-create under concurrency
pitfalls.detail: In READ COMMITTED, if another transaction inserts the same tag and commits after your statement's snapshot, DO NOTHING skips the insert and the fallback SELECT can't see the other row: zero rows come back. Treat an empty result as 'retry', or use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, which always returns the row at the cost of writing it.

pitfalls.title: A data-modifying CTE nobody reads still runs
pitfalls.detail: Data-modifying steps run exactly once and to completion even if the main query ignores them. A WITH (DELETE ...) added 'just to see' what it would return deletes.

quiz.q: `WITH u AS (UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'retest' WHERE status = 'failed' RETURNING id) SELECT status FROM test_cases WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM u)`: which status does the SELECT show for the updated rows?
quiz.why: The outer scan of test_cases uses the statement's snapshot, taken before the UPDATE. Only u's RETURNING rows carry the new values.

quiz.q: `WITH d AS (DELETE FROM tags RETURNING id) SELECT 1`: the main query never reads d. What happens?
options: An error about an unused CTE
quiz.why: Data-modifying statements in WITH are executed exactly once and to completion, regardless of whether their output is read.

quiz.q: How do the changes made by one WITH sub-statement reach the others and the main query?
options: Through a second snapshot taken after each step
quiz.why: All parts share one snapshot and run concurrently, so RETURNING is the only channel.

quiz.q: Before PG 18, what could `UPDATE ... RETURNING` show?
quiz.why: PG 18 added the old and new aliases; before that an UPDATE returned the new row only.

PostgreSQL docs: INSERT, ON CONFLICT clause
PostgreSQL docs: Read Committed Isolation Level (ON CONFLICT and snapshots)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A `WITH` clause may contain `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `MERGE`, not only
`SELECT`. A data-modifying step usually ends in `RETURNING`, and its returned rows act
as a temporary table that later steps and the main query can read. The main statement
can itself be a write. The result is several writes in one statement: one round trip,
and atomic even in autocommit.

Three rules make it predictable:

- **One snapshot.** Every step and the main query read the database as it was before
  the statement started. A step can't see another step's changes in the tables;
  `RETURNING` is the only channel.
- **Exactly once.** Each data-modifying step runs once and to completion, whether or
  not anything reads its output.
- **Top level only.** A data-modifying `WITH` must belong to the top-level statement.

That is the point of the feature: read what you wrote, in the same atomic statement.
Archive what you deleted, link children to the id you just generated, log the old and
new values of the rows you just changed.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go/TS with a driver:** the usual version is `BEGIN`, `INSERT ... RETURNING id`,
  read the id into a variable, `INSERT` the children with it, `COMMIT`: four round trips
  and a transaction to manage. The CTE is one statement; the id never leaves the server.
- **Java/JPA:** cascading a persist from a parent to its children sends one `INSERT`
  per entity, and the generated ids travel to the application in between. The ORM
  hides those round trips; the CTE removes them.
- **Triggers:** an audit trigger does the logging invisibly on every update. The CTE
  makes it explicit for the statements that need it, at the cost of being opt-in.
- **Any language with immutable snapshots:** the rule matches reading from a persistent
  data structure: every step got the same version, and the new version exists only in
  what the steps returned.

## Design notes

Use a data-modifying CTE when several writes form one logical operation and the later
ones need the earlier ones' output: archive moves, parent-with-children creation,
update-plus-audit. Make every step return exactly what the next one needs, and make the
main query read from `RETURNING` rather than from the tables.

Keep each row touched by one step. If two steps would modify the same row, merge them
into one statement; the docs leave the outcome unspecified.

Get-or-create with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` plus a fallback `SELECT` is the
cheapest form and correct without concurrent writers of the same key. With them, an
empty result means "someone else inserted it after my snapshot": retry, or use
`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING`, which always returns the row but writes it.

When a chain grows past three or four steps, or its steps need to branch on results,
move it into a transaction in Go or TS (or a function) where each step can be tested on
its own.

lessons.title: text vs varchar(n), integer vs bigint, numeric for money (never float)
lessons.summary: text and varchar(n) perform the same in PostgreSQL, and lengths count characters, not bytes. Use bigint wherever integer's 2.1 billion could run out, and numeric (or integer minor units) for money, because a float can't even hold 0.10 exactly.

examples.title: Characters vs bytes, and what varchar(n) actually enforces

annotations.note: Same storage and speed: varchar(n) is text plus a length check on write. Use it when the limit is a real rule, not as a guess; a guessed limit you later raise is a migration (cheap, see the ALTER lesson), a guessed limit you hit in production is an outage.

'şükrü' is 5 characters and 8 bytes (ş and ü take 2 bytes each in UTF-8), and it fits varchar(6). length() agrees with Python's len() and Go's utf8.RuneCountInString; Go's len() and C's strlen() report what octet_length() does.

The database's builtin C.UTF-8 collation upper-cases ipekç to IPEKÇ: the dotless capital, wrong in Turkish. COLLATE "tr-x-icu" applies Turkish rules and gives İPEKÇ. The same choice decides how ILIKE and lower() treat I and ı.
A cast is an instruction to fit the value, so it truncates to 6 characters without a word. Data that passes through such a cast loses its tail silently.
Storing is different: an over-long value fails with SQLSTATE 22001 and, as in any transaction, nothing after it runs. Better an error than a silently shortened name.

examples.title: integer vs bigint: division, widening, and overflow

annotations.note: Two integers divide as integers and the fraction is dropped. One numeric operand (2.0) makes the whole expression numeric, which picks a generous scale for the result.
sum(integer) returns bigint and sum(bigint) returns numeric, so totals don't overflow. avg() of integers returns numeric, which is why avg(x) beats sum(x) / count(*).

SQLSTATE 22003, integer out of range. C would hit undefined behaviour, Java and Go would wrap to -2147483648 and keep going. Postgres stops, and the real fix is the column type: bigint costs 4 more bytes per row, widening a big table later costs a full rewrite.

examples.title: numeric vs double precision for money

annotations.note: In Python and JS, 0.1 is a binary float (in Go, once it lands in a float64). In Postgres a literal with a decimal point is numeric, so 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 holds until you cast to float8. Since PostgreSQL 12 floats print their shortest exact form (0.30000000000000004); older versions rounded to 15 digits and printed 0.3, which hid the error.
numeric(12, 2) means 12 significant digits, 2 of them after the point: amounts up to 9,999,999,999.99. Choose the scale per field: 2 for TL prices, more for exchange rates or unit prices.
Ten float payments of 0.10 add up to 0.9999999999999999, and an equality check against 1 fails. numeric adds them in decimal and gets 1.00, the same answer an accountant would.

numeric rounds ties away from zero (19.995 becomes 20.00, 2.5 becomes 3); float8 rounds 2.5 to 2 (ties to even). If a business rule says how to round, apply it explicitly before storing instead of leaving it to the column's scale.
Eleven digits before the point don't fit numeric(12, 2): SQLSTATE 22003, numeric field overflow. Decimals round; whole digits never get dropped.

use_cases: text: names, emails, addresses, descriptions: anything without a business-defined maximum
varchar(n), or text with a CHECK: codes whose length is a real rule (ISO country codes, an IBAN's 34 characters)
bigint: primary keys, counters, byte sizes, anything that grows for years or gets summed
numeric(p, s): prices, balances, tax and exchange rates; integer minor units (kuruş in a bigint) when you never need fractions of the smallest unit
double precision: measurements and scientific values where a tiny relative error is acceptable
strengths: text has no penalty against varchar(n), so you don't guess maximum lengths up front; the docs call char(n) usually the slowest of the three
Length limits count characters, so varchar(6) means the same for 'ada' and 'şükrü', unlike a C char[6] or Go's len()
Integer overflow is an error (SQLSTATE 22003), not the silent wraparound of Java and Go or C's undefined behaviour
numeric is exact decimal arithmetic at the column level, like Java's BigDecimal; JS numbers and Go's float64 have no exact decimal type
weaknesses: numeric arithmetic is much slower than integer or float arithmetic; aggregating millions of rows notices it
integer columns run out at 2,147,483,647, and widening one later rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock
Character limits are not byte limits: varchar(255) can hold up to 4 bytes per character, which matters for client buffers and index size limits
Integer division truncates silently, so sum(x) / count(*) quietly loses the fraction

pitfalls.title: Money in double precision
pitfalls.detail: Sums drift (ten times 0.10 is 0.9999999999999999) and equality checks fail. The docs' Monetary Types page says it directly: floats should not be used to handle money.
pitfalls.good: price numeric(12, 2) NOT NULL  -- or price_kurus bigint NOT NULL

pitfalls.title: Counting on varchar(n) to reject long values
pitfalls.detail: Plain inserts fail with 22001, but an explicit cast (value::varchar(50)) truncates without an error. If the limit protects something, check it in a CHECK constraint, not through a cast.

pitfalls.title: integer keys and counters
pitfalls.detail: serial and integer ids stop at 2,147,483,647. Moving to bigint later is ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE bigint, a full rewrite of table and indexes. Start with bigint.

pitfalls.title: Averages by integer division
pitfalls.detail: Both operands integer means integer division.
pitfalls.good: SELECT avg(score) FROM results  -- or sum(score)::numeric / count(*)

pitfalls.title: Using length() for a byte budget
pitfalls.detail: length() counts characters. For anything measured in bytes (a protocol field, a fixed-size buffer in a C client) use octet_length(): Turkish letters take 2 bytes, emoji 4.

pitfalls.title: The money type
pitfalls.detail: Its output is formatted by the database's lc_monetary setting, and the docs warn that dumps may not load into a database with a different setting. numeric plus a currency column is portable and explicit.

quiz.q: Which column type keeps 0.10 + 0.20 exactly equal to 0.30?
options: Any of them: Postgres rounds for you
quiz.why: Only numeric stores decimal digits exactly; real and double precision are binary floats and can't represent 0.1.

quiz.q: handle is varchar(6). What happens with INSERT ... VALUES ('şükrüm'), 6 characters and 9 bytes?
quiz.why: varchar(n) limits characters, not bytes, so 6 characters fit regardless of their UTF-8 length.

quiz.q: hits is an integer column holding 2147483647. What does UPDATE ... SET hits = hits + 1 do?
options: Fails with integer out of range
quiz.why: Postgres checks integer arithmetic and raises SQLSTATE 22003; it neither wraps nor changes the column type.

quiz.q: What does SELECT -7 / 2 return?
quiz.why: Two integer operands give integer division, truncated toward zero as in Go, C and Java (Python's // would give -4).

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three type families cover most columns, and each wrong choice fails in its own way:

- **Strings.** `text`, `varchar(n)` and `char(n)` share one implementation. `varchar(n)`
  is `text` plus a length check, counted in characters. `char(n)` pads with spaces and,
  per the docs, is usually the slowest of the three. Too long is an error on insert, but
  a silent truncation in an explicit cast.
- **Whole numbers.** `smallint` (2 bytes), `integer` (4 bytes, ±2.1 billion) and `bigint`
  (8 bytes, ±9.2 × 10¹⁸). Arithmetic that leaves the range is an error, never a wrap.
- **Fractions.** `numeric(p, s)` is exact decimal arithmetic; `real` and `double
  precision` are IEEE 754 binary floats, fast but unable to store 0.1 exactly.

The goal of this lesson is a reflex: `text` unless a length is a rule, `bigint` unless
the range is provably small, `numeric` whenever someone will add the values up and
expect the books to balance.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++:** `char name[6]` is 6 bytes; `varchar(6)` is 6 characters, and there is no
  buffer to overflow: too long is an error. Signed overflow, undefined behaviour in C,
  is a clean SQLSTATE 22003 here.
- **Go:** `len(s)` counts bytes, like `octet_length()`; `utf8.RuneCountInString` counts
  what `length()` counts. Postgres `integer` is always 32 bits, so Go's `int` (64-bit on
  your machine) pairs with `bigint`, not `integer`.
- **Java:** `int`/`long`/`BigDecimal` map to `integer`/`bigint`/`numeric`. Java wraps on
  overflow; Postgres refuses.
- **Python:** ints never overflow, so Python code is the most likely to meet `integer out
  of range` for the first time in the database. `/` on two integers here behaves like
  C's, not like Python 3's.
- **JS/TS:** `number` is a float64. A `bigint` above 2⁵³ − 1 or a `numeric` amount parsed
  into a `number` loses precision, which is why drivers commonly hand them to JS as
  strings. Keep them strings (or `BigInt`) until you format them.

## Design notes

Lengths: default to `text`. When a length is a business rule, say so with a constraint,
`CHECK (char_length(code) = 2)`, or with `varchar(n)` if you prefer; raising a `varchar`
limit later is a catalog-only change, as the ALTER TABLE lesson shows. What to avoid is the
reflexive `varchar(255)` copied from other databases: it documents nothing and rejects the
one long name you didn't anticipate.

Integers: `bigint` for keys, counters and sizes. The 4 bytes you save with `integer` are
rarely worth the day you hit 2,147,483,647, because widening a column rewrites the table.

Money: `numeric(12, 2)` (scale per currency and field) or an integer number of minor units
(`price_kurus bigint`), always with the currency stored next to it when there could ever be
more than one. Never `double precision`, and not the `money` type, whose formatting follows
the server's `lc_monetary` setting. Rounding is a business rule: numeric rounds ties away
from zero, banks sometimes round to even, so make the rounding step explicit where a rule
applies instead of leaving it to the column's scale.

Turkish text: lengths are safe (characters, not bytes), but case mapping depends on the
collation. The database default here maps `i` to `I`; use `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` where Turkish
casing matters, as the search lessons do for ILIKE and full-text search.

lessons.title: timestamptz vs timestamp, date, interval; time zones done right
lessons.summary: timestamptz stores an instant and shows it in the reader's zone; timestamp stores wall-clock digits and silently drops any offset you give it. Use timestamptz for events, zone names like Europe/Istanbul instead of offsets, and AT TIME ZONE wherever a calendar day matters.

examples.title: The same input in timestamptz and timestamp, read from two cities

annotations.note: The session's TimeZone decides how timestamptz values are displayed and how input without an offset is read. The server default differs between machines (it is Europe/Istanbul on this one), so examples and applications set it explicitly.
Both types take 8 bytes with microsecond resolution. Despite its name, timestamp with time zone stores no zone: it converts the input to UTC and converts back to the session's zone on output.
The docs say it plainly: in a timestamp without time zone, PostgreSQL silently ignores any time zone indication. at_local keeps 09:00 and 08:30 as typed; the +03 and +01 are gone.
The review started at 07:30 UTC, after the standup at 06:00 UTC, but its wall-clock digits are smaller, so it sorts first. Every comparison, range query and duration on at_local has the same problem.
Same rows, Berlin session: at_tz now reads 07:00+01 and 08:30+01, the same instants in Berlin time. at_local can't follow, because it never knew which zone its digits belonged to.

examples.title: Calendar days, zone history, and offsets that mean the opposite

annotations.note: timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul' gives the wall-clock time in Istanbul (a timestamp), and only then is it cut to a date. Order 2 was placed on the 12th in UTC but on the 13th in Istanbul: a daily sales report that uses ::date silently follows the server's zone instead.

The other direction: timestamp AT TIME ZONE reads the digits as Istanbul time and returns the instant, shown here in UTC. Noon in January was 10:00 UTC in 2016 (+02) and is 09:00 UTC now (+03). A zone name gets both right; a hard-coded +03 gets 2016 wrong.

The zone name and INTERVAL '+03:00' agree on 09:00. 'UTC+3' is a POSIX-style specification, whose sign means the opposite of ISO 8601: three hours west of Greenwich, so 03:00. No error, just a wrong answer.

Same expression, two answers: 03:00 in a UTC session, 09:00 in an Istanbul session. In PostgreSQL 18 the current zone's own IANA abbreviations are recognized first, and tzdata's abbreviation for Turkey is literally "+03"; elsewhere the string falls through to POSIX rules. Spell zones as names or intervals and the question never comes up.

examples.title: date and interval arithmetic, DST, and what now() means

annotations.note: date minus date is an integer number of days, and date plus an integer is a date. No time of day and no zone: the right type for birthdays, due dates and holidays.

date + interval returns a timestamp. January 31 plus one month is February 28: the docs specify that the last day of the month is used when the day doesn't exist. Go's AddDate normalizes instead (October 31 plus one month is December 1).
age() answers in years, months and days, which is what a human means by "how old"; plain subtraction of timestamps would answer in days and hours.

'1 day' means the same local time tomorrow (12:00); '24 hours' means elapsed time (13:00, because an hour was skipped). The subtraction shows the day lasted 23:00:00. That is why interval stores months, days and microseconds as separate fields.

now(), current_timestamp and transaction_timestamp() are the transaction's start time. A batch insert with DEFAULT now() stamps every row identically, however long it runs; clock_timestamp() is the actual time at each call.

use_cases: timestamptz: created_at, paid_at, sent_at, log lines: anything that happened at an instant
date: birthdays, due dates, public holidays, billing days: a calendar day with no time or zone
timestamp plus a zone-name column: future appointments promised in local time ('Mondays 09:00 in Istanbul'), where the wall clock is the contract even if the zone's rules change
interval: durations, subscription lengths ('1 month'), retry back-offs, retention windows
strengths: One stored instant reads correctly in Istanbul and in Berlin; the conversion happens at the edges, like Java's Instant or Go's time.Time
IANA zone names carry history: Europe/Istanbul knows it was +02 in the winter of 2016 and +03 since
interval holds calendar units and elapsed time in one value; Go splits them into AddDate and time.Duration
Both timestamp types cost 8 bytes with microsecond resolution, so the correct choice is free
weaknesses: The name misleads: timestamp with time zone stores no zone. Keep the user's zone in its own column if you need it
Display depends on each session's TimeZone, so two clients print the same row differently unless they set it
Comparing timestamp with timestamptz converts implicitly through the session's zone, so results can change with a SET
Zone strings are parsed leniently: 'UTC+3' is accepted and means UTC−3

pitfalls.title: timestamp for events
pitfalls.detail: Offsets in the input are dropped and DEFAULT now() is stored as the server's local wall clock. The moment a second zone is involved (a server, a colleague, Docker running in UTC), the values become ambiguous.
pitfalls.bad: created_at timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
pitfalls.good: created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()

pitfalls.title: Offsets instead of zone names
pitfalls.detail: '+03' or INTERVAL '+03:00' is right for Istanbul today and wrong for its winters before 2016; 'UTC+3' is POSIX syntax for UTC−3; a bare '+03' changes meaning with the session's zone. Store and use names: Europe/Istanbul.

pitfalls.title: Daily reports with ::date
pitfalls.detail: Casting timestamptz to date uses the session's zone, so evening orders in Istanbul land on the wrong day when the server or pool runs in UTC.
pitfalls.good: GROUP BY (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul')::date

pitfalls.title: now() in long transactions
pitfalls.detail: now() is frozen at transaction start. A job that runs for ten minutes in one transaction stamps everything with its first second; use clock_timestamp() where the actual time matters.

pitfalls.title: Future local appointments stored as timestamptz
pitfalls.detail: The instant is computed with today's zone rules. When a country changes them, as Turkey did in 2016 by staying on +03 for good, appointments stored as instants drift by an hour. Store the local time plus the zone name and compute the instant when needed.

pitfalls.title: time with time zone
pitfalls.detail: A time of day with an offset but no date can't account for DST. The docs explicitly do not recommend timetz; use timestamptz, or time plus a zone name.

quiz.q: TimeZone is Europe/Istanbul. You insert '2026-11-13 10:00+01' into a timestamp (without time zone) column. What is stored?
quiz.why: A timestamp without time zone ignores any zone in its input; only the digits are kept.

quiz.q: What does a timestamptz column store?
options: The instant plus the zone it was written in
The instant (internally UTC); the zone is applied on output
quiz.why: Input is converted to UTC and the original zone is not retained; output converts to the session's TimeZone.

quiz.q: The session's TimeZone is UTC. Which expression gives the Istanbul calendar day of placed_at (a timestamptz)?
quiz.why: AT TIME ZONE with a zone name yields Istanbul wall-clock time first. ::date alone uses UTC, and 'UTC+3' is POSIX for UTC−3.

quiz.q: Why can ts + interval '1 day' differ from ts + interval '24 hours' for a timestamptz?
options: Across a DST change a calendar day lasts 23 or 25 hours
quiz.why: '1 day' keeps the local time of day; '24 hours' adds elapsed time. They differ exactly when the day isn't 24 hours long.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Date/Time Functions and Operators (AT TIME ZONE)
PostgreSQL docs: Date/Time Configuration Files (time zone abbreviations)
PostgreSQL docs: POSIX Time Zone Specifications

lessons.body:
## Concept

There are two different things people call "a time", and Postgres has a type for each:

- An **instant**: the moment a payment went through, the same moment everywhere on
  Earth. That is `timestamptz` (`timestamp with time zone`). Input is converted to UTC,
  output is converted to the session's `TimeZone`. No zone is stored.
- A **wall-clock reading**: "09:00", with no idea which clock it was read from. That is
  `timestamp` (`timestamp without time zone`). It stores the digits you gave it and
  silently ignores any offset in the input.

Around them: `date` (a calendar day, 4 bytes), `interval` (a duration kept as months, days
and microseconds, because months and days have no fixed length), and the `AT TIME ZONE`
operator that converts between instants and wall clocks for a named zone.

The most common Postgres data-type mistake is storing events in `timestamp`. It works
while every server, client and user shares one zone, and quietly corrupts ordering and
durations the day one of them doesn't.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java:** `timestamptz` ≈ `Instant`, `timestamp` ≈ `LocalDateTime`, `date` ≈
  `LocalDate`, `interval` ≈ `Period` and `Duration` in one value.
- **Python:** aware vs naive `datetime`. A naive datetime sent to a `timestamptz` column is
  read in the session's zone, which is usually not what you meant.
- **Go:** `time.Time` is an instant with a `Location` for display, which is `timestamptz`.
  Go has no zoneless wall-clock type. `time.Duration` is `'24 hours'`; `AddDate` is the
  calendar arithmetic, but it normalizes 2026-01-31 + 1 month to March 3 where Postgres
  clamps to February 28.
- **JS:** a `Date` is milliseconds since the epoch, an instant; `toString()` shows it in
  the browser's zone, as `timestamptz` output follows the session's.
- **C:** `time_t` is the instant, `struct tm` the wall clock.

## Design notes

Events get `timestamptz`, without exception. Set the session's `TimeZone` per connection
(`UTC` for services is a good default) so nothing depends on the server's configuration;
this machine's server default is `Europe/Istanbul`, a Docker image's is often UTC.

Keep a user's zone as a name (`Europe/Istanbul`), never as an offset. Names carry the
rule history; offsets don't, and string offsets are parsed by rules (POSIX signs, and in
PostgreSQL 18 the current zone's abbreviations) that surprise everyone once.

Future appointments are the exception to "always timestamptz". A meeting promised for
09:00 Istanbul time next spring is a wall-clock promise; store `timestamp` plus the zone
name, and compute the instant when you need it. Turkey's 2016 switch to permanent +03 is the
textbook case of rules changing under stored instants.

Reports by day, week or month: convert first, then truncate:
`date_trunc('day', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul')`. The whole lesson in one
habit: decide whose calendar you are counting in, and say it in the query.

lessons.title: uuid with uuidv7() (PG 18); identity columns vs serial
lessons.summary: Use bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for internal keys and uuid DEFAULT uuidv7() when ids are minted outside one database or shown to users; serial is the legacy shorthand. Version 7 UUIDs sort by creation time, random version 4 UUIDs don't.

examples.title: Identity columns: gaps, the backing sequence, and GENERATED ALWAYS

annotations.note: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard auto-increment. It implies NOT NULL but not uniqueness (the docs are explicit about that), which is what PRIMARY KEY adds. bigint, for the reasons in the previous lesson.

The rolled-back insert consumed id 3, so the next row gets 4. A sequence never takes a value back, because that would make every inserting transaction wait for the others. Gaps also come from crashes and from INSERT ... ON CONFLICT: sequence values are unique, not gapless.

An identity column still draws from a sequence (tickets_id_seq). The difference to serial is ownership: the column manages it, and you restart it with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN id RESTART instead of finding and altering a separate object.
SQLSTATE 428C9. With ALWAYS, an explicit id needs INSERT ... OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, so a hand-written id is always a visible decision. GENERATED BY DEFAULT would accept it silently, like serial.

examples.title: serial: a column default, and how imports break it

annotations.note: The docs say the serial types "are not true types, but merely a notational convenience": an integer column (so 2,147,483,647 is the ceiling), a sequence object, and a DEFAULT nextval(...). bigserial gives bigint.
The catalog sees an integer column with a default; is_identity is NO. Copying the table definition elsewhere, or granting other roles access, means dealing with that separate sequence too.
Explicit ids are just values overriding a default, so nothing objects. This is how migrations from other systems and test fixtures insert their rows.

SQLSTATE 23505: nextval() returns 1, which the import already used. The fix after any manual load is setval(pg_get_serial_sequence(...), max(id)); with an identity column the same holds after an OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE load, but at least the load had to say so.

examples.title: uuidv7() vs uuidv4(): sort order, embedded time, size

annotations.note: uuidv7() is new in PostgreSQL 18. No sequence and no coordination: any session, service or client can mint ids, and RFC 9562 defines the format, so ids made elsewhere are interchangeable with these.

A v7 UUID starts with a millisecond Unix timestamp, then (in PostgreSQL's generator) a sub-millisecond fraction, then random bits, and the generator never steps back within a session, so 1000 ids from one statement sort in creation order. v4 is 122 random bits: new keys land on random pages of the primary-key index instead of at its right edge, which costs cache and write volume on big tables.

Versions 7 and 4, read from the id itself. uuid_extract_timestamp() recovers a v7 id's creation time (to the millisecond) and returns NULL for v4. Handy for debugging; a leak if the id appears in a public URL and creation times are sensitive.

A uuid is 16 bytes, twice a bigint; as text it would be 36 characters plus overhead, compared case-sensitively. The optional shift argument moves the embedded time, so backfilled historic rows can get ids that sort where they belong.

use_cases: bigint identity: internal primary keys, join-heavy tables, ids people read aloud in support tickets
uuidv7: ids minted by clients or several services before the insert, rows merged from several databases, offline-first apps
uuidv4: public tokens and ids where neither order nor creation time may leak
strengths: Identity columns are standard SQL and, with GENERATED ALWAYS, refuse accidental hand-written ids; serial is a Postgres-only macro that refuses nothing
uuidv7 needs no central counter, yet keys still sort by creation time and append to the index like a sequence
uuid is a native 16-byte type with its own comparison and index support, not a 36-character string
Generating ids in the database (DEFAULT plus RETURNING) means the application needs no id library and no extra round trip
weaknesses: A uuid is twice the size of a bigint, in the table and again in every index and foreign key that refers to it
A v7 id reveals when its row was created
Sequences have gaps (rollbacks, ON CONFLICT, crashes), so no generated key is a gapless counter
UUIDs are hard to read in logs and impossible to dictate over the phone; ticket 4211 is not

pitfalls.title: serial (or BY DEFAULT identity) plus hand-written ids
pitfalls.detail: Imports and fixtures insert explicit ids, the sequence doesn't move, and the first ordinary insert collides. Resynchronize after every manual load.
pitfalls.good: SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('old_tickets', 'id'), (SELECT max(id) FROM old_tickets));

pitfalls.title: Using a sequence for invoice numbers
pitfalls.detail: The docs state that sequences cannot produce gapless numbering. If the law requires consecutive numbers, keep a counter row and update it in the same transaction as the invoice, accepting that those transactions serialize.

pitfalls.title: UUIDs stored as text
pitfalls.detail: More than twice the size, slower comparisons, and 'A0EE...' vs 'a0ee...' compare unequal as text. The uuid type accepts both spellings and stores one value.
pitfalls.bad: id text PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()::text
pitfalls.good: id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7()

pitfalls.title: Reading id order as commit order
pitfalls.detail: With any generated key, a transaction that took its id first can commit last. A consumer that remembers 'the highest id I have seen' can miss rows committed later with smaller ids.

quiz.q: An insert into a table with an identity id is rolled back. What happens to the id value it used?
options: It's lost; the next insert gets the following value
The rollback fails until the sequence is reset
quiz.why: nextval() results are not reclaimed when a transaction aborts, so sequences have gaps.

quiz.q: id is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY. Which insert of id 10 succeeds?
options: INSERT INTO t (id, title) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (10, 'x')
Neither: ALWAYS never accepts explicit values
quiz.why: ALWAYS accepts a user-specified value only when the INSERT says OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE.

quiz.q: Why are uuidv7 primary keys kinder to a B-tree index than uuidv4?
options: They start with a timestamp, so new keys arrive in order at the end of the index
quiz.why: Both are 16 bytes and practically unique; v7's time prefix makes inserts append like a sequence instead of scattering.

quiz.q: What does uuid_extract_timestamp(gen_random_uuid()) return?
quiz.why: gen_random_uuid() makes a version 4 UUID, which has no timestamp; the function returns NULL for versions other than 1 and 7.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Surrogate keys come in two families:

- **Counters**, drawn from a sequence. `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the
  standard way since PostgreSQL 10; `serial`/`bigserial` is the older shorthand that
  expands to a column default calling `nextval()`. Both use a sequence object, and
  sequences hand out each value once, gaps included, without waiting for other
  transactions.
- **UUIDs**, 128-bit values anyone can generate without asking anyone. PostgreSQL 18 adds
  `uuidv7()`, a time-ordered UUID (millisecond timestamp first), next to `uuidv4()` (an
  alias of `gen_random_uuid()`). Ordered ids keep the primary-key index appending at one
  end, the way a sequence does, without the sequence.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java, Python, JS:** the built-in generators you know (`UUID.randomUUID()`,
  `uuid.uuid4()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`) make version 4: random, unordered. Fine for
  tokens, poor as a clustered sort order.
- **ORMs:** "auto-increment" maps to an identity column. If an ORM or an old tutorial
  generates `serial`, it works, but it's the legacy form.
- **Go:** `DEFAULT uuidv7()` plus `INSERT ... RETURNING id` lets the database mint the id,
  so the service needs no UUID library just for keys.
- **C:** think of a uuid as a 16-byte array compared like `memcmp`; v7 puts a big-endian
  timestamp in the first 6 bytes, which is why byte order equals time order.

## Design notes

A sensible default: `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` for internal keys. Reach for
`uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()` when ids are created outside a single database (clients that work
offline, several services, merging data) or when sequential ids would leak volume ("order
4211" says you have had about 4,200 orders). Choose ALWAYS over BY DEFAULT unless loading
ids from elsewhere is routine; making the override explicit is the point.

v7 order is time order at millisecond granularity, which is what the docs promise.
PostgreSQL 18's generator additionally fills the next 12 bits with a sub-millisecond
fraction and keeps each new value above the previous one generated in the same session,
which is why the example's 1000 ids sort perfectly. The docs only list the parts
("millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random"); the per-session step is
in the source (src/backend/utils/adt/uuid.c, function get_real_time_ns_ascending), and
on PostgreSQL 18.7 here 100,000 ids from one statement, about 960 per millisecond, came
out strictly increasing. Across sessions there is no such promise: ids are ordered by
the clock reading they embed, millisecond then fraction, and random bits only decide
between ids generated within about a microsecond of each other. That is roughly the order in which they were
generated, not the order in which their transactions commit.

The embedded timestamp is the price of that order. If creation time is sensitive, keep v7
as the internal key and expose a separate random token, or use v4 and accept the index
cost.

lessons.title: jsonb, arrays, enums vs lookup tables vs CHECK
lessons.summary: jsonb suits attributes that really vary per row, arrays suit small lists read with the row; neither checks types or references. For a fixed set of values pick CHECK (simplest), an enum (ordered, compact, values never removable) or a lookup table (values that carry data or change often).

examples.title: json vs jsonb, querying attributes, and what jsonb doesn't check

annotations.note: jsonb parses the document once on input: whitespace, key order and duplicate keys are gone (only the last "a" survives). The docs advise jsonb for most applications; plain json only when the exact text must be kept.

The dividing line of this lesson. price exists for every product and is filtered, summed and constrained, so it is a column with a type. Tea has an origin, a cable has a length: those vary by category, so they go in jsonb.
-> returns jsonb (1000 is a JSON number), ->> returns text (Rize, not "Rize"). @> is containment and ? tests for a key; both can be served by a GIN index on attrs, which the JSON module covers.

A string where a number belongs, accepted without complaint. A CHECK such as jsonb_typeof(attrs -> 'weight_g') = 'number' would stop it; if you find yourself writing many such checks, the field wants to be a column.
SQLSTATE 22P02 at read time, far from the insert that caused it, and the whole report fails. This is the real cost of schemaless data: the validation you skipped on write is paid by every reader.

examples.title: Arrays: 1-based indexing, membership, unnest, and no foreign keys

annotations.note: text[] is an array of text. Declared sizes such as text[3] are accepted and ignored, per the docs. NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' keeps "no tags" as an empty array, so code never has to tell NULL and {} apart.

Indexing starts at 1. tags[0] and tags[3] are NULL, not an error: like JS's undefined, unlike Python's IndexError or Go's panic. For the empty array, array_length(tags, 1) is NULL while cardinality(tags) is 0, so WHERE array_length(tags, 1) = 0 never matches.
'sql' = ANY (tags) reads naturally for one value; tags @> ARRAY['go', 'sql'] means "has all of these". A GIN index on tags can serve @> but not = ANY, so write tags @> ARRAY['sql'] on large tables.

unnest expands each row's array into rows, and the function in FROM can refer to the table before it. This is how arrays rejoin set-based SQL: as soon as you aggregate over elements, you are treating them as rows.

'golang' next to 'go' is now a second tag, and nothing can stop it: a foreign key can't point into an array. The docs' own tip: arrays are not sets, and searching for elements can be a sign of misdesign. When tags need integrity or data of their own, use a junction table.

examples.title: One status, three designs: enum, lookup table, CHECK

annotations.note: An enum is a type: 4 bytes per value, labels case-sensitive, and two different enum types can't even be compared. Values can be added and renamed, but never removed or reordered without recreating the type.
A lookup table holds the values as rows. With the code itself as the primary key, tickets.as_lookup stays readable without a join; the join is only needed for the label and position.
A CHECK keeps the column plain text and the allowed list in the table's definition. Easiest to read, but only this table knows the list.

enum_order follows the declaration: open, in_progress, done. text_order is alphabetical: done, in_progress, open. If "sort by status" should mean workflow order, text needs a CASE or a position column.
Labels and order are data: translating a label or moving a status is an UPDATE, not a migration. Neither an enum nor a CHECK can attach a Turkish label to a value.

In a migration the type already exists, and the docs' rule applies: a value added inside a transaction block can't be used until that transaction commits. (This sandbox created the type in the same transaction, a case where Postgres allows the new value at once.)
Changing a CHECK means dropping and re-adding it, and the new one scans every row under an exclusive lock. On a large table, add it NOT VALID and validate separately, as the ALTER TABLE lesson shows.
SQLSTATE 23503: rows still say 'open'. Retiring a lookup value is explicit (migrate the rows, or add an active flag); for an enum there is no statement for it at all.

use_cases: jsonb: per-category product attributes, per-integration settings, raw webhook payloads kept for replay
arrays: tags or labels read and written with their row, small value lists without an identity of their own
CHECK (x IN ...): short, stable lists owned by one table
enum: stable, ordered states shared by several tables (severity, workflow stage)
lookup table: values with labels, translations, sort order or flags, or values that change at business speed
strengths: jsonb gives per-row flexibility without an entity-attribute-value table, and GIN indexes make @> and ? fast
An array keeps a short list inside the row: one read, no join, and GIN-indexable containment
enum values are 4 bytes, typo-proof, and sort in a meaningful order
A lookup table is the only option where values carry data and change with DML instead of DDL
weaknesses: Nothing inside jsonb or an array is type-checked or reference-checked unless you add CHECK constraints
Changing one key or element writes a new version of the whole row and locks it, which the docs flag for large documents
Enum values can't be removed or reordered without recreating the type, and an added value can't be used before it commits
A lookup table costs a foreign-key check on every write and a join for every label

pitfalls.title: jsonb for core fields
pitfalls.detail: Fields that every row has and that queries filter, join or sum on lose types, NOT NULL, foreign keys and planner statistics inside jsonb.
pitfalls.good: price numeric(12, 2) NOT NULL as a column; jsonb for the leftovers

pitfalls.title: Arrays of foreign keys
pitfalls.detail: author_ids int[] can't be checked against authors, and deleting an author leaves dangling ids. A junction table with two foreign keys can.
pitfalls.good: article_authors (article_id REFERENCES articles, author_id REFERENCES authors, PRIMARY KEY (article_id, author_id))

pitfalls.title: Testing an empty array with array_length
pitfalls.detail: array_length of an empty array is NULL, so the comparison is never true.
pitfalls.good: WHERE cardinality(tags) = 0

pitfalls.title: Adding an enum value and using it in one migration
pitfalls.detail: Migration tools usually wrap each migration in a transaction; the new value can't be used before ALTER TYPE commits. Put ADD VALUE and the UPDATE that uses it in separate migrations.

pitfalls.title: Comparing or grouping json values
pitfalls.detail: The json type has no equality operator, so =, DISTINCT and GROUP BY on json fail with 'operator does not exist: json = json'. jsonb has one.

pitfalls.title: Appending a literal to an array with ||
pitfalls.detail: tags || 'golang' reads the literal as an array and fails with malformed array literal. Use array_append(tags, 'golang') or ARRAY['golang'].

quiz.q: An object in a jsonb input has the same key twice. What is stored?
options: Only the last value for that key
quiz.why: jsonb doesn't keep duplicate keys; only the last value is kept. (json keeps the exact text, duplicates included.)

quiz.q: tags is text[] holding {go,sql}. What is tags[0]?
quiz.why: Arrays are 1-based and an out-of-bounds subscript returns NULL instead of raising an error.

quiz.q: Ticket statuses need a Turkish label each, and support staff add new ones every month. Which design fits?
options: Lookup table plus a foreign key
quiz.why: Only a lookup table lets values carry data (the label) and be added or retired with plain DML.

quiz.q: Why can't one migration transaction run ALTER TYPE status ADD VALUE 'archived' and then set rows to 'archived'?
options: A new enum value can't be used until the ALTER TYPE commits
ADD VALUE is not allowed in a transaction block
quiz.why: Since PostgreSQL 12 ADD VALUE may run in a transaction block, but the docs say the new value can't be used until the transaction has committed.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: ALTER TYPE (adding enum values)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Relational columns give you types, constraints and statistics per field. Three features
relax that, each for a specific shape of data:

- **`jsonb`**: a parsed JSON document per row, for attributes that differ from row to
  row. Queryable (`->`, `->>`, `@>`, `?`) and indexable, but nothing inside is checked.
- **Arrays** (`text[]`, `int[]`): an ordered list inside the row, for small lists you
  read and write with it. 1-based, and no foreign keys into them.
- **A fixed set of values** (a status, a severity) can be declared three ways: a
  `CHECK (x IN (...))` on a text column, an `enum` type, or a lookup table referenced by
  a foreign key. They differ in what changing the set costs.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript:** `'open' | 'in_progress' | 'done'` is the same idea as an enum or a CHECK,
  enforced at a different layer; a `jsonb` column is `Record<string, unknown>` and needs
  validating (zod) when it comes back, exactly like a `fetch` response.
- **Java:** Java enums are ordered like Postgres enums, but Java enums can carry fields.
  Postgres enums can't; that's what the lookup table is for.
- **Go:** Go has no enum type, only typed constants, so the database enum is stricter than
  your Go code. `jsonb` maps naturally to `json.RawMessage` or a struct via
  `encoding/json`.
- **Python/JS:** arrays here start at 1, and out-of-range reads return NULL, not an
  `IndexError`.
- **Document databases:** `jsonb` gives you a document per column inside a relational row,
  so you can keep transactions, joins and constraints for everything that is stable.

## Design notes

Structured where it's stable, JSON where it isn't. If every row has the field, or you
filter, join or sum on it, it is a column. `jsonb` earns its place for the long tail of
optional attributes and for payloads you store as received. The docs also suggest keeping
documents to a predictable structure and a manageable size, since every update rewrites
and locks the whole row.

Arrays are a denormalization: fine for tags that are just strings, wrong as soon as the
elements are references to other rows or need their own data.

For value sets, start with CHECK: it's plain text, visible in the table definition, and
changing it is ordinary DDL. Choose an enum when the order matters and the set is stable
across many tables. Choose a lookup table when values carry data (labels, translations,
positions, an active flag) or when people outside engineering add them.

lessons.title: ALTER TABLE done safely
lessons.summary: Some ALTER TABLE forms only touch the catalog; others rewrite every row and index while holding a lock that blocks even SELECT. Learn which is which, and the safe order for a required column: add nullable, constrain NOT VALID, backfill in batches, VALIDATE.

examples.title: Which changes rewrite the table or its index

annotations.note: relfilenode names the file a table or index is stored in, and files() reads both. A rewrite writes a new file and swaps it in, so the number changes. The numbers themselves differ on every run, so the log compares them instead of printing them.
