Catalog-only. A column without a default reads as NULL in old rows, and a non-volatile default is evaluated once and stored in the table's metadata (since PostgreSQL 11). Fast on a billion rows.

A volatile default (uuidv7(), clock_timestamp(), random()) differs per row, so every row is rewritten, and every index with it. now() is only stable: it is evaluated once, costs no rewrite, and gives every existing row the same timestamp.
A virtual generated column (the default kind since PostgreSQL 18) is computed when read, so adding one never rewrites. A STORED generated column, like an identity column, would.

Raising a varchar limit or dropping it is binary coercible: no rewrite, and because varchar and text sort identically, no index rebuild either. Shrinking a limit (varchar(200) to varchar(20)) rewrites both, since every value has to be checked.

A collation change leaves the table alone but rebuilds every index on the column, because the sort order changes. Switching a big table to Turkish ordering (tr-x-icu) costs index builds, not a table copy.

integer to bigint changes every row's bytes: a full rewrite of table and indexes under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, for as long as it takes. On a large table, add a bigint column, backfill it, and swap names in one short transaction instead.
DROP COLUMN only hides the column. The space comes back as rows are updated over time, or at the next rewrite.

examples.title: The lock each change holds, from pg_locks

annotations.note: In the sql runtime the table would be created in the same transaction, and CREATE TABLE already holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on it, which would hide what the ALTER takes. Here each statement commits on its own, so the table exists first, as in production.
pg_locks lists every lock; this view keeps the ones held by this session on accounts. Table locks are held until the transaction ends, so a query after the ALTER still sees them.

AccessExclusiveLock for a catalog-only change. It conflicts with every mode, plain SELECT included. The change itself is instant, but the ALTER must first wait for every open transaction that touched the table, and every query arriving after it queues behind it.
NOT VALID skips the scan of existing rows, but adding the constraint still needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, just for a moment.
VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which doesn't conflict with reads or with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. The long scan runs alongside normal traffic.
A plain CREATE INDEX holds SHARE: reads continue, but every write waits until the build finishes.

SQLSTATE 25001. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY doesn't block writes, but it works in several transactions of its own, so it can't run inside one. Migration tools that wrap each file in a transaction need an opt-out for it.

examples.title: Adding a required column without a long lock

annotations.note: Catalog-only. If one constant were right for every existing row, ADD COLUMN country text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'TR' would be catalog-only too, and you'd be done. Here the value depends on each row's phone number.

PostgreSQL 18 stores NOT NULL as a named constraint that can be added NOT VALID. It is enforced at once for new rows and for every updated row, even an update that doesn't touch country, so the application must already write the column before this step runs.
1000 rows without a country, and convalidated is false: the database knows the rule doesn't hold for old rows yet.
In production this is a loop over id ranges, committing after each batch, so no transaction holds thousands of row locks for long.
The scan happens here, under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE. If a NULL were left, VALIDATE would fail and change nothing; fix the rows and run it again.

Zero rows without a country and a validated constraint: a regular NOT NULL now. Before PostgreSQL 18 the same effect needed a CHECK (country IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, VALIDATE, then SET NOT NULL (which skips its scan when a valid CHECK proves the column has no NULLs), then dropping the CHECK.
SQLSTATE 23502. This insert would have failed at any point after step 2, which is what kept the backfill from racing new rows.

use_cases: Adding columns and constraints to tables that serve traffic while the migration runs
Reviewing a migration: predicting which statements rewrite or scan, and how long they hold which lock
Planning type changes (integer to bigint, a collation switch) on large tables
strengths: Many common changes are catalog-only: nullable columns, constant defaults, virtual generated columns, raising varchar limits, dropping columns
DDL is transactional: a migration's ALTERs, data fixes and constraint changes commit or roll back together (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is a documented exception)
NOT VALID plus VALIDATE splits a constraint into a brief exclusive step and a long step that runs alongside reads and writes
Rewrite behaviour is observable (relfilenode) and lock levels are documented per form, so migrations can be reasoned about before they run
weaknesses: Even catalog-only ALTERs need ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which blocks SELECT and queues all later queries behind it
Type changes such as integer to bigint rewrite the whole table and its indexes while holding that lock
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can't run in a transaction block and can leave an invalid index behind when it fails
Space from dropped columns isn't returned until rows are rewritten

pitfalls.title: DDL without lock_timeout
pitfalls.detail: An ALTER waiting behind a long-running query holds its place in the lock queue, and every query after it waits too: a metadata-only change becomes an outage. Set a short lock_timeout before DDL and retry on failure.
pitfalls.good: SET lock_timeout = '2s'; ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN note text;

pitfalls.title: A volatile default on a big table
pitfalls.detail: DEFAULT uuidv7(), gen_random_uuid() or clock_timestamp() rewrites the table. Add the column without a default, set the default separately (it then applies to new rows only), and backfill old rows in batches.
pitfalls.bad: ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN token uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7();
pitfalls.good: ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN token uuid; ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN token SET DEFAULT uuidv7(); -- then backfill, then NOT NULL NOT VALID + VALIDATE

pitfalls.title: Adding a constraint without NOT VALID
pitfalls.detail: ADD CONSTRAINT scans every row while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (or SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE for foreign keys, which still blocks writes). Add it NOT VALID, then VALIDATE in a separate transaction.

pitfalls.title: Plain CREATE INDEX on a live table
pitfalls.detail: It blocks all writes for the duration of the build. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block, and check for an INVALID index if it fails.

pitfalls.title: NOT VALID before the application writes the column
pitfalls.detail: A NOT VALID constraint is enforced for every new and updated row. If the old application version still writes rows without the column, its updates start failing. Deploy the writer first.

quiz.q: Which change rewrites the whole table on PostgreSQL 18?
options: ADD COLUMN plan text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free'
ALTER COLUMN name TYPE varchar(200) (from varchar(100))
ADD COLUMN token uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()
quiz.why: uuidv7() is volatile, so each existing row needs its own value; the others are catalog-only.

quiz.q: Your ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN is instant, yet the app stalls while it waits. Why?
options: It waits for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a long transaction, and new queries queue behind it
Postgres locks the whole database for DDL
quiz.why: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts even with SELECT; the waiting ALTER blocks everything that arrives after it. A short lock_timeout limits the damage.

quiz.q: Which lock does ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT take on the table?
quiz.why: Validation only checks existing rows (new ones are already checked), so it can let reads and writes continue.

quiz.q: What is the safe order for a new required column whose value is computed per row?
options: Add nullable, add NOT NULL NOT VALID, backfill in batches, VALIDATE
ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL, then backfill
quiz.why: Adding NOT NULL directly fails on existing rows (or scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE); NOT VALID guards new writes while old rows are fixed in batches.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: ALTER TABLE (see Notes on rewrites and locks)
PostgreSQL docs: Explicit Locking (table-level lock modes)
PostgreSQL docs: CREATE INDEX (Building Indexes Concurrently)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Every `ALTER TABLE` has two costs, and they are independent:

- **Work.** Catalog-only (instant), a **scan** of every row (adding a constraint, `SET NOT
  NULL`), or a **rewrite** of every row and index (most type changes, volatile defaults,
  stored generated and identity columns).
- **Lock.** Unless the docs say otherwise for a form, `ALTER TABLE` takes ACCESS
  EXCLUSIVE, the one mode that blocks plain `SELECT`. A few forms take less:
  `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` and `SET STATISTICS` take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, `ADD FOREIGN
  KEY` takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE.

A rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is downtime proportional to the table's size. Safe
migrations are built from catalog-only steps, scans under weak locks, and batched updates.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **ORM migrations (Django, Rails, Flyway):** they generate the DDL, but not the lock
  analysis. "Add a non-null column with a default" can be instant or a rewrite depending on
  whether the default is volatile; the migration file looks the same.
- **Java/Go deployments:** a migration runs while the old version of your service is still
  serving traffic. Expand first (add nullable, write both), contract later (constraints,
  drops), the same discipline as changing a public API.
- **Mutexes:** ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is a writer lock that also excludes readers, and the queue
  is fair: once a writer waits, later readers wait behind it, even though they wouldn't
  conflict with the current holder. The docs call this a "soft block" (under
  `pg_blocking_pids`, System Information Functions): a session waiting for a conflicting
  lock and "ahead of it in the wait queue" blocks the later one. On PostgreSQL 18.7, with
  one session holding ACCESS SHARE and an `ALTER TABLE` waiting, a third session's
  `SELECT` waited too, and `pg_blocking_pids` named the `ALTER`, not the reader.

## Design notes

Before running a migration, ask of each statement: catalog, scan or rewrite? Which lock,
and for how long? The rewrite example gives the common answers for PostgreSQL 18; the
ALTER TABLE notes in the docs are the reference.

Habits that follow:

- `SET lock_timeout` (a few seconds) before DDL, and retry. Waiting forever for ACCESS
  EXCLUSIVE is how a catalog-only change takes a site down.
- Keep each migration transaction short; Postgres DDL is transactional, so a failed
  migration rolls back, but a long transaction holds its locks to the end.
- Constraints: add NOT VALID, VALIDATE separately. Indexes: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY,
  outside a transaction block.
- Type changes on big tables: new column, backfill in batches, swap in a short
  transaction. Choose `bigint` and `text` up front and you rarely need this.

This sandbox runs every example in a throwaway transaction (or, for the lock example,
throwaway schema), so you can try any of these forms and look at `pg_locks` and
`relfilenode` yourself without affecting anything.

lessons.title: ACID, savepoints, MVCC: why readers don't block writers
lessons.summary: A transaction is all or nothing, and one failed statement aborts all of it unless a savepoint contains the damage. Postgres isolates transactions with row versions instead of read locks, so readers and writers never wait for each other; only two writers on the same row do.

examples.title: UPDATE writes a new row version; ROLLBACK TO just hides it

annotations.note: Transaction IDs change on every run, so xmin is compared, not printed. pg_current_xact_id() (PostgreSQL 13+) returns the 64-bit xid8; the cast gives the 32-bit form that xmin uses. Both rows were written by this script's one transaction, and xmax 0 means no transaction has deleted or replaced them.

Row a moved from (0,1) to (0,3): 60 is a new version. The 100 is still on the page, its xmax set to our transaction. We no longer see it, but a concurrent transaction would, until we commit. That old version is what lets readers proceed without waiting for writers.

SAVEPOINT starts a subtransaction. Its update gets a transaction ID of its own and writes version (0,4). ROLLBACK TO marks that subtransaction aborted, releases the locks taken since the savepoint, and leaves the outer transaction usable.

The docs say a nonzero xmax on a visible row usually means the deleting transaction hasn't committed yet, or that an attempted deletion was rolled back. Here it's the second case: rolling back did not restore the old version, it only marked the newer one's writer as aborted, so visibility checks skip it.
The aborted version still occupies slot 4, so the new version lands in slot 5. Versions from rolled-back work are garbage that VACUUM collects later (the last lesson of this module).

examples.title: Two sessions: the reader doesn't wait, the second writer does
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 0);

annotations.note: A has written new versions of both rows and holds a row lock on each until it ends. Nothing is visible to other sessions yet.

B never ran BEGIN, so each of its statements is its own transaction. Its snapshot shows the last committed versions, 100 and 0: no waiting, and never the in-between state where the 40 has left a but not reached b.

How the runner shows a wait: a step still running after 400 ms is printed as "[5] B: waiting" and the script moves on, as you would switch terminals; the result is printed under the same number when it arrives. B needs the row lock A holds on a, so it waits for A's commit or rollback.

A's COMMIT releases the locks and B's update completes right after it. Under READ COMMITTED a blocked UPDATE re-reads the row once the other transaction commits, so it adds 1 to A's 60, not to the 100 it saw when it started. Nothing was lost: 61 and 40.

examples.title: One error aborts the transaction; a savepoint contains it
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 0);

annotations.note: The duplicate key fails (23505), and from then on the whole transaction is aborted: every statement is refused with 25P02 until it ends. The successful insert of c is doomed too.

COMMIT on an aborted transaction doesn't raise an error. It rolls back and reports the command tag ROLLBACK. pgx turns that tag into pgx.ErrTxCommitRollback; code that ignores Commit's error believes it saved data that is gone.
With a savepoint in front of the risky statement, ROLLBACK TO undoes just that statement and clears the aborted state. The insert of c, made before the savepoint, survives.
A second connection sees c and d from the committed transaction and nothing from the failed one: all or nothing, and once COMMIT returned, durable.

use_cases: Any change that spans several statements and must happen completely or not at all: a transfer, an order with its lines, a schema migration
Imports that should skip bad rows instead of failing: a savepoint around the risky statement, ROLLBACK TO on error, carry on
Long reads (exports, reports) next to normal write traffic, without either side waiting for the other
strengths: Plain reads take no row locks: a long report never stalls updates, unlike a Java ReentrantReadWriteLock, where one writer waits for every reader to finish
ROLLBACK doesn't copy old values back; it marks the transaction aborted and visibility checks skip what it wrote
Most DDL is transactional too: a migration's CREATE, ALTER and data fixes commit or roll back together
Savepoints give statement-level recovery inside a transaction; PL/pgSQL's EXCEPTION blocks use the same subtransaction mechanism
weaknesses: Every UPDATE writes a whole new row version, usually with new index entries, so update-heavy tables grow until VACUUM reclaims the old versions
Any error aborts the entire transaction; recovering needs a savepoint, which costs a subtransaction
MVCC removes read/write blocking, not write/write blocking: writers to the same row still queue
Under the default READ COMMITTED each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so two reads in one transaction can disagree (next lesson)

pitfalls.title: Ignoring Commit's error
pitfalls.detail: COMMIT of an aborted transaction succeeds as a statement and reports ROLLBACK. pgx returns pgx.ErrTxCommitRollback for it, so the error from tx.Commit is the only signal that your writes are gone.

pitfalls.title: Catching an error and carrying on in the same transaction
pitfalls.detail: After any error every statement fails with 25P02 until ROLLBACK. If you expect a statement to fail (a duplicate during an import), put a savepoint in front of it, or better, write it so it can't fail.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO tags VALUES ('go');  -- may be a duplicate: aborts the transaction
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO tags VALUES ('go') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

pitfalls.title: A savepoint per row in a big loop
pitfalls.detail: Each savepoint is a subtransaction. The docs warn that overhead grows with the number kept open, and past 64 per backend lookups go to pg_subtrans on disk. Release savepoints you no longer need, and prefer ON CONFLICT or a staging table to a savepoint per row.

pitfalls.title: Leaving a transaction open
pitfalls.detail: An idle transaction keeps its row locks and stops VACUUM from removing versions it might still see. Never wait for user input, an HTTP call or a slow job inside a transaction; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is the server-side safety net.

quiz.q: Session A has updated row a but not committed. Session B runs SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'a'. What happens?
options: B waits until A commits or rolls back
B immediately gets the last committed value
quiz.why: B's snapshot doesn't include A's uncommitted version, and plain reads take no row locks, so it reads the previous version without waiting.

quiz.q: Inside a transaction an INSERT fails with a unique violation. What does the next SELECT do?
options: Runs normally: only the INSERT was undone
Fails with 25P02 until the transaction ends
quiz.why: Postgres aborts the whole transaction on an error. Only ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint taken before the error) makes it usable again.

quiz.q: What does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s do?
options: Undoes the work done after s and leaves the transaction open
Undoes the work done before s
quiz.why: The savepoint's subtransaction is aborted; everything before it is kept, and the transaction can continue and commit.

quiz.q: UPDATE accounts SET balance = 60 WHERE id = 'a' has committed. What happened on disk?
options: The row was overwritten in place
A new row version was written; the old one stays until VACUUM removes it once no snapshot can see it
The old version was moved to an undo log
quiz.why: Every update creates a new version with a new ctid. The old one is dead but stays in the table until VACUUM, which is what keeps it available to older snapshots.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: System Columns (xmin, xmax, ctid)
PostgreSQL docs: Asynchronous Commit (what COMMIT normally guarantees)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A transaction is the unit of correctness. Everything between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` is:

- **Atomic**: all of it takes effect or none of it does. In Postgres a single failed
  statement aborts the whole transaction; a **savepoint** lets you roll back to a point
  inside it and continue.
- **Consistent**: constraints are checked, so a committed state never violates them.
- **Isolated**: other sessions don't see your changes until you commit, and you don't
  see theirs half-done.
- **Durable**: by default `COMMIT` returns only after the transaction's WAL records are
  flushed to disk, so a reported commit survives a crash.

Postgres isolates with **MVCC** (multiversion concurrency control). An `UPDATE` never
changes a row in place: it writes a new **row version** and marks the old one as replaced.
Each statement reads from a **snapshot** that decides which versions it may see. A reader
therefore never needs a writer's lock: it takes the newest version its snapshot allows.
Only two writers on the same row wait for each other.

Examples 2 and 3 use the two-session runner: steps tagged `A:` and `B:` run on two
connections, in script order, like two psql terminals side by side.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/C++ locks:** a `ReadWriteLock` makes writers wait for readers. MVCC works like
  copy-on-write: a writer publishes a new version and readers keep the one they started
  with. In Go terms, it's closer to swapping an `atomic.Pointer` to an immutable struct
  than to a `sync.RWMutex`.
- **Python (psycopg) and Go (pgx):** the "poisoned transaction" is the classic surprise.
  psycopg raises `InFailedSqlTransaction` on the next statement after an error; that is
  SQLSTATE 25P02 from example 3. In pgx, check the error from `tx.Commit`.
- **Connection pools (pgxpool, node-postgres):** a transaction lives on one connection.
  Sending `BEGIN` through the pool and then another statement through the pool may use
  two different connections. Use the pool's transaction API (`pool.Begin` in pgx), which
  pins one connection until `Commit` or `Rollback`.
- **C:** think of `xmin` and `xmax` as a version stamp in every record header: "written by
  transaction X, superseded by transaction Y".

## How it works

Every row version carries the hidden columns from example 1: `xmin` (the transaction that
wrote it), `xmax` (the transaction that deleted or replaced it, or 0) and `ctid` (its
physical place, page and slot). Postgres also records for each transaction whether it
committed or aborted. Roughly, a version is visible to your snapshot if its `xmin`
committed before the snapshot was taken (or is your own transaction), and its `xmax` is
0, aborted, or not yet committed as far as the snapshot knows.

That is why `ROLLBACK` is cheap: it records "aborted" and every version the transaction
wrote becomes invisible. The cost comes later: dead versions stay in the table until
`VACUUM` removes the ones no snapshot can still see (lesson 7).

The `sql` runtime of example 1 runs your script inside one transaction that is always
rolled back, so it can show savepoints but not `COMMIT`; the two-session examples commit
for real, in a throwaway schema.

## Design notes

- **Keep transactions short.** Row locks are held until the end, and an open transaction
  holds back VACUUM. Do the HTTP call, the file upload or the user prompt before `BEGIN`
  or after `COMMIT`, never in between.
- **One place owns the boundary.** In Go, a small `WithTx(ctx, func(pgx.Tx) error)`
  helper begins, rolls back on error, and commits (the Go + PostgreSQL module builds it).
  Repositories take a `pgx.Tx` (or an interface it satisfies) instead of beginning
  their own.
- **Prefer statements that can't fail over savepoints.** `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, `WHERE
  NOT EXISTS`, or a staging table is cheaper and clearer than catching duplicates.
  Savepoints are for genuinely unpredictable failures inside a larger unit of work.
- MVCC only removes read/write blocking. When two transactions write the same rows, you
  still choose how they coordinate: isolation levels (next two lessons) or explicit row
  locks (lesson 4).

lessons.title: Isolation levels with live anomalies
lessons.summary: Under READ COMMITTED (the default), another transaction's commit can change what your next query sees. This lesson runs two sessions side by side so you watch the anomaly happen, then prevent it.

examples.title: Session B's read changes between statements in one transaction
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 0);

annotations.note: Session A opens a transaction and reads a's balance: 100. Under READ COMMITTED, each statement takes a fresh snapshot.
Session B, in its own transaction, moves 40 out and commits. No conflict: A only read.
A reads again inside the same transaction and sees 60. That is a non-repeatable read: one query, two answers.
REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot for the whole transaction, at its first statement rather than at BEGIN. A now reads 60.

B commits again (60 becomes 20), yet A's re-read still returns 60: the snapshot doesn't move. SERIALIZABLE goes further and aborts one transaction when concurrent reads and writes could not have happened in any serial order; that is the next lesson.

use_cases: Reports that must see one consistent snapshot (REPEATABLE READ)
Transfers and invariants that reads alone must not violate (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, next lesson)
strengths: Under MVCC plain reads never wait for writes and writes never wait for reads; only two writers on the same row wait for each other
Escalating isolation is one line — no code restructure
Anomalies are teachable because each level forbids a named, testable behavior
weaknesses: READ COMMITTED makes every statement its own consistency unit: multi-statement invariants leak
REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE can fail with a serialization error and need a retry loop

pitfalls.title: Re-reading inside a transaction and assuming consistency
pitfalls.detail: Under READ COMMITTED each statement gets a fresh snapshot. Use one snapshot (REPEATABLE READ) or lock rows.

pitfalls.title: Retrying nothing under SERIALIZABLE
pitfalls.detail: Serializable failures (40001) are normal: catch and retry the transaction.

quiz.q: Under READ COMMITTED, when does A's snapshot refresh?
quiz.why: Read committed takes a new snapshot for each statement — that's exactly the anomaly source.

quiz.q: Which level prevents the non-repeatable read above?
quiz.why: A transaction-pinned snapshot returns the same rows it read before.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Postgres implements isolation with MVCC: writers create new row versions, readers see
snapshots. READ COMMITTED (default) takes a snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ and
SERIALIZABLE pin one snapshot per transaction and reject what would break it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Mutexes: MVCC is "readers never block writers" — no lock table for plain reads.
- Goroutines/JS: the interleaving is real concurrency, but the *database defines* which
  interleavings are legal, per isolation level.
- Go memory model: think of isolation levels as happens-before guarantees you opt into.

## Design notes

Choose isolation per transaction, not per database: most traffic is fine at READ COMMITTED,
and the two or three flows with invariants (transfers, stock) either lock rows (FOR UPDATE)
or escalate to REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE with retries. The multi-session runner exists
because these behaviors only become visible — and only become trusted — when you watch both
sessions in a timeline.

lessons.title: Serializable isolation and retry loops
lessons.summary: REPEATABLE READ still lets two transactions each make a correct decision and together break a rule (write skew). SERIALIZABLE detects that pattern without blocking anyone and rolls one transaction back with SQLSTATE 40001, so the application must retry it from the start.

examples.title: Write skew under REPEATABLE READ: both checks pass, the rule breaks
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE doctors (name text PRIMARY KEY, on_call boolean NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO doctors VALUES ('alice', true), ('bob', true);

annotations.note: Each transaction gets one snapshot, taken at its first query. This is what many databases call snapshot isolation, and it already prevents the non-repeatable read from the previous lesson.
Both see two doctors on call. A plain read takes no lock and leaves no trace, so nothing records that A's decision depends on Bob's row.
REPEATABLE READ fails a transaction only when it writes or locks a row that another transaction changed after its snapshot. A and B write different rows, so no step waits and both commits succeed.
Each transaction was correct on its own; together they leave nobody on call. This is write skew, a serialization anomaly: the docs' isolation table lists it as possible under REPEATABLE READ.

examples.title: SERIALIZABLE aborts one of them with 40001; the retry decides again
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE doctors (name text PRIMARY KEY, on_call boolean NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO doctors VALUES ('alice', true), ('bob', true);

annotations.note: Under SERIALIZABLE each read also leaves an SIRead lock, a note of what was read (visible in pg_locks). It blocks nobody. This query scans the whole table, so the note covers the whole table.
A writes a row B read, and B writes a row A read: a read/write dependency in each direction. Still nothing waits; the server only records the dependencies.

No serial order of A and B can produce this result, so one of them must go. Here A commits first and B's COMMIT fails with 40001. In other interleavings the error can come at an earlier statement; the handling is the same. A failed COMMIT ends the transaction, so B can begin again at once.

The retry runs the whole transaction again, check included, and the check now sees one doctor on call. Replaying only the UPDATE would reproduce the bug: the decision depends on the read, which is why the docs say to retry the complete transaction.
The rule held, and no transaction ever waited for a lock. The price was one transaction's work thrown away, plus a retry loop in the application.

use_cases: Rules that span several rows and that no constraint can express: at least one on call, a budget spread across line items, a quota counted over many rows
Complex transactions where finding the exact rows to lock is error-prone
Teams that prefer one rule for every write path ('SERIALIZABLE plus a retry wrapper') to reasoning about locks in each one
strengths: Nothing blocks: SIRead locks never make anyone wait and can't take part in a deadlock, unlike SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Correctness doesn't depend on knowing which rows to lock; the database detects the dangerous pattern for you
Switching is one clause in BEGIN or one field in pgx.TxOptions; the SQL stays the same
weaknesses: Every transaction needs a retry loop, and its side effects outside the database (e-mails, HTTP calls) must wait until after commit or be safe to repeat

False positives: a sequential scan predicate-locks the whole table, and fine-grained locks are combined into coarser ones when lock memory runs short, so transactions that didn't really conflict can fail
Under heavy contention many transactions fail and redo their work; a hot row is often better served by an explicit row lock
The guarantee covers SERIALIZABLE transactions only, and doesn't extend to hot standby or logical replicas

pitfalls.title: Retrying the statement instead of the transaction
pitfalls.detail: The failed transaction made decisions from data that has since changed. Re-run everything from BEGIN, reads included, so the decision is made again on fresh data. PostgreSQL offers no automatic retry for exactly this reason.

pitfalls.title: Mixing isolation levels
pitfalls.detail: The docs promise consistency when SERIALIZABLE is used for all writes and for all reads that need a consistent view. A READ COMMITTED writer on the same tables slips past the checks. Set default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable' for the application role rather than relying on every call site.
pitfalls.good: ALTER ROLE app SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable';

pitfalls.title: Long serializable transactions
pitfalls.detail: SIRead locks are kept past commit until the overlapping transactions finish, so one long transaction raises the failure rate for everyone. Keep them short, and declare READ ONLY where you can.

pitfalls.title: A long report that keeps failing
pitfalls.detail: A read-only report can still be cancelled by a serialization failure. SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits for a safe snapshot when it starts, then runs with no risk of failure and without SSI overhead.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE, READ ONLY, DEFERRABLE;

quiz.q: Two REPEATABLE READ transactions each count the on-call doctors, then each takes a different doctor off call. What happens?
options: The second UPDATE waits for the first transaction
Both commit and nobody is on call
quiz.why: REPEATABLE READ only conflicts on rows both transactions write. Disjoint writes based on overlapping reads are write skew, which it allows.

quiz.q: Under SERIALIZABLE, what does B's SELECT do to A's later UPDATE of a row B read?
options: It blocks the UPDATE until B commits
Nothing visible: it leaves an SIRead lock that only matters for conflict detection
It takes a FOR SHARE lock on the rows
quiz.why: Predicate (SIRead) locks never block. They record reads so the server can spot read/write dependencies when the writes happen.

quiz.q: B fails with SQLSTATE 40001. What should the application do?
options: Start a new transaction and run the whole unit of work again, reads and decisions included
Retry the same transaction at READ COMMITTED
quiz.why: The error means B's view of the data is no longer valid. Only re-running the logic on a new snapshot gives a correct decision.

quiz.q: Why can a SERIALIZABLE transaction fail even though no other transaction wrote the rows it cares about?
options: Predicate locks can be coarse: a sequential scan locks the whole table, and many fine locks can be combined into a page or table lock
SERIALIZABLE takes table locks on every read
quiz.why: The docs warn that relation-level predicate locks increase the failure rate. Detection errs on the safe side; indexes and short transactions reduce false positives.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Data Consistency Checks at the Application Level
PostgreSQL docs: SET TRANSACTION (READ ONLY, DEFERRABLE)

lessons.body:
## Concept

REPEATABLE READ gives a transaction one snapshot and fails it if it writes a row that
someone changed after that snapshot. That prevents lost updates on the same row, but not
**write skew**: two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a *different* row, and
together they break a rule that each one checked.

SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL (true serializability since 9.1) is **Serializable Snapshot
Isolation (SSI)**. Transactions read from snapshots exactly as in REPEATABLE READ; in
addition the server records what each one read (SIRead or predicate locks) and notices when
another concurrent serializable transaction writes that data. When the reads and writes
form a pattern that no one-at-a-time order could produce, one transaction is rolled back
with SQLSTATE 40001 (`serialization_failure`).

Nothing waits. You pay with failed transactions instead, and the application must retry
them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Optimistic concurrency:** like a compare-and-swap loop in Go (`atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64`)
  or JPA's `@Version` check: do the work, detect the conflict at the end, retry. SSI goes
  further: it detects conflicts on data you only *read*, which a version column on the row
  you write can't see.
- **Python/JS/Go drivers and ORMs:** none of them retry for you, and neither does
  Postgres: the docs explain it can't, because the retry must re-run your decision logic.
- **Java `synchronized` / Go `sync.Mutex`:** pessimistic, you wait up front. SERIALIZABLE
  is the opposite trade: no waiting, occasional redo. Row locks (next lesson) are the
  pessimistic tool in SQL.

## How it works

In example 2, A read Bob's row and B later wrote it; B read Alice's row and A later wrote
it. Each of these is a *read/write dependency*: the reader must come before the writer in
any equivalent serial order. Two of them pointing in opposite directions form a cycle, so
no serial order exists and one transaction has to be rolled back.

SIRead locks live in shared memory, as tuple, page or relation locks. A sequential scan
always takes a relation-level one, and when memory for them runs short, many fine-grained
locks are combined into coarser ones. Coarser locks mean more transactions look like they
depend on each other, so some fail that were actually fine. The docs list the remedies:
declare `READ ONLY` where possible, keep transactions short, use a connection pool, help
the planner choose index scans, and raise `max_pred_locks_per_transaction` (and its
per-relation and per-page siblings) if promotion is the problem.

The two-session runner never shows `waiting` in this lesson: SSI never blocks.

## Design notes

Before reaching for SERIALIZABLE, check whether a **constraint** can state the rule:
uniqueness, a partial unique index ("one active subscription per user") or an exclusion
constraint ("no overlapping bookings") is enforced for every isolation level and never
needs a retry. "At least one doctor on call" can't be written as a constraint, so the
choice is between:

- **Explicit locks:** under READ COMMITTED, `SELECT name FROM doctors WHERE on_call FOR
  UPDATE` makes the second transaction wait, then return only the rows that still match,
  and decide on those. Correct, but you must find every code path that touches the rule.
- **SERIALIZABLE everywhere** plus one retry wrapper. Every path is covered, at the cost of
  occasional redo.

The wrapper, with pgx, in one place:

```go
// inSerializableTx runs fn in a SERIALIZABLE transaction and runs it again
// from the start when Postgres reports a serialization failure or a deadlock.
// fn may run several times: it must not have side effects outside the tx.
func inSerializableTx(ctx context.Context, pool *pgxpool.Pool, fn func(pgx.Tx) error) error {
	const maxAttempts = 5
	for attempt := 1; ; attempt++ {
		err := pgx.BeginTxFunc(ctx, pool, pgx.TxOptions{IsoLevel: pgx.Serializable}, fn)
		var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
		retryable := errors.As(err, &pgErr) &&
			(pgErr.Code == "40001" || pgErr.Code == "40P01") // serialization_failure, deadlock_detected
		if !retryable || attempt == maxAttempts {
			return err
		}
		backoff := time.Duration(attempt) * 20 * time.Millisecond
		select {
		case <-time.After(backoff + rand.N(backoff)): // jitter: don't collide again in lockstep
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return ctx.Err()
		}
	}
}
```

`BeginTxFunc` commits when `fn` returns nil and rolls back otherwise; a 40001 raised at
`COMMIT` comes back as its error too. Wrap errors inside `fn` with `%w`, or `errors.As`
won't find the `*pgconn.PgError`. The retry must contain the reads: if `fn` receives values
read before the transaction began, retrying it decides on stale data again.

lessons.title: Row locks: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, NOWAIT
lessons.summary: When application code reads a row, decides, and writes it back, a concurrent transaction can overwrite the result. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serializes exactly those rows; FOR NO KEY UPDATE does it without blocking foreign-key inserts, and NOWAIT or lock_timeout bound the wait.

examples.title: A lost update, then the same withdrawals with FOR UPDATE
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 100);

annotations.note: Both read 100. A plain read locks nothing, so nothing stops the other transaction from changing the row before you write.

Each writes a constant its application computed from a stale read. B's UPDATE has nothing to wait for (A already committed) and nothing to re-check: SET balance = 50 doesn't depend on the current value. A's withdrawal of 30 is overwritten.

FOR UPDATE takes the row lock at read time. How the runner shows a wait: B's read is still running after 400 ms, so it is printed as "waiting" and the script moves on to A's steps; B's result appears, under the same step number, as soon as A's COMMIT releases the lock.
Under READ COMMITTED, a FOR UPDATE that waited returns the row as the other transaction committed it: 70, not 100. B's decision is made on current data.
Account a ends at 50 instead of 20; account b, with the same two withdrawals, ends at 20.

examples.title: FOR UPDATE blocks inserts of child rows; FOR NO KEY UPDATE doesn't

annotations.note: The foreign-key check of an INSERT into payments locks the referenced account row in KEY SHARE mode, the weakest of the four: it only conflicts with deleting the row or changing its key.
An UPDATE that doesn't change a key column takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE, which doesn't conflict with KEY SHARE. B's payment goes in while A's update is uncommitted.
FOR UPDATE conflicts with all four modes, so the payment insert waits for A to finish, although A never meant to delete the account or change its id.
FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the lock A's UPDATE will take anyway. Taking it at read time protects the read-modify-write just as well, and inserts of child rows keep flowing.

examples.title: NOWAIT and lock_timeout: fail fast instead of queueing
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100);

annotations.note: NOWAIT applies to the row locks of this one statement: it fails with SQLSTATE 55P03 (lock_not_available) at once, so the caller can answer "busy, try again" instead of hanging.

lock_timeout bounds every lock wait, including the implicit row lock of a plain UPDATE, which has no NOWAIT clause. Same SQLSTATE, after 100 ms, still inside the runner's 400 ms window, so no "waiting" line. B runs in autocommit, so the error doesn't leave a transaction to roll back.
Row locks never block plain reads: B gets the last committed value, 100, while A still holds the lock.

use_cases: Read-modify-write when the new value is computed in application code: balances, stock levels, seat counts
Check-then-act on one row: 'if the order is still pending, ship it'
Endpoints that should answer 'busy, try again' instead of queueing (NOWAIT, lock_timeout)
strengths: Locks only the rows the query returns, and never blocks plain readers, unlike a Java synchronized method that serializes every caller
No lock table to fill up: row locks are recorded in the row itself, so there's no limit on how many rows one transaction can lock
Four strengths let you lock exactly as much as you need; foreign-key checks use the weakest, so ordinary updates don't block child inserts
Waits can be bounded per statement (NOWAIT) or per lock (lock_timeout), and the error has its own SQLSTATE, 55P03
weaknesses: Locks are held until the transaction ends; one slow transaction stalls everyone queued behind it
Locking a row writes to it (the lock is marked in the row), so SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on many rows causes disk writes
Transactions that lock the same rows in different orders can deadlock (lesson 6)
Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, locking a row that changed after your snapshot raises 40001 instead of returning the new version

pitfalls.title: Reading, then writing a value computed from the read
pitfalls.detail: If the new value can be computed in SQL, one UPDATE is atomic and needs no explicit lock: a blocked UPDATE re-evaluates on the newest committed version. Use FOR UPDATE when the decision really needs application code.
pitfalls.bad:
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'a';            -- app computes 100 - 50
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 50 WHERE id = 'a';

pitfalls.title: FOR UPDATE where FOR NO KEY UPDATE would do
pitfalls.detail: FOR UPDATE also blocks inserts of rows that reference the locked row, because their foreign-key check needs KEY SHARE. Unless you will delete the row or change its key, lock FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;
pitfalls.good: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;

pitfalls.title: Expecting FOR UPDATE to stop readers
pitfalls.detail: A plain SELECT reads the last committed version and never waits. If another code path decides on the same row, it must lock too, or put its condition into its UPDATE's WHERE clause.

pitfalls.title: No bound on lock waits in request handlers
pitfalls.detail: Without a limit a request queues behind a lock for as long as the holder runs. Set lock_timeout for the transaction and turn SQLSTATE 55P03 into a retry or an HTTP 409/503.

quiz.q: A holds FOR UPDATE on account a. B runs SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'a' with no locking clause. What happens?
options: B immediately gets the last committed balance
quiz.why: Row locks block writers and lockers only; plain reads use their snapshot.

quiz.q: id is the primary key and balance has no index. Which row lock does UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = 'a' take?
quiz.why: An UPDATE takes FOR UPDATE only when it changes a column with a unique index usable by a foreign key; otherwise FOR NO KEY UPDATE.

quiz.q: Under READ COMMITTED, B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE waited while A changed the balance from 100 to 70 and committed. What does B's query return?
options: 100, the value when B's statement started
An error, because the row changed
quiz.why: After the wait it locks and returns the updated row. Under REPEATABLE READ it would fail with 40001 instead.

quiz.q: What is the difference between NOWAIT and lock_timeout = '100ms'?
options: NOWAIT fails at once on a locked row in that statement's locking clause; lock_timeout lets any lock wait up to the limit
quiz.why: NOWAIT is a clause on one SELECT; lock_timeout is a setting that applies to every lock acquisition, including UPDATE's implicit row lock. Skipping is SKIP LOCKED (next lesson).

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, The Locking Clause
PostgreSQL docs: Enforcing Consistency with Explicit Blocking Locks
PostgreSQL docs: lock_timeout and other client settings

lessons.body:
## Concept

MVCC lets readers and writers ignore each other. That's exactly wrong for a
**read-modify-write** done in application code: read a balance, compute in Go, write the
result. Two such transactions read the same value, and the second write silently replaces
the first. This is the **lost update**.

A **row lock** makes the read part of the critical section. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks
the rows it returns until the transaction ends; a second locker waits, then (under READ
COMMITTED) gets the committed new version. Plain readers are never affected.

There are four strengths, strongest first. Writes take one implicitly; `SELECT` takes one
when you add the clause:

- **`FOR UPDATE`**: taken by `DELETE` and by an `UPDATE` that changes a key column.
  Conflicts with all four modes.
- **`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`**: taken by every other `UPDATE`. Conflicts with all but
  `FOR KEY SHARE`.
- **`FOR SHARE`**: a shared lock; conflicts with the two exclusive modes above.
- **`FOR KEY SHARE`**: taken by foreign-key checks. Conflicts only with `FOR UPDATE`.

"Key column" means a column with a unique index usable by a foreign key. To bound waiting,
`NOWAIT` makes one statement fail immediately and `lock_timeout` caps every lock wait;
both raise SQLSTATE 55P03.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Mutexes:** `FOR UPDATE` is a mutex per row, created on demand and released at
  `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` (or `ROLLBACK TO` a savepoint taken before it); there's no
  unlock call. Plain `SELECT`s don't take it, so only the code paths that ask for the
  lock respect it.
- **Java `synchronized` / Go `sync.Mutex` in the service:** stops working as soon as you
  run two instances. The row lock lives in the database, where every instance meets.
- **ORM pessimistic locking (JPA, Django, SQLAlchemy):** these APIs emit `SELECT ... FOR
  UPDATE` or one of its variants. Log the SQL once to see which mode you actually get.
- **Go `TryLock`:** `NOWAIT` is the database's `sync.Mutex.TryLock`, except that it reports
  failure as an error, not a boolean.

## How it works

Row locks aren't kept in a lock table: the locking transaction marks the row itself (its
`xmax`, from the first lesson), which is why there's no limit on how many rows you can lock
and why locking can cause disk writes. A transaction that wants a locked row waits for the
*holder's transaction* to end. To see who blocks whom, ask for each waiting session's
blockers:

```sql
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, wait_event_type, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
```

PostgreSQL 18 adds `log_lock_failures`, which logs `SELECT ... NOWAIT` lock failures, if
you need to see how often your fail-fast paths fire.

## Design notes

Pick the narrowest tool that's correct:

1. **One statement**, when the new value can be computed in SQL: `UPDATE ... SET balance =
   balance - 50 WHERE balance >= 50 RETURNING balance`. Atomic, no explicit lock.
2. **`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`** on the rows you'll update, when the decision needs application
   code. Use `FOR UPDATE` only when you'll delete the row or change its key.
3. **SERIALIZABLE** (previous lesson), when the rule spans rows you can't enumerate up
   front.

Lock late and briefly: read everything that needs no lock first, lock, decide, write,
commit. Every millisecond between the lock and the commit is a millisecond everyone else
waits. And put a bound on that waiting on every user-facing path: `SET LOCAL
lock_timeout` in the transaction, plus a mapping from 55P03 to a clear error.

lessons.title: A job queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
lessons.summary: A jobs table plus SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED gives you a work queue in which workers never wait for each other. Then choose how a crashed worker's job comes back: hold the lock for the whole job, or commit the claim and use a lease.

examples.title: Plain FOR UPDATE: the second worker queues behind the first

annotations.note: The row lock is the claim: as long as A's transaction is open, job 1 is A's. ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 asks for the oldest queued job.

How the runner shows a wait: B's step is still running after 400 ms, so it is printed as "waiting" and the script carries on with A. B's result appears under the same number once A commits. B is stuck on job 1 although jobs 2 and 3 are free; ten workers would all queue on the same row.
When A commits, B's query re-checks job 1 against WHERE status = 'queued', finds it done, and moves on to lock job 2. Correct, but B was idle for as long as A's job ran.

examples.title: SKIP LOCKED: workers never wait; a crash puts the job back

annotations.note: Rows that can't be locked immediately are skipped, so B gets job 2 straight away: no "waiting" line anywhere in this transcript.
B takes job 3 while job 1 is still running. SKIP LOCKED gives up strict FIFO order; for a work queue that's the point.
A killed worker's connection drops and the server rolls its transaction back, exactly like this ROLLBACK. The lock goes with it, and job 1 was never marked done: no cleanup code needed.
Job 1 is retried by B. In this design the lock is the job's "running" state, so a crash can never leave a stuck job. The price: one open transaction, and one connection, per running job.

examples.title: Claim and commit, with a lease and a reaper for crashed workers

annotations.note: The claim is one statement: the subquery picks and locks the oldest queued job it can get, the UPDATE marks it running with a deadline, and RETURNING hands it to the worker. After commit, status = 'running' keeps other workers away; the lock was only needed for the moment of the claim.
B claims while A's claim is still uncommitted. Job 1 is locked, so B skips it and takes job 2 instead of waiting for A.
The transaction ends right after the claim. The job then runs with no transaction open: no locks held, no connection pinned, and nothing holding back VACUUM, however long the job takes.

The cost of committing the claim: when A dies, nothing rolls back and job 1 stays 'running'. The lease is the deadline after which other workers may assume its owner is dead. The demo moves the deadline into the past instead of waiting five minutes.
The reaper puts expired jobs back in the queue. Run it every few seconds from any worker; it is idempotent.
Job 1 comes back with attempts = 2. Cap it: a job that keeps killing its worker should end up 'failed' for a human to look at, not retried forever.

use_cases: Background jobs stored next to the data they belong to: reports, e-mails, webhooks, imports (TraceLite's report generation)
An outbox table: rows written in the business transaction, delivered by a worker pool afterwards
Any table several consumers drain concurrently, where each row must be handled by one consumer at a time
strengths: Enqueueing is an INSERT in the same transaction as the business change: the job exists if and only if the change committed, which a separate message broker can't give you without extra machinery
Workers never wait for each other: each claim skips rows other workers hold
Crash recovery comes from transactions (example 2) or from a lease and a reaper (example 3), with no separate broker to run, monitor and back up
Queue depth, stuck jobs and retry counts are one SQL query away
weaknesses: Every job passes through several row versions (queued, running, done), so a busy queue table depends on autovacuum keeping up
Ordering is only approximately FIFO
Idle workers have to poll, or be woken with LISTEN/NOTIFY
Holding a transaction per running job (example 2) pins one connection per worker and holds back VACUUM for as long as jobs run

pitfalls.title: Plain FOR UPDATE in the claim
pitfalls.detail: Every worker queues on the oldest job's lock, so N workers process one job at a time. Add SKIP LOCKED.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE;
pitfalls.good: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

pitfalls.title: SKIP LOCKED outside a queue
pitfalls.detail: The docs are explicit: skipping locked rows gives an inconsistent view of the data. Never use it for counts, reports, uniqueness checks or anything that must see every row.

pitfalls.title: Long jobs inside the claim transaction
pitfalls.detail: Example 2's design suits jobs of seconds. A job that runs for minutes keeps a transaction open the whole time, which holds back VACUUM in the whole database and ties up a pooled connection. Commit the claim and use a lease (example 3).

pitfalls.title: A lease without a fence
pitfalls.detail: A worker that was only slow can finish after its lease expired and the job was claimed again. Make jobs idempotent, or let only the current attempt finish the job, using attempts as a fencing token.
pitfalls.good:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done', lease_until = NULL
WHERE id = $1 AND attempts = $2 AND status = 'running';

pitfalls.title: No index for the claim query
pitfalls.detail: Done jobs pile up, and the claim's scan wades through them. A partial index covers only the rows the claim looks at.
pitfalls.good: CREATE INDEX jobs_queued ON jobs (id) WHERE status = 'queued';

quiz.q: Without SKIP LOCKED, what does a second worker do when the oldest queued job is locked by the first?
options: Waits until the first worker's transaction ends
quiz.why: A plain FOR UPDATE waits for the lock holder, so workers process the queue one at a time.

quiz.q: In example 2's design (lock held for the whole job) the worker process is killed. What happens to its job?
options: It stays 'running' until a reaper resets it
The server rolls the transaction back, the lock is released and the job is queued again
quiz.why: The claim was never committed: the status change and the lock disappear with the transaction.

quiz.q: In example 3's design (claim committed) why do you need a lease?
options: Because a crashed worker leaves the job 'running' and no transaction will undo that
Because SKIP LOCKED requires a timestamp
quiz.why: Once the claim commits, only a deadline tells other workers the job's owner is gone.

quiz.q: Where is SKIP LOCKED the wrong tool?
options: Claiming the next outbox row to send
SELECT count(*) of open orders for a dashboard
Picking the next import file to process
quiz.why: A count must see every row; SKIP LOCKED leaves out the ones that happen to be locked.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, The Locking Clause (NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A job queue in Postgres is a table plus one query. Workers claim the oldest queued job
with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`: rows another worker has locked are skipped
instead of waited for, so every worker gets a different job immediately. `SKIP LOCKED`
(PostgreSQL 9.5+) exists for exactly this; the docs call it unsuitable for general work
but right for "multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table".

The claim is easy. The design decision is what happens when a worker dies mid-job:

- **Hold the lock for the job's duration** (example 2): claim, work, mark done, commit, all
  in one transaction. A crash rolls back and the job reappears by itself.
- **Commit the claim** (example 3): mark the job `running` with a lease, commit, work with
  no transaction open, then mark it done. A crash leaves the job `running` until the lease
  expires and a reaper re-queues it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go worker pools:** a buffered channel of jobs hands each job to exactly one goroutine.
  A `SKIP LOCKED` claim is the same "receive" across processes and machines, with the
  queue surviving restarts. The usual shape in Go: N goroutines, each looping claim, run,
  finish, and sleeping (or waiting for a `NOTIFY`) when the claim returns no row.
- **Java `BlockingQueue` / Python `queue.Queue`:** in-memory and lost on a crash. Here the
  queue is durable and transactional with your data.
- **Message brokers:** example 3's lease plays the role of a broker's acknowledgement
  deadline (SQS calls it a visibility timeout): a message that isn't confirmed in time is
  delivered again. What you gain over a broker is the enqueue happening in the same
  transaction as the business change.

## How it works

`SKIP LOCKED` (like `NOWAIT`) only changes how row locks are taken; the table-level lock is
taken normally. With `LIMIT 1`, locking stops once one row is returned. Each candidate row
is read through the snapshot as usual; if its row lock can't be taken immediately, the row
is left out of the result and the scan moves on.

In example 1, B's waiting query shows a READ COMMITTED detail: a row that matched the
`WHERE` clause at the snapshot is locked, but it isn't returned if it was changed meanwhile
and no longer matches. That's why B moves on to job 2 instead of getting job 1 twice.

## Design notes

Example 2's design (lock held for the whole job) is the simplest correct queue and fits
short jobs: there is no state machine to get wrong, and a crash can't leave a stuck job.
Its limits come from holding a transaction open while the job runs: one connection per
running job, and an old snapshot that keeps VACUUM from cleaning up behind it (lesson 7).

Example 3's design (claim, lease, reaper) fits jobs that take minutes, call external
services or must survive a deploy, like TraceLite's report generation. Its rules:

- The claim and the finish are separate short transactions; the job runs between them.
- A lease longer than the longest normal run, an `attempts` counter, and a cap that moves
  jobs to `failed`.
- Jobs must be idempotent, or finished only by the current attempt (the fencing pitfall).
  At-least-once is the honest guarantee.
- A partial index on queued jobs, and autovacuum settings tuned for a table where every
  row is updated several times (lesson 7).

To avoid polling, a worker can `LISTEN jobs` and the enqueuer can `NOTIFY jobs` in the
same transaction as the insert; the notification is delivered only if that transaction
commits. Keep a slow poll as a fallback anyway: notifications aren't stored, so a worker
that was restarting misses them.

lessons.title: Deadlocks (cause and prevention via lock ordering), advisory locks
lessons.summary: Two transactions that lock the same rows in opposite order deadlock; Postgres detects the cycle after deadlock_timeout and aborts one with 40P01. Locking in a consistent order prevents it. Advisory locks serialize work that has no row to lock.

examples.title: Opposite transfers deadlock, and Postgres breaks the cycle
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 100);

annotations.note: Each UPDATE locks its source row (FOR NO KEY UPDATE) until its transaction ends: A holds a, B holds b.

How the runner shows a wait: a step still running after 400 ms is printed as "waiting" and the next step is sent; the result appears later under the same number. A now waits for b, held by B; B waits for a, held by A. Neither wait can ever end on its own.

A waiting session checks for a deadlock after deadlock_timeout (1 s by default). A started waiting first, so its check runs first, finds the cycle, and A's UPDATE fails with 40P01; its transaction is aborted until this ROLLBACK. The docs warn that which transaction is aborted is hard to predict; this runner just makes it repeatable.
A's abort released its lock, so B's update went through and B commits: a = 120, b = 80. A's transfer is simply gone; the application has to retry it (40P01 is a retryable error).

examples.title: Locking both rows in key order turns the deadlock into a short wait
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 100);

annotations.note: A locks a, then b, before changing anything. ORDER BY fixes the lock order, and FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the mode the UPDATEs need anyway, so the first lock taken is already the strongest one needed, as the docs recommend.
B asks in the same order, so it waits at row a while holding nothing. A wait without a cycle just ends when the holder commits.
A's updates find their rows already locked by A itself: no waiting. COMMIT releases both, and B's lock request is granted.
B's transfer runs after A's, and both are applied: a = 110, b = 90. Same work as example 1, no deadlock, no retry.

examples.title: Advisory locks: transaction-level and session-level

annotations.note: The try variants answer at once. B's false means "someone else is running the report": skip it. The variants without try wait, like a row lock, and take part in deadlock detection like one.
COMMIT released A's lock. B's statement runs in autocommit, so its transaction-level lock lasted exactly one statement: it got the lock and released it again.
A session-level lock ignores transactions: the docs say a lock taken in a transaction that later rolls back is still held after the rollback. B still can't get it.
It ends only with an explicit unlock (one per lock call: they stack) or when the connection closes. With a connection pool, a forgotten unlock stays with the pooled connection, not with your request.

use_cases: Transfers and any transaction that updates several rows of one table: lock them in key order first
Run-once work across many app instances: one nightly report, one migration run, one cache rebuild (advisory locks)
Serializing work on something that has no row yet, such as 'one import per customer at a time' before the import row exists
strengths: Deadlocks are detected and broken automatically, unlike two Go goroutines locking mutexes in opposite order, which hang until something kills them
The victim gets its own SQLSTATE (40P01), which is safe to retry
Advisory locks are cheap, need no table and no cleanup: the server releases them at transaction or session end
Advisory waits take part in the same deadlock detection as row and table locks
weaknesses: Nothing happens until deadlock_timeout (1 s by default) has passed, and the aborted transaction's work is lost
You don't choose which transaction is aborted; the docs say not to rely on it
Advisory keys are bare numbers shared by every session in the database: nothing stops two features from picking the same one
Session-level advisory locks ignore transactions and can outlive the request that took them when connections are pooled

pitfalls.title: Locking rows in the order the request lists them
pitfalls.detail: A transfer from a to b and one from b to a lock in opposite order. Sort the keys and lock them in one statement before writing.
pitfalls.bad:
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $3 WHERE id = $1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $3 WHERE id = $2;
pitfalls.good:
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
-- then both UPDATEs, in any order

pitfalls.title: Trusting a multi-row UPDATE to lock in a sensible order
pitfalls.detail: UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) locks rows in whatever order the plan visits them, which can differ between two statements. Lock explicitly with ORDER BY first when several transactions update overlapping sets.

pitfalls.title: Session-level advisory locks with a pool
pitfalls.detail: pg_advisory_lock outlives COMMIT and ROLLBACK. If the code that should unlock never runs, the pooled connection keeps the lock and the next request that borrows it holds a lock it doesn't know about. Prefer the _xact_ variants; if you need session-level, unlock in a defer on the same connection.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(4242);  -- through a pool, unlock in some other request

pitfalls.title: Calling lock functions in a query with LIMIT
pitfalls.detail: The docs' example: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100 may lock more ids than it returns, because LIMIT isn't guaranteed to apply before the function runs. Select the ids in a subquery with the LIMIT, and lock in the outer query.

quiz.q: Transaction A updates row a then b; B updates b then a, concurrently. What happens?
options: After deadlock_timeout, one is aborted with 40P01 and the other continues
quiz.why: The waiting sessions run the deadlock check after deadlock_timeout; one transaction is aborted so the other can proceed.

quiz.q: What prevents the deadlock?
options: Every transaction locks the rows it needs in the same order, for example by key, before writing
quiz.why: A cycle needs two transactions that each hold a lock the other wants; a single global order makes that impossible.

quiz.q: A session runs BEGIN; SELECT pg_advisory_lock(7); ROLLBACK;. Is lock 7 still held?
options: Yes: session-level advisory locks ignore transactions
quiz.why: Session-level locks are held until pg_advisory_unlock or the end of the session; only the _xact_ variants follow the transaction.

quiz.q: Five app instances run the same nightly job; exactly one should do it and the others skip. Which call fits?
options: pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42) at the start of the job's transaction, skipping on false
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT on a random row
quiz.why: The try variant doesn't wait, and the transaction-level lock is released automatically when the job's transaction ends, even if the instance crashes.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Explicit Locking (Deadlocks, Advisory Locks)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **deadlock** is a cycle of waits: A holds a lock B wants while B holds a lock A wants.
Row locks are enough to form one, without any explicit locking: two transfers that update
the same two accounts in opposite order will do it.

Postgres doesn't let it hang. A waiting session checks for a cycle after
`deadlock_timeout` (1 second by default), and if it finds one, one transaction is aborted
with SQLSTATE 40P01 (`deadlock_detected`) so the others can continue. The aborted work is
lost and has to be retried.

The fix is ordering: if every transaction acquires the locks it needs in the same order,
no cycle can form. The docs add a second rule: take the strongest lock you will need on an
object first, rather than upgrading later.

**Advisory locks** are locks on numbers rather than rows, for coordinating things the
database doesn't model: "only one instance runs the nightly report", "one import per
customer at a time". They come in transaction-level (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`, released at
commit or rollback) and session-level (`pg_advisory_lock`, held until unlocked or
disconnect) forms, each with a `try` variant that returns false instead of waiting.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go mutexes:** the same rule you'd follow with two `sync.Mutex`es (always lock them in
  one order) applies to rows. The difference: Go doesn't detect a deadlock between two
  goroutines while others still run; the runtime only reports one when every goroutine is
  asleep. Postgres detects any cycle among waiting transactions.
- **Java:** `jstack` reports deadlocked threads but doesn't break the cycle. Postgres
  breaks it, and that turns your deadlock into an error your code must handle.
- **Distributed locks (Redis, ZooKeeper):** an advisory lock is a lock service you
  already run. Its lifetime is tied to a transaction or a connection, so a crashed client
  can't leave it held; there's no TTL to tune.

## How it works

Waiting is cheap and optimistic: a blocked session sleeps on the lock, and only after
`deadlock_timeout` does it run the (relatively expensive) check of the wait-for graph.
Only superusers, or roles granted the right to set it, can change `deadlock_timeout`; it
isn't a tuning knob for application code.

Advisory locks live in the same shared-memory lock table as table locks, so they show up
in `pg_locks` with `locktype = 'advisory'`, and the table is finite (sized by
`max_locks_per_transaction` and `max_connections`): don't take millions of them. The
`bigint` key and the `(int, int)` key pair are separate key spaces; the pair is handy for
"(kind of thing, id)".

## Design notes

Deadlock prevention, in order of preference:

1. **Fewer locks per transaction.** A transfer written as a single statement still locks
   two rows, but short transactions leave less room for interleaving.
2. **A global lock order.** Sort ids before locking (`slices.Sort(ids)` in Go, then `WHERE
   id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR NO KEY UPDATE`). Across tables, pick an order too, for
   example parent before child.
3. **Retry 40P01** like 40001, in the same wrapper (the serializable lesson's
   `inSerializableTx` already does). Deadlocks you didn't foresee will still happen.

Advisory locks: prefer the transaction-level `try` variant around a unit of work, so a
crash or a panic can't leave the lock behind. Keep the keys in one place in the code (a
`const` block), since collisions are silent. The session-level form is for work that must
stay exclusive across several transactions, such as a migration run that commits each
step: take it on one dedicated connection and unlock in a `defer`.

lessons.title: VACUUM, autovacuum and bloat
lessons.summary: Every UPDATE and DELETE leaves a dead row version behind. VACUUM makes that space reusable but rarely gives it back to the OS, an open transaction can stop it from removing anything, and HOT updates with a lower fillfactor avoid much of the garbage in the first place.

examples.title: Table size through updates, VACUUM, a mass DELETE and VACUUM FULL

annotations.note: Why TEMP: this playground database is shared with other runs, and an open transaction anywhere in it could stop VACUUM from removing rows (example 2). Other sessions' transactions don't hold back a temporary table. Autovacuum can't process temporary tables either, so nothing runs behind the script's back.
Each UPDATE writes a new version of every row. The pages are full (fillfactor 100), so the new versions go to new pages and the table doubles. Once the UPDATE commits, the old versions are dead.
Plain VACUUM removes the dead versions and records the space as free, but the file keeps its size: the free pages are at the start of the table, and VACUUM only hands back empty pages at the end.
The second round of updates fills the space VACUUM freed: no growth. This is the steady state autovacuum aims for, a table larger than its live data that stops growing.
Deleting half the rows frees space all over the table. VACUUM makes it reusable, and the file still doesn't shrink, because live rows remain up to the last page.
VACUUM FULL copies the live rows into a new file: half the original size. Meanwhile it holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which blocks even SELECT, and it needs disk space for the copy.
Byte counts depend on the page size and the platform; ratios to the first measurement are what this lesson is about, and they come out the same on every run.

examples.title: An open transaction keeps VACUUM from removing anything

annotations.note: REPEATABLE READ keeps the snapshot from its first query until the transaction ends. A is now idle in transaction with an old snapshot, like a report that is still running or a forgotten BEGIN.
The deleted rows are dead for everyone except A's snapshot, which predates the delete. VACUUM must keep them; VACUUM VERBOSE would say "5000 are dead but not yet removable". Nothing shrank.

A never read events. VACUUM can't know which tables an open snapshot will read next, so an old snapshot holds back cleanup in every table of the database. (Setup turned autovacuum off for events so it can't interfere with the demo.)

With A gone the rows are removable, the last pages become empty, and VACUUM truncates them: the one case where plain VACUUM returns space to the operating system. It needs a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to do so, and simply skips the truncation if it can't get it.

examples.title: HOT updates and fillfactor: three rounds of updates, no growth, no VACUUM

annotations.note: fillfactor = 50 makes INSERT fill pages only halfway. The rest of each page is reserved for updated versions of the rows on that page.
packed has no free space, so every update is a regular one: the new version goes to another page, with a new index entry. Without VACUUM in between, each round adds a full copy: 4.0 after three.

roomy's updates are HOT (heap-only tuple): the new version stays on the same page and the index isn't touched, because the only indexed column, id, didn't change. The next update prunes the old versions from the page in passing and reuses the space.
roomy didn't grow at all, with no VACUUM. The price is visible in the last column: it started twice as big. Lower fillfactor only on tables whose rows are updated often.

use_cases: Diagnosing a table that keeps growing while its row count stays flat
Tuning autovacuum per table for hot, update-heavy tables: counters, sessions, job queues
Finding the forgotten open transaction that blocks cleanup
Getting disk space back after a mass DELETE (VACUUM FULL in a maintenance window)
strengths: Cleanup is off the critical path: UPDATE and DELETE don't move old data anywhere, and readers never block
Plain VACUUM and autovacuum run alongside SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
HOT updates and page pruning remove many dead versions during normal reads and writes, with no VACUUM at all
Autovacuum is on by default and can be tuned per table with storage parameters
weaknesses: Dead versions occupy space until VACUUM runs, and indexes bloat along with the table
Plain VACUUM rarely shrinks a file; VACUUM FULL does, but blocks all access to the table while it rewrites it
One forgotten open transaction stops cleanup in the whole database
Vacuuming is not optional: every table must be vacuumed (frozen) at least once every two billion transactions, and Postgres forces it even with autovacuum off

pitfalls.title: Turning autovacuum off to save I/O
pitfalls.detail: Dead rows pile up, planner statistics go stale, and the anti-wraparound vacuum runs anyway, later and bigger. Tune instead: a lower scale factor makes autovacuum visit a big, busy table sooner.
pitfalls.good: ALTER TABLE jobs SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01);

pitfalls.title: VACUUM FULL on a live table
pitfalls.detail: It holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rewrite: every query on the table waits. Usually you don't need the space back; plain VACUUM keeps the size stable. If you must shrink, plan a maintenance window.

pitfalls.title: Sessions left idle in transaction
pitfalls.detail: A connection that ran BEGIN and then waits on the application holds back VACUUM everywhere. Find the oldest snapshots, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as a safety net.
pitfalls.good:
SELECT pid, state, xact_start, age(backend_xmin) AS xmin_age
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC;

pitfalls.title: Reading n_dead_tup right after a change
pitfalls.detail: pg_stat_user_tables is cumulative statistics: each backend flushes its counts when it goes idle, at most about once a second, so a query right after your DELETE may not see it yet. Use these numbers for monitoring trends, not as a check inside a script.

pitfalls.title: Indexing a column you update constantly
pitfalls.detail: An update that changes any indexed column can't be HOT. An index on last_seen_at turns every heartbeat into a new index entry plus a dead version for VACUUM. Index it only if queries really need it.

quiz.q: You deleted every other row of a big table and ran plain VACUUM. What happens to the file size?
options: It stays about the same: the space is now reusable but not returned
quiz.why: Plain VACUUM returns space only when whole pages at the end of the table are empty; scattered free space is kept for reuse.

quiz.q: VACUUM ran, yet the deleted rows are still there ('dead but not yet removable'). The most likely cause?
options: A transaction with a snapshot older than the delete is still open
The table has no primary key
quiz.why: VACUUM may only remove versions no snapshot can see. One old snapshot anywhere in the database is enough to keep them.

quiz.q: Why does fillfactor = 70 help a table whose rows are updated often?
options: It leaves room on each page, so updates can be HOT: same page, no new index entry, cleaned up without VACUUM
It makes VACUUM run more often
quiz.why: HOT needs free space on the old row's page and no change to indexed columns; fillfactor reserves that space.

quiz.q: When does plain VACUUM give disk space back to the operating system?
options: Only when pages at the end of the table become entirely empty and it can briefly lock the table exclusively
quiz.why: That truncation is the only shrinking plain VACUUM does; VACUUM FULL rewrites the whole table.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Vacuuming and autovacuum settings

lessons.body:
## Concept

MVCC never overwrites: an `UPDATE` leaves the old row version behind and a `DELETE` only
marks it deleted. Those dead versions take space until **VACUUM** removes them, and it can
remove a version only when no snapshot can still see it. That is the price of readers that
never wait.

What VACUUM does with the space depends on the form:

- **Plain `VACUUM`** (and autovacuum, which runs it for you) marks the space free for
  reuse inside the same table. It runs alongside normal reads and writes, and returns
  space to the OS only when whole pages at the end of the table are empty.
- **`VACUUM FULL`** writes a compact copy of the table and drops the old file. It gets the
  space back but holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which blocks every query on the table, until it
  finishes.

A table that is updated steadily and vacuumed regularly settles at some size above its
live data, and stays there. **Bloat** is when it keeps growing: autovacuum can't keep up,
or something stops it from removing anything.

VACUUM also has jobs beyond space: it updates the visibility map (which makes index-only
