pitfalls.good: catch (e) { toast(e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)); }

pitfalls.title: Wrapping without cause
pitfalls.detail: throw new Error("import failed") inside a catch discards the original error and its stack. Pass it on.
pitfalls.good: catch (e) { throw new ImportError(line, { cause: e }); }

pitfalls.title: return without await inside try
pitfalls.detail: The try block ends before the promise rejects, so catch never runs and finally runs too early. Use return await inside try/catch/finally.
pitfalls.good: try { return await save(id); } catch { ... }

pitfalls.title: Catching everything and logging
pitfalls.detail: A catch that logs and continues also hides TypeErrors and RangeErrors from bugs. Catch what you can handle, rethrow the rest, and leave the last word to a top-level handler or an error boundary (lesson ts.errors.result).

quiz.q: Under strict, what is the type of e in try { ... } catch (e) { }?
quiz.why: useUnknownInCatchVariables, part of strict since TS 4.4, types it unknown because any value can be thrown.

quiz.q: Promise.reject("timeout").catch((e) => e.message). What happens?
options: It compiles and evaluates to undefined
quiz.why: The lib declares the callback's reason as any, so the access compiles; a string has no message property, so the result is undefined.

quiz.q: Inside async function f() { try { return save(); } catch { return "handled"; } }, save() rejects. What does await f() do?
quiz.why: Without await, the promise leaves the try block before it rejects, so the catch never sees the rejection; f's promise adopts it.

quiz.q: Which line keeps the original error available to callers?
options: throw new Error("load failed", { cause: e })
quiz.why: Only cause keeps the error object itself, with its type, fields and stack. The first keeps only its text.

further_reading.title: TypeScript 4.4 release notes: unknown in catch variables

lessons.body:
## Concept

`throw` in JavaScript accepts any value: an `Error`, a string, a plain object, `undefined`.
TypeScript can't know what a call will throw, because signatures have no throws clause, so
since TS 4.4 the `strict` family includes `useUnknownInCatchVariables` and the catch
variable is `unknown`. You narrow it before use: `instanceof Error` for errors,
`typeof` for primitives, a fallback for everything else.

For your own failures, throw subclasses of `Error`. A subclass carries fields a caller can
act on (`id`, `line`), sets `name`, and works with `instanceof`. When a layer adds context,
it wraps instead of replacing: `new ImportError(line, { cause: e })` (ES2022) keeps the
original error attached, and code further up can walk the `cause` chain to find the error
it cares about.

Two rules complete the picture. Catch only what you can handle, and rethrow the rest
unchanged. And in async code, `try`/`catch` sees a rejection only if the `await` happens
inside the `try` block, which is why `return await` matters there.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: no checked exceptions and no typed catch blocks. `catch (NotFoundException e)` becomes
  `catch (e) { if (e instanceof NotFoundError) ... else throw e; }`. `cause` corresponds to
  `getCause()`.
- Python: `raise ImportFailed(line) from e` is `{ cause: e }`; `except NotFound as e:` is the
  `instanceof` check plus rethrow. Python, like Java, only lets you raise exception objects;
  JavaScript doesn't.
- Go: exceptions unwind for you where Go makes every layer write `if err != nil`.
  `{ cause: e }` is `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)`, the `findCause` loop is `errors.As`, and
  `finally` covers what `defer` does for cleanup. What you lose is the visible error result
  in every signature.
- C++: you can `throw 42;` there too, but catch clauses are typed and `catch (...)` gives you
  nothing to inspect. JavaScript has the one untyped catch, and you inspect the value.
- JS: nothing new at run time. TypeScript only stops you from pretending you know what was
  thrown.

## Design notes

Throw `Error` objects only, and give each failure callers branch on its own subclass with
the data they need; keep the hierarchy flat, one level under `Error` is usually enough.
Wrap at layer boundaries with `cause`, the same place Go code would add context with
`%w`. Handle errors where you can do something about them (retry, show a message, fall
back) and let the rest travel to one top-level handler that logs them once.

Exceptions are the right tool for bugs and for failures nobody nearby can handle. For
failures a caller is expected to handle every time, such as validation or "not found" in a
lookup, a return type that says so is often better: that is the Result pattern, the next
lesson, together with React's error boundaries for what slips through.

lessons.title: The Result pattern vs exceptions, compared with Go; React error boundaries
lessons.summary: A Result type puts expected failures in the signature, where the checker makes callers look before they use the value. Exceptions stay for bugs, and a React error boundary catches the render-time ones so one broken widget doesn't blank the page.

examples.title: A Result whose error is a union of known problems

annotations.note: The whole pattern is a discriminated union and two constructors; no library is needed. ok() returns Result<T, never> and err() Result<never, E>, and both fit any Result with matching T or E, because never is assignable to everything.
The failure modes are spelled out as data a caller can branch on, with the details each one needs. A thrown exception would carry this as a message string or an untyped property.
The signature tells the whole story: a Link or one of three problems. With exceptions the signature would say Link, and the failures would live in the doc comment.
An exhaustive switch over the problem kinds: add a fourth kind and this function no longer compiles (TS2366), so every new failure gets a message.
The value is unreachable until ok is checked: TS2339. Go's (Link, error) lets you read the zero-value Link without looking at err; here the type removes that option.

examples.title: Early returns, error unions, batch errors, and the exception boundary

annotations.note: The boundary between the two styles. JSON.parse throws, so the expected failure (SyntaxError) becomes a Result here, once. Anything else is unexpected and stays an exception, the same split as Go's errors and panics.

if (!parsed.ok) return parsed; is Go's if err != nil { return nil, err }: the failed Result passes through unchanged, since its error type fits the wider union. The return type lists every way readIds can fail.
A Record over the error union is an exhaustive message table: a new error code without a message is a compile error.
For batch input, check everything and return all problems at once, as Go's errors.Join does. An exception would stop at the first bad item.
The caller handles each failure where it occurs, with plain control flow. Note the cost: every call site has to unwrap, which exceptions spare you.

examples.title: A React error boundary, proven by two tests

annotations.note: This example runs as a Vitest test in jsdom, which is how you'd check a boundary in a real project. In React 18 development builds, an error a boundary catches is also reported to window error handlers (react.dev, componentDidCatch caveats), so a page's own window.onerror sees it too. StackLab's browser runner skips those reports and counts only errors no boundary caught.

Error boundaries must be class components; react.dev says there is no function-component equivalent yet. getDerivedStateFromError runs during rendering and only switches to the fallback. The state is a flag because throw null is legal and would look like no error.

getDerivedStateFromError must stay pure, so reporting belongs in componentDidCatch, with the component stack. It lists the component that threw (Coverage here) and its parent components; the JavaScript stack of a render error shows React's internals where the parents would be.
A real render bug: the API sent tests: null, and the as Row cast believed it. Types vanish at run time, so a boundary is still needed where data from outside meets rendering code.
Each widget has its own boundary, so the broken one shows its fallback and the working one stays. With no boundary at all, React removes the whole UI from the screen on a render error.

Boundaries don't see errors in event handlers or async code: by then React isn't rendering. Storing the error in state and throwing it on the next render hands it to the nearest boundary; the useErrorBoundary hook from react-error-boundary packages the same move.
The rejection arrives after the click handler returned, so findByRole waits for the re-render that throws. The fallback replaces the button, and the report names SaveButton.

use_cases: Results for failures callers handle every time: validating forms and imports, parsing user input, a lookup that may find nothing, a conflict on save
Collecting every problem in a batch (CSV import, bulk edit) instead of stopping at the first
Exceptions for bugs and for failures nobody nearby can handle: a violated invariant, a lost database connection deep in a call chain
Error boundaries around independent page regions: a dashboard widget, each message in a list, a route's content
strengths: Unlike Go's (T, error), the value is unreachable until the check, and E can be a precise union instead of the opaque error interface
Failure modes appear in signatures and editor hovers, where exceptions are invisible to TypeScript
Exhaustive switches and Record tables over the error union make a new failure kind a compile error at every place that must handle it
Error boundaries contain render bugs per subtree, the UI's version of Go's recover at a request boundary
weaknesses: Every call site unwraps; without Rust's ? operator, chains of early returns are as verbose as Go's if err != nil
Two error channels coexist: library code still throws, so boundaries between the styles need care
Promise<Result<T, E>> can still reject, so async code has both a Result and a rejection to consider
Error boundaries need a class component, don't catch event-handler or async errors on their own, and don't reset themselves

pitfalls.title: Wrapping everything in Result
pitfalls.detail: A Result for failures no caller can handle (a bug, an exhausted connection pool) only adds unwrapping. Keep Results for expected failures and let bugs throw to a boundary.

pitfalls.title: Catching every exception at the edge and returning it as a Result
pitfalls.detail: A catch that converts any error turns a TypeError from a bug into a validation message. Convert the specific failure you expect and rethrow the rest.
pitfalls.good: catch (e) { if (e instanceof SyntaxError) return err("invalid-json"); throw e; }

pitfalls.title: Expecting a boundary to catch event-handler and async errors
pitfalls.detail: Boundaries catch errors thrown while React renders. Handle errors in the handler, or store them in state and throw during render so the nearest boundary takes over.

pitfalls.title: A boundary that never recovers
pitfalls.detail: Once failed, the boundary keeps showing its fallback. Give it a key that changes when the input changes (a new route or record id) so React mounts a fresh one, or use react-error-boundary's resetKeys.

quiz.q: const r: Result<Link, LinkProblem> = parseLink(line). Why is r.value a compile error?
options: r might be the failure variant, which has no value property
quiz.why: r is a union; value exists only on the { ok: true } member, so you have to narrow with r.ok first.

quiz.q: Compared with Go's func parse(s string) (Link, error), what does the TS Result add?
options: The value can't be read until the error case is excluded, and the error type can be a precise union
quiz.why: Go returns both values and leaves checking to discipline; the discriminated union makes the unchecked read a type error.

quiz.q: A button's onClick handler throws. What does the surrounding error boundary do?
options: Nothing: the error didn't happen during rendering
quiz.why: Boundaries catch errors thrown while React renders; event handler errors propagate like any other exception.

quiz.q: Which failure fits an exception better than a Result?
options: The user typed an invalid e-mail
The requirement ID in the URL doesn't exist
A switch over your own status union reaches a value that can't exist
quiz.why: Only the last is a bug. The others are expected outcomes a caller must handle every time.

further_reading.title: react.dev: Catching rendering errors with an error boundary
react.dev: componentDidCatch (including development vs production behavior)
react.dev: Preserving and Resetting State (resetting with a key)
The Go Blog: Errors are values

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript has no checked exceptions: `function parseLink(line: string): Link` can throw
anything and the signature doesn't say so. The **Result pattern** moves expected failures
into the return type:

```ts
type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
```

It is an ordinary discriminated union. The caller must check `ok` before `value` exists,
`E` can be a union of tagged problems the caller switches over exhaustively, and a failed
Result passes upward with a plain `return`. Nothing is unwound; the failure is a value,
as in Go.

That doesn't retire exceptions. Libraries and the platform throw (`JSON.parse`, `fetch` on a
network error), and bugs throw. The working split: Results for outcomes a caller is
expected to handle every time, exceptions for bugs and for failures nobody nearby can do
anything about, and explicit conversion where the two meet.

In React, the last line of defense is an **error boundary**: a class component with
`static getDerivedStateFromError` (render a fallback) and `componentDidCatch` (report the
error). It catches errors thrown while its children render, so one broken widget shows a
message instead of unmounting the page. It doesn't see event handlers, async code,
server rendering or its own errors.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `(Link, error)` is the closest relative, with two differences. Go lets you read the
  `Link` without checking `err`, while the union makes that a type error; and Go's `error`
  is an interface inspected with `errors.Is`/`As`, while `E` here is a precise type. Go's
  split between errors and panics is the same split as Results and exceptions, and an
  error boundary is the UI's `recover` at a request boundary (lesson go.errors.panic-strategy).
- Rust: `Result<T, E>` with the `?` operator. TypeScript has no `?`, so propagation is an
  explicit `if (!r.ok) return r;`.
- Java: checked exceptions put failures in signatures too, but force handling through
  try/catch and don't compose with lambdas; a Result is an ordinary value that does.
- C++: `std::expected<T, E>` (C++23) is the same idea in the standard library.
- Python and JS: nothing built in; the pattern is a convention, which TypeScript's
  narrowing makes enforceable.

## Design notes

Choose per failure, not per codebase. A form validator, an import parser or a repository
lookup that may find nothing should return a Result whose error is a small union, and the
UI should map that union to messages in one exhaustive table. A violated invariant or a
lost connection deep in the stack should throw and travel to a boundary that logs it once.
Convert at the seams: wrap throwing library calls where their expected failures become
Results, and throw from a Result only where nobody can handle it.

Place error boundaries where a fallback makes sense to the user: around each route's
content, each independent widget, each item in a long list, not around every component.
Report from `componentDidCatch`, give the boundary a `key` that changes with the data it
shows so it can recover, and forward errors from handlers and effects into render when the
boundary should show them. The boundary is the backstop for bugs, not a substitute for
handling expected failures where they happen.

lessons.title: Primitives, literal types, any vs unknown vs never
lessons.summary: Seven primitive types, one of them a single double-precision number type, plus literal types that turn values into types. any switches checking off, unknown forces a check, and never is the type with no values.

examples.title: number, bigint and literal types

annotations.note: There is no int: number is Java's double / Go's float64 for everything. Integers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1).

The full-stack trap: Postgres bigint and Go int64 go beyond 2^53, and JSON.parse rounds to the nearest double without an error. The annotation says number and is right; the value is still wrong. Send such ids as strings.

bigint (ES2020) is arbitrary precision with its own literal suffix n. As with Go's numeric types (and unlike Java's int-to-long-to-double widening) the two never mix implicitly: tsc reports it at compile time, where plain JavaScript would throw a TypeError at run time.

A literal type is a type with one value. const keeps "GET" as its type because the binding can't change; let widens to string because it can, so a let can't be passed where only "GET" | "POST" is allowed.
The fix is an annotation with the union, not a cast: next can change, but only to a valid Method.

examples.title: string: UTF-16 code units and Turkish case mapping

annotations.note: A JS string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units, so length is not a character count and not a byte count. Go's len(s) counts UTF-8 bytes (9 here); a VARCHAR(n) in Postgres counts characters.
Unicode's default lowercase of İ (U+0130) is i followed by U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE, so the string grows by one and no longer equals "istanbul".
toLocaleLowerCase("tr") / toLocaleUpperCase("tr") apply the Turkish rules (I <-> ı, İ <-> i). Pass the locale explicitly: without an argument the result depends on the user's browser settings.
Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji, some CJK) take two code units. Spread or for...of iterates code points; slicing by index can cut one in half.

examples.title: any vs unknown vs never

annotations.note: any is assignable to and from everything and allows any operation, so loose.count + 1 compiles and concatenates. Worse, any spreads: total is any too, and the missing items field is only found when the code runs.
unknown accepts every value but allows nothing until you narrow it. typeof, the null check and `"count" in v` (narrowing since TS 4.9) prove the shape step by step, then v.count is usable.
never is the empty type. A function that cannot return normally returns never, which is assignable to every type, so `return fail(...)` fits a function returning number.
An intersection of incompatible primitives reduces to never: no value is both a string and a number. The same type shows up when a switch has handled every member of a union.

use_cases: number for counts, money in minor units (kuruş) and measurements; bigint or strings for 64-bit database ids
Literal unions for closed sets of strings: HTTP methods, statuses, event names
unknown for anything from outside the program: JSON.parse, catch variables, postMessage data
never for helpers that always throw and for exhaustiveness checks
strengths: Literal types give enum-like safety to plain strings with zero runtime cost, which Java needs an enum class and Go a named type plus constants for
unknown is a safe top type: unlike Java's Object (which you downcast with a cast that may throw) you narrow with ordinary runtime checks the compiler follows
bigint and number never mix implicitly, so a precision loss can't slip in through arithmetic
weaknesses: One floating-point number type: no int, no decimal; money and 64-bit ids need care (minor units, bigint, strings)
string.length counts UTF-16 code units, which is neither Go's bytes nor the characters a user sees
any is contagious and silent, and it enters through common APIs (JSON.parse, older libraries); it takes lint rules to keep it out

pitfalls.title: Large ids through JSON.parse
pitfalls.detail: Ids above 2^53 - 1 are silently rounded. Have the server send them as strings (Go: `json:"id,string"`, SQL: id::text) and keep them as strings in TS.

pitfalls.title: toLowerCase() on Turkish text
pitfalls.detail: "ISPARTA".toLowerCase() is "isparta", and "İ".toLowerCase() has a combining dot. Use toLocaleLowerCase("tr") for Turkish user input, and plain toLowerCase() only for ASCII identifiers.
pitfalls.good: login.toLocaleLowerCase("tr") === stored

pitfalls.title: Annotating parsed JSON instead of narrowing it
pitfalls.detail: `const x: Payload = JSON.parse(s)` turns any into a promise nobody checked. Type it unknown and narrow, or validate with a schema.

pitfalls.title: Using the wrapper types
pitfalls.detail: String, Number and Boolean (capitalized) are the object wrapper types. Always write string, number, boolean.

quiz.q: `let status = "ok";` What is the type of status?
quiz.why: let can be reassigned, so the literal widens to string. const status = "ok" would have type "ok".

quiz.q: On which value can you call .toUpperCase() without any check, and have tsc accept it?
quiz.why: any disables checking (and may crash at run time); unknown requires narrowing first, for example typeof v === "string".

quiz.q: What is "İ".toLowerCase().length?
quiz.why: Outside the Turkish locale, U+0130 lowercases to i plus U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE. toLocaleLowerCase("tr") gives the single letter i.

quiz.q: A Postgres bigint id 9007199254740993 arrives as a JSON number. What does JSON.parse return?
quiz.why: JSON numbers become doubles; the nearest double to 2^53 + 1 is 2^53, and no error is raised.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (unknown, never)

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript's primitive types are JavaScript's: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`,
`symbol`, `null` and `undefined` (always lowercase). On top of them sit **literal
types**: `"GET"`, `42` and `true` are types with exactly one value, and unions of them
(`"GET" | "POST"`) are how TypeScript models closed sets.

Three special types frame the rest of the type system:

- **`any`** opts out. Everything is assignable to it, it is assignable to everything, and
  every operation on it compiles. It is the escape hatch from untyped JavaScript.
- **`unknown`** is the safe top type. Everything is assignable to it, but you can do
  nothing with it until a runtime check narrows it.
- **`never`** is the bottom type, with no values. It is the return type of functions that
  cannot return and the type that is left after every case has been handled.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/C/C++/Go: there is no `int`, `long` or `float`. `number` is a 64-bit double, and
  `bigint` is a separate arbitrary-precision type, closer to `BigInteger` than to `long`.
- Java: there are no boxed `Integer` types to think about; `String`/`Number` (capitalized)
  exist but are wrapper types you never annotate with.
- Go: a string is UTF-8 bytes there and `len` counts bytes; here a string is UTF-16
  code units, like Java's `String.length()`. Go's `strings.ToLower` ignores Turkish
  rules too (I becomes i); `strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` is its
  `toLocaleLowerCase("tr")`.
- Python: `Any` in mypy is TS's `any`; `object` is the closest thing to `unknown`;
  `NoReturn`/`Never` is `never`. `Literal["GET", "POST"]` is a literal union.
- JS: same values, same `typeof` results. TypeScript adds literal types and the three
  special types.

## Design notes

Treat `any` as a code smell to contain, not a convenience: it disables checking for
everything it touches, and it spreads through assignments and return values. At the
edges of the program (JSON, `catch`, messages from other windows) use `unknown` and
narrow once, so the types inside the program are real. Prefer literal unions to plain
`string` whenever the set of valid values is known; the next lessons show how they
replace enums. And because `number` is a double, decide deliberately how money and
database ids cross the wire: minor units as integers for money, strings for 64-bit ids.

lessons.title: Arrays, readonly tuples, object types, optional and readonly properties
lessons.summary: Arrays, tuples and object types describe data; readonly and ? describe what may change and what may be missing. Both are compile-time only and shallow, so know when Object.freeze or a copy is the real guarantee.

examples.title: readonly arrays, tuples and the in-place sort bug

annotations.note: sort() (like reverse() and splice()) mutates the array it is called on, so the caller's data changes behind its back. In Go a slice parameter shares its backing array in the same way.

readonly number[] (also written ReadonlyArray<number>) is the same runtime array with the mutating methods removed from its type. toSorted (ES2023, needs lib es2023+; this app's own tsconfig.app.json uses ES2020 libs, where you'd write [...scores].sort()) returns a sorted copy.
A tuple type fixes length and per-position types; readonly forbids writes. The labels lat and lon are documentation only: they don't change compatibility and destructuring can use any names.
Object.entries yields [key, value] tuples, and destructuring in the callback parameter unpacks them. This is TS's answer to Go's multiple return values.

examples.title: Optional and readonly properties, and their limits

annotations.note: `minutes?: number` means the key may be absent, so every read is number | undefined and the caller picks a default. Unlike Go, there is no zero value: a missing number is undefined, not 0.
readonly applies to the property, not to the value in it. The tags reference can't be replaced, but the array can be pushed to. Use readonly string[] as well when the contents must not change either.
A known hole: readonly properties are ignored when checking assignability, so a mutable type can alias the same object. Readonly arrays are stricter: readonly T[] is not assignable to T[] (TS4104).

Object.freeze is the runtime guarantee, and its return type is Readonly<T>. In strict-mode code (every ES module) a write throws a TypeError; in sloppy scripts it is silently ignored. It is shallow as well: nested arrays and objects stay mutable.

use_cases: readonly T[] parameters on every function that only reads an array, so callers know their data is safe
Readonly tuples for fixed pairs: coordinates, [key, value], a hook's [value, setValue]
Optional properties for genuinely absent data (no estimate yet), not as a way to avoid modelling states
Object.freeze for module-level constants and configuration that must not change at run time
strengths: Unlike Java's unmodifiable views (which throw at run time), readonly arrays remove the mutators from the type, so the mistake is a compile error
Tuples give fixed-length, per-position types without a class, which Java needs a record for and Go a struct or multiple returns
Optional properties make absence part of the type, so a missing field is handled where it is read, not discovered as null later
weaknesses: readonly is shallow and compile-time only; deep immutability needs Readonly types at every level, as const, or a freeze at run time
readonly properties are not enforced on assignment to a mutable type, so an alias can write to them
Arrays and objects are reference types with no copy-on-assign, unlike Go structs; sharing is the default and copying is explicit

pitfalls.title: Mutating an array you were handed
pitfalls.detail: sort, reverse and splice change the caller's array. Use toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced (ES2023) or copy first, and type read-only parameters as readonly T[].
pitfalls.bad: function top(xs: number[]) { return xs.sort((a, b) => b - a)[0]; }
pitfalls.good: function top(xs: readonly number[]) { return xs.toSorted((a, b) => b - a)[0]; }

pitfalls.title: Treating readonly as immutability
pitfalls.detail: readonly stops assignments through that type only. Nested values remain mutable, and another alias without readonly can still write.

pitfalls.title: Optional property where a union of states belongs
pitfalls.detail: `{ data?: T; error?: string }` allows both or neither. If exactly one must be present, use a discriminated union (lesson ts.narrowing.discriminated-unions).

quiz.q: A function takes `xs: readonly string[]`. Can you pass it a `string[]`?
quiz.why: A mutable array can always be viewed read-only. The reverse, readonly string[] to string[], is a compile error (TS4104).

quiz.q: `interface C { readonly tags: string[] }`. Which statement compiles?
quiz.why: readonly protects the property binding, not the array it points to. Make it readonly string[] to block push too.

quiz.q: What does Object.freeze give you that a readonly type does not?
options: Enforcement at run time, one level deep
quiz.why: freeze makes the object's own properties non-writable at run time; nested objects are not frozen.

quiz.q: In `type LatLon = readonly [lat: number, lon: number]`, what do the labels change?
options: They turn the tuple into an object with lat and lon
They make the tuple incompatible with [number, number]
quiz.why: Tuple labels are documentation: the type is still a two-element array of numbers.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Object Types (optional, readonly, tuples)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Four building blocks cover most data you will type:

- **Arrays**: `string[]` (or `Array<string>`), and `readonly string[]`
  (`ReadonlyArray<string>`), which has no `push`, `sort` or other mutating methods.
- **Tuples**: arrays with a fixed length and a type per position, `[string, number]`,
  optionally labelled and readonly: `readonly [lat: number, lon: number]`.
- **Object types**: inline `{ id: string; title: string }`, or named with `interface`
  or `type`. `Record<string, T>` (or an index signature `{ [key: string]: T }`) types
  dictionaries; with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` their reads include `undefined`.
- **Property modifiers**: `?` marks a property that may be absent, `readonly` one that
  can't be assigned through this type.

`readonly` and `?` are checker-only, like every type. At run time an array is an array
and an object is an object; `Object.freeze` is the only built-in runtime enforcement.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C++: `readonly T[]` is closest to `const std::vector<T>&`: the callee can read but not
  modify. Like C++ `const` it is shallow for pointers inside, and it is weaker: a
  `readonly` property can be aliased as writable without any cast (example 2).
- Java: `final` fields ≈ `readonly` properties; `List.copyOf`/unmodifiable views ≈
  `readonly T[]`, except Java enforces at run time with an exception and TS at compile
  time with a missing method. Records ≈ readonly object types.
- Go: slices share their backing array just as JS arrays are shared references, but Go
  structs are copied on assignment; JS objects never are. There is no zero value: an
  absent optional property reads as `undefined`.
- Python: tuples are immutable at run time; TS tuples are ordinary arrays with a fixed
  type. `typing.Final` and frozen dataclasses are the nearest relatives of `readonly`
  and `Object.freeze`.
- JS: nothing changes at run time. `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with`
  (ES2023) are the copying versions of the mutating array methods.

## Design notes

Make read-only the default in signatures: a function that only reads an array or object
should say so with `readonly T[]` or `Readonly<T>`, which costs nothing and documents
the contract at every call site. Return fresh values rather than mutating inputs (the
copying ES2023 methods and spread make that cheap to write). Reserve `?` for data that
can legitimately be absent; when fields come and go together, model the states as a
discriminated union instead. Reach for `Object.freeze` when something outside the type
system (another module, a library, the console) could write to a shared value.

lessons.title: null/undefined under strictNullChecks; ?. and ??
lessons.summary: Under strictNullChecks, null and undefined are not members of every type: a value that may be absent says so (T | undefined, T | null), and the compiler makes you handle it. ?. and ?? are the operators that make handling it short.

examples.title: Absence in the type, narrowing, and the ! escape hatch

annotations.note: Two kinds of absence: `string | null` means the key is always there and null is a legitimate value (a nullable column); `phone?: string` means the key may be missing. Say which one you mean.

find() returns User | undefined, and the compiler refuses member access until a check narrows it. In Java this line compiles and throws a NullPointerException at run time; in Go a nil pointer dereference panics.
Narrowing is per value: mehmet is a User inside the if, but its nickname is still string | null, so the same rule applies one level down.

`!` asserts "not null or undefined" and is erased, so it checks nothing at run time. When the assertion is wrong you get exactly the crash strictNullChecks was meant to prevent. Every ! deserves a reviewer's look.

examples.title: ?. and ?? versus ||

annotations.note: || falls back on every falsy value, so a deliberate pageSize of 0 and an empty title are replaced. ?? (ES2020) falls back only on null and undefined, which is almost always what a default means.

?. stops the whole chain at the first null or undefined and yields undefined, so one ?? at the end supplies the fallback. The Turkish locale gives IŞIL for Işıl; plain toUpperCase() would give the same here, but not for a name with a dotted i.
`?.()` calls a function only if it exists: the idiomatic way to invoke an optional callback without an if.
??= (ES2021) assigns only when the current value is null or undefined: lazy initialisation in one line. The second assignment is skipped.

examples.title: null vs undefined at the edges (JSON, Go, defaults)

annotations.note: `x == null` is true for both null and undefined, the one place where loose equality is idiomatic. Use === everywhere else.
JSON has no undefined: JSON.stringify drops such properties and writes null in arrays. A value that must survive a round trip as "empty" has to be null.

This is what a Go handler sends: a nil *string becomes null, and an omitempty field disappears, which TS models as an optional property. pgx scans SQL NULL into a nil pointer, so NULL arrives as null too.
Default values fire for undefined only. greet(null) prints "Merhaba, null" and the null nickname survives destructuring. Normalise null with ?? if you want the default.

use_cases: Lookups that can miss: Array.find, Map.get, index reads with noUncheckedIndexedAccess
Nullable database columns and JSON fields from a Go API, typed T | null
Optional configuration and callbacks, read with ?. and defaulted with ??
strengths: Unlike Java, where any reference can be null and Optional is opt-in, or Go with its nil pointers and maps, the compiler tracks which values may be absent and refuses unchecked access
Narrowing is ordinary code: an if, an early return or ?? changes the type, without wrapper types like Optional<T>
?. and ?? make the safe version as short as the unsafe one
weaknesses: Two kinds of absence (null and undefined) with different behaviour in JSON, defaults and typeof; teams must agree which means what
`!` and `as` switch the check off locally with no runtime trace when they are wrong
Only as good as the data's types: JSON.parse returns any, so a field typed string can still be null at run time

pitfalls.title: || for defaults
pitfalls.detail: 0, "" and false are valid values that || replaces. Use ?? unless you really mean every falsy value.
pitfalls.good: const size = input.pageSize ?? 50;

pitfalls.title: Truthiness checks on numbers and strings
pitfalls.detail: if (count) skips 0 and if (name) skips "". Compare with undefined or null explicitly when 0 or empty are legitimate.

pitfalls.title: Expecting defaults to replace null
pitfalls.detail: Parameter and destructuring defaults apply to undefined only. A null from JSON or the database passes straight through.

pitfalls.title: Sprinkling ! to make errors go away
pitfalls.detail: Each ! is a claim the compiler can't verify. Prefer a check that handles the absent case, or throw a descriptive error at the point you know it can't happen.

quiz.q: `input.pageSize` is 0. What is `input.pageSize || 50`?
quiz.why: || replaces every falsy value, and 0 is falsy. `input.pageSize ?? 50` would keep 0.

quiz.q: user is undefined. What does `user?.address.city` evaluate to?
quiz.why: ?. short-circuits the entire rest of the chain, so .address.city is never evaluated.

quiz.q: `function f(x: number | null = 1) { return x; }`. What does f(null) return?
quiz.why: Default parameters are applied only when the argument is undefined.

quiz.q: What does the ! in `map.get(k)!.name` do at run time?
options: Throws a clear error if the value is missing
Nothing; it is erased and the access may still crash
quiz.why: The non-null assertion is type syntax only. If the value is undefined, .name throws a TypeError.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Everyday Types (null and undefined)

lessons.body:
## Concept

JavaScript has two "no value" values: `undefined` (a variable or property that was never
set, a missing argument, a function without `return`) and `null` (an explicit "empty").
With **`strictNullChecks`** (part of `strict`, on by default since TypeScript 6.0) neither
belongs to any other type. A value that may be absent says so in its type, as
`T | undefined`, `T | null` or an optional property `x?: T`, and the compiler rejects
member access until a check narrows the type back to `T`.

Two operators (ES2020) make the checks short:

- **`a?.b`** evaluates to `undefined` if `a` is null or undefined, skipping the rest of the
  chain. It also works for calls (`f?.()`) and index reads (`a?.[i]`).
- **`a ?? b`** gives `b` only if `a` is null or undefined; `??=` (ES2021) assigns on the
  same condition.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: without `strictNullChecks` TypeScript works like Java, where null is a member of
  every reference type. With it, it works like Kotlin's `String` vs `String?`, without
  needing an `Optional<T>` wrapper.
- Go: nil pointers, maps and interfaces are unchecked, and a missing map key silently
  gives the zero value. TS has no zero values: absent is `undefined`, and the type says
  when that can happen.
- C/C++: like a pointer the compiler forces you to null-check before dereferencing.
- Python: `Optional[str]` / `str | None` under mypy, with `?.` and `??` as operators
  Python lacks.
- SQL: TS `null` is not SQL `NULL`. `null === null` is true in JS, whereas `NULL = NULL`
  is NULL in SQL; use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` there.

## Design notes

Give each kind of absence one meaning: `undefined` (or an optional property) for "not
set / not provided", `null` only where the data itself has nulls, typically JSON from a
Go API and nullable database columns. Normalise at the boundary (`row.nickname ?? undefined`
or the reverse) instead of letting both flow through the program. Prefer narrowing to
assertions: an early `if (x === undefined) return ...` documents the absent case and keeps
the rest of the function on the happy path. And default with `??`, never with `||`, unless
you really want to replace `0`, `""` and `false` as well.

lessons.title: Enums vs literal unions with as const; type aliases vs interfaces
lessons.summary: Enums are the one everyday TypeScript feature that generates code, with quirks to match; a literal union derived from an `as const` array or object gives the same safety and is plain erasable JavaScript. Use interfaces for object shapes and type aliases for unions.

examples.title: What an enum is at run time, and where it leaks

annotations.note: A numeric enum compiles to an object holding both Debug -> 0 and 0 -> "Debug". Code that iterates Object.keys or Object.values over it sees six entries for three members, a classic source of duplicated dropdown options.

Since TS 5.0 an out-of-range literal is an error, but a value of type number is still assignable to a numeric enum. A 7 from the database type-checks as a Level, and the reverse lookup gives undefined.

String enums are an exception to structural typing: the literal "active" is not assignable to Status even though Status.Active is exactly "active" at run time. Every value from JSON needs a cast, and the cast checks nothing.

examples.title: The erasable replacement: as const and a derived union

annotations.note: as const (TS 3.4) makes the array a readonly tuple of literal types, and (typeof LEVELS)[number] reads the union of its elements back out. One source of truth: add a level to the array and the type follows.

includes on a tuple of literals only accepts those literals, so checking an arbitrary string needs a widened view. The `s is Level` return type is a type guard (lesson ts.narrowing.guards): a true result narrows s.

The other side of the Turkish rule: "INFO".toLocaleLowerCase("tr") is "ınfo" with a dotless ı, which matches nothing. Use the locale for words people read and plain toLowerCase() for ASCII identifiers.

The object form gives named members (Status.Active) like an enum, but the type is the plain union "active" | "suspended". A value and a type may share the name Status because they live in separate namespaces.

examples.title: interface vs type alias

annotations.note: Interfaces describe object shapes and extend each other; a union of them needs a type alias, because an interface can only name an object type. This interface-per-variant plus union is the discriminated union you will use constantly.

Two interface declarations with the same name merge. That is how libraries let you add fields to Window or to a request type, and also how a stray duplicate name silently changes a type. Type aliases can't be reopened: declaring one twice is a "Duplicate identifier" error.

extends checks the new members against the base and reports the conflict where it is written. An intersection reports nothing: the member becomes never, and the error appears later, at whichever value fails to fit.

use_cases: Closed sets of values that cross the wire (statuses, roles, log levels): a const array or object plus its derived union
Runtime lists of the allowed values (validation, dropdowns) from the same as const array as the type
interface for object shapes, especially ones others may extend or augment; type for unions, tuples, functions and computed types
strengths: Literal unions cost nothing at run time and accept plain strings from JSON without casts, unlike string enums
as const keeps the runtime list and the type in one place, which Go needs a named type, iota constants and a hand-written slice for
Unlike Java's enum classes, a union of string literals is just data: it serialises to itself and needs no valueOf/name mapping
weaknesses: Unions have no namespace of named members unless you add the as const object; refactoring a string value means finding its uses by type, not by symbol
Enums give named members and IDE navigation, but emit code, break Node's type stripping and erasableSyntaxOnly, and numeric ones accept any number
type vs interface overlaps heavily, so codebases need a convention; declaration merging can surprise when two files reuse a name

pitfalls.title: Iterating a numeric enum
pitfalls.detail: Object.keys/values on a numeric enum include the reverse-mapping keys. Iterate an as const array instead.

pitfalls.title: Casting JSON strings to string enums
pitfalls.detail: `value as Status` compiles for any string and validates nothing. With a literal union, validate once with a guard like isLevel.
pitfalls.good: if (!isStatus(row.status)) throw new Error(`bad status ${row.status}`);

pitfalls.title: Locale-aware lowercasing of identifiers
pitfalls.detail: toLocaleLowerCase() with a Turkish default locale turns "INFO" into "ınfo". Lowercase ASCII identifiers with toLowerCase(); keep the "tr" locale for human text.

pitfalls.title: Intersections instead of extends for overriding a member
pitfalls.detail: `A & { id: number }` with A.id: string yields never instead of an error. Use interface extends (or Omit<A, "id"> & ...) when a member's type changes.

quiz.q: With erasableSyntaxOnly on, which declaration is an error?
quiz.why: enum (including const enum) generates JavaScript, so tsc reports TS1294. The others are erasable.

quiz.q: `enum Status { Active = "active" }`. Does `const s: Status = "active"` compile?
quiz.why: String enum types are nominal: only Status.Active is assignable, not the equal string literal.

quiz.q: `const LEVELS = ["debug", "info"] as const`. What is `(typeof LEVELS)[number]`?
quiz.why: as const keeps the literal types; indexing the tuple type with number gives the union of its elements.

quiz.q: When must you use a type alias rather than an interface?
quiz.why: An interface can only declare an object type; unions, tuples and primitive aliases need type.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Everyday Types (type aliases vs interfaces, literal types)

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript offers two ways to model a closed set of values:

- **`enum`**: named members compiled to a JavaScript object. Numeric enums also get a
  reverse mapping; string enums are nominal (only `Status.Active` is a `Status`).
- **A literal union**: `type Level = "debug" | "info" | "warn"`. To get a runtime list or
  named members as well, declare an array or object `as const` and derive the union
  from it with `(typeof X)[number]` or `(typeof X)[keyof typeof X]`.

`enum` is one of the few TypeScript constructs that is not erasable, which is why
`erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8) rejects it, `const enum` included, and why Node's type
stripping refuses to run it. The `as const` pattern gives the same compile-time safety
in plain JavaScript.

The second half of the lesson is the everyday choice between **`interface`** and
**`type`**. Both name object shapes. Only `type` can name a union, tuple, function or
computed type; only `interface` can be extended with `extends` checks and reopened by
declaration merging.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: enums there are classes with behaviour. TS string enums are closer to a set of
  constants with nominal typing; literal unions are closer to a sealed set of string
  values with no class at all.
- C/C++: numeric enums behave like C's `enum`: any integer value converts in, so the
  enum type does not guarantee a valid member. Even C++'s `enum class` is stricter; it
  needs a `static_cast`.
- Go: there are no enums. `type Level string` plus constants (or `iota`) is the idiom,
  and like a numeric TS enum it accepts any value of the underlying type through a
  conversion. `as const` plus a union is the TS idiom that plays the same role.
- Python: `Literal["debug", "info"]` is the literal union; `enum.Enum` is closer to TS
  enums, minus the reverse-mapping quirk.
- SQL: Postgres has `CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM` and CHECK constraints; a literal union is
  the TS-side mirror of a `CHECK (status IN ('active', 'suspended'))`.

## Design notes

Default to literal unions. Declare the values once `as const`, derive the type, and
validate untrusted strings with a guard built on the same array. That keeps the code
erasable (Node, esbuild and every other per-file tool run it unchanged), JSON values
flow in without casts, and the list of allowed values is available at run time for
validation and UI. Reach for an `enum` only when a codebase already uses them
consistently.

For object shapes, pick one convention and keep it. The handbook's heuristic is "use
`interface` until you need features from `type`": interfaces keep their names in error
messages and `extends` is checked, while unions, tuples, functions and mapped types
need `type`. The difference matters in two places: an interface
can be merged and augmented, which libraries rely on, and `extends` reports a conflicting
member where an intersection silently produces `never`.

lessons.title: Parameter and return types; optional, default and rest parameters
lessons.summary: Parameters are the one place TypeScript cannot infer, so you annotate them; return types are inferred, and you pin them where they are a contract. ?, = and ... decide how a function may be called, and an options object takes over once optional arguments pile up.

examples.title: Annotate parameters; pin return types where they are a contract

annotations.note: A parameter's type is an input to inference, not a result of it. The compiler won't guess from how the body uses it, so under strict (noImplicitAny) a missing annotation is an error. Without strict it silently becomes any and nothing that touches it is checked.
The return type is inferred as string. For small internal functions, writing it out adds nothing and goes stale when the body changes.
Plain JS lets you pass fewer arguments (the rest become undefined) or more (they are ignored). TypeScript checks the count against the signature at every call site.

With ": number | undefined" the bad return is an error inside the function. Without the annotation, return null would compile and widen the inferred type to number | null | undefined, and the errors would appear in callers instead. The Turkish decimal comma is a real trap here: Number("12,5") is NaN and parseFloat("12,5") is 12.
To infer digitSum's return type the compiler would need digitSum's return type. It reports TS7023 instead of guessing; one annotation breaks the cycle.
toLocaleUpperCase("tr-TR") maps i to İ and ı to I. toUpperCase() uses the locale-independent Unicode mapping and turns both into I.

examples.title: Optional and default parameters

annotations.note: title?: string makes the argument omittable, so inside the function its type is string | undefined and you must narrow it before calling string methods. One function covers both call shapes where Java would need two overloads.
With a default, callers see locale?: string, but inside the function locale is a plain string, inferred from "tr-TR". No narrowing needed.
JS evaluates the default expression on every call that needs it, so each call gets its own array. Python evaluates def f(x=[]) once and shares that list across calls; that bug can't happen here.

Only undefined (passed explicitly or by leaving the argument out) selects the default. null is a real value: JS would hand it to toLocaleLowerCase, which throws a TypeError. Here tsc rejects the call before that can happen.

The same input lower-cased with two locales has different lengths. The locale is part of a text function's meaning, which is why it is a parameter with an explicit default instead of the machine's locale.

examples.title: Rest parameters, spread arguments and an options object

annotations.note: ...amounts collects all remaining arguments into a number[]. Called with no arguments it is an empty array, never undefined. Same idea as Java's varargs and Go's ...T.
number[] has no known length, so tsc can't prove that two numbers arrive for min and max. as const turns the literal into the tuple readonly [0, 100], whose length is part of its type.
The naive version. To change only the third setting, the caller must pass undefined twice, and the call site no longer says what 1 means.
Destructuring in the parameter list with a default per field gives named, order-free arguments. The trailing = {} makes the whole object optional. Adding a fourth option later breaks no caller.
Both functions produce the same delays. Only the call sites differ, and only one of them can be read without opening the definition.

use_cases: Annotate every parameter of a function declaration; annotate return types on exported functions, recursive functions, and results other modules rely on
Optional parameter for one trailing argument most callers leave out (a title, a separator)
Default parameter for a configuration-like argument with a sensible value (locale = "tr-TR", pageSize = 50)
Rest parameters for variadic helpers: total(...amounts), log(level, ...parts)
An options object once a function has two or more optional settings: retry policies, formatters, fetch wrappers
strengths: Unlike Java, one function covers calls with and without an argument; optional and default parameters replace chains of telescoping overloads
Unlike plain JS, a wrong argument count or type fails at compile time (TS2554, TS2345) instead of arriving as undefined at runtime
Unlike Python, a default expression is evaluated on each call, so a [] or {} default is never shared between calls
Options objects give named arguments with per-field defaults, which Go and Java only get through option structs or builders
weaknesses: Checks are compile-time only: plain JS callers, or data cast with as, can still pass anything, so validate input at the boundaries
Defaults fire only for undefined; a null from a JSON API is not replaced
Positional optionals scale badly: f(a, undefined, undefined, true) compiles and is unreadable
An inferred return type changes silently when the body changes; without an annotation the error shows up at distant call sites

pitfalls.title: Expecting a default to replace null
pitfalls.detail: Defaults apply only when the argument is undefined. JSON APIs send null for absent values. Convert at the boundary with ?? undefined; tsc rejects passing string | null to a defaulted string parameter, which shows you where.
pitfalls.bad: lower(text, settings.locale) // locale: string | null -> TS2345
pitfalls.good: lower(text, settings.locale ?? undefined)

pitfalls.title: Case-mapping Turkish text without a locale
pitfalls.detail: toLowerCase()/toUpperCase() use the locale-independent Unicode mapping: I becomes i, and İ becomes i plus a combining dot. toLocaleLowerCase() without an argument uses the runtime's default locale, so results differ between machines. Pass the locale, ideally as a parameter with a default.
pitfalls.good: name.toLocaleLowerCase("tr-TR")

pitfalls.title: Boolean and undefined holes in positional calls
pitfalls.detail: render(rows, undefined, true, false) compiles but hides which flag is which, and reordering the parameters breaks every caller silently if the types match. Use an options object once there is more than one optional argument.
pitfalls.good: delays({ factor: 1 })

quiz.q: function f(a: string, b?: number) — inside f, what is the type of b?
quiz.why: A missing argument arrives as undefined, so the checker adds undefined to the declared type and makes you narrow before using b as a number.

quiz.q: Given function lower(text: string, locale = "tr-TR"), which call uses the default locale?
quiz.why: Only undefined, explicit or from a missing argument, selects a default. null is rejected by tsc, and an empty string is a real argument value.

quiz.q: function f(x: string | undefined) and function g(x?: string). Which of f() and g() compiles?
quiz.why: f's parameter is required; its type merely allows undefined, so f() is TS2554 and callers must write f(undefined). The ? on g's parameter makes the argument omittable.

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript infers almost everything inside a function, including locals and the return
type. Parameters are the exception: their types are what inference starts from, so you
write them. Under `strict`, a parameter without a type is an error (TS7006), not an
implicit `any`. Two exceptions: a parameter with a default value takes its type from the
default, and a callback whose function type is already known gets its parameter types
from it (next lesson).

The return type is inferred from the `return` statements. Annotate it when it is a
contract: exported functions, recursive functions (which can't be inferred), and results
other code depends on. A wrong `return` is then an error at the definition, not at every
caller.

Three parameter forms change how a function may be called:

- `x?: T`: callers may leave it out; inside, `x` is `T | undefined`.
- `x = value`: callers may leave it out or pass `undefined`; inside, `x` is `T`, inferred
  from the default. The default expression runs on each call that needs it.
- `...xs: T[]`: any number of trailing arguments, collected into a real array.

Once a function has two or more optional settings, replace them with one options object,
destructured in the parameter list with a default per field.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: optional and default parameters replace telescoping overloads, and `...xs: T[]`
  is varargs. There is one implementation per function name; the next lesson shows TS
  overload signatures and why you rarely need them.
- C++: default arguments must be trailing. A TS default can sit anywhere (callers then pass
  `undefined` to get it) and can refer to earlier parameters: `(w: number, h = w)`.
- Python: an options object with destructuring plays the role of keyword arguments, and
  the mutable-default trap (`def f(x=[])`) doesn't exist. Python checks the argument
  count at runtime; TypeScript checks it at compile time, and plain JS not at all.
- JS: the runtime semantics are unchanged. TypeScript adds arity and type checks at call
  sites and the `T | undefined` view of optional parameters, then erases all of it.
- Go: no optional or default parameters and no overloading. Go uses an options struct or
  separate functions; `...T` is the same idea as a rest parameter.

## Design notes

Annotate at the boundaries and let inference handle the inside. Exported functions get
explicit return types so that a change in the body can't silently change the module's
API. The `isolatedDeclarations` option (TS 5.5) enforces this for every export whose type
isn't trivially obvious, so other tools can generate `.d.ts` files without running the
type checker.

Keep positional parameters for what every caller passes. One trailing optional parameter
is fine. After that, an options object names each argument at the call site, lets each
setting default independently, and lets you add a setting without breaking callers. It's
the TypeScript version of Go's options struct.

Text functions should take the locale as a parameter with an explicit default (`"tr-TR"`)
instead of relying on the runtime's default locale. The default locale differs between
your laptop, CI and a user's browser; an explicit parameter keeps the result the same
everywhere.

lessons.title: Function types, callbacks, closures, this, arrow vs function, void vs undefined
lessons.summary: Function types describe callbacks, and contextual typing fills in an inline callback's parameter types. Arrows capture this, methods passed as values lose it, void in a function type means "result ignored", and a union parameter usually beats overloads.

examples.title: Function types, contextual typing and void callbacks

annotations.note: A function type is structural: any function taking two strings and returning a number fits, with no functional interface to declare as in Java. Parameter names don't take part in compatibility.
The annotation on byLength flows into the arrow: a and b are strings without being annotated, and the return value is checked against number. That flow is called contextual typing.
sort() mutates the array in place and returns it, so copy first. sort(undefined) uses the default order, which is why an optional comparator can be passed straight through.

The default sort compares UTF-16 code units: ç (U+00E7), ı (U+0131) and ş (U+015F) all come after z. Intl.Collator("tr") applies the Turkish alphabet. Its compare is bound to the collator, so it survives being passed as a bare value, unlike the methods in the next example.
An inline callback gets its types from the parameter it is passed to. || chains comparators: a 0 from byLength (same length) falls through to the Turkish comparison.

A void return in a function TYPE means the caller won't use the result, so a function returning a number fits. This is what lets you write forEach((x) => arr.push(x)). The value still exists at runtime: typeof result is "number".
Because the result's type is void, tsc refuses to branch on it. The compiler won't let you depend on a value the type says to ignore.

A function literal declared with : void must not return a value, and () => undefined demands an actual undefined. Use void for callbacks whose result you ignore; use undefined when callers handle it as a value. Since TS 5.1, a function declared : undefined may omit return.

examples.title: Closures, this, and methods passed as values

annotations.note: Each makeCounter() call creates a fresh count, and the returned arrow keeps that variable alive, so a and b don't share state: 1 2 1. The closure captures the variable itself, which it may reassign; Java lambdas only accept effectively final locals.
In a method (and any function declared with function), this is set by the call: basket.add(x) passes basket. A bare reference to the method carries no receiver.
An arrow has no this of its own; it uses the one around it, which in a field initializer is the new instance. The cost: one function per instance instead of one shared on the prototype.

forEach calls basket.add with this undefined (modules and classes are strict mode), so this.items throws. tsc accepts the line; the type-aware typescript-eslint rule unbound-method reports it. Go's method values bind the receiver; JS method references don't.
Three fixes, in the order you'll meet them: an arrow field, an arrow wrapper at the call site (the most common), and bind.

A this parameter is a fake first parameter that esbuild and tsc erase. It only works on function declarations and expressions (arrows can't declare one). It catches the direct detached call, not a method passed as a callback.

examples.title: Overloads and the union parameter you usually want instead

annotations.note: Callers see the two overload signatures; the third signature belongs to the implementation and is invisible to them. tsc checks only that the implementation is compatible with the overloads, not that each branch returns what its overload promises.
The call resolves to the first overload that matches, so single is a number and many is a number[]. Callers don't have to narrow the result, which is the one thing overloads buy you.
A string | string[] argument matches neither overload on its own, so TS2769. The caller has to narrow first and call twice. Handbook rule: prefer union parameters to overloads when possible.
When the return type doesn't depend on the argument type, a union parameter does the same job with one signature and accepts the mixed case directly.
lib.dom.d.ts declares createElement with overloads: a generic one keyed by tag name plus a fallback taking any string and returning HTMLElement.

use_cases: Typing callbacks and handlers: comparators, listeners, React props such as onSelect: (id: string) => void
Closures for private state: counters, caches, debounced handlers
Arrow functions wherever the surrounding this is needed, including class fields passed as callbacks
Overloads only when the return type depends on the argument type: parse one vs parse many, createElement(tag)
strengths: Function types are structural: any function with matching parameters and return fits, unlike Java's named functional interfaces or C#'s delegate types
Contextual typing types inline callbacks from the API they are passed to, so callback code carries almost no annotations
A void return in a callback type accepts any function, so forEach((x) => arr.push(x)) needs no wrapper
this parameters document and check what a standalone function expects as this, at zero runtime cost
weaknesses: A method passed as a value loses this, and tsc does not catch it; Python's obj.method and Go's method values bind the receiver, JS's don't
Overload implementations are checked loosely: a branch can return number[] for the string overload and callers will believe it is a number
A void-typed result can still be a value at runtime, including a rejected Promise nobody awaits
Arrow-function fields cost one function object per instance and are not on the prototype, so subclasses can't call them through super

pitfalls.title: Passing a method as a callback
pitfalls.detail: arr.forEach(obj.method) runs the method with this undefined; it throws as soon as the method touches this. Wrap it in an arrow, bind it, or make it an arrow field. typescript-eslint's unbound-method rule (recommended-type-checked) reports it.
pitfalls.good: items.forEach((item) => basket.add(item))

pitfalls.title: Async callbacks where void is expected
pitfalls.detail: An async function returns a Promise, which a void-returning slot accepts and ignores: forEach neither waits for it nor sees its rejection. Use for...of with await, or Promise.all. typescript-eslint's no-misused-promises (recommended-type-checked) reports it.
pitfalls.good: await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => save(id)))

pitfalls.title: Optional parameters in callback types
pitfalls.detail: onRow: (row: Row, index?: number) => void tells every implementation that index may be missing. If you always pass it, declare it required: a function that takes fewer parameters is still assignable, so implementations can ignore index anyway.
pitfalls.bad: type OnRow = (row: Row, index?: number) => void
pitfalls.good: type OnRow = (row: Row, index: number) => void

quiz.q: type Listener = (e: string) => void. Does const f: Listener = (e) => e.length compile?
options: No: a void function must not return a value
Yes: void in a function type means the result is ignored
Only with an explicit : number on the arrow
quiz.why: Contextual typing with a void return type doesn't forbid returning something; the value is ignored. Only a function literal declared with : void must not return a value.

quiz.q: class C { n = 1; get() { return this.n; } } — what does [0].map(new C().get) do?
quiz.why: map calls the bare method with this undefined, and reading this.n throws. tsc does not check this for method references, so it compiles.

quiz.q: When are overload signatures the right tool?
options: Whenever a parameter accepts several types
When the return type depends on which argument type was passed
To bind a method to its instance
quiz.why: If the return type is the same for every argument shape, a union parameter is simpler and also accepts a union argument, which overloads reject.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Functions are values, and their types are written like arrows:
`(a: string, b: string) => number`. Only the parameter types, their order and the return
type matter; names are documentation. When TypeScript already knows which function type
a position expects (an annotated variable, a parameter of the function you're calling),
it types the function literal from it. This is **contextual typing**, and it's why inline
callbacks rarely need annotations.

A closure captures variables, not snapshots of their values. Arrow functions also take
`this` from where they are defined. Functions declared with `function`, and methods, get
`this` from each call, so `obj.method` passed as a value arrives without `obj`.

`void` and `undefined` differ as return types. In a function *type*, `void` means "the
caller ignores the result", and any function fits. A function literal declared `: void`
must not return a value. `undefined` is a value type: the function returns `undefined`
and the caller may rely on it.

Overload signatures give one function several call signatures, so the return type can
follow the argument type. When the return type is the same for every argument shape, a
union parameter does the job better.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: no functional interfaces to name. Any function with the right shape fits a
  function type. Closures may reassign captured locals; there's no "effectively final"
  rule. Overloads are signatures over a single body, not separate methods.
- C++: an arrow capturing variables is like a `[&]` lambda, but the garbage collector keeps
  captured variables alive, so nothing dangles.
- Python: `obj.method` is a bound method in Python. In JS it is a bare function that has
  forgotten `obj`, which is the single most surprising difference in this lesson.
- Go: `func(a, b string) int` is the same idea as a function type. Go's method values
  (`f := basket.Add`) bind the receiver, and Go has no overloading at all.
- JS/React: the runtime is unchanged. TypeScript checks callback shapes such as React props
  (`onChange: (value: string) => void`). Function components and hooks avoid `this`
  entirely, which is one reason modern TS code rarely meets these problems.

## Design notes

Prefer plain functions and arrows, and keep `this` inside classes. A class method that
will be handed to someone else (an event listener, `forEach`) is either an arrow field or
gets wrapped at the call site. Enable the type-aware typescript-eslint presets
(`recommended-type-checked`) to catch the cases tsc lets through: `unbound-method` and
`no-misused-promises`.

Type callback results as `void` when you ignore them; that keeps `(x) => arr.push(x)`
legal. Name a function type (`type Compare`) when it's part of an API, so signatures and
error messages refer to it by name.

Before writing overloads, try the alternatives in order: a union parameter (same return
type), two functions with different names (`parseAmount`, `parseAmounts`, often the
clearest), and generics (the generics module). Keep overloads for return types that
genuinely follow the argument type, list the most specific signature first, and remember
that the implementation's branches are not checked against each overload.

lessons.title: Generic functions and types, extends constraints, defaults
lessons.summary: A type parameter relates the types of several values, usually an input and the output, so every call keeps its precise type. Constraints state what T must have while T keeps the rest; defaults, const type parameters and NoInfer tune inference.

examples.title: any vs unknown vs a type parameter

annotations.note: Three signatures for "first element". any switches checking off for every caller, unknown is honest but makes every caller narrow, and T relates the input to the output: it appears twice, which is what makes a type parameter worth having.
any spreads: the result of firstAny is any, so calling a number method on a string compiles and throws at run time.

unknown refuses every use until you narrow it (TS2571). The generic version returns string | undefined, so string methods work and a number annotation is rejected. "izmir".toLocaleUpperCase("tr") is İZMİR; the locale-free toUpperCase gives IZMIR.

Each type parameter is inferred from its own argument. With nothing to infer from, first([]) would infer never and return undefined, so pass the type argument. Type arguments are all or nothing: pair<string>(...) is TS2558 (expected 2), unless the missing ones have defaults.

A const type parameter (TS 5.0) infers literal types as if the caller had written as const. The constraint must be a readonly array, or the inferred readonly tuple doesn't fit and inference falls back to string[]. (typeof locales)[number] turns the tuple into a union.

examples.title: Constraints keep the caller's type

annotations.note: Both functions require an id. Only the generic one returns what it was given: T extends HasId sets a lower bound, and T itself carries every other property of the caller's objects through to Map<string, T>.
The lossy version forgot price (TS2339). An argument without id fails the constraint: T falls back to HasId, and the object literal then has an excess property (TS2353).

A constraint is a minimum, not the type. The caller chooses T, which may be a subtype with more required properties, so { id: "new" } is not a T. Note that T appears only in the return type here, the warning sign from example 3.

T is inferred from items and then flows into the callback, so p is the full product type without an annotation. Intl.Collator("tr") sorts in the Turkish alphabet (Ç after C, I before İ, Ş after S); the default sort compares UTF-16 code units, which puts Ilık before Çay.

examples.title: Generic types, defaults, NoInfer and the return-only trap

annotations.note: A generic type alias. E = Error is a default: Result<number> means Result<number, Error>. Parameters with defaults must come after the ones without, as in function parameters.

parsePrice relies on the default, parsePort narrows the error to two string literals. The union is discriminated by ok (lesson ts.narrowing.discriminated-unions), so r.value and r.error are only reachable on the right branch.

NoInfer (TS 5.4) blocks inference from fallback, so T comes from the options list alone and "fr" is rejected. Without it, every argument is an inference candidate and T silently widens to include "fr".

T appears only in the return type, so it relates nothing: it is a cast with nicer syntax. JSON.parse returns any, which is assignable to T, so port is typed number while holding the string "8080", and + concatenates.
The honest signature returns unknown and makes the caller check. For real data, validate with a schema at the boundary (lesson ts.services.zod) and let the schema produce the type.

use_cases: Collection helpers that return what they were given: first, indexById, groupBy, sortBy, chunk
Containers and wrappers: Result<T, E>, Page<T>, Cache<K, V>, a typed event emitter
Functions that take callbacks over the caller's element type, such as sortBy(items, (p) => p.name)
Accepting anything with a required shape while returning the caller's exact type: T extends { id: string }
strengths: Inference does the work: callers rarely write type arguments, and the return type follows the arguments
Constraints can be any type, including an object shape, a literal union or a function type; Java bounds and Go constraints are declared interfaces
Type parameters are erased: one JavaScript function serves every T, with no boxing as in Java and no per-type instantiation as in C++ templates
const type parameters and NoInfer let a library shape inference without asking callers for as const or explicit type arguments
weaknesses: Erased means no new T(), no T.name and no runtime check that a value is a T; pass a factory, a schema or a type guard instead
A type parameter used only in the return type compiles and lies: the caller picks any T
No partial inference: supply every type argument or none (defaults aside)
Deeply generic signatures produce long error messages; two plain functions are often clearer than one clever generic

pitfalls.title: A generic return type with no matching input
pitfalls.detail: The handbook's rule: a type parameter that appears once relates nothing. parseJson<T> is an unchecked cast; return unknown and validate.
pitfalls.bad: function parseJson<T>(text: string): T { return JSON.parse(text); }
pitfalls.good: function parseJson(text: string): unknown { return JSON.parse(text); }

pitfalls.title: Constraining a type parameter instead of using it
pitfalls.detail: When T is the whole array, element reads resolve through the constraint and the return type degrades to any. Make the element the type parameter (the handbook calls this pushing type parameters down).
pitfalls.bad: function first<T extends any[]>(arr: T) { return arr[0]; }
pitfalls.good: function first<T>(arr: readonly T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; }

pitfalls.title: Generic where a plain type would do
pitfalls.detail: function greet<S extends string>(s: S): void relates nothing to S. Write (s: string): void; add the type parameter when a second position needs it.

pitfalls.title: Fabricating a T inside the function
pitfalls.detail: Returning { id: "new" } as T compiles with the cast and breaks for any caller whose T has more required fields. Take a factory parameter, or return the constraint type.
pitfalls.bad: function create<T extends HasId>(): T { return { id: "new" } as T; }
pitfalls.good: function create<T extends HasId>(make: (id: string) => T): T { return make("new"); }

quiz.q: first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined. What is the type of first(["a", "b"])?
quiz.why: T is inferred from the array literal, whose elements widen to string. Getting the literals needs a const type parameter or as const.

quiz.q: Why is function make<T extends HasId>(): T { return { id: "x" }; } an error?
options: Object literals can't be returned from generic functions
T may be a subtype of HasId with more required properties
HasId must be a class to be used as a constraint
quiz.why: The constraint is a lower bound chosen by the caller; { id } satisfies HasId but not every T.

quiz.q: Which signature is a cast in disguise?
options: <T extends string>(options: T[], fallback: NoInfer<T>) => T
quiz.why: Its T appears only in the return type, so nothing ties it to a real value; the caller asserts it.

quiz.q: pick<T extends string>(options: T[], fallback: T) is called as pick(["tr", "en"], "fr"). What happens?
quiz.why: Both arguments are inference candidates. NoInfer<T> on fallback makes the call an error.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (generic functions, guidelines)
TypeScript 5.0 release notes: const type parameters
TypeScript 5.4 release notes: the NoInfer utility type
Go tutorial: Getting started with generics

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **type parameter** is a placeholder the caller fills in, usually by inference:
`function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined`. Its job is to *relate* types:
the element type of the input is the type of the output. A parameter that appears once
relates nothing and is a sign the function doesn't need to be generic.

- **Constraints** (`T extends HasId`) set a minimum. Inside the function you may use what
  the constraint guarantees; outside, the caller's full type flows through. A constraint
  is a lower bound, so the function can't invent a value of type `T`.
- **Generic types** take parameters too: `type Result<T, E = Error>`, `interface Page<T>`,
  `class Cache<K, V>`. A **default** (`E = Error`) fills in an argument the user omits.
- **Inference** picks each type parameter from the arguments. When it guesses wrong, you
  can pass type arguments explicitly (all of them, or none), mark a parameter
  `const` (TS 5.0) to keep literal types, or wrap a parameter in `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) so
  it is checked against `T` but doesn't help infer it.

Type parameters are erased like every other type. One JavaScript function runs for every
`T`, which is why `new T()` and `x instanceof T` don't exist.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` reads the same, and Java also erases. Differences: the
  bound can be any TS type (an object shape, a union of literals, a function type), not
  only a declared interface; there are no wildcards, because variance is computed from
  structure; and primitives need no boxing.
- C++: templates generate code per instantiation and check the body per use. TS checks a
  generic body once, against the constraint, and generates nothing. The closest C++ idea
  is a concept, minus the code generation.
- Python: `def first[T](items: Sequence[T]) -> T | None` (PEP 695) is the same idea, also
  erased, also checked only by a separate tool.
- Go: `func First[T any](items []T) (T, bool)` matches closely. Go constraints are
  interfaces listing methods and type sets; TS constraints are arbitrary types. TS
  methods have always been able to declare their own type parameters, which Go methods
  gained in 1.27 (lesson go.generics.methods-when).
- JS: nothing changes at run time; generics exist only in the checker.

## Design notes
