Start concrete. Write `(items: readonly Product[]) => Product[]`, and introduce `T` the
second time you need the same logic for a different type, when the relation between
input and output is obvious. Apply the handbook's three rules: use the type parameter
itself rather than constraining a bigger one, use as few type parameters as possible,
and make each one appear at least twice.

Prefer the constraint that states what the body actually uses (`T extends { id: string }`),
and return `T` so callers keep their type. Reach for `const` type parameters and
`NoInfer` when you write library-style helpers whose callers shouldn't need `as const`
or explicit arguments. And when a type parameter would only describe data arriving from
outside (`fetchJson<T>()`), stop: that is a validation problem, solved at run time by a
schema, not by a type argument.

lessons.title: keyof, indexed access types, generic React components
lessons.summary: keyof T is the union of T's property names and T[K] the type stored under K, so a generic K extends keyof T ties a key to its value type. The same idea makes React components generic over the caller's row type, with every column checked.

examples.title: keyof, T[K], and why Object.keys returns string[]

annotations.note: keyof Product is the union of its property names as literal types; Product["price"] reads the type stored under a key, and [number] reads an array's element type. Both are computed from Product, so renaming a field updates every type derived from it.

K extends keyof T captures the literal key the caller passed, so get(cay, "price") is a number. The loose version accepts any key and must return the union of every property type, leaving the caller to narrow. A typo is a compile error in both.
T[K][] follows the key: pluck(rows, "name") is string[], and pluck(rows, "tags") is string[][]. The Turkish locale uppercases simit to SİMİT; toUpperCase() would give SIMIT.

Object.keys returns string[] on purpose. Structural typing lets a Product carry extra properties (stock here), so typing the keys as (keyof Product)[] would be a lie. Indexing with a plain string is TS7053; compare the key against known names first, which narrows it.

examples.title: A generic key keeps key and value together

annotations.note: keyof Settings and Settings[keyof Settings] are two independent unions, so any key may pair with any field's value type, including "pageSize" with "tr-TR".
K records which key was passed, and value must be Settings[K] for that K. The mismatched call is TS2345; the message shows the literal widened to string.
The loose call compiled and stored a string where every reader expects a number. Nothing at run time noticed, which is why the type has to.

A mapped type, { [K in keyof T]: ... }, builds one property per key, and T[K] gives each handler its own parameter type: v is a number for pageSize and a boolean for darkMode. Lesson ts.type-level.utility covers mapped types properly.

examples.title: A generic React table typed by keyof

annotations.note: In generic code keyof T is string | number | symbol, and a React key can't be a symbol, so columns use keyof T & string. render receives the whole row, typed T, which avoids the harder problem of typing a per-column value.
A generic comparator over any key. T[keyof T] could be anything, so it compares String() of each value with a Turkish collator; numeric: true also orders "9" before "10".

A generic component is a generic function that returns JSX. In a .tsx file a generic arrow must be written <T,>(props) => ..., because <T> parses as a JSX tag. Rows are keyed by rowKey, not by index, so sorting can't mix up row state.
A fixed time zone keeps the output identical on every machine; tr-TR medium dates abbreviate months: 1 Haz 2023.

T is inferred as Customer from rows, so rowKey's c is a Customer, sortBy must be a Customer key, each column key is checked, and render gets c.joined as a Date. <Table<Customer> ...> states T explicitly when inference can't.
flushSync makes React render synchronously, so the DOM can be read on the next line. The rows come out in Turkish order: Çağrı, Işıl, Şule.

use_cases: Typed property helpers: get, pluck, groupBy(rows, key), sortBy(rows, key)
Updating settings or form state with correlated key and value: set(form, key, value)
Reusable components over the caller's data: tables with column definitions, selects, lists, filters
Deriving types from data: keyof typeof labels, (typeof ROUTES)[number]
strengths: Property names become types, so renaming a field breaks every column definition and sort key at compile time; Java needs reflection or string constants, Go struct tags are unchecked strings
Generic components infer T from props: JSX call sites need no type arguments, and callbacks such as render get the row type for free
Indexed access types derive one type from another (Product["price"], Row["tags"][number]) instead of restating it
weaknesses: Object.keys and for...in give string, not keyof T; iterating keys safely needs a known key list or a narrowing check
keyof T in generic code includes number and symbol, so string operations need keyof T & string
Wrapping a generic component in memo or forwardRef loses its type parameter: memo(Table) infers T as unknown
Typing a per-column value (a formatter taking T[K]) needs mapped types and runs into correlated-union limits inside the component

pitfalls.title: Independent key and value unions
pitfalls.detail: (key: keyof S, value: S[keyof S]) accepts every pairing of key and value. Capture the key in a type parameter.
pitfalls.bad: function set(s: Settings, key: keyof Settings, value: Settings[keyof Settings]) { ... }
pitfalls.good: function set<K extends keyof Settings>(s: Settings, key: K, value: Settings[K]) { ... }

pitfalls.title: Casting Object.keys to keyof T
pitfalls.detail: The cast compiles, and at run time the array also holds the extra properties the object carried in. Iterate a list of the keys you know.
pitfalls.bad: for (const k of Object.keys(p) as (keyof Product)[]) show(k, p[k]);
pitfalls.good: for (const k of ["name", "price"] as const) show(k, p[k]);

pitfalls.title: Generic arrow components in .tsx
pitfalls.detail: const Table = <T>(props: TableProps<T>) => ... is parsed as a JSX element and fails to compile (TS17008). Add a trailing comma or use a function declaration.
pitfalls.good: const Table = <T,>(props: TableProps<T>) => <table />;

pitfalls.title: The array index as the row key in a sortable list
pitfalls.detail: When rows are reordered, index keys make React reuse the wrong row's state. Take a key function (rowKey) from the caller.

quiz.q: type M = { [k: string]: boolean }. What is keyof M?
quiz.why: JavaScript converts numeric keys to strings, so obj[0] is obj["0"] and a string index signature also accepts numbers.

quiz.q: Why does Object.keys(product) return string[] instead of (keyof Product)[]?
options: A Product value may carry more properties than the type lists
keyof is not available at run time
quiz.why: Structural typing allows extra properties, so the runtime key list can be longer than keyof Product.

quiz.q: set(s: Settings, key: keyof Settings, value: Settings[keyof Settings]). What does set(s, "pageSize", "tr-TR") do?
options: Compiles, and stores a string in pageSize
quiz.why: Key and value are separate unions. With <K extends keyof Settings> and value: Settings[K] the call is rejected.

quiz.q: In a .tsx file, which declaration of a generic component compiles?
quiz.why: <T> alone starts a JSX element. A trailing comma, a constraint (<T extends object>) or a function declaration avoids the ambiguity.

TypeScript 2.9 release notes: generic type arguments in JSX elements

lessons.body:
## Concept

Two type operators turn property names into types:

- **`keyof T`** is the union of `T`'s keys as literal types: `keyof Product` is
  `"id" | "name" | "price" | "tags"`. For a string index signature it is
  `string | number`, because JavaScript converts numeric keys to strings.
- **Indexed access `T[K]`** is the type stored under `K`: `Product["price"]` is `number`,
  `Product[keyof Product]` the union of all property types, and `T[number]` an array's
  element type.

Both arrived in TypeScript 2.1. Combined with a type parameter they give the key a memory:
`function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` infers `K` as the literal key
you passed, so the result has that property's type, and a typo is a compile error.

A React component is a function, so it can be generic too. `function Table<T>(props:
TableProps<T>)` infers `T` from the `rows` you pass, and every other prop (column keys,
sort key, render callbacks) is checked against that row type. TS 2.9 added explicit
type arguments in JSX, `<Table<Customer> ... />`, for the cases inference can't settle.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: there is no type for "a field name of `Product`". You use strings plus
  reflection, or method references (`Product::getPrice`) that can't be enumerated. `keyof`
  makes the field name itself a checked type.
- C++: closest are pointers to members (`&Product::price`), which do carry the member's
  type, but there is no way to get "all member names" as a type.
- Python: `Literal["id", "name"]` must be written by hand; `TypedDict` keys aren't
  derived automatically the way `keyof` derives them.
- Go: struct tags such as `json:"price"` are strings nobody checks, and generics can't
  abstract over field names. Code that needs "any field of T" uses reflection.
- JS/React: `Object.keys` and `for...in` behave as always, and TypeScript types their keys
  as `string` on purpose. Generic components are ordinary function components with a type
  parameter; nothing changes at run time.

## Design notes

Use `K extends keyof T` whenever a function takes a key and a value or returns a
property's value; it is the cheapest way to keep pairs consistent. Accept that
`Object.keys` returns `string[]`: when you need to iterate keys, iterate a list you control
(`["name", "price"] as const`) and let the list's literal types do the narrowing.

For components, make generic the ones that render the caller's data (tables, lists,
selects), and give them a small surface: rows, a key function, column definitions whose
`key` is `keyof T & string`, and render callbacks that receive the whole typed row.
Per-column value types (`format: (value: T[K]) => string`) are possible with mapped
types but quickly need helper functions to stay type-safe inside the component; reach for
them only when the row-level callback really isn't enough. Generic components also don't
survive `memo` or `forwardRef` with their type parameter intact, so memoize the data you
pass in rather than the component, or cast the wrapped component back to its generic
signature in one place.

lessons.title: TS = JS + erasable static types; what tsc 7 does vs what bundlers do
lessons.summary: Types exist only for the checker: the transpiler that feeds the browser deletes them without looking. tsc 7 checks the whole program; bundlers strip one file at a time and run code with type errors in it.

examples.title: What actually runs has no types in it

annotations.note: toString() prints the function as the engine received it: esbuild deleted `: User` and `: string` and changed nothing else. This is the whole contract of erasable syntax: the output is your code minus the types.

An interface is a compile-time name only, so there is nothing to typeof, iterate or reflect over. Java keeps class metadata at run time and C# keeps generics; TypeScript keeps nothing. Runtime type questions need runtime values (typeof on values, instanceof on classes, a validator).

The annotation on parsed is an unchecked promise. JSON.parse returns any, which is assignable to everything, so tsc is satisfied and "41" + 1 gives "411". Data crossing a boundary (fetch, JSON, localStorage) must be validated at run time; the zod lesson does it properly.

A real type error: delete the directive and tsc reports TS2322. The transpiler never asked, so the program runs and prints 80801. Vite, Node and this runner all behave this way; only tsc (in your editor and in CI) stops it.

examples.title: The few TS constructs that are not erasable

annotations.note: A union type alias is pure type syntax: it disappears and only the string "info" is left. This is why literal unions are the default replacement for enums (lesson ts.everyday-types.unions-enums).

enum is TypeScript-only syntax with runtime behaviour: the transpiler has to generate an object, here with a reverse mapping (0 -> "Low"). Node's type stripping refuses to run it (ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX), and erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc reject it up front.

`private readonly id` in the parameter list looks like a type annotation but is a field declaration plus an assignment. esbuild wrote `this.id = id` and a field `id;` that do not appear in your source.

The erasable spelling produces the same class, but every line of the output now exists in the source. `private` on a field is just a modifier the checker reads and the transpiler deletes; for privacy enforced at run time use a JavaScript #private field instead.

use_cases: Reading a stack trace or the browser debugger: the code you see is your TS with the types removed, so line-by-line debugging works without surprises
Choosing tsconfig flags for a project transpiled by Vite/esbuild or run directly by Node 22.18+/23.6+: erasableSyntaxOnly plus verbatimModuleSyntax
Deciding where validation must happen: every value that arrives as text (fetch, JSON.parse, localStorage, URL params)
strengths: Zero runtime cost: unlike Java or C# there is no type metadata or reflection data at run time, and the shipped JS is as small as hand-written JS

Transpiling is fast and per-file, so Vite's dev server serves a changed file in milliseconds without waiting for the checker; tsc 7 then checks the whole program several times faster than the JavaScript-based 6.0
Any JavaScript engine runs the output: browsers, Node, Deno, Bun, workers. There is no TypeScript runtime to install or version
weaknesses: Unlike Go, where a type error means no binary, a TS type error does not stop `vite build`, the dev server or this runner. The checker is a separate step you must wire into CI
No runtime types: you cannot ask an interface whether a JSON value matches it. Validation libraries (zod) exist to rebuild that at the boundary
Annotations on any-typed values (JSON.parse, catch variables without strict) are trusted blindly, so a wrong type can travel far before something breaks

pitfalls.title: Treating a green bundler build as a type check
pitfalls.detail: Vite, esbuild and Node strip types and never report type errors. In this repo `npm run build` does not run tsc; `npm run typecheck` does, and CI needs both.

pitfalls.title: Annotating parsed JSON and calling it validated
pitfalls.detail: `const u: User = JSON.parse(text)` compiles for any text. Parse to unknown and validate, or the first wrong field surfaces far from where it entered.
pitfalls.good: const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(text); const u = UserSchema.parse(raw);

pitfalls.title: Non-erasable syntax in code that Node runs directly
pitfalls.detail: enum, namespaces with values, parameter properties and `import =` make Node's type stripping throw ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Turn on erasableSyntaxOnly so tsc reports TS1294 in the editor instead.

quiz.q: `vite build` succeeds on a file that has a type error. Why?
options: Vite downgrades type errors to warnings
Vite transpiles each file by deleting the types and never runs the type checker
quiz.why: Bundlers strip types per file without type information. Only tsc (or your editor's language service) reports type errors.

quiz.q: Which of these produces JavaScript code rather than being erased?
quiz.why: An enum compiles to an object (with a reverse mapping for numeric members). The other three disappear completely.

quiz.q: `const u: User = JSON.parse(text)`: what verifies that text contains a numeric age?
options: The browser, when the annotated line runs
Nothing, unless you validate the value yourself
quiz.why: JSON.parse returns any and the annotation is erased. Neither the checker nor the runtime looks at the actual data.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: The Basics (Erased Types, Emitting with Errors)

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a layer of type syntax that is designed to be deleted. Two
different tools act on a `.ts` file, and they never talk to each other:

- The **checker**, `tsc`, reads the whole program (every file, every `.d.ts`), works out
  the types and reports errors. In a bundler project like this app it writes nothing:
  `npm run typecheck` is `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json`.
- The **transpiler** (esbuild inside Vite, Node's type stripping, the esbuild-wasm worker
  behind this Run button) looks at one file at a time, removes the type syntax and hands
  JavaScript to the engine. It does not know or care whether the types are right.

So nothing about a type exists at run time: no reflection, no checks on assignment, no
`typeof SomeInterface`. A type is a claim that the checker verified, or (via `any`)
didn't.

**TypeScript 7.0** (July 2026) is the same language with the compiler ported to Go:
type-checking runs in parallel, and the 7.0 announcement measured full builds 8 to 12
times faster than the JavaScript-based compiler. tsc 7 can still emit JavaScript, and
like every tsc it emits even when there are errors unless `noEmitOnError` is set. The
bundler-plus-`noEmit` split is a project choice, not a limit of the compiler. What 7.0
does not ship is the old JavaScript compiler API, which is why this repo keeps
TypeScript 6.0 installed beside it for typescript-eslint (ADR-0006).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: the closest analogue. Type hints are ignored at run time and mypy/pyright is a
  separate checker. TypeScript works the same way, except that the hints are stripped
  out of the file instead of being kept in `__annotations__`.
- Java: you know generic type erasure. TypeScript erases *everything*: classes survive
  (they are JavaScript), but interfaces, type aliases, generics and annotations leave no
  trace, so there is nothing like `getClass()` or reflection over a declared type.
- C/C++: types drive code generation there (overload resolution, layout, templates).
  In TypeScript the types never change the emitted code, apart from the few
  non-erasable constructs in example 2.
- Go: `go build` refuses to produce a binary with a type error. Vite, Node and this
  runner happily run TypeScript that tsc rejects. The gate is your editor plus CI.
- JS: the runtime is exactly the one you know. Nothing new executes.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  src["app.ts"] --> tsc["tsc 7 (whole program)"]
  tsc --> diag["type errors, or nothing (noEmit)"]
  src --> strip["esbuild / Vite / Node (one file at a time)"]
  strip --> js["app.js: same code minus types"]
  js --> engine["browser or Node"]
```

Erasable syntax is what a per-file transpiler can delete without understanding it:
annotations, `interface`, `type`, generics, `as` casts, `import type`. A short list of
older TypeScript features generate code instead: `enum`, `namespace` with values, class
parameter properties and `import x = require(...)`. tsc also flags the old `<T>value`
assertion syntax under `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Node's built-in type stripping (on by default
since Node 23.6 and 22.18) refuses the code-generating constructs outright, and the
`erasableSyntaxOnly` flag (TypeScript 5.8) makes tsc report them as TS1294 so you learn
it in the editor rather than at startup.

`isolatedModules` (on in this repo's tsconfig) is the matching guard for the
transpiler's blindness: it makes tsc reject code that a one-file-at-a-time tool can't
transpile correctly, such as re-exporting a type without `export type`.

## Design notes

Treat the two tools as two jobs. The transpiler gives you a fast edit-run loop; the
checker is a test suite for your types and belongs in CI next to the unit tests
(`npm run typecheck` here). Write only erasable syntax (`erasableSyntaxOnly` plus
`verbatimModuleSyntax`), so the JavaScript that runs is exactly what you wrote minus
the types, and the same file works unchanged under esbuild, Node, Deno or Bun. Finally,
because types vanish, every value that enters as text (fetch bodies, `JSON.parse`,
storage, URL parameters) is `unknown` in reality, whatever its annotation says:
validate it once at the boundary, and inside the program trust the types.

lessons.title: Essential tsconfig options and the strict flags
lessons.summary: strict (the default since TypeScript 6.0) is a family of checks; three flags outside it close the holes that bite most often: unchecked index reads, optional properties that may hold undefined, and imports whose fate depends on elision.

examples.title: What strict turns on, and what it catches

annotations.note: verbatimModuleSyntax (TS 5.0): imports without `type` stay in the output, imports with `type` disappear, and nothing in between is guessed. Node's type stripping and esbuild see one file and cannot know that Prefs is only a type, so the rule makes the source say it. It implies isolatedModules.

noImplicitAny is the flag that makes TypeScript a typed language rather than optional hints: a parameter tsc cannot infer must be annotated. Variables and return types are still inferred, so annotate parameters and exported signatures, not every local.

strictNullChecks puts undefined into find()'s return type. Without it, null and undefined are members of every type, which is Java's NullPointerException model. Lesson ts.everyday-types.null goes deeper.
useUnknownInCatchVariables (TS 4.4, part of strict): JavaScript can throw any value, here a string. The cast on line 33 compiles and prints undefined; narrowing with instanceof is the honest version.

examples.title: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and a Turkish lookup key

annotations.note: Record<string, string> promises a string for every key, which no object can keep. Without the flag tsc believes it; the `!` makes that belief visible. "IŞIK".toLowerCase() is "işik" (dotted i), so the lookup misses and the call crashes on undefined.

With the flag (TS 4.1, not part of strict) the read is string | undefined and the compiler forces the miss to be handled. Lowercasing with the "tr" locale maps I to ı and İ to i, which is what Turkish logins need.
Array index reads and destructuring get undefined too. for...of and map() don't, because they only visit elements that exist: prefer them to index loops and the flag costs little.

examples.title: exactOptionalPropertyTypes and the spread that erases a default

annotations.note: Without the flag, `theme?: T` also accepts an explicit undefined. The key then exists ("theme" in loose is true) and object spread copies it, overwriting the default with undefined.
With the flag (TS 4.4, not part of strict), `theme?: T` means absent or a real T. If you really mean "may be present and undefined", write `theme?: T | undefined` and the type says so.

Leaving the key out is the only way to say "not set", so the spread keeps the default. The same distinction matters for PATCH bodies, where a missing field means "don't change" and null means "clear".
JSON.stringify drops undefined properties, so both objects print as {}. Logging the object won't show the bug; the flag catches it at compile time.

use_cases: Starting a project: strict plus noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, verbatimModuleSyntax and erasableSyntaxOnly from day one, when turning them on costs nothing
Tightening an existing codebase one flag at a time: run tsc with the flag on the command line, count the errors, fix, then commit the tsconfig change
Reviewing a pull request that adds `!` or `as` around index reads: each one is a place where the checker was overruled
strengths: Unlike javac's or Go's fixed rules, strictness is adjustable per project, so a JS codebase can be migrated gradually and a new one can start strict
TypeScript 6.0 and 7.0 default strict to true, so a fresh tsconfig already checks null, implicit any and catch variables
noUncheckedIndexedAccess catches the missing-key class of bugs that Java only reports at run time (a null from Map.get) and Go hides behind zero values
weaknesses: The most useful extra flags are not part of strict, so `strict: true` alone still lets arr[i] and record[key] lie
noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds noise to index loops (`for (let i...)` reads are T | undefined even inside bounds); there is no bounds analysis
exactOptionalPropertyTypes trips over library types that write `x?: T` but would accept undefined: passing `{ x: maybe }` then needs a conditional spread or a cast

pitfalls.title: Assuming strict covers index reads
pitfalls.detail: strict does not include noUncheckedIndexedAccess or exactOptionalPropertyTypes. Turn them on explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Silencing the flag with `!` everywhere
pitfalls.detail: A `!` on every index read restores the unchecked behaviour with extra typing. Use for...of, a Map with .get(), or an explicit undefined check that does something sensible.
pitfalls.good: const role = roles[key] ?? "guest";

pitfalls.title: Relying on a missing tsconfig field meaning "off"
pitfalls.detail: Defaults changed in 6.0 (strict, module, target, types). Write the important options explicitly so the file reads the same under every compiler version.

quiz.q: Which flag is NOT turned on by `strict: true`?
quiz.why: noUncheckedIndexedAccess (and exactOptionalPropertyTypes) are separate opt-ins; the other three are members of the strict family.

quiz.q: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, what is the type of `names[0]` when `names: string[]`?
quiz.why: The flag adds undefined to every index-signature and array element read, because the index may be out of range.

quiz.q: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, what happens to `import type { User } from "./user"` in the JavaScript output?
options: It is rewritten to a side-effect import
quiz.why: Imports with the type modifier are erased; imports without it are kept verbatim. That is the whole rule.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`tsconfig.json` decides which program you are writing. The same file can be loosely typed
JavaScript or a tightly checked one depending on a handful of flags:

- **`strict`** is an umbrella for the "strict family": `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`,
  `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`,
  `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `noImplicitThis` and `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. New
  members join the family in later releases, so `strict: true` gets stricter when you
  upgrade. **Since TypeScript 6.0 it defaults to true** (also in 7.0). `alwaysStrict`
  went the other way: 6.0 took it out of the family and turned it on unconditionally, so
  `alwaysStrict: false` is deprecated in 6.0 and rejected by 7.0.
- **`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`** (4.1): `arr[i]` and `record[key]` include `undefined`.
- **`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`** (4.4): `x?: T` means "absent or a T", not "or undefined".
- **`verbatimModuleSyntax`** (5.0): imports and exports are emitted exactly as written,
  minus anything marked `type`.

None of the last three is part of `strict`.

This repo's `tsconfig.app.json` is a typical Vite setup: `strict`, `isolatedModules`,
`noEmit` with `allowImportingTsExtensions`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`,
`noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`. It does not turn on the three extra flags. Try them from the
command line without editing anything:
`node node_modules/typescript7/bin/tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json --noUncheckedIndexedAccess`
lists every index read the app takes on trust, such as `lines[i]` in a parsing loop or
`m[1]` from a regex match. Run it for the current count: it changes with the code.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `javac`'s rules are fixed. TypeScript's are configurable because it had to absorb
  untyped JavaScript gradually. `strictNullChecks` is the switch between Java's model
  (null is in every reference type) and Kotlin's (it isn't, unless you say `T?`).
- C/C++: comparable to `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, except that a TS flag changes what the
  type system believes (`T` vs `T | undefined`), not just which warnings print.
- Python: mypy's `--strict` is the same idea: opt-in checks bundled under one switch.
- Go: the compiler has no strictness knobs; its rules are the same for every module. A
  missing map key gives the zero value; in TS without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` it
  gives `undefined` typed as `T`.
- JS: the flags change nothing at run time. They only change which programs tsc accepts.

## Design notes

For new code, start with everything on: `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`,
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Each one
turns a whole category of runtime surprise (the missing key, the undefined that overwrote
a default, the import that only existed for types, the enum Node can't strip) into a
compile error, and the cost is lowest on an empty codebase. Tighten an existing project
one flag at a time from the command line, as above, and commit the flag together with
the fixes. Write important options explicitly even when they match today's default: the
6.0 default changes showed that "unset" means different things to different compiler
versions.

lessons.title: Structural typing vs nominal typing; where TS runs
lessons.summary: TypeScript compares types by their members, not their names: anything with the right shape fits, including values of unrelated classes. That follows from erasure, since at run time an object is only a bag of properties.

examples.title: Shapes decide compatibility, for better and worse

annotations.note: Pixel never mentions Point, and a plain object literal works too. In Java the class would need `implements Point`; here the checker compares members, and extra ones (color) don't matter.

Meters and Feet are the same type as far as tsc is concerned, so the units bug compiles. Go would reject it: `type Meters float64` and `type Feet float64` are distinct named types that need an explicit conversion.

A #private (or TS `private`) member makes a class behave nominally: no object literal or other class can supply Altitude's own #meters. Since only the constructor can produce one, instanceof Altitude is also a reliable runtime check.

examples.title: Extra properties pass the check and leak at run time

annotations.note: Excess-property checking applies only to a fresh object literal written directly against a type. There, an unknown key is almost certainly a typo, and nothing could ever read it through that type.

Through a variable, DbUser is a subtype of PublicUser (it has at least the required fields), so the call compiles. The annotation narrows what the code may read, not what the object contains, and JSON.stringify sends the hash.
Explicit mapping is the fix, as with a DTO in Java or a `json:"-"` tag in Go. In TS it is the only fix: no type annotation removes a property.

examples.title: Function types are structural too

annotations.note: map passes (value, index, array); parseInt's parameters (string, radix?) line up with the first two, so the types fit and the index becomes the radix: parseInt("10", 1) is NaN, parseInt("10", 2) is 2.
This is why the rule exists: a callback may ignore trailing arguments, as JavaScript callbacks always have. Java's functional interfaces need an exact arity; TypeScript accepts fewer parameters.
The reverse is unsafe and rejected: a function that needs a third argument would receive undefined from a caller that passes two.

use_cases: Passing a class instance, an object literal or a mock to the same function without interfaces or adapters
Test doubles: any object with the right methods is a valid fake, with no mocking framework or `implements` needed
Typing plain JSON data, which has no class to be nominal about
strengths: Unlike Java or C#, no `implements` ceremony: the consumer declares the shape it needs and every producer that has it fits, like Go's implicit interfaces
Matches how JavaScript actually works (duck typing), so existing JS patterns type-check without wrappers
Object literals, class instances and JSON-derived objects are interchangeable when they have the same fields
weaknesses: Same shape, different meaning compiles: Meters vs Feet, UserId vs OrderId (type aliases of string are fully interchangeable). Go's named types and Java's classes catch this; TS needs branded types
A wider object passes for a narrower type and keeps its extra fields at run time, so types never sanitize data
A value typed as a class need not be an instance of it: `const p: Pixel = { x: 1, y: 2 }` compiles and `p instanceof Pixel` is false

pitfalls.title: Expecting a type annotation to strip fields
pitfalls.detail: Returning a DbUser from a function typed PublicUser still sends every field. Map to a new object explicitly.
pitfalls.good: const body: PublicUser = { name: row.name };

pitfalls.title: Using instanceof on a value that was only typed as a class
pitfalls.detail: If a class has only public members, a plain object literal satisfies its type but fails instanceof. Narrow with a discriminant field or construct real instances.

pitfalls.title: ID aliases that mix silently
pitfalls.detail: `type UserId = string` is a name, not a new type. Passing an OrderId where a UserId is expected compiles; brand them (lesson ts.type-level.branded) when mixing them would be a real bug.

quiz.q: `interface Named { name: string }` and `class Dog { name = "Karabaş"; bark() {} }`. Does `const n: Named = new Dog()` compile?
options: No: Dog does not implement Named
Yes: Dog has a string name
quiz.why: Compatibility is structural: Dog has every member Named requires, and extra members are allowed.

quiz.q: `const u: PublicUser = { name, passwordHash }` fails, but `const u: PublicUser = row` with the same two fields compiles. Why?
options: Excess-property checks apply only to fresh object literals
quiz.why: A literal's extra key is unreachable through the target type and probably a typo; a variable may be used elsewhere with its full type, so only the shape is compared.

quiz.q: What makes an otherwise structural class type behave nominally?
quiz.why: Private members are only compatible with themselves, so nothing but the class (or a subclass) can supply them.

further_reading.title: TypeScript for Java/C# Programmers (structural type system)
TypeScript Handbook: Object Types (excess property checks)

lessons.body:
## Concept

In a **nominal** type system (Java, C#, C++) two types are compatible when their
declarations say so: same class, or a declared subclass or `implements`. In TypeScript's
**structural** system, a type is compatible with another when it has at least the
required members with compatible types. Names are only labels for shapes.

This is a direct consequence of erasure. At run time an interface does not exist and a
JavaScript object is a bag of properties, so the only thing a checker can promise about
a value is its shape. TypeScript chose to model JavaScript as it is, duck typing
included, and to check it statically.

**Where TS runs**: nowhere, strictly speaking. Browsers run the JavaScript that Vite
(esbuild) or this runner produces. Node runs `.ts` files itself by stripping types (on by
default since Node 23.6 and 22.18, stable since 24.12 and 25.2), and Deno and Bun accept
`.ts` directly by transpiling first. In every case the type checker ran earlier, in your
editor or CI, and the runtime sees the shapes only.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/C#: no `implements` needed, and two classes with the same public members are
  interchangeable. Private members bring nominal behaviour back for classes.
- C++: templates are the closest analogue, checked duck typing at compile time, but in
  TS it applies to every type, not only to template parameters.
- Go: interfaces are structural, exactly as here. Named types are not: `type Meters
  float64` cannot be passed as `Feet` without a conversion. TypeScript has no equivalent
  of Go's named types; a type alias is only another name for the same type.
- Python: `typing.Protocol` is structural typing for type checkers; TS works that way
  for every interface and object type.
- JS: you have always written duck-typed code. TS now checks that the duck has the
  members you use.

## Design notes

Lean on structure: declare the small shape a function needs next to the function (the
consumer-declared interface idea from Go), and accept any producer that has it. That
makes tests trivial, since a literal object is a valid fake. Add nominal guarantees
deliberately where mixing values is a real bug: `#private` members for classes and
branded types (lesson ts.type-level.branded) for IDs and units. And never use types
to control what leaves the process: what goes into a response or a log is decided by
code that copies fields, because a narrower type over a wider object still carries
every property.

lessons.title: typeof, instanceof and in narrowing
lessons.summary: TypeScript follows your runtime checks (typeof, instanceof, in, equality and truthiness) and narrows a union branch by branch. Each check tests exactly what JS tests: typeof null is "object", truthiness also drops 0 and "", and instanceof needs a class.

examples.title: typeof, truthiness and == null

annotations.note: Inside the if, code is a number. After the return, number can no longer reach the last line, so there code is a string. The same variable has a different type at different points: that is control flow analysis.
typeof null is "object", a JS accident the compiler models: in the object branch tags is string[] | null, so tags.length is TS18047. Arrays are "object" too; Array.isArray is the precise array check.

The naive version reports a stock of 0 as unknown, because 0 is falsy. tsc accepts both functions: truthiness is a legal narrowing, just a wrong one for numbers and strings. Objects are never falsy, so for them it is safe.

name == null is true for exactly null and undefined, which makes it the one loose comparison worth keeping. ESLint's eqeqeq rule allows it with { null: "ignore" }. An empty string passes through as a string.
The last line prints an array so the empty string stays visible as "". ilgaz becomes İLGAZ because tr-TR maps i to İ.

examples.title: instanceof for classes, in for shapes and unknown JSON

annotations.note: A class exists at runtime as a constructor with a prototype, which is what instanceof tests. Classes and built-in constructors (Date, Map, Error) can be checked this way; types that exist only for the compiler can't.

Under strict, a catch variable is unknown, which is why describe accepts unknown. instanceof narrows it step by step. Swap the two ifs and the HttpError branch never runs, because every HttpError is also an Error.
Type aliases and interfaces are erased, so instanceof has nothing to test (TS2693). "iban" in p narrows to the members that declare iban. An optional property would put a member in both branches.

v starts as unknown. typeof plus !== null gives object; "id" in v gives object and Record<"id", unknown> (TS 4.9; before that, v stayed object); typeof v.id narrows the property. Lesson 03 packages such checks into a reusable type predicate.

examples.title: Where narrowing holds, and where it stops

annotations.note: Since TS 4.4 a condition stored in a const still narrows, as long as the narrowed value is a const, a readonly property or a parameter that the function never assigns.

The assignment narrows prefix to string. The callback could run at any later time, so TS keeps the narrowing only because no assignment follows (TS 5.4). Add prefix = null after the map and prefix.trim() becomes TS18047: 'prefix' is possibly 'null'.
Since TS 5.5 the compiler infers the predicate c is string for this arrow, so filter returns string[]. Before 5.5 the result stayed (string | null)[].

No predicate is inferred for !!s: false could mean undefined or 0, so the type can't drop undefined. At runtime the 0 score really is gone, a bug the TS 5.5 release notes use as their example. Compare with !== undefined.

use_cases: Values from spreadsheets, forms and query strings that arrive as string | number
catch (e): narrow unknown to Error or to your own error classes with instanceof
Unions of object shapes you don't control and that have no tag field: narrow with in
A first pass over JSON.parse output before it reaches a type predicate or a schema validator
strengths: Ordinary JS checks drive the types: the same if does the runtime test and changes the static type, with no cast and no new variable
Narrowing follows control flow: early returns, assignments, &&, ||, ternaries and conditions stored in a const all count
The compiler models JS quirks such as typeof null === "object", turning a classic runtime bug into a compile error
weaknesses: A narrowing is only as precise as its runtime test: a truthiness check also removes 0 and "", and the compiler accepts it
instanceof needs a runtime class, so it can't test interfaces or type aliases, and it fails for objects from another realm (iframe, window)
Narrowing is local: it doesn't cross a function boundary unless you write a type predicate (lesson 03)
in proves that a key exists, not what type its value has; optional properties end up on both sides

pitfalls.title: Truthiness checks on numbers and strings
pitfalls.detail: if (qty) treats 0 as missing, and if (name) treats "" as missing. Compare with !== undefined, or use == null to exclude both null and undefined and nothing else.
pitfalls.good: qty !== undefined ? `${qty} left` : "unknown"

pitfalls.title: typeof x === "object" lets null through
pitfalls.detail: typeof null is "object". Add x !== null, or use Array.isArray when you mean an array.
pitfalls.good: if (Array.isArray(tags)) return tags.length;

pitfalls.title: instanceof across realms
pitfalls.detail: An array or Error created in another iframe or window fails instanceof Array or instanceof Error in yours, because each realm has its own constructors. Array.isArray works across realms.
pitfalls.good: Array.isArray(value)

pitfalls.title: Checking the base class first
pitfalls.detail: if (e instanceof Error) before if (e instanceof HttpError) makes the second branch dead code: every HttpError is an Error. Order the checks from the most specific class to the most general.

quiz.q: tags: string[] | null. Inside if (typeof tags === "object") { ... }, what is the type of tags?
quiz.why: typeof null is "object", so null survives the check. TS models this and reports TS18047 if you use tags.length there.

quiz.q: qty: number | undefined. Which condition is true for qty = 0?
quiz.why: 0 is falsy, so the truthiness checks treat it like undefined. Only the explicit comparison keeps it.

quiz.q: type Card = { last4: string }. Why does p instanceof Card fail to compile?
options: Card must be declared as an interface
Type aliases and interfaces are erased; instanceof needs a runtime constructor
instanceof only works on values of type unknown
quiz.why: instanceof walks the prototype chain looking for a constructor's prototype. Card has no runtime existence, so TS2693 says it only refers to a type.

quiz.q: arr: (string | null)[]. In TS 5.5 or later, what is the type of arr.filter((x) => x !== null)?
quiz.why: Since TS 5.5 the compiler infers the type predicate x is string for the arrow, and filter's predicate overload returns string[].

further_reading.title: TypeScript 4.9 release notes: unlisted property narrowing with in
TypeScript 5.5 release notes: inferred type predicates

lessons.body:
## Concept

A union type says what a value might be. Narrowing is the compiler following your runtime
checks to work out what it is on a given line. Every branch of an `if`, every early
`return` and every assignment updates the type; the handbook calls this **control flow
analysis**. The checks it understands are the ones you already write in JS:

- `typeof x === "string"` and the other `typeof` results: `"number"`, `"bigint"`,
  `"boolean"`, `"symbol"`, `"undefined"`, `"object"`, `"function"`
- truthiness (`if (x)`) and equality (`===`, `!==`, `== null`)
- `x instanceof C` for classes
- `"key" in x` for object shapes

Each narrows exactly as far as the runtime test goes, quirks included. The next lesson
covers the most useful special case, a literal tag field; lesson 03 shows how to turn
your own checks into type predicates.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: similar to pattern-matching `instanceof` (`if (o instanceof String s)`), but
  there is no new variable: `x` itself has the narrower type inside the branch. And it
  works for any union, not only along a class hierarchy.
- C/C++: no counterpart. Checking a tagged union's tag doesn't change the static type,
  and `dynamic_cast` hands you a new pointer.
- Python: the same idea as mypy or pyright narrowing after `isinstance()`. JS's `typeof`
  is much coarser than `isinstance`, and there is no runtime check for an interface.
- Go: a type switch (`switch v := x.(type)`) binds a new variable per case and works on
  interface values. TS narrows the variable you already have, for any union.
- JS: nothing changes at runtime. TypeScript reads checks you already write, and some
  classic bugs (`typeof null`, `catch` values that aren't `Error`s) now show up at
  compile time.

## Design notes

Narrowing is why idiomatic TypeScript needs few casts: write the check you'd write in JS
anyway, and the type follows it. When you own the data shape, prefer a literal tag field
over `in` checks on incidental keys (next lesson); it is more precise and survives
refactoring. When a check gets long, name it: first as a `const` (TS 4.4), then as a type
predicate (lesson 03), which is the only way to carry a narrowing across a function
boundary. Data from outside the program (`JSON.parse`, `localStorage`, `postMessage`)
starts as `unknown` and gets narrowed step by step or validated by a schema
(`ts.services.zod`), never cast.

lessons.title: Discriminated unions: the single most important pattern
lessons.summary: Give every variant of a union a shared literal tag field. The compiler then narrows the variant from the tag alone, and a switch over the tag can be checked for exhaustiveness with never.

examples.title: A run result as a discriminated union

annotations.note: status is a literal type "ok", not string. That literal is the discriminator: comparing it anywhere narrows the whole object type.
The failed variant carries an error and no rows. Impossible states like "ok with error message" or "failed with rows" are unrepresentable.
Narrowing happens on the tag alone — no type assertions, no casts. Inside case "failed", TypeScript knows error exists and rows doesn't.
The never default is a compile-time exhaustiveness check: add a variant without extending this switch and tsc refuses to build.

use_cases: API responses (ok/failed), state machines (idle/loading/ready/error), UI events
Anywhere you would otherwise have optional fields that are only sometimes present
strengths: Unlike optional-field soup (rows?: T[]; error?: string), variants document which fields belong together
switch + never catches every unhandled variant at compile time, for free
Narrowing works through any check on the tag: switch, if, ternary, destructuring
weaknesses: Requires discipline at the boundaries: network JSON needs runtime validation (zod) before you can trust the tag
Deep unions of unions can get noisy; keep variants flat where you can

pitfalls.title: Typing the tag as string instead of a literal
pitfalls.detail: status: string narrows nothing. The tag must be a literal type ('ok' | 'failed').

pitfalls.title: Optional fields instead of variants
pitfalls.detail: rows?: T[] invites checking nothing. With variants, using rows in the failed branch is a compile error.

pitfalls.title: Assertions (as) instead of narrowing
pitfalls.detail: res as FailedResult silences the compiler and lies at runtime. Narrow from the tag; assert only when you truly know more than tsc.

quiz.q: What makes a union 'discriminated'?
options: A literal-typed shared field identifies each variant
quiz.why: The literal tag is what lets control-flow analysis narrow the variant everywhere it's compared.

quiz.q: Adding a 'cancelled' variant without touching the switch — when does it break?
options: At compile time, via the never check
quiz.why: The default branch assigns the variant to never, which no type except never satisfies, so tsc errors.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A discriminated union is a union of object types that share one field — the *tag* — whose
type is a string (or number) literal unique to each variant. Checking the tag narrows the
object type: `if (r.status === "failed")` gives you the failed variant, with its fields and
nothing else.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: a tagged union (`struct { enum tag; union {…} }`) done by the type system, with the
  forgetting-to-check-the-tag bug made impossible.
- Java/Python: sealed interfaces / subclasses and instanceof; discriminated unions are the
  data-only, serialization-friendly version.
- JS: you've written this shape as plain objects with a `type` field (Redux actions). The
  difference is TypeScript checking the tag and the exhaustiveness.

## Design notes

Model a value as *exactly one variant* and make illegal states unrepresentable: a request
either has rows or an error, never both, never neither. Combined with a `never`-checked
switch, the compiler forces every consumer to grow when the union grows — this is the
frontend's equivalent of Go's "accept interfaces, return structs": a default shape for
everything that crosses feature boundaries.

lessons.title: Type guards, assertion functions, satisfies, never for exhaustiveness
lessons.summary: Beyond discriminated unions: custom type predicates teach the checker your own invariants, assertion functions throw instead of branching, satisfies validates without widening, and never catches a missed case at compile time.

examples.title: Predicates, assertions, satisfies and never

annotations.note: `shape is Circle` is a type predicate: when it returns true the checker narrows shape to Circle at every call site.
An assertion function either returns normally or throws. After a call that returned, the checker treats shape as a Circle, so the code continues without an else branch.

use_cases: Parse unknown JSON and narrow it to a tagged union before use
DOM event handlers: narrow EventTarget to HTMLInputElement
Config objects validated with satisfies while keeping literal types
strengths: Custom predicates teach the checker project-specific invariants once, then every call site narrows
never-exhaustiveness turns 'we added a variant' into a compile error at the switch, not a bug in production
satisfies validates without widening, keeping inference precise
weaknesses: A predicate can lie: the compiler trusts the runtime check it names, so the check must be tested
Assertion functions couple call sites to throw-based control flow
Chained predicates read worse than a discriminated union; prefer tagging data

pitfalls.title: Writing a predicate whose runtime check is weaker than the type
pitfalls.detail: `x is Circle` that only tests typeof x === 'object' narrows incorrectly and the compiler cannot tell. Keep the predicate next to its type and test it like any other invariant.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the never guard when a union grows
pitfalls.detail: A switch without a default: never branch compiles fine with the new variant and silently does nothing. Add the guard from day one so the next variant breaks the build instead.

quiz.q: What does `x is Circle` on a boolean-returning function do?
options: Narrows x to Circle where the function returns true
quiz.why: It is a type predicate: the checker narrows the argument in the true branch of every call site.

quiz.q: What is the point of `satisfies`?
options: It widens the value to the constraint
It validates the shape while keeping the narrower literal type
quiz.why: satisfies checks assignability without widening, so literal keys and tuple types survive.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Discriminated unions cover most narrowing, but four tools handle the rest:

- **Type predicates** (`x is T`) package a runtime check so the compiler can
  reuse it. Write once, narrow everywhere.
- **Assertion functions** (`asserts x is T`) throw instead of returning false —
  the right shape for "this is a programmer error, not a value to handle".
- **`satisfies`** checks a value against a type *without widening* it: the
  config object keeps its literal keys, so later reads stay precise.
- **`never`** in the default branch of an exhaustive switch turns a forgotten
  variant into a compile error — the check that keeps switches honest when the
  union grows.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

Java's `instanceof` narrows too, but only along class hierarchies; TS predicates
narrow along any shape you can express. Python's `isinstance` is runtime-only —
no checker learns from it unless you use `typing.TypeGuard`. C++ has no
equivalent; you cast and pray. JavaScript gives you none of this — TS adds the
whole layer on top of the same runtime. The `never` exhaustiveness trick has no
mainstream analogue: it is a static assertion that doubles as documentation.

## Design notes

Predicates shift trust from the checker to you: the compiler believes whatever
boolean you name, so the predicate's runtime logic must actually correspond to
the type — the one place in this lesson where lying is possible. That is why the
idiom pairs a predicate with a single implementation and a test, instead of
scattering ad-hoc casts.

lessons.title: Node running .ts via type stripping; erasable syntax only
lessons.summary: Node 22.18+ and 23.6+ run a .ts file directly by blanking out its type syntax with spaces: no build step, no tsconfig, no type check. Only erasable syntax survives that, which is exactly what erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc enforce.

examples.title: What Node does to a .ts file before V8 runs it

annotations.note: This file runs as it is, with no compile step. The interface and the `: City` and `: string` annotations are replaced by spaces, and the default value `upper = false` stays because it is JavaScript. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ and ı to I, giving DİYARBAKIR; plain toUpperCase() would give DIYARBAKIR.

stripTypeScriptTypes from node:module (22.13 and 23.2, a release candidate API) applies the same transformation to a string. Each output line is exactly as long as its input: the non-null `!`, the `as number` and the whole interface become spaces. Node's docs warn that its output may change between Node versions.

The stack frame names line 26 of this file. Because nothing moved, Node needs no source maps for stack traces or breakpoints. esbuild and tsc rewrite the code, so they need source maps to get the same result.
tsc reports TS2741 (property 'plate' is missing). Node never asks, so the call runs and prints "undefined Ankara". The type check is a separate step: your editor, and `tsc --noEmit` in CI.

examples.title: What Node refuses, and the erasable spelling of each

annotations.note: Each entry becomes a real file in the run's temp directory. Loading them with a dynamic import() makes every failure an exception for that file alone. A static import of enum.ts would stop the whole program before its first line ran, because modules are parsed and linked before any of them executes.

An enum makes the compiler emit an object, so Node refuses it. The as-const object plus a type with the same name gives the same `Level.Warn` at the call site. Only the value shows up in the exports below. The type was erased.

`public x` in a constructor's parameter list declares a field and assigns it, which is code the type stripper would have to write. The explicit field is erasable. A namespace with values compiles to an IIFE; a plain module is the modern namespace. A namespace holding only types is still allowed.

types.ts exports nothing at run time. `import { User }` is therefore a value import of a name that doesn't exist, and module linking fails. Node can't tell a type from a value without type information. `import type` is deleted entirely, and verbatimModuleSyntax makes tsc insist on it (TS1484).

Node resolves the specifier exactly as written: no .ts, .js or /index guessing, and no tsconfig paths. Write "./plain.ts". tsc accepts that with rewriteRelativeImportExtensions or allowImportingTsExtensions, and otherwise reports TS5097.

Plumbing for stable output: Node 22 wraps the parser's message in a code frame and Node 24 does not. Messages of other errors (here ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND) contain absolute paths, so only their code is printed.

use_cases: Scripts and small tools (migrations, data fixes, code generators, CI helpers) written in TS and run with `node script.ts`, no build step and no dev dependency
Small services and CLIs where the deployed code is the source tree, checked by `tsc --noEmit` in CI
The Node test runner (`node --test`) over .ts test files
Choosing tsconfig flags for a codebase that must also run under Vite/esbuild: erasableSyntaxOnly plus verbatimModuleSyntax keep one file valid for all of them
strengths: No build step, and unlike ts-node or tsx no package to install: Node is the only dependency, like `go run` needs only the Go toolchain
Stack traces and breakpoints point at the .ts source with no source maps, because types become spaces and nothing moves
Startup stays fast: the parser only finds and blanks out types. It doesn't check them and doesn't read tsconfig, so it never loads the whole program the way tsc does
The rules are the same erasable subset that esbuild, Vite and Deno handle without surprises, so the same file runs everywhere
weaknesses: No type check at all. Unlike `go run`, which refuses to build code with a type error, `node app.ts` runs code that tsc rejects
tsconfig.json is ignored: no paths aliases, no `target` downleveling, no JSX (.tsx files are refused)
No TypeScript inside node_modules: libraries still have to ship compiled JavaScript plus .d.ts files
Older TS codebases full of enums, namespaces and parameter properties need refactoring (or a full transpiler like tsx) before Node runs them

pitfalls.title: Treating `node app.ts` as a type check
pitfalls.detail: Node strips types without reading them. Run `tsc --noEmit` in CI and before commits; in this repo that is `npm run typecheck`.

pitfalls.title: Importing a type without `type`
pitfalls.detail: The import survives stripping, so Node looks for a runtime export that was never there and linking fails with a SyntaxError. Turn on verbatimModuleSyntax so tsc reports TS1484 at the import.
pitfalls.good: import { type User, loadUser } from "./users.ts";

pitfalls.title: Extensionless imports and tsconfig paths
pitfalls.detail: `import "./db"` and `import "@/db"` both fail with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Write the real file name, and for aliases use package.json subpath imports, which must start with #.
pitfalls.good: import { pool } from "#db"; // package.json: "imports": { "#db": "./src/db.ts" }

pitfalls.title: Expecting tsconfig's target to downlevel new syntax
pitfalls.detail: Node runs the syntax you wrote. `await using f = await open(path)` works on Node 24 but is a SyntaxError on Node 22, whatever tsconfig says. Check the oldest Node version you deploy to.

pitfalls.title: Non-erasable syntax that still compiles with tsc
pitfalls.detail: enum, namespaces with values, parameter properties, `import x = require()` and `<T>value` assertions all compile with plain tsc and fail in Node with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Set erasableSyntaxOnly so tsc reports TS1294 instead.

quiz.q: Which declaration runs under `node app.ts` unchanged?
options: const Level = { Info: "info", Warn: "warn" } as const
quiz.why: The as-const object is plain JavaScript plus an erasable `as const`. The other three make the compiler generate code, so Node throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

quiz.q: types.ts contains only `export interface User {}`. What does `import { User } from "./types.ts"` do under Node?
options: Linking fails with a SyntaxError: the module does not provide an export named 'User'
User is undefined at run time
quiz.why: Without `type`, the import is a value import. Node has no type information, so it keeps the import, and the interface left no runtime export behind.

quiz.q: Why do stack traces from a stripped .ts file point at the right line and column without source maps?
options: Node generates source maps in memory
Type syntax is replaced by spaces, so every remaining token keeps its position
quiz.why: Stripping blanks out types in place instead of rewriting code, so positions in the JavaScript V8 runs equal positions in your file.

quiz.q: A script has a type error that tsc reports. What does `node script.ts` do?
options: Prints the type error as a warning and runs
quiz.why: Node performs no type checking. Only tsc (or your editor) reports type errors.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`node app.ts` works. Since Node 23.6 and 22.18 type stripping is on by default, since
24.3 it no longer prints an experimental warning, and since 24.12 and 25.2 it is
marked stable. (It arrived behind `--experimental-strip-types` in 22.6.) Node parses
the file with a built-in TypeScript parser, replaces every piece of type syntax with
spaces, and hands the result to V8. That is all it does:

- **no type checking**: a file that tsc rejects still runs;
- **no tsconfig.json**: no `paths`, no `target` downleveling, no JSX;
- **no code generation**: only *erasable* syntax is accepted, meaning syntax that
  leaves valid JavaScript behind once it is blanked out.

The constructs that make the compiler generate code (`enum`, namespaces with values,
parameter properties, `import x = require()`) are refused with
`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`, and so is the old `<T>value` assertion syntax. tsc
5.8's `erasableSyntaxOnly` flag rejects the same set at edit time (TS1294), so your
editor tells you before Node does.

Module rules follow from "no type information, no tsconfig": a `.ts` file is ESM or
CommonJS according to the nearest package.json `"type"` (`.mts` is always ESM, `.cts`
always CommonJS), import specifiers need their real extension, type-only imports need
`import type`, `.tsx` is unsupported, and Node refuses TypeScript files anywhere under
`node_modules`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `go run main.go` compiles and type-checks; one type error and nothing runs. Node is
  the opposite: it runs first, and the check is a separate `tsc --noEmit` you have to
  wire into CI.
- Python: the closest match. CPython ignores type hints and mypy checks them separately.
  The difference is that Python keeps annotations in `__annotations__` at run time, while
  Node deletes them.
- Java: `java Main.java` (the source launcher, Java 11) compiles in memory with full type
  checking. Node does no checking and keeps no class metadata.
- JS/Node: before this, running TS meant a build step or a loader such as ts-node or
  tsx. Those are still the answer for JSX, `paths` aliases or enums; for erasable code,
  plain `node` is enough.
- C/C++: think of a preprocessor that only blanks out text, never expands anything.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  file["app.ts"] --> resolve["resolve the specifier exactly as written"]
  resolve --> nm{"under node_modules?"}
  nm -- yes --> refuse["refused"]
  nm -- no --> parse["TS parser (WebAssembly)"]
  parse --> erasable{"only erasable syntax?"}
  erasable -- no --> err["ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX"]
  erasable -- yes --> blank["types replaced by spaces"]
  blank --> v8["V8 runs the JavaScript"]
```

Node's own docs recommend TypeScript 5.8 or newer with this tsconfig, and every flag
in it mirrors one runtime rule:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
  }
}
```

- `erasableSyntaxOnly`: TS1294 on enum, value namespaces, parameter properties and `<T>x`.
- `verbatimModuleSyntax`: TS1484 when a type is imported without `type`.
- `module: nodenext`: TS2835 when a relative import has no extension.
- `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` (TS 5.7): allows `./db.ts` specifiers, and rewrites
  them to `.js` if you ever compile instead of strip.

tsc 7.0.2 reports each of these codes for the snippets in example 2.

## Design notes

Running TypeScript directly splits the toolchain into two independent jobs. Node
executes, and tsc is your test suite for types. Keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI; without it
nothing ever checks the types. Write only erasable syntax even where a bundler would
accept more. The rule costs little (literal unions instead of enums, explicit fields
instead of parameter properties, modules instead of namespaces), and in return the same
file runs unchanged under Node, esbuild, Vite, Deno and Bun, and the JavaScript that
executes is your code minus its types. The boundary is publishing: a package on npm
still ships compiled `.js` plus `.d.ts`, because Node won't strip types inside
`node_modules` and consumers may run older Node versions.

lessons.title: node:fs/promises and streams, side by side with Go equivalents
lessons.summary: The Go file-reading lesson again, in Node: readFile for the whole file, FileHandle.readLines() for constant memory, and stream.pipeline as the io.Copy that propagates errors and closes every stage. Chunks are bytes, so decode them with the stream, not one by one.

examples.title: readFile: the whole file as a Buffer, failures as rejections

annotations.note: The same output as the Go example, from the same app.log. Without an encoding readFile returns a Buffer (a Uint8Array of bytes, Go's []byte); toString("utf8") decodes it into a new string, the copy that string(data) makes in Go. The file ends with "\n", hence trimEnd() before split, where Go used TrimSpace.

There is no error return value: the promise rejects and await turns that into an exception. Under strict, `err` in catch is unknown, so it is cast to NodeJS.ErrnoException from @types/node, which Node itself never reads. Compare err.code with "ENOENT", the analogue of errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist). The message holds the absolute path and errno differs per OS, so print neither.

31 bytes, 26 characters: ğ, ı, Ş and Ç take two bytes each in UTF-8. A Buffer's length counts bytes like len() in Go; a string's length counts UTF-16 code units, which matches the character count for Turkish text but not for emoji (two units each). Node prints a Buffer as hex: 49 is "I", c4 9f is "ğ".

examples.title: Line by line with FileHandle.readLines()

annotations.note: open() is os.Open: it returns a FileHandle or rejects (ENOENT, EACCES) right here, before any reading starts.

readLines() wraps a read stream in a readline interface. The file is read 64 KiB at a time and memory stays flat however big it is, as with bufio.Scanner. Unlike Scanner, readline has no maximum line length: a file without newlines becomes one huge string.

No defer here: the read stream closes the file at end of input or on an error, and leaving the loop early (break or throw) closes it too. A FileHandle you open and never read from must be closed yourself, in finally, or with `await using` on Node 24.

Go randomizes map iteration on purpose; a JS Map always iterates in insertion order, so the output would already be deterministic. Sorting matches the Go version's output. Plain sort() compares UTF-16 code units, the right order for identifiers; for Turkish words use localeCompare with "tr" or Intl.Collator.

examples.title: Chunks, decoding and stream.pipeline

annotations.note: highWaterMark 4 forces 4-byte chunks (the default is 64 KiB) so the bug shows on a short line. Decoding each chunk alone turns a two-byte ı or ğ split across chunks into two U+FFFD characters. With real files it happens wherever a 64 KiB boundary falls inside a letter, which ASCII-only test data never catches.

With an encoding the stream decodes for you and keeps an incomplete trailing sequence until the next chunk arrives. readline and readLines() do the same. Go's Scanner can't hit this bug: it splits raw bytes at "\n", a byte that never occurs inside a multi-byte UTF-8 letter.

An async generator is a complete transform stage: it pulls a line, yields zero or more chunks, and pipeline() asks for the next line only when the file stream has accepted the output. That is backpressure. In Go the same pull happens because a Reader is read only when someone calls Read.

pipeline is Node's io.Copy with the error handling included. It connects the stages, passes along the first error, and resolves only after the write stream has finished writing errors.log, which is why the next line can read the file back.

The rejected pipeline destroyed the write stream, so no file descriptor leaks. partial.log still exists with 0 bytes, because createWriteStream had already opened and truncated it. When the target matters, write a temp file and rename it, exactly like the atomic write in the Go lesson.

use_cases: readFile: config files, templates, small JSON or CSV, fixtures in tests
open() + readLines(): logs, large exports, anything of unknown size read line by line
pipeline: copy, compress (zlib.createGzip), hash or filter data between files, sockets and HTTP bodies with backpressure and one error path
A CLI that reads stdin line by line: readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin }) takes the same loop as readLines()
strengths: Async iteration turns push-based streams into a pull loop that reads like Go's Scanner loop, and async generators make transforms plain functions
pipeline gives streams what io.Copy has: backpressure, one error, and every stage destroyed on failure
Waiting for the disk never blocks the event loop: fs promises run on the libuv threadpool, so one thread keeps serving other work in the meantime
Setting an encoding on the stream handles multi-byte UTF-8 split across chunk boundaries
weaknesses: Several API generations side by side (callbacks, *Sync, promises, streams, web streams), where Go has one io.Reader/io.Writer pair
Stream errors are 'error' events: with no listener the process crashes, and .pipe() doesn't forward them. You need pipeline() to get Go's single returned error
readline has no maximum line length; Go's Scanner stops at 64 KB with ErrTooLong instead of growing a string up to V8's limit (about 512 MiB of UTF-16, then ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG)
The libuv threadpool has 4 threads by default (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), so many slow file operations queue behind each other; goroutines have no such shared pool

pitfalls.title: Connecting streams with .pipe()
pitfalls.detail: .pipe() moves data but not errors: if the source fails, the destination stays open, and an 'error' event nobody listens to terminates the process. pipeline() forwards the error and destroys every stage.
pitfalls.good: await pipeline(createReadStream(src), createGzip(), createWriteStream(dst));

pitfalls.title: Decoding Buffer chunks one at a time
pitfalls.detail: chunk.toString() on each chunk corrupts any letter split across a boundary into U+FFFD. Pass encoding: "utf8" to the stream, use readline, or a TextDecoder with { stream: true }.

pitfalls.title: readFileSync in a server
pitfalls.detail: A *Sync call blocks the only JavaScript thread, so every other request waits for the disk. It is fine at startup or in a CLI; in request handlers use the promise API.

pitfalls.title: Relative paths resolve against process.cwd()
pitfalls.detail: They don't resolve against the script's directory, the same trap as in Go. Build paths from import.meta.dirname or new URL("./data.txt", import.meta.url) when the file ships next to the code.

pitfalls.title: Opening a FileHandle and relying on garbage collection
pitfalls.detail: Node may close an unclosed FileHandle on garbage collection and warn, and its docs say not to rely on it. Close it in finally or use `await using`.
pitfalls.bad:
const f = await open(path);
const header = await f.read(buf, 0, 16, 0);

quiz.q: You decode each chunk of createReadStream(path) with chunk.toString(). What can go wrong with Turkish text?
options: A two-byte letter split across two chunks turns into replacement characters
quiz.why: Each chunk is decoded alone, so a sequence cut in half is invalid in both halves and becomes U+FFFD. An encoding on the stream keeps the incomplete bytes for the next chunk.

quiz.q: Which is Node's counterpart of Go's `_, err := io.Copy(dst, src)`, error handling included?
quiz.why: pipeline propagates the first error from any stage and destroys the others; .pipe() forwards neither errors nor cleanup, and readFile loads everything into memory.

quiz.q: A 2 GB log has to be counted on a small VM. Which do you use?
options: open(path) and for await over readLines()
quiz.why: readLines holds one 64 KiB chunk and one line at a time. readFile would need the whole file in memory, and a 2 GB string exceeds V8's maximum string length anyway.

quiz.q: Why does the Go version sort map keys, while the Node version would be deterministic without sorting?
options: Go maps randomize iteration order; a JS Map iterates in insertion order
Both randomize; Node just happens to be lucky
quiz.why: Go deliberately randomizes map iteration. A JS Map iterates in insertion order, a guarantee of the language.

lessons.body:
## Concept

The Go lesson had two levels: `os.ReadFile` for the whole file, `os.Open` plus
`bufio.Scanner` for a constant-memory pass. Node has the same two, plus a third piece
that Go builds into `io.Reader` itself:

- `readFile(path)` returns a `Buffer` (bytes), or a string when you pass an encoding.
- `open(path)` returns a `FileHandle`; `for await (const line of handle.readLines())`
  is the Scanner loop.
- **streams** carry data in chunks between a source and a destination, and
  `stream.pipeline()` connects them with backpressure and a single error path, which is
  what `io.Copy` does in Go.

Everything here is asynchronous. `await` doesn't block a thread the way a Go read
blocks a goroutine: it hands control back to the event loop until the threadpool has
the data.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `os.ReadFile` ↔ `readFile`; `os.Open` + `bufio.Scanner` ↔ `open` + `readLines()`;
  `io.Copy`/`io.Pipe` ↔ `pipeline`; `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` ↔
  `err.code === "ENOENT"`; `defer f.Close()` ↔ `try`/`finally` (or `await using` on
  Node 24); `[]byte` ↔ `Buffer`.
- Python: `Path.read_bytes()` ↔ `readFile`; `for line in f` ↔ `readLines()`. Python's
  text mode decodes across buffer boundaries for you; Node does so only when you set
  an encoding.
- Java: `Files.readAllBytes` / `Files.lines`. Instead of an InputStream decorator
  hierarchy, Node composes stages with `pipeline` and async generators.
- C: the chunk-boundary bug in example 3 is the multibyte problem `mbrtowc` keeps
  conversion state for.
- Browser JS: `File.text()` and `File.stream()` (lesson ts.browser-dom.reading-files)
  are web streams. Node has those too (`Readable.toWeb`, `Readable.fromWeb`), but its
  fs and http APIs hand you Node streams.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  disk["app.log"] -->|"64 KiB reads on the libuv threadpool"| rs["ReadStream buffer"]
  rs -->|"for await pulls"| gen["async generator"]
  gen -->|"write; waits when full"| ws["WriteStream buffer"]
  ws --> out["errors.log"]
```

A readable stream reads ahead until its buffer holds `highWaterMark` bytes (64 KiB for
files), then stops until someone consumes. A writable stream reports "full" the same
way. `for await` and `pipeline` consume only as fast as the next stage accepts, so a
fast disk can't flood a slow network socket: that is backpressure. Without it, a
naive `on("data")` handler that writes to a slow destination buffers the whole file in
memory.

## Design notes

Same advice as in Go: keep file opening at the edge and give the logic an iterable. In
Go that is `func countLevels(r io.Reader)`. In TypeScript it is
`async function countLevels(lines: AsyncIterable<string> | Iterable<string>)`, since
`for await` accepts both kinds. Production passes `handle.readLines()` or a readline
over `process.stdin`; a test passes a plain array of strings, no file needed. Reach
for `pipeline` whenever two streams meet: it is the only form where errors and cleanup
are correct by construction. Choose `readFile` only when the size is bounded and
known.

lessons.title: A small CLI and a tiny HTTP server in Node, next to the Go version
lessons.summary: The same two programs as in the Go track: a CLI built on util.parseArgs and stdin, and an HTTP server built on node:http and fetch. The code looks alike; the runtime differs. Every Node request shares one thread, so CPU work in a handler stalls them all, and a throw in an async handler can kill the process.

examples.title: parseArgs, stdin, and an exit status from a testable main
examples.stdin:
2026-11-01T09:00:00Z INFO server started port=8080
2026-11-01T09:00:05Z WARN slow query took=1200ms
2026-11-01T09:01:10Z ERROR db connection lost
2026-11-01T09:01:12Z INFO reconnected attempts=2
2026-11-01T09:02:31Z ERROR payment failed order=111042

annotations.note: The Go idiom carried over: `func run(args []string, stdin io.Reader, stdout, stderr io.Writer) int`. Arguments and streams come in, an exit status goes out, and nothing touches process globals, so a test calls main directly instead of spawning a process.

parseArgs (node:util, stable since Node 20) parses an explicit array, like a Go FlagSet. strict is the default, so unknown options and missing values throw. Unlike Go's flag package, options may follow positionals, -min means the three short flags -m -i -n, and --json=false is an error (allowNegative enables --no-json instead).
Exit status 2 for a usage error, the convention Go's flag package follows too. The message goes to stderr; this demo prefixes it with (stderr) because only stdout is shown.

toUpperCase() is locale-independent, which is what identifiers and protocol words need. toLocaleUpperCase() with no argument uses the host's default locale, and under a Turkish locale "info" becomes "İNFO" (what toLocaleUpperCase("tr") returns), which matches no level. Go's strings.ToUpper is locale-independent as well.
The readLines() loop from the previous lesson, over stdin. It reads one line at a time, so `levels < huge.log` runs in constant memory, like a bufio.Scanner over os.Stdin.

Set process.exitCode and let the process end; don't call process.exit(), which terminates at once, even while writes to a piped stdout are still pending. Go has the mirror-image problem: os.Exit skips deferred calls. In both languages, return a status and exit in one place.

examples.title: node:http: one listener, raw URLs, and errors you must catch

annotations.note: createServer takes one listener for every request: there is no ServeMux, no patterns and no 405. Go 1.22's mux matches method and wildcard patterns and picks the most specific; in Node that is your code or a framework. Each request is a callback on the one JavaScript thread, not a goroutine of its own.

req.url is the raw request target, path plus query and still percent-encoded: /hello/Ay%C5%9Fe. Parse it with new URL against a fixed base (not the client's Host header) and decode segments yourself; Go's PathValue hands you "Ayşe" already decoded.
