No Content-Type was set, so Node sends none, where Go would sniff "text/plain; charset=utf-8".

json() from node:stream/consumers reads the whole body stream and parses it, with no size limit. A real server caps the body (Go: http.MaxBytesReader) and validates its shape (lesson ts.services.zod) instead of trusting the cast.

This catch is load-bearing. http.Server ignores the promise an async listener returns, so a throw becomes an unhandled rejection, and Node's default is to terminate the process, together with every other request in flight. Go's server recovers a panicking handler, logs it, and closes only that connection. Errors map to a status in one place: SyntaxError (bad JSON) and URIError (bad escape) give 400, anything else 500.
Port 0 on 127.0.0.1 lets the OS pick a free port, the job httptest.NewServer does in Go. listen() is asynchronous, so wait for the "listening" event before asking for the address.
fetch is built into Node 18+. /hello/%ZZ makes decodeURIComponent throw: without the catch above, that single request would have taken the whole server down.

close() stops accepting connections and, since Node 19, also closes idle keep-alive connections, so the process can exit. It does not cut requests that are still running; Go's Server.Shutdown(ctx) is the counterpart.

examples.title: One thread: what a busy handler does to every other request

annotations.note: spin is 300 ms of pure computation, a stand-in for parsing a large report, hashing or a heavy regex. The worker gets the same loop as source text because eval keeps this example in one file; a real project gives the worker its own .ts file, new Worker(new URL("./report.ts", import.meta.url)).

The output, line by line. Spinning on the event loop: /health cannot even start until /report ends, because timers, sockets and every other request share the one JavaScript thread. Awaiting I/O: the handler yields at await, and /health completes in the meantime. A worker thread: the same CPU work runs in parallel on another thread with its own event loop, and the main thread stays free. In Go all three would interleave: every request has its own goroutine, goroutines run on several OS threads, and since Go 1.14 even a tight loop is preempted.
A fresh server per strategy logs when each request starts and ends. /report signals as soon as its handler is running, then does its 300 ms of work.

The client runs in the same process, so it can only send /health once the server has handed control back to the event loop. A real client in another process would send /health right away; the request would then sit unread in the socket buffer, with the same result.

use_cases: Small CLIs and dev tools in the same language as the frontend: code generators, data fixes, release scripts
I/O-bound services (API gateways, BFFs, webhook receivers, proxies) where handlers mostly await databases and other services
Moving CPU-heavy work (image resizing, report generation, large JSON parsing) off the request thread with worker_threads
Comparing designs: the Go version of the same server is the default choice for CPU-heavy or highly concurrent services
strengths: Built-in parts are enough for small tools: parseArgs, readline, node:http and fetch need no dependencies, much like Go's flag and net/http
One thread means no data races: handler code needs no mutex around shared state (though it can change across an await), unlike Go handlers running concurrently on goroutines
Awaiting I/O is cheap: thousands of slow connections cost callbacks, not threads
Sane server timeouts by default (requestTimeout 300 s and headersTimeout 60 s since Node 18), where Go's zero http.Server has none
weaknesses: CPU work in any handler stalls every request; Go spreads handlers across all cores and preempts long-running goroutines
A throw that escapes an async handler terminates the process; Go's net/http recovers a panicking handler per connection
node:http has no routing, path parameters or 405 handling; real services add a framework, where Go 1.22's ServeMux covers most needs
No Content-Type sniffing, no decoded path values and no body size limit: more of HTTP is left to your code
A Go CLI ships as one static binary; a Node CLI needs Node installed (or a bundled single-executable application)

pitfalls.title: An async request handler without try/catch
pitfalls.detail: http.Server ignores the returned promise, so a rejected one is an unhandled rejection, which by default terminates the process. Wrap the handler body once, or use a framework that catches async errors and answers 500.

pitfalls.title: CPU-heavy work inside a request handler
pitfalls.detail: A synchronous loop, JSON.parse of a huge body, crypto.pbkdf2Sync or a catastrophic regex blocks every request and timer. Move the work to worker_threads (or a job queue), or split it into chunks that await between batches.

pitfalls.title: process.exit() at the end of a CLI
pitfalls.detail: It exits immediately, even while writes to stdout are still pending (Node's docs: pipes are asynchronous on Linux and macOS, terminals on Windows), so `mycli | grep x` can lose its last lines. Set process.exitCode and let the event loop drain.
pitfalls.good:
console.log(report);
process.exitCode = failed ? 1 : 0;

pitfalls.title: Using req.url as a path
pitfalls.detail: It is the percent-encoded request target including the query string. Compare and route on new URL(req.url, base).pathname, and decode each segment with decodeURIComponent inside a try, because a bad escape throws URIError.

pitfalls.title: toLocaleUpperCase() with no locale on flags and identifiers
pitfalls.detail: It follows the host's locale, so on a Turkish system "info" becomes "İNFO". Use toUpperCase() for identifiers and toLocaleUpperCase("tr") for Turkish text shown to people.

quiz.q: A Node handler runs a 2-second synchronous computation. What happens to a /health request that arrives during it?
options: It is served immediately on another thread
It waits until the computation finishes, like every other event
Node preempts the computation after 10 ms
quiz.why: All JavaScript in the process runs on one thread. Nothing else runs until the handler returns or awaits. Go would serve /health on another goroutine.

quiz.q: An async request listener throws and nothing catches it. What happens by default?
options: The connection is closed and the server keeps running
The rejection is unhandled and the process terminates
quiz.why: http.Server doesn't look at the listener's returned promise. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, which ends the process.

quiz.q: GET /hello/Ay%C5%9Fe reaches a node:http server. What is req.url?
quiz.why: req.url is the raw request target from the request line: path and query, still percent-encoded. Decoding is your job.

quiz.q: Why should a CLI set process.exitCode rather than call process.exit()?
options: process.exit() ends the process at once, possibly before pending stdout writes reach a pipe
exitCode is the only way to return a non-zero status
quiz.why: process.exit() terminates even while asynchronous writes are pending. With exitCode set, the process exits by itself once the event loop is empty, after the output is written.

further_reading.title: Node.js: Don't block the event loop (or the worker pool)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Both programs from the Go track, rewritten for Node. The code reads much the same;
what sits underneath differs.

- **CLI**: `util.parseArgs` parses an explicit argument array (Go: a `FlagSet`),
  `readline` over `process.stdin` reads lines (Go: `bufio.Scanner` over `os.Stdin`),
  and the exit status is set on `process.exitCode`. Put the logic in a function that
  takes argv and streams, exactly as you would write `run(args, stdin, stdout)` in Go.
- **Server**: `http.createServer` takes one listener for every request. You route on
  `new URL(req.url, base).pathname`, decode path segments, set Content-Type and catch
  errors yourself; Go's `ServeMux` and `net/http` do more of that for you.

The **runtime model** is the real difference. A Go server gives every request its own
goroutine; goroutines run in parallel on all cores and are preempted. A Node server has
one JavaScript thread and an event loop: a handler runs until it returns or reaches an
`await`, and while it computes, nothing else in the process runs. Waiting is cheap and
computing is shared. CPU work goes to `worker_threads`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `flag` ↔ `parseArgs`; `os.Exit(2)` ↔ `process.exitCode = 2`;
  `http.HandlerFunc` ↔ the request listener; `r.PathValue` ↔ your own regex plus
  `decodeURIComponent`; `httptest.NewServer` ↔ `listen(0, "127.0.0.1")`;
  `Server.Shutdown` ↔ `server.close()`. Go recovers handler panics, while an async Node
  handler that throws takes the process down.
- Java: a servlet container runs requests on a thread pool, closer to Go. Node is like
  a single-threaded Netty event loop where your handler code runs on the loop itself.
- Python: asyncio with aiohttp is the same model as Node: one thread, cooperative
  `await`, and CPU work in a process or thread pool.
- C: a `select`/`epoll` loop with callbacks, minus the manual buffer management.
- JS: the browser's event loop, with sockets in place of DOM events. The rule you know
  from the UI (don't block the main thread) applies to every client of the server.

## How it works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as client
  participant L as event loop (one JS thread)
  participant W as worker thread
  C->>L: GET /report
  L->>W: start the CPU work
  C->>L: GET /health
  L-->>C: 200 /health (the loop is free)
  W-->>L: work done
  L-->>C: 200 /report
```

The event loop runs one callback at a time: a request arriving, a timer firing, a
promise continuation. `await` ends the current callback and schedules the rest for
later, which is why the timer strategy in example 3 lets /health through. A worker
thread has its own V8 isolate and event loop. It shares no ordinary objects with
the main thread (only SharedArrayBuffer memory) and talks to it by messages (`postMessage`, or the
`exit` event used here), much like goroutines that share nothing and communicate
over a channel.

## Design notes

For a service that mostly waits on databases and other services, Node's model is
productive: one thread means no locks in handler code. Keep two rules. First, every
async handler needs a try/catch, or a framework that provides one, because an escaped
rejection ends the process. Second, CPU work above a few milliseconds per request
belongs in a worker or a job queue. If a service is CPU-bound, or needs many cores
without that bookkeeping, it is a good fit for Go, like this repo's own backend. For CLIs the choice comes down to distribution: Go ships one static
binary, while Node needs a runtime on the target machine but shares code and types with
the frontend. In both languages, write `main` as a function of argv and streams that
returns a status; that keeps the CLI testable.

lessons.title: Spread/rest and immutability
lessons.summary: Spread copies one level, so a functional update copies every object on the path to the change and shares the rest. structuredClone deep-copies data; no copy, deep or shallow, carries a class's behaviour.

examples.title: Shallow copies and the nested functional update

annotations.note: { ...c } is a new object, but its address property holds the same object as the caller's, so writing through copy.address changes the original and both lines say İzmir. Declaring Address's fields readonly turns line 24 into error TS2540, a cheap guard for data you mean to update functionally.

The functional update copies the customer and the address, the two objects on the path to the change, and shares everything else: d.tags is still c.tags. That structural sharing keeps updates cheap and is exactly what React's Object.is comparisons rely on. A changed branch gets a new reference, an unchanged one keeps its identity.

Spread defines properties left to right, so the last one wins. Put defaults first. A key that is present with the value undefined also wins; lesson ts.mental-model.tsconfig shows how exactOptionalPropertyTypes catches that.

Spread, filter and map already return new arrays. ES2023 added copying versions of the mutating methods: with(i, v) for arr[i] = v, plus toSorted, toReversed and toSpliced. The last value printed shows the original untouched.

examples.title: Rest to drop keys, spreading class instances and iterables

annotations.note: Rest collects everything not named, and tsc computes its type: the object type minus passwordHash, with no Omit to maintain. It is still a deny-list. A field added to User later, say totpSecret, flows into rest silently (see the pitfalls).

Object spread copies own enumerable properties. The getter and the method live on Price.prototype, so the copy has only amount and is not a Price. tsc models this correctly: the spread type has no methods and no getters, so the call on line 36 does not compile.

Array spread accepts any iterable. [...new Set(xs)] removes duplicates and keeps first-occurrence order; new Map([...m, entry]) is the copy-with-change for Maps. Object spread of a Map gives {}, because its entries are not properties.

.length counts UTF-16 code units (the emoji is a surrogate pair, 2 units), spread iterates code points (3). Neither counts what a reader sees: "İ".toLowerCase() without a locale is i plus U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE, two code points for one letter. The "tr" locale gives the plain i. Intl.Segmenter counts user-perceived characters.

examples.title: structuredClone vs a JSON round trip

annotations.note: Three copies of one order, then one mutation of the original. The shallow copy shares the lines array and sees qty 99; the structured clone has its own and still says 2.

A JSON round trip keeps only what JSON can express: the Date becomes an ISO string, the Map becomes {}, and the undefined property disappears. structuredClone keeps Date, Map, Set, RegExp, ArrayBuffer and typed arrays, Error types, undefined values and even cycles.
JSON.parse returns any, so viaJson.createdAt.getTime() type-checks and then throws. A deep copy through JSON loses both the runtime types and the static ones.

structuredClone does not walk the prototype chain and does not copy getters, setters or #private fields, so a class instance comes back as a plain object. Its declared signature is <T>(value: T) => T, which is why cloned is typed Money and format() compiles, then throws.
Functions (and DOM nodes) cannot be cloned at all: structuredClone throws a DOMException named DataCloneError. Data with callbacks needs a hand-written copy.

use_cases: State updates in reducers and React components: { ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }, and items.map((i) => (i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))
Merging options: { ...defaults, ...fromUser }
Removing a field for display or logging: const { passwordHash, ...rest } = user (for API responses, see the deny-list pitfall)
Snapshots of plain data: undo history, a draft copy of a form, test fixtures you are about to mutate: structuredClone
Deduplicating while keeping order: [...new Set(values)]
strengths: A copy-with-change is one expression, and structural sharing makes it cheap: unchanged branches keep their identity. Java records have no built-in copy-with-change; you call the constructor with every field again
tsc computes the types: a spread of two objects gives the merged type, and a rest pattern gives the object type minus the named keys
structuredClone is built into browsers and Node and handles Date, Map, Set, typed arrays and cycles, which a JSON round trip mangles; Python needs copy.deepcopy, Go a hand-written copy
weaknesses: Spread is shallow: each nested level needs its own spread, which gets noisy past two or three levels (normalized state or a library such as Immer are the usual answers)
Every update copies the whole object or array at that level; spreading an accumulator in a loop is quadratic
No copy carries behaviour: class instances become plain objects, and structuredClone's signature claims they don't
Immutability is a convention: readonly is compile-time and shallow, so a stray write through an alias still mutates the shared original

pitfalls.title: Mutating after a shallow copy
pitfalls.detail: The copy's nested objects are the original's. Copy each level you change, and declare the nested fields readonly so the compiler rejects the write.
pitfalls.good: const next = { ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } };

pitfalls.title: Rest as a deny-list for API responses
pitfalls.detail: Removing secrets with rest leaks every field added to the type later. For data leaving the process, list the fields you send.
pitfalls.good: return Response.json({ id: user.id, email: user.email });

pitfalls.title: Spreading the accumulator in reduce
pitfalls.detail: Each iteration copies everything collected so far: O(n²) for what should be O(n). Build the object once.
pitfalls.good: Object.fromEntries(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]))

pitfalls.title: JSON round trip as a deep copy
pitfalls.detail: Dates become strings, Map and Set become {}, undefined properties vanish, and the result is typed any. Use structuredClone for data; for class instances, give the class its own copy method.
pitfalls.good: const copy = structuredClone(order);

quiz.q: const b = { ...a }; b.address.city = "Ankara"; What happens to a.address.city?
quiz.why: Spread copies one level. b.address and a.address are the same object, and tsc only objects if city is declared readonly.

quiz.q: Which call gives an independent deep copy in which createdAt is still a Date?
quiz.why: Spread and Object.assign share createdAt (same Date object); the JSON round trip turns it into a string.

quiz.q: What do { ...defaults, ...fromUrl } and { ...fromUrl, ...defaults } differ in?
options: Which value wins for keys both define: the later spread
Only the key order of the result
quiz.why: Properties are defined left to right, so the last spread overwrites earlier ones. Defaults go first.

quiz.q: class Money { format() { ... } } — what is structuredClone(new Money())?
quiz.why: The prototype is not cloned, so format() is gone, but the lib signature returns T. The method call compiles and throws.

further_reading.title: MDN: The structured clone algorithm (what can't be cloned)

lessons.body:
## Concept

The same three dots do two jobs:

- **Spread** expands a value. In an array literal or argument list it iterates any
  iterable (`[...set]`, `Math.max(...xs)`). In an object literal it copies the source's
  own enumerable properties (`{ ...defaults, ...overrides }`, ES2018).
- **Rest** collects what is left: `const { id, ...rest } = obj`, `const [head, ...tail] = xs`,
  and rest parameters.

Every copy made this way is **shallow**. The new object has new property slots, but each
slot holds the same value as before, and for objects and arrays that value is a
reference. So a functional update of nested data copies each object on the path from the
root to the change and shares everything else. That is cheap, because untouched branches
are reused, and it is what makes `prev === next` a valid "did this change?" test in React.

TypeScript types all of it. `{ ...a, ...b }` gets the merged type with later properties
winning, a rest pattern gets the object type minus the named keys, and spreading a class
instance gives a type without its methods and accessors, which matches what happens at
run time.

For a real deep copy of **data**, use `structuredClone` (an HTML platform function,
available in browsers and Node). It copies `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, typed arrays and cycles.
It throws `DataCloneError` on functions and DOM nodes, and it ignores prototypes, getters
and `#private` fields, so class instances come back as plain objects.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C++: copying a struct copies its members, and a `std::vector` member is copied deeply.
  In JavaScript every object is reached through a reference, so `{ ...outer }` behaves
  like copying a struct of `shared_ptr`s: a new outer object, the same inner ones.
- Java: object spread is a shallow `clone()` without `Cloneable`. Java records are
  immutable, but changing one field means calling the constructor with all of them; in
  TS the "wither" is `{ ...rec, field: value }`.
- Python: `{**d, "k": v}` and `[*xs, x]` are the same idea. `copy.copy` vs `copy.deepcopy`
  maps to spread vs `structuredClone`, except that `deepcopy` keeps the class of each
  instance and `structuredClone` does not.
- Go: assigning a struct copies it, nested structs included, but slices and maps inside
  still share their backing storage: the same trap, one level further down
  (go.composite.structs).
- JS: `Object.assign({}, a, b)` is the pre-ES2018 spelling. The difference: it calls
  setters on the target and can mutate an existing object; spread only defines
  properties on the new one.

## Design notes

Treat state that other code can see as immutable and update it by copying the path to the
change. Two levels of spread are readable; when updates need four, the data is usually
nested more deeply than it should be. Normalize it (an `entities` map keyed by id instead
of arrays inside arrays) before reaching for a helper library. Annotate the shapes with
`readonly` (lesson ts.everyday-types.objects) so a mutation of shared data is a compile
error rather than a code-review finding.

Keep deep copies for the places that need a snapshot: undo stacks, a draft of a form the
user may cancel, data handed to a worker (`postMessage` uses the same structured clone
algorithm). Copying "just in case" hides ownership questions and costs time on every
call. Classes are where copying gets awkward. If instances must be copied, give the class
a method that returns a new instance (`withAmount(n)`), because neither spread nor
`structuredClone` will produce one.

lessons.title: Classes: #private vs private, readonly, abstract, parameter properties
lessons.summary: `#private` is enforced by the JavaScript engine; `private`, `protected`, `readonly` and `abstract` are compile-time checks that vanish. Parameter properties generate code and interact badly with field initializers, so erasable code declares fields explicitly.

examples.title: private vs #private, and when a class is nominal

annotations.note: Two kinds of private. `private pin` is a TypeScript modifier: tsc checks it, the transpiler deletes it, and pin is an ordinary property. `#balance` is a JavaScript private field (ES2022): not a property at all, so no bracket access, JSON, Object.keys or Proxy can reach it. For targets below ES2022, tsc emulates it with a WeakMap.

`#balance in x` (ES2022, supported since TS 4.5) is true only for objects this class's constructor initialized, so unlike instanceof it can't be fooled by Object.create(Account.prototype) or a copied prototype. tsc narrows x to Account after the check.

The private modifier rejects acc.pin, but the handbook deliberately allows acc["pin"] (an escape hatch for tests), and at run time pin shows up in JSON.stringify, Object.keys and every log line. #balance shows up nowhere; only the getter exposes it.

A private or #private member makes a class nominal: no object literal can provide it, so the look-alike is rejected. With only `private pin` the message would be "Property 'pin' is private in type 'Account' but not in type ...". Two different classes with the same private member are not interchangeable either.

Without private members a class is just a shape, compared structurally like any type. tsc accepts the literal as a Point, but instanceof says false. A function that takes a Point and branches on instanceof will misjudge well-typed callers.

examples.title: Parameter properties and initialization order

annotations.note: `constructor(private readonly id: string)` declares a field and assigns it, so the transpiler must write `this.id = id` that isn't in your source. That is why erasableSyntaxOnly (TS 5.8) reports TS1294 and Node's type stripping refuses the file. tsc also reports TS2729 on the label initializer; @ts-expect-error silences it so the program runs.

Fields are initialized in declaration order before the constructor body runs, and the parameter property is assigned in the body, so label reads undefined. This is define semantics (useDefineForClassFields), the default for target ES2022 and later. With an older target tsc moved initializers after the parameter assignments and this printed "Fatura 2026-001": the same source changes behaviour when the target is raised.

The erasable spelling: a #private field for the state, a readonly field assigned in the constructor, and a getter that exposes id without a setter. Every line that runs is in the source, in the order it runs.
readonly fields may be assigned in their declaration or in the constructor, nowhere else. A get accessor without a set is read-only as well; both writes are TS2540.

readonly is erased. Object.assign's signature does not check it, and at run time label is a plain writable property, so the write succeeds. The #id field can't be reached this way; Object.freeze(this) at the end of the constructor would block the label write too.

examples.title: Abstract classes vs an interface and a function

annotations.note: Template method: export() is the fixed algorithm, header() and row() are the steps that vary. Abstract members have no body and must be implemented by every concrete subclass. protected, like private, is checked by tsc only.
override is optional when implementing an abstract member. Under noImplicitOverride (TS 4.3) it is required when replacing a concrete method (TS4114), so writing it everywhere keeps the rule simple.

tsc refuses to instantiate the abstract class and lists every missing member of an incomplete subclass. The abstract keyword is erased: at run time Exporter is an ordinary class, and plain JavaScript could call new on it.

The same variation point as data: an interface for the shape and a function for the algorithm. Any object literal fits, there is no this to lose and no base class to read. Most TypeScript code takes this route, and tests just pass a different object.
The real value of override: if the base method is renamed, every subclass that still says override fails to compile instead of silently becoming a new, never-called method.

Classes exist at run time, interfaces don't. When code must ask "what is this value?" at run time (Error subclasses, values from another module), a class gives instanceof; an interface needs a discriminant property or a type guard.

use_cases: Many instances that share behaviour and guard an invariant: Money, a date range, a tokenizer with internal state, a rate limiter, a connection pool
Runtime identity: Error subclasses checked with instanceof
Platform contracts that require a class: custom elements (extends HTMLElement), React error boundaries
A fixed algorithm with a few varying steps that need shared protected state (template method)
strengths: #private is enforced by the engine: no reflection, bracket access or JSON can reach it, unlike TS private, Python's _name convention or Java private fields opened by reflection
Methods live once on the prototype, and instanceof works, which plain object types can't offer
readonly, abstract, override and protected are checked at compile time and cost nothing at run time
A private member makes a class type nominal exactly where you want it: no object literal can pass as an Account
weaknesses: private, protected, readonly and abstract exist only for tsc; JSON, Object.keys, bracket access and plain JavaScript callers ignore them
Parameter properties and field initializers interact through initialization order, and the outcome depends on target and useDefineForClassFields
Methods passed as callbacks lose this (lesson ts.functions.higher-order); objects of functions don't have that problem
Inheritance couples subclasses to base-class internals, and instances don't survive JSON, structuredClone or postMessage as instances

pitfalls.title: Treating private as secret
pitfalls.detail: A private field is an ordinary property at run time: it is logged, serialised and reachable with brackets. Use #private for anything that must not leak or be tampered with.
pitfalls.good: class Session { #token = ""; }

pitfalls.title: Field initializers that read parameter properties
pitfalls.detail: Under define semantics (target ES2022+) fields are initialized before the constructor body assigns parameter properties, so the initializer sees undefined. tsc reports TS2729; the erasable style avoids the trap entirely.
pitfalls.bad: class Invoice { label = `Fatura ${this.id}`; constructor(private id: string) {} }
pitfalls.good: class Invoice { readonly label: string; constructor(id: string) { this.label = `Fatura ${id}`; } }

pitfalls.title: Redeclaring an inherited field to narrow its type
pitfalls.detail: With define semantics a field declared in a subclass is re-initialized after super() returns, overwriting what the base constructor stored. tsc reports TS2612; `declare` narrows the type without emitting a field.
pitfalls.bad: class DogHouse extends AnimalHouse { resident!: Dog; }
pitfalls.good: class DogHouse extends AnimalHouse { declare resident: Dog; }

pitfalls.title: instanceof on a structurally typed class
pitfalls.detail: A class without private members accepts any object of the same shape, so instanceof can be false for a well-typed value. Discriminate with a kind property, or give the class a #private brand.

quiz.q: Which field is missing from JSON.stringify(obj) and Object.keys(obj)?
quiz.why: A #private field is not a property, so nothing that enumerates properties sees it. private is erased and leaves an ordinary property.

quiz.q: class A { label = `x${this.id}`; constructor(private id: string) {} } with target ES2022. What is new A("1").label?
quiz.why: Field initializers run before the constructor body, where the parameter property is assigned.

quiz.q: Why does erasableSyntaxOnly reject constructor(private id: string)?
options: private is not allowed on constructor parameters
It generates a field and an assignment, so deleting the types is not enough
Parameter properties are deprecated in TypeScript 6
quiz.why: Erasable syntax can be removed without changing behaviour; a parameter property has runtime effects the transpiler must generate.

quiz.q: class Point { x = 0; y = 0 } — does const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 } compile, and is p instanceof Point?
quiz.why: Classes are compared structurally unless they have private members, but instanceof checks the prototype chain at run time.

further_reading.title: react.dev: Component (error boundaries still need a class)

lessons.body:
## Concept

A TypeScript class is a JavaScript class plus annotations, and the annotations split into
two groups that behave very differently:

- **JavaScript features** survive into the running code: fields, methods, accessors,
  `static`, `extends`, and **`#private`** fields and methods (ES2022). A `#name` is a
  private slot the engine enforces; outside the class body it is a syntax error, and no
  reflection reaches it.
- **TypeScript modifiers** are checked by tsc and then erased: `private`, `protected`,
  `public`, `readonly`, `abstract`, `override`, `implements`. At run time a `private` field
  is a normal property, a `readonly` one is writable and an abstract class can be
  instantiated.

**Parameter properties** (`constructor(private readonly id: string)`) are the odd one
out: TypeScript-only syntax that generates a field and an assignment. They are not
erasable, which is why `erasableSyntaxOnly` and Node's type stripping reject them, and
they run at a surprising point in the initialization order.

That order, with define semantics (the default for target ES2022 and later): base class
fields, base constructor, then the derived class's fields in declaration order, then the
derived constructor body. A field initializer therefore can't see anything the constructor
body assigns.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `private` in TS is closer to a lint rule than to Java's access control, and even
  Java's can be opened by reflection. `#private` is stronger than both. Classes are
  structural unless they have private members, so `implements` is optional: any object
  with the right shape satisfies an interface.
- C++: no multiple inheritance, no destructors (memory is garbage collected), and every
  method is dispatched dynamically, like a virtual function. An abstract method is a pure
  virtual function; `override` is the same keyword with the same purpose.
- Python: `_name` is a convention like TS `private`; `__name` mangling is still reachable.
  `#name` is real privacy. Python's dataclass fields are initialized in `__init__`; JS
  fields are initialized before the constructor body.
- Go: no classes or inheritance. A struct with methods plus an implicitly satisfied
  interface is what most TS code achieves with plain objects and interfaces. Go's
  unexported fields are package-private and enforced by the compiler, roughly between TS
  `private` and `#private`.
- JS/React: classes are the same as in JavaScript. React recommends function components;
  error boundaries are the remaining case that needs a class component.

## Design notes

Reach for a class when you have many instances sharing behaviour and an invariant to guard
(a `Money` that never holds a fractional kuruş, a tokenizer's position), when you need
runtime identity (`instanceof` for error types), or when a platform demands one (custom
elements, error boundaries). For everything else, plain data plus functions in a module
is simpler: module scope already hides what isn't exported, closures give privacy, and
there is no `this` to lose.

When you do write a class, write it erasably: declare fields explicitly, assign them in
the constructor, use `#private` for state that must stay inside and a getter to expose it
read-only. Turn on `erasableSyntaxOnly` and `noImplicitOverride`. Prefer composition
(pass a `Format` object) to an abstract base class unless the varying steps genuinely
need shared protected state; an interface plus a function is easier to test and has no
initialization order to get wrong.

lessons.title: ES modules: import type, verbatimModuleSyntax, barrels, path aliases, .d.ts
lessons.summary: ES modules run once, share one instance per specifier and export live, read-only bindings. Mark type-only imports with `type` so every tool emits the same code, import from the defining file instead of a barrel, and configure path aliases for both tsc and the runtime.

examples.title: import type is erased before the code runs

annotations.note: ./billing.ts does not exist in this sandbox, yet the program runs: every transpiler (esbuild here, Node, tsc) deletes an `import type`. Under verbatimModuleSyntax an import without `type` stays in the output exactly as written, and here it would fail to load.

`import type` may name a value. CURRENCIES is a const in billing.ts, and `typeof CURRENCIES` derives a union from it without loading the module; reading it at run time is TS1361. This is how one module can depend on another's types without creating a runtime import cycle.
The imported types work as usual. The tr-TR currency format puts the symbol first and swaps the separators: ₺1.250,50, and €99,00 for euros.
A per-file transpiler can't tell whether Invoice is a type or a value in billing.ts, so verbatimModuleSyntax (like isolatedModules) makes the re-export say it. `export type` is erased with the rest.

examples.title: Live bindings, one instance per specifier, read-only namespaces

annotations.note: The sandbox runs one file, but import() accepts any URL its CSP allows, including data: URLs, so a second module can be written inline. Real code imports files; the semantics are the same.

import() of a computed string is typed Promise<any>, so the interface is a description you assert, exactly like a hand-written .d.ts file: tsc trusts it and never compares it with the JavaScript. If the module changes, nothing warns you.

counter.count reads the exporting module's variable, which increment() changed: a live binding. A named import (import { count }) is live in the same way. Destructuring copied the value at that moment, which is also what CommonJS's const { count } = require() and Python's from m import count give you.

A module is evaluated once per resolved specifier, and every importer gets the same instance: one "evaluated" line, same object. Module-level state is therefore a singleton, handy for caches and a trap for tests that expect a fresh copy.

Only the exporting module can assign its bindings. The namespace object rejects writes, and modules are strict, so the write throws. Without the cast tsc refuses the line (TS2540), because the interface declares count readonly to mirror that rule.

examples.title: What a barrel costs

annotations.note: Three feature modules that log when their body runs, and a barrel that re-exports all of them with export *, which is what a typical src/shared/index.ts looks like.
Importing the defining module evaluates that module and its own dependencies, nothing else.

Importing the same function through the barrel evaluates every module the barrel re-exports, in import order, before the import resolves. In a dev server each is a separate request; Vite's performance guide recommends direct imports for this reason. money is not evaluated again, and the function is the same object.

money and charts both export VERSION, so the name is ambiguous and export * exports neither. A namespace import just lacks it; a named import { VERSION } from the barrel fails at link time with a SyntaxError. tsc reports TS2308 on the barrel. Namespace keys are listed in sorted order.

use_cases: import type for everything used only in annotations, including types from API clients imported into components
Direct imports from the defining file in application code; a barrel only as the public entry point of a package
Path aliases (@/... in tsconfig paths plus the bundler's alias, or #/... in package.json imports) instead of ../../../ chains
.d.ts files for untyped JavaScript, bundler-injected globals such as import.meta.env, and non-code imports such as *.svg
strengths: verbatimModuleSyntax makes emit predictable: an import stays or goes based on what it says, not on what another file declares, so esbuild, Node and tsc produce the same JavaScript
Imports are static and linked before any code runs, so bundlers can tree-shake and editors can rename across files; CommonJS require() can appear anywhere, with any computed string
Bindings are live and read-only: importers always see the current value and can't overwrite another module's variables, unlike Python's from m import x copy
Declaration files type existing JavaScript without touching it, the way C headers describe a compiled library
weaknesses: Aliases need two configurations that must agree: tsconfig paths for tsc and the bundler or Node mapping for the runtime; tsc never rewrites import paths
Barrels make each importer pay for every sibling module, hide name clashes from namespace imports, and make import cycles more likely
Module state is a singleton per specifier, shared by every feature and every test in the same process
A .d.ts is trusted, not verified against the JavaScript it describes; a wrong declaration is a type error waiting at run time

pitfalls.title: Inline type modifiers still load the module
pitfalls.detail: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, import { type User } from "./user" becomes import {} from "./user": the module is still fetched and evaluated. When every name is a type, put type on the import itself.
pitfalls.bad: import { type User, type Role } from "./user.ts";
pitfalls.good: import type { User, Role } from "./user.ts";

pitfalls.title: Circular imports through a barrel
pitfalls.detail: Feature A imports from "@/shared", whose barrel re-exports a module that imports A. One of them runs first and reads a const or class that isn't initialized yet: ReferenceError: Cannot access 'X' before initialization. Import from the defining file, and keep dependencies pointing one way.
pitfalls.good: import { formatMoney } from "@/shared/money.ts";

pitfalls.title: baseUrl in a TypeScript 7 tsconfig
pitfalls.detail: baseUrl is deprecated in 6.0 (TS5101) and removed in 7.0 (TS5102). paths entries resolve relative to the tsconfig file and must start with ./ (TS5090).

pitfalls.title: paths without a runtime mapping
pitfalls.detail: tsc resolves @/x, the editor is happy, and the build or Node then fails to resolve the import. Add the same alias to the bundler (Vite resolve.alias) or use package.json imports, which Node, Vite and TypeScript all understand.

quiz.q: With verbatimModuleSyntax, what does import { type User } from "./user" compile to?
options: import {} from "./user": the module still loads
quiz.why: Only the type-marked name is dropped. To drop the whole import, write import type { User }.

quiz.q: c.ts exports let count = 0 and inc(). main.ts: import { count, inc } from "./c"; inc(); console.log(count). What prints?
quiz.why: Named imports are live bindings to the exporter's variable, not copies.

quiz.q: tsconfig has "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } and tsc emits JavaScript. What does import { x } from "@/util" become?
options: It stays "@/util"; the runtime or bundler must resolve it
quiz.why: paths only tells tsc how another tool will resolve the specifier; tsc does not rewrite it.

quiz.q: A barrel has export * from "./money" and export * from "./charts", and both export VERSION. What do importers get?
options: Neither: the name is ambiguous, and tsc reports TS2308
quiz.why: Ambiguous star exports are excluded. A namespace import lacks the name; a named import of it is a link-time SyntaxError.

further_reading.title: MDN: The module graph (evaluation order, caching, cycles, export * ambiguity)
TypeScript 6.0 release notes: baseUrl deprecation, #/ subpath imports

lessons.body:
## Concept

An ES module is a file with its own scope. Its `import` declarations are hoisted and
linked before any of its code runs; its dependencies are evaluated first, depth-first in
import order; and it is evaluated **once** per resolved specifier, so every importer
shares one instance. What it exports are **live, read-only bindings**: importers see the
exporter's variables, not copies, and only the exporter can assign them.

TypeScript adds imports that carry only types. Mark them, and choose the rule with
`verbatimModuleSyntax` (TS 5.0): anything with `type` is erased, anything without it is
kept exactly as written.

```ts
import type { Invoice } from "./billing.ts";       // erased entirely
import { formatInvoice, type Invoice } from "./billing.ts"; // becomes import { formatInvoice } ...
import { type Invoice } from "./billing.ts";       // becomes import {} from "./billing.ts": still loads
export type { Invoice } from "./billing.ts";       // erased
```

Before that flag, tsc *elided* imports it decided were only used as types, which needs
knowledge of other files. esbuild, Vite and Node see one file at a time, so the source has
to say it.

Three conventions shape how modules are laid out:

- **Barrels**: an `index.ts` that re-exports a folder (`export * from "./money.ts"`).
  Shorter imports, at a price: every importer evaluates every re-exported module, clashing
  names silently disappear, and import cycles get easier to create.
- **Path aliases**: `paths` in tsconfig tells *tsc* that `@/shared/money.ts` means
  `./src/shared/money.ts`. tsc never rewrites specifiers, so the runtime needs the same
  mapping (Vite `resolve.alias`, or `imports` in package.json).
- **Declaration files** (`.d.ts`): types with no implementation. They describe JavaScript
  libraries (bundled typings or `@types/*`), globals and non-code imports, and `tsc
  --declaration` emits them for libraries you publish.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: a `.d.ts` is a header: declarations the compiler trusts, for code compiled
  elsewhere. There is no preprocessor and no include-once guard to write; the module map
  guarantees one evaluation per specifier.
- Java: a module is closer to a file-level class with static members than to a package.
  Imports name files, not namespaces, and `import type` has no Java equivalent because
  Java's types exist at run time.
- Python: modules are also evaluated once and cached, but `from m import x` copies the
  binding, while an ES named import stays live. Python's circular imports fail with a
  partially initialized module; ES ones fail with a ReferenceError for `let`, `const`
  and `class`.
- Go: a Go package is a directory and every file in it shares one namespace; a TS module
  is a single file. Go forbids import cycles at compile time; JavaScript allows them and
  fails at run time. A barrel is roughly a package's exported API, which Go gets without
  a separate file.
- JS: CommonJS `require()` is an ordinary function call that returns the `module.exports`
  object, and `const { count } = require("./c")` copies values out of it. ESM imports are
  static declarations with live bindings, and ES modules allow top-level `await`.

## How it works

A feature folder and the configuration that makes `@/` work everywhere:

```ts
// src/shared/money.ts
export const CURRENCIES = ["TRY", "EUR", "USD"] as const;
export function formatMoney(n: number): string { /* ... */ }

// src/shared/index.ts  (a barrel: convenient, and every importer pays for all of it)
export * from "./money.ts";
export * from "./charts.ts";
// error TS2308: Module "./money.ts" has already exported a member named 'VERSION'. Consider explicitly re-exporting to resolve the ambiguity.

// src/features/billing/invoice.ts
import { formatMoney } from "@/shared/money.ts"; // direct: loads money.ts only
import type { Customer } from "@/features/customers/types.ts"; // erased
```

The tsconfig has no `baseUrl` (removed in TypeScript 7.0), and `paths` entries start with
`./` because they resolve relative to the tsconfig file:

```json
{ "compilerOptions": { "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } } }
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts: the same mapping for the bundler
resolve: { alias: { "@": fileURLToPath(new URL("./src", import.meta.url)) } }
```

This repo's `tsconfig.app.json` and `vite.config.ts` configure exactly this pair. The
runtime-native alternative is a subpath import in package.json, `"imports": { "#/*":
"./src/*" }`, used as `import { formatMoney } from "#/shared/money.ts"`. Node supports
the `#/` prefix since 24.14 and 25.4 (older versions need a name such as `#src/*`),
and TypeScript 6.0 resolves it under `moduleResolution` `nodenext` and `bundler`.

A declaration file in an app usually extends what the platform gives you:

```ts
// src/vite-env.d.ts in this repo: pulls in Vite's types for import.meta.env and asset imports
/// <reference types="vite/client" />

// a hand-written one for an untyped script
declare module "legacy-chart" {
  export function draw(el: HTMLElement, values: readonly number[]): void;
}
```

## Design notes

Turn on `verbatimModuleSyntax` and write `import type` whenever a whole import is types;
the `type` modifier inside braces is for mixed imports. The output then contains exactly
the imports you wrote, which keeps side effects and load order visible.

Import from the file that defines a thing. Keep barrels for the public surface of a
package that other packages consume, where one entry point is the point; inside an app,
a barrel per folder mostly buys import cycles and slower dev reloads. Choose one alias
scheme (`@/` with tsconfig plus bundler, or `#/` in package.json), configure it in every
tool that resolves imports, and make dependencies point one way: features import shared
code, never the reverse (lesson ts.architecture.folders).

Treat module-level `let` and singletons as global state with a module-shaped name. They
are shared by everything that imports them, survive between tests in the same worker,
and can't be reset from outside. Export functions that take their state as parameters,
or a factory, instead.

lessons.title: Typed components and props: children, ComponentProps
lessons.summary: A component is a function of one typed props object, and children is just another prop. Extend native elements with ComponentPropsWithoutRef and derive prop types from the types you already have instead of copying fields.

examples.title: Props, children and native button props

annotations.note: ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button"> is the prop type JSX itself uses for `<button>`, minus `ref`. The wrapper accepts onClick, disabled, aria-* and form without listing them, and stays in sync with @types/react. Why not ComponentProps: in React 18 a function component never receives `ref` (that needs forwardRef), so a type that allows it would accept a ref React then drops.

Take what you handle, forward the rest. The default `type="button"` matters: a native button's default type is submit, so a reusable button placed in a form would otherwise submit it. Default parameters replace `defaultProps`, which React 19 removed for function components.

children is an ordinary prop with a special JSX syntax. ReactNode is everything React can render: strings, numbers, elements, arrays, null, undefined and booleans. footer is a second slot: any ReactNode prop works like children.

toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ: SİPARİŞ. Plain toUpperCase() gives SIPARIŞ. For purely visual capitals, CSS `text-transform: uppercase` under `lang="tr"` applies the Turkish rule without touching the text (browser support varies).
A boolean on the left of &&, so 0 warnings renders nothing. The output has no `<strong>`.

The last output line is `

0

`. && returns its left operand when it is falsy, and React renders the number 0 (it skips only false, true, null and undefined). react.dev lists it as a pitfall of conditional rendering.
Both mistakes fail at compile time. Without the type, the second one is a runtime crash: React throws "Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {id})".

examples.title: Derive props instead of duplicating them

annotations.note: One declaration of the domain shape, ideally generated from the API contract. Everything below derives from it.

Pick<User, "name" | "city"> keeps the link to User: rename city to town and tsc flags this component. A hand-written `{ name: string; city: string }` would compile and drift. Being structural, any object with those two fields fits, test data included.

ComponentProps<typeof UserBadge> reads a component's props type, which also works for library components that don't export theirs. The intersection adds one prop; rest destructuring forwards the others.
Mutually exclusive props are a discriminated union on kind. Inside the if, props.href exists; after it, only onClick does. No optional href plus optional onClick plus a runtime "exactly one" check.
onClick never shows in the HTML: event handlers are attached by React on the client, not serialized as attributes.
Mixing the variants is a compile error that names the offending prop.

use_cases: Design-system primitives (Button, Input, Link) that wrap a native element and forward everything else with `...rest`
Layout components with slots: `children` plus named ReactNode props such as `footer`, `actions`, `aside`
Components fed by API types: `Pick<User, ...>` or `Omit<User, ...>` so a contract change surfaces in every consumer
Components with mutually exclusive modes (link vs button, controlled vs uncontrolled) as discriminated-union props
strengths: Unlike PropTypes (runtime warnings, ignored since React 19), prop types are checked at every call site at compile time, and JSX is just a typed function call
ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button"> gives a wrapper the full native API in one line, so aria-* and data-* attributes keep working without a whitelist
Derived types (Pick, ComponentProps<typeof X>) turn a renamed field into compile errors at every use, where copied fields in Java DTOs drift silently
Composition through children and slot props replaces the inheritance hierarchies of Swing or Android views
weaknesses: ReactNode is broad: you can't express 'only `<li>` children' in the type system (react.dev says so), so structural rules stay conventions
Error messages for union props and intersections with IntrinsicAttributes are long; the useful line is usually the last one
The ref story differs by version: React 18 needs forwardRef, React 19 makes ref a regular prop, and types written for one are subtly wrong for the other

pitfalls.title: Numbers on the left of &&
pitfalls.detail: `count && <Badge />` renders 0 when count is 0. Make the left side a boolean.
pitfalls.good: {items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />}

pitfalls.title: ComponentProps<"button"> on a React 18 function component
pitfalls.detail: The type includes `ref`, so `<Button ref={r}>` compiles, but React 18 drops the ref with a 'Function components cannot be given refs' warning and r.current stays null. Use ComponentPropsWithoutRef, or forwardRef when callers need the DOM node.

pitfalls.title: React.FC and implicit children
pitfalls.detail:
In @types/react 18 (this app's version), `FC

` does not add children. `text` is a compile error unless P declares `children: ReactNode`. Plain functions with a typed props parameter are the simpler default.

pitfalls.title: Copying fields into props interfaces
pitfalls.detail: A props interface that repeats `name: string; city: string` from a domain type will drift. Pick, Omit and ComponentProps<typeof X> keep the dependency visible to tsc.

quiz.q: React 18. `function Button(props: ComponentProps<"button">)` is rendered as `<Button ref={r} />`. What happens?
options: tsc accepts it and r.current is the button
tsc accepts it, React drops the ref and warns
quiz.why: ComponentProps<"button"> includes ref, but a React 18 function component only gets a ref through forwardRef. ComponentPropsWithoutRef makes the same line a compile error.

quiz.q: `{items.length && <List items={items} />}` with an empty array renders...
quiz.why: && returns its falsy left operand, 0, and React renders numbers. false, null, undefined and true render nothing.

quiz.q: Which type accepts a string, a number, an element, an array of elements and null as children?
quiz.why: ReactNode is the union of everything renderable; ReactElement is JSX elements only.

quiz.q: Why `Pick<User, "name" | "city">` instead of `{ name: string; city: string }`?
options: A change to User reaches the component and tsc flags what breaks
React requires prop types to be named
quiz.why: Types are erased, so there is no runtime difference. The derived type keeps the dependency on User visible to the compiler.

further_reading.title: React: Passing props to a component

lessons.body:
## Concept

A React component is a function that takes **one** argument, the props object, and returns
something React can render. Typing a component means typing that object: an `interface`
or `type`, destructured in the parameter list. JSX is a function call in disguise
(`<Card title="x">` compiles to `jsx(Card, { title: "x" })` with `"jsx": "react-jsx"`), so
the compiler checks every prop at every call site, including `children`, which is just a
prop that JSX fills from between the tags.

Three types do most of the work:

- `ReactNode` for anything renderable: `children`, and named slots like `footer`.
- `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button">` (and the other intrinsic element names) for components
  that wrap a native element and forward the rest with `...rest`.
- `ComponentProps<typeof SomeComponent>` to reuse the props of a component you already
  have, including library components that don't export a props type.

The goal is that props are **derived**: from domain types with `Pick`/`Omit`, from other
components with `ComponentProps`, from native elements with the intrinsic element types.
A field is declared once; everything else references it.

The examples use React 18.3, this app's version. React 19 changes two things here: `ref`
becomes a regular prop for function components (no `forwardRef`), and `defaultProps` and
`propTypes` for function components are gone.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java (Swing, Android views):** no class hierarchy, no `extends JButton`. A component is
  a function re-run with new props; `interface ButtonProps extends
  ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button">` extends a *type*, not the DOM element. Customization
  is composition: pass elements in through `children` and slot props.
- **C++:** think of props as a `const` parameter struct. The component must not modify it;
  React relies on that when it decides what to re-render.
- **Python:** like a function with keyword-only arguments typed by a `TypedDict`;
  `children` is one more keyword that the JSX syntax fills in for you.
- **JS/React:** you know the runtime. What's new is that a missing or misspelled prop is a
  compile error instead of a PropTypes console warning, and that "objects are not valid as
  a React child" is caught before the page loads.
- **Go:** `html/template` checks fields when the template executes; a typed component is
  checked when it is compiled. Go's habit of small interfaces declared by the consumer is
  the same idea as `Pick<User, "name" | "city">`: ask for exactly what you use.

## Design notes

Props are the public API of a component, so treat them like a function signature: as
narrow as the job, derived from the source of truth, plain data and callbacks rather than
service objects. This app's `src/shared/ui/LevelBadge.tsx` is a small example: its prop is
`{ level: Level }`, where `Level` is a union the badge declares itself (the curriculum's
identical one is assignable), and its style table is a `Record<Level, string>`, so a
fourth level is a compile error at every call site until the badge handles it.
`src/features/runner/RunPanel.tsx` types its props inline
(`{ example: RunnableExample; onRan: () => void }`), which is fine for a component nobody
wraps; the example's shape is a named, exported interface because the lesson page builds
one from a lesson.

For wrappers of native elements, forwarding `...rest` beats whitelisting props: a
whitelist silently drops `aria-describedby`, `id` or `form` and breaks accessibility in
ways no test of the happy path notices. Pick `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` on React 18 and add
`forwardRef` only when callers need the DOM node (focus management, measuring). Generic
components (`List<T>` with a typed render function) are the next step; they are covered in
the generics module.

lessons.title: useState and useReducer with discriminated unions
lessons.summary: State is a snapshot per render that you replace, never mutate. Model it as one discriminated union instead of independent flags, and move the transitions into a reducer when they need rules: impossible states then fail to compile.

examples.title: State is a snapshot: updater functions, and why mutation is invisible

annotations.note: useState infers number from 0. For an empty array it would infer never[], so the type argument string[] is needed there; with a union state, write the union as the type argument.
count is a constant of this render: the handler closed over 0. All three calls request "set to 1", so the first output line says count=1. Calling a setter never changes the variable in running code.
An updater function receives the pending state, so the three updates chain: count=4. Use the updater form whenever the next state is computed from the previous one, and always in async code.
push changes the array React already holds, then setTags passes the same reference. Object.is sees no change and React skips the re-render: the "mutate" line shows tags=go.

A new array re-renders, and the "sql" pushed earlier appears too: the mutation was real, only invisible. Mutation bugs surface later, in an unrelated update, which is what makes them expensive to find.
The harness: flushSync applies each click's updates before the next line reads the DOM. In application code you don't need it; React batches all updates of one event and re-renders once afterwards.

examples.title: One union-typed state instead of independent flags

annotations.note: A boolean and two optionals allow eight combinations, most of them nonsense. The union allows exactly four, and each one carries only the data that exists in it.
The guard reads this render's snapshot. The second click of a double click runs the handler of the re-rendered component, which sees "sending" and returns, so the server gets one request, not two.
Rendering switches on the tag. Inside case "failed" TypeScript knows state.error is a string; in any other case accessing it is a compile error, so no `error && ...` checks are needed.

Harness plumbing. The server answers asynchronously, so show() waits until the expected text is on screen, like Testing Library's findByText, instead of guessing how many event-loop turns React needs.
Three clicks, two requests: the double click was absorbed while sending, the retry after the failure was allowed.

examples.title: useReducer: every transition in one pure, testable function

annotations.note: State and actions are both discriminated unions. attempt lives only in the variants where it means something, and travels from failed to the next sending.

Each case first checks that the transition is legal from the current state, otherwise it returns the same object. The declared return type Submit doubles as an exhaustiveness check: add an action variant without a case and tsc reports TS2366 "Function lacks ending return statement".
After the guard, s is the sending variant and a is the succeed action: orderNo comes from the action because the state doesn't have one yet, and the compiler knows it.
No React needed to test the machine: fold a script of actions through the function. Returning the same object for an ignored action matters in React too: Object.is equality means no re-render.

useReducer infers state and action types from the reducer. dispatch has a stable identity, and a malformed action is a compile error. Two clicks still show "sending": the reducer, not the button, enforces the rule.

use_cases: Request lifecycles (editing, sending, failed, done) where each phase carries different data
Wizards and multi-step flows: the step and the data collected so far in one value
Components whose handlers all need the same rules (no submit while sending, no retry after success): a reducer keeps those rules in one place
Logic you want to unit-test without rendering: a reducer is a pure function of (state, action)
strengths: Unlike a bag of booleans, a union makes 'sending with an error' unrepresentable, and narrowing gives each branch exactly its fields
A reducer is a pure function: test it with plain calls, no DOM, no mocks, unlike a Java controller whose state lives in fields mutated by handlers
Replacing state instead of mutating it makes change detection a reference comparison (Object.is), which is what lets React skip work cheaply
dispatch has a stable identity, so passing it down or listing it in effect dependencies costs nothing
weaknesses: Updating nested immutable data by hand is verbose (spreads several levels deep); flatten the state or use a helper library if it hurts
A reducer adds indirection: for one or two independent values useState reads better
The snapshot model surprises newcomers: logging state right after setState prints the old value
Strict Mode calls reducers and updater functions twice in development, so any side effect inside them shows up doubled

pitfalls.title: Mutating state and passing the same reference
pitfalls.detail: React compares with Object.is and skips the update. Create a new array or object.
pitfalls.good: setTags([...tags, "ts"]);

pitfalls.title: Reading state right after setting it
pitfalls.detail: The variable belongs to the current render. Compute the next value into a local and use that.

pitfalls.title: Boolean flags that can contradict each other
pitfalls.detail: isLoading, isError and data as three useState calls allow states your UI can't render sensibly. One union-typed state cannot contradict itself.
pitfalls.good: const [state, setState] = useState<Submit>({ status: "editing" });

pitfalls.title: Side effects in reducers or updater functions
pitfalls.detail: They must be pure. Strict Mode calls them twice in development and keeps one result, so a request sent from a reducer goes out twice. Do I/O in the event handler, then dispatch the outcome.

quiz.q: count is 5. A click handler calls setCount(count + 1) twice. What does the next render show?
quiz.why: Both calls compute 5 + 1 from the same snapshot. setCount(c => c + 1) twice would give 7.

quiz.q: A handler does items.push(x); setItems(items). What happens?
options: React re-renders with the new item
React skips the re-render because the reference is the same
quiz.why: Object.is(items, items) is true, so React treats it as no change. The pushed item appears only when something else re-renders.

quiz.q: Why does the reducer return the same state object for an illegal transition instead of a copy?
options: The same reference tells React nothing changed, so it can skip the re-render
quiz.why: A copy would be a new reference and trigger a render with identical content. Returning state unchanged is the reducer's 'no-op'.

quiz.q: A reducer is typed (s: Submit, a: Action): Submit and switches on a.type with a return in every case. You add { type: "cancel" } to Action. What happens?
options: Nothing until a cancel action is dispatched
tsc reports that the function lacks an ending return statement
The reducer returns undefined silently in production only
quiz.why: The unhandled variant makes the end of the function reachable, and undefined isn't a Submit. A `const x: never = a` default branch gives the same guarantee with a clearer message.

further_reading.title: React: Extracting state logic into a reducer

lessons.body:
## Concept

`useState` gives a component a value that survives re-renders and a setter that
**requests** a new render with a new value. Three rules follow from that:

- The value is a **snapshot**: every render has its own constant `count`, and handlers created
  in that render see that constant forever. Calling the setter doesn't change it.
- Setters can take an **updater function** (`c => c + 1`); React queues them and applies them
  in order to the pending state.
- React decides whether anything changed with `Object.is`. **Replace** objects and arrays;
  mutating them and passing the same reference is ignored.

For anything with phases, type the state as **one discriminated union** rather than several
independent `useState` calls. `{ status: "failed"; error: string }` cannot also be
"sending", and only the failed branch can read `error`. When the transitions start to have
rules ("send is allowed from editing or failed, nothing else"), move them into a **reducer**:
`useReducer(reducer, initial)` keeps the state, and `reducer(state, action)` is a pure
function that returns the next state, or the same object when the action doesn't apply.
Actions are a discriminated union too, so a misspelled or incomplete action doesn't compile.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/C++:** there are no fields to assign. State lives in React, the component reads a
  copy per render. Think of an immutable value object you replace wholesale, not a bean you
  call setters on.
- **C:** the reducer is the classic `switch (state) { case ...: }` state machine, with the
  tagged union checked by the compiler instead of by convention.
- **Python:** like a frozen dataclass you rebuild with `dataclasses.replace`; mutating it in
  place is the bug.
- **JS/Redux:** a `useReducer` reducer is a Redux reducer scoped to one component, without the
  store, middleware or action-creator boilerplate. The typed action union replaces string
  constants.
- **PostgreSQL:** the snapshot idea is close to MVCC: a handler sees the state of the render
  it came from, as a REPEATABLE READ transaction sees its snapshot, and a new render is the
  next snapshot.

## Design notes

Ask "which combinations of my state variables are legal?" If the answer is "fewer than all
of them", the variables belong in one union. Derive everything else during render instead
of storing it: this app's `LessonQuiz` (`src/features/learning/LessonQuiz.tsx`) stores only
the chosen answers and computes the score on every render, so the two can never disagree.
The same file keeps `answers` and a separate `loaded` flag; a union such as
`{ phase: "loading" } | { phase: "ready"; answers: Answers }` would make "answers shown
before they loaded" unrepresentable.

`useState` versus `useReducer` is not about size but about where the rules live. Keep
`useState` while every update is "set this value". Switch to a reducer once several handlers
must agree on what is allowed; the reducer is then the single place to read the state
machine and the obvious unit to test. Keep I/O out of it: the handler calls the server and
dispatches what happened. Server data itself (lists, caches, refetching) is a different
kind of state with a better tool, covered in the TanStack Query lesson.

lessons.title: Effects and cleanup (and when you don't need an effect); custom hooks; context
lessons.summary: An effect keeps a component synchronized with something outside React, and its cleanup undoes exactly what its setup did. Values computed from props belong in render, not in an effect. Custom hooks share logic; context injects values down the tree.

examples.title: Setup, cleanup and Strict Mode's extra cycle

annotations.note: The external system: a socket, a timer, a map widget, a subscription. Effects exist for exactly this; if nothing outside React is involved, you probably don't need one.

Setup connects, the returned function disconnects. The dependency array [room] means "re-synchronize when room changes": React compares each dependency with Object.is and skips the effect otherwise, which is why the second render of #genel logs nothing.

StrictMode is on, as in this app's src/main.tsx. In development React runs one extra setup and cleanup cycle before the real setup, to prove the cleanup mirrors the setup: connect, close, connect. Production connects once.

On a dependency change the old cleanup runs first, with the old room, then the new setup. Unmount runs the last cleanup. The order is the contract: never two connections at once. In this runner the effects of a flushSync render run before it returns, which keeps the log in order; in a browser an effect not caused by an interaction generally runs after paint.

examples.title: You might not need an effect: derive during render

annotations.note: toLocaleUpperCase("tr") makes "ilkay ışık" İI. toUpperCase() would give II, a different person's initials in Turkish.
State that copies props, synchronized by an effect. The output shows the cost: a committed render with an empty label, then a second render. The DOM briefly shows a value that was never true.
The same value computed during render: one render, correct the first time, and it can't go stale when props change. If it were expensive, useMemo would cache it; an effect never would be the answer.
Harness: flushSync commits synchronously, then one timer turn lets the update scheduled by the effect render. Printing before and after makes the extra render visible.

examples.title: Context with a guard hook, and custom hooks built on it

annotations.note: A locale has no sensible default, so the context type says Locale | null and the default is null. A fake default like "en-US" would hide a missing provider until a Turkish user saw English sorting.
The pattern react.dev recommends: one hook reads the context, throws without a provider and returns the narrowed type, so no consumer handles null.

Custom hooks are functions whose names start with use and that call other hooks; useSorted qualifies only because it calls useLocale. They run on every render as part of the calling component, and each call has its own state: they share logic, not state.

[...items] copies before sort, which sorts in place: never mutate data you received. Intl.Collator("tr-TR") puts Ç after C, Ö after O and Ş after S; English collation treats them as accented C, O and S.

The same component under two providers: tr-TR gives Ceyhan, Çanakkale and 1.249,90; en-US gives Çanakkale, Ceyhan and 1,249.90. In React 19 you may write `<LocaleContext value={locale}>` instead of `.Provider`; React 18 needs `.Provider`.
Without a provider the guard throws during render, with a message that names the fix, instead of rendering wrong data.

use_cases: Effects: WebSocket or EventSource connections, timers, third-party widgets (maps, charts, editors), browser APIs such as IntersectionObserver
No effect: derived values, filtering and sorting for display, resetting state when an id changes (use a key), reacting to a click (do it in the handler)
Custom hooks: a named piece of stateful logic used by several components, such as useOnlineStatus, useLocale or useDebouncedValue
Context: values many components need and that change rarely: locale, theme, the current user, a QueryClient
strengths: Cleanup lives next to setup in one closure, like Go's defer after acquiring a resource, instead of split across componentDidMount and componentWillUnmount
Strict Mode's development-only remount finds a missing cleanup on the first run, not in production after a route change
Custom hooks compose by plain function calls, with no mixins or higher-order component wrappers
Context removes prop drilling for cross-cutting values without a global mutable singleton, and a test can wrap a component in any provider it likes
weaknesses: Effects are easy to overuse: an effect that only sets state from props costs an extra render and can show stale values
Dependency arrays compare by reference, so objects and functions created during render re-run the effect every time
A context value change re-renders every consumer, and memo doesn't stop it; frequently changing values belong elsewhere
Fetching in effects needs hand-written race handling, caching and retries; a data library or framework does it better

pitfalls.title: Fetching in an effect without ignoring stale responses
pitfalls.detail: When the input changes quickly, responses can arrive out of order and the last one to arrive wins, even if it is for an old input. Flag the old request in cleanup. Better still, let TanStack Query handle it.

pitfalls.title: Copying props into state with an effect
pitfalls.detail: One render with the stale value, then another. Compute it during render; reset state on identity change with a key.
pitfalls.bad:
const [full, setFull] = useState("");
useEffect(() => setFull(`${first} ${last}`), [first, last]);
pitfalls.good: const full = `${first} ${last}`;

pitfalls.title: Subscribing to an external store with useEffect and useState
pitfalls.detail: It works, but an update between render and subscription can be missed, and every component repeats the code. React 18's useSyncExternalStore is the purpose-built hook.
pitfalls.good: const value = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.get);

pitfalls.title: A new context value object on every render
pitfalls.detail: value={{ user, login }} is a new object each time the provider renders, so every consumer re-renders. Wrap it in useMemo (and login in useCallback) when the provider re-renders often.

quiz.q: An effect with dependency [room] logged connect a. The prop changes to b. What runs, in order?
quiz.why: React runs the previous cleanup with the old values before the next setup, so there is never a moment with two connections.

quiz.q: In development with StrictMode, a component with a connecting effect mounts. What does the log show?
quiz.why: React 18 runs one extra setup and cleanup cycle in development to check that cleanup mirrors setup. Production shows a single connect.

quiz.q: fullName is first + ' ' + last, both props. Where should it be computed?
options: In a useEffect that sets fullName state
During render, as a plain const
quiz.why: Derived values belong in render. An effect would commit one render with a stale value and then render again.

quiz.q: Why createContext<Locale | null>(null) plus a hook that throws, rather than createContext<Locale>("en-US")?
options: A missing provider fails loudly instead of silently using the wrong locale
quiz.why: The default is used only when no provider is above. A plausible default hides the mistake; the guard hook turns it into an immediate error and removes null from consumers' types.

further_reading.title: React: You might not need an effect
React: Reusing logic with custom hooks

lessons.body:
## Concept

Rendering must be pure: given props and state, return UI and touch nothing else. **Effects**
are the escape hatch for code that must run *because the component is on screen*:
connecting to a chat room, starting a timer, attaching a third-party widget.
`useEffect(setup, deps)` runs `setup` after React commits; if `setup` returns a function,
that **cleanup** runs before the next setup (when a dependency changed, compared with
`Object.is`) and once more on unmount. In development, `StrictMode` adds one extra
setup-cleanup cycle on mount to prove the cleanup undoes the setup.

Most code people put in effects doesn't need one. react.dev names the two big cases:
**transforming data for rendering** (compute it during render) and **handling user events**
(do it in the event handler, where you know what happened). Resetting state when an id
changes is a `key`, and subscribing to an external store is `useSyncExternalStore`.

A **custom hook** is a function named `useSomething` that calls other hooks. It shares
stateful *logic*; every call gets its own state. **Context** passes a value to every
component below a provider without threading props through each level: create it with
`createContext`, provide it with `<Ctx.Provider value={...}>` (React 18; React 19 also
accepts `<Ctx value={...}>`), and read it with `useContext`, ideally through one custom
hook that handles the missing-provider case.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go:** React context is **not** `context.Context`. Go's context carries cancellation,
  deadlines and request values explicitly as a first parameter; React context is implicit
  dependency injection through the component tree. The cleanup function is the closer
  analogy to Go: it is your `defer conn.Close()`, and the `ignore` flag in a fetching effect
  is checking `ctx.Err()` after a call returns.
- **Java/Android:** an effect is not `onCreate`/`onDestroy`. Think "keep this in sync with
  these values": it re-runs when the dependencies change, not only at mount and unmount.
  Context plays the role of a DI container scoped to a subtree, without annotations or
  reflection.
- **C++:** setup/cleanup is RAII expressed as a closure pair; the dependency array decides
  when the old object is destroyed and a new one is constructed.
- **Python:** a custom hook is like a context manager or decorator you compose freely, except
  that it must be called unconditionally, at the top level of a component or another hook.
- **JS (class components):** `componentDidMount`/`componentDidUpdate`/`componentWillUnmount`
  collapse into one effect per concern, so the setup and teardown of one subscription
  stay together.

## Design notes

Treat every `useEffect` in review as a question: which external system does it synchronize
