with? If the answer is "React state", delete it and compute during render or in the handler.
Fetching is the common exception that still deserves a library: an effect-based fetch needs
race handling, caching, deduplication and retries, which is the next-but-one lesson.

This app has a real example of each side. `LessonQuiz` (`src/features/learning/LessonQuiz.tsx`)
loads answers in an effect with a `live` flag set to false in cleanup, the `ignore` pattern
above. `src/features/learning/store.ts` subscribes components to a small module-level store
with `useState` plus `useEffect` (`useProgressStatus`, `useIsBookmarked`). That is the shape
react.dev suggests replacing with `useSyncExternalStore`, calling it less error-prone; one
concrete gap is that the effect subscribes after the commit, so a store change that lands
between render and subscription is not seen until the next change.
`RunPanel` (`src/features/runner/RunPanel.tsx`) used to reset its editor state in an effect
when the example changed, while its parent already gave it a `key` per example, so the
effect only repeated what remounting did. It was removed: with the key, the initial
`useState` values are the reset.

Keep context for values that are read widely and change rarely (locale, theme, the
QueryClient). A value that changes on every keystroke re-renders every consumer; give such
state a narrower home.

lessons.title: Controlled forms, lists and keys, accessibility basics
lessons.summary: A controlled input renders React state and reports every keystroke through onChange; the form validates on submit. useId wires labels and error messages for assistive technology, and list keys come from the data, never from the index.

examples.title: A controlled input with typed events and validation on submit

annotations.note: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> types e.target as an input, so .value is a string without a cast. onChange fires on every keystroke, like the DOM input event, not like the DOM change event, which waits for blur. Store exactly e.target.value: react.dev warns that storing anything else, or storing it asynchronously, makes the caret jump.

FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> for the submit handler. preventDefault stops the browser's navigation; the data stays in state. Trimming and Turkish upper-casing happen once, here, not in onChange: "izmir" is saved as İZMİR, where toUpperCase() would give IZMIR.

Wrapping the input in its label associates them without ids. The error paragraph has role="alert", so screen readers announce it when it appears. type="submit" states the default explicitly, so Enter in the field submits the form.

Test plumbing. Assigning input.value directly does not reach React's onChange; setting it through the prototype's setter and firing a bubbling input event is what a typing user (and Testing Library) produces.

This runner's iframe is sandboxed without allow-forms, and a browser then skips form submission entirely, submit event included. So the harness dispatches the event React listens to. In a normal page, clicking the button or pressing Enter does it.
The empty submit shows the error; the input keeps exactly what was typed, spaces included; the second submit saves the normalized value and clears the error.

examples.title: An accessible Field component with useId

annotations.note: The native input's props plus a label and an optional error: callers keep name, type, defaultValue and every aria-* attribute.

useId returns an id unique to this component instance and stable across renders, and it matches between server and client rendering, which a module-level counter can't promise. Derive related ids from it (`${id}-error`) rather than calling useId twice.

aria-invalid only once validation found a problem (MDN: not on empty fields before the user tried to submit). aria-describedby makes the message part of the input's description, read when it gets focus. ARIA's dedicated aria-errormessage is the alternative MDN points to.
input.labels is the browser's own label association, so this checks the wiring the way assistive technology sees it. The ids :r0: and :r1: are React 18's format; treat them as opaque.

examples.title: Keys: an index is not an identity

annotations.note: Turkish plate codes make natural keys: unique and stable. Database ids work the same way; for items created in the browser, generate an id when the item is created (crypto.randomUUID()), never while rendering.
Each Row holds state React keeps per position in the tree. The key decides which state belongs to which row after the list changes.

Removing the first city shifts every index. With key={i}, React sees rows 0 and 1 survive and row 2 disappear, so Ankara's note moves to İzmir: the first output line. With key={city.plate}, Ankara keeps its row and its note. No key at all behaves like the index, plus a console warning.
The harness types into Ankara's input, removes İstanbul and prints every row with its input's value, once per key strategy.

use_cases: Controlled inputs: live validation, inputs that depend on each other, formatting previews, disabling submit until valid
Uncontrolled inputs (defaultValue + FormData on submit): simple forms where nothing reacts to each keystroke
A shared Field component that owns label, id and error wiring for every form in the app
Keys from data ids: tables, todo lists, chat messages, anything that can be inserted, removed or re-sorted
strengths: The input shows exactly the state, so validation, formatting and conditional fields are plain functions of state, not DOM reads
Typed events (ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) give e.target the right element type, where plain DOM handlers in TypeScript need a cast
useId produces ids that survive server rendering and hydration, unlike Math.random() or a global counter
Keys let React move existing DOM nodes and state instead of recreating them, so focus, scroll position and typed text survive a re-sort
weaknesses: Every keystroke re-renders the form component; a large form with expensive children may need splitting or uncontrolled inputs
Validation, touched-state and error wiring are hand-written in React 18; libraries or React 19's form actions take some of it over
Accessibility is not enforced by the types: a label-less input compiles fine

pitfalls.title: Index as key in a list that changes
pitfalls.detail: Insertions, deletions and re-sorts attach state and DOM to the wrong items. Use an id from the data.
pitfalls.good: {items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}

pitfalls.title: Generating keys while rendering
pitfalls.detail: key={Math.random()} or key={crypto.randomUUID()} in render gives every row a new identity each time: all rows remount and typed input is lost. Create ids when the data is created.

pitfalls.title: value without onChange, or value that becomes undefined
pitfalls.detail: value without onChange renders a read-only field (React warns). Switching value from undefined to a string flips the input from uncontrolled to controlled (another warning). Initialize controlled values to "" and use value={x ?? ""}.

pitfalls.title: Transforming the value inside onChange
pitfalls.detail: Upper-casing or formatting in onChange stores something other than what the DOM holds; react.dev's troubleshooting lists it as a cause of the caret jumping. Normalize on submit or blur.
pitfalls.good:
onChange={(e) => setCity(e.target.value)}
// on submit: city.trim().toLocaleUpperCase("tr")

pitfalls.title: A button without a type inside a form
pitfalls.detail: A button's default type is submit, so an 'Add row' button in a form submits it. Give non-submit buttons type="button".

quiz.q: React's onChange on a text input fires...
options: When the input loses focus, like the DOM change event
On every edit, like the DOM input event
quiz.why: react.dev: it fires immediately when the value is changed by the user and behaves like the browser input event.

quiz.q: A list keyed by index has a text input in every row. You delete the first row. What happens to the text typed into the second row?
options: It stays with the second item
It appears next to the item that used to be third
quiz.why: The rows at indexes 0 and 1 survive with their state and the last row is removed. The item that was third now renders at index 1 and inherits the second row's input.

quiz.q: Why derive the error message id from useId instead of hard-coding id="city-error"?
options: Two instances of the component would produce duplicate ids
quiz.why: ids must be unique in the document; useId is unique per component instance and also matches between server and client rendering.

quiz.q: Where should a form trim and upper-case a city name?
options: In onChange, so the input shows the normalized value
On submit (or blur), leaving the input exactly as typed
In a useEffect watching the value
quiz.why: A controlled input must store e.target.value; changing it in onChange can make the caret jump. An effect would add a render for no reason.

lessons.body:
## Concept

An input is **controlled** when React decides what it shows: `value={city}` plus an
`onChange` that stores `e.target.value`. Every keystroke goes through state, so the form can
validate, format previews or enable buttons from plain state. An input is **uncontrolled**
when the DOM keeps the value (`defaultValue`) and you read it on submit with
`new FormData(e.currentTarget)`; that's simpler when nothing reacts to each keystroke.
Either way the form's `onSubmit` handler calls `e.preventDefault()` and owns what happens next.

Lists are rendered with `map`, and each item gets a **key**: a string or number, unique
among its siblings and stable over time. React matches elements between renders by key,
so the key decides which component state and which DOM node belong to which item after an
insert, delete or re-sort. Keys come from the data (a database id, a plate code), not from
the array index and never from `Math.random()` during render.

Accessibility basics are part of "a form that behaves": every input has a label (wrap it,
or `htmlFor` + `id`), ids come from `useId` so two instances never collide, and a failed
validation sets `aria-invalid` and points `aria-describedby` at the message.

React 19 adds form **actions** (`<form action={fn}>`, `useActionState`, `useFormStatus`).
This app runs React 18.3, where `onSubmit` is the API; the concepts above carry over.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS (DOM):** React's `onChange` is the DOM `input` event, not the DOM `change` event that
  fires on blur. In TypeScript, React's event types (`ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`) also
  save you the `e.target as HTMLInputElement` cast that plain DOM handlers need.
- **Java (Swing/JavaFX):** a controlled input is a text field bound one way to a model,
  with every edit routed through your handler; there is no two-way binding magic.
- **Python (Django forms, WTForms):** validation is a function from the submitted values to
  an errors object, as here; the difference is that it runs in the browser first and
  must be repeated on the server anyway.
- **Go:** the server still validates (`go.http.json-validation`); client validation is a
  convenience, never a security boundary. A shared schema such as zod on the client and
  the same rules on the server keeps the two honest.

## Design notes

Put the wiring in one component. A `Field` that takes `label` and `error` and forwards the
native input props makes the accessible version the easy version: nobody hand-writes
`aria-describedby` in each form, and changing how errors are announced is one edit. Keep
validation a pure function of the form values, called on submit (and later on blur if you
want earlier feedback); it is then trivially testable and reusable with a schema library.
MDN's advice on `aria-invalid` matches that timing: don't flag empty required fields before
the user has tried to submit.

For lists, decide identity when data is created, not when it is rendered. Server data
already has ids; client-created items get one at creation (`crypto.randomUUID()`), and
that id is the key. If a list never changes order and items have no state, index keys
happen to work, but nothing in the code says so, which is why reviewers flag them.

lessons.title: TanStack Query: caching, invalidation, optimistic updates
lessons.summary: Server data is a cache, not component state. useQuery reads it by key with deduplication and stale-while-revalidate refetching; useMutation changes the server, updates the cache optimistically, rolls back on error and invalidates what it touched.

examples.title: useQuery: one request for many components, cached by key

annotations.note: The fake server is an async function with an access log: the lesson iframe has no network, and the log makes every request visible. useQuery doesn't care where the promise comes from.

v5 accepts only the object form. queryKey is the cache identity: include every input the fetch depends on (here track), so ["titles", "go"] and ["titles", "ts"] are separate entries. staleTime says how long fetched data counts as fresh; the default is 0.

status is a union, "pending" | "error" | "success" (v5 renamed "loading" to "pending"), and the result type is a discriminated union on it: before the checks, data is string[] | undefined; after them, string[]. isFetching is separate: true during any fetch, including a background refetch while old data is on screen.

retry: false because the default retries a failed query three times with exponential backoff, which a lesson doesn't want. gcTime (called cacheTime before v5) is how long unused data stays cached, 5 minutes by default; Infinity here only so no timer outlives the run.
Harness: wait until no query is fetching, then one more timer turn, because TanStack hands results to components in a batched 0 ms timer and timers fire in the order they were set.
Three components, two keys, two requests: the two "go" components share one cache entry and one in-flight promise. No prop drilling, no global store, no request bookkeeping in components.

Unmounting doesn't drop the data. Remounting renders it immediately and, because it is stale (staleTime 0), refetches in the background: "(yenileniyor)" and a third request. This is stale-while-revalidate.
With staleTime 60 s the cached "ts" data still counts as fresh, so mounting causes no request at all. Choose staleTime per kind of data: how old may this be before the user would mind?

examples.title: useMutation: optimistic update, rollback, invalidation

annotations.note: The fake server holds each PATCH until the harness answers, so the output can show the screen while the request is in flight, then after success, then after a failure.
One constant for the key. Bigger apps use query-key factories, so queries and the mutations that invalidate them can't drift apart.

onMutate runs before the request. Cancel in-flight fetches of the key so an older response can't overwrite the optimistic data, snapshot the current list, write the expected result into the cache, and return the snapshot. Every component reading ["todos"] updates at once. The second parameter is the mutation context, whose client is the QueryClient; older v5 code calls useQueryClient() instead.

onError receives onMutate's return value and restores the snapshot. onSettled runs after success or failure and invalidates the key: mark it stale and refetch active queries, so the cache ends up as the server says, not as we guessed. invalidateQueries matches by prefix, so ["todos"] would also cover ["todos", { done: true }].

The component knows nothing about caching: it renders the query and calls mutate. toggle.isError shows the failure next to the rolled-back item. A button, not a clickable div, keeps it keyboard-accessible.
Mutations are kept in a cache of their own and have a gcTime too; Infinity again only so no timer outlives the runner.
First round: [x] immediately, the server agrees, the refetch confirms. Second round: [ ] immediately, the server fails with 503, the snapshot puts [x] back, and the refetch confirms that too.

use_cases: Lists and detail views backed by a REST or GraphQL API, shared by several components without a global store
Dashboards that should refresh when the user returns to the tab or reconnects
Toggles, likes, reordering and inline edits that should feel instant: optimistic updates with rollback
After a create or delete: invalidate the affected keys instead of hand-editing every cached list
strengths: Deduplication, caching, background refetch and retries come from one library, where a useEffect fetch needs race handling and still has no cache
The result is a discriminated union on status, so TypeScript forces the pending and error branches before data is usable
Server state stays out of Redux-style global stores; client state left in React is small and easy to reason about
Invalidation by key prefix says what changed, not how to fix every view; the next fetch makes the cache right
weaknesses: Another dependency with its own vocabulary (stale, inactive, gc, fetchStatus) and defaults that surprise: data is stale immediately and refetches on window focus
Query keys are untyped strings and arrays by default; a typo creates a separate cache entry silently
Optimistic updates are hand-written per mutation and easy to get subtly wrong (forgetting cancelQueries or the rollback)
Tests need a fresh QueryClient per test with retries off, or state leaks between tests

pitfalls.title: Leaving inputs out of the query key
pitfalls.detail: If the fetch depends on track but the key is just ["titles"], every track shares one cache entry and the UI shows the wrong data.
pitfalls.good: useQuery({ queryKey: ["titles", track], queryFn: () => fetchTitles(track) })

pitfalls.title: Copying query data into useState
pitfalls.detail: The copy stops updating when the cache refetches or a mutation invalidates it. Read data from the query result where you render it.

pitfalls.title: Optimistic update without cancelQueries
pitfalls.detail: A refetch already in flight can resolve after setQueryData and overwrite the optimistic value with older server data.

pitfalls.title: A QueryClient created inside a component
pitfalls.detail: new QueryClient() in render creates a new, empty cache on every render. Create it once at module level or in a useState initializer.

quiz.q: Two components call useQuery with the same queryKey while nothing is cached. How many times does queryFn run?
quiz.why: Both observers subscribe to the same cache entry, and the second one joins the in-flight fetch.

quiz.q: Cached data exists, staleTime is the default, and a component using it mounts. What happens?
options: It shows pending until a new fetch finishes
It shows the cached data and refetches in the background
It shows the cached data and never refetches
quiz.why: The default staleTime is 0, so the data is stale: render it immediately and revalidate. isFetching is true meanwhile.

quiz.q: Why return { previous } from onMutate?
options: onError receives it, so it can restore the cache if the request fails
quiz.why: The value is passed to onError, onSuccess and onSettled as onMutateResult; the snapshot is what a rollback restores.

quiz.q: After a successful mutation, why invalidate instead of trusting the optimistic value?
options: The optimistic value is discarded automatically
The server may have changed more than you predicted (timestamps, ordering, other users), so refetch the truth
invalidateQueries is required for the mutation to finish
quiz.why: The optimistic update is a guess for responsiveness; invalidation makes the cache converge to the server's state.

further_reading.title: React: You might not need an effect (fetching data)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Data that lives on a server is not your component's state: other users change it, it gets
old, several components show it at once. TanStack Query (v5, formerly React Query) treats it
as a **cache** owned by a `QueryClient` that you provide once at the top of the tree.

- `useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })` subscribes a component to one cache entry. The key is an
  array that identifies the data (`["titles", track]`); components with equal keys share one
  entry and one request. The result is a discriminated union on `status`
  (`"pending" | "error" | "success"`), plus `isFetching` for background refetches.
- Data is **stale** after `staleTime` (default 0). Stale data is still shown, and refetched
  when a new component mounts, the window regains focus or the network reconnects.
  Unused entries are garbage-collected after `gcTime` (default 5 minutes).
- `useMutation({ mutationFn, onMutate, onError, onSettled })` changes the server. After it,
  **invalidate** the keys it affected; for instant feedback, write the expected result into
  the cache in `onMutate` and roll back in `onError` (an **optimistic update**). The simpler
  alternative is optimistic *UI*: render `mutation.variables` while `isPending` and leave the
  cache alone.

The library's own documentation (guides on query keys, important defaults, invalidation
and optimistic updates) is at
[tanstack.com/query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/overview);
v5 needs React 18 or later.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Spring:** think of `@Cacheable` keyed by method arguments plus `@CacheEvict` after a
  write, moved to the client and made reactive: evicting (invalidating) a key re-renders
  every component that reads it once the refetch lands.
- **HTTP:** `staleTime` and background revalidation are the `stale-while-revalidate` idea
  from `Cache-Control`, applied per query key instead of per URL.
- **Redux/global stores (JS):** server responses copied into a store need hand-written
  loading flags, invalidation and refetch logic. Here the store is the cache and those
  concerns are configuration.
- **Go:** like a `singleflight.Group` (concurrent callers for one key share one call) in
  front of a TTL cache, but on the client and wired to rendering. The default of three
  retries with exponential backoff is the retry loop you'd write with `go.services.retries`.

## How it works

Each `useQuery` creates an observer for its key and subscribes to it with React's
`useSyncExternalStore`, the hook from the effects lesson for external stores. The
`QueryCache` maps a stable hash of the key to a query holding `data`, `error`, timestamps and
any in-flight promise. Fetches update the query, observers compute a new result, and the
library notifies subscribed components in batches. `invalidateQueries({ queryKey })` matches
every query whose key starts with the given prefix, marks it stale and refetches the ones that
are currently rendered.

## Design notes

Split state by owner. Server state goes through queries and mutations; URL state (filters,
pagination) goes into the URL (next lesson); what remains for `useState` and context is small:
open panels, draft input. Most "we need a global store" discussions dissolve after that split.

Treat query keys as an API. Put them in one module per feature (`todoKeys.all`,
`todoKeys.list(filter)`) so a mutation invalidates exactly the keys its queries use. Choose
`staleTime` from the data's nature: a curriculum that changes on deploy can be fresh for
minutes, a chat list for seconds. Keep `retry` on in the app and off in tests. Optimistic
updates pay off for small, high-frequency, likely-to-succeed actions (toggles, reorders);
for a payment, show the pending state honestly instead.

This app doesn't use TanStack Query yet: `src/features/learning` keeps progress in a
hand-written store with optimistic updates and manual rollback (`markLesson`,
`toggleBookmark` in `store.ts`). Comparing that file with the second example shows what
the library would take over: the rollback, the subscription, and the refetch after a write.

lessons.title: Routing and URL state; the rendering model and memoization; composition
lessons.summary: Put navigation state (which page, which filter) in the URL so back, reload and shared links work. A component re-renders when its parent does; memo, useCallback and passing children skip that work, and the first two are worth it only for a problem you have measured.

examples.title: The URL owns the filter: it survives navigating away and back

annotations.note: Two kinds of state side by side: level lives in the URL's search params, sorted in the component. params.get returns string | null: the URL is user input, so treat it like untrusted data (validate, default) before relying on its type.

filter returned a new array, so sorting it in place is safe. The Turkish collator gives defer, Sözlükler, Şablonlar. A plain sort() compares UTF-16 code units and gives Sözlükler, defer, Şablonlar: capitals before lowercase, Ş after every ASCII letter.
setSearchParams navigates: it pushes a history entry with the new query string (pass { replace: true } to replace it instead), and every component reading the params re-renders.
Link renders a real `<a href>`, so open-in-new-tab and copy-link work; a plain click is intercepted and becomes a client-side navigation.
useParams gives the :id segment as string | undefined. navigate(-1) is the history back button.

MemoryRouter keeps the history in memory: right for tests and for this iframe, which has no address bar. The app itself uses createBrowserRouter in src/main.tsx. useTransitions={false} is for the printout only: by default React Router applies navigations inside startTransition, which renders later than flushSync returns.

The last line is the point: after going to a lesson and back, the level filter is still applied, because it is part of the history entry. The sort is gone: LessonList unmounted on navigation and its useState died with it.

examples.title: What re-renders, and the two ways to skip it

annotations.note: Counting renders by mutating a Map during render breaks render purity on purpose, as instrumentation. Under StrictMode, development builds render each component twice and these counts would double.
memo(Chart) compares each prop with Object.is against the previous render and skips the component when all are equal. It is a performance hint, not a guarantee: correct code must not depend on it.

Each keystroke re-renders Search and every child it creates: plain renders 4 times (mount plus 3). memo skips when the props are equal (1 render). An inline arrow is a new function each render, so memo sees unequal props and renders anyway (4). useCallback returns the same function while its dependencies don't change (1).

Composition instead of memo. Pinning re-renders Panel and what Panel creates ("created inside": 4), but not its children: those elements were created by the parent, which didn't re-render, so React reuses them ("passed as children": 1). react.dev lists this as the first way to make memoization unnecessary.

Each press is its own flushSync, so each is one commit. The table is the measurement; in an app the React DevTools Profiler or the `<Profiler>` component gives timings, and only an interaction that feels slow justifies adding memo.

use_cases: URL state: filters, sort order, pagination, selected tab, search query, the open item: anything a user would bookmark, share or expect Back to restore
Component state: hover, open menus, draft input not yet applied, animation state
memo/useCallback/useMemo: a measured slow interaction where an expensive child re-renders with equal props, or a value used as an effect dependency
Composition (children, slot props): stateful wrappers such as panels, modals and layouts around content that shouldn't re-render with them
strengths: URL state is free persistence: reload, back/forward, deep links and shared links all work, with no storage code
Typed route params and search params as string | undefined and string | null force the parsing that server handlers in Go also need
React's model is simple to predict: a component renders when its own state changes (store subscriptions included), its parent renders, or a context it reads changes
Composition fixes most unnecessary renders structurally, without the dependency bookkeeping memo and useCallback need
weaknesses: Search params are strings only: numbers, booleans and arrays need parsing and validation on every read
memo is defeated by any new object, array or function prop, so it tends to pull useMemo and useCallback through the whole call chain
Memoization costs memory and comparisons on every render; applied everywhere it can make things slower and the code harder to read
React Router's own API changed between v5, v6 and v7; much code found online targets older versions

pitfalls.title: Mirroring URL state in useState
pitfalls.detail: Copying a search param into state means two sources of truth, and Back updates one of them. Read the param where you render and write it with setSearchParams.
pitfalls.good: const level = params.get("level"); // and setParams({ level }) to change it

pitfalls.title: Trusting the URL's type
pitfalls.detail: `params.get("page") as number` compiles and lies: it is a string or null. Parse and validate, with a default.
pitfalls.bad: const page = params.get("page") as unknown as number;
pitfalls.good: const page = Math.max(1, Number(params.get("page") ?? "1") || 1);

pitfalls.title: memo with inline object or function props
pitfalls.detail: `<MemoChart options={{ dense: true }} onSelect={() => pick(id)} />` creates new props every render, so memo never skips. Hoist constants, use useMemo/useCallback, or drop memo.

pitfalls.title: Memoizing by default
pitfalls.detail: react.dev: memo is only valuable when a component re-renders often with the same props and its rendering is expensive. Measure with the Profiler first; React Compiler, where adopted, applies memoization automatically.

quiz.q: A list filter is kept in useState in the list component. The user opens an item and presses Back. What does the list show?
quiz.why: Navigating away unmounted the list and its state. A filter in the search params is part of the history entry and comes back with it.

quiz.q: A parent re-renders. Its child receives no props at all and is not wrapped in memo. Does the child render?
options: Yes, rendering a parent renders the children it creates
quiz.why: Without memo React doesn't compare props; a parent's render re-renders its subtree. The DOM is only touched where output differs.

quiz.q: memo(Chart) still renders on every keystroke. The parent passes onSelect={() => select(id)}. Why?
options: memo only works on class components
The arrow is a new function each render, so the props are never equal
quiz.why: memo compares each prop with Object.is. Wrap the callback in useCallback, or don't rely on memo there.

quiz.q: A Panel with its own state wraps expensive content. Which change stops the content re-rendering when Panel's state changes, without memo?
options: Move the content into Panel's own JSX
Pass the content as children from Panel's parent
Store Panel's state in a ref
quiz.why: Elements passed as children are created by the parent; when only Panel re-renders, those elements are the same objects and React skips them.

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Routing** maps the URL to components. With React Router v7 (`react-router-dom`, this
app's version) you declare routes (`path="/lessons/:id"`), read the matched segment with
`useParams`, read and write the query string with `useSearchParams`, and navigate with
`<Link>` or `useNavigate`. The rule that makes routing pay off: **the URL owns navigation
state**. Which page, which item, which filter, which sort, which tab: if a user would
bookmark it, share it or expect Back to restore it, it belongs in the path or the search
params, not in `useState`. Component state is for what's transient: an open menu, a draft.

The **rendering model** decides how much work each change costs. A component renders when
its state changes, when a context it reads changes, or when its parent renders; React then
compares the output and touches only the DOM that differs. A parent's render re-renders the
children it creates, whether or not their props changed. Two tools skip that:

- **`memo(Component)`** skips rendering when every prop is `Object.is`-equal to last time,
  which makes `useCallback`/`useMemo` necessary for function and object props.
- **Composition**: a stateful wrapper that receives `children` from its parent re-renders
  without re-rendering those children, because they are elements the parent already created.

Composition is free and structural; memoization costs comparisons and code. Reach for memo
when a profile shows a slow interaction, not by default. React Compiler (stable, and
documented to support React 17 to 19) inserts this memoization automatically at build time.
React Router's own documentation, including the v7 modes (declarative, data, framework), is
at [reactrouter.com](https://reactrouter.com/home).

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go:** `mux.HandleFunc("GET /lessons/{id}", h)` with `r.PathValue("id")` (Go 1.22+) is the
  server-side twin of `path="/lessons/:id"` with `useParams()`. Both hand you strings, and
  `r.URL.Query().Get("level")` returns `""` for a missing parameter where
  `searchParams.get("level")` returns `null`.
- **Java (Swing/Android):** navigation is not a stack of view objects you push; it is a URL,
  and the view is a function of it. Android's deep links are the closest analogue.
- **Python (Django/Flask):** the URL conf moves to the client; the server serves one HTML
  page and an API.
- **C++:** memo is an output cache keyed by shallow equality of the inputs; like any cache it
  helps only when hits are common and recomputation is expensive.
- **JS:** URLSearchParams percent-encodes UTF-8, so `?q=şablon` travels as
  `?q=%C5%9Fablon`; `get("q")` decodes it back. Never build query strings by concatenation.

## Design notes

This app follows the URL-first rule for the big things: `src/main.tsx` maps
`/tracks/:trackId` and `/lessons/:lessonId` with `createBrowserRouter`, and its comment
cites ADR-0005. The same comment says `?example=` and tab params would come next; in
`src/features/lessons/LessonContent.tsx` the selected tab and example are still `useState`,
so a reload or a shared link always opens the Concept tab and the first example. Moving
them to `useSearchParams` is the change this lesson argues for, and it costs a few lines of
parsing (the param can be any string, so fall back to the defaults).

For performance, think in this order: keep state as low as possible (a keystroke in a
search box should re-render the search box, not the page), pass slow content as children,
derive instead of syncing with effects, and only then memoize the specific component the
Profiler points at. When you do memoize, check what the value feeds: a `useMemo` whose
result is a dependency of a `useCallback` or an effect keeps those stable, which is a
correctness concern as much as a speed one.

lessons.title: fetch basics and pitfalls: it doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx
lessons.summary: fetch rejects only when no HTTP response arrives; a 404 or a 500 fulfils the promise like a 200. Check response.ok, read the body exactly once, and pass a timeout signal, because fetch has no timeout of its own.

examples.title: A 404 and a 502 fulfil the promise; only a failed request rejects

annotations.note: The fake server has fetch's exact type and returns real Response objects, so the client code can't tell the difference. Response.json() builds a JSON body with Content-Type: application/json. Taking the fetch function as a dependency is also how tests swap the network out.

res.json() is typed Promise<any>, so returning it as Promise<User> compiles whatever arrives. The 404's error object becomes a "User" whose name is undefined, and the proxy's HTML page fails as a SyntaxError that looks like a bug in your code, not an outage.

ok is true only for status 200-299. Check it before touching the body, read error bodies as text (they may be HTML or empty), and keep the status on the error so callers can tell "not found" from "try again later".

This is what a rejection looks like: no response at all. The sandbox's CSP blocks the request, and offline, DNS failures and CORS refusals produce the same TypeError. The message is the browser's own ("Failed to fetch" in Chromium) and deliberately carries no details.

examples.title: The body is a one-shot stream: clone(), empty bodies, and the charset

annotations.note: The body is a ReadableStream, and text(), json(), blob() and arrayBuffer() consume it. Afterwards bodyUsed is true and any further read rejects with a TypeError.
clone() splits the stream so each copy can be read once. Clone before the first read. If only one copy is ever read, the other buffers the whole body in memory, so don't clone large downloads.
A 204 has no body, and the empty string is not JSON, so json() rejects with a SyntaxError. Any empty body does the same, whatever the status.

Read the text once and parse it yourself: the error can then quote what came back. The classic case: the session expired, the API redirected to the login page, fetch followed the redirect, and the result is a 200 with HTML.

text() always decodes as UTF-8 and ignores the charset parameter. In windows-1254 (labels iso-8859-9 and latin5 too) the byte 0xDE is Ş; as UTF-8 it is invalid and becomes U+FFFD. Read the bytes and decode with the declared charset. TextDecoder throws a RangeError for a label it doesn't know.

examples.title: Timeouts with AbortSignal, and one place that classifies every outcome

annotations.note: A fake with a delay that honours init.signal the way fetch does: an already aborted signal rejects at once, and an abort later stops the timer and rejects with signal.reason.
Every way a request can end, as a discriminated union. Callers switch on kind and the compiler checks they handled each case, which a catch block holding unknown can't give you.
fetch has no timeout option. AbortSignal.timeout() is the deadline, and AbortSignal.any() merges it with the caller's own cancel signal: whichever fires first decides the reason.

The signal stays attached to the response. If it fires after the headers arrived but before the body was read, the body read rejects, so the deadline covers the whole exchange, as http.Client.Timeout does in Go.

The DOMException's name says why the signal fired: TimeoutError for the deadline, AbortError for abort(). A TypeError means no response. Anything else, such as a 200 whose body isn't JSON, is a bug and propagates.
A cancel is not a failure: nobody wants the answer anymore. Keeping it a separate kind lets the UI skip the error message.

use_cases: Every call to your own API, through one small wrapper that owns the ok check, the timeout and the error type
Showing the server's error message: check the status first, then read the error body (often application/problem+json)
Downloading files and legacy exports: arrayBuffer() and TextDecoder with the charset the server declared
Logging raw responses in development: clone() before the parser reads the body
strengths: One API in browsers, workers and Node (built in since Node 18), replacing XMLHttpRequest and Node's http.request
Response is a constructible value, so fakes and tests return real Response objects without a mocking library
Cancellation and deadlines use the same AbortSignal as the rest of the platform, the way Go threads context.Context through I/O
Like Go's http.Get and unlike axios, an HTTP error status is a value: the caller decides which statuses count as failures
weaknesses: No timeout and no status check by default: every call site that forgets either is a latent bug, so wrap fetch once
res.json() returns Promise<any>, which silently satisfies any declared return type
Offline, DNS, CORS and CSP failures all arrive as one TypeError whose message differs between browsers
No upload progress events; XMLHttpRequest still has them (ts.services.advanced)

pitfalls.title: Treating a fulfilled fetch as success
pitfalls.detail: A 404, a 500 or a proxy's 502 page all fulfil the promise. Check res.ok (or the exact status) before reading the body.

pitfalls.title: json() on a 204 or an HTML page
pitfalls.detail: An empty body and an HTML error page both reject with a SyntaxError that hides the real cause. Read the text once, return undefined for an empty body, and include the status, the Content-Type and the start of the body in the error.

pitfalls.title: Reading the body twice
pitfalls.detail: The second read rejects with a TypeError. Keep the text you already read, or clone() before the first read.

pitfalls.title: No timeout
pitfalls.detail: Without a signal, a hung server keeps the request, and your spinner, pending for as long as the browser allows.
pitfalls.good: await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) });

pitfalls.title: Matching on error messages
pitfalls.detail: "Failed to fetch" is Chromium's wording; Firefox and Safari say something else. Check instanceof TypeError and the DOMException name instead.

quiz.q: await fetch("/api/orders/9") reaches the server, which answers 404 with a JSON error body. What happens?
options: The promise rejects with a TypeError
The promise fulfils; res.ok is false and res.status is 404
The promise rejects with an HTTP error carrying the status
quiz.why: fetch rejects only when no response arrives. Any status, including 404 and 500, fulfils the promise; checking ok is your job.

quiz.q: A fetch rejects with a TypeError. Which of these cannot be the cause?
options: The server didn't allow the cross-origin read (CORS)
The page's Content Security Policy blocks the URL
quiz.why: A 500 is a response, so the promise fulfils with ok === false. The other three leave fetch with no response to return.

quiz.q: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) }): the headers arrive after 1 s, the body takes 5 s more. What happens?
options: fetch fulfils and json() succeeds: the timeout only covers the request
fetch fulfils, then json() rejects when the signal fires at 3 s
quiz.why: fetch fulfils when the headers arrive, but the signal still governs the body: once it fires, reading the body rejects.

quiz.q: A logger and the parser both need the response body. What works?
options: Read it twice; the browser caches the body
Call res.clone() before the first read and give one copy to the logger
quiz.why: A body is a one-shot stream. clone() before reading gives two independently readable copies; reading the text once and sharing it works too.

lessons.body:
## Concept

`fetch(url, init)` returns a `Promise<Response>` that settles in two phases. The promise
fulfils as soon as the status line and the headers arrive. The body comes afterwards, as a
`ReadableStream` you consume with `text()`, `json()`, `blob()`, `arrayBuffer()` or
`formData()`.

The promise **rejects** only when there is no HTTP response to hand you:

- a `TypeError`: network failure (offline, DNS, connection reset), a cross-origin response
  that CORS doesn't let the page read, a URL the page may not fetch (blocked by its Content
  Security Policy), an invalid URL or invalid options. The browser deliberately reveals
  nothing more.
- a `DOMException` from the request's `signal`: `AbortError` after `abort()`,
  `TimeoutError` from `AbortSignal.timeout()`.

Everything else **fulfils**: a 404, a 500, a proxy's 502 page, a redirect that ends on the
login page. `response.ok` is `true` for status 200-299 only, and checking it is your job.

Three rules for the body:

- **Once.** Reading consumes the stream; `bodyUsed` turns `true` and a second read rejects.
  `clone()` before the first read if two consumers need it.
- **`json()` is `JSON.parse` over the text.** An empty body (204) or an HTML page rejects
  with a `SyntaxError`.
- **`text()` is always UTF-8**, whatever charset the `Content-Type` declares.

And one for time: `fetch` has **no timeout option**. Pass
`signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`; the same signal also aborts reading the body.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: `requests.get()` doesn't raise on a 404 either. `raise_for_status()` is the
  `if (!res.ok) throw` line, and as with `requests` without `timeout=`, nothing stops a
  hung server for you.
- **Java**: `HttpClient.send()` returns an `HttpResponse` for every status and throws only
  for I/O failures (`IOException`), so `if (res.statusCode() >= 400)` is the same check you
  write by hand.
- **Go**: `http.Get` returns `err == nil` for a 404, and you check `resp.StatusCode`: the
  same rule. Go's zero `http.Client` has no timeout either, and `Client.Timeout`, like the
  signal here, also covers reading the body. JavaScript has no `defer resp.Body.Close()`;
  if you don't need a body, `res.body?.cancel()` releases it early instead of leaving it
  to the garbage collector.
- **JS (axios)**: axios rejects on any non-2xx status by default and has a `timeout`
  option. Code ported from axios to fetch silently stops catching HTTP errors.
- **C (libcurl)**: `curl_easy_perform` returns `CURLE_OK` for a 404 unless you set
  `CURLOPT_FAILONERROR`.

## Design notes

Wrap fetch once and never call it raw from components. A small module (`api/http.ts`) owns
the base URL, the default timeout, the `ok` check, an error type that carries the status
and the start of the body, and the `Content-Type` check before parsing. It returns
`unknown`, not `any`: the next lesson validates that `unknown` with zod at exactly this
point.

Take the fetch function as a parameter with the real one as default
(`doFetch: typeof fetch = fetch`). The examples' fake servers use the same seam, and so do
unit tests; MSW, in the testing module, intercepts at the network layer instead, without
the seam.

Choose an error model deliberately. Throwing an `HttpError` suits TanStack Query, which
expects a rejected promise; an `Outcome` union suits code that must handle every case, and
the compiler checks the `switch`. In both, keep "cancelled" distinct and silent, treat
timeouts, 5xx and 429 as retry candidates (ts.services.advanced), and other 4xx as final.
Error bodies from well-behaved APIs are `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457); this app's
Go backend writes every error that way (`problem()` in `server/internal/httpapi`).

lessons.title: Runtime validation with zod at the trust boundary
lessons.summary: TypeScript types are erased, so nothing checks what arrives over the network. A zod schema is a run-time value that validates and normalizes the data, and the static type is derived from it: one definition, checked where data enters the app.

examples.title: A cast checks nothing; a schema checks and produces the type

annotations.note: JSON.parse returns any, so the cast compiles. At run time id is the string "7" and + concatenates: the bug surfaces as "71" somewhere far from the response that caused it.
The schema is an ordinary value that exists at run time. z.infer derives the static type from it, so there is no interface to keep in sync by hand.

safeParse returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }, a discriminated union, so data is typed only after the check. Every issue is collected, not just the first; each has a path and a machine-readable code, and prettifyError formats them for logs.

By default z.object drops keys it doesn't declare (admin is gone) and applies normalizations such as trim(). Dropping is the tolerant choice for responses: a server that adds a field doesn't break old clients.

parse() throws a ZodError instead of returning a result. strictObject turns unknown keys into an error, which suits data you fully own, such as a config file, rather than responses from a server that evolves.

examples.title: Input type vs output type: coerce, transform, default, refine

annotations.note: overwrite() rewrites the value and keeps the schema a ZodString. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ. zod's own toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() are locale-free: the output shows IZMIR, and lowercasing İSTANBUL gives i plus a combining dot.

coerce runs Number(input) before validating, so "2" becomes 2. It also turns "" and null into 0, which only min(1) catches. For booleans in query strings use z.stringbool(): z.coerce.boolean() turns "false" into true.
transform changes the type: a string goes in, a Date comes out. JSON has no date type, so the schema is the natural place to convert.

refine adds a rule across fields; path attaches the issue to "to", so a form can show it next to that field. It runs only when the object has the right types: a failed min() doesn't stop it, a wrong type does.
One schema, two types. z.input is what arrives (guests unknown, createdAt string, note optional); z.output is what the app gets (number, Date, string with a default). z.infer is z.output.
Go's encoding/json writes a time.Time in RFC 3339 with that value's own offset, +03:00 for Europe/Istanbul, and with the microseconds PostgreSQL stored.
A Date has millisecond precision, so the microseconds are gone. If a timestamp is used as a key or a pagination cursor, keep the string.
z.iso.datetime() accepts only a Z suffix by default, so a server writing +03:00 fails validation. Agree on UTC with Z, or pass { offset: true } as above.

examples.title: One validating entry point, discriminated unions, and a policy for bad items

annotations.note: discriminatedUnion selects the branch by the status field, so errors name the bad discriminator instead of listing every branch's failures. The inferred type is a TypeScript discriminated union.
A new server meets an old client, which happens with every deploy while users still run the previous bundle: a status this client was never written for.
The single point where unknown JSON becomes typed data. T is inferred from the schema's output type, so callers never write a type argument or a cast.
All or nothing: one unknown item fails the whole list, and the path [2].status says which item and which field.
Per item: keep the valid ones and report the rest. Choose per endpoint: a ledger whose total must add up can't drop rows silently, while a notification feed can.
Because the inferred type is a discriminated union, checking status narrows it: kurus exists only in the "paid" branch, and amounts stay integer kuruş until formatting.

use_cases: Responses from your own API: one validating getJson(url, schema) in the client module
Data the app didn't just create: localStorage, URL search params, postMessage payloads, WebSocket messages
Form input, with the same schema reused on submit; issue paths map to fields
Configuration and environment variables at startup, where a strict object catches typos
strengths: One definition gives both the run-time check and the static type, unlike Java's DTO class plus separate Bean Validation annotations
safeParse returns a discriminated union, so a failed parse can't be used by mistake
Transforms normalize at the edge (trim, Turkish uppercase, string to Date), so the rest of the code sees clean values
Every issue comes with a path, which makes contract breaks easy to locate and form errors easy to place
weaknesses: A library and a run-time cost on every parse; Go's encoding/json checks field types during decoding without any schema code
Schemas are a second definition when the types already come from an OpenAPI generator; keep them aligned (ts.services.openapi)
Built-in string helpers such as toUpperCase() are locale-free, which is wrong for Turkish text
Complex schemas slow down type checking and produce long editor tooltips

pitfalls.title: Casting instead of validating
pitfalls.detail: A cast tells the compiler to stop checking. The wrong data then fails far away, or not at all.
pitfalls.good: const order = Order.parse(await res.json());

pitfalls.title: z.coerce.boolean() on query strings
pitfalls.detail: Coercion is Boolean(input), and any non-empty string is true, "false" included. Use z.stringbool(), which accepts true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off.

pitfalls.title: Strict schemas for server responses
pitfalls.detail: strictObject or a closed enum turns every additive server change into a client outage. Strip unknown keys, and give enums a fallback with .catch() where an unknown value is survivable.

pitfalls.title: Validating the same data twice, or everywhere
pitfalls.detail: Validate once, where data crosses into the app. Inside, the types are trustworthy; re-validating internal calls costs time and suggests the boundary is in the wrong place.

quiz.q: const user = (await res.json()) as User, and the server sends "id": "7" where User says number. What happens at the cast?
options: Nothing: the string flows on until something misbehaves
quiz.why: A cast is erased at compile time; no code runs for it. The string surfaces later, for example as "71" from id + 1.

quiz.q: z.object({ id: z.number() }).parse({ id: 1, isAdmin: true }) returns?
quiz.why: Plain z.object strips unknown keys. z.strictObject would throw; z.looseObject would keep them.

quiz.q: A query string carries ?archived=false. What does z.coerce.boolean() produce?
quiz.why: Coercion is Boolean("false"), and every non-empty string is truthy. z.stringbool() parses "false" as false.

quiz.q: For z.object({ at: z.iso.datetime().transform((s) => new Date(s)) }), what are z.input and z.output of at?
quiz.why: The input is what the schema accepts (an ISO string); the output is what transform returns. z.infer gives the output.

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript types are erased: `JSON.parse` and `res.json()` return `any`, and a type
annotation or `as` cast on the result is a promise the compiler believes and nothing at run
time checks. Data from outside the program, such as an API response, a URL, localStorage or
a message from another window, crosses a **trust boundary**. It has to be checked there,
once, by code that exists at run time.

[zod](https://zod.dev) makes the check a value. A schema such as
`z.object({ id: z.number() })` validates input at run time and also *is* the type:
`z.infer<typeof Schema>` derives the static type, so the two can't drift apart.

- `parse(data)` returns the typed value or throws a `ZodError`; `safeParse(data)` returns
  `{ success: true, data }` or `{ success: false, error }`.
- `error.issues` lists every problem with its `path`, `code` and `message`;
  `z.prettifyError(error)` formats them.
- A schema can also normalize: `trim()`, `default()`, `z.coerce`, `overwrite()` and
  `transform()`. A schema therefore has an **input** type (`z.input`) and an **output** type
  (`z.output`, the same as `z.infer`).
- Objects strip unknown keys by default; `z.strictObject` rejects them, `z.looseObject`
  keeps them.

This lesson uses zod 4 (`import { z } from "zod"`). Version 3 differs in details:
`z.prettifyError`, `z.iso.*` and top-level `z.email()` are version 4 APIs.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go**: `json.Unmarshal` into a struct already rejects a string in an `int` field, but
  ignores unknown fields unless you call `DisallowUnknownFields`, turns missing fields
  into zero values, and leaves range checks to a hand-written `validate()` method. zod
  does the decoding checks and the validation in one place; TypeScript alone does neither.
- **Java**: Jackson maps JSON onto a class and Bean Validation annotations (`@NotNull`,
  `@Min`) check it. zod inverts the arrangement: the schema is the value, and the type is
  derived from it.
- **Python**: pydantic is the closest relative: a model validates, coerces and documents.
  pydantic's default lax mode turns `"7"` into `7`; zod coerces only where you write
  `z.coerce`.
- **JS**: hand-written type guards (`isUser(x): x is User`) do the same job for small
  shapes. They don't report which field failed, and the guard and the type can drift apart.

## Design notes

Validate at the edge and nowhere else. In a frontend the edges are few: the API client
(`getJson(url, schema)`), the code that reads storage and URL parameters, and message
handlers. Everything behind them can trust the types, which is the point of having them.

Be tolerant with what servers send and strict with what you own. Old clients outlive
deploys: a cached bundle will meet a newer server. Stripping unknown keys and giving
enums a fallback value (`z.enum(["paid", "failed", "unknown"]).catch("unknown")`; the
fallback must be one of the values) keeps additive server changes from becoming outages. Use strict objects for configuration files, where an unknown key is a
typo.

Decide what a contract break means per endpoint. For money, fail the whole response and
report it, because a broken contract is a bug and partial data would be wrong. For feeds,
skip the bad item and report it. Either way, send the issues to your error tracking: they
show the bug, while the user only needs "something went wrong".

When the types come from an OpenAPI generator (next lesson), the schema and the generated
type are two definitions. Annotate the schema with the generated type,
`const Order: z.ZodType<components["schemas"]["Order"]> = z.object({...})`, and tsc will
reject a schema whose output no longer matches the contract.

zod 4 implements the Standard Schema interface (a `~standard` property), so libraries that
accept "any Standard Schema" take a zod schema directly. For bundle-size-sensitive code
there is `zod/mini`, with a functional API that tree-shakes better.

lessons.title: Generating types from OpenAPI; a typed API client
lessons.summary: An OpenAPI document is the contract between server and client. openapi-typescript turns it into types with no run-time code, and a small generic client checks paths, parameters and per-status bodies at compile time. Nothing checks the server at run time, so drift needs a validator or a test.

examples.title: A generic client over generated paths: wrong paths and params don't compile

annotations.note: The shape openapi-typescript emits, abbreviated: paths keyed by the literal path template, then the method, then parameters and responses keyed by status code, each with content keyed by media type. The unabridged generated file works with the same client unchanged.
The client is pure indexing into the generated types. Reply maps every documented status S to { status: S; body } and takes the union of them, a discriminated union on status built from the contract.
P is inferred from the path literal, so path is checked against the contract and params gets that path's parameter type. Only the fetch function is injected, as in the earlier lessons.

Types are erased, so the client can't know at run time which statuses the spec lists, and this cast is unavoidable. A status the spec doesn't mention, such as a proxy's 502, is cast all the same. Check the status first, or validate (example 2).
Before the status check, body is Order | Problem; after reply.status === 200 it is Order. The error path is as typed as the happy path.
Mistakes that a hand-written fetch(`/order/${id}`) would send to the server fail the build instead. Renaming a path in the spec and regenerating turns every stale call site into a compile error.

examples.title: When the server drifts from the spec: nil slices and int64 ids

annotations.note: This is the generator's output for type: integer, format: int64. JSON numbers are doubles in JavaScript, so the format survives only as a comment.
Two classic Go-side deviations. encoding/json writes a nil slice as null, and an int64 as a number, however large. Both are legal JSON, and neither matches the spec.
The cast succeeds, as every generated client's does. The id is silently rounded to the nearest double, and items.length throws a TypeError far from the response that caused it.

Annotating the schema with the generated type ties the two definitions: if the spec changes and the schema no longer produces an Order, tsc rejects it. At run time the schema reports both problems with their paths. int() accepts only safe integers, so the rounded id fails instead of passing as the wrong number.

Fix the contract, not the client. Go initializes the slice (Items: []string{}), and large ids travel as strings (the ,string tag option, type: string in the spec). BigInt does exact arithmetic when you need it.

use_cases: A frontend and a Go backend developed in parallel: the spec in the repo is what both sides compile against
Calling a third-party API that publishes an OpenAPI document, without writing its types by hand
Typed error handling: per-status response types for 404, 409 and 422 problem bodies
CI checks: regenerate types and fail on a diff when the spec changed but the client didn't
strengths: One spec drives server stubs, client types, documentation and mock servers, instead of each side retyping the shapes
Renamed fields and removed endpoints become compile errors after regenerating, not production bugs
openapi-typescript emits types only, so the client costs no bundle size beyond your fetch wrapper
Per-status response types make the error paths as typed as the happy path
weaknesses: Generated types check nothing at run time: a server that deviates from its own spec goes unnoticed without validation
A spec written by hand next to the code drifts like any other copy: generate one side from the other, or test against it
JSON semantics leak through: int64 ids, nullable vs optional, Go's nil slices and omitempty
The generated types are deeply nested, and helpers that index into them are hard to read without a library such as openapi-fetch

pitfalls.title: Treating generated types as validation
pitfalls.detail: The types describe what the spec promises. If the server's real behaviour matters, validate responses at the client edge, at least in development and tests.

pitfalls.title: int64 ids as JSON numbers
pitfalls.detail: Above 2^53 - 1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), JSON.parse rounds silently. Send such ids as strings.
pitfalls.bad: ID int64 `json:"id"`   // spec: type: integer, format: int64
pitfalls.good: ID int64 `json:"id,string"`   // spec: type: string

pitfalls.title: Go nil slices and omitempty
pitfalls.detail: A nil slice marshals as null, and omitempty drops false, 0, "" and empty slices entirely, so a field the spec marks required can be null or missing. Initialize slices, and use omitempty only on optional fields.

pitfalls.title: Editing the generated file
pitfalls.detail: The next regeneration erases the edit. Change the spec, or wrap the generated types in your own module.

quiz.q: The client uses types generated by openapi-typescript. What checks at run time that a response matches components["schemas"]["Order"]?
options: The generated code validates each response
Nothing, unless you add a validator
quiz.why: openapi-typescript emits types only, and types are erased. The run-time check has to be code, such as a zod schema.

quiz.q: A Go handler returns ID int64 = 9007199254740993 as a JSON number. What does JSON.parse produce?
quiz.why: JSON numbers become doubles, and above 2^53 - 1 not every integer is representable: the value rounds to the nearest double, silently.

quiz.q: A Go struct has Items []string `json:"items"` and the handler never sets it. What does the client receive?
quiz.why: encoding/json writes a nil slice as null. The key would be missing only with omitempty, and [] needs an initialized empty slice.

quiz.q: In example 1, why does reply.body.customer fail to compile before checking reply.status?
options: body is unknown until it is validated
body is the union Order | Problem until the status narrows it
customer is optional in the spec
quiz.why: Reply has one member per documented status. Comparing status with 200 selects the member whose body is Order.

further_reading.title: package encoding/json (Go): nil slices, omitempty, the string option

lessons.title: Retries with backoff, timeouts, pagination, uploads with progress
lessons.summary: A production client retries only what is safe to repeat, with exponential backoff, jitter and the server's Retry-After; pages with server-issued cursors instead of offsets; and reports progress by counting streamed bytes, or by uploading in parts, because fetch has no upload progress events.

examples.title: Retries: what to retry, how long to wait, and the Idempotency-Key

annotations.note: sleep and random are injected, so the example runs instantly and prints the same delays every time. In production they are a setTimeout promise and Math.random; in tests, no fake timers needed.

Retry what may go away: timeouts (408), rate limits (429) and server-side trouble (500, 502, 503, 504). A 400, 401, 404 or 422 will say the same thing next time. The idempotent methods are the ones HTTP defines as safe to repeat; POST and PATCH are not.

A POST is repeatable only with an Idempotency-Key: the server stores the result under the key and answers a repeat with the stored result instead of charging twice. The header is an IETF draft and a widespread convention; the server has to implement it.

A deadline per attempt, so one hung connection doesn't use up the whole budget. In real code, merge it with the caller's signal through AbortSignal.any() so a cancel stops the retries too. clone(), because sending a request consumes its body: the same Request can't be sent twice.
Only "no response" is retried here: a network TypeError or this attempt's TimeoutError. A caller's abort or a bug in your own code is not a reason to try again.
A POST without a key that got no response has an unknown outcome: the server may have committed it. Saying so is the honest answer; retrying blindly is how users get charged twice.

Exponential backoff with full jitter: a random wait below a ceiling that doubles per attempt, so clients that failed together don't retry together. A Retry-After header wins. It can also be an HTTP date, which needs Date.parse and an injected clock; this sketch handles the seconds form only.
The key is created once per user intent (one click on Pay) and reused by every retry of that intent. A new key per attempt would defeat it.

examples.title: Offset vs cursor pagination, and following the server's next link

annotations.note: Offset paging counts rows: "skip 2". When a row is inserted in front, everything shifts by one, so page 2 repeats order 4. A deleted row shifts the other way and one is skipped. PostgreSQL also has to read and throw away every skipped row.

Cursor (keyset) paging remembers a position: "older than order 4". Inserts and deletes elsewhere don't move it, and an index on id finds the start directly (sql.indexes.stats-pagination). The cursor is opaque: the client treats it as a token, so the server may change its contents later.
The client follows the next URL the server returns until it is null, and never builds page URLs itself. An async generator fetches a page only when the loop asks for it, and break stops it.
The same insert in both runs. Offset shows 4 twice; cursor shows every order exactly once (the new one appears at the top on the next refresh).

examples.title: Download progress from the body stream; upload progress in parts

annotations.note: Progress is measured in bytes. Each of these Turkish letters is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 30000 characters are 60000 bytes: compute progress from file.size, not from string length.

Reading the body yourself instead of calling json() or blob(): each read() returns the next chunk the network delivered, so the count of bytes so far is the progress. Chunk sizes are up to the browser; here the fake server fixes them at 16 KiB.

Content-Length can be missing (a chunked response) or count the compressed bytes when Content-Encoding is gzip, while the stream yields decompressed ones. Treat it as a hint and fall back to an indeterminate progress bar.

fetch exposes no upload progress at all. Sending a file in parts gives progress that means "the server has this much", and a failed part is retried alone. S3 multipart uploads and the tus protocol work this way.
Blob.slice cuts at byte offsets and can split a multi-byte character. That is fine for upload parts, which the server reassembles before anyone decodes them; never decode a part on its own.

use_cases: Mobile and flaky networks: retry idempotent requests with backoff, give non-idempotent ones a key
Rate-limited third-party APIs: honour 429 and Retry-After instead of hammering
Infinite scroll and exports over live data: cursor pagination with server-issued next links
Large file uploads (videos, CSV imports) with a progress bar and resume after a dropped connection
strengths: Composable platform pieces: AbortSignal for deadlines, Request.clone() for re-sending, async generators for pages, streams for progress
Injected sleep and randomness make retry logic testable in microseconds, without fake timers
Server-issued cursors let the server change its paging scheme without a client release
Uploading in parts survives flaky connections: only the failed part is sent again
weaknesses: fetch has no built-in retry, no upload progress and no pagination helper; each is code you own and test
Retries multiply across layers and can turn a short outage into an overload the clients caused themselves
Cursor pagination can't jump to page 7 or show a total cheaply
Download progress depends on Content-Length, which compression and chunked responses make unreliable

pitfalls.title: Retrying requests that aren't safe to repeat
pitfalls.detail: A POST that timed out may have succeeded. Retry it only with an Idempotency-Key the server honours, created once per user action.
pitfalls.bad: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { try { return await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body }); } catch {} }
pitfalls.good:
const headers = { "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID() }; // once per click
await send(doFetch, new Request(url, { method: "POST", body, headers }), policy);

pitfalls.title: Retrying 4xx responses
pitfalls.detail: 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 won't change on a retry. Only 408 and 429 among the 4xx codes mean "try again later".

pitfalls.title: Fixed delays, or no cap
pitfalls.detail: Every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment. Use exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum number of attempts, and the caller's deadline.

pitfalls.title: Retrying at every layer
pitfalls.detail: Three attempts each in the browser, in a backend-for-frontend and in the service behind it make up to 27 requests to the last service. TanStack Query already retries failed queries three times by default; don't add a retrying fetch wrapper under it.

pitfalls.title: Offset pagination over data that changes
pitfalls.detail: Inserts duplicate items across pages and deletes skip them. Use a keyset cursor for feeds, exports and infinite scroll.

quiz.q: POST /payments timed out with no response. What does the client know?
options: Nothing: the server may or may not have committed it
quiz.why: A lost response says nothing about the server side. Without an Idempotency-Key the only safe move is to report the unknown outcome, or check the order's status.

quiz.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: So clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment
quiz.why: Without jitter, synchronized clients form waves that hit the recovering server together. A random wait spreads them out.

quiz.q: A list pages with ?offset=. A new item is inserted at the top between page 1 and page 2. What does the user see?
options: The last item of page 1 again at the top of page 2
quiz.why: Everything shifts down by one, so offset 2 now starts at the item that was at offset 1. A delete does the opposite and skips one.

quiz.q: How can a browser app show upload progress for a 500 MB file?
options: XMLHttpRequest's upload progress events, or uploading in parts with fetch
Reading response.body while the upload runs
quiz.why: fetch has no upload progress events. xhr.upload fires progress events; parts give progress that the server has confirmed.

lessons.body:
## Concept

The plain client from the first lesson becomes production-grade by adding four
behaviours, each a small piece of code you own.

**Retries.** Retry a request only when the failure may go away *and* repeating it is
safe. "May go away": no response at all, a timed-out attempt, 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and
504. "Safe": the method is idempotent (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE), or the request
carries an `Idempotency-Key` that the server uses to recognise a repeat. Wait between
attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `Retry-After` (seconds or an HTTP
date), and stop at a maximum number of attempts or at the caller's deadline.

**Timeouts.** Two of them: one per attempt (`AbortSignal.timeout`), and one for the whole
operation, which is usually the caller's signal. Combine them with `AbortSignal.any()`.

**Pagination.** Offset paging (`?offset=40`) is simple and lets users jump to a page, but
it shifts when rows are inserted or deleted, and it gets slower with depth. Cursor paging
(`?cursor=…`, keyset in SQL) is stable and fast, and the server should hand out the next
URL or cursor so the client never constructs one. Some APIs put that URL in a `Link`
header with `rel="next"`; reading it cross-origin requires the server to list `Link` in
`Access-Control-Expose-Headers`.

**Progress.** Download progress comes from reading `response.body` chunk by chunk and
counting bytes. Uploads are the gap: fetch has no upload progress events.
`XMLHttpRequest` still has them, and uploading in parts gives progress that the server
has confirmed:

```ts
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.upload.addEventListener("progress", (e) => {
  if (e.lengthComputable) bar.value = e.loaded / e.total;
});
xhr.open("POST", "/api/uploads");
xhr.send(file);
```

A listener on `xhr.upload` makes a cross-origin request preflighted (next lesson). A
`ReadableStream` request body (with `duplex: "half"`) lets you count bytes as fetch reads
them, but that measures what the browser took, not what the server received, and support
differs between browsers.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: urllib3's `Retry(total=..., backoff_factor=..., status_forcelist=...)`
  retries only `allowed_methods`, which by default excludes POST and PATCH, and respects
  `Retry-After`: the same policy as `send()` here.
- **C**: the curl tool's `--retry` treats a timeout and HTTP 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504
  (plus Cloudflare's 522 and 524) as transient, doubles its wait between attempts, and
  lets `Retry-After` override the wait.
- **Go**: the same loop, with `context` instead of `AbortSignal` (go.services.retries). A
  Go request body is also read once; `http.Request.GetBody` returns a fresh copy, the job
  `Request.clone()` does here. `http.Transport` itself replays a request after a network
  error on a reused connection only if it counts as idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE,
  or any request with an `Idempotency-Key` header.
- **Java**: teams reach for Resilience4j or Spring Retry. In the browser there is no
  standard library for this: write the loop, or let TanStack Query retry queries.
- **JS**: TanStack Query retries failed queries three times with exponential backoff by
  default and doesn't retry mutations; keep fetch-level retries out of code that runs under
  it.

## Design notes

Put the policy in one place, the API client, as data: attempts, base delay, which
statuses, which methods. Callers shouldn't sprinkle retry loops. Inject the clock, the
sleep and the random source; deterministic tests of retry logic are otherwise slow and
flaky.

Retry at one layer only, and give the whole operation a budget: a deadline signal from the
caller, merged with the per-attempt timeout. When the user navigates away, the cancel
should stop the waiting as well as the request.

Idempotency is a contract with the server. The client creates the key per user intent and
keeps it for that intent's retries (store it with the pending form if a reload must not
duplicate the order); the server stores the outcome under the key, typically with a unique
constraint and an upsert (sql.modifying.returning-upsert), and replays it.

For pagination, let the server own the cursor format and return the next link; for
progress, report what you can measure honestly: bytes read, parts acknowledged, or an
indeterminate spinner.

lessons.title: WebSockets, EventSource (SSE), CORS from both sides, tokens vs cookies (concepts)
lessons.summary: Server-sent events push text over one HTTP response; WebSockets carry messages both ways. CORS doesn't stop requests: the server labels its response and the browser decides whether the page's origin, even the opaque "null", may read it.

examples.title: Parsing a text/event-stream from a fetch body

annotations.note: EventSource can't send an Authorization header or use POST, so streaming APIs that need either are read with fetch and parsed by hand. TextDecoderStream decodes UTF-8 across chunk boundaries: a character split between two chunks is held until its second byte arrives.

A chunk can end in the middle of a line, so the last piece waits for the next chunk. The stream ends without a final blank line in this example, and the unfinished event is dropped, as EventSource drops it. The format also allows a lone CR as a line end; this sketch doesn't.

A line starting with a colon is a comment, which servers send as a keep-alive. A blank line dispatches: data lines are joined with \n, the last \n is removed, the type defaults to "message", and an event without data lines dispatches nothing.

Each line is field: value, with one leading space removed. The id carries over to later events (the second event shows #41 too), and EventSource sends it back as Last-Event-ID when it reconnects, so the server can resume. retry sets EventSource's reconnection delay.
The wrong way to decode a stream: a fresh TextDecoder per chunk turns each half of İ into U+FFFD. Any Turkish text breaks this way sooner or later; decode with one streaming decoder.

In a page, the body comes from fetch, with whatever method and headers the API needs. for await consumes the events as they arrive; break stops reading, and an AbortSignal on the fetch closes the connection.

examples.title: A WebSocket client: validated messages, resubscribe on reconnect

annotations.note: WebSocket gives you frames, not a protocol. Define the messages as a discriminated union and validate each one: a frame is untrusted input like any response body.
An exception thrown in an event listener is reported as uncaught, and the rest of that message's handling is lost. Turn bad JSON into a value the schema rejects.
The client depends on two members of WebSocket. The real class satisfies the type structurally, and the fake below does too, with no shared base class.
Server-side state such as subscriptions belongs to one connection. After a reconnect the server knows nothing, so the client subscribes again on every open, not once at startup.
Two malformed frames are dropped and the stream continues. Throwing here, or trusting a cast, would break the live view on the first odd message.

wasClean is false when the connection died without a close handshake; 1006 is the code the browser reports then, and no endpoint ever sends it. Reconnect with exponential backoff, and jitter in production, or every client hits a restarted server at once.

A real socket fires these events from the network. Here the example fires them itself, which makes the order deterministic. A real send() throws InvalidStateError while the socket is still connecting and silently drops data once it is closing or closed.

examples.title: CORS: when the browser preflights, and when the page may read the answer
