annotations.note: Real, not modelled: this sandboxed iframe (sandbox without allow-same-origin) has an opaque origin, which serializes as "null", and no access to cookies: reading document.cookie throws.
fetch's defaults: mode "cors" for cross-origin requests, and credentials "same-origin", so cookies go only to the page's own origin unless you pass credentials: "include".

Requests an HTML form could always send (GET, HEAD, POST with form or text bodies and a few plain headers) go out directly. Anything else, JSON bodies and Authorization headers included, is preceded by an OPTIONS preflight, and the real request is sent only if the answer allows it. Simplified: the real rules also limit header values.

The decision after the response arrives. A simple request has already reached the server and run, so CORS is no protection for its side effects. "*" never works with credentials; then the origin must match exactly and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must be "true".
A null-origin page can read "*" responses, and anything that allow-lists the string "null". Every sandboxed iframe, data: URL and file: page in the world has that origin, so never allow-list it.

use_cases: SSE: notifications, progress of server-side jobs, streamed generated text; one direction, plain HTTP, automatic reconnect
WebSocket: chat, collaborative editing, multiplayer state; both directions, low overhead per message
CORS: a SPA on app.example.com calling an API on api.example.com; a public read-only API answering with *
Same-origin instead of CORS: a reverse proxy (or Vite's dev proxy, as in this app) serving page and API from one origin
strengths: EventSource reconnects and resumes (Last-Event-ID) on its own, unlike a raw socket in Go or Java where you write that loop
SSE is ordinary HTTP: proxies, HTTP/2 multiplexing, cookies and server logs all just work
WebSocket is supported everywhere, bidirectional, and has little per-message overhead after the handshake
CORS lets the server opt in per origin and per credential mode, without the browser ever exposing a response by default
weaknesses: EventSource is GET-only with no custom headers; over HTTP/1.1 each stream holds one of the browser's 6 connections per domain
WebSocket has no backpressure, no built-in reconnect and no message schema; all three are your code
CORS failures reach JavaScript as an opaque TypeError; only the devtools console says why
CORS protects reading, not acting: simple cross-origin requests still execute on the server

pitfalls.title: Treating CORS as access control
pitfalls.detail: The server still receives and executes simple cross-origin requests, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely. Authenticate every request and protect cookie-authenticated writes against CSRF.

pitfalls.title: Reflecting any Origin with credentials
pitfalls.detail: Echoing the request's Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin together with Allow-Credentials: true lets every website read your users' data. Compare against an allow-list, send Vary: Origin, and never allow-list null.

pitfalls.title: Not checking Origin on the WebSocket handshake
pitfalls.detail: CORS doesn't govern WebSockets. The browser sends the page's Origin and the user's cookies with the handshake; a server that doesn't check Origin can be driven from any site (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).

pitfalls.title: Bearer tokens in localStorage
pitfalls.detail: Any script on the page, including an injected one, can read them. Prefer HttpOnly cookies, or keep a short-lived access token in memory only.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting to resubscribe after a reconnect
pitfalls.detail: Server-side subscriptions die with the connection. Send them again on every open event.

quiz.q: A page on https://app.example.com POSTs a form-encoded body to https://api.example.com, which sends no CORS headers. What happens?
options: The browser blocks the request before it is sent
The request reaches the server and runs; the page just can't read the response
The browser sends a preflight first
quiz.why: A form-encoded POST is a simple request: no preflight. CORS only decides whether the response is exposed to the page.

quiz.q: Which of these requests triggers a preflight?
quiz.why: application/json is not one of the three form content types, so the browser asks permission with OPTIONS first.

quiz.q: fetch(url, { credentials: "include" }) gets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. Can the page read the response?
options: No: credentialed responses need the exact origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Only if the cookie is HttpOnly
quiz.why: The wildcard is ignored for credentialed requests. The server must echo the specific origin and allow credentials.

quiz.q: Your app needs live order updates from server to browser, and requests carry a session cookie. What is the simplest fit?
quiz.why: One-way push over plain HTTP: EventSource sends cookies (same-origin, or with withCredentials), reconnects itself and resumes with Last-Event-ID.

further_reading.title: MDN: Origin header (when it is null)

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Server-sent events (SSE)** keep one HTTP response open and send UTF-8 text in a tiny
format (`text/event-stream`): `field: value` lines, events separated by a blank line.
`EventSource` parses it, dispatches `message` events (or named ones from the `event`
field), and reconnects on its own, sending the last `id` it saw as `Last-Event-ID`:

```ts
const es = new EventSource("/api/orders/events"); // same origin: cookies go along
es.addEventListener("order", (e) => render(JSON.parse(e.data)));
es.onerror = () => {
  // readyState CONNECTING: it is reconnecting; CLOSED: it gave up
};
es.close(); // when the view goes away
```

The constructor takes a URL and one option, `withCredentials` (send cookies to another
origin), nothing else: always GET, no custom headers. When an API needs POST or an
`Authorization` header, read the stream from fetch and parse it yourself (example 1).

**WebSockets** upgrade an HTTP request into a two-way channel of messages.
`new WebSocket("wss://…")` fires `open`, `message`, `error` and `close`; `send()` throws
while the socket is still connecting. There is no reconnect, no message schema and no
backpressure: when messages arrive faster than you handle them, they pile up in memory.
`WebSocketStream` was an attempt to add backpressure; MDN now points to WebTransport
instead.

**CORS** relaxes the same-origin policy, which lets a page *send* requests to other
origins but not *read* the answers. The browser attaches `Origin` to cross-origin
requests. For anything beyond what an HTML form could send, it first sends an `OPTIONS`
preflight. Then it reads the response's `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers and decides
whether the page may see the response. A refusal surfaces as a `TypeError` with no
details. `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` widens the short list of response headers a
page may read. An opaque origin, from a sandboxed iframe like the lesson runner, a
`data:` URL or a `file:` page, is sent as `Origin: null`.

**Tokens vs cookies** decides how a request proves who sends it:

- A **cookie** is sent by the browser automatically. `HttpOnly` hides it from JavaScript
  (an XSS bug can't steal it, though it can still make requests while the user is on the
  page), `Secure` keeps it off plain HTTP, and `SameSite` controls cross-site sending.
  Because it is automatic, cookie-authenticated writes need CSRF protection. Cross-origin,
  fetch sends it only with `credentials: "include"`, and the server must answer with the
  exact origin plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- A **bearer token** in an `Authorization` header is sent only when your code adds it, so
  there is no CSRF. But your JavaScript must be able to read the token, so XSS can steal
  it, and the header makes every cross-origin request preflighted. EventSource can't send
  it at all, and a WebSocket can't send custom headers either: there the token goes in the
  first message, or in the URL, where proxies and access logs record it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go**: a server sends SSE by writing `data: …\n\n` and flushing
  (`http.ResponseController.Flush`); go.http.uploads-streams shows the server side and
  go.http.cors-cookies-httptest the CORS middleware and cookies. The Go standard library
  has no WebSocket server; teams use a module such as `github.com/coder/websocket`.
- **Java**: Spring's `SseEmitter` and `@ServerEndpoint` (Jakarta WebSocket) are the server
  halves of this lesson. `HttpClient` has a WebSocket client too. Nothing in Java resembles
  CORS: it exists because a browser runs code from many mutually untrusting origins, all
  with the user's cookies.
- **Python**: `sse-starlette` or `websockets` on the server; a `requests` client ignores
  CORS entirely, which is the point: CORS restrains browsers, not clients.
- **C/C++**: a WebSocket is a framed TCP stream after an HTTP upgrade handshake; SSE is a
  chunked HTTP response you read line by line, as you would with `fgets`.

## How it works

A preflighted cross-origin request with a session cookie, from both sides:

```text
OPTIONS /orders/7              Origin: https://app.example.com
                               Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
                               Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type
204                            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
                               Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, PUT
                               Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type
                               Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
                               Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
                               Vary: Origin
PUT /orders/7                  Origin: https://app.example.com, Cookie: session=…
200                            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
                               Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
                               Vary: Origin
```

The preflight carries no cookies; its answer may be cached for `Max-Age` seconds.
`Vary: Origin` stops a shared cache from serving one origin's permission to another. On
the client the only line that matters is
`fetch(url, { method: "PUT", credentials: "include", headers, body })`.

## Design notes

Prefer one origin. A reverse proxy that serves the page and `/api` from the same origin
removes CORS, preflights and cross-site cookie questions in one move. This app does that:
the frontend calls `/api/...` on its own origin and Vite's dev server proxies it to the Go
backend, which sends no CORS headers at all (see `server.proxy` in `vite.config.ts` and
`API_BASE` in `src/shared/api.ts`).

When you do need CORS, keep the policy in one middleware on the server: an allow-list of
origins, credentials only where needed, `Vary: Origin`, and a short `Max-Age`. Never
reflect arbitrary origins and never allow-list `null`.

Pick the realtime channel by direction. Server-to-client only: SSE, with cookies for
authentication and `id` fields so a reconnect resumes without gaps. Both directions with
high message rates: WebSocket, with a validated message union, resubscription on every
`open`, backoff with jitter, a heartbeat to detect dead connections, and an Origin check
on the server's handshake. Either way, close the connection when the view unmounts.
Over HTTP/1.1 each open SSE stream occupies one of the browser's six connections per
domain, shared by all tabs; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection.

lessons.title: Vitest: it.each tables, Testing Library (behavior, not implementation)
lessons.summary: Vitest runs tests the way Vite runs code, and it.each turns a table of cases into one named test per row, the TS spelling of Go's table-driven tests. Testing Library drives components through roles, labels and clicks, so the tests survive a rewrite of the component's internals.

examples.title: it.each: a table of Turkish edge cases, one named test per row

annotations.note: The code under test. NFD splits ç, ğ, ş, ö and ü into a base letter plus a combining mark, and \p{M} removes the marks. Dotless ı has no decomposition, so it is mapped to i by hand. Lower-casing with "tr" turns I into ı and İ into i; plain toLowerCase() would turn İ into "i" plus U+0307, which only works here because marks are stripped afterwards.

it.each takes the table and returns a test function. Each row becomes its own test, and $title and $want write the row into the name, so a failure points at the row. The row type is inferred from the table, so a misspelled field in the callback is a type error in tsc (Vitest itself doesn't check types).

This row is the reason the table exists. Remove the replaceAll("ı", "i") line and it fails with "gd-r-kalesi": ı is not in [a-z], so it becomes a separator and the leading I-turned-ı is cut off. ASCII-only test data would never notice.
Array rows are spread into the callback's parameters, and %s formats them into the name in order. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") turns i into İ and ı into I; toUpperCase() would give "Istanbul".

examples.title: Testing Library: find by role and label, act like a user, wait for async UI

annotations.note: The component under test. It lives in the test file only because the runner takes one file; in a project, CityForm.tsx and CityForm.test.tsx sit side by side.

Testing Library unmounts after each test by itself only when the runner provides a global afterEach. Vitest's globals option is off by default, so without this line the second test finds two forms and fails with: Found multiple elements with the role "button" and name "Save".

Create the user before rendering. user.click fires the whole event sequence a real click produces (pointer, mouse, focus, click), and clicking a submit button submits the form. getByRole with a name finds the element the way a screen reader announces it; that is the top of Testing Library's query priority.
getBy throws when nothing matches, and its error prints the DOM. The onSave prop is the component's boundary, so checking it with vi.fn() tests behavior, not internals.
Promise.withResolvers (ES2024) gives the test a promise it settles when it wants. Until then the component sits in its "saving" state, which the test can observe.

getByLabelText finds the input through its label. user.type types character by character, so React's onChange runs per keystroke as in a browser. The saved value is trimmed and upper-cased the Turkish way: İZMİR, not IZMIR.

The state update happens after the promise resolves, so a plain getBy here would race it. findBy retries until the element appears (default 1000 ms), and Testing Library takes care of act() while it waits. queryBy returns null instead of throwing, the way to assert that something is absent.

examples.title: describe.each over two implementations: tests that survive a refactor

annotations.note: Version 1 keeps the draft in state; the input is controlled and renders that state on every keystroke.
Version 2 is a different design: the list lives in a reducer, and the input is uncontrolled. The DOM holds the draft and the component reads it through a ref on submit.
describe.each works like it.each, one level up: the whole suite runs once per row, and %s puts the version into every test name.

The test types, presses Enter ({Enter} submits the form), clicks Add, and reads list items and the field's value. It never touches state, hooks, refs or class names, which is why it passes for both versions. A test that spied on setDraft or called the reducer would have to be rewritten for the refactor.

use_cases: Pure functions with many edge cases (parsers, formatters, slug and case rules for Turkish text): one it.each table, one row per case
Component tests for forms, lists, dialogs and error states, written in terms of what the user sees and does
Pinning behavior before a refactor: the same suite run against the old and new implementation with describe.each
Fast feedback in watch mode while editing, with the same transform pipeline as the Vite dev server
strengths: it.each gives Go-style table tests with less ceremony: each row is a named test, and a failing row doesn't stop the others
Queries by role and label double as an accessibility check: a button without an accessible name cannot be found by getByRole("button", { name })
Tests written against roles and text survive refactors (useState to useReducer, controlled to uncontrolled), unlike tests that inspect state or CSS classes
Vitest uses Vite's transform, so ESM, TypeScript and JSX need no Babel or ts-jest setup
weaknesses: jsdom is not a browser: no layout (sizes are zero), no real navigation or CSS media queries, and user-event only simulates input. Some behavior needs a real browser (Playwright, next lesson)
Vitest strips types like Vite and never type-checks a runtime test; unlike `go test`, which compiles the package first, a type error in a test file passes unless tsc runs too
Async UI needs findBy or waitFor at the right places; a getBy that races a state update gives flaky failures
More setup than Go's built-in testing package: an environment (jsdom), user-event, and cleanup when globals are off

pitfalls.title: No cleanup between tests
pitfalls.detail: With Vitest's default globals: false, Testing Library can't register its afterEach, so every render stays in the document and queries start finding duplicates. Add afterEach(cleanup), or enable globals in the Vitest config.

pitfalls.title: Testing implementation details
pitfalls.detail: Selecting by class name, counting renders or asserting on internal state ties the test to today's code. Ask what the user perceives: a role, a label, a text.
pitfalls.good: expect(screen.getByRole("alert").textContent).toBe("Enter a city");

pitfalls.title: getBy to assert absence
pitfalls.detail: getBy throws when nothing matches, so `expect(getBy...).toBeNull()` can never pass. Use queryBy for absence and findBy for elements that appear later.
pitfalls.good: expect(screen.queryByRole("alert")).toBeNull();

pitfalls.title: fireEvent where a user would type
pitfalls.detail: fireEvent.change sets a value and fires one event. userEvent.type focuses, types each key and fires the events in a browser's order, so it catches handlers that a single change event skips. Prefer user-event; keep fireEvent for events users can't produce.

pitfalls.title: Trusting jsdom with browser behavior
pitfalls.detail: In this setup (jsdom 31, user-event 14.6) typing after form.reset() continued from the old text, although the field's value was already empty. In a browser the field is empty. When a test depends on real browser behavior (layout, focus order, form reset, navigation), test it in Playwright.

quiz.q: Which query does Testing Library recommend trying first?
quiz.why: Roles and accessible names are what users and assistive technology perceive; test ids are the last resort because users can't see them.

quiz.q: You want to assert that no error message is shown. Which query?
quiz.why: queryBy returns null when nothing matches. getBy throws, and findBy waits and then rejects.

quiz.q: A status message appears after an awaited save. `expect(screen.getByRole("status"))` right after the click fails now and then. The fix?
options: Add a setTimeout of 100 ms before the assertion
quiz.why: findBy retries until the element appears or the timeout passes; fixed sleeps are slow and still flaky.

quiz.q: Why use it.each over a loop of expect calls inside one test?
options: Each row is reported as its own named test, and one failing row doesn't hide the others
Loops are not allowed in Vitest tests
quiz.why: Like t.Run per row in Go, each row has its own name and result, and you can run one row with a name filter (-t).

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Vitest** runs test files through Vite's transform: TypeScript and JSX are stripped
and compiled, ESM works as it does in the app, and `expect` follows Jest's API.
`it.each(table)` (also spelled `test.each`) turns a table into one test per row, and
`describe.each` does the same for a whole suite. The [Vitest API
docs](https://vitest.dev/api/) list the name placeholders: `$field` for object rows,
`%s`, `%i`, `%#` for array rows.

**Testing Library** renders a component into jsdom and gives you queries that find
elements the way a user does: by role and accessible name (`getByRole`), by label
(`getByLabelText`), by visible text. **user-event** produces the input a user would
(click, type, Enter). The [guiding
principle](https://testing-library.com/docs/guiding-principles): the more your tests
resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you. Query
variants encode timing:

- `getBy…` returns the element or throws (zero or several matches);
- `queryBy…` returns `null` when nothing matches: use it to assert absence;
- `findBy…` returns a promise that retries until the element appears (1000 ms by
  default): use it after anything asynchronous.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `it.each` is the table-driven test. `for _, tc := range tests { t.Run(tc.name,
  ...) }` becomes a table plus a name template, and `go test -run 'TestSlug/Iğdır'` is
  `vitest -t "Iğdır"`. Unlike `go test`, Vitest never compiles your types: a type
  error in a test file still runs.
- Java: JUnit 5's `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource`. Testing Library has no
  close JUnit analogue; Selenium-style page objects are the nearest relative, built
  on roles instead of CSS selectors.
- Python: `pytest.mark.parametrize` for tables; Testing Library plays the role of a
  user-level driver that pytest's unit tests usually lack.
- JS: Jest's API almost one to one (`vi.fn` for `jest.fn`). Enzyme's shallow
  rendering and `wrapper.state()` are the implementation-detail style that Testing
  Library deliberately leaves out.

## How it works

`render()` mounts the component into `document.body` of a jsdom window that Vitest
creates per test file (the `environment: 'jsdom'` setting). Testing Library runs
`render` and user-event actions inside React's `act()`, and its async helpers
(`findBy`, `waitFor`) take care of act while they wait, so state updates and effects
are flushed before your next line runs. It also sets `IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT`,
which is why these tests print no act() warnings. Queries
read the DOM through the same accessibility rules a browser uses: a `<label>` names
its input, `role="alert"` is an alert, a `<button>`'s text is its name. A component
that is hard to query is usually hard to use with a screen reader too.

## Design notes

Test at the component's boundary. That boundary is its props and callbacks on one
side and the rendered DOM on the other, so assert on what the user sees and on what
the component reports outward (`onSave` called with "İZMİR"), never on how it got
there. Example 3 is the payoff: the state model and the input style both changed, and
the suite didn't. Keep pure logic (slugs, validation, Turkish case rules) out of
components and cover it with `it.each` tables; they are cheap to extend when a bug
report brings a new edge case. Component tests then only need to check the wiring.

lessons.title: MSW for the API; Playwright basics; type tests with expectTypeOf
lessons.summary: Mock the network, not fetch: MSW answers real requests from production code. Playwright drives a real browser and can answer its requests too, so end-to-end tests need no backend. expectTypeOf tests the types themselves, which no runtime test can see.

examples.title: MSW: production fetch code, mocked at the network boundary

annotations.note: This is production code that calls the real global fetch. There is no injected client and no vi.mock of a module, so the test exercises the URL building, encodeURIComponent and the status check exactly as shipped. res.json() returns any; real code validates it (lesson ts.services.zod).

setupServer describes the network: a method and a URL pattern map to a resolver that receives a standard Fetch API Request and returns an HttpResponse. searchParams.get decodes the query, so "Güneydoğu Anadolu" arrives with its ğ and ü intact, as a real server would see it.

onUnhandledFrame is MSW 3's name (MSW 2 called it onUnhandledRequest). The default "warn" lets an unmocked request through to the real network. "error" stops it, so a missing mock fails the test instead of calling a live service.

resetHandlers removes what server.use added, so one test's error scenario can't leak into the next. close() stops the interception after the last test. cleanup is the Testing Library unmount from the previous lesson.
findAllByRole waits for the effect, the intercepted fetch and the re-render. The test never mentions MSW: it renders and reads, like a user.
server.use prepends a handler for this test only, and the newest matching handler wins. The 503 path is tested without touching the component or the client.
With "error", an unmocked request rejects with "fetch failed", and MSW prints the method and URL on stderr. Without that option, this request would have gone out to the internet.

examples.title: Playwright: a real browser, with page.route as the backend

annotations.note: The app under test is a string of HTML with an inline script, because this runner has no app server. In a project, playwright.config's webServer starts the dev server and tests call page.goto("/").
page.route intercepts requests from the browser itself, including the navigation to https://app.test/, where nothing is listening. route.fulfill answers with any status, headers and body.
The browser-side counterpart of an MSW handler: read the request, answer with JSON (`json:` also sets the Content-Type). When several routes match, the most recently registered one wins.
Locators are lazy queries by role and label, the same vocabulary as Testing Library. press("Enter") submits the form through the browser's own implicit submission, in real Edge, not a simulation.

Web-first assertions retry until they pass or time out (5 s by default), so no findBy or sleep is needed. toHaveText with an array checks every list item in order. toBeHidden asks the browser's real rendering, something jsdom can't compute.
The failure path: one route answers 503, and the test checks what the user sees, an alert and an empty list.

examples.title: Type tests with expectTypeOf in a *.test-d.ts file

annotations.note: The kind of type worth testing: the path picks the response type through an indexed access. A careless refactor turns it into Promise<any> and every caller still compiles. `declare function` is enough, because a .test-d.ts file is only type-checked and never executed.

expectTypeOf(x) captures x's static type. .resolves unwraps a Promise, .parameter(0) reads a parameter, and toEqualTypeOf demands identical types. The @ts-expect-error line is a negative test: that call must not compile, and if it ever does, tsc reports an unused directive (TS2578) and the test fails.
Narrowing pinned down: on the union, data doesn't exist; after `if (r.ok)` it is a City. If someone loosens Result so that data is always present, this test fails.

toExtend checks assignability, the structural rule (extra properties allowed); toEqualTypeOf checks identity. expect-type 1.2 deprecated the older toMatchTypeOf in favor of toExtend and toMatchObjectType.

use_cases: Component and client tests against a mocked API: success, empty, 4xx/5xx, slow responses, malformed JSON
End-to-end tests of critical flows (login, checkout, a form wizard) in a real browser, with page.route for unreliable or paid third-party APIs
Type tests for library-style code: generic helpers, typed API clients, discriminated unions and mapped types that callers depend on
Sharing one set of MSW handlers between tests and local development (setupWorker in the browser) while the backend is unfinished
strengths: MSW leaves the client untouched: fetch, URL building, headers and JSON parsing run as in production, unlike vi.mock or a spy on fetch that replaces exactly the code you wanted to test
No port and no injected base URL: compared with Go's httptest.NewServer, which needs the client to accept srv.URL, MSW intercepts in process
Playwright runs real browser engines with auto-waiting locators and assertions, so the flakiness of manual waits mostly disappears
Type tests catch regressions no runtime test can, such as a generic quietly widening to any, and they cost nothing at run time
weaknesses: Mocks are a second description of the API and can drift from the real server; derive them from the OpenAPI contract or keep a few tests against the real backend
Playwright is slow next to jsdom: this two-test file takes about 8 s here, mostly starting Edge, against about 1 s for the jsdom files, so keep end-to-end tests few and focused
Type-test failures are tsc errors about generic constraints and can be hard to read; Vitest's typecheck mode still prints an experimental-feature notice
MSW patches globals in the test process: every test in a file shares one set of handlers, so overrides need resetHandlers discipline, and concurrent tests need server.boundary() to keep them apart

pitfalls.title: Mocking fetch instead of the network
pitfalls.detail: A spy on fetch must hand-build Response objects and breaks when the client changes (another header, a switch to a different client), while the request the server would have received is never checked.
pitfalls.good: server.use(http.get(`${API}/cities`, () => HttpResponse.json([])));

pitfalls.title: Copying an MSW 2 setup into MSW 3
pitfalls.detail: MSW 3 renamed onUnhandledRequest to onUnhandledFrame. tsc reports the old key as an unknown property (TS2353), but at run time it is ignored: the default "warn" applies, and unmocked requests go out to the real network.

pitfalls.title: Sleeping in Playwright tests
pitfalls.detail: A fixed wait is slow when the app is fast and flaky when it is slow. Web-first assertions retry until the condition holds.
pitfalls.good: await expect(page.getByRole("listitem")).toHaveCount(1);

pitfalls.title: MSW's browser worker and page.route together
pitfalls.detail: Requests answered by a Service Worker (MSW's setupWorker in a dev build) never reach page.route. Playwright's docs recommend serviceWorkers: "block" when you route requests yourself.

pitfalls.title: Type tests that never run
pitfalls.detail: *.test-d.ts files are checked only in typecheck mode (vitest --typecheck); a plain `vitest run` skips them, and nothing fails. This lesson's runner adds the flag. In a project, put --typecheck into the CI test command or enable typecheck in the Vitest config.

quiz.q: What does MSW replace in the code under test?
options: Nothing: it intercepts the request after the code made it, at the network layer
quiz.why: The client code runs unchanged; MSW answers the outgoing request (in Node by intercepting the request modules, in the browser with a Service Worker).

quiz.q: A test adds `server.use(...)` for a 503 and the next test unexpectedly sees 503 too. What is missing?
quiz.why: server.use prepends handlers until they are reset; resetHandlers returns to the handlers given to setupServer.

quiz.q: Why does `await expect(locator).toHaveText("...")` need no explicit wait in Playwright?
options: Playwright waits for network idle before every assertion
Web-first assertions retry until the condition holds or the timeout passes
The page is static, so nothing changes
quiz.why: Assertions on locators re-query and retry (5 s by default), which is what makes them robust against timing.

quiz.q: `expectTypeOf({ name: "a", plate: 1, extra: true })` passes which check against `City`?
quiz.why: The object is assignable to City (structural typing allows the extra property), but its type is not identical to City.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three tools, three boundaries:

- **MSW** (Mock Service Worker) mocks **the network**. You describe endpoints with
  handlers (`http.get(url, resolver)`); in Node, `setupServer` intercepts outgoing
  requests and answers them from the handlers. Your `fetch` code runs unchanged. See
  the [MSW docs](https://mswjs.io/docs).
- **Playwright** drives **a real browser** (here the installed Microsoft Edge,
  headless) through locators and auto-retrying assertions. `page.route` answers the
  browser's requests, the network mock one level up. See the
  [Playwright docs](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro).
- **Type tests** check **the types**. `expectTypeOf` from Vitest turns "this returns
  `Result<City[]>`" into an assertion that tsc verifies; files named `*.test-d.ts`
  are type-checked by `vitest --typecheck` and never executed. See Vitest's
  [testing types guide](https://vitest.dev/guide/testing-types).

A sensible split: many fast jsdom tests with MSW for components and clients, a
handful of Playwright tests for the flows that must work in a real browser, and type
tests for the types other code leans on.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `httptest.NewServer` runs a real server on a loopback port, and your client
  must accept `srv.URL`. MSW intercepts in process: no port, no injected URL, but a
  patched global. Go has no type tests because the compiler is one; the closest idiom
  is a compile-time assertion such as `var _ io.Reader = (*MyReader)(nil)`, which is
  what `toExtend` expresses.
- Java: MSW sits between Mockito (replace the client) and WireMock (a real HTTP
  server); Playwright fills Selenium's role, with auto-waiting built in.
- Python: `responses` or `respx` patch the HTTP library much as MSW patches Node's;
  Playwright has Python bindings with the same API.
- JS: `jest.mock("axios")` and hand-made `fetch` stubs are the pattern MSW replaced.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph vitest["Vitest (Node + jsdom)"]
    comp["component"] --> client["fetchCities()"] --> fetch1["fetch"]
    fetch1 -. intercepted .-> msw["MSW handlers"]
  end
  subgraph pw["Playwright test (Node)"]
    spec["spec"] -- "protocol" --> edge["Edge: page + script"]
    edge -- "fetch /api/cities" --> route["page.route handler (in the test)"]
  end
```

In Node, MSW hooks the modules that issue requests (the MSW README describes it as a
low-level interception algorithm, since Node has no Service Workers); in a browser it
registers a Service Worker. Playwright runs your test in Node and controls the browser
over a protocol; `page.route` pauses each matching request inside the browser and
lets the test continue, fulfill or abort it. For type tests, Vitest runs tsc with
`--noEmit` over the test files and maps each error to the `test()` block it falls in.
In this repo that is the `typescript` package (6.0); `npm run typecheck` uses 7.0.

## Design notes

Mock at the outermost boundary you can. The further out the mock sits, the more of
your real code each test covers: MSW keeps the client honest, and `page.route` keeps
the whole page honest. Keep handlers realistic (status codes, error bodies, Turkish
text in the payloads) and make unhandled requests fail. A mock that quietly lets a
request through, or answers everything with 200, gives you green tests that prove
nothing. Type tests earn their place on code with clever types: generic helpers, typed
clients, unions that callers narrow. If a type is simple enough that a reviewer sees
it at a glance, a type test adds nothing.

lessons.title: A ladder of tsconfig strictness; ESLint + typescript-eslint; Prettier
lessons.summary: Three tools, three jobs: tsc proves types, type-aware ESLint catches bugs that type-check fine, Prettier ends formatting debates. Climb the strictness ladder one measured rung at a time, and ratchet each new check in so existing errors never block a merge.

examples.title: Promise bugs that tsc accepts and type-aware lint rejects

annotations.note: filter's predicate may return anything, so tsc accepts a Promise; every Promise is truthy, so nobody is filtered out. tsc does catch the plain `if (isAdmin(x))` (TS2801), but not this, a negation, or a forEach.
forEach calls the async callback and drops the Promise it returns. Each callback stops at its first await, so countAdmins returns 0 before any of them resumes.

A floating promise: submit returns while saveDraft is suspended, and a rejection would surface as an unhandled rejection far from this line. If fire-and-forget is really meant, `void saveDraft()` says so and satisfies the rule.
The fixed versions. Promise.all runs the checks concurrently and keeps their order; by the last line saveDraft has finished, which shows the floating call did run, just not when submit assumed.

examples.title: Values that type-check and still print nonsense

annotations.note: A template literal accepts any type, so an object becomes "[object Object]" in a log line, an error message or a URL.
|| falls back on every falsy value, so an explicit 0 becomes 3. ?? falls back only on null and undefined. The rule fires only when the left side can actually be nullish, as an optional property can.

A switch statement that assigns instead of returning gives tsc nothing to check: the missing "archived" case compiles and renders an empty badge. switch-exhaustiveness-check is in no preset; enable it by name.

examples.title: Ratcheting a new check in: compare per-file counts against a baseline

annotations.note: unchecked-index.txt is tsc 7.0.2's real output for this repo with noUncheckedIndexedAccess on (2026-11-13). The baseline is invented to show all three verdicts; a real one is generated once and committed.

tsc's non-pretty format is file(line,col): error TSnnnn: message, one error per line plus indented continuation lines, which the regex skips. Counting per file, not per line, survives code moving around.
New errors fail; fewer errors pass and ask for a lower baseline, so the count can only go down. browserTs.ts fails here because it had no entry: a new index read without a check.
The run here only prints, because a non-zero exit fails the example. In CI the exit code is the whole point.

use_cases: Starting a project: strict tsconfig, type-aware recommended lint and a formatter on day one, when every rung costs zero errors
Tightening an existing codebase: measure each flag or rule from the command line, take the free ones immediately, ratchet the rest
Code review: lint catches floating promises and misused async callbacks so reviewers can look at design instead
Ending formatting discussions: Prettier on save and `prettier --check` in CI, ESLint left to bugs
strengths: Unlike Go, where gofmt and vet ship with the compiler, every rung is adjustable, so a JavaScript codebase can be migrated gradually and a new one can start at the top
Type-aware rules see what tsc knows: a Promise passed where void is expected, an object stringified in a template, a non-exhaustive switch statement
A ratchet makes a new check adoptable without a big-bang cleanup: existing errors are tolerated, new ones fail
Separating formatter and linter keeps each fast and uncontroversial; formatting never shows up as a lint error
weaknesses: Type-aware linting needs a TypeScript program per run: 3.8 s instead of 1.6 s on this repo's src, and much more on large codebases
typescript-eslint drives the TypeScript 5/6 JavaScript API, which TypeScript 7.0 doesn't ship, so a TS 7 project keeps TS 6 installed for its linter (ADR-0006)
strict and strict-type-checked are documented as not semver-stable: a minor typescript-eslint update can add errors
Three tools mean three configs and three places where an ignore list can be forgotten

pitfalls.title: Turning on the strictest preset in one commit
pitfalls.detail: On this repo, strict-type-checked plus stylistic-type-checked reports 53 problems in 15 files. Done in one go, that becomes a wall of eslint-disable comments. Take the free rungs, then ratchet.

pitfalls.title: Fire-and-forget without saying so
pitfalls.detail: A deliberately unawaited promise should be marked, and its errors handled, so readers and no-floating-promises can tell it from a forgotten await.
pitfalls.good: void saveDraft().catch(reportError);

pitfalls.title: Linting generated files
pitfalls.detail: ESLint 9 lints .js files by default. This repo's ignores list only dist, so `npm run lint` also lints the generated public/lesson-libs/bundle.js and reports errors from eslint-disable comments inside bundled libraries. Ignore build output explicitly.
pitfalls.good: { ignores: ['dist', 'public/lesson-libs'] }

pitfalls.title: Formatting rules in the linter
pitfalls.detail: ESLint deprecated its core formatting rules (indent, semi, quotes and others) in v8.53.0. Let a formatter own layout and turn off any lint rule that disagrees with it.

quiz.q: `logins.filter(async (l) => await isAdmin(l))` keeps every login. Which tool reports it?
quiz.why: no-misused-promises needs type information to know the callback returns a Promise where filter tests truthiness. tsc accepts it, and syntax-only rules can't see return types.

quiz.q: A new flag produces 27 errors in 5 files. With a per-file ratchet, which pull request fails?
options: One that leaves the 27 errors untouched
One that fixes two errors in one file
One that adds a new error in a file whose count was 0
quiz.why: The ratchet compares per-file counts with the baseline: unchanged or lower passes, higher fails. Old errors never block a merge; new ones always do.

quiz.q: Prettier and an ESLint rule disagree about where a line breaks. What is the fix?
options: Configure Prettier to match the ESLint rule
Turn the formatting rule off in ESLint and let Prettier decide
Run ESLint --fix after Prettier in CI
quiz.why: Formatting belongs to the formatter. Prettier's docs recommend eslint-config-prettier for exactly this, and ESLint itself deprecated its formatting rules.

quiz.q: Why does this repo keep TypeScript 6.0 installed next to TypeScript 7.0?
options: typescript-eslint's type-aware rules need the TypeScript JavaScript API, which 7.0 doesn't ship
quiz.why: ADR-0006: tsc 7 is authoritative for type-checking; typescript-eslint loads the 6.0 compiler API until TypeScript 7.1 ships its new API. Vite transpiles with esbuild and needs neither.

further_reading.title: TypeScript 6.0 release notes (new defaults and deprecations)

lessons.body:
## Concept

Three tools, three questions:

- **tsc**: is the program type-correct? Its strictness is set in `tsconfig.json`.
- **ESLint with typescript-eslint**: does the program contain patterns that are type-correct
  but almost always bugs? The rules that matter most are **type-aware**: they ask the
  TypeScript checker what a value is.
- **Prettier**: what should the code look like? A formatter with deliberately few options,
  run on save and checked in CI.

Strictness is a **ladder**: you climb it one rung at a time, measuring each rung first.
Measured on this repo with tsc 7.0.2 and ESLint 9.12 on 2026-11-13:

1. `strict: true`, the default since TypeScript 6.0. This repo is here, plus
   `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`.
2. Free rungs, zero errors then: `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters` (both explicitly
   `false` in `tsconfig.app.json`), `noImplicitReturns`, `noImplicitOverride`,
   `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Turning them on now keeps them at zero.
3. Small rungs: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` (3 errors in 2 files),
   `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` (2 in 2).
4. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: 27 errors in 5 files, 20 of them in
   `src/shared/ui/markdownBlocks.ts`. A ratchet rung.
5. Lint presets, in typescript-eslint's own order: `recommended` (this repo, no type
   information, 0 problems in `src`), `recommended-type-checked` (11 problems in 2 files),
   `strict-type-checked` with `stylistic-type-checked` (53 problems in 15 files), plus rules
   no preset enables, such as `switch-exhaustiveness-check`.

Measure a flag without editing anything:
`node node_modules/typescript7/bin/tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json --noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
A day later the same command reported 40 errors in 6 files, 31 of them in
`markdownBlocks.ts`, which had grown table support in the meantime. Un-ratcheted counts
drift with every change, which is why the ratchet compares each file with its own
baseline instead of one total.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go:** `gofmt` is Prettier with zero options, and the whole community accepted it. `go vet`
  is a type-aware linter shipped with the toolchain; staticcheck is the stricter rung.
  Go's compiler already rejects unused variables and imports, which TypeScript leaves to
  `noUnusedLocals`.
- **Java:** javac's `-Xlint` and Error Prone (bug patterns using type information) are the
  type-aware lint; Checkstyle the stylistic one; google-java-format the formatter.
- **C/C++:** `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` is the same ladder, `clang-tidy` the type-aware linter,
  `clang-format` the formatter.
- **Python:** mypy's flags and `--strict` mirror tsconfig; ruff or pylint lint; black is
  the "uncompromising" formatter, the closest relative of Prettier.
- **JS:** plain ESLint parses JavaScript only. typescript-eslint adds a TypeScript parser
  and, for type-aware rules, a running TypeScript program.

## How it works

The first two examples type-check cleanly with tsc 7 and pass this repo's own lint
configuration. Linted with `strict-type-checked`, `stylistic-type-checked` and
`switch-exhaustiveness-check`, using `parserOptions: { projectService: true }`, they report
(path prefix shortened):

```
01_promise_bugs.ts
  10:30  error  Expected a non-Promise value to be returned  @typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises
  16:18  error  Promise returned in function argument where a void return was expected  @typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises
  30:3   error  Promises must be awaited, end with a call to .catch, end with a call to .then with a rejection handler or be explicitly marked as ignored with the `void` operator  @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises

02_silent_values.ts
  12:23  error  'lesson' will use Object's default stringification format ('[object Object]') when stringified  @typescript-eslint/no-base-to-string
  12:23  error  Invalid type "Lesson" of template literal expression  @typescript-eslint/restrict-template-expressions
  15:40  error  Prefer using nullish coalescing operator (`??`) instead of a logical or (`||`), as it is a safer operator  @typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing
  20:11  error  Switch is not exhaustive. Cases not matched: "archived"  @typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check

✖ 7 problems (7 errors, 0 warnings)
```

`projectService` asks TypeScript's language service for each file's program, which is what
makes these rules possible and what makes them slower: 3.8 s for this repo's `src` against
1.6 s for the syntax-only configuration (tsc 7 type-checks the same files in about 0.26 s).
The service is TypeScript's JavaScript API. TypeScript 7.0 ships no such API (a new one is
planned for 7.1), so ADR-0006 keeps `typescript` 6.0 installed for typescript-eslint and
calls `node_modules/typescript7/bin/tsc` for type-checking.

## Design notes

Climb in this order: take every free rung now, because a flag at zero errors only costs
something once someone breaks it. Then ratchet the expensive rungs: commit per-file counts,
fail CI on increases, lower the baseline as files are touched. The third example is the
whole mechanism in twenty lines.

Two findings from measuring this repo. ADR-0006 records the owner's decision that
type-aware ESLint is on, but `eslint.config.js` still extends the syntax-only
`tseslint.configs.recommended`; switching to `recommendedTypeChecked` with `projectService`
is the next rung, and its 11 findings include the unnecessary double cast in
`src/features/learning/api.ts` discussed in ts.architecture.patterns. Second, the
`ignores` list holds only `dist`, so `npm run lint` also lints the generated
`public/lesson-libs/bundle.js` and reports errors from it.

Prettier is not installed in this repo. If it is added, keep its job separate: format on
save, `prettier --check .` in CI, and eslint-config-prettier (the integration Prettier's
documentation recommends) to switch off any lint rule that would fight it. Prettier's
documentation advises against running it as an ESLint rule (eslint-plugin-prettier): slower,
and formatting turns into red squiggles. ESLint 9.22 added `defineConfig()` in
`eslint/config`, and typescript-eslint now marks its own `tseslint.config()` helper as
deprecated in its favour. This repo's ESLint 9.12 predates it (the same helpers ship
separately as `@eslint/config-helpers`), so `tseslint.config()` stays until one of the two
dependency changes is made.

lessons.title: Vite: dev server, proxy, env variables, build, source maps, DevTools debugging
lessons.summary: Vite serves source files to the browser as native ES modules in development and bundles them for production. Neither mode type-checks. Its proxy keeps the API same-origin, its env variables are build-time strings, and source maps take DevTools back to your TypeScript.

examples.title: import.meta.env: strings at build time, parsed once at startup

annotations.note: import.meta is part of JavaScript (import.meta.url works in any module); env is Vite's addition. Code that runs outside Vite (this runner, a Node script, a Vitest test without Vite's config) sees undefined.

The values are what `vite build` substituted for this .env in the lesson's scratch build. vite/client declares ImportMetaEnv as Record<string, any> plus the built-in keys, so the compiler accepts any VITE_ name and any use of it.
"false" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy, and "20" + 1 is "201". In the real build both expressions were constant-folded to exactly these wrong answers.
The schema states what each variable means and converts it once. z.infer gives the rest of the app a real type (boolean, number) instead of any.
A bad value fails at startup with a precise message, instead of NaN travelling into a request ten screens later.

examples.title: Reading a real source map: minified column to TypeScript line

annotations.note: Real esbuild output and map. Minified, the whole program is one line and the parameter names are e, n and r; sourcesContent embeds the original TypeScript, so DevTools can show it without fetching the .ts file.
Each mapping number is base64 VLQ: variable-length, 5 bits per character with a continuation bit, sign in the lowest bit. Small deltas take one or two characters, which keeps maps compact.
Every field is relative to the previous segment, so the decoder keeps running totals. The optional fifth field indexes names: how the map remembers that t was totalMinutes.
A stack frame gives a generated line and column; the last segment at or before that column names the original position. DevTools does this for every frame, breakpoint and console location.

use_cases: Running the frontend against a local backend without CORS: proxy /api in server.proxy, as this app does
Per-environment configuration that is safe to publish: API base URLs, feature flags, build labels
Debugging production errors: build hidden source maps, keep them out of the deploy, feed them to the error tracker
Setting breakpoints in TypeScript in the browser's DevTools while the dev server runs
strengths: Unlike webpack-style dev servers that bundle before serving, Vite transforms only the modules the page requests, so dev startup stays roughly flat as the app grows
Env replacement at build time lets the minifier delete whole branches: the DEV-only code in the scratch build never reached the bundle
The proxy makes development same-origin, so the backend needs no CORS configuration it would never use in production
Source maps are a standard format, so the same map works in Chrome, Edge and Firefox DevTools and in error trackers
weaknesses: No type-checking anywhere in Vite: `vite build` ships code with type errors unless tsc runs separately
Env values are strings typed as any by default; nothing stops `VITE_DEBUG ? ... : ...` from always being true
Dev and build use different pipelines (per-module transforms vs a Rollup bundle in Vite 7), so a bug can appear in only one of them
server.proxy exists only in the dev server; production needs the same routing in a real reverse proxy or the backend

pitfalls.title: Secrets in VITE_ variables
pitfalls.detail: Everything Vite exposes is compiled into JavaScript that every visitor downloads. Keep keys on the server and call the server.

pitfalls.title: A proxy key that matches more than you meant
pitfalls.detail: Keys are prefix matches on the raw path, so '/api' also proxies '/apiary'. In this app a request to /apiary returns the Go backend's '404 page not found' instead of Vite's index.html fallback. End the key with a slash or use a ^ regular expression.
pitfalls.good: proxy: { '/api/': apiTarget }

pitfalls.title: Testing a flag with truthiness
pitfalls.detail: VITE_FEATURE=false is the string "false". Compare with === 'true' or parse the whole env once.
pitfalls.good: if (config.VITE_DEBUG) enableDebug(); // parsed to boolean at startup

pitfalls.title: Trusting `vite build` to catch type errors
pitfalls.detail: It strips types without checking them (lesson ts.mental-model.erasable). This repo's build script is plain `vite build`, so run `npm run typecheck` before it in CI.

quiz.q: `.env` contains `VITE_DEBUG=false`. What does `import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG ? "on" : "off"` produce in a production build?
quiz.why: The value is the string "false", which is truthy. Vite substituted it at build time and the minifier folded the expression to "on".

quiz.q: vite.config.ts has `server.proxy: { '/api': 'http://127.0.0.1:8080' }`. Which request does the dev server forward?
quiz.why: Non-regex keys are matched with startsWith on the request path. '/api/' or '^/api(/|$)' limits it to the API.

quiz.q: You set `build.sourcemap: 'hidden'`. What changes compared to `true`?
options: Map files are written, but the bundles don't reference them, so browsers won't load them
The map is inlined into each bundle
quiz.why: 'hidden' writes the maps without the sourceMappingURL comment: upload them to an error tracker and keep them off the public server.

quiz.q: `.env` sets `VITE_API_URL=/api` and `.env.production` sets `VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com`. Which value does `vite build` (mode production) compile in?
quiz.why: Vite loads .env, .env.local, .env.production and .env.production.local; variables in mode-specific files take precedence over the generic ones.

lessons.body:
## Concept

Vite (this repo: 7.3.7) has two modes that share a config file and little else:

- **Dev server** (`npm run dev`; `npm start` runs it for you). Nothing is bundled. The
  browser loads `index.html`, follows `<script type="module">`, and requests each module
  by URL. Vite transforms each file on request: esbuild strips the types (one file at a time,
  no type information, hence `isolatedModules` in `tsconfig.app.json`), bare imports such as
  `react` are rewritten to dependencies pre-bundled once into a cache, and hot module
  replacement swaps edited modules in place.
- **Build** (`vite build`). Rollup bundles the module graph, esbuild minifies, every
  `import.meta.env.*` is replaced by its value, dynamic `import()` becomes a separate chunk,
  file names get content hashes. Vite 8 (released 2026-03-12) replaced esbuild and Rollup
  with Rolldown and Oxc; the concepts below carry over.

Three features matter daily:

- **`server.proxy`** forwards matching paths from the dev server to another server. This
  app's `vite.config.ts` sends `/api` and `/healthz` to `http://127.0.0.1:8080` (or to
  `STACKLAB_API_PROXY_TARGET` under Compose), so the page and its API share an origin and the
  backend needs no CORS headers. The proxy is dev-only.
- **Env variables.** Vite loads `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.[mode]` and `.env.[mode].local`
  (mode-specific files win) and exposes only names starting with `VITE_` (configurable with
  `envPrefix`). Built-ins: `MODE`, `BASE_URL`, `DEV`, `PROD`, `SSR`. User values are
  **strings**, and they end up **in the bundle**.
- **Source maps.** In dev, each transformed TypeScript module carries an inline map. In a build,
  `build.sourcemap` is `false` by default; `true` writes `.map` files, `'inline'` embeds them,
  `'hidden'` writes them without the comment that tells browsers where to find them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++:** a source map is debug info: DWARF or a PDB maps machine addresses to source
  lines; a source map maps generated columns to TypeScript lines. `'hidden'` maps are the
  equivalent of shipping stripped binaries and keeping the symbols for your crash reporter.
- **Go:** `go build` type-checks and links everything. Vite's dev server never type-checks
  and never links; it serves files. The built `dist/` can be embedded in a Go binary with
  `embed` (lesson go.files-io.embed), which is how one Go server ships the SPA and its API
  from the same origin in production.
- **Java:** the closest analogues are a servlet container serving static files with hot
  reload in dev, and a fat-jar build for production. Env values are build-time constants
  like Maven resource filtering, not runtime `System.getenv`.
- **nginx users:** `location /api` is also a prefix match and also matches `/apiary`; the
  same `/api/` habit applies to Vite's proxy keys.
- **JS:** webpack-dev-server bundles in memory before the first page load; Vite relies on
  the browser's native module loader and transforms files on request, so startup stays fast
  as the app grows.

## How it works

Fetching a module from this app's running dev server shows the dev pipeline directly.
`GET http://127.0.0.1:5173/src/shared/api.ts` returns (map shortened):

```js
import.meta.env = {"BASE_URL": "/", "DEV": true, "MODE": "development", "PROD": false, "SSR": false};export const API_BASE = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL ?? "";

//# sourceMappingURL=data:application/json;base64,eyJ2ZXJzaW9uIjozLCJzb3VyY2VzIjpbImFwaS50cyJdLC...
```

The doc comment and the `as string | undefined` cast are gone, Vite has prepended the env
object, and the base64 map decodes to `{"version":3,"sources":["api.ts"],...}` with the
original file inside.

For the build, a scratch project had this `.env`:

```
VITE_API_URL=/api
VITE_DEBUG=false
VITE_PAGE_SIZE=20
SECRET_TOKEN=do-not-ship
```

and this `src/main.ts` (`format.ts` exports `formatTitle` and an unused `unusedHelper`;
`editor.ts` builds a 2000-line array):

```ts
import { formatTitle } from "./format";

const api: string = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL ?? "";
const debug = import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG;
console.log(formatTitle("istanbul"), api, typeof debug, debug ? "debug on" : "debug off");
console.log(import.meta.env.VITE_PAGE_SIZE + 1, import.meta.env.MODE);
if (import.meta.env.DEV) console.log("dev only");

document.querySelector("#open")?.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const { openEditor } = await import("./editor");
  console.log(openEditor());
});
```

`vite build --sourcemap` printed:

```
vite v7.3.7 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 6 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                 0.17 kB │ gzip: 0.14 kB
dist/assets/editor-C4QPI_bQ.js  0.15 kB │ gzip: 0.16 kB │ map: 0.40 kB
dist/assets/index-Bm7OXp9I.js   2.21 kB │ gzip: 1.13 kB │ map: 1.24 kB
✓ built in 136ms
```

and the entry chunk contains `console.log(P("istanbul"),L,"string","debug on");console.log("201","production");`.
The minifier folded both naive reads to wrong constants, the `DEV` branch is gone,
`unusedHelper` and `SECRET_TOKEN` appear nowhere, and `editor` became its own chunk because
it was loaded with `import()`. Adding `console.log(JSON.stringify(import.meta.env))` showed
that reading the whole object compiles to
`{BASE_URL:"/",DEV:!1,MODE:"production",PROD:!0,SSR:!1,VITE_API_URL:"/api",VITE_DEBUG:"false",VITE_PAGE_SIZE:"20"}`.

In DevTools, open Sources, find the `.ts` file under the dev server's origin, and set
breakpoints as usual; a `debugger;` statement also stops there when DevTools is open.
Stack traces in the console already point at TypeScript lines, because DevTools applies the
same lookup the second example performs.

## Design notes

Parse the env once, at the edge, the way the first example does, and export a typed
`config` object; nothing else in the app should read `import.meta.env`. For stricter types
without a schema, Vite's documentation shows declaring the keys on `ImportMetaEnv` in
`src/vite-env.d.ts`, and opting into `strictImportMetaEnv` through `ViteTypeOptions` so that
unknown keys stop being `any`. This app reads one variable, in
`src/shared/api.ts`, with a cast to `string | undefined`; that is the minimal honest
version.

The proxy key in this app is `'/api'`, which also forwards `/apiary`; harmless today, but
`'/api/'` says what is meant. And because `"build": "vite build"` never type-checks, the
order that keeps a broken build out of `dist/` is `npm run typecheck && npm run build`.
Production source maps are a policy decision: `'hidden'` plus an error tracker gives
readable stack traces without publishing the original source.

lessons.title: Bundle-size awareness; the TS 7 native compiler and what changed since 5/6
lessons.summary: Every kilobyte in the first chunk is downloaded, parsed and run before the page works: measure it, delete what the platform already provides, and split the rest with import(). TypeScript 7 is the same type checker as 6.0, rewritten in Go: far faster, with 6.0's deprecations removed and no compiler API until 7.1.

examples.title: Static imports vs import(): when a chunk is loaded, evaluated and cached

annotations.note: The [static] line prints before "main starts": static imports are fetched and evaluated before the importing module runs at all. Every static import in the entry module's graph is in the first chunk's critical path.
The chunk is a separate module with its own top-level work (2000 strings here, a code editor in a real app). Nothing about it is fetched or run until the import() expression executes.

The second click logs no "[chunk] evaluating": module records are cached by URL, so import() of an already-loaded chunk resolves without fetching or evaluating again. Lazy-loading costs a delay once, not on every use.
Two concurrent import() calls for one URL share one fetch and one instance. That is why splitting never duplicates module state such as a store or a cache.

A lazy boundary is an async boundary, so it needs a loading and an error state (lesson ts.architecture.explicit-states). After a deploy deletes old chunk files, a page loaded earlier fails exactly here.

examples.title: The cheapest dependency: what Intl and the standard library already do

annotations.note: Time zones and Turkish month and day names come from the browser's own ICU data. A fixed instant and an explicit timeZone make the output independent of the machine's clock and time zone setting.
Currency uses the lira sign and Turkish separators (1.234,50); ListFormat knows "ve". Both are data the browser already ships.
The Collator orders Ç after C, I before İ and Ş after S. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ; plain toUpperCase() maps it to I and turns "istanbul" into a different word.
Object.groupBy (ES2024) and structuredClone cover the common uses of lodash's groupBy and cloneDeep. structuredClone keeps Dates and Sets, which a JSON round-trip would not.

use_cases: Reviewing a dependency before adding it: what does it add to the first chunk, and does the platform already do it?
Moving rarely used screens (editors, charts, admin pages) behind import() so they cost nothing until opened
Explaining a 'chunk larger than 500 kB' warning from vite build: attribute the bytes to sources first
Upgrading a project from TypeScript 5.x/6.0 to 7.0: clear the 6.0 deprecations, keep TS 6 for tools that need the compiler API
strengths: Unlike a Go binary, where unused code costs disk space, unused JavaScript costs download and parse time on every cold load, so the payoff of removing it is direct
import() is part of the language: Vite turns each one into a chunk without configuration, and the browser caches modules by URL
Intl covers dates, time zones, numbers, currencies, plurals, lists, collation and relative time for Turkish and every other locale with no bundle cost
tsc 7 type-checks this repo in about 0.26 s against 1.5 s for tsc 6, and the TypeScript team reports roughly 8 to 12 times faster full builds on large projects
weaknesses: Each lazy chunk adds a network round trip and an async boundary that needs loading and error states
Tree-shaking keeps any top-level code with side effects, so a module imported 'for one function' can still bring its whole setup along
TypeScript 7.0 ships no compiler API: typescript-eslint, ts-morph and similar tools keep running on 6.0 until 7.1
Options removed in 7.0 are hard errors with no ignoreDeprecations escape hatch, so legacy configs must be migrated first

pitfalls.title: Statically importing data you only need on one page
pitfalls.detail: A generated JSON or TS module of content, translations or fixtures imported at the top of the app lands in the first chunk. Load it per page with import() or fetch it.
pitfalls.good: const trackLessons = await import(`./lessons/${track}.generated.ts`);

pitfalls.title: Lazy chunks without an error path
pitfalls.detail: After a deploy removes old chunk files, import() rejects for users still on the old page. Vite fires a vite:preloadError event on window; reload the page there and serve index.html with Cache-Control: no-cache.

pitfalls.title: Reading gzip size as the whole cost
pitfalls.detail: Compression shrinks the transfer, not the work: the engine parses and compiles the uncompressed bytes. Watch both columns in the build report.

pitfalls.title: Keeping legacy options through the switch
pitfalls.detail: ignoreDeprecations: "6.0" silences target es5, moduleResolution node10 and baseUrl in TypeScript 6.0. TypeScript 7.0 rejects them regardless. Migrate (baseUrl to paths, node10 to bundler or nodenext) before switching.

quiz.q: A route component is imported statically in main.tsx, but users rarely open that route. What changes if you load it with import() instead?
options: Nothing: Vite bundles all modules into one file anyway
Its code moves to a separate chunk fetched and evaluated the first time the route renders
It is fetched on page load but evaluated later
quiz.why: Each import() target becomes its own chunk. The browser requests it only when the expression runs, and caches the module afterwards.

quiz.q: A module has `console.log('registered')` at the top level and one export you never use. You import it with `import './plugin'`. What does a production build keep?
options: The top-level console.log, but not the unused export
quiz.why: Tree-shaking removes unused exports but must keep side effects. The lesson's scratch build kept exactly the console.log and dropped the export.

quiz.q: A tsconfig sets `baseUrl` and `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"`. What happens with tsc 6.0 and tsc 7.0?
options: 6.0 accepts it; 7.0 fails with TS5102 'Option baseUrl has been removed'
quiz.why: ignoreDeprecations only applies to 6.0's deprecation errors. In 7.0 the option no longer exists; the error suggests paths instead.

quiz.q: Why does a project on TypeScript 7 still install TypeScript 6.0?
options: Tools that call the compiler's JavaScript API, such as typescript-eslint, need it until 7.1
Vite needs TypeScript 6 to strip types
quiz.why: 7.0 ships the native tsc but no stable API. This repo keeps typescript@6.0 for typescript-eslint and calls node_modules/typescript7/bin/tsc for type-checking (ADR-0006).

further_reading.title: TypeScript 6.0 release notes: defaults, deprecations and the path to 7.0

lessons.body:
## Concept

**Bundle size** has two costs. The transfer is measured compressed (the `gzip` column in
Vite's build report); the parse, compile and run is paid on the uncompressed bytes, on every
cold load, on the user's CPU. The first chunk matters most, because nothing works until it
has run. Three levers, in order of payoff:

1. **Don't ship it.** The platform covers dates, time zones, money, plurals, lists,
   collation, deep copies and grouping (second example). Check before adding a library.
2. **Let tree-shaking remove it.** With static ES imports the bundler sees which exports are
   used and drops the rest. It must keep top-level code with side effects, so a module that
   does work at import time brings that work along; a package's `"sideEffects": false` in
   `package.json` lets the bundler drop its unused modules without proving them pure.
3. **Split it.** Every `import()` becomes a separate chunk, fetched and evaluated the first
   time the expression runs (first example). `React.lazy` wraps the same mechanism for
   components; routes are the natural seams.

**TypeScript 7.0** (released 2026-07-08) is the TypeScript compiler ported to Go. You still
install `typescript` and run `tsc`; the npm package is a small launcher plus a per-platform
package with a native binary (`@typescript/typescript-win32-x64`, a 24.5 MB `tsc.exe`, on
this machine). It type-checks in parallel (`--checkers`, default 4; `--singleThreaded` turns
that off). What changed for users came mostly in two steps:

- **6.0 changed defaults and deprecated the past**: `strict` true, `module` esnext, `target`
  the newest ES version, `types` `[]`, `rootDir` the tsconfig's directory; deprecated
  `target: es5`, `downlevelIteration`, `moduleResolution: node`/`node10`, `baseUrl`, and more.
- **7.0 removed what 6.0 deprecated**, made `stableTypeOrdering` permanent, reworked JSDoc
  checking of JavaScript, and ships **no compiler API**; a new, different API is planned
  for 7.1.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C/C++:** tree-shaking is the linker's dead-code elimination (`--gc-sections`), with one
  difference: a JavaScript module's top level is code that runs on import, like a static
  initializer, so the bundler must keep it. Lazy chunks are `dlopen` for the web.
- **Go:** the linker removes unreachable functions and the binary loads once. In the browser
  the "binary" is downloaded and compiled on every cold visit, which is why its size gets
  attention a Go binary's doesn't. Go's toolchain was always native; TypeScript 7 moves
  tsc from Node to a Go binary, the same speed story in reverse.
- **Java:** a fat JAR loads classes lazily on first use; a JavaScript bundle evaluates every
  statically imported module up front. `import()` gives back the lazy class loading.
- **Python:** heavy imports moved inside a function to speed up startup are the same
  technique as `import()`.
- **JS:** moment.js, lodash and numeral.js were sensible before `Intl` and modern built-ins
  were everywhere; in a new codebase each needs a reason.

## How it works

This app is the case study. Building it into a scratch directory
(`vite build --outDir <scratch> --sourcemap`, Vite 7.3.7, 2026-11-13) printed, in excerpt
and with the output path shortened to `...`:

```
✓ 1613 modules transformed.
...assets/esbuild.worker-Da5M7R_F.js     70.31 kB
...assets/index-lINU84IR.css             20.81 kB │ gzip:   4.55 kB
...assets/index-B52vhmod.js           2,267.25 kB │ gzip: 734.91 kB │ map: 3,616.10 kB

(!) Some chunks are larger than 500 kB after minification. Consider:
- Using dynamic import() to code-split the application
```

Attributing the main chunk's bytes to sources through its source map (the decoding from
lesson ts.tooling.vite, run over every segment) gives:

```
  1894 kB  83.5% src/features/lessons/lessons.bundle.generated.ts
   131 kB   5.8% react-dom
    92 kB   4.1% react-router
    50 kB   2.2% src/features/curriculum/curriculum.generated.ts
```

Five sixths of the JavaScript was lesson text and example code, imported statically by
`src/features/lessons/types.ts`, and it grew with every lesson written. On 2026-11-14 the
app took the third lever: a light index of every lesson stays in the first chunk, and each
lesson's content is a JSON file of its own, listed with `import.meta.glob` and loaded with
`import()` when the lesson opens. With all 229 lessons written, the same build went from

```
index-DuDG42j7.js   4,685.04 kB │ gzip: 1,529.43 kB      (before the split)
index-5QpmjKlJ.js     478.29 kB │ gzip:   151.92 kB      (after)
```

plus 229 lesson chunks, 19 kB at the median and 44 kB the largest. Other heavy parts were
lazy already: `esbuild.wasm` (14 MB, fetched by the worker on the first TypeScript run)
and `lesson-libs/bundle.js` (2.9 MB, fetched the first time a lesson imports one of its
libraries). A smaller scratch build showed the
tree-shaking rules: an unused export disappeared from the bundle, while a module imported
only for its side effect kept its top-level `console.log` and lost its unused export.

On the compiler side, the same `tsconfig` with legacy options, checked by both versions:

```
tsc 6.0.3:
tsconfig.json(3,15): error TS5107: Option 'target=ES5' is deprecated and will stop functioning in TypeScript 7.0. Specify compilerOption '"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"' to silence this error.
tsconfig.json(5,25): error TS5107: Option 'moduleResolution=node10' is deprecated and will stop functioning in TypeScript 7.0. Specify compilerOption '"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"' to silence this error.
  Visit https://aka.ms/ts6 for migration information.
tsconfig.json(6,5): error TS5101: Option 'baseUrl' is deprecated and will stop functioning in TypeScript 7.0. Specify compilerOption '"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"' to silence this error.
  Visit https://aka.ms/ts6 for migration information.

tsc 7.0.2:
tsconfig.json(3,15): error TS5108: Option 'target=ES5' has been removed. Please remove it from your configuration.
tsconfig.json(5,25): error TS5108: Option 'moduleResolution=node10' has been removed. Please remove it from your configuration.
tsconfig.json(6,5): error TS5102: Option 'baseUrl' has been removed. Please remove it from your configuration.
  Use '"paths": {"*": ["./*"]}' instead.
```

With `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` added, 6.0.3 exits cleanly and 7.0.2 prints the same
three errors. On this repo's `tsconfig.app.json`, `--extendedDiagnostics` reports a total of
1.32 s for 6.0.3 and 0.144 s for 7.0.2 (0.272 s with `--singleThreaded`). The permanent
stable type ordering is visible in messages: for a union declared as
`"title" | "level" | "minutes"`, tsc 6 prints it in that order and tsc 7 prints
`"level" | "minutes" | "title"` (lesson ts.architecture.patterns).

## Design notes

For this app, the attribution pointed at the step that was then taken: keep an index in the
first chunk and load lesson bodies on demand. Per lesson rather than per track, because a
lesson page needs exactly one lesson. The price is a loading state on the lesson page and
one request per lesson opened, cheap for a local app served from 127.0.0.1, and the index
still grows with the curriculum, by about 0.46 KB per lesson. The same pass removed
something the report couldn't show: `@monaco-editor/react`'s loader fetched Monaco 0.55.1
from cdn.jsdelivr.net at run time, while the installed `monaco-editor` (0.57.0) was used
only for types. `loader.config({ monaco })` with the installed package, plus Vite `?worker`
imports for its editor and TypeScript workers, put the editor into a lazy 4.1 MB chunk of
the build and took it off the network.

For TypeScript 7: clear every 6.0 deprecation first (this repo already replaced `baseUrl`
with `paths`, see the comment in `tsconfig.app.json`), then switch `tsc`, and keep 6.0 for
tools that load the compiler API, as ADR-0006 does. Expect identical diagnostics on code
that compiles cleanly under 6.0 with stable type ordering; differences show up in message
and declaration-emit ordering and in JavaScript files checked through JSDoc.

lessons.title: Mapped types and the built-in utilities: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Awaited...
lessons.summary: Write the domain type once and compute its variants: the create payload, the patch, the per-field error map, the result of an async function. Mapped types are the loop behind every built-in utility, and you can write your own in one line.

examples.title: One source type, its create and patch variants, and two traps

annotations.note: Omit is opt-out and Pick is opt-in. Add a required dueDate to Requirement and every create() call missing it stops compiling, while the patch type ignores it until someone decides it is editable. Choose per type which failure mode you want.

Readonly<Requirement> makes every property readonly, one level deep, at compile time only. Passing r1 to update(r: Requirement) still compiles: readonly properties are assignable to mutable ones, so the guarantee holds only while the value keeps its Readonly type.
The patch type has no id, and a fresh object literal gets the excess property check, so { id } is rejected. tsc 7 prints the expanded type, with the union members in its own order.

Omit is declared as Omit<T, K extends keyof any>, so any string is accepted. "createdOn" matches nothing and Oops is Requirement unchanged; the proof is that oops.createdAt still type-checks. Pick's K extends keyof T catches the same typo.

Optional means "may be missing", and without exactOptionalPropertyTypes it also admits an explicit undefined. The spread then overwrites title with undefined while r3 is typed as a Requirement whose title is a string.

examples.title: Writing your own mapped types

annotations.note: [K in keyof T] loops over T's keys and T[K] reads each property's type, so each validator gets its own parameter type: v is a string for title and a number for priority. Mapping over keyof T keeps T's readonly and ? markers, which is how Partial and Readonly are built.
The mapped type makes the rule set exhaustive: a form field without a validator is TS2739, the same check you would otherwise write as a unit test.

In generic code, validators[key] has the type (value: T[typeof key]) => ... and value[key] is exactly T[typeof key], so the call needs no cast. The loop walks the validators, not the value: structural typing lets the value carry extra properties, and they have no rule to run.
FieldErrors<T> has every key optional, so only failing fields appear. This shape is what a form component renders next to each input.

A - removes a modifier, as Required<T> removes ? with -?. The as clause (TS 4.1) renames or filters keys; mapping a key to never drops it. The condition is a conditional type over a template literal type, the next lesson's topic.
Types compose inside out: Public drops _etag, then Mutable removes readonly from what is left, so copy.id can be reassigned.

examples.title: Types read off values and functions with typeof, ReturnType and Awaited

annotations.note: as const makes the array a readonly tuple of literals, and [number] reads the union of its elements. The list stays available at run time for menus and validation, which a type-only union is not.

typeof in a type position reads the declared type of a value. ReturnType alone would give a Promise; Awaited unwraps it the way await does (TS 4.5), and an indexed access walks into the result. This is how you type the output of a library that doesn't export it.
A Record over a finite union requires every key, so a new status breaks the build at every table that has to handle it. A Map or Partial<Record<...>> would let the missing entry through to run time.

use_cases: Request types derived from the entity: Omit for create payloads, Partial<Pick<...>> for PATCH bodies
Per-field maps over a form or DTO: validators, error messages, dirty flags, column definitions
Lookup tables that must cover a whole union: labels, colors, status transitions as Record<Status, ...>
