Typing what a library returns without its cooperation: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof client.get>>, Parameters<typeof fn>, ComponentProps<typeof Button>
strengths: One source of truth: renaming or adding a field in the entity updates every derived type, where Java needs a separate CreateRequest and UpdateRequest class (or MapStruct code generation) kept in sync by hand
A PATCH type is Partial<Pick<...>> in one line; Go needs a second struct with pointer fields to tell a missing field from a zero value
Mapped types are ordinary code you can read and write, so a project-specific utility (Validators<T>, FieldErrors<T>) costs one line instead of a code generator
Record over a union makes lookup tables exhaustive at compile time, the type-level version of a switch with a never check
weaknesses: Omit doesn't check its keys and doesn't distribute over unions, two silent failures in the most used utility
Readonly is shallow and compile-time only; nothing freezes the object, and a Readonly<T> passes for a mutable T
Hovering a derived type often shows Partial<Pick<...>> instead of the resulting fields, and error messages print the expanded form, which gets long
Partial makes every field optional with no way to say which combinations are valid; a patch that must change at least one field needs a hand-written type or a runtime check

pitfalls.title: A typo in Omit removes nothing
pitfalls.detail: Omit<T, K extends keyof any> accepts any key, so the type silently stays whole. Use Pick where you can, or a one-line strict version.
pitfalls.bad: type Draft = Omit<Requirement, "id" | "createdOn">; // createdAt still required
pitfalls.good: type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;

pitfalls.title: Omit on a discriminated union keeps only the common fields
pitfalls.detail: keyof (A | B) is the keys both variants share, so Omit<TraceEvent, "id"> becomes { kind: ... } and every variant's own fields disappear. Apply it per member with a distributive conditional type (next lesson).
pitfalls.good: type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never;

pitfalls.title: Partial lets undefined overwrite real values
pitfalls.detail: { ...r, ...patch } with patch = { title: undefined } stores undefined in a field typed string. Turn on exactOptionalPropertyTypes (lesson ts.mental-model.tsconfig), or drop undefined entries before merging.

pitfalls.title: Record<string, T> lookups claim to always find something
pitfalls.detail: owners["REQ-EXPORT"] is typed string even when the key is missing. Use a Map, Partial<Record<string, T>>, or noUncheckedIndexedAccess so the miss shows up as undefined in the type.

quiz.q: You add a required dueDate: Date to Requirement. RequirementDraft = Omit<Requirement, "id" | "createdAt"> and RequirementPatch = Partial<Pick<Requirement, "title" | "status">>. What changes?
options: RequirementDraft requires dueDate, so create() calls without it stop compiling; RequirementPatch is unchanged
Nothing until you rebuild the derived types
quiz.why: Omit keeps every key it doesn't name, so new fields flow in; Pick keeps only the keys it names. Derived types are recomputed on every check.

quiz.q: What does Omit<Requirement, "createdOn"> do when Requirement has createdAt but no createdOn?
quiz.why: Omit constrains its keys only to keyof any, so an unknown key is accepted and matches nothing. Pick<Requirement, "createdOn"> would be TS2344.

quiz.q: async function load(): Promise<Row[]>. What is ReturnType<typeof load>?
quiz.why: ReturnType reads the declared return type, which is the Promise. Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>> gives Row[].

quiz.q: Which mapped type is Required<T>?
quiz.why: -? removes the optional modifier from each property; -readonly removes readonly, which is a different utility.

further_reading.title: TypeScript 4.5 release notes: the Awaited type

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **mapped type** builds an object type by looping over keys:
`{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` copies `T`, and changing the right-hand side, the modifiers or
the keys gives you every variant you need. The built-in utilities are mapped types you
don't have to write:

- `Partial<T>` and `Required<T>` add or remove `?`; `Readonly<T>` adds `readonly`.
- `Pick<T, K>` keeps the keys you name; `Omit<T, K>` keeps the rest.
- `Record<K, V>` builds an object with one `V` per key in `K`.

A second family reads types off other types and values: `typeof value`,
`ReturnType<typeof fn>`, `Parameters<typeof fn>`, and `Awaited<T>` (TS 4.5), which unwraps a
promise the way `await` does. With these the entity type is written once, and the create
payload, the patch body, the form's error map and the API result are computed from it,
so they can't drift apart.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: a `Requirement` record plus `CreateRequirementRequest` and `UpdateRequirementRequest`
  DTOs, kept in sync by hand or by a code generator. Here each one is a type expression,
  and adding a field to the entity updates them all at compile time.
- Go: a PATCH body is a second struct with pointer fields (`Title *string`) so a missing
  field differs from an empty one, and generics can't map over a struct's fields. No type
  is computed from another; each struct is written out.
- C++: templates compute types too, but standard C++ through C++23 cannot enumerate a
  struct's members, so there is no `Partial<T>`.
- Python: `TypedDict` with `total=False` is a hand-written `Partial`; the `typing` module
  has no `Pick` or `Omit`.
- JS: nothing changes at run time. Every one of these types is erased; the spread in
  `update` is the same code you would write without them.

## Design notes

Derive in one direction: the entity (or the generated API type) is the source, and request
types, view models and form state are computed from it. Choose `Omit` when a new field
should be required everywhere by default and `Pick` when new fields should stay out until
someone opts in; a write payload is usually safer as a `Pick`, since a new server-managed
field then can't slip into the request type.

Stop deriving when the derived type stops being readable. `Partial<Omit<Pick<A, ...>, ...>>`
nested three deep is harder to review than the four fields written out, and a type that
must express rules ("status `approved` requires an owner") isn't a mapping at all: that is
a discriminated union, lesson ts.type-level.branded. Two traps are worth a lint rule or a
local helper: `Omit` checks neither its keys nor union members, and `Partial` admits
`undefined` unless `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is on.

lessons.title: Conditional types, infer, template literal types
lessons.summary: A conditional type is an if-expression over types, distributed over unions; infer extracts parts of what matched, including parts of strings. They compute precise types for callers, but generic code that must produce them needs casts, which is where to stop.

examples.title: Extract, a guard that mirrors it, and infer

annotations.note: A conditional type with a naked type parameter runs once per union member and unions the results, so Extract keeps each event that matches on its own. The pattern `requirement.${string}` matches two of the three types.

approval accepts exactly one variant. The predicate repeats the type's rule in runtime code, and the checker trusts it: if the prefix in the type and the prefix in startsWith ever drift apart, nothing reports it. Keep them adjacent.

infer V declares a type variable that the match fills in, here the promise's value type, and the recursion unwraps Promise<Promise<T>> as well. The built-in Awaited is the same idea, generalized to any object with a callable then method, which is what await itself unwraps.

Comparing the discriminant narrows e to the approved variant, which is exactly EventOf<"requirement.approved">. Without the check e is the whole union, and the message names the first member that doesn't fit.

filter with a type predicate returns RequirementEvent[], so e.id type-checks after it. An inline (e) => e.type.startsWith(...) would leave TraceEvent[]: TS 5.5 infers predicates only from checks that narrow, and startsWith doesn't.
Distribution applies only when the checked type is a bare type parameter. One more consequence: IsText<never> is never, because never is the empty union and there is no member to run the check on.

examples.title: Building and parsing string types; Uppercase knows no locale

annotations.note: Each union in a template literal type is cross multiplied, so 2 x 2 gives 4 topics. The product grows fast, and the handbook recommends generating large string unions ahead of time rather than in the checker.

The leading ${string} matches up to the first colon, Name up to the next slash, and Rest takes the remainder, which recurses. ParamNames of the route is "reqId" | "testId", and Params maps that union to an object. React Router's generatePath types its params argument with the same technique.

The runtime loop parses the same grammar the type parses, and the final cast asserts they agree. That cast is the trust boundary of every type-level parser: test the function, because the checker can't compare the two.
After the undefined check m.reqId and m.testId are strings, and a misspelled parameter is a compile error with a suggestion instead of an undefined at run time.

The handbook says these intrinsic types use the JavaScript string functions and are not locale aware: Uppercase<"izmir"> is "IZMIR". A Turkish UI shows "İZMİR", which doesn't fit that type. Use Uppercase for machine identifiers (event names, HTTP methods, environment variables), never for display text.

examples.title: Knowing when to stop: a conditional return type vs a type map

annotations.note: Callers of parseCell get precise types, but inside the body K is still a type parameter: checking kind === "number" narrows the value, not K, so Parsed<K> stays unresolved and only a cast compiles. The cast accepts the wrong date branch just as readily.
The type map states the relation as data. Each parser is checked against its own entry, so returning the raw string for date is TS2322 at the definition.

Indexing a mapped type with a generic key lets the checker relate the call to CellTypes[K] directly, so the function needs no cast and no conditional type. Prefer this shape whenever the cases can be listed.
The cost of the cast at run time: due1 is typed Date but holds a string, and the first Date method called on it throws. due2 really is a Date.

use_cases: Narrowing a union by shape or string pattern: Extract<Event, { type: `user.${string}` }>, Exclude<Status, "deleted">
Reading types out of other types: element types, promise results, parameters of a callback, props of a component
String-keyed APIs: route params from path patterns, event and topic names, CSS custom property names
Library signatures where the result depends on an option, e.g. a query hook whose data type depends on a select function
strengths: Types can be computed from other types, including strings, which neither Java nor Go generics can do: a route pattern yields its params type, an event union yields per-event handler types
Distribution over unions makes filters like Extract and Exclude one-liners that keep every variant's own fields
infer names a nested part without restating the outer structure, so helpers keep working when the outer type changes
It all runs in the checker, so precise library APIs cost nothing at run time
weaknesses: Generic implementations can't produce a conditional type without casts, and casts silently accept wrong branches
Error messages print the computed types, which get long and hard to read as type-level code grows
Distribution is implicit: whether a union is split depends on whether the checked type is a bare type parameter
Recursive types have depth limits (TS2589) and cost editor responsiveness on large inputs

pitfalls.title: Accidental distribution
pitfalls.detail: ToArray<string | number> with T extends unknown ? T[] : never gives string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. Wrap both sides in brackets when you mean the whole union.
pitfalls.bad: type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
pitfalls.good: type ToArray<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;

pitfalls.title: A conditional return type that forces casts
pitfalls.detail: Inside the function K is unresolved, so every return needs `as Parsed<K>`, and a cast on the wrong branch compiles. List the cases in a type map and index into it, or write overloads.
pitfalls.bad: function parseCell<K extends Kind>(k: K, raw: string): Parsed<K> { return raw as Parsed<K>; }
pitfalls.good: function parseCell<K extends keyof CellTypes>(k: K, raw: string): CellTypes[K] { return parsers[k](raw); }

pitfalls.title: Uppercase and Capitalize for Turkish text
pitfalls.detail: They use JavaScript's locale-independent case mapping, so Capitalize<"istanbul"> is "Istanbul" while Turkish users expect "İstanbul". Keep these types for identifiers and case display text at run time with toLocaleUpperCase("tr").

pitfalls.title: Type-level parsers on unbounded input
pitfalls.detail: A recursive type that isn't tail recursive stops with TS2589 "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite" after about a hundred levels (tsc 7.0 fails on a 120-character string); tail-recursive types (TS 4.5) go further. Route patterns are fine; CSV rows, SQL or JSON documents belong in runtime code.

quiz.q: type IsText<T> = T extends string ? "text" : "other". What is IsText<"a" | 1>?
quiz.why: T is a bare type parameter, so the check runs per member: "a" gives "text", 1 gives "other", and the results are unioned.

quiz.q: What is Uppercase<"istanbul">?
quiz.why: The intrinsic string types apply JavaScript's toUpperCase, which is not locale aware; only toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ.

quiz.q: function f<K extends Kind>(k: K): Parsed<K> { if (k === "number") return 1; ... } fails with TS2322. Why?
options: Number literals are never assignable to conditional types
Checking k narrows the value but not the type parameter K, so Parsed<K> is still unresolved
The function needs an explicit type argument
quiz.why: Narrowing works on values. K could still be any Kind, or a union of them, so the checker can't pick a branch of Parsed<K>.

quiz.q: A template literal type interpolates Verb = "get" | "list" and then Entity = "Requirement" | "Test" | "Link". How many members does it have?
quiz.why: Unions in a template literal type are cross multiplied: 2 x 3 = 6.

lessons.body:
## Concept

A **conditional type** `T extends U ? X : Y` is an if-expression evaluated by the checker:
if `T` is assignable to `U`, the result is `X`, otherwise `Y`. Two rules make it useful:

- **Distribution.** When `T` is a bare type parameter and receives a union, the condition
  runs for each member separately and the results are unioned. `Extract` and `Exclude`
  are one-line conditional types built on this.
- **`infer`.** Inside the `extends` clause, `infer X` declares a type variable that the
  match fills in: the element of an array, the value of a promise, a parameter of a
  function. `ReturnType`, `Parameters` and `Awaited` are written this way.

**Template literal types** (TS 4.1) bring string manipulation into the type system. The
type `${Entity}.${Change}`, written between backticks like a template string, builds
every combination of two unions, and `infer` inside a template takes a string apart, so
`"/requirements/:reqId"` can yield the type `{ reqId: string }`. Conditional types can recurse, which makes small parsers possible.

All of this is evaluated by the checker and erased. The goal is precise signatures for
callers; the implementation behind them is ordinary JavaScript.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C++: closest to template metaprogramming: `std::conditional_t` is `T extends U ? X : Y`,
  partial specialization plays the role of `infer`, and SFINAE-style tricks have the same
  readability problems. TypeScript adds string types, which C++ templates can't take apart.
- Java and Go: generics substitute types but never compute them; there is no way to say
  "the parameter names in this path string". Go's generics deliberately stop at
  constraints, so code that needs this uses code generation instead.
- Python: `typing` has `Literal` and overloads but no conditional types; a type checker
  can't derive `{ "reqId": str }` from a string.
- JS: none of it exists at run time. A function typed with a conditional type still needs
  runtime code that does what the type claims, and nothing checks that the two agree.

## Design notes

Conditional types pay off at **call sites**: a caller writes
`match("/requirements/:reqId", path)` and gets `reqId` checked. They cost at
**implementations**: a generic function cannot narrow its type parameter, so returning a
conditional type means a cast on every branch, and a cast on the wrong branch compiles. When
the cases can be listed, state them as a type map and index into it (example 3), or write
one overload per case. Keep conditional return types for library signatures whose result
really is computed from the argument types, and test the implementation behind the casts.

Stop when the type is harder to understand than the bug it prevents. Signs: a reviewer
can't predict the type without hovering, error messages scroll, a recursive type runs into
the depth limit (TS2589), or the type-level parser duplicates a runtime parser you also
have to test. Keep type-level programs small and close to the boundary they describe,
and write the runtime half first.

lessons.title: Branded types (RequirementId) and making illegal states unrepresentable
lessons.summary: A brand gives a structural type a name the checker enforces, so a RequirementId can only come from the parser that validated it. Unions model each state with its own data. Both pay off where values get mixed up or states get confused, and stop paying beyond that.

examples.title: RequirementId and TestCaseId, parsed once and never swapped

annotations.note: Structural typing compares strings with strings, so two string parameters are interchangeable, and so are two type aliases of string. The call is backwards and nothing notices.

RequirementId is a string that also claims a property keyed by a unique symbol. No real string has it, so a plain string isn't assignable, and the two brands differ in that property's type. declare const emits nothing: the symbol exists only for the checker.

Smart constructors: the regex and the cast sit in one function, so every RequirementId in the program has passed the check. Code that receives one never re-validates, which is the point of parsing at the boundary.

Swapped arguments and raw strings are now TS2345. At run time req is just the string: typeof, JSON and every string method see no brand, and toLowerCase() returns a plain string, because a lowercased ID is no longer known to be valid.

toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ, so "REQ-LOGİN" fails the check. The same happens with toLocaleUpperCase() and no argument on a machine whose default locale is Turkish. Identifiers need locale-independent toUpperCase(); locale rules are for text people read.

examples.title: Each state with its own data, and "at least one" as a type

annotations.note: With optional fields the type admits a draft with an approver, and code that tests a field instead of the status believes it. Every reader has to know which combinations are real; the type doesn't say.

A tuple with a required first element and a rest: [] doesn't fit, so "approved with no tests" can't be constructed, and evidence[0] is a string, not string | undefined, even under noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
The union lists exactly three shapes. A draft has no approvedBy to set, so the nonsense value is a compile error, and an approval can't exist without evidence.

Transitions accept the state they need and return the state they produce. isNonEmpty is the parser for arrays: data from a query is a plain array, and the guard is the one place that proves it has an element.

The switch narrows r per case, so each branch can read only that state's fields. Add a fourth status without a case and the function could end without returning, which is TS2366 under the string return type.

examples.title: Where to stop: state in a type parameter vs a union of states

annotations.note: Typestate: the status lives in a type parameter and each transition is a function from one state to the next. It is a real technique, used by builders whose steps are fixed in the source.
When the code itself creates the value, the compiler tracks every step: approving a draft is TS2345.

Most domain objects come from a database or a request, so their state is a run-time value: Req<Status>. It is one object type with a union-typed property, not a union of objects, so checking row.status narrows the property and leaves row as Req<Status>.
A guard per question gets the type back. This is the cost of typestate on dynamic data: extra code whose only job is to convince the checker.

The union of the states is the discriminated union from example 2, and a plain comparison narrows it. TS 3.5 also lets Req<Status> be assigned to it without a cast, because each possible status matches one member.

use_cases: IDs of different entities that travel through the same code: RequirementId, TestCaseId, UserId in services, URLs and React props
Units and currencies that are all number: meters vs feet, kuruş vs lira, milliseconds vs seconds
Validated or normalized values that are expensive or risky to re-check: an e-mail address, a slug, sanitized HTML
Workflows where each state has its own data: draft, approved with approver and evidence, rejected with a reason
strengths: Zero run-time cost: a brand is erased, unlike a Java wrapper record that allocates an object per ID
Validation happens once, in the parser; everything downstream receives proof in the type instead of re-checking strings
Unions make impossible combinations compile errors at construction time, not bugs found by reading every if statement
Stricter than Go's named types in one respect: an untyped string constant converts to a Go `type RequirementID string` implicitly, while a literal never becomes a RequirementId without the parser
weaknesses: A brand is a convention the compiler enforces only until someone writes `as RequirementId`; nothing at run time backs it
Data from JSON, the database and URL parameters arrives as plain strings, so every boundary needs a parse step
String methods and arithmetic drop the brand, so transformed values need re-parsing or a deliberate cast
Each extra type-level guarantee costs readability, error-message length and onboarding time; past a point the casts and guards outnumber the bugs prevented

pitfalls.title: Forging brands with as
pitfalls.detail: A cast at the call site skips the validation the brand stands for. Keep `as RequirementId` inside the parser module and make every other path go through it; a lint rule or code review can enforce that.
pitfalls.good: const id = parseRequirementId(params.reqId); if (!id) return notFound();

pitfalls.title: Locale-dependent case mapping for identifiers
pitfalls.detail: toLocaleUpperCase() follows the default locale, and on a Turkish machine "req-login" becomes "REQ-LOGİN". Normalize identifiers with toUpperCase() or toLowerCase(); keep toLocaleUpperCase("tr") for display text.
pitfalls.good: const s = raw.trim().toUpperCase();

pitfalls.title: Optional fields standing in for states
pitfalls.detail: { status; approvedBy?; reason? } accepts combinations that never happen, and every consumer has to guess which ones are real. Write one union member per state.

pitfalls.title: Branding everything
pitfalls.detail: Brands on every string (Title, Description, Comment) turn ordinary code into a stream of parse calls and casts. Brand what actually gets mixed up or carries a validated invariant; leave free text as string.

pitfalls.title: Typestate on data whose state is only known at run time
pitfalls.detail: A Req<S> loaded from the database is Req<Status>, and checking its status doesn't narrow it. A discriminated union does the same job with a plain if.

quiz.q: id is a RequirementId holding "REQ-LOGIN". What does JSON.stringify({ id }) produce?
quiz.why: The brand exists only in the type. At run time the value is the plain string, and symbol-keyed properties wouldn't be serialized anyway.

quiz.q: id is a RequirementId. What is the type of id.toLowerCase()?
quiz.why: toLowerCase is declared on string and returns string. A transformed ID isn't known to satisfy the parser's rules, so losing the brand is correct.

quiz.q: row: Req<Status> where interface Req<S> { id: string; status: S }. Why does if (row.status === "review") approve(row) fail?
options: Narrowing doesn't work on string literals
Req<Status> is one object type, not a union, so the check narrows row.status but not row
approve needs an explicit type argument
quiz.why: Narrowing an object by a property needs a union of object types to pick from. Req<"draft"> | Req<"review"> | Req<"approved"> is one; Req<Status> is not.

quiz.q: Which change makes "an approved requirement without evidence" impossible to construct?
options: evidence?: string[] on an approved state
evidence: string[] on an approved state
evidence: readonly [string, ...string[]] on an approved state
quiz.why: Only the tuple with a required first element rejects []; string[] accepts an empty array.

lessons.body:
## Concept

TypeScript compares types by shape, so `type RequirementId = string` is only a second name
for `string`: any string fits, including a `TestCaseId`. A **brand** gives the type a
member no real string has, `string & { readonly [brand]: "RequirementId" }`, keyed by a
`unique symbol` that exists only for the checker. Now a plain string doesn't fit, two
brands don't fit each other, and the only way to get a `RequirementId` is a function that
checks the input and casts once. That function is the parser; everything after it trusts
the type.

The same idea applied to objects is **making illegal states unrepresentable**: instead of one
type with optional fields that allows every combination, write a union with one member per
state, each carrying exactly the data that state has. A draft can't have an approver; an
approval can't exist without evidence, and `readonly [T, ...T[]]` turns "at least one" into a
type.

This lesson also closes the type-level module, so it ends with the other half of the skill:
recognizing when an extra guarantee costs more than the bugs it prevents.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `type RequirementID string` is a distinct named type, closer to a brand than a TS
  alias is, but any code can convert with `RequirementID(s)`, and an untyped string
  constant such as `"REQ-LOGIN"` is assignable without a conversion. Enforcing a
  constructor takes a struct with an unexported field.
- Java: `record RequirementId(String value)` with checks in the compact constructor is
  nominal and enforced at run time, at the price of a wrapper object per value. A brand is
  enforced only by the checker and costs nothing at run time.
- C++: the strong-typedef idiom, a wrapper template with a tag type, is the same trick: a
  type parameter that exists only to make types distinct.
- Python: `typing.NewType("RequirementId", str)` is the closest analogue: distinct for the
  type checker, the plain value at run time.
- JS: it is a string. Every guarantee here disappears when the types are stripped, which
  is why parsers sit at the boundaries where data enters.

## Design notes

Brands earn their place where values of the same base type travel together and a mix-up
is a real bug: IDs of different tables, units, amounts in different currencies, validated
strings such as slugs or sanitized HTML. Create them only in parsers at the boundary (a
route handler, an API client, a zod schema: zod's `.brand()` uses the same `unique symbol`
technique, lesson ts.services.zod), and keep the casts in those parsers. For prefixed IDs
a template literal type is a cheaper middle ground:

```ts
type RequirementCode = `REQ-${string}`;
```

Plain strings and `TC-...` IDs are rejected and literals need no cast, though it checks only
the prefix.

Then stop. A useful ladder: plain types and discriminated unions first, since they catch
most domain mistakes; brands for the values that actually get confused; typestate, phantom
parameters and type-level parsers only for APIs whose states are fixed in the source, such
as builders. Signs you went too far: casts written to satisfy your own types, guards that
exist only to convince the checker, error messages longer than the function, and types
nobody else on the team dares to change. The goal is fewer bugs per unit of reading
effort, not the most precise type that compiles.

-- LEARN(design.paradigms.side-by-side): SQL states the result and the rules; the planner picks the loops.
CREATE TABLE runs (
  test   text PRIMARY KEY,
  req    text NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('passed', 'failed'))
);
INSERT INTO runs VALUES
  ('TC-1', 'REQ-LOGIN', 'passed'),  ('TC-2', 'REQ-LOGIN', 'failed'),
  ('TC-3', 'REQ-LOGIN', 'passed'),  ('TC-4', 'REQ-EXPORT', 'passed'),
  ('TC-5', 'REQ-SEARCH', 'failed'), ('TC-6', 'REQ-SEARCH', 'failed');

SELECT req,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') AS passed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed
FROM runs
GROUP BY req
ORDER BY failed DESC, req;

-- The map and the sort you wrote by hand in Go, chosen by the planner here.
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT req, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed
FROM runs GROUP BY req ORDER BY failed DESC, req;

-- The rule lives in the table, so it holds for every client and every write.
INSERT INTO runs VALUES ('TC-7', 'REQ-LOGIN', 'pased');
files.design/paradigms/03-polymorphism/example:
-- LEARN(design.paradigms.polymorphism): variants in one table: a kind column, per-variant columns, and a CHECK tying them together.
CREATE TABLE discounts (
  code         text PRIMARY KEY,
  kind         text NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('percent', 'fixed')),
  percent      int CHECK (percent BETWEEN 1 AND 100),
  amount_kurus bigint CHECK (amount_kurus > 0),
  -- Each kind has exactly its own columns: the tagged union, enforced.
  CONSTRAINT one_shape CHECK (
    (kind = 'percent' AND percent IS NOT NULL AND amount_kurus IS NULL) OR
    (kind = 'fixed' AND amount_kurus IS NOT NULL AND percent IS NULL))
);
INSERT INTO discounts VALUES
  ('DEV250', 'fixed', NULL, 25000),
  ('HOSGELDIN', 'fixed', NULL, 5000),
  ('KASIM15', 'percent', 15, NULL);

-- The switch over kind, written as a CASE in the query that needs it.
SELECT code,
       CASE kind
         WHEN 'percent' THEN 20000 - 20000 * percent / 100
         WHEN 'fixed' THEN greatest(20000 - amount_kurus, 0)
       END AS price_kurus,
       kind
FROM discounts
ORDER BY code;

-- A row with the wrong shape for its kind is refused, like the TS literal.
INSERT INTO discounts VALUES ('BOZUK', 'percent', 15, 5000);

-- +goose Up
CREATE TABLE projects (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  name       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT projects_name_length CHECK (char_length(name) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  project_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE,
  parent_id   uuid,  -- NULL: top level
  code        text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL CONSTRAINT requirements_code_format
                CHECK (code ~ '^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(-[A-Z0-9]+)*$' AND char_length(code) <= 40),
  title       text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT requirements_title_length CHECK (char_length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft'
                CONSTRAINT requirements_status_valid CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'approved', 'obsolete')),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_in_project UNIQUE (project_id, id),  -- target of same-project FKs
  CONSTRAINT requirements_not_own_parent CHECK (parent_id <> id),
  CONSTRAINT requirements_parent_fkey FOREIGN KEY (project_id, parent_id)
    REFERENCES requirements (project_id, id)
);
CREATE INDEX requirements_parent ON requirements (parent_id);
-- (test_cases, trace_links and test_runs follow; example 3 runs them)

-- add() inserts by project name and parent code, and reports what a Go store
-- would see: the SQLSTATE and the name of the constraint that refused the row.
CREATE FUNCTION add(project text, parent text, new_code text, new_title text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE refused_by text;
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO requirements (project_id, parent_id, code, title)
  SELECT p.id, (SELECT r.id FROM requirements r WHERE r.code = parent), new_code, new_title
  FROM projects p WHERE p.name = project;
  RETURN 'ok';
EXCEPTION WHEN others THEN  -- the failed INSERT is rolled back, the script goes on
  GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS refused_by = CONSTRAINT_NAME;
  RETURN SQLSTATE || ' ' || refused_by;
END $$;

INSERT INTO projects (name) VALUES ('Ödeme'), ('Raporlama');
SELECT attempt, add(project, parent, code, title) AS outcome
FROM (VALUES
  ('top level',                'Ödeme',     NULL,         'AUTH',       'Kimlik doğrulama'),
  ('child',                    'Ödeme',     'AUTH',       'AUTH-LOGIN', 'Parola ile giriş'),
  ('lower-case code',          'Ödeme',     'AUTH',       'auth-reset', 'Parola sıfırlama'),
  ('upper-cased in tr locale', 'Ödeme',     'AUTH',       'AUTH-LOGİN', 'Parola ile giriş'),
  ('same code, same project',  'Ödeme',     NULL,         'AUTH',       'Yetki'),
  ('parent in other project',  'Raporlama', 'AUTH-LOGIN', 'EXPORT-CSV', 'CSV indir'),
  ('200 characters, 400 bytes', 'Ödeme',    NULL,         'LONG',       repeat('ş', 200)),
  ('201 characters',           'Ödeme',     NULL,         'LONGER',     repeat('ş', 201)),
  ('same code, other project', 'Raporlama', NULL,         'AUTH',       'Rapor yetkisi')
) AS t (attempt, project, parent, code, title);

SELECT p.name, r.code, r.parent_id IS NULL AS top_level, octet_length(r.title) AS title_bytes
FROM requirements r JOIN projects p ON p.id = r.project_id
ORDER BY p.name COLLATE "C", r.code;  -- byte order: Ö (U+00D6) sorts after R

-- One project's requirements, abridged: the project already has AUTH.
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id        uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  parent_id uuid REFERENCES requirements,
  code      text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  title     text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO requirements (code, title) VALUES ('AUTH', 'Kimlik doğrulama');

-- The staging table, as example 3's COPY filled it.
CREATE TEMP TABLE import_rows (
  id     uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7(), -- minted before the requirement exists
  line   integer NOT NULL,
  code   text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL,
  title  text NOT NULL,
  parent text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL
) ON COMMIT DROP;
INSERT INTO import_rows (line, code, title, parent) VALUES
  (2, 'AUTH-LOGIN-2FA', 'İki adımlı doğrulama', 'AUTH-LOGIN'),
  (3, 'AUTH-LOGIN', 'Parola ile giriş', 'AUTH'),
  (4, 'AUTH', 'Kimlik doğrulama', ''),
  (5, 'AUTH-LOGIN', 'Parola', 'AUTH'),
  (6, 'EXPORT-CSV', 'CSV indir', 'EXPORT'),
  (7, 'LOOP-A', 'Döngü A', 'LOOP-B'),
  (8, 'LOOP-B', 'Döngü B', 'LOOP-A');

-- The checks no single row can make, as one query over the whole file.
WITH RECURSIVE reached AS (
  SELECT code FROM import_rows
  WHERE parent = '' OR parent NOT IN (SELECT code FROM import_rows)
  UNION
  SELECT s.code FROM import_rows s JOIN reached r ON s.parent = r.code
)
SELECT line, 'code' AS "column", 'already used in this project' AS detail
FROM import_rows s
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT FROM requirements r WHERE r.code = s.code)
UNION ALL
SELECT line, 'code', 'also on line ' || first
FROM (SELECT line, min(line) OVER (PARTITION BY code) AS first
      FROM import_rows) AS d
WHERE line > first
UNION ALL
SELECT line, 'parent', 'no requirement ' || parent || ' in the file or the project'
FROM import_rows s
WHERE parent <> '' AND parent NOT IN (SELECT code FROM import_rows)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM requirements r WHERE r.code = s.parent)
UNION ALL
SELECT line, 'parent', 'its chain of parents loops and never reaches the top'
FROM import_rows
WHERE code NOT IN (SELECT code FROM reached)
ORDER BY 1, 2;

-- The fixed file keeps lines 2 and 3. One INSERT creates the tree, although
-- the child comes before its parent.
DELETE FROM import_rows WHERE line > 3;
INSERT INTO requirements (id, parent_id, code, title)
SELECT s.id, coalesce(p.id, e.id), s.code, s.title
FROM import_rows s
LEFT JOIN import_rows p ON p.code = s.parent
LEFT JOIN requirements e ON e.code = s.parent;

SELECT r.code, p.code AS parent, r.title
FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN requirements p ON p.id = r.parent_id
ORDER BY r.code;

-- queries/report.sql: one row per requirement and linked test, in tree order, so
-- the rows of one requirement are adjacent. The tables and project Ödeme are in
-- this example's setup.
PREPARE report (uuid) AS
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, code, title, 0 AS depth FROM requirements WHERE project_id = $1 AND parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.code, c.title, t.depth + 1 FROM requirements c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
) SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code SET ord
SELECT t.code, t.title, t.depth,
  EXISTS (SELECT FROM requirements k WHERE k.parent_id = t.id) AS has_children,
  CASE WHEN count(tc.id) OVER w = 0 THEN 'uncovered'
       WHEN count(*) FILTER (WHERE last.result = 'failed') OVER w > 0 THEN 'failing'
       WHEN count(*) FILTER (WHERE last.result = 'passed') OVER w = count(*) OVER w THEN 'passing'
       ELSE 'incomplete' END AS coverage,
  tc.code AS test, last.result, last.finished_at
FROM tree t
LEFT JOIN trace_links l ON l.project_id = $1 AND l.requirement_id = t.id
LEFT JOIN test_cases tc ON tc.id = l.test_case_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT result, finished_at FROM test_runs WHERE test_case_id = tc.id
                   ORDER BY finished_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1) last ON true
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY t.id)
ORDER BY t.ord, tc.code;

EXECUTE report('01937b6e-0000-7000-8000-00000000000a');

  setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(description)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(description)), 'B')

CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;
CREATE EXTENSION unaccent;
CREATE FUNCTION tr_lower(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower($1 COLLATE "tr-x-icu");
CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower(unaccent('unaccent'::regdictionary, $1));
CREATE FUNCTION words_query(q text) RETURNS tsquery LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN plainto_tsquery('turkish', tr_lower(q)) ||
    (SELECT to_tsquery('simple', string_agg(quote_literal(w) || ':*', ' & '))
     FROM regexp_split_to_table(tr_lower(q), '[^[:alnum:]]+') AS w WHERE w <> '');
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  project_id int NOT NULL, code text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL, title text NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(title)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(title)), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(description)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(description)), 'B')
  ) STORED,
  CONSTRAINT requirements_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code));
CREATE INDEX requirements_search ON requirements USING gin (search);
CREATE INDEX requirements_title_key ON requirements USING gin (search_key(title) gin_trgm_ops);

INSERT INTO requirements (project_id, code, title, description) VALUES
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN',         'Parola ile giriş', 'Kullanıcı e-posta adresi ve parolasıyla giriş yapar.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT', 'Hatalı girişte hesap kilitleme', 'Beş hatalı parola denemesinden sonra hesap kilitlenir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-RESET',         'Parola sıfırlama', 'Sıfırlama bağlantısı e-postayla gönderilir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-RESET-EXPIRY',  'Sıfırlama bağlantısının süresi', 'Bağlantı bir saat sonra geçersizdir; yeni parola istenir.'),
  (1, 'PAROLA-KURAL',       'Parola kuralları', 'En az on iki karakter.'),
  (1, 'PROFILE',            'Profil sayfası', 'Kullanıcı adını ve parolasını değiştirebilir.');

-- queries/search.sql, SearchRequirements. $1 project, $2 what the user typed,
-- $3-$5 the last row's sort key (tier 0 on the first page), $6 page size + 1.
PREPARE search(int, text, int, int, text, int) AS
SELECT tier, score, code, title
FROM (
  SELECT r.code, r.title,
    CASE WHEN r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~' THEN 1
         WHEN r.search @@ q.words THEN 2
         ELSE 3 END AS tier,
    CASE WHEN r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~' THEN 0
         WHEN r.search @@ q.words THEN (1e6 * ts_rank(r.search, q.words))::int
         ELSE (1e6 * word_similarity(q.key, search_key(r.title)))::int END AS score
  FROM (SELECT upper($2 COLLATE "C") AS prefix, words_query($2) AS words, search_key($2) AS key) AS q,
       requirements AS r
  WHERE r.project_id = $1
    AND (r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~'
         OR r.search @@ q.words
         OR q.key <% search_key(r.title))
) AS hits
WHERE (tier, -score, code) > ($3, -$4, $5)
ORDER BY tier, score DESC, code
LIMIT $6;

-- Page 1 of "parola", three per page: the API asks for four.
EXECUTE search(1, 'parola', 0, 0, '', 4);
-- Page 2: after the third row's key, which nextCursor carried as [2, 607927, "AUTH-RESET"].
EXECUTE search(1, 'parola', 2, 607927, 'AUTH-RESET', 4);
-- Typed with a typo, and typed on an English keyboard.
EXECUTE search(1, 'sifirlma baglantisi', 0, 0, '', 4);

package main

import (
	"context"
	"embed"
	"fmt"
	"io/fs"
	"log"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
)

//go:embed migrations/*.sql
var migrationFiles embed.FS

func main() {
	// signal.NotifyContext in TraceLite; here a goroutine below plays the signal.
	ctx, sigterm := context.WithCancel(context.Background())

	// Start in dependency order: pool, migrations, jobs, listener, HTTP.
	db, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	check(err)
	names, _ := fs.Glob(migrationFiles, "migrations/*.sql")
	for _, name := range names { // goose.Up in TraceLite: only what isn't applied yet
		sql, _ := migrationFiles.ReadFile(name)
		_, err := db.Exec(ctx, string(sql))
		check(err) // exit rather than serve a schema the code doesn't expect
	}
	fmt.Printf("migrations: %d applied, from inside the binary\n", len(names))

	jobsCtx, stopJobs := context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(ctx))
	jobsDone := make(chan struct{})
	go func() { <-jobsCtx.Done(); close(jobsDone) }() // step 11's Pool.Run(jobsCtx), reduced to its lifetime
	fmt.Println("jobs: 4 workers claiming")

	started := make(chan struct{})
	srv := &http.Server{ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second, Handler: http.HandlerFunc(
		func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			close(started)
			time.Sleep(300 * time.Millisecond) // still running when the signal arrives
			w.Write([]byte(`{"items": [], "nextCursor": null}`))
		})}
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") // TRACELITE_ADDR
	check(err)
	go srv.Serve(ln)
	fmt.Println("http: serving")

	answer := make(chan string)
	go func() {
		resp, err := http.Get("http://" + ln.Addr().String() + "/api/projects")
		check(err)
		resp.Body.Close()
		answer <- resp.Status
	}()
	go func() { <-started; sigterm() }()

	<-ctx.Done()
	fmt.Println("signal: shutting down in reverse order")
	stopCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), 10*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	check(srv.Shutdown(stopCtx)) // no new connections; requests in flight finish first
	fmt.Println("http: stopped; the request in flight got", <-answer)
	stopJobs() // after HTTP: a last request may still have queued a job
	<-jobsDone
	fmt.Println("jobs: drained")
	fmt.Println("listener (step 9): closed")
	db.Close()
	fmt.Println("database pool: closed")
}

func check(err error) {
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

import "fmt"

type Config struct {
	Name    string
	Retries int
	Debug   bool
	Tags    []string
	Limits  map[string]int
}

func main() {
	var c Config // no constructor: every field starts at its zero value
	fmt.Printf("%q %d %t %v %v\n", c.Name, c.Retries, c.Debug, c.Tags, c.Limits)
	fmt.Println("nil slice:", c.Tags == nil, "nil map:", c.Limits == nil)

	// Zero values are usable, not just "empty":
	c.Tags = append(c.Tags, "beta")           // append allocates on demand
	fmt.Println(len(c.Limits), c.Limits["x"]) // reading a nil map is fine
	// c.Limits["x"] = 1 would panic: writing needs make(map[string]int)

	n := 3               // short declaration: infers int, function bodies only
	n, extra := 4, "new" // legal: extra is new, so n is only assigned
	a, b := 1, 2
	a, b = b, a // tuple assignment, no temp variable
	fmt.Println(c.Tags, n, extra, a, b)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	arr := [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5} // an array: fixed length, copied on assignment
	s := arr[1:3]                // a slice: pointer into arr, len 2, cap 4
	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))

	s[0] = 20 // writes through to arr
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr)

	s = append(s, 30) // room left in cap: append overwrites arr[3]
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr)

	s = append(s, 40, 50) // no room: new backing array, arr is left alone
	s[0] = 99
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr, "s:", s)

	// The classic bug: two appends to the same slice share its spare capacity.
	base := make([]int, 3, 10)
	a := append(base, 1)
	b := append(base, 2)
	fmt.Println("a:", a, "b:", b)

	// A full slice expression base[low:high:max] caps the capacity, so the
	// next append has to copy.
	a = append(base[:3:3], 1)
	b = append(base[:3:3], 2)
	fmt.Println("a:", a, "b:", b)
}

package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") // port 0: the OS picks a free one
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	base := "http://" + ln.Addr().String()

	// Shutdown waits for requests but never cancels them. Long-lived ones
	// (streams, long polls) need a signal: this context, canceled on Shutdown.
	serverCtx, stopStreams := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	started, release := make(chan bool, 2), make(chan bool)
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /report", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		started <- true
		<-release // slow work in progress
		io.WriteString(w, "report done")
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /events", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		started <- true
		<-r.Context().Done() // a stream ends when the client or the server does
		io.WriteString(w, "stream closed: server shutting down")
	})
	srv := &http.Server{
		Handler:           mux,
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
		BaseContext:       func(net.Listener) context.Context { return serverCtx },
	}
	srv.RegisterOnShutdown(stopStreams)
	served := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { served <- srv.Serve(ln) }()

	get := func(path string) <-chan string {
		out := make(chan string, 1)
		go func() {
			resp, err := http.Get(base + path)
			if err != nil {
				out <- path + ": no response"
				return
			}
			defer resp.Body.Close()
			body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
			out <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: %d %s", path, resp.StatusCode, body)
		}()
		return out
	}
	report, events := get("/report"), get("/events")
	<-started
	<-started // both requests are in flight

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	shutdown := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { shutdown <- srv.Shutdown(ctx) }()

	fmt.Println("Serve returned:", <-served)
	_, err = net.Dial("tcp", ln.Addr().String())
	fmt.Println("new connections refused:", err != nil)
	fmt.Println(<-events)
	close(release)
	fmt.Println(<-report)
	fmt.Println("Shutdown returned:", <-shutdown)
}

package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
)

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()

	cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	cfg.MaxConns = 2 // tiny on purpose, so the limit is easy to hit
	cfg.MaxConnLifetime = 30 * time.Minute

	pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg) // returns before any connection exists
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	if err := pool.Ping(ctx); err != nil { // the first real connection: fail fast here
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	// Two queries whose rows stay open: each keeps its connection checked out.
	rows1, _ := pool.Query(ctx, "SELECT pg_backend_pid()")
	rows2, _ := pool.Query(ctx, "SELECT pg_backend_pid()")
	pid := func(r pgx.Rows) (p int32) { r.Next(); r.Scan(&p); return p }
	fmt.Println("two server processes:", pid(rows1) != pid(rows2))
	fmt.Println("acquired:", pool.Stat().AcquiredConns(), "of", pool.Stat().MaxConns())

	short, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 200*time.Millisecond)
	defer cancel()
	var n int
	err = pool.QueryRow(short, "SELECT 1").Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println("third query:", err)

	rows1.Close() // hands its connection back to the pool
	err = pool.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT 1").Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println("after rows1.Close():", n, err)
	rows2.Close()
}

package main

import (
	"context"
	"database/sql"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
)

type User struct {
	ID        int64
	Name      string
	City      string
	BirthYear int32 // matches birth_year: case and underscores are ignored
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	conn, err := pgx.Connect(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer conn.Close(ctx)

	_, err = conn.Exec(ctx, `
		CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
			name text NOT NULL, city text NOT NULL, birth_year int NOT NULL);
		INSERT INTO users (name, city, birth_year)
		VALUES ('Ayşe', 'İzmir', 1990), ('Çağrı', 'Ankara', 1985), ('Işıl', 'İzmir', 2001)`)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	const byCity = "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users WHERE city = $1 ORDER BY id"
	rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, byCity, "İzmir") // errors resurface from CollectRows
	users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Printf("%+v %v\n", users, err)

	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT name FROM users ORDER BY id")
	names, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowTo[string])
	fmt.Println(names, err)

	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users WHERE id = $1", 99)
	_, err = pgx.CollectOneRow(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Println(err, errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows), errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows))

	// Someone adds a column; SELECT * now returns a field User doesn't have.
	if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx, "ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone text"); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id")
	_, err = pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Println(err)
}

package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	self, _ := os.Executable()
	if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "child" {
		gc := exec.Command(self, "grandchild")
		gc.Stdout = os.Stdout // the grandchild inherits the same output pipe
		_ = gc.Start()
		time.Sleep(time.Minute) // hangs until the timeout kills it
		return
	}
	if len(os.Args) > 1 { // grandchild: report its PID, then outlive the child
		fmt.Println(os.Getpid())
		time.Sleep(3 * time.Second)
		return
	}

	for _, grace := range []time.Duration{0, 300 * time.Millisecond} {
		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, self, "child") // default Cancel kills the child only
		var out bytes.Buffer
		cmd.Stdout = &out
		cmd.WaitDelay = grace
		start := time.Now()
		_ = cmd.Run()
		elapsed := time.Since(start)
		cancel()

		waited := elapsed > 2500*time.Millisecond
		fmt.Printf("WaitDelay=%v: Run waited for the orphaned grandchild: %v\n", grace, waited)
		if pid, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(out.String())); err == nil && !waited {
			p, _ := os.FindProcess(pid) // a manual tree kill, by PID
			fmt.Println("  grandchild still running, killed now:", p.Kill() == nil)
		}
	}
}

-- LEARN(sql.aggregation.group-by): one row per group; WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int              -- NULL: the run was skipped, nothing was timed
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'passed',  120), (2, 'auth',   'failed',  340),
  (3, 'auth',   'passed',  110), (4, 'export', 'skipped', NULL),
  (5, 'export', 'passed',  900), (6, 'search', 'failed',   75),
  (7, 'search', 'failed',   80), (8, 'search', 'skipped', NULL);

-- One output row per suite. count(*) counts rows; count(col) and avg skip NULLs.
SELECT suite,
       count(*)                AS runs,
       count(duration_ms)      AS timed,
       round(avg(duration_ms)) AS avg_ms
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- WHERE picks rows before grouping; HAVING picks groups after aggregation.
SELECT suite, count(*) AS failures
FROM test_runs
WHERE status = 'failed'
GROUP BY suite
HAVING count(*) >= 2
ORDER BY suite;

-- No GROUP BY: all input rows form one group, so even zero rows give one row.
SELECT count(*) AS runs, sum(duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM test_runs
WHERE suite = 'billing';

-- With GROUP BY, zero input rows make zero groups.
SELECT suite, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
WHERE suite = 'billing'
GROUP BY suite;

-- Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. Which status per suite?
SELECT suite, status, count(*) FROM test_runs GROUP BY suite;

CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int NOT NULL         -- 0 for skipped runs
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'passed',  120), (2, 'auth',   'failed',  340),
  (3, 'auth',   'passed',  110), (4, 'export', 'skipped',   0),
  (5, 'export', 'passed',  900), (6, 'search', 'failed',   75),
  (7, 'search', 'failed',   80), (8, 'search', 'skipped',   0);

-- One pass over the table, one row per suite, one column per status.
SELECT suite,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed')  AS passed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')  AS failed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'skipped') AS skipped,
       count(*)                                   AS total
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- The same counts the portable way: CASE inside the aggregate.
SELECT suite,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 'passed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS passed,
       count(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 END)      AS failed
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- count() returns bigint, and bigint / bigint truncates toward zero.
SELECT suite,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*) AS int_ratio,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*), 1)
         AS pass_pct
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- A FILTER that matches no row: count says 0, sum says NULL.
SELECT suite,
       count(*)         FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_runs,
       sum(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_ms,
       coalesce(sum(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed'), 0)
         AS failed_ms_or_0
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- array_agg keeps them.

       string_agg(owner, ', ' ORDER BY id) AS owners_text,
       array_agg(owner ORDER BY id)        AS owners_array,
       array_agg(DISTINCT owner ORDER BY owner) FILTER (WHERE owner IS NOT NULL)
         AS distinct_owners
FROM test_cases
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- point, so Ç, İ and Ş come after Z. Name the Turkish collation to fix it.

       string_agg(title, ', ' ORDER BY title COLLATE "tr-x-icu") AS turkish
FROM test_cases
WHERE suite = 'auth';

       coalesce(array_agg(title ORDER BY title), '{}') AS or_empty
FROM test_cases
WHERE suite = 'billing';

SELECT array_agg(DISTINCT owner ORDER BY id) FROM test_cases;

-- LEARN(sql.aggregation.grouping-sets): several groupings in one pass; GROUPING() tells them apart.
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  browser     text,             -- NULL: an API test, no browser involved
  duration_ms int NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'chrome', 120), (2, 'auth', 'firefox', 340),
  (3, 'auth',   NULL,      30), (4, 'auth', NULL,       40),
  (5, 'export', 'chrome', 900), (6, 'search', 'chrome', 80);

-- Detail rows, a subtotal per suite and a grand total, in one query.
-- Look at auth: two rows with browser NULL that mean different things.
SELECT suite, browser, count(*) AS runs, sum(duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)
ORDER BY suite, browser, GROUPING(browser);

-- GROUPING(col) is 1 where col was rolled up, so a subtotal's NULL can be
-- told apart from a NULL in the data. The two-argument form is a bitmask.
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(suite) = 1 THEN 'all suites' ELSE suite END
         AS suite_label,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(browser) = 1 THEN 'all browsers'
            ELSE coalesce(browser, 'api') END AS browser_label,
       GROUPING(suite, browser) AS level,
       count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)
ORDER BY GROUPING(suite), suite, GROUPING(browser), browser;

INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth', 'passed'), (2, 'auth', 'failed'), (3, 'auth', 'passed'),
  (4, 'search', 'failed'), (5, 'search', 'failed');

-- Two unrelated breakdowns and the total, as one result. Without grouping
-- sets this is three GROUP BY queries glued together with UNION ALL.
SELECT suite, status, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ())
ORDER BY GROUPING(suite, status), suite, status;

-- CUBE (a, b) is every subset: (a, b), (a), (b) and ().
SELECT GROUPING(suite, status) AS level, suite, status, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY CUBE (suite, status)
ORDER BY level, suite, status;

-- One scan of the table feeds all the groupings.
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT suite, status, count(*)
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ());

-- group, and DISTINCT ON keeps only that first row.
SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, ran_at, passed, id
FROM test_runs
ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC, id DESC;

-- Want the result in another order? Sort outside.

FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, ran_at, passed
  FROM test_runs

ORDER BY ran_at DESC, test_case;

-- LEARN(sql.basics.mental-model): a connection is one server process, one role, one database.

-- The server started a process for this connection. pg_stat_activity
-- has one row per server process; this row is yours.
SELECT backend_type, datname AS database, usename AS role, state
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE pid = pg_backend_pid();

-- The same facts from SQL functions. session_user is who logged in;
-- current_user is whose privileges apply (SET ROLE changes it).
SELECT current_database(), session_user, current_user;

-- Inside the database, the search path decides where unqualified names
-- resolve. The sandbox schema is renamed every run, so its suffix is
-- masked as <id>. current_schemas(true) adds the implicit entries.
SELECT regexp_replace(current_schema(), '_\d+_[0-9a-f]+$', '_<id>')
         AS current_schema,
       regexp_replace(current_schemas(true)::text, '_\d+_[0-9a-f]+', '_<id>')
         AS effective_path;

-- One server (a "cluster") holds many databases. Some catalogs are
-- shared by all of them, the rest exist once per database.
SELECT relname AS catalog, relisshared AS shared_by_all_databases
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('pg_authid', 'pg_database', 'pg_namespace', 'pg_class')
ORDER BY relisshared DESC, relname;

-- Roles are cluster-wide, so a database is owned by a role, and so is
-- every schema in it. A new database's public belongs to pg_database_owner
-- (PG 15+); StackLab's setup gave the playground's public to postgres.
CREATE SCHEMA reporting;
SELECT nspname AS schema, pg_get_userbyid(nspowner) AS owner
FROM pg_namespace
WHERE nspname IN ('public', 'reporting')
ORDER BY nspname;

SELECT datname AS database, pg_get_userbyid(datdba) AS owner
FROM pg_database
WHERE datname = current_database();

-- A connection sees exactly one database. Naming another one is an
-- error, not a join: there is no cross-database query.

-- LEARN(sql.basics.psql): \d and friends are catalog queries; this is one in plain SQL.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES customers,
  total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE VIEW big_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total >= 1000;
COMMENT ON TABLE orders IS 'One row per checkout';

-- \d with no pattern (= \dtvmsE): the relations visible on the search
-- path, minus the system schemas. \d+ adds size and the COMMENT text.
SELECT c.relname AS "Name",
       CASE c.relkind
         WHEN 'r' THEN 'table'    WHEN 'p' THEN 'partitioned table'
         WHEN 'v' THEN 'view'     WHEN 'm' THEN 'materialized view'
         WHEN 'S' THEN 'sequence' WHEN 'f' THEN 'foreign table'
       END AS "Type",
       pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) AS "Owner",
       obj_description(c.oid, 'pg_class') AS "Description"
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p', 'v', 'm', 'S', 'f')
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND n.nspname !~ '^pg_toast'
  AND pg_table_is_visible(c.oid)
ORDER BY "Name";
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id         int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      varchar(80) NOT NULL,
  total      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  tags       text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- \d orders, top half: columns with psql's type names and defaults.
SELECT a.attname AS "Column",
       format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod) AS "Type",
       CASE WHEN a.attnotnull THEN 'not null' ELSE '' END AS "Nullable",
       CASE a.attidentity
         WHEN 'a' THEN 'generated always as identity'
         WHEN 'd' THEN 'generated by default as identity'
         ELSE pg_get_expr(d.adbin, d.adrelid)
       END AS "Default"
FROM pg_attribute a
LEFT JOIN pg_attrdef d ON d.adrelid = a.attrelid AND d.adnum = a.attnum
WHERE a.attrelid = 'orders'::regclass
  AND a.attnum > 0 AND NOT a.attisdropped   -- skip system and dropped columns
ORDER BY a.attnum;

-- \d orders, bottom half: constraints. contype 'n' rows are the NOT NULLs,
-- which PG 18 stores here too; the query above already shows them.
SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND contype <> 'n'
ORDER BY conname;

-- The SQL-standard, portable view of the same columns: no modifiers in
-- data_type, and anything Postgres-specific is just 'ARRAY' or 'USER-DEFINED'.
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = current_schema() AND table_name = 'orders'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

-- psql patterns follow SQL's identifier rules, so look at the names the
-- catalog actually stores before blaming \dt for "missing" tables.
CREATE TABLE Payments (id int);     -- unquoted: folded to lower case
CREATE TABLE "Invoices" (id int);   -- quoted: stored exactly as written
CREATE TABLE Şubeler (id int);      -- unquoted, but Ş is not ASCII

SELECT c.relname AS stored_name, length(c.relname) AS chars,
       octet_length(c.relname) AS bytes
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname = current_schema() AND c.relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY c.relname;

-- to_regclass returns NULL instead of failing: a quick "does it exist?".
SELECT to_regclass('payments')   IS NOT NULL AS payments,
       to_regclass('PAYMENTS')   IS NOT NULL AS "PAYMENTS",
       to_regclass('invoices')   IS NOT NULL AS invoices,
       to_regclass('"Invoices"') IS NOT NULL AS "quoted Invoices",
       to_regclass('şubeler')    IS NOT NULL AS şubeler;

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          int  PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  net_cents   int  NOT NULL,

CREATE TABLE requirements (code text PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES ('REQ-1'), ('REQ-2');
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  case_code text         NOT NULL,
  req_code  text         NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  run_on    date         NOT NULL,
  seconds   numeric(6,2) NOT NULL CHECK (seconds >= 0),
  passed    boolean      NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (case_code, run_on)
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES ('TC-1', 'REQ-1', '2026-11-02', 4, true);

-- All text, no constraints: loading the file can't fail. In psql:
-- \copy staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) FROM 'kosular.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER, DELIMITER ';')
CREATE TABLE staging (
  row_no int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  case_code text, req_code text, run_on text, seconds text, result text
);
INSERT INTO staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) VALUES
  ('TC-2', 'REQ-1', '09.11.2026', '1.250,5', 'Geçti'), ('TC-3', 'REQ-2', '10.11.2026', '0,75', 'KALDI'),
  ('TC-4', 'REQ-9', '10.11.2026', '2', 'geçti'),       ('TC-5', 'REQ-1', '31.11.2026', '2,5', 'Gecti'),
  ('TC-6', 'REQ-2', '11.11.2026', '-1', 'Kaldı'),      ('TC-1', 'REQ-1', '02.11.2026', '4', 'Geçti'),
  ('TC-7', 'REQ-2', '12.11.2026', '3,1', 'Geçti'),     ('TC-7', 'REQ-2', '12.11.2026', '3,2', 'Geçti');

-- Every rule in one place: typed values, or NULL plus a reason.
CREATE VIEW checked AS
SELECT s.row_no, s.case_code, s.req_code, t.run_on, t.seconds, t.passed,
  array_remove(ARRAY[
    CASE WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM requirements r WHERE r.code = s.req_code) THEN 'unknown requirement' END,
    CASE WHEN t.run_on IS NULL THEN 'date is not DD.MM.YYYY' END,
    CASE WHEN t.seconds IS NULL THEN 'bad number' WHEN t.seconds < 0 THEN 'negative seconds' END,
    CASE WHEN t.passed IS NULL THEN 'result is not Geçti/Kaldı' END,
    CASE WHEN count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY s.case_code, t.run_on) > 1 THEN 'twice in file' END,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT FROM test_runs x WHERE (x.case_code, x.run_on) = (s.case_code, t.run_on))
         THEN 'already imported' END], NULL) AS problems
FROM staging s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT regexp_match(s.run_on, '^(\d\d)\.(\d\d)\.(\d{4})$') AS d,
                           replace(replace(s.seconds, '.', ''), ',', '.') AS n) p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT
  CASE WHEN pg_input_is_valid(p.d[3] || '-' || p.d[2] || '-' || p.d[1], 'date')
       THEN (p.d[3] || '-' || p.d[2] || '-' || p.d[1])::date END AS run_on,
  CASE WHEN s.seconds ~ '^-?(\d{1,3}(\.\d{3})+|\d+)(,\d+)?$' AND pg_input_is_valid(p.n, 'numeric(6,2)')
       THEN p.n::numeric(6,2) END AS seconds,
  CASE lower(s.result COLLATE "tr-x-icu") WHEN 'geçti' THEN true WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END AS passed) t;

-- Report first, move second (see the note on why the order matters).
SELECT row_no, case_code, array_to_string(problems, '; ') AS problems
FROM checked WHERE problems <> '{}' ORDER BY row_no;

INSERT INTO test_runs (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, passed)
SELECT case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, passed FROM checked WHERE problems = '{}';

SELECT * FROM test_runs ORDER BY run_on, case_code;

CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id    int  PRIMARY KEY,
  code  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  title text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id         bigint       PRIMARY KEY,
  req_id     int          NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  run_at     timestamptz  NOT NULL,
  seconds    numeric(6,2) NOT NULL,
  passed     boolean      NOT NULL,
  commit_sha text         NOT NULL,
  tester     text         -- NULL: an automated run
);

INSERT INTO requirements
SELECT i, 'REQ-' || lpad(i::text, 3, '0'),
       (ARRAY['Giriş', 'Arama', 'Rapor', 'Yetki', 'Dışa aktarım'])[1 + i % 5] || ' ' || i
FROM generate_series(1, 200) AS i;

-- 100,000 runs, one statement. md5 of the row number stands in for
-- random(): it looks random but is the same on every run.
INSERT INTO test_runs
SELECT i,
       1 + floor(200 * r.u ^ 2)::int,
       timestamptz '2026-01-01 09:00+03' + i * interval '257 seconds',
       round(0.2 + 30 * r.v ^ 4, 2),
       r.v < 0.9,
       left(md5((i / 25)::text), 10),
       CASE WHEN i % 4 = 0 THEN (ARRAY['ayşe', 'mehmet', 'zeynep'])[1 + i % 3] END
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS i,
     LATERAL decode(md5(i::text), 'hex') AS h(b),
     LATERAL (SELECT (get_byte(b, 0) * 256 + get_byte(b, 1)) / 65536.0 AS u,
                     (get_byte(b, 2) * 256 + get_byte(b, 3)) / 65536.0 AS v) AS r;

SELECT count(*) AS runs, count(DISTINCT req_id) AS reqs,
       count(DISTINCT commit_sha) AS commits,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE passed) / count(*), 1) AS pass_pct,
       round(100.0 * count(tester) / count(*), 1) AS manual_pct,
       min(run_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul')::date AS first_day,
       max(run_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Istanbul')::date AS last_day
FROM test_runs;

SELECT r.code, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs t JOIN requirements r ON r.id = t.req_id
GROUP BY r.code ORDER BY runs DESC, r.code LIMIT 3;

SELECT passed, round(avg(seconds), 2) AS avg_s, min(seconds), max(seconds)
FROM test_runs GROUP BY passed ORDER BY passed;

CREATE TABLE requirements (id int PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (

  requirement_id int REFERENCES requirements,  -- NULL: not linked yet

FROM requirements r
LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id
WHERE t.automated
ORDER BY r.id, t.id;

SELECT r.title AS requirement, t.title AS automated_test
FROM requirements r
LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id AND t.automated
ORDER BY r.id, t.id;

-- LEARN(sql.json.jsonb-operators): -> keeps jsonb, ->> gives text; JSON null is not SQL NULL.
CREATE TABLE ci_events (
  id      int   PRIMARY KEY,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL          -- a CI webhook body, stored as received
);
INSERT INTO ci_events VALUES
  (1, '{"build": {"number": 108, "branch": "main", "agent": {"os": "linux"}},
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
                    {"test": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85}],
        "tags": ["nightly", "smoke"], "retry_of": null}'),
  (2, '{"build": {"number": 9, "branch": "feature/kvkk"},
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 130}],
        "tags": []}');

-- Chain -> to walk down, or give #> / #>> the whole path. JSON arrays
-- are 0-based, and negative indexes count from the end.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'build' -> 'number'          AS number_jsonb,
       payload -> 'build' ->> 'branch'         AS branch_text,
       payload #>> '{build,agent,os}'          AS agent_os,
       payload -> 'results' -> 0 ->> 'test'    AS first_test,
       payload -> 'results' -> -1 ->> 'status' AS last_status,
       payload -> 'tags' ->> 0                 AS first_tag
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- A key holding JSON null and a missing key look alike through ->>.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'retry_of'               AS arrow,
       payload -> 'retry_of' IS NULL       AS arrow_is_null,
       payload ->> 'retry_of' IS NULL      AS text_is_null,
       payload ? 'retry_of'                AS has_key,
       jsonb_typeof(payload -> 'retry_of') AS json_type
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- ->> returns text, and text compares character by character.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'build' ->> 'number' > '100'      AS as_text,
       (payload -> 'build' ->> 'number')::int > 100 AS as_int,
       payload -> 'build' -> 'number' > '100'       AS as_jsonb
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- Text on the left, a number on the right: no operator matches.
SELECT id FROM ci_events WHERE payload -> 'build' ->> 'number' = 108;

CREATE TABLE ci_events (
  id      int   PRIMARY KEY,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_events VALUES
  (1, '{"build": {"branch": "main"}, "tags": ["nightly", "smoke"],
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
                    {"test": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85}]}'),
  (2, '{"build": {"branch": "feature/kvkk"}, "tags": ["smoke"],
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 130}]}'),
  (3, '{"build": {"branch": "main"}, "tags": [], "results": [], "retry_of": 1}');

-- @> asks: does the left document contain this shape? Nested objects match
-- at the same path; array elements match in any order; extra keys are ignored.
SELECT id,
       payload @> '{"build": {"branch": "main"}}'         AS on_main,
       payload @> '{"branch": "main"}'                     AS wrong_level,
       payload @> '{"tags": ["smoke", "nightly"]}'         AS both_tags,
       payload @> '{"tags": "smoke"}'                      AS scalar_tag,
       payload -> 'tags' @> '"smoke"'                      AS array_has_smoke,
       payload @> '{"results": [{"status": "failed"}]}'    AS any_failed
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- ? and friends test strings: top-level keys, or string elements of an array.
SELECT id,
       payload ? 'retry_of'                          AS has_retry,
       payload ? 'branch'                            AS nested_key,
       payload -> 'tags' ? 'smoke'                   AS smoke,
       payload -> 'tags' ?| ARRAY['nightly', 'perf'] AS any_of,
       payload -> 'tags' ?& ARRAY['nightly', 'smoke'] AS all_of
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- jsonb equality is structural and numeric: 120.0 = 120, key order is irrelevant.
SELECT '{"ms": 120.0, "test": "Giriş"}'::jsonb
         = '{"test": "Giriş", "ms": 120}'::jsonb AS equal,
       '{"ms": 120.0}'::jsonb                    AS kept_as_written;

-- The plain json type stores text and has none of these operators.
SELECT payload::json @> '{"tags": ["smoke"]}' FROM ci_events;

-- LEARN(sql.json.path-table): a jsonpath walks, filters and unwraps inside one document.
CREATE TABLE ci_reports (
  id     int   PRIMARY KEY,
  report jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES
  (1, '{"build": 108, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
            {"title": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85, "error": "timeout"}]},
         {"name": "export", "tests": [
            {"title": "CSV dışa aktarım", "status": "passed", "ms": 900}]}]}'),
  (2, '{"build": 109, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": "slow"}]}]}');

-- [*] iterates an array, ? (...) filters, @ is the item being tested.
-- jsonb_path_query returns one row per match; report 2 has none.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.status == "failed").title')
         AS failed
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- Collect matches as an array, pass values in as variables, test with @?.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*].title') AS titles,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.ms > $max).title',
                              '{"max": 500}')                       AS slow,
       report @? '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.status == "failed")'   AS any_failed,
       jsonb_path_query_first(report, '$.suites.size()')             AS suites
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- lax mode (the default) unwraps arrays without [*] and skips missing keys.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites.tests.title') AS unwrapped,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites.tests.error') AS errors
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- strict mode treats a missing key as an error.
SELECT jsonb_path_query_array(report, 'strict $.suites[*].tests[*].error')
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;

         title     text PATH '$.title',

SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE ci_reports (
  id     int   PRIMARY KEY,
  report jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES
  (1, '{"build": "108", "finished": "2026-11-13T06:12:00Z",
        "suites": [{"name": "auth", "slowest_ms": 120},
                   {"name": "export", "slowest_ms": 900}],
        "owner": null}'),
  (2, '{"build": "109", "suites": [{"name": "auth", "slowest_ms": 130}]}');

-- JSON_VALUE extracts one scalar and casts it with RETURNING; JSON_QUERY
-- returns JSON; JSON_EXISTS tests. PASSING binds path variables.
SELECT id,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.build' RETURNING int)               AS build,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.finished' RETURNING timestamptz)    AS finished,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.owner' DEFAULT 'nobody' ON EMPTY)   AS owner,
       JSON_QUERY(report, '$.suites[*].name' WITH WRAPPER)       AS suites,
       JSON_EXISTS(report, '$.suites[*] ? (@.slowest_ms > $max)'
                   PASSING 500 AS max)                           AS has_slow
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- By default every problem becomes NULL: two values where one was expected,
-- an object instead of a scalar, a missing key.
SELECT JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[*].name') AS two_values,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[0]')      AS an_object,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.nope')           AS missing
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;

-- Ask for errors where a NULL would hide a bug.
SELECT JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[*].name' ERROR ON ERROR)
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;

SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id         bigint      PRIMARY KEY,
  code       text        NOT NULL,
  title      text        NOT NULL,
  owner      text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id             bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  requirement_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  status         text   NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES
  (1, 'REQ-1', 'Giriş ekranı', 'Zeynep', '2026-11-13 09:00+03'),
  (2, 'REQ-2', 'Dışa aktarım', NULL,     '2026-11-13 10:30+03');
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (9007199254740993, 1, 'passed'), (11, 1, 'failed');

-- json keeps the keys in the order you wrote them; jsonb sorts them
-- (shorter first) and prints its own canonical spacing.
SELECT json_build_object('code', code, 'title', title, 'owner', owner, 'id', id)
         AS as_json,
       jsonb_build_object('code', code, 'title', title, 'owner', owner, 'id', id)
         AS as_jsonb
FROM requirements
WHERE id = 1;

-- A whole row: keys come from column names; - removes what the client
-- shouldn't get, jsonb_strip_nulls the fields that are null.
SELECT jsonb_strip_nulls(to_jsonb(r) - 'id') AS body
FROM requirements AS r
ORDER BY r.id;

-- One response document per requirement. timestamptz becomes ISO 8601 in
-- the session time zone; ids also go out as strings for JavaScript.
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'code', r.code,
         'created_at', r.created_at,
         'tests', (SELECT coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
                                     'id', t.id, 'id_str', t.id::text,
                                     'status', t.status) ORDER BY t.id), '[]')
                   FROM test_cases AS t
                   WHERE t.requirement_id = r.id)) AS body
FROM requirements AS r
ORDER BY r.id;
